## PARAGRAPH 10

# THE METHOD OF WARFARE

Generally, in the method of warfare, the fundamental principle consists in making government measures supremely prevalent. If this is done, then the people concerned will have no disputes, and having no disputes, they will have no thought of self-interest, but will have the interest of the ruler in mind. Therefore, a real king, through his measures, will cause people to be fearful in fights between various cities, but brave in wars against external foes.

<margin>5a</margin> If people have been trained to attack dangers with energy, they will, as a result, think lightly of death. Should the enemy be routed as soon as the engagement has begun, and should he not stop in his rout, abstain from further pursuit. Therefore does the “Art of War” say: “In a big battle, in the event of victory, pursue the fugitives not further than 10 *li*; in a small battle, in the event of victory, pursue the fugitives not further than 5 *li*.” When hostilities begin, weigh the...

<summary>This page outlines the Legalist approach to military discipline, emphasizing that domestic order and the suppression of internal strife are necessary prerequisites for external military success.</summary>
<keywords>Lord Shang, warfare, government measures, Art of War, li, Han Fei-tzŭ, Tso-chuan, Duke Wen, Sun-tzŭ</keywords>

Therefore it is said: "The great rule of an army is prudence." By estimating the strength of the enemy and by examining one's own hosts, victory or defeat may be known beforehand.

The army of a real king does not boast of victory, nor does it harbor rancor for defeat. That it does not boast of victory is because it ascribes it to its clever tactics; that it does not harbor rancor for defeat is because it knows why it has failed. # CHAPTER IV.

## ON THE DISTRIBUTION IN PHASE CALLED CANONICAL, IN WHICH THE INDEX OF PROBABILITY IS A LINEAR FUNCTION OF THE ENERGY.

Let us now give our attention to the statistical equilibrium of ensembles of conservative systems, especially to those cases and properties which promise to throw light on the phenomena of thermodynamics.
The condition of statistical equilibrium may be expressed in the form *

-> Σ ( dP/dp₁ ṗ₁ + dP/dq₁ q̇₁ ) = 0, (88) <-

where **P** is the coefficient of probability, or the quotient of the density-in-phase by the total number of systems. To satisfy this condition, it is necessary and sufficient that **P** should be a function of the *p*’s and *q*’s (the momenta and coordinates) which does not vary with time in a moving system. In all cases which we are now considering, the energy, or any function of the energy, is such a function.
-> P = func. (ε) <-
will therefore satisfy the equation, as indeed appears identically if we write it in the form
-> Σ ( dP/dq₁ dε/dp₁ - dP/dp₁ dε/dq₁ ) = 0. <-
There are, however, other conditions to which **P** is subject, which are not so much conditions of statistical equilibrium, as conditions implicitly involved in the definition of the coefficient of probability, whether the case is one of equilibrium or not. These are: that $P$ should be single-valued, and neither negative nor imaginary for any phase, and that expressed by equation (46), namely:

---
* See equations (20), (41), (42), also the paragraph following equation (20). The positions of any external bodies which can affect the systems are here supposed uniform for all the systems and constant in time.

It has the property that when the system consists of parts with separate energies, the laws of the distribution in phase of the separate parts are of the same nature—a property which enormously simplifies the discussion and is the foundation of extremely important relations to thermodynamics. The case is not rendered less simple by the divisor Θ (a quantity of the same dimensions as ε); on the contrary, it makes the distribution independent of the units employed. The negative sign of ε is required by (89), which determines also the value of ψ for any given Θ, namely:

# CANONICAL DISTRIBUTION

linear function of the energy, we shall say that the ensemble is canonically distributed, and shall call the divisor of the energy (Θ) the modulus of distribution.

The fractional part of an ensemble canonically distributed that lies within any given limits of phase is therefore represented by the multiple integral

->$\int \dots \int e^{\frac{\psi - \epsilon}{\Theta}} dp_1 \dots dq_n \quad (93)$<-

taken within those limits. We may express the same thing by saying that the multiple integral expresses the probability that an unspecified system of the ensemble (one of which we only know that it belongs to the ensemble) falls within the given limits.

Since the value of a multiple integral of the form (23) (which we have called an extension-in-phase) bounded by any given phases is independent of the system of coordinates by which it is evaluated, the same must be true of the multiple integral in (92), as appears at once if we divide up this integral into parts so small that the exponential factor may be regarded as constant in each. The value of ψ is therefore independent of the system of coordinates employed.

It is evident that ψ might be defined as the energy for which the coefficient of probability of phase has the value unity. Since, however, this coefficient has the dimensions of the inverse $n$th power of the product of energy and time, <note>See Chapter I, p. 19.</note> the energy represented by ψ is not independent of the units of energy and time. But when these units have been chosen, the definition of ψ will involve the same arbitrary constant as ε, so that, while in any given case the numerical values of ψ or ε will be entirely indefinite until the zero of energy has also been fixed for the system considered, the difference ψ-ε will represent a perfectly definite amount of energy, which is entirely independent of the zero of energy which we may choose to adopt.

<summary>This page defines the "modulus of distribution" (Θ) and clarifies that while individual energy values depend on the zero-point reference, the difference ψ-ε is physically definite.</summary>

# OF AN ENSEMBLE OF SYSTEMS.

It is evident that the canonical distribution is entirely determined by the modulus (considered as a quantity of energy) and the nature of the system considered, since when equation (92) is satisfied, the value of the multiple integral (93) is independent of the units and of the coordinates employed, and of the zero chosen for the energy of the system.

In treating of the canonical distribution, we shall always suppose the multiple integral in equation (92) to have a finite value, as otherwise the coefficient of probability vanishes, and the law of distribution becomes illusory. This will exclude certain cases, but apparently not such as will affect the value of our results with respect to their bearing on thermodynamics. It will exclude, for instance, cases in which the system or parts of it can be distributed in unlimited space (or in a space which has limits, but is still infinite in volume), while the energy remains beneath a finite limit. It also excludes many cases in which the energy can decrease without limit, as when the system contains material points which attract one another inversely as the squares of their distances. Cases of material points attracting each other inversely as the distances would be excluded for some values of Θ, but not for others. The investigation of such points is best left to the particular cases. For the purposes of a general discussion, it is sufficient to call attention to the assumption implicitly involved in the formula (92).*

The modulus Θ has properties analogous to those of temperature in thermodynamics. Let the system *A* be defined as one of an ensemble of systems of *m* degrees of freedom distributed in phase with a probability-coefficient

-> $e^{\frac{\psi_A - \epsilon_A}{\Theta}}$, <-

---
* It will be observed that similar limitations exist in thermodynamics. In order that a mass of gas can be in thermodynamic equilibrium, it is necessary that it be enclosed. There is no thermodynamic equilibrium of a (finite) mass of gas in an infinite space. Again, that two attracting particles should be able to do an infinite amount of work in passing from one configuration (which is regarded as possible) to another, is a notion which, although perfectly intelligible in a mathematical formula, is quite foreign to our ordinary conceptions of matter.

<summary>This page discusses the necessary constraints for a finite canonical distribution and introduces the analogy between the modulus Θ and thermodynamic temperature.</summary>

The most simple test of the equality of temperature of two bodies is that they remain in equilibrium when brought into thermal contact. Direct thermal contact implies molecular forces acting between the bodies. Now the test will fail unless the energy of these forces can be neglected in comparison with the other energies of the bodies. Thus, in the case of energetic chemical action between the bodies, or when the number of particles affected by the forces acting between the bodies is not negligible in comparison with the whole number of particles (as when the bodies have the form of exceedingly thin sheets), the contact of bodies of the same temperature may produce considerable thermal disturbance, and thus fail to afford a reliable criterion of the equality of temperature.

When the state of equality with the meditated reality is achieved in all three stages, <margin>two</margin> in the second [stage], the consciousness of the Lord <note>original: "īśāna-saṃvitti"</note> arises. (16)

<margin>two</margin> In the second [stage], the yogi becomes stable and equal to that. In the sixth [stage], he becomes the Lord of all; otherwise, he falls. (17)

<summary>This page details the advanced stages of the Water-concentration practice, focusing on stabilizing the internal vision of white light to achieve lordship over the water element and divine consciousness.</summary>

pages.166:
Thus, those who know the procedures should understand this [practice], which exists in fifteen forms across all Tantras, as it grants five types of fruits <term>siddhi</term>. (18)

The other fruits mentioned here and those that will be mentioned later are to be understood as incidental fruits, without doubt. (19)

Thus, the Water-concentration has been described with fifteen divisions. Now, listen to the Fire-concentration <term>āgneyī-dhāraṇā</term> for the sake of the yogi’s success in yoga. (20)

One should meditate on the body as a triangle filled with rows of red flames. O Goddess, after seven days, its sharpness arises. (21)

The practitioner is freed from all diseases arising from wind and phlegm in a month. He becomes sleepless, eats little, and produces very little waste. (22)

By his will, he can burn any object he touches, due to the intensity of the heat. After a year, having become like fire, he plays with fire at will. (23)

If angered, he burns everything, including mountains, forests, and woods. One should contemplate the self as raised upon a triangular mandala. (24)

The wise practitioner, through various methods of activity, becomes free from diseases in a week and becomes equal to fire in six months. (25)

In three years, he fully perceives the Fire-element <term>tejas-tattva</term>. Whatever is seen in the division of power becomes stable in its respective division. (26)

<summary>Shiva transitions from water to the Fire-concentration, describing how visualizing a fiery triangle can cleanse the body, cure ailments, and grant the practitioner the ability to manipulate fire.</summary>
<keywords>Fire-concentration, āgneyī, yoga, siddhi, triangle, tejas, healing, transformation</keywords>
pages.167:
As before, meditating on the self as having the radiance of fire while situated in the middle of the palate, he gradually sees all the Lords of the Fire-element. (27)

Meditating on the fire surrounded by smoke, having the shape of the sun-disk, one becomes equal to the Lord of the Fire-element within that [state]. (28)

Meditating on the light that destroys the net of darkness, having the splendor of smokeless fire, one should contemplate the "All" within it, and thus attain the state of reality. (29)

One should contemplate the light within, having the radiance of the midday sun. Once established in it, he attains the state of "That alone." (30)

One should manifest the light there, shining like a jewel-lamp. The yogi, having become identified with that, attains the state of the Lord of Mantras. (31)

By meditating on the light as both external and internal, he becomes one with it. Because of this, he does not fall from that state until the time of cosmic dissolution. (32)

At the time of dissolution, he attains the supreme, peaceful state of Shiva <note>original: "śāṅkaram"</note>. Thus, the Fire-concentration is described in fifteen ways. (33)

One should contemplate one's own body as black, round, marked with six dots, moving, and making a "chū-chū" sound, while resorting to the Air-concentration <term>vāyavī-dhāraṇā</term>. (34)

Movement, like that of wind, occurs due to the cessation of phlegm-based diseases. The yogi who practices this for six months with a focused inner self... (35)

<summary>This passage continues the Fire-concentration and introduces the Air-concentration, describing how different visualizations lead to mastery over the elements and eventual union with Shiva.</summary>
<keywords>Fire-concentration, Air-concentration, yoga, mantras, Shiva, visualization, elemental mastery</keywords>
pages.168:
...travels a hundred yojanas and returns within a moment without fatigue. By three years, he truly takes on the form of air. (36)

He can crush mountains and uproot trees. When angry, he can bring Indra <note>The King of the Gods</note> along with his servants, forces, and vehicles. (37)

He should meditate on his own body as having the color of dark collyrium. He attains everything mentioned previously in six months—there is no doubt. (38)

After two years, he sees the Air-element and becomes identified with it. He should remember the form as being like collyrium in the space between the eyebrows. (39)

He sees all the pure Lords of the Air-element. Meditating on it as having the luster of a sapphire covered by clouds and the shape of a sun-disk, (40)

he becomes equal to it. When he is absorbed in it, he should contemplate the "All" as having the luster of a broken sapphire. (41)

He attains identity with it and lordship over it. By meditating on that form pervading everything as light, he attains [great power]. (42)

Then he becomes unassailable, moving both upward and downward. Thus, this divine Air-concentration is described. (43)

After meditating on his body as air and remembering that state, the yogi attains emptiness in seven days. (44)

pages.169:
In just a month, even when seen by the lords of enjoyment, he is not bewildered. He is free from all diseases and devoid of wrinkles and gray hair. (45)

In six months, he can pass through even tiny openings like fire. In three years, he will become like the sky. (46)

At will, he can have a great body or a subtle body. He becomes uncuttable and unbreakable, and he sees the earth as full of holes. (47)

He should contemplate the body as produced from the sky, mixed with the essence of a hundred flowers. After a year, knowledge of the sky arises. (48)

He attains all previously mentioned fruits starting from seven days. Likewise, he should meditate in the forehead, extending twelve finger-breadths. (49)

He sees all the Lords of those elements standing before him. Meditating on the moon-disk eclipsed by Rahu <note>The celestial body causing eclipses</note>, he becomes equal to that. (50)

He should contemplate the "All" as being inside, like the moon-disk. He attains the state of the Lord of Mantras and, through moonlight, the state of the moon itself. (51)

Through that same moonlight flowing downwards, both internally and externally, the wise one attains the lordship of the Lords of Mantras and gains incomparable knowledge. (52)

By that same moonlight in the form of nectar flowing upwards, he attains independence and is not obstructed anywhere. (53)

pages.170:
Thus, the concentration on the five elements <term>pañca-tattva</term> has been declared. The pure state is consciousness itself, and there are five types of possession by it. (54)

By fixing the mind on these, one destroys one's own miseries. Whatever consciousness one desires, (55)

if one fixes the mind properly on it, one attains the fruit of that. Even though this is one, when contemplated through its secondary divisions, (56)

it becomes an obstacle; therefore, one should not dwell there. Those who dwell there will not attain the supreme fruit. (57)

<margin>p. 16/67</margin>
When the five-fold concentration is perfected, the eight qualities of the ghosts <term>piśāca</term> and the five [powers] ending with Indra are attained by the yogi, or even through their separation. (58)

One should practice these fifteen states in order. One should perfect the first in a year, the next in two, and another in one. (59)

Then another in six months, then with five, four, or three [months]. Then with two, one, a fortnight, ten days, or five days. (60)

With three, two, or one [days], the sequence is as before for one who desires in a distracted way. He attains the eternal state after enjoying the desired success. (61)

->Thus ends the thirteenth chapter of the Śrī Mālinī-Vijayottara Tantra, entitled "Conquest of the Elements."<-

Now, I shall explain the concentrations on the subtle elements <term>tanmātras</term>, starting with smell, for the sake of attaining their fruits. (1)

One should meditate on the smell-subtle element, which is yellow, the fourth part of the mountain-measure, situated at the tip of the nostrils, and marked with the sign of the thunderbolt <term>vajra</term>. (2)

After ten days, for the yogi whose mind is focused on nothing else, a certain scent arises, even if it is twofold or many-fold. (3)

Then, within a season, the pure scent becomes stable. In six months, he himself becomes the very nature of smell. (4)

Whichever smell he likes, he makes it intense there. In three years, he attains the success of the five elements as directed. (5)

If he then contemplates his own form there, he attains the science of the smell-veil in three years. (6)

Having slight radiance and free from the mandala, he sees all those who dwell within the smell-veil by meditating [on it]. (7)

<summary>The fourteenth chapter begins, introducing the "subtle element" <term>tanmātra</term> concentrations, starting with the sense of smell and the corresponding elemental veil.</summary>

pages.172:
Contemplating there like the disk mentioned in the Earth-element, he becomes equal to that when the two are stable as before. (8)

By contemplating the form there, making it shine as situated below, he attains lordship over it by the path previously mentioned. (9)

Remembering everything from here onwards like the Earth-element, he attains the fruit of that form residing in the smell-veil. (10)

Now I shall speak of the concentration on the taste-form <term>rasa-rūpa</term>, which is practiced by yogis, by which the yogi becomes able to taste all flavors. (11)

One should contemplate the taste-subtle element as resembling a water-bubble, situated at the tip of the tongue, having the tongue-tip as its support. (12)

One should contemplate the cool, six-fold flavor <note>sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, astringent</note> with an inward-turned self. Then, in just a month, the tasting of flavors begins. (13)

When, abandoning salty and other flavors, he attains sweetness, then the yogi who consumes that becomes a conqueror of death in six months. (14)

Freed from old age and disease, with black hair and unfailing radiance, he lives as long as the moon, stars, and sun exist, practicing here and there. (15)

Contemplating the form of the bubble mentioned before, what wonder is it that he attains the science of the veil-less state? (16)

<summary>The chapter continues with the taste-concentration, describing how mastery over the sense of taste leads to health, longevity, and the "veil-less" state of supreme knowledge.</summary>

# 18

->ألا أيها الليل الطويل ألا انجلي .. بصبح وما الإصباح منك بأمثل 48<-

"Oh you, long night, brighten with the dawn! Yet the morning is no better or superior to you in my opinion, for the pain of separation continues just the same."

<margin>Another instance of <term>tasri'</term> (rhyming the end of the two hemistichs in the opening line); see line 21.</margin>
<margin><term>Al-layl</term> is in the nominative case, being a single vocative (<term>munada mufrad</term>).</margin>
<margin><term>Ma</term> is used expletively with <term>amthal</term> (the predicate after the negative <term>ma</term>).</margin>

->فيالك من ليل كأن نجومه .. بأمراس كتان إلى صم جندل 49<-

"How wonderful you are as a night—a night whose stars are seemingly secured by hemp ropes to solid rock."

The night seems long to him; the light of the stars does not pale with the approach of dawn.

<margin><term>Faya-laka</term> = "What a wonder for you."</margin>
<margin><term>Min</term> is explanatory (<term>bayaniyya</term>) of the <term>ka</term> (the 'you' of address).</margin>
<margin><term>Ka-anna nujumuhu</term>, etc., is an adjective phrase describing the night.</margin>
<margin>Here, "secured" or "tied" is understood as the predicate after <term>ka-anna</term>, as it is obvious from the context.</margin>

In some copies, instead of this one line, there are two, as follows:—

->فيالك من ليل كأن نجومه .. بكل مغار الفتل شدت بيذبل<-
->كأن الثريا علقت في مصامها .. بأمراس كتان إلى صم جندل<-

"Oh wonder for you, a night whose stars are, as it were, tied firmly with strongly twisted rope to Mount Yazbul."
"As though the Pleiades were secured firmly in their position by means of hemp ropes to solid stones."

<margin><term>Maghar</term> is an adjective to <term>habl</term> (rope), which is understood; <term>summ</term> is the plural of <term>samma'</term> (solid), an adjective to <term>sukhur</term> (rocks), which is understood; <term>shuddat</term> is the predicate sentence to <term>nujumuhu</term> (its stars), the subject after <term>ka-anna</term>.</margin>
<margin><term>Ulliqat</term> is the predicate sentence to <term>Thurayya</term> (the Pleiades), the subject after <term>ka-anna</term>.</margin>

<summary>The poet addresses the long night, expressing that the arrival of morning offers no relief from his grief; he compares the stars to objects anchored to solid rock.</summary>
<keywords>Tasri', long night, stars, Pleiades, Mount Yazbul, metaphor</keywords>

> "And many a leather water-bag of the people, I have placed its strap over my shoulder, submissive, and repeatedly saddled with it."

->وَوَادٍ كَجَوْفِ الْعَيْرِ قَفْرٍ قَطَعْتُهُ .. بِهِ الذِّئْبُ يَعْوِي كَالْخَلِيعِ الْمُعَيَّلِ<-

> "And many a valley like the plain of 'Aer, a sterile desert, I have crossed, in which the wolf was howling like a gambler with a family to support."

<note><term>'Aer</term> is explained in two ways: (a) a substitute for the meter, for its synonym <term>himar</term> (ass), the name of a certain unbeliever who possessed a valley that God rendered waste for his infidelity; (b) the ass whose belly contains nothing useful.</note>

<note><term>Bihi al-dhi'bu</term>: <term>bihi</term> is the predicate, and <term>al-dhi'bu</term> is the subject.</note>
<note><term>Ya'wi</term> is an adjective sentence describing the wolf.</note>
<note><term>Khali'</term>: A gambler who always loses the game, or one repudiated by his family.</note>

52
->فَقُلْتُ لَهُ لَمَّا عَوَى إِنَّ شَأْنَنَا .. قَلِيلُ الْغِذَى إِنْ كُنْتَ لَمَّا تُمَوَّلِ<-

> "I said to him (the wolf) when he howled: 'Our condition is meager in terms of wealth, if you also have never been prosperous.'"

<note><term>Lamma</term> and <term>lam</term> are used expletively here.</note>

<note><term>Kunta</term> is the predicate sentence to <term>inna</term>.</note>
<note><term>Tumawwal</term> is in the jussive mood due to <term>lam</term>; it is a syncopated form of <term>tatamawwal</term>.</note>

> "And verily I started out in the early morning, while the birds were still in their nests, on a well-bred horse, long-bodied, outstripping the wild beasts in his gallop."

> "Attacking, fleeing, advancing, retiring, all at once; and in addition to these qualities, he is like a boulder of rock that the torrent has hurled down from on high, in his pace, force, and invulnerability."

The same applies to <term>dali'</term>, <term>mish</term>, <term>jiyash</term>, and <term>kumayt</term> in the following lines.</note>

Let η' and η'' be the indices of probability in two independent ensembles which are each in statistical equilibrium; then η' + η'' will be the index in the ensemble obtained by combining each system of the first ensemble with each system of the second. This third ensemble will of course be in statistical equilibrium, and the function of phase η' + η'' will be a constant of motion. Now when infinitesimal forces are added to the compound systems, if η' + η'' or a function differing infinitesimally from this is still a constant of motion, it must be on account of the nature of the forces added, or if their action is not entirely specified, on account of conditions to which they are subject. Thus, in the case already considered, η' + η'' is a function of the energy of the compound system, and the infinitesimal forces added are subject to the law of conservation of energy.

<margin>||</margin> Another natural supposition in regard to the added forces is that they should be such as not to affect the moments of momentum of the compound system. To get a case in which moments of momentum of the compound system shall be constants of motion, we may imagine material particles contained in two concentric spherical shells, being prevented from passing the surfaces bounding the shells by repulsions acting always in lines passing through the common center of the shells. Then, if there are no forces acting between particles in different shells, the mass of particles in each shell will have, besides its energy, the <note>The following phrase is circled in the original:</note> moments of momentum about three axes through the center as constants of motion.

Now let us imagine an ensemble formed by distributing in phase the system of particles in one shell according to the index of probability

-> A - ε/Θ + ω₁/Ω₁ + ω₂/Ω₂ + ω₃/Ω₃, (98) <-

where ε denotes the energy of the system, and ω₁, ω₂, ω₃, its three moments of momentum, and the other letters constants.

The same would be true if in the indices of each of the original ensembles we should substitute for the term or terms relating to any period which does not occur in the other ensemble, any function of the total energy related to that period, subject only to the general limitation expressed by equation (89). But in order that the ensemble of compound systems (with the added forces) shall always be approximately in statistical equilibrium, it is necessary that the indices of the original ensembles should be linear functions of those partial energies which relate to vibrations of periods common to the two ensembles, and that the coefficients of such partial energies should be the same in the two indices.†

# CANONICAL DISTRIBUTION

The properties of canonically distributed ensembles of systems with respect to the equilibrium of the new ensembles which may be formed by combining each system of one ensemble with each system of another, are therefore not peculiar to them in the sense that analogous properties do not belong to some other distributions under special limitations in regard to the systems and forces considered. Yet the canonical distribution evidently constitutes the most simple case of the kind, and that for which the relations described hold with the least restrictions.

Returning to the case of the canonical distribution, we shall find other analogies with thermodynamic systems, if we suppose, as in the preceding chapters,* that the potential energy (ε_q) depends not only upon the coordinates q₁ ... qₙ which determine the configuration of the system, but also upon certain coordinates a₁, a₂, etc., of bodies which we call *external*, meaning by this simply that they are not to be regarded as forming any part of the system, although their positions affect the forces which act on the system. The forces exerted by the system upon these external bodies will be represented by -dε_q/da₁, -dε_q/da₂, etc., while -dε_q/dq₁, ..., -dε_q/dqₙ represent all the forces acting upon the bodies of the system, including those which depend upon the position of the external bodies, as well as those which depend only upon the configuration of the system itself. It will be understood that ε_p depends only upon q₁, ..., qₙ, p₁, ..., pₙ; in other words, that the kinetic energy of the bodies which we call external forms no part of the kinetic energy of the system. It follows that we may write

-> \frac{d\epsilon}{da_{1}} = \frac{d\epsilon_{q}}{da_{1}} = - A_{1}, (104) <-

although a similar equation would not hold for differentiations relative to the internal coordinates.

* See especially Chapter I, p. 4.

<summary>This page introduces the concept of external coordinates in canonical distributions, setting the stage to derive formal analogies between statistical mechanics and thermodynamics.</summary>

# CANONICAL DISTRIBUTION

Now the average value in the ensemble of any quantity (which we shall denote in general by a horizontal line above the proper symbol) is determined by the equation

-> \bar{u} = \int \dots \int_{\text{phases}}^{\text{all}} u e^{\frac{\psi - \epsilon}{\Theta}} dp_1 \dots dq_n. (108) <-

Comparing this with the preceding equation, we have

-> d\psi = \frac{\psi}{\Theta} d\Theta - \frac{\bar{\epsilon}}{\Theta} d\Theta - \bar{A}_1 da_1 - \bar{A}_2 da_2 - \dots (109) <-

Or, since

-> \frac{\psi - \epsilon}{\Theta} = \eta, (110) <-

and

-> \frac{\psi - \bar{\epsilon}}{\Theta} = \bar{\eta}, (111) <-

-> d\psi = \bar{\eta} d\Theta - \bar{A}_1 da_1 - \bar{A}_2 da_2 - \dots (112) <-

Moreover, since (111) gives

-> d\psi - d\bar{\epsilon} = \Theta d\bar{\eta} + \bar{\eta} d\Theta, (113) <-

we have also

-> d\bar{\epsilon} = - \Theta d\bar{\eta} - \bar{A}_1 da_1 - \bar{A}_2 da_2 - \dots (114) <-

This equation, if we neglect the sign of averages, is identical in form with the thermodynamic equation

-> d\eta = \frac{d\epsilon + A_1 da_1 + A_2 da_2 + \dots}{T}, (115) <-

or

-> d\epsilon = T d\eta - A_1 da_1 - A_2 da_2 - \dots (116) <-

which expresses the relation between the energy, temperature, and entropy of a body in thermodynamic equilibrium, and the forces which it exerts on external bodies—a relation which is the mathematical expression of the second law of thermodynamics for reversible changes. The modulus in the statistical equation corresponds to temperature in the thermodynamic equation, and the average index of probability *with its sign reversed* corresponds to entropy. But in the thermodynamic equation the entropy (η) is a quantity which is

<summary>This page establishes the fundamental equivalence between the equations of canonical ensembles and the second law of thermodynamics, identifying the statistical modulus as temperature and the probability index as entropy.</summary>
<keywords>average value, canonical distribution, thermodynamics, entropy, second law of thermodynamics</keywords>
pages.69:
# OF AN ENSEMBLE OF SYSTEMS.

only defined by the equation itself, and incompletely defined in that the equation only determines its differential, and the constant of integration is arbitrary. On the other hand, the η̄ in the statistical equation has been completely defined as the average value in a canonical ensemble of systems of the logarithm of the coefficient of probability of phase.

We may also compare equation (112) with the thermodynamic equation

-> d\psi = -\bar{\eta} dT - A_1 da_1 - A_2 da_2 - \dots, (117) <-

where ψ represents the function obtained by subtracting the product of the temperature and entropy from the energy.

How far, or in what sense, the similarity of these equations constitutes any demonstration of the thermodynamic equations, or accounts for the behavior of material systems, as described in the theorems of thermodynamics, is a question of which we shall postpone the consideration until we have further investigated the properties of an ensemble of systems distributed in phase according to the law which we are considering. The analogies which have been pointed out will at least supply the motive for this investigation, which will naturally commence with the determination of the average values in the ensemble of the most important quantities relating to the systems, and to the distribution of the ensemble with respect to the different values of these quantities.

<summary>The author clarifies the definition of entropy in statistical mechanics versus thermodynamics and introduces the Helmholtz free energy analogy, proposing further investigation into the ensemble properties.</summary>

# PARAGRAPH 11

### THE ESTABLISHMENT OF FUNDAMENTALS

Generally, when utilizing soldiers, there are three stages to victory. Before hostilities break out, laws should be established <note>See paragraph 9, page 238.</note>; once laws are established, they must become customary; once they are customary <insert>custom becoming established</insert>, supplies must be provided. These three things must be accomplished within the country before soldiers can be sent abroad. To perform these three tasks, there are two conditions: the first is to uphold the law so it can be applied <note>Wang Shih-jun adds the word "execute" here based on the Ch’ung-wen text.</note>; the second is to appoint the right men so that the law can be established. 

Relying on the masses is merely assembling a mob; relying on outward appearances is just cleverness; relying on fame and sight is deceitfulness. If a leader relies on any of these three, his soldiers may be captured <note>Wang Shih-jun suggests that the character *yin* (cause) should be *gu* (firmly), which is often used for *gu* (therefore).</note>. Therefore it is said: “The strong are unbending; they fight for what they desire. By fighting, their strength develops to the full, and thus they are prepared. In this way, they have no rival in the four seas, and since order prevails, products are accumulated.”
pages.264:
By the accumulation of products, it is possible for the rewards to be great. If rewards are uniform, rank will be honored; if rank is honored, rewards will bring profit. Therefore it is said: “The army, being based on a state of order, produces a marvelous result; custom, being based on law, allows for ten thousand changes of circumstances; a condition of supremacy being based on the mind, it is outwardly manifested in a state of preparedness <note>The term *shi* (ornament/manifest) is difficult; it is used here in a positive sense. I follow the punctuation of Wang’s text. Yin reads: 'The army is born of order and is different from custom; it is born of law and can adapt to a myriad of changing situations; it is based on the mind and manifested in a state of preparedness.' However, that does not seem as good.</note>.” 

If these three points of view are all taken into consideration, the result will be that the strong may be firmly established. Thus, orderly government is the necessary result of strength, and strength is the result of orderly government; orderly government is the result of riches, and riches are the result of orderly government; riches are the result of strength, and strength is the result of riches. Therefore it is said: “The way to orderly government and strength is to discuss the fundamentals.”

## PARAGRAPH 12
### MILITARY DEFENCE

A state that has to fight on four fronts values defense, and a state that rests against the sea values attack. If a state that fights on four fronts is fond of raising soldiers <note>The word *ju* (raise) should be omitted.</note>, it will be in a dangerous position, as it has to resist four neighbors.
pages.265:
As soon as a country with four neighbors begins hostilities, those four countries mobilize armies; therefore, the country is in a dangerous position. If a state that has to fight on four fronts is unable to raise <note>The text has *she* (to house/stop); I prefer the reading *han* (to contain), as found in the Ch’ung-wen edition.</note>, from a city of ten thousand houses, an army of more than ten thousand men, then the state will be in a dangerous position. Therefore it is said: “A state that has to fight on four fronts should concern itself with defensive warfare.” 

In defending walled cities, the best method is to use the strength of the worn-out men to fight the fresh strength of the invaders. It is assaults upon walled cities that wear out the strength of men. As long as the walled cities have not all been razed, the invaders have no means of penetrating the country <note>Yü suggests reading: 'Unless the cities are entirely razed, the invaders have no way to enter.'</note>. This is what is meant by saying that the strength of worn-out men should fight the fresh strength of the invading force. But when the walled cities have all been razed and the foreign army thus finds the means of penetrating, then certainly it will be exhausted, and the people within the country will be rested. Fighting with rested strength against those of exhausted strength is what is meant by fighting with the strength of fresh men against the worn-out strength of the invading forces. All these are called the misfortunes attendant upon the besieging of walled cities.
pages.266:
It is regarded as a misfortune that, when capturing cities, the strength of the army is always worn out. In these three things, misfortune is due not to insufficient effort, but to mistaken generalship <note>The text seems corrupt; I suggest inserting 'obtain' before 'city'. I read *yue* instead of *ri* (day). The phrase 'It is regarded,' etc., is no doubt a commentary. The expression 'these three things' remains obscure. By the last phrase, one is reminded of the precept in Sun-tzŭ, Chapter 3: 'The worst policy of all is to besiege walled cities; the rule is not to besiege walled cities if it can possibly be avoided.'</note>. 

The way to hold a city is to have abundant strength. Therefore it is said: “When the invading force musters its levies, mobilize as many as three armies, and divide them according to the number of the chariots of the invading force.” Of these three armies, one should be formed of able-bodied men, one of able-bodied women, and one of the old and feeble men and women. These are called the three armies. Cause the army of able-bodied men, with abundant provisions and sharp weapons, to marshal themselves and await the enemy; cause the able-bodied women, with abundant provisions and ramparts at their backs, to marshal themselves and await orders, so as to make—at the approach of the invaders—earthworks as an obstruction, and traps, <term>chevaux-de-frise</term> <note>Portable obstacles made of spiked beams.</note>, and pitfalls, to pull down the supporting beams and to tear down the houses, to transport what is transportable, and to burn what is untransportable <note>The text is corrupt; I follow Sun in reading *zuo* (to clear away) for *geng* (plowing).</note>.
pages.267: ...so that the invaders are not able to make use of them in their attack. Cause the army of the old and feeble to guard the oxen, horses, sheep, and swine, and to collect all that is consumable—plants and water—to feed the others therewith, so as to obtain food for the able-bodied men and women. But see to it carefully that the three armies do not intermingle. If the able-bodied men mingle with the army of the able-bodied women, they will attach great value to the safety of the women, and wicked people will have opportunities for intrigue, with the result that the state will perish. Taking pleasure in the women’s company, the men will be afraid of disturbing reports, and so not even the brave will fight. If the able-bodied men and women intermingle with the army of the old and feeble, then the old will arouse the compassion of the able-bodied, and the feeble the pity of the strong. Compassion and pity in the heart cause brave people to be more anxious and fearful people not to fight <note>The text has been clarified by scholars including Yü and Sun, referencing Mo Ti: 'Up to a hundred paces outside the outer wall, cut away and remove completely all walls and trees... Pull down the houses... carry everything that might be used for the attack inside... burn the wood which cannot be transported.' Regarding the women's role, see also Mo Ti.</note>.
pages.268:
Therefore it is said: “See to it carefully that the three armies do not intermingle.” This is the way to have abundant strength.

### PARAGRAPH 13 <note>This section is largely identical to Han Fei-tzŭ, Chapter 20.</note>
## MAKING ORDERS STRICT <note>The term *chin* refers to a martingale for a horse, used for control.</note>

If orders are made strict, orderly government is not delayed, and if laws are equitable, officials are not wicked. Once the law is fixed, one should not damage it with virtuous words; if men of merit are appointed to office, people will have little to say, but if men of virtue are appointed to office, people will have much to say. The practice of good government begins with making judgments. Where five hamlets are the unit for judgments, supremacy is attained; where ten hamlets are the unit for judgments, there is merely strength <note>Commentators have often misunderstood this; it is not a measurement of distance.</note>. He who procrastinates in creating order will be dismembered. Govern by punishments and wage war by rewards; seek transgressors and do not seek the virtuous.
pages.269:
Therefore, if the law is fixed and not altered, then... If in the country there are no wicked people, there is no wicked trade in the capital. If affairs are many and secondary things <note>i.e., trade and non-essential commerce.</note> are numerous, if agriculture is neglected and criminals gain the upper hand, then the country will certainly be dismembered.

If the people have a surplus of grain, cause them to obtain office and rank by means of their cereals; if through their own efforts they can count upon obtaining office and rank, farmers will not be lazy.

If a tube of no more than four inches has no bottom, it can certainly not be filled <note>As noted in Huai Nan-tzŭ: 'A three-inch tube with no bottom cannot be filled by the whole world.'</note>; to confer office, to give rank, and to grant salaries without regard to merit is like having no bottom.

If a state, when poor, applies itself to war, the poison will originate on the enemy's side, and it will not have the "six parasites" <note>The six internal factors of decay.</note>, but will certainly be strong. If a state, when rich, does not apply itself to war, the poison is transferred to its own interior.
pages.270:
...and it will have the six kinds of parasites and will certainly be weak <note>I follow Yü in altering the text to 'The poison is transferred to the interior and the six parasites are born.' Wang Shih-jun suggests that 'poor' might be better as 'rich,' which aligns with the sense of the passage.</note>. If the state confers office and gives rank according to merit, it may be said to be planning with complete wisdom and fighting with complete courage. Such a country will certainly have no equal. If a state confers office and gives rank according to merit, then government measures will be simple and words will be few. This may be said to be abolishing laws by means of the law, and abolishing words by means of words. But if a state confers office and gives rank according to the six parasites, then government measures will be complicated and words will arise. This may be said to be bringing about laws...

<summary>This section details the military and administrative foundations of the state, emphasizing the necessity of strict law, the merit-based distribution of rank, and the danger of internal parasites that drain a state's strength. It also provides specific logistical advice for defensive warfare, including the segregation of different groups of the population to maintain combat efficiency.</summary>
<keywords>Lord Shang, Legalism, Military Defence, Meritocracy, Six Parasites, Siege Warfare, State Administration</keywords>

The phrase <term>ba'da ma muta'amali</term> is also interpreted as follows: <term>ba'da</term> is a syncopated form of the past tense verb <term>ba'uda</term>; 'It [the cloud], the object of my earnest observation, was far away.'</note>

<note>Another reading: <term>ba'da</term> = (distance) in the objective case as a vocative, with <term>ya</term> implied. It = <term>Ya bu'da ma muta'amali</term> = "O how great was the distance of the object of my earnest observation."</note>

"In looking for the rain, we guessed that the right of its downpour was over Qatan, while the left of it was upon Satar and beyond it upon Yadhbul."

These places are very far apart; hence the magnitude of the storm is described.

<note><term>Yadhbul</term> is <term>ghayr munsarif</term> (diptote), being a verb-form and a proper name, but here used as <term>munsarif</term> (triptote) for the necessity of the rhyme.</note>

->THE SECOND POEM<-

# THE SECOND POEM.

Ascribed to Tarafah, son of 'Abd-il-Bakrí, from the tribe of Bakr-ibn-Wáil. "Tarafah" is his title; his name is 'Amr-bin-ul-'Abd. He was one of the poets of the Age of Ignorance (Paganism) and lived after the time of Malik-ul-Zilleel, the author of the first Qasidah.

It is said that the poet's brother, Ma'bad, reproached him for neglecting their father's camels to indulge in poetical reveries. Ma'bad tauntingly asked, "Can your poetry recover the camels if they are lost?" The poet assured him it could. To test him, Ma'bad neglected the camels, which were then taken by the tribe of Muzar. Tarafah wrote this poem to seek the assistance of 'Amru, Qaboos, and a chieftain of Yaman, successfully recovering the camels along with an additional hundred as a reward.

The metre is *Al-Tawil*, the same as the first poem, as is the rhyme (<term>qafiyah</term>).

| | | | | | | | | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Li-Kholata | atlalun | bi-barqati | Thahmadi | taluhu | ka-baqi | al-washmi | fi | zahiri | al-yadi |
| Fa'ulun | mafa'ilun | fa'ulun | maf'ilun | fa'ulun | mafa'ilun | fa'ulun | maf'ilun | ... | ... |

1 لِخَوْلَةَ أَطْلَالٌ بِبَرْقَةِ ثَهْمَدِ .. تَلُوحُ كَبَاقِي الْوَشْمِ فِي ظَاهِرِ الْيَدِ

"There are traces of Kholah in the stony, sandy plain of Thahmad, which appear like the faint marks of tattooing on the back of the hand."

<summary>Introduction to the second Mu'allaqa by Tarafah, providing biographical and historical context for its composition.</summary>
<keywords>Tarafah, Kholah, Thahmad, biography, Qasidah</keywords>

Kholah is the name of his mistress. Traces refer to the marks left near a former encampment of her tribe, as in the first poem.

<note><term>Kholah</term> is read with a <term>fatha</term>, being a diptote (<term>ghayr munsarif</term>) because it is a feminine proper name. <term>Atlal</term> is the subject (<term>mubtada'</term>); <term>li-Kholata</term> is the predicate. <term>Taluhu</term> is an adjectival sentence modifying <term>atlal</term>.</note>

<note>In some copies, the second hemistich runs: <term>Zalaltu biha abki wa-ubki ila al-ghadi</term> = "Where I remained weeping and making others weep until the next day on account of the memories of the past."</note>

2 وَقُوفًا بِهَا صَحْبِي عَلَيَّ مَطِيَّهُمْ .. يَقُولُونَ لا تَهْلِكْ أَسًى وَتَجَلَّدِ

"My comrades, stopping their camels there near me, say, 'Do not die of grief, but bear it bravely.'"

This is a remarkable example of <term>al-tawarud</term> (coincidence). Both poets, Imru' al-Qais and Tarafah, happened to say the same line, differing only in the rhyme. It is said Tarafah was suspected of plagiarism and had to prove he composed it on the same day as Imru' al-Qais, but in a different place.

3 كَانَ حُدُوجَ الْمَالِكِيَّةِ غُدْوَةً .. خَلايَا سَفِينٍ بِالنَّوَاصِفِ مِنْ دَدِ
4 عَدُولِيَّةٌ أَوْ مِنْ سَفِينِ بْنِ يَامِنٍ .. يَجُورُ بِهَا الْمَلَّاحُ طَوْرًا وَيَهْتَدِي

"As if the Malikian camels, with the howdahs on the morning of her departure in the water-tracts of the village of Dad, were the big ships of 'Adoal, or the vessels of Ibni Yamin, which the sailors at times steer off-course and at times guide straight."

<note><term>'Aduliyyah</term> refers to a small town on the Persian Gulf where ships were built. The poet compares the camels traveling to ships tacking.</note>

<summary>Tarafah laments the loss of his beloved Kholah and compares the departure of her tribe to ships on the sea.</summary>

# Fourteenth Chapter

By meditating on that same luminous principle, devoid of any support, one achieves within a year everything that resides within the sphere of the senses. <note>original: "रस" (rasa) - refers to the essence or taste-related sensory perceptions.</note> (17) Contemplating the subtle forms and images mentioned previously, rising upward, one clearly attains all the outcomes resulting from the sphere of the senses. (18) Therefore, I shall now describe a beautiful and auspicious *dhāraṇā* <term>concentration technique</term> that grants divine vision and is based on the subtle element of form <term>rūpa-tanmātra</term>, for the purpose of achieving all spiritual powers. (19) When a yogi, sitting in solitude with closed eyes, perceives something that appears like the clouds of an autumn twilight, (20) and fixes their consciousness upon it for ten days, they will eventually perceive even the most subtle points of light within it. (21) Some of these are white, some red, others yellow or blue. Upon seeing these, one should meditate with a focused mind, without letting the thought wander. (22) After six months, one sees many forms within these lights. After three years, these same forms become radiant, steady, and brilliant. (23) By practicing this, after three more years, one perceives them in the shape of distinct images. Then, after another year, one sees the light itself, and after six more months, it takes the form of a human figure. (24)

<summary>This page introduces the *dhāraṇā* (meditation) focused on the subtle element of form, detailing a progression of light-based visions over years of practice leading to divine sight.</summary>
<keywords>Yoga, Dhāraṇā, Rūpa-tanmātra, Meditation, Divine Vision</keywords>
pages.174:
# In the Mālinī-Vijayottara Tantra

After practicing for three months, the light spreads throughout the entire body. Through the progression of time, one dwells within the previously mentioned sphere of forms. (25) One obtains all those fruits, and divine vision arises. This is the *dhāraṇā*—a conceptual technique described as a practical means. (26) Fifteen types of variations arise naturally within this practice. Since one attains certainty through this, what is the need for the ostentation of other scriptures? (27) Therefore, I will now tell you about the *dhāraṇā* related to the sense of touch, by which a yogi gains a "diamond-like body." <term>vajradeha</term> (28) One should imagine oneself situated within a hexagonal mandala, resembling dark antimony, with every part of the body vibrating. (29) Then, O Goddess, after ten days, the sensation of ants crawling will occur all over the skin. By meditating on that, (30) one attains a diamond-like body and receives the previously mentioned fruits, contemplating the previously described mandala and form. (31) Who could prevent the knowledge of the sphere of touch from arising? For the sake of the power of the master of that element, one should meditate on oneself within a diminished mandala. (32) Through this success, one will become a knower of all touch. With ears covered and eyes closed, one should practice with effort. (33)

<summary>This page details the practice of the 'diamond-like body' (vajradeha) dhāraṇā, focusing on the sensory perception of touch and the mastery of the hexagonal mandala.</summary>

# Fourteenth Chapter

<margin>Sound</margin>

One should focus their consciousness on the great sound heard therein. After ten days, the internal fire of digestion is ignited. (34) The knowledge of hearing from a distance arises after six months. When the sound heard at the end is faint and perceived bit by bit, (35) that should be known as the *sakala-ātmā* <note>original: "सकलात्मा" - refers to the soul connected to the body/limitations.</note>. Through persistent practice with a focused mind, one gains stability in the knowledge of the sphere of sound. (36) The sound that is heard again, resembling the blowing of a conch at its end, is the form of the *pralayākala* <note>original: "प्रलयाकल" - a stage of spiritual dissolution.</note>; it should be practiced by those desiring that fruit. (37) When that sound covers the subtle sound, it is called the *vijñānākala* <note>original: "विज्ञानाकल" - a stage of consciousness.</note>. That is the "Unconquered" <note>original: "अपराजिते" - referring to a specific state or divinity.</note>. (38) That which is heard at the end of the sound that delights the mind is known to yogis seeking yoga as the *mantra*. (39) Then, another sound is heard that resembles the quiet ringing of a bell. It is called the *mantreśa* <term>Lord of Mantras</term>, granting the fruit of all *siddhis* <term>spiritual powers</term>. (40) The sound that arises at the end of the bell-sound is the state of *mantreśa*; it is the great cause of all perfections. (41) Just as the sound produced by a lute struck by the wind, the sound that is there—one should know that as the *śāmbhava* <term>state of Shiva</term> position. (42)

<summary>This section explains the progression of internal sounds (nāda) encountered during meditation, leading to different stages of consciousness and spiritual mastery (Mantreśa).</summary>

->The Fifteenth Chapter<-

Now, I shall briefly explain the eleven *dhāraṇās* <term>concentrations</term> beginning with the organ of speech and ending with the mind. (1)

<margin>Organ of Speech</margin>
The wise practitioner should contemplate the syllable "Namaḥ" <note>original: "नमः" - a sacred salutation/bowing.</note> ending with speech. By adopting this silence, O Madhusudana, one attains it. (2)

Within six months, one's speech becomes flawless. Within a year, knowledge of the meaning of all scriptures arises. (3)

One's speech becomes adorned with poetry and rhetoric. In three years, one becomes a creator of scriptures oneself. (4)

In that same place, one should contemplate one's own body, white in color, and slightly illuminated by light. (5)

One should meditate on the essence from the moon-disk <note>original: "सोमबिम्ब" - the nectar-dripping moon in yogic physiology.</note> to the end of the light. By doing this in sequence, one attains all the fruits born of the sphere of speech. (6)

Taking that (focus) into the hand and keeping it there for six months, one can grasp objects even from across the ocean after three years. (7)

There, contemplating one's own body as a lotus, one should practice the fourteen-fold <note>original: "चतुर्दश" - referring to the 14-fold classification of practice.</note> path with devotion. (8)

<summary>This page begins the fifteenth chapter, detailing the practice of focus on the organ of speech (vāk) and the hand to achieve eloquence, scriptural mastery, and the ability to grasp distant objects.</summary>
<keywords>Vāgindriya, Dhāraṇā, Speech, Yoga, Siddhi</keywords>
pages.178:
# In the Mālinī-Vijayottara Tantra

By following the previously mentioned temporal rules and the previously described path, one attains all the fruits associated with the practice of the hand. (9)

Meditating on the method of "entering the feet" <note>original: "पादावेश" - a yogic practice involving movement or mobility.</note> with devotion for three years, one can travel the entire earth to the edge of the ocean without fatigue in a single moment. (10)

By practicing the fourteen-fold method and meditating on one's own body, one attains all the previously mentioned fruits associated with the practice of the feet. (11)

By stabilizing the principle of the mind in the anus, one will obtain freedom from disease within a month, if one relies on this. (12)

By practicing with devotion for three years, one attains a reputation for virtue <note>original: "पुण्यश्लोक" - famous for pious deeds.</note>. One will obtain the fourteen-fold fruits here as described before. (13)

One should meditate on the *linga* <term>phallus/symbol of energy</term> in its own form for a month, having mastered the senses. Within six months, one will easily obtain the power to manifest desires. (14)

In this fourteen-fold practice, the wise person who practices gains all the fruits born from the sphere of the *linga* as described before. (15)

One should meditate on one's own tongue, which has the color of the moon, for ten days. The yogi attains the experience of the tongue as if it were of their own essence. (16)

<summary>Continuing the fifteenth chapter, this page outlines specific yogic concentrations on the feet, anus, and tongue to achieve supernormal powers like instant travel, health, and manifested desires.</summary>
<keywords>Yoga, Linga, Dhāraṇā, Siddhi, Physiology</keywords>
pages.179:
The single-minded yogi tastes (the nectar) from a distance after six months. After three years, one directly attains the supreme nectar. (17)

By which this yogi becomes free from old age and death. Even if addicted to forbidden things, they are not overcome by sins. (18)

Contemplating everything else as before, starting with one's own body, one undoubtedly attains the fruit born from the sense of taste. (19)

Slowly contemplating one's own nose as having the color of gold, in ten days the experience of the "emptiness of smell" occurs. (20)

After six months, one smells the fragrance of objects even from a distance. If someone is evil, one should cause them to smell (the scent of) that. <note>original: A protective/defensive measure using scent.</note> (21)

After three years, the yogi who knows yoga, having obtained the divine scent, attains divinity, possessed of the qualities of freedom from old age and death. (22)

One should meditate on everything else as instructed. One attains the gradual fruits by residing in the sphere of smell. (23)

Contemplating one's own eyes as resembling the rising sun, in ten days one will experience blood-leaking from the eyes. (24)

Great pain arises in the forehead, O Great Goddess. One should not fear, nor should one abandon the practice. (25)

### PARAGRAPH 11
### THE ESTABLISHMENT OF FUNDAMENTALS

Generally, in utilizing soldiers, there are three stages to victory: before the outbreak of hostilities, laws should be fixed; once laws are fixed, they should become customary; when they have become customary, supplies should be provided. These three things must be accomplished within the country before soldiers can be sent abroad. To perform these three things, there are two conditions: the first is to support the law so that it can be applied; the second is to appoint the right men so that the law can be established. 

Relying on the masses is described as assembling a mob; relying on outward appearances is called mere cleverness; relying on fame and empty spectacle is called deceitfulness. If one relies on any of these three, one’s soldiers may be captured. Therefore it is said: "The strong are unbending; they fight for what they desire. By fighting, their strength develops to the full, and thus they are prepared. In this way, they have no rival in the four seas, and with order prevailing, products are accumulated."

<summary>This page outlines the foundational requirements for military success: establishing fixed laws, creating a culture of compliance, and ensuring logistical support before mobilizing.</summary>
<keywords>military strategy, law, logistics, discipline, Lord Shang</keywords>
pages.264:
By the accumulation of products, it is possible for rewards to be substantial. If rewards are uniform, rank will be honored; if rank is honored, rewards will bring profit. Therefore it is said: "The army, being based on a state of order, produces a marvelous result; custom, being based on law, brings about ten thousand changes of circumstance; a condition of supremacy, being based on the mind, is outwardly manifested in a state of preparedness." If these three points of view are all taken into consideration, the result will be that the strong may be firmly established. 

Thus, orderly government is the necessary result of strength, and strength is the result of orderly government; orderly government comes from riches, and riches from orderly government; riches come from strength, and strength from riches. Therefore it is said: "The way to orderly government and strength is to discuss the fundamentals."

## PARAGRAPH 12
### MILITARY DEFENCE

A state that has to fight on four fronts values defense, while a state that rests against the sea values attack. For if a state that fights on four fronts is fond of raising soldiers, it will be in a dangerous position, as it has to resist four neighbors.

<summary>This page connects state strength, economic prosperity, and orderly government, framing them as a cycle of fundamental requirements for national security and military success.</summary>
<keywords>orderly government, military defense, state strength, economic policy, rewards and ranks</keywords>
pages.265:
As soon as a country with four neighbors begins hostilities, four countries mobilize armies; therefore, the country is in a dangerous position. If a state that has to fight on four fronts is unable to raise, from a city of ten thousand houses, an army of more than ten thousand men, then the state is in a dangerous position. 

Therefore it is said: "A state that has to fight on four fronts should concern itself with defensive warfare." In defending walled cities, the best way is to use the strength of the worn-out men to fight the fresh strength of the invaders. It is assaults upon walled cities that wear out the strength of men. As long as the walled cities have not all been razed, the invaders have no means of penetrating the country. This is the meaning of the saying that the strength of worn-out men should fight the fresh strength of the invading force. But when the walled cities have all been razed and the foreign army thus finds the means of penetrating, it will certainly be exhausted, and the people within the country will be rested. Fighting with rested strength against those of exhausted strength is what is meant by fighting with the strength of fresh men against the worn-out strength of the invading forces. All these are the misfortunes attending the besieging of walled cities.

<summary>The text argues that states surrounded by enemies must prioritize defensive warfare, focusing on attrition by wearing down invading forces against fortified positions.</summary>
<keywords>defensive warfare, walled cities, siege tactics, attrition, military defense</keywords>
pages.266:
It is regarded as a misfortune that, in capturing cities, the strength of the army is always worn out. In these three things, misfortune is due, not to insufficient effort, but to mistaken generalship.

The way to hold a city is to have abundant strength. Therefore it is said: "When the invading force musters its levies, mobilize as many as three armies, and divide them according to the number of the chariots of the invading force." Of these three armies, one should be formed of able-bodied men, one of able-bodied women, and one of the old and feeble men and women. These are called the three armies. 

Cause the army of able-bodied men, with abundant provisions and sharp weapons, to marshal themselves and await the enemy. Cause the able-bodied women, with abundant provisions and ramparts at their backs, to marshal themselves and await orders, so as to make—at the approach of the invaders—earthworks as obstructions, traps, <term>chevaux-de-frise</term><note>A defensive obstacle consisting of a frame with protruding iron or wooden spikes.</note>, and pitfalls. They should pull down the supporting beams, tear down the houses, transport what is transportable, and burn what is untransportable so that the invaders are not able to make use of it in their attack.

<summary>The author details a three-tier defense system involving able-bodied men, women, and the elderly, emphasizing a scorched-earth policy to deny resources to besiegers.</summary>
<keywords>siege warfare, three armies, scorched earth, logistics, defensive infrastructure</keywords>
pages.267:
Cause the army of the old and feeble to guard the oxen, horses, sheep, and swine, and to collect all that is consumable of plants and water to feed them, so as to provide food for the able-bodied men and women. But be careful that the three armies do not intermingle. If the able-bodied men mingle with the army of the able-bodied women, they will become overly concerned with the women's safety, and wicked people will have opportunities for intrigue, with the result that the state will perish. Taking pleasure in the women's company, the men will be afraid of disturbing reports, and so not even the brave will fight. If the able-bodied men and women intermingle with the army of the old and feeble, then the old will arouse the compassion of the able-bodied, and the feeble the pity of the strong. Compassion and pity in the heart cause brave people to be anxious, and fearful people not to fight.

<summary>This page warns against the social dangers of mixing distinct military units, arguing that emotional attachments and pity hinder the combat effectiveness of the state's defenders.</summary>
<keywords>military discipline, social cohesion, morale, logistics, internal security</keywords>
pages.268:
Therefore it is said: "See to it carefully that the three armies do not intermingle." This is the way to have abundant strength.

## PARAGRAPH 13
### MAKING ORDERS STRICT

If orders are made strict, orderly government is not delayed; if laws are equable, officials are not wicked. Once the law is fixed, one should not damage it with virtuous words. If men of merit are appointed to office, people will have little to say, but if men of virtue are appointed to office, people will have much to say. 

The practice of good government begins with making judgments. Where five hamlets are the unit for judgments, supremacy is attained; where ten hamlets are the unit for judgments, there is merely strength. He who procrastinates in creating order will be dismembered. Govern by punishments and wage war by rewards; seek transgressors and do not seek the virtuous.

<summary>The focus shifts to the importance of strict legal enforcement and the necessity of basing governance on merit and punishment rather than abstract virtue.</summary>
<keywords>Legalism, strict governance, meritocracy, punishment, rewards, judicial units</keywords>
pages.269:
Therefore, if the law is fixed and not altered... If in the country there are no wicked people, there is no wicked trade in the capital. If affairs are many and secondary things—such as trade—are numerous, if agriculture is neglected and criminals gain the upper hand, then the country will certainly be dismembered.

If the people have a surplus of grain, cause them to obtain office and rank by means of their cereals; if through their own efforts they can count upon obtaining office and rank, farmers will not be lazy.

If a tube of no more than four inches has no bottom, it can certainly not be filled; to confer office, to give rank, and to grant salaries without regard to merit is like having no bottom.

If a state, when poor, applies itself to war, the poison will originate on the enemy's side; it will not have the six parasites<note>Refers to social groups or behaviors that consume state resources without contributing to agriculture or warfare, such as merchants or scholars.</note>, but will certainly be strong. If a state, when rich, does not apply itself to war, the poison is transferred to its own interior; it will have the six kinds of parasites and will certainly be weak.

<summary>This page argues that agriculture and warfare are the only two legitimate pursuits, warning that prosperity without military focus leads to internal decay via unproductive classes.</summary>
<keywords>agriculture, war, rank by merit, six parasites, internal decay, economic policy</keywords>
pages.270:
If the state confers office and gives rank according to merit, it may be said to be planning with complete wisdom and fighting with complete courage. Such a country will certainly have no equal. If a state confers office and gives rank according to merit, then government measures will be simple and words will be few. This may be said to be abolishing laws by means of the law and abolishing words by means of words. But if a state confers office and gives rank according to the six parasites, then government measures will be complicated and words will arise. This may be said to be bringing about laws...

<meta>Continuity: This page continues the discussion of statistical equilibrium and explores distributions based on constants of motion other than energy, such as momentum.</meta>
# OTHER DISTRIBUTIONS

[Whether the] statistical equilibrium which has been described is peculiar to it, or whether other distributions may have analogous properties.

Let η' and η'' be the indices of probability in two independent ensembles which are each in statistical equilibrium. Then η' + η'' will be the index in the ensemble obtained by combining each system of the first ensemble with each system of the second. This third ensemble will, of course, be in statistical equilibrium, and the function of phase η' + η'' will be a constant of motion. Now, when infinitesimal forces are added to the compound systems, if η' + η'' (or a function differing infinitesimally from this) is still a constant of motion, it must be due to the nature of the forces added, or—if their action is not entirely specified—due to conditions to which they are subject. Thus, in the case already considered, η' + η'' is a function of the energy of the compound system, and the infinitesimal forces added are subject to the law of conservation of energy.

<margin>||</margin> Another natural supposition regarding the added forces is that they should be such as not to affect the moments of momentum of the compound system. To get a case in which the moments of momentum of the compound system remain constants of motion, we may imagine material particles contained in two concentric spherical shells, being prevented from passing the surfaces bounding the shells by repulsions acting always along lines passing through the common center of the shells. Then, if there are no forces acting between particles in different shells, the mass of particles in each shell will have, besides its energy, the <note>The following phrase is circled in the original:</note> moments of momentum about three axes through the center as constants of motion.

Now let us imagine an ensemble formed by distributing in phase the system of particles in one shell according to the index of probability:

-> A - ε/Θ + ω₁/Ω₁ + ω₂/Ω₂ + ω₃/Ω₃, (98) <-

where ε denotes the energy of the system, and ω₁, ω₂, ω₃, its three moments of momentum, and the other letters represent constants.

<summary>This page introduces the concept of combining independent ensembles and explores how distributions based on constants of motion—specifically energy and moments of momentum—maintain statistical equilibrium.</summary>
<keywords>statistical equilibrium, probability indices, ensembles, constants of motion, moments of momentum</keywords>

# HAVE ANALOGOUS PROPERTIES.

In like manner, let us imagine a second ensemble formed by distributing in phase the system of particles in the other shell according to the index:

-> A' − ε' / Θ + ω₁' / Ω₁ + ω₂' / Ω₂ + ω₃' / Ω₃, (99) <-

where the letters have similar significations, and Θ, Ω₁, Ω₂, Ω₃ have the same values as in the preceding formula. Each of the two ensembles will evidently be in statistical equilibrium, and therefore so will the ensemble of compound systems obtained by combining each system of the first ensemble with each of the second. In this third ensemble, the index of probability will be:

-> A + A' − (ε + ε') / Θ + (ω₁ + ω₁') / Ω₁ + (ω₂ + ω₂') / Ω₂ + (ω₃ + ω₃') / Ω₃, (100) <-

where the four numerators represent functions of phase which are constants of motion for the compound systems.

Now, if we add to each system of this third ensemble infinitesimal conservative forces of attraction or repulsion between particles in different shells—determined by the same law for all the systems—the functions ω₁ + ω₁', ω₂ + ω₂', and ω₃ + ω₃' will remain constants of motion, and a function differing infinitely little from ε + ε' will be a constant of motion. It would therefore require only an infinitesimal change in the distribution in phase of the ensemble of compound systems to make it a case of statistical equilibrium. These properties are entirely analogous to those of canonical ensembles.*

Again, if the relations between the forces and the coordinates can be expressed by linear equations, there will be certain "normal" types of vibration of which the actual motion may be regarded as composed, and the whole energy may be divided:

The case is not so simple when some of the normal types of motion have the same periods. In this case, the addition of infinitesimal forces may completely change the normal types of motion. However, the sum of the partial energies for all the original types of vibration which have any same period will be nearly identical (as a function of phase, i.e., of the coordinates and momenta) with the sum of the partial energies for the normal types of vibration which have the same, or nearly the same, period after the addition of the new forces. If, therefore, the partial energies in the indices of the first two ensembles (101) and (102) which relate to types of vibration having the same periods have the same divisors, the same will be true of the index (103) of the ensemble of compound systems, and the distribution represented will differ infinitesimally from one which would be in statistical equilibrium after the addition of the new forces.*

The same would be true if in the indices of each of the original ensembles we should substitute for the term or terms relating to any period which does not occur in the other ensemble any function of the total energy related to that period, subject only to the general limitation expressed by equation (89). But in order that the ensemble of compound systems (with the added forces) shall always be approximately in statistical equilibrium, it is necessary that the indices of the original ensembles should be linear functions of those partial energies which relate to vibrations of periods common to the two ensembles, and that the coefficients of such partial energies should be the same in the two indices.†
