pages.66:
# CANONICAL DISTRIBUTION

The properties of canonically distributed ensembles of systems—with respect to the equilibrium of the new ensembles which may be formed by combining each system of one ensemble with each system of another—are therefore not peculiar to them in the sense that analogous properties do not belong to some other distributions under special limitations in regard to the systems and forces considered. Yet, the canonical distribution evidently constitutes the most simple case of the kind, and that for which the relations described hold with the least restrictions.

Returning to the case of the canonical distribution, we shall find other analogies with thermodynamic systems if we suppose, as in the preceding chapters,* that the potential energy (εq) depends not only upon the coordinates q₁, q₂, ..., qₙ which determine the configuration of the system, but also upon certain coordinates a₁, a₂, etc., of bodies which we call *external*. By this, we simply mean that they are not to be regarded as forming any part of the system, although their positions affect the forces which act on the system. The forces exerted by the system upon these external bodies will be represented by -dεq/da₁, -dεq/da₂, etc., while -dεq/dq₁, ..., -dεq/dqₙ represent all the forces acting upon the bodies of the system, including those which depend upon the position of the external bodies, as well as those which depend only upon the configuration of the system itself. It will be understood that εp depends only upon q₁, ..., qₙ, p₁, ..., pₙ; in other words, the kinetic energy of the bodies which we call external forms no part of the kinetic energy of the system. It follows that we may write:

-> \frac{d\epsilon}{da_{1}} = \frac{d\epsilon_{q}}{da_{1}} = - A_{1}, (104) <-

although a similar equation would not hold for differentiations relative to the internal coordinates.

* See especially Chapter I, p. 4.

<summary>This page defines the relationship between canonical distributions and thermodynamic systems by introducing "external" coordinates that influence potential energy.</summary>
<keywords>canonical distribution, thermodynamic systems, potential energy, external coordinates, kinetic energy</keywords>
pages.67:
# OF AN ENSEMBLE OF SYSTEMS.

We always suppose these external coordinates to have the same values for all systems of any ensemble. In the case of a canonical distribution—that is, when the index of probability of phase is a linear function of the energy—it is evident that the values of the external coordinates will affect the distribution, since they affect the energy. In the equation:

-> e^{-\frac{ψ}{Θ}} = \int \dots \int_{\text{phases}}^{\text{all}} e^{-\frac{ε}{Θ}} dp_1 \dots dq_n, (105) <-

by which ψ may be determined, the external coordinates a₁, a₂, etc., contained implicitly in ε, as well as Θ, are to be regarded as constant in the integrations indicated. The equation indicates that ψ is a function of these constants. If we imagine their values varied, and the ensemble distributed canonically according to their new values, we have by differentiation of the equation:

-> e^{-\frac{ψ}{Θ}} \left( - \frac{1}{Θ} dψ + \frac{ψ}{Θ^2} dΘ \right) = \frac{1}{Θ^2} dΘ \int \dots \int_{\text{phases}}^{\text{all}} ε e^{-\frac{ε}{Θ}} dp_1 \dots dq_n <-
-> - \frac{1}{Θ} da_1 \int \dots \int_{\text{phases}}^{\text{all}} \frac{dε}{da_1} e^{-\frac{ε}{Θ}} dp_1 \dots dq_n <-
-> - \frac{1}{Θ} da_2 \int \dots \int_{\text{phases}}^{\text{all}} \frac{dε}{da_2} e^{-\frac{ε}{Θ}} dp_1 \dots dq_n - \text{etc.,} (106) <-

or, multiplying by Θe^(ψ/Θ), and setting:

-> - \frac{dε}{da_1} = A_1, \quad - \frac{dε}{da_2} = A_2, \text{ etc.,} <-

-> - dψ + \frac{ψ}{Θ} dΘ = \frac{1}{Θ} dΘ \int \dots \int_{\text{phases}}^{\text{all}} ε e^{\frac{ψ - ε}{Θ}} dp_1 \dots dq_n <-
-> + da_1 \int \dots \int_{\text{phases}}^{\text{all}} A_1 e^{\frac{ψ - ε}{Θ}} dp_1 \dots dq_n <-
-> + da_2 \int \dots \int_{\text{phases}}^{\text{all}} A_2 e^{\frac{ψ - ε}{Θ}} dp_1 \dots dq_n + \text{etc.} (107) <-

<summary>This page details the mathematical derivation of ψ and shows how variations in external coordinates influence the canonical distribution of an ensemble.</summary>
<keywords>canonical distribution, probability of phase, external coordinates, integration, energy</keywords>
pages.68:
# CANONICAL DISTRIBUTION

Now, the average value in the ensemble of any quantity (which we shall denote in general by a horizontal line above the proper symbol) is determined by the equation:

-> \bar{u} = \int \dots \int_{\text{phases}}^{\text{all}} u e^{\frac{\psi - \epsilon}{\Theta}} dp_1 \dots dq_n. (108) <-

Comparing this with the preceding equation, we have:

-> d\psi = \frac{\psi}{\Theta} d\Theta - \frac{\bar{\epsilon}}{\Theta} d\Theta - \bar{A}_1 da_1 - \bar{A}_2 da_2 - \text{etc.} (109) <-

Or, since:

-> \frac{\psi - \epsilon}{\Theta} = \eta, (110) <-

and:

-> \frac{\psi - \bar{\epsilon}}{\Theta} = \bar{\eta}, (111) <-

-> d\psi = \bar{\eta} d\Theta - \bar{A}_1 da_1 - \bar{A}_2 da_2 - \text{etc.} (112) <-

Moreover, since (111) gives:

-> d\psi - d\bar{\epsilon} = \Theta d\bar{\eta} + \bar{\eta} d\Theta, (113) <-

we have also:

-> d\bar{\epsilon} = - \Theta d\bar{\eta} - \bar{A}_1 da_1 - \bar{A}_2 da_2 - \text{etc.} (114) <-

This equation, if we neglect the sign of averages, is identical in form with the thermodynamic equation:

-> d\eta = \frac{d\epsilon + A_1 da_1 + A_2 da_2 + \text{etc.}}{T}, (115) <-

or:

-> d\epsilon = T d\eta - A_1 da_1 - A_2 da_2 - \text{etc.}, (116) <-

which expresses the relation between the energy, temperature, and entropy of a body in thermodynamic equilibrium, and the forces which it exerts on external bodies—a relation which is the mathematical expression of the second law of thermodynamics for reversible changes. The modulus in the statistical equation corresponds to temperature in the thermodynamic equation, and the average index of probability *with its sign reversed* corresponds to entropy.

<summary>The author identifies the formal correspondence between his statistical mechanical equations and the thermodynamic equations, specifically linking the modulus to temperature and the negative index of probability to entropy.</summary>
<keywords>canonical distribution, average value, entropy, thermodynamic equilibrium, second law of thermodynamics</keywords>
pages.69:
# OF AN ENSEMBLE OF SYSTEMS.

But in the thermodynamic equation, the entropy (η) is a quantity which is only defined by the equation itself, and it is incompletely defined in that the equation only determines its differential, and the constant of integration is arbitrary. On the other hand, the η̄ in the statistical equation has been completely defined as the average value in a canonical ensemble of systems of the logarithm of the coefficient of probability of phase.

We may also compare equation (112) with the thermodynamic equation:

-> dψ = − η̄ dT − A₁ da₁ − A₂ da₂ − etc., (117) <-

where ψ represents the function obtained by subtracting the product of the temperature and entropy from the energy.

How far, or in what sense, the similarity of these equations constitutes any demonstration of the thermodynamic equations, or accounts for the behavior of material systems as described in the theorems of thermodynamics, is a question of which we shall postpone the consideration until we have further investigated the properties of an ensemble of systems distributed in phase according to the law which we are considering. The analogies which have been pointed out will at least supply the motive for this investigation, which will naturally commence with the determination of the average values in the ensemble of the most important quantities relating to the systems, and to the distribution of the ensemble with respect to the different values of these quantities.

<summary>This page clarifies the difference between the arbitrary constant in thermodynamic entropy and the concrete statistical definition provided by Gibbs, while setting the stage for further investigation into these analogies.</summary>
<keywords>entropy, canonical ensemble, probability of phase, thermodynamics, statistical mechanics</keywords>

# Chapter 14

By meditating on that same light, which is devoid of any support, within a year the practitioner obtains everything associated with the perception of taste. <note>original: "रस" (rasa) - refers to taste or essence.</note> 

By contemplating the image described in the earth-element <term>dhārā-tattva</term> and anything above it, one clearly obtains all the previously mentioned fruits born from the perception of taste. 

Now, I shall describe the auspicious <term>dhāraṇā</term> (fixation of mind) that grants divine vision, which relies on the subtle element of form <term>rūpa-tanmātra</term> for the sake of all accomplishments. 

When a yogi is alone with closed eyes, and perceives something that resembles the clouds of an autumn evening, if he fixes his mind there for ten days, he will begin to see even the most subtle points of light. Some are white, some red, others yellow, and still others blue. Having seen them, if one keeps one's mind focused there with undivided attention, after six months one sees many forms within them. 

After three years, these same forms become bright with radiance and remain steady. By continuing the practice for another three years, one sees them in the shape of images <term>bimba</term>. After another year, one sees light, and within six months of that, one perceives a human form. 

<summary>This section details the progression of meditative practices (dhāraṇā) focused on form and light, leading to the attainment of divine vision.</summary>
<keywords>Dhāraṇā, Yoga, Divine Vision, Meditation, Subtle Elements</keywords>

<meta>Continuity from page 173: Continuation of meditation on form.</meta>

After three months of practicing on this light, it spreads everywhere within a month. Following the sequence of time, one relies on the previously mentioned veil of form. One obtains all the fruits thereof, and divine vision arises. This is the <term>dhāraṇā</term> described as <term>kṛtaka</term> (constructed), which is devoid of conceptualization. 

The fifteen-fold division arises here of its own accord. Since one attains certainty in this, what is the use of the vanity of other scriptures? 

Now, I shall tell you about the <term>dhāraṇā</term> related to touch, by which a yogi becomes possessed of a diamond-like body (<term>vajradeha</term>). 

One should contemplate oneself as being within a six-pointed mandala, resembling black antimony, trembling in every part. O Goddess, after ten days, the sensation of ants crawling will be felt on one's skin everywhere. By continuing to contemplate that, one attains a diamond-like body and obtains the previously mentioned fruits as before. 

By contemplating the previously mentioned mandala shape and the primordial form, who can prevent the knowledge of the veil of the touch-element? One should meditate on oneself as being in the <term>hīna-maṇḍala</term> (a specific low-level mandala) for the perfection of the lord of that element. Through this perfection, one will become a knower of all touch. Closing the ears with effort and keeping the eyes closed, [one practices this].

<summary>This text introduces practices for developing a "diamond-like body" through meditation on the touch element and the use of a six-pointed mandala.</summary>
<keywords>Vajradeha, Mandala, Touch-element, Yoga, Siddhi</keywords>
pages.175:
<meta>Continuity from page 174: Continuation of meditation practices.</meta>

<margin>Sound</margin>

One should focus the mind on the great sound that one hears. By doing so, the internal fire <term>jāṭhara-vahni</term> ignites, and after ten days, the knowledge of hearing from a distance arises within six months. 

That which is heard as a faint sound at the end is to be known as the <term>sakalātmā</term> (the soul with parts). By practicing this with undivided attention, one gains the knowledge of the veil of sound and attains stability. 

The sound that is heard again like a conch shell at the end is the form of the <term>pralayākala</term> (a state of dissolution), which should be practiced by those desiring its fruits. When that sound overwhelms the previous subtle sound, it is called <term>vijñānākala</term>; at that time, O Unconquered One, [one attains this state]. 

That which is pleasing to the mind and perceived at the end is to be known as the <term>mantra</term> by yogis who seek the path of yoga. That which is heard after that, like the sound of a silent bell, is called <term>mantreśa</term> (lord of mantras), the giver of the fruits of all accomplishments. 

At the end of the cessation of the bell sound, the sound that arises is the position of <term>mantreśa</term>, the great cause of accomplishments. The sound that is like the music of a lute played by the wind—that should be known as the state of <term>śāmbhava</term>. 

<summary>This page details the stages of sound perception during meditation, leading to the realization of Mantra and the Śāmbhava state.</summary>
<keywords>Sound, Mantra, Mantreśa, Śāmbhava, Yoga</keywords>

Whether separately or in sequence, one should practice all of these. Having relied upon the veil of sound, one attains the perfection of being all-knowing <term>sarva-vit-siddhi</term>. 

Thus are described the five <term>dhāraṇās</term> (fixations) of the subtle elements.

pages.177:

->Now, the fifteenth chapter.<-

Now, I shall describe in summary the eleven <term>dhāraṇās</term> beginning with the organ of speech <term>vāk-indriya</term> and ending with the mind. 

<margin>Organ of speech</margin>

The wise one should contemplate the sound of "Namah" (obeisance) ending with speech in oneself. Having taken this upon oneself, one attains silence, O slayer of Madhu (Krishna). 

Within six months, one’s speech becomes flawless in all places. Within a year, the knowledge of the meaning of all scriptures arises. 

One's speech becomes adorned with poetry and rhetoric. Within three years, the practitioner himself becomes a creator of scriptures. 

In that same [practice], one should contemplate one's own body accordingly, becoming white and slightly illuminated by light. One should remember it as ending with the light of the moon-disk within the taste. By following this sequence, one obtains all the fruits born of the veil of speech. 

Having taken that in the hand, and after six months, it stays in the essence. One grasps objects without doubt, even from beyond the ocean, after three years. 

Contemplating the lotus-like form beginning with one's own body, one should focus on the fourteen-fold division with devotion.

<summary>Introduction to the fifteen-fold (or eleven-fold as mentioned) dhāraṇās, beginning with practices related to the organ of speech and the hand.</summary>
<keywords>Vāgindriya, Dhāraṇā, Scripture, Yoga, Meditation</keywords>
pages.178:
<meta>Continuity from page 177: Continuation of specific dhāraṇā practices.</meta>

By following the previously mentioned rules of time and the path, one obtains all the fruits associated with the practice of the hand. 

By meditating on the method of the feet for three years with devotion, one can tirelessly walk to the ends of the ocean in a single moment. 

Having worshiped the fourteen-fold divisions and practicing on one's own body, one obtains all the previously mentioned fruits related to the practice of the feet. 

By fixing the element of the mind in the anus, one will attain freedom from disease within a month. 

By practicing with devotion for three years, one attains the state of having a "pure story" (fame). Here, one will obtain the fourteen-fold fruits as before. 

By remembering the phallus (<term>liṅga</term>) in its true form for a month, one subdues the senses. In six months, one easily attains the power to fulfill one's desires <term>icchā-kāmitva</term>. 

In the fourteen-fold division, when practiced, the great-minded one obtains all the fruits born of the veil of the phallus, as before. 

By contemplating one's own tongue, which has the luster of the moon, for ten days, the yogi attains the experience as if it were the essence of the self. 

<summary>Describes specific meditative practices for the feet, anus, phallus, and tongue to attain various siddhis.</summary>
<keywords>Yoga, Linga, Siddhi, Dhāraṇā, Meditation</keywords>
pages.179:
<meta>Continuity from page 178: Continuation of tongue and sense-based meditations.</meta>

One tastes the distant object in six months with a focused mind. Within three years, one directly obtains the supreme nectar. 

By this, the yogi becomes free from old age and death. Even if he engages in forbidden things, he is not overcome by sins. 

Contemplating everything else as before—starting from one's own body—one undoubtedly obtains the fruit arising from the essence of taste. 

By contemplating one's own nose, which has the luster of gold, slowly for ten days, the experience of the void of smell occurs. 

Within six months, one smells the scent of an object even from a distance. One should cause the scent to be smelled by him for whom it will be bad. 

Within three years, the knower of yoga, having obtained the divine scent, deserves divinity, being free from the qualities of old age and death. 

One should contemplate everything else just as it was taught, and one obtains the sequential fruit by dwelling on the veil of smell. 

Contemplating one's own eyes as having the luster of the rising sun, in ten days one will experience the flow of blood from the eyes. Great pain arises in the forehead of the practitioner. O great Goddess, one should not be afraid, nor should one abandon the practice. 

<summary>Explains meditations on the senses of taste, smell, and sight to attain divine perceptions and freedom from decay.</summary>
<keywords>Yoga, Taste, Smell, Vision, Siddhi, Deathless</keywords>
pages.180:
<meta>Continuity from page 179: Conclusion of the sense-based meditation chapter.</meta>

By abandoning [fear], blindness is averted; therefore, one should practice with effort. Within six months, the great yogi attains divine vision. 

The alert practitioner sees the earth as if it were porous, all the way to the foundation, and upward as well, like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand. 

Within three years, the yogi sees the end of the universe. The knowledge of the <term>yoginīs</term> within that, residing in the body, arises. 

By remembering one's own body and the other things as previously mentioned, is it any wonder that one obtains everything from the vision of the eyes? 

By remembering the skin to be as smooth as the leaf of a black antimony (or anjan) plant, with no waves, within a month it will not be possible to kill the practitioner even with weapons. 

Within six months, it is not burnt even by the most intense fire. By practicing for three years, the yogi is never afflicted by diamond, stone, or poison, having attained old age-lessness and immortality. 

The fourteen-fold divisions of the touch-vision knowledge should be known with their fruits according to the previous timing. However, here one should contemplate the body as covered by one's own body. 

Applying one's own consciousness to the space of hearing <term>śrotrākāśa</term>, the wise one obtains the knowledge of hearing from a distance within six months. 

<summary>Describes the attainment of supernatural physical invulnerability and the ability to hear across distances through advanced meditation.</summary>
<keywords>Divine Vision, Invulnerability, Siddhi, Śrotrākāśa, Yoga</keywords>

<meta>Continuity from page 37/61: Continuing the discussion of statistical equilibrium and its potential extension to other types of probability distributions.</meta>
# OTHER DISTRIBUTIONS

statistical equilibrium which have been described are peculiar to it, or whether other distributions may have analogous properties.

Let η' and η'' be the indices of probability in two independent ensembles which are each in statistical equilibrium; then η' + η'' will be the index in the ensemble obtained by combining each system of the first ensemble with each system of the second. This third ensemble will of course be in statistical equilibrium, and the function of phase η' + η'' will be a constant of motion. Now when infinitesimal forces are added to the compound systems, if η' + η'' or a function differing infinitesimally from this is still a constant of motion, it must be on account of the nature of the forces added, or if their action is not entirely specified, on account of conditions to which they are subject. Thus, in the case already considered, η' + η'' is a function of the energy of the compound system, and the infinitesimal forces added are subject to the law of conservation of energy.

<margin>||</margin> Another natural supposition in regard to the added forces is that they should be such as not to affect the moments of momentum of the compound system. To get a case in which moments of momentum of the compound system shall be constants of motion, we may imagine material particles contained in two concentric spherical shells, being prevented from passing the surfaces bounding the shells by repulsions acting always in lines passing through the common centre of the shells. Then, if there are no forces acting between particles in different shells, the mass of particles in each shell will have, besides its energy, the <note>The following phrase is circled in the original:</note> moments of momentum about three axes through the centre as constants of motion.

Now let us imagine an ensemble formed by distributing in phase the system of particles in one shell according to the index of probability

-> A - ε/Θ + ω₁/Ω₁ + ω₂/Ω₂ + ω₃/Ω₃, (98) <-

where ε denotes the energy of the system, and ω₁, ω₂, ω₃, its three moments of momentum, and the other letters constants.

<summary>This page introduces the idea that distributions other than the canonical ensemble might exhibit properties of statistical equilibrium, specifically when constants of motion like energy or moments of momentum are involved.</summary>
<keywords>statistical equilibrium, probability index, constants of motion, moments of momentum, concentric shells</keywords>

# HAVE ANALOGOUS PROPERTIES.

In like manner let us imagine a second ensemble formed by distributing in phase the system of particles in the other shell according to the index

->A' − ε' / Θ + ω₁' / Ω₁ + ω₂' / Ω₂ + ω₃' / Ω₃, (99)<-

where the letters have similar significations, and Θ, Ω₁, Ω₂, Ω₃ the same values as in the preceding formula. Each of the two ensembles will evidently be in statistical equilibrium, and therefore also the ensemble of compound systems obtained by combining each system of the first ensemble with each of the second. In this third ensemble the index of probability will be

->A + A' − (ε + ε') / Θ + (ω₁ + ω₁') / Ω₁ + (ω₂ + ω₂') / Ω₂ + (ω₃ + ω₃') / Ω₃, (100)<-

where the four numerators represent functions of phase which are constants of motion for the compound systems.

Now if we add in each system of this third ensemble infinitesimal conservative forces of attraction or repulsion between particles in different shells, determined by the same law for all the systems, the functions ω₁ + ω₁', ω₂ + ω₂', and ω₃ + ω₃' will remain constants of motion, and a function differing infinitely little from ε + ε' will be a constant of motion. It would therefore require only an infinitesimal change in the distribution in phase of the ensemble of compound systems to make it a case of statistical equilibrium. These properties are entirely analogous to those of canonical ensembles.*

Again, if the relations between the forces and the coordinates can be expressed by linear equations, there will be certain "normal" types of vibration of which the actual motion may be regarded as composed, and the whole energy may be divided

The consideration of the above case of statistical equilibrium may be made the foundation of the theory of the thermodynamic equilibrium of rotating bodies—a subject which has been treated by Maxwell in his memoir "On Boltzmann's theorem on the average distribution of energy in a system of material points." <meta>Continuity from page 64: Discussing cases where vibration periods might be identical.</meta>
# HAVE ANALOGOUS PROPERTIES.
<meta>Handwritten checkmark in right margin next to the first full paragraph.</meta>

ensemble of compound systems after the addition of the supposed infinitesimal forces will differ infinitesimally from one which would be in statistical equilibrium.

<margin>✓</margin>
The case is not so simple when some of the normal types of motion have the same periods. In this case the addition of infinitesimal forces may completely change the normal types of motion. But the sum of the partial energies for all the original types of vibration which have any same period, will be nearly identical (as a function of phase, i.e., of the coordinates and momenta) with the sum of the partial energies for the normal types of vibration which have the same, or nearly the same, period after the addition of the new forces. If, therefore, the partial energies in the indices of the first two ensembles (101) and (102) which relate to types of vibration having the same periods, have the same divisors, the same will be true of the index (103) of the ensemble of compound systems, and the distribution represented will differ infinitesimally from one which would be in statistical equilibrium after the addition of the new forces.*

The same would be true if in the indices of each of the original ensembles we should substitute for the term or terms relating to any period which does not occur in the other ensemble, any function of the total energy related to that period, subject only to the general limitation expressed by equation (89). But in order that the ensemble of compound systems (with the added forces) shall always be approximately in statistical equilibrium, it is necessary that the indices of the original ensembles should be linear functions of those partial energies which relate to vibrations of periods common to the two ensembles, and that the coefficients of such partial energies should be the same in the two indices.†

---

* It is interesting to compare the above relations with the laws respecting the exchange of energy between bodies by radiation, although the phenomena of radiations lie entirely without the scope of the present treatise, in which the discussion is limited to systems of a finite number of degrees of freedom.

† The above may perhaps be sufficiently illustrated by the simple case where n = 1 in each system. If the periods are different in the two systems, they may be distributed according to any functions of the energies: but if the periods are the same they must be distributed canonically with the same modulus in order that the compound ensemble with additional forces may be in statistical equilibrium.

<summary>The author clarifies that when systems share vibration periods, they must follow specific canonical distribution requirements to maintain statistical equilibrium upon combination.</summary>

pages.66:
<meta>Continuity from page 65: Summarizing the implications of canonical distribution for thermodynamic systems.</meta>
# CANONICAL DISTRIBUTION

The properties of canonically distributed ensembles of systems with respect to the equilibrium of the new ensembles which may be formed by combining each system of one ensemble with each system of another, are therefore not peculiar to them in the sense that analogous properties do not belong to some other distributions under special limitations in regard to the systems and forces considered. Yet the canonical distribution evidently constitutes the most simple case of the kind, and that for which the relations described hold with the least restrictions.

Returning to the case of the canonical distribution, we shall find other analogies with thermodynamic systems, if we suppose, as in the preceding chapters,* that the potential energy (ε_q) depends not only upon the coordinates q_1 … q_n which determine the configuration of the system, but also upon certain coordinates a_1, a_2, etc. of bodies which we call *external*, meaning by this simply that they are not to be regarded as forming any part of the system, although their positions affect the forces which act on the system. The forces exerted by the system upon these external bodies will be represented by - dε_q / da_1, - dε_q / da_2, etc., while - dε_q / dq_1, … - dε_q / dq_n represent all the forces acting upon the bodies of the system, including those which depend upon the position of the external bodies, as well as those which depend only upon the configuration of the system itself. It will be understood that ε_p depends only upon q_1, … q_n, p_1, … p_n; in other words, that the kinetic energy of the bodies which we call external forms no part of the kinetic energy of the system. It follows that we may write

->dε / da_1 = dε_q / da_1 = - A_1, (104)<-

although a similar equation would not hold for differentiations relative to the internal coordinates.

* See especially Chapter I, p. 4.

<summary>This page introduces the external coordinates that affect system potential energy and bridges the gap between statistical mechanical systems and thermodynamic systems.</summary>
<keywords>canonical distribution, thermodynamic systems, potential energy, external coordinates, kinetic energy</keywords>
pages.67:
<meta>Continuity from page 66: Mathematical derivation of the effects of external coordinates on the canonical distribution.</meta>
# OF AN ENSEMBLE OF SYSTEMS.

We always suppose these external coordinates to have the same values for all systems of any ensemble. In the case of a canonical distribution, i.e., when the index of probability of phase is a linear function of the energy, it is evident that the values of the external coordinates will affect the distribution, since they affect the energy. In the equation

-> e^(-ψ/Θ) = ∫ … ∫_{phases}^{all} e^(-ε/Θ) dp_1 … dq_n, (105) <-

by which ψ may be determined, the external coordinates, a_1, a_2, etc., contained implicitly in ε, as well as Θ, are to be regarded as constant in the integrations indicated. The equation indicates that ψ is a function of these constants. If we imagine their values varied, and the ensemble distributed canonically according to their new values, we have by differentiation of the equation:

-> e^(-ψ/Θ) ( - 1/Θ dψ + ψ/Θ² dΘ ) = 1/Θ² dΘ ∫ … ∫_{phases}^{all} ε e^(-ε/Θ) dp_1 … dq_n <-
-> - 1/Θ da_1 ∫ … ∫_{phases}^{all} (dε/da_1) e^(-ε/Θ) dp_1 … dq_n <-
-> - 1/Θ da_2 ∫ … ∫_{phases}^{all} (dε/da_2) e^(-ε/Θ) dp_1 … dq_n - etc., (106) <-

or, multiplying by Θ e^(ψ/Θ), and setting

-> - dε/da_1 = A_1, - dε/da_2 = A_2, etc., <-

-> - dψ + ψ/Θ dΘ = 1/Θ dΘ ∫ … ∫_{phases}^{all} ε e^((ψ - ε)/Θ) dp_1 … dq_n <-
-> + da_1 ∫ … ∫_{phases}^{all} A_1 e^((ψ - ε)/Θ) dp_1 … dq_n <-
-> + da_2 ∫ … ∫_{phases}^{all} A_2 e^((ψ - ε)/Θ) dp_1 … dq_n + etc. (107) <-

<summary>The author derives the differential relationships involving ψ, the modulus Θ, and external coordinates, showing how they relate to the energy and force variables.</summary>
<keywords>canonical distribution, external coordinates, differential equations, integration, phase distribution</keywords>
pages.68:
<meta>Continuity from page 67: Identifying average values of quantities within the ensemble.</meta>
# CANONICAL DISTRIBUTION

Now the average value in the ensemble of any quantity (which we shall denote in general by a horizontal line above the proper symbol) is determined by the equation

-> ū = ∫_{phases}^{all} … ∫ u e^((ψ - ε)/Θ) dp_1 … dq_n. (108) <-

Comparing this with the preceding equation, we have

-> dψ = (ψ/Θ) dΘ - (ē/Θ) dΘ - Ā_1 da_1 - Ā_2 da_2 - etc. (109) <-

Or, since

-> (ψ - ε)/Θ = η, (110) <-

and

-> (ψ - ē)/Θ = η̄, (111) <-

-> dψ = η̄ dΘ - Ā_1 da_1 - Ā_2 da_2 - etc. (112) <-

Moreover, since (111) gives

-> dψ - dē = Θ dη̄ + η̄ dΘ, (113) <-

we have also

-> dē = - Θ dη̄ - Ā_1 da_1 - Ā_2 da_2 - etc. (114) <-

This equation, if we neglect the sign of averages, is identical in form with the thermodynamic equation

-> dη = (dε + A_1 da_1 + A_2 da_2 + etc.) / T, (115) <-

or

-> dε = T dη - A_1 da_1 - A_2 da_2 - etc., (116) <-

which expresses the relation between the energy, temperature, and entropy of a body in thermodynamic equilibrium, and the forces which it exerts on external bodies—a relation which is the mathematical expression of the second law of thermodynamics for reversible changes. The modulus in the statistical equation corresponds to temperature in the thermodynamic equation, and the average index of probability *with its sign reversed* corresponds to entropy.

<summary>This page demonstrates the formal identity between the statistical equations derived and the fundamental laws of thermodynamics, specifically the relation between energy, entropy, and temperature.</summary>
<keywords>average values, canonical distribution, entropy, modulus, thermodynamic equilibrium, second law of thermodynamics</keywords>
pages.69:
<meta>Continuity from page 68: Concluding the derivation and preparing for further investigation of ensembles.</meta>
# OF AN ENSEMBLE OF SYSTEMS.

But in the thermodynamic equation the entropy (η) is a quantity which is only defined by the equation itself, and incompletely defined in that the equation only determines its differential, and the constant of integration is arbitrary. On the other hand, the η̄ in the statistical equation has been completely defined as the average value in a canonical ensemble of systems of the logarithm of the coefficient of probability of phase.

We may also compare equation (112) with the thermodynamic equation

-> dψ = - η̄ dT - A_1 da_1 - A_2 da_2 - etc., (117) <-

where ψ represents the function obtained by subtracting the product of the temperature and entropy from the energy.

How far, or in what sense, the similarity of these equations constitutes any demonstration of the thermodynamic equations, or accounts for the behavior of material systems, as described in the theorems of thermodynamics, is a question of which we shall postpone the consideration until we have further investigated the properties of an ensemble of systems distributed in phase according to the law which we are considering. The analogies which have been pointed out will at least supply the motive for this investigation, which will naturally commence with the determination of the average values in the ensemble of the most important quantities relating to the systems, and to the distribution of the ensemble with respect to the different values of these quantities.

<summary>The author compares statistical and thermodynamic entropy and sets the stage for further investigation into the physical significance of these mathematical analogies.</summary>
<keywords>statistical mechanics, thermodynamics, entropy, ensemble, probability of phase</keywords>

71 <foreign lang="ar">فَبَاتَ عَلَيْهِ سَرْجُهُ وَلِجَامُهُ .. وَبَاتَ بِعَيْنِي قَائِمًا غَيْرَ مُرْسَلِ</foreign>

"He spent the night with his saddle and bridle on; he spent the night standing before my eyes, not sent off to the stable."

*   <term>قَائِمًا</term> (standing) and <term>غَيْرَ</term> (not) are in the accusative case, acting as <term>حَال</term> (adverbial state/condition).
*   <term>عَلَيْهِ سَرْجُهُ</term> (upon him is his saddle), etc., functions as an adverbial sentence of state (<term>حَال</term>); <term>لِجَامُهُ</term> (his bridle) and <term>سَرْجُهُ</term> (his saddle) are the subject and predicate respectively.

72 <foreign lang="ar">أَصَاحِ تَرَى بَرْقًا أُرِيكَ وَمِيضَهُ .. كَلَمْعِ الْيَدَيْنِ فِي حَبِيٍّ مُكَلَّلِ</foreign>

"Oh, my companion, do you see the lightning, whose glitter I am showing you—like the flashing of two hands in thick, clustered, crowned clouds."

*   <term>أَصَاحِ</term> (O companion) is <term>مُرَخَّم</term> (truncated) from <term>صَاحِب</term> (companion), with the final <term>ب</term> suppressed; it retains its original vowel, the <term>كَسْرَة</term> (i).
*   <term>أُرِيكَ وَمِيضَهُ</term> (I show you its glitter) is an adjectival sentence modifying <term>بَرْقًا</term> (lightning).
*   <term>تَرَى</term> (do you see) is interrogative, with <term>هَل</term> (is it that) or <term>أ</term> (an) implied.
*   <term>مُكَلَّل</term> (crowned/encircled) = either crowned, encircling, or flashing with lightning.

Another reading is <term>أَحَارُ</term> = <term>أَحَارِثُ</term> (Hárith).
Another reading is <term>أَعِنِّي عَلَى بَرْقٍ</term> = "Assist me in seeing the lightning."

73 <foreign lang="ar">يُضِيءُ سَنَاهُ أَوْ مَصَابِيحُ رَاهِبٍ .. أَمَالَ السَّلِيطَ بِالدَّبَالِ الْمُفَتَّلِ</foreign>

"Its radiance shines, or [it shines] like the lamps of a monk who has dipped well-twisted wicks into the oil."

*   <term>أَمَالَ السَّلِيطَ بِالدَّبَالِ</term> (he tilted the oil with the wicks) is an example of an inverted construction. It acts as an adjectival sentence modifying <term>رَاهِبٍ</term> (monk).
*   Another reading is <term>أَهَانَ السَّلِيطَ</term> (he did not spare the oil), meaning he used it lavishly.
*   <term>أَهَانَ</term> means he considered it of no value.
*   <term>مَصَابِيحُ</term> (lamps) is in the genitive case, coordinate with <term>لَمْعِ</term> (flashing) in the previous line.

<summary>This page continues the philological and grammatical analysis of the first Mu'allaqat, focusing on the description of a horse and the imagery of lightning in the desert.</summary>
<keywords>Arabic poetry, Al-Mu'allaqat, linguistics, grammar, philology</keywords>
pages.56:
Or in the objective case, with the <term>ك</term> (like/as) implied; or in the nominative case, serving as the subject to <term>يضيء</term> (it shines), coordinate with <term>سناه</term> (its radiance); or connected to the implied word qualified by the <term>ك</term> in the preceding line.

74 <term>قعدت له وصحبتي بين ضارج .. وبين العذيب بعد ما متأملي</term>

"I sat down for it with my companions between Zárij and 'Uzaib after watching it [the lightning] attentively."

*   <term>صحبتي</term> (my companions, plural of <term>صاحب</term>) is in the nominative case, coordinate to the implied first-person pronoun in <term>قعدت</term> (I sat).
*   <term>ما</term> is an expletive (a filler word for emphasis), and <term>متأملي</term> (my observing) functions as a verbal noun.
*   <term>بعد ما متأملي</term> is also interpreted as: <term>بعد</term> is a shortened form of the past tense verb <term>بَعُدَ</term> (it was far); it means the cloud, the object of my earnest observation, was far away.

Another reading: <term>بُعْدَ</term> (distance) is in the objective case, treated as a vocative (<term>منادى</term>), with <term>يا</term> (O) implied. It means: "O, how great was the distance of the object of my earnest observation!"

75 <term>علي قطن بالشيم ايمن صوبر .. وايسره علي الستار فيذبل</term>

"In looking for the rain, we guessed that the right side of its downpour was over Qatan, while the left side of it was over Satár and beyond that upon Yazbul."

These locations are very far apart, highlighting the massive scale of the storm.
*   <term>علي قطن</term> (over Qatan), with <term>ايمن</term> (right side) implied.

Another reading: <term>عَلَيَّ قَطَنًا</term>. It then means: "As we guessed from observing the lightning and other signs of rain, its right-side downpour was over Qatan, etc."

*   <term>يذبل</term> (Yazbul) is <term>غير منصرف</term> (diptote), due to being a proper noun and having the form of a verb, but it is treated as <term>منصرف</term> (triptote) here due to the requirements of the rhyme.

<summary>The author analyzes verses 74-75, discussing geographical markers in the desert and the grammatical treatment of locations in Arabic poetry.</summary>
<keywords>Arabic grammar, Al-Mu'allaqat, Qatan, Satár, Yazbul, geography</keywords>
pages.57:
76 فَأَضْحَى يَسِحُّ المَاءُ حَوْلَ كُثَيْفَةٍ .. يَكُبُّ عَلَى الأَذْقَانِ دَوْحَ الكَنَهْبُلِ

"The storm began to pour its waters around Kuthaifah, overturning the large Kanahbul trees upon their faces [the ground]."

*   <term>أَذْقَان</term> (plural of <term>ذَقَن</term>, literally 'a chin'). Here, it signifies the upper branches of the tree.
*   Another reading is <term>مِنْ كُلِّ دِيقَةٍ</term> (from what collects at each interval of raining); and also <term>مِنْ كُلِّ ثُلْعَةٍ</term> (from each watercourse).
*   <term>يَسِحُّ</term> (it pours) is the predicate after <term>أَضْحَى</term> (it became/commenced). <term>يَكُبُّ</term> (it overturns) is an adverbial sentence of state (<term>حَال</term>). The <term>الهاء</term> (pronoun) refers back to the verb.

77 وَمَرَّ عَلَى القَنَانِ مِنْ نَفَيَانِهِ .. فَأَنْزَلَ مِنْهُ العِصْمَ مِنْ كُلِّ مَنْزِلِ

"Then it passed over the hills of Qanán with such spray that it was so violent it forced the mountain goats to descend from every haunt."

*   He describes the violence of the storm.
*   <term>عِصْم</term> (plural of <term>أَعْصَم</term>) refers to a gazelle or mountain goat with white forelegs above the pastern, or a color distinct from the rest of its body.
*   Another reading of the first hemistich: <term>وَأَلْقَى بِبَيْسَانَ مَعَ اللَّيْلِ بُرْكَةً</term> = "It settled itself on Mount Busyán at night." <term>أَلْقَى بُرْكَةً</term> means it placed its chest down like a camel.
*   <term>بَيْسَان</term> (Busyán) is normally a diptote (<term>غَيْرُ مُنْصَرِف</term>), but used here as a triptote (<term>مُنْصَرِف</term>) by poetic license.

78 وَتَيْمَاءَ لَمْ يَتْرُكْ بِهَا جِذْعَ نَخْلَةٍ .. وَلَا أُطُمًا إِلَّا مُشَيَّدًا بِجَنْدَلِ

"And at Taimáa, it did not leave a single date palm trunk standing, nor any building except those strengthened with hard stones."

*   <term>تَيْمَاءَ</term> is the object of the verb. <term>لَمْ يَتْرُكْ</term> (it did not leave) is directed from the implicit subject to govern the verb. <term>هَا</term> refers back to it. <term>مُشَيَّدًا</term> (strengthened) is an adjective modifying <term>أُطُمًا</term> (building).

<summary>This page details the violent imagery of a rainstorm described in the poem, using precise Arabic grammatical analysis of the verses.</summary>
<keywords>Al-Mu'allaqat, Arabic poetry, storm, lexicography, philology</keywords>
pages.58:
79 كَأَنَّ ثَبِيرًا فِي عَرَانِينِ وَبْلِهِ .. كَبِيرُ أُنَاسٍ فِي بِجَادٍ مُزَمَّلِ

"As if Thabeer [a mountain] at the first downfall of its rain were a great chieftain of the people, wrapped in a striped cloak."

*   <term>عَرَانِين</term> (plural of <term>عِرْنِين</term>) refers to the prominent part of something, especially the bridge of the nose. <term>وَبْل</term> is the plural of <term>وَابِل</term> (heavy rain).
*   <term>مُزَمَّل</term> (wrapped), being an adjective qualifying <term>كَبِير</term> (great one), should have been in the nominative case, but it is affected by its proximity to <term>بِجَاد</term> (striped cloak), which is in the genitive case.
*   Another reading: <term>كَأَنَّ أَبَانًا فِي أَفَانِينِ وَدْقِهِ</term> = "As if Abán in the diversities of its showers."

80 كَانَ ذُرَى رَأْسِ الْمُجَيْمِرِ غُدْوَةً .. مِنَ السَّيْلِ وَالْأَغْثَاءِ فَلْكَةُ مِغْزَلِ

"As if in the morning the summit of the peak of Mujaimir, due to the flood and the debris around it, were the whirl of a spindle."

*   Another reading: <term>الْغُثَاءِ</term> (the debris).
*   <term>غُدْوَةً</term> serves as the adverb of time.
*   <term>فَلْكَةُ</term> (whirl of a spindle) is the predicate of <term>كَانَ</term> (was), with <term>ذُرَى</term> (summit) being the subject.

81 وَأَلْقَى بِصَحْرَاءِ الْغَبِيطِ بَعَاعَهُ .. نُزُولَ الْيَمَانِي ذِي الْعِيَابِ الْمُحَمَّلِ

"And the cloud poured out its goods—that is, rain—on the desert of Ghabeet; it resembled the arrival of a Yemeni merchant with his trunks loaded with rich goods."

*   The desert became bright with grass and flowers.
*   <term>نُزُولَ</term> (arrival/descent) is in the accusative case as a <term>مَفْعُول مُطْلَق</term> (absolute object).

82 كَانَ مَكَاكِيَّ الْجِوَاءِ غَدِيَّةً .. صُبِحْنَ سُلَافًا مِنْ رَحِيقٍ مُفَلْفَلِ

"As if in the morning the small birds of the valley of Jiwáa had taken a morning draught of old, pure, spiced wine."

<summary>This page covers descriptive verses involving mountains, floods, and nature, utilizing metaphorical comparisons to human activities and objects.</summary>
<keywords>Thabeer, Mujaimir, Ghabeet, Jiwáa, Arabic poetry, metaphors</keywords>

Spiced wine is believed to have a significant effect on conversational ability. The birds were, as it were, intoxicated with delight.
*   <term>غدية</term> is a diminutive of <term>غداة</term> (morning), used here as an adverb of time.
*   <term>صبحن</term> (they were given a morning drink) serves as the predicate sentence after <term>كان</term> (as if).

83 <foreign lang="ar">كَأنَّ السِّباعَ فِيهِ غَرقَى عَشِيَّةً .. بِأَرْجَائِهِ القُصْوَى أَنَابِيشُ عُنْصُلِ</foreign>

"As if in the evening the wild beasts in it—drowned in the furthest parts of it, that is, the valley of Jiwáa—were the root-bulbs of the wild onion."

They were covered with sand and dirt.
*   <term>غرقَى</term> (drowned) is the plural of <term>غريق</term> and acts as the state (<term>حَال</term>).
*   <term>عشية</term> (evening) is the adverb of time.
*   <term>انابيش</term> (root-bulbs) acts as the predicate after <term>كان</term> (as if).

[A small floral ornament centered on the page.]

->القصيدة الثانية<-

# THE SECOND POEM.

Ascribed to Tarafah, son of 'Abd-il-Bakrí, from the tribe of Bakr-ibn-Wáil. "Tarafah" is his title; his name is 'Amr-bin-ul-'Abd. He was one of the poets of the Pagan era, living after the time of Malik-ul-Zilleel, the author of the first Qasidah.

Legend says that the poet's brother, Ma'bad, reproached him for neglecting their father’s camels to indulge in poetry. Ma'bad once asked, "Can your poetry recover the camels if they are lost?" Tarafah insisted it could. To test him, Ma'bad neglected the camels, and they were taken by the tribe of Muzar. Tarafah wrote this poem, seeking assistance from 'Amru, Qáboos, and a Yemeni chieftain, and successfully recovered the camels, plus a hundred more as a reward.

The meter is the second form of <term>الطويل</term> (Al-Tawil), the same as the first poem; the rhyme (<term>قافية</term>) is also the same.

[Table of prosody for the first line]

1 لِخَوْلَةَ أَطْلَالٌ بِبَرْقَةِ ثَهْمَدِ .. تَلُوحُ كَبَاقِي الْوَشْمِ فِي ظَاهِرِ الْيَدِ

"There are traces of Kholah [his mistress] in the stony plain of Thahmad, which appear like the remains of tattooing on the back of the hand."

<summary>This page introduces the second Qasidah by Tarafah, providing biographical background and the circumstances of the poem's composition regarding the lost camels.</summary>
<keywords>Tarafah, 'Abd-il-Bakrí, Bakr-ibn-Wáil, Qasidah, Al-Mu'allaqat, Kholah</keywords>
pages.61:
Kholah is the name of his mistress. Traces refer to the ruins left near a former encampment of her tribe, as in the first poem.
*   <term>خولة</term> (Kholah) is read with a <term>فتحة</term> (a-vowel), acting as a diptote (<term>غير منصرف</term>) due to being a feminine proper noun.
*   <term>أطلال</term> (traces) is the subject (<term>مبتدأ</term>); <term>لخولة</term> (for Kholah) is the predicate.
*   <term>تلوح</term> (they appear) is an adjectival sentence modifying <term>أطلال</term>.

In some manuscripts, the second hemistich is:
> ظَلَلْتُ بِهَا أَبْكِي وَأَبْكِي إِلَى الْغَدِ = "Where I remained weeping and causing others to weep until the next day, due to memories of the past."

2 وَقُوفًا بِهَا صَحْبِي عَلَيَّ مَطِيَّهُمْ .. يَقُولُونَ لا تَهْلِكْ أَسًى وَتَجَلَّدِ

"My comrades, stopping their camels near me there, say, 'Do not die of grief, but bear it bravely.'"

This is a notable example of <term>التوارد</term> (coincidental similarity). Both poets, Imraul-Qais and Tarafah, happened to write the same line independently, differing only in the rhyme. It is said Tarafah had to prove he wrote the line on the same day as Imraul-Qais, but in a different place, to avoid accusations of plagiarism.

3 كَانَ حُدُوجَ الْمَالِكِيَّةِ غُدْوَةً .. خَلايَا سَفِينٍ بِالنَّوَاصِفِ مِنْ دَدِ
4 عَدُولِيَّةٌ أَوْ مِنْ سَفِينِ بْنِ يَامِنٍ .. يَجُورُ بِهَا الْمَلَّاحُ طَوْرًا وَيَهْتَدِي

"As if the Málikian camels, with the howdahs [litters] on the morning of her departure in the water-tracts of Dad, were the big ships of 'Adoal or the vessels of Ibni Yámin, which the sailors at times steer off course and at times guide straight."

<summary>This page analyzes the opening lines of Tarafah's poem, discussing the theme of lost love and the metaphorical comparison of camel litters to ships.</summary>
<keywords>Kholah, Tarafah, Imraul-Qais, Arabic poetry, camels, howdahs</keywords>
pages.62:
*   <term>حُدُوج</term> (howdahs, plural of <term>حِدْج</term>, a camel litter for women) is in the objective case, serving as the subject (<term>اسم</term>) after <term>كان</term> (as if); the predicate is <term>خلايا</term> (ships), which is in the nominative.
*   The phrase <term>بالنواصف من دد</term> relates to <term>حدوج</term>, not <term>سفين</term>.
*   <term>عدولية</term> is in the genitive case, acting as an adjective for <term>سفين</term>.
*   <term>يجور بها</term>, etc., is an adjectival sentence describing the ships.

5 يَشُقُّ حُبَابَ المَاءِ حَيْزُومُهَا .. كَمَا قَسَمَ التُّرْبَ المُفَايِلُ بِاليَدِ

"Their bows cleave the ripples of the sea, just as the divider of the sand heaps separates the dust with his hand."

*   <term>المفايِل</term> (the divider) acts as the agent of the action. This refers to the game of <term>فَيَال</term>, where a small object (like a coin) is hidden in sand, and the "divider" separates the sand into heaps to find it.
*   This line is an example of <term>الايطاء</term> (Al-Ita'), a defect where the same rhyming word (<term>اليد</term>) is repeated within nine lines.

6 وَفِي الحَيِّ أَحْوَى يَنْفِضُ المَرِدَ شَادِنٌ .. مُظَاهِرَ سِمْطَيْ لُؤْلُؤٍ وَزَبَرْجَدِ

"And in the tribe there is one like a young gazelle, with deep-colored lips, shaking the Arák tree for fruit, while wearing double strings of pearls and emeralds."

*   The standard word order is: <term>وفي الحي شادن احوى ينفض المرد</term>.
*   <term>مظاهر</term> (wearing) and <term>خذول</term> (next line) are adjectives modifying <term>شادن</term> (gazelle).

7 خَذُولٌ تَرَاءَى رَبْرَبًا بِخَمِيلَةٍ .. تَدَاوَلُ أَطْرَافَ البَرِيرِ وَتُؤْدِي

"A doe who has left her young and is grazing with a herd in a lush thicket, turning over the Arák berries and walking slowly."

<summary>This page concludes the analysis of Tarafah's imagery, focusing on maritime metaphors and a descriptive passage about a gazelle, including notes on poetic defects.</summary>
<keywords>Al-Mu'allaqat, Arabic grammar, prosody, Al-Ita', Arák tree</keywords>

pages.90:
CHAPTER IV

THE PSYCHOLOGY OF THE NIKAYAS—continued

III. FEELING

The last-named feature is the reason why, in the lengthy collection of Suttas <note>Scriptural discourses</note> devoted to the ‘Sixfold Sphere of Sense,’ we get so open and steady a contemplation of the psychology of sense, and so limited a range of psychological result. We are told that the six senses give man his world—his everything—and that they are the world, everything.

“I will teach you *Sabbam* [the all, everything]... What is that? Eye and visible object, ear and sound, nose,” and so on to *mano* <term>the mind or mental sense</term> and its objects.

“I will teach you the arising and the passing away of the world... What are they? Because of eye and visible form arises visual consciousness; the encounter of the three is contact..., thence feeling, thence craving, from the extinction of which comes extinction of grasping and the extinction of this whole mass of ill.” <note>original: "Samyutta-N. iv. 1 ff., ‘Salayatana.’"</note>
pages.91:
FEELING 75

“That by which one becomes cognizant of the world, and has conceits about the world, that is called, in the Ariyan <note>Noble</note> discipline, the world... namely, by cognizance through sight, hearing, smell, taste, touch, and *mano*.”

“I say that the end of the world is not to be learnt, to be seen, or to be arrived at by traveling to the end of the world, nor is an end to be made of ill by failing to get there... It is within this fathom-long carcass, percipient and intelligent, that I declare to be the genesis of the world, the ceasing of the world, and the way going to the cessation of the world.”

We should err if we read any Idealism <note>The philosophical theory that reality is mentally constructed</note> into the last quotation; it is anticipated by a context coinciding mainly with the foregoing quotation, which is again closely connected with those before it. The elements of ultimate reality, I do not say existed, but were constantly becoming and passing away, in the macrocosm as in the subjective microcosm <note>The individual human world</note>. But that microcosm apprehended them by way of its sense-doors. They presented the ‘world’ to the individual by representing it.

“Where there is eye and visible objects, visual consciousness, and the things that may be learnt through visual consciousness, there is the world, or the notion of world. Where there is ear,” etc.
pages.92:
76 BUDDHIST PSYCHOLOGY

Those sense-doors were presenting it to him night and day from birth till death, and, by the all-powerful lever of feeling, were pushing him this way and that, as mighty Ganga <note>The Ganges River</note> was ever bearing down bubbles of foam and driftwood. And nothing that sense-cognition could show was able to end Sorrow and Pain finally and altogether.

So we hear more often about how sense affected the person than about what it told them. I have attributed this emphasis to the aesthetic vivacity of the ancient Northern Hindus, as betrayed by their literature. There is also this negative condition under which Buddhist doctrine was put forward and organized: the absence of any advance in natural science.

Modern psychology has made its most marked forward strides during periods of scientific advance and excitement. And the strides were usually made by men of scientific, especially medical, training. Hartley, for example, was a physician; Tetens, a physicist and mathematician; Priestley was a chemist; Cabanis was a professor of medicine; Locke was a student of natural science and a physician; Weber, Fechner, and Spencer are other notable instances. Such thinkers were more interested in the mechanism of sense as so many avenues of knowledge, and as a department of the science of the living organism. Their interest was intellectual. The ‘dynamics’ of consciousness were relatively uninteresting until the influence of Schopenhauer <note>German philosopher who emphasized the will</note> had leavened thought.
pages.93:
FEELING 77

To revert to older days, it is clear from Aristotle’s works that a considerable activity in biological inquiry was being carried on at the time, and not only by Aristotle himself, the ‘master of those who know.’ He too evinces a relatively mild interest in the dynamics of feeling and will. He delivered lectures on Ethics, but it is not a little instructive to compare his somewhat pedagogic treatment of Pleasure with the immense ground-wave importance attached to pain and pleasure, sorrow and happiness, in Buddhist psychological ethics. He writes six and a half sections, out of a total of ten, in the *Nicomachean Ethics*, before resuming thus: “The consideration of pleasure and pain... is one of the subjects we are bound to discuss, for we said that moral virtue and vice have to do with pleasures and pains, and most people say that happiness implies pleasure.” In the *De Anima* and the *De Sensu*, his chief interest is in biological and intellectual conclusions.
pages.94:
78 BUDDHIST PSYCHOLOGY

But in the Buddhist canonical books, amid all the allusions to contemporary activities, there is no indication of any activity in scientific research going on, with the exception of astrology and medicine, and of medicine practiced rather as an art than as being advanced by systematic investigation and experiment.

The art of the physician and the surgeon figures frequently in narrative, in sanitary regulation (e.g., in the Vinaya books), and in parable. The Founder himself is called the Great Healer, the World’s Physician. The most central of all Buddhist ethical doctrines—the Four Ariyan <note>Noble</note> Truths—is formulated on the plan of a medical diagnosis: namely, the nature of a malady, its cause, its cessation, and its curative regimen. And we may not be greatly wrong if we judge that, however we regard the grasp of universal causation by the mind of the Sakyamuni <note>The Buddha</note>, it was due to (1) the absence of a contemporary body of science, and (2) the presence of a developed medical tradition, that the doctrine of causation took the peculiar form and standpoint that it did for us.

Thus: anything due to an assignable cause was terminable if you could stop the working of the cause. But you could stop it because nothing became a cause arbitrarily or supernaturally.
pages.95:
FEELING 79

Now, for the doctor, for the patient, and for the patient’s own folk, the ‘anything’—the One Thing—is *Dukkha*, Ill (the word means everything that is the contrary of *Sukha*—happiness, pleasure). And all or any *dukkha* can be made to cease if (1) it is rightly diagnosed, (2) its cause or the conditions of its genesis and persistence are ascertained, (3) the nature of the state contrary to it is realized, and (4) the ‘cure’ is consistently carried out.

The medical inspiration, or at least standpoint, was pointed out several years ago by Dr. Kern: “It is not difficult to see that these four *Satyas* <note>Truths</note> are nothing else but the four cardinal articles of Indian medical science, applied to the spiritual healing of mankind, exactly as in the Yoga doctrine. E.g., in *Yogasutra* ii. 15, Commentary: ‘Just as the doctor’s code is fourfold: illness, cause of illness, health, and medicine, so too is this code fourfold, to wit: *samsara* <note>endless cycle of living and dying</note>, its cause, emancipation (*moksha*), and the way thereto.’” The learned writer, however, in this valuable *apercu* <note>original: "insight"</note>, specializes unnecessarily and, moreover, leaves us to draw a mistaken inference.
pages.96:
80 BUDDHIST PSYCHOLOGY

I have heard a physician pointing out the analogy between the Four Truths and his own British medical code, simply from hearing them stated as Buddhist religious doctrine, without allusion being made to his own profession. Talking of physicians tempts me to quote from the letter of a notable British Buddhist as bearing on this point: “The operation and hospital-experience was indeed a very formidable affair—so terribly impressive in its insistence on the *Dukkha*-Truths, that I marvel... after that experience, that the realization of the truth of them is not more common, at least among those who have to do with hospitals. Perhaps indeed this most impressive object-lesson is responsible for the large proportion of medical men among those Occidentals who are... deeply interested in Buddhism.”

Moreover, to quote the late Commentary on the *Yogasutras* as an authority for the statement that Indian medical procedure suggested a fundamental doctrine of Buddhism is much like saying that J. S. Mill’s inclusion of the syllogism in his *Formal Logic* proves it to have been in existence when Aristotle was teaching. There were ‘cardinal articles’ of medical clinic, not only in India, but in all countries before either the *Yogasutras* (let alone the Commentary) or other records, more certainly pre-Buddhistic, were compiled. Today has been unbroken; no one has filched the slightest part of it from me. The whole time has been divided between rest and reading. A brief space has been given over to bodily exercise, and on this ground, I can thank old age—my exercise costs very little effort; as soon as I stir, I am tired. And weariness is the aim and end of exercise, no matter how strong one is. Do you ask who my pace-makers are? One is enough for me—the slave Pharius, a pleasant fellow, as you know; but I shall exchange him for another. At my time of life, I need one who is of still more tender years. Pharius, at any rate, says that he and I are at the same period of life; for we are both losing our teeth. <note>See Epistle 12 for a similar witticism.</note> Yet even now I can scarcely follow his pace as he runs, and within a very short time, I shall not be able to follow him at all; so you see what profit we get from daily exercise. Very soon does a wide interval open between two persons who travel different ways. My slave is climbing up at the very moment when I am coming down, and you surely know how much quicker the latter is. Nay, I was wrong; for now my life is not coming down; it is falling outright. Do you ask, for all that, how our race resulted today? We raced to a tie—something which rarely happens in a running contest. After tiring myself out in this way (for I cannot call it exercise), I took a cold bath; this, at my house, means just short of hot. I, the former cold-water enthusiast, who used to celebrate the new year by taking a plunge into the canal, who, just as naturally as I would set out to do some reading or writing, or to compose a speech, used to inaugurate the first of the year with a plunge into the Virgo aqueduct <note>Constructed by Marcus Agrippa; now the fountain of Trevi.</note>, have changed my allegiance, first to the Tiber, and then to my favorite tank, which is warmed only by the...

sun, at times when I am most robust and when there is not a flaw in my bodily processes. I have very little energy left for bathing. After the bath, some stale bread and breakfast without a table; no need to wash the hands after such a meal. Then comes a very short nap. You know my habit; I avail myself of a scanty bit of sleep—unharnessing, as it were. For I am satisfied if I can just stop staying awake. Sometimes I know that I have slept; at other times, I have a mere suspicion.

Lo, now the din of the Races sounds about me! My ears are smitten with sudden and general cheering. But this does not upset my thoughts or even break their continuity. I can endure an uproar with complete resignation. The medley of voices blended in one note sounds to me like the dashing of waves, or like the wind that lashes the tree-tops, or like any other sound which conveys no meaning.

What is it, then, you ask, to which I have been giving my attention? I will tell you. A thought sticks in my mind, left over from yesterday—namely, what men of the greatest sagacity have meant when they have offered the most trifling and intricate proofs for problems of the greatest importance—proofs which may be true, but none the less resemble fallacies. Zeno, that greatest of men, the revered founder of our brave and holy school of philosophy, wishes to discourage us from drunkenness. Listen, then, to his arguments proving that the good man will not get drunk: 

> "No one entrusts a secret to a drunken man; but one will entrust a secret to a good man; therefore, the good man will not get drunk." 

Mark how ridiculous Zeno is made when we set up a similar syllogism in contrast with his. There are...

many, but one will be enough: "No one entrusts a secret speech to a man who is asleep; but one does entrust it to a good man; therefore, the good man does not sleep." <margin>See Epistle 49: "What you have not lost, you have; you have not lost horns; therefore, you have horns."</margin> 

10 Posidonius tries to plead the cause of our Zeno in the only way he can, but I do not believe it can be done even in this way. He says that the word "drunk" is used in two ways: first, when someone is heavy with wine and lacks self-control; second, if one is accustomed to becoming drunk and is prone to this vice. He claims Zeno was referring to the one who is habitually drunk, not the one who is currently drunk. And to such a person, he argues, no one would entrust secrets that might be blurted out due to wine. 

11 This is false. The first interrogation includes the one who is currently drunk, not just the one who might become so. You will admit there is a big difference between being "drunk" and being a "drunkard." A person who is currently drunk might be in that state for the first time and not have the vice, while an habitual drunkard is often sober. Therefore, I understand it as the word usually signifies, especially when used by a man who professes diligence and weighs his words. Add to this that if Zeno meant this and wanted us to understand it that way, he used the ambiguity of the word to create a fallacy, which should not be done when seeking the truth. 

12 But even if he did mean that, the conclusion—that secrets are not entrusted to one who is prone to drunkenness—is false. Just think how many soldiers, who are not always sober, have been entrusted with private messages by their general, tribune, or centurion.

many, but one will be enough: "No one entrusts a secret to a man when he is asleep; but one entrusts a secret to a good man; therefore, the good man does not go to sleep." Posidonius pleads the cause of our master Zeno in the only possible way; but it cannot, I hold, be pleaded even in this way. For Posidonius maintains that the word "drunken" is used in two ways—in the one case of a man who is loaded with wine and has no control over himself; in the other, of a man who is accustomed to get drunk, and is a slave to the habit. Zeno, he says, meant the latter—the man who is accustomed to get drunk, not the man who is drunk; and no one would entrust to this person any secret, for it might be blabbed out when the man was in his cups. This is a fallacy. For the first syllogism refers to him who is actually drunk and not to him who is about to get drunk. You will surely admit that there is a great difference between a man who is drunk and a drunkard. He who is actually drunk may be in this state for the first time and may not have the habit, while the drunkard is often free from drunkenness. I therefore interpret the word in its usual meaning, especially since the syllogism is set up by a man who makes a business of the careful use of words, and who weighs his language. Moreover, if this is what Zeno meant, and what he wished it to mean to us, he was trying to avail himself of an equivocal word in order to work in a fallacy; and no man ought to do this when truth is the object of inquiry.

But let us admit, indeed, that he meant what Posidonius says; even so, the conclusion is false—that secrets are not entrusted to an habitual drunkard. Think how many soldiers who are not always sober have been entrusted by a general or a captain or a centurion with messages which might not be divulged!

# 81
### FEELING
<sig>6</sig>

I suggest that an advance in the systematic study of the mind is especially liable to be influenced by—and to mold itself upon—that body of more or less systematic physical knowledge which carries the most weight with the thoughtful society of its time and place. For the subject matter of mental science is, as we know, not accessible to strictly collective observation; introspection belongs to the individual, and in the individual, no two instances of a phenomenon can be shown as absolutely identical. Hence, it is largely (though I do not say *only*) when some onward stride in physical science draws the rest of human knowledge in its wake that the laws of the mind are freshly investigated, as something that must also be brought into the line of march.

Where there is no such advance in psychical investigation, some system of dogmatic metaphysics is probably holding the cultured imagination of the age captive through the spell of some myth of "The Word." When the mind breaks free and looks deeper, it will naturally have recourse to more positive ideas as guides and supports for its fresh concepts.

Now, in the healing lore and craft of the day—the only one, I repeat, that comes prominently to the front in the episodes and detailed rules in the <term>Vinaya</term> <note>The code of monastic discipline for Buddhist monks and nuns.</note>—the revolt of thought embodied in the Buddhist movement found its noblest inspiration.

<summary>This page discusses how advancements in mental science are often shaped by the dominant physical or medical theories of the era, arguing that Buddhist psychology sought to align its investigation of the mind with the empirical, clinical spirit of its time.</summary>
<keywords>Mental science, introspection, physical science, dogmatic metaphysics, Vinaya, Buddhist movement</keywords>

82 BUDDHIST PSYCHOLOGY

The word *dukkha* <term>Dukkha</term> <note>Usually translated as suffering, ill, or unsatisfactoriness.</note> covers all that is meant by "not well"—ills and pains of the body, ills and misery of the mind—in a word, *dis-ease*. Its presence is the doctor’s *casus belli* <note>original: "cause of war/reason for conflict"</note> and *raison d'être* <note>original: "reason for being"</note>; its cause and extinction are his quest. For its absence, there may be several positive expressions. And yet, there is nothing else in life so mortally positive as *dukkha*. And it is easy, alas! for many to conceive its mere absence as sufficient for happiness. *Nibbana* itself, a quasi-negative term, was at times employed as "health," as well as happiness. And the Founder <note>The Buddha.</note>, in one of his more emphatic utterances about his mission, expressed that mission as one of healing:

"Both then and now, just this do I reveal:
—*dukkha* and the extinction of *dukkha*." <note>Majjhima-Nikaya i. 509; Sutta-Nipata, verse 749.</note>

The physical healer finds the causes of dis-ease in the mutual interaction of man and his environment. Buddhism too found therein the causes of all that made for unhappiness. Sense-impressions were the avenues whereby came satisfactions (*pasāda*) fraught with peril. Consciousness, with its three main roots or conditions—greed or appetite, enmity, and delusion—pushing it, reacted on its impressions as feeling, desiring for, and grasping after all that tended to the...

<summary>The author explains the centrality of the concept of 'dukkha' (dis-ease) in Buddhist thought, drawing a direct parallel between the medical professional's work and the Buddha's mission of diagnosing and treating human suffering.</summary>
<keywords>Dukkha, Nibbana, the Founder, sense-impressions, greed, enmity, delusion</keywords>

FEELING 83

...expansion and conceit of this "Me" and "Mine." And as it behooved the physician to keep in view all possible sources of any disease, neglecting none, so was Buddhism searching and exhaustive in its treatment of the avenues of sense, ignoring none of the five that conveyed information, nor the sixth <note>The mind (mano).</note> that coordinated and revived what the former brought.

The great intermediary between the (relatively) passive reactions to the manifold stimulus of sense and the following more or less deliberate reactions, Buddhism discerned—correctly enough—in Feeling. This might be pleasant, painful, or neither. And it did not follow that where feeling was pleasant (*sukha*), the symptoms of disease (*dukkha*) were absent. For the *sukha* born of sense was the most efficient handmaiden of *dukkha*, if *dukkha* be broadly understood as both physical and moral ill, and all that this does, or may involve, of mental suffering and moral deterioration.

As Ledi Sadaw, the eminent *Thera* <note>Senior monk.</note>, writes: "We must distinguish between *dukkha* of the category (or, in Buddhist idiom, of the essential mark) of something unpleasant experienced (by way of sense), physical or psychical, and the *dukkha* we use in the triad: impermanence (*anicca*), ill, and non-soul (*an-atta*). By this *dukkha*, we mean a state of peril and danger, without peace, security, or blessing." <note>Yamaka, ii. Appendix, p. 248 (London, Pali Text Society, 1913).</note>

<summary>The author analyzes how Buddhism distinguishes between simple pleasant feelings and the deeper, pervasive state of 'dukkha,' emphasizing that even pleasant sensations can be part of the cycle of suffering.</summary>
<keywords>Feeling, sukha, dukkha, sense-avenues, Ledi Sadaw, impermanence, non-soul</keywords>

84 BUDDHIST PSYCHOLOGY

This, in other words, is the distinction a physician—or at least a patient—might draw between sensations of pain and disease. The presence, the growth, or the decline of the pain is not always accompanied by the presence, increase, or cessation of the disease. And this distinction we have to draw throughout the whole of Buddhist literature dealing with sense, with feeling, and the effects of feeling. Otherwise, we find ourselves landed in much inconsistency of expression, as I shall show.

That feeling is the inevitable response to awareness of a new stimulus is affirmed up and down the *Nikayas*, notably in the *Samyutta-Nikaya* regarding the sphere of sense (vol. iv. 1 ff.), e.g.:

"Where there are hands, there taking and setting down appears; where there are feet, there coming and going appears; where there are limbs, there folding and stretching appears; where there is a stomach, there hunger and thirst appears. Just so, *bhikkhus* <note>Monks.</note>, where there is sight (or eye), or hearing . . . there arise subjective pleasure and pain, conditioned by sense-stimulus (literally: contact, *samphassa*)." <note>Samyutta-Nikaya iv. 171.</note>

The contrary is then stated, both of the analogies and the analogues: ". . . Where there is not sight, etc., neither pleasure nor pain, conditioned by sense-stimulus, arises."

<summary>This page reinforces the Buddhist view of feeling as a necessary byproduct of sense-stimulus, using physiological analogies to explain the link between sense organs and the resulting mental states of pleasure or pain.</summary>
<keywords>Samyutta-Nikaya, sense-stimulus, contact (samphassa), pleasure, pain, bhikkhus</keywords>

FEELING 85

This quotation is conclusive enough to represent all other passages stating the concomitance of sensations and feeling, understood as our psychology of sense understands pleasure and pain (or at least pleasure and "unpleasure"). That the senses convey pleasure as well as its opposite is not only allowed and affirmed by doctrinal teaching, but the pleasure is also recognized as very genuine and good by the most eminent of the teachers. The Founder affirmed at times that none lived more at ease (*sukham seti*) than himself, however much he had forsworn most of the so-called good things of life. His chief apostles forgather with him one fine evening in the Gosinga Wood, delighting in the "divine perfumes" of the dewy moonlit scene, where the tall sal-trees stand clad in golden bloom. Temperance was prescribed for maintaining the physical comfort (*phāsuvihāra*) of health.

But when the disciple is bidden to look upon *sukha* as, or *qua* <note>original: "as/in the capacity of"</note> *dukkha*, then we know that the wider concept is to be understood after the *guḍ* <note>The author uses this to refer to the "hidden" or "deeper" meaning.</note>. And this is no less the case when things unpleasant to the "average sensual man" are valued by a different scale and held to constitute higher pleasure.

<summary>The author clarifies that while Buddhism acknowledges the validity of physical pleasure, it ultimately asks the disciple to view all transient joys through the lens of 'dukkha' to avoid attachment.</summary>
<keywords>Concomitance, pleasure, unpleasure, the Founder, Gosinga Wood, temperance, sukha, dukkha</keywords>
