86 BUDDHIST PSYCHOLOGY

"Things seen and heard, tastes, odors, what we touch,
Perceive, all, everything desirable,
Pleasant and sweet, while one can say 'It is,'

These are deemed *Sukha* by both gods and men,
And where these cease to be, they hold it woe.

"What other men call *Sukha*, that the saints
Call *Dukkha*; what the rest so name,
That do the Ariyans <note>Noble ones.</note> know as happiness.
Behold a norm that’s hard to apprehend!
Hereby are baffled they that are not wise." <note>Sutta-Nipata, verse 759 f.; compare Samyutta-Nikaya iv. 127.</note>

If we would not be baffled, it is with this wider implication that we must read those passages wherein each sense is declared to be *dukkha*, and not productive of either this or its contrary. If, using Ledi Sadaw’s definition, we read into such passages as "seeing . . . is sorrow . . ." the wider sense of *dukkha*, thus:

"The eye, brother, is a faculty of peril and danger, bringing, as such, no peace, security, or blessing; it is to understand this that the holy life under the Exalted One is lived,"

and so on for the other senses, why, then we may not be unwilling to admit even for laymen the truth in this "monkish" statement.

<summary>This page presents a paradoxical teaching: what the world calls happiness, the saints identify as suffering. The author argues that this is not a denial of pleasure, but a realization of the inherent insecurity of sensory experience.</summary>
<keywords>Ariyans, Sukha, Dukkha, Ledi Sadaw, senses, perception</keywords>
pages.103:
CHAPTER V

THE PSYCHOLOGY OF THE NIKAYAS—continued

IV. IDEATION

The systematic analysis of mind in the *Nikayas* is pursued no further than the recipient and coordinating work of *mano* <note>The mind or mental faculty.</note> as *sensus communis* <note>original: "common sense/shared faculty of perception."</note>. Sequences in consciousness are occasionally pursued further, but without overmuch terminological consistency, and irregularly. Here are a few instances:

"Because of some tendency, there arises perception, opinion, thinking, volition, wish, aspiration. And according as the tendency is low, mediocre, or lofty, so will all these be." <note>Samyutta-Nikaya ii. 153.</note>

The process of conversion in religion is described as one of "hearing, attending, remembering, comparing, discerning, desire, zeal, pondering, endeavor."

"Thinking results in desire; through desire, objects are divided into what we like and what we dislike, hence envy and selfishness, hence quarreling and fighting." <note>Digha-Nikaya ii. 278 f. (condensed).</note>

<summary>This section introduces the Buddhist analysis of 'Ideation' (mental processes), noting that the texts provide scattered but insightful descriptions of how thoughts, desires, and perceptions arise and influence behavior.</summary>
<keywords>Ideation, mano, sensus communis, consciousness, tendency, volition</keywords>
pages.104:
88 BUDDHIST PSYCHOLOGY

"Conditioned by contact arises feeling; what one feels, one perceives; what one perceives, one thinks about; what one thinks about, one is obsessed withal." <note>Majjhima-Nikaya i., iii.</note>

These samples reveal the persistent effort, in the *Suttas*, to carry on the method—systematically observed in treating of sense—of setting forth mind and character as orderly, causal process. The method is emphatically Buddhist. The most notable example of it is the important formula of natural causation, as exemplified in the process of life being bound up with *dukkha*. In the mental process, the resolution of afferent <note>Carrying inward to the brain/mind.</note> or receptive consciousness into efferent <note>Carrying outward from the brain/mind.</note> or discharging consciousness is clearly affirmed. Sense and feeling stirred by sense are converted into motor presentations—as desire, etc. But we meet with no closer analysis of intellectual process, of what has, in our own psychology, been called representative and re-representative cognition, or ideation. In the last sample, we only hear that "what we perceive," i.e., notice (*saññā-khandha* <note>The aggregate of perception.</note>), we "think about" (*vitakketi*).

<summary>The author concludes that Buddhist psychology successfully maps the causal chain from sense-perception to motor action (desire/will), even if it lacks the complex terminology of modern western theories of representative cognition.</summary>
<keywords>Suttas, causal process, afferent consciousness, efferent consciousness, motor presentations, saññā-khandha, vitakketi</keywords>

71 <foreign lang="ar">فَبَاتَ عَلَيْهِ سَرْجُهُ وَلِجَامُهُ .. وَبَاتَ بِعَيْنِي قَائِمًا غَيْرَ مُرْسَلِ</foreign>

“He passed the night with his saddle and bridle on; he passed the night standing in my sight, not sent away to the stable.”

<term>qā’iman</term> (standing) and <term>ghayra</term> (other than/not) are in the accusative case, serving as the <term>ḥāl</term> (state or adverbial condition). 
<term>‘alayhi sarjuhu</term> (upon him is his saddle), etc., functions as an adverbial phrase of state; <term>lijāmuhu</term> and <term>sarjuhu</term> are the subject and predicate respectively.

72 <foreign lang="ar">أَصَاحِ تَرَى بَرْقًا أُرِيكَ وَمِيضَهُ .. كَلَمْعِ الْيَدَيْنِ فِي حَبِيٍّ مُكَلَّلِ</foreign>

“Oh my companion, do you see the lightning, whose flashing I am showing you; it is like the flickering of hands in thick, crown-like clouds.”

<term>aṣāḥi</term> is a shortened form (<term>murakhkham</term>) of <term>ṣāḥib</term> (companion), the final <term>b</term> being dropped; it retains its original vowel, the kasra.
<term>urīka wamīḍahu</term> (I show you its flashing) is an adjectival phrase modifying <term>barqan</term> (lightning).
<term>tarā</term> (do you see) is interrogative, implying an omitted <term>hal</term> or <term>a</term>.
<term>mukallal</term> can mean crowning, encircling, or flashing with lightning.

Another reading is <term>aḥāru = aḥārithu</term>, referring to the name Hārith.
Another reading is <term>a‘innī ‘alā barqin</term> = assist me in seeing the lightning.

73 <foreign lang="ar">يُضِيءُ سَنَاهُ أَوْ مَصَابِيحُ رَاهِبٍ .. أَمَالَ السَّلِيطَ بِالدَّبَالِ الْمُفَتَّلِ</foreign>

“Its glory shines, or [it is] like the lamps of a monk who has tilted the oil onto the well-twisted wicks.”

<term>amāla al-salīṭa bi-al-dabāli</term> (he tilted the oil onto the wicks) is an example of an inverted construction. It acts as an adjectival phrase modifying <term>rāhib</term> (monk).
Another reading is <term>ahāna al-salīṭa</term> = he did not spare the oil; he used it lavishly.
<term>ahāna</term> = considered as of no value.
<term>maṣābīḥu</term> (lamps) is in the genitive case, coordinated with <term>lam‘i</term> in the preceding line.

pages.56:
Or it may be in the objective case, with the <term>k</term> [like] implied; or in the nominative case, serving as the subject to <term>yuḍī’u</term> (shines), coordinated with <term>sanāhu</term>; or it relates to the implied word qualified by <term>k</term> in the preceding line.

74 <term>qa‘adtu lahu wa-ṣuḥbatī bayna Ḍārijin .. wa-bayna al-‘Udhaybi ba‘da mā muta’ammalī</term>

"I sat with my companions waiting for the rain between Ḍārij and 'Udhayb, after regarding the lightning attentively."

<term>ṣuḥbatī</term> (companions) is in the nominative case, coordinated with the implied first-person pronoun in <term>qa‘adtu</term> (I sat). <term>mā</term> is an expletive, and <term>muta’ammalī</term> means "my observing attentively." 
<term>ba‘da mā muta’ammalī</term> is also interpreted thus: <term>ba‘uda</term> is a syncopated form of the past tense; the cloud, the object of my earnest observation, was far away.

Another reading: <term>bu‘da</term> (distance) is in the objective case, serving as a vocative with an implied <term>yā</term>. It means: "O, how great was the distance of the object of my earnest observation."

75 <term>‘alayhi Qaṭanu al-shaymi aymanu ṣawbirin .. wa-aysaruhu ‘alā al-Sitāri fa-Yadhbulī</term>

"In looking for the rain, we guessed that the right of its downpour was over Qaṭan, while its left was upon Sitār and beyond it upon Yadhbul."

These locations are very far apart, which describes the magnitude of the storm.
<term>‘alā Qaṭan</term> is subordinate to <term>ayman</term> (the right side).

Another reading: <term>‘alā Qaṭanan</term>. It then means: "As we guessed from the observation of the lightning and other signs of rain, its right downpour topped Qaṭan," etc.

<term>Yadhbul</term> is typically a diptote (non-declinable), being a proper noun with the verbal form, but here it is used as a triptote (declinable) due to the necessity of the rhyme.

76 فَأَضْحَى يَسِحُّ المَاءُ حَوْلَ كُثَيْفَةٍ .. يَكُبُّ عَلَى الأَذْقَانِ دَوْحَ الكَنَهْبُلِ

“The storm began pouring its waters over Kuthaifah, overturning the large Kanahbul trees onto their 'chins' [upper branches].”

<term>adhqān</term> is the plural of <term>dhaqan</term>, literally "a chin," but here it signifies the upper branches of the tree.

Another reading: <term>min kulli dīqatin</term> = from what collects at each interval of raining; and also <term>min kulli thul‘atin</term> = from each watercourse.

<term>yas iḥḥu</term> is the predicate after <term>aḍḥā</term>. <term>yakubbu</term> acts as an adverbial phrase of state (<term>ḥāl</term>).

77 وَمَرَّ عَلَى القَنَانِ مِنْ نَفَيَانِهِ .. فَأَنْزَلَ مِنْهُ العِصْمَ مِنْ كُلِّ مَنْزِلِ

“Then the spray of it passed over the hills of Qanān, and was so violent that it forced the wild goats to descend from every haunt.”

<term>‘iṣm</term> is the plural of <term>a‘ṣam</term> = a gazelle or mountain goat whose forelegs are white above the pastern, or a color different from the rest of its body.

Another reading for the first hemistich: <term>wa-alqā bi-Baysāna ma‘a al-layli burkatan</term> = "It settled itself on Mount Baysān at night." <term>alqā burkatan</term> = placed its chest [on the ground], like a camel.

<term>Baysān</term> is a diptote, but used here as a triptote by poetic license.

78 وَتَيْمَاءَ لَمْ يَتْرُكْ بِهَا جِذْعَ نَخْلَةٍ .. وَلَا أُطُمًا إِلَّا مُشَيَّدًا بِجَنْدَلِ

“And at Taimā’ it did not leave a single date-palm trunk standing, nor any fortress except those strengthened by hard stones.”

<term>Taimā’a</term> is in the accusative case, governed by an implied verb. <term>lam yatruk</term> refers back to it. <term>mushayyadan</term> is an adjective to <term>uṭuman</term> (fortress).

79 كَأَنَّ ثَبِيرًا فِي عَرَانِينِ وَبْلِهِ .. كَبِيرُ أُنَاسٍ فِي بِجَادٍ مُزَمَّلِ

“As if Thabeer, at the first downfall of its rain, were an elder of the people wrapped in a striped cloak.”

<term>‘arānīn</term> is the plural of <term>‘irnīn</term>, the prominent part of anything, especially the bridge of the nose. <term>wabl</term> is the plural of <term>wābil</term> (downpour).

<term>muzammal</term> (wrapped), as an adjective qualifying <term>kabīr</term> (elder), should be in the nominative case, but it is affected by its proximity to <term>bijādin</term> (cloak), which is in the genitive case.

Another reading: <term>ka’anna Abānan fī afānīni wadqihi</term> = As if Abān, in the variety of its showers.

80 كَانَ ذُرَى رَأْسِ الْمُجَيْمِرِ غُدْوَةً .. مِنَ السَّيْلِ وَالْأَغْثَاءِ فَلْكَةُ مِغْزَلِ

“As if, in the morning, the peak of Mujaimir, due to the flood and the debris around it, were the whirl of a spindle.”

Another reading: <term>al-ghuthā’i</term>. <term>ghudwatan</term> is an adverb of time. <term>falkatu</term> is the predicate after <term>kāna</term>, with <term>dhurā</term> being the subject.

81 وَأَلْقَى بِصَحْرَاءِ الْغَبِيطِ بَعَاعَهُ .. نُزُولَ الْيَمَانِي ذِي الْعِيَابِ الْمُحَمَّلِ

“And the cloud poured its goods [rain] out onto the desert of Ghabeet; it resembled the arrival of a Yemeni merchant with his trunks loaded with rich clothes.”

The desert became bright with grass and flowers. <term>nuzūla</term> is in the accusative case, as a cognate accusative (<term>maf‘ūl muṭlaq</term>).

82 كَانَ مَكَاكِيَّ الْجِوَاءِ غَدِيَّةً .. صُبِحْنَ سُلَافًا مِنْ رَحِيقٍ مُفَلْفَلِ

“As if, in the morning, the small birds of the valley of Jiwā’ had taken a morning draught of old, pure, spiced wine.”

<term>ghadiyyatan</term> is a diminutive of <term>ghadāh</term>, used as an adverb of time.

->The Second Poem<-

# THE SECOND POEM.

Ascribed to Ṭarafah, son of 'Abd-il-Bakrī, from the tribe of Bakr-ibn-Wā’il. Ṭarafah is his title; his name is 'Amr-bin-ul-'Abd. He was one of the poets of the Age of Ignorance [Paganism] and lived after the time of Mālik-ul-Zilleel, the author of the first Qaṣīdah.

It is said that the poet's brother, Ma'bad, reproached him for neglecting their father’s camels to indulge in poetical reveries. Ma'bad taunted him, asking if his poetry could recover the camels if they were lost. Ṭarafah assured him it could. To test him, Ma'bad neglected the camels, which were then seized by members of the tribe of Muẓar. The poet wrote this poem, appealing to 'Amru, Qābūs, and a chieftain of Yaman for assistance, and succeeded in recovering the camels, plus a hundred more as a reward.

The meter of this poem is the second of the <term>ṭawīl</term> [long meter], the same as the first poem; the rhyme [qāfiyah] is also the same.

| | | | | | | | | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Li-Khawlata | aṭlālun | bi-barqati | Thahmadi | talūḥu | ka-bāqī | al-washmi | fī | ẓāhiri | al-yadi |

1 لِخَوْلَةَ أَطْلَالٌ بِبَرْقَةِ ثَهْمَدِ .. تَلُوحُ كَبَاقِي الْوَشْمِ فِي ظَاهِرِ الْيَدِ

"There are traces of Khawlah in the stony, sandy plain of Thahmad, which appear like the remains of tattooing on the back of the hand."

<summary>This page introduces the second Mu'allaqah, attributed to Ṭarafah, and provides the historical context regarding the poet's life and the circumstances of the poem's composition, followed by the first line of the text.</summary>
<keywords>Ṭarafah, 'Abd-il-Bakrī, Bakr-ibn-Wā’il, 'Amr-bin-ul-'Abd, Mālik-ul-Zilleel, Ma'bad, Muẓar, Qaṣīdah, meter, Al-Mu'allaqat, Khawlah, Thahmad</keywords>
pages.61:
Khawlah is the name of his mistress. 
"Traces" refer to the marks left near a former encampment of her tribe, as in the first poem. 
<term>Khawlata</term> is read with a <term>fatḥah</term>, being a diptote due to its feminine gender and status as a proper name. <term>aṭlālun</term> (traces) is the subject (<term>mubtada’</term>); the predicate is <term>li-Khawlata</term> (belonging to Khawlah). 
<term>talūḥu</term> (they appear) is an adjectival phrase modifying <term>aṭlālun</term>. 

In some copies, the second hemistich reads: 
> ẓalaltu bihā abkī wa-ubkī ilā al-ghadi = Where I remained weeping and making others weep until the next day on account of the memories of the past.

2 وَقُوفًا بِهَا صَحْبِي عَلَيَّ مَطِيَّهُمْ .. يَقُولُونَ لا تَهْلِكْ أَسًى وَتَجَلَّدِ
"My comrades, stopping their camels there near me, say: 'Do not die of grief, but bear it bravely.'"

This is a remarkable example of <term>tawārud</term> [coincidence]. Two poets, Imru’ al-Qays and Ṭarafah, happened to compose the same line, differing only in the rhyme, independently. It is said that Ṭarafah was suspected of plagiarism and had to prove that he composed the line on the same day as Imru’ al-Qays, but in a different location.

3 كَانَ حُدُوجَ الْمَالِكِيَّةِ غُدْوَةً .. خَلايَا سَفِينٍ بِالنَّوَاصِفِ مِنْ دَدِ
4 عَدُولِيَّةٌ أَوْ مِنْ سَفِينِ بْنِ يَامِنٍ .. يَجُورُ بِهَا الْمَلَّاحُ طَوْرًا وَيَهْتَدِي

<term>ḥudūj</term> is in the objective case, acting as the subject (<term>ism</term>) after <term>kāna</term>, with <term>khalāyā</term> being the predicate in the nominative case. The prepositional phrase <term>bi-al-nawāṣif min Dadi</term> modifies <term>ḥudūj</term>, not <term>safīn</term>. <term>‘Adūliyyah</term> is in the genitive case, acting as an adjective for <term>safīn</term>. <term>yajūru bihā</term>, etc., acts as an adjectival phrase modifying <term>safīn</term>.

5 يَشُقُّ حَبَابَ المَاءِ حَيْزُومُهَا .. كَمَا قَسَمَ التُّرْبَ المُفَايِلُ بِاليَدِ

“Their bows cleave the ripples of the water, as the divider [the <term>mufāyil</term>] separates the sand-heaps with his hand.”

<term>Mufāyil</term> is an agent from the third conjugation of <term>fāyala</term>, referring to the player of the game called <term>fiyāl</term>. This game involves hiding an item like a coin or ring in sand, which is then divided into heaps; the player who finds the item wins the stakes.

This line is an example of a defect in rhyme called <term>īṭā’</term>, or the repetition of the same rhyming word (<term>al-yad</term>), used with the same meaning within nine lines.

“And in the tribe there is one like a young gazelle, with deep-colored lips, shaking the Arāk tree to obtain its fruit, while wearing double strings of pearls and emeralds.”

pages.97:
# FEELING

It is often suggested that progress in the systematic study of the mind is likely to be influenced by—and to model itself upon—the body of physical knowledge that appears most impressive to the thoughtful society of that time and place. This is because the subject matter of mental science is not accessible to collective observation; introspection is an individual act, and no two instances of a mental phenomenon in different individuals can be shown to be absolutely identical. Consequently, it is usually—though I do not say *only*—when some major advance in physical science drags the rest of human knowledge in its wake that the laws of the mind are freshly investigated, as something that must also be brought into line with current progress.

Where there is no such progress in psychological investigation, some system of dogmatic metaphysics likely holds the cultured imagination of the age captive through the spell of some "Word-myth." When the mind eventually breaks free and looks deeper, it will naturally turn toward more positive ideas as guides and supports for its fresh concepts.

Now, in the healing lore and craft of that day—the only one, I repeat, that comes prominently to the forefront in the episodes and detailed rules of the <term>Vinaya</term> <note>The disciplinary code for Buddhist monks</note>—the revolt of thought embodied in the Buddhist movement found its noblest inspiration.

82 BUDDHIST PSYCHOLOGY

The word <term>dukkha</term> <note>Often translated as "suffering" or "ill," but implies a broader state of unsatisfactoriness.</note> covers all that is meant by "not well"—the ills and pains of the body, the ills and misery of the mind; in a word, *dis-ease*. Its presence is the doctor’s *casus belli* <note>original: "cause of war"</note> and *raison d'être* <note>original: "reason for being"</note>; its cause and extinction are his mission. While there may be several positive expressions for its absence, there is, alas, nothing else in life as mortally positive as *dukkha*. It is easy for many to conceive of its mere absence as sufficient for happiness. <term>Nibbana</term> <note>The state of liberation from suffering</note> itself, a quasi-negative term, was at times employed as "health" as well as "happiness." The Founder, in one of his most emphatic statements about his mission, expressed it as one of healing:

"Both then and now, just this do I reveal:
—*dukkha* and the extinction of *dukkha*." <note>Majjhima-Nikaya i. 509; Sutta-Nipata, verse 749.</note>

The physical healer finds the causes of disease in the mutual interaction of a person and their environment. Buddhism also found there the causes of everything that made for unhappiness. Sense impressions were the avenues through which satisfactions (*pasāda*) came, though they were fraught with peril. Consciousness, driven by its three main roots or conditions—greed (appetite), enmity, and delusion—reacted to its impressions through feeling, desire, and grasping after everything that tended toward the expansion and conceit of this "Me" and "Mine."
pages.99:
FEELING 83

Just as it behooved the physician to keep in view all possible sources of a disease—neglecting none—so was Buddhism searching and exhaustive in its treatment of the avenues of sense. It ignored none of the five that conveyed information, nor the sixth that coordinated and revived what the former brought.

Buddhism correctly discerned that the great intermediary between the (relatively) passive reactions to the manifold stimuli of sense and the subsequent, more deliberate reactions, was *Feeling*. This feeling might be pleasant, painful, or neither. It did not follow that where the feeling was pleasant (*sukha*), the symptoms of disease (*dukkha*) were absent. In fact, the *sukha* born of sense was the most efficient servant of *dukkha*, if *dukkha* is understood broadly as both physical and moral ill—and all that this involves regarding mental suffering and moral deterioration.

As Ledi Sadaw, the eminent *Thera* <note>Senior monk</note>, writes: "We must distinguish between *dukkha* of the category (or, in Buddhist terminology, the essential mark) of something unpleasant experienced via the senses—whether physical or psychological—and the *dukkha* we use in the triad: impermanence (*anicca*), ill, and non-soul (*an-atta*). By this *dukkha* we mean a state of peril and danger, lacking peace, security, or blessing." <note>Yamaka, ii. Appendix, p. 248 (London, Pali Text Society, 1913).</note>
pages.100:
84 BUDDHIST PSYCHOLOGY

This is the distinction a physician—or at least a patient—might draw between sensations of pain and the disease itself. The presence, growth, or decline of pain is not always accompanied by the presence, increase, or cessation of the disease. We must maintain this distinction throughout all Buddhist literature dealing with sense, feeling, and the effects of feeling. Otherwise, we will fall into significant inconsistencies of expression, as I shall demonstrate.

That feeling is the inevitable response to the awareness of new stimuli is affirmed throughout the <term>Nikayas</term> <note>The main collections of early Buddhist teachings</note>, notably in the *Samyutta-Nikaya* regarding the sphere of sense:

"Where there are hands, there taking and setting down appears; where there are feet, there coming and going appears; where there are limbs, there folding and stretching appears; where there is a stomach, there hunger and thirst appears. Just so, monks, where there is sight (or eye), or hearing... there arise subjective pleasure and pain, conditioned by sense-stimulus." <note>Samyutta-Nikaya iv. 171.</note>

The converse is then stated for both the analogies and the analogues: "...Where there is no sight, etc., neither pleasure nor pain, conditioned by sense-stimulus, arises."
pages.101:
FEELING 85

This quotation is conclusive enough to represent all other passages stating that sensations and feelings coexist, understood much as our modern psychology of sense understands pleasure and unpleasure. That the senses convey pleasure as well as its opposite is not only allowed and affirmed by doctrinal teaching, but this pleasure is also recognized as very genuine and good by the most eminent of the teachers. The Founder affirmed at times that no one lived more at ease (*sukham seti*) than he, despite having forsworn most of the so-called "good things" of life. His chief apostles gathered with him one fine evening in the Gosinga Wood, delighting in the "divine perfumes" of the dewy, moonlit scene, where the tall *sal*-trees stood clad in golden bloom. Temperance was prescribed for maintaining the physical comfort of health.

However, when the disciple is told to look upon *sukha* as <term>dukkha</term>, then we know that the wider concept is to be understood. 

<note>I owe the term 'unpleasure', borrowed from German science, to my university colleague, Mr. T. H. Pear.</note>
pages.102:
86 BUDDHIST PSYCHOLOGY

This is also the case when things unpleasant to the "average sensual man" are valued by a different scale and are held to constitute a higher pleasure:

"Things seen and heard, tastes, odours, what we touch,
Perceive, all, everything desirable,
Pleasant and sweet, while one can say 'It is,'
These are deemed *Sukha* by both gods and men,
And where these cease to be, they hold it woe.

What other men call *Sukha*, that the saints
Call *Dukkha*; what the rest so name,
That do the <term>Ariyans</term> <note>The Noble ones, those who have attained spiritual realization</note> know as happiness.
Behold a norm that’s hard to apprehend!
Hereby are baffled they that are not wise." <note>Sutta-Nipata, verse 759 f.; cp. Samyutta-Nikaya iv. 127.</note>

If we do not wish to be baffled, we must read those passages wherein each sense is declared to be *dukkha* with this wider implication. If, using Ledi Sadaw’s definition, we read into such passages as "seeing... is sorrow" the wider sense of *dukkha*, it becomes:

"The eye, brother, is a faculty of peril and danger, bringing, as such, no peace, security, or blessing; it is to understand this that the holy life under the Exalted One is lived."

If we do this, we may not be unwilling to admit the truth of this "monkish" statement, even for laypeople.
pages.103:
CHAPTER V

THE PSYCHOLOGY OF THE NIKAYAS—continued

IV. IDEATION

The systematic analysis of the mind in the *Nikayas* is pursued no further than the recipient and coordinating work of *mano* <note>The mind or 'sense-center'</note> acting as a *sensus communis* <note>original: "common sense/shared faculty of perception"</note>. Sequences in consciousness are occasionally pursued further, but without much terminological consistency. Here are a few instances:

"Because of some tendency, there arises perception, opinion, thinking, volition, wish, aspiration. And according as the tendency is low, mediocre, or lofty, so will all these be." <note>Samyutta-Nikaya ii. 153; see Commentary.</note>

The process of religious conversion is described as one of "hearing, attending, remembering, comparing, discerning, desire, zeal, pondering, endeavour." <note>Majjhima-Nikaya i. 480; ii. 173.</note>

"Thinking results in desire; through desire, objects are divided into what we like and what we dislike, hence envy and selfishness, hence quarrelling and fighting." <note>Digha-Nikaya ii. 278 f. (condensed).</note>
pages.104:
88 BUDDHIST PSYCHOLOGY

"Conditioned by contact arises feeling; what one feels, one perceives; what one perceives, one thinks about; what one thinks about, one is obsessed with." <note>Majjhima-Nikaya i., iii.</note>

These samples reveal the persistent effort in the <term>Suttas</term> <note>Buddhist discourses</note> to continue the method—systematically observed in the treatment of sense—of setting forth mind and character as an orderly, causal process. This method is emphatically Buddhist. The most notable example is the important formula of natural causation, exemplified by the process of life being bound up with *dukkha*. In the mental process, the resolution of receptive consciousness into discharging consciousness is clearly affirmed. Sense and feeling, stirred by sense, are converted into motor presentations (such as desire). But we meet with no closer analysis of the intellectual process—what has been called representative cognition, or ideation, in our own psychology. In the last sample, we only hear that "what we perceive," i.e., notice (*sañña-khandha*), we "think about" (*vitakketi*).

<summary>This section explores the Buddhist psychological view of 'feeling' (vedana) as an intermediary between sense-stimuli and deliberate reactions, distinguishing between sensory pain and the broader state of 'dukkha' (unsatisfactoriness), while also introducing the causal mental processes involved in ideation.</summary>
<keywords>Feeling, Dukkha, Sense-stimulus, Psychology, Nikayas, Ideation, Mind, Causality</keywords>

<margin>16</margin> Therefore, let us put away those rhetorical exercises:
"A mind bound by drunkenness is not under its own control. Just as wine vats themselves are burst by new wine, and the heat forces everything that lies at the bottom to the top, so when wine boils up, whatever lies hidden at the bottom is brought forth and into the open. As those laden with wine cannot hold their food when they have overindulged, so they cannot hold a secret. That which is their own and that which belongs to others, they pour out alike." <margin>17</margin> But although this usually happens, so too does the opposite: that we deliberate about necessary matters with those whom we know to drink more freely. Therefore, the argument often used as a defense—that one who is accustomed to getting drunk cannot be trusted with a secret—is false.

How much better it is to openly condemn drunkenness and expose its vices, which even a decent person would avoid, let alone a perfect and wise man, who is content to satisfy his thirst, and who, even if occasionally led on by merriment for the sake of others, still stops short of <margin>18</margin> drunkenness. For we shall see later whether the mind of the wise man is disturbed by too much wine and performs the acts typical of the drunkard. Meanwhile, if you want to prove that a good man should not get drunk, why use logical syllogisms? Say how shameful it is to pour into oneself more than one can hold and not to know the capacity of one’s own stomach; how many things drunkards do that would make sober men blush; and that drunkenness is nothing but voluntary madness. Extend that drunkard’s condition over several days; would you have any doubt about his madness? It is no less severe now, just shorter in duration. Recall the example of Alexander of Macedon, who killed Clitus, his dearest and most loyal friend, during a banquet, and once he understood his crime, wished to die—as he certainly ought to have done.

Every vice is both inflamed and uncovered by drunkenness; it removes the modesty that stands in the way of evil impulses. For many abstain from forbidden things more because of the shame of sinning than from good intentions. <margin>20</margin> When an excessive amount of wine has taken possession of the soul, whatever evil was hidden emerges. Drunkenness does not create vices, but it exposes them; then, the lustful man does not even wait for the bedroom, but grants his desires what they demand without delay; then, the unchaste man confesses and publishes his sickness; then, the insolent man does not restrain his tongue or his hand. Arrogance grows in the haughty, cruelty in the savage, and spite in the envious. <margin>21</margin> Every vice is loosened and brought to light. Add to this the ignorance of oneself, the doubtful and poorly articulated words, the wandering eyes, the unsteady gait, the dizziness of the head, the very houses looking as if they were moving, as if some whirlwind were spinning the whole building, and the torments of the stomach when the wine effervesces and distends the very bowels.

<summary>Seneca argues against the idea that a drunkard can be trusted with secrets, citing the reliability of Cossus and the inherent dangers of drunkenness.</summary>
<keywords>Cossus, drunkenness, secrets, rhetoric, vice, Seneca</keywords>

So let us abolish all such harangues as this: "No man in the bonds of drunkenness has power over his soul. As the very vats are burst by new wine, and as the dregs at the bottom are raised to the surface by the strength of the fermentation; so, when the wine effervesces, whatever lies hidden below is brought up and made visible. As a man overcome by liquor cannot keep down his food when he has over-indulged in wine, so he cannot keep back a secret either. He pours forth impartially both his own secrets and those of other persons." This, of course, is what commonly happens, but so does this—that we take counsel on serious subjects with those whom we know to be in the habit of drinking freely. Therefore this proposition, which is laid down in the guise of a defense of Zeno’s <term>syllogism</term>, is false—that secrets are not entrusted to the habitual drunkard.

How much better it is to arraign drunkenness frankly and to expose its vices! For even the middling good man avoids them, not to mention the perfect <term>sage</term>, who is satisfied with slaking his thirst; the sage, even if now and then he is led on by good cheer which, for a friend’s sake, is carried somewhat too far, yet always stops short of drunkenness. We shall investigate later the question whether the mind of the sage is upset by too much wine and commits follies like those of the toper; but meanwhile, if you wish to prove that a good man ought not to get drunk, why work it out by logic? Drunkenness kindles and discloses every kind of vice, and removes the sense of shame that veils our evil undertakings. <note>This is the firm conviction of Seneca, himself a most temperate man.</note> For more men abstain from forbidden actions because they are ashamed of sinning than because their inclinations are good. When the strength of wine has become too great and has gained control over the mind, every lurking evil comes forth from its hiding-place. Drunkenness does not create vice, it merely brings it into view; at such times the lustful man does not wait even for the privacy of a bedroom, but without postponement gives free play to the demands of his passions; at such times the unchaste man proclaims and publishes his malady; at such times your cross-grained fellow does not restrain his tongue or his hand. The haughty man increases his arrogance, the ruthless man his cruelty, the slanderer his spitefulness. Every vice is given free play and comes to the front. Besides, we forget who we are, we utter words that are halting and poorly enunciated, the glance is unsteady, the step falters, the head is dizzy, the very ceiling moves about as if a cyclone were whirling the whole house, and the stomach suffers torture when the wine generates gas and causes our very bowels to swell.

<meta>This page continues the technical analysis of planetary periods (Dasas), explaining the calculation of sub-periods and the proportional distribution of influence among planets in the 120-year cycle.</meta>

# JATAKACHUNDRIKA.

In the science of Astrology, the period of the most powerful planet in the angular houses (<term>Kendras</term>) is the first to be calculated. The *Vimsottari* (120 years) and *Astottari* (108 years) systems are prevalent in Southern and Northern India respectively. The terms of years ascribed to the planets also differ. In Southern India, *Oodudasa*—or periods calculated according to the rising constellation at the time of birth—is in vogue, and is easy to determine. In another system, the most powerful planet, including the lord of the Ascendant (<term>Lagna</term>), begins as the lord of the first period. 

The strength of the planets must be determined by the sources of power prescribed in astrological texts—such as <term>Sthanabala</term> (positional strength), <term>Digbala</term> (directional strength), <term>Kalabala</term> (temporal strength), <term>Viryabala</term> (intrinsic strength), <term>Chestabala</term> (motional strength), <term>Nysargikabala</term> (natural strength), and the various good and evil <term>Vergas</term> (divisional charts). I refer the reader to the first chapter of my English translation of the *Sarwartha Chintamani* for full details on this important branch of knowledge. 

Find out the <term>Nakshatra</term> (constellation) at the time of birth and see how much of it has passed and how much remains. Take the Sun’s period, which is 6 years; this represents the Sun’s general period. Then we have the *Vidasa* (sub-period), the *Bhookti* (sub-sub-period), the *Antardasa* (sub-sub-sub-period), and the *Antarantara* (a smaller division). Finally, we have the *Sookshma* (very small division) and the *Prana* (the smallest planetary sub-division), enabling us to make hourly or even half-hourly predictions. 

Take the *Ravi Dasa* (Sun's period) of 6 years. Planets have an invariable proportion in the distribution of their periods and sub-periods. The Sun receives 6 years out of the 120-year total. Within his 6-year period, his sub-period bears the same proportion as his general period bears to the 120 years. When he has 6 years out of 120, how much will he have in 6 years? 6 × 6 / 120 years = 36 / 120 years. Since the denominator is larger, we reduce the fraction to months: 36 × 12 / 120 = 36 / 10 = 18 / 5 = 3 and 3/5 months. We convert the 3/5 of a month into days: 3/5 × 30 days = 18 days. Thus, the sub-period of *Ravi* (the Sun) within the Sun's general period is 3 months and 18 days. In all other minute divisions, *Ravi* maintains this constant proportion of 6 to 120. If we take *Ravi's* sub-sub-period: 3 and 3/5 months = 18 / 5 × 6 / 120 months.

->= 18 / 5 × 1 / 20 = 18 / 100 = 9 / 50 months =<-
->9 / 50 × 30 days = 27 / 5 = 5 and 2/5 days.<-

Now, if we require further subdivisions, we must follow the same rule.

### **STANZA XXIX.**

Planets who are with the lords of the periods, planets who occupy the houses of the lords of the periods, and planets who are otherwise equal in strength to the lords of the periods, give similar results to those of the lords of the periods themselves during their respective sub-periods.

### **NOTES.**

The *Dasa* (major period) and its subdivisions must be calculated with reference to the rising constellation at the time of birth, which is called the *Janma Nakshatra*. I have already provided the *Dasas* for the 27 constellations. If *Krittika* is rising at birth, it commences with the period of the Sun. In judging planetary influences, the reader must bear in mind the various sources of strength and weakness a planet possesses. If one planet occupies the house of another, and the latter is the lord of the period (*Dasanatha*), the former gives results similar to those given by the *Dasanatha*. Those planets in conjunction with the *Dasanatha* also produce similar results. The owner of the house occupied by the *Dasanatha* produces results similar to the *Dasanatha* himself. Other planets that possess strength or weakness equal to the *Dasanatha* yield similar results. Planets are considered similar in strength when they occupy houses of the same nature, or possess lateral, periodical, or positional advantages. This is a guide for the student to measure planetary influence. All planets emit light—even if it is reflected solar rays. The effects of a pure solar ray must differ from the effects of the same ray when reflected...

## STANZA XXX.

In the periods and sub-periods of other planets not connected with the lord of the general *Dasa*, the results are to be predicted based on whether they are opposed to him and inclined to produce contrary effects.

## NOTES.

In Stanza 29, the author stated that in the general period of a planet, we expect results similar to *him* if we are in the sub-periods of planets associated with him, in his house, or who own the house the <term>Dasanatha</term> (period lord) occupies. Every horoscope contains two or three sets of planets. One set is directly connected to the <term>Dasanatha</term> by conjunction, aspect, or occupation. Another set is directly opposed to the lord of the general <term>Dasa</term>, seeking to manifest their own nature or modify the results of the <term>Dasanatha</term>. A third set is indifferent. 

The author explains the results of sub-periods belonging to planets opposing the <term>Dasa</term> lord. If the <term>Dasanatha</term> promotes good health, but the lord of the <term>Bhookti</term> (sub-period) promotes sickness, the result is that the health of the <term>native</term> (the person whose chart it is) becomes indifferent. If the <term>Dasanatha</term> provides wealth, but the <term>Bhooktinatha</term> (sub-period lord) is inclined to steal it away, the person will possess money but eventually lose it, or have it in small quantities. ## STANZA XXXI.

In the *<term>Dasa</term>* of the lord of the 5th or 9th houses (who is not otherwise powerless), the lord of the 1st, 4th, 7th, or 10th houses—even if unconnected with the *<term>Dasanatha</term>*—produces good. Similarly, a *<term>Bhooktinatha</term>* who is the owner of one or more quadrants and is not otherwise weakened produces good during the *<term>Dasa</term>* of the lord who governs the 5th or 9th houses.

### NOTES.

This stanza is capable of several interpretations. The *<term>Dasa</term>* of the lords of the 5th and 9th houses is generally declared to be good. However, those lords might also rule the 6th, 8th, or 12th houses (inauspicious signs), be in conjunction with evil planets, receive malicious aspects, or be debilitated. In such cases, one must subtract from their general ability to do good. Suppose we are in the sub-period of a quadrant lord during such a *<term>Dasa</term>*; what is the result? The author suggests that if the sub-period lord owns a quadrant (*<term>Kendra</term>*) and has none of the aforementioned evil influences, he produces good results despite having no connection to the *<term>Dasanatha</term>*. The author does not explicitly provide for the reverse case.

<summary>This page explains the beneficial influence of quadrant lords during the periods of 5th and 9th house lords, highlighting how the quality of a house affects planetary outcomes.</summary>
<keywords>Stanza 31, Dasa, Bhooktinatha, Dasanatha, Kendras, quadrants, 5th house, 9th house</keywords>

# JATAKACHUNDRIKA.

...as the lord of the 5th or 9th houses? Take again the lord of the 5th or 9th house in the *Dasa* of a lord of the quadrants. Does he produce good results if not otherwise powerless? Other cases may also be put forth, but I refer the reader to the general principles laid down at the beginning of this work. All planets—good or evil—who own the 5th or 9th houses produce good, whereas not all planets who own quadrants are productive of auspicious results. It seems clear that the value of planets ruling the 5th or 9th house is greater than the value of those governing quadrants (1-4-7-10). Benefics ruling quadrants often produce evil, while malefics governing *Kendras* are productive of favorable results. Regardless of whether they are inherently good or evil, planets produce good results when they own the 5th or 9th houses.

->Success begins in the Dasas of death-inflicting planets.<-
->Evil planets in those sub-periods not only work against this success but also bring death to the native. || 32 ||

### STANZA XXXII.

Success comes in the *Dasas* of death-inflicting planets. Evil planets in those sub-periods not only negate this success but also bring death to the *native*.

### NOTES.

The lords of the 2nd and 7th houses are death-inflicting planets, and these houses are called *Maraka* (death) houses. The lords of these houses give success during their own *Dasas*. However, when the *Bhooktis* of evil planets intervene, the success predicted will be negated, and they may bring death. Planets in conjunction with death-inflicting lords provide prosperity. Those not with them but favorably disposed provide limited fortune. Those who are not in conjunction and are maliciously disposed bring ruin and death. The term "evil planets" has two meanings: <term>Guru</term> (Jupiter), <term>Sukra</term> (Venus), <term>Poornachundra</term> (full Moon), and well-associated <term>Buda</term> (Mercury) are generally termed "benefics." Conversely, <term>Sani</term> (Saturn), <term>Kuja</term> (Mars), <term>Ravi</term> (Sun), <term>Kshinachundra</term> (new Moon), and poorly associated <term>Buda</term> are called "malefics."

<summary>This page defines Maraka (death-inflicting) houses and explains how the interaction between benefics and malefics influences whether a period brings success or danger.</summary>

<meta>This page clarifies the terminology of good and evil planets and introduces Stanza 33.</meta>

# JATAKACHUNDRIKA.

...Good planets may become "evil" when they own the 1st, 3rd, 4th, 6th, 7th, 8th, 10th, 11th, or 12th houses, when they receive evil aspects, or when they are debilitated. Conversely, evil planets may become "good" when they are lords of the 1st, 4th, 5th, 7th, 9th, or 10th houses. We say good planets own evil houses and produce evil, while evil planets own good houses and produce good. There is some confusion in Sanskrit texts regarding these terms, but with closer study, the student will see that "good" and "bad" have limited meanings depending on the context. The word <term>Rajayoga</term> (a combination for success) is also used vaguely; some astrologers limit it to political or official success, while others define it as success in any walk of life.

->Good planets in conjunction with the lords of the death-inflicting houses give success.<-
->Those who are not in conjunction give moderate results, while those who are not in conjunction and do not produce success bring ruin. || 33 ||

## STANZA XXXIII.

Good planets in conjunction with the lords of the death-inflicting houses provide success. These same planets, when not in conjunction with the lords of death, provide moderate success in their sub-periods. Powerful planets give good success in the <term>Bhooktis</term> even when they are not in conjunction with the owners of the death-inflicting houses.

### NOTES.

Stanzas 33 and 34 refer to <term>Dasas</term> and the <term>Bhooktis</term> that intervene during them. The <term>Dasa</term> might be generally good, but if the sub-period is governed by a planet that is evil by nature or opposed to the <term>Dasanatha</term>, the period will not be favorable. If the lord of the major period is good and the lord of the sub-period is bad, the good of the former is canceled, and the result is indifferent. If one is good and the other is indifferent, there will be moderate success; if both are good, success is certain; if both are bad, the results will be disastrous.

<summary>This page elaborates on the classification of planets as benefics or malefics based on house ownership and explains how these classifications determine the outcomes of sub-periods.</summary>
<keywords>Stanza 33, Rajayoga, Bhooktis, Dasas, Dasanatha, benefics, malefics</keywords>

# JATAKACHUNDRIKA.

...If the sub-lords are in conjunction with the major lords, they produce good. If they are not in conjunction but are otherwise good, they produce partial success. If they are bad and not in conjunction with the major lords, they produce ruin and death.

->Planets disposed to give Rajayoga will do so in their sub-periods,<-
->which intervene during the general periods of planets with which they are not associated. || 34 ||

## STANZA XXXIV.

Planets which are disposed to give *Rajayoga* will do so in their sub-periods, which intervene during the general periods of planets with which they are not associated.

### NOTES.

This stanza is plain. A planet that is "good" for several reasons wishes to produce success for the <term>native</term>. His own <term>Dasa</term> may not occur during the person's lifetime. However, the sub-periods of planets, being shorter, occur many times. It has been remarked that planets in combination with "good" planets also give success. This may be due to the purification of their rays by conjunction with a nobler planet, or because the weaker planet's rays become inactive due to the power of the stronger one. Either way, the result is auspicious. If there is no conjunction between the major and sub-period lords, the result depends on the nature of the individual planet.

->When Rahu and Kethu occupy favorable houses and are not in conjunction with any other planets,<-
->they give success in their respective sub-periods according to their relative strength. || 35 ||

### STANZA XXXV.

When <term>Rahu</term> and <term>Kethu</term> occupy favorable houses and are not in conjunction with any other planets, they give success in their respective sub-periods according to their relative strength.

# JATAKACHUNDRIKA.

### NOTES.

<term>Rahu</term> and <term>Kethu</term> (the Dragon’s Head and Dragon’s Tail) own no independent mansions. They are called shadow (<term>chaya</term>) planets or dark (<term>Thamo</term>) planets. However, later writers have assigned them places of exaltation and debilitation. "Exaltation" means the state in which a planet is capable of producing the greatest possible good. "Debilitation" is the opposite state (<term>Neecha</term>), where the planet is inclined to do harm. In the state of exaltation (<term>Oocha</term>), a planet is in full glory and produces success. When eclipsed or disturbed, the rays become useless and produce misery. From Aries (<term>Mesha</term>) to Virgo (<term>Kanya</term>), <term>Rahu</term> is considered powerful. From Libra (<term>Thula</term>) to Pisces (<term>Meena</term>), <term>Kethu</term> is considered good. Taurus (<term>Vrishabha</term>) is especially strong for <term>Rahu</term>, while Scorpio (<term>Vrischika</term>) is so considered for <term>Kethu</term>.

->If the lords of the Dasa are evil and the lords of the sub-period are favorable but unconnected with them, they produce evil.<-
->The sub-periods of favorable planets who are connected with them become mixed in result. || 36 ||

->Sub-periods of those who produce Rajayoga produce mixed results,<-
->but those who are not in conjunction produce extremely evil results. || 37 ||

### STANZAS XXXVI & XXXVII.

If the lords of the <term>Dasa</term> are evil and the lords of the sub-period are favorable but unconnected with them, they produce evil. If the favorable lords of the sub-periods are connected with them, the results are mixed. If the lords of the sub-periods are "Rajayoga" creators, they yield mixed results, but if they are not in conjunction, they yield extremely evil results.

<keywords>Rahu, Kethu, exaltation, debilitation, Stanza 36, Stanza 37, Dasa, Bhookti</keywords>

# FEELING

I suggest that an advance in the systematic study of mind is especially likely to be influenced by, and to mold itself upon, that body of more or less systematic physical knowledge which bulks most impressively in the more thoughtful part of the society of that time and place. For the subject matter of mental science is, as we know, not accessible to strictly collective observation; introspection is of the individual, and in the individual no two instances of a phenomenon can be shown as absolutely coincident. Hence it is largely—I do not say only—when some onward stride in physical science draws the rest of human knowledge in its wake, that the laws of mind are freshly investigated, as something that must also be brought into the line of march.

Where there is no such advance in psychical investigation, some system of dogmatic metaphysic is probably holding the cultured imagination of the age captive, through the spell of some myth of the Word. When the mind breaks free and looks deeper, there will naturally be a recourse, for its fresh concepts, to more positive ideas as guides and supports.

Now in the healing lore and craft of the day—the only one, I repeat, that comes prominently to the front in episode and in details of rules in the <term>Vinaya</term><note>The Vinaya is the regulatory framework for the Buddhist monastic community.</note>—the revolt of thought embodied in the Buddhist movement found its noblest inspiration.

<summary>This page argues that advancements in mental science are often modeled after contemporary physical sciences, and posits that Buddhist psychology was deeply influenced by the medical knowledge of its time.</summary>
<keywords>mental science, introspection, Buddhist movement, physical science, Vinaya, history of psychology</keywords>

The word <term>dukkha</term><note>Dukkha is often translated as suffering, unsatisfactoriness, or ill.</note> covers all that is meant by "not well"—ills and pains of body, ills and misery of mind; in a word, disease. Its presence is the doctor’s *casus belli*<note>original: "casus belli" (a cause or justification for war).</note> and *raison d'être*<note>original: "raison d'être" (reason for being).</note>; its cause and extinction is his quest. For its absence there may be several positive expressions. And yet there is nothing else in life so mortally positive as <term>dukkha</term>. And it is easy, alas! for many to conceive its mere absence as sufficient for happiness. <term>Nibbana</term> itself, a quasi-negative term, was at times employed as "health," as well as happiness. And the Founder, in one of his more emphatic utterances about his mission, expressed that as one of healing:

"Both then and now just this do I reveal:
—<term>dukkha</term> and the extinction of <term>dukkha</term>."<note>Majjhima-Nikaya i. 509; Sutta-Nipata, verse 749.</note>

The physical healer finds the causes of disease in the mutual interaction of man and his environment. Buddhism too found therein the causes of all that made for unhappiness. Sense-impressions were the avenues whereby came satisfactions (<term>pasada</term>) fraught with peril. Consciousness, with its three main roots or conditions—greed or appetite, enmity, delusion—pushing it, reacted on its impressions as feeling, desire for, and grasping after all that tended to the

And as it behooved the physician to keep in view all possible sources of any disease, neglecting none, so was Buddhism searching and exhaustive in its treatment of the avenues of sense, ignoring none of the five that conveyed [stimuli], nor the sixth that coordinated and revived what the former brought.

The great intermediary between the (relatively) passive reactions to the manifold stimulus of sense and the following more or less deliberate reactions, Buddhism discerned, correctly enough, in Feeling. This might be pleasant, painful, or neither. And it did not follow that where feeling was pleasant (<term>sukha</term>), the symptoms of disease (<term>dukkha</term>) were absent. For the <term>sukha</term> born of sense was the most efficient handmaiden of <term>dukkha</term>, if <term>dukkha</term> be broadly understood as both physical and moral ill, and all that this does, or may involve of mental suffering and moral deterioration.

As Ledi Sadaw, the eminent Thera (Senior in the Order) writes:<note>Yamaka, ii. Appendix, p. 248 (London, Pali Text Society, 1913).</note> "We must distinguish between <term>dukkha</term> of the category (or, in Buddhist idiom, of the essential mark) of something unpleasant experienced (by way of sense), physical or psychical, and the <term>dukkha</term> we use in the triad: impermanence (<term>aniccha</term>), ill, and non-soul (<term>an-atta</term>). By this <term>dukkha</term> we mean a state of peril and danger, without peace, security or blessing."

84 BUDDHIST PSYCHOLOGY

This, in other words, is the distinction a physician, or at least a patient, might draw between sensations of pain and disease. The presence, the growth, the decline of the pain is not always accompanied by the presence or increase or cessation of the disease. And this distinction we have to draw throughout the whole of Buddhist literature dealing with sense, with feeling, and the effects of feeling. Else we find ourselves landed in much inconsistency of expression, as I shall show.

That feeling is the inevitable response to awareness of new stimulus is affirmed up and down the Nikayas, notably in Samyutta-Nikaya on the sphere of sense (vol. iv. 1 ff.), e.g.:

"Where there are hands, there taking and setting down appears; where there are feet, there coming and going appears; where there are limbs, there folding and stretching appears; where there is stomach, there hunger and thirst appears. Just so, <term>bhikkhus</term><note>Monks.</note>, where there is sight (or eye), or hearing . . . there arise subjective pleasure and pain, conditioned by sense-stimulus (literally contact, <term>samphassa</term>)."<note>Samyutta-Nikaya iv. 171.</note>

The contrary is then stated, both of the analogies and the analogues: ". . . Where there is not sight, etc., neither pleasure nor pain, conditioned by sense-stimulus, arises."

<summary>The author illustrates the Buddhist understanding of how sense-stimulus leads inevitably to feeling, citing canonical texts to prove the causal link.</summary>

That the senses convey pleasure as well as its opposite is not only allowed and affirmed by doctrinal teaching, but the pleasure is also recognized as very genuine and good by the most eminent of the teachers. The Founder affirmed at times that none lived more at ease (<term>sukham seti</term>) than himself, however much he had forsworn most of the so-called good things of life.<note>Anguttara-Nikaya i. 136; Samyutta-Nikaya iv. 127.</note> His chief apostles forgather with him one fine evening in the Gosinga Wood, delighting in the "divine perfumes" of the dewy moonlit scene, where the tall sal-trees stand clad in golden bloom.<note>Majjhima-Nikaya i. 212f.; Samyutta-Nikaya iv. 104, and passim.</note> Temperance was prescribed for maintaining the physical comfort (<term>phasu-vihara</term>) of health.<note>Bud. CHAPTER V

THE PSYCHOLOGY OF THE NIKAYAS—continued

IV. IDEATION

THE systematic analysis of mind in the Nikayas is pursued no further than the recipient and coordinating work of <term>mano</term> as <term>sensus communis</term><note>original: "sensus communis" (common sense or central faculty of perception).</note>. Sequences in consciousness are occasionally pursued further, but without overmuch terminological consistency, and irregularly. Here are a few instances:

"Because of some tendency there arises perception, opinion, thinking, volition, wish, aspiration. And according as the tendency is low, mediocre or lofty, so will all these be."<note>Samyutta-Nikaya ii. 153; see Commentary.</note>

The process of conversion in religion is described as one of "hearing, attending, remembering, comparing, discerning, desire, zeal, pondering, endeavor."<note>Majjhima-Nikaya i. 480; ii. 173.</note>

"Thinking results in desire, through desire objects are divided into what we like and

<summary>This page introduces the Buddhist psychological analysis of 'ideation', noting how the Nikayas describe mental sequences such as perception, volition, and desire.</summary>
<keywords>ideation, Nikayas, mano, consciousness, mental process, volition</keywords>
pages.104:
88 BUDDHIST PSYCHOLOGY

what we dislike, hence envy and selfishness, hence quarrelling and fighting."<note>Digha-Nikaya ii. 278 f. (condensed).</note>

"Conditioned by contact arises feeling; what one feels, one perceives; what one perceives, one thinks about; what one thinks about, one is obsessed withal."<note>Majjhima-Nikaya i., iii.</note>

These samples reveal the persistent effort, in the Suttas, to carry on the method, systematically observed in treating of sense, of setting forth mind and character as orderly, causal process. The method is emphatically Buddhist. The most notable example of it is the important formula of natural causation, as exemplified in the process of life being bound up with <term>dukkha</term>. In the mental process, the resolution of afferent or receptive consciousness into efferent or discharging consciousness is clearly affirmed. Sense and feeling stirred by sense are converted into motor presentations; as desire, etc. But we meet with no closer analysis of intellectual process, of what has, in our own psychology, been called representative and re-representative cognition, or ideation. In the last sample, we only hear that 'what we perceive,' i.e. notice (the <term>sanna-khandha</term><note>The aggregate of perception.</note>), we 'think about' (<term>vitakketi</term>).

<summary>The text concludes this section by highlighting the Buddhist focus on causal mental sequences, while noting the limitations of their analysis compared to modern representative cognition.</summary>
<keywords>causation, mental process, Suttas, afferent, efferent, sanna-khandha, vitakketi, ideation</keywords>

So let us abolish all such harangues as this: "No man in the bonds of drunkenness has power over his soul. As the very vats are burst by new wine, and as the dregs at the bottom are raised to the surface by the strength of the fermentation; so, when the wine effervesces, whatever lies hidden below is brought up and made visible. As a man overcome by liquor cannot keep down his food when he has over-indulged in wine, so he cannot keep back a secret either. He pours forth impartially both his own secrets and those of other persons." This, of course, is what commonly happens, but so does this—that we take counsel on serious subjects with those whom we know to be in the habit of drinking freely. Therefore this proposition, which is laid down in the guise of a defence of Zeno's <note>Zeno of Citium, founder of Stoicism</note> syllogism, is false—that secrets are not entrusted to the habitual drunkard.

How much better it is to arraign drunkenness frankly and to expose its vices! For even the middling good man avoids them, not to mention the perfect sage, who is satisfied with slaking his thirst; the sage, even if now and then he is led on by good cheer which, for a friend's sake, is carried somewhat too far, yet always stops short of drunkenness. We shall investigate later the question whether the mind of the sage is upset by too much wine and commits follies like those of the toper; but meanwhile, if you wish to prove that a good man ought not to get drunk, why work it out by logic? Recall the example of Alexander of Macedon, who stabbed Clitus, his dearest and most loyal friend, during a banquet, and upon realizing the crime, wished to die—he certainly ought to have.

Drunkenness both inflames and reveals every vice, removing the sense of shame that hinders evil attempts. For more men abstain from forbidden things out of shame of sinning than from good will. When an excessive amount of wine has taken possession of the mind, whatever evil lay hidden emerges. Drunkenness does not create vices, but draws them out; at that time, the lustful person does not even wait for the bedroom, but yields to his desires as much as they demand without delay; at that time, the unchaste person proclaims and publishes his malady; at that time, the petulant person restrains neither his tongue nor his hand. Arrogance grows in the insolent, cruelty in the savage, malice in the spiteful. Every vice is loosened and comes forth. Think of Alexander of Macedon <note>For a dramatic account of the murder see Plutarch's *Alexander*, ch. 51.</note>, who stabbed Clitus, his dearest and most loyal friend, at a banquet; after Alexander understood what he had done, he wished to die, and assuredly he ought to have died.

Drunkenness kindles and discloses every kind of vice, and removes the sense of shame that veils our evil undertakings <note>This is the firm conviction of Seneca, himself a most temperate man.</note>. For more men abstain from forbidden actions because they are ashamed of sinning than because their inclinations are good. When the strength of wine has become too great and has gained control over the mind, every lurking evil comes forth from its hiding-place. Drunkenness does not create vice, it merely brings it into view; at such times the lustful man does not wait even for the privacy of a bedroom, but without postponement gives free play to the demands of his passions; at such times the unchaste man proclaims and publishes his malady; at such times your cross-grained fellow does not restrain his tongue or his hand. The haughty man increases his arrogance, the ruthless man his cruelty, the slanderer his spitefulness. Every vice is given free play and comes to the front. Besides, we forget who we are, we utter words that are halting and poorly enunciated, the glance is unsteady, the step falters, the head is dizzy, the very ceiling moves about as if a cyclone were whirling the whole house, and the stomach suffers torture when the wine generates gas and causes our very bowels to swell.

# Notes on Arab Music and Musical Instruments.

By Henry George Farmer.

1.

### SCIENCE OF ARAB MUSIC.

Since the downfall of Arab government and civilization in Spain, the Arabs (at least those of Mauretania) seem to have lost the scientific understanding of their music.* Shaw, in his "Travels in Barbary" (1757), says the Arabs and Moors do not write down their compositions and have no formal science of music, everything being learned by ear. Yet, he adds, "the greatest uniformity and exactness is always preserved throughout their performances."

---

* In Persia, however, in the eighteenth century, a traveler speaking of native musicians said, "they learn by rule and play by note."—Pinkerton's "Collection of Voyages," etc.

<summary>This page introduces the scholarly notes by Henry George Farmer, noting that while some Arab populations lost the formal written science of music, historical accounts suggest they maintained high performance standards through oral tradition.</summary>
<keywords>Arab music, Henry George Farmer, Mauretania, oral tradition, performance practice</keywords>
pages.192:
Niebuhr ("Travels in Arabia," 1790) says they "use no notes but sing by ear." Addison ("West Barbary," 1671) says he was told that *formerly* every mosque had a layman who "understood the cadences of the Alcoran" <note>original: Al-Qur'an/Quran</note> and could chant it in its original meter. Jones ("Lyric Airs," 1804) says that the Turks are equally ignorant of the use of written notes, yet they have a practical theory for all that, and "there is no school of music in the West of Europe, where it (music) is more discussed" than in Turkey. "The lack of notes . . . does not prevent them from composing and executing concertos of great length." Lane ("Modern Egyptians") says the Arabs of Egypt have very few books on music, and these are not understood by their modern musicians.

---

2.

SIMILARITY TO CATHOLIC CHANT.

"We cannot fail . . . to be struck with the remarkable similarity which the melodies of the Koran bear to the responses and chants of the Catholic liturgy." (Naumann, "History of Music.") A traveler in Algeria (Lumsden, "Trip to Algerine Territory," 1847) refers to visiting a mosque and hearing the Imam <note>original: Imaun</note> "chanting portions of the Koran in a manner which reminded me forcibly of many parts of the Catholic mass." Addison ("West Barbary," 1671) speaks of the mosque music in Morocco as "a delightful piece of devotion."

<summary>The author collects historical observations on the lack of written musical notation in Arab cultures and notes the stylistic parallels between Islamic liturgical chanting and Catholic church music.</summary>
<keywords>notation, oral tradition, Koran, Catholic liturgy, liturgical chant, Islam</keywords>
pages.193:
### 3.

*THE TROUBADOURS.*

"The Provençal singers (the troubadours) resembled the Arabian, not only in sentiments and character, but also in the very forms of their minstrelsy. As the Arabians had their dual verses, so had the Provençals their *Coblas*, or ‘couplets.’ . . As the duality of the verse had led to those amicable ‘Contentions,’ or poetic duels, of which we have spoken among the Arabian singers, so had the Provençals their *Tensos*. . . No less the manner of using the rhymes. For as the Arabians had their *Casidas* or long poems all on one rhyme, and their short bespangled and dainty *Maouchahs* or ‘embroideries,’ so also had the Provençals . . . Even the names they gave their songs . . . are but Arabian names translated." (Rowbotham, "History of Music.")

<summary>This section highlights the strong structural and thematic influence of Arabian poetry and musical traditions on the European troubadour movement.</summary>
<keywords>troubadours, Provençal, Arabian influence, poetic forms, musical history</keywords>
pages.194:
### 4.
### ARAB INFLUENCE IN SPAIN.

"There is a striking degree of similarity between many of the airs which I have heard in Egypt and some of the popular melodies of Spain." (Lane, "Modern Egyptians.") "Not only do we meet with certain terms and expressions in the popular songs of Spain," says Engel in his "Study of National Music," "which forcibly remind us of Arabic music, but also several Spanish instruments are of Arabic origin." 

Strange to say, Engel failed to mention the dances of Spain, which bear a wholesale imprint from the Arab: the *Sarabande*, *Villarro*, *Pabana*, *Chaconne*, *Villota*, *Maya*, *Giga*, *Gallarda*, etc. Engel points out that whilst there is little trace of Arab music in the Catholic church music in Spain, there is considerable influence to be seen in the music of the Jewish synagogue. This latter is also testified by De Sola in his "Ancient Melodies of the Spanish and Portuguese Jews" (1857).

<summary>The text explores the lasting impact of Arab musical culture on Spanish popular music, dance, and Jewish synagogue liturgy, citing various scholars and common musical forms.</summary>
<keywords>Spanish music, Arab influence, musical instruments, folk dance, synagogue music</keywords>

Again, the idea seems to be repeated. It may be that the author is emphasizing this point. There is, however, a nice distinction drawn by the author. He seems to differentiate between good planets (*Shubhagrahas*) and planets which are said to be powerful or *yoga karakas* (producers of fortune). The meaning of the latter expression seems to be that those planets which are not inherently good in nature, but become powerful by association or otherwise, are called *yoga karakas*. *Guru* (Jupiter), *Sukra* (Venus), *Poornachundra* (the Full Moon), and well-associated *Buda* (Mercury) are called *Shubhagrahams*. But when they are debilitated, badly associated, or occupying evil houses, they produce evil and may be called evil planets. 

There is also the general term "evil" applicable to *Kuja* (Mars), *Ravi* (the Sun), *Sani* (Saturn), badly associated *Buda*, and *Kshinachundra* (the Waning Moon) along with *Ravi* and *Kethu*. These also may produce good or bad results depending on whether they own good or evil houses, combine with good or evil planets, and whether they are in states of exaltation or debilitation. Therefore, *Shubhagraham* are different from *Yogakarakagrahams*.

The distinction deserves to be specially remembered, as the *Phalam* (results) to be predicted depends largely upon these considerations. *Sani*, for instance, can own the 9th and 10th houses and thus become very powerful; if he is also exalted and well-associated, he will produce splendid results. If *Guru* owns the 8th and 11th houses, he becomes evil and produces bad results. ### Stanza XXXVIII.

The lord of the Period who has jurisdiction to inflict death does not do so in the sub-periods of favorable planets who are in conjunction with him. He causes death in the sub-periods of malefic planets who are not in conjunction with him.

## NOTES.

There are two combinations contemplated here, and they must be specially borne in mind. First, we have to determine who is the most painful planet capable of inflicting death, and then, if his general Period is long, we must determine in whose *Bhookti* (sub-period) death is caused. Life is the most important question for any person; therefore, his longevity must first be considered and determined. Then, the good and bad results in his life have to be predicted. Prospects in life have no value unless we know the length of our existence. 

The author says that in the *Dasa* (Period) of the *Maraka* (death-inflicting) planet, the *Bhookti* of a favorable planet who is in conjunction with him does not produce death, but the *Bhookti* of an evil planet who is not in conjunction with the *Dasanatha* (lord of the period) will produce certain death. The question may be raised: does the *Bhookti* of an evil planet who is in conjunction with the *Maraka Dasanatha* produce death or favorable results? From a careful perusal of the above verses, it appears clear that the periods and sub-periods of even the worst planets, when they are in conjunction with each other, do not inflict such evil as the periods and sub-periods of planets who are not in conjunction. Therefore, there is some good in the very act of conjunction or combination, which should not be lost sight of by the student of astrology. I have already stated the results of the sub-periods of favorable planets when they are not in conjunction with the planets whose periods govern the native for the time being.

---

->During each other's periods, in their own sub-periods, Saturn and Venus (Sani and Sukra) give good or bad results inversely, specifically. || 39 ||

Venus and Saturn (*Sukra* and *Sani*) give good or bad results in their respective periods and sub-periods inversely.

## NOTES.

These two planets seem to have a peculiar affinity and produce good or evil in an intense form inversely in their *Dasas* and *Bhookties*. If *Sani* is good and his *Dasa* governs a man, the *Bhookti* of *Sukra*, when he is well-disposed, produces excellent results. The author says that even if there are other *Bhookties* equally favorable like that of *Sukra*, they will not produce such splendid results as *Sukra* can. Thus, in the *Dasas* of *Sani* and *Sukra* and their intervening sub-periods, the greatest fortune may be expected if they are favorably disposed. Whatever may be the occupation of the planets or their association, *Sani* and *Sukra* will produce the most intense effects during their periods and sub-periods, which no other two planets could produce. 

The author has taken us far into the fields of astrology and has shown by brief but very expressive stanzas the results of many principles guiding the life of the creature. He has shown the relative merits of the planets, the periods of successes and failures, the principles upon which death may be safely predicted, and a general survey of other items which give strength or weakness to the planets. These are all general results; now, in the 40th stanza and subsequent ones, he is going to summarize the results that a person born in each of the 12 Zodiacal signs is likely to enjoy. This will help the student see at once which planets are favorable and which are not when judging the different *lagnas* (rising signs) in which people are born.

### STANZA XLI Mesha—Aries.

A person born in ***Mesha Lagna*** (Aries rising at the time of birth) has ***Sani*** (Saturn), ***Buda*** (Mercury), and ***Sukra*** (Venus) ill-disposed towards him. ***Guru*** (Jupiter) and ***Ravi*** (the Sun) are auspicious. ### NOTES.

Here the author has drawn the readers' attention to three most important points to be consulted in estimating the good and evil results likely to happen to a person born while <term>Mesha</term> is rising. <term>Sukra</term> is the lord of the 2nd and 7th houses, <term>Buda</term> is the lord of the 3rd and 6th houses, and <term>Sani</term> is the lord of the 10th and 11th houses.

It has already been pointed out that the lords of the 3rd, 6th, 8th, 11th, and 12th houses are bad. Therefore, *Buda* (Mercury), being the lord of the 3rd and 6th houses for a person born in *Mesha*, becomes evil. *Sukra* (Venus) owns the 2nd and 7th houses. Good planets owning quadrants (the 1st, 4th, 7th, 10th houses) are evil if they own the 7th, and the 7th is a quadrant. *Sani* (Saturn) owns the 10th and 11th houses; the 11th is bad, but the 10th house (a quadrant) owned by an evil planet like *Sani* is good. *Buda* is perfectly bad, but in the cases of *Sukra* and *Sani*, out of the two houses each owns, one is evil and the other good. However, *Buda*, *Sani*, and *Sukra* are not friends of the lord of *Mesha*, which is *Kuja* (Mars). This point is fully explained in the *Astrological Self Instructor* and *Primer* published by me in English. 

*Guru* (Jupiter) and *Ravi* (the Sun) are declared to be good. *Ravi* owns the 5th house from *Mesha*, and *Guru* owns the 9th and 12th houses. It has been shown that the lords of the trines (angular points of an equilateral triangle) are productive of good results. *Ravi* owns only one house and is perfectly good; *Guru* owns the 9th as well as the 12th, of which the 9th is good and the 12th is bad. *Guru*, *Ravi*, and *Kuja* (lord of *Mesha*) are friends, and thus, even though *Guru* owns an evil house, he will, in the main, produce good. The third point the author refers to is the non-production of *Raja Yoga* by the combination of the lords of the 9th and 10th houses. This sounds contrary to his own principles enunciated in Stanza 16, where he says that *Rajayogam* is produced by the combination of the lords of quadrants and trines. But in this case, these two planets not only own the 9th and 10th houses, but they are also lords of the 12th and 11th houses, whose combination acts against the production of *Rajayogam* (see p. 24). Therefore, the author says clearly that for a person born in *Mesha*, the simple conjunction of *Sani* and *Guru* is not sufficient to produce political success. We must look to other combinations. The line of argument is simple, and the reader is requested to note its force when consulting horoscopes.

### **STANZA XLII.**

But on the other hand, *Guru* (Jupiter) when combined with *Sani* (Saturn) not only does not give good, but will actively produce evil. *Sukra* (Venus) does not himself kill the native, although he possesses death-inflicting powers.

### **NOTES.**

It was pointed out (see Stanza 41) that *Guru*, being the lord of the 9th and 12th houses, has both good and bad combined within himself.

In the combination of *Sani* and *Guru*, the author asked us not to expect any good results, and he here tells us that there will be evil in their combination, especially on the part of *Guru*. This requires a clear explanation. Let us take an example. We know that a planet has good and evil influences due to various causes explained in astrological works. If a planet is capable of giving one rupee worth of good and also one rupee worth of evil, the result will be that the planetary influence is neutral—good cancelling out the evil. However, astrological writers assure us that the result is not neutral but bad. They are of the opinion that when good and evil influences of a planet are equal, we must predict evil, albeit in a milder form. Remembering this principle, we shall see why *Guru* is bad in combination with *Sani*. *Guru* owns the 9th and 12th houses, of which the 12th for *Guru* and the 11th for *Sani* are evil houses. Here, the evil is equal to the good these two planets have, as one of the two houses each planet owns is good while the other is bad. We can understand that the combination is bad, but why should *Guru* be particularly declared bad in producing evil in the combination, while *Sani* also contributes to bring about the combined evil result? *Guru* is an auspicious planet by nature, and evil influences seem to affect him more; *Sani* is an evil planet, and good influences seem to make him better. *Guru* owns one good and one bad house, which neutralize each other, but he has an evil association—namely, being in conjunction with *Sani*. Therefore, there is something more than good and bad counteracting each other, and *Guru* is declared to produce evil because of his evil combination. *Sani* has a better prospect; his owning good and evil houses counterbalances the two results, but he is in conjunction with *Guru*, a declared good planet, and his position is improved.

<summary>This page analyzes the complex interaction between Jupiter (Guru) and Saturn (Sani) for an Aries birth, explaining why the combination is considered inherently harmful.</summary>
