### STANZA XLIII.

Evil planets like *Sani* &c. will cause death to the person; try and find out the results—good and bad—which might happen to the person born in *Mesha* carefully and with reference to the principles of astrology.

### NOTES.

In the previous stanza, we pointed out that when *Guru* and *Sani* combine, *Guru* will inflict evil. Now we have to determine who will kill the <term>native</term>. The author says "evil planets like *Sani* &c." He takes *Sani* first and includes *Buda* (Mercury) and occasionally *Chundra* (the Moon). *Buda* is bad as he owns the 3rd and 6th houses. But *Chundra* is the lord of the 4th. If he is full, he will be classified as good; his owning one of the <term>quadrants</term> is bad, and he may, by evil combinations, produce death. But if he is weak, then his owning the quadrant is auspicious, and he will do good. These are the planets who determine the death of a person born while the sign <term>Mesha</term> (<term>Aries</term>) is rising. I have given notes at considerable length, but the fuller the explanations offered, even at the risk of repetition, the better it is for beginners who read these...

### 5.

### HISTORY OF ARAB MUSIC.

The early Arab musicians were possibly of the wandering minstrel type, like the "Calenders" <note>members of a dervish order</note> we read of in the "Arabian Nights." Such at first was Mabed, one of the most famous of the early Arab musicians. Similar to the Western minstrels, they were as much poets as musicians. "This," says Lane, <note>Edward William Lane, British Orientalist</note> "was sufficient to satisfy a people passionately fond of poetry, whose first object is to understand the meaning of the verses which are chanted." Indeed, the song in these days, says Christianowitch, <note>Alexander Christianowitch, music historian</note> was a sort of <term>recitative</term> <note>a style of delivery in which a singer adopts the rhythms of ordinary speech</note> with a light refrain. Thus the music of the Arabs, bound in subjection to the words, would necessarily make slow progress. Then again, it is clear from the teachings of Mahomet that music was <term>tabu</term> <note>forbidden</note>, at any rate as regards

Salvador was under the impression that Greek influence upon Arab music dates from so early a period as this. But there can be little doubt that at this period the Arabs were more persuaded by the Persians† than the Greeks, for since the Arab conquest of Persia in the seventh century, there had been a gradual absorption of the musical theory and practice of the conquered race.

However, that be as it may. We do know that in the eighth century music had become a necessary adjunct to Arab life. Some of the early caliphs were accomplished musicians. Such was Yazid (680), a composer, and Walid I (705), a performer on the lute. The caliphs Abul Abbas (749) and Mansur (754) are spoken of as patrons of music, whilst Mahdi (775) was not only a musician himself, but his children were also accomplished in the art.

Bagdad had become the capital of the great Arab Empire which stretched from the borders of Tartary in the East to Spain in the West, and here were gathered the finest musical talent in all Arabia. It was the golden age of Arab music. Here was held the refined and dazzling court of the son of Mahdi, the famous Caliph Haroun El Raschid (786), a name immortal in Eastern song and story, and the unlimited patronage of art and music at his court is still on the lips of the Arab minstrel today. Haroun never built a mosque but what he attached a school to it. Schools and colleges, including those specially set apart for music, sprang up throughout the empire. Tudela, in his "Itinerary," says he found in Alexandria more than twenty schools for philosophy alone. Cairo, too, had its colleges, and in Fez and Morocco the most magnificent buildings were assigned for educational purposes, whilst Arab Spain vied with the mother country in its zeal for art, science and education.

In the fourteenth century the Arabian-Persian arts and sciences were put forth with considerable vigor, and music especially came under quite a revival. The leader of this revival was an Arab of Bagdad named Saffieddin Abd El Monim, whose principal work, the "Schereffije," was written in the Arab tongue. Not that there had been any dearth of musical theorists with the Arabs since those we mentioned. Following Chalil and El Kindi, in the eighth and ninth centuries, came the Hispano-Arab writers, chief of whom was Al Farabi. Then we have Abd El Moumini (eleventh century), Mohammed Ben Ahmed El Haddah (twelfth century), and Mohammed Schirasi (thirteenth century). But the fourteenth century was, with the Eastern Arabs and Persians, most propitious for the cultivation of the arts and sciences, as they were now under the beneficial rule of the Mongols. And from this period has come down to us several works on the science of Arabian-Persian music, and three especially; those of Saffieddin, Mohammed Ben Abu Bekr Ben Scerouni and Abd El Khadir. Just as those who are heavy with drink cannot hold their food when they have had too much, so they cannot keep a secret either. They pour out their own secrets and those of others alike." 

<margin>17</margin> But although this often happens, it is also common for us to deliberate on serious matters with those we know to enjoy drinking. Therefore, the argument often used as a defense—that a person accustomed to getting drunk cannot be trusted to keep a secret—is false.

So let us abolish all such harangues as this: “No man in the bonds of drunkenness has power over his soul. As the very vats are burst by new wine, and as the dregs at the bottom are raised to the surface by the strength of the fermentation; so, when the wine effervesces, whatever lies hidden below is brought up and made visible. As a man overcome by liquor cannot keep down his food when he has over-indulged in wine, so he cannot keep back a secret either. He pours forth impartially both his own secrets and those of other persons.” This, of course, is what commonly happens, but so does this—that we take counsel on serious subjects with those whom we know to be in the habit of drinking freely. Therefore this proposition, which is laid down in the guise of a defense of <term>Zeno’s syllogism</term>, is false—that secrets are not entrusted to the habitual drunkard.

How much better it is to arraign drunkenness frankly and to expose its vices! For even the middling good man avoids them, not to mention the perfect <term>sage</term>, who is satisfied with slaking his thirst; the sage, even if now and then he is led on by good cheer which, for a friend’s sake, is carried somewhat too far, yet always stops short of drunkenness. Drunkenness inflames and uncovers every vice; it removes the sense of shame that acts as a barrier to evil intentions. For more people abstain from sinning out of a fear of shame than from a genuine good will. When an excess of wine has taken possession of the mind, whatever evil lay hidden emerges. Drunkenness does not create vices, it brings them forward. At such a time, the lustful man does not even wait for the bedroom, but allows his desires to have whatever they demand without delay; then the unchaste man confesses and publishes his disease; then the insolent man does not restrain his tongue or his hand. Arrogance grows in the haughty, cruelty in the savage, and malice in the spiteful. Every vice is loosened and brought to light. Add to this the loss of self-awareness: the hesitant and unclear words, the wandering eyes, the faltering step, the dizziness of the head, and the buildings themselves seeming to move as if some whirlwind were spinning the whole house around, and the stomach's torment as the wine effervesces and distends the very bowels. Drunkenness kindles and discloses every kind of vice, and removes the sense of shame that veils our evil undertakings. For more men abstain from forbidden actions because they are ashamed of sinning than because their inclinations are good. When the strength of wine has become too great and has gained control over the mind, every lurking evil comes forth from its hiding-place. Drunkenness does not create vice, it merely brings it into view; at such times the lustful man does not wait even for the privacy of a bedroom, but without postponement gives free play to the demands of his passions; at such times the unchaste man proclaims and publishes his malady; at such times your cross-grained fellow does not restrain his tongue or his hand. The haughty man increases his arrogance, the ruthless man his cruelty, the slanderer his spitefulness. Every vice is given free play and comes to the front. Besides, we forget who we are, we utter words that are halting and poorly enunciated, the glance is unsteady, the step falters, the head is dizzy, the very ceiling moves about as if a cyclone were whirling the whole house, and the stomach suffers torture when the wine generates gas and causes our very bowels to swell.

Consider the disasters brought about by public drunkenness; it has betrayed the most keen and warlike nations to their enemies; it has opened gates that had been defended by years of persistent warfare; it has driven those who were most stubborn and refused the yoke into the power of others; it has conquered in battle those who were otherwise invincible. What glory is there in drinking a great deal? When you have claimed the prize, and the others have collapsed in sleep or are vomiting, refusing your toasts; when you are the last survivor of the party; when you have conquered everyone with your magnificent capacity—you have still been defeated by the wine barrel. pages.195:
<meta>This page begins a new section of the text, transitioning from a previous discussion of Moroccan song rhythms into an overview of early Arab musical history.</meta>

### 5.

HISTORY OF ARAB MUSIC.

The early Arab musicians were possibly wandering minstrels, similar to the "Calenders" <note>A type of wandering dervish or mendicant monk often featured in the "Arabian Nights."</note> we read about in the *Arabian Nights*. Such at first was Mabed, one of the most famous of the early Arab musicians. Much like Western minstrels, they were as much poets as they were musicians. "This," says Lane <note>Edward William Lane, a noted 19th-century British Orientalist.</note>, "was sufficient to satisfy a people passionately fond of poetry, whose first object is to understand the meaning of the verses which are chanted." Indeed, the song in those days, says Christianowitch <note>Alexander Christianowitch, author of *Esquisse historique sur la musique arabe*.</note>, was a type of recitative <note>A style of delivery in which a singer adopts the rhythms of ordinary speech.</note> with a light refrain. Thus, the music of the Arabs, bound in subjection to the words, would necessarily make slow progress. Then again, it is clear from the teachings of Mahomet that music was *tabu*—or forbidden—at any rate as regards
pages.196:
the practice of the faith. The prophet had said: "Music and singing cause hypocrisy to grow in the heart, as water makes corn grow." "Your prayers, if music form a part of them, will end but in piping and hand-clapping."

Although we read of the Caliph Omar (634), who was said to be a composer, and the Caliph Othman (644), the patron of the musician Ibn Soureidj, music continued under the ban of the prophet until the reign of Caliph Ali (656), when, as Salvador <note>Francisco Salvador-Daniel, the author of this work.</note> points out, music, together with art and literature in general, began to be freely cultivated. Under the reign of the Caliph Moawiya (661), a large portion of Greece had been annexed by the Arab armies, and the Caliph, who was surrounded at his court by poets, writers, and scientists, now commanded translations of the works of the Greeks, including those on music. How much they profited by these works, says Lane (*Modern Egyptians*), is well known. "It appears," continues Lane, "that they formed the system of music which has prevailed among them for many centuries partly from Greek, and partly from Persian and Indian treatises. From the Greek language are derived the most general
pages.197:
Arabic term for music, namely, 'mooseeka,' <note>Original: "mooseeka."</note> and the names of some of the Arab musical instruments; but most of the technical terms . . . are borrowed from the Persian and Indian languages."

Salvador was under the impression that Greek influence upon Arab music dates from as early as this period. But there can be little doubt that at this time the Arabs were more influenced by the Persians <note>Ibn Khaldoun, *Asiatic Journal*, Volume XX.</note> than the Greeks, for since the Arab conquest of Persia in the seventh century, there had been a gradual absorption of the musical theory and practice of the conquered race.

However, that may be. We do know that in the eighth century music had become a necessary adjunct to Arab life. Some of the early caliphs were accomplished musicians. Such was Yazid (680), a composer, and Walid I (705), a performer on the lute. The caliphs Abul Abbas (749) and Mansur (754) are spoken of as patrons of music, while Mahdi (775) was not only a musician himself, but his children were also accomplished in the art. <note>Hammer-Purgstall, on the other hand, says the word "mooseeka" is derived from the Persian.</note>
pages.198:
Bagdad had become the capital of the great Arab Empire, which stretched from the borders of Tartary in the East to Spain in the West, and here the finest musical talent in all Arabia was gathered. It was the golden age of Arab music. Here was the refined and dazzling court of the son of Mahdi, the famous Caliph Haroun El Raschid (786), a name immortal in Eastern song and story. The unlimited patronage of art and music at his court is still on the lips of the Arab minstrel today. Haroun never built a mosque without attaching a school to it. Schools and colleges, including those specifically set apart for music, sprang up throughout the empire. Tudela, in his *Itinerary*, says he found in Alexandria more than twenty schools for philosophy alone. Cairo, too, had its colleges, and in Fez and Morocco, the most magnificent buildings were assigned for educational purposes, while Arab Spain vied with the mother country in its zeal for art, science, and education.

## NOTES.

Two combinations are contemplated here, which must be kept in mind. First, we must determine which planet is the most likely to inflict death (*Maraka*), and then, if his major period (*Dasa*) is long, we must determine in whose sub-period (*Bhookti*) death is caused. Life is the most important concern, so longevity must be considered and determined first. Only then can other results be predicted. Prospects in life have no value if we do not know the span of our existence. The author states that during the *Dasa* of the *Maraka* planet, the *Bhookti* of a favorable planet in conjunction with him does not produce death, but the *Bhookti* of an evil planet not in conjunction with the *Dasanatha* will cause certain death. The question may arise: does the *Bhookti* of an evil planet in conjunction with the *Maraka Dasanatha* produce death or favorable results? It appears that the periods and sub-periods of even the worst planets, when in conjunction with each other, do not inflict as much evil as when they are not in conjunction. Therefore, there is a protective element in the act of combination that students of astrology should not overlook. I have already discussed the results of the sub-periods of favorable planets when they are not in conjunction with the planet governing the current period.

### STANZA XLI Mesha—Aries.

A person born in ***Mesha Lagna*** (Aries rising at birth) finds ***Sani*** (Saturn), ***Buda*** (Mercury), and ***Sukra*** (Venus) ill-disposed. ***Guru*** (Jupiter) and ***Ravi*** (the Sun) are auspicious. The simple combination of ***Guru*** and ***Sani*** produces no beneficial results.

### NOTES.

The author draws attention to three important points for someone born when <term>Mesha</term> is rising. <term>Sukra</term> (Venus) rules the 2nd and 7th houses, <term>Buda</term> (Mercury) rules the 3rd and 6th, and <term>Sani</term> (Saturn) rules the 10th and 11th. It has been established that the lords of the 3rd, 6th, 8th, 11th, and 12th houses are bad. Therefore, Buda, ruling the 3rd and 6th for an Aries native, is evil. Sukra owns the 2nd and 7th; good planets owning quadrants are often considered evil, and the 7th is a quadrant. Sani owns the 10th and 11th—the 11th is bad, but the 10th (a quadrant) owned by an evil planet like Sani is good.

But, on the other hand, *Guru* (Jupiter), when combined with *Sani* (Saturn), not only fails to give good results but will actively produce evil. *Sukra* (Venus) does not himself kill the <term>native</term>, even though he possesses death-inflicting powers.

### **NOTES.**

It was noted (Stanza 41) that *Guru*, being the lord of the 9th and 12th houses, possesses both good and bad qualities.

In the combination of *Sani* and *Guru*, the author warns us not to expect good results, stating instead that their combination will be evil, particularly on the part of *Guru*. Let us take an example. A planet has good and evil influences. If a planet is capable of producing one rupee's worth of good and one rupee's worth of evil, the influence is neutral—the good cancels the evil. However, astrological writers suggest that the result is not neutral but actually bad. They hold that when good and evil influences are equal, we must predict evil, albeit in a milder form. This explains why *Guru* is bad in combination with *Sani*. *Guru* owns the 9th and 12th houses; the 12th for *Guru* and the 11th for *Sani* are evil houses. Here, the evil is equal to the good these planets possess. While the combination is bad, why is *Guru* specifically declared to be the source of evil? *Guru* is an auspicious planet by nature, and evil influences affect him more deeply; *Sani* is an evil planet, and good influences improve him. *Guru* has an evil association—being in conjunction with *Sani*. Because of this, *Guru* is declared to produce evil. *Sani*, however, has a better prospect; his position is improved by being in conjunction with *Guru*, a naturally good planet.

We may conjecture that the Yule straw, which Swedish peasants use for various superstitious purposes, comes, at least in part, from the same sheaf used to make the Yule Boar. This Yule straw is long rye-straw, a portion of which is always set aside for this season. It is strewn over the floor at Christmas, and the peasants attribute many virtues to it. For example, they believe that scattering some of it on the ground will make a barren field productive. Furthermore, at Christmas, the peasant sits on a log, and his eldest son or daughter (or the mother, if the children are too young) places a wisp of the Yule straw on his knee. He draws out single straws and throws them one by one up to the ceiling; the number that lodge in the rafters represents the number of sheaves of rye he will have to thresh at harvest.

The reader has likely noted the complete parallel between the human-like (anthropomorphic) and animal-like (theriomorphic) conceptions of the corn-spirit. This parallel may be briefly summarized here: When the corn waves in the wind, it is said that the "Corn-mother" or the "Corn-wolf" is passing through the stalks. Children are warned against straying into cornfields because the "Corn-mother" or "Corn-wolf" is there. In the last corn cut or the last sheaf threshed, either the Corn-mother or the Corn-wolf is thought to be present. The last sheaf is itself called the "Corn-mother" or the "Corn-wolf" and is shaped to resemble a woman or a wolf. The person who cuts, binds, or threshes the last sheaf is referred to as the "Old Woman" or the "Wolf," depending on the name given to the sheaf. Just as in some places a sheaf made in human form—called the "Maiden" or "Mother of the Maize"—is kept from one harvest to the next to ensure the corn-spirit's blessing, so in other places the "Harvest-cock" or the flesh of a goat is kept for a similar purpose. As the grain from the "Corn-mother" is mixed with seed-corn in the spring to make the crop abundant, so are the feathers of the cock, or in Sweden the Yule Boar, kept until spring to be mixed with the seed-corn for the same purpose. Other animal forms assumed by the corn-spirit include the stag, roe, sheep, bear, ass, fox, mouse, stork, swan, and kite.<note>1 *Die Korndämonen* (The Corn Demons), p. 1.</note> If one asks why the corn-spirit is thought to appear as so many different animals, we may reply that for primitive man, the simple appearance of an animal or bird among the crops is sufficient to suggest a mysterious connection between that creature and the grain. When we remember that in older times, before fields were fenced, all kinds of animals were free to roam through them, it is no wonder that the corn-spirit was identified even with large animals like horses and cows, which today would rarely be found straying in the corn. This explanation applies particularly to cases where the animal embodiment is believed to lurk in the last standing patch of grain. At harvest, various wild animals—hares, rabbits, partridges, etc.—are commonly driven by the progress of the reapers into the last patch of standing corn, only to flee when the patch is cut. Reapers often stand around this last patch armed with sticks or guns to kill the animals as they dart out of their final refuge.

Now, to primitive man, for whom magical shape-shifting is perfectly credible, it seems natural that the spirit of the corn, driven from his home, should escape in the form of the animal seen rushing out of the last patch of corn as it falls under the reaper’s scythe. Thus, identifying the corn-spirit with an animal is analogous to identifying him with a passing stranger. Just as the sudden appearance of a stranger near a harvest-field or threshing-floor is, to the primitive mind, evidence that he is the spirit of the corn escaping from the cut grain, so the sudden appearance of an animal from the cut corn is enough to identify it with the corn-spirit fleeing his ruined home. These two identifications are so similar that they can hardly be separated. Anyone seeking a different principle to explain the latter must also account for the former.

Regardless of the explanation, the fact remains that in peasant folklore, the corn-spirit is very commonly represented in animal form. Might this fact explain the relationship certain animals held with the ancient deities of vegetation: Dionysus, Demeter, Adonis, Attis, and Osiris?

To begin with Dionysus: we have seen he was represented sometimes as a goat and sometimes as a bull. As a goat, he can hardly be separated from the minor divinities—the Pans, Satyrs, and Silenuses—who are all closely associated with him and are represented in goat form. Pan was regularly portrayed in art with the face and legs of a goat.<note>1 Herodotus, ii. 46.</note>

Some *Ljeschie* are spirits of the corn as well as the wood; before harvest, they are as tall as the corn-stalks, but after the harvest, they shrink to the height of the stubble.<note>1 B. Similarly, the Fauns, though wood-spirits, were believed to foster the growth of crops.<note>2 Servius on Virgil, *Georg.* i. 10.</note> As Mannhardt argues, the Pans, Satyrs, and Fauns belong to a widely diffused class of wood-spirits conceived in goat-form.<note>3 Above, p. 12 sqq.; A. W. F. ch. iii.</note> The tendency of goats to stray into woods and nibble tree bark—which they are known to destroy—is an obvious reason why wood-spirits are often supposed to take the form of goats. The inconsistency of a vegetation god eating the very vegetation he represents is not one that troubles the primitive mind. Such inconsistencies arise only when the deity ceases to be thought of as living *within* the vegetation and begins to be regarded as its owner or lord, for the idea of ownership naturally leads to the idea of subsistence. We have seen that the corn-spirit, originally considered immanent in the corn, later comes to be seen as its owner, who is reduced to poverty if deprived of it.<note>4 Above, vol. i. p. 379 sq.</note>

pages.47:
# III THE BULL-DIONYSUS

The representation of wood-spirits in goat-form appears to be both widespread and, to the primitive mind, natural. Therefore, when we find that Dionysus—a tree-god—is sometimes represented in goat form,<note>1 Above, vol. i. p. 326 sq.</note> we can hardly avoid the conclusion that this representation is simply part of his character as a tree-god, rather than a fusion of two independent cults—one a tree-god cult and the other a goat-god cult. If such a fusion occurred for Dionysus, it must also have occurred for the Pans and Satyrs of Greece, the Fauns of Italy, and the *Ljeschie* of Russia. That such a fusion of disconnected cults occurred once is possible; that it occurred twice independently is improbable; and that it occurred three times is practically incredible.

Dionysus was also represented, as we have seen,<note>2 Above, vol. i. p. 325 sq.</note> in the form of a bull. We are led to expect that his bull form is just another expression of his character as a vegetation deity, especially since the bull is a common embodiment of the corn-spirit in Northern Europe,<note>3 Above, p. 19 sqq.</note> and his association with Demeter and Proserpine at Eleusis shows he had strong agricultural affinities. The only other possible explanation is that the bull-conception was originally distinct and was merged due to something like the union of two tribes (a view suggested by Mr. Andrew Lang).

<summary>Frazer concludes that the various animal forms of Dionysus are expressions of his nature as a vegetation deity, rather than the result of the fusion of unrelated cults.</summary>
<keywords>Dionysus, tree-god, goat, bull, corn-spirit, Demeter, Proserpine, Andrew Lang, vegetation deity</keywords>

### 5.

HISTORY OF ARAB MUSIC.

The early Arab musicians were possibly of the wandering minstrel type, like the "Calenders" <note>A group of wandering dervishes mentioned in the *Arabian Nights*.</note> we read of in the "Arabian Nights." Such at first was Mabed, one of the most famous of the early Arab musicians. Similar to the Western minstrels, they were as much poets as musicians. "This," says Lane, <note>Edward William Lane, *Arabians of the Middle Ages*.</note> "was sufficient to satisfy a people passionately fond of poetry, whose first object is to understand the meaning of the verses which are chanted." Indeed, the song in these days, says Christianowitch, <note>Alexandre Christianowitch, *Esquisse Historique de la Musique Arabe*.</note> "was a sort of recitative with a light refrain." Thus the music of the Arabs, bound in subjection to the words, would necessarily make slow progress. It was the golden age of Arab music. In the fourteenth century the Arabian-Persian arts and sciences were put forth with considerable vigour, and music especially came under quite a revival. Our *moral sense* perceives this excellence, and we call the laws of the DEITY "good" when we imagine they are contrived to promote the public good in the most effectual and impartial manner. The DEITY is called "good," in a moral sense, when we apprehend that his whole providence tends to the universal happiness of his creatures; from which we conclude his benevolence and delight in their happiness.

Some tell us:

But they must excuse us from agreeing to this until they make us understand the meaning of this metaphor, "essential rectitude," and until we discern whether anything more is meant by it than a perfectly wise, uniform, and impartial benevolence.

<margin>Difference between Constraint and Obligation.</margin>
Hence we may see the difference between *constraint* and *obligation*. There is, indeed, no difference between *constraint* and the second sense of the word *obligation*—namely, a system that makes an action eligible from self-interest—if we only mean external interest, distinct from

The reader need scarcely be told that by *constraint* we do not understand an external force moving our limbs without our consent, for in that case we are not agents at all. Rather, we mean that constraint which arises from threatening and presenting some evil to make us act in a certain manner. And yet there seems to be a universally acknowledged difference between even this sort of constraint and *obligation*. We never say we are "obliged" to do an action we consider base, even if we are "constrained" to it. We never say that divine laws, through their sanctions, *constrain* us, but rather *oblige* us. Nor do we call obedience to the DEITY "constraint," unless by a metaphor, though many acknowledge they are influenced by the fear of punishment. And yet, suppose an almighty evil being should require treachery, cruelty, or ingratitude under grievous penalties; we would call this *constraint*. The difference is plainly this: When any sanctions cooperate with our *moral sense* in exciting us to actions we count morally good, we say we are *obliged*. But when sanctions of rewards or punishments oppose our *moral sense*, we say we are *bribed* or *constrained*. In the former case, we call the lawgiver "good" as designing the public happiness; in the latter, we call him "evil" or "unjust" for the supposed contrary intention.

<summary>Hutcheson distinguishes between "obligation" (which aligns with moral sense and benevolence) and "constraint" (which is forced upon us by external threats or contrary to moral sense).</summary>

But if all our ideas of moral good or evil were derived solely from opinions of private advantage or loss in actions, I see no possible difference that could be made in the meaning of these words.

VI. FROM this sense, too, we derive our *rights*.
<margin>Ideas of RIGHTS.</margin> Whenever it appears to us that a faculty of doing, demanding, or possessing anything—universally allowed in certain circumstances—would, on the whole, tend to the general good, we say that any person in such circumstances has a *right* to do, possess, or demand that thing. And according to whether this tendency to the public good is greater or less, the right itself is greater or less.

<margin>*Perfect Rights.*</margin>
The rights called *perfect* are of such necessity to the public good that the universal violation of them would make human life intolerable; they actually make those miserable whose rights are thus violated. On the contrary, to fulfill these rights in every instance tends to the public good, either directly or by promoting the innocent advantage of a part. Hence it plainly follows: "That to allow a violent defense or prosecution of such rights, before civil government is constituted, cannot in any particular case be more detrimental to the public than the violation of them with impunity."

<sig>T 3</sig>

And as to the general consequences, the universal use of force in a *state of nature*, in pursuit of *perfect rights*, seems exceedingly advantageous to the whole by making everyone dread any attempts against the *perfect rights* of others.

<margin>*Right of War, and Punishment.*</margin>
This is the moral effect that attends proper injury or a violation of the *perfect rights* of others: namely, a right to war and all violence necessary to force the injurious party to repair the damage and provide security against such offenses for the future. This is the sole foundation of the rights of punishing criminals and of the violent prosecution of our rights in a *state of nature*. These rights—originally belonging to the persons injured or their voluntary/invited assistants according to the judgment of impartial arbitrators in a *state of nature*—are, by the consent of the persons injured, transferred to the magistrate in a *civil state*, and thus form the true foundation of his right to punish. Instances of *perfect rights* are those to our lives; to the fruits of our labors; to demand the performance of contracts upon valuable considerations from men capable of performing them; to direct our own actions for public or innocent private good before we have submitted them to the direction of others; and many others of a like nature.

*Imperfect rights* are such that, if universally violated, would not necessarily make men miserable. These rights tend to the improvement and increase of *positive good* in any society but are not absolutely necessary to prevent *universal misery*. The violation of them only disappoints men of the happiness expected from the humanity or gratitude of others but does not deprive men of any good they already possessed. From this description, it appears that "a violent prosecution of such rights would generally occasion greater evil than the violation of them." Besides, allowing force in such cases would deprive men of the greatest pleasure in actions of kindness, humanity, and gratitude, which would cease to appear amiable when men could be constrained to perform them. Instances of *imperfect rights* are those which the poor have to the charity of the wealthy; which all men have to services of no trouble or expense to the performer; which benefactors have to returns of gratitude, and such like.

The violation of *imperfect rights* only argues a man to have such weak benevolence that he does not study to advance the positive good of others when it is even slightly opposite to his own. But the violation of *perfect rights*...

to escape them by his magic powers. First, he changed himself into the form of the youthful Zeus, then he transformed into an aged Chronos. His appearance shifted rapidly. He was a baby, then a youth, a lion, a horse, a horned snake, a tiger, and lastly, a bull. It was in the form of a bull that he finally died.

Hera, seeing that her plot was succeeding, enticed Zeus away from his great tower of vigilance so that his all-seeing eye might not behold the crime. After they had destroyed the body of Dionysius, the Titans sought a device to conceal their crime. As there was no way in which they could dispose of the body, they resolved to devour it so that no one might ever discover their evil deed. The Titans therefore dismembered the bull-formed body of Dionysius, first boiling the parts in water and then broiling them over a fire. High on Olympus, Zeus became aware of the odor of cooking flesh, and his great eye sought out the cause. Looking down, he beheld the Titans devouring the body of his son. He immediately dispatched Athena, or Minerva, who, swooping down from the heavens, caught up the heart of Dionysius before it had been consumed and brought it to the feet of Zeus. High Heaven then hurled his thunders at the giants; great bolts of lightning brought death to the Titanic conspirators. As the tempest of the wrath of Zeus at last subsided, only the charred bodies of the murderers remained.

It was from the ashes of the Titans that the race of man was formed, their bodies molded from the burned remains of the giants. With these ashes were also mingled the blood and body of Dionysius, so that all men contain within their fabric the substance of the Titans and the essence of the divine child. Zeus took the heart of Dionysius back to himself again, re-

storing the Dionysian principle to his own essence, to await the time when he could devise a way to send it forth again for the perfection of mankind.

A great time passed, and the scene changed from heaven to earth. Zeus, assuming the form of a bull <note>In many classical accounts, Zeus transformed into a white bull to carry Europa away.</note>, abducted Europa. Agenor, her father, dispatched his son Cadmus in search of the lost maiden. Agenor told Cadmus not to return without Europa on pain of death. As no mortal could outwit the celestial Zeus, Cadmus failed in his search and, fearing to return to his own country, consulted an oracle as to the proper course of his future action. The oracle bade the young man "be observant; and when he should see a cow, follow the animal, and wherever it stopped to rest, build a city and name it Thebes." Following the instructions exactly, Cadmus blessed the ground where the cow rested and prepared a libation <term>a drink offering poured out in honor of a deity</term> to his patron goddess, Minerva. It was on the site of the proposed city that he slew the great serpent sacred to the god Ares (Mars). After he had killed the monster, Cadmus, obeying the instructions of Minerva, his patron deity, sowed the teeth of the dragon in the earth, and there grew up immediately an army of soldiers. At first, these sons of Mars appeared as though they were about to attack Cadmus, but, obeying divine instruction, he hurled a rock among them, and they fell upon one another in civil strife. At the end of the battle, but five of the warriors remained alive, and these survivors of the army of the serpent's teeth united with Cadmus to build the sacred city of Thebes with its seven gates.

Cadmus is a mysterious person believed by some of the earlier mythologists to be identical with the Egyptian Hermes and by others with the patriarch Noah. His name is from the Phoenician *Cadm*, which means "East," and he may be in-

terpreted to represent not a person at all, but the Eastern Wisdom Teaching itself, which came out of Asia and established the Grecian civilization, represented by a city with seven gates.

According to the continuation of the myth, Cadmus married Harmonia, a maiden of great beauty and virtue; that is, wisdom is united to all that is harmonious, peaceful, and virtuous in the world. Five children resulted from this union, representing the five elements, the five senses, and the five rational powers of the soul. The first and most fortunate of these children was Semele, a personification of the Great Mother, devoted to the service of the gods, and like the immaculate mothers of all Messiahs, a virgin of the temple. Zeus, beholding her, resolved that she should be the mother of the reborn Dionysius.

There are several accounts of the myth by which the divine child was conceived. One of the most unusual describes how Zeus sent to Semele the heart of his son powdered in wine. Thus, by an immaculate conception, the light of the world was born again of a virgin mother. But Juno was not finished with her conspiring. She took the form of old Beroe, Semele's Epidaurian nurse, and in this guise succeeded in implanting doubts in Semele's mind concerning the father of her unborn child. Juno, as Beroe, explained to Semele that if she were indeed the bride of Zeus, she should demand as proof that the god appear to her in all his Olympian splendor. Semele listened to the evil advice, and when Zeus next came to her in mortal form, she demanded of him a favor. Zeus promised to grant her any wish, and she bound him to his word by the great oath of the river Styx <note>An unbreakable oath sworn by the gods upon the underworld river Styx.</note>. Semele then demanded that the father of the gods should come to her in all his heavenly

<summary>Cadmus marries Harmonia, and their daughter Semele is impregnated by Zeus; Juno tricks Semele into demanding Zeus appear in his true, deadly form.</summary>
<keywords>Cadmus, Harmonia, Semele, Dionysius, Juno, Beroe, Zeus</keywords>
pages.14:
glory. Zeus implored her not to demand this of him, but she insisted, and the given oath could not be broken. Bowed with sorrow, Zeus then returned to the Olympian Mount and vested himself in the mildest of his splendors. He did not don the great vestments of his terrors with which he shattered the giants, but only the simpler robes known among his attendant gods as the lesser panoply of power.

Zeus thus arrayed descended from the heights in a chariot of luminous flame surrounded by vast circles of fire and blazing with the splendor of the Æons <term>eternal beings or emanations of divine power</term>. The vibrant glory of Zeus destroyed the house of Semele; the walls of the city were shaken, tongues of flame darted in every direction, and Semele was entirely consumed by the heavenly fire. The flames would have accomplished a still greater damage had not a miracle occurred. The pillars of the fallen house were suddenly covered by grape and ivy leaves, and the whole ruin was immediately hidden by a thick, fire-resisting foliage.

Zeus, perceiving the disaster, immediately changed his form and gently sought among the ruins for the body of Semele. Having discovered it, he rescued therefrom his still living, unborn son. Zeus then made for the child an artificial womb in his own thigh, wherein Sabazius <note>A Thracian/Phrygian deity often identified with Dionysius.</note> fastened the infant with golden clasps. Dionysius remained in the thigh of Zeus for two months to complete the period of gestation. During this period, Zeus is said to have walked with a limp because he was pricked by the child's horns.

Having completed the prenatal period, Dionysius was delivered upon a fawnskin and bears the epithet *Bimater* <note>Latin: "twice-born." Original: "Bimater."</note> because he was twice born. Zeus then entrusted the education of his child to Hermes, or Mercury, who carried Dionysius far from

pages.15:
the plotting of the Olympian court to the mysterious garden of Nysa in Arabia the Happy. In the midst of this garden was a great hill or mountain called Meros. Here the infant Dionysius fed upon lion's milk and grew up to manhood, cared for and tutored by the Nysæan nymphs and other mysterious creatures of the elements. Among his companions were the dryads and satyrs, and he taught them the divine songs and dances. Among the preceptors of young Dionysius there were none more doting and indulgent than old Silenus, the most aged of the satyrs and the rotund deity of pleasure. In Roman art, obese, jovial Silenus, riding tipsily upon an ass's back, is often confused with Bacchus. Zeus variously rewarded the guardians and tutors of his son. The Nysæan nymphs were placed by Zeus among the constellations and are called the Hyades by modern astronomy. Silenus received worship suitable to a demigod.

Juno continued her efforts to destroy Dionysius. He journeyed from place to place to escape her plottings. On one occasion, she sent an Amphisbaena—a two-headed serpent—to destroy him in his sleep. Awaking in time, he killed the reptile with a vine twig. Juno then struck the young god with madness. Deprived of his reason, Dionysius wandered about the world for years. At last, his sanity was restored by initiation into the Phrygian Rites of Cybele, the Great Mother.

The greatest among the exploits of Dionysius was his expedition to India. This journey required three years. Silenus and other superphysical creatures accompanied him, and as he traveled, gods and heroes, priests and worshippers joined him until a great procession moved across the surface of the earth. In terms of modern geography, his expedition started in Egypt, and his course was first Northwest through what is now Spain

He then turned back through North Africa to Ethiopia, crossed the Red Sea, traversed the Near East, and finally came to Asia proper, where the journey continued until he reached the source of the Ganges river. Here he caused two great pillars to be erected, bearing upon them the record that the expedition had reached the extremity of the habitable world. For the most part, the journey made by Dionysius was a peaceful one, but on one occasion he was opposed by an Indian army mounted upon elephants. On this occasion, Silenus saved the expedition, for it is said that the braying of his ass stampeded the elephants. In honor of this, the animal was raised to heaven and became a constellation after its death. Having conquered the world with his cult, Dionysius returned to his own city, seven-gated Thebes.

*The Bacchi* <note>Referring to the play "The Bacchae" by Euripides.</note> of Euripides describes the fate of Pentheus, king of Thebes and grandson of Cadmus by his daughter Agave. Cadmus, though still alive, being of great age and philosophic mind, and having no male heir, had given the kingdom to his daughter's son. When Dionysius reached Thebes, he discovered that his mother's memory had been hardly used. The divine origin of her son was denied, and she was regarded as the victim of some ardent but dishonorable suitor. When the people of Thebes learned of the approach of Dionysius and his company of Bacchi, they went forth joyfully to meet him, despite the remonstrances of Pentheus, who was determined that the new cult should find no place in his kingdom. The king became more and more violent in his antipathy. He demanded that Dionysius be brought to him in chains and dispatched soldiers and attendants to effect his capture. The prisoner, who had preserved a dignified poise, explained that he was Acetes of Mæonia, a pilot by profession. One day his ship stopped at the island of Dia for a supply of fresh water. The sailors, returning to the vessel, brought with them a noble and beautiful youth whom they had found sleeping on the shore. The seamen decided first to hold the young man for ransom but afterwards changed their minds and determined to sell him into slavery in Egypt. Acetes was suspicious of the whole transaction. He felt a mysterious power about the youth and remonstrated with the deity in disguise. “Naxos is my home,” explained the beautiful prisoner. “Take me there and you shall be rewarded.” The sailors agreed but headed the ship in the opposite direction. Just before they reached Egypt, a miracle occurred. The vessel suddenly stopped in mid-ocean, and neither sail nor oars could move it. Then wine began pouring out of the hold of the ship, and vines began to twine themselves about the mast. Grape and ivy tendrils soon spread over the entire deck. Music filled the air. The young prisoner was suddenly transformed into the god Dionysius himself. On his brow was a chaplet of vine leaves, his spear was wreathed with ivy, and tigers and panthers played at his feet. The sailors fell on their knees in terror before the sight. Suddenly, he was transformed into a raging lion. To escape, the sailors jumped into the sea and were changed into dolphins. Only Acetes, the pilot, was spared because he alone had recognized the presence of the divine power.

## NOTES.

There are two combinations contemplated here, and they must be specially borne in mind. First, we have to determine who is the most painful planet to inflict death, and then, if his general Period is long, we must determine in whose *Bhookti* death is caused. Life is the most important question for any person; therefore, his longevity must first be considered and determined. Then, the good and bad results in his life have to be predicted. The author says that in the *Dasa* of the *Maraka* (death-inflicting) planet, the *Bhookti* of a favorable planet who is in conjunction with him does not produce death, but the *Bhookti* of the evil planet who is not in conjunction with the *Dasanatha* will produce certain death. The question may then be raised: does the *Bhookti* of the evil planet who *is* in conjunction with the *Maraka Dasanatha* produce death or favorable results? From a careful perusal of the above verses, it appears clear that the periods and sub-periods of even the worst planets, when they are in conjunction with each other, do not inflict such evil as the periods and sub-periods of planets who are *not* in conjunction. ### **STANZA XLII.**

But on the other hand, *Guru* (Jupiter), when combined with *Sani* (Saturn), not only does not give good results but will actively produce evil. *Sukra* (Venus) does not himself kill the native, although he possesses death-inflicting powers.

### **NOTES.**

It was pointed out (see Stanza 41) that *Guru*, being the lord of the 9th and 12th houses, has both good and bad qualities combined within himself.

In the combination of *Sani* and *Guru*, the author asked us not to expect any good results, and he here tells us that there will be evil in their combination, especially on the part of *Guru*. This requires a clear explanation. Let us take an example. We know that a planet has good and evil influences due to various causes explained in astrological works. If a planet is capable of giving one rupee worth of good and also one rupee worth of evil, the result will be that the planetary influence is neutral—good canceling out the evil. However, astrological writers assure us that the result is not only not neutral, but is bad. They are of the opinion that when good and evil influences of a planet are equal, we must predict evil, but in a milder form. Remembering this principle of their explanation, we shall see why *Guru* is bad in the combination with *Sani*. *Guru* owns the 9th and 12th houses, of which the 12th for *Guru* and the 11th for *Sani* are evil houses. Here the evil is equal to the good these two planets have, as one of the two houses each planet owns is good while the other is bad. We can understand that the combination is bad, but why should *Guru* be particularly declared bad in producing evil in the combination, while *Sani* also contributes to bring about the combined evil result? *Guru* is an auspicious planet by nature, and evil influences seem to affect him more; *Sani* is an evil planet, and good influences seem to make him better. *Guru* owns one good and one bad house, and they neutralize each other's effects, but he has an evil association—viz., being in conjunction with *Sani*. There is therefore something more than good and bad counteracting each other, and *Guru* is declared to produce evil because he has an evil combination. But *Sani* has a better prospect. # III THE BULL-DIONYSUS

The bull-formed Dionysus “had either been developed out of, or had succeeded to the worship of a bull-totem.”<note>1 A. Lang, *Myth, Ritual, and Religion*, ii. 232.</note> Of course this is possible. But it is not yet certain that the Aryans ever had totemism. On the other hand, it is quite certain that many Aryan peoples have conceived deities of vegetation as embodied in animal forms. Therefore, when we find amongst an Aryan people like the Greeks a deity of vegetation represented as an animal, the presumption must be in favor of explaining this by a principle which is certainly known to have influenced the Aryan race rather than by one which is not certainly known to have done so. In the present state of our knowledge, therefore, it is safer to regard the bull form of Dionysus as being, like his goat form, an expression of his proper character as a deity of vegetation.

The probability of this view will be somewhat increased if it can be shown that in other rites than those of Dionysus, the ancients slew an ox as a representative of the spirit of vegetation. This they appear to have done in the Athenian sacrifice known as “the murder of the ox” (*bouphonia*). It took place about the end of June or the beginning of July—that is, about the time when the threshing is nearly over in Attica. According to tradition, the sacrifice was instituted to procure a cessation of the drought and barrenness that had afflicted the land. The ritual was as follows: Barley mixed with wheat, or cakes made of them, were laid upon the bronze altar of Zeus Polieus on the Acropolis. Oxen were driven round the altar, and the ox which went up to the altar and ate the offering on it was sacrificed. The axe and knife with which the beast was slain had been previously wetted with water brought

We call an action absolutely good if it is characterized by *benevolence*, or a *tendency* toward the public *natural happiness* of *rational agents*. Our *moral sense* perceives this *excellence*. We describe the *laws* of the DEITY as *good* when we believe they are designed to promote the *public good* in the most effective and impartial manner. The DEITY is described as *good*, in a *moral sense*, when we understand that his *whole providence* tends toward the *universal happiness* of his *creatures*; from this, we conclude he possesses *benevolence* and takes *delight* in their *happiness*.

SOME tell us:
> “That the goodness of the divine *laws* consists in their *conformity* to some *essential rectitude* of his nature.”
But they must excuse us from agreeing to this until they explain the meaning of the metaphor *essential rectitude*, and until we discern whether it means anything more than a *perfectly wise, uniform, and impartial benevolence*.

HERE we may see the difference between *constraint* and *obligation*. There is, indeed, no difference between *constraint* and the second sense of the word *obligation*—that is, a *constitution* or system that makes an *action* eligible based on *self-interest*—if we only mean an *external interest* distinct from...

The reader need scarcely be told that by *constraint* we do not mean an *external force* moving our limbs without our consent, for in that case we are not *agents* at all. Rather, *constraint* arises from threatening or presenting some *evil* to force us to act in a certain way. Yet, there seems to be a universally acknowledged difference between even this sort of *constraint* and *obligation*. We never say we are *obliged* to perform an *action* we consider base, though we may be *constrained* to it. We never say that *divine laws*, through their *sanctions*, *constrain* us, but rather that they *oblige* us; nor do we call obedience to the DEITY *constraint* (unless speaking metaphorically), even though many admit they are influenced by the fear of *punishment*. If an almighty *evil being* were to require *treachery, cruelty,* or *ingratitude* under threat of severe *penalties*, we would call this *constraint*. The difference is clearly this: when *sanctions* cooperate with our *moral sense* by encouraging us toward *actions* we consider *morally good*, we say we are *obliged*. But when the *sanctions* of *rewards* or *punishments* oppose our *moral sense*, we say we are *bribed* or *constrained*. In the former case, we call the *lawgiver* good, as he intends the *public happiness*; in the latter, we call him *evil* or *unjust* for the presumed contrary...

VI. FROM this sense, too, we derive our *rights*. Whenever it appears to us that *a faculty of doing, demanding, or possessing anything, universally allowed in certain circumstances, would in the whole tend to the general good*, we say that any person in such circumstances has a *right* to do, possess, or demand that *thing*. And according to whether this tendency to the public good is greater or less, the *right* is greater or less.

<margin>*Perfect Rights.*</margin>
The rights called *perfect* are of such necessity to the public good that the *universal violation of them would make human life intolerable*; it actually makes those miserable whose *rights* are thus violated. On the contrary, to fulfill these *rights* in every instance tends to the public good, either directly or by promoting the innocent advantage of a *part*. Hence it plainly follows: “That to allow a violent defense, or prosecution, of such *rights* before *civil government* is constituted, cannot in any particular case be more detrimental to the public than the violation of them with impunity.”

<summary>This page defines the origin of "rights" based on their tendency to promote the public good and identifies "perfect rights" as those essential for the preservation of human life and society.</summary>

Section 7.
And as for the general consequences, the universal use of force in a *state of nature*, in pursuit of *perfect rights*, seems exceedingly advantageous to the *whole* by making everyone dread any attempts against the *perfect rights* of others.

<margin>*Right of War and Punishment.*</margin>
This is the *moral effect* that attends a *proper injury*, or a violation of the *perfect rights* of others: namely, a right to *war* and all violence necessary to compel the *injurious* party to repair the damage and provide security against such offenses in the future. This is the sole foundation of the rights of punishing criminals and of the violent prosecution of our rights in a *state of nature*. These rights originally belonged to the persons injured (or their voluntary or invited assistants, according to the judgment of impartial arbitrators in a *state of nature*). By the consent of the persons injured, these rights are transferred to the *magistrate* in a *civil state*, which is the true foundation of his right to punish. Instances of *perfect rights* include those to our *lives*; to the *fruits* of our *labors*; to demand the performance of *contracts* for valuable consideration from those capable of fulfilling them; and to *direct* our own *actions* for public or innocent private good before we have submitted them to the direction of others.

IMPERFECT *rights* are such that, if universally violated, would not necessarily make men miserable. These *rights* tend to the improvement and increase of *positive good* in any society but are not absolutely necessary to prevent *universal misery*. The violation of them only disappoints men of the happiness expected from the *humanity* or *gratitude* of others, but does not deprive them of any good they previously possessed. From this description, it appears: “That a violent prosecution of such *rights* would generally occasion greater *evil than the violation of them*.” Furthermore, allowing force in such cases would deprive men of the greatest pleasure in acts of *kindness, humanity,* and *gratitude*; these would cease to appear amiable when men could be constrained to perform them. Instances of *imperfect rights* include those the *poor* have to the *charity* of the *wealthy*; which all *men* have to *offices* (favors) of no trouble or expense to the *performer*; which *benefactors* have to returns of *gratitude*, and so on.

### THE MYTH OF DIONYSIUS

Later, Dionysius himself was captured and brought before Pentheus, but the god could not be harmed by any mortal power. His prison was destroyed by lightning, and the god, surrounded by an aura of glory, returned to his worshippers among the hills. Pentheus, disguising himself in woman’s clothing, went to the mountains to spy upon the Bacchic rites but was discovered and torn to pieces by the infuriated Bacchanales <note>Bacchantes; the female followers of Dionysus.</note>.

It was on the island of Naxos that Dionysius discovered Ariadne, daughter of Minos, king of the Cretans, who had been deserted there by her unfaithful lover, Theseus. Dionysius crowned her with a magnificent coronet of gold and jewels, and when she died soon after, while giving birth to the son of Theseus, Dionysius lifted the crown to heaven and placed it among the constellations.

From this point on, the legend of Dionysius is very fragmentary. According to most accounts, he devoted the rest of his earthly existence to the perfecting of the Theban state. There is an account of his descent into the underworld to rescue the soul of his mother from the abode of the dead. Having released Semele from the darkness of Hades, he escorted her to Olympus, where she became one of the immortals. Dionysius continued the dissemination of his teachings, and having established his priests and shrines and revealed his secret doctrine, he ascended at last to the throne of his father, with whom he is eternally reunited. In the words of the ancient poet:

> “One Zeus, one Dionysius.”

<summary>This page concludes the Dionysian myth, covering the god's triumph over Pentheus, his union with Ariadne, the rescue of his mother Semele from the underworld, and his final ascension to Olympus.</summary>

# Interpretation of the Dionysius Myth

According to the Greek historians, the elements of the Orphic tradition <note>A mystical religious movement in ancient Greece associated with Orpheus.</note> were derived from the metaphysical speculations of the Brahmins. Oriental doctrines, in the course of time, were carried westward into Egypt. It is explicitly stated that Osiris, in the form of the sacred bull Apis, was brought from India to become the god of the Egyptians. By Osiris, we are in this instance to understand the western migration of the mystical philosophies of Asia. Having taken up its abode in the double empire of the Nile, Himalayan occultism drew to itself the wisest and noblest of the Egyptians, with the result that the most sacred and obscure sciences flourished for thousands of years in the congenial atmosphere of enlightened Egypt. The doctrines transplanted from Asia fared so well in the land of the Pharaohs that Egypt gained a reputation of being the most enlightened of western nations, and from the Delta of the Nile, the occult sciences spread among all the civilizations flourishing in Mesopotamia or along the shores of the Mediterranean.

The most enlightened of the Greeks acknowledged the eastern origin of their cultural system. Priests, philosophers, and lawgivers traveled from the Grecian provinces to the older

<summary>The author traces the origins of the Orphic tradition and Dionysian mystery rites back to Eastern metaphysical systems, particularly India and Egypt.</summary>
<keywords>Orphic tradition, Brahmins, Osiris, Apis, Egypt, Mesopotamia, occult sciences</keywords>
pages.21:
### THE MYTH OF DIONYSIUS

civilizations in search of such forms of essential learning as are necessary for the establishment of an enduring culture. Thus, we find that such men as Thales, Solon, Pythagoras, and later Plato, dissatisfied with the educational opportunities of their race, journeyed to Egypt to be initiated into the secrets of religion and science—secrets to be learned only from the hierophants of Memphis, Abydos, Thebes, and the other great colleges of Egyptian learning.

The Egyptian method of teaching seems to have been of the interpretative kind. Initiates received keys which unlocked the elaborate systems of mythology that had accumulated during the formative periods of cultural systems. In their migrations from Asia thousands of years before, the progenitors of the Grecians had brought with them an elaborate pantheon of divinities, a complicated mythology, and a confused mass of obscure legend. The esoteric <note>Intended for or likely to be understood by only a small number of people with a specialized knowledge.</note> keys to this undigested mass of material had been lost in the waste of time, with the result that during the Homeric period, for example, a profound literalism darkened the face of truth.

From the sacred arts of the Egyptians, a few of the noblest of the Greeks gained the skill to unravel the tangled skein of Grecian fable. Institutions of interpretation were set up among the Greeks. These institutions were called Mysteries, and under the ennobling influence of these Mysteries, Greece rose to an unparalleled height of philosophic and metaphysical idealism.

It is said that Orpheus first brought the Eastern wisdom to the Grecians. Nothing is known concerning the origin or person of Orpheus save that his name indicates that he was a dark man. The doctrine which he brought is termed Dionysian. Chief among his teachings are those of rebirth and

<summary>This page discusses how Greek philosophers traveled to Egypt to learn from their mystery schools, moving away from literal interpretations of mythology toward an esoteric understanding facilitated by the Mysteries.</summary>

pages.22:
### THE MYTH OF DIONYSIUS

the perfection of the inner consciousness through specific religious or philosophic disciplines. The greatest interpreters of the Orphic or Dionysian revelation were Pythagoras and Plato. Through Platonism, Dionysius worship influenced Christianity and contributed a powerful impetus to the ethics and aesthetics of the modern world.

As we have already noted, mysticism is essentially a method of interpretation. It is an ensouling of material factors. Through mysticism, emphasis is transferred from material effects to their spiritual causes. Mystical philosophy is a training in discernment. The mind is instructed in the technique of values. Permanent elements are elevated above impermanent elements. Motive is elevated above action, principle is elevated above personality, and the inward experience of the soul is elevated above all the phenomenal complexities of physical existence. Of course, by this philosophy, the mind turns away from the obvious toward the hidden truths that sustain the world.

In the light of the above, it is evident that metaphysics as an interpretation of life can only flourish in a highly evolved social order. The more ignorant a person is, the more he dignifies the obvious. Ignoring both the past and the future, the uninformed person focuses his attention entirely upon the material factors of personal experience. Mysticism recognizes the often obscure but all-potent factors of cause and consequence. Greek mysticism escapes not only materiality, with its limiting perspective, but also literal theology with its personalization of all spiritual principles. The Mysteries explain not only the spiritual factors behind material action but the universal principles behind the theogonies <note>Systems of the generation or origin of the gods.</note> of the exoteric religions.

<summary>The author explains the nature of mysticism as an interpretative tool that prioritizes spiritual causes over material effects, and distinguishes it from literal or exoteric religious practice.</summary>

### THE MYTH OF DIONYSIUS

The keys used by the Greeks to interpret their mythologies are equally applicable to any system of religious mythology existing in our present time. All religions are capable of mystical interpretation. The inward sense is the true meaning in every case. The modern trend is away from literal theologies with their limiting and competitive aspects. Mysticism reveals a universal truth underlying all religious systems. "The letter of the law killeth, but the spirit of the law giveth life." <note>A biblical reference to 2 Corinthians 3:6.</note> As races mature under the compelling force of experience, mysticism is released through the racial consciousness. There is a mystical truth behind every physical fact, even as there is a moral force behind every aspect of universal law. As materialism leads inevitably to an emphasis upon material values, so mysticism leads inevitably to an emphasis upon metaphysical values. During the periods of mystical enlightenment, the noblest part of man expresses itself and civilization makes its greatest progress in essential values.

The question is frequently asked: why, if a great spiritual truth is concealed under myths and fables and the mythologies themselves are but allegories, was not the fact of this matter taught from the beginning? Why have men been permitted to deceive themselves and each other when the knowledge of the inner truths might have brought peace and enlightenment to the whole world ages ago? There are two important answers to these very reasonable questions.

In the first place, the keys which unlock the mystical interpretations of the world's fables also unlock certain other secrets extremely dangerous to unenlightened and unrefined humanity. It has been proven through ages of bitter experience that any extension of knowledge, without a corresponding extension of the moral faculties, produces exploitation and disaster.

<summary>This page argues for the universal applicability of mystical interpretation to all religious mythologies and addresses the historical reasons for why such "hidden truths" were not openly shared with the masses.</summary>
<keywords>mysticism, mythology, spiritual truth, allegories, materialism, moral faculties</keywords>
pages.24:
### THE MYTH OF DIONYSIUS

The little that we have already discovered about the working of universal law has too often left us the victims of the unscrupulous. It was for this reason that the ancient initiates tested with the greatest severity the integrity of all who desired to participate in metaphysical knowledge.

In the second place, mystical interpretation is not merely the communication of the key by which all universal mysteries may be unlocked. Mysticism is the awakening of the mystical consciousness within the individual himself. Mysticism is more than a secret. It is a spiritual experience, which can only come to a person who has achieved a certain maturity of attitude and a definite integrity of living and thinking. Metaphysics is not merely a formula; it is a realization which, unless lived, dies out of the life, leaving the consciousness more impoverished than before. Mysticism belongs to the experiences of maturity, and to the immature, it is a hopeless and unappreciable whim. The enlightened metaphysician lives a conviction and by this action perfects the conviction within himself. Religion is the living of a rational conviction, but this fact is not discernible to those who are still bound to the illusion of the significance of creeds and dogmas.

With this as a prologue, let us now consider the interpretation of the Dionysian myth outlined in the previous chapter.

The eternal Principle of Existence is designated Unaging Time, a duration in which there is neither past nor future, and all extensions are suspended in an eternal Now. Unaging Time is Absolute Existence. This principle the Egyptians honored by the title “the Thrice Deep Darkness.” The Jewish Cabbalists <note>Practitioners of Kabbalah, Jewish mysticism.</note> denominated this principle Ain Soph, and the Lamaists contemplated it under the term Adi Buddhi. Unaging

<summary>The author emphasizes that mysticism is a lived experience requiring moral maturity, not just a set of secrets, and begins the specific interpretation of the Dionysian myth, starting with the concept of 'Unaging Time'.</summary>
<keywords>mystical consciousness, metaphysics, Unaging Time, Absolute Existence, Cabbalists, Ain Soph, Adi Buddhi</keywords>
pages.25:
### THE MYTH OF DIONYSIUS

Time is the Absolute-conditioned divinity, the God of all gods, the Father of all generations divine and human, the Cause of all activity, and the Sustainer of worlds. Unaging Time is the One Immortal incapable of dissolution, above definition or defilement. In their adoration of Immovable Duration, the Orphics were monotheistic, for they acknowledged one indivisible source of all the diversity which fills the realm of aging time.

Pythagoras, defining the Orphic principles, created the term "the Monad" to distinguish the attributes of Unaging Time. By the Monad, Pythagoras meant unity or wholeness, an all-inclusive identity. The Pythagoreans further taught that from the immeasurable profundity of the Monad emerged the Duad, duality or condition, manifesting from what the Gnostics <note>Early Christian-era mystic sects.</note> called Bythos—the Profundity.

The elements of the Duad are termed Ether and Chaos, or as the Chinese express it, Yin and Yang, revealed out of Tien. Ether and Chaos are the polarities, the parents of extremes and opposites, the root of the principle of confusion. To signify their antipathy for the Duad, the Pythagoreans always spat upon the ground when mentioning the number two. The Ether of the Orphics was a luminous, self-moving principle. Activity was intrinsic to it, and it moved through the Great Deep in a vast circular course. Chaos was Mut or Mud, the Ilus or Primordial Slime, from which was to crawl the dragon form of the world with the time cycles traced upon its scales, as in the mythology of Central America. Ether, the mighty whirling life, caught up the humid particles of Chaos and, whirling them for countless ages, fashioned by the whirling the Great Egg of the world. The great Spiritual Agent moving in Ether was termed by the Egyptians Ptah the

<summary>The author describes the Orphic concept of the "Monad" (unity) giving rise to the "Duad" (duality), represented by the interaction of Ether and Chaos to form the "Great Egg" of the world.</summary>
<keywords>Orphics, Pythagoras, Monad, Duad, Gnostics, Bythos, Ether, Chaos, Yin and Yang, Ptah</keywords>
pages.26:
### THE MYTH OF DIONYSIUS

Artificer. Upon a potter’s wheel, Ptah shaped the world egg in the Abyss, which the Scandinavians called Ginnungagap, the cleft in space. Ether whirling the substances of Chaos and gradually forming them into a universal system would seem to indicate that the Orphics were aware of the nebular hypothesis <note>A scientific theory suggesting that the solar system formed from a rotating cloud of gas.</note>.

The Orphic Egg is frequently depicted with the serpent of Ether coiled about it. In the doctrines of the Hindus, there is the radiant or golden Egg, Hiranyagarbha, from which the Creator of the universe himself is born. In the Grecian account, the upper hemisphere of the egg is golden and the lower is silver, and within the egg itself the potencies of the universe abide together in the form of the primordial Being, Phanes. The egg is the symbol of individualization. Within it is the germ from which springs the objective universe. The potentialities latent in space incarnate in the egg-born gods. Ether, Chaos, and the Egg are the first triad, and from the Egg springs forth the luminous body of the informed divinity.

Phanes is the Sovereign Intellect of the world. In him are all the radiances of the mind. He is luminous intellection vested in the splendors of the Divine Thought. Winged, many-headed, yet unbodied, he is Living Reason, the personification of the rational urge which orders the world, bending the cosmic divergencies to the purpose of self-reasoning law. Phanes is Shang-te, the Logos of the Chinese. He is the Grand Man of the Zohar. He is many-headed Brahma born from the navel of Vishnu. Phanes, first born from the womb of Meru, establishes the divine order of the gods. He is Sovereign Truth from which descend the many forms of wisdom sustaining the various creations that emerge from the all-embracing mind of the egg-born Lord.

<summary>The author concludes this section by explaining the symbolism of the "Orphic Egg" and the emergence of Phanes as the Sovereign Intellect or the rational ordering principle of the universe.</summary>
<keywords>Ptah, Ginnungagap, nebular hypothesis, Orphic Egg, Hiranyagarbha, Phanes, Sovereign Intellect, Logos, Brahma, Vishnu</keywords>
