# Interpretation of the Dionysius Myth

According to Greek historians, the elements of the Orphic tradition were derived from the metaphysical speculations of the Brahmins. Oriental doctrines, in the course of time, were carried westward into Egypt. It is explicitly stated that Osiris, in the form of the sacred bull Apis, was brought from India to become the god of the Egyptians. By "Osiris," in this instance, we are to understand the western migration of the mystical philosophies of Asia. Having taken up its abode in the double empire of the Nile, Himalayan occultism drew to itself the wisest and noblest of the Egyptians, with the result that the most sacred and obscure sciences flourished for thousands of years in the congenial atmosphere of enlightened Egypt. The doctrines transplanted from Asia fared so well in the land of the Pharaohs that Egypt gained a reputation of being the most enlightened of western nations. From the Delta of the Nile, these occult sciences spread among all the civilizations flourishing in Mesopotamia or along the shores of the Mediterranean.

The most enlightened of the Greeks acknowledged the eastern origin of their cultural system. Priests, philosophers, and lawgivers traveled from the Grecian provinces to the older...

<summary>This page introduces the theory that Greek religious traditions, specifically the Orphic and Dionysian, originated in Eastern metaphysical thought and were transmitted through Egyptian civilization.</summary>
<keywords>Dionysius Myth, Orphic tradition, Brahmins, Osiris, Apis, Himalayan occultism, Mesopotamia</keywords>
pages.21:
<meta>Continues from the discussion of Greek scholars traveling to Egypt for wisdom.</meta>
civilizations in search of such forms of essential learning as are necessary for the establishment of an enduring culture. Thus, we find that such men as Thales, Solon, Pythagoras, and later Plato—dissatisfied with the educational opportunities of their own race—journeyed to Egypt to be initiated into the secrets of religion and science that could be learned only from the hierophants <note>high priests who interpreted sacred mysteries</note> of Memphis, Abydos, Thebes, and the other great colleges of Egyptian learning.

The Egyptian method of teaching seems to have been of the interpretive kind. Initiates received keys that unlocked the elaborate systems of mythology that had accumulated during the formative periods of cultural history. In their migrations from Asia thousands of years before, the progenitors of the Greeks had brought with them an elaborate pantheon of divinities, a complicated mythology, and a confused mass of obscure legend. The esoteric <note>intended for a small, initiated group</note> keys to this undigested mass of material had been lost in the passage of time, with the result that during the Homeric period, for example, a profound literalism darkened the face of truth.

From the sacred arts of the Egyptians, a few of the noblest of the Greeks gained the skill to unravel the tangled skein of Grecian fable. Institutions of interpretation were set up among the Greeks. These institutions were called "Mysteries," and under their ennobling influence, Greece rose to an unparalleled height of philosophic and metaphysical idealism.

It is said that Orpheus first brought the Eastern wisdom to the Greeks. Nothing is known concerning the origin or person of Orpheus, save that his name indicates that he was a dark man. The doctrine which he brought is termed "Dionysian." Chief among his teachings are those of rebirth and...

<summary>This page explains how Greek scholars traveled to Egypt to learn the "keys" to interpreting ancient myths, and introduces Orpheus as the bringer of the Dionysian doctrine.</summary>
<keywords>Thales, Solon, Pythagoras, Plato, Egypt, hierophants, Memphis, Abydos, Thebes, Egyptian, Grecians, Homeric, Mysteries, Orpheus, Dionysian</keywords>
pages.22:
<meta>Continues from the mention of rebirth and inner consciousness.</meta>
the perfection of the inner consciousness through specific religious or philosophic disciplines. The greatest interpreters of the Orphic or Dionysian revelation were Pythagoras and Plato. Through Platonism, Dionysian worship influenced Christianity and contributed a powerful impetus to the ethics and aesthetics of the modern world.

As we have already noted, mysticism is essentially a method of interpretation. It is an ensouling of material factors. Through mysticism, emphasis is transferred from material effects to their spiritual causes. Mystical philosophy is a training in discernment. The mind is instructed in the technique of values. Permanent elements are elevated above impermanent elements. Motive is elevated above action, principle is elevated above personality, and the inward experience of the soul is elevated above all the phenomenal complexities of physical existence. By this philosophy, the mind turns away from the obvious toward the hidden truths that sustain the world.

In light of the above, it is evident that metaphysics, as an interpretation of life, can only flourish in a highly evolved social order. The more ignorant a person is, the more he dignifies the obvious. Ignoring both the past and the future, the uninformed person focuses his attention entirely upon the material factors of personal experience. Mysticism recognizes the often obscure but all-potent factors of cause and consequence. Greek mysticism escapes not only materiality, with its limiting perspective, but also literal theology, with its personalization of all spiritual principles. The Mysteries explain not only the spiritual factors behind material action but the universal principles behind the theogonies <note>theories concerning the origin of the gods</note> of the exoteric <note>public or common</note> religions.

<summary>This page defines mysticism as a tool for discerning spiritual causes over material effects, and argues that this metaphysical approach is essential for a mature society.</summary>
<keywords>Dionysius, Orphic, Pythagoras, Plato, Platonism, mysticism, metaphysics, theogonies, exoteric religions</keywords>
pages.23:
The keys used by the Greeks to interpret their mythologies are equally applicable to any system of religious mythology existing in our present time. All religions are capable of mystical interpretation; the inward sense is the true meaning in every case. The modern trend is away from literal theologies with their limiting and competitive aspects. Mysticism reveals a universal truth underlying all religious systems. "The letter of the law killeth, but the spirit of the law giveth life" <note>A biblical reference, 2 Corinthians 3:6</note>. As races mature under the compelling force of experience, mysticism is released through the racial consciousness. There is a mystical truth behind every physical fact, just as there is a moral force behind every aspect of universal law. As materialism leads inevitably to an emphasis upon material values, so mysticism leads inevitably to an emphasis upon metaphysical values. During periods of mystical enlightenment, the noblest part of man expresses itself, and civilization makes its greatest progress in essential values.

The question is frequently asked: if a great spiritual truth is concealed under myths and fables, and the mythologies themselves are but allegories, why was this not taught from the beginning? Why have men been permitted to deceive themselves and each other when the knowledge of the inner truths might have brought peace and enlightenment to the whole world ages ago? There are two important answers to these very reasonable questions.

In the first place, the keys that unlock the mystical interpretations of the world's fables also unlock certain other secrets extremely dangerous to unenlightened and unrefined humanity. It has been proven through ages of bitter experience that any extension of knowledge, without a corresponding extension of the moral faculties, produces exploitation and disaster.

<summary>This page argues for the universal validity of mystical interpretation across all religions and explains why such knowledge was historically kept secret: the danger of power without moral development.</summary>
<keywords>mysticism, mythology, Dionysius, spiritual truth, allegories, materialism, metaphysical values, Greeks</keywords>
pages.24:
The little that we have already discovered about the working of universal law has too often left us the victims of the unscrupulous. It was for this reason that the ancient initiates tested with the greatest severity the integrity of all who desired to participate in metaphysical knowledge.

In the second place, mystical interpretation is not merely the communication of a key by which all universal mysteries may be unlocked. Mysticism is the awakening of the mystical consciousness within the individual himself. Mysticism is more than a secret; it is a spiritual experience that can only come to a person who has achieved a certain maturity of attitude and a definite integrity of living and thinking. Metaphysics is not merely a formula; it is a realization that, unless lived, dies out of the life, leaving the consciousness more impoverished than before. Mysticism belongs to the experiences of maturity; to the immature, it is a hopeless and unappreciable vagary. The enlightened metaphysician lives a conviction, and by this action, perfects the conviction within himself. Religion is the living of a rational conviction, but this fact is not discernible to those who are still bound to the illusion of the significance of creeds and dogmas.

With this as a prologue, let us now consider the interpretation of the Dionysian myth outlined in the previous chapter.

The eternal Principle of Existence is designated "Unaging Time," a duration in which there is neither past nor future, and all extensions are suspended in an eternal "Now." Unaging Time is Absolute Existence. The Egyptians honored this principle by the title “the Thrice Deep Darkness.” The Jewish Cabbalists <note>students of Jewish mysticism</note> denominated this principle "Ain Soph," and the Lamaists contemplated it under the term "Adi Buddhi." Unaging...

<summary>This page clarifies that mysticism is a lived experience rather than just a set of secrets, and begins the interpretation of the Dionysian myth by defining the "Unaging Time" or Absolute.</summary>
<keywords>Dionysius, metaphysics, mysticism, Unaging Time, Absolute Existence, Thrice Deep Darkness, Ain Soph, Adi Buddhi</keywords>
pages.25:
<meta>Continues from the definition of Unaging Time.</meta>
Time is the Absolute, conditioned divinity, the God of all gods, the Father of all generations (divine and human), the Cause of all activity, and the Sustainer of worlds. Unaging Time is the One Immortal, incapable of dissolution, above definition or defilement. In their adoration of "Immovable Duration," the Orphics were monotheistic, for they acknowledged one indivisible source of all the diversity that fills the realm of aging time.

Pythagoras, defining the Orphic principles, created the term "the Monad" to distinguish the attributes of Unaging Time. By "the Monad," Pythagoras meant unity or wholeness, an all-inclusive identity. The Pythagoreans further taught that from the immeasurable profundity of the Monad emerged "the Duad," duality or condition, manifesting from what the Gnostics called "Bythos"—the Profundity.

The elements of the Duad are termed Æther and Chaos, or as the Chinese express it, Yin and Yang, revealed out of Tien. Æther and Chaos are the polarities—the parents of extremes and opposites, the root of the principle of confusion. To signify their antipathy for the Duad, the Pythagoreans always spat upon the ground when mentioning the number two. The Æther of the Orphics was a luminous, self-moving principle. Activity was intrinsic to it, and it moved through the Great Deep in a vast circular course. Chaos was Mut or Mud, the Ilus or Primordial Slime, from which was to crawl the dragon form of the world with the time cycles traced upon its scales, as in the mythology of Central America. Æther, the mighty whirling life, caught up the humid particles of Chaos and, whirling them for countless ages, fashioned by the whirling the Great Egg of the world. The great Spiritual Agent moving in Æther was termed by the Egyptians Ptah, the...

<summary>This page describes the transition from the absolute Monad to the dualistic world of Æther and Chaos, utilizing Pythagorean and other ancient philosophical concepts to explain the origin of the cosmos.</summary>
<keywords>Orphics, Pythagoras, Monad, Duad, Gnostics, Bythos, Æther, Chaos, Yin, Yang, Tien, Ptah</keywords>
pages.26:
<meta>Continues from the description of Ptah.</meta>
Artificer. Upon a potter’s wheel, Ptah shaped the world-egg in the Abyss, which the Scandinavians called Ginnungagap, the cleft in space. Æther, whirling the substances of Chaos and gradually forming them into a universal system, would seem to indicate that the Orphics were aware of the nebular hypothesis <note>a theory that the solar system formed from a rotating cloud of gas</note>.

The Orphic Egg is frequently depicted with the serpent of Æther coiled about it. In the doctrines of the Hindus, there is the radiant or golden Egg, Hiranyagarbha, from which the Creator of the universe himself is born. In the Grecian account, the upper hemisphere of the egg is golden and the lower is silver, and within the egg itself, the potencies of the universe abide together in the form of the primordial Being, Phanes. The egg is the symbol of individualization. Within it is the germ from which springs the objective universe. The potentialities latent in space incarnate in the egg-born gods. Æther, Chaos, and the Egg are the first triad, and from the Egg springs forth the luminous body of the informed divinity.

Phanes is the Sovereign Intellect of the world. In him are all the radiances of the mind. He is luminous intellection vested in the splendors of the Divine Thought. Winged, many-headed, yet unbodied, he is Living Reason, the personification of the rational urge that orders the world, bending the cosmic divergencies to the purpose of self-reasoning law. Phanes is Shang-te, the Logos of the Chinese. He is the Grand Man of the Zohar. He is the many-headed Brahma born from the navel of Vishnu. Phanes, first-born from the womb of Meru, establishes the divine order of the gods. He is Sovereign Truth from which descend the many forms of wisdom sustaining the various creations that emerge from the all-embracing mind of the egg-born Lord.

<summary>This page details the symbolism of the "Orphic Egg" as the origin of the universe and introduces Phanes as the Sovereign Intellect or the rational governing principle of the cosmos.</summary>
<keywords>Artificer, Ptah, Ginnungagap, Æther, Chaos, Orphics, nebular hypothesis, Orphic Egg, Hiranyagarbha, Phanes, individualization, triad, Sovereign Intellect, Divine Thought, Living Reason, Shang-te, Logos, Zohar, Brahma, Vishnu, Meru</keywords>

### CHAPTER I.

->*Brothels and Introducing Tea-houses.*<-

**Art. 1.** — The business of brothel-keeping or the operation of <term>hikite-jaya</term> (introducing tea-houses) shall only be carried on in places approved by the Metropolitan Police Board. No new establishments will be permitted outside of the <term>yūkwaku</term> (a quarter set apart for licensed prostitution).

**Art. 2.** — Persons wishing to open a brothel (<term>kashi-zashiki</term>) or an introducing tea-house shall submit a petition to the Metropolitan Police Board through the local Police Station and obtain a license. The same formality must be observed if one wishes to relocate the business. The petition must contain the following details:

> (*a*). Place of registration, rank or status, residence, full legal name, and age.
>
> (*b*). Name of the brothel or tea-house.
>
> (*c*). Address of the business.
>
> (*d*). A floor plan of the building. (The arrangement and size of rooms, as well as the width, number, and location of staircases, must be specified).

**Art. 3.** — When proposing to erect buildings to be used as brothels or tea-houses that exceed three stories in height, a petition with detailed construction plans and specifications must be submitted to

pages.487:
the Metropolitan Police Board through the local Police Station, and permission must be obtained before beginning work. For buildings of two stories or fewer, only the floor plans need to be submitted to the Police Board. The same requirements apply when rebuilding or repairing existing structures.

Every house (containing floor space up to 30 <term>tsubo</term> <note>A Japanese unit of area, approximately 3.3 square meters</note>) used as a brothel or tea-house must have at least two staircases, each 4 feet wide. An additional staircase must be added for every additional 30 <term>tsubo</term>.

**Art. 4.** — After the permission mentioned in Art. 3 is granted and the buildings are completed, the local Police Station must be notified. The premises will then be inspected, and the building shall not be used until the police authorities have sanctioned it.

**Art. 5.** — Should the keeper of a brothel or tea-house be found infringing these regulations—thereby endangering public safety, committing offenses against public morals and good order, or lending his or her name to others—the license shall be withdrawn or the business suspended.

**Art. 6.** — If a keeper, without reasonable cause, does not commence business within three months of receiving a license or ceases operations for more than one year, the license shall be declared null and void.

**Art. 7.** — Two or more brothels or tea-houses are not permitted to operate in partnership.

## EXPOSITION CONTINUED,
### IN WHICH SUNDRY INQUIRIES AND OBJECTIONS ARE STATED AND ANSWERED.

The following pages were written in the State of Ohio, and printed in a pamphlet with the preceding, under the superintendence of R. McNemar and D. Spinning, in 1832. As they will afford further information to the candid inquirer, they are now reprinted with a few corrections and amendments.

**NOTWITHSTANDING** much has been published for the information of mankind, relative to the faith and practice of the United Society of Believers; yet we find many among the most candid and intelligent, who are still at a loss, and often anxiously, and we hope honestly, seeking further information, especially on matters of a practical nature. For the satisfaction of such, the following pages have been written; and as truth is our object, we shall aim at presenting it in so plain a dress that it may be easily comprehended by persons of common capacity.

In the first place, it is a question with many, whether this Society has for its primary object the things of this world, or that which is to come.

This question is, of all others, of the greatest importance, and ought to be first settled. It is strangely supposed, that if our main object were to prepare for a

<summary>This page concludes the preface of the 1830 edition and introduces the 1832 "Exposition Continued," which aims to answer practical questions regarding Shaker faith and life.</summary>
<keywords>United Society of Believers, Exposition, religious principles, Calvin Green, Seth Y. Wells</keywords>
pages.22:
future state, we would show a greater indifference about the things of time; but, instead of this, we are as zealous to provide a good living, and to have everything about us in the best order and of the most durable quality; hence we have been publicly denounced as “a set of worldly-minded, cunning deceivers.”

To this strange kind of reasoning, we need only reply that all our zeal in improving temporal things, and taking satisfaction in the enjoyment of them, will not prove that we have no greater enjoyments in prospect; and we think that the manner in which we use temporal things may serve as positive proof that we consider them of but little value in comparison with the things of eternity.

Where is the man of the world who could be induced by anything earthly to confess all his most secret sins, and take up a full cross against all manner of sin and uncleanness in his knowledge, and live the life of self-denial that we live? This single appeal may satisfy the conscience of any man that nothing but motives purely religious can possibly induce any person to join this Society and perseveringly conform to its rules and orders.

1. *The confession of sins.* This, being the initiating act, opens a large field of inquiry, and some weighty objections, especially among Protestants, who have imbibed a disgust to almost every point of order held sacred by the Church of Rome. It is questioned whether the order of the gospel be to confess to God alone, in general terms, or to name the particular acts, thing by thing, in the presence of witnesses appointed to hear, remit, and counsel, as the case may be.

The idea of confessing to man, or of any man having power to forgive sin, is generally viewed by Protestants as the greatest presumption. But were it not for the abuses of this sacred order by the Catholic Church, no Protestant, nor any other person of candor, could read the Scriptures attentively and not see that an oral confession of sins, as established in this Society, was practiced both under the law and the gospel. The confession, if sin-

<summary>The author addresses the objection that the Society is "worldly-minded" due to their industrious nature, explaining that their work is secondary to their religious devotion and introduces the requirement of confession of sins.</summary>
<keywords>temporal goods, self-denial, confession of sins, Protestants, religious motives</keywords>
pages.23:
cere, is indeed made to God, and it is by his order that the penitent is released, and his sins forgiven him.
> “Whosesoever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them, and whosesoever sins ye retain, they are retained.”

A striking evidence of the propriety and justice of this order of confession may be observed in mankind under various circumstances. A sinner, under deep tribulation and remorse of conscience, will often apply to some confidential friend, in whose piety and goodness he can safely trust, to unburden his mind by laying open those crimes which occasion his remorse, and will often find relief in so doing. This is frequently the resource of awakened sinners on a dying bed. Criminals, also, under a just sentence of death, and expecting soon to be launched into eternity, will often make an open confession of their crimes, and seem to leave the world with much more peace of mind than they otherwise would have done. These things clearly show that there is a witness in the soul of man, implanted by the finger of God, to point out the true order of confession.

2. *Self-denial* comes next in order. The remission of sins that are past only serves to place the candidate on the ground of further trial. By bringing his deeds to the light, he sees what kind of a creature he is, and what he shall do with himself is now the question. The answer is, “Deny thyself.” Can anything be more objectionable? Self is the supreme object of every natural man; nothing is so near and dear to him as himself; of course, to deny himself appears the greatest inconsistency imaginable. Hence it becomes a deep labor to reconcile the mind, in any degree, to a course so directly opposite to that of nature.

The candidate views and reviews his whole life, his actions and his principles of action, and compares them with their opposites now set before him in the precepts of the gospel and the example of believers; the infallible result of which, in every honest man, is self-abhorrence and sincere inquiry, “Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?” “Take up thy cross,” is the answer.

<summary>This page defends the practice of oral confession of sin as a natural relief for the conscience and explains the necessity of self-denial as the next step in the gospel life.</summary>
<keywords>confession, remission of sins, self-denial, conscience, repentance</keywords>
pages.24:
3. **The Cross of Christ** comes next into consideration. Here is the grand halting-place with the generality: they are unwilling to purchase salvation at so dear a rate. But to an honest soul there is no time to hesitate, no room for evasion or getting round the cross; no alternative but to make a full surrender, an entire sacrifice. It might, perhaps, be understood that great latitude is given to the young believer, to hold and manage his own property, family, etc. It is only so considered after the manner of men; the faith of the gospel makes no reserve. Whoever denies self, denies all that belongs to self. The grand requisition to discipleship embraces “all that he hath.” He himself is not his own, and what can he have that he can call his own?

Thus, the honest soul, having received the faith of the gospel, confessed his sins, denied himself, and taken up his cross, is placed on the proper ground of probation, to follow Christ in the regeneration; which leads to a further inquiry into those several steps which are considered more or less objectionable by the generality of mankind.

1. The first step which the believer takes, in conformity to the example of Christ, is to withdraw from the communion and fellowship of the world. “Two cannot walk together except they be agreed.”

The disagreement between the spirit of Christ and the spirit of the world is irreconcilable; therefore, the first step that goes to test our faith is prompt obedience to the call of Christ, which ever was, is, and ever will be, “Come ye out from among them, and be ye separate.” Hence begins the first order of the Society.

No consideration of an earthly nature can bind the believer to his former associates, nor separate him from the company of those to whom he is united in spirit. The terms laid down by the Captain of our salvation are unalterable. No worldly honor, no earthly interest, no natural affection, is taken for an excuse; but whatever cannot be adjusted and disposed of in an orderly manner must be forsaken. “If any man come to me and hate

<summary>The author describes the "Cross of Christ" as the requirement for total surrender of self and possessions, followed by the first step of separating from the world's fellowship.</summary>
<keywords>Cross of Christ, discipleship, regeneration, separation, faith</keywords>
pages.25:
not his father and mother, his wife and children, and brethren and sisters, yea, and his own life also, he cannot be my disciple."
> "He that loveth father or mother more than me is not worthy of me; and he that loveth son or daughter more than me, is not worthy of me; and he that taketh not his cross and followeth after me, is not worthy of me." (Matt. x: 37.)

We have no system of rules to prescribe the form and manner of proceeding in this matter; each individual acts according to circumstances. If there is a neighborhood of Believers, they are under no necessity of selling or forsaking their houses or lands, or deserting their families.

They establish their own rules of operation, and unbelievers rarely mix with them, unless it be to persecute and afflict them. Any that live remote, if they are not driven off, may take their time for settling their temporal concerns, and moving within the bounds of the Society. If they are single persons, they are accommodated in some of the families of Believers; those who have families move them somewhere near, if they are willing to come, and provide for them if they are able; if not, they depend on their brethren for help.

When a family is divided, and part hold with Believers and part with unbelievers, it furnishes occasion for many objections, which may all be answered in the words of Christ— 
> "I am not come to send peace but rather division." (Luke xii: 51.)

2. When thus separated from the world, and located in the order of the Society, the next step is to test their union and relation to each other. Their first faith was to make a full and unreserved surrender to God, and it now remains to prove the sincerity of their dedication. If God is in heaven and we upon earth, how is he to receive this dedication and surrender? This question is answered by Christ himself: 
> "Whatsoever ye do unto the least of these my brethren, ye do it unto me."

The matter then is to regulate and adjust the general interest to the best advantage, for the mutual support

<summary>This page clarifies that Shakers do not force families to desert one another, explains how new members relocate, and introduces the concept of dedicating property to the Society as a form of serving Christ.</summary>
<keywords>family relations, separation, relocation, dedication of interest, Christ</keywords>
pages.26:
and benefit of all. This is a radical principle that pervades the whole concern, from its embryo to its greatest maturity, and holds a selfish nature to the cross in every arrangement that takes place.

The arrangement of persons is a matter of the first importance, to organize them in family order, to assign to each individual the lot and place which he is best qualified to fill, and in which he can improve his talents to the best advantage. This, however wise and economical, is not without serious objection, particularly on the ground of disorganizing families, and dissolving the ties of nature. But those who esteem the gospel relation as the most valuable treasure, must gain it, though it be at the expense of those partial affections so highly prized by the children of this world.

3. When a family, in gospel relation, is thus constituted, the next inquiry is: What step is taken to arrange their temporal interest and mutual labors, so as to prevent confusion? What example has Christ given in this respect? Answer—In the first gathering of Believers, under the ministry of the Apostles, while they had all things common, there was cause of murmuring, till deacons were appointed to see that justice was done to all.
According to this example, when property is united together and appropriated to common purposes, it is placed under the care and management of a deaconship, who are to be responsible for the same.

A covenant is entered into between the parties, in which the use and benefit of the property, and the services of all and each, are freely devoted to the common support of the family; but to prevent fraud or imposition, no transfer of property is made to the deacons or to any other person.

As this order is merely probationary, the utmost caution is used to prevent imposition. Each individual who brings property with him has it valued by disinterested men, takes an inventory of it signed by the appraisers, delivers it to the care and custody of the deacons, and if

pages.27:
he should afterwards call for it, he receives it without interest, and gives a receipt and acquittance from all further demands.

The reasons for retaining this joint property on the ground of individual and separate claims, are to afford each a sufficient time of trial, and to secure a just settlement of all individual accounts. As long as there is any ground of claim upon the individual, his property remains in his own power, liable for his debts and other personal purposes. It is therefore in this order that all matters are adjusted relating to the settlement of property, all accounts settled with creditors, and donations given or appropriations made to heirs. But above every temporal consideration, it is here that the following lines begin to be realized:

"Our flesh and sense must be denied,
Passion and envy, lust and pride:
While justice, temp'rance, truth and love,
Our inward piety approve." — Isaac Watts.

Few objections are ever brought against the order of such a family, relative to their domestic economy; but the case of the withdrawing of members sometimes excites the tender sympathies of the world. For such to receive barely what they brought in; no interest; no wages! How will this comport with the injunctions of Scripture, not to defraud the hireling of his wages: or how will it bear the scrutiny of the laws of the land?

Answer. We have ever, from the beginning, discarded the idea of hiring each other, or paying any wages to any member of the Society; therefore, no objection can arise on the ground of defrauding a hireling: and as for paying interest, it is pointedly prohibited by the moral law.

"Thou shalt not lend upon usury to thy brother, usury of money, usury of victuals, usury of anything that is lent upon usury." — "Lord, who shall abide in thy tabernacle? Who shall dwell in thy holy hill?" Mark the answer. "He that putteth not out his money to usury."

As for the laws of the land, they will be considered

<keywords>property withdrawal, usury, interest, communal economy, biblical law</keywords>
pages.28:
hereafter, in reference to a higher order, which is the next subject of inquiry.

4. The fourth and last step which is marked out for our journey through time, is into Church order, where the spirits of men are to be tried as by fire, "and the fire shall try every man's work of what sort it is" (1 Thess. iii: 13); their characters will be fairly tested, and their destiny for a future state decided. Every order short of this is merely preparatory, and admits of some reserve; but whoever advances into church relation ought to calculate to make no reserve, and "to go no more out" (Rev. iii: 12). He must enter this order as Noah entered the ark, to ride the foaming billows of time, and terminate his voyage on the peaceful shores of eternity.

To this ark of safety the true Believer steadily and gradually progresses, making straight paths for his feet, until he arrives at the door of admission.

When a competent number have passed through a sufficient trial of their faith in the junior order, and are unitedly prepared to establish and support Church relation, they have only to ratify and confirm their inward agreement by executing what is, by way of eminence, called the Church Covenant. Our limits will not admit of inserting this Covenant entire; we shall therefore only state the outlines of its stipulations.

The parties solemnly announce their faith, and the object of their associating together in that order. They agree to live together as brethren and sisters of one family, possessing one consecrated interest, and equally enjoying the benefits of the same; to conform to the order of the Church heretofore known and approved. The several orders of ministry, elders, deacons and trustees, and the duties of each are severally designated, as also the duties and obligations, rights and privileges of the members respectively. They further, in the most explicit terms, relinquish all claim to personal or private property, and wages for their services, and debar, not only themselves, but their heirs and assigns forever, from all private claims

<summary>This page introduces the final "Church order" of the Shaker society, emphasizing the "Church Covenant" as a total commitment and the final step in the believer's journey.</summary>
<keywords>Church order, Church Covenant, probation, commitment, consecrated interest</keywords>

It is a result of complaints like these that we are unappreciative in our comments upon the gifts of heaven; we complain because they are not always granted to us, because they are few and unsure and fleeting. Hence we have not the will either to live or to die; we are possessed by hatred of life, by fear of death. Our plans are all at sea, and no amount of prosperity can satisfy us. And the reason for all this is that we have not yet attained to that good which is immeasurable and unsurpassable, in which all wishing on our part must cease, because there is no place beyond the highest. Do you ask why virtue needs nothing? Because it is pleased with what it has, and does not lust after that which it has not. Whatever is enough is abundant in the eyes of virtue.

Dissent from this judgment, and duty and loyalty will not abide. For one who desires to exhibit these two qualities must endure much that the world calls evil; we must sacrifice many things to which we are addicted, thinking them to be goods. Gone is courage, which should be continually testing itself; gone is greatness of soul, which cannot stand out clearly unless it has learned to scorn as trivial everything that the crowd covets as supremely important; and gone is kindness and the repaying of kindness, if we fear toil, if we have acknowledged anything to be more precious than loyalty, if our eyes are fixed upon anything except the best.

But to pass these questions by: either these so-called goods are not goods, or else man is more

or else man is more fortunate than God, since God has no enjoyment of the things that are prepared for us. For neither lust, nor the elegance of feasts, nor wealth, nor anything of those things that ensnare man and lead him into base pleasure, pertains to Him. Therefore, it is either not unbelievable that goods are lacking to God, or else the very fact that they are absent from God is proof that they are not goods. Add to this that many things which wish to appear as goods befall animals more abundantly than men. They use their food more greedily, they are not equally fatigued by sexual indulgence, and they possess a greater and more stable strength. It follows that they are much more fortunate than man. For they live without wickedness and without fraud. They enjoy pleasures which they both capture more easily and without any fear of shame or regret.

Consider, therefore, whether that should be called a good in which God is surpassed by man. Let us keep the Supreme Good in the soul; it grows obsolete if it is transferred from the best part of ourselves to the worst—that is, to the senses, which are more active in dumb animals. Our happiness must not be placed in the flesh; those are true goods which reason provides, solid and everlasting, which cannot fall away or even grow less or be diminished. Other things are goods only by opinion; they have a name in common with true goods, but they do not possess the property of "good." Therefore, let them be called "advantages," and, to speak in our own tongue,

For lust pertains not to God, nor do elegant banquets, nor wealth, nor any of the things that allure mankind and lead him on through the influence of degrading pleasure. Therefore, it is either not incredible that there are goods which God does not possess, or else the very fact that God does not possess them is in itself a proof that these things are not goods. Besides, many things which are wont to be regarded as goods are granted to animals in fuller measure than to men. Animals eat their food with better appetite, are not in the same degree weakened by sexual indulgence, and have a greater and more uniform constancy in their strength. Consequently, they are much more fortunate than man. For there is no wickedness, no injury to themselves, in their way of living. They enjoy their pleasures and they take them more often and more easily, without any of the fear that results from shame or regret.

This being so, you should consider whether one has a right to call anything good in which God is outdone by man. Let us limit the Supreme Good to the soul; it loses its meaning if it is taken from the best part of us and applied to the worst, that is, if it is transferred to the senses; for the senses are more active in dumb beasts. The sum total of our happiness must not be placed in the flesh; the true goods are those which reason bestows, substantial and eternal; they cannot fall away, neither can they grow less or be diminished. Other things are goods according to opinion, and though they are called by the same name as the true goods, the essence of goodness is not in them. For a clear exposition of this topic, see Cicero, *On Ends* (De Finibus), iii. 52 ff.</margin> Otherwise, let us know that they are our chattels, not parts of ourselves; let them be with us, but in such a way that we remember they are outside ourselves. Even if they are with us, they should be counted among the subordinate and lowly things for which no one should puff himself up. For what is more foolish than for someone to take pleasure in what he himself did not create? Let all those things come to us, but not stick to us, so that if they are taken away, they leave without any tearing of ourselves. Let us use them, not boast of them, and let us use them sparingly as if they were entrusted to us and about to depart. Whoever possessed them without reason did not hold them for long; for prosperity itself, if it is not tempered, crushes itself. If one has trusted in the most fleeting goods, one is quickly deserted, and even if not deserted, one is distressed. Few have been allowed to lay aside prosperity gently; the rest fall along with the things amid which they had risen, and are weighed down by the very things that had exalted them. Therefore, prudence will be applied to impose a limit or frugality upon them, since unchecked license overthrows its own wealth. Things without limit have never lasted unless moderated by that guiding reason. The outcome of many cities will show you this, whose luxurious empires fell in their very prime, and whatever was gained by virtue, intemperance has destroyed.

Do you desire to know what this instrument of defense is? It is that he should not be angry at what happens to him, and should know that those very things by which he seems to be harmed pertain to the preservation of the universe and are among the things that fulfill the course and duty of the world. Let a man be pleased with whatever has pleased God; for this very reason let him admire himself and his own things—because he cannot be overcome, because he holds evils themselves under his control, and because he subdues chance, pain, and injury by means of reason, than which nothing is more powerful. Love reason! The love of this will arm you against the hardest things. The wildness of young animals drives them into the hunter's spears, and their ferocity and unthinking impulse keep them untamed; sometimes, a desire for glory has cast youthful minds into the contempt of both iron and fire; the appearance and shadow of virtue push some to voluntary death. How much stronger is reason than all these, how much more constant, so much more vehemently will it make its way through fears themselves and dangers.

The siege of your country, the death of your children, the enslavement of your parents will disturb you." I will set down what is usually answered on our behalf against these critics; then I will add what else I think ought to be answered.

The condition is different for those things which, when removed, substitute some inconvenience in their place; just as good health, when corrupted, shifts into poor health; the loss of eyesight afflicts us with blindness; not only does speed perish when the hamstrings are cut, but weakness takes its place. This is not the danger in the things we mentioned a little while ago. Why? If I have lost a good friend, I do not have to suffer treachery in his place, nor if I have buried good children, does impiety succeed them. Furthermore, the death is not of the friends or children themselves, but of their bodies. A "good" perishes in only one way: if it changes into an "evil"—which nature does not allow, because every virtue and every work of virtue remains uncorrupted. Furthermore, even if friends have perished, and even if children who were tested and responsive to a father's wishes have died, there is something to fill their place. You ask what it is? That which had made them good in the first place: virtue. It allows no place to be empty, it holds the whole mind, it takes away the longing for all things;

Raymond Lully <note>The *Doctor Illuminatus* (c. 1232–1315), a philosopher and polymath.</note> is said to have written five hundred separate treatises; the list may be seen in the first volume of an unfinished and impossible attempt to collect them into a folio edition, the editor supplying not only the precise years but the months in which they were composed. What Raymond did, as they say, could not have been impossible for Moses. But, in fact, the *doctor illuminatus* wrote only a small percentage of that gorgeous list, and reasonable criticism regards the spendthrift Israelite <note>Referring to Moses de Leon.</note> as a possible compiler and polisher who may have played a little at "writing out of his own head"—and that is all. This is not because it views the *Zohar* as the work of Simeon ben Jochai, or even of R. Abba, but because it recognizes R. Moses as a human being.

Graetz, the German historian of Jewry, whose distinctive criticism of Kabbalistic literature has gained much popularity, lays down a principle of criticism that ought to be written in capital letters at the head of most indictments of the *Zohar*: namely, that it is not compulsory for a hostile critic to be more careful in his arguments than those who plead in its defense. Without seeking to determine what is "compulsory" in criticism, it may be observed that there is no binding law to enforce serious consideration for a scholar who adopts that principle. What Graetz did openly has been done tacitly or unconsciously by others. There is, of course, little unanimity in hostile—or indeed any—Kabbalistic criticism. Just as, on the one hand, a defender of the *Zohar* challenges the *Bahir* excerpts, so have the latter been exalted as the prototype and actual inspirer of the former work. This view, though in any case of little moment, involves the existence of the *Bahir* prior to the alleged date when the *Zohar* was produced out of the head of Moses de Leon, like Minerva out of the head of Jupiter, ready-made and at one leap. Morinus, who has left perhaps the most sensible review of the subject, bases his opinion that the *Bahir* was a product of the thirteenth century on the silence of writers prior to that date, and especially of Moses Nachmanides, a Kabbalistic Jew of Jerusalem whose literary labors belong to the period before and after 1250. The proof is that the Italian Jew Recanati, a contemporary of Moses de Leon, used these quotations, and, misled by the name, inferred that they were from the Jerusalem Talmud <note>Original: *Yerushalmi*.</note>, but afterwards discovered them in the *Bahir*, to which a Palestinian origin is ascribed. By how much the lost treatise predated Azariel we have no grounds for conjecturing, but the position of Wolf and Morinus is destroyed by the fact recorded here, which leaves the *Bahir* where we should be disposed to place it: between the date when the *Sepher Yetzirah* is first mentioned and the publication of the *Zohar*.

The name *Bahir* refers to Job 37:21: "And now men see not the bright light which is in the clouds," according to the Authorized Version, or according to Dr. Durell's amended rendering, "And now men see not the light which is above (or within) the clouds, etc." Hence, "light in darkness" is a good equivalent of the Hebrew word. The subject matter of the book, which is in the form of a dialogue between certain enlightened doctors, is the mystery inherent in the divine names; it contains a very full exposition of the celebrated *Shemahamphoras* <term>Shemahamphoras</term> (the "Explicated Name" of God), the explained name of the deity. It belongs, therefore, to the least philosophical part of Kabbalism, and we can understand and sympathize with the instinctive dislike of Franck to accept the excerpts by which it is known to us. Facts, however, must have precedence over personal preferences, and though the later history of the doctrine of divine names may well make an admirer of the higher Kabbalism ashamed of

> "It is written: 'The silver is mine and the gold is mine, saith the Lord of Hosts.' What does this mean? It is like a king having two treasures, one of silver and one of gold. The first he put to his right and the second to his left, saying: 'This is prepared so that it is easy to spend it.' He has done everything in an easy way. Hence it is said: 'Thy right hand, O Lord, is become glorious in power' (Exodus 15:6). If a man may rejoice in his inheritance, it is good, but if not, it is said: 'Thy right hand, O Lord, hath dashed in pieces the enemy' (*Ibid*). What does this signify? Surely this is the gold. It is written: 'The silver is mine and the gold is mine.' Why do they call it gold? Because three measures are included in it. [That is to say, the word consists of three letters, Z H B, *Dzain*, *He*, *Beth*]. The *Dzain* is seven measures [*i.e.*, this letter represents the number 7]; the *He* is Unity [*i.e.*, A Ch D V Th, Unity = 419 = 5 according to Kabbalistic addition, and 5 is the number of *He*]; the *Beth* [representing the number 2] signifies *Chokmah* and *Binah*, and they are called *Neshamah* because of the last five *Sephiroth*. The *Neshamah* has five names: *Nephesh*, *Ruach*, *Neshamah*, *Chaiah*, and *Jechidah*." <note>Zohar, Cremona ed., part i. fol. 116b and 117a.</note>

The second excerpt concerns the Fall of Man, and its quotation is of some importance for the purpose of this study.

> "It is written: 'Now the serpent was more subtle than any beast of the field' (Genesis 3:1). R. Isaac said: 'That [the serpent] is the evil inclination.' R. Judah said: 'It is a real serpent.' When they came to R. Simeon, he said unto them: 'Surely it is all one; This is Samaël <note>Samaël: A figure often associated with Satan or the angel of death in Jewish mysticism.</note>, and he has been seen upon a serpent, but his shadow and the serpent are Satan, yet all are one. When Samaël descended from heaven, riding on this serpent, and his shadow was seen, all creatures fled from him, but coming to the woman with soft words he brought death to the whole world. Surely with wiles he invoked curses on the world and despoiled the first tree which the Holy Blessed One created in the world. [The reference here is apparently to the Sephirotic tree and, by implication, to the primordial Adam. Compare the Kabbalistic thesis of Picus de Mirandola: *Peccatum Adæ fuit truncatio Malkuth ab arbore Sephirotico* <note>Original Latin: "The sin of Adam was the cutting off of Malkuth from the Sephirotic tree."</note>.] The *Neshamah* of the male comes from male, and of the female from female [*i.e.*, from the male and female sides of the Sephirotic tree]. This is why the serpent had recourse to Chavah <note>Eve.</note>. He said unto himself: 'Because her soul is from the North I can persuade her quickly.' [The North, says Myer, is the left side, facing eastward in worship; it is therefore the side of wrath and severity, connected by the Kabbalists with the idea of the female. But the *Tikkune Ha Zohar* terms *Netzach* and *Hod* the *latera Aquilonis* <note>Original Latin: "Sides of the North."</note>. There is no consistency in these attributions.] And the persuasion has been because he came on her."

<header>THE VILLAGE GODS OF SOUTH INDIA</header>

The goddess is roughly represented on one side of it by pieces of silver and blotches of <term>kunkuma</term> <note>a red turmeric powder used for religious markings</note>, a red paste stuck on to represent the eyes, nose, mouth, etc. Sticks of incense were placed all around the lamp, and on the top were about four betel leaves stuck upright, forming a sort of cup with a wreath of white flowers below them. An <term>ārati</term> <note>a ritual of waving lights before a deity</note> was brought to me at Mysore by the <term>pūjāris</term> <note>priests or temple ministrants</note> for my inspection. It was a quaint object and seemed like the relic of some harvest festival from bygone days.

A common symbol of the village deities is simply a stick or a spear. It is very common in the Tamil country to see one or more iron spears stuck into the ground under a tree to represent a village deity. The idea seems to be that the deity is represented by their weapons. In the Telugu country, <term>Potu-Razu</term> <note>a male guardian deity, considered the brother or husband of the village goddess</term>, the brother or husband of the village goddess, is sometimes represented by a stone, and sometimes by a thin wooden stake like an attenuated post, about four or five feet high and roughly carved at the top. It faintly resembles a spear and is called <term>śūlam</term>, which in Telugu means a spear. <note>original: "Siva’s spear is called śūal in Sanskrit, and his trident is triśūla, three-spike."</note> Sometimes this stake stands beside a slab of stone representing <term>Potu-Razu</term>. At one village, the symbol of <term>Potu-Razu</term> is a painted wooden image about three feet high, representing a warrior sitting down with a sword in his hand, carrying a lime and nine glass bangles belonging to his sister, <term>Ellamma</term> <note>a powerful mother goddess</note>. Beside each foot is the figure of a cock, and a large painted mask is kept in the shrine for the <term>pūjāri</term> to wear at festivals as he dances around the image of <term>Potu-Razu</term>. However, elaborate images of <term>Potu-Razu</term> of this kind are not very often found.

Another symbol akin to these stakes and spears is the <term>Nattan Kal</term> <note>a planted stone or post</note> in the Tamil country. <term>Nattan</term> means "planted" and <term>Kal</term> means "a stone" or "post." The <term>Nattan Kal</term> is the first post of a wedding booth, set up at an auspicious moment, painted red and white, and adorned...
pages.41:
<header>THE CULT</header>

with various decorations, and worshipped with offerings of coconuts and flowers. The symbolism is obscure. The name is also applied to a small stone set up at the entrance to a village, which, according to a writer in *The Indian Interpreter* who reviewed the first edition of this book in the January 1917 issue, "is said to represent all the other <term>Nads</term> <note>territorial or clan divisions</note> which are comprised in the particular district to which that place belongs," and is worshipped on the occasion of a marriage. The reviewer thinks that "it is evident that it points back to a time when people were not so numerous or so widely separated, and when all could come to the marriage festivities," and that "when that time passed some means had to be found for the representation of the others." For this purpose, a stone was erected to symbolize the clan, and worship was offered to it. It is probable, however, that the stone placed at the entrance of Tamil villages is akin to the <term>Boddu-rayee</term>, or navel-stone, set up at the foundation of a village in the Telugu country, as described below on page 60, which probably represents—like the boundary-stone—the spirit of the land on which the village is built.

The <term>Nattan Kal</term> set up for the wedding booth may, in the same way, represent the spirit who presides over the procreation of children, and may possibly be a phallic emblem, like the <term>lingam</term> <note>an abstract or aniconic representation of the Hindu deity Shiva</note> of <term>Śiva</term>.

Why stones or posts should represent spirits in this way is difficult to explain. I have provided what seems to me a possible explanation below on page 148. But it must be admitted that all explanations can only be regarded as more or less probable hypotheses.

The shrines and images of <term>Kogillu</term>, a village in the <term>Mysore</term> country not far from <term>Bangalore</term>, are typical of that part of the country. At the extreme entrance to the village, near a tank, stands a small shrine of stone and mud sacred to the goddess <term>Pūjāmma</term> (she who is worshipped). On the stone door-posts are carved figures of serpents. Within the shrine there is no image of any kind, but on the left-hand side of the door is a platform covered with garlands of white flowers,
pages.42:
<header>THE VILLAGE GODS OF SOUTH INDIA</header>

with a small earthenware lamp upon it, which is kept burning day and night as a symbol of the goddess.

To the right of this shrine stands a smaller one dedicated to a goddess called <term>Dalamma</term>. No one in the village could tell me who the goddess was nor what her name meant. There was no image, lamp, or symbol of any kind in her shrine. An old picture frame, hung up on the wall to the left without any picture in it, was the only attempt at decoration or symbolism. Just within the doorway was a shallow trough about one and a half feet long, one foot broad, and two inches deep, where the worshippers break their coconuts.

In front of the larger shrine stood an enclosure about five or six yards square, enclosed by a stone wall, with four slabs of stone in the center on which a platform is erected, covered by a canopy of cloth and leaves during the annual festival. The lighted lamp is then brought out from the shrine, placed under the canopy, and worshipped as the symbol of the goddess. Apparently, cattle are tethered in the enclosure at other times, and when I saw it, there were no obvious marks of sanctity about it. About twenty yards off stands the <term>Cattle Stone</term>, a slab of rough stone about five feet high and three feet broad, set upon a stone platform about one and a half feet high. When the cattle get sore feet, their owners pour curds over the <term>Cattle Stone</term> for their recovery.

Near the <term>Cattle Stone</term>, in a field on the outskirts of the houses, stands a square stone pillar, about five feet high and half a foot in thickness, without any carving or ornament on it whatever. It represents <term>Maramma</term>, the goddess of smallpox and other epidemics, a most malignant spirit. Apparently, she had been brought to this village by some people who had migrated from another village called <term>Hethana</term>; whence she is called <term>Maramma-Hethana</term>. Buffaloes and sheep are offered to her whenever epidemics break out.

The <term>grāma-devatā</term> <note>village deity</note> herself—she has no other name—has no permanent image in this village. The gold-
pages.43:
<header>THE CULT</header>

smith makes an image of clay in the form of a woman, about one or one and a half feet high, every year at the annual festival, which takes place after harvest. She is then placed in the center of the village under a canopy of green boughs. One striking feature of this festival is that on the first day, a woman comes from every household to the place of worship with a lighted lamp made of rice flour, called <term>āratī</term>; they all together wave their lamps in a circle from left to right above their heads and from right to left below. When the festival is over, the washerman of the village, who acts as <term>pūjārī</term>, accompanied by all the villagers, takes the image to the tank, walks into the water, and leaves it there. In some villages in the Mysore State, the <term>āratī</term> is presented by the men, the heads of the households, and not by the women. But in all the annual festivals in these parts, the presentation of the <term>āratī</term>, which often seems to be regarded as a symbol of the deity herself, forms an important part of the ceremonial.

*Ministrants.* One of the most striking features of the worship of the village deities is the absence of anything like a priestly caste in connection with it. Every other department of village work belongs to a special caste, and in the ordinary worship of <term>Vishnu</term> and <term>Śiva</term>, the priestly caste of the <term>Brāhmans</term> is supreme. But in the worship of the village deities, the <term>pūjārīs</term> are drawn from all the lower castes indiscriminately, though in any one village the <term>pūjārīs</term> of a particular goddess nearly always belong to one particular caste.

I have occasionally found a <term>Brāhman</term> in charge of a <term>grāma-devatā</term> shrine in the Tamil country. But then, as I have noted above, the <term>Brāhman pūjārī</term> never takes any part in the animal sacrifices, and, even so, is degraded by his connection with the shrine. In the Telugu country, the potters and the washermen, who are <term>Śūdras</term> <note>the fourth caste in the Hindu hierarchy</note> of low caste, often officiate as priests, and
pages.44:
<header>THE VILLAGE GODS OF SOUTH INDIA</header>

an important part, especially in the buffalo sacrifices, is taken by the <term>Mālās</term> and <term>Mādigās</term>. <note>The Mālās and Mādigās are the chief groups of outcasts in the Telugu country.</note>

A <term>Mādiga</term> nearly always kills the buffalo and performs the unpleasant ceremonies connected with the sprinkling of the blood, and there are certain families among the <term>Mālās</term>, called <term>Asādis</term>, who are the nearest approach to a priestly caste in connection with the village deities. They have the hereditary right to assist at the sacrifices, to chant the praises of the goddess while the sacrifices are being offered, and to perform certain ceremonies. But in the more primitive villages, where it may be presumed that primitive customs prevail, it is remarkable how great a variety of people take an official part in the worship: the potter, the carpenter, the toddy-drawer, the washerman, <term>Mālās</term> and <term>Mādigās</term>, and even the <term>Brāhman Karṇam</term> <note>village accountant</note>, all have their parts to play.

In the Tamil country this is not so marked, and the details of the worship are left far more to the regular <term>pūjārī</term>. It is noticeable that the office of <term>pūjārī</term> is by no means an honorable one, and this is especially the case among the Tamils, where <term>Brāhman</term> influence is strong and the shedding of blood is regarded with aversion. Even among the <term>Brāhmans</term> themselves, though they owe their influence to the fact that they are the priestly caste, the men who serve these temples are regarded as having a lower position in the caste than those <term>Brāhmans</term> engaged in secular pursuits.

Among the <term>Canarese</term> in the Bellary district, the <term>Asādis</term> take a similar part in the worship to the <term>Asādis</term> in the Telugu country. In the whole of the Bellary district, there are about sixty families of them living in three separate villages. They form practically a separate caste or section of the Outcastes. They eat food given them by the <term>Mādigās</term> and take their girls in marriage. The <term>Asādi</term> girls, however, never marry, but

are made <term>Basavīs</term> <note>women consecrated to a deity, often living as temple prostitutes</note>—that is, they are consecrated to the goddess and become prostitutes. Certainly, the degradation of religion in India is seen all too plainly in the degradation of the priesthood.

*Festivals.* There is no act of uniformity and no ecclesiastical calendar regulating the festivals or forms of worship of village deities, and no universal custom as to the appointment of ministrants. In some villages, where there is a permanent shrine, offerings of rice, fruit, and flowers, with incense and camphor, are made every day by the villagers who have made vows to the goddess, through the <term>pūjārī</term>. Often offerings are made once or twice a week, on fixed days, consisting chiefly of grain, fruit, and flowers, and occasionally of goats, sheep, and fowls. In many places there is a fixed annual festival, which sometimes takes place after harvest when the people are at leisure and have plenty of food; but there is no regular rule as to the time, and the custom varies widely in different districts. In most places, however, there is no regular annual festival, but sacrifices are offered whenever an epidemic or any other calamity occurs which may make it expedient to propitiate the goddess. In some villages, old men complained to me that whereas formerly sacrifices were offered yearly, now, owing to the decay of religion, they are only offered once in four or five years. So, again, there is no uniformity as to the duration of a festival. Generally it lasts about a week, but in the Tamil country it is sometimes a very elaborate affair, lasting for a fortnight, three weeks, or even a whole month; so too in some parts of the Canarese country, the <term>Māri</term> <note>goddess of smallpox/disease</note> festival, which is held in February, lasts for about four weeks. But a long festival is an expensive luxury that only a large town or a well-to-do village is able to afford. Speaking generally, the object of the festival is simply to propitiate the goddess.

<meta>Continuity with page 130: The text continues the discussion of why upright men face hardship, shifting toward the Stoic definition of the "Supreme Good."</meta>

# EPISTLE LXXIV.

...upright men often suffer misfortunes,<note>See Epistle LXXIII, section 14: "Jupiter cannot use them [external goods] as his own."</note> and that the time which is allotted to us is but short and scanty, if you compare it with the eternity which is allotted to the universe.

It is a result of complaints like these that we are unappreciative in our comments upon the gifts of heaven; we complain because they are not always granted to us, because they are few and unsure and fleeting. Hence we have not the will either to live or to die; we are possessed by hatred of life and by fear of death. Our plans are all adrift, and no amount of prosperity can satisfy us. And the reason for all this is that we have not yet attained to that good which is immeasurable and unsurpassable, in which all wishing on our part must cease, because there is no place beyond the highest. Do you ask why virtue needs nothing? Because it is pleased with what it has, and does not lust after that which it has not. Whatever is enough is abundant in the eyes of virtue.

Dissent from this judgment, and duty and loyalty will not abide. For one who desires to exhibit these two qualities must endure much that the world calls evil; we must sacrifice many things to which we are addicted, thinking them to be "goods." Gone is courage, which should be continually testing itself; gone is greatness of soul, which cannot stand out clearly unless it has learned to scorn as trivial everything that the crowd covets as supremely important; and gone is kindness and the repaying of kindness, if we fear toil, if we have acknowledged anything to be more precious than loyalty, if our eyes are fixed upon anything except the best.

But to pass these questions by: either these so-called goods are not goods, or else man is more
pages.132:
# THE EPISTLES OF SENECA

fortunate than God, since God has no use for the things that are provided for us. Lust, elegant banquets, wealth, and any of the other things that entice man and lead him toward base pleasure have no relevance to Him. Therefore, it is either not unbelievable that God lacks these "goods," or the very fact that God lacks them is proof that they are not goods at all. Add to this that many things which are thought to be goods are granted more abundantly to animals than to humans. They use their food more greedily, they are not equally exhausted by sexual indulgence, and their strength is greater and more consistent. It follows that they would be much happier than man. For they live without wickedness and without fraud. They enjoy their pleasures, which they grasp more fully and easily, without any fear of shame or regret.

16 Therefore, consider whether that should be called a "good" by which man surpasses God. Let us keep the Supreme Good within the soul; it withers if it is transferred from our best part to our worst, and moved to the senses, which are more active in dumb animals. Our happiness is not to be placed in the flesh. The true goods are those which reason bestows—solid and eternal—which cannot fall, nor even decrease or be diminished. Other things are goods only in opinion; they share a name with true goods, but they do not possess the true essence of goodness. Therefore, let them be called "advantages," and, to speak in our own tongue,

<margin>a Cf. Ep. lxxiii. § 14 *Jupiter cannot use them.*</margin>
pages.133:
# EPISTLE LXXIV.

"preferred" things. Let us, however, recognize that they are our chattels, not parts of ourselves; and let us have them in our possession, but take heed to remember that they are outside ourselves. Even though they are in our possession, they are to be reckoned as things subordinate and poor, the possession of which gives no man a right to pride himself. For what is more foolish than being self-complacent about something which one has not accomplished by one's own efforts? Let everything of this nature be added to us, and not stick fast to us, so that, if it is withdrawn, it may come away without tearing off any part of us. Let us use these things, but not boast of them, and let us use them sparingly, as if they were given for safe-keeping and will be withdrawn. Anyone who does not employ reason in his possession of them never keeps them long; for prosperity of itself, if uncontrolled by reason, overwhelms itself. If anyone has put his trust in goods that are most fleeting, he is soon bereft of them, and, to avoid being bereft, he suffers distress. Few men have been permitted to lay aside prosperity gently. The rest all fall, together with the things amid which they have come into eminence, and they are weighted down by the very things which had before exalted them. For this reason foresight must be brought into play, to insist upon a limit or upon frugality in the use of these things, since license overthrows and destroys its own abundance. That which has no limit has never endured, unless reason, which sets limits, has held it in check. The fate of many cities will prove the truth of this; their sway has ceased at the very prime because they were given to luxury, and excess has ruined all that had been won by virtue.

# THE EPISTLES OF SENECA

We must arm ourselves against these occurrences. However, there is no wall so impregnable against Fortune that it cannot be taken by storm; we must be built up from within. If the inner part is safe, a man may be struck, but he cannot be captured.

20 Do you wish to know what this instrument of defense is? It is the ability to refrain from being angry at anything that happens to one, and to know that those very things which seem to cause injury belong to the preservation of the universe and are among the things that complete the course and duty of the world. Let man be pleased with whatever has pleased God; let him marvel at himself and his own resources for this very reason: that he cannot be conquered, that he holds even "evils" beneath him, and that by reason—than which nothing is stronger—he subdues chance, pain, and injury. Love reason! The love of it will arm you against the hardest things. The ferocity of wild beasts drives them into the hunter's spears out of love for their young, and their wildness and heedless impulse keep them indomitable; sometimes a desire for glory has driven young spirits to despise both the sword and the fire; the mere vision and shadow of virtue drives some to a voluntary death. Insofar as reason is stronger and more constant than all these, so much more forcefully will it emerge through fears themselves and through dangers.

22 "You achieve nothing," someone says, "by denying that there is any good other than the honorable; this defense will not make you safe from Fortune and immune to her. For you say that among goods..."
pages.135:
# EPISTLE LXXIV.

"are dutiful children, a well-governed country, and good parents; you cannot look upon the dangers of these things with a secure mind. You will be disturbed by the siege of your country, the death of your children, and the enslavement of your parents." I will set down what is usually answered for us against these points; then I will add what I myself think should be answered.

The situation is different regarding things which, when taken away, replace themselves with some disadvantage; for instance, good health, if corrupted, turns into a malady; if the sharpness of our eyes is extinguished, it subjects us to blindness; in this case, not only does speed vanish when the tendons are cut, but weakness takes its place. This is not the danger in the things we listed a moment ago. Why? If I have lost a good friend, I do not have to suffer treachery in his place; nor, if I have buried good children, does impiety take their place. Furthermore, what is lost there is not the friends or the children themselves, but their bodies. A "good" perishes in only one way: if it turns into an "evil"—which nature does not allow, because every virtue and every work of virtue remains uncorrupted. Furthermore, even if friends have perished, even if children who were tested and responsive to a father's prayers are gone, there is something to fill their place. Do you ask what it is? That which had made them good in the first place: virtue. This allows no space to remain empty; it occupies the whole soul and takes away the longing for all else.
