# THE SAFFRON-FLOWER 203

Taking pity on them, one of Genji's servants went to their assistance and quickly opened it. Genji remembered the poem in which <term>Po Chü-i</term> <note>A famous Chinese poet whose works were highly influential in Japanese court culture.</note> describes the sufferings of villagers in wintry weather and he murmured the lines: "The little children run naked in the cold; the aged shiver for lack of winter clothes." All at once, he remembered the chilly appearance that unhappy bloom had given to the princess's face, and he could not help smiling. If ever he were able to show her to Tō no Chūjō, what strange comparison, he wondered, would Chūjō use concerning it? He remembered how Chūjō had followed him on the first occasion. Had he continued to do so? Perhaps even at this minute he was under observation. The thought irritated him.

Had her defects been less striking, he could not possibly have continued these distressing visits. But since he had actually seen her in all her tragic uncouthness, pity gained the upper hand, and from then on, he kept in constant touch with her and showed her every kindness. In the hope that she would abandon her sables, he sent her presents of silk, satin, and quilted stuffs. He also sent thick cloth such as old people wear, so that the old man at the gate might be more comfortably dressed. Indeed, he sent presents to everyone on the estate, from the highest to the lowest. She did not seem to have any objection to receiving these donations, which, under the circumstances, was very convenient, as it enabled him for the most part to limit their very singular friendship to good offices of this kind.

Utsusemi, too, he remembered, had seemed to him far from handsome when he had peeped at her on the evening of her sudden flight. But she at least knew how to behave, and that saved her plainness from being obtrusive. It was hard to believe that the princess belonged to a class so far above that of Utsusemi. It only showed how little...

these things have to do with birth or station. For in idle moments he still regretted the loss of Utsusemi, and it rankled in him yet that he had, in the end, allowed her unyielding persistency to win the day. <insert>He only wants what he can't have.</insert>

And so the year drew to its close. One day when he was at his apartments in the Emperor's Palace, Myōbu came to see him. He liked to have her do his hair and handle small commissions for him. He was not in the least in love with her, but they got on very well together, and he found her conversation so amusing that even when she had no duty to perform at the Palace, he encouraged her to come and see him whenever she had any news. "Something so absurd has happened," she said, "that I can hardly bring myself to tell you about it," and she paused, smiling. "I can hardly think," answered Genji, "that there can be anything you are frightened of telling me." "If it were connected with my own affairs," she said, "you know quite well that I should tell you at once. But this is something quite different. I really find it very hard to talk about." For a long while he could get nothing out of her, and only after he had scolded her for making so unnecessary a fuss did she at last hand him a letter. It was from the princess. "But this," said Genji, taking it, "is the last thing in the world that you could have any reason to hide from me." She watched with interest while he read it. It was written on thick paper drenched with a strong perfume; the characters were bold and firm. With it was a poem: "Because of your hard heart, your hard heart only, the sleeves of this my Chinese dress are drenched with tears." The poem must, he thought, refer to something not contained in the letter.

He was considering what this could be when his eye fell on a clumsy, old-fashioned clothes-box wrapped in a painted canvas cover. "Now," said Myōbu, "perhaps you...

understand why I was feeling rather uncomfortable. You may not believe it, but the princess means for you to wear this jacket on New Year's Day. I am afraid I cannot take it back to her; that would be too unkind. But if you like, I will keep it for you and no one else shall see it. Only please, since it was to you that she sent it, just have one look at it before it goes away." "But I should hate it to go away," said Genji; "I think it was so kind of her to send it." It was difficult to know what to say. Her poem was indeed the most unpleasant jangle of syllables that he had ever encountered. He now realized that the other poems must have been dictated to her, perhaps by Jijū or one of the other ladies. And Jijū, too, it must surely be who held the princess's brush and acted as writing-master. When he considered what her utmost poetic endeavor would be likely to produce, he realized that these absurd verses were probably her masterpiece and should be prized accordingly. He began to examine the parcel; Myōbu blushed while she watched him. It was a plain, old-fashioned, buff-colored jacket of finely woven material, but apparently not particularly well cut or stitched. It was indeed a strange present, and spreading out her letter, he wrote something carelessly in the margin. When Myōbu looked over his shoulder, she saw that he had written the verse: "How comes it that with my sleeve I brushed this saffron-flower<note>1</note> that has no loveliness either of shape or hue?"

What, wondered Myōbu, could be the meaning of this outburst against a flower? At last, turning over in her mind the various occasions when Genji had visited the princess, she remembered something<note>2</note> which she had herself noticed one moonlit night, and though she felt the joke was rather unkind, she could not help being amused. With practiced...

ease she threw out a verse in which she warned him that in the eyes of a censorious world, even this half-whimsical courtship might fatally damage his good name. Her impromptu poem was certainly faulty, but Genji reflected that if the poor princess had even Myōbu’s very ordinary degree of alertness, it would make things much easier; and it was quite true that to tamper with a lady of such high rank was not very safe.

At this point, visitors began to arrive. "Please put this somewhere out of sight," said Genji, pointing to the jacket; "could one have believed that it was possible to be presented with such an object?" and he groaned. "Oh, why ever did I show it to him?" thought Myōbu. "The only result is that now he will be angry with me as well as with the princess," and in very low spirits she slipped out of his apartments.

Next day, she was in attendance upon the Emperor, and while she was waiting with other gentlewomen in the ladies’ common-room, Genji came up, saying: "Here you are. The answer to yesterday’s letter. I am afraid it is rather far-fetched," and he flung a note to her. The curiosity of the other gentlewomen was violently aroused. Genji left the room humming "The Lady of Mikasa Hill,"<note>1</note> which naturally amused Myōbu very much. The other ladies wanted to know why the prince was laughing to himself. Was there some joke...? "Oh, no," said Myōbu; "I think it was only that he had noticed someone whose nose was a little red with the morning cold. The song he hummed was surely very appropriate." "I think it was very silly," said one of the ladies. "There is no one here today with a red nose. He must be thinking of Lady Sakon or Higo no Uneme." They were completely mystified. When...

# THE SAFFRON-FLOWER 207

Myōbu presented Genji's reply, the ladies of the Hitachi Palace gathered round her to admire it. It was written negligently on plain white paper but was nonetheless very elegant. "Does your gift of a garment mean that you wish a greater distance than ever to be kept between us?"<note>1</note>

On the evening of the last day of the year, he sent back the box which had contained his jacket, putting into it a court dress which had formerly been presented to him: a dress of woven stuff dyed grape-color, and various stuffs of yellow-rose color and the like. The box was brought by Myōbu. The princess's ancient gentlewomen realized that Genji did not approve of their mistress's taste in colors and wished to give her a lesson. "Yes," they said grudgingly, "that's a fine deep red while it's new, but just think how it will fade. And in Madam's poem, too, I am sure, there was much more good sense. In his answer, he only tries to be smart." The princess shared their good opinion of her poem. It had cost her a great deal of effort, and before she sent it she had been careful to copy it into her notebook.

Then came the New Year's Day celebrations; and this year there was also the New Year's "mumming," a band of young noblemen going round dancing and singing in various parts of the Palace. After the festival of the White Horse on the seventh day, Genji left the Emperor's presence at nightfall and went to his own apartments in the Palace, as though intending to stay the night there. But later he adjourned to the Hitachi Palace, which had on this occasion a less forbidding appearance than usual. Even the princess was rather more ordinary and amenable. He was hoping that, like the season, she too had begun anew, when he saw that sunlight was coming into the room. After hesitating for a while, he got up and went out into the front room. The...

people will revert to the witchcraft of savages or peasants, which may be revived in some obscure American village and pursued by the gullible and simple-minded. When that happens, the desired phenomena will be provided through the sleight of hand of charlatans. Since it is easy to prove the quackery of paid "mediums"—and that, in any case, is a <term>vera causa</term> <note>original: "vera causa"; Latin for "true cause," meaning an established or proven reason for an effect</note>—the theory of "Survival and Revival" seems adequate. Yet, there are two circumstances that suggest the situation is not so straightforward. 

The first is the constant reporting of "spontaneous" and sporadic abnormal phenomena: clairvoyance (whether in or out of a hypnotic trance), effects on the mind and senses apparently produced by the action of a distant mind, hallucinations that coincide with remote events, physical prodigies that defy the law of gravity, or inexplicable sounds, lights, and other occurrences in certain places. These are precisely the things that medicine men, mediums, and classical diviners have always claimed to provoke and produce through specific arts or rituals. 

Secondly, whether or not these performers occasionally succeed without resorting to fraud, the "spontaneous" phenomena are attested by a volume and quality of evidence—ancient, medieval, and modern—that would demand serious attention in any other field. Living, sane, and scientifically trained men today—not to mention the ingenious and intelligent, if superstitious, observers of the past, Catholic collectors of contemporary evidence regarding saintly miracles, and witnesses, judges, and juries in witchcraft trials—are all undeniably "telling the same story."

<summary>Lang argues that while fraud explains many mediumistic feats, the persistence of reported "spontaneous" paranormal events across history and among sane observers suggests a deeper psychological phenomenon worth investigating.</summary>
<keywords>necromancy, mediums, survival and revival, spontaneous phenomena, clairvoyance, witchcraft</keywords>

<header>COCK LANE AND COMMON-SENSE.</header>

<margin>0 0 1</margin>
We can easily devise an explanation for the stories told by savages, fanatics, peasants, those under religious influence, witches, and the victims of witches. That is simple. But why are sane, modern, scientific observers—and even cynical modern skeptics—telling the same story, and specifically the old "savage" story? What makes them repeat the stories they do? We are not asking so much, "Are these stories true?" as "Why are these stories told?" Professor Ray Lankester <note>original: E. Ray Lankester, a prominent British zoologist and evolutionary biologist</note> poses the question this way, and we are still struggling for an answer.

Meanwhile, modern science has actually accepted as real some strange psychological phenomena that both science and common sense rejected between 1720 and 1840. Historically, these accepted phenomena are always reported as accompanying the even stranger—and still rejected—occurrences. We are thus faced with a curious question of evidence: To what extent do educated modern observers share the same illusions as Native Americans, Kaffirs, Eskimos, Samoyeds, Australians, and Maoris? To what extent does the alignment of their testimony with that of cultures so differently situated and trained justify curiosity, interest, and perhaps a suspension of judgment?

The value of these facts must be determined by physiologists, physicians, physicists, and psychologists. It is clear that the alleged phenomena—both those now accepted and those still rejected—attend, or are said to attend, people of a unique physical constitution. It is not for nothing that Iamblichus, when describing the constitution of his diviner or seer and the phenomena they display, should exactly describe a man like St. Joseph of Cupertino, whose miracles were recorded in the *Acta Sanctorum* <note>original: "Acta Sanctorum"; the "Acts of the Saints," a massive collection of documents concerning the lives and miracles of Catholic saints</note> (1603–1663).

<summary>Lang questions why modern scientific observers report phenomena similar to those reported by "savage" cultures and suggests that these accounts, often tied to specific physical types, merit closer study.</summary>
<keywords>Ray Lankester, Iamblichus, psychological phenomena, cross-cultural testimony, St. Joseph of Cupertino</keywords>
pages.33:
<page-num>9</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTION.</header>

Certain scientific and (as a layperson might assume) qualified individuals claim to have seen and even tested, in modern instances, the very phenomena insisted upon by Iamblichus, the Bollandists <note>original: The Bollandists, a group of Jesuit hagiographers dedicated to the critical study of saints' lives</note>, and a great company of witnesses in all climates, ages, and levels of culture. However, these few scientific observers are dismissed by the vast majority of physicists and psychologists. It is with this majority—if they choose to find the time and can muster the inclination for the task of prolonged and patient experimentation—that the ultimate decision regarding the significance of these facts must rest. The problem cannot be solved or settled by amateurs, nor by "common sense," which:

> Delivers brawling judgments all day long,
> On all things, unashamed.

Ignorance, however respectable and however contemptuous, is certainly not an infallible oracle on any subject. Meanwhile, most representatives of physical science—perhaps all official representatives—hold themselves aloof, not merely from performances or pretenses that can only be criticized by professional conjurers, but from the entire mass of reported abnormal events. Because the occurrences are admitted, even by believers, to depend on fluctuating and uncertain personal conditions, the reluctance of physicists to examine them is very natural and understandable.

<summary>Lang notes that while some scientists verify these phenomena, the majority of the scientific establishment ignores them, preferring to dismiss the subject rather than commit to long-term investigation.</summary>
<keywords>Iamblichus, Bollandists, scientific methodology, academic skepticism</keywords>
pages.34:
<page-num>10</page-num>
<header>COCK LANE AND COMMON-SENSE.</header>

Whether the determination to avoid research into these matters, and to denounce their investigation as having dangerous moral consequences, is scientific or simply "obscurantist," every person may decide for themselves. The pursuit of truth is usually supposed to be indifferent to consequences. Meanwhile, until science offers an opinion—until *Roma locuta est* <note>original: "Roma locuta est, causa finita est"; "Rome has spoken, the case is closed"—an old phrase suggesting a definitive, authoritative judgment</note>—and provided it does not simply assert a prejudice after a hurried inquiry (or no inquiry at all), mere literary and historical students cannot be expected to provide a verdict.

Spiritualists, and even less convinced individuals, have frequently denounced official men of science for not conducting more careful and prolonged investigations into this murky region. It is not enough, they say, to unmask one imposture or to sit in the dark four or five times with a "medium." This matter demands the close scrutiny of years and the most patient and persevering experimentation.

This sounds very plausible, but the few official men of science whose names the public recognizes (and it is astonishing how famous a scientist may be among peers while remaining unknown to the public) can easily answer their accusers: "What," they might cry, "are we to investigate? It is absurd to ask us to abandon our specialized studies and sit for many hours, over many years, likely in the dark, with an epileptic person and a few hysterical believers. We are not magicians or judges of stage magic." Furthermore, is a man like Professor Huxley or Lord Kelvin supposed to travel the country, examining every cottage where there are rumors of curious noises and where stones and...

<summary>Lang discusses the tension between spiritualists demanding scientific validation and scientists who reject these "dark" investigations as beneath their expertise and professional dignity.</summary>
<keywords>Spiritualism, scientific skepticism, Professor Huxley, Lord Kelvin, research methodology</keywords>
pages.35:
<page-num>II</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTION.</header>

...other missiles are thrown by invisible hands? That is the business of the police. If the police are baffled, as they were in a "Cock Lane" style affair at Port Glasgow in 1864 and in Paris in 1846, we cannot expect men of science to act as amateur detectives.<note>The Port Glasgow story is in the *Report of the Dialectical Society*, p. 200. The flooring was torn up; walls, ceilings, and cellars were examined by the police, and attempts were made to imitate the noises, without success. In this case, as at Rerrick in the late seventeenth century and elsewhere, "the appearance of a hand moving up and down" was seen by the family, "but we could not catch it: it quietly vanished, and we only felt cold air." The house was occupied by a gardener, Hugh McCardle. The names of witnesses, a police sergeant, and others are appended.</note> Again, it is hardly to be expected that our chosen modern leaders of opinion will devote themselves to cross-examining ladies and gentlemen who tell ghost stories. Barristers and solicitors would be better suited for that task. Thus, almost nothing remains for physical science to investigate except the conduct and utterances of the hysterical, the epileptic, the hypnotized, and other subjects who are occasionally said to display an abnormal extension of their perceptive faculties, such as through clairvoyance. To the unscientific mind, it seems conceivable that if someone like [Daniel Dunglas] Home could have been kept in an establishment like the Salpêtrière <note>original: "Salpetrière"; a famous Paris hospital known for its psychiatric wards and research on hysteria</note> for a year and studied like other hysterical patients, his claims might have been decided once and for all. Instead, he performed only a few *speciosa miracula* <note>original: "speciosa miracula"; Latin for "showy miracles"</note> under tests set by one or two English men of science, and believers and skeptics are still left to argue over him.

<summary>Lang argues that scientists are ill-equipped to investigate "ghost" sightings, noting that such tasks fall more logically to police or legal professionals, while proposing that clinical study of "mediums" might yield more definitive results.</summary>
<keywords>Cock Lane affair, Port Glasgow, Salpetrière, Daniel Dunglas Home, clairvoyance, clinical investigation</keywords>
pages.36:
<page-num>12</page-num>
<header>COCK LANE AND COMMON-SENSE.</header>

...and skeptics are still left to wrangle over him; they usually introduce questions of moral character. A few men of science in England, such as Dr. Gregory around 1851 and Dr. Carpenter, along with a larger number on the continent, have examined and are still examining these peculiarities. Their reports are often sufficiently astonishing to the lay mind.

No doubt when—if ever—a large and imposing body of these reports is presented by a crowd of scientific witnesses of esteemed reputation, official science will dedicate more time and study to the topic than it is currently inclined to do. Mr. [Alfred Russel] Wallace has asserted that "whenever the scientific men of any age have denied, on *a priori* <note>original: "a priori"; Latin for "from the earlier"—reasoning from theoretical deduction rather than empirical observation</note> grounds, the facts of investigation, they have always been wrong."<note>Report of Dialectical Society, p. 86.</note> He adds that Galileo, Harvey, Jenner, Franklin, Young, and Arago—when he "wanted even to discuss the subject of the electric telegraph"—were "vehemently opposed by their scientific contemporaries," "laughed at as dreamers," "ridiculed," and so on, much like the early observers of Paleolithic axes and similar prehistoric remains. This is true, of course, but just because some correct ideas were once laughed at, it does not follow that everything laughed at is correct. People who try to square the circle, discoverers of perpetual motion, and those inquiring into the origin of language have all been ridiculed and ruled out of court—the first two groups, at least, quite justly. Now, official science apparently regards all these long-rumored abnormal occurrences as being in the same category as Keely’s Motor and Perpetual Motion, rather than in the same category as the wave theory of light or the circulation of the blood.

<summary>Lang explores the resistance of "official science" to new discoveries, comparing the dismissal of paranormal reports to the historical rejection of now-accepted scientific breakthroughs.</summary>
<keywords>Dr. Gregory, Dr. Carpenter, Alfred Russel Wallace, scientific history, Galileo, paradigm shifts</keywords>
pages.37:
<page-num>13</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTION.</header>

Clairvoyance, ghosts, or the suspension of the laws of gravity are things so widely contradictory to general experience and ascertained laws that they are pronounced impossible; like perpetual motion, they are not granted a hearing.

As for the undeniable phenomenon that, in every land, age, and condition of culture, and in every stage of belief or disbelief, some observers have persistently asserted their experience of these occurrences; as for the phenomenon that the testimonies of Australian blacks, Samoyeds, Hurons, Greeks, European peasants, Catholic and Covenanting clergy, and even some scientifically trained modern physicians and chemists are all aligned, official physical science leaves these things to anthropology and folklore. Yet the coincidence of such strange testimony is a singular fact in human nature. Even people with open minds can, at present, say no more than that there is a great deal of smoke—a puzzling quantity, if there be no fire—and that either human nature is very easily deluded by simple sleight of hand, or that, in all stages of culture, minds are subject to identical hallucinations. The whole hocus-pocus of "spirit-writing" on slates and in pellets of paper has been satisfactorily exposed and explained as a rather simple kind of *leger-de-main* <note>original: "leger-de-main"; French for "sleight of hand"</note>. But this was a purely modern sort of trickery; the old universal class of "useless miracles," said to occur spontaneously, still presents problems of undeniable psychological interest.

<summary>Lang highlights the consistency of paranormal testimonies across vastly different cultures and eras, arguing that while much of "spiritualism" is fraud, the underlying spontaneous reports warrant serious psychological investigation.</summary>
<keywords>clairvoyance, anthropology, folklore, cross-cultural testimony, hallucinations, spirit-writing</keywords>
pages.38:
<page-num>14</page-num>
<header>COCK LANE AND COMMON-SENSE.</header>

For example, if it is granted—as Dr. Carpenter apparently did—that in certain circumstances, people who are wide awake can perform intelligent actions and produce intelligent expressions automatically without being conscious of what they are doing, then that fact is nearly as interesting and useful as the fact that we are descended from protozoa. Dr. Carpenter says that in "table-talking," "cases have occasionally occurred in the experience of persons above suspicion of intentional deception, in which the answers given by the movements of tables were not only unknown to the questioners, but were even contrary to their belief at the time, and yet afterwards proved to be true." Such cases, he argues, offer typical examples of "unconscious cerebration" <note>original: "unconscious cerebration"; a 19th-century term for the theory that the brain can perform complex tasks or retrieve memories without the conscious mind being aware of them</note>. In several of them, it was clearly shown that the answers, although contrary to the questioners' beliefs at the time, were true to facts they had once known but had forgotten. The remnants of these forgotten impressions gave rise to cerebral changes that prompted the responses without the agents being conscious of the hidden sources of their actions. It is apparently to be understood that, since the existence of latent, unconscious knowledge was traced in "several" cases, the explanation therefore held good in all cases, even where it could not be established as a fact.

Let us see how this theory works out in practice.

<summary>Lang introduces the concept of "unconscious cerebration" as a scientific explanation for mysterious phenomena like table-talking, while questioning if this theory truly covers all reported cases.</summary>
<keywords>Dr. Carpenter, unconscious cerebration, table-talking, memory, psychological theories</keywords>

pages.217:
# THE TALE OF GENJI

The double doors at the end of the eastern wing were wide open. The roof of the verandah had fallen in, so the sunshine poured straight into the house. A little snow was still falling, and its brightness made the morning light look even more exquisitely brilliant and sparkling. She watched a servant helping him into his cloak. She was lying halfway out of the bed, her head hanging slightly downwards, with her hair falling in great waves to the floor. Pleased with the sight, he began to wonder whether she would not one day outgrow her plainness. He began to close the door of the women’s apartments, but suddenly feeling that he owed her amends for the harsh opinion of her appearance he had formed earlier, he did not quite shut the door. Instead, he brought a low stool toward it and sat there, putting his disordered head-dress to rights. One of the maids brought him an incredibly battered mirror-stand, Chinese combs, a box of toilet articles, and other things. It amused him to discover that in this household of women, a little male gear still survived, even in such a decrepit state.

He noticed that the princess, who was now up and dressed, was looking quite fashionable. She was, in fact, wearing the clothes which he had sent her before the New Year, but he did not at first recognize them. He began, however, to have a vague idea that her mantle, with its rather conspicuous pattern, was very like one of the items he had given her. "I do hope," he said presently, "that this year you will be a little more conversational. I await the day when you will unbend a little toward me, more eagerly than the poet longs for the first nightingale. If only, like the year that has changed, you too would begin anew!" Her face brightened. She had thought of a remark, and trembling from head to foot with a tremendous effort, she brought out the quotation: "When plovers chirp and all things grow anew." "Splendid," said Genji. "This is a sign that the new year has indeed
pages.218:
# THE SAFFRON-FLOWER 209

begun," and smiling encouragingly at her, he left the house. She followed him with her eyes from the couch on which she lay. Her face, as usual, was half covered by her arm; but the unfortunate flower<note>Referring to the "Saffron-Flower" princess, known for her red nose.</note> still bloomed conspicuously. "Poor thing, she really is very ugly," thought Genji in despair.

When he returned to the Nijō-in, he found Murasaki waiting for him. She was growing up to be as handsome a girl as one could wish, and promised well for the future. She was wearing a plain, close-fitting dress of cherry color; above all, the unstudied grace and ease of her movements charmed and delighted him as he watched her come to meet him. In accordance with the wishes of her old-fashioned grandmother, her teeth were not blackened, but her eyebrows were delicately touched with stain. "Why, when I might be playing with a beautiful child, do I spend my time with an ugly woman?" Genji kept asking himself in bewilderment while they sat together playing with her dolls. Next, she began to draw pictures and color them. After she had painted all sorts of queer and amusing things, "Now I am going to do a picture for you," said Genji, and drawing a lady with very long hair, he put a dab of red on her nose. Even in a picture, he thought, pausing to look at the effect, it gave one a most uncomfortable feeling. He went and looked at himself in the mirror, and as though dissatisfied with his own fresh complexion, he suddenly put on his own nose a dab of red such as he had given the lady in the picture. He looked at himself in the mirror. His handsome face had in an instant become ridiculous and repulsive. At first the child laughed. "Should you go on liking me if I were always as ugly as this?" he asked. Suddenly she began to be afraid that the paint would not come off. "Oh, why did you do it?" she cried. "How horrible!" He pretended to rub it without effect. "No," he said ruefully, "it will not come off. What a sad end to our game! I
pages.219:
# 210 THE TALE OF GENJI

wonder what the Emperor will say when I go back to the Palace?" He said it so seriously that she became very unhappy, and longing to cure him, she dipped a piece of thick, soft paper in the water-jug which stood by his writing-things and began scrubbing at his nose. "Take care," he cried, laughing, "that you do not serve me as Heichū<note>A historical figure known for his extravagant attempts to win his lady's affection.</note> was treated by his lady. I would rather have a red nose than a black one." So they passed their time, making the prettiest couple.

In the gentle spring sunshine, the trees were already shimmering with a haze of new-grown buds. Among them, it was the plum-trees that gave the surest promise, for already their blossoms were uncurling like lips parted in a faint smile. Earliest of them all was a red plum that grew beside the covered steps. It was in full color. "Though fair the tree on which it blooms, this red flower fills me with a strange misgiving,"<note>Original: "Though fair the tree on which it blooms, this red flower fills me with a strange misgiving." This is a poem comparing the princess to a red plum blossom; while the tree (her birth) is noble, the flower (her appearance) is unsettling.</note> sang Genji with a deep sigh.

We shall see in the next chapter what happened in the end to all these people.
pages.220:
# CHAPTER VII
# THE FESTIVAL OF RED LEAVES

The imperial visit to the Red Sparrow Court was to take place on the tenth day of the Godless Month.<note>The tenth month of the lunar calendar.</note> It was to be a more magnificent sight this year than it had ever been before, and the ladies of the Palace were very disappointed that they could not be present.<note>They were not allowed to leave the palace.</note> The Emperor, too, could not bear that Fujitsubo should miss the spectacle, and he decided to hold a grand rehearsal in the Palace. Prince Genji danced the "Waves of the Blue Sea." Tō no Chūjō was his partner; but though both in skill and beauty he far surpassed the common run of performers, yet beside Genji he seemed like a mountain fir growing beside a cherry-tree in bloom. There was a wonderful moment when the rays of the setting sun fell upon him and the music grew suddenly louder. Never had the onlookers seen feet tread so delicately nor head so exquisitely poised; and in the song which follows the first movement of the dance, his voice was as sweet as that of the Kalavinka<note>The bird that sings in Paradise.</note> whose music is Buddha’s Law. So moving and beautiful was this dance that at the end of it the Emperor’s eyes were wet, and all the princes and great gentlemen wept aloud. When the song was over and, straightening his long dancer’s sleeves, he stood waiting for the music to begin again—and at last the more lively tune of the second movement struck up—then indeed,
pages.221:
# THE TALE OF GENJI

with his flushed and eager face, he merited more than ever his name of Genji the Shining One. The Princess Kōkiden did not at all like to see her step-son’s beauty arousing so much enthusiasm, and she said sarcastically, "He is altogether too beautiful. Presently we shall have a god coming down from the sky to fetch him away."<note>In allusion to a boy-prince of seven years old whom the jealous gods carried off to the sky. See the Ōkagami.</note> Her young waiting-ladies noticed the spiteful tone in which the remark was made and felt somewhat embarrassed. As for Fujitsubo, she kept on telling herself that were it not for the guilty secret which was shared between them, the dance she was now witnessing would be filling her with wonder and delight. As it was, she sat as though in a dream, hardly knowing what went on around her.

Now she was back in her own room. The Emperor was with her. "At today’s rehearsal," he said, "the 'Waves of the Blue Sea' went perfectly." Then, noticing that she made no response, "What did you think of it?" "Yes, it was very good," she managed to say at last. "The partner did not seem to me bad either," he went on; "there is always something about the way a gentleman moves and uses his hands which distinguishes his dancing from that of professionals. Some of our crack dancing-masters have certainly made very clever performers of their own children; but they never have the same freshness, the same charm as the young people of our class. They expended so much effort on the rehearsal that I am afraid the festival itself may seem a very poor affair. No doubt they took all this trouble because they knew that you were here at the rehearsal and would not see the real performance."

Next morning she received a letter from Genji: "What of the rehearsal? How little the people who watched me knew of the turmoil that all the while was seething in my brain!"
pages.222:
# THE FESTIVAL OF RED LEAVES

And to this he added the poem: "When sick with love I yet sprang to my feet and capered with the rest, knew you what meant the fevered waving of my long dancing-sleeve?" Next he enjoined secrecy and prudence upon her, and so his letter ended. Her answer showed that despite her agitation, she had not been wholly insensible to what had fascinated all other eyes: "Though from far off a man of China waved his long dancing-sleeves, yet did his every motion fill my heart with wonder and delight."

To receive such a letter from her was indeed a surprise. It charmed him that her knowledge should extend even to the Court customs of a land beyond the sea. Already there was a regal note in her words. Yes, that was the end to which she was destined. Smiling to himself with pleasure, he spread the letter out before him, grasping it tightly in both hands as a priest holds the holy book, and gazed at it for a long while.

On the day of the festival, the royal princes and all the great gentlemen of the Court were in attendance. Even the Heir Apparent went with the procession. After the music-boats had rowed around the lake, dance upon dance was performed, both Korean and of the land beyond the sea. The whole valley resounded with the noise of music and drums. The Emperor insisted upon treating Genji’s performance at the rehearsal as a kind of miracle or religious portent and ordered special services to be read in every temple. Most people thought this step quite reasonable; but Princess Kōkiden said crossly that she saw no necessity for it. The Ring<note>Those who stand in a circle round the dancers while the latter change their clothes.</note> was, by the Emperor’s order, composed indifferently of commoners and noblemen chosen out of the whole realm for their skill and grace. The two Masters of Ceremony, Sayemon no Kami and Uyemon no Kami, were
pages.223:
# THE TALE OF GENJI

in charge of the left and right wings of the orchestra. Dancing-masters and others were entrusted with the task of seeking out performers of unusual merit and training them for the festival in their own houses. When at last, under the red leafage of tall autumn trees, forty men stood circle-wise with their flutes, and to the music that they made, a strong wind from the hills sweeping the pine-woods added its fierce harmonies—while from amid a wreckage of whirling and scattered leaves the Dance of the Blue Waves suddenly broke out in all its glittering splendor—a rapture seized the onlookers that was akin to fear.

The maple-wreath that Genji wore had suffered in the wind, and thinking that the few red leaves which clung to it had a desolate air, the Minister of the Left<note>The high official in charge of the court, often a political rival to the Right.</note> plucked a bunch of chrysanthemums from among those that grew before the Emperor's seat and twined them in the dancer's wreath.

At sunset, the sky clouded over and it looked like rain. But even the weather seemed conscious that such sights as this would not for a long while be seen again, and until all was over, not a drop fell. His Exit Dance, crowned as he was with this unspeakably beautiful wreath of multicolored flowers, was even more astonishing than that wonderful moment on the day of the rehearsal and seemed to the thrilled onlookers like the vision of another world. Humble and ignorant folk sitting afar on tree-roots or beneath some rock, or half-buried in deep banks of fallen leaves—few were so hardened that they did not shed a tear. Next came the "Autumn Wind," danced by Lady Jōkyōden's son,<note>Another illegitimate son of the Emperor; Genji’s step-brother.</note> who was still a mere child. The remaining performances attracted little attention, for the audience had had its fill of wonders and felt that whatever followed could but spoil the recollection of what had gone before.
pages.224:
# THE FESTIVAL OF RED LEAVES

That night, Genji was promoted to the First Class of the Third Rank, and Tō no Chūjō was promoted to intermediate standing between the First and Second Classes of the Fourth Rank. The gentlemen of the court were all promoted one rank. But though they celebrated their good fortune with the usual rejoicings, they were well aware that they had only been dragged in Genji's wake, and wondered how it was that their destinies had come to be linked in this curious way with those of the prince who had brought them this unexpected piece of good fortune.

Fujitsubo now retired to her own house, and Genji, waiting about for a chance of visiting her, was seldom at the Great Hall and was consequently in very ill favor there. It was soon after this that he brought the child Murasaki to live with him. Aoi heard a rumor of this, but it reached her merely in the form that someone was living with him at his palace, and she did not know that it was a child. Under these circumstances, it was quite natural that she should feel much aggrieved. But if only she had flown into an honest passion and abused him for it, as most people would have done, he would have told her everything and put matters right. As it was, she only redoubled her icy aloofness and thus led him to seek those very distractions of which it was intended as a rebuke. Not only was her beauty so flawless that it could not fail to win his admiration, but also the mere fact that he had known her since so long ago, before all the rest, made him feel toward her a tenderness of which she seemed quite unaware. He was convinced, however, that her nature was not at bottom narrow and vindictive, and this gave him some hope that she would one day relent.

Meanwhile, as he got to know little Murasaki better, he became the more content both with her appearance and her character. She at least gave him her whole heart. For the present, he did not intend to reveal her identity even to the

In the ostrich, all these things are clearly visible; in which, besides the external orifice of the common cavity, which a veil <note>original: "velabrum"</note> covered, I found another round orifice inside the anus, constricted and as if closed by a sphincter.

But, omitting these, let us deal with what concerns our purpose.

<margin>Orifice of the womb.</margin>
The orifice of the womb, or vulva; that is to say, the passage from the common cavity into the womb of the hen, is like a certain soft, loose, wrinkled, and circular protrusion; as if it were the closed extremity of a foreskin, or a prolapse of some internal tunic of the vulva. It is located (as I have said) between the anal opening and the rump, and it inclines slightly to the left; and this is considered by <term>Ulysses Aldrovandus</term> to be for the more convenient intercourse and easier entry of the cock's genital member. I, however, have observed more often that the hen, depending on whether the cock has mounted her from the right or left side, turns her vent indifferently toward that side. In the cock, I do not find a penis, which <term>Fabricius</term> also could not find, although it appears most manifestly in the goose and the duck. In its place, however, in the cock, I find an orifice (not unlike that in the hen), yet smaller and narrower; just as the same is seen in the swan, the goose, and the duck. The member of the goose and duck, however (while they are mating), is extended from this orifice.

This also happens in birds that are tame and allow themselves to be handled; when swelling with desire, they extend this orifice, and you will find it resistant and somewhat hard if you move your finger toward it.

Furthermore, <term>Aristotle</term> is the authority that females can conceive eggs from this, and I myself have experienced this in the thrush, the blackbird, and others; and this,

at first learned by chance and to my own loss.

My wife kept a remarkable and learnedly talkative parrot as a pet for a long time. It was so familiar that it would wander freely through the house wherever it pleased; it would look for its absent Mistress; when it found her, it would fawn upon her with a cheerful voice; it would answer when called, fly to her, grasp her clothing and feet in turn, climb to her highest shoulder, and from there descend along her arm to station itself always upon her hand. When ordered to speak or sing, it complied, even at night and in the dark. Often, playful and lascivious, it would approach the lap of the one sitting, where it wanted its head stroked and its back smoothed; by shaking its wings and with a gentle noise, it testified to the utmost joy of its spirit. I interpreted all these things as proceeding from a long-accustomed familiarity and obedience, for I assumed it was a male because of the exceptional excellence of its speech and song.

For among birds, females rarely sing or provoke one another with their voice; but we observe that only the males charm the females with the sweet modulation of their voices and entice them to the service of Venus. And therefore <term>Aristotle</term> says: <note>"Partridges, if they stand facing the males, and the wind blows from where the males stand, they conceive and mate. They also frequently become heavy in the womb from the voice of the males if they are excited and swelling with lust. The same can be accomplished by the flight of the males overhead; namely, while the male himself sends down the fertilizing spirit into the female."</note>

Not long after these pleasant caresses, the parrot, which had lived healthy for many years, fell ill; and finally, after frequent convulsions arose, it breathed its last in the lap of its Mistress, where it had played so often, to her great regret. Having dissected the carcass (to investigate the cause of death), I found an egg almost perfect in the womb, but corrupted due to the lack of a male. This often happens to little birds kept in cages that desire the company of a male.

By these and other examples, I am led to believe that the cock and the pheasant not only charm the females with their song, but also contribute to the conception of eggs: for at night, at the crowing of the cock, some of the hens sitting nearby shake themselves, flapping their wings and heads, as if seized by a gentle horror and gesticulating because of intercourse.

Thus, many birds, the more lustful they are, the more fecund they are; and sometimes they conceive eggs without a male (because of the richness of their food or for some other cause); but they rarely finish or lay them without his operation; instead, they are held by more serious diseases and finally perish. The hen, however, not only conceives eggs but also lays them, and perfect ones at that; but they are <term>hypenemia</term> <gloss>wind-eggs</gloss> and unfruitful. Similarly, many insects (among whom are silkworms and butterflies) conceive and lay eggs without the meeting of a male (as do fish), but they are useless and wind-eggs.

## ANTONIUS TASSARA 
## TO THE READER, GREETINGS.

<note>A woodcut depicts the letter 'C' adorned with floral patterns.</note>

Since, by the instigation of that spirit who gave cause for the first death of men, who shakes the elements, disturbs the minds of men, deludes human curiosity, and transforms himself into an angel of light, adorning himself with the habit and the name of a just man, mortals have very often turned aside from the path of reason and the straight way of living; preferring power to equity and appetite to reason, they would be overwhelmed by every evil; and they would never reach the knowledge of truth, but rather resist it, just as Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses: that One, who has mercy on human frailty, who is the revealer of terrible things, the searcher of hearts, and the lord of sciences, from whom the elements of the whole world have proceeded and by whom their disposition has been brought into the sphere of the earth; [he] inspired with his spirit Moses, the first lawgiver of the Hebrew people, Phoroneus, Androdamus of Rhegium, Philolaus of Corinth, Hippodamus of Miletus, Solon, Draco, Lycurgus, Numa Pompilius, M. Mutius, P. Manilius, L. Brutus, and innumerable others with one
pages.11: spirit, so that they might promulgate laws, constitutions, sanctions, and judgments, separate the equitable from the iniquitous, discern the lawful from the unlawful, segregate the honest from the dishonest, restrain human audacity, curb the capacity for doing harm, and check the idle play of other things. Therefore, since notaries do not preserve intact what they themselves have established with counsel in the sacred canons and have affixed in worldly laws, acting indeed against their most wholesome institutions: I do not consider it inconvenient to collect certain cases worthy of correction, lest they come to be judged severely by the holy fathers and be condemned by the Holy Spirit, by whose instinct and gift they were created: since they seem not incongruously to sin against the Holy Spirit, by whose will and grace sacred laws have been ordained for the common pledge of mortals; nor do I believe that this present booklet will incur the mark of arrogance, since, as Blessed Gregory says, just as it is laudable and discreet to show reverence to those who came before us, so it is a matter of uprightness and fear of God, if anything in them needs correction, not to postpone it with any dissimulation, lest the whole
pages.12: (which God forbid) body be invaded by disease, if the weakness has not been cured in the head. And it is also held in the sacred scriptures that when Balaam the soothsayer went to curse the people, the Angel of the Lord stood against him in the way upon the donkey on which he was sitting, and with drawn sword stopped it from its journey: and while he was beating it with lashes, it broke out into a voice, and rebuked the madness of the prophet. Likewise, when David had committed adultery and murder, the Prophet Nathan was sent by God to rebuke him: because it is worthy for everyone to render an account of his stewardship; as Christ, the Truth of the Lord, says; who also, when he was the shepherd of shepherds, said to his own sheep (of whom he says, "I am not sent but unto the lost sheep of the house of Israel"), amidst the reproaches and lashes that he was suffering from them, "If I have spoken evil, bear witness of the evil; but if well, why do you strike me?" And Samuel also (as is read in the first book of Kings) said to the people: "Speak to me before the Lord, whether I have taken any man's ox or his ass, or if I have falsely accused anyone, if I have oppressed anyone, or if I have received a bribe from anyone's hand, and I will restore it to you." They said to him,
pages.13: "You have not falsely accused us, nor have you oppressed us, nor have you taken anything from the hand of any man." He said to them, "The Lord is witness that you will not find anything in my hand." And therefore, for the common utility of these notaries, I have taken care to send them, according to our poor weakness, into the treasury of the Lord, as Blessed Jerome testifies in his commentary on Malachi, that if anyone learned and erudite in the law can instruct others, understanding God as the giver, and giving thanks to those through whom he has been instructed by God, he shall humble himself and bring food into the granary of God, that is, he shall minister the nourishment of scripture to the people: immediately the floodgates of heaven will be opened upon him, and spiritual rain will be poured out, and he will command his clouds to rain a shower upon him, and he will enjoy an abundance of all things. Therefore, those exercising the office of notary ought to acquire this present booklet even for a monetary price: because just as the night does not extinguish the stars of the heaven, so worldly iniquity will not obscure their minds clinging to this booklet: and if the things contained in this booklet taste of wisdom, they will be made wise by the Lord; but if they do not know, they will not be known by the Lord,
pages.14:
as Paul attests, that he who is ignorant shall be ignored; and just as it does not befit the members to depart from the head, but according to the testimony of Scripture all members follow the head, so it will not befit them to deviate from this booklet, since in it are contained the traditions which we have received of old from the fathers, which to infringe is an abominable disgrace. Farewell.

### SUMMARY.

1 *In the election of notaries, three things are primarily to be considered.*
2 *The maturity of age, by reason of public office, to be looked for in notaries.*
3 *The maturity of age is to be investigated in public offices even if a worthy person is found.*
4 *Legal persons are to be elected to the office of notary, so that parties cannot easily allege they are suspect.*
5 *Notaries are equal to the deed of two, even in matters not pertaining to their office.*
6 *The gravity of morals is to be looked for in notaries.*
7 *One lacking the knowledge of letters oppresses many.*
8 *Three degrees of literal knowledge.*
9 *Notaries must be established in sufficiency.*

### *10 Choosing less suitable notaries, [one must] undergo the due penalties.*

<margin>1</margin>
Let notaries, having the power of election, hold in memory that three things are primarily to be considered in their creation: namely, the maturity of age, the gravity of morals, and the knowledge of letters. Argued from the chapter *cum in cunctis*, in the Decretals, *de electione*. Since it is of such great weight that the business of men receives its increase from it, argued from the law *legatis*, § *ornatricibus*, in the *Digest*, *de legatis*. And therefore, since the use of the notary is frequent, useful, and daily, great care must be taken in their creation, according to the text in law 1, in the *Digest*, *de diversis et temporalibus actionibus*; law *legavi*, in the *Digest*, *de libertis legatis*; law 1, § *dixerit aliquis*, in the *Digest*, *de publicis*; law *iusto*, in the *Digest*, *de usucapionibus*; law 1, in the *Digest*, *de in integrum restitutionibus*. <margin>2</margin> Therefore, the maturity of age is to be looked at first, because it is a public office, and a notary is called a public person. Law 2, in the *Digest*, *rem pupilli salvam fore*; law *orphanotrophos*, in the *Codex*, *de episcopis et clericis*; law *non aliter*, in the *Digest*, *de adoptionibus*; note the gloss in the chapter *quanquam*, *de usuris*, book 6; Bartolus in law *generali*, in the *Codex*, *de tabellionibus*, book 10. <margin>3</margin> For a public office,
pages.17: he who is not established in mature age cannot be elected. Law *ad Rempublicam*, in the *Digest*, *de muneribus et honoribus*. And if a worthy person is found before that age, as is the strange text in the chapter *si quis triginta*, in the 78th distinction. And it is persuaded by the fact that such an office was found for the public utility and favor of men; if they were elected before mature age, such favor would be turned into hatred, since the judgments of men are said to be weak before mature age. Law 1, *Digest*, *de minoribus*. Which indeed ought not to be, [according to] law *quod favor*, *Codex*, *de legibus*, chapter *odia*, *de regulis iuris*, book 6; law *cum quidam*, *Digest*, *de liberis et posthumis*. <margin>4</margin> And therefore, this quality being considered, legal men shall be appointed to such an office, according to what is held in the chapter *quoniam contra falsam*, *de probationibus*, in the law *si à bonae fidei*, *Codex*, *de rei venditione*; otherwise the parties could most easily allege them to be suspect, according to the singular gloss in § *quia saepe*, in the *Authenticae*, *de triente et semisse*. <margin>5</margin> And this is especially to be investigated since notaries are equivalent to the deed of two, as Baldus attests in the *Authentica*, *sed cum testator*, *Codex*, *ad legem falcidiam*; law *militibus*, *Codex*, *de militari testamento*.

Smith, Jones, Brown, and Robinson are sitting with their hands on a table. All, <term>ex hypothesi</term> <note>original: "ex hypothesi"; Latin for "by hypothesis" or "assuming this premise."</note>, are honorable men, "above suspicion of intentional deception." They ask the table where Green is. Smith, Jones, and Robinson have no idea; Brown firmly believes that Green is in Rome. The table begins to move, kicks, and answers—by means of an alphabet and knocks—that Green is at Machrihanish <note>A village in Scotland.</note>, where, upon investigation, he is proven to be. Later, Brown is able to show (let us hope by documentary evidence) that he had heard Green was going to Machrihanish instead of to Rome as he had intended, but this remarkable change of plans on Green’s part had entirely faded from Brown’s memory. Now we are to assume, <term>ex hypothesi</term>, that Brown is the soul of honor and, like Mr. Facey Rumford <note>A character from a novel by R.S. Surtees, known for being blunt and honest.</note>, "wouldn’t tell a lie if it was ever so." The practical result is that, while Brown’s consciousness informs him, loud and clear, that Green is in Rome, "the residue of a forgotten impression" makes him (without his knowing it) move the table—which he does not intend to do—and forces him to say, through the tilts of the table, that Green is at Machrihanish, even while he believes Green is in Rome.

The table-turners were laughed at, and many, if not all of them, deserved ridicule. But see how even this trivial superstition illuminates our knowledge of the human mind! A mere residue of a forgotten impression—a lost memory which Brown would have sworn in a court of justice had never been in his mind at all—can move his muscles while he supposes they are *not* moving. It can...

If Brown’s residue of an impression can make Brown’s muscles move a table to give responses of which he is ignorant, why should not the residue of a forgotten impression—that it would be a pleasant thing to shoot Mr. Gladstone or Lord Salisbury—make Brown unconsciously commit that mistake <note>original: "solecism"; here used to mean a social or moral blunder.</note>? At all events, if the unconscious self can do as much as Dr. Carpenter believed, we cannot tell how many other marvels it may perform; we cannot know until we investigate further. If this is so, it is perhaps hardly wise or scientific to taboo all investigation. More than twenty years ago, an attempt was made by a body called the "Dialectical Society" to investigate the phenomena styled spiritualistic. This well-meant essay had most unsatisfactory results. <note>Report on Spiritualism, Longmans, London, 1871.</note>

First, a committee of inquiry was formed on the motion of Dr. Edmunds. The committee was heterogeneous. Many of the names now suggest little to the reader. We remember Mr. Bradlaugh, but he chiefly attended a committee that sat with D. D. Home, and it is admitted that nothing of interest occurred there. Then we find the Reverend Maurice Davies, who was accustomed to write books of little distinction on semi-religious topics. Mr. H. G. Atkinson was a person interested in mesmerism. Kisch, Moss, and Quelch, with Dyte and Isaac Meyers, Bergheim and Geary, Hannah, Hillier, and Reed (their names go naturally in blank verse) were, doubtless, all most estimable men, but scarcely boast of scientific fame. Serjeant Cox, a believer in the phenomena, if not in their spiritual cause, was of the company, as was Mr. Jencken, who married one of the Miss Foxes, the first authors of modern thaumaturgy <note>Miracle-working or magic.</note>. Professor Huxley and Mr. G. H. Lewes were asked to join, but declined to march to Sarras, the spiritual city, with...

This was neither surprising nor reprehensible, but Professor Huxley's letter of refusal appears to indicate that matters of interest—and, perhaps, logic—are differently understood by men of science and men of letters. <note>Report, p. 229.</note> He gave two reasons for refusing, and others may readily be imagined by the sympathetic observer. The first was that he had no time for an inquiry involving much trouble and (as he justly foresaw) much annoyance. Next, he had no interest in the subject. He had once examined a case of "spiritualism" and detected an imposture. "But, supposing the phenomena to be genuine, they do not interest me. If anybody would endow me with the faculty of listening to the chatter of old women and curates in the nearest cathedral town, I should decline the privilege, having better things to do." Thus, it would not interest Professor Huxley if some new kind of telephone should enable him to hear all the conversation of persons in a town (if a cathedral town) more or less distant. He would not be interested by the "genuine" fact of this extension of his faculties because he would not expect to be amused or instructed by the contents of what he heard. Of course, he was not invited to listen to a chatter which, on one hypothesis, was that of the dead, but to help to ascertain whether or not there were any genuine facts of an unusual nature, which some persons explained by the animistic hypothesis. The results of the Dialectical Society's inquiry were somewhat comic. The committee reported that marvels were alleged, by the experimental sub-committees, to have occurred. Sub-committee No. 1 averred that "motion may be produced in solid bodies without material contact, by some hitherto unrecognized force." Sub-committees 2 and 3 had many communications with mysterious intelligences to vouch for, and much erratic behavior on the part of tables to record. No. 4 had nothing to report at all, and No. 5, which sat four times with Home, had mere trifles of raps. Home was ill, and the <term>séances</term> were given up.

He complained that convinced spiritualists had "captured" the editing sub-committee, as people say, and had issued a report practically spiritualistic. He himself had met nothing more remarkable than impudent frauds or total failure. "Raps, noises, and movements of various kinds," he had indeed witnessed, and he heard wondrous tales from truthful people, "but I have never been able to see anything worthy of consideration, as not being accounted for by unconscious action, delusion, or imposture." On many nervous systems, the mere sitting idly round a table, and calling the process a <term>séance</term>, produces evil effects.

<margin>1006</margin>As to the idea of purposely evoking the dead, it is at least as impious, as absurd, as odious to taste and sentiment, as it is insane in the eyes of reason. This protest the writer feels obliged to make, for while he regards the traditional, historical, and anthropological curiosities here collected as matters of some interest, in various aspects, he has nothing but abhorrence and contempt for modern efforts to converse with the spirits <note>original: "manes"; Roman deities of the dead or spirits of ancestors.</note>, and for all the profane impostures of "spiritualism."

On the question of the real existence of the reported phenomena hereafter chronicled, and on the question of the significance <note>original: "portée"; scope or reach.</note> of the facts, if genuine, the writer has been unable to reach any conclusion, negative or affirmative. Even the testimony of his senses, if they ever bore witness to any of the *magnificent miracles* <note>original: "speciosa miracula"; a phrase from Horace meaning "striking miracles."</note>, would fail to convince him on the affirmative side. There seems to be no good reason why one observer should set so much store by his own impressions of sense, while he regards those of all other witnesses as fallible. The double doors at the end of the eastern wing were wide open, and because the roof of the verandah had fallen in, the sunshine poured straight into the house. A little snow was still falling, and its brightness made the morning light appear even more exquisitely brilliant and sparkling. Genji watched a servant helping the princess into her cloak. She was lying half out of the bed, her head hanging a little downward, and her hair falling in great waves to the floor. Pleased with the sight, he began to wonder whether she would not one day outgrow her plainness. He started to close the door of the women’s apartments, but suddenly feeling that he owed her amends for the harsh opinion of her appearance which he had formed before, he did not quite shut the door. Instead, he brought a low stool toward it and sat there, putting his disordered head-dress to rights. One of the maids brought him an incredibly battered mirror-stand, Chinese combs, a box of toilet articles, and other things. It amused him to discover that in this household of women, a little male gear still survived, even in so decrepit a state.

He noticed that the princess, who was now up and dressed, was looking quite fashionable. She was, in fact, wearing the clothes which he had sent her before the New Year, but he did not at first recognize them. He began, however, to have a vague idea that her mantle, with its rather conspicuous pattern, was very like one of the things he had given her. 

“I do hope,” he said presently, “that this year you will be a little more conversational. I await the day when you will unbend a little toward me, more eagerly than the poet longs for the first nightingale. If only, like the year that has changed, you too would begin anew!” 

Her face brightened. She had thought of a remark, and trembling from head to foot with a tremendous effort, she brought out the quotation: “When plovers chirp and all things grow anew.” 

“Splendid,” said Genji. “This is a sign that the new year has indeed
pages.218:
begun,” and smiling encouragingly at her, he left the house, she following him with her eyes from the couch on which she lay. Her face, as usual, was half covered by her arm; but the unfortunate flower <note>Referring to the "Saffron-Flower," a nickname for the princess due to her prominent red nose.</note> still bloomed conspicuously. “Poor thing, she really is very ugly,” thought Genji in despair.

When he returned to the Nijō-in, he found Murasaki waiting for him. She was growing up to be as handsome a girl as one could wish, and she promised well for the future. She was wearing a plain, close-fitting dress of cherry color; above all, the unstudied grace and ease of her movements charmed and delighted him as he watched her come to meet him. In accordance with the wishes of her old-fashioned grandmother, her teeth were not blackened, but her eyebrows were delicately touched with stain. 

“Why, when I might be playing with a beautiful child, do I spend my time with an ugly woman?” Genji kept on asking himself in bewilderment while they sat together playing with her dolls. 

Next, she began to draw pictures and color them. After she had painted all sorts of queer and amusing things, “Now I am going to do a picture for you,” said Genji, and drawing a lady with very long hair, he put a dab of red on her nose. Even in a picture, he thought, pausing to look at the effect, it gave one a most uncomfortable feeling. He went and looked at himself in the mirror, and as though dissatisfied with his own fresh complexion, he suddenly put on his own nose a dab of red such as he had given to the lady in the picture. He looked at himself in the mirror. His handsome face had in an instant become ridiculous and repulsive. At first, the child laughed. 

“Should you go on liking me if I were always as ugly as this?” he asked. 

Suddenly, she began to be afraid that the paint would not come off. “Oh, why did you do it?” she cried. “How horrible!” 

He pretended to rub it without effect. “No,” he said ruefully, “it will not come off. What a sad end to our game! I
pages.219:
wonder what the Emperor will say when I go back to the Palace?” 

He said it so seriously that she became very unhappy, and longing to cure him, she dipped a piece of thick, soft paper in the water-jug which stood by his writing-things and began scrubbing at his nose. 

“Take care,” he cried, laughing, “that you do not serve me as Heichū <note>A famous Heian-period lover known for his dramatic gestures.</note> was treated by his lady. I would rather have a red nose than a black one.” 

So they passed their time, making the prettiest couple.

In the gentle spring sunshine, the trees were already shimmering with a haze of new-grown buds. Among them, it was the plum-trees that gave the surest promise, for already their blossoms were uncurling like lips parted in a faint smile. Earliest of them all was a red plum that grew beside the covered steps. It was in full color. 

“Though fair the tree on which it blooms, this red flower fills me with a strange misgiving,” <note>The reference, of course, is to the princess. "Though fair the tree" refers to her high birth.</note> sang Genji with a deep sigh.

We shall see in the next chapter what happened in the end to all these people.

<summary>Genji spends time with the plain princess, then returns home to play with the young Murasaki, playfully teasing her by painting his nose red, before reflecting on the arrival of spring and the princess's high but disappointing station.</summary>

pages.220:
# CHAPTER VII
# THE FESTIVAL OF RED LEAVES

The imperial visit to the Red Sparrow Court was to take place on the tenth day of the Godless Month <note>The tenth month of the lunar calendar, when the gods were believed to leave their shrines to congregate at Izumo.</note>. It was to be a more magnificent sight this year than it had ever been before, and the ladies of the Palace were very disappointed that they could not be present. <note>They were not allowed to leave the palace.</note> The Emperor, too, could not bear that Fujitsubo should miss the spectacle, and he decided to hold a grand rehearsal in the Palace. Prince Genji danced the “Waves of the Blue Sea.” Tō no Chūjō was his partner; but though both in skill and beauty he far surpassed the common run of performers, yet beside Genji, he seemed like a mountain fir growing beside a cherry-tree in bloom. There was a wonderful moment when the rays of the setting sun fell upon him and the music grew suddenly louder. Never had the onlookers seen feet tread so delicately nor head so exquisitely poised; and in the song which follows the first movement of the dance, his voice was sweet as that of the Kalavinka <note>The bird that sings in Paradise.</note> whose music is Buddha’s Law. So moving and beautiful was this dance that at the end of it, the Emperor’s eyes were wet, and all the princes and great gentlemen wept aloud. When the song was over and, straightening his long dancer’s sleeves, he stood waiting for the music to begin again and at last the more lively tune of the second movement struck up—then indeed,
pages.221:
with his flushed and eager face, he merited more than ever his name of Genji the Shining One. The Princess Kōkiden <note>The Emperor’s consort and Genji’s antagonist.</note> did not at all like to see her step-son’s beauty arousing so much enthusiasm, and she said sarcastically, “He is altogether too beautiful. Presently we shall have a god coming down from the sky to fetch him away.” <note>An allusion to a boy-prince of seven years old whom the jealous gods carried off to the sky, as recorded in the Ōkagami.</note> 

Her young waiting-ladies noticed the spiteful tone in which the remark was made and felt somewhat embarrassed. As for Fujitsubo, she kept on telling herself that were it not for the guilty secret which was shared between them, the dance she was now witnessing would be filling her with wonder and delight. As it was, she sat as though in a dream, hardly knowing what went on around her.

Now she was back in her own room. The Emperor was with her. “At today’s rehearsal,” he said, “The ‘Waves of the Blue Sea’ went perfectly.” 

Then, noticing that she made no response, “What did you think of it?” 

“Yes, it was very good,” she managed to say at last. 

“The partner did not seem to me bad either,” he went on; “there is always something about the way a gentleman moves and uses his hands which distinguishes his dancing from that of professionals. Some of our crack dancing-masters have certainly made very clever performers of their own children; but they never have the same freshness, the same charm as the young people of our class. They expended so much effort on the rehearsal that I am afraid the festival itself may seem a very poor affair. No doubt they took all this trouble because they knew that you were here at the rehearsal and would not see the real performance.”

Next morning she received a letter from Genji: “What of the rehearsal? How little the people who watched me knew of the turmoil that all the while was seething in my brain!”
pages.222:
And to this he added the poem: 

“When sick with love I yet sprang to my feet and capered with the rest, knew you what meant the fevered waving of my long dancing-sleeve?” 

Next, he enjoined secrecy and prudence upon her, and so his letter ended. Her answer showed that despite her agitation, she had not been wholly insensible to what had fascinated all other eyes: 

“Though from far off a man of China waved his long dancing-sleeves, yet did his every motion fill my heart with wonder and delight.”

To receive such a letter from her was indeed a surprise. It charmed him that her knowledge should extend even to the Court customs of a land beyond the sea. Already there was a regal note in her words. Yes, that was the end to which she was destined. Smiling to himself with pleasure, he spread the letter out before him, grasping it tightly in both hands as a priest holds the holy book, and gazed at it for a long while.

On the day of the festival, the royal princes and all the great gentlemen of the Court were in attendance. Even the Heir Apparent went with the procession. After the music-boats had rowed round the lake, dance upon dance was performed, both Korean and of the land beyond the sea. The whole valley resounded with the noise of music and drums. The Emperor insisted upon treating Genji’s performance at the rehearsal as a kind of miracle or religious portent, and ordered special services to be read in every temple. Most people thought this step quite reasonable; but Princess Kōkiden said crossly that she saw no necessity for it. The Ring <note>Those who stand in a circle round the dancers while the latter change their clothes.</note> was, by the Emperor’s order, composed indifferently of commoners and noblemen chosen out of the whole realm for their skill and grace. The two Masters of Ceremony, Sayemon no Kami and Uyemon no Kami, were
pages.223:
in charge of the left and right wings of the orchestra. Dancing-masters and others were entrusted with the task of seeking out performers of unusual merit and training them for the festival in their own houses. When at last, under the red leafage of tall autumn trees, forty men stood circle-wise with their flutes, and to the music that they made, a strong wind from the hills sweeping the pine-woods added its fierce harmonies, while from amid a wreckage of whirling and scattered leaves the Dance of the Blue Waves suddenly broke out in all its glittering splendor—a rapture seized the onlookers that was akin to fear.

The maple-wreath that Genji wore had suffered in the wind, and thinking that the few red leaves which clung to it had a desolate air, the Minister of the Left <note>Referring to the Sadaijin.</note> plucked a bunch of chrysanthemums from among those that grew before the Emperor's seat and twined them in the dancer's wreath.

At sunset the sky clouded over and it looked like rain. But even the weather seemed conscious that such sights as this would not for a long while be seen again, and till all was over not a drop fell. His Exit Dance, crowned as he was with this unspeakably beautiful wreath of many-colored flowers, was even more astonishing than that wonderful moment on the day of the rehearsal and seemed to the thrilled onlookers like the vision of another world. Humble and ignorant folk sitting afar on tree-roots or beneath some rock, or half-buried in deep banks of fallen leaves—few were so hardened that they did not shed a tear. Next came the 'Autumn Wind' danced by Lady Jōkyōden's son <note>Another illegitimate son of the Emperor; Genji’s step-brother.</note> who was still a mere child. The remaining performances attracted little attention, for the audience had had its fill of wonders and felt that whatever followed could but spoil the recollection of what had gone before.
pages.224:
That night Genji was promoted to the First Class of the Third Rank and Tō no Chūjō was promoted to intermediate standing between the First and Second Classes of the Fourth Rank. The gentlemen of the court were all promoted one rank. But though they celebrated their good fortune with the usual rejoicings, they were well aware that they had only been dragged in Genji's wake and wondered how it was that their destinies had come to be linked in this curious way with those of the prince who had brought them this unexpected piece of good fortune.

Fujitsubo now retired to her own house and Genji, waiting about for a chance of visiting her, was seldom at the Great Hall and was consequently in very ill favor there. It was soon after this that he brought the child Murasaki to live with him. Aoi <note>Genji’s wife.</note> heard a rumor of this, but it reached her merely in the form that someone was living with him at his palace, and she did not know that it was a child. Under these circumstances it was quite natural that she should feel much aggrieved. But if only she had flown into an honest passion and abused him for it as most people would have done, he would have told her everything and put matters right. As it was, she only redoubled her icy aloofness and thus led him to seek those very distractions of which it was intended as a rebuke. Not only was her beauty so flawless that it could not fail to win his admiration, but also the mere fact that he had known her since so long ago, before all the rest, made him feel toward her a tenderness of which she seemed quite unaware. He was convinced, however, that her nature was not at bottom narrow and vindictive, and this gave him some hope that she would one day relent.

Meanwhile, as he got to know little Murasaki better, he became the more content both with her appearance and her character. She at least gave him her whole heart. For the present, he did not intend to reveal her identity even to the

<summary>Genji gives a breathtaking performance of the "Waves of the Blue Sea" at the imperial festival, sparking both jealousy and awe, while simultaneously struggling with his clandestine feelings for Fujitsubo and his distant relationship with his wife, Aoi.</summary>
<keywords>Genji, Fujitsubo, Aoi, Murasaki, Festival of Red Leaves, court promotion, dance, court intrigue</keywords>
