# EXERCISE VI.

the internal cavity of the uterus, it is hardly likely; for I could find no passage inside with either a probe or a bristle; nor did Fabricius manage to find one. Indeed, according to the same witness, not even blown air penetrates into the uterus. This, I think, was the reason why he described the history of the uterus while proceeding from the internal parts to the external ones. Furthermore, <margin>Page 30.</margin> having weighed this structure of the uterus, he denies that semen reaches the cavity of the uterus, or constitutes any part of the egg. In this opinion, I also willingly declare my agreement.

Indeed, you will find nothing in a fertile egg (which is not found in an infertile one <note>original: "subventaneum"</note>) that is added or changed, from which it might be certain that the rooster’s semen has entered the uterus and touched the egg. Furthermore, although without the rooster’s mating all eggs are ineffective and infertile, through his actions (even some time after copulation) the subsequent eggs, of which no beginning or material yet exists, turn out to be fertile.

<margin>Page 37.</margin> Fabricius, to explain the manner in which the rooster’s semen renders eggs fertile, says the following: *Since semen does not appear in the egg, and yet is extended by the rooster into the uterus; the question is, why is the rooster’s semen sent into the uterus if it does not enter the egg? Likewise, if it is not present in the egg, how is the egg rendered fertile from the rooster’s semen, which it does not contain? My opinion is that the rooster’s semen, sent into the beginning of the uterus, affects the entire uterus, and at the same time all the yolks falling into it, and finally the whole egg, making it fertile: and it does this by its own power, or radiating spiritual substance; in the way in which we see,*
pages.76:
# On the Generation of Animals.

from the testicles and semen, other animals are also rendered fertile. For if anyone recalls to mind that incredible transmutation by which an animal is affected when castrated, while it loses vigor, strength, and fertility in its whole body, he will easily concede that what we say happens to the uterus of a hen. But that it is absolutely true that the virtue of fertilizing eggs and also the uterus proceeds from the rooster’s semen is evident from what women do; having a hen at home without a rooster, they send it elsewhere to a rooster for one or two days; for from this short time, the fertility of all the eggs is secured for the whole <margin>On the generation of animals, book 3, chapter 1. Page 38.</margin> year. This is also confirmed by Aristotle, who holds that when birds have once mated, they continue to have almost all eggs fertile. Furthermore, that the fertilizing virtue of the semen might not in any way evaporate, but rather remain longer in the uterus to be shared with the whole, Nature herself enclosed and deposited it in a cavity, a bursa <note>pouch</note> near the anus, appended to the uterus and endowed with an opening, so that the semen being detained therein, its virtue might be preserved and communicated to the entire uterus.

I, however, suspected the truth of the aforementioned experiment; and the more so, because I saw the words of the Philosopher quoted in bad faith; for he did not say, *Birds, when they have once mated, continue to have almost all eggs fertile,* but, *they continue to have almost all eggs*; Fabricius added <term>fertile</term> on his own. It is one thing for birds to conceive eggs from coitus, and another for eggs to be fertilized from coitus. And that this is clear from the
pages.77:
# EXERCISE VI.

preceding words of Aristotle, where he says: *In the genus of birds, even those eggs which arise through coitus cannot for the most part be increased unless the bird's coitus is continued.* The reason for this is that, just as in women the <term>menstruum</term> <gloss>menstrual discharge/waste</gloss> is drawn out by coitus with a male (for the warmed uterus draws it, and the passages are opened), so it happens in birds while the menstrual waste gradually approaches, which cannot exit because it is small and is contained above by the girdle, but collapses into the uterus itself. For this egg is increased, just as the fetus of viviparous animals, because it flows in through the umbilical cord. For when birds have once mated, they continue to have all eggs always, but they are very small and imperfect, and therefore infertile; for the perfection of the egg is to be fertile. If, therefore, without continued coitus of the bird, not even those eggs which were conceived by coitus are increased, or (as Fabricius interpreted) are perfected; much less will those eggs which birds continue to have without coitus be rendered fertile.

But so that no one may think that by these words (*for the warmed uterus draws it, and the passages are opened*) it is concluded that the uterus can draw the rooster’s semen into its cavity; it must be known that it is not said by the Philosopher that the uterus draws semen from outside; but in women, through veins and passages opened by heat, menstrual blood is drawn from their own body; and similarly in birds, blood is drawn to the uterus warmed by continued coitus, and from there eggs are increased; just as the fetuses of viviparous animals are accustomed to be through the umbilical cord.
pages.78:
# On the Generation of Animals.

But what he adds concerning that cavity, or *bursa*, in which he assumes the rooster’s semen is harbored for an entire year; those things have already been refuted by us; where we asserted that no semen is contained in it, and that it is present in the rooster just as it is in the hen.

Therefore, although I could easily believe (if by fertility we understand the production of more and larger eggs) that the hens of poor women (to whom it is proven that a sufficiency of food is lacking) would lay fewer and smaller eggs unless they were with a rooster; (according to that saying of the Philosopher: *But if they have once mated with a rooster, then for the whole year they will continue to have larger, better, and more numerous eggs.* To which end the abundance and quality of food also contribute very much.) yet that hens, from a few matings with a rooster, should lay all eggs fertile for the whole duration of a year, this seemed less likely to me. For if a few acts of coitus were sufficient for such long-lasting generation, Nature (which does nothing in vain) would have made males in the class of birds less lustful; and the rooster would not solicit his hens for coitus so often every day, even when they are unwilling.

We know that a hen, as soon as she has laid an egg and leaves the nest, cries out with a shrill voice, and entices the rooster to coitus; who, responding with an equally loud and sobbing voice, anxiously seeks her, and having found her, suddenly compresses her: which surely, Nature would not have willed to happen unless for the sake of procreation.

The male pheasant, kept in an aviary, so
pages.79:
# EXERCISE VI.

burns with violent lust that, unless he has several females (at least six) with him, he will mistreat them with too frequent repeated coitus, hindering fertility rather than promoting it. I once saw a female pheasant, so exhausted by a rooster shut in with her (whom she could not avoid by hiding or fleeing), and bare of feathers on her back from his frequent assaults, that at last, agitated in a miserable way, she perished from sorrow. Yet, in the same bird dissected, I indeed found the rudiments of eggs.

I also observed a male duck, lacking a mate and living with hens, burning with such lust that he would pursue a young hen in every direction for several hours, peck at her with his beak, and finally, exhausted, would mount her and perform the act of defilement.

A rooster victorious in battle exercises his lust not only on the mates of the defeated one, but also on the living bird itself.

Similarly, some females are so prone to lust that they nip their males with little bites (as if whispering the joys of Venus into their ear), mount them, and invite them to coitus with other arts: in which number are doves and sparrows.

It does not seem likely, therefore, that a few acts of coitus, performed at the beginning of the year, suffice for the fertility of all the eggs following throughout its entire course. I, however, once (to provide a defense for Fabricius here) in the spring season (intending to investigate something certain about the time and necessity of fertilizing coitus)
pages.80:
# On the Generation of Animals.

kept two hens separated from the rooster for four days, which meanwhile had each laid three eggs, no less prolific than other eggs. And again I separated another hen, which laid an egg on the tenth day from then; and another on the twentieth day, and both were fertile. Thus it appears that one or two acts of coitus can render the whole year, and all the eggs of that year, fertile.

I will also say what I observed at that time. When I restored each hen (separated for some time, as I said) to the rooster; of which one was pregnant with an egg and the other had recently laid, the rooster met the latter more quickly, and greedily compressed her three or four times: but he circled the former more often, appearing to salute her by rubbing his feet and wings, and to congratulate her on her arrival; nevertheless, having returned to the former, he mounted her again and again, and repeated the act by force: meanwhile neglecting the pregnant one, whom he in no way solicited for Venus. I wondered by what signs he so distinguished which one would benefit from coitus, and for which one it would be importunate. Truly, it is not at all clear how males (even from a distance) understand, whether by sight, hearing, or smell, that females are struck by the heat of desire and desire coitus. Some, even if they only hear their voice, or smell the place where they have urinated, or even just their tracks, are immediately ignited with lust, and pursue the same for coitus. But concerning this matter, elsewhere, in the treatise on the love, lust, and coitus of animals, more fully

there will be a place for speaking. Now I return to my purpose.

### *On the belly of the hen and other birds.*

### EXERCISE VII.

From the external orifice, therefore, through the vulva, we have arrived at the hen’s uterus, or matrix; in which the egg is perfected, surrounded by albumen, and covered by a shell: before we speak of its site and position, some things concerning the peculiar <term>anatomy</term> <gloss>dissection/structure</gloss> of the belly of birds must be brought forward here and discussed beforehand. For I have observed in feathered animals that the stomach, intestines, and other viscera are situated and constituted differently in the lower part of their belly than in the class of walking animals.

Almost all birds have a double stomach; of which one is called the <term>crop</term> <gloss>ingluvies/craw</gloss>, the other the <term>stomach</term> <gloss>ventriculus/gizzard</gloss> properly so called. In the former, food eaten is reserved and prepared; in the latter, it is processed and passes into chyle <note>the milky fluid consisting of lymph and emulsified fats</note>: our countrymen call the former *the crop, or craw*; the latter, *the gisard*. In the crop, birds retain whole grains devoured; from there, when moistened with drunk water, macerated, and softened, they later transmit them into the stomach; so that they may be ground and crushed in the same place. For the sake of which, almost all feathered animals swallow sand, small stones, and certain other harder things, keeping them in the stomach together with food; (while meanwhile nothing such is found in the crop) and they have this stomach made of two very thick
pages.82:
# On the Generation of Animals.

and most robust muscles (in smaller birds, fleshy or ligamentous); so that in this way, like two millstones joined by two hinges, they can grind food and crush it; and the small stones supply the place of the molar teeth, which they lack. In this way, they process their food and create chyle; and afterwards, pressure having been applied (in the way we are accustomed to squeeze juice or porridge from crushed herbs or fruits), the softer and more liquid part is lifted upward; and they transfer it into the beginning of the intestines (which in them is located near the entrance of the gullet, in the upper part of the stomach). That this is so done appears in many kinds of birds; in whose stomachs, if stones or other harder and rough things have remained for a long time, they are seen to be so worn and smoothed by their continuous motion that they are inept for the attrition of food, and therefore are rejected. Hence, when birds pick up stones, they test them with their tongue; and if they feel nothing rough, they reject them. In this way, you will find iron, silver, and pebbles worn down and almost consumed in the stomach of the Ostrich, and also in the Cassowary. And therefore it is commonly believed that they digest iron and are nourished by it.

In falcons, eagles, and other birds living on prey, if you place your ear nearby while the stomach is empty, you may perceive manifest sounds of stones ingested there and colliding with one another. Nor do falcons swallow stones for the sake of cooling (which is the common error of falconers).

# INTRODUCTION.

Smith, Jones, Brown, and Robinson are sitting with their hands on a table. All of them, *ex hypothesi* <note>original: "by hypothesis"</note>, are honorable men, “above suspicion of intentional deception.” They ask the table where Green is. Smith, Jones, and Robinson have no idea, but Brown firmly believes that Green is in Rome. The table begins to move, kicks, and answers—by the aid of an alphabet and knocks—that Green is at Machrihanish, where, upon investigation, he is proven to be. Later, Brown is able to show (let us hope by documentary evidence) that he had heard Green was going to Machrihanish instead of to Rome as he had intended; however, this remarkable change of plans on Green’s part had entirely faded from Brown’s memory. Now we are to assume, *ex hypothesi*, that Brown is the soul of honor and, like Mr. Facey Rumford <note>a character from a novel by R.S. Surtees, known for his stubborn honesty</note>, “wouldn’t tell a lie if it were ever so.” The practical result is that, while Brown’s consciousness informs him, trumpet-tongued, that Green is at Rome, “the residue of a forgotten impression” makes him (without his knowing it) wag the table, which he does not intend to do, and forces him to say through the tilts of the table that Green is at Machrihanish, while he believes that Green is at Rome.

The table-turners were laughed at, and many, if not all of them, deserved ridicule. But see how even this trivial superstition illuminates our knowledge of the human mind! A mere residue of a forgotten impression—a lost memory which Brown would have sworn in a court of justice had never been in his mind at all—can work his muscles while he supposes that they are *not* working, can
pages.40:
# COCK LANE AND COMMON-SENSE.

make a table move at which three other honorable men are sitting, and can tell all of them what none of them knows. Clearly, the practice of table-turning in court might be tried by conscientious witnesses who have forgotten the circumstances on which they are asked to give evidence. As Dr. Carpenter remarks, quoting Mr. Lecky, “our doctrine of unconscious cerebration <note>the theory that the brain performs intellectual work without the person being aware of it</note> inculcates toleration for differences not merely of belief, but of the moral standard.” And why not toleration for “immoral” actions? If Brown’s residue of an impression can make Brown’s muscles move a table to give responses of which he is ignorant, why should not the residue of a forgotten impression—that it would be a pleasant thing to shoot Mr. Gladstone or Lord Salisbury <note>prominent British politicians of the Victorian era</note>—make Brown unconsciously commit that solecism <note>a social blunder or mistake</note>? It is a question of degree. At all events, if the unconscious self can do as much as Dr. Carpenter believed, we cannot tell how many other marvels it may perform; we cannot know until we investigate further. If this is so, it is perhaps hardly wise or scientific to taboo all investigation. If a mere trivial drawing-room amusement, associated by some with an absurd “animistic hypothesis” <note>the belief that inanimate objects are imbued with life or spirit</note>, can, when explained by Dr. Carpenter, throw such unexpectedly blinding light on human nature, who knows how much light may be obtained from a research into more serious and widely diffused superstitious practices? The research is, undeniably, beset with the most thorny of difficulties. Yet whosoever agrees with Dr. Carpenter must admit that, after one discovery so singular as “unconscious cerebration” in its effect on tables, someone is bound

# INTRODUCTION.

to go further in the same field and try for more. We are assuming, for the sake of argument, the accuracy of Dr. Carpenter’s facts. ¹

More than twenty years ago, an attempt was made by a body called the “Dialectical Society” to investigate the phenomena styled spiritualistic. This well-meant essay had most unsatisfactory results. ²

First, a committee of inquiry was formed on the motion of Dr. Edmunds. The committee was heterogeneous. Many of the names now suggest little to the reader. We remember Mr. Bradlaugh, but he chiefly attended a committee which sat with D. D. Home <note>a famous 19th-century physical medium</note>, and it is admitted that nothing of interest occurred there. Then we find the Rev. Maurice Davies, who was wont to write books of little distinction on semi-religious topics. Mr. H. G. Atkinson was a person interested in mesmerism. Kisch, Moss, and Quelch, with Dyte and Isaac Meyers, Bergheim and Geary, Hannah, Hillier, Reed (their names go naturally in blank verse), were, doubtless, all most estimable men, but scarcely boast of scientific fame. Serjeant Cox, a believer in the phenomena (if not in their spiritual cause), was of the company, as was Mr. Jencken, who married one of the Miss Foxes—the first authors of modern thaumaturgy <note>the performance of miracles or magic</note>. Professor Huxley and Mr. G. H. Lewes were asked to join, but declined to march to Sarras, the spiritual city, with

This was neither surprising nor reprehensible, but Professor Huxley’s letter of refusal appears to indicate that matters of interest, and perhaps logic, are differently understood by men of science and men of letters. ¹ He gave two reasons for refusing, and others may readily be imagined by the sympathetic observer. The first was that he had no time for an inquiry involving much trouble and (as he justly foresaw) much annoyance. Next, he had no interest in the subject. He had once examined a case of “spiritualism” and detected an imposture. “But, supposing the phenomena to be genuine, they do not interest me. If anybody would endow me with the faculty of listening to the chatter of old women and curates in the nearest cathedral town, I should decline the privilege, having better things to do.” Thus, it would not interest Professor Huxley if some new kind of telephone should enable him to hear all the conversation of persons in a town (if a cathedral town) more or less distant. He would not be interested by the “genuine” fact of this extension of his faculties, because he would not expect to be amused or instructed by the contents of what he heard. Of course, he was not invited to listen to chatter, which, on one hypothesis, was that of the dead, but to help to ascertain whether or not there were any genuine facts of an unusual nature, which some persons explained by the animistic hypothesis. To mere “belletristic triflers” <note>those concerned with literature for its own sake rather than science</note>, the existence of genuine abnormal and unexplained facts seems to have been the object of inquiry, and we must peni-

tently admit that if genuine communications could really be opened with the dead, we would regard the circumstance with some degree of curious zest, even if the dead were on the intellectual level of curates and old women. Besides, not all old women are imbeciles; history records cases of a different kind, and even some curates are as intelligent as the apes whose anatomy and customs, about that time, much occupied Professor Huxley. In Balaam’s conversation with his ass <note>a reference to the biblical story in Numbers 22</note>, it was not so much the fact that *mon âne parle bien* <note>original: "my donkey speaks well"</note> which interested the prophet, as the circumstance that *mon âne parle* <note>original: "my donkey speaks"</note>. Science has obviously soared very high when she cannot be interested by the fact (if a fact) that the dead are communicating with us, apart from the value of what they choose to say.

However, Professor Huxley lost nothing by not joining the committee of the Dialectical Society. Mr. G. H. Lewes, for his part, hoped that with Mr. Alfred Russel Wallace to aid (for he joined the committee) and with Mr. Crookes (who apparently did not), “we have a right to expect some definite result.” Any expectation of that kind was doomed to disappointment. In Mr. Lewes’s own experience, which was large, “the means have always been proved to be either deliberate imposture... or the well-known effects of expectant attention.” That is, when Lord Adare, the Master of Lindsay, and a cloud of other witnesses thought they saw heavy bodies moving about of their own free will, either somebody cheated, or the spectators beheld what they did behold, because they expected to do so,

# COCK LANE AND COMMON-SENSE.

even when, like M. Alphonse Karr and Mr. Hamilton Aidé, they expected nothing of the kind. This would be Mr. Lewes's natural explanation of the circumstances, suggested by his own large experience.

The results of the Dialectical Society's inquiry were somewhat comic. The committee reported that marvels were alleged, by the experimental sub-committees, to have occurred. Sub-committee No. 1 averred that “motion may be produced in solid bodies without material contact, by some hitherto unrecognized force.” Sub-committees 2 and 3 had many communications with mysterious intelligences to vouch for, and much erratic behavior on the part of tables to record. No. 4 had nothing to report at all, and No. 5, which sat four times with Home, had mere trifles of raps. Home was ill, and the *séances* <note>meetings for communication with spirits</note> were given up.

So far, many curious phenomena were alleged to have occurred, but now Dr. Edmunds, who started the whole inquiry, sent in a separate report. He complained that convinced spiritualists had “captured” the editing sub-committee, as people say, and had issued a report practically spiritualistic. He himself had met nothing more remarkable than impudent frauds or total failure. “Raps, noises, and movements of various kinds,” he had indeed witnessed, and he heard wondrous tales from truthful people, “but I have never been able to see anything worthy of consideration, as not being accounted for by unconscious action, delusion, or imposture.” Then the editors of the *Report* contradicted Dr.

D. Home, by the Master of Lindsay (Lord Crawford), and by other witnesses who had seen Home grow eight inches longer and also shorter than his average height; fly in the air; handle burning coals unharmed; cause fragrance of various sweet scents to fill a room, and, in short, rival St. Joseph of Cupertino <note>a saint said to have had the power of levitation</note> in all his most characteristic performances. Unluckily, Mr. Home, not being in the vein, did not do one of these feats in the presence of Mr. Bradlaugh and sub-committee No. 5. These results are clearly not of a convincing and harmonious description, and thus ended the attempt of the Dialectical Society. Nobody can do otherwise than congratulate Professor Huxley and Mr. Lewes on their discreet reserve. The inquiry of the Dialectical Society was a failure;

<meta>Continuity: Continues the description of Genji's morning at the Hitachi Palace, where he finds the princess and decides to treat her with more kindness.</meta>

The double doors at the end of the eastern wing were wide open, and because the roof of the veranda had collapsed, the sunlight poured straight into the house. A little snow was still falling, and its brightness made the morning light even more exquisitely brilliant and sparkling. He watched a servant helping him into his cloak. The princess was lying halfway out of the bed, her head hanging a little downward, and her hair falling in great waves to the floor. Pleased with the sight, he began to wonder whether she would not one day outgrow her plainness. He began to close the door of the women’s apartments, but suddenly feeling that he owed her amends for the harsh opinion of her appearance which he had previously formed, he did not quite shut the door. Instead, he brought a low stool toward it and sat there, putting his disordered head-dress to rights. One of the maids brought him an incredibly battered mirror-stand, Chinese combs, a box of toilet articles, and other things. It amused him to discover that in this household of women, a little male gear still survived, even in so decrepit a state.

He noticed that the princess, who was now up and dressed, was looking quite fashionable. She was, in fact, wearing the clothes which he had sent her before the New Year, but he did not at first recognize them. He began, however, to have a vague idea that her mantle, with its rather conspicuous pattern, was very like one of the things he had given her. 

“I do hope,” he said presently, “that this year you will be a little more conversational. I await the day when you will unbend toward me, more eagerly than the poet longs for the first nightingale. If only, like the year that has changed, you too would begin anew!” 

Her face brightened. She had thought of a remark, and trembling from head to foot with a tremendous effort, she brought out the quotation: “When plovers chirp and all things grow anew.” 

“Splendid,” said Genji. “This is a sign that the new year has indeed
pages.218:
begun.” Smiling encouragingly at her, he left the house, while she followed him with her eyes from the couch on which she lay. Her face, as usual, was half-covered by her arm, but the <term>unfortunate flower</term> <note>A reference to the princess's red nose, often described as a "saffron-flower."</note> still bloomed conspicuously. 

“Poor thing, she really is very ugly,” thought Genji in despair.

When he returned to the Nijō-in, he found Murasaki waiting for him. She was growing up to be as handsome a girl as one could wish, and promised well for the future. She was wearing a plain, close-fitting dress of cherry color; above all, the unstudied grace and ease of her movements charmed and delighted him as he watched her come to meet him. In accordance with the wishes of her old-fashioned grandmother, her teeth were not blackened, but her eyebrows were delicately touched with stain. 

“Why, when I might be playing with a beautiful child, do I spend my time with an ugly woman?” Genji kept on asking himself in bewilderment while they sat together playing with her dolls. 

Next, she began to draw pictures and color them. After she had painted all sorts of queer and amusing things, “Now I am going to do a picture for you,” said Genji. Drawing a lady with very long hair, he put a dab of red on her nose. Even in a picture, he thought, pausing to look at the effect, it gave one a most uncomfortable feeling. He went and looked at himself in the mirror, and as though dissatisfied with his own fresh complexion, he suddenly put a dab of red on his own nose, just like the one he had given to the lady in the picture. He looked at himself in the mirror. His handsome face had in an instant become ridiculous and repulsive. At first, the child laughed. 

“Should you go on liking me if I were always as ugly as this?” he asked. 

Suddenly she began to be afraid that the paint would not come off. “Oh, why did you do it?” she cried. “How horrible!” 

He pretended to rub it without effect. “No,” he said ruefully, “it will not come off. What a sad end to our game! I
pages.219:
wonder what the Emperor will say when I go back to the Palace?” He said it so seriously that she became very unhappy, and longing to cure him, she dipped a piece of thick, soft paper in the water-jug which stood by his writing-things and began scrubbing at his nose. 

“Take care,” he cried, laughing, “that you do not serve me as Heichū <note>A legendary romantic figure in Japanese literature known for his excessive, often performative, displays of emotion.</note> was treated by his lady. I would rather have a red nose than a black one.” 

So they passed their time, making the prettiest couple.

In the gentle spring sunshine, the trees were already shimmering with a haze of new-grown buds. Among them, it was the plum-trees that gave the surest promise, for already their blossoms were uncurling like lips parted in a faint smile. Earliest of them all was a red plum that grew beside the covered steps. It was in full color. 

“Though fair the tree on which it blooms, this red flower fills me with a strange misgiving,” <note>The "red flower" is a mocking reference to the princess's nose; the "fair tree" refers to her noble birth.</note> sang Genji with a deep sigh.

We shall see in the next chapter what happened in the end to all these people.

# CHAPTER VII
# THE FESTIVAL OF RED LEAVES

The imperial visit to the Red Sparrow Court was to take place on the tenth day of the Godless Month <note>The tenth month of the lunar calendar.</note>. It was to be a more magnificent sight this year than it had ever been before, and the ladies of the Palace were very disappointed that they could not be present. <note>Women were traditionally restricted from such public spectacles.</note> The Emperor too could not bear that Fujitsubo should miss the spectacle, and he decided to hold a grand rehearsal in the Palace. 

Prince Genji danced the “Waves of the Blue Sea.” Tō no Chūjō was his partner; but though both in skill and beauty he far surpassed the common run of performers, yet beside Genji he seemed like a mountain fir growing beside a cherry-tree in bloom. There was a wonderful moment when the rays of the setting sun fell upon him and the music grew suddenly louder. Never had the onlookers seen feet tread so delicately nor head so exquisitely poised; and in the song which follows the first movement of the dance, his voice was sweet as that of the Kalavinka <note>A mythical bird in Buddhist tradition, said to have a beautiful, melodious voice.</note> whose music is Buddha’s Law. So moving and beautiful was this dance that at the end of it the Emperor’s eyes were wet, and all the princes and great gentlemen wept aloud. When the song was over and, straightening his long dancer’s sleeves, he stood waiting for the music to begin again and at last the more lively tune of the second movement struck up,—then indeed,
pages.221:
with his flushed and eager face, he merited more than ever his name of Genji the Shining One. The Princess Kōkiden did not at all like to see her step-son’s beauty arousing so much enthusiasm and she said sarcastically, “He is altogether too beautiful. Presently we shall have a god coming down from the sky to fetch him away.” <note>Referring to folklore where exceptionally beautiful children are taken by the gods.</note> Her young waiting-ladies noticed the spiteful tone in which the remark was made and felt somewhat embarrassed. As for Fujitsubo, she kept on telling herself that were it not for the guilty secret which was shared between them, the dance she was now witnessing would be filling her with wonder and delight. As it was, she sat as though in a dream, hardly knowing what went on around her.

Now she was back in her own room. The Emperor was with her. “At today’s rehearsal,” he said, “the ‘Waves of the Blue Sea’ went perfectly.” Then, noticing that she made no response, “What did you think of it?” 

“Yes, it was very good,” she managed to say at last. 

“The partner did not seem to me bad either,” he went on; “there is always something about the way a gentleman moves and uses his hands which distinguishes his dancing from that of professionals. Some of our crack dancing-masters have certainly made very clever performers of their own children; but they never have the same freshness, the same charm as the young people of our class. They expended so much effort on the rehearsal that I am afraid the festival itself may seem a very poor affair. No doubt they took all this trouble because they knew that you were here at the rehearsal and would not see the real performance.”

Next morning she received a letter from Genji: “What of the rehearsal? How little the people who watched me knew of the turmoil that all the while was seething in my brain!”
pages.222:
And to this he added the poem: 

“When sick with love I yet sprang to my feet and capered with the rest, 
knew you what meant the fevered waving of my long dancing-sleeve?” 

Next he enjoined secrecy and prudence upon her, and so his letter ended. Her answer showed that despite her agitation she had not been wholly insensible to what had fascinated all other eyes: 

“Though from far off a man of China waved his long dancing-sleeves, 
yet did his every motion fill my heart with wonder and delight.”

To receive such a letter from her was indeed a surprise. It charmed him that her knowledge should extend even to the Court customs of a land beyond the sea. Already there was a regal note in her words. Yes, that was the end to which she was destined. Smiling to himself with pleasure, he spread the letter out before him, grasping it tightly in both hands as a priest holds the holy book, and gazed at it for a long while.

On the day of the festival the royal princes and all the great gentlemen of the Court were in attendance. Even the Heir Apparent went with the procession. After the music-boats had rowed round the lake, dance upon dance was performed, both Korean and of the land beyond the sea. The whole valley resounded with the noise of music and drums. The Emperor insisted upon treating Genji’s performance at the rehearsal as a kind of miracle or religious portent, and ordered special services to be read in every temple. Most people thought this step quite reasonable; but Princess Kōkiden said crossly that she saw no necessity for it. The Ring <note>Those who stand in a circle round the dancers while the latter change their clothes.</note> was by the Emperor’s order composed indifferently of commoners and noblemen chosen out of the whole realm for their skill and grace. The two Masters of Ceremony, Sayemon no Kami and Uyemon no Kami, were
pages.223:
in charge of the left and right wings of the orchestra. Dancing-masters and others were entrusted with the task of seeking out performers of unusual merit and training them for the festival in their own houses. When at last under the red leafage of tall autumn trees forty men stood circle-wise with their flutes, and to the music that they made a strong wind from the hills sweeping the pine-woods added its fierce harmonies, while from amid a wreckage of whirling and scattered leaves the Dance of the Blue Waves suddenly broke out in all its glittering splendor—a rapture seized the onlookers that was akin to fear.

The maple-wreath that Genji wore had suffered in the wind, and thinking that the few red leaves which clung to it had a desolate air, the Minister of the Left plucked a bunch of chrysanthemums from among those that grew before the Emperor's seat and twined them in the dancer's wreath.

At sunset the sky clouded over and it looked like rain. But even the weather seemed conscious that such sights as this would not for a long while be seen again, and until all was over, not a drop fell. His Exit Dance, crowned as he was with this unspeakably beautiful wreath of many-colored flowers, was even more astonishing than that wonderful moment on the day of the rehearsal and seemed to the thrilled onlookers like the vision of another world. Humble and ignorant folk sitting afar on tree-roots or beneath some rock, or half-buried in deep banks of fallen leaves—few were so hardened that they did not shed a tear. Next came the 'Autumn Wind' danced by Lady Jōkyōden's son, who was still a mere child. The remaining performances attracted little attention, for the audience had had its fill of wonders and felt that whatever followed could but spoil the recollection of what had gone before.
pages.224:
That night, Genji was promoted to the First Class of the Third Rank and Tō no Chūjō was promoted to intermediate standing between the First and Second Classes of the Fourth Rank. The gentlemen of the court were all promoted one rank. But though they celebrated their good fortune with the usual rejoicings, they were well aware that they had only been dragged in Genji's wake and wondered how it was that their destinies had come to be linked in this curious way with those of the prince who had brought them this unexpected piece of good fortune.

Fujitsubo now retired to her own house and Genji, waiting about for a chance of visiting her, was seldom at the Great Hall and was consequently in very ill favor there. It was soon after this that he brought the child Murasaki to live with him. Aoi heard a rumor of this, but it reached her merely in the form that someone was living with him at his palace and she did not know that it was a child. Under these circumstances, it was quite natural that she should feel much aggrieved. But if only she had flown into an honest passion and abused him for it as most people would have done, he would have told her everything and put matters right. As it was, she only redoubled her icy aloofness and thus led him to seek those very distractions of which it was intended as a rebuke. Not only was her beauty so flawless that it could not fail to win his admiration, but also the mere fact that he had known her since so long ago, before all the rest, made him feel towards her a tenderness of which she seemed quite unaware. He was convinced, however, that her nature was not at bottom narrow and vindictive, and this gave him some hope that she would one day relent.

Meanwhile, as he got to know little Murasaki better, he became the more content both with her appearance and her character. She at least gave him her whole heart. For the present he did not intend to reveal her identity even to the

<summary>Genji and his companions perform at the magnificent Festival of Red Leaves, where Genji's dancing reaches a transcendent level of beauty. Amidst his rising court success, Genji's relationship with his wife, Aoi, remains strained, while his affection for the young Murasaki deepens.</summary>

or that his semen enters the interior cavity of the womb, is hardly likely; for I could find no path inside with a probe or a bristle, and it did not happen that Fabricius found any either. Indeed, by his own testimony, not even blown air penetrates the womb. This was the reason, I believe, why he described the history of the womb by progressing from the interior parts to the exterior. Furthermore, having weighed this structure of the womb, he denies that the semen reaches the cavity of the womb or constitutes any part of the egg. In this opinion I also willingly profess my name. Indeed, you will find nothing in a fertile egg (which is not found in an infertile one) either added or changed from which it might be certain that the rooster's semen had entered the womb and touched the egg. Furthermore, although all eggs are vain and infertile without the rooster's union, yet by his labor (even some time after copulation) the subsequent eggs, of which there is no yet existing principle or matter, turn out fertile.

<margin>Page 37.</margin> Fabricius, in order to explain the manner by which the rooster's semen renders eggs fertile, has these words: *Since semen does not appear in the egg, and yet it is presented by the rooster into the womb; it is asked, why the rooster's semen is sent into the womb if it does not enter the egg? Likewise, if it is not present in the egg, how is a fertile egg produced from the rooster's semen, which it does not contain? My opinion is that the rooster's semen, sent into the beginning of the womb, renders the entire womb, and at the same time also all the yolks falling into it, and finally the whole egg, fertile; and that it does this by its own faculty, or by a radiating spiritual substance; in the way in which we see,*
pages.76:
<header>On the Generation of Animals.</header>

by witnesses, that other souls are also rendered fertile by semen. For if anyone recalls to memory that incredible transmutation by which an animal is affected when castrated, while it loses the fat, strength, and fertility in its whole body, he will easily grant that which we say happens to the womb of a hen alone. But that it is entirely true that the power of fertilizing eggs and also the womb proceeds from the semen of the rooster is evident from that which women do, having a hen at home deprived of a rooster; they send it to a rooster elsewhere for a day or two: for from this small amount of time the fertility of the juice of all the eggs [is provided] for the whole time of the year. This is what Aristotle also confirms, who holds that when birds have once mated, they persist in having almost all eggs fertile. Furthermore, that the fertilizing power of the semen might not in any way be able to exhale, but might persist longer in the womb and be imparted to the whole, nature itself enclosed and deposited it in a cavity, a bursa <note>an anatomical pouch or sac</note>, near the vent and attached to the womb, and endowed with an entrance so that, with the semen being detained therein, its power might be preserved and communicated to the entire womb.

I, however, suspected the truth of the aforesaid experiment, and the more so because I saw the words of the Philosopher <note>referring to Aristotle</note> recited in bad faith; for he did not say, *Birds, when they have once mated, persist in having almost all eggs fertile*, but, *they persist in having almost all eggs*; Fabricius added <term>to fæcunda</term> <gloss>as fertile</gloss> on his own. But it is one thing for birds to conceive eggs from coitus, and another for eggs to be fertilized from coitus. And that is from the

preceding words of Aristotle more clearly evident, where he says: *In the genus of birds, entirely, not even those eggs which arise through coitus can for the most part be increased, unless the bird's coitus is continued.* The reason for this matter is that, as in women through coitus the male draws out the menstrual excretion (for the warmed womb draws out the humor, and the passages are opened), so it happens in birds while the menstrual excretion gradually approaches, which cannot depart outward because it is little and is contained above at the girdle <note>referring to the narrow part of the oviduct</note>, but it collapses into the womb itself. For this egg is increased, just as the fetus of viviparous animals, because it flows through the navel. For when birds have once mated, they persist in having almost all eggs always, but very small and imperfect, and therefore infertile; if indeed the perfection of an egg is to be fertile. If, therefore, without continued coitus of the bird, not even those eggs which were conceived through coitus are increased, or (as Fabricius has interpreted) are perfected; much less will those eggs which birds persist in having without coitus be rendered fertile.

But lest anyone think that by these words (*for the warmed womb draws out, and the passages are opened*) it is concluded that the womb can draw the rooster's semen into its cavity, it should be known that it is not said by the Philosopher that the womb draws semen from outside; but in women, through veins and passages opened by heat, menstrual blood is drawn from their own body; and similarly in birds, blood is drawn to the womb warmed by continued coitus, and from thence the eggs are increased; just as the fetuses of viviparous animals are accustomed to be through the navel.

But what he adds concerning that cavity, or *bursa*, in which he presumes the rooster's semen is harbored for an entire year; these things have already been refuted by us before; where we asserted that no semen is contained in it, and that it is present in the rooster just as in the hen.

Wherefore, while I could easily believe (if by fertility we understand the production of more and larger eggs) that the hens of poor little women (for whom it is proven there is a lack of an abundance of feed) will produce fewer and smaller eggs unless they are with a rooster (according to that saying of the Philosopher: *But if they have once mated with a rooster, then they will persist in having larger, better, and more numerous eggs throughout the whole year.* To which end the abundance and quality of feed also contribute most). I thought, however, it seemed less likely to me that hens lay all eggs fertile for the whole span of a year from a few matings with a rooster. For if a few coitions were sufficient for such long-term generation, Nature (which does nothing in vain) would have made males in the avian genus less lustful; nor would the rooster so often daily solicit his hens for coitus, even against their will.

We know that a hen, as soon as she has laid an egg and leaves the nest, cries out with a clamorous voice and lures the rooster to coitus; who, responding in like manner with a raised and gasping voice, anxiously seeks her, and having found her, suddenly mounts her: which surely, Nature would not have willed to happen, except for the sake of procreation.

A male *pheasant*, kept in an aviary, is so
pages.79:
<header>EXERCISE VI.</header>

inflamed with intense lust that, unless he has many females (at least six) with him, he maltreats them by frequent repeated coitus, hindering fertility rather than promoting it. I once saw a female pheasant, because of a rooster kept with her (whom she could not avoid either by hiding or by fleeing), so exhausted, and bare of feathers on her back because of his frequent assaults, that at length, agitated in a miserable manner, she failed from sorrow. Yet in the same one, when dissected, I did indeed find the rudiments of eggs.

I also observed a male duck, lacking a mate and living with hens, inflamed with such lust that he would pursue a young hen everywhere for some hours, peck at her with his beak, and at last, when she was exhausted, mount her and perform the act of lewdness.

A rooster, victor in battle, exercises his lust not only on the mates of the defeated, but also on the living bird himself.

Similarly, some females are so inclined to lust that they peck at their males with little bites (as if they were whispering the joys of Venus into their ears), leap upon them, and invite them to coitus with other arts: in which number are pigeons and sparrows.

It does not seem likely, therefore, that a few coitions, celebrated at the beginning of the year, are sufficient for the fertility of all the subsequent eggs throughout its entire course. I, however, sometimes (in order to provide a defense for Fabricius here) in the spring season (intending to investigate something certain about the time and necessity of fertilizing coitus) kept two hens separated from the rooster for four days, which in the meantime each had laid three eggs, no less prolific than other eggs. And again I separated another hen, which on the tenth day from then laid an egg; and another on the twentieth day, and both were fertile. So that it may seem that one or another coition can render the entire year, and all eggs of that year, fertile.

I will also say what I observed at that time. When I restored each hen (separated for some time, as I said) to the rooster; of which one was pregnant with an egg, the other had recently laid, the rooster met the latter more quickly, and greedily mounted her three or four times: the other one, however, he circled often, appearing to greet her by rubbing his feet and wings, and to congratulate her on her arrival; nevertheless, having returned to the former, he mounted her again and again, and repeated the act by force: neglecting meanwhile the pregnant one, whom he in no way solicited for Venus <note>sexual intercourse</note>. I wondered by what signs he could thus distinguish to whom coitus would be beneficial and to whom it would be unwelcome. Truly, it is not at all plain how, whether by sight, hearing, or smell, males (even from afar) understand that females are struck by the gadfly of desire and crave coitus. Some, even if they hear only their voice, or smell the place where they have urinated, or only their tracks, are immediately inflamed with lust and pursue them for coitus. But about this matter elsewhere, in a treatise on the love, lust, and coitus of animals, [it will be] more fully

the place to speak. Now I return to the proposed subject.

### *On the belly of the hen and other birds.*

### EXERCISE VII.

From the external orifice, therefore, through the vulva, we have arrived at the hen's womb, or matrix; in which the egg is perfected, surrounded by albumen, and covered with a shell: concerning whose site and position, before we speak, some things concerning the peculiar *anatomy* of the belly of birds must be brought here and premised. For I have observed in feathered creatures that the stomach, intestines, and other viscera are situated and constituted differently in the lowest part of their belly than in the genus of walking animals.

Almost all birds have obtained a double stomach; of which the one is called the *crop*, the other the *stomach* <note>gizzard</note> properly so called. In the former, eaten food is reserved and prepared; in the latter, it is concocted and passes into chyle: our countrymen call the former *the crop, or craw*; the latter, *the gizzard*. In the crop, birds retain whole grains swallowed; from there, when softened, macerated, and emollient with drunk water, they later transmit them into the stomach; so that they may be ground and broken up in the same place. For the sake of which thing, almost all feathered creatures swallow little grains of sand, pebbles, and other harder things, and keep them in the stomach together with the food (while meanwhile nothing such is found in the crop); and they have this stomach [formed] from two very thick
pages.82:
<header>On the Generation of Animals.</header>

and very robust muscles (in smaller birds, fleshy or ligamentous); so that in this way, as if by two millstones joined by double hinges, they can grind the food and pound it; and the pebbles take the place of molar teeth, which they lack. In this manner they prepare the food and make it into chyle; and afterwards, when compression has been made (just as we are accustomed to express juice or porridge from crushed herbs or fruits), the softer and more liquid part is lifted upward; and they transfer it into the beginning of the intestines (which is placed in them near the entrance of the gullet, in the upper part of the stomach). That it is done so appears in many genera of birds; in whose stomachs, if pebbles or other harder and rough things have remained for a longer time, they are seen to be so worn and smoothed by their continuous motion that they are unfit for the attrition of food, and for that reason are rejected. Hence birds, when they pick up pebbles, test them with their tongue; and, if they have felt nothing rough, they reject them. In this way you will find iron, silver, and pebbles worn and almost consumed in the stomach of the *Ostrich*, and also in the *Cassowary*. And for that reason, it is commonly believed that they digest iron and are nourished by it.

In falcons, eagles, and other birds living on prey, if you place your ear near while the stomach is empty, you may perceive the clear sounds of the pebbles thrown in there, colliding with one another. Nor indeed do falcons swallow pebbles for the sake of cooling (which is the common error of falconers).

# INTRODUCTION.

Smith, Jones, Brown, and Robinson are sitting with their hands on a table. All, <term>ex hypothesi</term> (by hypothesis), are honorable men, “above suspicion of intentional deception.” They ask the table where Green is. Smith, Jones, and Robinson have no idea; Brown firmly believes that Green is in Rome. The table begins to move, kicks, and answers—by aid of an alphabet and knocks—that Green is at Machrihanish, where, upon investigation, he is proven to be. Later, Brown is able to show (let us hope by documentary evidence) that he had heard Green was going to Machrihanish instead of to Rome as he had intended, but this remarkable change of plans on Green’s part had entirely faded from Brown’s memory. Now we are to take it, <term>ex hypothesi</term>, that Brown is the soul of honor, and, like Mr. Facey Rumford <note>A fictional character known for his moral uprightness.</note>, “wouldn’t tell a lie if it was ever so.” The practical result is that, while Brown’s consciousness informs him, trumpet-tongued, that Green is at Rome, “the residue of a forgotten impression” makes him (without his knowing it) move the table, which he does not intend to do, and forces him to say through the tilts of the table that Green is at Machrihanish, while he himself believes that Green is at Rome.

The table-turners were laughed at, and many, if not all of them, deserved ridicule. But see how even this trivial superstition illuminates our knowledge of the human mind! A mere <term>residuum</term> (remnant) of a forgotten impression—a lost memory which Brown would have sworn in a court of justice had never been in his mind at all—can work his muscles while he supposes that they are *not* working; it can
pages.40: make a table move at which three other honorable men are sitting, and can tell all of them what none of them knows. Clearly, the experiment of table-turning in court might be tried by conscientious witnesses who have forgotten the circumstances on which they are asked to give evidence. As Dr. Carpenter remarks, quoting Mr. Lecky, “our doctrine of unconscious cerebration inculcates toleration for differences not merely of belief, but of the moral standard.” And why not toleration for “immoral” actions? If Brown’s remnant of an impression can make Brown’s muscles move a table to give responses of which he is ignorant, why should not the remnant of a forgotten impression that it would be a pleasant thing to shoot Mr. Gladstone or Lord Salisbury <note>Prominent 19th-century British politicians.</note> make Brown unconsciously commit that social error? It is a question of degree. At all events, if the unconscious self can do as much as Dr. Carpenter believed, we cannot tell how many other marvels it may perform; we cannot know until we investigate further. If this is so, it is perhaps hardly wise or scientific to taboo all investigation. If a mere trivial drawing-room amusement, associated by some with an absurd “animistic hypothesis” <note>The belief that inanimate objects or phenomena are possessed by spirits or souls.</note>, can, when explained by Dr. Carpenter, throw such unexpectedly blinding light on human nature, who knows how much light may be obtained from a research into more serious and widely diffused superstitious practices? The research is, undeniably, beset with the most thorny of difficulties. Yet whosoever agrees with Dr. Carpenter must admit that, after one discovery so singular as “unconscious cerebration,” in its effect on tables, someone is bound

to go further in the same field and try for more. We are assuming, for the sake of argument, the accuracy of Dr. Carpenter’s facts. <note>For ourselves, we have never seen or heard a table give any responses whatever, any more than we have seen the ghosts, heard the raps, or viewed the flights of men in the air which we chronicle in a later portion of this work.</note>

More than twenty years ago, an attempt was made by a body called the “Dialectical Society” to investigate the phenomena styled spiritualistic. This well-meant essay had most unsatisfactory results. <note>Report on Spiritualism, Longmans, London, 1871.</note>

First, a committee of inquiry was formed on the motion of Dr. Edmunds. The committee was heterogeneous. Many of the names now suggest little to the reader. Mr. Bradlaugh we remember, but he chiefly attended a committee which sat with D. D. Home, and it is admitted that nothing of interest occurred there. Then we find the Rev. Maurice Davies, who was wont to write books of little distinction on semi-religious topics. Mr. H. G. Atkinson was a person interested in mesmerism. Kisch, Moss, and Quelch, with Dyte and Isaac Meyers, Bergheim and Geary, Hannah, Hillier, and Reed (their names go naturally in blank verse) were, doubtless, all most estimable men, but scarcely boast of scientific fame. Serjeant Cox, a believer in the phenomena, if not in their spiritual cause, was of the company, as was Mr. Jencken, who married one of the Miss Foxes, the first authors of modern thaumaturgy <note>The working of miracles or magic.</note>. Professor Huxley and Mr. G. H. Lewes were asked to join, but declined to march to Sarras, the spiritual city <note>A legendary city in Arthurian romance associated with the Holy Grail.</note>, with
pages.42: the committee. This was neither surprising nor reprehensible, but Professor Huxley's letter of refusal appears to indicate that matters of interest, and, perhaps, logic, are differently understood by men of science and men of letters. <note>Report, p. 229.</note> He gave two reasons for refusing, and others may readily be imagined by the sympathetic observer. The first was that he had no time for an inquiry involving much trouble, and (as he justly foresaw) much annoyance. Next, he had no interest in the subject. He had once examined a case of “spiritualism” and detected an imposture. “But, supposing the phenomena to be genuine, they do not interest me. If anybody would endow me with the faculty of listening to the chatter of old women and curates in the nearest cathedral town, I should decline the privilege, having better things to do.” Thus, it would not interest Professor Huxley if some new kind of telephone should enable him to hear all the conversation of persons in a distant town. He would not be interested by the “genuine” fact of this extension of his faculties, because he would not expect to be amused or instructed by the contents of what he heard. Of course, he was not invited to listen to chatter, which, on one hypothesis, was that of the dead, but to help to ascertain whether or not there were any genuine facts of an unusual nature, which some persons explained by the animistic hypothesis. To mere “literary triflers,” the existence of genuine abnormal and unexplained facts seems to have been the object of inquiry, and we must peni-
pages.43:
tently admit that if genuine communications could really be opened with the dead, we would regard the circumstance with some degree of curious zest, even if the dead were on the intellectual level of curates and old women. Besides, all old women are not imbeciles; history records cases of a different kind, and even some curates are as intelligent as the apes, whose anatomy and customs, about that time, much occupied Professor Huxley. In Balaam’s conversation with his ass <note>Refers to the biblical story in Numbers 22, where Balaam's donkey speaks to him.</note>, it was not so much the fact that *mon âne parle bien* <note>Original: "my donkey speaks well."</note> which interested the prophet, as the circumstance that *mon âne parle* <note>Original: "my donkey speaks."</note>. Science has obviously soared very high when she cannot be interested by the fact (if a fact) that the dead are communicating with us, apart from the value of what they choose to say.

However, Professor Huxley lost nothing by not joining the committee of the Dialectical Society. Mr. G. H. Lewes, for his part, hoped that with Mr. Alfred Russel Wallace to aid (for he joined the committee) and with Mr. Crookes (who apparently did not), “we have a right to expect some definite result.” Any expectation of that kind was doomed to disappointment. In Mr. Lewes’s own experience, which was large, “the means have always been proved to be either deliberate imposture... or the well-known effects of expectant attention.” That is, when Lord Adare, the Master of Lindsay, and a cloud of other witnesses thought they saw heavy bodies moving about of their own free will, either somebody cheated, or the spectators beheld what they did behold because they expected to do so,
pages.44:
even when, like M. Alphonse Karr and Mr. Hamilton Aidé, they expected nothing of the kind. This would be Mr. Lewes's natural explanation of the circumstances, suggested by his own large experience.

The results of the Dialectical Society's inquiry were somewhat comic. The committee reported that marvels were alleged, by the experimental sub-committees, to have occurred. Sub-committee No. 1 averred that “motion may be produced in solid bodies without material contact, by some hitherto unrecognized force.” Sub-committees 2 and 3 had many communications with mysterious intelligences to vouch for, and much erratic behavior on the part of tables to record. No. 4 had nothing to report at all, and No. 5, which sat four times with Home, had mere trifles of raps. Home was ill, and the *séances* (spiritualist meetings) were given up.

So far, many curious phenomena were alleged to have occurred, but now Dr. Edmunds, who started the whole inquiry, sent in a separate report. He complained that convinced spiritualists had “captured” the editing sub-committee, as people say, and had issued a report practically spiritualistic. He himself had met nothing more remarkable than impudent frauds or total failure. “Raps, noises, and movements of various kinds,” he had indeed witnessed, and he heard wondrous tales from truthful people, “but I have never been able to see anything worthy of consideration, as not being accounted for by unconscious action, delusion, or imposture.” Then the editors of the *Report* contradicted Dr.
pages.45: Edmunds on points of fact, Mr. A. R. Wallace disabled his logic, <note>Mr. Wallace may be credited with scoring a point in argument. Dr. Edmunds had maintained that no amount of evidence would make him believe in certain obvious absurdities, say the lions in Trafalgar Square drinking out of the fountains. Mr. Wallace replied: “The asserted fact is either possible or not possible. If possible, such evidence as we have been considering would prove it; if not possible, such evidence could not exist.” No such evidence exists for the lions; for the phenomena of so-called spiritualism, we have consentient testimony in every land, period and stage of culture. That certainly makes a difference, whatever the weight and value of the difference may be.</note> Mr. Geary dissented from the Report, the editors said that his statements were incorrect and that he was a rare attendant at séances, and Serjeant Cox vouched for more miracles. A great many statements of the most astounding description were made by Mr. Varley, an electrician, by D. D. Home, by the Master of Lindsay (Lord Crawford), and by other witnesses who had seen Home grow eight inches longer and also shorter than his average height, fly in the air, handle burning coals unharmed, cause fragrance of various sweet scents to fill a room, and, in short, rival St. Joseph of Cupertino <note>A 17th-century saint reported to have the gift of levitation.</note> in all his most characteristic performances. Unluckily, Mr. Home, not being in the vein, did not do one of these feats in the presence of Mr. Bradlaugh and sub-committee No. 5. These results are clearly not of a convincing and harmonious description, and thus ended the attempt of the Dialectical Society. Nobody can do otherwise than congratulate Professor Huxley and Mr. Lewes on their discreet reserve. The inquiry of the Dialectical Society was a failure;
pages.46:
the members of the committees remained at variance; and it is natural to side with the skeptics rather than with those who believed from the first, or were converted (as many are said to have been) during the experiments. Perhaps all such inquiries may end in no more than diversity of opinion. These practical researches ought not to be attempted by the majority of people, if by any. On many nervous systems, the mere sitting idly round a table, and calling the process a *séance*, produces evil effects.

<margin>1006</margin>As to the idea of purposely evoking the dead, it is at least as impious, as absurd, as odious to taste and sentiment, as it is insane in the eyes of reason. This protest the writer feels obliged to make, for while he regards the traditional, historical, and anthropological curiosities here collected as matters of some interest in various aspects, he has nothing but abhorrence and contempt for modern efforts to converse with the *manes* (the spirits of the dead), and for all the profane impostures of “spiritualism.”

On the question of the real existence of the reported phenomena hereafter chronicled, and on the question of the <term>portée</term> (significance) of the facts, if genuine, the writer has been unable to reach any conclusion, negative or affirmative. Even the testimony of his senses, if they ever bore witness to any of the *speciosa miracula* (splendid miracles), would fail to convince him on the affirmative side. There seems to be no good reason why one observer should set so much store by his own impressions of sense, while he regards those of all other witnesses as fallible. On the other hand, the writer feels unable to set wholly aside the concurrent

## C A P. I I.

### S U M M A R I U M.
pages.22:
1 *The statement of a witness testifying regarding a loan, and not knowing what a loan is, is not valid.*
2 *That notaries cannot claim ignorance.*
3 *That substantial clauses must be applied specifically and expressly in instruments.*
4 *That a woman renouncing the Velleian decree is deceived.*
5 *That someone cannot certify another, if he himself is in need of the same certification.*
6 *That notaries who do not know the force of the clauses placed in instruments at the time the contract was celebrated, are to be punished for falsity.*

**It should be set forth** to the notaries, that if they have placed substantial clauses of instruments in them and have ignored their force, when questioned: and these are causes concerning the fact of the contractors, that the contract is null by the law itself: for example, if in the instrument of some woman they assert that the woman herself was certified regarding the Velleian <note>The <term>Senatus Consultum Velleianum</term> <gloss>a Roman law forbidding women from assuming debt for others</gloss></note>, and when asked what the Velleian is, they do not know how to respond, then the instrument is null by the law itself, as Albericus notes in the final law in the penultimate paragraph <note>Digest 16.1.1</note> of the Digests on the Velleian. Bartolus notes in a similar case in the first law <note>Digest 12.1.1</note> of the Digests on if a certain thing is claimed, where he says † that if a witness testifies regarding a loan, and when asked

And in consultation 115, which begins *Viso processu*, in the 3rd volume. † And this is especially urged, because a notary cannot claim ignorance as Bartolus says in the law *Divus Claud*, <note>Digest 48.10.1</note> in the Digests on the false. Baldus in law 1, <note>Digest 1.3.1</note> in the Digests on laws, and this is the reason, because ignorance does not fall upon one's own act, law *Quisquis*, <note>Code 4.44.2</note> Code on the rescission of a sale, law *Quanquam*, <note>Digest 16.1.1</note> in the Digests on the Velleian Senate Decree, final law in the Digests on his own. And consequently, since he cannot claim ignorance, and he was ignorant of the vigor of the clauses placed in the instrument, we must say the instrument itself is vitiated, † because substantial clauses of instruments must be applied specially and expressly. Law *Seia*, <note>Digest 32.1.41</note> in the Digests on gold and silver legacies, law *Iulianus*, <note>Digest 43.3.1</note> in the Digests on exhibiting, law *Cum hi*, paragraph *Praetor*, <note>Digest 43.16.1</note> in the Digests on translation, final law in the Digests on divorces. # TO THE MAJESTY OF THE EMPEROR
# FERDINAND III.
## On the Egyptian Oedipus of Father Athanasius Kircher.
## SONG
### BY THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS AND EXCELLENT
### LORD
# POMPEO COLONNA
## PRINCE OF GALLICANO.

<note>A large historiated decorative initial 'S' features a figure amidst dense floral and vine-like scrollwork.</note>

SIR, you whose heavy Diadem
You honor with merit more than it honors you with a throne,
You in whose breast dwell
Honest, virtuous, and holy desires;
You who are a true connoisseur of goodness
Among the many cares with which you govern a World,
Of acute wit and profound knowledge,
You are a follower of doctrine and virtue;

<margin>Whence</margin> it happens that with your example you often
Anticipate the high laws, and both good and just
With sentiments of piety from the August page
Before governing others you govern yourself;
<margin>You</margin> who know well that he who governs on earth
Must feed, not oppress the flock,
And that he who greedily leans to another style
Stays away from the right path and errs;
<margin>You</margin> who finally are turned to every good study,
And understand the art of every Magistery,
Look at the volume of Athanasius part by part,
And you will see every knowledge gathered therein.
<margin>Oedipus</margin> he is, who reveals for the common good
Of every Oedipus the most hidden enigmas,
And the arcana reserved for the wisest
He offers and unveils to every understanding.

+++
pages.25:
After its oblique and twisted path
Where like a Hydra the Nile spreads its mouths,
Seen only until now as a giant and great thing
It finally discovers its cradle and makes itself a child.

You will see, Sir, in the commended deeds
Of those Kings who bowed to the laws
A clear, vivid image expressed
Of that which you did in your reign.

And so many Deities in the form of animals
Isis, Anubis, Apis, or Serapis, or Osiris,
And so many other deliriums born to the World
Only from Egypt can their origins be known.

But in those Sages there was not such foolishness
That in those Gods for whom the Altars smoked
They did not enclose hidden and rare mysteries,
Of which the learned Athanasius now gives an account.

Further on then a School will offer itself to you
To satiate the most hungry wits,
Since written with those obscure signs
Every word contains a science.

The Character that in every creature
Its maker impressed but not seen
Thus by everyone, now by everyone known
Will be with its virtue and its nature;

No otherwise can we believe
Than that the name corresponding to the virtue
Of every thing down here with a wise mind
The first Father Adam placed then.

Vulgar medicine is held here as vain
Which only drives away evil with its contraries,
And that one is procured only for the common good
Which through its own virtue smooths the humors.

O flashing lamps of light
To trace the arcana, now in the beasts,
In the birds, in the stones, now in the woods,
In the mute fish; now in the flowered fields

Athanasius will send them! Now rejoice
O sons of Aesculapius, for you will be able to restore
The lost method of healing well with such aid
For the benefit of the sick.

Ghi
pages.26:
He who ever placed his foot in the Elements
Of the learned Euclid can now well hope
In spite of those Sages, he too to make
The bird of Archytas and the globe of Archimedes.

He who was by chance intent on walking
In the rich and ample gardens of Hermes;
With a slow, solitary, and late step
Will arrive to admire the golden borders:

But the greedy one, at whom I am accustomed to laugh,
Who pretends to raise mountains of gold
Will read that his labor promises
Hunger, cold, stench, toil, and smoke.

To flee together and foresee disasters
He who is curious to know desires,
Will well be able here with natural Magic
Sculpted beforehand, to make the Stars propitious.

From the beasts and birds, from the elements,
From every thing finally created in the World
He who has a thirsty desire to guess
Could almost retell future events;

Provided that the fool does not desire to know
The truth from the enchantments of Hell;
Since here he will read that it is a vain thought
To hope for the truth from the King of lies.

Of the Mysteries up there of the Creator,
And of the spirits stripped of matter,
How the great Planet that distinguishes the hours
Is moved and crosses so much space.

He who yearns to have knowledge, now will be satisfied
That at last, with double glory, from Athanasius
Paths not trodden before are now joined
Sagaciously, the Christian and the Magus.

The wonders of famous Egypt
Hidden among mysteries are now manifest,
And the obscure and misunderstood Characters
That ancient Memphis has written on Obelisks.

Rome, I do not know what more can return to your glory
Than that such great masses are your ornament,
Or rather that he who renders their mute sentiment
Clear to you, fully dwells in you.
pages.27:
To make such long journeys now there is no need
    To know what mysteries it hides within itself
    When a man governs, or when an Island is in the waves;
Or when the star Canopus shines in the Sky.
In vain you push your steps toward Egypt
    On a perilous and long harsh path,
    O curious one, for here even the Sphinxes
Speak in an intelligible language.
From the sepulchers the preserved corpses
    Rise also to reveal arcana,
    That it was not delirium or vain thought
To be almost like children anointed and swaddled.
Happy wit, that with clear flight
    You cross the path of glorious fame
    Since he who has an ardent desire for every knowledge
You know how to satiate with a single volume.
Pythagoras and Plato, to acquire
    Uncommon doctrine, see Egypt,
    But from now on everyone will stop their foot
For just having seen your Oedipus is enough.
Through the sea of knowledge you now welcome us
    Expert helmsman with a safe Ship
    Since with a placid and sweet breeze
We travel through Egypt within your pages.
Oppressed among the events of fortune
    Which in vile servitude has wrapped its greatness,
    Its memories buried among oblivion
Egypt itself will have as a gift from you.
You, great FERNANDO, alone will know nothing
    More than what your mind already understood,
    But these papers will make clear to others
A memory at least of what you do.

# TO THE MOST GLORIOUS
# FERDINAND III.
# CAESAR ALWAYS AUGUST.

### ELEGY

### By Ferdinand of Fürstenberg, Canon of Hildesheim and Paderborn,

<note>An ornamental woodcut initial 'N' is decorated with intricate floral and scrollwork patterns.</note>

NOT the lineage of the *AUSTRIANS* descended from the blood <margin>of Gods,</margin>
*Nor an Empire closed by the ends of the world,*
Nor would I dare to mention immortal triumphs,
*And wars worthy of the Maeonian <note>Homeric</note> trumpet:*
Whether *CAESAR* destroys the fortresses conquered by victorious eagles
*Under the happy auspices of the Swabians;*
Whether he vindicates the *Danube* <note>original: Istrum</note> that badly obeys Roman
*Laws; or whether he repels Northern powers.*
Let others sing of that, those supported by the buskin <note>tragic acting boot/tragedy</note>
*Of whom the Muse rises, and labors on the epic of heroes.*
It pleases me to go more safely in the path of unwarlike elegies, and small
*Songs, sounding not from on high,*
And to celebrate customs, and the sacred arts of *CAESAR*.
*This subject matter suits my numbers.*
He loves pious poets, and the gifts of pious poets,
*Affable, with the cloud of his brow laid aside.*
He, the glory and guardian of the Heliconian Sisters <note>the Muses</note>,
*Adorns the learned Divinities with his riches.*
Who does not know the arduous temples of Cecropian Minerva <note>Athena</note>
*That were built? Who does not know the proud roofs of the Clarian God <note>Apollo</note>?*
Where the Viadrus <note>Oder river</note>, crowned with reed-hair,
*Washes the temples dedicated to the Aonian choirs.*
Where, marveling widely at Pandionian <note>Athenian</note> Athens,
*The Danube, slower, lingered with stirred waters:*
And where the thresholds rising at *CAESARIAN* expense
*Make the royal Prague equal to the Cyrrhaean ridges <note>Mount Parnassus</note>.*
There: just as Jupiter, after the wars of Enceladus,
*Takes off his hands armed with threatening fire;*
And just as Atlas, tired by the long weight,
*Placed the high axis on his Herculean shoulders:*
*CAESAR*, weary of the reins that rule the lands,
*Often reclines the vast burden of the Empire.*
