But after the benefit provided by Caesar two years ago: and with the new Academy established: you seem to be prescribing to us: what we ought to add to the classical exercises.
Therefore, the compilation of the Academic letters has been entrusted to me: so that according to my own judgment: what I feel about establishing the Academy: I may explain that to friends in letters.
And in this matter, I hold your will and consent: as a deed excellently performed: and I prefer it to a military victory or triumph. For a battle, as soon as it is engaged, ceases to be: but the establishment of some Lyceum, or Stoa, or Academy: as soon as it is instituted, begins to be: and it promises longevity: and hopes for immortality: and brings forth daily fruits of glory from daily seeds of labor, for an age that will last as long as the world stands, perpetual.
For this reason, the matter which has been entrusted to me
pages.8:
and undertaken by me, I will not depart from it: before I have brought it to you in its completed state.

And although I shall write nothing different from those things, which I have handed down in the book on the correct opening of schools of letters: yet I shall ascend a little higher: and proceed further: so that from these things it may appear, what I then hoped for, or what I foresaw.

I will, however, set before me those most flourishing Athens: which at one time had both the most famous leaders of military affairs: and the highest exponents of past deeds: also excellent poets: and perfect orators: and in three places, three families of the greatest philosophers: in the Academy, the Stoa, and the Lyceum: which men, how great they were in industry, diligence, and learning: are proof of the books which they wrote: and which are numbered by Diogenes Laertius, and by Suidas: and can be understood from the authorities of the remaining writers.

And in the compilation of this, whatever it is to be:
pages.9:
written work: it has seemed good to call upon you and to summon you to me, so that I may show to men, that you are the patrons of the liberal arts: and that what we establish, and what we do, we undertake with you as our authors. Farewell. Strasbourg.

## TO THE SCHOLARCHS:

For if anyone recalls to memory that incredible transmutation by which an animal is affected when castrated, while it loses vigor, strength, and fertility in the whole body, he will easily concede that what we say happens to the uterus of the hen alone. But that it is entirely true that the power of fertilizing eggs, and also the uterus, comes from the rooster's semen, is evident from what women do: having a hen at home deprived of a rooster, they send it to a rooster elsewhere for a day or two. From this short time, the fertility of all the eggs [is obtained] for the whole <margin>On the Gen. of An. book 3, ch. 1, p. 38.</margin> year's time. This is also confirmed by Aristotle, who holds that when birds have once mated, they continue to have almost all their eggs fertile. Furthermore, that the fertilizing power of the semen might not in any way be able to exhale, but might remain in the uterus for a longer time and be imparted to the whole, nature herself has enclosed and stored it in a cavity, a pouch near the vent, and attached to the uterus, and endowed it with such an entrance that, with the semen detained within, the power of the same might be preserved and communicated to the whole uterus.

I, however, suspected the truth of the aforesaid experiment, and all the more so because I saw the words of the Philosopher <note>referring to Aristotle</note> recited in bad faith: for he did not say, *Birds, when they have once mated, continue to have almost all their eggs fertile*, but, *they continue to have almost all their eggs [fertile]*: Fabricius added <term>fertile</term> on his own account. For it is one thing for birds to conceive eggs from coitus, and another for eggs to be fertilized from coitus. And that this is clear from the preceding words of Aristotle, where he says: *In the genus of birds, even those eggs which arise through coitus cannot for the most part grow, unless the mating of the bird is continued.*

The cause of this matter is that, as in women, by the coitus of the male, menstrual excrement is drawn away (*for the heated uterus draws [it], and the passages are opened*), so it happens in birds while the menstrual excrement gradually approaches, which cannot depart outwardly, since it is little and is held above at the girdle <note>referring to the narrow part of the oviduct</note>, but it collapses into the uterus itself. For this egg grows, just as the fetus of viviparous animals, because it flows in through the navel. For when birds have once mated, they continue to have almost all their eggs, but they are very small and imperfect, and therefore infertile; since the perfection of an egg is to be fertile. If, therefore, without the continued mating of the bird, not even those eggs which were conceived through coitus grow, or (as Fabricius has interpreted) are perfected; much less will those eggs be rendered fertile which birds continue to have without coitus.

Lest anyone should think that by these words (*for the heated uterus draws [it], and the passages are opened*) it is concluded that the uterus can attract the rooster's semen into its cavity, it should be known that it is not said by the Philosopher that the uterus attracts semen from without; but in women, through the veins and passages opened by heat, menstrual blood is drawn from their own body; and likewise in birds, blood is drawn to the uterus heated by continued coitus, and from thence the eggs are grown; just as the fetuses of viviparous animals are accustomed to [be nourished] through the navel.

### *On the Ventricle of the Hen and Other Birds.*

### EXERCITATIO VII.

From the external orifice, therefore, through the vulva, we have arrived at the hen's uterus, or matrix; in which the egg is perfected, surrounded by albumen, and covered by a shell: before we speak of its situation and position; some things about the peculiar *anatomy* of the birds' belly must be brought here and prefaced. For I have observed in feathered [animals], the ventricle <note>referring to the stomach</note>, intestines, and other viscera are situated and constituted differently in their lower belly than in the genus of walking animals.

Almost all birds have a double ventricle; of which one is called the *ingluvies* <note>original: "ingluvies" - crop</note>, the other the *ventricle* properly so-called. In the former, eaten food is reserved and prepared; in the latter, it is digested and passes into chyle <note>original: "chylum" - chyle</note>: ours call the former, *the crop, or craw*; the latter, *the gisard* <note>original: "gisard" - gizzard</note>. In the crop, birds retain whole grains that have been devoured; and from thence, when softened, macerated, and emollited by drunk water, they transmit them afterwards into the ventricle; so that there they may be ground and comminuted. For the sake of which, almost all feathered animals swallow little sands, pebbles, and other harder things, and keep them in the ventricle together with the food; (while in the meantime nothing of the sort is found in the crop) and they have this ventricle [made] of two very thick

and most robust muscles (in smaller birds, fleshy or ligamentous) compacted; so that in this way, as with two millstones, tied together by two hinges in turn, they can grind the food and pound it; and the pebbles take the place of molar teeth, which they lack. In this way, they prepare the nourishment, and chylify; and afterwards, when compression has been made (just as we are accustomed to express juice or mash from crushed herbs or fruits), the softer and more liquid part is lifted upwards; and they transfer it into the beginning of the intestines (which in them is placed next to the entrance of the esophagus, in the upper part of the ventricle). That it happens in this way is apparent in many genera of birds; in whose ventricles, if pebbles or other harder and rougher things have remained too long, they are seen to be so worn down and smoothed by their continuous motion that they are inept for the attrition of food, and therefore are cast out. Hence, when birds pick pebbles, they test them with their tongue; and, if they feel nothing rough, they reject them. In this way, you will find iron, silver, and pebbles worn down and almost consumed in the ventricle of the *Ostrich* <note>original: "Struthionis"</note>, and also in the *Cassowary* <note>original: "Caffovvare"</note>. And therefore it is commonly believed that they digest iron and are nourished by it.

In falcons, eagles, and other birds living on prey, if you move your ear near when the ventricle is empty, you may perceive clear sounds of pebbles ingested there, and colliding with each other. For falcons do not swallow pebbles for the sake of cooling (which is the common error of falconers).

SINCE IT IS THE CUSTOM of our Academy that we attempt to teach everything that the human mind can attain, it behooves us teachers to have learned everything, a state we have not yet reached. For I do not see that any of us could have promised that to himself, nor, as I feel, has anyone done so. Or if he has promised it, he did so more out of zeal and desire than out of knowledge of a difficult and arduous matter. If someone were to read all the books of Plato, or even those of Aristotle, or Plutarch as well: how many are there who do not think they have heard, inquired into, and known everything? Yet how many and how great are the things they lacked? I believe indeed, and I believe truly: if one were to gather and arrange in order the doctrines of all philosophers, whether they be Epicureans, or Academics of both the old and new Academy, or Stoics—of all these, I say, and of the rest of the wise men of all Greece—yet one would see that they wished for everything rather than were able to, and that they had divided rather than explained whatever philosophy professes. And even if there were nothing else: they could certainly say nothing about God, nothing about the creation of the world, nothing about the nature of man, and nothing about the return of men into life. The poets dared to name the sons and daughters of Jupiter, but how...
pages.16:
much did they, along with the philosophers, wander away from the investigation of true knowledge, to say nothing of cognition. Now, in the later physical and mathematical sciences, many things have been discovered that were unknown to the first wise men. And although this is so: yet since a philosopher virtually professes everything, and all have labored to attain the goal of knowing and handing down everything: why should the same be denied to us that was granted to them? Or why are we able to achieve less than they by means of industry? Are books lacking to us? Is leisure, or funding, or resources lacking? Or, finally, is talent lacking? If we yield to the ancients in this, it is due more to the corruption of discipline and our own sloth than to the capacity of nature, the goodness of which is no less a gift and benefit from God than the harvest and the grain supply. Ages have indeed produced men, one after another, who are more numerous, sharper, and more learned: just as some years are surpassed by others in fertility. And even if the Arabs possess more men of talent than Germany possesses: yet for that reason, the benevolence of God, who is the illuminator of the human mind, should not be taken away. For every light of genius proceeds from God.
Therefore, let Athens have been learned, and let poets, mathematicians, and philosophers have flourished there: yet they did not always flourish in the same way. Nor for that reason is it denied to us because that was granted to them before us; and they have left behind for us the monuments of literature, which teach us how many and how great are the things they encompassed in doctrine: learned men understand them, and how much has been added by those who followed the first, and how much can be added to the later ones by us: there are those who consider, and who notice the path by which one arrives at this faculty.
But, as he says, when two come together, there is need for <term>syzētēseōs</term> <gloss>discussion/inquiry</gloss>: and just as he speaks of a bad matter, so let us speak of a good one: mutual efforts must be traded between us: so that if we individuals cannot attain everything perfectly, we may yet attain individual things moderately, each for himself...
pages.17:
each person should cultivate what is certain according to his own talent: let him reach for the rest as far as he is able: and let him learn from his other colleagues: so that what individuals do not possess, the whole may possess. Therefore, if you wish to be authors to me and my colleagues: you could bring it about that we establish a distribution among ourselves of the arts and the books that we read: so that in a few years, we may possess everything, not in books and libraries, but in our minds and memories, divided, known, and acquired among us: things which are indeed preserved in the books of the ancients. Let the theologians, therefore, divide among themselves the authors whom they might read at home, whether they be Greeks, such as these ecclesiastical historians: such as Chrysostom, Basil, Nazianzen, and the others: or Latins, such as Tertullian, Lactantius, Cyprian, Jerome, and Augustine.
Let the mathematicians and physicists do the same with their own writers. As for me, to the precepts of speaking, and to Cicero and Demosthenes, I shall gladly add this year the books of Plato and Aristotle on the Republic, and on laws, and what they have handed down regarding morals. Let others work hard on the historians and poets: so that, instructed by these, in daily meetings and conversations: in disputations and schools: in rhetorical declamations, it may appear: how many and how great are the things the human mind can attain if it tries: and if it enters upon the right path and method: how great are the progresses the mind of man can make: with shared studies: divided labors: distinct intervals of hours: and finally, with reason and good method.

## TO LAURENTIUS TUPIUS, DOCTOR OF LAWS.

<note>A decorative initial 'C' features elaborate scrollwork and foliage motifs inside a square frame.</note>
I believe it is also very troublesome for you to repeat the <term>Institutiones</term> <gloss>Institutes</gloss> of the Emperor Justinian so often: and unpleasant for those who listen to you, to know nothing from you except the Institutes. And it also hinders the praises of our Academy: that we have so few interpreters of law in our gymnasium. I know it was ordained thus by our ancestors: and that they retained the same rule: to have but one explainer of laws: and it was believed by them that students of law are more dissolute than other students: who devote themselves primarily to good letters and to theology.
And although in other academies some who cultivate this study lead their lives somewhat wantonly: although why do I say cultivate? They do not cultivate it, those who live basely: but they violate it with vices: and they neglect one of the first precepts of this doctrine. For where is that saying? TO LIVE HONESTLY. Although, therefore, there are some who live more wantonly: yet we are able to restrain them by our laws. And we have discovered by experience that, because of the scarcity of hours: not only the adolescents, but even the teachers themselves are not just slowed down, but are corrupted by leisure...
pages.18:
rather than languishing: so that they depart from us before it is advantageous for either party. I pass over the fact that this scarcity, which is akin to poverty, also harms the children of our citizens.
Therefore, if my advice were to have a place, I would advise that you share the <term>Pandectas</term> <gloss>Pandects/Digest of Justinian</gloss> with Beuther, Hugo Blotius, and Vuilueshemius: so that we may be compared with the remaining academies in this part of philosophy as well.
You have the sources of your law in the books of the philosophers on the Republic and on morals: books which will hereafter be diligently explained in our schools. You will do a great service if you also bring your own streams back to their origin: and they derive their streams to you from their own sources.
By this path and this method, the study of <term>Jurisprudentiae</term> <gloss>jurisprudence/law</gloss> would turn out more pleasantly: and the labor would be easier: and the doctrine of laws would become fuller.
For just as the view of springs is more pleasant and their taste sweeter than that of streams: and just as the little fish in those rivulets that come from the springs...

for they are joined by the law of charity, and owe this duty only to themselves, not to another. But do you wish to abstain? He shows how you can do so piously: first <term>ἐκ συμφώνου</term> <gloss>by consent</gloss>, that is, so that you have a willing wife, and you become a pleader and lead with words, not refusing your own person to one who is not unwilling. Then <term>πρὸς καιρὸν</term> <gloss>for a time</gloss>, that is, let it be done opportunely, with a certain and most pious occasion offered. For these he supplies arguments for a husband pleading with his wife for her company. Thirdly, he brings forward certain cases in which this might be done, but in these he ought to establish nothing without the other's consent. For marriage has the form of an Aristocracy and a Monarchy. In fasting and private prayers they can obtain this from each other by mutual agreement. He understands, however, solemn fasting and prayers, in which the whole Church was accustomed to assemble, such as in times of persecution, pestilence, famine, and similar cases. Following the example of the Synagogue, the Church would proclaim certain days of prayer, and join fasting to these, so that they might pray more holily and ardently; they could abstain from the marriage bed by consent. Otherwise, the whole life of a Christian man ought to be adorned with fasting and prayers; Christ taught that one must always pray, and He commended fasting so that our bodies might not be burdened by drunkenness.

Fourthly, he commands them to come together again. Marriage is not dedicated to pleasures alone, but is for the most part consecrated to the cross and to labors: therefore, by mutual meeting, they ought to soothe the troubles of life.
pages.219:

The reason is added: Lest Satan tempt you, that is, lest he introduce occasions for whoring. For he does not sleep, but seeks opportunities to contaminate marriages. Here consider the force of the argument. The Apostle does not wish, even for the sake of prayers and fasting, that is, most holy exercises, that one be away from the bed for too long. What, therefore, shall we say about annual pilgrimages? About military service rashly undertaken, and other infinite occasions by which marriages are rashly corrupted, etc.

Finally, he adds, *Because of your intemperance*. He notes the luxury of the Corinthians and the intemperance that is born from it, for without Ceres and Bacchus, Venus grows cold. You will say the same today about our customs: We are intemperate, therefore we ought to be all the less absent from the marriage bed, as we show ourselves easy to temptations. Remain at home, therefore.

6. *But I say this by way of indulgence, not by way of commandment.*

<term>Συγγνώμη</term> <gloss>Indulgence/forgiveness</gloss> is the mitigation of supreme law without sin; it establishes what is good and equitable, relaxing the rigor of the law in certain cases. Thus Aristotle, Ethics book 6, chapter 11. <term>Συγγνώμη</term> <gloss>Indulgence</gloss> is a judgment <unclear>that</unclear>

<term>αἰτιολογία</term> <gloss>reasoning/account</gloss> which is correct <term>περὶ ἐπιστολῆς</term> <gloss>concerning the epistle</gloss>. For the Apostle here measures the weakness of the Corinthians and opposes the cunning of Satan; therefore, when he had said they should withdraw for prayers and fasting, and soon come together again, he says this is not a commandment but a consideration of equity, for the sake of avoiding evil. If they wish to prolong the time, and can bear the temptations, he makes it free for them. Therefore, he does not make a general commandment that all must contract marriage. Moses compelled everyone to marry. Paul corrects this and brings a mitigation, as Christ also did, because there are those who have the gift of chastity; let them abstain, and he grants permission to the married, that in other cases they may abstain from the marriage bed, provided they are honest.

7. *For I would that all men were as I wish myself to be.*

<margin>Rendering of the cause.</margin>
<term>Αἰτιολογία</term> <gloss>Reasoning</gloss> is why he speaks according to the mitigation of the law, for equity and good, as if he were to say, because your weakness does not bear it. I would indeed wish you to be like me, that is, all equal to celibacy, but I see that it is an impossible thing, therefore I grant you permission; I would rather have you live in matrimony.

The second is the commendation of celibacy, by which he wishes all to be celibate after his own example; but just as he corrected the first, so he soon corrects this one also according to present circumstances. Everyone, he says, has his own gift. Therefore, mar-
pages.221:
<margin>Celibacy and marriage are gifts of God.</margin>
riage is also a gift, no less than celibacy. Furthermore, both are from God: therefore both are honest, and in this they are equal, nor is it an obstacle that they are particular to us even though they are from God. For this one declares the origin and author: the other the use and possession: finally, those two gifts vary in use: celibacy is a rarer gift, common to few, more expeditious in these miseries, a simulation of the celestial life where He will reign. Marriage, however, is a commoner good, more troublesome, proper to this life, serving the infirmity of the Church. Here, while the Apostle refers himself from the rare and impossible, turning himself to circumstances, he commands those who do not have the gift to pass to marriage. It is a gift, therefore no one can take this upon himself of his own accord: where the gift is not, its nature should not be followed, lest we strive for things impossible and illicit. You are born for marriage, do not strive for a celibate life, lest you run outside the olive groves. You have the gift of celibacy, follow this, do not entangle yourself in the troubles of marriage. This is Paul's <term>συγγνώμη</term> <gloss>indulgence</gloss>, which we all ought to follow. But today they cast a noose. They demand the vow of celibacy indiscriminately, which they can neither maintain for long nor maintain chastely. Some sweep the traces of a woman to expel the dust: meanwhile hearts burn with the flames of Venus, life is most filthy, morals most corrupt: they redeem prostitutes with money, nor is there any other kind of life more corrupt than the priestly order. Meanwhile, they think it is excellently provided for celibacy if they do not have legitimate wives.

8. *But I say to the unmarried and to the widows, it is good for them if they remain as I am.*

The second question is about those who are outside of marriage: the sum is that it would be expedient for the Corinthians if they could abstain from the troubles of marriage after the example of Paul. He does not confirm this but rather corrects it; the reason, however, is manifest. Because in that kind of life there would be fewer inconveniences, easier flight in persecutions, fewer impediments to divine matters, and similar things which contribute to the commendation of celibacy.

<margin>About those who are outside of marriage</margin>

Next, an apt distribution is to be observed. The celibate life <note>original: "coelibatus vita"</note> embraces a twofold genus of men: <term>ἀγάμους</term> <gloss>the unmarried</gloss>, that is, those who have never been in marriage, who have never celebrated weddings; and <term>χήρας</term> <gloss>widows</gloss>, that is, matrons, who although they may have been married at some time, yet now are not. In both classes there have always been some who were adorned with this gift, and therefore for these alone <term>καλὸν ἐστιν</term> <gloss>it is good</gloss>, that is, it is useful to remain in that state. For individuals live both more commodiously and more happily in the state for which they have the gift than that for which they are not adorned with the gift. Finally, he proposes his own example, from which Jerome refers to Eustochium concerning the preservation of virginity among the celibate. For those are not to be heard who invent that he had a wife, since when discussing continence and persuading it, he introduced perpetual chastity. I wish, however, that all were
pages.223:
COMMENTARIES

as I am, as below: But I say to the unmarried and to widows, it is good for them if they remain as I also. Chrysostom and Ambrose are of the same opinion. And indeed he could not propose his own example to the celibate unless he himself were such. But as for what is written in Philippians 4 and 3, <term>γνήσιε σύζυγε</term> <gloss>sincere yokefellow</gloss>, it is such that it can easily be referred to a man whose faith and diligence in teaching the Gospel he had experienced. And to me, therefore, it seems more probable that the Apostle did not use his own right in many places, which he nevertheless easily concedes to others. Thus he did not accept a stipend from the Churches <margin>Inf. 9.</margin>, but worked with his own hands. Thus he would prefer to abstain from meat forever; so he did not lead about a sister as a wife, not that he disapproved of such things in others, but that he would prefer to become all things to all men.

Those who establish the contrary have grave authors also, whom they follow. Clement of Alexandria in the 3rd book of the Stromata affirms that Paul had a wife, and interprets that phrase in Philippians 4 as concerning his wife, whom he did not lead about because he had no need of great service from her. Eusebius, book 3, chapter 10 of Church history, cites almost the same from Clement, etc. Some reconcile this question thus: that when writing this to the Corinthians he perhaps did not have a wife, but otherwise had married for certain reasons. Or that he changed her into a sister; and therefore his example holds place here, because he lived as a celibate in body and soul with a sister.

To me, Paul's discourse concerning celibacy seems too open to admit a wife; I know he claims for himself the right to the power of a sister, but I do not have an open word that he used that right. It is open, however, concerning his celibacy among the celibate: It is good for them if they have remained as I. 9. *But if they do not contain, let them contract marriage.*

Thirdly, he commended the celibate life; therefore, thirdly, he tempers the praises of it with a truly Christian correction. Why he wishes the celibate life for all, will appear below in verse 29 and the following. And Eusebius, in Demonstration of the Gospel, book 1, chapter 9, pursues this more copiously from this very place, namely that the circumstance of time being afflicted and contracted, demanded this more. For the celibate are more prepared for flight, and have fewer inconveniences, cares, temptations, etc., with which marriage is burdened. When he had turned his mind to these things, he wished a celibate life for all. And soon looking back at the believers themselves, he easily perceived that his wish did not have place: therefore, correcting it, he says: if they do not contain, that is, if they do not have the gift of continence

They have nothing, therefore, of which they may glory concerning celibacy: for individuals rightly and laudably follow the commandment of their own gift: he who tries to do otherwise sins against God who distributes the gifts, against the grace of the gift, and against the Apostle who piously and rightly distinguishes among the gifts, and commands what is possible to each. To the celibate, <term>γαμησάτωσαν</term> <gloss>let them marry</gloss> does not apply: thus, he who does not have the gift of celibacy, it does not pertain to him; it is good if he has remained as I; the same rule ought not to be applied to all, just as the same shoe does not fit both feet. For that one, the celibate life is better; for this one, it is better to live in marriage; both are good in different respects: but they cease to be good if they are interchanged, as is done today. Those who do not have the gift of celibacy are constrained to it. Hence, from colleges have been made brothels, from virgins prostitutes, from monks defilers of others' beds, corrupters of virgins, and something even more nefarious.

<margin>Necessity is a just cause for marriage</margin>
Let us observe that the just cause for marriage is finally necessity itself, that is, if they experience that they do not have the gift of continence. Hence it is that he says if they do not contain, that is, if they cannot, if they perceive themselves to be conquered. He establishes this as a certain and firm <term>κριτήριον</term> <gloss>criterion</gloss>, that they do not have the gift of celibacy. Therefore, he counsels these from their own convenience, let them live in marriage

## BY FRANCESCO GOZADINO, BISHOP OF ZAKYNTHOS AND CEPHALONIA.

<note>A large decorative drop cap initial 'Π' featuring a central shield with vertical bars (heraldic pales), surrounded by an ornate frame.</note>

Octavianus Augustus, moved by the love of <unclear>Caesar</unclear>, [sought] the ancient wisdom in the obelisks raised by him, which were <unclear>unveiled</unclear>, [and] the whole of Egypt, buried and despaired of, laden with rich works and all accompanying suffering. Just as he published the hieroglyphic learning, <unclear>experience</unclear> (having sent them to Rome), for the divine service of the interpretation of secret things. But the burden fell upon him alone, to whom much of the mystical learning of all the ancients, having been, as it were, overwhelmed and submerged in the streams of Lethe. Ferdinand III, Augustus, happier than that Octavian, obtained what was then hidden, and succeeded in having it happen successfully with that same zeal and expense, the other—he, at that time, I do not know how he is borne to him—Athanasius the German, Kircher, and those <unclear>witnessing</unclear> in riddles, and <term>Oedipus</term> <term>revived</term>, sent by Royal mandate, did not set out for the distant places of wisdom, but visited, where until then they were untrodden and inaccessible, he revealed and <unclear>excavated</unclear> the treasure. For whether by virtues, in which Ferdinand trusts in his desires, and by the African commands, the forbidden or <term>Mimetic</term> <gloss>Imitative</gloss> secret depths, he opened the seals of the orgies, and the mysterious letters of the ancient temples, and the inscription, setting forth the imperial alliance, or he unfolded the soul of his soul in great generosity. Therefore we proclaim you a thrice-happy Caesar, as indeed by the achievements of your gentle brothers, and those of the most eminent <unclear>brought forth</unclear> completed in such things, whoever might wish or be able to practice, or perform the work, men with the thoughts of the mind. Long ago, Augustus displayed the sphere to you as being able to do it, with the <unclear>unoffered</unclear> Obelisks. But you, by your ability, because you were raised up not only on luxurious stones, but also obtained it otherwise from yourself, so that by your grant and your nod, eternally and silently, the sweet-speaking verses of the obelisks and the wealth of two thousand years, you explored and raised up the Egyptian wisdom. And it was right that the wretched one should clothe himself in the chariot of the world. And to turn to the reflections of this fame, bringing together, and joining with, the entire human race, with flashes of lightning, with revelers, and with triumphs, and establishing the property of the world as you are the ambassador of angels, and heralds.

# TO FERDINAND III.

## CAESAR,

### KING THRICE-GREATEST,

### FATHER OF THE FATHERLAND, &c.

->Happiness.<-

->*Francesco Gozadinus, Bishop of Zakynthos and Cephalonia.*<-

<note>A decorative drop cap 'O' featuring a seated scholar or saintly figure writing at a desk, surrounded by ornate scrollwork.</note>

Octavianus AUGUSTUS Caesar, stirred by the desire to acquire the ancient wisdom which was reported to be inscribed upon the obelisks erected by him, explored the whole of Egypt through the work of learned men, so that if he could find any interpreter skilled in hieroglyphic doctrine, he might summon him to Rome for the office of interpreting secret things. But he could not obtain his wishes, all the mystical doctrine of the Ancients having long since been submerged as if by a certain river of Lethe. FERDINAND III, Caesar Augustus, so much happier than that Octavian, by how much happier auspices he achieved that which the other could not attain by any prayers or expenses, while by some fate it fell to him to have Athanasius Kircher, a new Interpreter, an Oedipus revived; who, spurred by the Caesarian command, flew with a shining intellect to the regions of Wisdom, [and] uncovered treasures hitherto inaccessible. He, the first, relying on the orders of Ferdinand, entered more deeply into the hidden recesses of the Memphitic shrines, opened the secret seals of the sacraments, [and] interpreted the mysterious volumes of the ancient Priests with Caesarian obstetric munificence. SINCE IT IS THE CUSTOM of our Academy to attempt to teach everything that the human mind can grasp, it behooves us instructors to have learned everything, a state we have not yet attained. For I do not see any of us who could have promised this to himself, nor, as I feel, does anyone keep his promises. Or if he has promised, he has done so more out of zeal and desire than out of knowledge of a difficult and arduous subject. If someone were to read all the books of Plato, or even those of Aristotle and Plutarch, how many are there who would not think they had heard, questioned, and known everything? Yet how many and how great are the things they lacked? I truly believe, and believe it to be the truth, that if anyone were to collect the doctrines of all philosophers—whether they be Epicureans, or Academics of both the old and new Academy, or Stoics—I say, of all these and the rest of the wise men of all Greece, and arrange them in order, he would still see that they wished for everything rather than were able to achieve it, and that they had divided rather than explained whatever philosophy professes. And even if there were nothing else, they were certainly unable to say anything about God, nothing about the creation of the world, nothing about the nature of man, and nothing about the return of men into life. The poets dared to name the sons and daughters of Jove, but how
pages.16:
much they wandered, along with the philosophers, from the pursuit of true knowledge, to say nothing of understanding. Now, in the later physics and mathematics, many things have been discovered that were unknown to the first wise men. And even though this is so, since the philosopher professes, as it were, everything, and all have striven to attain this, so that they might know and transmit everything: why should the same not be granted to us as was to them? Or why should we be less able than they to acquire it through industry? Do we lack books? Do we lack leisure? Do we lack stipends or resources? Or, finally, do we lack talent? If we yield to the ancients in this, it is due more to the corruption of discipline and our own sloth than to the capacity of nature, whose goodness is no less a gift and benefit of God than that of the crops and the harvest. Ages have indeed brought forth others, and more numerous, and sharper, and more learned men, just as some years are surpassed in fertility by others. And though the Arabs may have more men of talent than Germany has, the kindness of God, who is the illuminator of the human mind, must not therefore be taken away. For every light of genius proceeds from God.
Thus, Athens may have been learned, and poets, mathematicians, and philosophers may have flourished there, yet they did not always flourish in the same way. Nor is it denied to us for that reason, because that was granted to them before us, and they left us the monuments of literature which teach us how many and how great are the things they comprised in their learning. Learned men understand these things, and consider how much has been added by those who came later to the first, and how much can be added by us to those who came later. They are the ones who reflect, and who observe the path by which one arrives at this capacity.

And just as he says in a bad matter, so let us speak in a good one: we must offer each other mutual effort, so that if we cannot individually attain everything perfectly, we may nevertheless individually attain things moderately, and each person may cultivate his own path according to his talent, touching upon the others as far as he can, and learning from his other colleagues, so that what individuals do not possess, the whole group may possess. Therefore, if you wish to be the authorities for me and my colleagues, you could bring it about that we institute a distribution among ourselves of the arts and books that we read, so that in a few years, we may possess everything—not just in books and libraries, but in mind and memory—divided, known, and acquired among ourselves, which indeed has been preserved in the books of the ancients. Let the theologians, therefore, divide among themselves the authors whom they read at home, whether they be the Greeks, such as the ecclesiastical historians—like Chrysostom, Basil, Nazianzen, and the rest—or the Latins, such as Tertullian, Lactantius, Cyprian, Jerome, and Augustine.
Let the mathematicians and physicists do the same with their own writers. As for me, to the precepts of speaking, and to Cicero and Demosthenes, I will gladly add this year the books of Plato and Aristotle on the Republic, and on the laws, and what they transmitted about morals. Let others work hard on the historians and poets, so that, instructed by these in daily gatherings and conversations, in disputations and schools, and in rhetorical declamations, it may appear how many and how great are the things the human mind can attain if it tries, and if it enters upon the right reason and path: how many advances the soul of man can make through shared studies, distributed labors, distinct intervals of hours, and, finally, through reason and a good method.

# TO CAROLUS MIEGIUS
## CONSUL AND SCHOLARCH.

<note>A large ornate woodcut initial 'Q' contains a grotesque face or sun-like mask centered within the letter, surrounded by decorative foliate patterns.</note>
SINCE IT IS THE CUSTOM of our Academy that we attempt to teach all things, insofar as the human mind is able to attain them, it behooves us teachers to have learned all things, a state which we have not yet achieved. Nor indeed do I see any one of us who has been able to promise this to himself, nor, as I perceive, has anyone made such a promise.
pages.16: or if he has promised, he has done so more out of zeal and desire than out of knowledge of a difficult and arduous subject. If someone were to read all the books of Plato, or even those of Aristotle, or even Plutarch, how many are there who would not think that they had heard, inquired into, and known everything? But how many and how great were the things they lacked? I believe indeed, and I believe it to be true: if one were to collect and arrange into order the doctrines of all philosophers, whether they be Epicureans, or Academics—both of the old and of the new Academy—or Stoics; if, I say, one were to collect the doctrines of all these and of the other wise men of all Greece, he would nevertheless see that they wished for everything rather than were able to possess it, and that they had divided rather than explained whatever philosophy professes. And even if there were nothing else: they certainly could not say anything about God, nothing about the creation of the world, nothing about the nature of man, nothing about the return of men to life. The poets dared to name the sons and daughters of Jupiter; but how
pages.17: far they wandered, along with the philosophers, from the pursuit of true knowledge, to say nothing of cognition. Now, in the later fields of Physics and Mathematics, many things have been discovered which were ignored by the first wise men. And even though this is so, since the individual philosopher professes, as it were, all things, and since all have labored to attain the goal of knowing and handing down everything, why should the same not be granted to us as was granted to them? Or why should we be able to achieve less than they through industry? Are books lacking to us? Is leisure? Are stipends or resources? Or, finally, is talent? If we yield to the ancients in this, it happens more from the corruption of discipline and our own sloth than from the capacity of nature, whose bounty is no less a gift and benefit of God than is the grain and the harvest. Ages have indeed produced—one after another—more, and sharper, and more learned men, just as some years are surpassed by others in fertility. And even if the Arabs have more ingenious men than Germany
pages.18:
has, the kindness of God, who is the illuminator of the human mind, must not therefore be taken away. For every light of genius proceeds from God. 
Therefore, Athens may have been learned, and poets, mathematicians, and philosophers may have flourished there; yet they did not always flourish in the same way. Nor for that reason is it denied to us because that was granted to them before us. They have left behind for us monuments of literature which teach us how many and how great the things are that they have encompassed in their learning. Erudite men understand these things, and they consider and observe how much has been added to the first by those who came later, and how much can be added by us to those who follow. And there are those who observe by what path this faculty is reached. 
But as he says, <term>σὺν δύ' ἐρχομένῳ</term> <gloss>when two go together</gloss>, there is a need for <term>συζητήσεως</term> <gloss>discussion</gloss>, and as he speaks in a bad matter, so let us speak in a good one: we must trade our efforts with one another so that, if we cannot individually attain everything perfectly, we may nevertheless individually attain things moderately,
pages.19:
and truly let each one cultivate them according to his own talent; let him touch upon the others as far as he can, and learn from his other colleagues, so that what individuals do not have, the whole body may possess. Therefore, if you wish to be authors to me and my colleagues, you could make it possible for us to institute a distribution among ourselves of the arts and books that we read, so that in a few years we may possess everything, not in books and libraries, but in our minds and memories—divided, known, and acquired among us—which are preserved in the books of the ancients. Let the theologians, therefore, divide among themselves the authors whom they read at home, whether they be the Greeks, as are these ecclesiastical historians—like Chrysostom, Basil, Nazianzen, and the rest—or the Latins, such as Tertullian, Lactantius, Cyprian, Jerome, and Augustine. 
Let the mathematicians and physicists do the same with their writers. For my part, I shall gladly apply this year to the precepts of rhetoric and to Cicero and Demosthenes
pages.20:
the books of Plato and Aristotle on the Republic and on Laws, and what they handed down regarding morals. Let others labor in the same way on historians and poets, so that, instructed by these in daily meetings and conversations, in disputations and schools, and in rhetorical declamations, it may appear how many and how great the things are that the human mind can attain if it strives, and if it enters upon the right reason and path: what great progress the mind of man can make through shared studies, distributed labors, distinct spans of time, and, finally, through a good method and manner.

## TO LAURENTIUS TUPIUS, DOCTOR OF LAW.

<note>A decorative initial 'C' features elaborate scrollwork and foliage motifs inside a square frame.</note>
I believe it is quite troublesome for you as well to repeat so often the Institutes of Emperor Justinian, and unpleasant for those who listen to you to
pages.21:
to know nothing from you beyond the Institutes. And it also detracts from the praises of our Academy that we have so few interpreters of Law in our gymnasium. I know that this was established by our ancestors, and I know that we have retained the same, except for having only one explainer of laws, and it was believed by them that students of Law are more dissolute than other students who devote their effort primarily to good literature and Theology. 
And even though in other Academies some who cultivate this study conduct their lives more petulantly—though why do I say "cultivate"? Those who live basely do not cultivate it, but violate it with vices and neglect one of the primary precepts of this doctrine. For where is that saying: TO LIVE HONESTLY? Even though, therefore, there are some who live more petulantly, we can nevertheless restrain them with our own laws. And we have discovered by experience that, because of the scarcity of hours, not only are the adolescents corrupted by leisure, but the teachers themselves are also
pages.22:
not languishing; they depart from us sooner than is expedient for both parties. I pass over the fact that this scarcity, which is akin to poverty, also harms the children of our citizens. 
Therefore, if my counsel were to have place, I would advise that you share the Pandects with Beuther, Hugo Blotius, and Vuilueshemius, so that we might be compared with the remaining Academies in this part of philosophy as well. 
You have the sources of your Law in the books of the philosophers on the Republic and on morals, which books will hereafter be explained diligently in our schools. You will do well if you also reduce your streams back to their origin, and they derive their streams to you from their own sources. 
By this path and by this rationale, the study of Jurisprudence would turn out more pleasantly, and the labor would be easier, and the doctrine of laws would become fuller.

10. *But to those who are bound by marriage, I say, not I, but the Lord.*

The third passage is on avoiding divorce in marriage: the proposition is, The bond of marriage is most tight and therefore indissoluble.

<header>COMMENTARII</header>

First, weigh the manner of his speech here. Not I, he says, but the Lord. Does Paul therefore declare one thing, and the Lord another? Not at all: the Apostle brought forth the preceding things without an expressed word of God, <margin>Matt. 19. 11</margin> although Christ had said something similar: Not all receive this word, he who is able to receive it, let him receive it. Thus, the Apostle determines the consequences concerning unequal marriage. Where, therefore, he did not have an expressed commandment of God, he attributes the decision to himself. Here, however, he has the commandment of Christ concerning the constancy of marriage outside the case of adultery, as in lighter cases, in which Moses had even indulged the Jews, which indulgence Christ correcting, said that it was not so from the beginning, but that the two would be one flesh. The same the Apostle commands here, that marriage is indissoluble among the faithful in such cases. Meanwhile, both these and the following are decisions of the Holy Spirit. For the Apostle is an instrument of the Holy Spirit, and through his mouth He pronounces these things. Moreover, he binds the faithful more tightly to keep the bond of marriage when he introduces the Lord as the author. The Lord says this in Matt. 5 and 19, with which the doctrine of the Apostle agrees. Let a wife not depart from her husband for a light cause, namely, under the pretext of religion, because of a changed manner of life, and similar causes. In which a bill of divorce could have had a place according to Moses. Then, if she chooses to depart entirely, let her remain unmarried, or be reconciled to her husband. He prohibits a new marriage, because the former
pages.228:
<header>IN EPIST. AD COR.</header>

still endures, and cannot be dissolved for a just cause, and therefore he commands widowhood for her in the hope of reconciliation. Thirdly, he commands the husband similarly: Let not a husband send away his wife: for it could have seemed that he granted a certain greater right to the husband than to the wife, which Ambrose also follows; therefore, he commands the same to the husband, that he should not send away his wife, namely for a light cause, after the manner of the Jews, for whom it was customary even to send away pious wives if their morals, or beauty, or something else were blamed. And among the Heathens also it was quite familiar to exchange marriages. In these things, therefore, the commandment of the Apostle is valid: let not the husband send away the wife. But as for that question: Is it therefore not allowed in any way to repudiate a wife once taken? <margin>That divorce is not dealt with here explicitly.</margin> We answer that it is not dealt with here. For the Apostle is not instituting a dispute concerning divorce, or concerning its legitimate causes, but his purpose is to persuade first that marriages are to be kept as sacredly as possible, and therefore indissolubly. He who maintains this does not deny that there is a certain manner which can dissolve marriages sacredly entered into. But what that manner is for which it can be dissolved, Christ indicates in Matt. 5 and 19, namely, fornication; for that makes it so that the two are no longer one flesh. Also, what the Apostle teaches here, if an infidel person does not wish to live with a believer anymore, the believer is not held to servitude. It is beyond controversy that for these causes marriage is broken, and therefore justly dissolved. Truly, he did not look to the just causes of divorce, but rather to the unjust, and therefore he defers concerning indissolubility. We have explained the passage concerning divorces separately; see our topics.

12. *But to the rest I say, not the Lord, if any brother has an infidel wife who consents, etc.*

<margin>Concerning unequal marriage.</margin> The fourth passage is concerning unequal marriage, that is, in which one person is a believer, the other remaining in their old religion, or Jewish, or Heathen. The passage contains two things, a <term>propositio</term> <gloss>proposition</gloss> and a <term>causa</term> <gloss>reason</gloss>. The proposition is proposed in several ways. For he renders the right equal to both persons. The meaning of the proposition is: An unequal marriage is also to be kept indissolubly by the pious. How he understands this, he explains concerning the husband who has an infidel wife who nevertheless wishes to live with the Christian man. Similarly, concerning the wife who has an infidel husband who nevertheless does not think the wife should be abandoned because of the new religion. Thus, the right is equalized, and therefore it looks only to the faithful persons. For the Apostle could not give commandments to infidels. Furthermore, he says that he says these things, because Christ had given no commandment in these cases regarding the new Christian profession. Meanwhile, it is the rule of the Holy Spirit, of whom the Apostle is the organ.
pages.230:
<header>IN EPIST. AD COR.</header>

14. *For the infidel husband is sanctified in the wife.*

<margin>Why a believer should not desert an infidel spouse.</margin>
This is a confirmation of the proposition set forth, if a believer ought not to desert an infidel spouse. Why? Because the worse part, that is, the infidel, is sanctified through the better, that is, the believing spouse. He takes the argument from the nature of the faith of the better person. It is proper to faith to sanctify us to God, that is, it declares us sanctified by God; and it does not reside only in one person, namely the believer, but because the believer is one flesh with the infidel spouse, consequently the sanctification flows over even to the worse part. And indeed, the infidel will have infinite occasions of repenting, and even of converting himself to Christ the Savior. Nevertheless, the Apostle did not say "he shall be sanctified," or "let him be sanctified," but "he is sanctified." For it is a most certain argument of the hope of his conversion also, since he does not wish to depart. Therefore, that sanctification has a place only in those who do not wish to dissolve the marriage: in others, not in the same way. Furthermore, the children born from this are holy; if the marriage were broken, they would be rendered impure. Therefore, it is not to be broken because of religion. Their children are called holy because, notwithstanding the infidelity of the other part, they belong to the Church of Christ. For it is said to individual believers, I will be your God, and of your children. Therefore, for the sanctification of the children, it is sufficient if one parent is a believer.
pages.231:
<header>COMMENTARII</header>

It is. The children are also called holy because they can also be consecrated to Christ through education. Wherefore, for the utility of the children also, such a marriage is not to be broken. Thirdly, because God has called you to peace. Therefore, no society among men instituted for a good end is to be rashly torn apart by the pious. He adds this reason to the objection. <margin>Question.</margin> For the believer will ask: you do not want me to desert an infidel spouse, I being a believer, but what if he does not wish to live with me? Shall I follow him? Or shall I be bound to keep celibacy unless I am reconciled to him? The Apostle answers, I do not want this at all: but I do not want you to be the cause, so that the marriage may remain ratified; but if the infidel does not wish it, very well, let him depart; you will be free from the marriage, he himself so deciding. God has called us to peace. Therefore, the marriage ought not to be broken by you. And, He has called us to peace. Therefore, leave the departing infidel; do not call him into court; do not prosecute your cause against him. Keep peace in both ways.

Fourthly, from the hope of conversion. An unequal marriage ought not to be broken by the believer, because there is hope that the infidel can be gained by honest conversation. For effort must be given so that we gain everyone for the Lord, let alone a spouse. Therefore, the spouse is to be borne more in this case. It is to be observed in these arguments that the Christian religion does not disturb political affairs, such that it holds marriages previously entered into as ratified: nay, it teaches that even unequal ones are to be borne patiently.

Then, that in a just marriage the consent of cohabitation is necessarily required, without which it cannot subsist entirely. 3. From which it is also brought about that the marriages of the impious are not sacred in the least. For while each person lacks sanctification, they are impure. So one must judge concerning all their works. Meanwhile, they have their political virtues, which, however, do not please God. Fourthly, great is the dignity of faith, to which is attributed the power of sanctifying that which is not yet holy, such as an infidel spouse, children born from an unequal marriage, etc.

17. *Unless as God has partitioned to each, as God the Lord has called.*

The fifth passage is concerning one's station being diligently kept by each. For among the Corinthians there seemed to be some morose men who, to those converted from Judaism, immediately imposed the changing of their whole life in external ceremonies, or from Gentilism, immediately demanded a new manner of living from those converted. Or perhaps there were also others who did not seem pious enough to themselves unless they cast off all previous life ceremonies entirely. The Apostle meets these in this place and decides that there is no need for such austerity; that the religion of Christ does not abolish the status of life; this he teaches learnedly by proposing, explaining, confirming, concluding. We shall resolve the individual things to the proposition.

<header>COMMENTARII</header>

We shall resolve the individual things to the proposition. Let that be the proposition.

<term>Πρότασις</term> <gloss>Proposition</gloss>. Because of the profession of the Gospel, it is not necessary to change one's manner of life immediately, but each one's own vocation, with religion saved, is to be diligently protected and preserved. The Apostle said this: to <term>περιπατεῖν</term> <gloss>walk</gloss> as God has called each one, that is, to persist in his own kind of life in which the profession of the Gospel found him. And the word <term>περιπατεῖν</term> <gloss>walk</gloss> is to produce the fruits of the active life, so that you may understand that it is of piety to produce actions conformable to the profession. For it is not enough to contemplate and speak much concerning piety: action is needed. And the particle <term>εἰ μὴ</term> <gloss>unless</gloss> is to be connected with <term>ὡς</term> <gloss>as</gloss>. For it is a limited proposition and restricted by a certain condition: Unless as God has distributed, one must walk; that is, not otherwise, not by our own judgment, a vocation is not to be feigned for us, but that which the Lord has imposed is to be retained. In which sense he pricks the superstition of the Corinthians who, because of the profession of religion, immediately wanted to change everything.

But let us consider the arguments by which this can be shown that we have proposed from the Apostle: One's own station is to be kept by each after the acknowledgement of the truth. Why? Because God has so distributed the kinds of life. It is a firm reason from divine ordination and disposition, which is to be studiously observed by the pious. The Apostle urges the argument with gemination and change of words, <term>θεὸς ἐμέρισεν</term> <gloss>God has distributed</gloss>, and <term>κύριος κέκληκεν</term> <gloss>the Lord has called</gloss>. He says the same thing indeed.

# ON NATURAL
## AND
# SUPERNATURAL
## THINGS

### Chapter One.

Since I have now undertaken to write of the primary <term>tincture</term> <gloss>a substance capable of transmuting metals</gloss>, the root of Metals and Minerals, and also of spiritual things, and how Metals and Minerals are first conceived and born corporeally: I have judged it necessary to preface a discourse in which I shall reveal that all things reside in two classes, namely in natural and in supernatural things. For that which is visible, comprehensible, and clothed in its own form, that is natural; but that which is incomprehensible and spiritual is called supernatural, as it is something that must be apprehended and judged by faith alone, such as the creation and, above all, the eternity of GOD, infinite, unsearchable, and immense, which nature cannot grasp nor human reason attain. This, therefore, is supernatural: that which reason cannot perceive but must apprehend by faith,
pages.4:
and it is an entirely celestial thing, which looks toward Theology, which judges souls. Furthermore, the Angels of GOD belong to supernatural things, endowed with clarified bodies, performing that by the permission of their creator which otherwise consists in the powers of no creature, since their works, which they exhibit, are hidden from the world, and no less do the works of infernal spirits lie hidden, which are permitted to them by divine allowance. But above all, the great works of GOD are perceived and known supernaturally, because they can be judged and comprehended by no human thoughts, as is principally the highest grace and benevolence of GOD, which, touched by love, He imparted to men in an infinite and unsearchable manner, as also many other miracles through Christ our Redeemer and Savior, issued variously and frequently in confirmation of His omnipotence and glory, such as when He raised Lazarus from the dead, the daughter of Jairus, and the son of the widow of Nain: He restored speech to the mute, hearing to the deaf, and sight to the blind, all of which are supernatural mighty works of GOD, just as His conception, resurrection, descent into hell, and ascension into heaven are most hidden and patent only through faith.

To supernatural things are also referred the ascension of Elijah into heaven and that of Enoch, likewise the Rapture of St. Paul into the third heaven. Moreover, many supernatural things occur through imagination, visions, and dreams, as often many miracles proceed through imagination, just as variegated sheep were born by the benefit of spotted rods placed into the water. GOD warned the Magi in the East through a dream not to return to Herod.
pages.5:
Furthermore, the number of persons and their threefold gifts, and the supernatural star, import something singular and mystical.

Nor was it a natural dream that befell the wife of Pilate, who falsely judged our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ to death. That vision of the Angels made to the shepherds at the birth of Christ, and likewise to the women at His sepulcher, is by no means to be considered natural.

What of the fact that many other supernatural things happened frequently through the prophecies of the Prophets and the Saints? Likewise, the voice of the ass speaking to Balaam was not consistent with nature, just as the interpretation of dreams by Joseph exceeded the powers of nature. GOD also very often protects us from infinite evils by the ministry of His Angels and snatches us from necessities and dangers, for the repulsion of which the powers of nature would not otherwise suffice.

These, therefore, and many other things pertain to Theology and are celestial, which the soul ought to attend to. To these follow the supernatural things of the visible creatures of GOD, such as we perceive in the firmament, in the Planets and stars, together with the Elements, which also surpass our reason; yet we observe their course through the speculation of calculation, which is a matter of Astronomical doctrine. Such creatures, however, perform their operations in a visible, yet incomprehensible manner, in the manner of a magnet, from which proceed just as many miracles, far removed from nature. But hold this: that heaven flows into the earth, and the earth in turn responds to heaven, for the earth also
pages.6:
fosters seven Planets, which are generated by the seven celestial ones, though by a certain spiritual impression, since all stars beget Minerals, and these things therefore occur in an incomprehensible and spiritual way, and thus they seem to be supernatural, by the example of two people loving one another. The human body is visible and physical, but love is invisible, spiritual, incomprehensible, and supernatural, to be compared only to magnetic attraction, for invisible love, lured by cupidity through spiritual imagination, is calmed only when its thirst is quenched.

In a similar way, when the love of heaven inclines toward the earth, and the affection of the earth tends toward man, as the love of the macrocosm to the microcosm, since the latter depends upon the former, when the earth now conciliates to itself the love of heaven by the desire of its own invisible imagination, a conjunction results of the superior with the inferior, by the example of male and female, who are fashioned by us under one body. After which conjunction, the earth, impregnated by such an influence, begins to bring forth, according to the influx that has been made; which offspring is then, after conception, cooked by the Elements and matured to perfection, which is reckoned and counted among supernatural things, how the operation of a supernatural thing descends into a natural thing.

Among supernatural things are also placed all Magical and Cabbalistic arts, which proceed from the true light of nature, not from those which smack of superstition or the illicit conjuration of enchanters, but I understand here such Magic
pages.7:
as the Magi from the East were instructed in, who judged from divine inspiration and lawful art, from that which the ancients before us obtained and which the Egyptians and Arabs possessed, who before the invention of writing marked and observed things through signs, characters, and other things of that kind. Nor is the use of these expiations forbidden, which we read in scripture that Christ Himself employed: *And taking the children, He laid His hands upon them and blessed them.* But that which in these things is contrary to GOD and His word is deservedly to be repudiated and not permitted, because it is certain that it is done not by GOD but by the Devil himself. But supernatural things that are not adverse to GOD or His word are referred to Magic, which is without the loss of the soul.

Regarding visions, which very often befall the men of GOD, they also deservedly claim a place for themselves among things alien to nature. For whatever man ought to attain in his mind by speculation is supernatural; on the contrary, that which man can touch, discern, and grasp is natural.

The third order of natural and supernatural things consists in Medicine, in the virtue of any thing, which Medicine of any thing must first be elicited from some speculable, comprehensible, and natural body and promoted into an emended spiritual and supernatural operation, so that the spirit, which was infused and granted to the body in the beginning for living, may be freed and penetrate to operate, just as the spiritual nature and fire, to which its vents are left, for burning, and nothing is an impediment to it which might suffocate, extinguish, and interrupt the flaming life,
pages.8:
than otherwise, with the separation of soul and spirit from the body neglected, no virtual and convenient operation, as necessity would require, can by any means follow. For whatever is comprehensible to the eye and is inseparable and corporeal exists as natural and corporeal. But as soon as separation has been made, with life departing from the body, the thing attains its full operation. And with the natural body separated, the spiritual nature is liberated to penetrate and is turned into a spiritual and supernatural medicine. And briefly, all palpable things, without exception, are natural, but they are to be raised into a supernatural state if we are to destine them for Medicine; for the supernatural includes only the living virtue of operating, while the natural possesses a dense and sensible form. For when Adam was created, he was lifeless and endowed with no life of any virtue, but as soon as the vivifying spirit approached, it displayed its living virtue and faculty in supernatural admiration, and thus in every thing the natural and the supernatural are as one thing coupled and tied in their own domicile, so that to each its own perfection may remain. For all created things in this universe are certain supernatural ones, as far as animated and spiritual things are concerned, while some are natural and supernatural, which concerns the Elements as well as the firmament, likewise Minerals, vegetables, and Animals, which becomes known from generation when the soul exits from the body and leaves it a vacant domicile.

Furthermore, you will now notice that the Macrocosm and microcosm were conflated, formed, and created from the <term>prima materia</term> <gloss>first matter</gloss> by omnipotence in the beginning,
pages.9:
in which the eternal spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters. The Macrocosm, however, heaven and earth, was first founded, then the microcosm, namely man, formed from the macrocosm after the water was separated from the earth; the water was the matter over which the eternal spirit of GOD was borne. From the most noble earth, as its quintessence, the microcosm was fashioned, through the aqueousness of the earth remaining, but all these were natural only. After the warm divine inspiration, however, the supernatural immediately intervened, and thus the supernatural and natural were conjoined to each other. The Macrocosm is fleeting and perishable, even if a new world should be constituted, but the microcosm is eternal. The Macrocosm, as perishable, will be reduced to nothing from whence it was made, but the microcosm will be clarified through the spirit of GOD because it possesses it, and from the former earthly water it will make a celestial clarified water; then it will appear that the first matter had been changed into the last and the last into the first. The cause, however, of the destruction of the macrocosm is that the spirit of the Lord will change His seat and domicile in it and transfer it into the microcosm. For man is the temple of the HOLY SPIRIT unless he contaminates himself and adjudges himself to hell, by which very act a discord intervenes and GOD flees from him, whom He created in His own image and dedicated as a temple to Himself. Furthermore, everything is also contained in the microcosm that is given in the macrocosm, namely heaven and earth with the Elements, and those things which are akin to these and joined from the firmament.

We also find that three things, made from nothing, arose in the first creation: the animal, the spiritual, and the visible essence, which served in the place of Mercurial water, sulphureous exhalation, and earthy
pages.10:
<margin>salt.</margin> These three exhibited a full and perfect body of all things. In which, most importantly, all four Elements are perfectly given, as I have already warned for a long time in my writings, and especially where I treated of the microcosm.

But that I may deliver more on natural and supernatural, spiritual and corporeal things, we accept that the Canaanite woman was healed from the flow of blood of ten years, by touch alone, by which she touched the garment of the son of GOD, whose disease was natural, but the medicine was supernatural, because she had obtained help from Christ by faith.

Likewise, a remarkable and most supernatural miracle is presented to us in those three men, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, thrown into the fiery furnace by the order of King Nebuchadnezzar, who nevertheless were liberated therefrom unharmed and safe by divine aid.

The confusion of tongues, likewise, and the introduction of diverse idioms, which occurred in the construction of the Babylonian tower that was to be raised to heaven, was considered by the name of a supernatural miracle.

Moreover, it was a supernatural thing that the Israelites were forced to lap water like dogs with tongues protruding, when they were compelled to join battle with Pharaoh's army by the command of GOD. So also the sending forth of the dove from Noah's ark, carrying in its mouth a green olive leaf as a sign of grace, was a divine and supernatural legation.

That Moses, a man of GOD, struck his staff upon the hardest rock and brought forth water from it, eluded all human reason, and no less did it exceed the powers of nature.

pages.30: <meta>continues from previous page: [He] also explores, O Nature, your strengths and the seeds of things with learned and diligent ingenuity. What tremor causes astonished cities to tremble with their citizens; what drives the ebbing tides of the sea; what force nourishes the riches stored in the deepest earth, or your gems, O ingenious shell-fish; how far distant is the sea, congealed by Arctic cold, from the sources of the great Nile; how far distant is the Indus, divided from the western Gades, as it plunges its born waters into the Erythraean salt-sea; whence light winds are born, and why Aetna feeds the ruins of the mountain, having ejected pitchy globes; whence flows the salty liquid of the deep, and whence the healthy vein of the Baian water draws its warmth. Having finally searched through all the miracles of the earth, he leaves the ground below with a winged mind, and having traversed the Olympus painted with stars, he flies over the bright signs of the ethereal house. Here the Marathonian Virgin <note>Virgo Marathonia: likely referring to the constellation Virgo, often identified with Astraea or Justice</note> submits to him her double balance, and the neighboring Lion <note>Leo: the constellation Leo</note> submits its own stars, and Orion grants the sword taken from his side, the due rewards of a CAESAREAN knighthood. Here he tracks the path of the Sun, and [seeks] the hidden causes: why pale Cynthia <note>Cynthia: the Moon</note> mourns with black horses; why the Africans thirst; why the seven kingdoms of the North are scorched by winter delayed by Hyperborean frost; why shadows flee Syene <note>Syene: modern Aswan, famous in antiquity for the noon-day sun casting no shadow at the summer solstice</note> when the Crab is scorching; why the greater limit varies the day from the lesser. But what part of learning and of your praises is it, O AUSTRIAD <note>Austriad: a member of the House of Austria, specifically Ferdinand III</note>, to know the stars of the great pole, and the lands stretched out with the surrounding sea where the Sun illuminates the East and the West? If even Wisdom is revealed to you through the eloquent papers of the recovered history of the Nile, nor are the sacred things hidden in reverend shrines unknown to you, nor the marbles ennobled by sculpted beasts. Indeed, Egypt, having dared to entrust learning to stones, had fashioned foreign images, so that the secrets of the gods, manifest to the masters, might keep the common crowd away with dubious images. And so that late posterity, with the years slipping by, might eventually recognize the untouched work of ancient art. O vain cares of men! O blind hearts to the future! So many monuments in royal ruin. The barbarian drinker of the Armenian Araxes, Cambyses, laid waste the Pharian fields,</meta>
pages.31:
and the fleeting age, with silent centuries, could turn even the saved relics: but long time will not steal the eternal honors from your merits, O renowned Rome, you who collect the breathing ruins of Pelusium, and lift them to the stars in the middle of the forum. Nor will dark night cover your oblivion, O GREATEST CAESAR, nor your genius. For if there is any praise, because under your leadership, antiquity, having been opened, reveals the dark bays of Memphis; because you reveal the secret faces of the Inachian heifer <note>Inachian heifer: Io, often identified with Isis in syncretic Egyptian-Greek thought</note>, because the mystical form of the dog and of the sacred bull, and whatever other monsters of famous Canopus remain to be seen, surpass the ancient notes: the last dweller of the Nile will read the titles of the AUSTRIADS, and will shake the tinkling sistra <note>Sistrum: a sacred percussion instrument used in the cult of Isis</note> with a joyful sound. Now Solyme, now the Arab will learn, and the marbles will speak of the gifts scattered by the CAESAREAN hand. Am I mistaken? Or will the fates add to the AUSTRIAN trophies the sacred signs torn from the Paraetonian vaults? Or, O FERDINAND, does Victory now prepare to write your name upon the stones of the Pyramids? Certainly, glory, emulating the Pellaean <note>Pellaean: referring to Alexander the Great</note> palms, calls the idle hands of Europe to pious wars.

Octavian Augustus, having been seized by a love for the wisdom of Caesar, [sought] the ancient wisdom uncovered in the obelisks raised by him, the whole of Egypt, buried and despaired of, full of rich ministrations and all accompanying sufferings. [He sought] whatever the hieroglyphic experience of learned teachings had published, having sent them to Rome, for the divine service of the revelation of secrets. But the burden fell only upon him, to whom much of the mystical education of all the ancients [was known], as if it had been flooded and submerged by the streams of Lethe. Ferdinand III, O Augustus, more fortunate than that Octavian, obtained what was then hidden, and even then, by that zeal and expense, [he] succeeded in having it successfully accomplished. The other [Kircher], I do not know how he is carried by him, Athanasius the German Kircher, and the witnesses to the riddles, and an <term>Oedipus</term> <gloss>solver of riddles</gloss> <term>reborn</term> <gloss>brought to life again</gloss>, having been urged on by a Royal command, he jumped into the dwelling places of wisdom, not [having] a bright mind, and he visited [them], where until then an impenetrable and inaccessible treasure had been revealed and <unclear>unearthed</unclear>. Whether by virtues, in which you, Ferdinand, trusting in your wishes, and by the African commands, the forbidden or <term>Mimetic</term> <gloss>imitative/symbolic</gloss> hidden depths of the shrine, having opened the seals of the rites mystically, and the mysterious letters and inscription of the ancient sacred things, having set forth the imperial alliance, or he unfolded [it] with the body of the soul of great bounty. Therefore we proclaim you a most fortunate Caesar, as one who, by the achievements of the soft brothers <note>referring perhaps to the Habsburg relations or the Jesuit brotherhood</note> and by the most illustrious [deeds] carried out, [this] has been completed on such things, whoever might wish, or be able to practically arrange, or to perform the work [that] people [do] with the thoughts of the mind. In the past, Augustus showed the sphere himself, in the <unclear>unbidden</unclear> Obelisks. But you, by the ability according to him, [did] not only raise stones on expensive bases, but also you obtained [it] otherwise, so that by your generosity and your nod, eternally and silently, the sweet-speaking lines of the obelisks, and with wealth always [to] the un-suffering, and hidden from two thousand years [ago], you explored and resurrected the Egyptian wisdom. And [he who was] miserable had to rightly clothe the chariot of the inhabited world. And to think of turning back from the vehicles of this fame, [with] the whole human race, in the followers of the lightning, and in the triumphs, and establishing the idiom of the inhabited world, as you, the elder, [send] messengers and heralds.
