<note>A decorative drop cap 'O' featuring a seated scholar or saintly figure writing at a desk, surrounded by ornate scrollwork.</note>

Octavian AUGUSTUS Caesar, having been struck by the desire to acquire ancient wisdom, which was said to be inscribed upon the obelisks erected by him, explored the whole of Egypt through the work of learned men, so that if he could find an interpreter skilled in hieroglyphic doctrine, he might summon him to Rome for the office of interpreting arcana. But he could not obtain his wishes, all the mystical doctrine of the Ancients having long since been submerged, as if by a certain river of Lethe. FERDINAND III, Caesar Augustus, was so much more fortunate than that Octavian, by how much more fortunate omens he achieved that which the other could not obtain by any wishes or expenses, while by some fate Athanasius Kircher fell to him as a new interpreter, an <term>Oedipus</term> <gloss>riddle-solver</gloss> <term>reborn</term> <gloss>brought back to life</gloss>; who, stimulated by the Caesarean command, flew with a brilliant intellect to the regions of Wisdom and uncovered treasures hitherto inaccessible. He, trusting in the commands of Ferdinand, was the first to enter more deeply into the hidden recesses of the Memphitic shrines, and he opened the secret seals of the sacraments; he interpreted the mysterious volumes of the ancient Priests, with Caesarean bounty acting as midwife. Therefore, we proclaim You, Caesar, fortunate, since you burn with a great and very grand desire to accomplish [great things], and such a man has fallen to You, who both wishes and is able to urge the concepts of your great mind into execution: Augustus once placed the scope of his power in the raising of vast masses of Obelisks; but You are even more powerful than this, who not only raise great stones, but also this has fallen to You beyond others, that by your help and work, the mute stones of the Obelisks

At any time it will happen that you achieve anything

**Cho.** <term>IN</term> these matters, there is need of great prudence;

**Chr.** But before I make an opening of my speech,
O women, if there were even the smallest part of mind

And call me into the companionship of danger?
Little have you weighed that you are a woman, not born a man, and far
Unequal in strength and power to the enemies.
Furthermore, fortune and the divine powers favor them,
While we experience adverse things daily.
Who would destroy such a man without his own most grievous
Damage and extreme calamity?
Look again and again, sister, lest we, while plotting such
Deeds, procure for ourselves evils
Greater than these, if by chance someone overhearing such sounds
Should reveal them.
What does it profit to achieve glory and fame,
If we are forced to end our life disgracefully?
I do not consider death itself grave, but, when you
Desire to die, not to be able to achieve it.
Therefore, I beg you, before we and our lineage
Go down to the depths entirely;
Restrain your anger, and curb these impulses of your mind.
I, in turn, will ensure that all these things now spoken by you
Remain unspoken and secret.
You, just instruct your mind more prudently,
And finally, weighing your own strengths, since you can accomplish
Nothing as a weakling, begin to yield
To the princes and the more powerful.

The same condition of necessity is expressed in the comparison: it is better for them to marry than to burn <note>referring to 1 Corinthians 7:9</note>, which is to say: one gift is one thing, another kind of life requires another, so that we understand "to burn" not as a small flame: for no one is so chaste that he does not experience flames at times, a fact which the most chaste admit, nor would that necessity exist. But he takes "to burn" to mean more serious temptations, in which there is a certain danger of fornication; to avoid this, he suggests a healthier counsel. First, they sin who move toward marriage not because of such necessity, but out of a desire for wealth, honors, or a certain ambition, seeing that the splendor of name and family comes from marriages. These have not yet encountered these flames. Next, they sin who, under the pretext of celibacy—which they observe not at all—despise marriage. Political men labor under the former vice, valuing weddings not so much by necessity as by ambition. The sacred order labors under the latter, from which hypocrisy has taken possession of the monasteries. They have celibacy on their lips, fornication in their laps, and lust in their hearts, etc.

10. *But to those who are married I command, yet not I, but the Lord.*

The third point is about avoiding divorce in marriage: the proposition is that the bond of marriage is most tight and therefore indissoluble.
pages.227:
COMMENTARII

First, weigh the type of speech here. "Not I," he says, "but the Lord." Does Paul then proclaim one thing, and the Lord another? By no means: the Apostle put forth the previous points without an explicit word of God, <margin>Matt. 19:11</margin> although Christ had said something similar: "Not all can receive this word; let him who can receive it, receive it." Thus, the Apostle determines the consequences concerning unequal marriage. Where, therefore, he did not have an explicit commandment of God, he attributed the decision to himself. Here, however, he has the command of Christ regarding the constancy of marriage outside the case of adultery, as in lighter cases, in which Moses had even granted indulgences to the Jews; correcting that indulgence, Christ said that it was not so from the beginning, but that the two would be one flesh. The Apostle here commands the same thing, that marriage is indissoluble among the faithful in such cases. In the meantime, both these and the following are decisions of the Holy Spirit. For the Apostle is an instrument of the Holy Spirit, and he pronounces these things through His mouth. He binds the faithful more tightly to preserving the bond of marriage when he introduces the Lord as the author. The Lord says this in Matthew 5 and 19, with which the doctrine of the Apostle agrees. Let not the wife depart from her husband for a light cause, namely, for a pretext of religion, because of a changed way of life, and similar causes. In such cases, a bill of divorce could have had a place according to Moses. Furthermore, if it pleases her to depart altogether, let her remain unmarried, or be reconciled to her husband. He prohibits a new marriage, because the first
pages.228:
IN EPIST. AD COR.

still endures, and cannot be dissolved for a just cause, and therefore he commands widowhood for her in the hope of reconciliation. Thirdly, he commands the husband similarly: "Let not the husband put away his wife": for he might have seemed to grant a certain greater right to the husband than to the wife, which Ambrose also follows; therefore he commands the same to the husband, not to put away his wife, namely for a light cause, after the custom of the Jews, for whom it was customary even to put away pious wives if their manners displeased, or their appearance, or if something else was alleged. And among the Gentiles, too, it was quite common to change unions. In these cases, therefore, the precept of the Apostle is valid: let the husband not put away his wife. But as for that question: Is it then not allowed in any way to repudiate a wife once taken? <margin>That this is not a discourse on divorce by profession.</margin> We answer that this is not being treated here. For the Apostle is not instituting a dispute about divorce, or its legitimate causes, but he is concerned with persuading that marriages must be kept most sacredly and therefore indissolubly. Whoever defends this does not deny that there is a certain mode that can dissolve marriages once entered into sacredly. But what that mode is for which it might be dissolved, Christ indicates in Matthew 5 and 19, namely fornication, for that makes it so that two are no longer one flesh. Likewise, as the Apostle teaches here, if an unbelieving person does not wish to live any longer with a believer, the believer is not bound to servitude. It is beyond controversy that for these causes marriage is broken, and therefore can be lawfully dissolved. But he did not look to just causes of divorce, but rather to unjust ones, and therefore he deals with indissolubility. We have explained the place concerning divorces separately; see our topics.

<margin>Concerning unequal marriage.</margin> The fourth place is about unequal marriage, that is, in which one person is a believer, while the other remains in their old religion, whether Jewish or Gentile. The place contains two parts, <term>protasin</term> <gloss>proposition</gloss> and <term>aition</term> <gloss>reason</gloss>. The proposition is proposed in several ways. For he returns equal right to both persons. The meaning of the proposition is: even an unequal marriage must be preserved indissolubly by the pious. He explains how he understands this regarding a husband who has an unbelieving wife who nonetheless wishes to dwell with a Christian man. Similarly, regarding a wife who has an unbelieving husband who nonetheless thinks his wife should not be abandoned on account of the new religion. And so the right is equalized, and therefore looks only toward the faithful persons. For the Apostle could not give precepts to unbelievers. Furthermore, he says that he speaks these things, because Christ had given no command in these cases for the new Christian profession. In the meantime, it is a rule of the Holy Spirit, whose instrument the Apostle is.
pages.230:
IN EPIST. AD COR.

14. *For the unbelieving husband is sanctified by the wife.*

<margin>Why a believer should not desert an unbelieving spouse.</margin>
This is a confirmation of the proposition set forth, that if a believer ought not to desert an unbelieving spouse. Why? Because the worse part, that is, the unbeliever, is sanctified through the better, that is, the believing spouse. He takes the argument from the nature of the faith of the better person. It is proper for faith to sanctify us to God, that is, it declares us sanctified by God, nor does it reside only in one person, namely the believer, but because the believer is one flesh with the unbelieving spouse, consequently the sanctification flows over even to the worse part. And indeed, the unbeliever will have infinite opportunities of repenting and converting even to Christ the Savior. Nevertheless, the Apostle did not say "will be sanctified," or "let him be sanctified," but "is sanctified." For it is a most certain argument for hoping even for their conversion, since he does not wish to depart. Therefore, that sanctification has a place only in those who do not wish to break the marriage; in the others, it is not the same. Furthermore, the children born from this are holy; if the marriage were broken, they would be rendered impure. Therefore, it should not be broken because of religion. Their children are called holy because, notwithstanding the infidelity of the other part, they belong to the Church of Christ. For it is said to individual believers: "I will be your God, and the God of your children." For the sanctification of the children, therefore, it is enough if one parent is a believer.

Thirdly, because God has called you to peace. Therefore, no society established among men for a good end is to be rashly torn apart by the pious. He attaches this reason to the objection. <margin>Question.</margin> For the believer will ask: you do not want me to desert an unbelieving spouse, I being a believer, but what if he does not wish to live with me? Shall I follow him? Or will I be bound to keep celibacy unless I am reconciled to him? The Apostle answers: I do not wish this at all; but I do not want the marriage to be broken at least on your part, provided it remains valid; if the unbeliever does not wish it, very well, let him depart, you will be free from the marriage, he himself deciding thus. God has called us to peace. Therefore, the marriage should not be broken by you. And, He has called us to peace. Therefore, leave the unbelieving one who departs, do not bring them to court, do not pursue your case against them. Preserve peace in both ways.

Fourthly, from the hope of conversion. An unequal marriage should not be broken by the believer, because there is hope that the unbeliever can be gained through honest conduct. For effort must be given so that we may gain anyone for the Lord, let alone a spouse. Therefore, the spouse is to be borne more patiently in this case. It is to be observed in these arguments that the Christian religion does not disturb political matters, so much so that it holds as valid marriages previously entered into: indeed, it teaches one to bear unequal ones patiently.

17. *Unless as God has distributed to each, as the Lord has called each.*

The fifth place is about each person diligently keeping their own station. For among the Corinthians, some sullen men seemed to exist who, upon the conversion of Jews, immediately imposed an alteration of their whole life in external ceremonies, or, in the case of those converted from gentilism <note>paganism</note>, they immediately demanded a new way of living. Or perhaps there were others who did not seem pious enough to themselves unless they threw away all their previous ceremonies of life entirely. The Apostle meets them in this place, and decides that there is no need for such austerity, that the religion of Christ does not abolish one's state of life; he teaches this learnedly by proposing, explaining, confirming, and concluding. We resolve each part into the proposition.

pages.233:
COMMENTARII

But let that proposition be.

<term>Protasin</term> <gloss>proposition</gloss>. On account of the profession of the Gospel, it is not necessary to change one's way of life immediately; but each person's own calling, with religion kept safe, must be diligently guarded and preserved. The Apostle said <term>peripatein</term> <gloss>to walk</gloss>, as God has called each one, this is, to persist in his own way of life in which the profession of the Gospel discovered him. And the word <term>peripatein</term> is to produce the fruits of an active life, so that you may understand it to be a matter of piety to produce actions conforming to the profession. For it is not enough to contemplate and speak much about piety: there is a need for action. And the particle "unless" should be connected with "as." It is a limited proposition and restricted by a certain condition: "Unless as God has distributed," one must walk; this is, not otherwise, not by our own judgment, a calling is not to be feigned for ourselves, but the one which the Lord has imposed is to be retained. In this sense, he censures the superstition of the Corinthians who wanted to change everything immediately on account of the profession of religion.

But let us consider the arguments by which this which we have proposed from the Apostle can be shown: each one's station is to be kept after the acknowledgment of the truth. Why? Because God has distributed the kinds of life in this way. It is a firm argument from divine ordination and disposition, which must be studiously observed by the pious. The Apostle urges the argument with repetition and change of words, <term>theos emerisen</term> <gloss>God distributed</gloss> and <term>kurios kekleken</term> <gloss>the Lord has called</gloss>. He indeed says the same thing.

the matter exceeded, when salt water turned into the sweetest drink: The dry passage of the Israelites through the Red Sea, as well as the sprouting of Aaron’s rod, occurred in a supernatural way.

And in summary, the bursting forth of Christ from the sealed tomb, that appearance made to the two going to the village of Emmaus, and the manifestation through closed doors were divine and supernatural things. Many other examples from the sacred codex could still be brought forward, if brevity did not have to be observed.

Among supernatural things are numbered all the portents of metallic mines, the bodily appearances of spirits, phantoms, pygmies, and dwarves, which very often place themselves before our sight and portend good or evil, destruction or wealth; likewise all the figures and other impressions of metals which are found under the earth, formed among men, fish, and other living things through the imagination of the three principles, matured and cooked by the earth and other Elements. To this also pertain the monsters of the earth and such things which are given in strange forms under the earth at set times, outside of which they can nowhere else be detected, although at another time they may truly appear again and present themselves to our eyes.

To this also are referred all visions which are accustomed to happen through waters, mirrors, crystals, and other media, through seals and characters, which nevertheless differ greatly; for some are only natural, yet exhibiting supernatural visions. The rest, arising from incantations, are neither natural nor supernatural but Diabolical, and therefore are counted among Demonic Magic, and are deservedly forbidden by all Christians.
pages.12:
by right, moreover, all those media contrary to the holy scriptures, the word of GOD, and His command are rejected and refuted by true and natural <term>Cabalists</term> <gloss>those who study the mystical tradition of the Torah</gloss>. And I warn of this so that a sure distinction and a certain order may be established between natural, supernatural, and contranatural things.

Similarly, all <term>Naiads</term> <gloss>water nymphs</gloss>, <term>Sirens</term>, <term>Succubi</term>, and other <term>Nymphs</term> and their kin hold a place among supernatural things; likewise the terrestrial spirits and those that inhabit the air, presenting themselves to hearing, sight, and touch, sometimes announcing death or other evil, and sometimes signifying fortunes and treasures in certain places by their appearances. Added to these, moreover, are the fiery spirits, showing themselves in the form of fire and a burning torch, all of whom are incorporeal spirits and yet not infernal, who lie in wait for the souls of men like eternal treasures, as the Stygian <term>Lucifer</term> and his excommunicated followers are accustomed to do. But these are Spirits who are presented to the wonder of men beyond nature, uniquely nourished, fed, and pastured by the Elements, and afterwards they cease in this earthly world, dying and vanishing together, deprived of a redeemed soul. I add no more of these now, but postpone their further treatment to another time and more convenient place, where I will arrange a singular treatise on visions and their spiritual appearances, which the greater part of the world judges to be contrary to nature, although in truth they are indeed natural, but are detected as supernatural regarding their operations and their strange qualities.

To confirm my purpose more, I assert that there are many things in medicine manifesting and perfecting their operation in a supernatural way, merely in a magnetic manner, through a certain spiritual attractive virtue which is drawn in by the benefit of the air, because this is the medium between medicine and the ailment, just as the magnet perpetually turns itself toward the southern star, even if it is many thousands of miles distant from it. Nevertheless, such great spiritual operation and inclination intervenes here that, by means of this link—namely, the air—such great distances meet; but since an attractive virtue of this kind is commonly known, it has passed into mere habit, and its function alone is sustained, nor is any further occult quality observed from which an operating virtue of this kind draws its origin. In like manner, wounds and ailments can be healed even if a man oppressed by such things and the physician are separated by a long interval, not by expiations, charms, and other illicit means contrary to GOD and nature, but by those in which the magnetic attractive virtue lies hidden. As if a wounded person, departing from here, leaves to the physician the weapons by which he was hurt or anything from the gore shed from the wound, from which afterwards legitimate means of healing are duly administered, as is customary with the binding of wounds, he will without any doubt recover firmly; nor are these charms, but such healing is accomplished uniquely by the attractive virtue of the medicine, which is carried by the air to the wound to purify the wound and perfect its spiritual operation.

These words will perhaps seem difficult to many and alien to the powers of nature, and many will attack this doctrine
pages.14:
as entirely hostile to nature, whence very many will descend into most serious mutual altercations: whether this remedy is natural or not, possible or not, or whether it is a fascination. But this controversy must be settled by this: that such a cure is indeed natural, but the mode of operating is supernatural and spiritual, because it occurs by a certain attractive and incomprehensible reason alone; furthermore, that this mode of healing proceeds without fascination is proven by this very fact, because it is joined with no fascination nor any other contranatural medium that contradicts GOD the creator and His word, but is entirely natural, resulting from its supernatural, invisible, incomprehensible, spiritual, and attractive virtue, which, having obtained its origin from the stars, perfects its operation through the Elements.

Finally, I can defend this cure from the charge of fascination, since it is established that the Devil prefers to rejoice in the calamity and misfortune of the human race rather than provide any help for the salvation of men, which otherwise, without divine permission, in no way consists in his own powers. Many things would still have to be added to this magnetic form, but to avoid various errors, I now stop and keep silent until I have relayed certain things about the natural miracles of the world.

Coarse and crude minds, though stuffed with the opinion of philosophy, and all those who have corrupted senses, know no distinction in these things, but the wise and skilled can most easily distinguish natural things from supernatural ones.

Let one note and observe this similarity through a coarser
pages.15:
example of a certain kind. There are many living things that are devoid of all life during the winter time, but as soon as summer returns, natural heat generates new life so that the body arises in the same substance in which it previously exercised vital motion, just as a herb that dies in winter revives again in spring. The death of these things is therefore judged to be natural, but the repair of the new life through its own knowledge is supernatural. But in truth, because man is accustomed to all these things, the smallest part, which further remains to be weighed and investigated, sets upon them, leaving aside both natural and supernatural things.

Very many are also accustomed to pass over with dry foot the character of man, which itself is also supernatural; likewise those monsters which bring stains into the world together, all these are indeed natural but display themselves supernaturally from the imagination that has arisen, which supernatural form and character the mother impressed upon the infant by accident through her imagination, as indeed we often see, that some manners are instilled in certain men which they can never renounce, however much they strive to be unaccustomed to them. Such an innate power of man is natural; the conception in the mother’s womb, which the imagination of these things provided, is supernatural and subject to those things which the heaven impressed.

Finally, I do not deny that no one can support things that exceed the powers of nature with unshaken foundations and undoubted causes, to avoid injury to the truth, unless those things are first known which become known to us from their physical course, as they have drawn their birth and their form from supernatural things
pages.16:
; thus it will afterwards happen that, having perceived these, an infallible experiment will prove that he has snatched the palm from those who deny all faith in supernatural things. It will likewise refute the opinions of many who, disputing about natural things and not grasping the foundation, do nothing but act out trifles and rashly produce their contentions.

## The First Tincture and Root of Metals.

### Chapter Two.

But in order that I may finish my undertaking, GOD permitting, and take up the doctrine concerning the first tincture, root, and generation of Metals and Minerals, it must be known that the tincture and root of all Metals is also a supernatural, volatile, and fiery Spirit, which sustains itself in the air and naturally seeks its seat in water and earth, where it can rest and work. This Spirit is found in all Metals, and more abundantly in others than in gold, since that, because of its cooked, matured, and fixed body, is solid, firm, and compact, and therefore, besides what the body requires, it cannot receive more. But the other Metals are destitute of such a fixed body, and their pores are open and widely dispersed; therefore the Spirit of the tincture can penetrate and occupy them more copiously. But since the bodies of other metals are unfixed, the Tincture also cannot subsist with wandering bodies,
pages.17: but is forced to yield. Since, therefore, the Tincture of gold exists no more abundantly than in Mars and Venus, or male and female, once their bodies are destroyed, the spirit of the tincture is driven from there, which enriches the enclosed prepared gold with blood and volatilizes it through food and drink. Hence, volatile gold, saturated with its food and drink, acquires its own blood, dries it with its native heat by the aid of vaporous fire, and a certain mutual victory is given, which brings about the greatest fixity, so that gold may turn into a most fixed medicine; because of the redundancy of blood, it cannot exhibit any body, unless in turn the most abundant body is added to it, where the superfluous fixed blood is diffused, which added metallic body is penetrated like fire because of the immense heat of the fixed leonine blood, is cleansed of all impurity, and is immediately cooked into the fullest maturity and fixity. Thus the servant gathers riches for the Master, because this one cannot desire anything more for his garment, since nature has granted him the only robe of honor, and no less, in turn, can the King dispense inheritance and lasting courtly attire to his retainers from the kingdom where he has previously collected tribute from his subjects, so that Lord and servant can dwell together. Do not, however, wonder that the King needs the mutual help of his retainers, for the cause is the unfixedness of their bodies; many things indeed they receive into themselves, but they can provide little faith. But where the King can become a participant in that thing, he is able to dispel cold and heat better than impure metals. Thus, through such reception, he becomes the particular victor of all the rest with glorious
pages.18: triumph of wealth and health for a long life. I believe now that you have sufficiently perceived, in place of a beginning, this doctrine concerning natural and supernatural things, concerning the first tincture of the root of Metals and Minerals, upon which the cornerstone has been built and the truest rock founded in kind, where nature has too deeply hidden and concealed her gifts. In the fiery and tinctured spirits, which color it has obtained from the heaven of the stars through the operation of the Elements, and thus could further tinge and fix those things which were not yet tinctured and fixed, since the Moon is destitute of the habit of the golden crown and fixity, as also are Saturn, Jupiter, and Mercury. And although Mars and Mercury by no means have need of a garment, but can communicate this to the other five, I say nevertheless that they can do nothing, without the lion, because they are not sufficiently instructed in the fixity of their Mercury and the subtlety of their salt, which makes for wealth, unless they are defeated in the contest by the lion, so that they have carried off a triumph on both sides, raised moreover into no small improvement, which improvement lies hidden in the signed star or in its magnet, whence the metals themselves have received all their gifts. I will now proceed to generation in particular, how the <term>Archaeus</term> <gloss>the formative vital force</gloss> exhibits its virtue, pours it forth, and brings it into the light, whence all the forms of Metals and Minerals are presented to the eyes and are formed and furnished with body by the incomprehensible and volatile fiery spirits of Minerals. Therefore, now receive it thus, attend with study, lest by forgetting you lose great things, nor pass by most useful things and on the contrary observe naked letters at great length, with the main path neglected. First, weigh the type of speech here. "Not I," he says, "but the Lord." Does Paul, therefore, proclaim one thing, and the Lord another? By no means. The Apostle brought forth the preceding things without an explicit 
<margin>Matt. 19. 11</margin> word of God, although Christ said something similar: "Not all can grasp this word; let him who can grasp it, grasp it." Thus, the Apostle determines the consequences regarding unequal marriage. Where, therefore, he did not have an explicit commandment of God, he attributed the decision to himself. Here, however, he has the commandment of Christ concerning the constancy of marriage outside the case of adultery, as in lighter cases, in which Moses had even granted indulgence to the Jews—an indulgence which Christ corrected, saying it was not so from the beginning, but that two would become one flesh. The Apostle commands the same thing here: that marriage is indissoluble among the faithful in such cases. Meanwhile, both these and the following are decisions of the Holy Spirit. For the Apostle is the organ of the Holy Spirit, and through his mouth, he pronounces these things. He binds the faithful more tightly to keep the marriage bond when he introduces the Lord as its author. The Lord says this in Matthew 5 and 19, to which the doctrine of the Apostle agrees. Let not a wife depart from her husband for a light cause, namely, under the pretext of religion, because of a changed way of life, and similar causes. In these cases, a bill of divorce could have had a place according to Moses. Then, if she chooses to depart altogether, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband. He prohibits a new marriage because the previous one

Thirdly, he commands the husband similarly: "Let not a husband dismiss his wife." For it might have seemed that a certain greater right was conceded to the husband than to the wife, which Ambrose also follows; therefore, he also commands the husband not to dismiss his wife for a light cause, in the manner of the Jews, to whom it was customary to dismiss even pious wives if their manners or appearance displeased them, or if something else was claimed. And it was also very familiar to the heathens to exchange marriages. In these cases, therefore, the command of the Apostle is valid: "Let not a husband dismiss his wife." But as for that question: is it then in no way allowed to repudiate a wife once taken? 
<margin>That this place does not deal with divorce professionally.</margin> We respond that it is not dealt with here. For the Apostle does not institute a discussion about divorce or its legitimate causes, but he is concerned with persuading them that marriages should be kept most sacredly and thus indissolubly. He who maintains this does not deny that there is a certain way that can dissolve marriages that were entered into sacredly. But Christ indicates what that way is for which it might be dissolved in Matthew 5 and 19, namely, fornication; for that makes it so that the two are no longer one flesh. Likewise, what the Apostle teaches here: if an unbelieving person does not wish to live with a believer, the believer is not bound to servitude. It is beyond controversy that marriage is broken for these causes, and thus may be rightly dissolved. But he did not look to the just causes of divorce, but rather to the unjust ones, and therefore he differs on the indissolubility. We have explained the passage on divorce separately; see our topics.

12. *But to the rest I say, not the Lord, if any brother has an unbelieving wife who consents, etc.*

<margin>Concerning unequal marriage.</margin> The fourth passage is on unequal marriage, that is, in which one person is a believer while the other remains in their old religion, whether Jewish or Heathen. The passage includes two parts: a <term>propositio</term> <gloss>proposition</gloss> and an <term>aition</term> <gloss>a cause/reason</gloss>. The proposition is proposed in several ways. For he renders the right equal for both persons. The meaning of the proposition is: even an unequal marriage must be kept indissolubly by the pious. How he understands this he explains concerning a husband who has an unbelieving wife who nevertheless wishes to dwell with her Christian husband. Similarly concerning a wife who has an unbelieving husband who nevertheless does not think his wife should be abandoned because of her new religion. Thus, the right is equalized, and therefore it looks only to the faithful persons. For the Apostle could not give commandments to unbelievers. Furthermore, he says that he speaks these things because Christ had given no commandment in these cases regarding the new Christian profession. Meanwhile, it is the rule of the Holy Spirit, of whom the Apostle is the organ.

14. *For the unbelieving husband is sanctified in the wife.*

<margin>Why a believer ought not to desert an unbelieving spouse.</margin>
This is a confirmation of the proposition set forth: if a believer ought not to desert an unbelieving spouse. Why? Because the worse part, that is, the unbeliever, is sanctified through the better, that is, the believing spouse. He takes the argument from the nature of the faith of the better person. It is the property of faith to sanctify us to God, that is, it declares us sanctified by God; and it does not reside only in one person, namely the believer, but because the believer is one flesh with the unbelieving spouse, consequently, the sanctification flows over even to the worse part. And truly, the unbeliever will have infinite opportunities to repent and to convert even to Christ the Savior. Yet the Apostle did not say "shall be sanctified" or "let him be sanctified," but "is sanctified." For it is a most certain argument for the hope of his conversion, provided he does not wish to depart. Therefore, that sanctification has a place only in those who do not wish to break off the marriage; in the others, not as much. Furthermore, the children born from this are holy; if the marriage were broken, they would be rendered impure. It is not, therefore, to be broken on account of religion. Their children are called holy because, notwithstanding the infidelity of the other part, they belong to the Church of Christ. For it is said to each of the faithful, "I will be God to you, and to your females." For the sanctification of the children, therefore, it is enough if one parent is faithful

17. *Unless as God has distributed to each, as God has called each.*

The fifth passage is about the station each person must diligently keep. For among the Corinthians there seemed to be some morose men who, to those converted from Judaism, immediately imposed a total change of life in external ceremonies, or from those converted from Heathenism, they demanded a new manner of living. Or perhaps there were also others who did not seem pious enough to themselves unless they cast off all their former ceremonies of life in their entirety. The Apostle meets them at this point and decides that there is no need for such austerity, that the religion of Christ does not abolish one's station in life. He teaches this learnedly by proposing, explaining, confirming, and concluding. We shall resolve each to the proposition.

Shine forth? To whom, with resources and paternal inheritance stripped away,
Nothing remains, but the ability to pour tears
And groans and to grieve perpetually.
Besides, that you might grow old as a long-lived virgin, devoid of marriage and the partner of a bed, nor believe
That it will come to pass at any time, that you might attain any
Of these things. For Aegisthus is not so lacking in counsel,
A man who would suffer that your or my
Lineage should ever flourish with his own manifest
Loss, or grow. And if you do not refuse to obey my
Exhortations,
First indeed you will give effort so that, in the underworld
Where they now act, you might revere and honor my father and brother equally.

<header>SOPH. ELECTRA</header>

With the piety that is fitting.
Then, just as you are free, born from parents who were
The highest kings, so in the future
You will be called, and you will be deemed worthy of that
Honor: and you will be joined to marriage of such worthy
Lineage. <term>NANQVE</term> <gloss>For</gloss> who of mortals
Does not direct eyes toward honorable and noble things?
What more? You will procure glory and perennial honor for yourself
And for me, by obeying these my warnings. What citizen, what guest,
Seeing us, will not receive us with such proclamations?
Behold two sisters, who dared to preserve the ancestral
Home and to assert it into its pristine state, who, of their own
Improvident and prodigal life, have bravely
Given to death those enemies who were once
Blessed in all things. It is right that these be loved by all,
That these be uniquely honored, that these be celebrated in public
Assemblies and festivals throughout the whole city
For the sake of the distinguished glory of fortitude,
That they be affected with honor. This, and anyone else will speak
Other things to this sentiment,
Nor will glory desert the dead or the living.
But obey me now, most dear sister,
Bring help to your parent, bestow effort upon your brother,
Deliver me and yourself from present evils:
Meanwhile keeping before your eyes how shameful it is
To live disgracefully, born of a noble lineage. <margin>pe sit</margin>

**Cho.** <term>IN</term> <gloss>In</gloss> these matters there is need of great prudence,
This is useful for the one counseling and for the one hearing.

**Chr.** But before I make an opening of speech,
O women, if this one possessed even the smallest part
Of a sane mind, which she does not, she would take care
Of her own safety. For by what trust,
By what hope, pray, does she herself arm herself with such rash
Audacity, and call me into the fellowship of danger?
Little do you seem to have weighed that you are a woman, not a man,
And unequal in strength and power to the enemies by far.
Fortune, moreover, and the powers of the gods favor them,
Which we experience as adverse every day.
Who would destroy such a man without his own most grave
Loss and extreme calamity?
Look out also again and again, sister, lest we, while plotting
Such deeds, procure worse evils for ourselves, if by chance someone
Hearing such sounds should expose us.
What does it profit to attain glory and fame,
If we are compelled to end life disgracefully?
Nor do I deem death grave, but, when you desire to die,
Not to be able to attain that.
Therefore I beseech you before we go to ruin
And our lineage utterly;
Restrain your anger, and curb these impulses of your mind.
I in turn will see to it that all words now from you
Remain unsaid and secret.
You only prepare your mind more prudently,
And at last, weighing your own strength, since you are weak and can do nothing,
Begin to yield to those who are leaders and more powerful.

<summary>Chrysothemis refuses Electra's proposal, urging caution and prudence to avoid their mutual destruction.</summary>

I beseech you to hear, Apollo, with a benign divinity.
The visions which I have seen in twin dreams
During the night, if they be of good omen, Apollo,
Make them true: but if of evil, turn them back onto the head
Of my enemies again: nor let me be driven out from these riches, if by deceit
Some might plot that,
Ever allow; grant that I may live without annoyance, and that I may hold these homes and the scepters of the Atridae
Which are uniquely pleasant to friends whose company delights
Me, with these children also surviving, whoever act peacefully with me
And do not exhibit any business, as is fitting.
These, I beseech, Phoebus, perceive with inclined ears,
And assent to these our vows, being merciful,
And to other things which I do not now declare openly
Even while I am silent. For I believe that you have
All things known. AND SINCE you are a God, nothing
Of human affairs can be hidden from you.

*Pæd.* O women, guests, I beseech you, tell me,
Is this the royal house of the tyrant Aegisthus?
*Cho.* It is, guest, indeed, you have not guessed badly.
*Pæd.* Then, is that the spouse whom I see?
For from her countenance the royal character shines forth.
*Cho.* She herself: you conjecture rightly, she is present here.
*Cly.* Queen, hail: I bring a message to you and
To Aegisthus, a most joyful one from a friend.
*Cly.* Your speech is pleasing to me. But first explain
Who, guest, among mortals has sent you here?
*Pæd.* Phanoteus from Phocis, reporting grave matters.
*Cl.* What matters, guest? Declare: for from a most dear man,

*Pæd.* Orestes has died, and that I assert in brief.
*Elec.* Woe, woe is me, wretched, I have perished utterly today.
*Cl.* What do you say? What do you say, guest? Beware, do not offer your ear to her.
*Pæd.* Orestes has died, just as I said before, I now say.

And he could turn even the saved relics into dust
As the silent age fled over the centuries:
But long time shall not take away your eternal honors,
Renowned Rome, for your merits,
You who gather the breathing ruins of Pelusium
And lift them to the stars from the middle of the forum.
Nor shall oblivion hide your deeds, **GREATEST CAESAR**,
Nor shall black night suppress your genius.
For if there is any praise, because under your leadership ancient history
Openly reveals the dark inlets of Memphis,
Because the father reveals the secret appearances of the Inachian heifer,
Because the mystical form of the dog and the sacred ox,
And what other monsters of famous Canopus besides
Surpass those to be seen in ancient marks:
The last dweller of the Nile shall read the titles of the **AUSTRIANS**,
And shall shake the tinkling sistra <note>a sacred rattle used in the cult of Isis</note> with a joyful sound.
Now Solyma <note>Jerusalem</note>, now the Arab shall learn, and the clear marbles will speak
Of the gifts scattered by the **CAESAREAN** hand.
Am I mistaken? Or will the fates also add to the **AUSTRIAN** trophies
The sacred signs torn from the Paraitonian domes?
Or, **FERDINAND**, is Victoria already happily preparing
To write your name on the stones of the Pyramids?
Glory certainly calls the rival, in the manner of the Pellaean <note>referring to Alexander the Great</note> palms,
For the idle hands of Europe to pious wars.

<header>ELOGIUM III.</header>

# G R E E C E.

## TO FERDINAND THE THIRD,
### THE UNCONQUERED,
### CAESAR,
### EMPEROR DIVINELY APPOINTED,
### AND THRICE-GREATEST KING,
### MOST PIOUS,
### FATHER OF THE FATHERLAND,
### GOOD, FORTUNATE, AND BENEFACTOR,
### GLORY, LIFE, AND EVERLASTING HEALTH.

->According to the Greek salutation set forth<-

## BY FRANCESCO GOZADINO, BISHOP OF ZAKYNTHOS AND CEPHALONIA.

<note>A large ornamental letter 'P' depicting a central shield with heraldic stripes.</note>

Octavian Augustus, moved by a love for Caesar <note>referring to Julius Caesar</note>, sought out the ancient wisdom hidden in the obelisks erected by him, and the entirety of Egypt, which had been buried and despaired of, owing to the neglect of rich service and all the accompanying sufferings. He wished that whatever the experience of the hieroglyphic art had produced (having sent them to Rome) might be brought to the divine service of explaining the secrets. But the burden fell upon him alone, as the mystical knowledge of all the ancients had been overwhelmed and baptized in the currents of Lethe <note>the river of forgetfulness</note>. Ferdinand the Third, Augustus, you are more fortunate than that Octavian, for you have successfully managed to bring to light what was then hidden, with the same zeal and expense. The other man, indeed, did not know how it might be brought to him, but Athanasius Kircher, the German, and the <term>Oedipus</term> <gloss>solver of riddles</gloss> <term>palimpsychus</term> <gloss>resurrected soul</gloss>, urged by royal command, did not depart from the bright intellect into the outskirts of wisdom, and wandered where until then the treasure, inaccessible and impossible, was revealed and <unclear>unearthed</unclear>. For whether by virtues, in which you, Ferdinand, trust by your will, and by the ancient commands, he opened the secret depths of the <term>mimetic</term> <gloss>imitative</gloss> sanctuary, and revealed the seals of the mysteries and the mysterious writings and inscription of the ancient sacred things, displaying the imperial standard, or he unfolded the soul of great gifts in the body. Therefore we proclaim you a most blessed Caesar, as one who, by the achievements of your brothers and the most illustrious men <unclear>brought forth</unclear> to completion in such matters, whosoever might wish, or be able, to practically arrange, or to perform the work, the thoughts of the mind, with men. Long ago Augustus showed the sphere to himself powerfully, by the <unclear>unknown</unclear> Obelisks. But you, by a power like his, not only raised up stones with lavish foundations, but also obtained something else from yourself, so that by your generosity and your nod, the sweetly-speaking lines of the obelisks have eternally and silently become rich for the <unclear>invulnerable</unclear> ones, and out of two thousand years of secrecy, you have searched out and resurrected the Egyptian wisdom. And indeed it was right for the wretched one to wear the chariot of the world. And to turn away from the consideration of the vehicles of this fame of yours, mingling and parading the whole human race with flashes of lightning, choruses, and triumphs, and establishing the identity of the world as if you were a messenger and herald.

<summary>This Greek encomium compares Emperor Ferdinand III to Augustus, praising his patronage of Athanasius Kircher in successfully deciphering ancient Egyptian hieroglyphs.</summary>
<keywords>Ferdinand III, Augustus, Athanasius Kircher, Hieroglyphics, Obelisks, Egypt, Oedipus, Wisdom</keywords>

# TO FERDINAND III.

## CAESAR,

### KING THRICE-GREATEST,

### FATHER OF THE FATHERLAND, &c.

->Wishing happiness.<-

->*Francesco Gozadino, Bishop of Zakynthos and Cephalonia.*<-

<note>A decorative 'O' featuring a scholar writing at a desk.</note>

Octavian Augustus Caesar, stirred by the desire to acquire the ancient wisdom which was inscribed on the obelisks erected by him, searched the whole of Egypt through the work of learned men, so that if he could find an Interpreter skilled in hieroglyphic doctrine, he might summon him to Rome for the office of interpreting arcane matters. But he could not obtain his wishes, as all the mystical doctrine of the ancients had long since been submerged as if by some river of Lethe. Ferdinand III, Caesar Augustus, is so much more fortunate than that Octavian, in as much as he achieved with happier omens what the other could not achieve with any wishes or expense, while by some fate Athanasius Kircher happened to him, a new Interpreter, a resurrected Oedipus; who, stimulated by Caesarean command, flew with a brilliant intellect to the regions of Wisdom, and uncovered treasures hitherto inaccessible. He, first, relying on the orders of Ferdinand, entered more deeply into the hidden recesses of the Memphitic shrines, opened the secret seals of the sacraments, and interpreted the mysterious volumes of the ancient Priests, with Caesarean munificence acting as midwife. Therefore, we proclaim You, Caesar, happy, who, when you burn with a great and grand desire to perform, have obtained such a man who both wishes and is able to urge the concepts of your great mind into execution: Augustus once placed the scope of his power in erecting vast masses of Obelisks; but You are even more powerful than this, for you do not only raise great stones, but this also happened to You above others, so that by your help and work the mute stones of the Obelisks spoke, and with open mouths belched forth the wisdom of the Egyptians, already hidden for two thousand years. Behold, therefore, you triumph, deservedly carried on the wagon of encomiums with the human race applauding, and every language of the Orbis terrarum sends its messengers to You, so that they may extol your name to the stars.

<summary>The text celebrates the Emperor's success in uncovering ancient Egyptian wisdom, positioning him as superior to Augustus through his patronage of Athanasius Kircher.</summary>

And in sum, the breaking forth of Christ from the sealed tomb, that appearance made to the two walking to the village of Emmaus, the manifestation through closed doors, was a divine and supernatural event. Many other examples could still be brought forth from the sacred code, if one did not have to sacrifice them for the sake of brevity.

Included among supernatural things are all the prodigies of metallic mines, the bodily apparitions of spirits, phantoms, pygmies, and dwarves, which very often present themselves to sight and portend good or evil, ruin or wealth. Likewise, all the figures and other impressions of metals, which are found under the earth among human beings, fish, and other living creatures, formed through the imagination of the three principles, matured and baked by the earth and other elements; to which also belong the monsters of the earth and things of that kind, which are given in wondrous forms under the earth at set times, outside of which they can be detected nowhere else, although at another time they may truly appear again and present themselves to our eyes.

Hither also are referred all visions, which are accustomed to be made through waters, mirrors, crystals, and other media, by seals and characters, which nevertheless differ greatly; for some are merely natural, yet exhibit supernatural visions. The rest, arising from enchantments, are neither natural nor supernatural, but Diabolical, and are therefore enumerated among Demoniacal Magic, and are deservedly interdicted to all Chris-

tians, and by right all such media contrary to the sacred scriptures, to the word of GOD, and to His commandment, are rejected and refuted by true and natural <term>Cabalists</term> <gloss>those who study the mystical tradition</gloss>. And I warn of this so that a sure distinction and a certain order may be established between natural, supernatural, and contranatural things.

Likewise, all <term>Naiads</term> <gloss>water nymphs</gloss>, <term>Sirens</term>, <term>Succubi</term>, and other <term>Nymphs</term>, and whatever is akin to them, obtain a place among supernatural things, as do also those earthly spirits that inhabit the air, offering themselves to hearing, sight, and touch, sometimes foretelling death or some other evil, at other times signifying fortunes and treasures in certain places by their apparitions. Added to these, furthermore, are fiery spirits, showing themselves in the form of fire and a burning torch, all of which are incorporeal spirits and yet not infernal, lying in wait for the souls of men as if they were eternal treasures, just as the Stygian <term>Lucifer</term> and his excommunicated companions are accustomed to do. But these are spirits which, presented to men for wonder above nature, are uniquely nourished, fostered, and fed by the elements, and afterwards cease in this earthly world, dying and vanishing together, deprived of a redeemed soul. I will add no more about these things now, but I defer their further discussion to another time and more convenient place, where I will compile a singular treatise on visions and their spiritual apparitions, which the greater part of the world judges to be contrary to nature, when in truth they are indeed natural, but are perceived as supernatural regarding their operations and wondrous qualities.

To confirm my proposal more, I assert that there are many things in medicine that manifest and complete their operation in a supernatural manner, only in a magnetic way, through a certain spiritual attractive virtue, which is enticed by the benefit of the air, because this is the medium between the medicine and the vice, just as the magnet always turns itself toward the northern star <note>original: "australi" (literally 'southern', though traditionally assigned to the pole/star)</note>, even if it be many thousands of miles distant from it. Nevertheless, such great spiritual operation and inclination intervenes here, that by means of this bond, namely the air, such distances concur. But because an attractive virtue of this kind is commonly known, it has passed into mere custom, and it alone sustains its function, nor is any further occult quality observed from which an operating virtue of this kind draws its origin. In a like manner, wounds and vices can be healed, even if the man oppressed by such and the Physician are separated by a long interval, not by incantations, spells, and other illicit means contrary to GOD and nature, but by those in which a magnetic attractive virtue lies hidden. For if a wounded person, departing from here, leaves to the Physician the arms with which he was injured or any of the gore that issued from the wound, from which legitimate means of healing are then duly administered by him, as is accustomed to be done with the binding of wounds, he will recover firmly without any doubt. These are not spells, but such a healing is accomplished uniquely by the attractive virtue of the medicine, which is carried to the wound by means of the air to purify the wound and to complete its spiritual operation.

These words will perhaps seem difficult to most and alien to the powers of nature, and many will fight against this doctrine
pages.14:
as if it were entirely contrary to nature, whence very many will descend into the most serious mutual altercations: whether this remedy is natural or not, whether it is possible or not, or whether it is a fascination <note>a magical influence or sorcery</note>. But this controversy is to be settled by this: that such a cure is indeed natural, but the mode of operating is supernatural and spiritual, because it is done solely by a certain attractive and incomprehensible reason. Furthermore, that this mode of healing proceeds without fascination is proven by this very fact: because it is joined with no fascination nor any other contranatural medium that protests against GOD the creator and His word, but is entirely natural, resulting from its own supernatural, invisible, incomprehensible, spiritual, and attractive virtue, which, having obtained its origin from the stars, completes its operation through the Elements.

Finally, I can defend this cure from fascination, since it is established that the Devil prefers to rejoice in the calamity and misfortune of the human race rather than to provide any help for the salvation of men, which fact, moreover, does not consist in his own powers at all without divine permission. Much more could be added to this magnetic form, but to avoid various errors, I now pause and hold my silence until I have related some things about the natural miracles of the world.

Coarse and rude minds, though stuffed with the opinion of philosophy, and all who have corrupted senses, know no distinction in these things; but the wise and skilled can distinguish natural things from supernatural ones most easily.

Let one note and observe this analogy through a coarser
pages.15:
example. There are many living creatures that are devoid of all life during the winter time, but as soon as summer returns, the natural heat generates new life, so that the body rises again in that substance in which it previously exerted vital motion, just like an herb, which dies in winter and revives anew in spring. The death of these things is therefore judged to be natural, but the restoration of new life through its own knowledge is supernatural. But truly, because man is accustomed to all these things, the smallest part approaches what ought to be further weighed and examined, dismissing both natural and supernatural things.

Very many are also accustomed to pass over the disposition of man with a dry foot <note>a classical idiom for passing over something hastily or without consideration</note>, which itself is also supernatural, as well as those monsters which bring spots into the world together; all these are indeed natural but show themselves supernaturally out of a rising imagination, which supernatural form and disposition the mother imprinted on the infant by accident through her imagination, as we indeed see quite often, that some customs are imbued in certain men, which they can never renounce, however much they may labor to break the habit. This kind of innate force of man is natural, but the conception in the mother’s womb, which the imagination of these things provided, is supernatural and subject to those things which the heaven imprinted.

Finally, neither do I deny this, that no one can support what exceeds the powers of nature with unshaken foundations and undoubted causes to avoid an injury to truth, unless those things are first known which become known to us from their physical course, for they have drawn their birth and their form from supernatural things

## The First Tincture and Root of Metals.

### Chapter Two.

BUT so that I may complete my undertaking, with GOD permitting, and take up the doctrine concerning the first tincture, root, and generation of Metals and Minerals, it must be known that the tincture and root of all Metals is also a supernatural, volatile, and fiery Spirit, which sustains itself in the air and naturally seeks its seat in water and earth, where it can rest and operate. This Spirit is found in all Metals, and more abundantly in others than in gold, for the reason that because of its baked, matured, and fixed body, it is solid, firm, and compact, and therefore, besides what the body requires, it cannot receive more. The other metals, however, are destitute of such a fixed body, but their pores are open and widely dispersed; therefore, the Spirit of the tincture can penetrate and occupy them more copiously. But since the bodies of other metals are unfixed, the Tincture also cannot subsist with wandering bodies
pages.17: but is compelled to yield. Since, therefore, the Tincture of gold exists nowhere more abundantly than in Mars <note>Iron</note> and Venus <note>Copper</note>, or the male and female, once their bodies are destroyed, the spirit of the tincture is driven from there, which enriches the enclosed, prepared gold with blood and volatilizes it through food and drink. Hence, the volatile gold, satiated with its food and drink, acquires its own blood and dries it with its native heat by the aid of vaporous fire, and a certain mutual victory is given, which conciliates the greatest fixity, so that gold may turn into a most fixed medicine. Because of the redundancy of blood, it can exhibit no body unless in turn a very large body is added to it, where the superfluous fixed blood is diffused; this added Metallic body, because of the immense heat of the leonine fixed blood, is penetrated like fire, is cleansed from all impurity, and is immediately baked into the fullest maturity and fixity. And so the servant gathers riches for the Lord, because the latter can desire nothing first from his own garment, since nature has bestowed upon him a single garment of honor; nor can the King, in turn, dispense inheritance and lasting courtly attire to his attendants from the kingdom, where he previously collected tribute from his subjects, so that the Lord and the servant may dwell together. Do not, however, wonder that the King needs the mutual help of his attendants, for the cause is the unfixedness of their bodies; for they receive many things into themselves, but can provide little faith. But where the King can become a participant in that matter, he is able to banish cold and heat better than impure metals. Thus, through such reception, he becomes the victor of all the rest, with a glorious
pages.18: triumph of wealth and health for a long life. I believe you have now sufficiently perceived, in place of a principle, this doctrine concerning natural and supernatural things, about the first tincture of the root of Metals and Minerals, upon which the cornerstone has been built and the truest rock in its kind founded, where nature has too deeply hidden and concealed her gifts. In the fiery and tinctured spirits, which color she obtained from the heaven of the stars through the operation of the Elements, and so was able to further tinge and fix those which were not yet tinctured and fixed, since the Moon <note>Silver</note> is destitute of the habit of a golden crown and fixity, as is also Saturn <note>Lead</note>, Jupiter <note>Tin</note>, and Mercury <note>Quicksilver</note>. And although Mars <note>Iron</note> and Mercury may need no garment, but could communicate this to the other five, I say, however, that without the lion <note>the prepared gold/tincture</note>, since they are not sufficiently instructed by the fixity of their Mercury and the subtlety of their salt, they can accomplish nothing that makes for wealth, unless they are conquered by the lion in the contest, so that they might carry off a triumph on both sides, raised moreover to no small improvement, which improvement lies hidden in the signed star or in its magnet, whence all the metals themselves received their gifts. I will proceed now to generation in particular, how the <term>Archaeus</term> <gloss>the vital, formative principle of nature</gloss> exhibits its virtue, pours it out, and draws it into the light, whence all the forms of Metals and Minerals are presented to the eyes and are formed and fortified with bodies by the incomprehensible and volatile fiery spirits of Minerals. THE trees also differ in such matters according to the bearing of fruit; for some bear from the <term>new</term> <gloss>shoots</gloss>, others from the <term>old</term>, others from both. ## Kind Reader.

<note>A decorative drop cap 'N' set within a square frame containing intricate foliate scrollwork.</note>After I have now taught the Catechism in churches and schools for the twentieth year without interruption by the command of my superiors, and—as they say—have had to pay enough "tuition" <note>idiomatic: learning through experience</note> until I found a way that is at once pleasant, useful, and convenient for the still-blossoming youth, and also beneficial to the parents, I have, after long practice, ensured that this *Catechismus Practicus* lacks nothing, neither regarding suitable examples, nor short explanations, hymns, or other exercises.

But because this book is intended mostly for children, no one should look here for subtle wit or hair-splitting or sharp-drawn matters, because such subtleties are of very little use to dear youth.

Here, Christian doctrine is placed before children in a childish way, and before the simple in a simple way: right and
pages.23:
plainly laid before the eyes: also sometimes a thing is broken up and presented in two, three, or four ways, so that the still-tender youth may grasp the necessary parts for salvation in either this or another pleasant way. Also, so that the knowledge of divine things takes root deeper and deeper, is imprinted into hearts as soft as wax, and sticks quite firmly, through short examples, now through short questions and answers, then through hymns in different melodies, concerts, and rounds: so that the catechist has many sorts of means, ways, and skills in hand to help only this one, or only that one, with pleasant variety, without which weariness would immediately arise beyond measure. The catechist and schoolmaster should by no means be ashamed to be childish with children, and to deal simply with simple little people, because the wisdom of the eternal Father also lowered Himself and accepted our weakness, willed to accommodate Himself to our understanding, offering milk to some and strong food to others, with the highest patience and humility.

that it surpassed the nature of the thing, when salt water turned into the sweetest drink: The dry passage of the Israelites through the Red Sea, as well as the sprouting of Aaron's rod, also occurred in a supernatural way.

And in summary, the emergence of Christ from the sealed sepulcher, that appearance made to the two walking to the castle of Emmaus, the manifestation through closed doors, were divine and supernatural things. Many other examples could be brought from the sacred code, if one did not have to attend to brevity.

To supernatural things are ascribed all the portents of metallic mines, bodily apparitions of spirits, ghosts, pygmies, and dwarfs, who very often present themselves to our sight and portend good or evil, ruin and wealth; likewise all the figures and other impressions of metals which are found underground, formed through the imagination of the three principles among humans, fish, and other living creatures, matured and cooked by the earth and the other elements, to which also pertain the monsters of the earth and things of that kind, which are given in strange forms underground at stated times, outside of which they can be found nowhere else, although at another time they may truly appear again and be presented to our eyes.

Hither are also referred all visions accustomed to be made through waters, mirrors, crystals, and other media, through seals and characters, which nevertheless differ greatly, for some are merely natural, yet exhibit supernatural visions. The rest, arising from incantations, are neither natural nor supernatural but Diabolical, and therefore are numbered among Demoniacal Magic, and by all Christians deservedly
pages.12:
are forbidden; and by right all those media contrary to the Holy Scriptures, the word of GOD, and His commandment are reproved and refuted by true and natural <term>Cabalists</term> <gloss>those versed in traditional, mystical interpretations of scripture</gloss>. And I warn of this so that a sure distinction and a certain order may be established between things natural, supernatural, and contranatural.

Similarly, all <term>Naiads</term> <gloss>water nymphs</gloss>, <term>Sirens</term>, <term>Succubi</term> <gloss>female demons that haunt men in sleep</gloss>, and other <term>Nymphs</term>, and what is akin to them, obtain a place among supernatural things; likewise earthly spirits and those who inhabit the air, offering themselves to hearing, sight, and touch, sometimes announcing death or other evil, and sometimes signifying fortunes and treasures in certain places by their apparitions. To these are added fiery spirits, showing themselves under the form of fire and a burning torch, all of whom are incorporeal spirits and yet not infernal—those who lie in wait for the souls of men as if they were eternal treasures, as the Stygian <term>Lucifer</term> and his excommunicated fellows are wont to do—but they are spirits of such a kind that, presented to humans for admiration above nature, they are uniquely nourished, fed, and pastured by the elements, and afterwards cease in this earthly world, dying and vanishing together, deprived of a redeemed soul. I add no more about these things now, but reserve their further treatment for another time and a more convenient place, where I shall prepare a singular treatise on visions and their spiritual apparitions, which the greater part of the world judges to be contrary to nature, when in truth they are indeed natural, though they are found to be supernatural with regard to their operations and their strange qualities.
pages.13:
In order to confirm my proposition more fully, I assert that there are many things in medicine manifesting and performing their operation in a supernatural way, merely in a magnetic manner, through a certain spiritual attractive virtue, which is attracted by the benefit of the air, because this is the medium between medicine and the ailment, just as the magnet perpetually turns itself to the southern star, even if it is many thousands of miles distant from it. Nevertheless, such a great spiritual operation and inclination intervenes here that, by means of this link—namely the air—such great distances concur. But because such an attractive virtue is commonly known, it has passed into mere custom, and it alone performs the task, nor is any further occult quality observed from which an operation of such a virtue draws its origin. In a similar way, wounds and ailments can be healed, even if the person so oppressed and the Physician are separated by a long interval, not by exorcisms, charms, and other illicit media contrary to GOD and nature, but by those in which a magnetic attractive virtue lies hidden. As if a wounded person, departing from here, leaves to the Physician the weapons with which he was injured, or anything from the blood that flowed from the wound, from which the legitimate means of healing are afterwards duly administered, as is wont to be done with the binding of wounds, he will recover firmly without any doubt. These are not charms; rather, such healing is accomplished uniquely by the attractive virtue of the medicine, which is carried to the wound by means of the air, to purify the wound and complete its spiritual operation.

These words will perhaps seem difficult to many and alien to the forces of nature, and many will attack this doctrine
pages.14:
as if it were entirely hostile to nature, from which many will descend into the most serious mutual altercations: whether this remedy is natural or not, whether it is possible or not, or whether it is a charm. But this controversy must be settled by this: that such a cure is indeed natural, but the mode of operating is supernatural and spiritual, since it happens by a certain attractive and incomprehensible reason alone; furthermore, that this mode of curing proceeds without charm is proved by this very fact, because it is joined with no charm nor any other contranatural medium, while it claims to be of the Creator GOD and His word, but is entirely natural, resulting from its own supernatural, invisible, incomprehensible, spiritual, and attractive virtue, which, having obtained its origin from the stars, performs its operation through the elements.

Finally, I can defend this cure from charm, since it is evident that the Devil rather rejoices in the calamity and misfortune of the human race than provides any help for the salvation of men, which otherwise, without divine permission, in no way consists in his powers. Many things could still be added to this magnetic form, but to avoid various errors, I now pause and hold my silence, until I have related some things about the natural miracles of the world.

Coarse and crude minds, yet stuffed with the opinion of philosophy, and all those who have corrupted senses, know no distinction in these things, but the wise and skilled can most easily distinguish natural things from supernatural ones.

Let one note and observe this similarity through a coarser

It will also confute the opinions of many who, disputing about natural things and not grasping the foundation, do nothing but act trifles and rashly produce their contentions.

## The First Tincture and Root of Metals.

### Chapter Two.

BUT in order to complete my undertaking, with GOD permitting, and to take up the doctrine concerning the first tincture, root, and generation of Metals and Minerals, it must be known that the tincture and root of all Metals is also a supernatural, volatile, and fiery Spirit, which sustains itself in the air and naturally seeks its seat in water and earth, where it can rest and operate. This Spirit is found in all Metals, and more abundantly in others than in gold, for gold, because of its cooked, matured, and fixed body, is solid, firm, and compact, and therefore, beyond what the body requires, it can receive no more. The other metals, however, are destitute of such a fixed body, but their pores are open and widely dispersed; therefore the Spirit of the tincture can penetrate and occupy them more copiously. But because the bodies of the other metals are unfixed, the Tincture also with wandering bodies
pages.17: cannot subsist, but is forced to yield. Therefore, since the Tincture of gold exists in none more abundantly than in Mars and Venus, or male and female, when their bodies are destroyed, the spirit of the tincture is driven thence, which enriches the secluded, prepared gold with blood and volatilizes it through food and drink. Hence, volatile gold, saturated with its own food and drink, acquires its own blood, and dries it with its native heat, by the help of vaporous fire, and a certain mutual victory is given, which procures the greatest fixity, so that gold may turn into the most fixed medicine; due to the redundancy of blood, it cannot exhibit any body, unless in turn a most abundant body is added to it, where the superfluous fixed blood is diffused, which added Metallic body is penetrated like fire because of the intense heat of the fixed leonine blood, is cleansed from all impurity, and is forthwith cooked into the fullest maturity and fixity; and thus the servant gathers riches for the Lord, because the latter can desire nothing further from his own cloth, since nature has bestowed upon him the only garment of honor, nor, conversely, can the King dispense inheritance and lasting courtly attire to his satellites from the kingdom, where he previously collected tribute from his subjects, so that the Lord and servant can cohabit. Do not, however, marvel that the King is in need of mutual help from his satellites, for the cause is the lack of fixity in their bodies; for they receive much into themselves, but can provide little faith. But where the King can become a participant in that thing, he is able to repel cold and heat better than impure metals. Thus, through such reception, he becomes the particular victor of all the rest with a glorious
pages.18: triumph of wealth and health for a long life. I believe you have now sufficiently perceived, in place of a beginning, the natural and supernatural doctrine concerning this first tincture of the root of Metals and Minerals, upon which the cornerstone is built and the truest rock is founded in general, where nature has hidden and concealed her gifts too deeply. In the fiery and tinctured spirits, which color it has obtained from the heaven of the stars through the operation of the elements, it was thus able to tinge and fix those things which were not yet tinctured and fixed, since the Moon is destitute of the habit of the golden crown and fixity, as are Saturn, Jupiter, and Mercury. Although Mars and Mercury have no need of a garment, but can communicate this to the other five, I say, however, that without the lion, since they are not sufficiently instructed by the fixity of their Mercury and the subtlety of their salt, they can provide nothing that makes for wealth, unless they are conquered by the lion in the contest, so that they both report a triumph, having been raised moreover to no small improvement, which improvement lies hidden in the signed star or in its magnet, from which the metals themselves received all their gifts. I shall now proceed to generation in particular, how the <term>Archaeus</term> <gloss>the formative, vital principle of nature</gloss> exhibits its virtue, pours it out, and brings it into the light, from which all forms of Metals and Minerals are presented to the eyes and are formed and furnished with a body by the incomprehensible and volatile fiery spirits of Minerals. ## Gracious Reader.

<note>A decorative drop cap 'N' is featured, containing intricate foliate scrollwork.</note>Having now taught the Catechism in churches and schools for the twentieth year without cessation by the command of my superiors, and having had to pay—as the saying goes—enough "tuition" <note>meaning practical experience gained through hardship</note> until I found a way that is at once pleasant, useful, and convenient for the still-blossoming youth, and also profitable for the parents, I have, after long practice, arranged this practical Catechism so that the catechist lacks nothing in terms of suitable examples, short explanations, hymns, or other exercises.

Because this book is intended mostly for children, no one should look here for subtle wit or sharp, pedantic matters, since such subtleties are of very little use to dear youth.

Here, Christian teaching is made childish for children and simple for the simple: rightly and
pages.23:
simply laid before the eyes: also, at times, a thing is presented and treated in two, three, or four ways so that the tender youth may grasp the necessary parts for salvation, either in this way or in another. Furthermore, so that the knowledge of divine things may take root more deeply the longer it is impressed upon wax-soft hearts and hold firm, it is presented only through short examples, now through short questions and answers, then through hymns in different melodies, concerts, and rounds: so that the catechist may have many kinds of means, ways, and tricks in hand to help this one or that one with pleasant variety, without which tedium will very quickly arise. The examiner and teacher should by no means be ashamed to be childish with children and simple with simple folk, because the Wisdom of the eternal Father also stooped down and took on our weakness, and chose to align Itself with our understanding, offering milk to some and strong meat to others, with the highest patience and humility.

### STATUS.

I establish the status as definitive, because the Apostle defines in what thing the true cause of justification consists, which has value before God. The genus is manifold, but the principal and predominant one is entirely Demonstrative. For the highest certainty is brought forth regarding the article of justification, which does not consist in anything else than demonstration <note>original: "apodixi"</note>. But one must remember that this is <term>χειροτονίαν</term> <gloss>an authoritative decree/ordination</gloss>, that is, which leans upon divine oracles; it is not <term>λογικὴ</term> <gloss>logical</gloss> [discourse] which we leave to Philosophy, and it is completed by a certain Analogy of things. pages.49: commends himself to the Romans, likewise commends the Romans to God, and in the end, also commends the saints to them as if they were brothers. The Parenetic, by which he exhorts them to the study of good works and commends the reborn for the new virtues of the Holy Spirit. <term>Εὐκτικόν</term> <gloss>Eucharistic/Prayerful</gloss>, by which he makes vows for the pious and prays unceasingly, as in the first chapter.
