PARTS OF THE EPISTLE.

The partition is either taken from the precepts of art or from the underlying subject matter that is explained. The precepts of art propose these parts to us. The title, which consists of the person writing and the one to whom it is written; to these a sweet prayer is added, and it is common in sacred letters for some longer discourse regarding the calling or the kind of doctrine to be inserted, which the Apostle Paul observed at the beginning. Then there is the exordium. Thirdly, the proposition. Fourthly, the narration or confirmation, or refutation, or the like. Fifthly, the greetings or some epilogue. Sixthly, finally, the subscription concerning the place, the messenger, or the person writing, containing something; thus indeed the precepts of art establish it. However, the matter often varies this, as in
pages.51:
this epistle, if you look at the subject matter, you will have those parts. The first is that men are not justified by works, which consists entirely of removal. The second is that men are justified by faith, which consists entirely of assertion. The third is that the merit of Christ pertains also to the Gentiles, from whom the Jews have fallen away in large part, by their own particular fault. The fourth is that reborn men adorn their profession with every study of good works. The fifth, finally, the greetings and commendations follow in place of an epilogue. But let us connect all the parts in order in this way:
1. First, the Epistle has a proper epigraph, that is, a title.
2. In the second place, it has an Eucharistic Exordium, to which a vow has been added.
3. In the third place is the Protasis: that men, according to the doctrine of the Gospel, are to be justified
pages.52: not according to the doctrine of men; I take this from the first chapter, verses 16 and 17. The fourth part is the Anasceue, that is, the refutation that men are not justified by works. Establish the beginning of the refutation from verse 18 of the first chapter, up to verse 21 of the third chapter. The fifth part is the Catasceue, the confirmation, the proposition of which is affirmative, that we are justified by faith in Christ. The beginning of that is from verse 21 of the third chapter, and it is continued through the following chapters, up to the beginning of the ninth chapter. The sixth part, therefore, is the <term>δηλωσις</term> <gloss>declaration/manifestation</gloss>, that is, the explanation of the whole dispute. For when he had taught that the Gentiles are not justified by moral works, and yet are to be justified, it was worth the effort to explain the passage concerning the vocation of the
pages.53: Gentiles. Thus, when he had taught that the Jews are not justified by the works of the law, it was necessary to show why the Jews were rejected, having been given it <note>original: "ipsi datis"</note>. Therefore, he treats this argument for the clarity of the dispute in chapters 9, 10, and 11. The seventh part, therefore, follows in order, namely the Parenesis <note>original: "Parænesis"</note> to the works of a reborn man: for he shows what the pious owe, both to their neighbor, to the magistrate, and to their household. Thus, here the ethical, political, and economic topics concur, and certain indifferent things <note>original: "adiaphora"</note>; these are treated in chapters 12, 13, 14, and the beginning of 15. Let the eighth part be established in chapter 15, verse 15, and it is the Epilogue, in which he deals with private matters, such as excusing himself for his prolixity. Likewise, that he commends the brothers, and adds besides friendly and copious greetings, re-greetings, and those are explained up to the end
pages.54:
of the end. In the last place is the Hypograph, the subscription, where we are admonished concerning the place where the Epistle was written, and concerning the messenger, although these things seem to be added not by Paul, but by others.

## Kind Reader.

Since I have now, for the twentieth year without interruption, taught the catechism in churches and schools by order of my superiors, and have had to pay what one calls "tuition" <note>a literal translation of "Lehrgeld," implying he learned through his own mistakes</note> until I found a way which is simultaneously pleasant, useful, and convenient for the still-blossoming youth, and also beneficial for the parents: I have, after long practice, composed this practical catechism so that the catechists might not lack suitable examples, short explanations, songs, or other exercises.

Because this book is intended mostly for children, no one should seek here subtle wit or sharp-witted and intricate matters, because such subtleties are of very little use to the dear youth.

Here, the Christian doctrine is presented in a childish way for children, and simply for the simple: rightly and
pages.23:

Furthermore, so that the knowledge of divine things might root more deeply the longer it is applied, being impressed upon wax-soft hearts, and remain quite firmly fixed, using only short examples, now through short questions and answers, then through songs in different melodies, concerts, and rounds: so that the catechist might have various means, ways, and techniques in hand just to help this one or that one, with lovely variety, without which resentment will arise over the masses very quickly. The opinion of those has always seemed plausible to me, MOST REVEREND, MOST EXALTED, and MOST ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE,

who affirm that the World, conglobated into the form of a perfect Sphere, adorned with eternal, restless, and wonderously swift-moving stars, planets, and circles, and with a sweet concert and harmony of motions, joined by a marvelous and indissoluble marriage and flux of all things (which the ancients called the *Archetypal World* made in likeness, and easily the Prince of the *Hyloperimetra* <note>meaning: measurements of matter/physical boundaries</note>), was created in the month of *March* at the point of *Aries*. They offer a twofold argument, not easily weakened: because in the month of *March*, around the point of *Aries*, the *Incarnation of the Divine Word*, which is a certain repair of the World from original sin, was begun by a stunning miracle of nature: and because at this same time the earth produces green herbs, and all generations of buds, especially solicitous of their primeval origin, as if they were aware of their early beginning, exult and luxuriate on the plains of the fields. I add, because the *Prince of the Planets* tends toward his own beginning at this same time, toward our zenith. Wherefore it is indeed consistent that the *Universe* acknowledged its own infancy in this very month, and indeed on the seventh day; for on the seventh day, He rested from the work that He had wrought. Thus, when that supreme *Former* of all things was about to create You, *Phoenix* of Prelates (with nature serving and acting as handmaid), in His own likeness (for He made man in His own image and likeness), and to the idea of the *microcosm*,

your

your microcosm, He willed that you be created and generated in the month of March, around the point of Aries, on the seventh day and in an odd year, endowed with incredible prudence, ineffable wisdom, and unspeakable piety. For that searcher of hearts knew that through You, in the world, and in the circle of the four Bishoprics over which you preside as a most deserving and worthy Prelate and Prince, a certain repair would come, not from original sin, but from pestilential and depraved opinions. And you would have done and accomplished this, had not the common enemies and disturbers of the Empire disrupted the matter, which, however, even though it was disturbed and thrown into confusion, you, as a sexagenarian and beyond, unceasingly and tirelessly and repeatedly, diligently ensure it be brought into the port of tranquility. He willed that You be created and generated at no other time than on an odd day and year (for even if by chance it might seem that the calculation of Your Nativity varied by an odd year or day, I would dare to say that by calculating the periods from the very infancy of the World, starting from the month of March, and leaving aside the Gregorian or even older correction of years, one would undoubtedly find that the day and year of Your Nativity was and existed as the seventh). Since the repair of the World was begun in the month of March, and it was decreed in the Divine Idea that the renewal and repair of depraved and pestilential opinions in Your Bishoprics should be begun in that same month, through You and Your Nativity. What more? You rejoice
pages.6:

in infancy, from the infancy of the World. You rejoice in the odd and septenary number, for GOD rejoices in the odd number, and "You," said GOD, "are gods." You rejoice in the seventh number, so that you may enjoy the privilege of the seventh, through whose happiness even those who are born in the seventh month (under the dominion of Diana, the very mother of humidity) are vital, so that you may live a long life. You rejoice in the seventh number, so that you may enjoy the Physician's privilege (for Physicians recognize the seventh as the King in the calculation of critical days), so that in this seventh year, after the morbid battle of Mars, you may be recognized as King and Prince. You rejoice in the seventh number, so that you may experience this sixty-seventh year of Your Nativity, which you are entering, as most happy, and may enjoy the privilege of those to whom, in ages past, when the seventh sun had returned, names were imposed with the most auspicious omen, so that in this seventh year of Your renewed Nativity, by a most auspicious omen, the Name of Repairer of the Orthodox Faith may be imposed upon You. You rejoice in the odd number (since "You are gods"), but not in every one, but in the number nine, dedicated and consecrated to Jupiter the Governor (for it is acknowledged that this number dominates at the very birth in the ninth month), so that You, in this same year, one thousand six hundred and fifty-nine, may rule like Jupiter. You rejoice in the odd number, by supreme privilege, for even Christ donned our mortal nature in an odd year from the founding of the World and the City: indeed, in the year 3963 from the World, from the City

->PREFACE.<-

"Difficult are the things that are beautiful," said Solon. Plato asserted that goodness accompanies difficulty. But Aristotle, Prince and Leader of philosophers, testified that virtue and art reside in difficult things. Indeed, it is true; thus, while the art and science of Medicine is most beautiful, it exists as a difficult thing, which, however, goodness and utility accompany: such as health itself, peace of mind, and among the wise, the highest honor. Moved and stirred by these things, the most august Emperors of the Romans, the most invincible Kings, and the highest Pontiffs of our ages, delighted greatly in this study. For that Augustus Caesar gladly used a medical composition invented by himself, which later many Physicians translated into their own books. Nero, that tyrant and indeed unpraised, yet truly most learned, is said to have placed a part of his study in this genre. Tiberius Caesar, according to Galen, composed troches for shingles. The antidotes of Adrian and Justinian are celebrated to this very day. Avicenna, Prince of the Arabs, in the remedies written by himself, praises the testimony of King Chabit in several places. In the commentaries of Serapis, Iacibusa, King of the Medes, and likewise King Chemur, are counted as witnesses of Medicine. I pass over Juba, King of Mauretania, who adorned the herb named Euphorbia with wonderful praises. I pass over Lysimachus, Gentius, and Eupator, Kings not ignorant of the medical art, who left their own names given to plants to be remembered for an eternal age. I pass over that one of Phoebus...

DISPOSITION ON THE FORMER
Epistle to the Corinthians.

*Who the Corinthians were.*

Corinth was named from Corinthus, the son of Marathon, who was either the founder or the enhancer of the city. Once it was the most famous and flourishing of the cities of Greece, for which reason Cicero did not hesitate to call it the light of all Greece. He describes its very location most elegantly in the <margin>In the Oration for the Manilian Law.</margin> Oration against Rullus in these words: "There is hardly a trace of Corinth left." For it was placed in the narrows and throats of Greece, so that it held the bolts of the region by land, and two seas, which were mostly for navi-
pages.60:
<header>IN EPIST. PAVLI. 55</header>
<sig>D. iiii.</sig>

gation, were almost joined, although they were separated by a very thin margin, etc. By these words he indicates that the Aegean Sea washes it from the east, where those sailing from Asia were received at the port of Cenchreae. The Ionian, however, is from the west, where those arriving were received at the port of Lechaeum. From this it is also that Horace sang:

<margin>Horace.</margin>
> Others will praise famous Rhodes, or Mitylene,
> Or Ephesus, or the walls of bimarian <note>located between two seas</note> Corinth—

This suitability of location, and wealth, and a singular corruption of morals had brought together into this city. For merchants from all of Asia and Europe flocked there as if to a common marketplace. And there was a very famous temple of Venus there, in which prostituted women made a living by their bodies,

from which those noble courtesans, whom Athenaeus and profane authors everywhere mention, were almost all Corinthians. And proverbs still exist among authors by which their morals are censured, such as "to behave like a Corinthian" <note>meaning to live profligately</note> and "it is not permitted to everyone to go to Corinth." From this corruption of morals, it undoubtedly followed that by the just judgment of God it was later destroyed, which we first read in histories was done by the Romans, through Lucius Mummius, before the Numantine War. The occasion for overthrowing that city was that they had defiled the ambassadors of the Roman people with filth. Afterwards, however, it was restored by Caesar, and again made noble by the studies of humanity, wealth, and corruption of morals. ### Epistle.

In this corruption of morals, the Lord also had a Church, whose origin exists in Acts chapter 18, from which place, and from the first chapter of this Epistle, and likewise the 7th, the occasion can be gathered: that the Apostle wrote this Epistle moved by a grave cause. For such a kind of plant also exists, which cannot grow unless in moisture; but others grow, though they are not the same, but inferior. Of all trees, to speak simply, and of plants, there happen to be more species in each genus; for there is almost nothing that is simple. But as many as are called cultivated and wild have this as the most evident and greatest difference, for example, the Fig tree and the wild Fig tree; the Olive and the wild Olive; the Pear and the wild Pear; and as many as are in each of these, in the fruits and leaves and the other forms and parts. But of the wild ones, most are nameless, and few are experienced [in them]; but of the cultivated and named ones, there are more, and the perception [of them] is more common; I mean, for example, the Grapevine, the Fig, the Pomegranate, the Apple, the Pear, the Laurel, the Myrtle, and the others. For the usage being common makes one consider the differences together. And this is also specific to each: some distinguish the wild ones by male and female, either solely or mostly; but the cultivated ones by more forms. And it is easier to grasp and enumerate the species of the former; but of the latter, it is more difficult due to their multitude. But indeed, one must try to observe the differences of the parts and of the other substances from these things; but about their origins, one must speak after these, for this is, as it were, next in order to the things already said.

# NOTES

## ON BOOK ONE.

---

### *The constituent parts of plants.*

#### CAP. I.

"Perhaps not in the same way." The utmost brevity, as **D. Moldenhawer** rightly observed, in the comparison of animals with plants at the end of this chapter; concerning which Aristotle should be consulted in *History of Animals* 5.3.

"Therefore nothing is strange." See about this matter in *On the Causes of Plants* 2.20, 22, 23; 5.2.

"By equal," i.e. interval. Equidistant.

#### CAP. II.

"These are the first and greatest." Thus Aristotle in *History of Animals*: as many of the parts, being wholes, have other parts of their own within them; for instance, the head, etc.

"Longer-lived in the roots." Those whose root is perennial. Bot.

"With a single," i.e. stem. Endowed with a simple trunk. See Pliny, *Natural History* 14.1.30.

"Similar-parted." "Dissimilar-parted." Aristotle should be consulted on this matter in *On the Generation of Animals* 1.1 and the *Lexicon of Theophrastus*.

"Any part whatever from the same things." The individual parts from the same vessels, fibers, membranes, etc.

"The greatest parts are almost these." End of chapter two in Bodaeus.

"Other things from which these come;" the author proceeds to the similar-parted [parts].

#### CAP. III.

"Menestor." An author on herbal matters whose works are not extant.

"Namelessly," simply "the moisture."

"Innate moisture and heat." Moldenhawer treats very copiously of the warm principle of life in *Tentamen*, p. 83. He calls it "generative heat."

<summary>This page contains scholarly notes on Book One of Theophrastus, focusing on plant anatomy, Aristotelian comparisons, and terminology.</summary>
<keywords>Theophrastus, Botany, Aristotle, Moldenhawer, plant anatomy, notes</keywords>
pages.139:
<header>NOTES ON BOOK ONE.</header>

*On the Causes of Plants* 1.4. Compare also Galen. By Aristotle, it is called "natural heat" 2.3.

"But other different species." Different, that is, from "moisture and heat." Beginning of chapter 4, Bodaeus.

"Fibers—veins." The author’s marvelous sagacity in describing these very thin vessels; which, however, in our century have been brought to their "acme" <gloss>perfection</gloss>. Moldenhawer treats most copiously of this matter in *Tentamen*, p. 91.

"Wood, flesh." See Moldenhawer, p. 108.

"The pith" is compared to "marrow in bones." But briefly, however, and narrowly, as he is accustomed, the author describes the "pith" of vegetables; clearly, however, if you weigh the force of the words. Mention is made elsewhere, 1.9; 4.2. *On the Causes of Plants* 5.6, 7, 24.

### CAP. IV.

"In which it is possible." In those which admit division.

"Contrary to the direction." By means of cultivation, etc. A frequent usage in Theophrastus.

"The coppice olives." The word "copades" is interpreted as coppice-wood, but here perhaps concerning a beheaded tree.

### CAP. VI.

"Of all, one must always take"—an obscure reading, if it is sound: the meaning is, "one must always take the differences of all [things] by their places" with respect to climate, etc.

"Another [difference] according to the other genus of fluids," i.e. aquatic plants differ among themselves with respect to "places."

"Smaller—larger." The former are seaweeds and laver; the latter are called "little trees" elsewhere; gorgonians, corallines. See 4.8.

### CAP. VII.

"Thickness." Here it indicates the thickness or mass of the trunk. It is opposed to "thinness," or slenderness.

"From which the composition [is]." With respect to the component parts. It is opposed to "those according to the conditions and powers."

### CAP. VIII.

"In the pith." See chapter 3, p. 9, line 6. N.B. Chapter IX in Bodaeus.

"Some do not have it—and the Elder." In the younger branches of the Elder, there is no pith.

<summary>Notes on Book One of Theophrastus continue, covering plant tissues, the role of moisture and heat, and specific terminology for plant structures.</summary>
<keywords>Theophrastus, botany, plant anatomy, pith, moisture, heat, scholarly notes</keywords>
pages.140:
<header>NOTES ON BOOK ONE.</header>

"All piths are black." The significance of the word "black" escaped Scaliger. See Bodaeus, p. 24, and the *Lexicon of Theophrastus*.

"In general, some do not have it." The discussion is about fungi; see the systematic catalogue, which have no affinity with other plants. See Bodaeus, p. 27.

"They also differ in their roots." See about this matter Pliny 16.31.

"Fringed." Pliny says "fimbriated," but there is another sense of the word "thysanoi," ribbons, bundles of fibers. Pollux. See the *Lexicon of Theophrastus*.

### C A P. IX.

"In those above the earth," i.e. "parts."

"For the root," i.e. the root in general.

### C A P. X.

"Crowning altars." Perhaps it should be read "saying heaps," gathering mounds.

"They bear fruit." Add "below": under the earth, concerning tubers. See the illustration of "Arachidnas" in Bodaeus, p. 35.

"The fruit," i.e. the tuber from the root.

"Before the parts above," i.e. "parts."

"These contribute greatly." It should be noted that the word "nature" should be taken in the plural.

"The juices of all are similar." Beginning of the chapter in Bodaeus.

"For from the shoots." A wonderful description of the habit of the <term>Ficus Indica</term> <gloss>Banyan tree</gloss>.

"If in deep soil." The meaning is, if some material intervenes between the seed and the earth, "it bends the root toward the earth" until it touches.

### C A P. XI.

"In which both are," i.e. "genders." Even if a sexual distinction occurs in the palm, commonly the words "male" and "female" are attributed to varieties of species, as they are observed to be more robust and fruitless, or the contrary.

"The most peculiar are those of the Apple tree." These words included in parentheses **crept in from the margin**, as I suspect, and interrupt the description of the habit of the "Fir." Even though it is hardly possible to conjecture what the author means with respect to "faces of wild beasts," Pliny interprets the place thus in *Natural History* 16.30: "A kind of branch is peculiar to the apples, for they render the snouts of wild beasts, with smaller ones adhering to one largest."

<summary>Further notes on the anatomy and classification of various plants, including the banyan tree and the structure of tubers, with philological corrections.</summary>
<keywords>Theophrastus, botany, Banyan tree, plant anatomy, philology, Pliny, tubers</keywords>
pages.141:
<header>NOTES ON BOOK ONE.</header>

"Of the nodes, some are blind." Observe that the word "ozos" occurs in a double sense, as branch and node on the trunk.

"Because nothing is placed in between." Because there are no intervals. Scaliger.

"Special hollows." See the word "elos" in the *Lexicon of Theophrastus*. A species of Hypoxylon, as I suspect. See 4.16.

"It is therefore." The chapter should be added to the previous one as it is a continuation.

"Increasing in length." The discussion is about the trunk: which is either tall and not branching, or which "divides straight." I also suspect that what follows, "the others similar to these," should be read thus: "but the root [is] similar to these." Thus Virgil: "As much as it rises to the ethereal breezes with its top, so much it reaches to Tartarus with its root."

"Becomes thin," i.e. by cultivation.

### CAP. XII.

"And some are evergreen." Here begins chapter 15 in Bodaeus.

"To participate in the winter." To last until the middle of winter.

### CAP. XIII.

"Like the hand." Pliny in the same place 16.24 says, "veins in the surfaces," "incisions underneath," that is, hollow lines, as in the palm of the hand.

"Whichever is toward the branch," i.e. from the turning of the leaves it is doubtful which side is the upper and which the lower; "for the supineness" with respect to position is different from the nature of the leaf.

"Not to be altered in the same way." It is opposed to conversions "by way of the veins or fibers," i.e. not in a constant, regular manner.

"Going through the depth" is to be interpreted concerning the thickness of the leaf.

"Saw-toothed." Perhaps "comb-toothed" or "slaughter-toothed." See the *Preface to the Illustrations of Theophrastus*, p. v. Also the description of the "Fir," book 3.

"Of the oak from the trunk." Pliny observes the same about the leaves of the Oak, *Natural History* 16.24. Bodaeus says he has never observed it. I suspect an error in the text: perhaps it should be read "Cyprian." See about the "Cyprian Fig," 4.2.

<summary>Notes on the growth patterns of trees, the structure of leaves, and the clarification of potential textual errors regarding botanical descriptions.</summary>
<keywords>Theophrastus, botany, plant morphology, leaves, trunk, philology</keywords>
pages.142:
<header>NOTES ON BOOK ONE.</header>

"The whole stem leafless." He accurately describes the scape of botanists.

"By itself." From itself: concerning a sessile leaf. Bot.

"Having enclosed in between [the fruit]." Fruit in the middle of the leaf.

### CAP. XIV.

"To those not annual [parts]." Persisting parts of the plant, such as the trunk, branches, etc. "For nothing [is] without this [moisture]."

"Of the flowers, some from the bark." Strange, what Theophrastus intends by flowers from the bark and nerves. Surely an error of the text, and it should be read for "flowers," "others" (i.e. stalks). Concerning flowers see 21, 22.

### CAP. XV.

"The seed immediately after the containing part." Seed with a simple covering. In this chapter six kinds of seeds are noted, the enumeration of which is confused and very long. These are: 1. simple seeds with covering; Palm. 2. from kernel and flesh—drupes. 3. in a pod—siliquose. 4. in a certain membrane, membranaceous follicle, such as the Pear, Apple. 5. angiosperms, with loose, rigid pericarp; Poppy. 6. gymnosperms, without covering; umbellifers.

"Such as the grape." Here the text of the passage is very corrupt. The distinction of Theophrastus of several grains contained in a common thing, such as a grape or seed-pip in the grape: and likewise in the seed. N.B. The kernels of the Pomegranate are opposed to the individual grains of Wheat, etc. "And least of all would the apple-seeds seem to be." Least of all, however, should be added to these the apple-seeds which in the interior part of the fruit are wrapped in membranes.

"But in the same way each of these." See the error of the scribe in transcribing above, "since [it is] not to each one taking."

### CAP. XVI.

"In those concerning juices." *History of Plants* 6.

"Of lettuce." The juice is called "watery" less correctly. Perhaps an error of the text, as above for "nappy" <gloss>opode</gloss> concerning the juice of the Fig and Poppy, "milky" should be placed.

"Which is proper." The meaning is that the peculiar juice of any plant "has a certain similarity" in itself before the concoction and maturation happen in the fruit, which is brought about by the help of the pericarp.

<summary>Notes on plant reproductive parts, seed classification, and the nature of plant juices, highlighting common textual corruptions.</summary>
<keywords>Theophrastus, botany, seeds, plant anatomy, juices, philology, taxonomy</keywords>
pages.143:
<header>NOTES ON BOOK ONE.</header>

"Of some, sweet-smelling." See more fully about odors in Theophrastus, *On the Causes of Plants* 1.6, as also about juices.

### CAP. XVII.

"Outside the sea." The Red Sea is understood.

"Having a sketch." The common columbine is indicated by the name "Iasione" by most botanists; and the description, although intricate, marvelously agrees with the convolutions of the petals: also "it is not separated in the flower."

N.B. To some perhaps the conjecture of Bodaeus will be more pleasing, that the Convolvulus sepium etc. is indicated here, in which sense "a sketch only of the majority" is to be interpreted concerning the amplitude of the flower.

"They appear perforated." The marvelous "accuracy" of the author, when the flower is perforated, i.e. it falls off without a stigma, the beginning fruit remains; when it is "scorched or soaked," either by too much sun or rain, it "sheds the fruit with it." See the observation below, "as many of the flowers as have, as it were, a spindle, are fertile."

"On the mouths themselves." The discussion is about syngenesious plants; "mouth" therefore [is] the common receptacle in this class.

"Like a spindle." Concerning the stigma of the orange flower.

"To show the fruit immediately," i.e. without a flower or petals.

### CAP. XVIII.

"The unripe fig." <term>Ficus Carica</term>, etc. is numbered by Linnaeus among the Trioecious. "The wild fig tree," from which "the wild figs" (which are perhaps "the unripe figs") [come], is the Male tree; the "Fig tree" is the Monoecious tree.

### CAP. XIX.

"Such are." A summary and recapitulation of this book.

"More species in each genus." More species under one genus. A truly Linnaean distinction!

"Cultivated and wild." Here the distinction is taken from sex: but what does it mean? That wild plants are distinguished by sex, but cultivated ones indeed by "more peculiarities"; does he indicate varieties of fruits?

pages.10: and human [law], by which the sacrosanct and inviolable envoys, especially in times of peace, were expected to be; and there were either none, or very few, who, mindful of the liberty of ancient Germany and the dignity of the Empire, were seriously moved by the care of these matters. And yet, for reasons of duty, you had to return to the upper regions of Germany. You said that you did not at all neglect your dangers, which you understood were set before you; and in these, you grieved that you were all but abandoned by those by whom it should least have been done. Yet, with every asseveration, you confirmed: that you wished to pursue your calling, which you knew to be from GOD, with as much zeal as you could, and that you did not fear the traps or violence of the Roman Pontiff, or of the most powerful enemies who hung upon his nod, so much as to doubt that you would be safe under the protection and guardianship of GOD alone. For why, you said, should I fear men in such a cause, pertaining to the glory of GOD and the salutary union of the Churches of CHRIST? When we are forbidden by divine command to fear the Devil himself, the enemy of all the pious?
pages.11:
I am divinely forbidden to fear the cunning, the rage, and the power of this most wicked enemy. If I wish to be a true Christian, I should not fear him; why, then, should I allow myself to be turned away from the straight path of my calling by the traps, hatreds, and most unjust machinations of hostile men, however well-equipped they may be to cause harm? Should I fear the Antichrist and his servants, I, who have professed the name of **CHRIST** and, with God’s help, have learned to despise the Devil, the prince of this age?

This voice, in harmony with that Apostolic one: “Greater is He who is in you, than he who is in the world,” and, “Everything that is born of **GOD** overcomes the world,” and, “This is the victory that overcomes the world: our Faith,” so penetrated my soul that I was both exceedingly grateful to you for this invincible strength of the Christian heart, and I prayed to **GOD** with a true groan that He might increase the Spirit of fortitude in you more and more, and grant security to you and yours on your most dangerous journey. From which, when you had escaped many traps,
pages.12:
not without divine miracle, you returned to us unharmed, your example could not but strengthen in my mind the belief handed down by so many divine promises:
->God knows not how to abandon the one who trusts in Him.<-
And because I have entered upon this commemoration, and all the pious are accustomed to being marvelously strengthened by past events against the insults of future dangers to which our life is constantly exposed, I cannot pass over in silence the mention of that divine liberation which occurred to you almost at the very beginning of your undertaken embassy, when, not far from France, as you departed with your companions, a shipwreck befell you, and all things threatened you with immediate death. Yet from that extreme danger, God most kindly preserved you, your companions, and all the things you were carrying with you. This benefit of God was so much greater and more illustrious, the more happily that other danger was divinely dispelled, which, having scarcely escaped from the shipwreck,
pages.13: you encountered, at that very same time, not without great consternation among your companions: when pirates made a most fierce attack upon the small boats into which you had transferred yourself and your possessions. They, however, upon the arrival of Scottish ships (which, as they were unknown to you, so you and yours were unknown to them), were immediately broken by a certain Panic terror and forced to take to flight, as God unexpectedly—and truly, as they say, <term>ἀπὸ Μηχανῆς</term> <gloss>from the machine/deus ex machina</gloss>—provided you help from on high, scattering and eluding those pirates as if they were gaping crows, who in their own minds had already devoured you and your treasures, which you were carrying with you into Germany by the command of your most Serene King. Which treasures, when you had later brought them to us, I beheld with these my own eyes, and I marveled at such a wealth of most precious gems, such a number of most excellent jewels, and finally, such a quantity of gold offered voluntarily by a most excellent King—and one who is in truth the most Christian—to Germany, not only as a most certain pledge but also as a most liberal subsidy, to testify to his most pious will
pages.14:
and his burning zeal in helping the common affairs of the Evangelical Churches.

The piety and liberality of this holy King is worthy of all the greater praise for all posterity, the more the kindness of God must also be proclaimed, who willed that those most opulent treasures should by no means perish in a shipwreck or become prey to pirates, and who rescued you, together with all those you had joined to yourself as companions, from the jaws of death, and brought you safe into Germany.

Where, with what dexterity, labor, zeal, solicitude, faith, and integrity you handled the affairs of your embassy—which pertained to the injury of no man, but looked toward the peace, quiet, and union of the Churches—among the Evangelical princes, the letters of the kings and princes themselves, in which they respond to your most Serene King, are witnesses. Witnesses also are many learned and honored men, not only in courts but also in the Republics to which you went, who will not allow either the praise of the royal piety
pages.15:
or the memory of your virtues to die out among them in any age whatsoever.

Although some time has elapsed until now, and perhaps in the future there will not be a lack of obstacles before the matters for the sake of which you undertook the embassy are brought fully to their hoped-for end and outcome—as no great things were ever both started and completed at once—yet it is of great benefit that the will of your Churches, desirous of peace and concord, has become known to our people even in this embassy of yours. And it is of great importance to you to know that the minds of most of the German Princes are not averse to the mutual union of the Evangelical Churches, however much certain ill-disposed theologians—who place their own ambition and other most unjust desires before the public welfare—do not cease to cry out against Synods, and with their intemperance to exacerbate controversies that have arisen regarding religion, and with brutal bolts of anathema
pages.16:
to strike so many heads of innocent men and so many Churches which are among you, neither heard nor ever legally convicted.

Against the tribunitial clamors of these <term>ματαιολόγων</term> <gloss>vain-talkers</gloss> (by which they show clearly enough to all who understand how much they distrust their own cause), the testimonies of the princes themselves, who are of chief authority in Germany, should by right and merit be opposed with far milder ones regarding your Churches. Such is this one alone, which exists in the letters of the Elector of Saxony to the King of France himself, written out expressly and clearly in these very words, with the great praise and approbation of all the pious and those who judge rightly:

“We faithfully and diligently warn, ask, and beseech: That the Royal ears may not be open to the seditious voices of most wicked men, and that they may not allow themselves to be incited by them against **THEIR OWN FAITHFUL CITIZENS, WHO ARE LOVERS OF TRUE PIETY**, who have suffered all things until now so that they might render to **GOD** the Best and Greatest His honor, and to your Royal Serenity
pages.17:
the obedience and subjection that is due. Whom these pests of mankind, the Pontificians, hate for this reason alone and desire to see extirpated, so that, with the strength of the kingdom of France exhausted and trampled upon, your most Serene Royal Majesty might be exposed to the tyranny and lust of the Roman Pontiff, to the irreparable loss of your affairs, your reputation, and, what is the head of all, your soul.” And entirely similar to these are the things contained in the letters of the most Serene King of Denmark to that same King of France.

Let these pests of mankind, therefore—not only of the Pontifical sort, but also of that kind of ambitious theologian who has hitherto abused the authority of princes throughout Germany—see how far they stand from the judgments of these very Princes. For they continue to burden your Churches with feigned and fabricated crimes, and they furiously reject all paths and methods suitable for establishing legitimate peace and concord in the Church (like madmen who turn away from the remedies for their own insanity).

DISPOSITION OF THE FIRST
Epistle to the
Corinthians.

*Who the Corinthians were.*

Corinth was named after Corinthus, the son of Marathon, who was either the founder or the illustrator of the city. Once it was the most famous and flourishing of the cities of Greece, whence Cicero did not hesitate to call it the light of all Greece. He describes its location most elegantly in the Oration against Rullus <note>original: "In Oratione pro Lege Manilia" <gloss>In the Oration for the Manilian Law</gloss></note>, in these words: "Hardly a trace of Corinth remains." For it was situated in the straits and jaws of Greece, so that the land held the bolts of the region, and it nearly joined two seas that were most navigation-
pages.60:

ally distinct, while they were separated by a very narrow interval, etc. By which words he indicates that the Aegean sea washes it from the east, where those sailing from Asia were received in the port of Cenchreae. Indeed, that the Ionian sea is from the west, where those arriving were received in the port of Lechaeum. Hence it is also that Horace sang:

<margin>Horace.</margin>
> "Others will praise glorious Rhodes, or Mitylene,
> Or Ephesus, or the walls of bimarian <note>meaning: between two seas</note> Corinth—"

This suitability of the place, and its wealth, and a singular corruption of morals had brought [people] into this city. For merchants from all of Asia and Europe flocked there as if to a common marketplace. And there was a most famous temple of Venus there, in which women practiced prostitution for profit with their bodies,
pages.61:

whence those noble courtesans, whom Athenaeus and profane authors everywhere mention, were almost all Corinthians. And there exist still today proverbs among authors by which their morals are taxed, such as "to behave like a Corinthian" <note>original: "Corinthiari"</note> and "it is not permitted for everyone to go to Corinth." From this corruption of morals, it flowed undoubtedly that by the just judgment of God it was later destroyed, which we first read in histories was done by the Romans, through Lucius Mummius, before the Numantine war. The occasion for overturning that city was that they had defiled the ambassadors of the Roman people with excrement. Later, however, it was restored by Caesar and again made noble by the studies of humanity, wealth, and corruption of morals. Whoever desires more, let him see Strabo, book 8; Livy, book 5 of the fifth decade;

### OCCASION OF THE
### Epistle.

In this corruption of morals, the Lord also had a Church, the origin of which exists in Acts chapter 18, from which passage, and the first chapter of this Epistle, and likewise chapter 7, the occasion can be gathered, namely that the Apostle wrote this Epistle moved by a grave cause. The occasion, therefore, was offered in this way. The Apostle had taught there for a full year and six months, and that with great fruit and success; for he had done this by divine command, and at the same time it was signaled to him

pages.10:
Orator, the King of the Persians, who proposed to mortals for eternal memory the Syrup called "of apples" (corruptly called "King Sabor" by some) to purge the melancholy and black humors offending in the <term>microcosm</term> <gloss>the human body as a world in miniature</gloss>. I pass over Archelaus, Hiero, and Philemetor, Kings who wrote about plants in Greek. I pass over the antidote of that most invincible King Mithridates, praised by all by common calculation to this day, discovered by Pompey in his secret repositories. In our own centuries, however, it is read in the monuments of histories that Nicholas and Eusebius the Fifth, Supreme Pontiffs, were Physicians by art and profession. Since it is most beautiful, therefore, it is little wonder if it is also difficult, and because of this, there seem to be so many and such varied opinions in the medical republic, that about this, that Horatian sentiment is recited by some. Book 2 of the Satires.

> There are as many thousands of studies as there are heads.
> A thousand kinds of men, and a varied use of things.
> Each has his own will, nor does one live by a single vow.

Yet one should not believe that this most noble science suffers any shipwreck from this (for by reason of its beauty and difficulty, opinions are indeed varied in theory, but in practice, the sense and calculation of all are the same). Rather, it is directed more and is strengthened more to protect and preserve the human Republic, to repair and overcome diseases; which goodness also accompanies. Hence, since I had proposed to defend certain Theses for the Medical College, as a Physician in Prague, in the year 1652, and had published them (as is usually done, promulgated in types), some friends who considered them difficult and beautiful for practice began to exhort me, that by adding
pages.11:
reasons I should corroborate them, for the good of mortals. I myself, who struggle with difficulty for the sake of so many critics <note>original: "zoilorum" - referring to Zoilus, a classic critic of Homer, used here as a term for carping critics</note> in such a <term>palaestra</term> <gloss>wrestling school or arena</gloss>, refused the advice. Yet, having found an opportune occasion (since I had also seen very learned men doubting about something in practice), I decided to follow the advice, and I consign them here in the same order as I defended them in Prague. If anyone, nauseated, rejects this my labor, let him know that I did not write for him, and if he has better things, let him offer them, and let him not doubt that I shall return the highest thanks; and that my intention was none other than that I wished to exercise myself in a thing difficult, most beautiful, and necessary for the common good of mortals. For if Emperors, Caesars, Kings, and Pontiffs exercised themselves in this same thing, because of its beauty and the goodness that accompanies it, why should it not be permitted to a Physician, let others enjoy it at their pleasure.

# PREFACE TO THE CONCLUSIONS,
### which is
# THE FIRST CONCLUSION.

<note>Large ornamental drop-cap initial 'O' decorated with floral and foliate patterns.</note>
All men desire to know naturally. Some indeed desire to know their origin, others wish to possess knowledge, and others have it in mind to learn something else. I myself, in order to satisfy this naturalness in some way, bring forth some things from the vast field of the Medical faculty, and first, what is formed in the very first formation of man, or one might say the fetus, whether it is the heart, the fountain of human life, or the liver, the workshop of blood, or the brain, the most divine member called so by Plato in the *Timaeus*, and I assert that the liver is formed first, then the heart, and finally the brain.

There are many things, I confess, to be discussed in this Conclusion, namely, how it expands in the infused seed, adheres, lives, and the like, which would pertain to the present matter; furthermore, whether it lives in potentiality or in act; whether a natural spirit is given, or whether it proceeds from the liver. But setting these aside, I descend to my main intent, (supposing from Aristotle, Book 1 of *The Parts of Animals*, chapter 1, that the seed is generation: and generation is the first participation with the warm, nutritive soul, from *On Youth and Old Age*, chapter 14; likewise, Book 1 of *On the Generation of Animals*, chapter 18, if the parts are
pages.13:
distracted in the seed, how does it live? Likewise, Book 2 of *On the Generation of Animals*, chapter 3, the seed and the conceptus nonetheless live just as plants do, nor is Galen contrary) see: what that first member is, among the principal ones, which is generated first and more conveniently, and lives with a vegetative life; so that this conclusion of ours may be firmer, we shall take authorities from Hippocrates and from others. Afterwards, if anything is to be brought against it, I shall resolve it.

    Hippocrates, therefore, in his book *On the Formation of the Fetus*, and his faithful interpreter Galen here, recounts a certain case (by which he intends to prove that the liver is generated first; I, however, shall bring forth both its structure and what it is for, so that everything may be more corroborated), which is as follows.

    "But I saw the seed, which had remained in the places for six days, and had later fallen out, and from those things which then appeared to me in it, I conjecture the rest: but how I saw the seed on the sixth day, I shall tell. A certain maid of a woman (she was a notable singer, who used to visit men, whom it was not proper to conceive in her womb, lest she be rendered more contemptible; but that singer had heard that which women were accustomed to say among themselves, that where a woman is about to conceive, the seed no longer goes out from the woman’s womb; but is contained within; when she had heard this, she observed and watched always, and by chance, when she felt that the seed had not gone out, she revealed it to her mistress, which, when it reached our ears, we ordered that she jump to the ground (another text reads, onto her buttocks, and better), and she did that about seven times, and the seed, not without some noise, was shaken out and flowed to the ground, which, when the woman had seen, she inspected, and wondered; but what it was like, I shall say, just as if someone were to pull apart the outer shell of a raw egg, so that through the inner membrane, the inner humidity would shine through, such it was plainly in some way, and a certain red and round thing was within, but in the membrane certain white and thick fibers were seen to be present, wrapped in a thick and red <term>sanie</term> <gloss>sanious or bloody matter</gloss>, and on the outside around the membrane were bloody bruises: in the middle something thin was gaping, which seemed to me to be the navel, by which the fetus would first breathe with spirit, both going out and coming in, by it the membrane, which contained the seed, was entirely produced." This is the series of Hippocrates’ history, with Galen and Bernardo Feliciano as interpreter. Which, also the same Galen, and from Galen, Feliciano,
pages.14:
explain entirely, and indicate what all things signify, but, omitting others, in chapter 3, around the middle, they interpret that red thing thus, saying, that red, round thing which shone in the chorion in the seed, Hippocrates said was six days old, it is to be believed it was the liver, still indistinct and unformed: and a little later they add, but earlier (so says Galen/Feliciano from him), when I was writing commentaries about the seed, and was forced to say something about the order of the formation of the individual members, I said the heart, just like the liver in the first days of the fetus, was, as it were, a certain foundation, most necessary for this, induced by its use in adults and perfect beings to be brought forth: but when afterwards I learned that the opinion of all others, both Physicians and Philosophers, was (behold the ingenuity of Galen admitting his own error, behold upon what foundations he leaned to change his opinion) that the fetus is dispensed only as a plant until its express formation, it seemed more probable to me if we should maintain that there was no necessity for the heart in the beginning, but that it was formed after the liver: and towards the end of the chapter he adds; but indeed, just as the heart is to be believed to have been made later than the liver, and therefore the liver was placed closer to the womb of the pregnant woman (which anatomy itself demonstrates most truly), so it was fitting that the brain also be placed further from the heart, inasmuch as it is also fabricated later; giving the reason why the brain is also fabricated last, saying, that this is to be thought to happen because there is no need for a brain to the fetus: for it is not necessary for it to see, nor to hear, nor to taste, nor to smell anything, nor likewise to work with hands or feet, nor to use any other voluntary function at all. In a similar way, there was no necessity for the sense of touch, no necessity for imagination, none for thought, none for memory; therefore, the brain was fabricated third in the order of time. (Beautifully said about the necessity of the last formation of the brain itself; if he had provided the same for the heart, it would be less burdensome for us, but we shall demonstrate it with our strength). These both Hippocrates and Galen said; but may I be permitted, to confirm this, to add this Case History which I saw.

---

->A certain Marchionilla of Tochov in Bohemia, January 14, 1653, after the tenth day of conception, suffered an abortion,<-
pages.15:
which desiring to see, or rather, being eager and curious to see the constitution of the fetus, she caused me to be called, and the midwife, in my presence, at my command, and with me demonstrating the method, cuts the abortion into parts, and while she was cutting the chorion, a certain bloody mass was seen, without any motion, without any sense, (as appeared from the section), intertwined and divided by various filaments, outside the chorion membrane, and certain other filaments were conspicuous; who will doubt that that bloody mass was not the liver, and those filaments were the rudiments of the veins and the navel? It appeared without sense, without motion; what else will you present or assign to me than the liver? Wherefore it remains that the liver is generated first, and that nothing can be devised more conveniently for the vegetative soul, as a member in which it might reside, than the liver. But let this be confirmed both from the structure of the liver and from its use.

The substance of the liver is fleshy, similar to blood recently poured out and coagulated, whence the word <term>parenchyma</term> <gloss>the functional tissue of an organ</gloss> was derived by Erasistratus, it is wrapped in a simple and sufficiently thin membrane, clinging tightly to the viscera on all sides, it consists of veins in a double order: the Upper, which are branches of the vena cava and lead blood into its large trunk, like a royal road; the Lower, which are greater in number, are branches of the portal vein, from which also the umbilical vein in the fetus, by which the fetus is nourished, arises.

Moreover, its function and duty is to nourish the body to the very end of life; for from the natural spirit arising from the liver, both the vital and animal spirits receive nourishment (although Manardus, and with him Ioan. Hier. Bronzerius, in his Treatise, Book of Epistles 15, first epistle, seem to deny this: yet they conceded, and Bertachius in the third book, *On Spirits*, chapter three, from Galen, Book 1 of *Natural and Spiritual Faculties*).
pages.16: Capiuaccius <insert>~~pro~~</insert> (in *Reading of Aphorisms* 50, and others from Galen) for whose cause of necessity and use, Galen rightfully, in *Method of Medicine*, Book 7, last chapter, brings forth these things about the liver: the work of the liver is most necessary to all parts, and in Book 11 of *Metaphysics*, chapter 16, he says it is most dangerous if the strength of the liver is dissolved, for this indeed is what provides nourishment to the heart and to all other parts: hence infants have more vigorous vegetative faculties, less vigorous sensitive ones, and still less intellectual ones, inasmuch as they obtain such utility from the liver: wherefore Franciscus Vlmus Baiensis, in his *Treatise on Urines*, a Physician not to be scorned, collecting the office and necessity of the liver, did not doubt to call this member the most noble. Therefore, having considered its substance, having considered its function, use, and duty, what was more fitting to be generated in the very first formation of the fetus than the liver itself? For the natural faculty (which I do not doubt to also call the natural spirit) permeates through all members, not only through the arteries themselves and the veins, but also through flesh, nerves, ligaments, bones, and all other things that constitute our body, whence it happens that also in diseases of all parts, we can have both continuous and certain signs, and can have an opinion about the disposition of the whole, simultaneously from this natural faculty, from the liver, the tinder and seat of this and the natural spirit: wherefore shall we not also grant it to be the foundation of the <term>microcosm</term> <gloss>the world in miniature</gloss>, and the first principle in the microcosm? From the liver, or from the natural faculty arising from the liver, we not only have the manifest diseases of this principle, but we can also have the internal causes of the diseases of other principal members represented. Let the brain labor, let the heart itself labor, some <term>pathognomonic</term> <gloss>characteristic of a specific disease</gloss> signs offer themselves (which I neither deny nor is it right to deny) by which you might be able to gather that these parts are laboring; however, unless the liver, through the subservient stomach, concocts the nourishment provided to it and carries it to the heart and to the brain, what help will you provide; if you concede to them that you can assist the laboring parts by topical [remedies] (which to deny is to deny reason and experience itself, as you will see when I demonstrate a single example of a person lacking a liver), why would you not grant it the principle at least of the vegetative soul, and that it is generated more fittingly first in the formation of the fetus?
pages.17: Many similar and better things could be elicited in the medical field for the dignity of such a principle; however, it must be conceded to the Reader, so that he may refresh his spirit, what I, too, writing, am permitted to do; and therefore, having set aside medical study, let us descend into the field of recreation, to the sacred, mysterious fables of antiquity, for from these, perhaps, our opinion will also be corroborated. Those who left behind a written genealogy of the gods fabulate thus about Venus and Mars. Venus was seen by Phoebus in adultery with Mars; the adultery of the spouse was revealed to Vulcan by the same inspector. A Council was convened among the gods concerning this matter of such great business (having first caught both adulterers in iron nets): Neptune, Mercury, and Apollo took part in the Council; it was decreed that they have the gods as liberators; Apollo interceded, Mercury interceded, but in vain Neptune interceded. The divinities were liberated. If it pleases us to look accurately into these fables and veils of fictions, we shall easily understand that the heat of fire, that Vulcan, is very agreeable to the mystery, and that Venus is placed in marriage to our mortality; he is procreated from Jove out of Juno, that is, from Heaven, acting with motion and light (for such is our native heat, spherical and conformable to the element of the stars, as is judged by the most learned) from the Air, and is precipitated into the surrounding Island of the Sea, indeed into the earth, into Venus, namely, of our mortality, encompassed by Water (through generation), into marriage, where at first it is nourished from apes, which it is sufficiently established are of the most prone nature to imitate the actions of rational beings and to feign. Let us move on to the confirmation, where 5 types of passages occur: first, concerning the justice which is by faith and the justice which is by works; concerning grace; concerning predestination; concerning the certainty of promises and that they are universal; concerning the love of God; concerning the origin of sin and whence its knowledge is derived; concerning the use of the law; concerning divine election; and concerning the morals and nature of the reborn. There follows the declaration of the argument in chapter 9, where notable passages occur: first, concerning the prerogative of the ancient people, to which he soon adds a passage concerning the calling of the gentiles, as well as the rejection of the Jews, the right of divine election, and predestination and its powers. Afterwards, in chapter 10, the passage is treated more copiously regarding the rejection

of Israel, and concerning the grace of God, which is the true cause of election and justification. In the <term>Parænesis</term> <gloss>exhortation</gloss>, there are very many passages, and they are conveniently distinguished into three orders. For there are ethical passages, such as the Gospel properly considers, concerning concord, consensus in the articles of faith, fraternal love, the diversity of gifts and their legitimate use, and even the love of enemies. Then there are political passages, where the law of magistrates is treated, concerning the condition of subjects, the ownership of property, public burdens, taxes, census, and similar things, and the honoring of leaders. Added to these in chapter 14 are new ones that pertain to ethical matters, such as tolerating the infirm. There follow then the <term>Adiaphora</term> <gloss>matters indifferent</gloss>, such as what should be thought concerning

food, drink, feast days, and similar topics. In chapter 15, regarding the arrogance of the faithful, by which they are accustomed to despise those who are weaker, which passage again pertains to the ethical. Afterward follows the Epilogue, which contains elegant passages, such as a passage of civility, excusing the boldness and length of the writing. Then a passage worth knowing, concerning the propagation of the Gospel doctrine during the times of the Apostle. Also a passage concerning his travels. Also concerning the contribution of the faithful for the needs of the poor. Also a passage concerning the intercession of the saints, but the way in which the living intercede for the living. Furthermore, there is an elegant passage concerning the customary manner of greeting among the pious. Also, regarding recommending pious brothers to the absent, and thus the Epistle is concluded.

*Who the Corinthians were.*

Corinth was named after Corinthus, the son of Marathon, who was either the founder or the one who made the city famous. It was once the most famous and flourishing of the cities of Greece, for which reason Cicero did not hesitate to call it the light of all Greece. He also describes its location most elegantly in his speech against Rullus, with these words: "Hardly a trace of Corinth remains." For it was situated in the straits and jaws of Greece, in such a way that it held the bolts of the land, and two seas that were greatly <margin>In the speech for the Manilian Law.</margin> different for navigation were almost joined, while being separated by a very thin boundary, etc.

With these words he indicates that the Aegean Sea washed it from the east, where those sailing from Asia were received in the port of Cenchreae. The Ionian Sea, however, was from the west, where those arriving were received at the port of Lechaeum. Hence it is also what Horace sang:

<margin>Horace.</margin>
> "Others will praise famous Rhodes or Mytilene,
> Or Ephesus, or the walls of two-harbored Corinth—"

This convenience of location, and wealth, and a singular corruption of morals had brought people to this city. For from all of Asia and Europe, merchants flowed there as if to a common market. And there was a most famous temple of Venus there, in which women practiced prostitution for money with their bodies,

whence those noble courtesans, whom Athenaeus and pagan authors everywhere commemorate, were almost all Corinthians. And there still exist proverbs among authors by which their morals are taxed, such as "to behave like a Corinthian" and "not everyone is allowed to go to Corinth." From this corruption of morals, it undoubtedly followed that by the just judgment of God it was later destroyed, which we read in histories was first done by the Romans under Lucius Mummius before the Numantine War. The occasion for overthrowing that city was that they had defiled the envoys of the Roman people with excrement. Later, however, it was restored by Caesar and made noble again, by studies of the humanities, wealth, and corruption of morals. Whoever desires more, let him see Strabo in book 8, Livy in book 5 of the fifth decade,

And their madness, according to Paul, will become evident to all, and the fruit of the pious efforts of your Serene King will break forth at last, even against the will of the Devils, for he who seeks the peace of the Churches through you, if controversies are first rightly judged. Thinking about this, there often came to my mind that most beautiful saying of Nazianzen, who, having delivered an Oration in praise of Cyprian, said: "Divine wisdom knows how to lay the foundations of great things long before, and to procure contrary outcomes through contrary means, so that it may excite a greater admiration of itself among mortals." <note>original: "οἶδε πόῤῥωθεν καταβάλλεσθαι τῶν μεγάλων πραγμάτων ἡ θεῖα σοφία τὰς ὑποθέσεις καὶ διὰ τῶν ἐναντίων τὰ ἐναντִια οἰκονομεῖσθαι ἵνα καὶ μᾶλλον θαυμάζεται."</note>
pages.19: But to return to where I digressed: I truly rejoice with my whole heart that God has kept you safe and sound until this day on which you wrote to us from England. And I vehemently congratulate you on so many and such great testimonies of divine presence, which have been shown to you divinely throughout your entire embassy. And I pray together with you to our Son of GOD, Immanuel, the head and most faithful guardian of His Church, that He may bless your most holy labors more and more each day, and keep you safe for a very long time. And likewise that He may strengthen your Serene KING, a second Josiah. Regarding his constancy and fortitude in defending and professing the true religion, the letters of most trustworthy men clearly testify to us, even after your departure from Germany, against the fabrications of the most vain rumors which, while you were still present in Germany, had been spread by wicked and
pages.20:
corrupt men, in the courts of many princes, to hinder the success of your embassy. You said that some of these you knew, and that you had perceived and explored the vanity of these rumors, and that you said others wished to believe the fables—even though they wished to please others—which facts and time (which is the daughter of truth) were to refute. Thus far indeed excellently, with GOD confirming the spirit of the Royal Serenity, the piety of such a king has dispersed and scattered all the mists of lies with its own brightness and light.

But as I have the firmest persuasion that He who began His good work in you and in your Serene King will also perfect it until the day of JESUS CHRIST: so, to approve and celebrate that heroic and most holy voice of yours—by which you said to me at the time when various tempests and dangers were seen to hang over you from every side, that in a good cause, the conscience of a right will ought to be despised by Christians no less than the Devil himself, through the trust of Divine protection—I think I can present no more fitting an epilogue to this than to append that most noble Psalm of Martin Luther, which, as it is most sung in the German Churches, so it has an admirable <term>energeia</term> <gloss>efficacy/power</gloss> for stirring the soul, which I remember also moved you sweetly when I once recited a part of it to you, rendered in Stigelian rhythms in this way:

If this world were teeming with demons,
Like worms in the earth,
We would not fear anxiously,
We shall conquer in the end, strenuously.
Let the prince of this world be proud,
Let him gnash his teeth and rage,
The deceiver knows not how to harm,
Since he is broken by even a little word.
pages.21: But neither did it displease Sleidan to insert that entire song into his history of our times, expressed in these words: "GOD is a firm fortress and bulwark for us. That old enemy of the human race now acts with all his might, and employs all kinds of engines. Our power is indeed small, and we cannot sustain such an onslaught for long. But for our sake, that hero whom GOD himself chose for Himself has taken up arms and fights. If you ask who that is, know that it is CHRIST JESUS, in whose hands it must be that victory and triumph lie. Because even if this whole fabric of the world were overflowing with devils, yet we do not fear, and with most certain trust we await a happy outcome. For however much Satan may rage and prowl, he will accomplish nothing against us. For he has been judged, and all his armor falls with a single word. They will not take this Word from us, our adversaries; but however unwilling, they will leave it. For GOD dwells in our camp and in our battle line, who protects us and our gifts with His spirit. If they take away life, if goods, if children and wife, bear it patiently. For nothing is added to them thereby, but an immortal kingdom is prepared for us."
pages.22: I had written this letter privately to you, illustrious and noble Lord SEGUR, and I had written it in such a way that I seemed to be dealing with you as if in a present conversation, with a mind rejoicing at the auspicious news of your safe return to England. Nevertheless, I could not resist my friends, who wished for this to be printed as a testimony, not only of my own but of many good men’s true and undissembled judgment of your virtues, and of praise <note>original: "καὶ εὐφημίας"</note>, and to be prefixed to a book which Lord Brocardus had put to the press at this same time. In it, so that he might satisfy your commands, he strove to illustrate that mystical song of Solomon with his own interpretation. As I trust that its reading will be neither useless nor unpleasant to pious and learned men who will wish to judge the essence of the matter candidly, so I ask and pray with the reverence I owe that you do not let this letter, as a witness of my observance and love toward you, be burdensome or troublesome to you, and that you embrace me constantly with your accustomed benevolence.

and loving,

### CAP. XIX.
->*Repetition of the Differences of Plants.*<-

The differences of the entire substance are clearly evident: some are cultivated, others wild; some fruit-bearing, others barren; some evergreen and others deciduous, as has been said; some entirely leafless; some flowering, others flowerless; some early-sprouting and early-fruiting, others late-sprouting and late-fruiting; and likewise those things similar to these. <gloss>i</gloss> Such are the differences in the parts; but that one is most peculiar, and in a certain way the greatest distinction, just as it is in
