# NOTES

## ON THE FIRST BOOK.

### *Constituent parts of Plants.*

#### CAP. I.

*Perhaps not in the same way.* Utmost brevity, as **Dr. Moldenhawer** rightly observed, in the comparison of Animals with Plants at the end of this chapter; concerning which Aristotle, Hist. Anim. v. 3, should be consulted.

*So there is nothing strange.* See on this matter Lib. de Caus. Plant. ii. 20, 22, 23. v. 2.

*By an equal distance*, sc. interval. Equidistant.

#### CAP. II.

*And they are first and greatest.* Thus Aristotle, Hist. Anim.: as many parts as, being whole, have other parts of their own within them; for example, the head, etc.

*More durable in the roots.* Those whose root perennates. Bot.

*Regarding the one*, sc. being. To be provided with a simple trunk. See Pliny, Nat. Hist. xiv. 1. 30.

*Homoeomerous. Anhomoeomerous.* Consult Aristotle on this matter, De Gen. Anim. i. 1, and the Lexicon of Theophrastus.

*Any part from the same things.* Individual parts [composed] from the same vessels, fibers, membranes, etc.

*The greatest parts are almost these.* End of chapter ii in Bodaeus.

*Others from which these are*; the Author proceeds to the homoeomerous.

#### CAP. III.

*Menestor.* An author on herbal matters, whose works are not extant.

*Namelessly*, simply the moisture.

*Innate moisture and heat.* Moldenhawer deals very copiously with the warm principle of life in *Tent.* p. 83. He calls it generative heat.
pages.139:
de Caus. Plant. i. 4. Confer also Galen. Called by Aristotle *natural heat*. ii. 3.

*But other different kinds*. Distinct, that is, from *moisture and heat*. Beginning of chapter iv, Bod.

*Fiber—veins*. The Author's remarkable sagacity in describing these most tenuous vessels, which, however, in our century have been brought to their *acme* <gloss>peak/perfection</gloss>. Mold. *Tent.* p. 91 deals very copiously with this matter.

*Wood, flesh*. See Mold. p. 108.

*Marrow* is compared to *marrow in bones*. But briefly, however, and narrowly, as he is accustomed to, the Author describes the *marrow* <gloss>pith</gloss> of vegetables; clearly, however, if you weigh the force of the words. Mention is made elsewhere, i. 9. iv. 2. De Caus. Plant. v. 6, 7, 24.

### CAP. IV.

*In which it is possible*. In those which admit of division.

*Beside the cultivation*. By means of cultivation, etc. A frequent usage in Theophrastus.

*Olive cuttings*. The word *kopades* is interpreted as coppice wood, but here perhaps of a decapitated tree.

### CAP. VI.

*One must always take all*— An obscure reading, if it is sound: the meaning is, *one must always take the differences of all [things] by places* with respect to climate, etc.

*Different according to the different genus of moistures*, i.e., aquatic plants differ among themselves with respect to *places*.

*Smaller—larger*. The former are Sea-wracks and Sea-lettuce; the latter are called elsewhere *small trees*; Gorgonians, Corallines. See iv. 8.

### CAP. VII.

*Thickness*. Here it indicates the thickness or mass of the trunk. It is opposed to *thinness*, slenderness.

*From which is the composition*. With respect to the component parts. It is opposed to *those according to conditions and powers*.

### CAP. VIII.

*Marrows*. See chapter iii, p. 9, l. 6. N.B. Chapter IX in Bodaeus.

*Some do not have—and the Elder*. There is no pith in the younger branches of the Elder tree.
pages.140:
*All marrows are black.* The significance of the word *black* escaped Scaliger. See Bod. p. 24 and the Lexicon of Theophrastus.

*In general some do not have.* The discussion is about Fungi: see the Systematic Catalogue, which have no affinity with other plants. See Bod. p. 27.

*They differ also in roots.* See on this matter Plin. xvi. 31.

*Fringed.* Fimbriated, Pliny, but there is another sense of the word *thysanoi*, ribbons, tufts of fibers. Poll. See the Lexicon of Theophrastus.

### C A P. IX.

*Those above ground*, sc. *parts*.

*For the root*, i.e., the root in general.

### C A P. X.

*Crowning the altars.* Perhaps one should read *gathering heaps*.

*They bear fruit.* Add *below*: under the earth, concerning tubers. See the illustration of *Arachidnas*, Bod. p. 35.

*The fruit*, sc. the tuber from the root.

*Earlier than those above*, sc. *parts*.

*These contribute greatly.* It is to be noted that the word *nature* should be taken in the plural.

*Of all [plants] the juices are likewise.* Beginning of the chapter in Bodaeus.

*For from the shoots.* An amazing description of the habit of the Indian Fig, L. Engl. "The Banyan Tree."

*If the material is deep.* The meaning is, if some material intervenes between the seed and the earth, *it divides the root toward the earth*, it bends the root toward the earth until it reaches it.

### C A P. XI.

*In which are both*, sc. *genders*. Although sexual distinction occurs in the Palm, commonly the words *male*, *female* are attributed to the varieties of the species, as they are observed to be more robust and fruitless, or the contrary.

*Most peculiar are those of the Apple tree.* These words included in parentheses **crept in from the margin**, as I suspect, and interrupt the description of the habit of the *Fir*. Although it is hardly possible to conjecture what the Author means with respect to the *faces of wild beasts*, Pliny interprets the place thus in Nat. Hist. l. xvi. c. 30: "The Apple tree has a peculiar kind
pages.141:
"of branches; for they show the snouts of wild beasts, with smaller ones adhering to one "very large one."

*Of knots, some are blind.* Observe that the word *ozos* occurs in a double sense, as a branch, and a knot in the trunk.

*Because nothing is placed in between.* Because there are no intervals. Scal.

*Peculiar hollows.* See the word *nail* in the Lexicon of Theophrastus. Species of Hypoxylon, as I suspect. See iv. 16.

*There is then.* A chapter to be added to the previous one as it is a continuation.

*Growing in length.* The discussion is about the trunk, which is either tall and not branching, or which *is split straight*. I also suspect that what follows, *those things similar to these*, should be read as follows: *and the root similarly to these*. Thus Virgil: "As much as it extends its top to the ethereal breezes, "so much does it extend its root to Tartarus."

*Becomes thin*, sc. *by cultivation*.

### CAP. XII.

*And further, some are evergreen.* Here begins chapter xv in Bodaeus.

*To partake of the winter.* To last until the middle of winter.

### CAP. XIII.

*Like the hand.* Pliny in passage xvi. 24 says, *veins on the flat sides*, "incisions underneath," that is, hollow lines, as in the palm of the hand.

*Which part toward the twig*, i.e., from the conversion of the leaves, it is doubtful which side is upper, which lower; *for the hollowness* with respect to position is different from the nature of the leaf.

*Not to be altered in the same way.* It is opposed to conversions *by means of veins or fibers*, i.e., not in a constant, regular way.

*Going through the depth* to be interpreted concerning the thickness of the leaf.

*Saw-toothed.* Perhaps *comb-like* or *slaughter-like*. See the Preface to the Illustration of Theophrastus, p. v. Also the description of the *Fir*, l. iii.

*Of the Oak from the trunk.* Pliny observes the same thing about the leaves of the Oak, Nat. Hist. xvi. 24. Bodaeus says he has never observed it. I suspect an error in the text: perhaps it should read *Cyprian*. See concerning the *Cyprian Fig* iv. c. 2.
pages.142:
*The whole stem is leafless.* He accurately describes the scape of the Botanists.

*By itself.* From itself: concerning a sessile leaf. Bot.

*Encompassing between*. Fruit in the middle of the leaf.

### CAP. XIV.

*For those [parts] not annual.* Persistent parts of a plant, such as the trunk, branches, etc. *For nothing [is] without this [moisture].*

*Of the flowers, some from the bark.* An amazing thing, what Theophrastus means. Flowers from the bark and nerves. Surely an error of the text, and one should read for *of the flowers*, *of the others* (sc. stems). Concerning Flowers, see c. 21, 22.

### CAP. XV.

*The seed immediately after the containing part.* Seed with a simple covering. In this chapter six kinds of seeds are noted, the enumeration of which is confused and very long. These are: 1. simple seeds with a covering; Palms. 2. from a nut and flesh—Drupes. 3. in a pod—siliquose. 4. in some membrane, membranous follicle, such as the Pear, Apple. 5. angiosperms <gloss>vessel-seeded</gloss>, with a loose, rigid pericarp; Poppy. 6. gymnosperms <gloss>naked-seeded</gloss>, without a covering; umbelliferous plants.

*Such as the berry.* Here the text of the passage is very corrupt. The distinction of Theophrastus of many grains contained in some common [vessel], such as a berry or grape-stone: and likewise in the seed. N.B. The nuts of the Pomegranate are opposed to the individual grains of Wheat, etc. *Least of all would those of Apples seem [to be].* Yet they should not be joined to the Apples, which are wrapped around by membranes in the inner part of the fruit.

*But similarly each of these.* See the error of the scribe in transcribing above, *since for each one taking [it]*.

### CAP. XVI.

*In those on juices.* Hist. de Caus. Plant. l. vi.

*Of Lettuce.* The juice is said to be watery, which is less correct. Perhaps an error of the text, as above for *milky* <gloss>should be placed</gloss> concerning the juice of the Fig and Poppy.

*Which is proper.* The meaning is that the peculiar juice of any plant *has some likeness* in itself before cooking and maturation happens in the fruit, which is effected by means of the pericarp.
pages.143:
*Some are sweet-smelling.* See more fully concerning odors in Theophrastus, *de Caus. Plant.* l. i. 6, as also concerning juices.

### CAP. XVII.

*Outside the sea.* The Red Sea is understood.

*Having a diagram.* The common Columbine is indicated by most Botanists under the name of *Iasione*; and the description, although intricate, marvelously fits the convolutions of the petals: also *it is not separated in the flower*.

N.B. Perhaps Bodaeus's conjecture will please some more, that the Bindweed, etc., is indicated here, in which sense *only a diagram of the majority* is to be interpreted concerning the amplitude of the flower.

*They appear perforated.* The Author's remarkable *precision*, when the flower is perforated, i.e., falls off without the stigma, the beginning fruit remains; when *it is burnt or soaked*, or affected by too much sun or rain, *it throws off the fruit*. See the observation below: *as many of the flowers as have, as it were, a spindle, are fertile*.

*On the mouths themselves.* The discussion is about syngenesious plants; therefore *mouth* is the common receptacle in this class.

*As if a spindle.* Concerning the stigma of the flower of the Citron tree.

*Immediately to show the fruit*, i.e., without a flower or petals.

### CAP. XVIII.

*The olynthus* <gloss>wild fig</gloss>. The Fig tree, etc., is counted by Linnaeus among the Trioecious plants. *The Oleaster*, from which [come] the *erina* (which perhaps are the *olynthoi*), the Male tree; *the Fig tree* the Monoecious tree.

### CAP. XIX.

*And such are*. A summary and recapitulation of this book.

*More species under each genus*. More species under one genus. A truly Linnaean distinction!

*Cultivated and wild*. Here the distinction is taken from sex: but what does it mean? That wild plants are distinguished by sex, but cultivated ones indeed by *more peculiar things*; does he indicate varieties of fruits?

This hope of a happy harvest should not at all be shaken for us by the fact that the seeds of peace and concord, scattered in this your embassy, seem to lie hidden for a while. For nature itself willed that there be one time for sowing and another for reaping.

Reflecting on this, there often comes to mind that most beautiful saying of Nazianzen, who, in the Oration delivered in praise of Cyprian, says: Divine wisdom knows how to lay the foundations of great matters long before, and to procure contrary outcomes through contrary means, so that it might excite greater admiration for itself among mortals <note>original: "οἶδε πόῤῥωθεν καταβάλλεσθαι τῶν μεγάλων πραγμάτων ἡ θεῖα σοφία τὰς ὑποθέσεις"</note>.
pages.19:
and through opposites to govern opposites, so that it may be even more admired.

But to return to where I digressed: Indeed, I rejoice with my whole heart that God has kept you safe and sound until the day you wrote to us from England. And I vehemently congratulate you on the many and great testimonies of divine presence, which have been shown to you divinely throughout your entire embassy. And I pray with you to the Son of GOD, our Immanuel, the head and most faithful guardian of His Church, that He may bless your most holy labors more each day, and keep you safe for a very long time. And likewise that He may strengthen your Most Serene KING, another Josiah. Regarding his constancy and fortitude in defending and professing the true religion, letters from most trustworthy men—even after your departure from Germany—testify to us clearly, contrary to the inventions of the vainest of rumors, which, while you were still present in Germany, had been spread by wicked and per<column-break/>verse men in the courts of many princes to impede the success of your embassy.
pages.20:
Some of whom you said you knew, and that you held the vanity of those rumors to be perceived and proven, and that you said you wanted to believe the tales—which events and time (which is the daughter of truth) were to refute—only to gratify others. As indeed, until now, with GOD confirming the spirit of the Royal Serenity, the piety of such a king has dispersed and scattered all the mists of lies with its own brightness and light.

But as I am most persuaded that He who began His good work in you and in your Most Serene King will also perfect it until the day of JESUS CHRIST, so, to approve and celebrate that heroic and most holy voice of yours—by which you told me at the time when various storms and dangers seemed to hang over you from all sides that in a good cause, the conscience of a right will ought to be despised by Christians no less than the Devil himself, through confidence in Divine protection—I believe I can append no more suitable epilogue to this than that most noble Psalm of Martin Luther, which, just as it is most frequently sung in the German Churches, so it has an admirable <term>energeia</term> <gloss>efficacy/activity</gloss> for stirring the soul, which I remember also affected you sweetly when I once recited a part of it to you, rendered in Stigel’s rhythms in this way:

> If this world were swarming 
> With demons like worms,
> We would not fear anxiously,
> We will win in the end stoutly.
> Let the prince of the world be proud,
> Let him gnash his teeth and rage,
> The scoundrel knows not how to harm,
> Since he is broken by even a little word.

But it did not weary Sleidan to insert that whole song into the history of our times, expressed in these words: GOD is a firm fortress and rampart for us. That ancient enemy of the human race now acts with all his might, and employs all kinds of engines. Our power indeed is small, nor can we withstand such an attack for long. But for our sake that hero whom GOD Himself has chosen for Himself has taken up arms and fights. If you ask who that may be, know that it is CHRIST JESUS, with whom the victory and triumph must rest. Because even if this whole fabric of the world were teeming with devils, we do not grow terrified, and with most certain confidence we await a joyful outcome. For however much Satan may rage and prowl, he will accomplish nothing against us. For he has been judged, and by a word alone all his armor falls. Our adversaries will not snatch this Word from us, but will leave it, however unwillingly. For GOD dwells in our camp and battle line, who protects us and our gifts with His spirit. If they take away life, if goods, if children and wife, you may bear it patiently. For nothing is added to them by that, but for us a kingdom is prepared that is immortal.

pages.23: I had written this letter privately to you, Illustrious and generous Lord SÉGUR, and indeed I wrote it as if I were speaking to you in a present conversation, my mind rejoicing at the auspicious news of your safe return to England. Nevertheless, I ought not to have resisted my friends, who wanted this, as a testimony of the true and not feigned judgment—not just of myself, but of many good men—regarding your virtues, and of praise, to be printed and prefixed to the book which Lord Brocardus had put to the press at this same time. In this book, so that he might satisfy your commands, he sought to illustrate that mystical Song of Solomon with his interpretation. Just as I am confident that its reading will be neither useless nor unpleasant to pious and learned men who will wish to judge the matter as a whole with an open mind, so I ask and pray with the reverence I owe you that you do not let this letter be a burden or a nuisance to you as a witness of my respect and love toward you, and that you continue to embrace me with your accustomed benevolence.
pages.24:
Fare well, Hero, most worthy of the perpetual praise and celebration of all good men. And continue to labor vigorously in the work of the Lord, as you do, to receive at some time the crown of justice, which the Lord, the just judge, will render on that day to you and to all who love His coming. At Bremen, in the beginning of the Year of Christ 1585. Which I pray to GOD, with the innermost groans of my soul, may be wholesome for the whole Church and the Republic, and happy and holy for us all.

To Your Illustrious 
Generosity.

Sincerely honoring 
and loving you,

Christophorus Pezelius, Doctor.

## *Most illustrious Baron, Jacques Ségur*
## *Pardailhan, Prefect of the King*

In the year 1579, and frequently thereafter, you urged me to write something on the Song of Solomon. I, however, who both owe it to you and desire in all things—insofar as I am able and capable—to obey you, always refused for two primary reasons which I brought to you. First, because the exposition of that Song seemed to me at the time to be only for those who existed during a time of peace achieved among the entire Christian people: when the Church had attained her bridegroom, so that she might speak of herself and her own things properly, and those who were rapt in it, above others, in the love of CHRIST. Second, in other books, however I may have exposed them, I seemed to be impelled to write, and an argument was given to my mind, certain and without my own great meditation and deliberation. But because the same did not happen with this Song, such that suddenly to me

pages.46: is the connection of power and object. Generation in creatures is a form with which an agent produces known forms. Corruption is a form with which a corrupting agent deprives ancient forms. Privation exists in the middle of these. Theology is a science that speaks of God. Philosophy is a science through which the intellect contracts itself to all sciences. Geometry is an art invented to measure lines, angles, and figures. Astronomy is an art with which the astronomer recognizes the virtues and motions that the heaven has effectively in inferior things. Arithmetic is an art invented to count many units. Music is an art invented to order many concordant voices in one song. Rhetoric is an art invented with which the rhetorician adorns and colors his words. Logic is an art with which the logician finds the natural conjunction between subject and predicate. Grammar is an art of finding the method of speaking correctly and writing correctly. Morality is a habit for acting well or badly. Politics is an art with which the citizens provide for the public utility of the city. Justice is an act regulated in man by a habituated justice. Medicine is a habit with which the physician provides for the health of the patient. Regime is a form with which a prince rules his people. Militia is a habit with which the soldier helps the prince so that he may be able to maintain justice. Commerce is the ha
pages.47:
bit with which the merchant knows how to buy and sell.
Navigation is an art with which sailors know how to navigate through the sea. Conscience is a form with which the intellect afflicts the soul regarding things committed. Preaching is a form with which the preacher informs the people to have good morals by avoiding bad ones.
Prayer is a form with which the one praying speaks to God sanctifyingly. Memory is an entity with which entities are recollectable.

¶ Regarding the second part which is about questions.
This part is divided into twelve parts or places arranged and proportioned to questions according to the diversity of the matter from which they are, for in one place or part is signified the solution of one question and in another place the solution of another question, on account of which we will apply the questions to the aforesaid places in various ways and this in two ways. Namely, we will make some questions which we will solve and others which we will not solve; similarly, we will do likewise and leave those for the artist who is well-perceiving so that he himself may well abstract the solution from that part or place to which we transmit the questions, for in that part or place the solution is signified. Here, indeed, we will make and solve a few questions for the sake of brevity, for this art is abstracted from the great art so that it may treat things more briefly and so that the intellect may apprehend many things under few words, and thus in
pages.48:
the intellect is more universal, and through the solutions of these questions placed or given here, the solution of other questions can be given in its own way. The places or parts to which we will transmit the questions are twelve, as has already been said above, namely: the first figure, the second figure, the third figure, the fourth figure, definitions, rules, table, evacuation of the third figure, multiplication, mixing of the fourth figure's principles and rules with the hundred forms underneath. And first, we will speak of the first part or place.

### Regarding the questions of the first figure.

Question: Whether there is any entity in which the subject and predicate are converted in identity of essence, nature, and number through the whole first figure. And it must be answered that yes, for otherwise the conversion of subject and predicate and the quality of essence would be destroyed absolutely, and eternity would be superior through infinity, and its goodness, greatness, power, etc., would be inferior through finiteness, which is impossible. It is asked: what is that entity in which the subject and predicate are converted? And it must be answered that God is that entity; indeed, such a conversion cannot be except in an infinite and eternal subject. It is asked: whether the divine goodness has in itself as great a bonification as the divine intellect has intellection? It is asked: why God has in himself as great an agency as existence? It is asked: God, of what is He as much as He is Himself
pages.49:
It is asked: why man and animal are not converted? And to this it must be answered from the fact that conversion cannot happen between greater and lesser but between equals. It is asked: whether in an angel its power, intellect, and will are converted? And it must be answered that no, otherwise he could have as infinite and eternal an act as God.

<note>A paragraph mark denotes the beginning of the next section.</note> Regarding the questions of the second figure.

Questions of the second figure can be made in three ways, just as man and lion, which are distinguished by difference in species and agree by concordance in genus and are contrariated by contrariety, namely through corruptible and incorruptible, and so on for others in their own way. It is asked: whether difference is more general than concordance and contrariety? To which it must be said that yes, because wherever there is concordance and contrariety, there is difference, but not vice versa in all; for in many things there is found difference and concordance, and yet in them there is not contrariety naturally, as in spiritual entities. It is asked: which is the greater principle, concordance or contrariety? It must be said that concordance, for positive principles descend from concordance, but privative ones from contrariety. It is asked: whether this definition is more offensive by saying thus: "man is a rational animal that bonifies," or "man is an entity to which it properly belongs to be man," than this: "man is a mortal rational animal"? And it must be answered that yes, the reason
pages.50: for this is because being man belongs only to man; rationality and mortality, however, belong to many. Through the triangle of principle, middle, and end, questions can be made in three ways. The first way is when it is asked why there is one first cause and not more. To which it must be answered from the fact that one end is infinite. The second way is when it is asked whether the middle existing between subject and predicate has continuous or discrete quantity. And it must be answered that it has continuous quantity with respect to the middle of the extremities, but discrete with respect to the middle of conjunction and measurement. The third way is when it is asked what kind of end is the ultimate in a subject, and it must be answered that it is the proper end, but not the appropriated one. Through the triangle of majority, equality, and minority, questions can be made in three ways through majority, such as when it is asked why God is above the angel and the angel above man. And it must be answered that God is above the angel because divine goodness and divine greatness, etc., differ by infinity from quantity and by eternity from time; the goodness, however, of an angel and its greatness, etc., are not, but they themselves are above the goodness and greatness of man, etc., because the place in which they are differs from division and reception, but the goodness, greatness, etc., of the body of man do not. The second way is when it is asked in the soul why intellect, will, and memory are equal by essence, to which it must be answered
pages.51:
from the fact that by the first cause, by the equality of His goodness, greatness, etc., He is intelligible, recollectable, and lovable equally, and in this step the intellect recognizes that a demonstration can be made in three ways: by "that," or by "why," or by equality or by equivalence. The third way is when it is asked why sin is more around nothingness than any other entity; and it must be said that it is because of this, because it is more repugnant to the end of existing. It is asked whether the difference that is between sensual and sensual is greater than that which is between sensual and intellectual, and than that which is between intellectual and intellectual. Furthermore, whether that difference which is between principle and middle is greater than that which is between middle and end. Similarly, one can ask about the difference which is between substance and substance, etc. And it must be answered through those things which are signified in the aforementioned triangles subjectively and objectively by means of the rule of B.

### Regarding the questions of the third figure.

It is said in the third figure that every principle is applied to another, and therefore it is asked: whether contrariety is only applicable to goodness, greatness, etc., as much as concordance? And it must be said that no; for contrariety is applied to them by depriving and contrariating; concordance, however, by positing and concordating. It is said in the third figure: "goodness is great," and "what is a good great goodness?" And it must be answered
pages.52:
that a great goodness is that which, without contrariety and minority, agrees with all principles and their correlatives. It is asked: "goodness, where is it?" Go to chamber B.I. and receive the significations. It is asked: "goodness, of what is it?" It is asked: "goodness, how is it?" Go to chambers B.D. and B.K. and receive their significations, and so on for others. Likewise, it is asked when the intellect is universal and particular.

¶ Regarding the questions of the fourth figure.

It is asked through chamber B.C.D. whether any goodness is great infinitely like eternity? And it must be answered that yes, otherwise the whole greatness of eternity would not be good through chamber B.E.F. It is asked whether God is as powerful through His goodness as through His intellect? Go to that chamber and receive the significations of His correlatives and His definitions. It is asked whether an angel produces an angel since it is superior, just as man produces man since it is inferior? It must be answered that no, because he would evacuate his own essence; for an angel does not receive increase from outside, but man does, by reason of his body.

¶ Regarding the questions through the definitions of the principles.

It is asked whether God is a necessary entity. It is asked whether unity can be infinite without an infinite act. It is asked whether God is one singular. It is asked whether God could be evil. Go to the definition of goodness, greatness, and eternity, and hold those things which are signified to you, for if goodness is
pages.53:
great and eternal, then it is necessary that goodness be the reason of the good that produces a great and eternal good; and so on for other questions which can be made through the definitions of the principles.

¶ Regarding the questions through the rules.

It is asked whether believing precedes understanding. It is asked which definition is better and clearer, that which is given by power and its specific act, or that which is given by genus and difference? And it must be answered that that which is given by power and its specific act, for by that, the cognition of the subject and its specific act is indeed had, whereas by the other, not at all, except partially. It is asked whether power has an act outside its own essence. It is asked whether the intellect is an agent in memory and a patient in the will. Whether the intellect can have an object without sense. Whether the divine power can have an infinite act. Whether an act can be without difference. Whether an act is possessed by the power or by the object or by both. Whether substance can exist by itself without its causes. Whether the will has power in the intellect through believing and the intellect in the will through understanding. Whether in the soul the will and memory are equal. Whether the intellect without its correlatives can be universal or particular. Whether the intellect, when it makes science, makes it through property and difference.

the orator, King Sapor of the Persians, who, regarding the melancholic and dark sins of the humors in the microcosm, proposed for the eternal memory of mortals the Syrup of Apples <note>original: "Syrupum de pomis"</note>, <note>a digestive/cordial syrup used to treat imbalances</note> (corrupted by some as King Sabor’s syrup) to be cast down. I pass over Archelaus, Hiero, and Philometor, kings who wrote in Greek about plants. I pass over that antidote of the most invincible King Mithridates, praised by all by common consent to this day, which was found by Pompey in his shrines. In our own centuries, it is read in the monuments of history that Nicholas and Eusebius V, supreme pontiffs, were physicians by art and profession. Since it is so beautiful, it is hardly surprising if it is also difficult, and therefore, in the medical republic, there seem to be so many and such varied opinions that, regarding this, the saying of Horace from Book 2 of his Satires is recited by some:

> There are as many kinds of studies as there are heads.
> A thousand species of men, and a variegated use of things.
> To each his own will, and one does not live by a single vow.

Yet it must not be believed that this most noble science suffers any shipwreck thereby (for while opinions in theory are indeed varied due to the nature of its beauty and difficulty, in practice the judgment of all is the same, the calculation the same). Rather, it is directed and more firmly established for protecting and preserving the human republic and for repairing and defeating diseases, which is accompanied by the good. Hence, captivated by the same beauty, which is both difficult and beautiful, when I had proposed certain Theses for the Medical College at Prague in the year 1652 to be defended—and had published them to the public in print, as is customary—not a few friends who considered them difficult and beautiful for practice began to exhort me to add reasons to them.
pages.11:
to corroborate them for the good of mortals. I, who struggle with difficulty in such an arena against so many critics, declined the advice. Yet, having found a timely opportunity (since I had seen even the most learned men doubting something in practice), I decided to follow the advice and I set them down in the same order in which I defended them at Prague. If anyone, feeling nauseated, rejects this labor of mine, let him know that I did not write for him. If he has better things, let him offer them, and he need not fear that I shall return the greatest thanks; it was never my intention, other than to have exercised myself on a subject that is difficult, most beautiful, and necessary for the common good of mortals. For if Emperors, Caesars, Kings, and Pontiffs have exercised themselves regarding the same, due to its beauty and the attendant good, why should it not be permitted for a physician, and let others enjoy it as they please.

# PREFACE TO THE CONCLUSIONS,
### which is
# THE FIRST CONCLUSION.

<note>Large ornamental drop-cap initial 'O' decorated with floral and foliate patterns.</note>
All men naturally desire to know. Some indeed desire to know their own origin, others crave to be skilled in science, and others have a mind to learn something else. I, in order to satisfy this natural tendency in some way, bring forward a few things from the vast field of medical faculty. Firstly, as to what is formed in the very first formation of man, or one might say the fetus: whether it is the heart, the fountain of human life; or the liver, the workshop of blood; or the brain, the most divine member, as called by Plato in the *Timaeus*. I assert that the liver is formed first, then the heart, and finally the brain.

There are many things, I admit, to be discussed in this conclusion: namely, how this is dilated in the injected seed, how it adheres, lives, and the like, which would pertain to the present matter; furthermore, whether it lives in potency or in act; whether a natural spirit is given, or whether it proceeds from the liver. However, setting these aside, I descend to my main intent (supposing from Aristotle, Book 1 of *Parts of Animals*, Chapter 1, that seed is generation, and generation is the first participation with the heat of the nutritive soul; from *On Youth and Old Age*, Chapter 14; likewise, Book 1 of *On the Generation of Animals*, Chapter 18, if the parts are dis-
pages.13:
tracted in the seed, how does it live? Likewise, Book 2 of *On the Generation of Animals*, Chapter 3, the seed and the conception live no less than plants, nor is Galen contrary). See: what is that first member, from the stated principles, which is generated first and most conveniently, and lives with a vegetative life? To make this conclusion of ours firmer, we shall draw authorities from Hippocrates and others. Afterward, if anything must be brought to the contrary, I shall resolve it.

Hippocrates, therefore, in his book *On the Formation of the Fetus*, and his faithful interpreter Galen, recount a certain case here (by which he intends to prove that the liver is generated first; I, however, shall bring forward both its structure and its purpose, so that everything may be more corroborated), which is as follows:

"But I saw the seed, which had remained in the place for six days and had subsequently fallen out, and from those things which then appeared to me in it, I conjecture the rest. How I saw the seed on the sixth day after, I shall tell. A certain maid of a woman (she was a notable singer who visited men, whom it did not befit to conceive in her womb, lest she be rendered contemptible; but that singer had heard what women are accustomed to say among themselves: when a woman is about to conceive, the man's seed no longer exits from the womb, but is contained within). When she had heard this, she observed it always, and by chance, when she felt that the seed had not exited, she revealed it to her mistress. When this reached our ears, we ordered her to jump onto the ground (another text reads, 'onto her buttocks,' and it is better). She did this about seven times, and the seed, not without a certain noise, was shaken out and flowed onto the ground. When the woman saw it, she inspected it and was amazed. What it was like, I shall say: just as if one were to tear the outer shell of a raw egg, so that through the inner membrane the inner humidity would shine through, such in a certain way it plainly was. There was a red and round thing inside; in the membrane, however, certain white and thick fibers were discerned, wrapped in a thick and red matter, and externally around the membrane were bloody bruises. In the middle, something thin was gaping, which seemed to me to be the navel, by which the fetus first breathed with the spirit going both out and in. From it, the membrane which contained the seed was entirely produced." This is the series of the history of Hippocrates, according to the interpretation of Galen and Bernardo Feliciano. Which, and the same Galen, and from Galen, Feliciano,
pages.14:
explain in their entirety, and indicate what all things signify. Truly, omitting other things, in Chapter 3, around the middle, they interpret that red thing thus, saying: "It is to be believed that that red, round thing which appears in the chorion in the six-day seed of Hippocrates was the liver, still indistinct and unformed." And shortly after, they add: "Before, however" (thus Galen/Feliciano from him), "when I was writing commentaries on the seed, and was forced to say something about the order of formation of the individual members, I said the heart, just as the liver, in the first days of the fetus, was as if a certain foundation, driven to this by the use of the same, most necessary in adults and perfect ones to be brought forward. But when I subsequently learned that it was the opinion of all others, both physicians and philosophers" (behold the sincerity of Galen admitting his own error, behold the foundations upon which he relied to change his opinion), "that the fetus is dispensed merely as a plant until express formation, it seemed more probable to me if we were to sustain that there is no necessity for the heart in the beginning, but that it is formed after the liver." And toward the end of the chapter, he adds: "But truly, just as it must be believed that the heart was made after the liver, and therefore the liver was constituted nearer to the womb of the pregnant woman (which anatomy itself demonstrates is very true), so it was fitting that the brain also be constituted further from the heart, since it is fashioned later." He gives the reason why the brain also is fashioned last, saying: "It is to be thought that this is done because the fetus has no need for a brain: for it does not need to see, nor hear, nor taste, nor smell anything, nor does it work with its hands or feet, nor use any other voluntary function at all. In a similar way, there was no necessity for the sense of touch, no imagination, no thought, no memory; therefore, in the third order of time, the brain was fashioned." (He speaks beautifully about the necessity of the final formation of the brain; if he had provided the same for the heart, it would be less burdensome for us, but we shall demonstrate it to the best of our ability.) These are the accounts of both Hippocrates and Galen; to me, however, let it be permitted to add this History of a Case which I saw to confirm it.

---

->A certain Marchioness of Tochau in Bohemia, January 14, 1653, after the tenth day of conception, suffered a mis-
pages.15:
carriage. Desiring to see it, or better said, being desirous and curious to see the constitution of the fetus, she had me called, and the midwife. In my presence, by my order and demonstration, she cuts the abortion into parts, and while she was cutting the chorion, a certain bloody mass was seen, without any motion, without any sense (as appeared from the section), interwoven and divided by various filaments. Outside the chorion membrane, other certain filaments were conspicuous. Who will doubt that that bloody mass was the liver, and those filaments were the rudiments of the veins and the navel? It appeared without sense, without motion; what else can you present or assign to me but the liver? Therefore, it remains that the liver is generated first, and nothing more convenient can be conceived for the vegetative soul than the member in which it resides: the liver. But let this be confirmed both from the structure of the liver and from its use.

The substance of the liver is fleshy, similar to blood recently shed and congealed, whence the word *parenchyma* <gloss>the functional tissue of an organ</gloss> was derived by Erasistratus. It is wrapped in a simple and sufficiently thin membrane, clinging tightly to the organ on all sides. It consists of veins in a double order: the Superior, which are branches of the *vena cava* <gloss>great vein</gloss> and lead the blood into its large trunk like a royal road; and the Inferior, which are more numerous and are branches of the *vena porta* <gloss>portal vein</gloss>, from which the umbilical vein also arises in the fetus, by which the fetus is nourished.

Its task and duty is to nourish the body to the very end of life; for from the natural spirit arising from the liver, both the vital and the animal spirits receive nourishment (although Manardus and with him Ioan. Hier. Bronzerius, in his book of letters, Book 15, first letter, seem to deny this in their treatise; yet they conceded it, and Bertachius in his third book, *On Spirits*, Chapter 3, on Galen, Book 1, *On Natural and Spiritual Faculties*).
pages.16: Capiuaccius (in his reading of the *Aphorisms*, 50, and others from Galen), because of whose necessity and use, Galen rightfully proffers these things about the liver in the last chapter of his 7th *Method*, "The work of the liver is most necessary to all parts." And in the 16th chapter of the 11th *Metaphysics*, he says: "It is most dangerous if the strength of the liver is dissolved, for this is what provides nourishment both to the heart and to the other parts." Hence, infants have more vigorous vegetative faculties, less vigorous sensitive ones, and even less intellectual ones, inasmuch as they derive such utility from the liver. Wherefore, Franciscus Vlmus Baiensis, a physician not to be despised, in his *Treatise on Urines*, collecting the duty and necessity of the liver, did not hesitate to call this the most noble member. Considering, therefore, its substance, considering its function, use, and duty, what was necessary to be generated first and most conveniently in the very first formation of the fetus, if not the liver itself? For the natural faculty (which I do not hesitate to call the natural spirit) permeates all members, not only through the arteries themselves and the veins, but also through the flesh, nerves, ligaments, bones, and everything else that constitutes our body. Whence it happens that even in the diseases of all parts, we can have both continuous and certain signs, and from this natural faculty—from the liver, the tinder and seat of this natural spirit—we can have knowledge of the disposition of the whole. Wherefore, shall we not concede that it is the foundation of the microcosm and the first principle in the microcosm? From the liver, or from the natural faculty arising from the liver, we not only have the open diseases of this principle, but also the internal causes of the diseases of the other principle members are represented. Let the brain labor, let the heart itself labor; certain pathognomonic signs present themselves (which it is not right to deny or contradict), by which you can conclude that these parts are laboring. But if the liver does not digest the nourishment presented to it through the subservient stomach, and convey it to the heart and to the brain, what help will you provide? If you believe that you can help those who are laboring with topicals,
pages.17: if you concede that (which to deny is to deny reason itself and experience—you will see, when I demonstrate a unique example, the case of a man lacking a liver), why will you not concede that the vegetative principle of the soul is more appropriately generated first in the fetus formation? Many similar and better things could be elicited in the medical field for the dignity of such a principle; truly, for the sake of the reader, so that he may refresh his mind, it must be granted—as it is permitted to me, the writer—that, leaving aside the medical study, we may descend into the field of recreation to the sacred secret fables of antiquity. From these, perhaps, our opinion will also be corroborated. Those who have left behind a written genealogy of the gods fable thus about Venus and Mars: that Venus was seen by Phoebus in adultery with Mars, and the adultery of the spouse was revealed to Vulcan by that same observer. Upon this matter of such great importance among the gods (having first captured both adulterers with iron nets), a Council was convened. Neptune, Mercury, and Apollo participated in the Council. It was decreed that the gods should have the children; Apollo interceded, Mercury interceded, but in vain did Neptune intercede. The divinities are freed. If it pleases one to accurately examine these fables and veils of fiction, we will easily understand that the heat of fire—that Vulcan—is very consonant with the mystery of our mortality placed in the marriage of Venus. He is procreated from Jove and Juno, that is, from Heaven, by the acting motion and light (for such is our native heat, spherical and considered by the most learned to be conformable to the element of the stars), and is brought forth from the Air and precipitated into the surrounding Island of the Sea—that is, into the earth, into the Venus of our mortality, understood by Water (through generation)—into a marriage, where at first he is nourished by monkeys, which it is sufficiently clear are of a most prone nature for imitating the actions of rational beings and for acting. Here, I say, he possesses Venus through the mixture of the humid. By the beauty of this Venus

and reject them. But unless our sins deserve otherwise, they will not prevail in the end: And as Paul says, their folly will become evident to all, and will eventually erupt—even against the will of the devils—into the fruit of the pious efforts of your Most Serene King, who through you seeks the peace of the Churches, if the controversies are first judged correctly. This hope of a happy harvest should not at all be shaken for us by the fact that the seeds of peace and concord, scattered in this legation of yours, seem to lie hidden for a while. For nature herself has willed that there be one time for sowing and another for reaping.

Thinking about this, there often comes to mind that most beautiful saying of Nazianzen <note>Gregory of Nazianzus</note>, who, in the oration delivered in praise of Cyprian, said: Divine wisdom knows how to lay the foundations of great things long beforehand, and to bring about contrary things through their opposites, so that it may excite greater admiration in mortals: <note>original Greek: οἶδε πόῤῥωθεν καταβάλλεσθαι τῶν μεγάλων πραγμάτων ἡ θεῖα σοφία τὰς ὑποθέσεις</note>
pages.19:
and to manage contrary things through their opposites, so that it might be even more admired.

But to return to where I left off: Indeed, I rejoice with my whole heart that God has kept you safe and sound until the day you wrote to us from England. And I vehemently congratulate you on the many and great testimonies of divine presence that were divinely shown to you throughout your entire legation. And I pray with you to the son of GOD, our Immanuel, and the most faithful head and guardian of His Church, that He may bless your most holy labors more each day, and keep you safe for a very long time; and likewise strengthen your Most Serene KING, another Josiah. Regarding his constancy and fortitude in defending and professing the true religion, the letters of most trustworthy men clearly testify to us, even after your departure from Germany, against the fabrications of the most vain rumors, which, while you were still present in Germany, were spread by wicked and per-
pages.20:
dite men in the courts of many princes to impede the success of your legation. You said that some of them knew, and had perceived and investigated, the vanity of these rumors, and that to satisfy others, they chose to believe the tales that circumstances and time—which is the daughter of truth—would refute. As indeed, up to this point, with GOD confirming the spirit of His Royal Serenity, the piety of such a great king has dispelled and scattered all the mists of lies with its own brilliance and light.

But just as I am most fully persuaded that He who began His good work in you and your Most Serene King will complete it until the day of JESUS CHRIST: so too, to prove and celebrate that heroic and most holy voice of yours—by which you told me at that time, when various tempests and dangers seemed to hang over you on every side, that in a good cause, the conscience of a right will should make Christians despise the impious men no less than the Devil himself through trust in Divine protection—I believe I can append no more suitable epilogue to this than to add that most noble Psalm of Martin Luther. As it is most frequently sung in the German Churches, so it has a wonderful <term>energia</term> <gloss>force/efficacy</gloss> for exciting the spirit, which I remember also moved you sweetly when I once recited a part of it to you, rendered in Stigelian rhythms in this manner:

> If this world were swarming
> With demons like worms,
> We would not fear anxiously,
> We will prevail in the end with strength.
> Let the prince of the world be proud,
> Let him gnash his teeth and rage,
> The scoundrel cannot harm us,
> Since he is broken by a mere word.

But it did not displease Sleidanus to insert that entire song, expressed in these words, into the history of our times: GOD is for us a firm fortress and bulwark. That ancient enemy of the human race now acts with all his might,
pages.21: and employs every kind of machine. Our power is indeed small, nor can we sustain such an attack for long. But that hero whom GOD Himself has chosen for Himself has taken up arms and fights for us. If you ask who he is, know that it is CHRIST JESUS, in whose hands victory and triumph must reside. Because even if this entire fabric of the world were to abound with devils, we do not dread it, and with most certain trust we await a joyful outcome. For however much Satan may fret and rage, he will accomplish nothing against us. For he has been judged, and his entire armory collapses at a single word. They will not snatch this Word from us, our adversaries, but will leave it behind, however unwilling they may be. For GOD is present in our camp and battle line, who protects us and our gifts with His spirit. If they take away life, goods, children, and wife, bear it patiently. For nothing is added to them by this, but for us, an immortal kingdom is prepared.
pages.22: I had written this letter privately to you, illustrious and generous Lord SEGUR, and I had written it in such a way that I seemed to be dealing with you as if in a present conversation, with a spirit rejoicing at the auspicious news of your safe return to England. Nevertheless, I could not refuse my friends who wanted this, as a testimony of the true and not feigned judgment—not only of myself but of many good men—regarding your virtues, and of <term>euphemia</term> <gloss>good repute</gloss>, to be printed with types and prefixed to the book which Lord Brocardus had put to the press at this same time. In this book, to satisfy your requests, he strove to illustrate that mystical song of Solomon with his interpretation. Just as I trust that the reading of this will be neither useless nor unpleasant to pious and learned men who will wish to judge the matter fairly, so I pray and beseech you with the reverence I owe, that you do not allow this letter, a witness of my respect and love for you, to be burdensome or troublesome to you, and that you continue to embrace me with your accustomed benevolence.

At Bremen, at the beginning of the year of Christ 1585. Which I pray to GOD with the deepest groans of my soul to be salutary for the whole Church and the Republic, and happy and holy for us all.

Does the intellect dispose toward loving and remembering, and vice versa? Does the intellect have the ability to believe and understand at one and the same time? Does the intellect create science within itself? It is asked by what means the intellect creates a <term>species</term> <gloss>mental image/form</gloss>. Does the intellect, with its <term>species</term>, command the will and memory to objectify that <term>species</term>? Just as we apply the questions of the rule to the intellect, so they can be applied to other powers in their own way.

### Regarding the questions of the table.

It is asked whether the world is eternal. Go to column b, c, d, and hold the negative, and you will find in chamber b, c, t, b that if it is eternal, there are many eternities differing in <term>species</term>, and they are concordant through chamber b, c, t, e, against chamber b, c, d, which is impossible; whence it follows that the negative question is to be held, and the rule b proves this. It is asked whether God can only be as infinite by His magnitude as by His eternity; go to column c, d, e, and to chamber c, d, t, c, holding the affirmative against chamber c, d, t, d. Whether God can be as much by eternity as by intellect; go to column d, e, f, and to chamber d, e, t, d. Whether God is as powerful by His power as by His understanding and loving; go to column e, f, g, and hold the affirmative by chamber e, f, t, e, and by chamber e, f, t, f, and by chamber e, f, t, g, until the entire column is completed. Whether in God His intel-
pages.55:
lect and will are greater than His virtue; go to column f, g, h, and hold the negative for all the chambers of that column, drawing out the meanings of the chambers. Whether the divine truth is just as virtuous through equal correlatives as the divine will; go to column g, h, i, and hold the affirmative through all the chambers of that column. Whether in God His virtue and His truth and His grace have that by which they are equal and removed from time, place, and minority; go to column h, i, k, and hold the affirmative through all the chambers.

¶ Regarding the questions of the evacuation of the third figure.

In chamber b, c, it is said that goodness is great. Now it is asked whether goodness is great, and what is its magnitude, and goodness, and magnitude, in what do they concord? And whether they can concord without difference? And it must be answered that goodness is great, as appears by the definition of magnitude. And its magnitude is having correlatives, as is evident through the second species of rule c, and they concord, because goodness is great through magnitude and vice versa. Now, they could not indeed concord without the difference of their correlatives. And let these things suffice regarding the evacuation of the third figure for the sake of brevity. For through these things which we have said about it, the artist can solve and make questions through the other chambers.
pages.56:
¶ **Regarding the questions of the multiplication of the fourth figure.**

It is asked by what mode the intellect conditions itself toward being general through general understanding. Go to the multiplication of the fourth figure and see by what mode the intellect multiplies the conditions with which it multiplies objects and its understanding, so that through many and great sciences it becomes general and endowed with many habits. And let these things suffice regarding the multiplication of the fourth figure for the sake of brevity.

**Regarding the questions of the mixture of principles and rules.**

It is asked whether goodness is discursive through magnitude, duration, etc., and vice versa. And it must be answered that it is, as was signified through the third figure by making the subject the predicate. It is asked what goodness is in magnitude, duration, etc. To which it must be answered that it is great in magnitude and durable in duration. It is asked what goodness has in magnitude, etc., to which it must be said that in itself it has its correlatives, great in magnitude and durable in duration. And just as we exemplify about goodness, so it can be exemplified about other principles in their own way. And let these things suffice regarding mixture in its own way.

**Regarding the questions of the nine subjects. And first about God.**

It is asked whether God is. And it must be answered that He is. It has been proven in the questions of the first figure. It is asked: what is God? And it must be answered that God
pages.57:
is a being that acts in itself as much as He is. Through the second species of rule c, it is asked what God has in Himself essentially. To which it must be answered that He has His correlatives, without which He could not have immense and eternal reasons. Through the third species, it is asked what God is in another. To which it must be said that He is creating, governing, and such. Through the fourth species of rule c, it is asked what God has in another. And it must be said that He has in another power and dominion, and in men, judgment and the act of grace, mercy, patience, and piety. And let these things suffice regarding God for the sake of brevity.

¶ Regarding the questions of the angels.

It is asked whether angels exist. And it must be answered that they do. For if that which is less like God exists, much more so does that which is more like God exist. Furthermore, if there is something which is composed of the intellectual and the corporeal, much more so is that which is composed of the intellectual and the intellectual. Furthermore, if angels did not exist, the scale of difference and concord would be evacuated, and consequently the world, which is impossible. It is asked of what the angel is and whose it is. And it must be answered by rule d that it is of itself; its essence indeed cannot be punctual nor lineal. And by the second species of the same rule, it is of its spiritual correlatives, and of its <term>tivi</term> <gloss>active</gloss> and <term>biles</term> <gloss>receptive</gloss> from which it is composed
pages.58:
and <term>tiu</term> <gloss>active</gloss> is active, and through <term>biles</term> <gloss>receptive</gloss> it is receptive, and through <term>are</term> <gloss>the act of being</gloss> it is the act existing between the <term>tiu</term> and <term>biles</term>; through the third species it must be said that the angel is of God. And let these things regarding the angels suffice for the sake of brevity.

# Regarding the questions of the Heaven.

It is asked whether the heaven moves itself. And it must be answered that it does, so that its principles may have substantial and proper correlatives through their constellations. Whether the heaven moves itself to a place; and it must be answered that it does, in itself and in lower things, circularly, but not outside itself; the reason for this is that outside itself it has no action, nor can it have. Whether an angel moves the heaven; and it must be answered that it does not, because if it did, the <term>tivi</term> <gloss>actives</gloss> would already be lower and the <term>biles</term> <gloss>receptives</gloss> higher, and also by its form it would then not move the elements or the elemental things, but by its matter, which is impossible. It is asked whether the heaven has a motive soul. And it must be answered that it does; for otherwise the sensitive and vegetative would not have motive souls, nor would the elements have motion. It is asked through the first species of rule e, why the heaven exists. And it must be said that it is because it is constituted from its form and matter. Through the second species of rule e, it is asked why the heaven is; and it must be said: so that lower beings may have motion. And let these things regarding the heaven suffice for the sake of brevity.
pages.59:
¶ Regarding the questions of the fourth subject, which is man.

It is asked whether man can have greater knowledge of God by affirming or by denying; and it must be answered that by affirming, for God is not through those ends by which He is, but through those ends by which He cannot be. It is asked why man acts through a specific form; go to the second species of rule e, and the solution is implied there. Whether man, augmenting his acts, augments his essence; and it must be answered that no man acts upon himself. It is asked when man desires to remember and cannot remember, which of these fails first, the memory or the intellect; to which it must be said that the memory itself yields its <term>species</term> <gloss>mental image</gloss> to the intellect more quickly by nature than to the will. It is asked of what soul and body men are composed. And it must be answered that in man, corporeal and spiritual goodness compose one goodness, and so of others. It is asked what is the life of man; to which it must be answered that it is that form which is composed of the vegetative, sensitive, imaginative, and rational. What is the death of man; it must be answered that it is the dissolution of the elemental, vegetative, sensitive, imaginative, and rational power. It is asked whether man is visible; and it must be said that he is not, for sight cannot see anything except color and shape. It is asked whether in man the intellect and memory are the same power; and it must be answered
pages.60:
that they are not, because if they were the same power, the intellect would not then be successive in acquiring <term>species</term> <gloss>mental images</gloss>, nor would it consign them to oblivion, nor would it be ignorant of them. Again, because it would be too strong in the object against the liberty of the will. And let these things said about man suffice for the sake of brevity.

### Regarding the questions of the imaginative power.

Whether the imaginative power imagines imaginable things in its own way just as the sensitive power senses sensible things. It is asked what is the reason why the imaginative power abstracts <term>species</term> <gloss>mental images</gloss> from sensible things. It is asked what the imaginative power is. Whether the imaginative power has correlatives. Whether the imaginative power augments itself by augmenting its act. Whether the imaginative power is a higher power than the sensitive. Whether the imaginative power has specific instincts and appetites. By what mode the sensitive power impedes the act of the imaginative power. Why the imaginative power is not as powerful in sensible or sensed things as the sensitive; go to the subject of the imaginative power. It is asked whether the sensitive power senses the imaginative power. And it must be answered that lower powers do not act upon higher ones.

### Regarding the questions of the sensitive power.

It is asked which power of these senses hunger and thirst, either the gustatory or the tactile. And it must be answered that it is the one that most disposes the object. Whether the gustatory thus senses hunger or thirst with instinct and appetite, just as the visual [senses] the colored with
pages.61:
color. Go to the second species of rule c. It is asked from what the sensitive power senses sensed things. And it must be answered that every particular sense senses its sensible object through a specific form, just as a colored subject subsisting in a crystal colors it. Whether the sensitive power has punctual and lineal quantities. And it must be answered that the sensitive power attains an object from far away just as quickly as from near by. Whether the sensitive power, just as it has a common sense, so has a common power, instinct, and appetite. It is asked what the sensitive power is. With what the sensitive power is particular and common. From what the sensitive power lives and is nourished. Whether the sensitive power is sensed; go to the subject of the sensitive power.

### Regarding the vegetative power.

Whether the vegetative power acts through its <term>species</term> <gloss>mental image</gloss>. Whether the vegetative power has any reason by which it is common and particular, just as the sensitive. Whether the quantity of the vegetative power is punctual or lineal. It is asked what the vegetative power is and what it has in itself through the second species of rule c. It is asked from what the vegetative power lives and is nourished and grows, and in what subject it is planted. What is the death of the vegetative power; go to the subject of the vegetative power in which the solutions of the aforementioned questions are implied.

### CAP. XIX.
->*The Classifications of Plants Reconsidered.*<-

SUCH differences in the whole substance appear to be clear: some are cultivated, some wild; some fruit-bearing, others barren; some evergreen and others deciduous, as has been said, and some entirely leafless. Some are flowering, some flowerless, some early-sprouting and early-fruiting, and others late-sprouting and late-fruiting; and likewise for everything similar to these. There are such differences in the parts as well, but the most peculiar and in a sense the greatest division is the one that exists also among animals, namely, that some are aquatic and others terrestrial. For there is such a class of plants, which cannot grow unless in moisture; while others grow, though not in the same way, but worse. For all trees, simply speaking, and for all plants, there happen to be many species within each genus; for there is almost nothing simple. But those that are called cultivated and wild exhibit this as the most obvious and greatest difference, for example: Fig and Wild Fig; Olive and Wild Olive; Pear and Wild Pear; and whatever else occurs in each of these, in the fruits, the leaves, and the other forms and parts. But of the wild plants, most are nameless and few are expert in them; of the cultivated and named ones, there are more, and the knowledge of them is more common; I mean, for example, the Vine, Fig, Pomegranate, Apple, Pear, Laurel, Myrtle, and others. For their use being common makes it easier to observe their differences. This is also peculiar to each: for they divide the wild ones by male and female, either solely or mostly; but the cultivated ones by more forms. It is easier to grasp and enumerate the species of some, but more difficult for others because of their great variety. But one must attempt to observe the differences of the parts and other substances from these things; regarding their origins, we must speak next, for this follows as if in order from what has been said.

### *Constituent Parts of Plants.*

#### CAP. I.

"Perhaps not in the same way." Utmost brevity, as correctly observed by <note>D. Moldenhawer</note>, in the comparison of animals with plants at the end of this chapter; concerning which, one should consult Aristotle, <term>Historia Animalium</term> <gloss>History of Animals</gloss> v. 3.

"So that nothing is out of place." See on this subject the book <term>De Causis Plantarum</term> <gloss>On the Causes of Plants</gloss> ii. 20, 22, 23. v. 2.

"At equal," sc. distance. Equidistant.

#### CAP. II.

"They are primary and greatest." Thus Aristotle, <term>Historia Animalium</term>: "Whatever parts, being whole, have other parts within them that are peculiar; such as the head, etc."

"More durable in their roots." Whose root is perennial. <term>Bot</term>.

"To one," sc. being. To be equipped with a simple trunk. See Pliny, <term>Naturalis Historia</term> xiv. 1. 30.

<term>Homoiomerēs</term> <gloss>having similar parts</gloss>. <term>Anomoiomerēs</term> <gloss>having dissimilar parts</gloss>. One should consult Aristotle on this subject, <term>De Generatione Animalium</term> i. 1, and the Lexicon of Theophrastus.

"Any part whatever from the same things." The individual parts are from the same vessels, fibers, membranes, etc.

"The greatest parts are almost these." End of chapter ii in <note>Bodæus</note>.

"Other things from which these are;" the author proceeds to the <term>homoiomerē</term>.

#### CAP. III.

<note>Menestor</note>. An author on botanical matters, whose works do not exist.

"Innate moisture and heat." Regarding the warm principle of life, <note>Moldenhawer</note> treats this very copiously in <term>Tentamen</term>, p. 83. He calls it <term>thermon gonimon</term> <gloss>generative heat</gloss>.

### CAP. IV.

"In which it is possible." In those things that admit of division.

"Beyond the cultivation." By means of culture, etc. Frequent usage in Theophrastus.

"Olive cuttings." The word <term>kopades</term> is interpreted as coppiced woods, but here perhaps of a decapitated tree.

### CAP. VI.

"Of all things one must always take"—an obscure reading, if it is sound: the meaning is, "of all things one must always take the differences by their places" regarding climate, etc.

"One thing according to one genus of moistures," i.e., aquatic plants differ among themselves with respect to "places."

"Smaller—larger." The former are seaweeds and laver; the latter are called "little trees" elsewhere; Gorgonians, Corallines. See iv. 8.

### CAP. VII.

"Thickness." Here it indicates the mass or bulk of the trunk. It is opposed to "slenderness."

"From which the composition." With respect to the constituent parts. Opposed to "those things according to the conditions and powers."

### CAP. VIII.

"Piths." See chapter iii, p. 9. l. 6. N.B. Chapter IX of <note>Bodæus</note>.

"Some do not have—and the Alder." In the younger branches of the Elder tree there is no pith.

pages.140:
"All piths are black." The meaning of the word <term>melas</term> <gloss>black</gloss> escaped Scaliger. See <note>Bodæus</note>, p. 24, and the Lexicon of Theophrastus.

"In general, some do not have." The discourse is about fungi: see <term>Catalogus Systematicus</term> <gloss>Systematic Catalog</gloss>, of which there is no affinity with other plants. See <note>Bodæus</note>, p. 27.

"They differ also in their roots." See regarding this matter Pliny, xvi. 31.

"Fimbriate." Fringed, Pliny, but there is another sense of the word <term>thysanoi</term>, ribbons, bundles of fibers. <note>Pollux</note>. See Lexicon of Theophrastus.

### CAP. IX.

"In those above the ground," sc. "parts."

"For the root," i.e., the root in general.

### CAP. X.

"Crowning the altars." Perhaps one should read "gathering heaps," collecting piles.

"They bear fruit." Add "below": underground, regarding tubers. See illustration of the <term>Arachidna</term> <gloss>earthnut</gloss>, <note>Bodæus</note>, p. 35.

"The fruit," sc. the tuber from the root.

"Before those above," sc. "parts."

"These contribute significantly." It is to be noted that the word "nature" should be taken in the plural.

"Of all things, the juices are likewise." Beginning of the chapter in <note>Bodæus</note>.

"For from the shoots." A wonderful description of the habit of the Indian Fig, L. Engl. "The Banyan Tree."

"If in deep soil." The meaning is, if some material intervenes between the seed and the earth, "it divides the root toward the earth," it bends the root toward the ground until it reaches it.

### CAP. XI.

"In which are both," sc. "genera." Although sexual distinction occurs in the Palm, commonly the words "male," "female" are attributed to varieties of species, insofar as they are observed to be more robust and fruitless, or the contrary.

"The most peculiar are those of the Apple tree." These words included in a parenthesis "crept in from the margin," as I suspect, and interrupt the description of the habit of the <term>Elate</term> <gloss>silver fir</gloss>. Although it is hardly possible to conjecture what the author means with respect to "the faces of beasts," Pliny interprets the passage thus, <term>Naturalis Historia</term> l. xvi. c. 30: "The Apple tree has a peculiar kind of branch, for they represent the snouts of wild beasts, with smaller ones adhering to one very large one."

pages.141:
"Branches, some are blind." Observe that the word <term>ozos</term> <gloss>branch/node</gloss> occurs in a double sense, as a branch, and a node in the trunk.

"Because nothing is placed in between." Because there are no intervals. <note>Scaliger</note>.

"Peculiar cavities." See the word <term>hēlos</term> <gloss>nail/stud</gloss> in the Lexicon of Theophrastus. A species of <term>Hypoxylon</term> <gloss>a type of fungus</gloss>, as I suspect. See iv. 16.

"It is, therefore." A chapter to be added to the previous one as it is a continuation.

"Growing in length." The discourse is about the trunk: which is either tall and not branching, or which "is split straight." I also suspect that what follows, "those similar to these," should be read thus: "a root similar to these." Thus Virgil: "As much as it stretches its top to the ethereal breezes, so much does it stretch its root to Tartarus."

"They become thin," sc. "by cultivation."

### CAP. XII.

"And some are evergreen." Here begins chapter xv of <note>Bodæus</note>.

"To participate of the winter." To last until the middle of winter.

### CAP. XIII.

"Like the hand." Pliny in the passage xvi. 24 says, "veins on the underside," that is, hollow lines, as in the palm of the hand.

"Which toward the twig," i.e., from the conversion of the leaves, it is doubtful which part is upper, which lower; "for the concavity" with respect to position is different from the nature of the leaf.

"Not to be altered in the same way." Opposed to the conversions "through the veins or fibers," i.e., not in a constant, regular way.

"Deeply going" is to be interpreted concerning the thickness of the leaf.

"Saw-edged." Perhaps "comb-edged" or "teethed." See Preface to the Illustration of Theophrastus, p. v. Also the description of the <term>Elate</term> <gloss>silver fir</gloss>, l. iii.

"Of the Oak from the trunk." Pliny observes the same regarding the leaves of the Oak, <term>Naturalis Historia</term> xvi. 24. <note>Bodæus</note> says that he himself has never observed it. I suspect an error in the text: one should perhaps read <term>Kyprias</term> <gloss>Cyprian</gloss>. See regarding the <term>Sykē Kypria</term> <gloss>Sycamore Fig</gloss>, iv. c. 2.

pages.142:
"The whole stem leafless." He accurately describes the scape of botanists.

"Through itself." From itself: of a sessile leaf. <term>Bot</term>.

"Holding in between." Fruit in the middle of the leaf.

### CAP. XIV.

"To those not annual [parts]." Persistent parts of the plant, such as the trunk, branches, etc. "For nothing is without this [moisture]."

"Of the flowers, some from the bark." A wonder what Theophrastus means. Flowers from the bark and nerves. Surely an error of the text, and one should read instead of "of the flowers," "of the others" (sc. stalks). Regarding flowers, see c. 21, 22.

### CAP. XV.

"The seed immediately after the containing part." Seed with a simple covering. In this chapter six kinds of seeds are noted, whose enumeration is confused and very long. These are: 1. simple seeds with a covering; Palms. 2. from a nut and flesh—Drupes. 3. in a pod—siliquose. 4. in some membrane, membranaceous follicle, such as Pear, Apple. 5. <term>angiospermata</term> <gloss>seeds in vessels</gloss>, with a loose, rigid pericarp; Poppy. 6. <term>gymnospermata</term> <gloss>naked seeds</gloss>, without a covering; umbellifers.

"Such as the berry." Here the text is very corrupt. Theophrastus's distinction of several grains contained in something common, such as a grape or stone in a grape: and likewise in a seed. N.B. Stones of the Pomegranate are opposed to the single grains of Wheat, etc. "And least of all would the apple kinds seem." Nevertheless, the apple kinds are least to be added to these, which are surrounded by membranes in the inner part of the fruit.

"But likewise of these, each." See the error of the scribe in transcribing above, "for one taking each."

### CAP. XVI.

"In the books on juices." <term>Historia de Causis Plantarum</term>, l. vi.

"Of lettuce." The juice is called "watery" less correctly. Perhaps an error of the text, as above, for "milky" (which should be put regarding the juice of the Fig and Poppy).

"Which is proper." The meaning is that the peculiar juice of any plant "has some similarity" in itself before the cooking and maturation occurs in the fruit, which is effected by the help of the pericarp.

pages.143:
"Some are sweet-smelling." See more fully regarding odors in Theophrastus, <term>De Causis Plantarum</term>, l. i. 6, as also regarding juices.

### CAP. XVII.

"Outside the sea." The Red Sea is intended.

"Having a diagram." The common columbine is indicated by most botanists under the name <term>Iasione</term>; and the description, although intricate, wonderfully agrees with the convolutions of the petals: also "it is not separated in the flower."

N.B. To some perhaps <note>Bodæus's</note> conjecture will be more pleasing, that the Bindweed, etc., is indicated here, in which sense "a diagram only of the majority" is to be interpreted concerning the breadth of the flower.

"They appear perforated." The author’s wonderful "accuracy," when the flower is perforated, i.e., falls off without a stigma, the beginning fruit remains; when "it is burned or wet," whether it is affected by too much sun or rain, "it drops the fruit." See the observation below, "as many of the flowers as have, as it were, a spindle, are fertile."

"On the mouths themselves." The discourse is about syngenesious plants; the "mouth" therefore is the common receptacle in this class.

"Like a spindle." Regarding the stigma of the orange flower.

"Immediately to show the fruit," i.e., without flower or petals.

### CAP. XVIII.

"The wild fig." The common fig, etc., is counted by Linnæus among the trioecia. The "wild fig," from which "wild figs" (which perhaps are the "olunthoi" <gloss>wild figs/abortive figs</gloss>) are produced, is the male tree; the "fig" is the monoecious tree.

### CAP. XIX.

"But such." A summary and recapitulation of this book.

"More species under each genus." More species under one genus. A truly Linnæan distinction!

"Cultivated and wild." Here the distinction is taken from sex: but what does it mean? That wild plants are distinguished by sex, but cultivated ones by "more peculiar things"; does he indicate the varieties of fruits?
