pages.54:
Does the intellect organize itself to love and remember, and vice versa? Can the intellect believe and understand at one and the same time? Does the intellect create knowledge within itself? It is asked by what means the intellect creates a species <note>an intellectual representation or image</note>. Does the intellect, with its species, command the will and memory to objectify that species? Just as we apply the questions of the rule to the intellect, they can be applied to other faculties in their own way.

### On the questions of the table.

It is asked whether the world is eternal. Go to column b, c, d, and hold the negative, and you will find in chamber b, c, t, b, that if it is eternal, there are many eternities <note>original: "eternitates"</note> differing by species, and they are concordant through chamber b, c, t, e, against chamber b, c, d, which is impossible; whence it follows that the negative question is to be held, and this the rule b proves. It is asked whether God can be infinite as much by his magnitude as by his eternity; go to column c, d, e, and to chamber c, d, t, c, holding the affirmative against chamber c, d, t, d. Whether God can be as much by eternity as by intellect; go to column d, e, f, and to chamber d, e, t, d. Whether God is as powerful through his power as through his understanding and loving; go to column e, f, g, and hold the affirmative for chamber e, f, t, e, and for chamber e, f, t, f, and for chamber e, f, t, g, until the whole column is finished. Whether in God his intel
pages.55:
lectus and will are greater than his virtue; go to column f, g, h, and hold the negative for all the chambers of that column, extracting the meanings of the chambers. Whether the divine truth is in itself as virtuous through equal correlatives as the divine will; go to column g, h, i, and hold the affirmative for all the chambers of that column. Whether in God his virtue and his truth and his grace possess that by which they are equal, and remote from time, place, and minority; go to column h, i, k, and hold the affirmative for all the chambers.

¶ On the questions of the evacuation of the third figure.
In chamber b, c, it is said that goodness is great. Now it is asked whether goodness is great and what is its magnitude, and goodness, and magnitude, in what they agree. And whether they can agree without difference. And it must be answered that goodness is great as appears by the definition of magnitude. And its magnitude is to have correlatives; as is clear through the second species of rule c, and they are concordant, because goodness is great through magnitude and vice versa. Now, indeed, they could by no means agree without the difference of their correlatives. And let these things suffice concerning the evacuation of the third figure for the sake of brevity. For through these things which we have said about it, the artist can solve and make questions through other chambers.
pages.56:
¶ **On the questions of the multiplication of the fourth figure**
**It** is asked by what mode the intellect conditions itself to be general for general understanding. Go to the multiplication of the fourth figure and see by what mode the intellect multiplies the conditions with which it multiplies objects and its understanding, so that through many and great knowledges it becomes general and clothed in many habits. And let these things concerning the multiplication of the fourth figure suffice for the sake of brevity.

**On the questions of the mixing of principles and rules.**
**It** is asked whether goodness is discursive through magnitude, duration, etc., and vice versa. And it is to be answered that it is so, as is signified by the third figure, making the predicate of the subject. It is asked what goodness is in magnitude, duration, etc. To which it is to be answered that it is great in magnitude and durable in duration. It is asked what goodness has in magnitude, etc., to which it must be said that in it it has its correlatives, great in magnitude and durable in duration. And just as we exemplify about goodness, so it can be exemplified about other principles in their own way. And let these things concerning the mixture suffice in their own way.

**On the questions of the nine subjects. And first of God.**
**It** is asked whether God is. And it must be answered that he is. It is proven in the questions of the first figure. It is asked: What is God? And it must be answered that God
pages.57:
is an entity that acts in itself as much as he is himself. Through the second species of rule c, it is asked what God has in himself essentially. To which it is to be answered that he has his correlatives without which he could not have immense and eternal reasons. Through the third species, it is asked what God is in another. To which it must be said that he is creating, governing, and the like. Through the fourth species of rule c, it is asked what God has in another. And it must be said that he has in another power and dominion, and in men, judgment and the act of grace, mercy, patience, and piety. And let these things concerning God suffice for the sake of brevity.

¶ On the questions of the angels.

It is asked whether angels are. And it must be answered that they are. For if that which is less is seen to be from God, it is; and much more so, that which is seen to be more similar to God. Furthermore, if there is something which is composed of the intellectual and the corporeal, much more so is that which is composed of the intellectual and the intellectual. Moreover, if angels indeed were not, the scale of difference and concordance would be evacuated, and consequently the world, which is impossible. It is asked of what the angel is and whose it is. And it must be answered by rule d that it is of itself; its essence indeed cannot be punctual nor lineal. And by the second species of the same rule, it is of its spiritual correlatives, and of its <unclear>biles</unclear> and <unclear>are</unclear> <note>These terms likely refer to specific technical divisions in Lull's system</note> from which it is composed
pages.58:
correlatives, it is active; and through the <unclear>biles</unclear> it is receptive; and through the <unclear>are</unclear> it is an act existing between the <unclear>tiuos</unclear> and the <unclear>biles</unclear>. By the third species, it must be said that the angel is of God. And let these things concerning the angels suffice for the sake of brevity.

# On the questions of the Heavens.

**It** is asked whether the heaven moves itself. And it must be answered that it is so, so that its principles may have substantial and proper correlatives through its constellations. Whether the heaven moves itself to a place; and it must be answered that it is so in itself and in inferior things, circularly, but not outside itself. The reason for this is because outside itself it has no action, nor can it have. Whether an angel moves the heaven; and it must be answered that it is not, because if it moved, already the <unclear>tiui</unclear> by the movement of the correlatives would be lower, and the <unclear>biles</unclear> higher; and also by its form it would not now move elements nor elementated things, but by its matter, which is impossible. It is asked whether the heaven has a motive soul. And it must be answered that it is so, for otherwise sensitive and vegetative things would not have motive souls, nor would elements have motion. It is asked by the first species of rule d, e, why the heaven is. And it must be said that it is from the fact that it is constituted from its form and matter. Through the second species of rule e, it is asked why the heaven is; and it must be said that it is so that lower entities may be able to have motion. And let these things concerning the heaven suffice for the sake of brevity.
pages.59:
¶ On the questions of the 4th subject, which is man.
It is asked whether man can have greater knowledge of God by affirming or by denying; and it is to be answered that by affirming, for God is not through those ends by which he is, but through those ends by which he cannot not be. It is asked why man acts through a specific form; go to the second species of rule e, and there the solution is implied. Whether man, increasing his acts, increases his essence; and it is to be answered that no man acts upon himself. It is asked when man desires to remember and cannot remember, which of these fails first, either memory or intellect; to which it must be said that memory indeed more quickly renders the ancient species <note>memories/impressions</note> to the intellect than to the will. It is asked of what soul and body men are composed. And it is to be answered that in man, corporeal and spiritual goodness compose one goodness, and so of others. It is asked what the life of man is, to which it must be answered that it is that form which is composed of the vegetative, sensitive, imaginative, and rational. What is the death of man? It must be answered that it is the dissolution of the elementative, vegetative, sensitive, imaginative, and rational power. It is asked whether man is visible, and it must be said that no. For sight can see only color and figure. It is asked whether in man intellect and memory are the same power. And it must be answered
pages.60:
¶ not, because if they were the same power, the intellect would not then be successive in acquiring species, nor would it hand them over to oblivion, nor would it be ignorant of them. Again, because it would be too strong in the object against the liberty of the will. And let these things said concerning man suffice for the sake of brevity.

### On the questions of the imaginative.

Whether the imaginative imagines imaginable things in its own way just as the sensitive senses sensible things. It is asked what is the reason why the imaginative abstracts species from sensible things. It is asked what the imaginative is. Whether the imaginative has correlatives. Whether the imaginative increases itself by increasing its act. Whether the imaginative is a higher power than the sensitive. Whether the imaginative has specific instincts and appetites. Through what mode the sensitive hinders the act of the imaginative. Why the imaginative is not as powerful in sensible things or sensed things as the sensitive; go to the subject of the imaginative. It is asked whether the sensitive senses the imaginative. And it is to be answered that lower powers do not act upon higher ones.

### On the questions of the sensitive.

It is asked which power of these senses hunger and thirst, either taste or touch. And it must be answered that it is the one which more disposes the object. Whether taste thus senses hunger or thirst with instinct and appetite, just as sight senses the colored with
pages.61:
color. Go to the second species of rule c. It is asked from what the sensitive senses sensed things. And it must be answered that every particular sense senses its own sensible object through a specific form, just as a colored subject subsisting in crystal colors it. Whether the sensitive has punctual and lineal quantities. And it must be answered that the sensitive reaches an object from afar just as quickly as from near. Whether the sensitive, just as it has a common sense, so has a common power, instinct, and appetite. It is asked what the sensitive is. The sensitive, with what it is particular and common. From what the sensitive lives and is nourished. Whether the sensitive is sensed; go to the subject of the sensitive.

### On the vegetative.

Whether the vegetative acts through its species. Whether the vegetative has some reason through which it is common and particular just as the sensitive. Whether the quantity of the vegetative is punctual or lineal. It is asked what the vegetative is and what it has in itself through the second species of rule c. It is asked from what the vegetative lives and is nourished and grows, and in what subject it is planted. What is the death of the vegetative; go to the subject of the vegetative, in which the solutions of the aforementioned questions are implied.

# PREFACE TO THE CONCLUSIONS,
### which is
# THE FIRST CONCLUSION.

<note>Large ornamental drop-cap initial 'O' decorated with floral and foliate patterns.</note>
All men desire to know naturally. Some, indeed, desire to know their own origin; others yearn to be skilled in knowledge; others have it in mind to learn something else. To satisfy this natural tendency somewhat, I bring forward from the vast field of the medical faculty some things, and first, what is formed in the very first formation of man, or you may say the fetus: whether the heart, the fountain of human life; or the liver, the workshop of the blood; or the brain, the most divine member, as called by Plato in the *Timaeus*. And I assert that the liver is formed first, then the heart, and finally the brain.

There are many things, I admit, to be discussed in this conclusion: namely, how this is dilated, adheres, and lives in the implanted seed, and similar things that would pertain to the present matter; further, whether it lives in potency or in act; whether a natural spirit is given, or whether it proceeds from the liver. However, setting these aside, I descend to my main intent (supposing from Aristotle, *On the Parts of Animals*, Book 1, Chapter 1, that seed is generation, and that generation is the first participation with the warm nutritive soul; *On Youth and Old Age*, Chapter 14; and likewise *On the Generation of Animals*, Book 1, Chapter 18, if the parts were extracted in the seed, in what manner does it live? Likewise, Book 2, *On the Generation of Animals*, Chapter 3, the seed and the conception live no less than plants, nor is Galen contrary to this). See: what that first member is, among the aforementioned, which is generated first and more conveniently, and lives with a vegetative life. To make this conclusion of ours firmer, we shall draw authorities from Hippocrates and others. Afterward, if anything is to be brought forward to the contrary, I shall resolve it.

Hippocrates, therefore, in his book *On the Formation of the Fetus*, and his faithful interpreter Galen, recount a case here (by which he intends to prove that the liver is generated first; I, indeed, shall bring forward both its structure and its purpose, so that everything may be more corroborated), which is as follows.

What it was, I myself shall say: just as if one were to tear off the outer shell of a raw egg, so that the inner humidity would shine through the interior little membrane, such in some way it clearly was; and there was a certain red and round thing within it; but in the membrane, certain white and thick fibers were seen to be present, wrapped in a truly thick and red substance, and on the outside, around the membrane, were bloody bruises; in the middle, something thin gaped open, which seemed to me to be the navel, through which the fetus would first breathe, with spirit passing both out and in; from it, the membrane that contained the seed was entirely produced." But, others omitted, in Chapter 3, around the middle, they interpret that red thing thus, saying: "That red, round thing which appears in the chorion in the seed, Hippocrates said was six days old, it must be believed to have been the liver, still indistinct and unformed." And a little later they add: "But previously (thus Galen and Felicianus from him), when I was writing commentaries on the seed, and was forced to say something about the order of the formation of individual members, I said the heart, just as the liver is in the first days of the fetus, was, as it were, a certain foundation, driven to this by the use of it, most necessary in adults and perfect beings: but when I later learned that it was the opinion of all others, both physicians and philosophers (behold the ingenuity of Galen admitting his own error; behold the foundations upon which he relied to change his opinion) that the fetus until express formation is dispensed just as a plant, it seemed more probable to me if we should maintain that there was no necessity for the heart in the beginning, but that it is formed entirely after the liver." And toward the end of the chapter he adds: "But indeed, just as it must be believed that the heart was made later than the liver, and for that reason the liver was established closer to the pregnant womb (which anatomy itself demonstrates as most true), so also it was fitting that the brain be established further from the heart, inasmuch as it is also fabricated later," giving the reason why the brain is also fabricated last, saying: "That which is made, one must believe, is because the fetus has no need of a brain: for it does not need to see, nor hear, nor taste, nor smell anything, nor likewise to work with hands or feet, nor to use any other voluntary function at all. In a similar way, there was no necessity for the sense of touch, no imagination, no thought, no memory; therefore, the brain was fabricated third in the order of time." (Beautifully said regarding the necessity of the final formation of the brain itself; if he had provided the same for the heart, it would be less burdensome for us, but we shall demonstrate it with all our strength.) These are both Hippocrates and Galen. But may it be permitted to me, for the confirmation of this, to add this Case History which I have seen.

pages.15:
miscarriage, and desiring to see—or rather, I should say, being curious and desirous of seeing the constitution of the fetus—she had me called, and the midwife. This woman, in my presence, at my command, and with me demonstrating the manner, cut the miscarriage into parts. And while she was incising the chorion, a certain mass of blood, without any motion, without any sensation (as was apparent from the section), interwoven and divided by various filaments, was perceived. Outside the chorion membrane, other certain filaments were conspicuous. Who will doubt that that bloody mass was the liver, and that those filaments were the rudiments of the veins and the navel? It appeared without sensation, without motion; what else will you present or assign to me than the liver? Wherefore it remains that both the liver is generated first, and that nothing can be thought of more conveniently for the vegetative soul—the member in which it might reside—than the liver. But let this be confirmed both from the structure of the liver and from its use.

The substance of the liver is fleshy, similar to blood recently shed and congealed, whence the word *parenchyma* was derived by Erasistratus. It is enveloped by a simple and sufficiently thin membrane, adhering tightly to the organ on all sides. It consists of a double order of veins: the Superior ones, which are offshoots of the *vena cava*, and lead the blood into its ample trunk, as if it were a royal road; the Inferior ones, which are more numerous, are the branches of the *vena portae*, from which also the umbilical vein in the fetus, by which the fetus is nourished, arises.

Moreover, its function and duty is to nourish the body until the end of life; for from the natural spirit arising from the liver, both the vital and the animal spirits receive nourishment (although Manardus and, with him, Ioan. Hier. Bronzerius, in his *Treatise*, Book 15, first epistle, seem to deny this; yet they have conceded it, and Bertachius in the third, *On Spirits*, chapter three, *On Galen* 1. *On Natural and Spiritual Faculties*.)

Hence, infants have more vigorous vegetative faculties, less vigorous sensitive ones, and even less intellectual ones, inasmuch as they obtain such utility from the liver. Therefore, Franciscus Vlmus Baiensis, a physician not to be despised, in his *Treatise on Urines*, collecting the office and necessity of the liver, did not hesitate to call this member the most noble. Therefore, having considered its substance, having considered its function, use, and duty, what should have been generated first, and more conveniently, in the very first formation of the fetus than the liver itself? For the natural faculty (which I do not hesitate to name the natural spirit) permeates through all members, not only through the arteries themselves and the veins, but also through the flesh, nerves, ligaments, bones, and all the rest that constitute our body. Whence it happens that even in the diseases of all parts, we can have both continuous and certain signs, and from the disposition of the whole, we can have knowledge at the same time from this natural faculty, from the liver, the tinder and seat of this natural spirit. Why then should we not concede it to be the foundation of the microcosm, and the first principle in the microcosm? From the liver, or from the natural faculty arising from the liver, we have not only the diseases of this principle manifest, but we can also have represented the internal causes of the diseases of the other principle members. Let the brain labor, let the heart itself labor; some pathognomonic signs present themselves (which I neither deny nor is it right to deny) by which you are able to conclude that these parts are laboring; however, if the liver does not digest the nourishment provided to it by the serving ventricle and carry it to the heart and to the brain, what aid will you provide? For from these, perhaps, our opinion will also be corroborated. Those who have left behind a written genealogy of the gods spin such fables about Venus and Mars. Venus was seen by Phoebus in adultery with Mars; the adultery of his wife was revealed to Vulcan by that same inspector. A council was convened among the gods concerning this matter of such great moment (having first captured both adulterers with iron nets); Neptune, Mercury, and Apollo took part in the council. It was decreed that the gods should have their freedom; Apollo interceded, Mercury interceded, but in vain; Neptune interceded and the deities were liberated. how those things might be discovered, I could explain to you. But I shall see to myself. Now I propose this, which I have persuaded myself of: although it may not be an art, yet there is nothing more illustrious than a perfect orator. For, to omit the practice of speaking, which dominates in every peaceful and free state, there is such great pleasure in the faculty of speaking itself that nothing more delightful can be perceived by the ears or minds of men. For what song can be found sweeter than the measured pronunciation of an oration? What poem is more apt than the artful conclusion of words? What actor is more pleasant in imitating than an orator in undertaking the truth? What, moreover, is more subtle than acute and frequent thoughts? What more admirable than a matter illustrated by the splendor of words? What more full than an oration accumulated with every kind of thing? For there is no matter that is not the orator's own, provided that it ought to be spoken of ornately and gravely. It is his, when giving counsel on the greatest matters, to provide an explained opinion with dignity; it is his, as well, both to incite a languid populace and to moderate one that is unbridled. By the same faculty, the fraud of men is called to ruin, and integrity to salvation. Who can exhort more ardently to virtue? Who can recall more sharply from vices? Who can disparage the wicked more harshly? Who can praise the good more ornately? Who can break greed more vehemently by accusing? Who can soothe grief more gently by consoling? Indeed, history, the witness of times, the light of truth, the life of memory, the teacher of life, the messenger of antiquity—by what other voice, if not the orator's, is it commended to immortality? For if there is any other art that professes knowledge of words...

<summary>Antonius asserts that while oratory may not be a formal art, it remains a supreme skill for its ability to sway minds, preserve history, and serve as a tool for both virtue and statecraft.</summary>

pages.477:
# DE ORATORE

or of things to be done or selected; or if anyone is said to form an oration—and to vary and distinguish it with certain badges, as it were, of words and thoughts—unless he is an orator; or if any way is taught, unless by this one art, regarding arguments, or thoughts, or finally description and order: let us admit that either this, which this art professes, is foreign to it, or that it is common with some other art. But if this reasoning and doctrine are found in this one alone, it does not follow that, if others who are skilled in other arts have spoken well, it is any less the property of this one. Just as an orator can speak about the matters that belong to other arts, provided he has learned them—as Crassus was saying yesterday—so too do the men of other arts speak more ornately about their own subjects if they have learned something from this art. For, if some farmer has spoken eloquently about rustic matters, or a physician about diseases, or a painter about painting, or has written about them, the eloquence is not on that account to be attributed to that art. In eloquence, because there is great power in the talents of men, many achieve something of all kinds and arts even without doctrine. But as to what is the property of each—although it can be judged when you see what each one teaches—yet nothing can be more certain than this: that all other arts can perform their function without eloquence; the orator cannot maintain his name without it. So that others, if they are eloquent, have something from this man; but the orator, unless he has equipped himself with his own domestic resources, cannot seek the resources of speech from elsewhere. Then Catulus said, "Although, Antonius, your course of speech should not be hindered by an interruption..."

<summary>Antonius argues that true eloquence is the exclusive domain of the orator, even if practitioners of other arts occasionally borrow its techniques.</summary>
<keywords>eloquence, orator, art, doctrine, Crassus, Catulus, Antonius</keywords>

For I cannot help but exclaim, as that man says in the <term>Trinummus</term> <gloss>a comedy by Plautus</gloss>: you have seemed to me to express the power of the orator so subtly, and to praise it so copiously. This is indeed what an eloquent man ought to do very well, to praise eloquence; for in order to praise it, he ought to employ that very thing which he praises. But proceed further. For I agree with you that this whole matter of speaking eloquently belongs to you; and if anyone does it in another art, he is using a benefit taken from elsewhere, not his own or one proper to him." But Crassus said, "The night, Antonius, has polished you for us and restored you as a man. For in yesterday's conversation, you had described the orator to us as a rower or a porter of some single work, as Caecilius says, a man destitute of humanity and unrefined." Then Antonius said, "For yesterday, I had proposed this to myself: that if I had refuted you, I would take these students away from you. Now, with Catulus and Caesar listening, I seem to owe it not so much to fight with you, as to say what I myself think. It follows, therefore, since we must establish this man of whom we speak in the forum and before the eyes of the citizens, that we see what business we give him, and to what office we wish him to be appointed. For Crassus yesterday, when you, Catulus, and Caesar were not present, placed briefly in the distribution of the art the same thing that most Greeks have placed; nor did he reveal what he himself thought, but what was said by them: that there are two primary kinds of questions in which eloquence is involved: one infinite, the other certain. The infinite one seems to me to be that in which something is sought in a general way..."

<summary>Catulus praises Antonius for his eloquent defense of oratory, and Antonius begins to outline the nature of the orator's role and the division of rhetorical questions.</summary>

pages.479:
# DE ORATORE

as for example: whether eloquence should be sought, whether honors should be sought. The certain one, however, is that in which something is sought regarding persons and in a constituted and defined matter; such are the things which are involved in the forum and in the disputes and cases of citizens. These seem to me to be placed either in settling a lawsuit or in giving counsel. For that third kind, which was touched upon by Crassus and, as I hear, by that very Aristotle who most illuminated these things, even if it is necessary, is still less essential." "What is that?" said Catulus. "Are they panegyrics <note>original: "laudationes"</note>? For I see that as a third kind." "So it is," said Antonius, "and in that kind, I know that both I and all who were present were vehemently delighted when your mother, Popillia, was praised by you. I believe this honor was bestowed upon her as the first woman in our state. But it does not seem to me that everything we speak about should be recalled to art and to precepts. For from those sources from which all precepts of speaking ornately will be taken, it will also be permissible to adorn a panegyric; and there is no need for those elements. For if no one transmits them, who is there who does not know what things in a man are to be praised? For once those things are posited, which Crassus said at the beginning of that oration of his which he held against his colleague the Censor—which things are given to men by nature or fortune; that in those things he could bear to be surpassed with an even mind; but in those things which men could prepare for themselves, he could not bear to be surpassed—whoever praises anyone will understand that he must set forth the gifts of fortune. These are: lineage, wealth, relatives, friends, power, health, beauty, strength, genius, and other things which are either of the body or external. If he had them, he used them well; if he did not have them, he lacked them wisely; if he lost them, he bore it moderately. Then, what things he whom he praises did or endured wisely, liberally, bravely, justly, magnificently, piously, gratefully, humanely, or finally with any virtue."

<summary>Antonius discusses the third type of oratory, panegyric, arguing that it does not require formal precepts but draws upon the same natural principles as other types of speech.</summary>
<keywords>Aristotle, panegyrics, Popillia, Crassus, virtue, fortune</keywords>

These things, and those which are of that kind, he who wishes to praise anyone will easily see; and he who wishes to disparage will see the opposites." "Why, therefore, do you hesitate," said Catulus, "to make this a third kind, since it is included in the nature of things? For it should not be omitted from the number just because it is easier." "Because I do not wish," he said, "to treat everything that sometimes falls to the orator, however excellent it may be, as if nothing could be said without its own precepts. For testimony must also often be given, and sometimes even more accurately, as it was necessary for me to do against Sex. Titius, a seditious and turbulent citizen. In giving that testimony, I explained all the plans of my consulship by which I had resisted that Tribune of the plebs for the sake of the republic, and I exposed what I judged to have been done by him against the republic. I was detained for a long time; I heard much; I answered much. Does it please you, then, when you are teaching about eloquence, to also transmit something about giving testimony as if it were an art?" "Certainly there is no need," said Catulus. "What if, as often happens to the greatest men, mandates must be explained either in the senate by a commander, or to a commander, or to a king, or to some people by the senate? Is this part of cases also to be considered as needing to be numbered or instructed by its own precepts because a more accurate kind of oration must be used in such cases?"

<summary>Antonius argues against including testimony and diplomatic mandates as formal types of oratory, suggesting that an eloquent man can handle these tasks without specialized rhetorical rules.</summary>
<keywords>testimony, Sex. Titius, consulship, Tribune of the plebs, republic, eloquence</keywords>
pages.481:
# DE ORATORE

"Not at all," said Catulus. "For the ability acquired from other things and cases will not be lacking to an eloquent man in such matters." "Therefore," he said, "those things which must often be done eloquently—and which I mentioned a little while ago when I was praising eloquence as belonging to the orator—neither have any place of their own in the division of parts, nor a certain kind of precepts. Yet they must be done no less eloquently than those things which are spoken in a lawsuit: reproof, exhortation, consolation. There is none of these that does not require the highest ornaments of speaking, but these matters do not seek precepts from art." "I clearly agree," said Catulus. "But come now," said Antonius, "what kind of orator, and what kind of man in speaking, do you think it requires to write history?" "If as the Greeks have written," said Catulus, "a great one. If as our own, there is no need for an orator; it is enough not to be a liar." "And yet," said Antonius, "so that you do not despise our own, the Greeks themselves wrote thus in the beginning, as our Cato, as Pictor, as Piso. For history was nothing other than the compilation of annals. For the sake of retaining this matter and the public memory, from the beginning of Roman affairs up to the pontificate of P. Mucius, the Pontifex Maximus committed all the events of each year to writing, brought them forth onto a tablet, and set up the board at his house so that the people might have the power of knowing; and these are even now called the Great Annals <term>annales maximi</term> <gloss>official annual records of the Roman priests</gloss>. Many have followed this manner of writing; they left behind nothing but monuments of times, men, places, and deeds without any ornaments. Therefore, just as Pherecydes, Hellanicus were among the Greeks..."

<summary>Antonius and Catulus discuss the nature of historical writing, contrasting the plain annals of early Roman historians with the more eloquent tradition of the Greeks.</summary>
<keywords>history, Cato, Pictor, Piso, annals, Pontifex Maximus, P. Mucius, Pherecydes, Hellanicus</keywords>

and very many others: such were our Cato, and Pictor, and Piso. They neither hold the means by which an oration is adorned—for these things have only recently been brought here—and, as long as it is understood what they are saying, they think the only praise for speaking is brevity." He raised himself a little and added a greater tone of voice to history, that excellent man, Crassus's associate, Antipater. The rest were not adorners of deeds, but merely narrators. "It is," said Catulus, "as you say. But that very Caelius neither distinguished history by the variety of places, nor did he polish that work with the arrangement of words and a light and equitable flow of speech, but, as a man neither learned nor especially apt for speaking, he hewed it as he could. Yet he surpassed, as you say, those before him." "It is no wonder," said Antonius, "if that matter has not yet been illustrated in our language. For no one among our people studies eloquence except to shine in cases and in the forum. Among the Greeks, however, the most eloquent men, removed from forensic cases, applied themselves to writing history, just as they were illustrious in other matters. For we have received that even Herodotus, who was the first to adorn this kind, was not involved in cases at all. And yet his eloquence is such that it greatly delights me, as much as I can understand things written in Greek. And after him, Thucydides, in my opinion, easily surpassed everyone in the art of speaking. He is so dense with the frequency of facts that he almost matches the number of his thoughts with the number of his words; he is, furthermore, so apt and pressed with his words that you do not know whether the facts are illustrated by the oration or the words by the thoughts."

<summary>Antonius critiques Roman historiography while praising the Greek masters Herodotus and Thucydides for their unique blend of eloquence and substance.</summary>

# DE ORATORE

"Yet we have not even received him, although he was involved in the republic, from the number of those who used to plead cases. It is said that he wrote those books when he was removed from the republic and, as is wont to happen to every best man at Athens, when he had been driven into exile. The Syracusan Philistus followed him; he, while being a most intimate friend of the tyrant Dionysius, spent his leisure time in writing history; he has most of all, as it seems to me, imitated Thucydides. But later, as if from the most famous workshop of a rhetorician, two outstanding in talent, Theopompus and Ephorus, driven by their teacher Isocrates, betook themselves to history; they never touched cases at all. Finally, Xenophon, that Socratic, having started from philosophy, and later Callisthenes, a companion of Alexander, wrote history; and this one indeed in an almost rhetorical manner, but the former used a certain softer tone, one that does not have that impetus of an orator; perhaps less vehement, but still, as it seems to me, somewhat sweeter. The youngest of all these is Timaeus, but as far as I can judge, by far the most learned, most abundant in the variety of his facts and thoughts, and not unpolished in the composition of his words. He brought great eloquence to his writing, but no forensic practice." When he had said these things, Catulus said, "What is this, Caesar? Where are those who deny that Antonius knows Greek? How many historians did he name? How expertly, how properly did he speak about each one?" "By Hercules," said Catulus, "admiring that, I now cease to wonder at that which I was wondering at much more before: that he..."

# PREFACE

## PREFACE OF CUTHBERT TONSTALL, BISHOP OF DURHAM, TO THE READER.

<margin>Jer. 9.</margin>
<note>An ornate decorative initial 'Q' containing floral scrollwork within a circular frame.</note>Who will give water to my head, and a fountain of tears to my eyes, so that I may weep day and night for the misery of the age of our holy mother the Church? For whereas in past centuries she was infested by many and various heresies, <margin>dist. 7. di. 1. Can. haer.</margin> she slaughtered them all with the sword of the spirit as soon as they were born, prostrating them in such a way that it was thought their roots could not sprout again for those who followed. But now those that seemed buried by long oblivion not only raise their heads and revive, but also bring forth new and numerous offspring, more pestilential than themselves. New monsters of dogmas also emerge, and their new heralds, <term>pseudapostoloi</term> <gloss>false apostles</gloss>, not like Paul, <margin>2 Cor. 10.</margin> unskilled in speech but not in knowledge, rather breathing out their poison with great virulence of tongue. They have nothing in their mouths but that the light of the Gospel is finally appearing, that old darkness has been chased away, and that evangelical liberty has been restored. Yet these men, in place of wisdom and knowledge, display gross ignorance of divine matters; and that ignorance is supplied and sustained by supreme arrogance, a brazen face, and incomparable impudence. Indeed, they promise that they will render the most abstruse passages of the Prophets and the Apocalypse clearer than light, and what will they not do? As if they had been snatched up above the third heaven, like Paul himself, <margin>2 Cor. 12.</margin> they dare to blather anything rashly, and do not fear to chatter words that a man not bereft of his mind would be ashamed to utter. They fill the world with their books and papers, and the more unskilled each one is, the more they arrogate knowledge to themselves, daring anything. They strive to strip the most holy Eucharist of its dignity and reduce it to the order of common and edible bread and wine. Truly, they who assert that it has neither the presence of Christ nor any truth of His body, and they defend this in published books.
pages.8:
# PREFACE

They reject the meaning of the words of Christ accepted by the Apostles, and the consensus of the holy mother Church, which follows its own leaders in this matter. They affirm that they follow the words of the Holy Scripture, that they embrace them alone, and that they cling to them as if to sacred anchors. They do this with the intention that, if anyone should charge them with any error, they may flee to a meaning of words invented from their own brains, maintaining that they alone follow the straight path.
<margin>Lib. 1. cap. 1. aduers. haeres.</margin>
Irenaeus, however, says: just as if someone, having dismantled the image of a king fashioned from precious gems by an admirable artist, and having fashioned that beautiful form of human appearance into the ridiculous figure of a fox, should wish it to be considered in place of the king's image because of the splendor of the gems: in the same way, these men, fitting the words of God to their own fables, demand that faith be placed in their own inventions. For which of the heretics has ever set up some part of the Sacred Scripture, twisted from its true meaning, as a shield? The result is that each one constitutes himself his own sole judge, and admits no other, indeed, not even the Church of Christ, the spouse, the very pillar of truth. They contend that General Councils, even ecumenical ones, have clearly erred when they dissent from their own delusions; they assert that one must stand by the words of the Scripture and not depart from them. And although there are often many in one house holding different and conflicting opinions, yet no one of them is found with such modesty as to yield to another; each one contends that the truth stands with himself alone. Thus, they force the truth, which is consistent with itself and cannot dissent from itself, to collapse in the streets. Alas for the miserable condition of our holy mother the Church, which is now forced to endure preachers from the pulpit who <margin>Isa. 5.</margin> turn black into white, who call darkness light and light darkness, who call evil good and good evil, who call bitter sweet and sweet bitter. But while I consider with myself what should be done in such great evils, that saying of Ecclesiastes occurs first: All things have a time, and there is a time to be silent, and a time to speak. If I remain silent, I fear that I must say with the prophet Isaiah, Woe <margin>Isa. 6.</margin>
pages.9:
# TO THE READER.

to me because I have kept silent. I fear that if I bury the talent, whatever it may be, that was given to me in the earth, I will be rebuked and hear, "Why did you not give my money to the bank, so that I, on my arrival, might have exacted it with interest?" And also that saying: "He who does not gather with me, scatters." What if someone should also object, saying: "You see many impious men who not only think themselves learned, but many babblers and brawlers who thrust mere trifles in their papers upon the common people, unworthy to have good hours spent on reading them, and you see the truth itself attacked by those very things before your eyes; and you, a shepherd of Christ's flock, will you not defend the truth? Will you not keep wolves away from the fold of Christ with all your might?" Meditating on these things long and deeply with myself, I finally decided to break the silence, to follow Christ as my leader, who does not abandon those who hope in Him, and to repel the weapons thrown too impiously at the sacred mysteries with the shield of the word of God, seeking not the rivulets and stagnant pools of evils, but the very fountains and springs from which all these evils emanated. Furthermore, in general, among all the attackers of the Catholic faith in this turbulent storm, nothing is so frequent in their mouths as the proclamation of faith, yet if you look deeper, they have no faith in their hearts. For although you may object with the words of Christ, clearer than any light, for the truth of the mysteries, they immediately flee to a perverse meaning invented by them, alien to all truth, as they believe there is nothing so high or recondite in divine things that they cannot attain it by their own reason. They measure all the works of God by human reason, and rather than confess that Christ did something beyond their grasp, they twist everything to tropes and figures. <margin>John 1.</margin> As if Christ, the Son of God from eternity, through whom all things were made, incarnate as man in time, could not do anything by divine power beyond other mortals. But if those who seek to drink in the rays of the Sun with physical eyes do not accomplish what they intend, but are deprived of the very light by which they thrive and sustain innumerable inconveniences, how much more will he be blinded who seeks to fix his gaze on that eternal light, and to attain it with mortal reasons?
pages.10:
And since every intellect must be brought into captivity by faith in obedience to Christ, human genius so exalts itself against the height of God that it judges impossible that which it cannot investigate by searching out its reason, unmindful of that word of Christ: "With God all things are possible." Therefore, unless You, Christ, restrain the stupid audacity of those men who so wantonly insult Your mysteries, and protect Your Church from their insane rashness, no one who attempts to defend Your spouse will succeed. But if You, without whom mortals can do nothing that is right, rising up, favor our undertakings, <margin>Ps. 67.</margin> Your enemies will be dissipated immediately, and those who hate You will flee from Your face, and all other things will follow in tranquility. Relying, therefore, on Your help, O Christ, we pray that You illuminate us with the light of Your grace, and we will undertake the intended matter safely without fear, so that we may prove from Your own words that the truth of Your body and blood is in the Eucharist, and with Your favor, without whom we can do nothing, we will endeavor to eradicate the perverse dogmas of those who oppose this truth from the minds of the deceived faithful.

Farewell.

In the Year of our Lord 1551.

# ON CHRIST JESUS
## SON OF GOD AND SON OF MAN
## in one person, and in two natures: and of
## His holy conversation among men, death,
## resurrection, and ascension into heaven.

<note>An ornamental initial letter 'A' entwined with vine and leaf motifs.</note>Before we attempt to treat any of the mysteries, we think it will be beneficial to insert here at the beginning what Epiphanius collected in summary at the end of his work, which he entitled *Panarium* <gloss>Bread Basket/Medicine Chest</gloss>, concerning the holy conversation of Christ among men on earth, His death, resurrection, and ascension into heaven. This is so that, once the immense greatness of the mysteries of Christ, the Son of God and Son of man, the creator of the mysteries themselves, is known, along with His inenarrable power and ineffable love with which He pursues the human race, we may more fully embrace, venerate, and admire these mysteries instituted by Him for our sake. The words of Epiphanius are those which follow.

<margin>Baruch 3.</margin>
<margin>Luke 4.</margin>
> After these things, He was seen on earth, and He lived among men. And because He returned from the Jordan, He was manifest and truly tempted by the devil in the desert, and He hungered afterwards on account of the consequence and truth of His coming in the flesh. And because He chose disciples, and preached the truth, and cured the sick,
pages.12: slept, hungered, traveled, performed the signs of God, raised the dead, restored sight to the blind, and made the lame and paralytic strong. And because He preached the truth, the Gospel itself, the kingdom of heaven, His own kindness toward men, and likewise that of the Father and the Holy Spirit. And because He underwent the passion for us in truth, in the flesh, and in perfect humanity. He suffered in truth on the cross, the presence of His deity remaining, but not turned toward suffering, but alien to and immutable by passion. Thus these two consequences are clearly considered in Christ suffering for us in the flesh, the truth of the passion having arisen while remaining in the deity, not with man existing by himself and the deity by itself, but with the deity present simultaneously, yet not suffering because of the sincerity and incomparability of its essence, while He Himself suffered in the flesh and felt death in the flesh, yet lived always in the deity, and raised the dead, the body being buried in truth. And because He remained lifeless for three days without breathing and without movement, and was wrapped in a shroud, and placed in a tomb closed by a stone with seals added, the deity not being enclosed, the deity not being buried, but together with the holy soul descending to the underworld, and taking away from there the captivity of souls, breaking the sting of death, bursting through the locks and adamantine bars, and dissolving the sorrows of death by His own power: so that
pages.13:
He returned with His soul, the soul not being left in the underworld, when neither did the flesh itself see corruption, since the deity always present to it raised it up, so that the Lord and God Himself rose again, the Word and Son of God with soul and body, and the entire organ united to His organ into the Spirit Himself, that is to say, existing as a spiritual body, which at one time had been subject to touch, and handed over to scourges by the voluntary will of the deity, and permitted to be tempted by the devil, and to feel hunger and sleep, and weariness, sadness, and grief. This holy body itself is united henceforth to the deity: the deity being endlessly present simultaneously to that holy body which suffered such things.

For He rose again and united it into Himself into one spirit, into one unity, into one glorification, into one deity of His own.

<margin>John 20.</margin>
For He appeared in truth, and was handled by Thomas; and He took food with the Apostles, and lived with them for forty days and forty nights; indeed, He entered while the doors were closed, and having entered, He showed the nerves and bones, the mark of the nails and the mark of the lance, that it was truly His body, and that it was joined into one unity and into one deity, no longer waiting to suffer, no longer dying, as the holy Apostle says:

<margin>Rom. 6.</margin>
The Lord rose again, He no longer dies, death no longer has dominion over Him, remaining always passible, impassible, and devoid of passion
pages.14: divine with body and soul, and the entire humanity. And because He, existing as God Himself, ascended into the heavens and sits at the right hand of the Father in glory, not having put off the holy body, but having united it into a spiritual one in the perfection of one deity: just as it will also be regarding our bodies, <margin>1 Cor. 15.</margin> which are now sown animal bodies, they will rise as spiritual bodies: which are now sown in corruption, they will rise in incorruptibility: which are now sown in death, they will rise in immortality. If, therefore, our bodies are thus, how much more that holy, and inenarrable, and incomparable, and sincere one, which is united to God, which is one henceforth and uniform? Just as the Apostle also testifies concerning this, <margin>2 Cor. 5.</margin> saying: "Even if we knew Christ according to the flesh, yet now we no longer know Him." Not that He severed the flesh from the deity, but that it remains and is united to God: not, however, according to the flesh anymore, but according to the spirit, <margin>Rom. 1.</margin> as he says, "of sanctification from the resurrection from the dead of Jesus Christ our Lord," having this God simultaneously devoid of passion, and who suffered and was buried, and who rose again, and ascended into glory, to come to judge the living and the dead, as he says in truth, of whose kingdom there will be no end. For this our holy mother Church believes, just as it was truly preached and truly established: That we shall all fall asleep and rise again with this body, with this soul, with

Whether the intellect disposes to love and remember, and conversely. Whether the intellect can believe and understand at one and the same time. Whether the intellect creates knowledge within itself. It is asked by what means the intellect creates species. Whether the intellect with its species commands the will and memory to present that species. Just as we apply the questions of the rule to the intellect, so they can be applied to other powers in their own way.

### Questions of the table.

It is asked whether the world is eternal. Go to column b.c.d. and take the negative, and you will find in chamber b.c.t.b that if it is eternal, there are many eternities <note>original: "drentes spe" — likely a corruption of "diferentes species" or "diferentes eternitates"</note> and they are concordant through chamber b.c.t.e against chamber b.c.d., which is impossible. Whence it follows that the negative question is to be held, and this the rule b proves. It is asked whether God can be as infinite through his greatness as through his eternity. Go to column c.d.e. and to chamber c.d.t.c, holding the affirmative against chamber c.d.t.d. Whether God can be as much through eternity as through intellect. Go to column d.e.f. and to chamber d.e.t.d. Whether God is as powerful through his power as through his understanding and loving. Go to column e.f.g. and take the affirmative by chamber e.f.t.e and by chamber e.f.t.f. And by chamber e.f.t.g until the whole column is finished. Whether in God his intel
pages.55:
lect and will are greater than his virtue. Go to column f.g.h. and take the negative through all the chambers of that column, drawing out the meanings of the chambers. Whether divine truth is as virtuous through equal correlatives as divine will. Go to column g.h.i. and take the affirmative through all the chambers of that column. Whether in God his virtue and his truth and his grace have that by which they are equal, and removed from time and place and minority. Go to column h.i.k. and take the affirmative through all the chambers.

¶ Of the questions of the exhaustion of the third figure.
In chamber b.c. it is said that goodness is great. Now it is asked whether goodness is great and what is its greatness, and goodness, and greatness, in what they agree. And whether they can agree without difference. And it must be answered that goodness is great, as is clear by the definition of greatness. And its greatness is to have correlatives, as is clear by the second species of rule c, and they agree: because goodness is great through greatness and conversely. Indeed, they could in no way agree without the difference of their correlatives. And let these things suffice concerning the exhaustion of the third figure for the sake of brevity. For through these things which we have said of it, the artist can solve and make questions through the other chambers.
pages.56:
¶ **Of the questions of the multiplication of the fourth figure**
It is asked by what mode the intellect conditions itself to be general through general understanding. Go to the multiplication of the fourth figure and see by what mode the intellect multiplies the conditions with which it multiplies objects and its understanding, so that through many and great sciences it becomes general and clothed with many habits. And let these things concerning the multiplication of the fourth figure suffice for the sake of brevity.

**Of the questions of the mixture of principles and rules.**
It is asked whether goodness is discursive through greatness, duration, etc., and conversely. And it must be answered that it is, as is signified through the third figure by making the subject the predicate. It is asked what goodness is in greatness, duration, etc. To which it must be answered that in greatness it is great, and in duration it is durable. It is asked what goodness has in greatness, etc. To which it must be answered that in it, it has its correlatives, great in greatness and durable in duration. And just as we exemplify concerning goodness, so it can be exemplified concerning other principles in their own way. And let these things concerning mixture suffice in their own way.

**Of the questions of the nine subjects. And first of God.**
It is asked whether God is. And it must be answered that he is, as proven in the questions of the first figure. It is asked what God is. And it must be answered that God
pages.57:
is the being that acts as much in itself as it itself is. Through the second species of rule c, it is asked what God has in himself essentially. To which it must be answered that he has his correlatives, without which he could not have immense and eternal reasons. Through the third species, it is asked what God is in another. To which it must be answered that he is creating, governing, and such. Through the fourth species of rule c, it is asked what God has in another. And it must be answered that he has in another power and dominion, and in humans judgment and the act of grace, mercy, patience, and piety. And let these things concerning God suffice for the sake of brevity.

¶ Of the questions of angels.

It is asked whether angels exist. And it must be answered that they do. For if that which is less like God exists, much more so that which is more like God. Furthermore, if there is something that is composed of intellectual and corporal, much more so that which is composed of intellectual and intellectual. Moreover, if angels did not exist, the scale of difference and concordance would be exhausted, and consequently the world, which is impossible. It is asked of what the angel is and whose it is. And it must be answered by rule d that it is of itself; its essence cannot be punctual nor linear. And by the second species of the same rule, it is of its spiritual correlatives, that is, of its actives, passives, and acts, from which it is composed
pages.58:
active, and through passives it is receptive, and through acts it is an act existing between actives and passives. By the third species, it must be said that the angel is God's. And let these things concerning angels suffice for the sake of brevity.

# Of the questions of the Heavens.

Whether the heaven moves itself. And it must be answered that it does, so that its principles may have substantial and proper correlatives through their constellations. Whether the heaven moves itself to a place, and it must be answered that it does, in itself and in lower things, circularly, but not outside itself. The reason for this is because outside itself it has no action, nor can it have. Whether an angel moves the heaven, and it must be answered that it does not; because if it moved it, then the actives by the flow of correlatives would be below and passives above, and also by its form it would not move the elements nor the elementals, but by its matter, which is impossible. It is asked whether the heaven has a motive soul. And it must be answered that it does; for otherwise the sensitive and vegetative would not have motive souls, nor would the elements have motion. It is asked by the first species of rule e, why is the heaven. And it must be said that it is because it is constituted from its form and matter. Through the second species of rule e, it is asked why the heaven is, and it must be said so that lower beings may have motion. And let these things concerning the heaven suffice for the sake of brevity.
pages.59:
¶ Of the questions of the 4th subject, which is man.
It is asked whether man can have greater knowledge of God by affirming or by denying, and it must be answered that by affirming, for God is not through those things without which he himself is, but through those without which he cannot be. It is asked why man acts through a specific form; go to the second species of rule e, and there the solution is implied. Whether man, augmenting his acts, augments his essence; and it must be answered that no man acts upon himself. It is asked when man desires to remember and cannot remember, which of these fails first, either memory or intellect; to which it must be said that memory itself renders the species of antiquity more quickly by nature to the intellect than to the will. It is asked of what soul and body men are composed; and it must be answered that in man, corporal and spiritual goodness compose one goodness, and so of others. It is asked what the life of man is, to which it must be answered that it is that form which is composed of vegetative, sensitive, imaginative, and rationative. What is the death of man; it must be answered that it is the dissolution of the elementative, vegetative, sensitive, imaginative, and rationative power. It is asked whether man is visible, and it must be answered that he is not; for vision can see only color and figure. It is asked whether in man, intellect and memory are the same power, and it must be answered
pages.60:
no, because if they were the same power, the intellect would not be successive in acquiring species, nor would it hand them over to oblivion, nor would it be ignorant of them. Again, because it would be too strong in its object against the liberty of the will. And let these things said concerning man suffice for the sake of brevity.

### Of the questions of the imaginative.

Whether the imaginative imagines imaginable things in its own way just as the sensitive senses sensible things. It is asked what is the cause why the imaginative abstracts species from sensible things. It is asked what the imaginative is. Whether the imaginative has correlatives. Whether the imaginative augments itself by augmenting its act. Whether the imaginative is a higher power than the sensitive. Whether the imaginative has specific instincts and appetites. By what mode does the sensitive impede the act of the imaginative. Why is the imaginative not as powerful in sensible or sensed things as the sensitive; go to the subject of the imaginative. It is asked whether the sensitive senses the imaginative. And it must be answered that lower powers do not act upon higher ones.

### Of the questions of the sensitive.

It is asked which of these powers senses hunger and thirst, either the taste or the touch. And it must be answered that it is that which disposes the object the most. Whether the taste senses hunger or thirst with instinct and appetite, just as vision senses the colored with
pages.61:
color. Go to the second species of rule c.
It is asked from what the sensitive senses sensible things. And it must be answered that every particular sense senses its sensible object through a specific form, just as a colored subject subsisting in crystal colors it. Whether the sensitive has punctual and linear quantities. And it must be answered that the sensitive reaches an object from afar just as quickly as from near. Whether the sensitive, just as it has a common sense, so also has a common power, instinct, and appetite. It is asked what the sensitive is. With what is the sensitive particular and common. From what does the sensitive live and is nourished. Whether the sensitive is sensed; go to the subject of the sensitive.

### Of the vegetative.

Whether the vegetative acts through its species.
Whether the vegetative has any reason by which it is common and particular just as the sensitive.
Whether the quantity of the vegetative is punctual or linear. It is asked what the vegetative is and what it has in itself through the second species of rule c.
It is asked from what the vegetative lives and is nourished and grows, and in what subject it is planted. What is the death of the vegetative; go to the subject of the vegetative in which the solutions to the aforesaid questions are implied.

# Guillaume Budé to Richard Pace, Greetings.

I would be ashamed not to have written back to you for so long, having been challenged again, if my negligence could in any way be blamed on a fault of mine. On the fifth day before the Ides of December <note>December 9th</note>, while you were staying in Bruges, you wrote that you were awaiting the publication of your book on the *fruit which is perceived from learning*, and that you would soon send me a copy. Upon receiving your letter, I heard a rumor that you were to leave for the City of Rome on the very first opportunity to undertake an embassy. Therefore, although I was eager to establish a friendship with you through this type of service and the exchange of letters for the future, I decided it was better to hold off until I had more certain news about you. Recently, however, the royal herald <term>caduceator</term> <gloss>herald/messenger</gloss> wrote to me from the King's entourage that while he was there, you had asked him if he knew Budé, and how he was faring. Through your words, he bade me ask if there was anything I needed that might be found in Britain, which might fall within your office to provide. You were, he said, eager to render me some strenuous and kind service. He added how much you flourished in authority and wealth in that kingdom, and how much favor you enjoyed with the King. I was so cheered by this news that I have kept your letter almost in my bosom, showing it to every friend I encountered, and even thrusting it before the eyes of some who usually blame my excessive love of letters as something harmful.
pages.12: I certainly seem to myself to be foolish at times in such matters out of joy, and to come into the public eye more magnificently than my own spirits deserve, being a man who is not exactly a great admirer of himself, nor a sufficiently kind evaluator of his own industry, as I seem to those who are fair and good judges of the things that come out of my workshop to judge them as worth less than they could be if only the favor due them had come to us. However, since I have established the system of my ledgers, which I have been keeping for a long time in this trade of <term>Philologia</term> <gloss>love of learning/scholarship</gloss>, in such a way that I have never assigned a single page to profit, but have always desired to fill the whole book with the contributions of friends, the matter has turned out for me (unless I am mistaken) in such a way that I can compensate for a loss of fortune, which is not to be despised, with the wealth of a copious and manifold friendship. But since I have sought many friends, and among them distinguished men, in my own country, by whose authority I have often been able to bring protection and even subsidies to my own fortunes and those of my people if I had turned my mind and eye to the task, it happens that I know not how I think my reason for this insane love of letters, which many even think to be madness, is better sustained by foreign friendships, and I exult more in those friends whom I cannot use to make my affairs sound or more ample, nor even enjoy for the sake of the mind, and visit familiarly. Whence it happens that I bring forth and sell the letters of foreigners among our own people like exotic and more marketable goods.
pages.13: Nothing could have been more opportune than this latest letter of yours, which caused me to kiss my book *De Asse* <note>On the Roman Coinage</note>, which has won me such and so many friends in one region, and has augmented my circumstances with such a splendid addition. For you say that Linacre, More, Tunstall, and Latymer, along with some others, are your associates in love and even (if I can bring myself to believe it) admiration for me. While Tunstall and Linacre are already joined to me through an exchange of letters, perhaps the others will become better known to me in time, if the occasion should arise. I learned from reading your recently published book that these same men are your great friends, and in that book, most learned Pace, you proved your genius and scholarship to me. I marvel at and kiss that spirit of yours, so devoted and addicted to the study of letters that, even though admitted into the innermost court, you have not sent the Muses away, nor ceased to speak well of their followers. For this reason, I think I must take greater care not to admit such a fault against my own reputation, that I should seem to you to have yielded in this private, small-town leisure while you are busy with courtly duties. Unless, perhaps, this praise is proper to your King, to whom you gave most clear testimony in your book: not only as a man of a mind inclined toward learned men, but also as one not lightly imbued with learning itself.
pages.14: As for this latter point, while I have brought myself to believe it with some temperament of faith rather than discarding it as if rendering testimony too kindly to your benevolent and munificent King, I still think it is, by the very nature of the fates, royal in this age to admire letters, to honor those who study them, and to hold learning itself in high esteem. I have persuaded myself of this regarding that King beyond a doubt, because he always has Linacre, Pace, Tunstall, More, Latymer, and, as it were, a certain Palladian cohort in his palace, so that, girded and instructed by this bodyguard, the King appears in public and proceeds to councils as a more majestic figure than other kings. Whether this is true, or whether I am inflating it by imagining it greater than it is, it is nonetheless a pleasure to believe that it is really so, and I confess to you frankly that our own royal court has not produced such an example within the memory of men now living, otherwise it would be far the leader of all in the West. By my faith, I consider this to be attributed more to the fixed and unchangeable decree of the Fates than to the fault of our own kings and princes: that it is not so much that they themselves wish learned men to be kept away from their court, as that the learned themselves voluntarily remove themselves far from the court, by a fatal discord, no doubt, between courtly and elegant wits. And although very many courtiers marvel at this and are indignant, no one has yet appeared who deserves well of both the republic and the world of letters, so as to resolve that foul discord and accommodate the dignity of letters to the French court.
pages.15: ...although Guy de Rochefort, the Chancellor, aspired to that glory, if the Fates and the Parcae <note>the Fates</note> had allowed it. For it is thought to be more than a hope that it should occur to princes voluntarily after the passing of King Charles, who, it is believed, had begun to divert a portion of his liberality toward the favor of letters. As for the one who now reigns, just as he is by nature more fortunate and abundant, and all the gifts of body and mind are much more wealthy and instructed, so his studies and kindness have been diverted elsewhere by some sinister fate. As far as I am concerned, I have now been away from courtly life for more than eighteen years, during which I could enjoy my studies more lengthily and freely; for toward the end of his life, Charles had summoned me to court, as I was already becoming known for the recommendation of my literary studies, in which I had made some progress. But I had already begun to be on the tongues of men primarily for my study of the Greek language, which I then loved without a rival. Because our people wondered at this, a rumor had spread through the court (for I was already the King’s Secretary, not just one of his secret clerks), even though I practiced my studies of letters in hiding, far from observers and teachers, so do not wonder that I made little progress in so much time. About eight months after the death of that same King, when I felt myself degenerating while in his entourage, I found an opportunity and withdrew myself from court, and ever since I felt that I had returned to my own true nature, no one has been able to persuade me...
pages.16: ...to return to study again, even if I have visited the court for a few days at times, and have meanwhile performed an embassy to Rome. Therefore, as for what you write to me about peace, as if I have some role in the business of courtly affairs, I will not allow you to be mistaken any longer. I want you to understand that I have no business with the court, and absolutely no commerce with courtiers. What I think of them, you can easily understand from my digressions in my book *De Asse*, if you ever intend to occupy a few of your hours badly. I perform the duties of war and peace in much the same way. Kings are accustomed to have their secretaries partly in this city, where the centenary court has its seat, and partly in their entourage, but with free passage for everyone to and fro. I have joined myself to the urban ones, as I said, since the time I bade farewell to the court. For here our family has its household gods, not the most obscure; of whom eighteen children born of the same parents, twelve of us survived as heirs to our father. Therefore, I can help you with your wishes for peace, but not with my counsel. For I only spend time among the courtiers at the time when the King is staying in this city, from which he has been absent for a year now. However, since it is not given to me as it is to you in the Prince’s council to judge concerning the maintenance of leagues and peace, it will be a pleasure to whisper in your ear what I think and hear regarding these same matters, since I see that plans for peace are close to your heart, as a man who is peaceful and a lover of humanity.
pages.17: No one of sense would deny that the face of peace is pleasant and festive, and its name, striking and sweet. You, my dear friend, say that you disagree entirely with both kingdoms about leaving things as they are. This is why you embrace and wrap yourself in peace, as being a good thing for discourse and one that surrounds learning; while you loathe war as a destroyer and ward it off as something that is, in fact, an enemy of philosophy, and which has severely damaged the affairs of both our kingdoms in times past. There are those, however, among the more shameless who, while perhaps clever at guessing what concerns war and what concerns treaties, are not, I think, disposed with the same love of life as you and I. They say the Britons are now content to rest in what has been agreed upon and to be satisfied with the present, until the matters concerning the oath are more securely established for them; yet, once this is well and perfectly secured, they say you will no longer stand firmly by what has been agreed, but will seize upon any opportunity that arises. This is what they say, as is often the way with those who make treaties. I, for my part, join you in praying that things well and beautifully established may remain firmly in place, if not for a longer time, at least while we are still alive, so that we may know how to write back to one another as long as it is permitted to us, and whether it pleases you and your friends there to make our friendship known among those who are now educated and those who will be born hereafter, just as it has been from above according to the...

Furthermore, it has been truly preached, and certainly confirmed, and is believed, that some shall rise to eternal life, and others to eternal judgment, as it is written in the Gospels. Thus far Epiphanius.

To this must be added what Cyril writes in the Ephesian creed: We do not say that the flesh is changed into the nature of the deity, nor that the ineffable nature of the Word of God is transferred into the nature of flesh. For it is entirely immovable and immutable, remaining the same forever according to the scriptures. And when He was made visible, while still an infant and in the cradle and the bosom of the virgin mother, He filled every creature, as God, and sat with the Begetter. For the Godhead is without quantity and without magnitude, and cannot be circumscribed. Thus far Cyril.

# ON MYSTERIES
## AND SACRAMENTS.

<note>A woodcut depicts a bearded man in robes and a crown, seated at a desk, representing a biblical figure such as King David or Solomon.</note>When about to speak on mysteries, it is necessary to explore above all what a mystery is and what it contains, lest, by speaking many words about mysteries, I act like one running outside the racecourse set for the contenders, who merely exhausts himself in vain by laboring, and gains nothing but weariness: so, too, I myself, not containing myself within the bounds of the mysteries while arguing, would be unable to grasp the palm while wandering from the goal.

First, therefore, it must be observed that "mystery" is a Greek term, although frequently used by the Latins, and it signified something secret, or that under which something secret lies hidden, which is not perfected except by some hidden rite of holy things. For "mysteries" are sometimes called the secret and hidden affairs of men, which it is considered sacrilege to speak of in public, as it is with Solomon in Proverbs: "Do not associate with him who reveals mysteries and walks deceitfully, and opens his lips." And in Ecclesiasticus: "To uncover the mysteries of a friend is the despair of an unhappy soul." Likewise, the sacred secrets of God are called mysteries, as it is with Matthew regarding him who sows his seed: where Christ says to His disciples, "To you it is given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to the rest..."

<margin>1 Tim. 3</margin>God he says, "Great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifested in the flesh, justified in the spirit, seen by angels, preached to the Gentiles, believed in the world, received up in glory." And

And John in the Apocalypse

Sacred signs are also called "mysteries" by the Greeks and "sacraments" by the Latins, as Paul to the Ephesians
<margin>Eph. 5</margin>speaking of the union of husband and wife says: "This is a great sacrament, but I speak in Christ and the Church." In which sense mysteries are sometimes taken by the Latins: as Paul says to the Corinthians,
<margin>1 Cor. 4</margin>"Let a man so consider us, as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God." Furthermore, it is not our intention to treat of every kind of mystery in this work, lest we seem to think more highly than is sober: and we are conscious of not having drawn from the Spirit of God so much that we might be able to understand all the hidden and secret mysteries of God as is proper, or to pursue and illustrate each one with appropriate words.

Therefore, in this treatise, we shall affirm that the truth of the body and blood of the Lord is in the sacrament of the Eucharist, if Christ grants it to us, using both terms, "mystery" and "sacrament," interchangeably, but more frequently the name "sacrament," which is more familiar to Latin ears. But before we approach our undertaking, that concordant opinion of the most approved ancients regarding the sacraments must be conveniently opened here, which is of this sort: *Sacraments are sacred signs and symbols of God's will toward us. And they are, in the New Testament, certain and efficacious signs and vehicles of divine grace, conferring grace upon those who receive them worthily.*
