Since the sacraments are efficacious signs of the grace of God and our sanctification, they consist of two things: namely, of the sign itself, that is, an external element shadowing forth invisible grace, and of the Word, through which the Holy Spirit secretly works that grace. For because we are dull on account of our flesh (whose mass weighs down the strength of the mind) to receive the spiritual grace of God, and are in need of some external aid by which our fragility may be both excited and instructed: therefore, for the healing of human infirmity, God has applied the spiritual medicine of His grace, veiled in certain sensible signs: which the Greeks call symbols or mysteries, and some Latins call sacraments, others sacramental signs. These sacraments, so that no one might doubt their power and efficacy, Christ confirmed with His Word and promise:

Furthermore, the Word of God offers to us the promise of grace: but the sacramental sign is like a seal of the Word of God, exhibiting the thing promised. Therefore, just as the promise is useless to us unless it is grasped by faith: so the sacramental sign is likewise useless to us unless it is believed that we shall receive that which has been signified. For otherwise, if nothing that is not apparent is received through the sign of the sacrament, then the sign itself will be ineffectual, and it will be said that nothing of more remarkable efficacy and greater grace has been added to our New Testament sacraments from the virtue of Christ's passion than was present in those sacraments which were in the Old Testament.

And Catulus, said Antonius, I do not hunt for some utility for speaking, I am accustomed to reading these books, and several others, for the sake of delight when there is leisure. What then is it? I will confess: nevertheless, something happens—just as when I walk in the sun, even if I walk for another reason, I am colored by nature—so, when I have read those books more studiously at Misenum <note>a town on the Bay of Naples, a favorite resort for wealthy Romans</note> (for at Rome it is scarcely permitted), I feel my speech is, as it were, colored by their song. But, so that this may not seem to you to extend too broadly, I understand at least this much in Greek, which they who wrote it wanted to be understood by the common people. If I ever fall upon your philosophers, deceived by the indices of the books, because they are generally inscribed about known and illustrious things, about virtue, about justice, about honesty, about pleasure, I understand absolutely no word at all: they are so tied up in narrow and concise disputations. As for poets, as if they spoke some other language, I do not attempt to touch them. With those, as I said, I amuse myself, who have written of deeds or their own speeches, or who speak in such a way that they seem to have wished to be familiar to us, who are not the most learned. But I return to that point. Do you see how great a duty history is for the orator? I do not know if it is the greatest in the flow of speech and variety. Nor do I find it anywhere separately instructed by the precepts of the rhetoricians: for these things are situated before the eyes. For who does not know that the first law of history is to not dare to say anything false; then, not to dare to say anything true; so that there is no suspicion of favoritism in writing, nor any suspicion of enmity? These, of course, are the foundations.

The rationale of matters requires an order of time and a description of regions: it also desires, since in great matters worthy of memory, counsels are expected first, then actions, and afterwards the outcomes, that it be signified regarding the counsels what the writer approves, and in deeds it should be declared not only what was done or said, but also in what manner; and, when the outcome is spoken of, that all causes—whether of chance, wisdom, or rashness—be explained; and of the men themselves, not only their deeds, but also, for those who excel in fame and name, their life and character. The rationale of words, and the style of speech, must be diffuse and extended, and flowing with a certain equable gentleness, without this judicial harshness and without the barbs of forensic sentiments. Do you see if there are any precepts for these many and such great matters that may be found in the arts of rhetoricians? In the same silence, many other duties of orators have lain dormant: exhortations, consolations, precepts, and admonitions; all of which must be handled most eloquently, but have no place in those parts which have been handed down. And in this genre, there is also that infinite forest; because many (as even Crassus has shown) have given the orator two genres for speaking; one regarding a certain, defined cause, such as those which are concerned with lawsuits or deliberations: (let one add, if anyone wishes, even praise), the other, which almost all writers call by name, but no one explains: the infinite question of the genre without time and without person. When they speak of what this is, and how great it is, they do not seem to me to understand.

But see to it that the hydra and the skin do not become a problem for you in those two genres; lest Hercules and other greater works be left among those matters which you omit. For it does not seem to me to be less work to speak about universal kinds of defendants than about the causes of individuals, and much greater still to speak about the nature of the gods than about human lawsuits. It is not so, said Antonius: for I will tell you, Catulus, not as a learned man, but—which is greater—as one experienced. The oratory of all other matters, believe me, is a game for a man who is not dull, not unexercised, and not lacking in common letters and more refined humanity. In the contentions of causes there is a certain great work, and I do not know if it is by far the greatest of human works: in which the power of the orator is judged by the unskilled for the most part by the outcome and victory: where an armed adversary is present, who must both be struck and repelled: where often he who is to be the master of the case is a stranger and angry, or even a friend to the adversary and an enemy to you; when he must be taught or untaught, or repressed or incited, or moderated by speech in every way according to the time and the cause: in which often benevolence is to be brought to hatred, or hatred to benevolence: who must be twisted, as if by some machine, now to severity, now to a relaxation of mind, now to sadness, now to joy. One must use the gravity of all sentiments and the weights of all words. There must be added a varied action, vehement, full of spirit, full of soul, full of pain, full of severity.

Nor, by Hercules, without reason. All those who give precepts about the art of speaking seem to me to do this. For what they themselves have not experienced, that they teach others: but perhaps they err less in this, that they do not attempt to teach you, like Hannibal, but boys or adolescents. You err, Catulus, said Antonius. For I myself have fallen in with many Phormios by now. For who among those Greeks is there who thinks that any one of us understands anything? And to me, indeed, they are not so troublesome. I easily suffer and endure them all. For either they bring something that does not displease me, or they bring it about that I regret less that I have not learned. But I dismiss them not as insultingly as that philosopher was dismissed by Hannibal: and perhaps for that reason I have even more of a problem. But nevertheless, their doctrine, as far as I can judge, is ridiculous. For they divide the whole matter into two parts: into the controversy of the cause and that of the question. They call the matter placed in the dispute of affairs and controversy a "cause," and the matter placed in infinite doubt a "question." They give precepts about the cause. For I can make the judge benevolent toward me more easily when I am in the flow of speech than when all things are unheard; and docile not when I promise that I will demonstrate, but when I teach and explain; and attentive, indeed, we can bring about by frequently rousing the minds of the judges through the whole action, not by an initial proclamation. However, to treat of all types of mysteries in this work is not my intention, lest I seem to be wise beyond sobriety; and I am not conscious of having drawn so much from the Spirit of God that I could either understand all the hidden and secret mysteries of God as is fitting, or pursue each one with apt words and illustrate them once understood.

Therefore, in this treatise, we are to assert that the truth of the body and blood of the Lord is in the sacrament of the Eucharist, if Christ grants it to us, and we shall use both terms, mystery and sacrament, indifferently, but more frequently the name "sacrament," which is more familiar to Latin ears. But before we begin our undertaking, that agreeing opinion of the most approved ancients concerning the sacraments should be set forth here conveniently, which is of this sort: *Sacraments are sacred signs, and symbols, of God's will toward us. And in the New Testament, they are certain and efficacious signs, and vehicles of divine grace, conferring grace upon those who receive them worthily.*

Since sacraments are effective signs of God's grace and our sanctification, they consist of two things: namely, of the sign itself, that is, the external element, shadowing forth the invisible grace, and of the word, through which the Holy Spirit works that grace secretly. For because we are dull toward receiving the spiritual grace of God due to our flesh (by whose mass the strength of the mind is weighed down), and we are in need of some external aid, by which our fragility might be both aroused and instructed: therefore, for the healing of human infirmity, God has applied the spiritual medicine of His grace, veiled by certain sensible signs: which the Greeks call symbols or mysteries, some Latins call sacraments, others call them sacramental signs. Christ confirmed these sacraments with His word and promise, so that no one might doubt their power and efficacy:
pages.21:

<sig>C</sig>

the effect of which divine promise and operation is never wanting to those signs, unless an obstacle intervenes through the vice and unworthiness of the recipient. Such are baptism, the sacrament of penance, the Eucharist, or the sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord, and other sacraments: each of which has its own promises, supported by the Word of God as the firmest foundation, and appropriate and suitable to its own nomenclature. Baptism has the promise of grace, regeneration, and the kingdom of heaven annexed to it, as in this place:

<margin>Ioan. 3.</margin>
> *Amen, amen, I say to you, unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of heaven:*

and in another place,

<margin>Mar. ult.</margin>
> *He who believes and is baptized will be saved.*

The sacrament of penance has the promise of the remission of sins, and of restoration into the fellowship of the mystical body of Christ, which is the Church: as here,

<margin>Ioan. 20.</margin>
> *Whose sins you remit, they are remitted to them.*

Furthermore, the Eucharist, or the sacrament of the body and blood, has the promise of eternal life, and of abiding in Christ: as in John,

<margin>Ioan. 6.</margin>
> *He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life: and I will raise him up on the last day. For my flesh is food indeed, and my blood is drink indeed: he who eats my flesh, and drinks my blood, abides in me, and I in him: as the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father: so also he who eats me,*
pages.22:

he himself also will live because of me. Therefore, the worthy reception of the Eucharist constitutes us as members of Christ, just as, on the contrary, through its unworthy reception, which carries judgment with it, we make ourselves members of Satan.

Furthermore, the Word of God offers us the promise of grace: the sacramental sign is like a seal of the Word of God, exhibiting the thing promised. Therefore, just as the promise is useless to us unless it is apprehended by faith: so the sacramental sign is similarly useless to us unless it is believed that we will receive what is signed. For otherwise, if nothing that does not appear is received through the sign of the sacrament, then the sign itself will be ineffectual, and it will be said that nothing of more distinguished efficiency, or of greater grace, has been added to our New Testament sacraments from the power of Christ's passion than was present in those sacraments that were in the Old Testament.

<margin>Luc. 22. Mat. 26.</margin>
In the holy sacrament of the Eucharist, however, to whose worthy reception the promise of grace is annexed, two things are to be considered: namely, both the sign exposed to our senses, and at the same time the true body of Christ, to be known not by the judgment of the senses, but by faith, as appears through the words of the Savior Himself, saying:

> This is my body, which is given for you: This is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins.

Which words, from the very cradle of the Catholic Church after Christ suffered, without any allegory,

This king of ours also seems to abide by the aforementioned treaties, those made with other nations, and those with us, as far as I can see. He initiates nothing new before perceiving that either you or some others have violated the treaty regarding him, and he deliberates on his own behalf. But if you should decide to write back to me hereafter for the sake of our connection, I would willingly accommodate myself to this courtesy, since you began to love me of your own accord and provoked me with your letters, for which reason I love you wondrously. Since Linacre and Tunstall have bound me to them by this kind of service and have received my reply, I would like you to greet them in my words, and return a greeting to More—if you please, with interest—who greeted me in your letters by way of his own messages to Linacre. Farewell, man most dear to literature, and enroll me in your list. Paris, the fifth day before the Kalends of May, in the year 1518.

### Guillaume Budé to Richard Pace, Greetings.

Nicolas Bérauld, who delivered this letter to you, a man most learned in both languages <note>original: "utraque lingua" referring to Latin and Greek</note> and now highly deserving of good literature, is also otherwise a very close friend of mine. When I began to hear that he would be going there in the company of the Bishop of Paris, I thought it my duty to entrust a letter for him to you, even
pages.19:
though I had written a long enough letter to you a few days ago and had entrusted it to a relative of mine who is a companion of that same company. I did not want Bérauld, a man familiar to me and at one time a guest of your Erasmus, to be in Britain without your knowledge, since you seem to me to be a great lover of studious men. Whatever service and courtesy you extend to him while he is in a foreign province, I shall not refuse to count it all as an expense to myself. Yet, knowing the kindness with which you are endowed, I do not doubt that you would have done this of your own accord if you could have once discovered that a man of such character and such learning was there. And when you find the time to get to know him, you will desire everything for his sake so much that you will not ask me to count what you have bestowed upon him as a favor to me. Nevertheless, I would like him to be commended to you in my name, as much as my friendship allows me to commend my friends through your kindness. Farewell. Paris, the day after the Feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Mother of God <note>original: "Assumption of the Blessed Mother of God"</note>.

Good immortal gods, what is this I hear? Oh, how many? How great? What panegyrics? What theatrical speeches, what discourses worthy of applause from you and me, has the celebration of the betrothal now stirred up among us, and how lavishly, elegantly, magnificently, kindly, eloquently, and fluently was the fame of our embassy received? Oh, your elegant King, greater than any proclamation, more outstanding than any mention of praise, who has bestowed such ample gifts of body and soul, such egregious generosity, and such gracious courtesy toward all, and who has made the munificence of a benign nature appear visible and complete through his dexterity of manners, majestic presence, heroic appearance, and the integrity of his countenance. As soon as our people returned from there, they began to speak of that splendid magnificence of arrangement, and how rightly and orderly it was constituted. They were received by almost everyone with eager ears, but truly every person of gravity followed with gaping—if I may say so—ears and astonished faces the fact that this most serene prince is accustomed to frequent his court with the presence of every most learned man and those most outstanding in the power of speech, and, as it were, to distinguish and adorn his own court with these distinctions, a spectacle which the royal presence itself provides for foreigners to behold. He is indeed, in my opinion, worthy that his fame, illuminated by these lights, should shine forth wherever the boundaries of the Christian name extend, and be consecrated to eternal memory by the monuments of the learned.
pages.21: according to my plan, than to leave behind for such a great King a memorable eulogy, as a testimony of my mind inclined toward his majesty, which has indeed deserved so honorably of literature, if what we have heard is true. For he who has raised the honor of the humanities—which had been reduced to the plebeian order, whether by the neglect of other nations or especially by our own customs and institutions—to a higher degree of prestige, even by providing an example in his own person and establishing a royal eloquence, has most beautifully snatched the glory of the thing away from kings of his own time and those to come. For he is the first of kings in many centuries to have understood and seen that the power and authority of eloquence is such that it exalts kings among the heavens and the underworld according to their merits. If this virtue, so worthy of being embraced, offered itself so easily, and could be retained with a certain present sweetness, and if the splendor and beauty of virtue itself could earn applause among all types of men, those knowledgeable and those ignorant of the liberal arts alike, undoubtedly princes, nobles, and primary men, taught by such a great example, would soon begin to compete in preserving the majesty of the higher letters, as I see that the sense of our own countrymen is now affected since our legates returned. For there is no one among us now who is not ashamed and regretful of his own ignorance. But your speech, most learned Richard,
pages.22:
delivered in the most ample assemblies of others, is celebrated to such an extent that that opulent and shining display used in transacting business was made all the more honorable and magnificent by your eloquence. If you hope that we will do the same in this part of organizing affairs, I fear that we cannot satisfy you, as we are among those for whom the reward for scholarly industry has never been established, due to the notable obscurity and indignity of French affairs. Nicolas Bérauld, now very dear to you (as I have gathered from your letters), has set out for the court with the President of Paris, aided egregiously by your support and recommendations, and is now raised by undoubted hope. The King is said to be approaching to receive the legates expected from there. Farewell, my Pace, and greet my Tunstall, More, Linacre, and the others for me. Paris, the Nones of November.

## Guillaume Budé to Richard Pace, Greetings.

Having received your third letter, I have marveled at your diligence in this way of cultivating friendship, which I have hardly yet experienced as equaled in any of my friends. I hope you have now successfully recovered from the fever. It will be right that the concern for how well you live your life and how firm a health your body possesses should henceforth belong to me, since I hold that so very benevolent spirit of yours within it. So much more gladly...
pages.23: ...have you offered yourself to friendship, the more spontaneously and nobly you have presented yourself. And indeed, when I enumerate my friends from abroad, you deserve to be ranked among the very first, and it seems to me that you have not only inscribed your own name into the catalog of my friends of your own accord, but have also performed the customary duties with both hand and heart. Therefore, I consider a great addition to have been made to my accounts by your name, those more sacred ones which I have decided to deposit in the citadel of Pallas, not in the temple of Saturn. Therefore, since you so kindly indulge me in the service of friendship, you have incurred a great debt of gratitude from me. But see how far you have already stepped forward. For what will happen if I summon you not by a formal stipulation, but by your own spontaneous promise, when I have been beautifully secured by the testimony of the herald and by letters sealed by you? And so that you cannot finally plead that you have been circumvented, you did not hesitate to promise the same thing again after a rather long interval; when those who bind themselves in this way begin to reject their duty later and make their agreements void, the constitutions of the laws permit one to reproach them with the shame of a repeated promise and the bond of a doubled obligation. Therefore, when I recognize and embrace that candor of your mind as you simply promise yourself to my service, then I shall indeed account for your courtesy and generous humanity in such a way that I shall exact the promise only thus far, and ease your burden: as far as
pages.24: you can fulfill it cheerfully and without great difficulty, and not even at the very first moment, but when I have collected older debts, of which I still have many good and suitable ones, and whose judgment and arbitration I can constitute in my own forum if controversies arise from them. I have the calculation of the calendar of these names arranged in such a way that I think it well for me if I keep the written contracts safe at home, as I am glad that my resources are situated in such a way that I can long boast that the day for many rich names has already passed, and yet I would not want them to come, nor if it had come, could I exact them without blushing or sadness. I hear that a most ample embassy regarding a matter both grand and pacificatory is soon to go there. I would like it to be decided so auspiciously that peace may be confirmed from it for my age and yours, so that I may be able to experience and act with you on more equal terms (if the matter should turn out so) in an action on behalf of a friend, which any one might marvel at as not being explicitly declared by civil law, although he should certainly think and note that the action on behalf of a partner lies most broadly in the <term>Pandects</term> <gloss>the Digest of Roman Law</gloss>. But in that embassy, the Bishop of Paris will hold either the first or second place, as is the rumor; it was not yet certain when I wrote this whether he would make his way through this city, and
pages.25:
he has long been among the courtiers, where he spends most of his time. He is a man learned among few, endowed with the prudence of many things, a supporter and advocate of literary men, and a student of your Erasmus, with whom I share a relationship more than a customary life, as I dwell in the city. I believe you will observe him dutifully, even with the recommendation of this matter, especially since, as I conjecture, it will be necessary or opportune for you to speak often with the legates while performing your duty. Farewell, and return a hundredfold greeting to Tunstall, Linacre, and More, who have greeted me with your words or letters. Paris, the Kalends of August.

A pair of British hounds was offered to me by you through the young man Lupset, who is learned in both languages and, as I see, popular among the learned. Although this was a very welcome and pleasant gift for me, and indeed ample and magnificent in its outcome (for I hope I have produced a clear and happy munificence in gifting those individuals), yet that pair of letters was not a little more pleasant, in reading which I recognize and embrace your genius, as I once heard of it by report and as I have come to know it from your <term>Utopia</term> <gloss>More's work on an ideal society</gloss>.

And Catulus, said Antonius, I am not some hunter of utility for speaking when I am in the habit of reading these books and several others, but rather I do it for the sake of pleasure when there is leisure. What then is the case? I will confess: there is something nevertheless—just as when I walk in the sun, even if I walk for a different reason, it happens by nature that I am tanned; so, when I have read those books quite studiously at Misenum <note>a Roman naval base and resort</note> (for in Rome it is scarcely permitted), I feel my oration is, as it were, colored by their song. But, lest this seem to you to extend more widely; I understand these things at least in the Greek works which those who wrote them themselves wished to be understood by the common people. If I ever fall upon your philosophers, deceived by the indices of the books, because they are generally inscribed about known and illustrious things, about virtue, about justice, about honesty, about pleasure; I understand absolutely no word: they are so bound up in narrow and concise disputations. As for the poets, I do not attempt to touch them at all, as if they spoke in some other language. With those, as I said, I amuse myself who have written about deeds or their own orations, or who speak in such a way that they seem to have wished to be familiar to us, who are not the most erudite. But I return to that point. Do you see how great a duty of the orator is history? I do not know if it is the greatest in the flow of oration and in variety. Nor do I find it anywhere set apart and instructed by the precepts of the rhetoricians: for they are placed before our eyes. For who does not know that the first law of history is that one should not dare to say anything false: next, that one should not fear to say anything true, so that there is no suspicion of favor in writing, nor any of spite? These, of course, are the foundations
pages.485: note is known to all. But the building itself is placed in matters and words. The rationale of matters requires the order of times and the description of regions: it also desires, since in great matters worthy of memory, first counsels are expected, then acts, then outcomes, that it be signified regarding the counsels what the writer approves, and that in deeds it be declared not only what was done or said, but also in what manner; and, when the outcome is discussed, that all the causes, whether of chance, or of wisdom, or of rashness, be explained; and not only the deeds of the men themselves, but also of those who excel in fame and name, [that one speak] about the life and nature of each one. The rationale of words, however, and the genus of oration must be pursued as diffuse and extended, and flowing with a certain equable gentleness without this judicial harshness and without the barbs of forensic sententiae <note>concise, pointed expressions or arguments</note>. Do you see if there are any precepts for these so many and such great matters that may be found in the arts of the rhetoricians? In the same silence, many other duties of orators have lain dormant: exhortations, consolations, precepts, admonitions: all of which must be treated most eloquently, but have no place in those parts which have been handed down. And in this genre there is also that infinite forest; because most people (as Crassus also showed) have given the orator two genres for speaking: one about a certain, defined cause, such as those that are involved in lawsuits or in deliberations: (let one add, if one wishes, also praise) the other, which almost all writers call by name, but no one explains: the infinite question of a genre without time and without person. When they speak of what this is and how much it is; they do not seem to me to understand
pages.486: to understand. For if it is the orator's duty that, whatever matter is posited infinitely, he can speak about it: it will be necessary for him to speak about how great the magnitude of the sun is, what the shape of the earth is: he will not be able to refuse to speak about mathematics or musical matters once this burden is undertaken. In short, for him who professes that it is his duty to speak not only about those controversies which are marked by times and persons, that is, about all forensic matters, but also about the infinite questions of genera; there can be no genus of oration that is excluded. But if we wish to add that wandering, free, and broadly extending part of questions to the orator; so that we think the orator ought to speak about things good or bad; things to be sought or to be avoided; honest or shameful; useful or useless; about virtue, about justice, about continence, about prudence, about greatness of spirit, about liberality, about piety, about friendship, about faith, about duty, and about other virtues and their contrary vices; and likewise about the state, about empire, about military affairs, about the discipline of the city, about the characters of men: let us assume that part as well, but in such a way that it is circumscribed by modest boundaries. For my part, I think that all things which pertain to the use of citizens, the character of men; which are engaged in the custom of life, in the rationale of the republic, in this civil society, in the common sense of men, in nature, in customs; must be embraced by the orator; if not so that he might answer separately about these things in the manner of philosophers; then certainly so that he can weave them prudently into a cause; but that he should speak about these very things in such a way as those who have established rights, laws, and cities have spoken,
pages.487: simply and splendidly, without any series of disputations and without the barren contention of words. In this place, let there be no surprise if no precepts for so many and such great things are set down by me: I decide it this way, just as in the other arts, when the most difficult things of each matter have been handed down, it is not necessary for the rest to be handed down because they are either easier or similar; as in painting, he who has fully learned to paint the appearance of a man is able, even if he has not learned it, to paint anyone of any form or age; nor is there danger that someone who paints a lion or a bull excellently would not be able to do the same in many other quadrupeds; nor is there any art at all in which all things that can be accomplished by that art are handed down by the teacher; but those who have learned the genera themselves of the primary and certain things pursue the rest by themselves not inconveniently: similarly, I think that in this rationale or practice of speaking, he who has attained that power, so that he can move the minds of those who hear with some power of deciding, whether about the republic, or about his own matters, or about those against whom or for whom he speaks, to his own judgment; this person will not seek more about that whole genre of remaining orations as to what he should say, just as that Polycletus, when he was fashioning Hercules, did not ask how he should fashion the skin or the hydra, even if he had never learned to do these things separately. Then Catulus. You seem to me, Antonius, to have been able to clearly see before your eyes what he who was to be an orator ought to learn; and what, even if he had not learned it, he would take up from that which he had learned. For you have reduced the whole man into only two genres of causes. The rest
pages.488: you have left to practice and similarity. But see to it that in those two genres the hydra and the skin do not become your Hercules, and that other greater works are not left behind in those things which you omit. For it does not seem to me to be less work to speak about the universal genera of the accused than about the causes of individuals, and much greater to speak about the nature of the gods than about human lawsuits. It is not so, said Antonius: for I will tell you, Catulus, not as a learned man, but, which is greater, as one experienced. The oration of all other matters, believe me, is a game for a man who is not dull, not unpracticed, and not experienced in general literature and more polished humanitas <note>refined culture or humanity</note>. In the contentions of causes there is a certain great work, and I do not know if it is by far the greatest of human works: in which the power of the orator is judged by the unskilled for the most part by the outcome and the victory: where there is present an armed adversary who must be both struck and repelled: where often he who is to be the master of the case is a stranger and angry, or even a friend to the adversary and an enemy to you; when he must either be taught or untaught; or repressed or incited; or moderated by every means for the time and the cause by oration: in which often benevolence must be led to hatred, and hatred to benevolence: who must be twisted as if by some machine, now to severity, now to the relaxation of the spirit, now to sadness, now to joy. The weight of all sententiae and the gravity of all words must be used. There must be added a varied action, vehement, full of spirit, full of breath, full of pain, full of severity.
pages.489: full of severity. If anyone in these works has grasped that art, so that he can fashion the statue of Minerva as Phidias could: he will certainly not labor over how the same craftsman learns to do those lesser works on a shield. Then Catulus. The more great and miraculous you have made those things, the greater the expectation holds me as to by what rationales or by what precepts such a great power is acquired: not that it concerns me now: (for my age does not desire it; and we have followed a different genre of speaking: we who have never extorted opinions from the hands of judges by some power of oration, but rather, with their minds calmed, we have received only as much as they themselves allowed) but nevertheless I seek those things of yours for no use of my own, but led only by a desire for knowing. Nor do I have need of some Greek teacher who might chant to me common precepts; when he himself has never looked upon the forum, never looked upon any trial: as that Peripatetic Phormio is said to have done: when Hannibal, expelled from Carthage, had come to Antiochus as an exile; and because his name had great glory among all, he had been invited by his hosts to hear the one I mentioned, if he wished; and when he had said that he did not mind: the man, who was fluent, is said to have spoken for several hours about the duty of a commander and about all military matters. Then, when the others who had heard him were vehemently delighted; they asked Hannibal what he himself judged about that philosopher. This Carthaginian is said to have answered, not in the best Greek, but nevertheless freely: that he had often seen many delirious old men, but he had never seen anyone who was more delirious than Phormio.
pages.490: seen anyone. And by Hercules, not without cause. For what could be more arrogant or loquacious than for a Greek man, who had never seen an enemy, never seen a camp, and in short had never touched the smallest part of any public duty, to give precepts about military matters to Hannibal, who had contended for empire for so many years with the Roman people, the victor of all nations? This, it seems to me, all those who give precepts about the art of speaking do. For they teach others what they themselves have not experienced: but perhaps they err less in this, that they do not try to teach you, like Hannibal, but boys or young men. You err, Catulus, said Antonius. For I myself have already fallen upon many Phormios. For who among those Greeks is there who thinks that any one of us understands anything? And indeed they are not so annoying to me. I easily endure and bear with them all. For they either bring something that does not displease me, or they cause me not to repent less that I have learned. However, I dismiss them not as insultingly as that philosopher did to Hannibal: and perhaps I have more trouble for that reason. But nevertheless, their doctrine, as much as I can judge, is quite ridiculous. For they divide the whole matter into two parts, into the controversy of a cause and that of a question. They call the matter placed in the disceptation of things and controversy a Cause: but they call the matter placed in infinite doubt a Question. They give precepts about the cause. About the other part of speaking, a wondrous silence. Finally, they make, as it were, five limbs of eloquence: to find what you should say: to arrange what has been found: then to adorn with words: then to commit to memory:
pages.491: then at the end to act and to pronounce. A matter surely not hidden. For who would not have seen this on his own, that no one can speak aptly unless he has both what he should say, and in what words, and in what order he should say it, and has remembered these things? And I do not criticize these things, but I say that they are placed before our eyes, just as likewise those four, five, or six parts, or even seven (since they are arranged differently by others) into which all oration is distributed by them. For they bid us to begin in such a way that we make the one who is listening well-disposed to us, and docile, and attentive: Then to narrate the matter in such a way that the narration is verisimilar, open, and brief: After this to divide the cause or to propose; to confirm our side with arguments and rationales, then to refute the contrary. Then, however, others place the conclusion of the oration and, as it were, the peroration. Others bid us, before one reaches the peroration, to digress for the sake of adorning or amplifying, then to conclude and perorate. I do not even criticize these things: for they are neatly distributed, but nevertheless, which was necessary for men inexperienced in truth, not expertly. For what precepts they wanted to be for beginnings and narrations, these are to be preserved throughout the entire oration. For I can also make a judge well-disposed to me more easily when I am in the course of the oration than when all things are unheard; and docile, not when I promise that I will demonstrate, but when I teach and explain; and attentive, indeed, we can achieve through the whole action by stirring up the minds of the judges, not by a first announcement. Furthermore, that they bid the narration to be verisimilar, and open, and brief—

To these must be added what Cyril writes in the Ephesian symbol <note>i.e., the Acts of the Council of Ephesus</note>: "We do not say that the flesh is changed into the nature of divinity, nor that the ineffable nature of the Word of God is transferred into the nature of flesh. And when he was made visible, while still an infant in the cradle and at the breast of the Virgin mother, he filled all creation as God, and sat with the Father. For the divine power is without quantity, without magnitude, and cannot be circumscribed." Thus far Cyril.

# ON MYSTERIES
## AND SACRAMENTS.

<note>A decorative woodcut initial letter 'D' contains a figure of a bearded man wearing a crown and robes, seated at a desk or throne within an ornate rectangular frame.</note>Intending to speak of mysteries, it is necessary before all else to explore what a mystery is and what it comprehends. Otherwise, one who is about to speak many words about mysteries, like one running outside the stadium set for the competitors, exerts himself in vain with labor and achieves nothing besides weariness. So, he who does not contain himself within the boundaries of mysteries while discussing them, while wandering from the target, cannot grasp the palm of victory.

<margin>Prov. 20</margin>
<margin>Ecclus. 27</margin>
<margin>Matt. 13</margin>
Therefore, it must first be observed that "mystery" is a Greek term, although frequently used by the Latins, and it signifies something secret, or that under which something secret lies hidden, and which is not perfected except by some hidden rite of holy things. For mysteries are sometimes called those secret and hidden things of men, which it is considered sacrilege to reveal to the common people, as it is in Solomon in Proverbs: "Do not associate with him who reveals mysteries, walks deceitfully, and opens his lips." And in Ecclesiasticus: "To uncover the mysteries of a friend is the despair of an unhappy soul." Likewise, the holy secrets of God are called mysteries, as it is in Matthew regarding the one sowing his seed, where Christ says to his disciples: "To you it is given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to the rest..."
pages.18:
<header>ON THE TRUTH OF THE BODY AND BLOOD OF THE LORD</header>

<margin>1 Cor. 2</margin>
it is in parables. And in Paul to the Corinthians writing about the preaching of the Word of God: "We speak the wisdom of God hidden in a mystery, which God predestined before the ages for our glory." And to Timothy regarding the incarnation of the Word of God, he says: "Great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifested in the flesh, justified in the spirit, seen by angels, preached to the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up in glory." And to the Romans regarding the same incarnation: "According to the revelation of the mystery kept secret for eternal times, which has been made manifest through the scriptures of the prophets, according to the command of the eternal God for the obedience of faith." Paul also commemorates such secret things of God to the Romans, saying:

<margin>Rom. 11</margin>
"For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, lest you be wise in your own estimation, that blindness in part has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and so all Israel should be saved." And to the Corinthians he writes about the resurrection: "Behold, I tell you a mystery: We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a point of time, in the moment of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed. For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality." The same mystery he also mentions writing to the Thessalonians, saying: "For this we say to you in the word
pages.19:
<header>IN THE EUCHARIST, BOOK I.</header>

of the Lord, that we who are living and remain unto the coming of the Lord will by no means precede those who have fallen asleep, because the Lord himself, at the command and with the voice of the Archangel and with the trumpet of God, will descend from heaven, and the dead who are in Christ will rise first: then we who are living and remain will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord." And John in the Apocalypse explains the mystery of the seven stars. If Paul and John had not opened these secrets of God to us, they would still lie unknown to us.

Sacred signs are also called mysteries by the Greeks and sacraments by the Latins, as Paul speaking to the Ephesians about the union of husband and wife says:

<margin>Eph. 5</margin>
"This is a great sacrament, but I speak concerning Christ and the Church." In this sense, mysteries are sometimes taken by the Latins, as Paul says to the Corinthians:

<margin>1 Cor. 4</margin>
"Let a man so consider us as the ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God." However, I have no intention to treat all types of mysteries in this work, lest I appear to be wise beyond what is sober. Nor am I conscious of having drawn so much from the spirit of God that I am able to understand all the hidden and latent secrets of God as is fitting, or to pursue each one in apt words and clarify them once understood.

Therefore, in this treatise, if Christ grants it to us, we will assert that the truth of the body and blood of the Lord is in the sacrament of the Eucharist. We will use both terms, "mystery" and "sacrament," interchangeably, but more frequently the name of "sacrament," which is more familiar to Latin ears. But before we begin our undertaking, that consonant opinion of the most approved ancients regarding the sacraments should be opened here, which is of this kind: *Sacraments are sacred signs and symbols of God's will toward us. And in the New Testament, they are certain and effective signs and vehicles of divine grace, conferring grace upon those who receive them worthily.*
pages.20:
<header>ON THE TRUTH OF THE BODY AND BLOOD OF THE LORD</header>

<margin>Wisd. 9</margin>
Since the sacraments are effective signs of God's grace and our sanctification, they consist of two things: namely, the sign itself, that is, the external element, which adumbrates <gloss>shadows forth</gloss> invisible grace, and the Word, through which the Holy Spirit secretly works that grace. For because we are dull toward receiving the spiritual grace of God due to our flesh (by the weight of which the strength of the soul is burdened), and we are in need of some external aid by which our frailty may be both aroused and instructed, therefore, for the healing of human infirmity, God has applied the spiritual medicine of his grace, veiled by certain sensible signs: which the Greeks call symbols or mysteries, some Latins call sacraments, and some call sacramental signs. These sacraments, lest anyone should doubt their power and efficacy, Christ confirmed with his own word and promise:
pages.21:
<header>IN THE EUCHARIST, BOOK I.</header>
<sig>C</sig>

of which promise and divine operation the effect is never lacking, unless an obstacle intervenes through the fault and unworthiness of the receiver. Of such a kind are baptism, the sacrament of penance, the Eucharist (or the sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord), and the other sacraments. Each of these has its own promises, supported by the Word of God as the most firm foundation, and suitable and appropriate to its nomenclature. Baptism has the promise of grace, regeneration, and the kingdom of heaven annexed to it, as in this place:

<margin>John 3</margin>
> "Amen, amen, I say to you, unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter the kingdom of heaven,"

and in another place:

<margin>Mark, end</margin>
> "He who believes and is baptized will be saved."

The sacrament of penance has the promise of the remission of sins and of restoration into the society of the mystical body of Christ, which is the Church, as here:

<margin>John 20</margin>
> "Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them."

Furthermore, the Eucharist, or the sacrament of the body and blood, has the promise of eternal life and of dwelling in Christ, as in John:

<margin>John 6</margin>
> "He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life: and I will raise him up in the last day. For my flesh is food indeed, and my blood is drink indeed: he who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him: as the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father, so he who eats me,

he also will live because of me."
pages.22:
<header>ON THE TRUTH OF THE BODY AND BLOOD OF THE LORD</header>

Therefore, the worthy reception of the Eucharist constitutes us as members of Christ, just as, conversely, through its unworthy reception, which brings judgment with it, we make ourselves members of Satan.

Furthermore, the Word of God offers us the promise of grace; the sacramental sign is, as it were, a seal of the Word of God, exhibiting the thing promised. Therefore, just as the promise is useless to us unless it is apprehended through faith, so the sacramental sign is likewise useless to us unless it is believed that we will receive what has been signified. For otherwise, if nothing that is not apparent is received through the sign of the sacrament, then the sign itself will be ineffective. And it will be said that nothing of more remarkable efficacy and greater grace has been added to our sacraments of the New Testament, through the power of Christ's passion, than was present in those sacraments which were in the Old Testament.

<margin>Luke 22, Matt. 26</margin>
However, in the holy sacrament of the Eucharist, to whose worthy taking is annexed the promise of grace, two things must be considered: namely, both the sign exposed to our senses and, at the same time, the true body of Christ, to be recognized not by the judgment of the senses but by faith, as appears through the very words of the Savior, saying:

> "This is my body, which is given for you: This is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins."

These words, from the very infancy of the Catholic Church after Christ suffered, without any allegory,

This King of ours seems to abide by the aforementioned treaties, both those concluded with other nations and those with us, at least as far as I can see. He innovates nothing, before having perceived that either you or some others have breached the treaty regarding him, and he acts according to his own counsel.
Otherwise, if you should decide to write to me henceforth for the sake of our spirits, I would gladly accommodate myself to this service, since you began to love me of your own accord and provoked me with your letters, a thing for which I love you wonderfully.
Since Linacre and Tunstall have bound me to themselves by this sort of service, and have received my reply, I would like to ask you to greet them in my name; and render a greeting to More, or rather pay it back with interest, who greeted me in your letters by the messengers with Linacre. Farewell, man most friendly to letters, and write me into your register. Paris, the fifth day before the Kalends of May, in the year 1518.

### Guillaume Budé to Richard Pace. Greeting.

Nicolas Bérauld, who delivered this letter to you, a man most learned in both languages <note>original: "utraque lingua" referring to Latin and Greek</note> and already no mean contributor to good letters, is also otherwise a very dear friend to me. When I began to hear that he was going to travel there in the company of the Bishop of Paris, I thought it my duty to give him a letter for you, even
pages.19:
if I had written a long enough letter to you a few days ago, and entrusted it to a certain kinsman of mine who is a companion of the same retinue. For I did not want Bérauld, a man familiar to me and at one time a guest of your Erasmus, to be in Britain without your knowledge, since you yourself seemed to me to be a very great lover of scholarly men. Whatever service and courtesy you extend to him while he is staying in a foreign province, I shall not refuse to let you charge it all to me. Although (given the humanity I have discovered you possess) I do not doubt that you would have done so of your own accord, if you could once have learned that a man of such talent and such learning was there; and indeed when you have time to get to know him, you will be so desirous of doing everything for his sake that you will not ask me to count what you have bestowed upon him as a favor to me. And yet, I would like him to be commended to you in my name, so that he may be among those whom I am most permitted to commend to my friends through your kindness. Farewell, Paris, the day after the Assumption of the sublime divine Mother of God.

->Guillaume Budé to Richard<-
->Pace. S.P.D.<-

<note>A decorative large capital letter P begins the paragraph.</note>

Good immortal gods, what do I hear? Oh, how many? How great? What panegyrics? What theatrical speeches, worthy of applause by you and me, has the celebration of the betrothal excited among us; and the fame of our embassy, received with such richness, splendor, magnificence, kindness, elegance, and eloquence! Oh, your elegant King, greater than any praise, more excellent than any commemoration of merit, who has accommodated such great and ample gifts of body and mind with such noble generosity, remarkable goodwill, and graceful courtesy toward all; who has rendered the munificence of a kind nature worth seeing, embellished by the dexterity of his manners, his august majesty, heroic appearance, and the uprightness of his countenance. Our people, having returned from there, began at once to commemorate that splendid magnificence of the preparations and the proper and orderly arrangement; when they were received by almost all with receptive ears, every serious man indeed followed that account with gaping (so to speak) mouth and awestruck countenance: that this most serene prince is accustomed to frequent his retinue with the presence of every most learned man and every man most excellent in the faculty of speech, and thus to distinguish and adorn his court with those ornaments; which appearance they themselves provide to the venerable royal court, and to be viewed by outsiders; he himself is in my opinion worthy, that his fame, illuminated by those lights, might shine in every direction, as far as the boundaries of the Christian name extend, and might one day be consecrated to eternal memory by the monuments of men of genius. Indeed, as far as I am concerned, I would do nothing more willingly, nor more eagerly, if ever the occasion for writing should arise
pages.20: my intent, so that I may leave behind for such a great King a certain memorable eulogy, as a testimony of my mind inclined toward his majesty: that he has indeed served letters nobly and honorably, if what we have heard is true. For he who has raised the honor of the humanities, which had been reduced to the common level, both by the neglect of other nations and especially by our own customs and institutions, to a height of greater dignity, even by the example set forth in himself and the institution of royal eloquence, he has most beautifully snatched the glory of the thing away from contemporary and future kings alike. For he is the first of kings in many centuries to have understood and seen that the force and authority of eloquence are such that it may raise kings among the gods above and those below, according to the merits of each. If this virtue offered itself so easily to be embraced, and to be retained with a certain immediate sweetness, whose splendor and appearance would earn applause from every kind of man, those acquainted with the liberal disciplines just as those who are ignorant of them, undoubtedly princes, nobles, and primary men, educated by such a great example, would soon begin to strive to preserve the majesty of the higher letters, as I see the sense of our own people is now affected since our ambassadors have returned. For now, there is no one among us who is not ashamed and regretful of his own ignorance. But your speech, most learned Richard,
pages.21:
held in the most ample assemblies of others, is celebrated to such a degree: as that rich and resplendent apparatus employed for the conduct of affairs; your eloquence has been greatly honored by it, and has seemed more magnificent. If you hope that we will do equal things in this part of preparing matters, I fear that we might not be able to satisfy you, for among us the value of industrious work has never stood, due to the notable obscurity of French affairs because of that loss and indignity. Nicolas Bérauld, now most dear to you (as I have understood from your letters), has set out for the court with the President of Paris, aided remarkably by your votes and recommendations, and raised by the hope of it, which is not in doubt. The King is said to be arriving now, to receive the ambassadors expected from there. Farewell, my Pace, and greet my Tunstall, my More, Linacre, and the others for me. Paris, the Nones of November.

## Guillaume Budé to Richard Pace. Greeting.

Having now received your third letter, I have marveled at your diligence in this way of cultivating friendship, the like of which I have scarcely experienced in any of my friends thus far. I wish you are now successfully recovered from your fever. For it will be right for me to be concerned henceforth for how well you spend your life, and how firm a health your body enjoys, since I hold that so benevolent spirit of yours within it. By how much the more <unclear>[...]</unclear>
pages.22: willingly and more nobly you have offered yourself to friendship, by so much more happily... and indeed even when I count up my friends from abroad, you are justly ranked among the very first, and you seem to me not only to have written your name of your own accord into the catalog among those of yours, but also to be performing the customary duties with hand and heart. Therefore, I count a great addition to have been made to my accounts in your name: those indeed more sacred ones, which I have decided to deposit not in the temple of Saturn, but in the citadel of Pallas. Therefore, because you indulge yourself so kindly toward me in the duty of a friend, you have incurred a huge debt of gratitude from me. But see how far you have already stepped forward. For what will happen if I summon you not on the basis of a formal stipulation, but of a spontaneous promise: since I have been beautifully secured, both by the testimony of the herald and by letters signed by you; and so that you cannot finally plead that you were circumvented, you have not hesitated to promise the same thing again, and after a fairly long interval; since for those who bind themselves thus, if they subsequently begin to shirk their duty and make their agreements void, the constitutions of the laws permit the shaming of a repeated promise and the bond of a doubled obligation to be cast against them. Therefore, while I recognize and embrace that candor of spirit with which you promise yourself simply to the service, I will nonetheless take such account of your courtesy and generous humanity, that I shall demand the promise only so far: that your word may be burdened only to the extent that
pages.23: you can happily and without great trouble fulfill it, and not even that at the very first opportunity, but when I have called in older debts; which I still have many good and suitable ones, and whose judgment and adjudication I could establish in my own forum if disputes should arise from them. Moreover, I have the reckoning of this calendar of names arranged in such a way that I think I have done well if I keep the written bonds safe at home; being one who rejoices that my resources are situated in such a way that I can long boast that the day of many wealthy debtors has arrived, and yet I would not want it to come, nor if it had arrived, could I demand it without shame or sorrow. I hear that a most ample embassy regarding a matter both grand and pacificatory is soon to go there. I would like it to have been decreed so auspiciously that peace might be confirmed from it for my age and yours; so that I might be able to test and act on more equal terms with you (if things should turn out that way) by an action on behalf of a friend, which any person might wonder that none is specifically mentioned in the civil law: one who might certainly think and notice that an action for a partner lies most broadly in the Pandects of the law. But in that embassy, the Bishop of Paris will obtain either the first or second place, as is the rumor: whether he was going to make his way through this city, it was not yet certain when I wrote this, and
pages.24:
he had already been among the courtiers for a long time, where he spends the greater part of his time. He is a man learned among the few, and endowed with the prudence of many things, an embracer and supporter of lettered men, and a student of your Erasmus: with whom I have a relationship more than a custom of life, for I dwell in the city. I believe that you will observe him dutifully, even by the recommendation of this very thing, especially since in performing your duty (as I conjecture) it will often be necessary or opportune for you to speak with ambassadors. Farewell, and return a hundredfold greeting to Tunstall, Linacre, and More, who greeted me with your words or letters. Paris, the Kalends of August.

->Guillaume Budé to Thomas More. Greeting.<-

A pair of British hounds was offered to me from you by Lupset, a young man learned in both languages and (as I see) favored among the learned. Although this was for me a most pleasing and delightful gift, and even from the result ample and magnificent (for I hope I have produced a bright and fortunate munificence in giving each of those away), nonetheless that pair of letters was not a little more delightful, in the reading of which I recognize and kiss your genius, as once heard of in speech, so now known from your <term>Utopia</term> <gloss>Nowhere/Ideal State</gloss>.

pages.484:
<header>LIBER SECVNDVS.</header>

<meta>continues from previous page: ...that although he did not know these things, he could speak so powerfully.</meta> And, Catulus, said Antonius, it is not because I am hunting for any utility in speaking that I am accustomed to read these books and several others, but for the sake of pleasure when there is leisure. What then? I will confess: yet something happens, just as when I walk in the sun, even if I walk for another reason, I am naturally tanned; so, when I have read these books at Misenum <note>original: "ad Misenum"</note> (for at Rome it is hardly permitted) quite studiously, I feel my oratory is, as it were, colored by their song. But, lest this seem to you to extend more widely; I understand these things only in the Greeks, which the authors themselves wished to be understood by the common people. If I ever come across your philosophers, deceived by the indices of the books, because they are inscribed on known and illustrious subjects, on virtue, on justice, on honesty, on pleasure; I understand absolutely nothing: they are so bound up in narrow and concise disputes. As for the poets, as if they spoke in some other language, I do not try to touch them. With those, as I said, I amuse myself, who wrote history, or who wrote their own speeches; or who speak in such a way that they seem to have wished to be familiar to us, who are not the most learned. But I return to that point. Do you see how great a task history is for the orator? I do not know if it is the greatest in the flow of speech and variety. Nor do I find it anywhere separately instructed by the precepts of the rhetoricians: for they lie before our eyes. For who does not know that the first law of history is that one should not dare to say anything false: then, that one should not dare not to say what is true, so that there is no suspicion of bias in writing, nor of enmity? These, of course, are the foundations.

<summary>Antonius explains that he reads historical and oratorical works for pleasure, and notes that while these texts improve his own oratorical style, philosophical works are too dense to be easily understood. He asserts that history is a significant duty of the orator, governed by the primary law of truthfulness.</summary>
<keywords>Antonius, Catulus, history, rhetoric, Misenum, truth in writing</keywords>
pages.485:
<header>DE ORATORE</header>
<meta>continues from previous page: ...foundations</meta> are known to all. But the structure itself is placed in matters and words. The arrangement of matters requires the order of times and the description of regions: it also desires, since in great and memorable matters the counsels are first expected, then the deeds, afterwards the outcomes, and that it be signified regarding the counsels what the writer approves, and in the deeds it be declared not only what was done or said, but also in what manner; and, when the outcome is told, that all the causes be explained, whether of chance, or of wisdom, or of rashness; and not only the deeds of the men themselves, but also of those who excel in fame and name, concerning each one's life and character. The arrangement of words, however, and the style of speech, must be pursued as loose and extended, and flowing with a certain even gentleness, without this judicial harshness and without the barbs of forensic sentiments. Of so many and such great matters, do you see any precepts that are found in the arts of the rhetoricians? In the same silence, many other duties of orators have lain, exhortations, consolations, precepts, admonitions: all of which must be handled most eloquently, but they have no place in those parts which have been handed down. And in this category there is also that infinite forest; because most people (as Crassus also showed) have given the orator two types of speaking; one concerning a certain and defined cause, such as those which are involved in lawsuits or in deliberations: (let him add, if one wishes, even praise) the other, which almost all writers call, but no one explains, an infinite question of the kind without time and without person. When they say what this is, and how great, they do not seem to understand.

<summary>Antonius details the requirements for historical writing, including the need for chronological order and character analysis. He criticizes the lack of rhetorical guidance for other oratorical tasks like consolation and deliberation, and critiques the vague definition of "infinite questions."</summary>
<keywords>history, rhetoric, structure, Crassus, infinite questions</keywords>
pages.486:
<header>LIBER SECVNDVS.</header>
<meta>continues from previous page: ...understand.</meta> For if it is the orator's duty, whatever matter is positioned infinitely, to be able to speak about it: it will be necessary for him to speak about how great the magnitude of the sun is, what the shape of the earth is: concerning mathematics, concerning musical matters, he will not be able, having taken on this burden, to refuse to speak. Finally, for him who professes that it is his duty to speak not only about those controversies which are marked by times and persons, that is, about all forensic matters, but also about the infinite questions of types; there can be no kind of speech that is excluded. But if we wish to add to the orator that wandering, free, and wide-ranging part of questions; so that we think the orator ought to speak about good or bad things; about those to be sought or avoided; about the honest or the base; about the useful or the useless; about virtue, about justice, about continence, about prudence, about greatness of soul, about liberality, about piety, about friendship, about faith, about duty, and about the opposite vices; and likewise about the republic, about empire, about military affairs, about the discipline of the state, about the morals of men: let us take up that part as well, but in such a way that it is circumscribed by modest boundaries. For my part, I think that everything which pertains to the use of citizens, the custom of men; which is involved in the practice of life, in the reasoning of the state, in this civil society, in the common sense of men, in nature, in morals; ought to be comprehended by the orator; if not so that he may respond separately about these things in the manner of philosophers; then certainly so that he can prudently weave them into a case; however, that he may speak about these very things just as those who established rights, laws, and states have spoken,

<summary>Antonius argues that an orator must have a broad grasp of human affairs, including philosophical and political concepts, to properly weave them into forensic discourse, even if he does not treat them as a philosopher would.</summary>
<keywords>oratory, politics, philosophy, civic life, law, ethics</keywords>

<header>DE ORATORE</header>
<meta>continues from previous page: ...spoken,</meta> simply and splendidly, without any series of disputes and without a dry contention of words. At this point, let there be no surprise if no precepts are laid down by me regarding so many and such great matters: I hold this view, that in other arts, when the most difficult parts of each thing have been handed down, the rest, because they are either easier or similar, do not need to be handed down; as in painting, he who has fully learned to paint the likeness of a man, is able to paint one of any shape or age, even if he has not learned; nor is there any danger that he who paints a lion or a bull excellently might not be able to do the same for many other quadrupeds; nor is there any art at all in which everything that can be achieved by that art is handed down by the teacher; but those who have learned the types themselves of the primary and certain things, pursue the rest on their own not unskillfully: similarly I believe in this reasoning, or exercise of speaking, he who has attained such power, that he can move to his own will the minds of those who, whether concerning the republic or his own affairs, or those against whom or for whom he speaks, listen with some power of deciding; this man will not seek more about that whole kind of remaining speeches than that famous Polycletus, when he was fashioning a Hercules, would seek how to fashion a skin or a hydra, even if he had never learned to do these things separately. Then Catulus said, You seem to me, Antonius, to have been able to place before my eyes what it was necessary for him who was to be an orator to learn; what, even if he had not learned it, he would assume from that which he had learned. For you have reduced the whole man into only two types of causes. The rest

<summary>Antonius uses the analogy of painting and sculpture to argue that a truly skilled orator, having mastered the difficult essentials, can naturally handle the remaining aspects of the art without requiring explicit instruction for every detail.</summary>
<keywords>Polycletus, art, education, oratory, skill, analogy</keywords>

<header>LIBER SECVNDVS.</header>
<meta>continues from previous page: ...The rest</meta> you have left to exercise and imitation. But watch out, lest in those two types the hydra and the skin be for you; but that Hercules and other greater works be left among those things which you omit. For it seems to me that the work of speaking about the universal types of defendants is no less than that of speaking about the individual causes, and much greater still to speak about the nature of the gods than about human lawsuits. It is not so, said Antonius: for I will tell you, Catulus, not as a learned man, but as one who is, which is greater, experienced. The oratory of all other matters, believe me, is a game for a man who is not dull, nor unexercised, nor lacking in common letters and a more polished humanity. In the contentions of causes there is a certain great work, and I do not know if it is by far the greatest among human works: in which the power of the orator is often judged by the unskilled by the outcome and the victory: where an armed adversary is present, who must both be struck and repelled: where often the one who is to be the master of the matter is a stranger, and angry, or even a friend to the adversary, and an enemy to you; when he must either be taught or untaught; or repressed, or incited; or moderated by speech in every way according to the time and the cause: in which often benevolence is to be led to hatred, and hatred to benevolence: who must be twisted as if by some machine, now to severity, now to a relaxation of mind, now to sadness, now to joy. One must use the weight of all sentiments, the gravity of all words. There must be added varied action, vehement, full of spirit, full of soul, full of pain,

<summary>Antonius clarifies his position, arguing that while general discourse is important, the intense, adversarial nature of forensic litigation—where an orator must manipulate the emotions of a judge—represents the true peak of oratorical labor.</summary>
<keywords>forensic oratory, litigation, emotion, rhetoric, Antonius, Catulus</keywords>
pages.489:
<header>DE ORATORE</header>
<meta>continues from previous page: ...full of severity.</meta> In these works, if anyone has comprehended that art, so that he can fashion a statue of Minerva as if he were Phidias: he certainly will not labor over how the same craftsman learns to do those lesser works on a shield. Then Catulus said, The more great and wonderful you have made those things, the greater the expectation holds me as to by what reasons, or by what precepts that great power is acquired: not that it concerns me now: (for my age does not desire it: and we have followed a different kind of speaking: we have never extorted sentiments from the hands of judges by some force of oratory, but rather, with their minds calmed, we have accepted only what they themselves allowed) but yet I seek those things of yours, not for my use, but led by the desire to know. Nor do I have need of some Greek teacher who might sing of common precepts to me; when he himself has never looked upon the forum, never looked upon any trial: as that peripatetic Phormio is said to have done: when Hannibal, expelled from Carthage, had come to Ephesus to Antiochus as an exile; and because his name was of great glory among all, he was invited by his hosts to hear the one I mentioned, if he wished; and when he had said that he was not unwilling: the fluent man is said to have spoken for several hours about the duty of a commander, and about all military affairs. Then, when the others who had heard him were vehemently delighted; they asked Hannibal what he himself thought about that philosopher. This Carthaginian is said to have answered, not in the best Greek, but yet freely: that he had often seen many doting old men, but he had seen no one who doted more than Phormio.

<summary>Catulus expresses admiration for the oratorical skill described by Antonius. He critiques the theoretical nature of Greek rhetoricians by recounting the story of Hannibal dismissing the lecture of the philosopher Phormio, who knew nothing of real war.</summary>
<keywords>Phidias, Minerva, Phormio, Hannibal, Antiochus, theory vs. practice</keywords>
pages.490:
<header>LIBER SECVNDVS.</header>
<meta>continues from previous page: ...doted more than Phormio.</meta> And by Hercules, he was not wrong. For what could be more arrogant or loquacious than to give instructions on military affairs to Hannibal, who had contended for empire for so many years with the Roman people, the victor of all nations, to a Greek man who had never seen an enemy, never seen a camp, and finally had never touched the smallest part of any public duty? It seems to me that all those who give instructions on the art of speaking do this. For they teach others what they themselves have not experienced: but perhaps they err less in this, that they do not try to teach you, like Hannibal, but boys, or young men. You err, Catulus, said Antonius. For I myself have already encountered many Phormios. For who among those Greeks is there who thinks that any of us understands anything? And to me, indeed, they are not so annoying. I easily suffer and endure them all. For they either bring something that does not displease me: or they make it so that I do not regret less not having learned. I dismiss them, however, not as insultingly as that Hannibal did the philosopher: and perhaps I even have more trouble because of that. But yet their doctrine, as far as I can judge, is ridiculous. For they divide the whole matter into two parts, into the controversy of a cause, and that of a question. They call a cause a matter placed in the dispute of affairs and controversy: A question, however, a matter placed in infinite doubt. They give precepts about the cause. About the other part of speaking, a wonderful silence. Finally, they make five parts, as it were, of eloquence: to find what you say: to arrange what is found: then to adorn with words: then to commit to memory:

<summary>Antonius shares his frustration with Greek rhetorical teachers who lack practical experience, noting that he handles them with more patience than Hannibal did. He begins to outline the standard five-part division of eloquence taught by these rhetoricians.</summary>
<keywords>rhetoric, Antonius, Catulus, Hannibal, Phormio, pedagogy</keywords>
pages.491:
<header>DE ORATORE</header>
<meta>continues from previous page: ...then to commit to memory:</meta> then finally to act and to deliver. A matter certainly not hidden. For who would not see, of his own accord, that no one can speak aptly unless he has both what he should say, and in what words, and in what order he should say it, and has remembered those things? And these things I do not criticize, but I say that they have been placed before our eyes, as are likewise those four, five, or six, or even seven parts, (since they are distinguished differently by others) into which all oratory is distributed by them. For they order one to begin in such a way that we make the one who hears us benevolent to us, and docile, and attentive: Then to narrate the matter so that the narration is probable, so that it is open, so that it is brief: After that, to divide the cause, or to propose; to confirm our points with arguments and reasons, then to refute the contrary ones. Then, however, others place the conclusion of the speech, and as it were the peroration. Others order, before one perorates, to digress for the sake of adorning or amplifying, then to conclude and to perorate. I do not even criticize these things: for they are neatly distributed, but yet, as was necessary for men lacking the truth, not skillfully. For the precepts which they wished to be of beginnings and narrations are to be preserved throughout the entire speeches. For I can make the judge benevolent to me more easily when I am in the flow of the speech than when everything is unheard; docile, however, not when I promise that I will demonstrate, but when I teach and explain: attentive, indeed, we can make them through frequent stirring of the minds of the judges throughout the entire action, not by a first announcement. Furthermore, that they order the narration to be probable, and open, and brief—

<summary>Antonius continues his critique of rhetorical instruction, arguing that the standard advice on speech structure—such as introductions and narration—is superficial and should be applied throughout a speech rather than treated as distinct, mechanical steps.</summary>
<keywords>rhetoric, speech structure, narration, peroration, eloquence, Antonius</keywords>
