Since Linacre and Tunstall have bound me to them by this kind of service, and have received an answer, I would like you to greet them for me in my words, and return a greeting to More, also with interest, who greeted me in your letters by the messengers with Linacre. Farewell, man most friendly to letters, and write me into your register. Paris, April 27th, 1518.

### Guillaume Budé to Richard Pace. Greetings.

Nicolas Bérauld, who delivered this letter to you, a man most learned in both tongues and already no small contributor to good letters, is also for other reasons a most dear friend to me. When I began to hear that he was going there in the company of the Bishop of Paris, I thought it my duty to give him a letter for you, even
pages.19:
if I had written a sufficiently long letter to you a few days ago and had entrusted it to a certain kinsman of mine, a companion of the same company. For I did not wish Bérauld, a man familiar to me and once a guest of your Erasmus, to be in Britain without your knowledge, as you yourself seem to me to be most loving toward studious men. Whatever service and courtesy you show him while he is in a foreign province, I will not refuse to charge the full account to myself. Although (given the humanity I have found you to possess), I do not doubt that you would have done this of your own accord if once you could have learned that a man of such character and such learning was there; and indeed, whenever you have the leisure to become acquainted with him, you will so desire everything for his sake that you will not ask that I consider it a favor to me what you have bestowed upon him. Yet, no less would I wish him to be commended to you in my name, so that he may be commended to me as much as my friends can be, through your kindness. Farewell, Paris, the day after the Assumption of the sublime Mother of God.

<note>A large, decorative capital letter P begins the paragraph.</note>

O immortal gods, what do I hear? Oh, how many? How great? What panegyrics? What theatrical speeches, worthy of applause by you and me, has the celebration of the betrothal excited among us! Our legation's reputation was received lavishly, elegantly, magnificently, kindly, elegantly, and eloquently. O your elegant King, greater than any proclamation, more outstanding than any commemoration of praise! He has provided such great and ample gifts of body and mind, an extraordinary and excellent willingness, and a gracious kindness toward all. He has made the munificence of a kindly nature seem accumulated and worthy of viewing through the dexterity of his manners, his august majesty, his heroic appearance, and the uprightness of his character. As soon as our men returned from there, they began to recount that splendid magnificence of the arrangements, and how rightly and orderly it was constituted. Not only were they received by all ears with inclination, but also every most serious person followed that account with gaping (so to speak) mouth and amazed face: that this most serene prince is accustomed to frequent his court with the presence of every most learned man and those most outstanding in the power of speech, and, as it were, to distinguish and adorn his court with these insignia. Such a sight they provide for a venerable royal court, and for foreigners to behold! He himself, in my opinion, is worthy that his fame, illuminated by these lights, may shine forth in every direction wherever the ends of the Christian name extend, and may be consecrated to eternal memory by the monuments of geniuses. For my own part, I would do nothing more willingly, nor more readily, if ever the opportunity for writing should occur
pages.20: my intent, so as to leave behind for such a great King a memorable eulogy, as a testimony of my mind inclined toward his majesty; he has indeed deserved honorably for letters, if what we have heard is true. For he who has raised the honor of the liberal arts, reduced to a common level both by the neglect of other nations and especially by our own customs and institutions, to a degree of higher summit, also producing an example in himself and an institution of royal eloquence, has indeed most beautifully snatched the glory of the thing for his contemporaries and for kings to come. Indeed, he is the first of kings in many centuries to have understood and seen that such is the power and authority of eloquence that it raises kings among the gods above and those below, according to the merits of each. If such a virtue were to offer itself so easily to be embraced, and to be retained with a certain immediate sweetness, such that the splendor and appearance of virtue itself would earn applause for itself through all kinds of men, both those acquainted with the liberal arts and those ignorant of them, undoubtedly princes, nobles, and primary men, taught by such a great example, would soon strive to preserve the majesty of higher letters; as, indeed, I see the sense of our own countrymen is now affected, ever since our legates returned. For there is no one among us now who is not ashamed and regretful of his own ignorance. But your speech, most learned Richard
pages.21:
held in the most ample assemblies of others, is celebrated to such a degree: as that opulently and pre-shining arrangement used in handling affairs was, and was adorned by your eloquence, and seemed all the more magnificent. If you hope that we will do the same in this part of setting up affairs, I fear that we are unable to satisfy you, among whom the reward of labor has never stood for eloquent industry, due to the notable obscurity of French affairs. Nicolas Bérauld, now most dear to you (as I learned from your letters), has set out for the court with the President of Paris, aided egregiously by your votes and recommendations, and encouraged there by no uncertain hope. The King is now said to be arriving, to receive the legates expected from there. Farewell, my Pace, and greet for me Tunstall, and my More, Linacre, and others. Paris, the Nones of November.

## Guillaume Budé to Richard Pace. Greetings.

Having now received your third letter, I have marveled at your diligence in this kind of cultivating friendship, to which I have scarcely experienced an equal in any of my friends. I wish that you are now successfully recovered from the fever. For it will be right that the concern for how prosperously you live, and how firm a health your body possesses, should pertain to me in the future, since I have such a benevolent mind toward you in it. So much the more gladly <unclear>[...]</unclear>
pages.22: the more voluntarily and nobly you have offered yourself to friendship. And indeed, when I enumerate my friends from abroad, you are justly placed among the very first, and you seem to me not only to have written your name into the catalog of your own accord, but also to perform the customary duties with both hand and heart. Therefore, I deem that a great addition has been made to my accounts in your name; indeed, to those holier ones, which I have decided to deposit in the citadel of Pallas, not in the temple of Saturn. Therefore, that you so kindly indulge me in the service of a friend, you have incurred a huge debt of gratitude from me. But see where you have now stepped. For what will happen if I call upon you not by formal contract, but by spontaneous promise? Since I have been well secured, both by the witness of a herald and by letters signed by you; and so that you cannot finally plead that you have been circumvented, you did not hesitate to promise the same thing again, and after a fairly long interval; since, for those binding themselves in this way, if they begin to shirk their duty later and make the agreements void, the constitutions of the laws permit one to object to the shame of a repeated promise and the bond of a doubled obligation. Therefore, when I acknowledge and embrace that candor of your mind, whereby you simply promise yourself to the service, then indeed I will take such account of your kindness and generous humanity that I will demand the promise only so far as
pages.23: you can discharge it cheerfully and without great difficulty, and not even at the very first opportunity: but when I have called in older debts, of which I still have many good and suitable ones, and whose judgment and adjudication I can establish in my own forum, if controversies arise from them. I have the account of this calendar of names so arranged that I think it is going well for me if I keep the contracts safe at home; as one who rejoices that my wealth is situated in it, so that I can boast for a long time that the day has already passed for many wealthy names, nor would I wish them to come, nor even if they had come, could I demand them without shame or sadness. I hear that a most ample legation is about to go there soon, concerning a matter both great and pacificatory. Which I wish to have been decreed so auspiciously that peace may be confirmed from it for my age and yours; so that I may be able to experience and act with you on more equal terms (if the matter turns out so) by an action on behalf of a friend: such, however, as anyone might marvel that no one has explicitly published in the civil law, who might indeed certainly think and notice that an action for a partner extends most broadly in the Pandects of the law. But in that legation, the Bishop of Paris will hold either the first or second place, as is the rumor: whether he was going to make his way through this city was not yet certain when I wrote this, and
pages.24:
he has been among the courtiers for a long time now, where he spends the greatest part of his time. He is a man learned among the few, and endowed with the prudence of many things, an embracer and supporter of the literate, and studious of your Erasmus, with whom I have a relationship more than a habit of life, I who dwell in the city. I believe that you will dutifully observe him, even for the sake of a recommendation of this matter, especially since, in fulfilling your office (as I conjecture), it will often be either necessary or opportune for you to speak with the legates. Farewell, and return a greeting a hundredfold to Tunstall, Linacre, and More, who have greeted me in your words or letters. Paris, the Kalends of August.

->Guillaume Budé to Thomas More. Greetings.<-

A pair of British hounds was offered to me on your behalf by Lupset, a young man learned in both tongues and (as I see) gracious among the learned. Although this was a very pleasing and delightful gift to me, and indeed ample and magnificent by the outcome (for I hope I have produced an excellent and fortunate munificence in gifting each of them), yet by no means less delightful was that pair of letters, in which, while reading them, I recognize and kiss your genius, as I once heard of it, and as I have known it from your Utopia.

# Fearing the Buddha
<gloss><term>Chuandeng Lu</term> <gloss>Record of the Transmission of the Lamp</gloss>: A partridge flew up and trembled on the railing of the Buddha hall. # Ancestor Buddha
<gloss><term>Chuandeng Lu</term></gloss>: Zen Master Yixuan of Zhenzhou arrived at the Bear-Ear Pagoda. The pagoda master asked: "Do you pay respect to the Buddha first, or to the ancestor first?" He replied: "Both [the Buddha and the ancestor] are not respected."

# Lightning-struck Buddha
<gloss><term>Chuandeng Lu</term></gloss>: The Fuzhou pagoda was struck by lightning. Someone asked: "Why was it struck by lightning?" The master said: "It is the working of Heaven." The monk said: "Since it is the working of Heaven, why [the Buddha]...?" The master said: "Where in the action do you see the Buddha?"

<gloss><term>Chuandeng Lu</term></gloss>: Zen Master Hai asked: "There are those who ask the Buddha... [if one] asks about the Dharma and answers... [it is] called a one-character Dharma gate. I do not know if this is correct or not."

# Total Buddha
<gloss><term>Chuandeng Lu</term></gloss>: Zen Master Baoji of Panshan in Youzhou said: "The total mind is the Buddha, [the total human] is the human. Human and Buddha are not different; only then is it the Way."

Sitting and rising, it is always following; in speech and silence, we dwell together.'"

# Road Buddha
<gloss><term>Hou Hanshu</term> <gloss>Book of the Later Han</gloss>, Biography of Wang Yun</gloss>: A man of the commandery was a 'Road Buddha' <note>A nickname for someone considered mediocre or without reputation.</note>; he was young and had no name or conduct, but the governor Wang Qiu summoned him to be an official. Yun faced the anger and insisted on arguing, and Qiu was enraged and arrested Yun, wanting to kill him. Inspector Deng Sheng heard of this and galloped to summon him as a military aide, and thus Yun became famous, and the 'Road Buddha' was discarded because of this.

In the <term>Sishierzhang Jing</term> <gloss>Sutra of Forty-two Chapters</gloss>, the Buddha said: "To feed ten billion arhats is not as good as feeding one Pratyeka Buddha." 
In the <term>Bodhisattva Benxing Jing</term> <gloss>Sutra of the Original Acts of Bodhisattvas</gloss>: "Even if one were to transform countless billions of people to become Pratyeka Buddhas, if someone for one hundred years made offerings with the four necessities, the merit would be very great; yet it is not as good as someone who, with a joyful heart, praises one four-line verse of the Tathagata's merit, which is immeasurable." 
In the <term>Zhiyue Lu</term> <gloss>Record of Pointing at the Moon</gloss>: "Koubing was a bathing monk of the ancient Buddha. Jianning Xinfeng's Ong family's son's mother dreamed of a monk, Feng. Kashyapa Buddha... Luoyang, Shen Jiongran carried a staff to seek lodging, people pointed and said: 'This is the Buddha.'" 
"Afterwards, she became pregnant. Song Yun and Huisheng were sent to the Western Regions; one day they arrived at the place where the Tathagata plucked his eye to give to a person. There was also a stupa and temple. On a stone in the temple, there was a Buddha's footprint." 
Bai Juyi's poem "Visiting Wuzhen Temple" says: "Formerly, the Buddha sat here in nirvana."

# Western Regions Buddha
In the <term>Youyang Zazu</term>: "In the Western Regions, at the Diamond Seat, there is a boundary mark; two statues of the bronze Avalokitesvara are present. The people of the country pass down that when the Bodhisattva's body is submerged, the Buddha's Dharma will also be exhausted. By the end of the Sui, it was already submerged past the chest."

# Buddha
In the <term>Gui Tian Lu</term> <gloss>Records of Returning to the Fields</gloss>: "When the Taizu Emperor first visited the Xiangguo Temple, he arrived before the Buddha image to burn incense and asked if he should bow or not. The monk official Zanning replied: 'The Buddha does not bow to the past Buddha.' The Emperor smiled and understood this, and thus it became a fixed custom."

# Past Buddha
See above. In the <term>Chuandeng Lu</term>: "The Venerable One said: 'The one who sits with me is the Past Banyan Tree King Tathagata.' The crowd said: 'Our master's divine power is truly believable.' He said: 'The past Buddha is...' They were secretly suspicious. Sengqie knew the masses were slow to believe, so he slowly extended his right hand into the earth, reaching the diamond wheel limit, taking the nectar water to bring to the assembly in a glass vessel. The great crowd saw it and at that moment admired him, repented, and paid respects."

<gloss>From the <term>Gui Er Lu</term> <gloss>Record of Valued Hearing</gloss>: There was an official from Sichuan in the capital, requesting an appointment, staying for three or four years. This poem spread, and because of it, he obtained a position and left.</gloss>

# The Pure Soul of Madam Jiang (Volume 2)

<margin>Holding hands to part, then parting to compose poetry, the sentiment is extremely sweet, yet it is also merciful and painful. Could this truly be a final parting?</margin>

The high courtesy shown by Ding <note>referring to Fu Yue, a legendary sage-minister</note> toward others is just like the assistance given to King Wen <note>referring to Jiao Ge, another legendary figure of the Shang dynasty</note>. If a person can obtain even a spoonful of water, they can prolong their remaining breath, let alone a journey to Wenzhou and Fujian that takes no more than half a month. Go forward with determination; why harbor doubts? <gloss>The fox's nature is one of suspicion.</gloss> The scholar followed this advice. When the spring of the third month of the Gengyin year of the Zhizheng era arrived, the scholar prepared his luggage at the Diankou pass and composed a short poem in four rhymed lines to sigh at his own situation. He chanted:

> Lacking the destiny for fame and rank, I mount my horse;
> In vain, I carry my scholar's cap into old age.
> Asking if my return robes are still here,
> The rivers and lakes shall serve as the travels of Zichang. <gloss>Referring to Sima Qian, whose courtesy name was Zichang.</gloss>

Madam Jiang also composed a short poem:

> Bees and butterflies gather in busy, chasing teams;
> Travelers are dyed by the fragrance of a hundred flowers.
> Even if you go without a companion of your own kind,
> The spring breezes of the Yi River shall let you wander freely.

After the poems were finished, they parted ways. The scholar said to Shuying, "Take good care of yourself. In a month or so, I shall return." The scholar traveled toward the coast, and on the twenty-first day, he reached Fujian. He heard that his old friend had...

<column-break/>

<margin>Planning to visit an old friend only reveals that his family finances were truly desperate; his broad travels were also a matter of helplessness.</margin>

### The Pure Soul of Madam Jiang

Wei Jie of Wenzhou was a man of letters. He practiced Confucianism and mastered his studies, was well-versed in historical anecdotes, and was appointed as a student at the prefectural school. His wife, Madam Jiang, named Shuying, was passably familiar with the classics and histories. The couple lived alone and were always respectful toward each other, possessing the legacy of the ancient figures Liang Hong and Meng Guang. <gloss>Famous for their mutual respect as husband and wife.</gloss> However, since Jie occupied himself with the brush and ink as a Confucian scholar and was not from a merchant family, and since Shuying managed the household with simple, coarse clothing, how could they provide for their daily meals? Consequently, their family estate was particularly destitute, to the point where they could barely survive. An old friend named Shen Tianxi held the position of <term>darughachi</term> <gloss>a Mongol administrative official</gloss> in the Fujian circuit. Jie planned to go and visit him, but when he wanted to depart, he worried about leaving his home empty, and he lacked the travel funds to sustain himself. His mind was caught between the decision to go or stay for a long time. Shuying stepped forward and said, "Poverty will surely lead to success; if not, one will return to prosperity. This is the natural order. Fu Yue was not yet met, so he hid himself in the construction of walls; Jiao Ge was not yet met, so he lived among the fish and salt sellers. When the time and opportunity arrived, they were raised up and employed."

# The Snowing Injustice of the Maid of Qu

<margin></margin>
At the beginning of the dynasty, there was the case of the Censor of the Four Horses, and later the incorruptible, unbiased official Shangguan; this story is essentially an enactment of that.
</margin>

## The Snowing Injustice of the Maid of Qu

In the Renxu year of the Hongzhi era, the Yunnan Regional Inspector, Shangguan Shouzhong, conducted himself with integrity. He cut off all contact with the households of the powerful and treated others with impartiality, suppressing the influence of treacherous factions. When hearing legal cases, the straight and the crooked were immediately distinguished, and when resolving doubts, his vision was sagacious and clear. At that time, he was inspecting the customs of the Yunnan domain; having traveled everywhere, he felt no sense of dread. One evening, he stayed at the Gongsi station. He sat alone with a bright candle, having no way to dismiss his feelings, and thus chanted a regulated poem:

> The disused horses have been gone long, the grass is deep;
> The ruined walls and fallen ramparts lean against the dangerous peak.
> The bedside is full of dust where the spiders gather;
> Outside the curtain, the wind is desolate, and the crickets chirp.
> The traveler's pillow cannot bear the breaking of fragrant dreams;
> The scattered quilt deeply feels the early arrival of the cold.
> I feel only pity for the few plum blossoms under the moon;
> They know the one single heart of my entire life.

He also chanted another regulated poem:

> For years, my lowly office has kept me running to the frontier; <gloss>Border regions.</gloss>
> In the mirror, the west wind shows two temples of graying silk.
> The mountain lodge is bright with moon, the rooster crows early;
> In the sea and sky, the clouds are cold, and the geese return...

<column-break/>

<margin></margin>
The first line speaks of the rising sun turning upon the ten thousand trees, an idea of new beginnings; the last line about the cold valley is like the saying of a Daoist scholar, which is an idea of desolation.
</margin>

...late. Half my life's undertakings have been empty; ten thousand miles of mountain passes find the guest weary.
My worries are extreme at the small window as the remnants of dreams break;
The cuckoo cries out from the highest branch.

After chanting, suddenly a faint breeze brushed against the window, and dark fog billowed. Listening quietly, it sounded like someone speaking; it gradually formed a voice that chanted:

> The night moon hangs like a golden mirror, <gloss>A mirror.</gloss>
> The spring breeze unfurls the brocade sail.
> If the river flowers had feelings,
> They would fly to adorn my embroidered robes.

Before he could ask, she chanted the "Fragrant Tree Song":

> The morning sun turns the vast creation, <gloss>Sun beginning to emerge is called 'Xu'.</gloss>
> The garden has ten thousand new trees.
> The painted screen shows morning beauty;
> The colorful railing moves spring at night.
> The wild paths are all worth viewing;
> The neighbors are not at all poor.
> I only pity the bottom of the cold valley;
> The bitter leaves are still suspected of being dust.

Official Shangguan heard this and recognized that it was the voice of a soul from the beyond. Furthermore, examining her poetry, he sensed a feeling of injustice. He knew that she must have a hidden grievance that she could not voice herself, so he declared, "You spirit of the beyond, what injustice do you have? Can you state it?" From outside the window, she wept and said, "I am not a person of the living world, but from the realm of..."

...shadowy halls. My father and I have carried grievances in the human world for a long time. I have not yet come to face my situation and tell of my feelings. I humbly beg for your detailed investigation." The inspector saw a beautiful woman kneeling under the lamp. A moment later, she held up a silk handkerchief and wept, saying, "I am the daughter of the Xu Inspector of Qinzhou. Unhappily, five years ago, I accompanied my father to his post. When we were passing through this district, a man named Pian saw my beauty and conceived a treacherous plan. He poisoned my father to death <gloss>Died by poison.</gloss> and sank his corpse into the river. Then he wanted to assault me. <gloss>I steadfastly refused.</gloss> I hanged myself with my silk handkerchief, and he buried my body under the artificial hill in the back garden. Alas, all living things love life and hate death; the human heart is the same in this. Reward the good and punish the evil; the way of heaven should be thus. My father was on orders to go to his official post; what crime did he have? My body was following my father to his post; what name is there for me to die? This base man and his evil party destroyed reason and harmed people. This is something the laws of the living must execute and the underworld will not pardon. If he continues to live peacefully, where is the sagely law of Yu? <gloss>This is in imitation of the great prison cases of Lord Zhang; Zhang Shizhi would still have handled it accordingly.</gloss>

<column-break/>

<margin></margin>
Execute the man Pian in the marketplace, and then the souls of the father and daughter of the Xu family will be avenged.
</margin>

...in the high gate of Lord Yu, <gloss>Referring to Yu Dingguo, a famous official of the Han dynasty.</gloss> let my father and me die without suffering further. My father's and my grievances are sunk but not muddied. It is only today." After she finished speaking, she suddenly transformed into wind and left, leaving no trace to follow. The official listened in detail and could not help but be filled with indignation and rage, hating that he could not immediately summon the man and record his crimes. His heart was filled with suspense, and he sat waiting for dawn. The official reflected on how he could deal with the situation; if he punished him without proof, there would be no cause. If he interrogated him, there would be no evidence. Thus, he devised a plan in his heart. The next morning, when the man Pian and his cohorts were gathered, the official commanded them, "Five years ago, there was an Inspector named Xu who committed a breach of the constitutional laws, and it was appropriate for him to die. By mistake, he escaped and fled to this place. I have received an imperial decree that whoever can execute him will be rewarded with one hundred taels of silver. Have any of you ever known of this?" The man Pian and the others replied in unison, "We have already killed him and sank his corpse in the river." Shouzhong was greatly pleased, took their written confessions, threw them into prison, reported the matter to the imperial court, and they were all executed in the marketplace. Both near and far were amazed by this.

At this time, the night was deep, and the world was silent. The slanted moon had already sunk, and there was no light or clarity. Between the darkness and gloom, while walking in the wild fields west of the room, he suddenly heard the sound of crying. It was faint, coming from far and then near. The listener also felt desolate and miserable. The scholar then hid in a secluded place to observe her movements. <gloss>To observe.</gloss> Just then, a beautiful woman arrived slowly. She walked while weeping. As he listened and watched, her fat and skin were moist and abundant; her appearance was enchanting, possessing a kind of beauty that startled the observer. She said repeatedly, "My good man, my good man, I do not know where you are now." The scholar was originally a man who lived without restraint, and when he saw her beauty, he felt joyful <gloss>Unable to restrain himself; flat tone.</gloss> and rushed out before her. He teased her, saying, "Your good man is here. Why do you cry?" The woman did not seem very surprised. She straightened her appearance and thanked him, saying, "This is my good fortune." The scholar asked, "Why are you walking at night and weeping with such annoyance?" She said, "I am of the Gu family in the east village. Unfortunately, my husband passed away early, and I have been a widow. I served my mother-in-law, but because we did not get along, I was driven out by her."

<column-break/>

<margin></margin>
First, it narrates Concubine Gu's favor while she was alive, then narrates her death, both of which serve as the foundation for the spiritual essence in the later text.
</margin>

## The Spiritual Essence of Concubine Gu

During the reign of Emperor Guangzong of the Song dynasty, there was a favorite concubine surnamed Gu. She was selected to enter the palace. Her nature was agile, and she was quite knowledgeable about books and histories. She also dabbled in poetry and its laws. At the time, she was praised as virtuous within the palace. When she reached the end of her life, she was buried outside the Yongjin Gate in Hangzhou, on Magpie's Nest Mountain. Things changed and time moved on, and it became nothing more than a pile of mounds in the wilderness. By the second year of the Jingtai era, a scholar from Shanyin named Chen Yance, with the courtesy name Chengzhi, was also a man of wind and moon. He responded to the times, nourished things, and entrusted his boldness to the great mountains. <gloss>Refers to famous mountains.</gloss> He chanted to the moon and recited to the wind, keeping his secluded thoughts in poetry and rhyme. One day, he had business in Qiantang and lived abroad at Yongjin Gate. He thought of the journey to the Qiantang River and strolled, chanting a regulated poem:

> I have driven north and south, the years and months are distant;
> The traveler's feelings and thoughts are both far away.
> White sands and green bamboos on the wild riverbanks;
> Yellow reeds and water by the bridge outside the temple.
> A few sails cast toward the extreme shores; <gloss>The river mouth is called 'Pu'.</gloss>
> Several sounds of the fisherman's flute rise with the cold tide;
> The state of the world is like floating clouds.

<summary>This page contains a story about Concubine Gu, whose spiritual essence appears to a scholar named Chen Yance after her death, reflecting on her past life and current state as a lonely grave.</summary>
<keywords>Concubine Gu, Chen Yance, Hangzhou, Qiantang River, ghost story, spiritual essence</keywords>

They then met together, fully exhausting the quiet endearments. She once patted the scholar’s back and recited two regulated verses, saying: "Pear blossoms cover the ground as the bright moon comes, / Vainly I listen for the imperial carriage, its sound like thunder. / The silver pitcher is broken, difficult to mend again, / The golden lock is opened, yet I return empty-handed. / Drifting clouds uselessly pine for the dream of Gaotang, / Who pities the talent of Xie Yun when chanting of snow? <gloss>An allusion to her own situation.</gloss> / Do not cast spring longing into the incense burner, / Casting it aside in leisure until it turns cold to ash." Again she said: "Flowers clear, fragrant dust recalls the old track, / Clever orioles pass the songs and bells beyond the flute. / Scarlet silk socks line the narrow, double-hooked feet, / Golden-threaded clothes are scented with a hundred fragrances. / Dew cools the cloud gallery, chanting of cassia leaves, / The bright moon in the water palace watches the lotus. / Now, past events are hard to recall, / Grief cuts through the twelve peaks of Mount Wu." When she finished reciting, Juan wept and said, "That I secretly meet with you in violation of the prohibitions is because my intent is long-lasting; I do not want to be forgotten. I hope you will not neglect our love, like clouds and rain, and cause it to break. Even in the Nine Springs <gloss>the underworld</gloss>, my heart will be at peace." The scholar swore he would not betray their original promise. They associated with each other for nearly half a month. The scholar suddenly felt suspicious. The next day, he observed the meeting place and saw only tangled grass and tall trees, standing there as a desolate grave. Upon visiting the village elders, he learned this was the tomb of Concubine Yuan, from the era of Emperor Guangzong of the Song dynasty.

# Presentation of the Concubine’s Image

<margin>Wan'e died at twenty; this is what is meant by a jade person being crushed by the earth. How sad!</margin>

During the pseudo-Han dynasty, Chen Youliang had a concubine surnamed Zheng, named Wan'e. Her jade-like substance and icy posture were the most beautiful of her generation. Moreover, she was familiar with literature and music. The pseudo-Han emperor loved her extremely. She died at the age of twenty and was buried at the Pipa Pavilion in Jiangzhou. <gloss>Jiangzhou is modern-day Jiujiang.</gloss> At the time, two maids were buried with her: one named Xichan and one named Jin’e. Because the concubine was noble and beautiful, even after entering the underworld, her spirit would sometimes appear in the daylight. Those living nearby would see her walking or hear the sound of her singing; there was no one who did not mourn for her. During the early Hongwu era, Shen Shao of Wujiang was in the bloom of youth and possessed a beautiful appearance. His poetry was modeled after Sa Tianxi <gloss>an expert at poetry</gloss>, and his calligraphy was modeled after Guo Bojing <gloss>an expert at calligraphy</gloss>. Both were praised by his peers. He once harmonized with Tianxi's two poems about Jiading and Wuzhong, saying: "Seven marshes and three rivers reach for a hundred miles, / Willows and lotuses reflect the lake. / Passing the water gate, I arrive at Panmen, / Half-covered red curtains in the painted towers. / The miwu herb grows past the swimming mandarin ducks, / The east wind sheds all the crabapple flowers. / In the fragrant paths of the Guanwa Palace, deer run, / In the dark night, I see lanterns of red gauze. / Below the Three Worthies Shrine, the eastern river continues <gloss>The Shrine of the Three Worthies.</gloss> / Above the grave of Zhenniang, the wind blows through the bamboo. / After Xi Shi left, the sandal-wood shoes were forgotten, / Year after year, in deep spring, the burn marks are green. / In the southeastern landscape, the prosperous neighborhood, / A piece of sheng and xiao music brushes the river water. / A young girl writes spring on a white ramie shirt, / Cassia oars and orchid paddles in the mirror-like light. / Dancing stages and singing pavilions face the gull sand, / White walls partially emerge from cherry blossoms. / Butterflies gather fragrance and will not leave, / Striking down the light and thin silk fans. / Who will continue the Wu songs this night? / In the willow shadows, blowing through the Ke pavilion bamboo. / Fan Li’s flat boat leaves and does not return, / Only the spring waves reflect the green of men." His other poems were all of this type. However, because his family was wealthy, he did not wish to seek officialdom. People knew this and sought to profit from his wealth. Some wanted to nominate him as a filial and incorrupt official, others wanted to guarantee him as a student disciple, and the clamor left him with no peace. Although Shao...

It was faint, now far and now near, sometimes high and sometimes low. The three looked at each other, startled and confused. They listened for a long time, and then it was silent. After the wine was finished and they returned to the boat, they did not know the cause. Shao alone was fond of strange things. The next day, he went to investigate the truth, but found nothing at all. Just as he was about to return, a strange fragrance suddenly assailed him. Shao stood and waited. Soon, a beautiful woman in palace dress appeared, her appearance like a heavenly immortal, with two young maids leading her. Shao suspected it was a noble family's house.

<column-break/>
<margin>At first, he said there was a human scent; after searching, Shao appeared and offered an apology. The beautiful woman ordered them to share the mat. Shao approached the mat and asked her surname. The beautiful woman said: "I am Concubine Zheng Wan'e of the Han Chen lord. I died at twenty and was buried here. This one maid, Xichan, and one, Jin'e, were also buried with me at that time." Shao had always possessed courage and valued romantic feelings, so he did not consider it strange. The beautiful woman ordered Xichan to fetch wine and pour it in the pavilion. She sang a lyric titled "Nian Nu Jiao." The lyric said: "Dense, dense the grain, sighing for the rivers and mountains that seem old. / Heroes turned to dust, stone horses and bronze camels amid the thorns. / How many cold summers have passed through? / Iron spears turn to ash, flags and birds scatter. / Where can one look for the wine cups? / Dumb and silent, shouting and roaring, even now they still speak of the Hegemon of Western Chu. / Haggard in the jade tent, facing the lamp, covering my face, tears fly like red rain."</margin>

He secretly slipped a letter of his heart into the incense burner and burned it to provide for the beautiful woman’s merit in the underworld. ## The Consort Writes of Her Grievances

The Han Consort Ming was Wang Qiang. She was selected to enter the court of the Hu barbarians. Because of the pipa, she wrote of her grievances and later died, being buried in that land in a green grass mound. In the Jin dynasty, during the Guimao year of the Dading reign, Wanyan Shouyi of the Shangjing clan was a refined scholar. He had an errand <gloss>an affair</gloss> and went out. Seeing the tomb of Consort Ming, he felt moved in his heart and sighed, cupping his hands, saying, "Heroic, heroic! Treacherous ministers misled you! Alas, in the Han lands of the desert, you drank the pain and hatred of a thousand years!" Once he left, he pushed it aside as a past event. By evening, he was returning and traveled past the Consort’s tomb. He raised his eyes to look and saw a magnificent residence standing tall and alone. <gloss>Kui means high.</gloss> The painted beams and carved pillars were not of human dimension; the vermilion curtains and emerald screens resembled the immortal residence in heaven. Shouyi was both startled and suspicious. Before he could examine it in detail, he saw a beautiful woman with teeth like pearls and a graceful posture coming out from inside, saying, "Young master, will you temporarily humble yourself to bow and drink tea?" Shouyi...

<column-break/>

<margin>Shouyi’s pen portrays the Consort Ming living among the outer barbarians; if the barbarians were like the cold moon, she looked outward, her love departed, finally obtaining work to tell her story. It is also a strange encounter.</margin>

...before he could respond, the beauty asked again. Having no other choice, he followed her, entering the central hall. He took a seat as the host, and they drank tea, followed by wine. The beauty stood and thanked him, saying, "Today, I was honored by your clear gaze, and you expressed words of injustice. Although my body has rotted with the plants and trees in the Nine Springs, I feel gratitude and will not forget it." Shouyi was about to inquire about her surname and her words from the day, but the beauty suddenly rose and said, "I beg to tell my own heart’s feelings. Young master, please do not be alarmed. I am not a person of this contemporary world; I am Consort Ming, Wang Qiang, Zhaojun, of the Great Han dynasty. Since the treacherous minister <gloss>It is said he refers to Mao Yanshou.</gloss> forced me to marry the barbarians, I left the emperor in tears. The emperor missed my appearance and regretted it, but it had already been sent to the barbarians; regrets were of no use. After I arrived at the barbarian court, I held my pipa every day and wrote of my grievances, dying of depression. Even today, I am still a ghost relying on the longing for my hometown." She chanted a seven-character four-line regulated poem to lament herself, saying: "Ten thousand miles of yellow clouds, the desert grass is withered, / The pipa has no words, the bright moon is alone. / The King’s barrier..."

# The Presentation of the Lady of Jieyu

<margin></margin>
The elegant lady died at twenty; this is truly what is called a jade person crushed by the earth. How moving!
</margin>

Chen Youliang of the pseudo-Han dynasty had a Lady of Jieyu <note>an imperial concubine title</note> named Zheng Wane. She possessed a jade-like constitution and an icy grace, with a beauty unmatched in her time. She was also familiar with literature and skilled in music and rhythm. The pseudo-Han treated her with the utmost favor. She died at the age of just twenty and was buried at the Pipa Pavilion in Jiangzhou <gloss>Jiangzhou is modern-day Jiujiang</gloss>. At that time, two serving maids were buried with her: one named Xichan and the other named Jin’e. Although the Lady of Jieyu was noble and beautiful, after entering the underworld, her spirit would sometimes appear in broad daylight. Those living nearby would occasionally see her walking about or hear the sound of her playing music, and none were without feelings of grief. In the early Hongwu era, Shen Shao of Wujiang, a young man of twenty, was also handsome and talented. He studied poetry under Sa Tianxi <gloss>a master of poetry</gloss> and calligraphy under Guo Bojing <gloss>a master of calligraphy</gloss>, both of whom were praised by their contemporaries. Once, he harmonized with Tianxi’s two poems about passing through Jiaxing and writing on Wu: The first said, "The Seven Marshes and the Three Rivers connect for a hundred li; the willows and lotuses reflect the lake—"

<column-break/>

<margin></margin>
These two poems about Wu, although using the scenery to express his feelings, also contain gratitude and longing; they were not written lightly.
</margin>

"—water. Past the water gate, then it is Pan Gate; behind half-hidden red curtains in the painted towers, the *miwu* herbs have grown over the mandarin ducks. The east wind has blown away all the pear blossoms; in the Guanwa fragrance path, deer run, and in the clear night, lanterns can be seen. Below the Temple of the Three Worthies <gloss>a shrine to three sages</gloss>, the eastern flow continues; above the grave of Zhenniang, the wind blows through the bamboo. After Xi Shi left, the wooden sandals were overturned; year after year, the spring deepens, and the fire-scars turn green. In the prosperous region of the southeast, a stretch of flute and string music brushes the river water. The young maiden writes of spring on a white ramie shirt; the magnolia oars and orchid paddles are in the mirror’s reflection. The dance stages and song pavilions face the gull sands; the whitewashed walls are half-hidden by cherry blossoms. The butterflies picking fragrance do not leave, fluttering down on the light, round silk fans. Who will continue the Wu songs tonight? In the willow shadows, the flute blows through the Ke Pavilion bamboos. Fan Li’s flat boat is gone and will not return; only the spring waves reflect the green of the people."

<margin>Sighing at the tomb, lamenting the mistake of the treacherous official—this has been the public sentiment for a thousand years.</margin>

## The Beautiful Concubine Writes of Regret

The Honorable Concubine of the Han was Wang Qiang. Because she entered the barbarian lands according to the registers, she wrote of her regret using the *pipa*. Later, she was buried in that land, and the grass on her tomb turned green. In the Guiwei year of the Dading era of the Jin Dynasty, Wanyan Shouyi, a refined scholar from the capital, had business to attend to <gloss>circumstances</gloss>. He saw the tomb of the Honorable Concubine and felt moved in his heart. He cupped his hands and sighed, saying, "How heroic! How heroic! The treacherous official ruined you! Han lies in the northern desert, drinking the sorrow and regret of a thousand years! How bitter!" After he left, he simply let it pass as a thing of the past. By evening, he was returning and passed by the Concubine’s tomb. He raised his eyes to look and saw a magnificent residence standing tall and alone <gloss>kui means tall</gloss>. The painted beams and carved rafters were not of human standards; the red curtains and emerald screens resembled the celestial abodes of heaven. Shouyi was both surprised and suspicious. Before he could investigate in detail, he saw a beautiful woman with fragrant breath and a graceful figure come out from within, saying, "Young master, would you like to humble yourself and come in for tea?" Shouyi—

Whether the accidents are one or many, C, therefore, is never found in A because of them, but one of its causes K is in A C. C is not like that, for C is found in A without another existence preceding it essentially. As for A, if it were in potency C, then at that time there would be in A another type homogeneous with C, but that is by accident, not by essence, and that type is not a cause for the existence of C in A. As for A needing another cause to be C, which is the mover, that is only for each individual of the substances, since the forms of the individuals are opposites in one matter numerically and it is impossible for opposites to gather together at one time, and this is outside what we intended. Let the first matter be A, and let C be a certain place as one of the types of difference in K; it is not found in A without a cause preceding its existence in A, otherwise the accidents would be separate from the substance. Let the preceding meaning be C F N. If the subsistence of C is by it, then C is in N according to the natural course. If its subsistence is not by it, then K in C is outside of nature, and its existence in it is outside of nature, by compulsion or otherwise. Since it is a place, it is necessarily by compulsion, because the types of place are opposites, and their genus is not separate from substance, but rather equivalence necessarily follows it. That is clear to anyone who has engaged in this philosophy even the slightest bit. Its existence in it is only because of an obstacle, for K and its opposite are not among the opposites that belong to the subject equally, like sitting and standing for Zayd. Thus, if K precedes in A another existence, which is either another existence, or the relation of the world to it, it is a cause insofar as it is a part of what the subsistence of K depends on. Let the obstacle be Q. Thus K is found in A with the existence of C or Q necessarily. It is not possible for K to exist in A without C or Q, not even in speech, so how could it in existence? If C ceases—and the cessation of C is necessarily by change, and it may be by nature and other causes—then K will cease. If C ceases, if it ceases at once, it ceases at once. If it ceases...

If K is an accident in H by accident, if K is in A, the existence of Q precedes. With the cessation of Q, K ceases. If Q ceases part by part, its cessation is simultaneous with the cessation of K. If it ceases at once, and that is possible, then at that moment the cessation of K follows. However, if something has an opposite, and if there is no intermediate between them, K ceases at once. Let its opposite be L, or because we assumed K to be in H outside of nature. Therefore, L is for H by nature, K became in H since there is no intermediate between K and L. H is not free from them, like the one and the many, the even and the odd. If there are intermediates between them, it is clear that H is in potency L. It may be possible to move, because everything that moves is in potency that toward which it moves, so in it is the moved thing. Because what is in potency A is in act K, and K is divisible, therefore it is necessarily required that in A there be L. It requires the existence of another thing that necessitates that, as we said, which is either A or H. But it is not Q; it is H in H that necessitates for it to be in it K, and by it A becomes worthy of K. Therefore, it was necessary to be in A at the moment. But since L and K are opposites and divisible, that was not at a moment; it was in time. Therefore, it was found part after part in continuity, without being clearer in one of the parts. This is motion. Therefore, H is the mover for it in this way.

A questioner may ask about K and L if there is no intermediate between them, when did L become in H? If it was at the moment when H ceased, and H was always K, then H became K and L together. They are opposites, and that is not possible. If it was at another moment, and between every two moments is time, then H was free from K and L, and there became an intermediate between them. That is all contrary to what was assumed. The discussion on this is part of the discussion on motion. It has been explained that motion has no parts in the sixth <note>book</note> of the "Physics" <note>original: "al-Sama'"</note>. And it has been explained that the moment...

...is only for the future, not for the past. Let us turn from speaking about it to the observer of change, as it is not part of its path in this discussion.

It has been explained, then, how stones move. In general, everything that moves moves one of the two opposite movements essentially. As for the eternal bodies, we do not find among their movements any opposites. That has been explained in the first <note>book</note> of his book "On the Heavens and the World" <note>original: "Fi al-Sama' wa al-'Alam"</note>. Everything that moves one of the opposite movements is a natural body, and its form, which is a part, is called nature in particular. Every change has one opposite, and sometimes more than one. It may be opposed by rest only; an example of this is learning, for its opposite is remaining in ignorance. It may be opposed by another change along with rest, such as ascending, for it is opposed by remaining below, and it is opposed by descending, which is the movement to below. Movement may be opposed by movement in ways other than these two. That has been summarized in the fifth <note>book</note> of the "Physics". Movement in place has opposite endpoints: ascending and descending. It belongs to every hylomorphic <note>possessing matter</note> body, and primarily to the elements <term>al-ustuqusāt</term> <gloss>elements</gloss>. Each of them has one of the types of this movement essentially, such as descending for earth and ascending for fire. It belongs to other bodies because of them, for every hylomorphic body <note>Folio 345a</note> is either one of them or composed of more than one—an example of this is the bodies of plants and animals, for they are composed of earth and water; oil and wax are composed of them and air and smoke; and vapor is composed of water and earth. Aristotle has summarized the types of these in many places.

As for other bodies that have not been given a principle more complete than this from the principles of the existence of the elements—rather, the principles of their existence are homogeneous to those—they have no local movement essentially except these two types only, such as gold, wax, plant bodies, and animal bodies when souls have departed from them, such as juniper wood and ebony wood. Therefore, other movements are found in them by accident: either outside of nature or by compulsion.

pages.49:
<header>Abd al-Rahman Badawi</header>
<meta>[36]</meta>

The genera of local movement are three: the genus whose endpoints are ascending and descending; the second is the genus whose endpoints are advancing and retreating; and the third is the genus whose endpoints are moving to the right and moving to the left. These three genera are the genera of simple local movement. Any movement other than these is composite, like the movement of a river. As for the circular movements of an animal, it is a movement on a multi-angled shape and is composite in terms of combination and mixture. Summarizing that is outside of what we are concerned with.

Movement in place is called in the language of the Arabs some of its types "transfer" <term>al-naqla</term> <gloss>transfer or migration</gloss>, and it is voluntary movement. Sometimes it is said now and then for every type of its types as a transfer. Let us call it transposition. Regarding transposition, what of it is above and below, we have spoken about it. As for the other two genera, they are found for the animal especially. Not every type of them is found for every type of animal, as the types of transposition were found for the elements. Rather, both opposites are found equally for one and the same animal numerically, but not at every time. The reason for the difference in that is that above and below are limited by nature: for below is the center, and above is the concave of the sphere of the moon or another body below it. It is not possible in the center to be above, nor in the concave of the sphere of the moon to be below, for their quiddity requires that. As for the right, it is not limited in itself, for the existence of a place as a right is only by relation to the mover. By that, one place is a right for one and a left for another at one time, and it is a right and a left for one and the same animal numerically, but at two times, not at one time. Every animal is a body with distinct directions. Every body with distinct directions, the first place in which it is has distinct relations to other places. Every type of animal has types of place natural to it; an example of this is the bird, which has natural places in the air and places on the earth. Places in the water may also be found for it. That has been summarized...

As for whether its places in the air are similar to its places in matter or not, summarizing that is appropriate in the discussion on the local movements of animals. We have halted this discussion on the existence of the moved thing in the animal by nature <note>a blank space appears in the source text</note> ... except that it is an animal, for every animal is a body with distinct directions, so its places have distinct relations to one another. This is for the animal insofar as it is an animal. The most complete animal in distinguishing directions is man, for the directions of every straight body are six. As for plants, above and below have been distinguished in them, but contrary to the position of the world. We will speak about that after this. As for non-rational animals, front and back have been distinguished in those that are striving. Shellfish are not striving. In most of these, right and left have been distinguished. As for above and below, it has not been distinguished in them that the directions are circular, nor do they have legs. Also, the position of the bottom of the animal is its legs, as if its above is its back, and the back in man is behind him. Man, among all hylomorphic existents, is where all directions are distinguished: for his front is distinguished from his back, his above from his below, and his right from his left. These genera—I mean the genera of local movement—may be by the will of the animal, and they may be for it by necessity. As for by necessity, like the falling of someone who has tumbled from a height, for this is one of the types of what is said by necessity. That has been summarized in ethics <note>referring to Nicomachean Ethics</note>, and moving a patient from his bed. It may be by will: like the movement of a man to the market. As for the movement of necessity other than the first genus, the mover for the animal may be outside it. It may be in the first genus, like moving a patient from the house to the balcony <note>original: "al-shurfa"</note>. As for the places of the animal, while they are determined by relation to it, every place must have its determination, for the corner is a place determined by the craft, and the handle is a place determined by grasping. Summarizing the types of animal places is appropriate in the discussion on local movements.

pages.224:
<margin></margin>
A miraculous encounter and predestined union. There are many historical precedents for those who have borne witness to such things. There are accounts of meetings in the wilderness and encounters where one is invited to a tavern, but one has never heard of such earthly pleasures being enjoyed as those of Master Chen.
</margin>

Master Chen said, "If so, where will you go?" The beauty replied, "I am going to my uncle’s house to take refuge." Master Chen used this opportunity to entice her with words. The beauty did not refuse. Master Chen asked for a marital union, and the beauty agreed. Master Chen wished to bring her to his lodgings <note>a place for travelers</note>, but he was worried because there were many people living there, fearing that it would ruin the affair. Having no other choice, they undressed, spread their clothes upon the ground, and came together. <note>Covered by the sky and pillowed by the earth, what need is there for the flowery candles of a bridal chamber? The carpet of green grass is far better than a lotus-embroidered quilt.</note> When it was time to part, they were deeply attached and could not bear to leave one another. <note>"She" read as "shè," to let go.</note> Master Chen grasped her hand and said, "I do not know when I will be able to untie your silk sash again." The beauty smiled and said, "Having this meeting in this very place is enough. You need not regret anything." From that night on, Master Chen waited for her; as soon as he arrived, she would already be there. No one ever surpassed her. Every time she welcomed him, she would say to him, "Why are you so late coming to me?" Then they would come together, exhausting the utmost depths of their intimate affection. Once, she patted Master Chen’s back and recited two poems, saying:

"The pear blossoms fill the ground as the moonlight arrives,
In vain I hear the palace carriage rumble like thunder.
The silver bottle is broken, hard to ever re-join,
The golden key is unlocked—

<column-break/>
<margin></margin>
These two poems are recited with a clear and ancient elegance. They enter into the realm of true poetry; one should not treat them lightly simply because the circumstances are unusual.
</margin>

And now it returns to emptiness. In the drifting clouds, I idly dream of the Gao-Tang dream,
Who pities the talent of Xie Yun <note>a Tang dynasty poetess, used here by the ghost to describe herself</note> in composing poetry about snow?
Do not send a spring heart to the incense burner,
Cast away idly, it cools into ash."

She also said:
"The flowers are clear, the fragrant dust remembers the old path,
Clever orioles sing beyond the flute, through the songs and bells.
Crimson silk socks line the slenderness of her arched feet,
Golden-threaded robes are scented with a hundred perfumes.
The dew is cold on the cloud-corridors as I chant of the cassia leaves,
The moon is bright on the water-palace where I view the lotus blossoms.
Now, the past is truly difficult to recall,
Sorrow breaks my heart at the twelve peaks of Mount Wu."

After reciting, the beauty wept and said, "I have violated the prohibitions to share this secret time with you because I intended for it to last long, and I did not want to forget you. I hope you will not let the warmth of our love be severed. Even in the Nine Springs <note>the underworld</note>, my heart will be able to close its eyes in peace." Master Chen swore not to betray their initial agreement. They associated with each other for nearly half a month. Master Chen suddenly became suspicious. The following day, he observed the meeting place. He saw only a wild mound of earth, rising high amidst thick grass and towering trees. Upon inquiring with the village elders, he learned that this was the tomb of a consort of the Song Emperor Guangzong.

pages.226:
# The Imperial Consort Presents Her Image

<margin></margin>
The elegant lady died at twenty; she is truly what one would call a jade person crushed into the earth. How moving!
</margin>

During the Pseudo-Han dynasty, Chen Youliang had an imperial consort named Zheng Wane. Her jade-like quality and icy demeanor were the most beautiful in her generation; furthermore, she was well-versed in literature and skilled in music and rhythm. The pseudo-Han court favored her immensely. She died at the age of only twenty and was buried at the Pipa Pavilion in Jiangzhou. <note>Jiangzhou is modern-day Jiujiang.</note> At the time of her funeral, two ladies-in-waiting followed her in death, one named Xichan and one named Jin'e. Although the consort was noble and beautiful, once she entered the underworld, her spirit would sometimes appear during the day. Those living nearby would occasionally see her walking, or hear the sounds of her singing and playing instruments, and there was no one who did not mourn her. 

At the beginning of the Hongwu era, Shen Shao of Wujiang was in the prime of his youth. He was also handsome, studied poetry under Sa Tianxi <note>a master of poetry</note>, and studied calligraphy under Guo Bojing <note>a master of calligraphy</note>. Both were praised by their contemporaries. He once harmonized with Tianxi's two poems written when passing through Jiaxing about the Wu region, saying:

<column-break/>
<margin></margin>
Although these two poems about the Wu region are written to match the scenery and express his feelings, they are also filled with deep emotion and yearning, not written carelessly.
</margin>

"The Seven Lakes and Three Rivers connect for a hundred miles,
Willow catkins and lotus blossoms reflect in the lake.
Past the water gate is the Pan Gate, half-hidden by red curtains,
In the painted tower, the <term>mimi</term> <gloss>a type of aromatic herb</gloss> grows past the place where mandarin ducks swim.
The east wind has dropped all the pear blossoms in the flower pavilion,
At the fragrance path, deer and elk roam.
On a clear night, the lanterns see the crimson gauze,
Below the Three Sages Shrine, the east water continues to flow.
Above Zhenniang’s tomb, the wind blows through the bamboo,
After Xi Shi left, the sandal-wood shoes are deserted.
Year after year, deep in spring, the burn marks are green."

His other poems were of this same caliber. However, because his family was wealthy, he did not wish to serve in government. People knew of this, and being greedy for his wealth, some wanted to nominate him as a "filial and incorrupt" candidate, while others wanted to guarantee him a place as a student of the imperial academy. They came one after another until he had no peace of day or night. Although Shao...

<margin>Shen Sheng is certainly not someone who uses a rhinoceros horn as a bribe, or who calculates with the sharpness of an awl. Could it be that he is like a great ship carrying ten thousand millions in heavy cargo? What does that have to do with anything?</margin>

was not stingy with his money, he was truly weary of the disturbances. He thought of escaping and so invited his cousins, Master Chen and Master Liang, to take a great ship <note>both are names for types of boats</note> loaded with ten thousand millions in cargo to travel between the Xiang and Han rivers. They stopped at Jiujiang, loving the beauty of Mount Lu and viewing the purity of Lake Pengli. They lingered at the Pen River, mourning the ancients and seeking the secluded. By chance, the autumn rain had just cleared, and the water and sky were the same color. Together with the two Masters, Chen and Liang, they visited the Pipa Pavilion to recite the poems of the white-haired Master Sima <note>referring to Bai Juyi, who wrote the Pipa Xing</note> about the wind and moon of the reed flowers, and to ponder the rhymes of the capital lady’s silver bottle and iron cavalry. At the time, the moon was bright, the wind was fine, and the people were quiet in the deep of the night. Suddenly, they heard singing sounds beneath the moon, appearing suddenly near and then far, sometimes high and sometimes low. The three men looked at each other in astonishment and listened for a long time until it became silent. When the wine was finished and they returned to the boat, they did not know the cause. Shao alone was curious. The next day, he went to investigate the truth but found absolutely nothing. Just as he was about to return, a strange fragrance suddenly assailed him. Shao waited and stood by. A moment later, a beautiful woman dressed in palace attire, whose appearance was like a celestial immortal, arrived, preceded by two young maids. Shao suspected it was a household of high rank,

The beautiful woman ordered him to share the mat, so Shao joined her on the mat and asked for her surname. The beautiful woman said, "I am the consort of the Han King Chen, Zheng Wane. I died at twenty and was buried here. This one maid, Xichan, and one, Jin'e, were the ones who followed me in death at that time." Shao naturally possessed courage and also valued romantic affairs, so he did not find it strange. The beautiful woman ordered Xichan to fetch wine and pour it at the pavilion. The music is silent, the shouts are still, even now they tell of the Western Chu Overlord, haggard in the jade tent, covering his face before the lamp as tears fly like red rain..."

The beauty looked miserable and said, "Just speak of the wind and the moon; there is no need to speak deeply of these things." She then improvised a poem, saying:

Amidst the silver screens and golden rooms, I am in a dream.

The beauty heard this and sighed, saying, "You can be called a soulmate." Thereupon, they urged each other to sit and drink, and slept together in the pavilion just like in the human world. Suddenly it was dawn. At parting, the beauty said, "Tonight you must return to your lodging and plan for a long-term arrangement." Shao nodded <note>agreed</note> and returned to his lodgings. He sent his cousins, Chen and Liang, back first, while Shao remained alone. That evening, he went again, and Jin'e was already there. She said, "This was used by my master; now I offer it to you to show my feelings are not thin." After staying for over a month, they were inseparable like glue and lacquer. One day, the beauty...
pages.229:
<margin></margin>
The beauty did not wish to cause Master Shen to meet an untimely death, nor did she want to cause herself grave punishment in the underworld. Although the limbs and body are separated from the heart, the spirit itself remains clearly and unforgettably present.
</margin>

ordered him to go to the market to find blue sheep’s milk to moisten his eyes <note>the corners of the eyes</note>. Shao did as he was told, and after finding it, he applied it for thirty days. The beauty could rise during the day; sometimes they would hold hands and wander in the gardens, or lean on each other’s shoulders, laughing and singing in the pavilion. They did not realize that spring came and autumn went, and four years had passed. Although fish swimming side by side and birds with intertwined wings could not sufficiently describe their intimate affection, early that winter, the beauty wept and bade him farewell. ## The Bright Consort Writes of Her Resentment

The Bright Consort of the Han was Wang Qiang. She received a summons and entered the land of the Xiongnu. Because she wrote of her resentment upon the <term>pipa</term> <gloss>a four-stringed plucked instrument</gloss>, she was eventually buried in that land in a tomb of green grass. In the year of the Guiwei of the Dading era of the Jin dynasty, Wanyan Shouyi, a refined gentleman from the imperial clan in the capital, had business and went out <note>business/matters</note>. He saw the tomb of the Bright Consort and felt moved in his heart. He cupped his hands and sighed, saying, "How heroic, how heroic! The treacherous officials misled you! To have died in the desert north of the borders, carrying the painful hatred of a thousand years! How pathetic!" After leaving, he left it as a matter of the past, but at dusk, he returned along the road, passing the consort’s tomb. He raised his eyes to look at it and saw a magnificent dwelling standing alone <note>"kui" means high/lofty</note>. The painted beams and carved pillars were not of human standards, and the vermilion curtains and emerald screens resembled the dwelling of a celestial being in heaven. Shouyi was both startled and suspicious. Before he could investigate further, he saw a beautiful woman with teeth like fragrant jade, her appearance graceful and charming, emerge from within and say, "Young gentleman, would you like to lower yourself to come in for some tea?" Shouyi

He looked at her from the outside, and having fallen in love, he finally obtained the chance to speak with her. After they finished talking, he took his leave, and after they departed, he became an official. This was indeed a miraculous encounter.</margin>

did not have time to reply when the beauty invited him again. Having no other choice, he followed her inside. The beauty rose to thank him, saying, "During the day, I was honored to receive your clear gaze and your expressions of indignation. Even though I have been rotting among the grass and trees for nine springs, I am moved and will not forget it." Shouyi was just about to ask for her name and about the words spoken during the day when the beauty suddenly stood up and said, "I ask to relate my own heart’s grievances. I hope you will not be startled. I am not a person of this present world. I am the Bright Consort of the Great Han, Wang Qiang, Zhaojun. Since the treacherous official <note>referring to Mao Yanshou of the Han</note> forced me to marry into the barbarian lands, I bade farewell to the Emperor and left. Since perfection and deficiency do not exist in themselves, but are rather states that attach to things—as if they were genera—they only exist in their subjects. Every perfection must be revered. This is a primary proposition recognized by all. However, whether this or that is a perfection is something that requires clarification. What is a perfection for one group may be a deficiency for another. This is evident to anyone who has examined various laws, opinions, and traditions. A thing may be a perfection in relation to one thing, and a deficiency in relation to another. This is perfection by relation. These may sometimes be a perfection, and at other times not a perfection. But this is not called perfection; rather, the name "good" is applied to it. For goods are either synonymous with perfection or more general than it. Things that are perfections may be so by convention and law; thus, among some, written and unwritten opinions include perfection by convention, and this is considered perfection in the common opinion of all. That which is by convention is variable: what was a perfection for one group is not a perfection for others. Therefore, those raised among a certain people feel their souls revere things that others disdain. For this reason, if something is a perfection in existence, and a certain person is among a people who have become accustomed to their souls not revering that which is a perfection, and then it becomes clear to him that this matter is a perfection, his soul does not revere it, nor does he honor it, nor does he see that he has attained anything. Thus, that knowledge is discarded by that person, and he pays no attention to it except out of necessity of speech, just as the sick feel the bitter as sweet, and see one as two. Likewise, the sick of soul see perfection as deficiency and see deficiency as perfection. Just as there is no way for these sick people to feel the sweet as sweet until they are cured, likewise the sick of soul cannot see the good as good until their souls are healthy. Just as among the sick are those who feel the sweet as bitter and judge it to be bitter, and among them are those who feel it as bitter but know it is sweet, or judge that the defect is within them—so it is a duty for him, even if he does not disdain it, to cast it aside,
pages.53:
and the second does not merely disdain it. Neither of them understands about the sweet what is appropriate to be understood about it. Likewise, the sick of soul are afflicted with exactly this; they do not know the good, nor are they moved by the good, and the spiritual form of things <note>1</note> which is good does not move these people at all. If it does move them, it is only to flee from those of well-known ways of life, and what is found in the six-hundreds <note>2</note> of the Hijra from the history of the Arabs, all of which store diseases in souls. For this reason, they do not know the perfection that is free from potentiality; they only know stillness. And this is when it is purely in potentiality. Longing for them accompanies this, and they feel it because longing is a pain. They know of perfection only what is accompanied by motion, because pleasure exists at that point. If perfection is achieved and completed, they do not feel it. Similarly, the healthy person does not feel his health, nor does he see that he has been given something of value, whereas the sick feel it and see it as the greatest of perceived things, since they were healthy in potentiality. The feeling of the perfection-state of stillness—if it is permissible to call it stillness, for it is a stillness not accompanied by the potentiality of motion—is a very excellent thing. It is necessary to train oneself in feeling it until it becomes a habit. If this type becomes a habit, it has an effort in human existence that is of very great value. This is something that must precede and be placed before the discussion of supreme happiness.

Just as we said regarding being affected, so we must examine and count in how many ways it is said that the agent acts, and how we perceive the appetitive part in action, for the appetitive soul is acted upon. We do not act by the appetitive soul, but by another part that is in actuality, because the appetitive is only in potentiality. It might be thought that the discussion regarding it was not exhausted in "Generation and Corruption," just as happened regarding the right side, for Aristotle only spoke about it in "Meteorology" regarding what follows.
