For this reason, he said in "Animals" <note>1</note> that the discussion on the right side was not exhausted, and every affected thing, rather every moving thing, is in actuality another thing. For if it were not something in actuality at all, potentiality would be something existing in actuality, and prime matter would have a necessity, and possibility would exist by itself and be something subsisting in its own essence. This is obvious to anyone who has engaged in natural science, even the slightest engagement. The moving thing is some substance, or rather, it is some body, because every moving thing is divisible; but that is by motion in a direction intermediate between what is by essence and what is by accident. Aristotle considers that to be by accident. For if it were by essence in some way, it would not be first. The mover by potentiality is something by essence and first. It moves from the aspect of what is in potentiality, even if that which is in potentiality were found to be something separate from bodies, moving itself, and that thing became either a substance, or quantity, or quality, or place, or other categories. But what is in potentiality must necessarily—as we have said—be something in actuality. And we have said it is another thing in potentiality. Therefore, it is in actuality one of the categories, and it is in potentiality one of the categories. Let what is in potentiality be P, and what is in actuality be A, and the discussion K. It is clear to anyone who has practiced natural science, even the slightest practice, that what is in potentiality, from the aspect of what is in potentiality, is not under a category, for everything under a category
pages.55: —whatever category it may be—is something existing in actuality. The categories, therefore, are opposed by potentiality just as what is in actuality is opposed in A, K if they are under one category in A, K as two opposing species. If they were two substances, they would have no name, but Aristotle and Abu Nasr <insert>al-Farabi</insert> may call them "opposites" when the need arises. However, opposites require a single subject in actuality. These two do not have a subject in actuality. If they are under one of the nine categories, what is in potentiality necessarily exists as a substance; it has a third existence by which it is a subject for A, K. In A, L if they are under quantity, they are more similar to the opposites of the first class. Therefore, it is said of growth that it is motion, and that it is change, more than is said of stillness. The two opposing species of quantity are similar in two ways: one is that they are species accompanied by the privations of their genera, as is found in the form of substances. The second is that they have subjects existing in actuality capable of the species of quantity. The species of substance do not have subjects; rather, they are the subjects. Indeed, if the mover is said to have subjects, it is by way of equivocation. They differ from opposites in that the species of quantity do not have two limited extremes that can be named. For the largest dog cannot have the size of an elephant, and the smallest cannot have the size of an ant. The species of the size of substances are many and various, and their extremes are not limited unless it is by relation to them, in which case opposition occurs, as it occurs to the extremes of temperament in quality. This has been summarized in "Temperament" <note>1</note>. As for A, K, if they are qualities and are under one of the four genera of quality, they have a subject existing in actuality. Each of the species of that genus is accompanied by a privation of its genus <note>2</note>, and in them are two species that are extremes, not by relation but absolutely. It is impossible for a species to exist further
pages.56:
from that extreme in its opposition, and it is not so in what is quantity. Let the smallest size, the dog for example, be A, and the largest size be R. Whatever is found in A or T, A, R. Every species of quantity found in the dog is closer to R than the size of A is to D; and there is no size further from A than D. If that were found, it would be smaller than R, let it be E. So the size of R is closer to A than E. So D is not an extreme in M unless M is a universal, as it is a species of substance. So the sizes A, K are not extremes by relation in reality and by essence to the first subject, which is in potentiality—namely, prime matter—but they proceed in its manner, because a part of its parts is matter. And A, A are not extremes from what they are or from the aspect of a relation that has attached to them. Thus, they are not extremes in existence. For everything to which something exists from the aspect of what that thing is, it exists for it in existence. And what exists for it while it is in a certain state, and that thing exists for another thing that does not have that state, it is not said that it is so in existence. Rather, if it has it in existence, it is by way of resemblance. Also, if A, K are not under one category, it is possible for A, K to be necessarily, otherwise it would be merely in opinion and not something existing. If that is not possible, then K, A is not a subject for the other, except as it is said that the illumination in potentiality is cold, because illumination follows the heat of fire. Summarizing these classes and counting them is easy for whoever desires it, and we suffice with this summary by way of definition.

All opposites, when they are in their subjects, necessarily entail the privations of their opposites in them. Privations are of classes: among them is the privation of substance, the privation of quantity, and the privation of quality. I do not mean that substance is privated at all, nor quantity. If something is not quantity, such as intellect, this is negation and not privation. Abu Nasr has <insert>[346 b]</insert> summarized the way in which it is said to be privation. Privation is attributed to the category in two ways: one is its negation, like our saying: "The sky is neither heavy nor light"; the other is the removal of the negation of a species of it from
pages.57:
a subject in which that species could exist. This is more deserving of the name of privation than the first. It is then said in other ways, the most deserving of which for the name of privation is the privation summarized in the opposites in the book "Categories." This second type that we have mentioned is what Abu Nasr <al-Farabi> mentions and says: Aristotle counts the privation of every category in it: so the privation of substance is in the category of substance, and the privation of quantity is in the category of quantity.

It is clear with the slightest reflection for anyone who has engaged in natural science that prime matter cannot be devoid of some categories so that it does not have one species of them. The first of these is substance. This was clarified in the first book of the "Physics," for if it were devoid of it, prime matter would have a form. Next is quantity, for it is not even one substance—because it is not a body. How far from the truth is someone who composes size from what is indivisible! For if it were so, a substance would exist with no quantity for it. This is impossible. It has been clarified in the beginning of the sixth book of the "Physics," and it is clearer upon reflection. You must know that "size" is said of the circular and the straight by equivocation, and that circular size is what has a center. We have summarized this in the commentary on the meanings of the seventh book of the "Physics." Then, after that, in matter is the genus of passive quality: such as heat, cold, moisture, and dryness. For this reason, every hylomorphic <note>made of matter</note> substance is a body. Body is said by equivocation of what moves in a circle and what moves in a straight line; their matter is not the same in species as the forms, but they are proportional to the proportion of the forms, and the matter that accepts motion in a straight line is matter by priority. As for that which accepts circular motion, it is always a subject and is not matter or material. Rather, it is called matter and material by proportion, just as this is called a subject by resemblance and proportion. Prime matter is not free from the genus of passive quality, and it is impossible for it to be devoid of it. Therefore, when Aristotle wants to indicate all of them, he says: "every tangible body." Likewise, the quality of quantity, which is shape
pages.58:
and form. Likewise, place. Likewise, position. Likewise, time. Likewise, relation. These nine categories are such that it is clear that prime matter is not devoid of them, although some are whiter than others.

As for action and passion, it has been doubted. But when its matter is examined, it appears to be so. As for the category of "having" <note>1</note>, it exists in the soul; and it may be found in inanimate objects what is thought to be "having," yet when its matter is examined, it appears that it is not under this category.

Likewise, color: it may be thought of some bodies that they are devoid of color, such as air and glass, and clearer than that are tastes and smells. Their subject may not be devoid of all their species. But even if that is so, these do not exist for substance by its essence primarily, but they exist secondarily, and after various existing things under <note>3</note> another category precede them in the subject. It is as if these, even if they are not species of that, are like the species; an example of this is tastes. for perfection due to it being perfection, and holding imperfection in contempt due to it being imperfection. Since perfection and imperfection are not in themselves existing entities, but rather conditions that attach to things—as if they were genera—they only exist within their subjects. Therefore, every perfection demands our reverence. This is a primary proposition acknowledged by all. As for whether this or that is a perfection, that requires clarification. What is a perfection for one group may be an imperfection for others. This is evident to anyone who has examined the various laws, opinions, and traditions. A thing may be a perfection in relation to one thing and an imperfection in relation to another. This is perfection by relation. Something may be a perfection at one time and not a perfection at another. However, this is not called perfection; rather, the name "good" is applied to it. For "goods" are either synonymous with perfection or more general than it. Things that are perfections may be so by convention and law; thus, written and unwritten opinions contain perfection by convention. Consequently, they are perfection according to some, and according to recognized perfection, they are so for everyone. What exists by convention varies: what is perfection to one group is not perfection to others. Therefore, those raised among a certain people have souls that revere things that others hold in contempt. Thus, if there is something that is a perfection in existence, and a human being among a certain people has become accustomed to not revering that thing which is a perfection, and it is then clarified to him that it is indeed a perfection, his soul will not revere it, nor will he honor it, nor see that he has attained anything. Such knowledge, for that person, remains disregarded; he cares nothing for it except for the sake of the argument, just as the sick perceive the bitter as sweet and see one thing as two. Likewise, the sick of soul see perfection as imperfection and imperfection as perfection. Just as there is no way for these sick people to perceive the sweet as sweet until they are cured, the sick of soul cannot see the good as good until their souls are healthy. Just as among the sick there are those who perceive the sweet as bitter and judge it to be bitter, and others who perceive it as bitter yet know it to be sweet—or judge that the defect is in themselves—it is incumbent upon the latter, even if he does not hold it in contempt, to discard it.

The second does not merely hold it in contempt. Neither of them understands the nature of the sweet as it should be understood. Likewise, the sick of soul are afflicted with this very same state; they do not know the good, and the good does not move them. The spiritual image <note>original: "al-ṣūra al-rūḥāniyya"</note> of things <note>(1)</note> that are good does not move these people at all. If it does move them, it is only toward fleeing from the followers of the well-known paths and the things present in the year six hundred <note>(2)</note> of the Hijra of Arab history. All of this deposits diseases in the souls. Therefore, they do not know the perfection that is devoid of potentiality, but only know rest <note>term: <term>sukūn</term> <gloss>rest/immobility</gloss></note>. This is when it is purely in potentiality. Excitement accompanies this for them; they feel it because excitement is a form of pain. They recognize of perfection only that which is accompanied by motion, because pleasure exists at that point. If perfection is attained and completed, they do not feel it. Similarly, the healthy person does not feel his health, nor does he see that he has been given something of value; the sick, however, feel it and see it as the greatest of all perceptions, as they were healthy in potentiality. The feeling of "perfectional rest"—if it is permissible to call it rest, as it is a rest not accompanied by the potentiality of motion—is a very noble matter. One must discipline oneself in sensing it until it becomes a habit. If this type becomes a habit, it has an immensely valuable influence on human existence. This is a matter that must precede the discussion on the supreme happiness <note>term: <term>al-sa‘āda al-quṣwā</term> <gloss>supreme happiness</gloss></note>.

Just as we said regarding affection <note>term: <term>infi‘āl</term> <gloss>affection/being acted upon</gloss></note>, we must examine and count in how many ways it is said that the agent acts, and how we sense the desiderative part <note>term: <term>al-juz’ al-nuzū‘ī</term> <gloss>the desiderative or appetitive part of the soul</gloss></note> in action. For the desiderative soul is acted upon; we do not act through the desiderative soul, but through another part that is in actuality, because the desiderative part is only in potentiality. It might be thought that the discussion on this was not finished in *On Generation and Corruption*, just as happened in the case of the "right side," for Aristotle only spoke of it in *Meteorology* regarding what follows.

For this reason, he said in [book] "Y" <note>note: i.e., the 15th book of *On Animals*</note> of *Animals* that the discussion on the right side was not finished, and that every thing acted upon—in fact, every thing in motion—is in actuality [346a] something else. For if it were not something in actuality at all, potentiality would be something existing in actuality, and prime matter <note>term: <term>hayūlā</term> <gloss>prime matter</gloss></note> would necessarily exist, and possibility would be subsistent by itself and something subsistent in its own essence. This is evident to anyone who has practiced natural philosophy, even if only slightly. The thing in motion is some essence, or rather some body, because every thing in motion is divisible; but that is due to motion in a way that is intermediate between what is by essence and what is by accident. Aristotle considers that to be among the accidental. For if it were by essence in some way, it would not be first. The mover in potentiality is something by essence and first. It moves insofar as it is in potentiality, such that if what is in potentiality were found to be something separate from bodies, it would move by itself and that thing would become either an essence, a quantity, a quality, a place, or some other of the categories <note>term: <term>maqūlāt</term> <gloss>categories</gloss></note>. However, what is in potentiality necessarily requires—as we have said—that it be something in actuality. We have said it is something else in potentiality. It is therefore in actuality one of the categories, and in potentiality one of the categories. Let what is in potentiality be P, what is in actuality be A, and the thing by account be C. It is clear to anyone who has practiced physical science, even if only slightly, that what is in potentiality, insofar as it is in potentiality, is not under a category, for everything that is under a category—

<note>Editorial note: The translator lists various references to Aristotle's works *On the Parts of Animals* and *On the Progression of Animals* where the right side is discussed, noting it is considered more noble, warmer, stronger, and the initiator of motion.</note>
pages.55:
<header>‘Abd al-Raḥmān Badawī [42]</header>

—whatever category it may be—is something existing in actuality. The categories are therefore contrasted by potentiality just as they are contrasted by what is in actuality in A, C. If they were under one category in A, C, they would be two contrasted types. If they were two essences, they would have no name, but Aristotle and Abū Naṣr <insert>al-Fārābī</insert> might call them "contraries" when the need arises. However, contraries require one subject in actuality. These two do not have a subject in actuality. If they are under one of the nine categories that are in potentiality, they necessarily exist as an essence <note>term: <term>jawhar</term> <gloss>essence/substance</gloss></note>, so they have a third existence through which they are a subject for A, C. In A, L, if they are under quantity <note>term: <term>kam</term> <gloss>quantity</gloss></note>, they are more similar to contraries than the first type. For this reason, it is said that growth is motion, and that it is change more than is said of rest. The two contrary types of quantity are similar in two ways: first, they are types accompanied by the privations of their homogeneous counterparts, as is found in the form of essences. Second, they have subjects existing in actuality that are capable of receiving types of quantity. Essence types do not have subjects; rather, they are the subjects. Indeed, if the mover is said to have subjects, it is by way of skepticism. They differ from contraries in that types of quantity do not have two limited extremes from which one can speak. The largest dog cannot have the size of an elephant, and the smallest cannot have the size of an ant. Thus, types of the size of essences are many and varied, and their extremes are not limited except in relation to one another, so a contrariety occurs to them, as occurs to the extremes of temperament <note>term: <term>mizāj</term> <gloss>temperament/mixture</gloss></note> in quality. This has been summarized in *On Temperament*. As for A, C, if they are qualities and under one of the four genera of quality, they have a subject existing in actuality. Accompanied by each type of that genus is a privation homogeneous to it, and in them are two types that are extremes, not by relation but absolutely. It is impossible to find a type further

<note>Footnotes: (1) i.e., in the treatise "On Temperament". (2) ‘T’ reads: "its homogeneous counterparts".</note>
pages.56:
<header>New Epistles by Ibn Bājja [43]</header>

from that extreme than its counterpart, and this is not the case for what is quantity. Let the smallest size be that of a dog, for example, upon A, and the largest size be upon R. What exists in A or T, A, R. Every type of quantity that exists in a dog is closer to R than the size A is to D; there does not exist a size further from A than D. If that were found, it would be smaller than R; let it be E. The size R is closer to A than E. Thus D is not an extreme in Q, unless Q is universal, for it is a type of essence. The sizes A and C are not extremes by relation in reality and by essence to the first subject, which is in potentiality, i.e., the prime matter; rather, they behave as it does, because one of its parts is matter. A and A are not extremes in terms of what they are, or from the aspect of a relation that has attached to them. Thus they are not extremes in existence. For everything that exists and has some state from the aspect of being that thing, that thing exists for it. And what exists for it while it is in a certain state, and that thing exists for something else that does not have that state, it is not said to be such in existence. Rather, if it has it in existence, it is by way of analogy. Also, if A and C are not under one category, it is possible for it necessarily to be A, C; otherwise, it would be arbitrary and nothing existing. If that is impossible, then C, A are not one of them a subject for the other, except as it is said that the light is cold in potentiality, because the light implies the hot from the fire. The summary and enumeration of these types is easy for anyone who desires it, and we suffice with this summary by way of definition.

All contraries, if they are in their subjects, necessarily require in them the privations of their opposites. Privations are of types: among them is the privation of essence, the privation of quantity, and the privation of quality. I do not say that essence is ever non-existent, nor quantity. If there is something that is not a quantity, such as the intellect, this is a negation and not a privation. <insert>[346b]</insert> Abū Naṣr has summarized the mode by which it is called privation. Privation is attributed to the category in two ways: among them is its negation, as we say: "The sky is neither heavy nor light"; and among them is the lifting of the negation of a type of it from
pages.57:
<header>‘Abd al-Raḥmān Badawī [44]</header>

a subject that could contain that type. This is more deserving of the name "privation" than the first. It is then said in various ways, the most deserving of which is the privation summarized in the contraries in the book *Categories* <note>original: "Categoriae" or "Qāṭāghūrīyās"</note>. This second type that we mentioned is what Abū Naṣr <Fārābī> mentions, saying: Aristotle considers the privation of every category within it: the privation of essence is in the category of essence, and the privation of quantity is in the category of quantity.

It is clear upon the slightest reflection by anyone who has practiced natural science that prime matter cannot be devoid of some categories such that it would not contain one type of them. The first is essence. This was made clear in the first book of *Physics* <note>original: "Sama‘ Ṭabī‘ī"</note>, for if it were devoid of it, prime matter would possess a form. Following this is quantity, for it is not a single essence—because it is not a body. How far removed is he who composes size from what is not divisible! For if it were so, there would exist an essence without quantity. This is impossible. This has been made clear in the beginning of the sixth book of *Physics*, and made more clear upon reflection. You must know that "size" is said of the spherical and the straight by ambiguity, and that the spherical size is what has a center. We have summarized this in our commentary on the meanings of the seventh book of *Physics*. Then, after that, in the matter <note>term: <term>hayūlā</term> <gloss>prime matter</gloss></note> is the genus of qualitative affection: such as heat, cold, moisture, and dryness. Therefore, every material essence is a body. "Body" is said by ambiguity of what moves in a circle and what moves in a straight line; their matter is not one in type, as it depicts it, but they relate as the relation of forms. The matter that accepts motion in a straight line is the matter by priority. As for that which accepts circular motion, it is always a subject and is not matter, nor prime matter. Rather, it is called matter and prime matter by analogy, just as this is called a subject by similarity and analogy. Prime matter is not devoid of the genus of qualitative affection, and it cannot be stripped of it. Therefore, when Aristotle wants to indicate all of them, he says: "every tangible body." Likewise, the quality of quantity, which is shape
pages.58:
<header>New Epistles by Ibn Bājja [45]</header>

and form. Likewise for "where" <note>term: <term>ayna</term> <gloss>where/place</gloss></note>, position, "when," and relation. It is clear that prime matter is not devoid of these nine categories, though some are clearer than others.

As for action and passion <note>term: <term>fi‘l wa-infi‘āl</term> <gloss>action and passion/being acted upon</gloss></note>, there has been skepticism regarding them. However, when the matter is examined, it appears to be so. As for the category of "having" <note>(1)</note>, it is found in the soul; and it may be found in inanimate objects that which one thinks is "having," except that when the matter is examined, it appears it is not under this category.

Likewise for color: it may be thought of some bodies that they are devoid of color, such as air and glass. More evident than this are tastes and smells <note>(2)</note>, for their subject may not be devoid of all their types. Even so, these are not present to the essence in itself first; rather, they are found secondarily, and after various things under <note>(3)</note> another category have preceded them in the subject. It is as if these, even if they are not types of those, are like types. An example of this is tastes; for even if they are not types of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness, they are not outside of them, because they are heat to which another matter has attached, by which <note>(4)</note> that heat became a type of another genus, as occurred in the discussion on moving spheres: for the consideration of them is not a geometrical one resulting in geometrical theory, but it is rather under geometrical theory. We have summarized this in our remarks in *On the Soul*.

What we have said has been summarized in another way, which is that every body is composed of form and subject. The subject of the eternal bodies is specific to the subject. The subject of the generated and corruptible is called prime matter and matter and things similar to these. Every body
pages.59:
<header>‘Abd al-Raḥmān Badawī [46]</header>

that is corruptible is an element <note>term: <term>usṭuqus</term> <gloss>element</gloss></note> or composed of two or more elements. Everything composed of things contains what belongs to those things. The things necessary for the elements are necessary for every material body. The things necessary for the elements from the categories are that they are essences, possess sizes, possess qualitative affections, possess positions and places <note>(1)</note>, that they have "when," that they are relative, and that they act and are acted upon. Every body necessarily contains these genera of categories. As for the rest of what is found in material bodies, they revert to these—an example of this: roughness and dryness <note>(2)</note>, hardness, softness, and smoothness. As for the rest of what is found in material bodies, they revert to these. An example of this <unclear><...></unclear> <note>(3)</note> is that they are varieties of moisture and dryness. For when dryness is joined by an accident, it becomes roughness and dryness. From moisture comes smoothness and softness. Aristotle has mentioned this in the second book of *On Generation and Corruption*. Likewise for taste and smell, for these two genera contain moisture and dryness as matter. As for colors, the discussion on them is a different discussion. When the matter is examined, it appears that this genus is found in the elements. A full investigation of this is in a place other than this.

It has been made clear in the seventh book of *Physics* that alteration only occurs in the sensible things. Let anyone who wishes refer to that in the words of Aristotle there, and what the commentators have said about it. Action and passion are only in the primary qualities, which are those by which generation and corruption occur, and they are the four, and they have been enumerated in many places. We have clarified in places other than this that "potentialities" are said by equivocation of: the passive and the active, and we have defined each of these two genera. The active potentialities are necessarily

God, they turned away their heads, and you see them 
averting (others) while they are arrogant.

a Perpetual Forgiver." And whatever you put forward for yourselves

If it is a proper noun, such as <term>subḥān</term> <gloss>glorification</gloss> for glorification, and <term>fajjār</term> <gloss>wickedness</gloss> and <term>ḥammād</term> for the night, and <term>al-ḥamda</term>, then it does not work by consensus. Or ambiguous in it, then the <term>maṣdar</term> does not work by consensus, such as "The <term>qulū</term>—if your affliction is a man, I offer peace as a greeting of injustice." And after its genitive, meaning the <term>maṣdar</term>, its object which it was annexed to, just as its verb is installed <column-break/> its action, if it is annexed to the subject, which is the most common, like "preventing it, an excuse, right of the cattle," or is it completed by raising its action if it is annexed to the subject, which is frequent if the subject is not mentioned, such as "Man is not weary of the prayer of good." And it is rare if it is mentioned, such as "the exertion of Ali Zafar," and some restricted it to poetry, and it was refuted by his saying, "Peace be upon him, and the pilgrimage to the House of whoever is able to find a way to it." Then it may be annexed to the adverb <term>ẓarf</term> by expansion, so it works after it, the raising and the installing, such as "the love of a day for a sensible person," so it is more accurate. And the genitive of what follows is what was genitive, observing the wording, such as "I was amazed at the striking of Zayd, the noble, Umar." And whoever observed in the following the position, so he raised the follower of the subject and installed the follower of the object which were genitive in wording, so its action was good.
pages.66: as his saying, "The exhaustion of passion, its covenant, the possible virtue," and his saying, "Fear of bankruptcy, and in the sleeping one." It is permissible in the follower of the object which is genitive, the annexation of the subject with what was mentioned, the raising on the estimation of the <term>maṣdar</term> with a letter connected to a verb to install its subject. This is the **Chapter on the working of the active participle** <term>ism al-fāʿil</term>. It is, as he said in the commentary on <term>al-Kāfiya</term>, what was derived from a <term>maṣdar</term> balancing the present tense to indicate its subject, not suitable for annexation to it. And in the chapter on the working of the passive participle <term>ism al-mafʿūl</term>, the wording of the active participle in action, its meaning is from the triliteral, genitive, implied, running on the original attribute, and with it, and not about it if it was in the meaning of <term>bi-maʿzilin</term> <gloss>isolated</gloss>, because it is not correct for its wording to be similar to the wording of the verb indicated by the present and future tense, which is the present tense. If it was not, if its connection was 'al', then it remains <column-break/> in what is built, otherwise it does not work in it, contrary to Al-Kisa'i. And if it follows an interrogation, such as "is the striker Zayd, Umar?" or a vocative letter, such as "O rising, a mountain!" and it is in the corruption of the omitted adjective and with its described [noun]. And that is why it was not mentioned in <term>al-Kāfiya</term>, and negation, such as "not is the striker Zayd, Umar," and it came as an adjective, such as "I passed by a man striking Zayd," and it was permissible "striking Umar," or a predicate of the subject whose predicate is such, such as "Zayd is striking Umar," because in its meaning it is clear that "Zayd is honoring Umar, I thought Umar is striking, striking Khalid." And it may be omitted by custom, so the action which it described is strengthened, such as "of the people, the beasts, and the cattle, different are their colors," meaning a different sort. And if the active participle is connected to 'al', then in the past and other than it, its action <margin>because of its occurrence in a position that requires interpretation by a verb...</margin> is approved according to the majority. Al-Rummani went to

pages.52:
# <Treatise on the Appetitive Faculty>

...to perfection in terms of its being perfection, and disdain for deficiency in terms of its being deficiency. Since perfection and deficiency are not existent in themselves but are states that attach to things, it is as if they are genera; therefore, they only exist within their subjects. Thus, every perfection must be revered. This is a primary proposition acknowledged by all. However, whether this or that is a perfection is something that requires clarification. For a thing might be a perfection for some people and a deficiency for others. This is clear to anyone who examines the various laws, opinions, and customs. Something might be a perfection in relation to one thing and a deficiency in relation to another. This is conditional perfection. These may at one time be perfection and at another not. However, this is not called perfection, but is rather given the name of "the good." For "the good" is either synonymous with perfection or is more general than it. Things that are perfections may be so by convention and law; thus, some written and unwritten opinions contain perfection by convention, and so they are a perfection for some people, while others are universally accepted as perfection. What is by convention is varied: what is a perfection for one group is not a perfection for another. Therefore, one who is raised among a certain group will have a soul that feels reverence for things that others disdain. For this reason, if there exists something that is a perfection in reality, and a person is among a group that has become accustomed to not feeling reverence for that which is a perfection, and it then becomes clear to him that the matter is a perfection, his soul will not feel reverence for it, nor will he honor it, nor will he perceive that he has attained anything. Thus, that knowledge will be discarded by that person, and he will not concern himself with it except by necessity of speech. Just as the sick perceive bitter as sweet and see one thing as two, so too do the sick of soul see perfection as deficiency and deficiency as perfection. And just as there is no way for these sick people to perceive the sweet as sweet until they are cured, so too is it impossible for the sick of soul to see the good as good until their souls are healthy. Just as among the sick there is one who perceives the sweet as bitter and judges it to be bitter, and another who perceives it as bitter but knows it is sweet or judges that the affliction is in him—so it is incumbent upon him, even if he does not disdain it, to discard it,
pages.53:
and the second does not simply disdain it. Both of them do not understand what is to be understood about the sweet. Likewise, the sick of soul are afflicted with this very same thing; they do not know the good, and the good does not move them. The spiritual image <note>original: "الصورة الروحانية"</note> of the things that are good does not move them at all. If it does move them, it moves them to flee from the people of well-known ways of life. What is present in the six-hundredth year of the Hijra from the history of the Arabs—all of it deposits diseases in the souls. Therefore, they do not know the perfection that is devoid of power, and they only know stillness. This is if it is in potentiality alone. Longing for them accompanies this, and they feel it because longing is a pain. They recognize of perfection only that which is accompanied by motion, because pleasure exists at that point. If the perfection is attained and completed, they do not feel it. Likewise, the healthy do not feel their health, nor do they see that they have been given anything of value, whereas the sick feel it and see it as the greatest of perceptions, since they were healthy in potentiality. The feeling of the perfection of stillness—if it is permissible to call it stillness, because it is a stillness not accompanied by the power of motion—is a very excellent thing. One must exercise in perceiving it until it becomes a habit. If this type becomes a habit, it has a very great impact on human existence. This is something that must be preceded and placed before the discussion of supreme happiness.

Just as we said regarding being acted upon, we must likewise examine and enumerate the ways in which it is said that the agent acts, and how we perceive the appetitive part in actuality. For the appetitive soul is acted upon, and we do not act through the appetitive soul, but through another part that is in actuality, because the appetitive is in potentiality only. It might be thought that the discussion about it was not exhausted in "Generation and Corruption," just as occurred in the case of the right, for Aristotle only spoke of it in "Meteorology" regarding what follows.
pages.54: the sea resulting from the elements, and for this reason, he said in the fifteenth book of "Animals" that the discussion on the right has not been exhausted, and that everything that is acted upon, or rather everything that is moved, is in actuality [346 a] something else. For if it were not in actuality anything at all, potentiality would be something existing in actuality, and prime matter would necessarily exist, and possibility would be a thing standing by itself and a thing standing by its own essence. This is apparent to anyone who has practiced natural science in the slightest. The moved is some substance, or rather some body, because everything that moves is divisible; but that is movement in a way intermediate between that which is by essence and that which is by accident. Aristotle considers that to be by accident. For if it were by essence in some way, it would not be primary. The mover in potentiality is something by essence and primarily. It moves from the aspect that it is in potentiality, such that if what is in potentiality were found to be a thing separate from bodies, it would move by itself and that thing would become either a substance, a quantity, a quality, a place, or some other of the categories. However, it is necessary—as we have said—that what is in potentiality be something in actuality. We have said that it is another thing in potentiality. It is therefore in actuality one of the categories, and it is in potentiality one of the categories. Let what is in potentiality be P, let what is in actuality be A, and let the statement be S. It is clear to anyone who has practiced natural science in the slightest that what is in potentiality, from the aspect that it is in potentiality, is not under a category, for everything that is under a category
pages.55: —whatever category it may be—is existent in actuality. The categories are therefore opposed by potentiality just as they are opposed by what is in actuality. In A and S, if they are under one category, they are two opposing species. If they were substances, they would not have names, but Aristotle and Abu Nasr <insert>al-Farabi</insert> may call them "contraries" when the need for that arises. However, contraries require one subject in actuality. These two do not have a subject in actuality. If they are under one of the nine categories, what is in potentiality is necessarily existent; it has a third existence by which it is a subject for A and S. If in A and S they are under quantity, they are more similar to contraries of the first kind. Therefore, it is said of growth that it is motion, and it is more of a change than what is said of stillness. The two contraries of quantity resemble each other in two ways: first, they are species accompanied by the privations of their homogeneous kinds, as is found in the form of substances. Second, they have subjects existent in actuality that are receptive to the species of quantity. The species of substance do not have subjects; rather, they are the subjects. Indeed, if it is said that the mover has subjects, it is by way of equivocation. The contraries differ in that the species of quantity do not have two limited extremes that can be spoken of, for the greatest of dogs cannot have the size of an elephant, and the smallest cannot have the size of an ant. The species of the size of substances are many and varied, and their extremes are not limited unless it is in relation to them, so that opposition occurs to them, just as it occurs to the extremes of temperament in quality. This has been summarized in "Temperament." As for A and S, if they are qualities and are under one of the four genera of quality, they have a subject existent in actuality. Each of the species of that genus is accompanied by a privation homogeneous to it, and in them are two species that are extremes, not by relation, but absolutely. It is not possible to find a species further
pages.56:
than that extreme in its opposition, and it is not so in what is quantity. Let the smallest size, the dog for example, be A, and the greatest size be R. Whatever exists in A or T, A, R. Every species of quantity that exists in the dog is closer to R than the size A of D; there is no size further from A than D. If that were found, it would be smaller than R; let it be E. Thus the size R is closer to A than E. Therefore, D is not an extreme in M unless M is a universal; it is a species of substance. The sizes A and K are not extremes by relation in reality and by essence to the first subject, which is in potentiality, namely prime matter; rather, they proceed in its manner, because a part of its parts is matter. A and A are not extremes from the aspect of what they are or from the aspect of a relation that has attached to them. They are therefore not extremes in existence. For everything that has some state from the aspect of being that thing, it has it in existence. And what it has, while it is in a state, and that thing exists for another thing that does not have that state, it is not said that it is so in existence. Rather, if it has it in existence, it is by way of analogy. Also, if A and K are not under one category, it is possible for A and K to be, otherwise it would be a matter of opinion and not an existent thing. If that is not possible, then K and A are not one a subject for the other, except as it is said that the light is cold in potentiality, because the light implies the heat of the fire. The summarization and enumeration of these types is easy for whoever wishes it, and we suffice with this summary by way of definition.

All opposites, when they are in their subjects, necessarily have the privations of their opposites. Privations are of types: among them is the privation of substance, the privation of quantity, and the privation of quality. I do not say that substance is deprived entirely, nor quantity. If there is something that is not a quantity, such as intellect, then this is negation and not privation. Abu Nasr has <insert>[346 b]</insert> summarized the way in which it is called privation. Privation is attributed to the category in two ways: one is its negation, such as our saying, "The sky is neither heavy nor light"; the other is the removal of the negation of a species of it from
pages.57:
a subject in which that species can exist. This is more entitled to the name of privation than the former. Then it is said thereafter in ways, the most entitled of all to the name of privation being the privation summarized in the opposites in the book "Categories." This second type that we have mentioned is what Abu Nasr <al-Farabi> mentions and says: Aristotle considers the privation of every category within it: the privation of substance is in the category of substance, and the privation of quantity is in the category of quantity.

It is clear with the slightest reflection for anyone who has practiced natural science that it is not possible for prime matter to be bare of some categories so that it does not have one species of them. The first of these is substance. This is what was clarified in the first book of the "Physics," for if it were bare of it, prime matter would be possessed of a form. It is followed by quantity, for it is not a single substance—it is not a body. How far removed is one who composes size from that which is indivisible! For if it were so, a substance would be found that has no quantity. This is impossible. It has been clarified in the first of the sixth book of the "Physics" and is more clarified upon reflection. You must know that size is said of the circular and the straight by equivocation, and that circular size is what has a center. We have summarized this in the interpretation of the meanings of the seventh book of the "Physics." Then, after that, in prime matter is the genus of passive quality: such as heat, cold, moisture, and dryness. Therefore, every hylomorphic substance is a body. Body is said by equivocation of that which moves circularly and that which moves straightly; their matter is not one in species as they depict it, but they correspond to the correspondence of forms and matter that accepts motion in a straight line, which is matter by precedence. As for that which accepts circular motion, it is always a subject and is not prime matter or matter. Rather, it is called prime matter and matter by analogy, just as this is called a subject by likeness and analogy. Thus, prime matter is not free from the genus of passive quality, and it cannot be stripped of it. For this reason, when Aristotle wants to point to all of them, he says: "every tangible body." Likewise the quality of quantity, which is shape
pages.58:
and form. Likewise place. Likewise posture. Likewise time. Likewise relation. These nine categories are clear in their state: prime matter is not bare of them, although some are whiter than others.

As for action and passion, it has been doubted. But when its state is examined, it appears that it is so. As for the category of "having" <note>original: "له"</note> <note>original: "مقولة الملك"</note>, it is found in the soul; and it may be found in inanimate objects what is thought to be "having," but when its state is examined, it appears it is not under this category.

Likewise color: it may be thought of some bodies that they are devoid of color, such as air and glass, and clearer than that are tastes and smells, for their subject may not be free from all their types. But even if that is the case, these are not existent for the substance by itself primarily, but they are found secondarily and after various existents that are under another category precede them in the subject. It is as if these, even if they are not species of those, are like species. An example of this is tastes, for even if they are not species of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness, they are not outside of them, because they are heat to which another matter has attached, by which that heat has become a species of another genus, as occurred in the discussion of moving spheres: for the consideration of them is not geometric, attainable for geometric consideration, but it is under geometric consideration. We have summarized this in our treatises "On the Soul."

What we have said has been summarized in another way, which is that every body is composed of form and subject. The subject of the eternal bodies is specifically called the subject. The subject of the generated and corruptible is called prime matter, matter, and what is similar to these things. Every body
pages.59:
that is corruptible is an element or composed of two elements or more. Everything composed of things contains what belongs to those things. The things necessary for the elements are necessary for every hylomorphic body. The things necessary for the elements from the categories are that they are substances, that they are possessed of size, that they are possessed of passive qualities, that they are possessed of postures and places, that they have time, that they are relations, and that they act and are acted upon. Every body necessarily contains these genera of categories. As for the rest of what is found for hylomorphic bodies, they return to these—an example of this is roughness and dryness <note>original: "القحل"</note>, hardness, softness, and smoothness. As for the rest of what is found for hylomorphic bodies, they return to these. An example of this <unclear>. . .</unclear> are varieties of moisture and dryness. For when dryness is joined by an accident, it becomes roughness and dryness. From moisture comes smoothness and softness. Aristotle mentioned this in the second book of "Generation and Corruption." Likewise, taste and smell, for these two genera contain moisture and dryness like prime matter. As for colors, the discussion on them is another discussion. When the matter regarding them is examined, it appears that this genus is found for the elements. The exhaustive investigation of that is in another place.

It has been clarified in the seventh book of the "Physics" that alteration only occurs in the sensible things. Let whoever wishes pause upon that in the words of Aristotle there, and what the commentators have said about it. Action and passion only occur in the primary qualities, which are those by which generation and corruption occur, and they are four, and they have been enumerated in many places. We have clarified in places other than this that powers are said by participation of: the passive and the active, and we have defined each of these two genera. The active powers are necessarily

this [is] false. Exalted are You! So protect us from the punishment of the Fire. Allah is but one God; exalted is He above having a son. To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. It is the name of the column of Solomon’s temple, placed to the west on the north side where the apprentices assembled to receive their wages.

Q. What is your password?
A. TUBALCAIN. This word, the name of the 3rd son of Lamech who first invented the art of melting and working metals (Gen: 4.22), comes from the Hebrew *hobbil* which means the eldest and from *Cain* which signifies acquisition. He lived in the world and from the era [of] 666.
Who made you a M.?
My own free will.
Why did you have yourself received as a M.?
Because I was in darkness, and I wanted to see the light.
What is it?
A free man, exercising virtue and detesting vice.
Who introduced you?
A friend, whom I then recognized as a brother.
How were you admitted into the lodge?
By ... great knocks.
What do they signify?
These words of the scripture *Quærite et invenietis* <gloss>Seek and you shall find</gloss>.
Where were you prepared?
In darkness.
Before entering the ... what was required of you?
My age, my name, and my own free will.
What was done with you afterwards?
With the sincere desire I had to be received, I was made to enter the ...
What does the one who introduced you do with you?
He puts me in the hands of a stranger whom I then recognized as the brother second warden.
How were you at that time?
Neither naked nor dressed, but nevertheless in a
<column-break/>
decent manner, deprived of light, and stripped of all metals.
Why neither naked nor dressed?
To show that virtue does not need ornaments to appear with brilliance.
Why stripped of all metals?
Because metals are the symbol of vice and to teach me to strip myself of them to receive the brother, and because when one built the Temple of Solomon one heard the sound of no tool. 3 Kings 6:7.
How did one not hear the sound of any tool?
Because the cedars of Lebanon were sent all ready to be used and the stones had been cut in the quarries. 3 Kings 5:10.
What did you perceive upon entering the lodge?
Nothing that the human mind can understand, because I was in darkness.
What does the second warden do with you?
He made me travel from the east to the west by the north, and from the east to the west by the south.
How many times did you make this journey?
Three times, T. V. <note>Very Worshipful</note>
What did you find on your journey?
Many pains and difficulties, which proves that one does not reach the path of virtue without experiencing them.
What was done with you afterwards?
I was led to the east, near the R. V. <note>Respectable Venerable</note>
What was done with you?
He made me place my right knee on my right hand on [symbol: square] and I held with my left a [symbol: heart] on the [symbol: heart].
What were you doing in this posture?
I was contracting my obligation.
What is it? ......

What did you do after?
I was led back, between the two wardens, to the west and told to make my final reflections and I persisted.
What did you ask for?
The light, which was granted to me.
What did you see at that time?
Three great lights placed in J.
What do they represent?
* and the V:. <note>Venerable</note>
What are they for?
To light the workers during their work, after the work and the V:. at all times, to guide them with his wise advice.
What did you do next?
The V:. made me advance toward him by three apprentice steps, made me ratify my obligation and gave me the signs, grips and passwords, go dressed in a white leather apron and gave me two pairs of gloves, one for a man and one for a woman.
What does the apron signify?
It denotes the candor of our manners.
The man's gloves?
To teach me that a brother should never dip his hands in the blood of the innocent.
The woman's gloves?
To destroy the prejudices of the vulgar regarding our order, and to show that although we do not admit them among us, we hold them in no less regard.
Did you only perceive the three great lights?
I also saw all the brothers, the sword bared
<column-break/>
presenting the point, to show me that they were ready to pierce my breast if I became refractory to my engagements, and on the contrary to defend me even to shedding their blood if I were faithful to them.
What do you come to do in the lodge?
Conquer my passions, submit my will and make new progress in the light.
Where does the V:. sit in the lodge?
At the east.
Why?
Because it is in this part of the world that the sun opens its career to light the whole world; the V:. therefore also sits toward this part to light the brothers with his advice and open the lodge.

At the west to help the V:. to close the lodge, pay the workers and send them back content.

From the Saint John lodge.

The V:. of the lodge greets you by 3 times.

Good welcome to the visitor brothers and members who compose the lodge.
What do you ask for?
A place among you.

In what lodge have you been received?
In a just and perfect lodge.

The V∴, the 1st and 2nd Ward∴, 2 companions and 2 apprentices.
What is it that renders a lodge just and perfect?
They form it, compose it, and render it just and perfect.
Where is your lodge situated?
In the valley of Jehoshaphat, at the foot of a high mountain.
What shape has the lodge?
An oblong square.
What length?
From the east to the west.
What width?
From the south to the north.
What height?
Cubit, toises and feet without number.
What depth?
From the surface of the earth to the center.

A sky of celestial color, sprinkled with stars.
What does it represent?
The azure vault of the sky which covers the earth and the sea, where the brothers are dispersed.
What surrounds your lodge?
The union of the brothers.
How many jewels are there?
Six, three movable, and three immovable.
What are the movable ones?
The square which the V∴ wears, the level which the 1st Warden wears, and the plumb line which the 2nd Warden wears.
What are these jewels used for?
The square to give form, the level to make equal, the plumb line to raise perpendiculars on their base.
What are the immovable jewels?
The rough ashlar for the apprentices, the cubical stone with a point for the companions, and the tracing board for the masters.
How many ornaments are there?
Three, the indented tassel, the blazing star, and the mosaic pavement.
What is the indented tassel for?
It is the interior ornament of the lodge.
What does the blazing star signify?
The supreme majesty of the divinity.
What does the mosaic pavement signify?
The union of the brothers who, although separated, nevertheless make but one body.
pages.8:
On what is your lodge supported?
On the three columns, strength, wisdom, and beauty.
Who represents these columns?
The V∴ represents wisdom to undertake, the 1st Warden the strength to sustain, and the 2nd Warden the beauty to adorn.
Can every Master not possess these three perfections?
Yes, and he even must, for wisdom must be in his heart, strength in his union with his brothers, and beauty in his character.
How many doors are in your lodge?
Three doors: the 1st at the south, the 2nd at the west, and the 3rd at the east.
How many windows?
As many, situated above each door.
Why are there none in the north?
Because, as the sun lights this part little, it was judged proper to place none there.

At the north, to receive the order of the companions and keep away the profane.
Where do the companions sit?
At the west, to receive the order of the masters and watch over the apprentices.
To whom is the lodge dedicated?
To Saint John the Baptist, because he was the forerunner of the light.
How have you been received as a companion?
<column-break/>
By passing from the J column to the B column.

The J column to assemble the companions and the B column the companions.
Where were they situated?
At the west; the 1st on the north side, and the 2nd on the west side.
What height did they have?
They were 35 cubits in all, including the base, the column, the capitals, and the crown (2 Chron: 3:15); the base was eight cubits, the column 18 (3 Kings 7:15) (Jer: 52:21). The capitals were 5 cubits (3 Kings 7:16) (2 Chron: 3:15) (Jer: 52:21); the crown in the shape of a lily was 4 cubits (3 Kings 7:19), which makes 35 cubits in all.
What was the circumference of these columns?
Twelve cubits (3 Kings 7:15) (Jer: 52:21).
Were they hollow?
Yes, and their thickness was 4 fingers (Jer: 52:21).
Note: The cubit is a foot and a half of our measure, and the finger is worth eight and a quarter lines.
Why were they hollow?
To contain the tools of the apprentices and companions.
With what were they adorned?
With capitals and crowns surmounted by pomegranates without number.

# CHAPTER V.

## *History of Horus.*

Many authors have confused Horus or Orus with Harpocrates; but I will not discuss here the reasons that may have determined them to do so. The most accepted opinion is that Horus was the son of Osiris and Isis, and the last of the Gods of Egypt, not that he was the last in merit, but for the determination of his cult, and because he is in effect the last of the chemical Gods, being the Hermetic gold, or the result of the <term>œuvre</term> <gloss>work/process</gloss>. It is this Orus or Apollo, for whom Osiris undertook such a great voyage, and endured so many labors and fatigues. It is the treasure of the Philosophers, of the Priests and of the Kings of Egypt; the Philosophical child born of Isis and Osiris, or if you prefer, Apollo born of Jupiter and Latona. But, it will be said, some authors have regarded Apollo, Osiris and Isis as children of Jupiter and Juno; Apollo cannot, therefore, be the son of Isis and Osiris. Some authors even say that the Sun was the first King of Egypt, then Vulcan, then Saturn, and finally Osiris and Horus. All this,
pages.331: I admit, could cause embarrassment, and present insurmountable difficulties in a historical system; but regarding the Hermetic <term>œuvre</term> <gloss>work</gloss>, there are none at all. A new proof that it was the object of all these fictions. The agent and the patient in the <term>œuvre</term> being homogeneous, they reunite to produce a third similar to them, proceeding from both; the Sun and the Moon are its father and mother, says Hermes, and the other Philosophers after him. These names of Sun and Moon given to several things cause an ambiguity that occasions all these difficulties; it is from this source that all the qualities of father, mother, son, daughter, grandfather, brother, sister, uncle, husband and wife have sprung; and so many other similar names, which serve to explain the pretended incests and adulteries so often repeated in the ancient Fables. One would need to be a Hermetic Philosopher, or a Priest of Egypt to develop all this; but Harpocrates recommends secrecy, and one should not hope that it will be violated, at least clearly. What one can conclude from the good faith and ingenuity rather than from the indiscretion of some Adepts, is that the matter of the <term>œuvre</term> is the radical principle of everything; but that it is in particular the active and formal principle of gold; this is why it becomes Philosophical gold through the operations of the <term>œuvre</term> imitated from those of Nature. This matter forms in the bowels of the earth, and is carried there by the water of rains animated by the universal spirit spread in the air, and this spirit draws its fertility from the influences of the
pages.332: Sun and of the Moon, which by this means become the father and mother of this matter. The earth is the matrix where this seed is deposited, and is found thereby to be its nurse. The gold that forms from it is the terrestrial Sun. This matter, or the subject of the <term>œuvre</term> <gloss>work</gloss>, is composed of two substances, one fixed, the other volatile: the former igneous and active; the latter humid and passive, to which have been given the names of Heaven and Earth; Saturn and Rhea; Osiris and Isis; Jupiter and Juno; and the igneous principle or fire of nature which is enclosed therein, has been named Vulcan, Prometheus, Vesta, etc. In this manner, Vulcan and Vesta, which is the fire of the humid and volatile part, are properly the father and mother of Saturn, just as the heaven and earth are, because the names of these Gods are not given only to the matter still raw and indigestible taken before the preparation that the Artist gives it in concert with Nature; but also during the preparation and the operations that follow it. Whenever this matter becomes black, it is the Philosophical Saturn, son of Vulcan and Vesta, who are themselves children of the Sun, for the reasons we have stated. When the matter becomes gray after the black, it is Jupiter: if it becomes white, it is the Moon, Isis, Diana; and when it has reached red, it is Apollo, Phoebus, the Sun, Osiris. Jupiter is therefore the son of Saturn, Isis and Osiris the children of Jupiter. But as the gray color is not one of the principal ones of the <term>œuvre</term>, most of the Philosophers do not make mention of it, and passing all at once from the
pages.333:
black to the white, Isis and Osiris are brought closer to Saturn, and naturally become his first-born children, in accordance with the Inscriptions that we have reported. Isis and Osiris are therefore brother and sister, whether one regards them as principles of the <term>œuvre</term>, or one considers them as children of Saturn or of Jupiter. Isis is even found to be the mother of Osiris, since the red color is born from the white. But, it will be said, how are they husband and wife? If one pays attention to all that we have said, one will see that they are so from all points of view from which one can consider them; but they are so more openly in the production of the Philosophical Sun called Horus, Apollo, or sulfur of the sages; since it is formed of these two substances, fixed and volatile, reunited into a fixed whole, named Orus.

When one makes an abstraction of the preparation, or first operation of the <term>œuvre</term>, (which is quite customary among the Philosophers, who do not begin their treatises on the Sacerdotal, or Hermetic, Art until the second operation) as the Philosophical gold is already made; and one must use it as the base of the second <term>œuvre</term>; then the Sun is found to be the first King of Egypt; it contains the fire of nature in its bosom: and this fire acting on the materials, produces putrefaction, and blackness; here again is Vulcan, son of the Sun, and Saturn, son of Vulcan. Osiris and Isis will come next, finally Orus through the reunion of his father and his mother.

It is to this second operation that one must apply
pages.334:
these expressions of the Philosophers; one must marry the mother with the son. That is to say, that after its first decoction one must mix it with the raw matter from which it emerged, and cook it again until they are reunited, and make but one. During this operation the raw matter dissolves and putrefies the digested matter: it is the mother who kills her child, and puts him in her womb to be reborn, and to resuscitate. During this dissolution the Titans kill Orus, and his mother then brings him back from death to life. The son, then less affectionate toward his mother than she was toward him, say the Philosophers <note>(a)</note>, puts his mother to death, and reigns in her place. That is to say, that the fixed or Orus fixes the volatile or Isis, who had volatilized him; for to kill, to bind, to close, to inhume, to freeze, to coagulate, or to fix are synonymous terms in the language of the Philosophers; just as to give life, to resuscitate, to open, to untie, to travel signify the same thing as to volatilize.

Isis and Osiris are therefore justly reputed the principal Gods of Egypt with Horus who in fact reigns last, since he is the result of all the Sacerdotal Art. It is perhaps this that has caused him to be confused by some with Harpocrates, God of secrecy, because the object of this secret was none other than Orus, whom one also had reason to call the Sun or Apollo, since he is the Sun or the Apollo of the Philosophers. If the Antiquarians had studied Hermetic Philosophy,

## CHAPTER VI.

### *History of Typhon.*

Diodorus <note>(a)</note> makes Typhon born of the Titans. Plutarch <note>(b)</note> says he is the brother of Osiris and Isis: some others advance that he was born from the Earth, when Juno irritated struck it with her foot; that the fear he had of Jupiter made him flee to Egypt, where, unable to endure the heat of the climate, he threw himself into a lake where he perished. Hesiod gives us a most atrocious depiction of him <note>(c)</note>, which Apollodorus seems to have copied. The Earth, they say, outraged with fury that Jupiter had struck the Titans with his thunderbolts, joined with Tartarus, and making one last effort, she gave birth to Typhon. This dreadful monster had a greatness and a strength superior to all the others combined. His height was so enormous that he far surpassed the highest mountains, and his head penetrated to the stars. His extended arms reached from the orient to the occident, and from his hands came one hundred furious dragons,

Countless vipers issued from his legs and thighs, and folding back in various convolutions, stretched the entire length of his body, with hisses so horrible they astonished the most intrepid. His mouth exhaled nothing but flames; his eyes were burning coals, and his voice was more terrible than thunder; at times he bellowed like a bull, at times he roared like a lion, and sometimes he barked like a dog. <margin><insert>CaG</insert></margin> The whole upper part of his body was bristling with feathers, and the lower part was covered in scales. Such was this Typhon, formidable even to the Gods, who dared to throw rocks and mountains against Heaven while letting out frightful howls. The Gods were so terrified by this that, not believing themselves safe in Heaven, they fled to Egypt and sheltered themselves from the pursuits of this monster by hiding under the forms of various animals.

Attempts have been made to explain what ancient authors said about Typhon from moral, historical, and physical perspectives. The applications made have sometimes been quite successful, but it has never been possible for mythologists to explain his fable in its entirety within a single system. His marriage with <term>Echidna</term> made him the father of various monsters worthy of their origin, such as the Gorgon, Cerberus, the Hydra of Lerna, the Sphinx, the Eagle that devoured the unfortunate Prometheus, the dragons guarding the Golden Fleece and the Garden of the Hesperides, etc.

Mythologists, to extricate themselves from the embarrassment into which this fable cast them—as it became for them one of the most obscure mysteries of mythology <note>(a)</note>—have taken to saying that the Greeks and Latins, ignorant of the origin of this fable, only obscured it further by wishing to transport it, according to their custom, from the history of Egypt into their own. Founded upon the traditions they had learned through their trade with the Egyptians, they made Typhon into a monster equally horrible and bizarre, whom the jealous Juno had caused to emerge from the earth to take revenge on Latona, her rival.

What Diodorus <note>(b)</note> and Plutarch <note>(c)</note> report to us about this is not to the taste of the Abbé Banier; no doubt because they are not favorable to his system in this regard. These two authors, he says <note>(d)</note>, "did not fail, according to the genius of their nation, to mingle many ridiculous fictions into what they report; and, moreover, being little exact in chronology, and knowing only very confusedly the first histories of the world renewed after the Deluge, among which is undoubtedly the one I am explaining (that of Typhon), they are guides that should only be followed with great caution." If they mingled in some circumstances to adapt it to the fables of their own country, they preserved the foundation, which is equally fabulous. In vain does Gerard Vossius <note>(a)</note> claim that Og, King of Bashan, is the same as Typhon, based on the resemblance of the two names; for, he says, that of Typhon comes from <term>τύφω</term> <gloss>to burn/set on fire</gloss>, and that of Og signifies *he burned*, *he scorched*. In vain does M. Huet <note>(b)</note> make him the legislator of the Hebrews, who became odious to the Egyptians through the loss of their firstborn sons. The Abbé Sevin is no more correct in putting him in the place of Cush, nor the Abbé Banier in that of Sebon, following on this occasion the sentiment of Plutarch, who relies on the authority of Manethon. It would not be possible to reconcile Plutarch with himself. Bochart succeeded better <note>(c)</note> than all the authors above by thinking that Typhon is the same as Enceladus; but he guessed without knowing why, since he was ignorant of the reason that prompted the poets to name them interchangeably for one another, and to have them both perish in the same manner. The poets, much better than the historians, preserved for us the true foundation of the fables, and, properly speaking, disfigured them less than the historians, because they were content to report them, embellishing them sometimes in truth, but without bothering to discuss why, how, and

But finally, what is to be concluded from so many different opinions? That we must seek what we ought to think of Typhon in the features upon which the historians, poets, and mythologists agree, or in which they differ little. The poets and mythologists all say in concert that Typhon was cast under Mount Etna, and the ancients who did not place his tomb there chose for it sulphurous places known for subterranean fires, such as in Campania, or near Mount Vesuvius, as Diodorus claims <note>(a)</note>, or in the Phlegraean Fields, as Strabon recounts <note>(b)</note>, or in a place in Asia where water sometimes issues from the earth, and at other times fire, according to Pausanias <note>(c)</note>. In a word, in all the mountains and all other places where there were sulphurous exhalations. Finally, the Egyptians recounted that he had been struck by lightning and that he had perished in a whirlwind of fire.

Let us compare all this with some circumstances of the life of Typhon, and unless one wishes to obstinately close one's eyes to the light, one will be forced to admit that the entire history of this alleged monster is but an allegory, which is part of that which the priests

Since, according to the Abbé Banier himself <note>(a)</note>, the Greek and Latin poets and historians have preserved for us among their most absurd fables the traditions of Egypt, it is to these primitive traditions that we must hold. They teach us that Typhon was the brother of Osiris; that he persecuted him even to the point of causing him to die in the manner we have mentioned; that he was subsequently vanquished by Isis, assisted by Horus; and that he finally perished by fire. The historians also report that the Egyptians held the sea in abomination because they believed that it was itself Typhon, and they called it *foam* or *spittle of Typhon* <note>(b)</note>, names they also gave to sea salt. Pythagoras, instructed by the Egyptians, said that the sea was a tear of Saturn. The reason they had for this was that the sea, according to them, was a principle of corruption, since the Nile, which provided them with so many goods, was vitiated by its mixture with it. These traditions also teach us that Typhon caused Horus to perish in the sea, into which he cast him, and that Isis, his mother, resurrected him after having pulled him out.

We have said that Osiris was the igneous, gentle, and generative principle that Nature employs in the formation of mixtures, and that Isis was the radical humidity; for one must not confuse the one with the other, since they differ between themselves as

smoke and flame, light and air, sulphur and mercury. Radical humor is, in mixtures, the seat and nourishment of the innate heat, or natural and celestial fire, and becomes like the bond that unites it with the elementary body; this igneous virtue is like the form and the soul of the mixture. This is why it performs the office of the male, and the radical humor, as humidity, performs the function of the female; they are thus like brother and sister, and their reunion constitutes the base of the mixture. But these mixtures are not composed of radical humor alone; in their formation, homogeneous, impure, and terrestrial parts join with it to complete the body of the mixture; and these coarse and terrestrial impurities are the principle of its corruption, because of their combustible, acrid, and corrosive sulphur, which acts incessantly upon the pure and incombustible sulphur. These two sulphurs, or fires, are thus two brothers, but enemy brothers; and by the daily destruction of individuals, we have reason to be convinced that the impure prevails over the pure. These are the two good and bad principles of which we spoke in the first and second chapters of this book.

This being posited, it is not difficult to conceive why they made Typhon into a frightful monster, always disposed to do evil, and who had the audacity even to wage war against the Gods. Metals abound in this impure and combustible sulphur, which gnaws them by turning them into rust, each in its own species. The Gods had given their names to the metals; and this is why

Herodotus <note>(a)</note> says that the Egyptians counted at first only eight great Gods, that is to say, the seven metals and the principle of which they were composed. Typhon was born of the earth, but of the coarse earth, being the principle of corruption. He was the cause of the death of Osiris, because corruption only occurs through the solution that we have explained when speaking of the death of this Prince. The feathers that covered the upper part of Typhon’s body, and his height, which carried his head to the clouds, indicate his volatility and his sublimation into vapors. His thighs, his legs covered with scales, and the serpents that issue from them on all sides, are the symbol of his corrupting and putrefactive aqueousness. The fire that he throws from his mouth marks his corrosive combustibility and designates his pretended brotherhood with Osiris, because the latter is a hidden, natural, and vivifying fire, while the other is a tyrannical and destructive fire. This is why d'Espagnet calls him the tyrant of Nature and the fratricide of natural fire, which fits Typhon perfectly. For the philosophers, serpents are the ordinary hieroglyph of dissolution and putrefaction; thus, it is agreed that Typhon does not differ at all from the serpent Python, killed by Apollo. It is also known that Apollo and Horus were taken for the same God.

This monster was not content to have caused the death of his brother Osiris; he also cast his nephew Horus into the sea after seizing him.

One could not designate more clearly the resolution into water of the philosophical Horus or Apollo than by saying he was cast into the sea; the blackness, which is the mark of perfect solution and of the putrefaction called death by the adepts, is seen in this Queen of Ethiopia. This corrupted and putrefied matter is precisely that foam or spittle of Typhon in which Horus was cast and submerged. It is truly a tear of Saturn, since the black color is the philosophical Saturn. Isis finally resurrected Horus; that is to say, the philosophical Apollo, after having been dissolved, putrefied, and become black, passed from blackness to whiteness, called resurrection and life in the Hermetic style. The father and mother then reunited to fight Typhon, or corruption, and after having vanquished him they reigned gloriously, first the mother or Isis—that is to say, the whiteness—and after her Horus her son, or the redness. Some say that Typhon threw himself into a marsh where he perished; others that he was struck by Jupiter’s lightning and perished by fire. Countless vipers emerged from his legs and thighs, and, folding themselves in various convolutions, extended along the entire length of his body, with hissings so horrible that they astonished the most intrepid. His mouth exhaled only flames; his eyes were burning coals, with a voice more terrible than thunder; sometimes he bellowed like a bull, sometimes he roared like a lion; and sometimes he barked like a dog. <margin><insert>CaG</insert></margin> The upper part of his body was bristling with feathers, and the lower part was covered in scales. Such was this Typhon, formidable even to the Gods, who dared to throw rocks and mountains against Heaven while making hideous howls; the Gods were so terrified by this that, not believing themselves safe in Heaven, they fled to Egypt and took shelter from the pursuit of this monster by hiding there in the form of various animals.

Attempts have been made to explain what the ancient authors said about Typhon morally, historically, and physically. The applications that have been made of it have sometimes been quite successful; but it has never been possible for mythologists to explain his fable in its entirety within the same system. His marriage with <term>Echidna</term> <gloss>a mythological monster</gloss> made him the father of various monsters worthy of their origin, such as the Gorgon, Cerberus, the Hydra of Lerna, the Sphinx, the Eagle that devoured the unfortunate Prometheus, the Dragons guarding the Golden Fleece and the Garden of the Hesperides, etc.
