Mythologists, in order to get out of the embarrassment into which this fable threw them—which for them became one of the most obscure mysteries of mythology <note>(a)</note>—have taken it upon themselves to say that the Greeks and the Latins, ignorant of the origin of this fable, only obscured it further by wanting to transfer it, according to their custom, from the history of Egypt into their own. Based on traditions they had learned through their trade with the Egyptians, they made Typhon into a monster equally horrible and bizarre, whom the jealous Juno had caused to emerge from the earth to take revenge on her rival, Latona.

What Diodorus <note>(b)</note> and Plutarch <note>(c)</note> report to us about this is not to the taste of the Abbé Banier; no doubt because they are not at all favorable to his system in this regard. These two authors, he says <note>(d)</note>, "did not fail, according to the genius of their nation, to mingle several ridiculous fictions into what they report; and furthermore, they are not very exact in their chronology, and knowing only very confusedly the first histories of the world renewed after the Deluge, among which is undoubtedly that which I am explaining (of Typhon), they are guides that should only be followed with great caution." Although the Abbé Banier is right to think that these authors were not well-versed in the essence of the history of Typhon, it is nonetheless true that they had collected what they

If they mixed in some circumstances to adapt it to the fables of their own country, they preserved the foundation, which is found to be equally fabulous. In vain does Gerard Vossius <note>(a)</note> claim that Og, King of Bashan, is the same as Typhon, based on the resemblance of the two names; for, he says, that of Typhon comes from <term>τύφω</term> <gloss>to smoke, to burn, to kindle</gloss>, and that of Og means *he burned, he scorched*. It would not be possible to reconcile Plutarch with himself. Bochart succeeded better <note>(c)</note> than all the aforementioned authors by thinking that Typhon is the same as Enceladus; but he guessed without knowing why, since he was ignorant of the reason that led the poets to name them interchangeably for one another, and to have them both perish in the same manner. The poets, much better than the historians, have preserved for us the true foundation of the fables, and have, strictly speaking, defaced them less than the historians, because they were content to report them, embellishing them, it is true, sometimes, but without bothering to discuss why, how, and

But finally, what can one conclude from so many different opinions? That one must seek what we ought to think of Typhon in the traits upon which the historians, the poets, and the mythologists are in agreement, or in which they differ little. The poets and the mythologists all say in concert that Typhon was precipitated under Mount Etna, and the ancients who did not place his tomb there chose for this purpose sulfurous places known for their subterranean fires, such as in Campania, or near Mount Vesuvius, as Diodorus claims <note>(a)</note>, or in the Phlegraean Fields, as Strabo recounts <note>(b)</note>, or in a place in Asia where water sometimes issues from the earth, and at other times fire, according to Pausanias <note>(c)</note>. In a word, in all the mountains and all the other places where there were sulfurous exhalations. Finally, the Egyptians recounted that he had been struck by lightning and that he had perished in a whirlwind of fire.

Let us compare all this with some circumstances of Typhon’s life, and unless one wishes to stubbornly close one's eyes to the light, one will be forced to admit that the entire history of this alleged monster is but an allegory, which is part of the one that the priests

Since, according to the Abbé Banier himself <note>(a)</note>, the Greek and Latin poets and historians have preserved for us among their most absurd fables the traditions of Egypt, it is to these primitive traditions that we must hold. They teach us that Typhon was the brother of Osiris; that he persecuted him until he caused him to die in the manner we have mentioned; that he was then conquered by Isis, aided by Horus; and that he finally perished by fire. The historians also report that the Egyptians held the sea in abomination because they believed it was Typhon himself, and called it *foam* or *spittle of Typhon* <note>(b)</note>, names they also gave to sea salt. Pythagoras, instructed by the Egyptians, said that the sea was a tear of Saturn. The reason they had for this was that the sea, according to them, was a principle of corruption, since the Nile, which provided them with so many goods, was corrupted by its mixture with it. These traditions also teach us that Typhon caused Horus to perish in the sea, into which he threw him, and that Isis, his mother, resurrected him after drawing him out.

We have said that Osiris was the igneous, gentle, and generative principle that Nature employs in the formation of mixtures; and that Isis was its radical moisture; for one must not confuse the one with the other, since they differ from each other like

smoke and flame, light and air, sulfur and mercury. The radical humor is, in mixtures, the seat and nourishment of the innate heat, or natural and celestial fire, and becomes like the bond that unites it with the elemental body; this igneous virtue is like the form and soul of the mixture. This is why it performs the office of the male, and the radical humor, as moisture, performs the function of the female; they are therefore like brother and sister, and their reunion constitutes the base of the mixture. But these mixtures are not composed of the radical humor alone; in their formation, homogeneous, impure, and earthly parts join with it to complete the body of the mixture; and these gross and earthly impurities are the principle of its corruption, because of their combustible, acrid, and corrosive sulfur, which acts constantly upon the pure and incombustible sulfur. These two sulfurs, or fires, are therefore two brothers, but enemy brothers; and by the daily destruction of individuals, one has reason to be convinced that the impure prevails over the pure. These are the two good and evil principles of which we have spoken in the first and second chapters of this book.

This being posited, it is not difficult to conceive why Typhon was made into a terrifying monster, always disposed to do evil, and who even had the audacity to make war against the Gods. Metals abound in this impure and combustible sulfur, which gnaws at them by turning them into rust, each in its own species. The Gods had given their names to the metals; and this is why

Herodotus <note>(a)</note> says that the Egyptians counted at first only eight great Gods, that is to say, the seven metals and the principle of which they were composed. Typhon was born of the earth, but of the gross earth, being the principle of corruption. He was the cause of the death of Osiris, because corruption is only effected through the solution that we have explained while speaking of the death of this Prince. The feathers that covered the upper part of Typhon's body, and his height, which carried his head to the clouds, indicate his volatility and his sublimation into vapors. His thighs, his legs covered with scales, and the serpents that emerge from them on all sides are the symbol of his corrupting and putrefactive aqueousness. The fire he throws from his mouth marks his corrosive adustibility and designates his pretended brotherhood with Osiris, because the latter is a hidden, natural, and vivifying fire, while the other is a tyrannical and destructive fire. This is why d'Espagnet calls him the tyrant of Nature and the fratricide of the natural fire, which fits Typhon perfectly. Among the philosophers, serpents are the ordinary hieroglyph for dissolution and putrefaction; thus, it is agreed that Typhon does not differ from the serpent Python, killed by Apollo. It is also known that Apollo and Horus were taken for the same God.

This monster was not content with having caused his brother Osiris to die; he also cast his nephew Horus into the sea after seizing him.

One could not have designated the resolution into water of the Philosophical Horus or Apollo more clearly than by saying he was precipitated into the sea; the blackness which is the mark of the perfect solution and of the putrefaction called death by the Adepts is seen in this Queen of Ethiopia. This corrupted and putrefied matter is precisely that foam or spittle of Typhon, in which Horus was thrown and submerged. It is truly a tear of Saturn, since the black color is the Philosophical Saturn. Isis finally resurrected Horus; that is to say, the Philosophical Apollo, after having been dissolved, putrefied, and become black, passed from blackness to whiteness, called resurrection and life in the Hermetic style. The father and mother then reunited to fight Typhon, or corruption, and after having conquered him they reigned gloriously, first the mother or Isis, that is to say, the whiteness, and after her Horus her son, or the redness. Without resorting to so many explanations, the very supposed tombs of Typhon make us understand what was thought of this monster, father of so many others, which we will explain in the chapters that concern them. Some say that Typhon threw himself into a marsh where he perished; others that he was struck by lightning by Jupiter, and that he perished by fire. From an eye that He ascends higher and higher, and the truth below, the Messiah, as it is written, "And in the greatness of your majesty you overthrow those who rise against you" <note>Exodus 15:7</note>. **Rabbi Isaac** said: This verse is for the time that the Holy One, blessed be He, descends upon the nations who contend against Him, as it is written, "And He shall roar and shout together against him and against His Messiah." And war shall be waged against Jerusalem, the holy city, and to destroy many against it, which the Holy One, blessed be He, smites with many afflictions upon their faces as before. And it is written, "Against His people and against His sanctuary." And the Holy One, blessed be He, smites them to satisfy them, as it is written, "He who sits in the heavens shall laugh, the Lord shall have them in derision" <note>Psalm 2:4</note>. At that time, the Holy One, blessed be He, descends upon them and removes them from the world, as it is written, "And this shall be the plague wherewith the Lord will plague all the people that have fought against Jerusalem" <note>Zechariah 14:12</note>... from the name of the Lord... the sages... hot heat... the Holy One, blessed be He, to descend to them, and all of them... of Nebuchadnezzar and Sennacherib and all the other kings who destroyed His house and reached it before, and they shall be gathered, many of all the other nations, and the Holy One, blessed be He, smites to take vengeance upon them at the stirring of Jerusalem, which they deserve... it is written... to descend to them... as it is written, "And in the greatness of your majesty you overthrow those who rise against you." Seventy nations and they are hidden; immediately, as long as they spread, they suckle those powerful sides, the nations are found in their nature. When He sees the time of the dominion of every praise, and the praise is hidden in the time for Israel, all the end of the vision of that root, that all the nations are ruled over by them now, He will resurrect them in Him. When the dominion is pressed upon them, that portion of the name falls, for it has no building to arouse to us and to stand the name of all of them. And on this, the small mouth is stupid to give the name of praise, the name that is not, "Who is like You" in all that survey of the vision of the hour, that he sees the name taken, that all of it is the root of all the rest, and to them because He passed with them in the word, "Who is like You among the gods, O Lord, glorious in holiness" <note>Exodus 15:11</note>. Let us establish the matter, "Who is like You among the gods, O Lord?" **Rabbi Yose opened:** "I have seen all the works that are done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and vexation of spirit" <note>Ecclesiastes 1:14</note>. Could it be even the work of the Holy One? As it is written, "And the work of righteousness shall be peace" <note>Isaiah 32:17</note>. Rather, it is to establish: "All the works that are done under the sun," it is written, the rest is righteousness, which is above the sun. And this, "All is vanity and vexation of spirit," what is it talking about? And if you say "All is vanity and vexation of spirit," as we have established, that it is in the spirit of wisdom, as it is written, "All is vanities." And those vanities that are above, what is the work in that which is written here, "All is vanity and vexation of spirit"? And is it not a matter that is under the sun that he said? A little, and it is straw <margin>Like the argument of the memory</margin>, its sound is compromised below. that constantly darted their three-pointed tongues. Countless vipers emerged from his legs and thighs, and, folding themselves in various convolutions, spread over the whole length of his body with hissings so horrible that they astonished the most intrepid. His mouth exhaled only flames; his eyes were burning coals, and with a voice more terrible than thunder, he would sometimes bellow like a bull, sometimes roar like a lion, and sometimes bark like a dog. <margin><insert>CaG</insert></margin> The whole upper part of his body was bristled with feathers, and the lower part was covered in scales. Such was this Typhon, formidable even to the Gods, who dared to hurl rocks and mountains against Heaven while uttering frightful howls. The Gods were so terrified that, not believing themselves safe in Heaven, they fled to Egypt and took shelter from the pursuit of this monster by hiding there in the form of various animals.

Efforts have been made to explain what ancient authors said of Typhon, whether morally, historically, or physically. The applications made have sometimes been quite successful; but it has never been possible for mythologists to explain his fable in its entirety within the same system. His marriage with <term>Echidna</term> made him the father of various monsters worthy of their origin, such as the Gorgon, Cerberus, the Hydra of Lerna, the Sphinx, the Eagle that devoured the unfortunate Prometheus, the dragons guarding the Golden Fleece and the Garden of the Hesperides, etc.
pages.339:
<header>FABLES</header>

Mythologists, in order to extricate themselves from the difficulty into which this fable cast them—as it became for them one of the most obscure mysteries of mythology <note>(a)</note>—have taken it into their heads to say that the Greeks and Latins, ignorant of the origin of this fable, only obscured it further by wishing, according to their custom, to transport it from the history of Egypt into their own. Founded upon the traditions they had learned through their trade with the Egyptians, they made of Typhon a monster as horrible as it was bizarre, which the jealous Juno had caused to emerge from the earth to avenge herself upon Latona, her rival.

What Diodorus <note>(b)</note> and Plutarch <note>(c)</note> report to us about this is not to the taste of the Abbé Banier; no doubt because they are not, in this, favorable to his system. These two authors, he says <note>(d)</note>, "did not fail, according to the genius of their nation, to mingle several ridiculous fictions in what they reported; and besides being inaccurate in chronology, and only knowing very confusedly the first histories of the world reborn after the Deluge, among which is undoubtedly the one I am explaining (that of Typhon), they are guides that must be followed only with great caution." Although the Abbé Banier is right to think that these authors were not well-versed in the essence of Typhon's history, it is no less true that they had collected what they

If they mixed in some circumstances to adapt it to the fables of their own country, they preserved the foundation, which is equally fabulous. In vain does Gerard Vossius <note>(a)</note> claim that Og, King of Bashan, is the same as Typhon, based on the resemblance of the two names; for, he says, that of Typhon comes from <term>τύφω</term> <gloss>to burn, to set on fire</gloss>, and that of Og signifies *he burned*, *he scorched*. In vain does M. Huet <note>(b)</note> make him the legislator of the Hebrews, who became odious to the Egyptians through the loss of their firstborn sons. The Abbé Sevin is no more correct to put him in the place of Cush, nor the Abbé Banier in that of Sebon, following in this instance the sentiment of Plutarch, who relies on the authority of Manetho. It would not be possible to reconcile Plutarch with himself. Bochart succeeded better <note>(c)</note> than all the authors mentioned above by thinking that Typhon is the same as Enceladus; but he guessed without knowing why, since he was ignorant of the reason that compelled the poets to name them interchangeably for one another, and to have them both perish in the same manner. The poets, much better than the historians, have preserved for us the true foundation of the fables, and have, strictly speaking, less disfigured them than the historians, because they were content to report them, sometimes embellishing them, it is true, but without bothering to discuss why, how, and

at what time these things could have occurred; whereas the historians, seeking to accommodate them to history, suppressed features, mixed in their own conjectures, sometimes substituted other names, etc.

But finally, what to conclude from so many different opinions? That we must seek what we ought to think of Typhon in the traits upon which historians, poets, and mythologists agree, or in which they differ little. The poets and mythologists all say in concert that Typhon was cast under Mount Etna, and the ancients who did not place his tomb there chose for it sulphurous places, known for their subterranean fires, such as in Campania or near Mount Vesuvius, as Diodorus <note>(a)</note> claims, or in the Phlegraean Fields, as Strabo <note>(b)</note> recounts, or in a place in Asia from which water sometimes emerges from the earth and fire at other times, according to Pausanias <note>(c)</note>. In a word, in all the mountains and all other places where there were sulphurous exhalations. The Egyptians finally related that he had been struck by lightning and had perished in a whirlwind of fire.

Let us compare all this with certain circumstances of Typhon's life, and unless one wishes to shut one's eyes stubbornly to the light, one will be forced to agree that the entire history of this supposed Monster is but an allegory, which forms part of that which the priests

Since, according to the Abbé Banier himself <note>(a)</note>, the Greek and Latin poets and historians have preserved for us, among their most absurd fables, the traditions of Egypt, it is to these primitive traditions that we must hold. They teach us that Typhon was the brother of Osiris; that he persecuted him even to his death in the manner we have mentioned; that he was then conquered by Isis, assisted by Horus; and that he finally perished by fire. Historians also report that the Egyptians held the sea in abomination because they believed it was Typhon himself, and called it *foam* or *saliva of Typhon* <note>(b)</note>, names they also gave to sea salt. Pythagoras, instructed by the Egyptians, said that the sea was a tear of Saturn. The reason they had for this was that the sea, according to them, was a principle of corruption, since the Nile, which provided them with so many goods, became corrupted by its mixing with it. These traditions further teach us that Typhon caused Horus to perish in the sea, where he cast him, and that Isis, his mother, resurrected him after drawing him out.

We have said that Osiris was the igneous, gentle, and generative principle that Nature employs in the formation of mixed bodies; and that Isis was its radical moisture; for one must not confuse one with the other, since they differ from each other like

smoke and flame, light and air, sulfur and mercury. Radical moisture is, in mixed bodies, the seat and nourishment of the innate heat, or natural and celestial fire, and becomes like the bond that unites it with the elemental body. This igneous virtue is like the form and soul of the mixture. This is why it performs the office of the male, and the radical moisture performs, as moisture, the function of the female; they are therefore like brother and sister, and their union constitutes the base of the mixture. But these mixtures are not composed of radical moisture alone; in their formation, homogeneous, impure, and terrestrial parts join with it to complete the body of the mixture; and these gross and terrestrial impurities are the principle of its corruption, because of their combustible, acrid, and corrosive sulfur, which acts incessantly upon the pure and incombustible sulfur. These two sulfurs, or fires, are therefore two brothers, but enemy brothers; and by the daily destruction of individuals, one has reason to be convinced that the impure prevails over the pure. These are the two good and evil principles of which we spoke in the first and second chapters of this book.

This being established, it is not difficult to conceive why they made Typhon a frightful monster, always disposed to do evil, and who even had the audacity to make war upon the Gods. Metals abound in this impure and combustible sulfur, which gnaws at them, causing each to turn into rust in its own way. The Gods had given their names to the metals; and this is why

Herodotus <note>(a)</note> says that the Egyptians counted at first only eight great Gods, that is to say, the seven metals and the principle of which they were composed. Typhon was born of the earth, but of gross earth, being the principle of corruption. He was the cause of Osiris's death, because corruption only occurs through the dissolution that we explained when speaking of the death of that Prince. The feathers that covered the upper part of Typhon's body, and his height that carried his head to the clouds, indicate his volatility and his sublimation into vapors. His thighs, his legs covered with scales, and the serpents that emerge from them on all sides are the symbol of his corrupting and putrefactive aquosity. The fire he casts from his mouth marks his corrosive combustibility and designates his supposed fraternity with Osiris, because the latter is a hidden, natural, and vivifying fire, while the former is a tyrannical and destructive fire. This is why d'Espagnet calls him the tyrant of Nature and the fratricide of natural fire, which perfectly suits Typhon. Serpents are, for the philosophers, the ordinary hieroglyph of dissolution and putrefaction; thus, it is agreed that Typhon does not differ at all from the serpent Python, killed by Apollo. It is also known that Apollo and Horus were taken for the same God.

This Monster was not content to have caused the death of his brother Osiris; he also cast his nephew Horus into the sea, after seizing him.

What are the five perfect points of your reception?
Foot... knee... chest... the embrace and the kiss of peace.
Give me the explanation of this sign?
It teaches us that we must all walk in the same footsteps, that we must bow before one another, that our hearts must be united together and form but one; that we must support one another; that our souls must merge so as to form only the same thought.

Why do you call the M<note>Masons</note> children of the W<note>Widow</note>?
Because... your M<note>Master</note> was the son of a widow of the tribe of Naphtali (1 Kings 7:14) and we regard ourselves as his descendants. The father... was named Ur.

On the tracing board.

Chalk, charcoal, and the trough.

<column-break/>

What do they signify?
Chalk signifies zeal, charcoal fervor, and the trough constancy.
How many workers were at the temple?
Thirty thousand (1 Kings 5:13).
How many masters?
Three thousand (ibid. 16).
How many A. and C.<note>Apprentices and Companions</note>?
Twenty-six thousand.
What wood was used for the framework?
The cedars of Lebanon (ibid. 10).
Who sent them to Solomon?
Hiram King of Tyre (ibid. 10).
What gratitude did Solomon show for this?
As there was famine in the Kingdom of Tyre, Solomon in gratitude sent twenty thousand measures of wheat, which measure in Hebrew is called *hemoo* and in Greek *coros*. As this measure weighed 600 pounds of 16 ounces and the *carte* weighs 100, it results from the multiplication performed that there were 12,000,000 *cartes* of wheat; he also sent him as much grain; he also sent him twenty thousand measures of wine which amounts to 120,000 pounds of 16 ounces and twenty thousand sacks of oil which makes 40,000 pounds (2 Chronicles 2:10). He also gave him twenty cities in Galilee on the borders of Tyre (1 Kings 9:11). Hiram, who did not find these cities to his liking (by the name of Cabul which he gave them, meaning swampy), made reproaches to him which let us know that politics had no part in this present, but rather a perfect fraternity.

What does <term>YHWH</term> signify?
It is the incommunicable name among the Jews; it was forbidden under pain of death to pronounce it, and they substituted the word *Adonai* <term>Adonai</term> <gloss>My Lord</gloss>. In <term>YHWH</term>, J. signifies the present, H. the past, V. the future. This name means the one who is, who has been, and who will be eternally.
How were you purified?
In the salutary water that flows from the sea of brass, emblem and figure of the sacred water of baptism which draws its source from the Jordan.
Have you been disunited?
Yes, by natural imperfection.
How were you reunited?
By the triple alliance: the first, that of the Eternal with Abraham (Genesis 15:18) by circumcision (Genesis 17:10); the 2nd, that which He made in the desert of Sinai with His people (Exodus 24:8). H. It did not happen by chance that the all-wise Creator of all things, when He wished to make Himself known to the created beings, also explained Himself through measure and numbers; for example, He specified such things Himself in the erection of the Tabernacle in the wilderness, the Temple in Jerusalem, and the New Jerusalem, and wished for everything to be arranged so precisely according to them. There must be something in the measure and numbers that testifies to Divine Wisdom; otherwise, it would have been all the same to GOD, or could have been, whether the Tabernacle
pages.27:
# Divine Art of Calculation and Measurement.

had been a cubit narrower or shorter, longer or wider, than the commander Moses would have arranged according to the space required for the performance of the divine service. <margin>Exodus 25:9, 40; 26:30.</margin>
> See to it that you make it according to its pattern, which you saw on the mountain. And again: Thus you shall set up the dwelling according to the manner in which you saw it on the mountain.

Praise be to the Eternal, the First, in the house of study of the great, deceased, and noble rabbi, the preacher Rabbi Abraham ben Isaac, grandson of the honored Mordechai of the age. In this Psalm, it is supreme above all Psalms. The tribe "I will give thanks to the Lord with all my heart" corresponds to the tribe of David. The tribe "All good" that your eyes... from the heavens of the nations of the world. The tribe "All freewill" corresponds to the tribe that was occupied in the understanding of Torah.

A Psalm, a song for the Sabbath day.
On the Sabbath day they would say this Psalm in the Temple, and it has in it the essence of the Sabbath, as we shall explain. Our teachers erred, thinking it refers to the pillar (the human being), for it is all Sabbath and rest, and all the days of action. And furthermore, they said in the Midrash that Adam the First said this Psalm when the Sabbath arrived and he sinned and was corrupted, and on the Sabbath he was sanctified from Eden, and the Holy One, blessed be He, gave him ways that he would die, and when the Sabbath entered and removed him from the human (state), then he sang a song of praise for the Sabbath and said... and he said the Psalm. The Sabbath said: "Because you said," he said [in praise] (for it is good to give thanks to the Lord, for the human is good to give thanks) more than other days of the week, for the human is good from the depths of the world, its elevation and all the bodily aspects, and he is occupied in wisdom and in the service of God... that the Supreme Name shall find a place and rest... to tell in the day of rest, and there is no mercy... to tell the mercy that You did with us, that You gave us the order of the Sabbath for rest, and the faith that Your mercy is established for us at all times. And one of the mercies is that You made for us the Sabbath day. Behold, when we come to tell of Your mercy, we rest this... and the reason for "in the morning," for in all the days of the week a man rises in the morning for his work, and this morning is holy for rest and for the delight of the body and the soul, and this is the essence of mercy.

<margin>A Psalm, a song for the Sabbath day. This Psalm was said by Adam the First on the Sabbath when he saw the light in which he was created and saw the world perfected.</margin>

pages.7:
# VOYAGE
## Of the Reverend Father
## ANTONIO FERNANDEZ,
### T O
# GINGIRO;

->Conducted in Embassy with TECUR EGZY, sent by the Emperor of Ethiopia.<-

->In the Year 1613.<-

<note>Ornamental woodcut initial letter 'I' decorated with intricate foliate and scrollwork patterns.</note>

<margin>1613</margin>
**I**n the year 1607, a little after Sultan Segued was confirmed on the throne of the Empire of Ethiopia, Father Pays, encouraged by the favors that he received daily from that Ruler, and by the inclination that he saw in him to embrace the Catholic religion, wrote to Philip III, King of Spain, asking him to express some sentiment to this Ruler regarding the favors he was showing his subjects, and to encourage him through his letters to pursue our religion.

<margin>Emperor of the Abyssinians wants to send an embassy to Spain,</margin>
The Emperor received the answers that came from Spain with great joy. He was not satisfied with just answering them, but he also wanted to send an Envoy to the King of Spain
pages.8:
<header>VOYAGE OF</header>

<margin>1613</margin> with orders to travel through the Kingdom of Narea and from there to proceed to the coast of Melinde, and from there to Goa, to embark there on the Portuguese ships.

<margin>Chooses an Envoy, whom Father Antonio Fernandez accompanies.</margin> He made this intention known to the Jesuit Fathers, showing them the necessity of this embassy, the dangers they had to face, traveling through the lands that belonged to the Turk, and that they would not show mercy to his Ambassador if they had the slightest suspicion or scent of this mission and of the support of Portugal. He testified to them at the same time that he very much wished that one of the Jesuit Fathers accompany his Envoy, so that he might be better received in both India and Europe. The lot of this journey, for which all the Fathers offered themselves, fell to me. I had the luck to be well known to the Emperor for my prudence and zeal, which I had shown in all kinds of occurrences for his service. He chose Tecur Egzy (which is to say, Well-beloved of God) as head of the Embassy, being a person of esteem and great understanding, who had always shown a very great zeal for the Catholic faith. He foresaw, as well as I, the great difficulties of such a long journey, straight through the lands of Moors, Turks, Kaffers <note>infidels/heathens</note>, and other savage nations or country-people. Meanwhile, he did not fail to prepare everything that was in his power to make this journey succeed.

When I had received the letters of the Emperor, along with all the necessities for such a journey, I departed from Dambea in the beginning of March 1613, to go to Goiam to join the Ambassador, Tecur Egzy, who had gone there to settle his domestic affairs.
pages.9:
<header>ANTONIO FERNANDEZ.</header>

settle. I had 10 Portuguese with me, of whom 4 had offered to accompany me to India, and the 6 others to Narea. The Viceroy of Goiam, brother of the Emperor, who had recently become a Roman Catholic, received me with many expressions of friendship, allowing me to stay in his field camp until the Galles and the Xares, whom he had sent for to serve as guides to Narea, had arrived. This ruler showed many bounties to the guides, and promised them even more when they had brought us certain tidings that we had arrived with the Ambassador to Narea without misfortune. He took his leave of me with a speech that was full of zeal and wisdom to encourage me for this mission.

<margin>Departure of the Embassy.</margin> We departed from Ombrama, where the camp of the Viceroy was, on April 15, 1613, with 40 men as an escort, armed with assegais and shields. After 2 or 3 days of travel, moving West through the land of the Gongas, we arrived at Sinafse, which is one of the principal settlements of those regions. Here it was that we first began to recognize the difficulties of this expedition, for having requested a guide-party there to accompany us to the borders of Ethiopia, these people refused. We gave notice of this to the Viceroy through one of our Portuguese; he immediately sent 3 bands of soldiers there for our escort, and to punish the Gongas. But upon the knowledge that they received of the complaints the Ambassador had made to the Viceroy, they provided us with guides, with whom we arrived within 3 days at Mine, where one crosses the Nile, at the place of the bend that it makes there to run toward Egypt.
pages.10:
<header>VOYAGE OF</header>

<margin>1613</margin>
<margin>Difficult crossing of the Nile.</margin>
The same is at that place so large and running so fast that the Ambassador was forced to be ferried over on a raft that had been tied together poorly enough from pieces of wood, and supported by some hollowed-out pumpkins (calabashes), alongside men who swam before it to pull it forward, and others who pushed it from behind. We spent a whole day crossing the Nile back and forth like this.

The next day the Ambassador let the Viceroy know that we had passed the Nile, and requested that he call back his 3 bands of soldiers, as we had no more need of them. From there we traveled steadily Southward to Narea. On this road, which is about 50 miles long, we ran great danger of being shot at by the Galles and other savages (barbarians).

<margin>Danger near some Kaffers.</margin>
The following day we came into a land of the Kaffers, who pass for subjects of the Emperor of Ethiopia; nonetheless they came out of their huts like so many cruel beasts out of their dens and holes, weapons in hand, to plunder us and rob us of everything. In vain did one use the authority and the name of the Emperor; one had to defend oneself, which restrained them and made them come to a negotiation. They allowed the passage and received, in return for it, some caps and some pieces of salt in the shape of whole-loaves. A rainstorm, which arrived at a good time, contributed much to this, preventing them from being able to join with the inhabitants of a large village that was nearby. The Ambassador took his time, hurried away, and doubled his steps.
<margin>Defense.</margin>

That same day the guide, or pathfinder, whom we had hired to lead us through
pages.11:
<header>ANTONIO FERNANDEZ.</header>

<margin>1613</margin>
<margin>Miserable detours.</margin>
by-roads, so that we might not fall into the hands of the Kaffers, brought us through a very dense forest and to climb down a very steep rock, at the foot of which the river Maleg runs. We found ourselves at its banks in the evening; the next day we found no shallow place, or ford, which gave us reason for suspicion as if the Guide had the intention of playing a dirty trick on us, in the middle of a forest and wilderness through which we still had to go, and where he had once brought a great Lord of the land, whom he had also promised to guide but caused him to fall into the hands of his enemies. For these reasons I kept a very close watch on all his actions, without letting him notice anything regarding the suspicion I had of him.

<margin>Arriving at a ford.</margin>
The day after that we found a ford and entered the Kingdom of Narea, which begins from the banks of this stream. From here we traveled with more security, because we were now already very far from the Kaffers. First we climbed the mountain Ganca, or Gonca, which is very high, where one of the principal Captains of Narea has his residence. He received us with great expressions of friendship because the Viceroy of Goiam had recommended us to him highly, but even more because of the gifts that the Envoy and I presented to him on behalf of the same Viceroy.

<margin>And into the Kingdom of Narea.</margin>
The Kingdom of Narea is the most Southern of all the lands of the Empire of Ethiopia. One usually counts 200 miles from Masua to Narea, being a road that runs mostly always toward the South-West, that is to say until Minè, which belongs to the Empire of Goiam, where one must cross the Nile for the second time to go to Narea, and from there one goes straight toward the South.
pages.12:
<header>1613 6 VOYAGE OF</header>

<margin>Location of some places.</margin>
The middle of Dambea is at 13 and a half degrees North latitude, Mine at 12 degrees, and Narea lies at 8 degrees of the same latitude. The Kingdom of Narea is not as large as some make it, confusing it with the land of the Kaffers that surrounds it, and which extends to the coast of Melinde. It has the coast of Angola to the South-West and West, and just as the inhabitants of Narea trade with the Kaffers who lie on their borders, so they also have much gold that they buy from them, exchanging for it cloths, salt, and other goods.

<margin>Inhabitants of Narea are civilized people.</margin>
Narea does not have more than 30 or 40 miles of extent. Its inhabitants are the most civilized of all the peoples who are near Ethiopia; they do not resemble the Kaffers in the least, have a handsome figure, no thick lips, a pointed nose, nor are they very black. Besides that, they are people who keep their word, are no liars, nor hypocrites like the Amaras. Their land is very fertile in foodstuffs and in all kinds of cattle. They give gold by weight for what they buy, in place of minted money, just as is done throughout Ethiopia;

<margin>Have iron-money.</margin>
nonetheless they also have small iron plates, which are marked, 2 fingers wide, and 3 long, which are current as minted money.

<margin>And the faith of the Abyssinians.</margin>
These peoples were formerly heathens; but they received Baptism and the faith of the Abyssinians about 60 years ago, along with their errors.

<margin>Are also brave.</margin>
Not one of our Fathers has yet had the opportunity to go to Narea and to bring the Catholic faith there. They are brave, protect their land well, and notwithstanding that the Galles have made themselves masters of the greatest part of Christian Ethiopia, and that they constantly attack them, they have still not been able to win anything from them, and that without them ever having had any help or assistance from the Emperor.
pages.13:
<header>ANTONIO FERNANDEZ. 1613</header>

to whom they pay tribute, but with their own axes; for to come to them, his bands would necessarily have to march through the middle of the lands that are inhabited by the Galles, his enemies, besides that he has enough to do to pacify or suppress the continuous riots that arise in the kingdoms that are closer to his residence or strongholds.

From the Mountain Ganca, or Gonca, we marched toward the Court of the Benero, that is, Governor of Narea. After 6 days of travel we arrived there, the first days through a region that the Galles had entirely plundered only a few days before, and the others through a well-cultivated and populated land. <margin>The Ambassadors were received coldly by the Governor of Narea.</margin> The Governor received us coldly enough because, as I was told there, a certain schismatic monk who was with the Benero, and who was Vicarius, or deputy of the Abuna, or Patriarch of Ethiopia there, had spoken against me. This monk feared that I might have come to take away from him, with this office, a significant income that he drew from it. I went to visit him, and to take this suspicion out of his head, I asked him for his favor with the Benero to obtain a prompt dispatch. I added a gift to it, <margin>The reason why.</margin> which helped not a little to take out of his head his evil suspicion that he had conceived regarding the arrival of me and the Ambassador.

The Benero was not so easy to win over, because he saw deeper into the matter. He had great suspicion regarding the object of this embassy. He asked several questions of the Ambassador, and me, to get more scent and light from it, and although the hidden reason was known only to both of us, since it is very difficult to explain entirely to someone

pages.443:
The Indians continued their shouts and cries, calling the religious a thousand insults and liars; but they remained quiet in their little house, without leaving it or speaking a word to the Indians. As a good amount of time had passed and they saw that the Indians were not carrying out their intent, and it being now past midnight, they began to pray the Matins of the glorious Saint Michael, entrusting themselves to his patronage. They finished them, and heard no noise at all. They looked through the cracks of the house and discovered no Indians, nor any sign of what had preceded, at which they were amazed, without knowing the cause. God our Lord soon brought them out of this doubt, removing at once the anguish they were in, which seems a miraculous event.

They had given news to the Adelantado <note>governor</note> in Mérida that the Indians of Petu <note>Peto</note>, fourteen leagues further to the East from where this was happening, had rebelled and were denying obedience. To certify the truth and apply the convenient remedy, he dispatched some soldiers with a commander, who was then called a <term>caudillo</term> <gloss>leader/captain</gloss>. To have to pass to Petu, although they could have gone another way, God undoubtedly guided them to where the religious were, arriving when they were praying Matins surrounded by the Indians, who, as they heard the noise of horses and the voices of Spaniards, abandoned the siege and all fled, leaving the religious alone. The Spaniards came then in search of them, and as they heard the footsteps of horses and Castilian voices calling them by their names, they came out joyfully to welcome them for their arrival. They asked them where they were going, and they replied to Petu, for the remedy of the aforementioned uprising. The religious told them to calm down and rest without going further, and although they did not then reveal to them what had happened with the Indians, they warned them to have a sentinel and guard until dawn, and that afterwards they would see each other again, because it was important. The Spaniards said their goodbyes, and the two blessed fathers went to the church, where they sang the *Te Deum laudamus* <note>We praise Thee, O God</note> with great devotion, giving thanks to our Lord for having delivered them from a danger so close to death, with
pages.444:
a means that only His Divine Majesty seemed to have arranged for them, and from there they went to rest until the morning.

Dawn came, and as the sun rose, they signaled with the bell for Mass, as was their custom, and so that the Indians would gather for doctrine. The Spaniards came to hear Mass and to know what the religious had insinuated to them: but neither Indians nor boys appeared, because with the fear they had fled behind the Sierra, taking their little children with them: they only saw one boy who was as if lurking. Father Villalpando recognized that it was the one who had given him the afternoon before the news of the determination the Indians were in, and calling him, he came very happily and said to him: "Father, how are you alive? Now I say that your God is very great and powerful. My parents have gone to the mountain to protect themselves from these Spaniards, and in order to come to see you, I fled, to keep my word, for I am very happy to find you alive: here I want to stay with you." Father Villalpando was touched hearing such reasons from such a small child, and he took him into his arms, giving him his blessing, and truly, at such a young age, with the little capacity that we experience in them, it causes admiration the conversations and reasons he had with the religious, if it is not that we say that the grace of the Holy Spirit received in baptism was acting, what it seems that nature could not yet, or for the consolation of these religious, or for the confusion of the adults, or for the manifestation of His power. Father Villalpando then related to the Spaniards the whole event, and how that boy had given them news of it, for which they gave many thanks to God, as much for the fidelity of that creature as because he had brought them for the remedy of such grave harm, without having news of it.

The commander, certified of the case, then gave notice to the Adelantado of what was happening, and he stayed with the religious while the order of what he should do came to him, so that the Indians would not have some insolence. Once it was known in the city that the Indians of Petu had not had any disturbance, that they were quiet
pages.445:
and peaceful, and the great danger in which the religious had been at the hour the soldiers dispatched for Petu arrived there, caused notable admiration to the Adelantado and to all, for not having been able to find out who had sown the rumor in Mérida of the uprising of Petu: with which everyone understood it to have been a divine disposition to free the religious from that danger, who it was not understood needed any human favor.

The case gave much worry to the Adelantado and to all, lest this example be an occasion to incite the other Indians to whose notice it might reach, and thus he sent an order so that it might be known who the principal aggressors had been, and who had motivated such an iniquitous resolution, so that the commander, trying to catch them, would send them as prisoners to Mérida with collars and guards to punish their sacrilegious crime. The lord of Maní (who Father Lizana says was called Ah Kukum Xiu, from which it seems Tutul Xiu, who made peace with the Spaniards, had already died) had not been present or consented to it, and upon knowing what happened, he came to see the fathers. He clearly manifested his good intention and the sorrow he had for the event, because when the commander told him the order that the Adelantado had given, and that he should thus seek the delinquents for him, because if he did not do so he would take him prisoner, the good <term>cacique</term> <gloss>chief</gloss> already had twenty-seven of the most guilty Indians caught, and he delivered them all to him. The commander did not trust any person other than himself to take them into the presence of the Adelantado, and for fear that by taking those principals as prisoners there might be a new disturbance, he named another commander, who, remaining there with more soldiers, would take care of it, and he with some departed with the prisoners for the city of Mérida.

Seeing that those miserable Indians were going where they would receive the punishment deserved for their crime, the holy Father Villalpando, as he loved them in Christ and was desirous of their well-being, decided to go in their company, in case his presence could mitigate the rigor of justice. Father Benavente remaining, he went with them to the city of Mérida, where as soon as they arrived, they were
pages.446:
put in the public jail, and the Adelantado was very pleased seeing the blessed father. Legal proceedings were carried out against the Indians, who, convinced and confessing their crime, were sentenced to be burned. Their spiritual father felt it deeply, and with fervent charity another milder and, in his opinion, effective means occurred to him to provoke the Indians to amendment and to ensure the future. He dealt with the Adelantado that, in order to achieve it, the accused be put to the ultimate terror in sight of such a horrible punishment; and that when they understood the punishment was about to be executed upon them, he would ask for their pardon in their sight, and that he should delay granting it, so that it would appear he was doing so obliged by his pleas, and that he should afterwards give the pardon, with which he understood more would be gained than by punishing them. The Adelantado, who by nature was not cruel and had great veneration for Father Villalpando, assented to his advice and arranged for it to be executed as he ordered.

The time arrived in which the punishment was to be carried out; a great fire was made, and they brought the Indians into the presence of the Adelantado, who was attending there. A great crowd of Indians gathered to see the execution of a punishment so little experienced among them, and the Adelantado ordered that they throw the delinquents alive into the fire, since they had wanted to burn the religious alive. The venerable Father Villalpando then knelt before the Adelantado, making many supplications for them. The Adelantado showed anger that he was hindering the punishment, and with greater insistence, he asked that he grant them life, alleging for them that they were repentant and would amend the past. He persevered in this pious action until the Adelantado felt himself obliged by it and ordered that the punishment cease, so that, tied as they were, they should be delivered to him so he could do with them according to his will. He gave many thanks to the Adelantado for the favor he was doing him in yielding to his pleas, and for the favor to the delinquents in pardoning them. He received them as his own, and untying them, he took them with him to the convent, where instead of some grave punishment they expected, placed in the hand of the very person they had wanted to give such
pages.447:
an atrocious death (ignoring to what extent Christian charity extends), they found in their spiritual father caresses and kindness.

### CHAPTER IX.

*More religious come from Mexico and Spain, and the first custodial chapter of this province is celebrated.*

A great effect resulted from the charitable love with which Father Villalpando dealt with his children, whom he was regenerating in the Lord, because returning to Maní with them, they gave much credit to what he said to them. He soon left the city of Mérida for the towns of the Sierra, it seeming to him that the time he took to arrive could be an occasion for the Indians to cool in the new spirit of Christians they had begun to conceive. As everyone already knew what had happened, when they arrived in Maní they were received with great joy and rejoicing, because they did not expect to see any of them again, considering the gravity of their crime. The delinquents proclaimed how Father Villalpando, instead of asking for justice against them, had freed them from punishment, interceding for their lives with mercy. As that mode of retribution was so little used in their infidelity—that the aggrieved party should ask for it for the delinquent—it caused supreme admiration in the Indians, resolving that it was not possible that he who did such things was not good, nor could he fail to love them very much. With this, they formed a great concept of the venerable father, giving credit to what he told them. They held for him singular respect and obedience in what he commanded them, which was then executed without reply or delay of any kind. In whatever distress they found themselves, they had recourse to him as to the remedy for their ills, and with most pious bowels he received and comforted them. So much can virtue do even in the sight of gentile minds.

Tamed by the sweet force of charity, the minds of the Indians, and persuaded that those who had slaves should give them freedom, they were going about executing it, with which Father Villalpando already found more
pages.448:
disposition to give them holy baptism, which it seemed they desired with true affection. In a few days the number of the baptized was great, and among them the Lord of Maní, who was named Don Francisco Xiu in contemplation of the Adelantado, and all that region was very calm, gladly attending to the teaching of Christian doctrine. At this time, Father Lizana says, it seemed to the Lord of Maní, Don Francisco Xiu, that the seat of Maní was more suitable for founding the convent, for being more in the middle of the region and having more stone and materials for the building than in that of Oxkutzcab; and that thus it would be well for the religious to move there, as was done. I have already said what I feel in regard to this. What is certain is that in the town of Maní a site was marked out for a church and convent, which is where it is now founded, although everything at that time was done in the manner of the houses of the Indians.

The news that Father Villalpando had given by his letters (which it remains said he wrote from Campeche, as soon as he arrived, saying the great number of souls that were in this new conversion, and how help of ministers was necessary for it) caused the very reverend Father Commissary General Fray Francisco de Bustamante to send another six religious to this land, who arrived in it by the end of the year forty-eight. Coming as commissary and prelate was Father Fray Juan de la Puerta, a son of the holy province of Castilla: neither did Father Lizana report the names of the others, nor have I found it written to assign them. The arrival of these religious found Father Villalpando occupied in the administration of Maní and its regions. It caused great consolation to him and his companion, Father Benavente, whom he left in Maní, and he departed for Campeche on foot and barefoot, as he went out to receive them. As they were not coming to be idle, they had already left Campeche, and thus he found them on the road. They rejoiced greatly seeing the apostolic man, and all together they walked to the city of Mérida to see the Adelantado, and from there to distribute themselves according to what the present need demanded. Before they arrived,
pages.449:
the devotion of the Adelantado had foreseen knowing what day they were to enter, and thus he went out personally to receive them on the road with a very brilliant accompaniment of the most noble conquerors, in whose company the religious entered Mérida, with most of the Spaniards and many Indians concurring, who with their joy and rejoicing manifested the happiness they had to see them.

The religious went straight to their convent, and entering the poor and small church they had then, they prayed, giving thanks to God for the fulfillment of their journey. For not having the capacity to lodge them there, the Adelantado took them with him, providing them with lodging in his house, where he had them for some days, treating them well. The blessed Father Villalpando went with all speed to Maní to see his new children, whose memory was always impressed on his soul, wherever he resided, and the newly arrived remained in the house of the Adelantado. Considering that their lodging had to be for some time, although they were in a secular house, they chose a room where, having placed an altar, it might serve them as a choir. There they gathered for their religious exercises and to pray the divine office at its hours, as they could in the most reclusive convent; with which, satisfying their obligations, great edification of the secular state resulted, and an increase of the devotion that the Adelantado and the other conquerors had for our holy habit. The consolation of all increased that the following year, by the month of August, Father Fray Juan de Albalate arrived, who had gone to Spain with six other religious, whom the Royal Council of the Indies had given him for the administration of these natives, and thus this was the first mission that came from Spain directly assigned to this province. The religious who came in it were the fathers Fray Alonso de Alvarado of the holy province of Santiago, Fray Diego de Landa, Fray Francisco Navarro, Fray Antonio de Valdemoro, Fray Antonio de Figueras, and Fray Pedro de Noriega, all five of that of Castilla, and of whom it is treated later, although not as it should be for lack of writings that distinguish for us their apostolic
pages.450:
lives and heroic labors. With this increase of religious, it was decided to celebrate a custodial chapter, which, because it was the first, I will particularize, as Father Lizana writes it and as it happened in truth. Father Lizana says: "that Father Fray Juan de la Puerta, commissary of the religious who came from Mexico, brought an order to celebrate a custodial chapter with the friars who might be in the land, and to elect a custodian and definitors, so that the election that had been made of the custody might move forward, and that, having convoked the friars from Campeche and Maní at the beginning of the year 49 for the Easter of the Holy Spirit, they celebrated their chapter in the city of Mérida, and the venerable man Fray Luis de Villalpando was elected custodian, who until then had been no more than commissary; definitors were the blessed Father Fray Lorenzo de Bienvenida, who entered through Bakhalál, and Father Fray Miguel de Vera, whom they called the patched one, and their elections confirmed, Father Bienvenida, first definitor, was elected guardian of the convent of our Father Saint Francis of Mérida, and Father Vera, second definitor, of Campeche, and Father Pesquera of the recently arrived, with Father Fray Juan de Herrera and Father Fray Angel Maldonado, were named for the doctrines of Maní and its region, and the rest of the friars were distributed in Mérida and Campeche; all of which already concluded, Father Fray Juan de la Puerta was named by consent of all the friars as procurator to the court of the Emperor, and that he should bring friars to this province." I do not know how he allowed himself to be carried away by reports or conversations he might have heard; for as it has been done now for these writings, by resorting to the archive of the province for the capitular table that today remains, it would have told him with certainty what happened, which was in this form.

The very Reverend Father Commissary General came personally to visit the religious and see the progress there was in the new conversion of the Indians, and having done the first and experienced the second, having also already arrived the mission from Spain that has been mentioned, he celebrated the first custodial chapter on the twenty-ninth of September of fifteen hundred

The evening is the gathering of the assembly, regarding which it is said: we have seen many souls, as it is written regarding the souls, that they saw such and such, and Moses took upon himself the evening, for they were gathered from one, and each of you shall come to me and show what they have acquired and what they have divided before Moses, and they shall stand before him. What is this? This is the <term>ma'an</term> <gloss>manna</gloss>, the work of which is such that one <term>shamarq</term> <gloss>measure</gloss> is found that is sold to that servant and to every single soul from his house. It is that which is found, the <term>shamarq</term> <gloss>measure</gloss> which is for the servant like that vessel, and it is called <term>omer</term> <gloss>measure of grain</gloss>. And every soul from his house saw the servant as it is, for the <term>ma'an</term> <gloss>manna</gloss> was living, and if he accepted it, he acquired it, and it is written: "An omer for each head, according to the number of your souls" <note>Exodus 16:16</note>. **All of this corresponds** to what is written: "At evening, you shall know that the Lord has brought you out from the land of Egypt" <note>Exodus 16:6</note>, and it is written: "And in the morning, you shall see the glory of the Lord" <note>Exodus 16:7</note>. "At evening, you shall know"—how much you shall know, these things, you shall see them every day, they are found as a burden received to stir up kindness <term>Chesed</term> <gloss>Loving-kindness</gloss> in the world. And at that time, when it is evening, this hangs in the world. And we have established that at such a time, the prayer of the Afternoon <term>Minchah</term> <gloss>Afternoon prayer</gloss> was established. Why is this mentioned? "At evening, you shall know that the Lord," etc. When this is stirred up in the world, you shall know that at that time, the kindness of the Lord is with you, to save you from pain. "And in the morning, you shall see the glory of the Lord," for at that time kindness is stirred up in the world, and He gives you to eat **all that exists**. What is written above? They are found upon the mountain of the Creator. At that time, it is said: "evening," for at that time kindness is stirred up in the world, as it is said: "You shall know that the Lord brought you out from the land of Egypt." You shall know that it is the kindness that He did with you in your exodus from Egypt. "And in the morning, you shall see the glory of the Lord"—the glory of the Lord, truly. Why the soul? The Lord is your souls, the Lord of all days upon the mouth of the Creator, the burdens when you live, the life of the world, they rely upon them and turn the mercies to this, as it is said: **"Blow"** <note>Reference to the shofar or divine call</note> concerning that which is established by the vessel and the water which is established to eat in the world to come, and the life of the world is called rivers, and He gathered until there was found in it one part, one for the day and one for the King's needs in the holiness of the day before. And that night is the union of the <term>Matronita</term> <gloss>the Queen/Shekhinah</gloss> with the King, and every two days they are blessed, all so, and one alone in the human soul. # And the Lord said to Moses
Pass on before the people, and take with you some of the elders of Israel, and your staff, with which you struck the river, take in your hand, and go. Behold, I will stand before you there upon the rock at Horeb, and you shall strike the rock, and water shall come out of it, and the people shall drink. And Moses did so before the eyes of the elders of Israel. And he called the name of the place Massah and Meribah, because of the quarrel of the children of Israel and because they tested the Lord, saying: "Is the Lord among us or not?" Then came Amalek and fought with Israel in Rephidim. And Moses said to Joshua: "Choose for us men, and go out, fight with Amalek; tomorrow I will stand on the top of the hill with the staff of God in my hand." And Joshua did as Moses said to him, to fight with Amalek; and Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill. And it was when Moses lifted up his hand, Israel prevailed; and when he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed. But Moses' hands were heavy; and they took a stone, and put it under him, and he sat on it; and Aaron and Hur supported his hands, one on one side, and one on the other; and his hands were steady until the going down of the sun. And Joshua defeated Amalek and his people with the edge of the sword. And the Lord said to Moses: "Write this for a memorial in the book, and rehearse it in the ears of Joshua, that I will utterly blot out the memory of Amalek from under heaven." And Moses built an altar, and called the name of it Adonai-Nissi <note>The Lord is my banner</note>. And he said: "For the hand is upon the throne of the Lord; the Lord will have war with Amalek from generation to generation." <note>Exodus 17:5-16</note>

<margin></margin>
Rabbi Hiyya began: "The angel of the Lord camps around those who fear Him, and delivers them" <note>Psalm 34:8</note>. Blessed are the righteous, for the Holy One, blessed be He, desires them more than all else. Come and see how guilty the people of the world are, who go and transgress; above, justice and kindness support them everywhere. For it is taught: regarding Isaac, the Holy One, blessed be He, did not demand from him—once he thought of Him—the Holy One. What is written? "Then came Amalek, etc." <note>Exodus 17:8</note>. I know the serpent <term>nachash</term> <gloss>serpent</gloss>, he knows that he is split, and he praises him and makes offerings to him, and the Holy One did not demand from him. As they say, the serpent cuts, upon it he thought. I know his hand and the receipt. What is written? "And it became heavy, and he could not" <note>Reference to Moses' hands</note>. And for this, the Holy One did not demand from him, even though he was filthy with the throne of which it is written, the prince and the fool. He shook the hand of the Lord, and so in every place. And the Holy One demands the insult of the righteous more than all else. Here, Moses is a prince, Moses, and the voice rises to meet Him. He is aroused to demand your insult, and not so—even "pass on before the people and the elders." Who is it that will go to meet him? Is it by his own authority that he is sustained? No, by His authority. "And your staff, with which you struck the river"—staff, because it was refined through miracles, and it supports the power, sending to the water with it first. It is as it is said: "The way of a serpent upon a rock" <note>Proverbs 30:19</note>. It is for the gate; until then, the gate, take and go. Here, where it is written: "Behold I will stand before you there upon the rock at Horeb, and you shall strike the rock, etc." <note>Exodus 17:6</note>. Rock, just as you say: "The Rock, His work is perfect" <note>Deuteronomy 32:4</note>. And we have learned: Moses knew how the serpent stands upon a rock and took the wisdom from it. Rabbi Yehuda: To be silent is to take the horn; even so it is written: "And you shall strike the rock for your salvation, and from the right and from the drink of the cup..." It is certainly so, for there is no name among those holy names of the Holy One, blessed be He, that does not perform miracles and mighty deeds, and He covers all, for He is the Prince of the worlds, like that which comes out here from the water. Rabbi: So it is here, it is written: "The Rock, the Rock and brings forth water." From the source of the name, the voice steps, covering in his presence, and cuts the blackness. Even though this is in every place, Rock and Rock, and so the Holy One does not erase, for He does not erase the structure, and it is this that is written: "Behold He struck the rock, and the waters flowed." And it is not that He erases, He strikes the rock, and the Holy One is within it, as it is said: "He does not dry up..." The voice is thus written: "The Rock, your begetter, you forgot." And we have learned: "Strike the begetter," the shell of God, the voice is certainly so, for the children of the world to come know the Rock, and from it they are aroused before Him, and to erase them, the King will pass before Him. Even the weak, as the afflicted see, and not looking at it, and we look at their portion, and until the Rock that begot you. Rabbi Isaac: There is a Rock and there is a Rock. From the side of the male, the name brings out the Rock of Kindness, and it strikes the Rock of this world, which is all silence, and it strikes the hand of the One who is the offspring of Israel, as it is written: "The Rock, your begetter," for the Rock sends to the world, the Rock of Kindness emerges. From the side of the left, the Strength emerges, and this portion is as it is said: "Who can tell the mighty acts of the Lord? Who can tell His mighty acts?"

That which they saw in the Shekhinah that stands yet in the sanctuary, and for this, "the God of," and "under His feet, like the work of a brick of sapphire," that below it is the image of the memory of the brick, striking them, who were kneading in the mud, and now, today, it is born in its fullness, and they were living the scrolls of Pharaoh and making for him bricks of bricks, and now, sapphire, and it shines to it, and to the darkness under the feet of the Shekhinah, as it is written: "And upon the likeness of His feet, as a living soul." Rabbi Hiyya said: "The brick of sapphire," the light of the sapphire is like the light of the sun, that burn to every side, receive its foundations like sapphire, and in this heaven, the world is full, the heavens, the heart of white. What is the world of the heavens (to the end of seventy)? And those seventy princes are faithful, and every side, here is their life, the world of the heavens, the world of the heavens. Rabbi Yehuda said: All of them are dark in that light that is before, that burn, surrounding the Shekhinah, one truth, the explanation of the Creator, and they are the ones that surround the Shekhinah, as it is written: "The heavens, the clarity, around it." All this was, and also them, and the light that lacks borders, to the world, from the river of the worlds, that there, it lacks borders (to the end), they are sent as the scale, it rises as the light, as the great and strong appearance, and all of them are light in their dwellings, when it is broken in the desert. And this is the world of the heavens, the world of the heavens, truly, and all those light, seventy of them, the light of their dwellings, and nine, the light of them, that they are sent, that surround the signs in it, like that prince and the congregation, that the soles that surround below them, surround the Shekhinah. They burn in this congregation, "around, the clarity around it." **"And Moses built an altar"** as you saw, and called its name: The Lord is my banner, and explained, Moses, upon all those who were in it, and he was not separated, and He kept for us and ordered for us the understanding, and he saw upon that which was done in that time. What is written? "For the hand is upon the throne of the Lord; the Lord will have war with Amalek from generation to generation" <note>Exodus 17:16</note>. And they are, they are alive (to the worlds), you have no, there is not in them from that seed, cut, and the Holy One, blessed be He, there is no in them standing. Rabbi Isaac said: regarding this, "The sinners will be consumed from the earth, and from the," and from the, receive in it, the time, thus, "we shall blot out the memory of Amalek," Amen.

<summary>This page concludes the mystical reflection on the covenantal sign of the sapphire brick and the heavens, and reiterates the promise of the eventual destruction of Amalek as a manifestation of divine justice.</summary>
