pages.15:
<header>of the Baron von Trenck.</header>
<sig>A 4</sig>

should, that I should make room for him. He also shoved me back with such impetuosity that I, in anger, grabbed my torch with both hands and smashed it to pieces on his head in the church, whereupon I had to avoid both my order and the school and study at home. In this manner we traveled to the command that my father had received, which is the <term>border fortress</term> of Brod on the Sava River; but I and my brothers were sent to Possega <term>ad studia</term> <gloss>for studies</gloss> with the Jesuits, though against my desire, from where we always came home for the <term>vacancies</term> <gloss>vacations</gloss>.

Anno 1725 I had to endure the following danger to my life again: My father was visited by a certain engineer colonel, Count C*** and his family, as a neighbor; and since there was a pretty young girl in his retinue, with whom my eldest brother fell in love, we all three decided to escort her back, which also happened. But as we were driving back the next day from Diacovar, where we stayed overnight, it happened that the first wheel struck a log and we all fell out of the carriage. My eldest brother, however, who was steering the horses in place of the coachman, fell under the horses and was broken on the wheel in such a way that
pages.16:
<header>Life and Deeds</header>

<note>Small ornamental flourishes flank the word "und" in the header.</note>

he died two hours later on the way in the forest, after he had given the final sign of life and farewell to my father, who had received news of it and arrived at this misfortune just in time, with open eyes, but spoke no more words, and passed away immediately thereafter.

My grandmother, who was a Countess von Witt and loved us all tenderly, was so frightened and saddened by this fatal case that she also died of it 6 weeks later. My mother also had to succumb to a similar fate shortly thereafter, namely in the year 1726. Of all these deaths, none saddened me more than that of my dear brother, whom I also, for lack of a clergyman, prepared quite well for death, with the exception of confession and communion. My old father, however, was inconsolable over three such sensitive losses, as indeed he never proceeded to <term>vota secunda</term> <gloss>second marriage vows</gloss>. Meanwhile, he still kept both us brothers at our studies, though not away from home; which was once again the cause that I had to escape a danger to my life. For once, on the Sava River, which flowed right past our house, in wintertime, when the marshes were frozen and the ice was floating on the river with a multitude of ducks, I took a small boat,
pages.17:
<header>of the Baron von Trenck.</header>
<sig>A 5</sig>

with which I could travel perfectly, and drove with my shotgun through the ice, which I avoided quite skillfully, at the ducks, and shot three of them dead and one’s wing off. As I then chased the wounded duck, and forgot the danger in which I was, an ice floe shoved me with such force onto another like it, that I sat quite by accident on the other floes and saw my little boat shattered into pieces and drifting away. Who would have thought that I would escape this time too? My father and brother, together with good friends, threw their hands over their heads and called out to me that I should commend myself to God, which I also did. I floated in this way soon half a mile downstream, and the ice floe, because there was a narrow place there, wedged itself; and since it was not possible due to the amount of ice to come to my aid with a ship, over 300 people ran to help my <term>spectaculum</term> <gloss>spectacle</gloss>. The ice floe had hardly stopped when a Pandur <note>A member of the irregular infantry serving under Baron von Trenck.</note> with a rope in his hand, out of love for me, dared to reach me and safely led me out of my danger. I remained unpunished by my father here as well.

A few weeks after this experienced danger, I was in a boat with my
pages.18:
<header>Life and Deeds</header>

brother on a duck hunt, and as the boatman steered us both close to the ducks, and my brother, who was kneeling in the boat before me, did not want to shoot but wanted to be even closer, I took the shotgun and shot behind him; I hit the ducks, but at the same time I shot the garment from my brother from the right side down to the skin, and two lead pellets into his arm. If I had held a finger lower, I would have shot his arm completely away. Hereupon I received severe beatings from my father, and my brother, when the new battalions were raised, became an ensign under Wallis.

Shortly thereafter, namely on the 10th of July, 1727, the now deceased Hungarian <term>Palatinus</term> <gloss>Palatine</gloss>, Count Nicolaus Palfi, took me into his regiment as an ensign. From this time on my luck began to contend with misfortune, and misfortune with luck, <term>vice versa</term> <gloss>conversely</gloss>. The first misfortune was that, when my father sent me to Esseg to equip myself there, I became so deathly ill with a fever that my father, through the provision administrator still in Esseg at the time, our secretary at the time, Herr von Hess, sent the money <term>pro funeribus</term> <gloss>for the funeral</gloss>, and the hussars to accompany my body, to Diacovar, where I lay sick; but I was, through the help of good medicine,
pages.19:
<header>of the Baron von Trenck.</header>

soon cured, and thus had to travel to Belgrade to my regiment. I was barely 4 months in Belgrade when I already had a <term>rencontre</term> <gloss>encounter/duel</gloss> with an ensign of the regiment, who at first made me retreat; but finally, with a blow over the nose and skull, then four blows to the hand, he had to settle down. I also received three blows to the hand, and the hilt of my Parisian sword was hacked down by this strong man, although I was, so to speak, a child, so that it remained lying on my wounded hand. The same year I again had an affair with a Silesian volunteer named Gersdorff, whom I wounded through the hand.

Anno 1728 I had an affair with a certain Count Paradiso, from whom I had won 380 florins, and he did not want to pay me, over which I insulted him, and he struck at me with his hand, though he only touched my head by the tip of the hair. I drew my sword, but he jumped out of the coffee house, in which there were about 30 officers, and as I made my way through the officers with my sword in hand and wanted to go out the door, he lunged at me outside the door; I, however, wanted to parry him with my left arm and received a thrust through it; but this did not stop me from attacking him, and
pages.20:
<header>Life and Deeds</header>

and he, or I, would certainly have reached the <term>extremum</term> <gloss>end/fatal conclusion</gloss> had not about 6 officers thrown themselves upon me and hindered the affair in such a way. I later defamed him again, and could never learn where he went, for I have not been paid by him to this day. Perhaps, when this comes before his eyes, he will announce himself. I had two more small skirmishes in this year, which however ended without injury, consequently I will not make further mention of them.

Anno 1729, however, I again had an affair with the Auditor of the Prince Alexander of Württemberg’s regiment then stationed in Belgrade, by the name of Beyer, whom I finished off with two thrusts into his right side, for which he had to have himself cured for 6 weeks. It then happened that my battalion, in which I served, had to march to Esseg, and we arrived there in the month of October of this year. Here I must recall that I have hitherto traveled with my father through all of Sicily, the Neapolitan, Apulian, Roman, Venetian, Triestine, Carniolan, Styrian, Licanian, Croatian, Slavonian, Serbian, Austrian, Sirmian, Hungarian, and a part of Bosnia.
pages.21:
<header>of the Baron von Trenck.</header>

I had barely arrived in Esseg when I again, although I had never given any cause for it, got into an affair with my own cousin, named Tillier, with whom I fought twice, and wounded him both times.

Anno 1730, however, I fought again with Baron F***, whom I also wounded through the arm, and although I had liked to see beautiful girls since the year 1727, I was still not skilled enough for intrigues, but rather I satisfied my desire with everything young that came before my eyes, without giving myself any trouble. In this year, however, I fell in love with a certain young lady of good lineage, but since the father and mother, in whose house she was, kept a very good watch on her, I had to content myself initially only with the pleasure that I walked past her window at night and, this was the signal, cleared my throat sharply, whereupon she immediately came running to the window and spoke a few words with me to comfort us both. This <term>rendezvous</term> <gloss>meeting</gloss> I frequented very diligently and constantly; in such a way that I had wished that it were always night, in order to be able to talk with my beautiful young lady, until I finally brought it so far that she found the opportunity to let me into her bedroom. What could be more foolish than the two of us
pages.22:
<header>Life and Deeds</header>

lovers to see? I could not speak anymore for love, but only kissed her hands constantly and pressed her to me: she, however, as a young lady of 14 years at that time, smiled. I was also not bold enough to involve myself further in love, and thus left my young lady. As great as the love of this person for me was, so great also became the <term>esteem</term> <gloss>respect</gloss> she held for me, as I gave her no cause to commit an excess. I was thus loved by her in such a way that I could always, and whenever I wanted, come to my beauty at night. I chatted so much of love with her at every rendezvous, and held her beauty and coldness up to her, that she said to me at the seventh rendezvous, quite enraptured: (of which I will also remember my life long,) "Baron Trenck! I am no longer in a position to resist your love, do with me what you want, yet save my honor." Hereupon she fell into my arms quite enraptured and with tear-filled eyes; I kissed her, and she me again, with which we were satisfied, whereas certainly another more indiscreet lover than I, who had the motto <term>le respect arrête mes désirs</term> <gloss>respect stops my desires</gloss> always firmly imprinted, would not have let it rest there. I believed now that I would once be happy

pages.14:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
<margin>1613</margin>
to hide a matter, of which he already has doubts; so he immediately grasped that this journey was intended to help the <term>Portugysen</term> <gloss>Portuguese</gloss> enter his kingdom from <term>Indien</term> <gloss>India</gloss>, that they would make themselves masters of it, and force him to embrace the <term>Catholijke Religie</term> <gloss>Catholic Religion</gloss>. Hereupon he summoned the Great Lords of his Court and shared his thoughts with them very secretly. They all agreed that they must not allow the Ambassador and me to travel the path we had in mind, as it was the direct one, and that we must be made to take another and very inconvenient path, through many detours and the land of <term>Baly</term>.

<margin>Forced to take an inconvenient detour.</margin>
After much discussion back and forth, he finally said to us in conclusion that he would never let us pass along the road we intended, but rather through <term>Baly</term>, to which one had to submit, for we were determined to continue this enterprise.

<margin>The Kingdom of Baly.</margin>
<term>Baly</term> is a kingdom that formerly belonged to the <term>Keyserrijk van Ethiopiën</term> <gloss>Empire of Ethiopia</gloss>, but the <term>Galles</term> and <term>Mahometanen</term> <gloss>Muslims</gloss> possess it at present. It borders the <term>Rijk van Adel</term> <gloss>Kingdom of Adel</gloss> and lies to the east of the <term>Rijk van Narea</term> <gloss>Kingdom of Narea</gloss>. From this I could easily infer that I could not complete this journey, and that after I had encountered all these difficulties in the lands of the <term>Keyser</term> <gloss>Emperor</gloss>, I had even greater ones to expect in the lands of the <term>Kaffers</term> <gloss>infidels/non-believers</gloss>, who have no other law than their own profit. Nevertheless, considering that it was for the service of <term>God</term>, I took the road to <term>Baly</term>, trusting myself to His mercy.

<margin>Setting off.</margin>
The Ambassador and I, leaving the court of <term>Narea</term>, took our way eastward and arrived on the first day at the place where the <term>Kapiteyn</term> <gloss>Captain</gloss> was, whom the <term>Benero</term> had appointed as our guide. In the beginning, he received us quite well, hoping to get a fine gift from us, but that which we bestowed upon him,
pages.15:
<margin>1613</margin>
not matching his hope and expectation, he made us wait 8 days for him, after which he gave us 80 men to accompany us to the borders of the Kingdom of Narea. We went with this escort
<margin>Arriving in a desolate land.</margin>
4 long days' journey through a desolate and abandoned land, due to the incursions of the <term>Galles</term>. Our escort then turned back, and as the road we still had to travel was very dangerous, we let some scouts go ahead of us to give us a signal as soon as they caught sight of <term>Galles</term> from afar, so that we might have time to go and hide ourselves in the woods.

At midday we began to climb down a very high and rugged mountain, and the Envoy from <term>Gingiro</term> told us that before we proceeded to climb down, we must hide until evening so that by night we could pass through the fields where the <term>Galles</term> grazed their cattle.

<margin>Very bad road, coping very poorly.</margin>
At 4 o'clock in the afternoon we set off under the cover of a dense rain squall, which drove the <term>Galles</term> to their huts but also soaked us weary travelers and made us suffer much cold. Our worry and anxiety doubled when night came, because the thicket through which we passed was very dense near the ground, difficult to get through by day and even worse by night. We lit a fire in the woods and chewed a little roasted barley, which is the common food of the travelers of that land, and very early the next day, after we had climbed down a steep mountain, we arrived at the River <term>Zebée</term>.

<margin>Crossing a very dangerous bridge.</margin>
This stream runs faster than the <term>Nijl</term> <gloss>Nile</gloss>, and at the place where we had to cross it, it made a terrifying noise, falling from a mountain between very sharp cliffs, between which the water was crushed into foam
pages.16:
<margin>1613</margin>
The bridge over which we were forced to pass such fast and dangerous currents was made of a piece of wood. It went across the river, notwithstanding that it was remarkably wide, and the height of this bridge was so great that when one looked down from it, one discovered nothing but an abyss. The great length of the piece of wood made it tremble under the feet of our people, and yet everyone wanted to cross it first; for as soon as one is on the other side of this river, one has no more to fear from the <term>Galles</term>, for whom the fear was so great that it extinguished all other fears. We thanked <term>God</term> on the other side of the bridge that He had delivered us from the bloodthirsty hands of the <term>Galles</term>. We could not let our mules go across this bridge; therefore we left them there that night on the bank of the river with 2 men to guard them, with orders to cross the bridge if the <term>Galles</term> came and to break it down behind them. But the next day, 2 inhabitants of the land showed them a ford where they managed to get them across with great difficulty.

<margin>Granted an audience by the King of Gingiro.</margin>
Shortly after this, the Ambassador arrived at a dwelling from which we announced our arrival to the King of <term>Gingiro</term> and asked him for permission to present the letters that we had to deliver to him on behalf of the <term>Keyser van Ethiopiën</term> <gloss>Emperor of Ethiopia</gloss>. But this King, being besides very given to his sorcery, made us wait there for 8 days, at the end of which we received permission to come to his court, where we arrived in one day. We found this monarch ready to receive us, seated or rather enclosed in a cage; for it was a type of cage or crate about 25 hand-breadths high and 30 wide; it was round on top, having
pages.17:
<margin>1613</margin>
the shape of a wheel. The King sat on a carpet that was spread out on this wheel. All his courtiers stood upright below this throne, where he granted the audience. He was dressed in a very fine cloth, the whiteness of which made the blackness of his face stand out even more, in which one did not otherwise see those features that one notices in the <term>Kaffers</term>. He immediately asked for the letter from the <term>Keyser</term>. He climbed down from his throne to come and get it, asked how he was faring, and climbed back onto his throne, <margin>Who reads the letter from the Keyser.</margin> after which he read the letter and spoke for some time with us through an interpreter, to whom, whenever the <term>Keyser</term> or the King said something for us to hear, the interpreter would kiss the tips of his fingers, and after he had bowed down to the earth, he would go to interpret it to me, who was at some distance from the throne. And when he was to bring the answer from me back to the King, he first used the same formality. The conversation lasted a long time. Finally, the King let it be said to me and the Envoy that we should go and rest, and that the essence of the <term>Keyser</term>'s letter consisted of this: that he would gladly entertain us and have us accompanied by a good guard to the borders of his kingdom, which he said he would very gladly do.

The next day I presented some gifts to the King. He showed much pleasure in them, as they were a rare thing in that land. When I was ready to depart from there, the King sent me, in consideration of my gift, a young daughter of one of the Great Lords of his kingdom to serve me as a slave. I excused myself from receiving her, saying that I was by no means accustomed to taking women with me. The King took satisfaction in the difficulty I raised and sent
pages.18:
<margin>1613</margin>
<margin>And a beautiful mule.</margin>
me a slave, whom I also accepted, not with the thought of drawing any service from him, but rather in the hope of baptizing him. He also gave me a beautiful mule, which came in very handy for me on the journey, as well as people to help us cross the flood **Zebée** again and from there to travel to the Kingdom of **Cambate**.

<margin>Strange type of ferrymen.</margin>
For that purpose, we departed from the court of the King of **Gingiro** and arrived that same day at the bank of the river **Zebée** to cross it. The people whom the King had given us, being very skilled in this type of crossing, made a contrivance (machine) that was not much safer than the piece of wood. They slaughtered a cow and put the baggage into the hide, which would serve 2 purposes: one to get across, the other to serve as ballast for the "ship" that they made from the hide of this cow, sewing it shut tightly. Then they blew it up stiff and attached 2 pieces of wood or sticks to it, like those of a litter. 4 people went to sit on these sticks, 2 in front and 2 behind this raft-work. One forbade them to move, and they arranged themselves by equal weight so that they kept this strange vessel in an equal balance. In front of it swam a brave swimmer, who was very experienced in this art, who had a rope around his waist that was also attached to the apparatus, with which he pulled it forward. 2 other swimmers pushed it from behind as well. A whole day was spent on this crossing.

<margin>River Zebée.</margin>
<margin>The Kingdom of Gingiro described.</margin>
The stream **Zebée** surrounds almost entirely the Kingdom of **Gingiro** and makes it like a peninsula, as one sees on the map of **Ethiopiën** <gloss>Ethiopia</gloss>, and from there it goes to lose itself in the sea toward the coast of **Melinde**.

This kingdom is small; the inhabitants are
pages.19:
<margin>1613</margin>
black like the <term>Kaffers</term>, but they do not have the facial features of these; they are, like all heathens, very inclined toward sorcery, and they have such uncommon customs and habits that I shall undoubtedly deserve forgiveness for having described them.

<margin>Custom of those of Gingiro.</margin>
<term>Gingiro</term> means an ape or a monkey, and truly the black color of this monarch, his gestures, appearance, and manners were entirely similar to those of these animals. These peoples also have that of the apes, that they kill their kings, and those of their people who come wounded from battle, because, they say, it is better for them to die than to remain among their enemies in life with such signs of defeat.

<margin>Which are very ridiculous.</margin>
But although these kings, thus sitting on their <term>Jucquoir</term> <gloss>seat/throne</gloss> like an owl on a stool, resemble apes or monkeys very closely, they are nonetheless of an exalted spirit and a very keen perception. When the King is to go outside his palace, it is early in the morning before the sun rises, and if it happens that the sun is up before he is out, he keeps himself locked in his palace for that whole day, does not go onto the throne to grant audience, nor does he give any order to anyone, because, they say, 2 suns cannot endure each other in the world at one time, and because he does not wish to concede that priority to it, he avenges himself on it the next day and goes out before the sun is up.

<margin>Wonderfully strange ceremonies in the election.</margin>
The ceremonies that they observe to elect their kings are likewise entirely uncommon. They wrap the corpse of their dead king in costly fabrics and then put it into the hide of a cow that has been freshly skinned. Immediately, all those who might stand for the crown, such as the children of the deceased and the princes of the blood, hide themselves in a
pages.20:
<margin>1613</margin>
desolate forest and act as if they want to flee that honor that they desire. The electors, who are considered great sorcerers, hold council, go forest-wards, search for the chosen one, and by devilish art make a shape of a bird of prey as large as an eagle, which they call <term>Liber</term>, descend. This bird flies with a great shriek to the place where the one who is chosen is. The electors also immediately go thither and find him surrounded by lions, tigers, snakes, panthers, and more such beasts, which they make appear around this newly chosen monarch through sorcery, who defends and wards himself off like a mad bull against those who wish to take him along; he even sometimes wounds or kills them, for those who seek him do not leave him until they have gotten him and carried him along with force and violence. Leading him away thus, one must fight with the people of a lineage who for a long time have claimed to have the right to place the chosen monarch on the throne. The strongest or the victors have this privilege, which gives them a good share in the favor of the new <term>Gingiro</term>.

<margin>As also in the coronation of a king.</margin>
The ceremony of the coronation is to bring the King into the palace and place him under a tent. On the 7th day after the death of the last king, the sorcerers bring a worm, which they say came out of the nostrils of the dead man, which worm they wrap in a piece of silk fabric, and the new king pulls its head off with his teeth. This having been done, they bury the dead king after they have carried him through the sown fields, which they beg him to bless. Having arrived at the burial place of the old kings, which is in a small grove, they dig a hole in the earth and lay him in it without covering him, but he remains lying exposed to the air,
pages.21:
<margin>1613</margin>
because, they say, the earth is not worthy to cover the body of their king, who in greatness does not yield to the sun, and also for that purpose so that the sky might serve as a more glorious gravesite. On the day of the burial, they slaughter many cows by the grave, so that their blood drips onto the corpse of the king. They still throttle a head of cattle there daily as long as the new king is alive, which is to the great profit of their priests, or rather of their sorcerers, who indeed let the blood of the cow run into the grave but well supply their tables with what is left over.

To come to the new king while he bites the head off the worm, the people make a cry of joy and cheers to his praise, wishing him a long life. The festival ends after they have placed him on that construction of a throne described by us above; for the new king immediately has all those fetched who were favorites of his predecessor, saying to them: <note>as they had been his friends so strongly during his lifetime, it was also fair that they should accompany him into the other world, so that they might continue their services,</note> and under this pretext, he has all of them have their necks broken. He chooses others again, fills the government offices that are vacant, and that does not prevent these first and most important positions from being highly coveted, and it makes the courtiers have a very great interest in the preservation of their prince.

At the time of the election, they lay all the houses in which the deceased king has lived, with all his household effects and tools, without excluding anything, however costly it may be, into ashes and charcoal. They do the same when any special or common person dies,

pages.451:
HISTORIA DE YUCATAN. 

and forty-nine years, in which the venerable Father Fray Luis de Villalpando was elected custodian, exactly one year after the Indians in Maní had tried to burn him with his companion. The definitors were the father custodian himself as first, Father Fray Lorenzo de Bienvenida as second, Father Fray Francisco Navarro as third, and Father Fray Miguel de Vera as fourth. By this same table, it appears that the convent of the city of Mérida already had a name, its elected guardian being the aforementioned Father Fray Juan de la Puerta: that of Campeche, its guardian Father Fray Diego de Bejar: that of Maní, guardian Father Fray Juan de Albalate; and that of Cunkal, guardian the venerable father custodian, and that of Ytzamal, guardian the definitor Father Fray Lorenzo de Bienvenida. Not only are the guardians assigned in this capitular table, but also the companions who were to live with them in each convent: a custom that was observed in this province until the provincial chapter held in the year 1603, from which time it seems to have remained at the discretion of the reverend fathers provincial to assign the companions and residents of each convent, according to the need that arises in it. The chapter was presided over by the very Reverend Father Fray Francisco de Bustamante, as evidenced by the table signed with his name and sealed with the seal of his office of commissary general. This was like the birth of this holy province of San José of Yucatan, for which reason I have written of it with such singularity, in which, with the five convents that have been named, it remained in the form of a custody, subject while it was so to that of Mexico.

Although Father Fray Juan de la Puerta was elected guardian of the convent of the city of Mérida in the chapter, as the religious were still so few for such a number of towns as there were in Yucatan, since for the whole province of Valladolid, so populous and with so many people, a foundation of a convent had not been able to be made, it was discussed that a religious of the province should go as procurator to Spain, representing the need that existed for them, and it seems they agreed that Father Fray Juan de la Puerta was the most suitable for a matter of such importance.

<summary>This page describes the organization of the Custody of San José of Yucatan in 1549, detailing the election of Fr. Luis de Villalpando as custodian and the distribution of friars among the convents of Mérida, Campeche, Maní, Cunkal, and Ytzamal.</summary>
<keywords>San José of Yucatan, Custody, Luis de Villalpando, religious organization, convents, 1549</keywords>
pages.452:
LIBRO QUINTO. 435

of such importance as Father Fray Juan de la Puerta.
The Adelantado <note>title of governor and military leader during the conquest</note> was of the same opinion as the religious, and thus gave him letters for the Emperor and the Royal Council of the Indies, in which he signified the great fruit being made in the conversion of these Indians and the urgent need they had for the help of ministers.
Father Fray Juan de la Puerta received the dispatches that the province and the Adelantado gave him, and granting him Father Fray Angel Maldonado as his companion, he went to Mexico, where the very Reverend Father commissary general, who had great satisfaction with his virtue and prudence, confirmed the office of procurator that the province had given him, and entrusted other business to him, for which he gave him sufficient instructions and papers, with which he went to Spain in the Fleet of the following year of 1550. I have not found the result of this trip, it only seems to me that this religious was later elected bishop of this bishopric, as was said in the fourth book.

Nothing notable had happened regarding the secular state until this time: but as the new laws, which had been given for these kingdoms, ordered that no governor or royal official should have Indians in <term>encomienda</term> <gloss>a grant of indigenous labor and tribute</gloss>, and the Adelantado, as a conqueror, retained his own, a new order came so that they would be taken from him. Father Lizana says that this year of forty-nine, the <term>licenciado</term> <gloss>holder of a law degree</gloss> Herrera came from Spain (with Father Albalate, who brought the religious), assigned as <term>oidor</term> <gloss>judge</gloss> of the Royal Audiencia of Mexico, and that he visited this land and held the <term>residencia</term> <gloss>a formal judicial review of an official's conduct</gloss> of the Adelantado. I am persuaded that the one who held his residence was the <term>licenciado</term> Santillan, an <term>oidor</term> who resided in the same audience, because in a royal provision of the sixteenth day of the month of June of the same year of one thousand five hundred and forty-nine, he is given the power, so that

<summary>The Adelantado supports the mission of Fr. Juan de la Puerta to Spain to seek more missionaries. Meanwhile, legal proceedings are initiated against the Adelantado by the Royal Audiencia, leading to an order to remove his indigenous labor grants.</summary>
<keywords>Adelantado, Fr. Juan de la Puerta, encomienda, Royal Audiencia, residencia, law, indigenous labor</keywords>
pages.453:
HISTORIA DE YUCATAN.

coming to Yucatan, he should take away the Indians he held, and investigate other excesses that the Adelantado was said to have committed during the time of his government, so that if the other gentleman were holding his residency, it does not seem there would be need for this new commission. In it, it is referred to as a preamble, that in fraud of the new laws, many Indians were commended, in the name of the wives, sons, and daughters of the governors and royal officials, with which they enjoyed the Indians as if said prohibition of laws did not exist, descending to the singular motive of this commission, it is said:

"And we are informed that although it was provided by our said royal audience that the said Indians should be taken from the wife, sons, and daughters of the said Adelantado Montejo, it had not been done nor fulfilled: rather they say that the greater part of that land is in the said Adelantado Montejo and in his wife, and in Don Francisco de Montejo, and in his wife, and in a stepson of his, the son of his wife, and for this, many frauds and ruses have been made. Especially they say that having given a provision so that the Indians should be taken from the said Adelantado and his sons and daughters; he managed with the one who carried it to hand it over to him so that it could not be used, and of another provision he carried, in which it was ordered that they should not interfere in the jurisdiction of the town of the Victoria of the Rio de Grijalva in order to collect from the Indians, whom they ordered to be taken, all the tributes of a year in advance, belonging to us. And that the title with which he had caused the said tributes to be collected had been by saying that he had given them to a nephew of his, and for this, he had shown deposit certificates and the date of them from time past. And that to do the aforementioned, he had caused the provisions to be delayed. And that the fraud which the said governor was committing against us and our royal treasury having been seen by an ordinary mayor of the said town of the Victoria: he and a councilman, who was called Alonso Bazan, as our officials, took the person who for the said Adelantado was collecting the tributes, and what from

<summary>This page contains a formal royal document accusing the Adelantado Montejo and his family of circumventing the "New Laws" regarding indigenous labor grants and embezzling royal funds in the town of La Victoria.</summary>
<keywords>Adelantado Montejo, New Laws, encomienda, fraud, royal treasury, La Victoria, Alonso Bazan</keywords>
pages.454:
LIBRO QUINTO. 437

them had proceeded, and they put it in the chest of the three keys. And that known by the Adelantado, he went to the said town with an armed hand, after the said provision had been notified to him, so that he would not be judged, and arrested the said mayor and councilman, and took them as prisoners to Yucatan. And he newly raised other officials, his own servants, to have charge of our treasury, and tried to have them hold him as governor in it, in order to take revenge on the officials and give the Indians he held to persons of the said town, paying for them; which he did, as he sold some native Indians for interests they gave him. And that likewise we are informed that the said Adelantado Montejo is making a sugar mill in Champoton, and for it, he has taken and takes the land from the Indians of that province, and took away their farmlands, the said towns being mine, agreeing to relieve the said taxpayers by occupying them in commercial ventures. And that above all the aforementioned, the said Adelantado has not given any <term>repartimiento</term> <gloss>assignment of indigenous labor</gloss> to any conqueror, but to all his relatives and wives and children, to stepsons and grandsons: they say not only to the legitimate ones, but to the bastards. And they say that he made the Indians of Champoton and Campeche go to war and make slaves, and so they say many of them were made, likewise women against our laws made by us, and that they are sold against all reason and justice, which is a cause for the said provinces to be depopulated. And that not content with all the aforementioned things, the said Adelantado makes houses, ranches, and commercial ventures in the said provinces with our Indians: not being able to, nor having to do so, and tiring them and making them work excessively. And that likewise other persons have done and committed many and grave crimes in the said provinces worthy of imprisonment and punishment, to which it was convenient to provide and remedy as an important thing."

Such was the account that had been made to the Emperor in the Royal Council of the Indies of what had happened in Yucatan; but it seems to have been excessive, since for what is said in it of the Adelantado not having commended Indians to any conqueror

<summary>The royal accusation continues, detailing the Adelantado's use of armed force against officials, illegal slave-trading of indigenous people, and the exploitation of Indian labor for his own economic benefit in sugar mills and ranches.</summary>
<keywords>Adelantado Montejo, Champoton, Campeche, slave trade, indigenous labor, economic exploitation, royal accusation</keywords>
