HISTORIA DE YUCATAN.

at all, but to his relatives, there are still today many deposit certificates to the contrary, which were exhibited as soon as they finished subjugating them, which their descendants originally observe for greater qualification of their merits in the conquest. Regarding making slaves of the Indians and selling them, what was happening has already been said and is written in the third book. But as there is never a lack of someone to complain (or it is very rare) about those who govern, it had happened at present, and joining the retention of the Indians, which the Adelantado enjoyed as a conqueror: having to be removed by the general laws and the Emperor desiring to certify himself of the truth, this royal provision was dispatched, which by its context seems to be of residency, and in it, immediately to the referred account, it is said:

"And seen by those of our Council of the Indies, wanting to provide for it, trusting in you that you are such a person that you will keep our service, and the right to each one of the parties and that with all care and diligence you will try to understand what by us will be commanded and committed to you: it is our mercy and will to entrust and commit it to you, and by the present, we entrust and commit it to you. Because we command you that as soon as you see this, you go with the staff of our royal justice to the said provinces of Yucatan, Cozumél, and before all things, take away the Indians that the said Adelantado Montejo and his wife and children might have, and those of our officials of the said provinces: except for the male children to whom such Indians were commended, the such children already being married, and living on their own at the time they were commended to them. Which do and fulfill, even if the <term>encomiendas</term> <gloss>indigenous labor grants</gloss> of the such wives and sons and daughters were made, before the new laws or after. And because we have provided the said new laws or ordinances for the good of the conquerors and their children, so that they can live and remain in those parts, that the Indians that were taken by disposition of the said new laws and ordinances be placed in the royal crown and from their tributes

<summary>The text presents the official royal response to the accusations against the Adelantado. It orders a judge to proceed to Yucatan, remove the indigenous grants from Montejo and his family, and place those resources under the administration of the royal crown.</summary>
<keywords>Adelantado Montejo, Royal Council of the Indies, New Laws, encomienda, royal crown, judge, Cozumél</keywords>
pages.456:
LIBRO QUINTO. 439

it be given for the sustenance and entertainment of the said conquerors, and if they are dead, of their children who do not have <term>repartimientos</term> <gloss>labor grants</gloss>: you shall provide that the tributes that the towns of Indians that you thus take from the said Adelantado and from his wife, sons, and daughters, and from our officials of the said provinces of Yucatan and Cozumél yield; meanwhile, that we provide for the perpetuity of those provinces what is convenient: you shall distribute among the conquerors who did not have a <term>repartimiento</term>, and among their children and some good settlers. Which thus do and fulfill, notwithstanding any petitions that might be interposed against this letter of ours. You shall inform yourself how and in what manner such things contained above in this letter of ours have passed, and what frauds have been committed against our royal treasury, and what persons did and committed the aforementioned, or any thing or part of it, and of the other crimes that have been done in the said province, and by whose command they did it and who gave them advice, favor, and help for it, and those whom you find guilty in it, arrest their bodies, and thus imprisoned, the parties to whom it touches being called and heard, you shall do justice on it by your sentence or sentences, as well interlocutory as definitive, &c." And afterwards, it proceeds by putting all the clauses that are accustomed to be put in similar commissions. It only singles out that for the execution, as well of what is contained, as of any other thing that is committed to him, he should assist for the time that might be assigned to him by the viceroy Don Antonio de Mendoza.

Through this order, the time arrived for the Adelantado to provide residency for his having governed Yucatan in war and peace. The judge who was to hold his residency arrived in Campeche, and having given notice to the Adelantado of his arrival, he sent his son Don Francisco with other principal residents of the city of Mérida, so that in his name they would bid him welcome and receive him. Having arrived in Campeche, they visited the judge, who with many courtesies thanked the Adelantado for the one he had had, sending his son, and that which the other gentlemen had manifested by going to

<summary>The royal provision outlines the legal instructions for the judge sent to investigate the Adelantado, including the redistribution of indigenous labor and the requirement for a formal judicial review. The Adelantado welcomes the judge to Campeche.</summary>
<keywords>Adelantado Montejo, judge, residency, royal treasury, Don Antonio de Mendoza, Campeche, Mérida</keywords>
pages.457:
HISTORIA DE YUCATAN.

visit him. They came together to the city of Mérida, and manifesting the superior order that the judge carried, he was received to the exercise of his commission. He published the residency, and in the interim that it was to be done, the judge assumed the government of this land. Although there were complainants against the Adelantado, generally the event was felt, as much by the religious as by laymen and Indians, because he was a very gentlemanly person in his proceeding and a noble person, a friend of the poor, benign, and endowed with many good gifts, which made him lovable even if he had some defects as a man: who is perfect in everything? It was already seen in the third book what the principal conquerors wrote together in the council to the Emperor about him and his son Don Francisco, just after the city of Mérida was founded, when they dispatched the first procurator general to the kingdoms of Spain.

CHAPTER XI.

->The Indians are taken from the Adelantado. He goes with his<-
->residency to Spain, and dies: and his successors are mentioned.<-

The residency of the Adelantado having been published, the administration of justice and government of Yucatan remained with the judge who was acting it, in whose time it happened that some negro slaves of the Spaniards fled to the mountains, and joined by those who were already up in arms, a troop of up to twenty or more; they entered some towns of the Indians, to whom they did much evil and damage, taking from them what they could, and committing other crimes that demanded quick remedy. So that this might have the end that was necessary, the judge appointed Alonso Rosado, a conqueror, as head and leader of the Spaniards, that they should seek them and bring them as prisoners, and not yielding to imprisonment, to use the last remedy by shooting them or killing them by whatever means could be done. Alonso Rosado left with his men, and suffering some hardships through the mountains, he caught sight of the fugitive blacks, who finding themselves without weapons, and surrounded by the Spaniards with them, surrendered and were brought as prisoners to the city of Mérida. Delivered

<summary>The judge arrives in Mérida and initiates the residency of the Adelantado, which is viewed with general regret. Subsequently, the new government suppresses a group of fugitive enslaved Africans who were terrorizing local indigenous communities.</summary>
<keywords>residency, Adelantado, Don Francisco de Montejo, Mérida, Alonso Rosado, fugitive slaves, indigenous communities</keywords>
pages.458:
LIBRO QUINTO. 441

to the judge, he put them in jail, until by legal means they were punished according to their crimes. The imprisonment of these blacks was reputed as a considerable service in this land; because besides the damages that were avoided with it, a rumor that was already running was quelled, that some Indians were attempting to rebel against the Spaniards, with the heat and encouragement that those slaves gave them, fearful that they were to come into the hands of justice and be punished, as they were afterwards.

It happened also that many Indians from the southern part of this province, which they call the Sierra, had retired to the interior of the land (which is distant between this and that of Guatemala) fleeing from the contact with the Spaniards and from Christian teaching. Considering the judge the great disservice that was being done to God and the King with this flight, he ordered the captain Francisco de Montejo, who as was said was one of the conquest, to enter through those unpopulated areas and try to attract them to the towns of their nature. That captain left with people from the city and walked through the mountains and settlements, gathering many Indians with peaceful means. Some were distant more than seventy leagues from the city, and forty from the nearest settlement. Among these distant ones, the captain learned of a troop of Indians gathered in groups, and not being able to go, he entrusted it to Alonso Rosado, one of those who went with him, and who arrested the blacks before, giving him some Spaniards so that they might go with him. They found the Indians and persuaded them in such a way that they gave themselves up in peace and he brought them to the captain. A very considerable number of Indians was gathered with this departure, which was distributed to the towns of their nature, with which this land of Yucatan remained quiet for then. The one and the other is evident from the authentic proofs that were made and I have read.

It is said that the time of the residency lasted three months, in which the judge ordered some things for the utility of the Indians and their good treatment, and for the increase of their Christianity. He reformed others regarding the Spaniards, who as in republics recently founded

<summary>The colonial authorities suppress a potential indigenous rebellion linked to the escaped slaves and successfully repatriate indigenous groups who had fled to the interior mountains. The residency period lasts three months.</summary>
<keywords>indigenous rebellion, Sierra, Guatemala, Francisco de Montejo, Alonso Rosado, Christianization, residency, colonial administration</keywords>

pages.15:
<header>of the Baron von Trenck.</header>
<sig>A 4</sig>

should have shown, that I should make room for him. He pushed me back with such vehemence that, out of anger, I grabbed my torch with both hands and smashed it to pieces on his head inside the church. Following this, I had to avoid both my order and the school, and study at home.

Thus we traveled to the command that my father had received, which is the <term>border fortress</term> of Brod on the <term>Save river</term>. My brothers and I were sent to the Jesuits in Possega <term>ad studia</term> <gloss>for studies</gloss>, though against my desire; from there we always came home for the <term>vacations</term>.

In the year 1725, I again had to endure the following mortal danger: My father was visited by a certain Colonel Engineer, Count C***, and his family, as a neighbor. As there was a pretty young girl in his suite, with whom my eldest brother fell in love, we all three decided to escort her back, which we did. 

But as we were driving back the next day past Diacovar, where we had stayed overnight, it happened that the front wheel struck a log, and we all fell out of the carriage. My eldest brother, however, who was handling the horses in place of the coachman, fell under the horses and was run over in such a way that
pages.16:
<header>Life and Deeds</header>
<note>Small ornamental flourishes flank the word "und" in the header.</note>

he died on the way in the forest two hours later. After my father, who had received news of this and arrived at this misfortune just in time, reached him, he gave the final sign of life and farewell with open eyes, but spoke no more words, and passed away immediately thereafter.

My grandmother, who was a Countess von Witt and loved us all tenderly, was so shocked and saddened by this fatal <term>casum</term> <gloss>event/case</gloss> that she died from it 6 weeks later. My mother had to succumb to a similar fate soon after, specifically in the year 1726. Of all these deaths, none saddened me more than that of my dear brother, whom I had properly prepared for death, with the exception of confession and communion, due to the lack of a clergyman. My old father, however, was inconsolable over three such painful losses, and he never proceeded to <term>vota secunda</term> <gloss>second vows/remarriage</gloss>. Meanwhile, he still kept us both brothers studying, though not away from home, which was again the cause of my having to escape a mortal danger. For once, in the wintertime, on the Save river that flowed right past our house, when the marshes were frozen and the ice was floating on the river with a multitude of ducks, I took a small boat,
pages.17:
<header>of the Baron von Trenck.</header>
<sig>A 5</sig>

boat, with which I could row perfectly, and I rowed with my musket through the ice, which I dodged quite skillfully, toward the ducks. I shot three of them dead and shot the wing off one. As I then chased after the wounded duck and forgot the danger I was in, an <term>ice floe</term> struck another large one of the same kind so violently that I found myself, quite by chance, sitting on the other floe and saw my little boat shattered to pieces and drifting away. Who would have thought that I would escape this time, too? My father and brother, along with good friends, threw their hands over their heads and called to me that I should commend myself to God, which I did. I floated downstream for nearly half a mile in this manner, and because there was a narrow spot there, the ice floe jammed. Since it was not possible to come to my aid with a ship due to the mass of ice, over 300 people ran along to help with the spectacle. The ice floe had hardly stopped when a <term>Bandur</term> <gloss>a member of a Slavic military unit</gloss>, with a rope in his hand, risked himself for me out of love and successfully led me out of my danger. I remained unpunished by my father here as well.

A few weeks after this danger I had experienced, however, I was in a small boat with my
pages.18:
<header>Life and Deeds</header>

brother on a duck hunt. When the boatman rowed us close to the ducks, and my brother, who was kneeling in front of me in the boat, did not want to shoot but wanted to be even closer, I took the musket and fired behind him. I hit the ducks, but at the same time, I shot the clothing off my brother from the right side down to the skin, and two shots into his arm. Had I held my finger lower, I would have shot his arm off completely. For this, I received a severe beating from my father, and my brother, as the new battalions were raised, became an ensign under Wallis.

Shortly thereafter, namely on July 10, 1727, the now deceased Hungarian Palatine, Count Nicolaus Palfi, took me into his regiment as an ensign. From this time on, my luck began to struggle with misfortune, and misfortune with luck, as it were, <term>vice versa</term> <gloss>conversely</gloss>. The first misfortune was that when my father sent me to Esseck to equip myself, I became so deathly ill with a fever that my father sent the money <term>pro funeribus</term> <gloss>for the funeral</gloss> and the hussars to accompany my body to Diacovar, where I lay sick, via the commissary, our secretary at the time, Herr von Hess, who is still in Esseck. However, I was soon cured through the help of good medicine
pages.19:
<header>of the Baron von Trenck.</header>

and thus had to travel to Belgrade to join my regiment. I had been in Belgrade for barely 4 months when I already had a <term>rencontre</term> <gloss>encounter/duel</gloss> with an ensign from the regiment who at first made me retreat, but eventually had to settle down after receiving a slash over the nose and skull, and then four slashes to the hand. I also received three slashes on the hand, and the hilt of my Parisian sword was struck down by this strong man—even though I was still, so to speak, a child—so that it remained lying on my wounded hand. The same year, I again had an affair with a Silesian volunteer named von Gersdorff, whom I wounded through the hand.

In the year 1728, I had an affair with a certain Count Paradiso, from whom I had won 380 florins. He did not want to pay them to me, over which I insulted him; he struck at me with his hand but only touched my head by a lock of hair. I drew my sword, but he jumped out of the coffee house, inside of which were about 30 officers. As I pulled myself through the officers, sword in hand, and wanted to go out the door, he lunged at me from outside. I wanted to parry with my left arm, and I received a thrust through it; but this did not stop me from attacking him, and
pages.20:
<header>Life and Deeds</header>

and he, or I, would certainly have reached the extreme had about 6 officers not thrown themselves upon me and hindered the affair in that way. I later defamed him again and could never learn where he went, for I have not been paid by him to this day. Perhaps, if this comes before his eyes, he will report himself. I had two other small skirmishes this year, but they ended without injury, so I will not make any further mention of them.

In the year 1729, however, I again had an affair with the regimental auditor of the Prince Alexander of Württemberg's regiment, then stationed in Belgrade, by the name of Beyer, whom I finished off with two thrusts to the right side, for which he had to have himself treated for 6 weeks. It then happened that my battalion, in which I served, had to march to Esseck, and we arrived there in the month of October of this same year. Here I must recall that I have hitherto traveled with my father through all of Sicily, the Neapolitan, Apulian, Roman, Venetian, Triestine, Carniolan, Styrian, Lican, Croatian, Slavonian, Serbian, Austrian, Syrmian, and Hungarian lands, and a part of Bosnia.
pages.21:
<header>of the Baron von Trenck.</header>

I had barely arrived in Essek when I again had an affair with my own cousin, named Tillier, although I had never given any cause for it, with whom I fought twice, wounding him both times.

In the year 1730, however, I fought again with Baron F***, whom I also wounded through the arm. Although I had enjoyed looking at pretty girls since 1727, I was not yet skillful enough for intrigues, but rather satisfied my desire with anyone young who came before my eyes, without exerting myself. In this year, however, I fell in love with a certain young lady of good standing. But as the father and mother in whose house she lived kept a very close watch on her, I initially had to settle for the pleasure of walking past her window at night and clearing my throat sharply—this was the signal—whereupon she would immediately come running to the window and speak a few words with me, just to comfort both of us. I frequented this <term>rendez-vous</term> <gloss>meeting</gloss> very diligently and constantly; I would have wished that it were always night just to be able to talk to my beautiful young lady, until I finally managed to find an opportunity for her to let me into her bedroom. What could have been more foolish than to see us
pages.22:
<header>Life and Deeds</header>

two lovers? Out of love, I could no longer speak, but only kissed her hands constantly and pressed her to me. She, however, as a young lady of 14 at the time, smiled. I was not so bold as to engage further in love, and thus I left my young lady. As great as this person's love for me was, so great also became the <term>esteem</term> <gloss>high regard</gloss> she held for me, as I gave her no cause to commit an excess. I was so loved by her that I could come to my beauty at any time at night that I wished. At every rendezvous, I chatted so much to her about love and held her beauty and coldness before her that, at the seventh rendezvous, she said to me, completely enchanted (which I will remember for the rest of my life): "Baron Trenck! I am no longer in a state to resist your love; do with me what you will, only save my honor." Upon this, she fell into my arms, completely enchanted and with tear-filled eyes. I kissed her, and she kissed me back, with which we were satisfied—even though certainly another, more indiscreet lover than I, who always firmly imprinted the motto: <term>le respect arrête mes désirs</term> <gloss>respect halts my desires</gloss> in such cases, would not have left it at that. I now believed that I would finally be happy

pages.14:
# VOYAGIE VAN <note>Voyage of</note>

<margin>1613</margin>
to be able to hide a matter from one about whom he is already suspicious, he immediately concluded that this journey served to bring the *Portuguese* into his kingdom via *India*, that they would make themselves masters of it, and force him to embrace the *Catholic Religion*. Upon this, he summoned the great lords of his court and very secretly shared his thoughts with them. They all agreed that one should not permit the *Ambassador* and me to take this road which we had planned, as it was the direct one, and that we should be made to take another and very inconvenient route through many detours and the land of *Baly*.

<margin>Forced to take an inconvenient detour.</margin>
After much debate back and forth, he said to us finally in conclusion that he would never let us pass along the road we intended, but certainly through *Baly*, to which one would have to adjust, for we were determined to continue this undertaking.

<margin>The Kingdom of *Baly*.</margin>
*Baly* is a *Kingdom* that formerly belonged to the *Empire of Ethiopia*, but the *Gallas* and *Mahometans* possess it at present. It borders the *Kingdom of Adel* and lies to the east of the *Kingdom of Narea*. From this, I could easily conclude that I could not complete this journey, and that, after I had encountered all these difficulties in the lands of the *Emperor*, I had even greater ones to expect in the lands of the *Kaffers* <gloss>Infidels/Heathens</gloss>, who have no other *Law* than their own advantage. Nevertheless, considering that it was for the service of *God*, I took the road to *Baly*, trusting in His mercy.

<margin>Set out on the road.</margin>
The *Ambassador* and I, departing from the court of *Narea*, took our road eastward and arrived on the first day at the place where the *Captain* was, whom the *Benero* <gloss>a local chieftain/official</gloss> had assigned us as a guide. At first, he received us quite well, hoping to get a fine gift from us, but that which we presented to him,
pages.15:
# ANTONIO FERNANDEZ.

<margin>1613</margin>
did not correspond to his hope and expectation. Because of this, he let us wait for him for 8 days, after which he gave us 80 men to accompany us to the borders of the Kingdom of Narea. We went with this escort

<margin>Entering a wild land.</margin>
for 4 long days' journey through a wild and deserted land to avoid the raids of the Gallas. Our escort then turned back, and since the road we still had to cover was very dangerous, we let some scouts run ahead of us to give us a signal as soon as they spotted Gallas from afar, so that we might have time to go and hide in the woods.

At midday, we began to climb down a very high and rugged mountain, and the Envoy of Gingiro told us that, before we continued to climb down, we must hide until evening so that we could pass by night through the fields where the Gallas grazed their cattle.

<margin>A very bad road, suffering great poverty.</margin>
At 4 o'clock in the afternoon, we set out on the road under the cover of a dense rainstorm, which drove the Gallas to their huts, but also soaked us weary travelers and caused us to suffer much cold. Our care and distress doubled when the night came because the brush through which we passed was very dense near the ground, difficult to get through by day, and even worse by night. We lit a fire in the woods and chewed a little roasted barley, which is the common food of travelers in that land. The next day, very early, after we had climbed down a steep mountain, we came to the river Zebée.

<margin>Crossing a very dangerous bridge.</margin>
This stream flows faster than the Nile, and at the place where we had to cross it, it made a terrifying noise, falling from a mountain between very sharp rocks, between which the water was crushed into foam.
pages.16:
# VOYAGIE VAN A.

<margin>1613</margin>
The bridge over which we were forced to pass such fast and dangerous waters was made of a piece of wood. This went across the river, notwithstanding that it was remarkably wide, and the height of this bridge was so great that, when one looked down from it, one discovered nothing there but an abyss. The great length of the piece of wood caused it to tremble under the feet of our people, and yet everyone wanted to be the first across, for as soon as one is on the other side of this river, one no longer has to fear the Gallas, for whom the fear was so great that it numbed all other fears. We thanked God on the other side of the bridge that He had delivered us from the bloodthirsty hands of the Gallas. We could not let our mules go over this bridge, therefore we left them there that night on the bank of the river with 2 men to guard them, with orders to cross the bridge if the Gallas came, and to break it down behind them. But the next day, 2 inhabitants of the land showed them a ford where they managed to get them across with great difficulty.

<margin>Obtaining an audience with the King of Gingiro.</margin>
The Ambassador arrived shortly after this at a dwelling from which we made our arrival known to the King of Gingiro, and we asked for permission to present to him the letters which we had to deliver on behalf of the Emperor of Ethiopia. But this King, being besides that very devoted to his sorcery, made us wait there for 8 days, at the end of which we received permission to come to his court, where we arrived in one day. We found this monarch ready to receive us, sitting or rather enclosed in a cage, for it was a type of cage or crate of about 25 hand-breadths high and 30 wide. It was round on top, having
pages.17:
# ANTONIO FERNANDEZ.

<margin>1613</margin>
the appearance of a wheel. The King sat on a carpet which was spread out on this wheel. All his courtiers stood below this throne upright, where he gave the audience. He was clothed in a very fine cloth, the whiteness of which made the blackness of his face stand out all the more, in which one otherwise did not see those features that one notices in the Kaffers. He immediately asked for the letter from the Emperor. He climbed down from his throne to come and get it, asked how he was doing, and climbed back onto his throne,

<margin>Reading the Emperor's letter.</margin>
after which he read the letter and spoke for some time with us through an interpreter, to whom, as often as the Emperor or the King said something to be told to us, the interpreter kissed the tips of his fingers and, after he had bowed down to the earth, went to interpret it to me, who was at some distance from the throne. And to bring the answer from me back to the King, he first used the same ceremony. The conversation lasted a long time. Finally, the King let it be said to me and the Envoy that we should go and rest, and that the substance of the Emperor's letter consisted of this: that he would certainly like to entertain us, and would like to have us escorted with a good guard to the borders of his Kingdom, which (he said) he would do very gladly.

The day after, I presented some gifts to the King. He showed much pleasure in them, as they were a rare thing in that land. As I stood ready to depart from there, the King sent me, in consideration of my gift, a young daughter of one of the great men of his kingdom to serve me as a slave. I excused myself from receiving her, saying that I was by no means accustomed to taking women with me. The King was satisfied with the difficulty I made, and sent
pages.18:
# VOYAGIE VAN

<margin>1613</margin>
<margin>And a fine mule.</margin>
me a slave, whom I also accepted, not with the thought of getting any service from him, but in hope of baptizing him. He also gave me a fine mule, which served me very well on the trip, as well as people to help us cross the river Zebée again and from there to travel to the Kingdom of Cambate.

<margin>Strange kind of ferrymen.</margin>
We departed for that purpose from the court of the King of Gingiro, and arrived that same day at the bank of the river Zebée to cross it. The people that the King had given us, being very skilled in this kind of crossing, made a device (machine) that was not much safer than the piece of wood. They slaughtered a cow and put the luggage in the hide, which would serve two purposes: the one to get across, the other to serve as ballast for the ship that they made from the hide of this cow, sewing it tightly closed. After that, they blew it up stiff and then made 2 woods or sticks fast to it, similar to those of a sedan chair. 4 people went to sit on these sticks, 2 in front and 2 behind this raft-work. One forbade them to move, and one arranged them to be of equal weight so that they kept this strange vessel in an equal counterweight. In front of it swam a brave swimmer, who was very well experienced in this art, who had a rope around his body that was also fastened to the apparatus with which he pulled it forward. 2 other swimmers also pushed it from behind. A whole day was spent on this crossing.

<margin>River Zebée.</margin>
<margin>The Kingdom of Gingiro described.</margin>
The stream Zebée surrounds almost entirely the Kingdom of Gingiro and makes it like a peninsula, as one sees in the map of Ethiopia, and from there it goes to lose itself in the sea towards the coast of Melinde.

This Kingdom is small; the inhabitants are
pages.19:
# ANTONIO FERNANDEZ.

<margin>1613</margin>
black like the Kaffers, but they do not have the facial features of the latter. They are, like all heathens, very inclined to sorcery, and they have such uncommon customs and habits that I shall surely deserve to be excused for having described them.

<margin>Custom of those of Gingiro.</margin>
Gingiro means an Ape or a Monkey, and truly the black color of this monarch, his gestures, countenance, and manners were entirely similar to those of these animals. These people also have that of the apes, that they kill their kings, and those of their people who come wounded from the battle, because, they say, they ought to die sooner than keep their lives with such marks of reproach of the advantages of their enemies.

<margin>Which are very ridiculous.</margin>
But although these kings, sitting thus on their <term>Jucquoir</term> <gloss>throne</gloss> like an owl on a perch, look very oddly like apes or monkeys, they are nevertheless of a high spirit and of a very sharp perception. When the King is to go outside his palace, it is early in the morning before the sun rises. And if it happens that the sun is up before he is out, he keeps himself locked in his palace for that whole day, does not go onto the throne to give audience, and does not give the same order to anyone, because, they say, two suns cannot endure each other in the world at one time. And because he does not want to grant that precedence, he takes revenge for it the next day and goes out before the sun is up.

<margin>Wonderfully strange ceremonies in the election.</margin>
The ceremonies they observe to elect their kings are likewise entirely uncommon: they wrap the corpse of their dead king in precious fabrics and then put it in the hide of a cow that has been freshly skinned. Immediately, all those who might aspire to the crown, such as the children of the deceased and the princes of the blood, hide themselves in a
pages.20:
# VOYAGIE VAN

<margin>1613</margin>
wild forest and pretend as if they wanted to flee that honor, which they crave. The electors, who are held to be great sorcerers, hold council, go towards the forest, search for the chosen one, and by devilish art make a shape of a bird of prey as large as an eagle, which they call *Liber*, descend. This bird flies with a great cry to the place where the one who is chosen is. The electors also go there immediately, and they find him surrounded by lions, tigers, snakes, panthers, and more such beasts, which they make come around this newly chosen monarch by sorcery, who defends himself and resists like a mad bull against those who want to take him along. He wounds and sometimes even kills them, for those who search for him do not leave him until they have gotten him and have led him along with force and violence. Leading him thus, one must fight with the people of a clan who, from long ago, claim to have the right to put the chosen monarch on the throne. The strongest or the victors have this privilege, which gives them a good share in the favor of the new *Gingiro*.

<margin>As also in the coronation of a king.</margin>
The ceremony of the coronation is to bring the King into the palace and to set him under a tent. On the 7th day after the death of the last King, the sorcerers bring a worm which they say came out of the nostrils of the dead one, which worm they wind in a cloth of silk fabric, and the new King pulls the head off it with his teeth. That having been done, they bury the dead King after they have carried him through the sown fields, which they beg him to bless. Having arrived at the burial place of the old Kings, which is in a small grove, they dig a hole in the earth and lay him in it without covering him, but he remains lying exposed to the air,
pages.21:
# ANTONIO FERNANDEZ.

because, they say, the earth is not worthy to cover the body of their King, who in greatness does not yield to the sun, and also for that purpose so that the Heaven might serve as a more glorious grave-site. On the day of the funeral, they slaughter many cows by the grave so that the blood of these drips onto the corpse of the King. They still slaughter a head of cattle there daily as long as the new King is alive, which is to the great advantage of their priests, or rather their sorcerers, who do let the blood of the cow flow into the grave but well provide their tables with what remains of it.

<margin>1613</margin>

To get to the new King while he bites the head off the worm, the people make a cry of joy and acclamations to his praise, wishing him a long life. The feast ends after they have placed him on that construction of a throne described by us above, for the new King immediately has everyone fetched who were favorites of his predecessor, saying to them: *whereas they were his friends so strongly during his life, it was also fair that they accompany him in the other world, so that they might be able to continue their services*, and he has them all under this pretext have their necks broken. He elects others again, fills the state offices that are vacant, and that does not prevent these first and most important offices from being sought after strongly, and it causes the courtiers to have a very great interest in the preservation of their Prince.

At the time of the election, they lay all the houses in which the deceased King lived, with all his furniture and implements, without excluding anything, however precious it may be, in ashes and charcoal. They do the same when any private or common person dies,

pages.451:
HISTORIA DE YUCATAN.
<sig>28</sig>

and forty-nine years, when the venerable father Friar Luis de Villalpando was elected <term>custodio</term> <gloss>custodian/superior of a Franciscan custody</gloss>, exactly one year after the Indians in Maní had tried to burn him along with his companion. The <term>definidores</term> <gloss>councilors/definitors</gloss> were the said custodian himself as the first, Father Friar Lorenzo de Bienvenida as second, Father Friar Francisco Navarro as third, and Father Friar Miguel de Vera as fourth. By this same record, it appears that the city of Mérida already had the name of a convent, with the aforementioned Father Friar Juan de la Puerta elected as its guardian; Campeche, with Father Friar Diego de Bejar as its guardian; Maní, with Father Friar Juan de Albalate as guardian; Cunkal, with the venerable custodian as guardian; and Ytzamal, with the <term>definidor</term> <gloss>councilor</gloss> Father Friar Lorenzo de Bienvenida as guardian. Not only are the guardians assigned in this chapter table, but also the companions who were to live with them in each convent: a custom that was observed in this province until the provincial chapter held in the year 1603, from which time it seems to have been left to the discretion of the reverend provincial fathers to assign the companions and residents of each convent according to the need that arises there. The chapter was presided over by the Very Reverend Father Friar Francisco de Bustamante, as evidenced by the table signed with his name and sealed with the seal of his office of Commissary General. This was like the birth of this holy province of San José de Yucatan, for which reason I have written about it with such detail, as it remained in the form of a custody with the five convents that have been named, remaining subject to that of Mexico while it was one.

Although Father Friar Juan de la Puerta was elected guardian of the convent of the city of Mérida at the chapter, since the religious were still so few for the number of towns that existed in Yucatan—as for the entire province of Valladolid, which was so populous and had so many people, a convent foundation had not been able to be made—it was discussed that a religious from the province should go as a procurator to Spain to represent the need for them. It seems they agreed that Father Friar Juan de la Puerta was the most suitable for a matter
pages.452:
LIBRO QUINTO. 435

of such importance.
The <term>Adelantado</term> <gloss>governor/military commander</gloss> was of the same opinion as the religious, and thus he gave him letters for the Emperor and the Royal Council of the Indies, in which he expressed the great fruit being made in the conversion of these Indians and the urgent need they had for the help of ministers.
Father Friar Juan de la Puerta received the dispatches that the province and the <term>Adelantado</term> gave him, and, being granted Father Friar Angel Maldonado as his companion, he went to Mexico, where the Very Reverend Father Commissary General, who had great satisfaction in his virtue and prudence, confirmed the office of procurator that the province had given him and entrusted him with other business, for which he gave him sufficient instructions and papers, with which he went to Spain in the Fleet of the following year, 1550. I have not found the result of this trip; it only seems to me that this religious was later elected bishop of this bishopric, as was said in the fourth book.

->CHAPTER X.<-
->The order is given to take the <term>residencia</term> <gloss>judicial review of an official's conduct</gloss>,<-
->and to remove the Indians from the <term>encomienda</term> <gloss>grant of native labor</gloss> of the<-
-><term>Adelantado</term>, and the reason for both.<-

Nothing notable had occurred regarding the secular state until this time, but since the new laws that had been given for these kingdoms commanded that no governor or royal official should hold Indians in <term>encomienda</term>, and the <term>Adelantado</term>, as a conqueror, retained his, a new order came for them to be taken away. Father Lizana says that in this year of forty-nine, the Licentiate Herrera came from Spain (with Father Albalate, who brought the religious), assigned as a judge of the Royal <term>Audiencia</term> <gloss>high court</gloss> of Mexico, and that he visited this land and held the <term>residencia</term> of the <term>Adelantado</term>. I am persuaded that the one who took his <term>residencia</term> was the judge Licentiate Santillan, who resided in the same <term>audiencia</term>, because in a royal provision of the sixteenth day of the month of June of the same year of one thousand five hundred and forty-nine, he is given the authority to
pages.453:
HISTORIA DE YUCATAN. 436

come to Yucatan, remove the Indians he held, and investigate other excesses that the <term>Adelantado</term> was said to have committed during the time of his government, so if the other gentleman were holding his <term>residencia</term>, it does not seem there would be a need for this new commission. In it, it is stated as a preamble that, in fraud of the new laws, many Indians were held in <term>encomienda</term> under the names of the wives, sons, and daughters of the governors and royal officials, whereby they enjoyed the Indians as if there were no such prohibition of laws. Descending to the singular motive of this commission, it is said:

> "And we are informed that, although it was ordered by our said Royal <term>Audiencia</term> that the said Indians be taken away from the wife, sons, and daughters of the said <term>Adelantado</term> Montejo, it had not been done or fulfilled. Instead, they say that the greater part of that land is in the hands of the said <term>Adelantado</term> Montejo and his wife, and Don Francisco de Montejo and his wife, and a stepson of his, the son of his wife, and for this, many frauds and ruses have been committed. Especially they say that having given a provision so that the Indians be taken away from the said <term>Adelantado</term> and his sons and daughters, he found a way with the person carrying it to have it handed over, so that it could not be used, along with another provision he was carrying, in which it was ordered that they should not interfere in the jurisdiction of the town of La Victoria del Rio de Grijalva in order to collect from the Indians, whom they ordered to be taken away, all the tributes of a year in advance, which belonged to us. And the title with which he had had the said tributes collected had been by saying that he had given them to a nephew of his, and for this, he had shown deposit certificates with dates from long before. And that to do the aforementioned, he had had the provisions detained. And that the fraud, which the said governor was committing against us and our royal treasury, having been seen by an ordinary mayor of the said town of La Victoria, he and a councilman, who was called Alonso Bazan, as our officials took the person who was collecting the tributes for the said <term>Adelantado</term>, and what had proceeded
pages.454:
LIBRO QUINTO. 437

from them, and put it in the chest of the three keys. And that when the <term>Adelantado</term> found out, he went to the said town with an armed hand, after the said provision had been notified to him, so that he would not be judged, and he arrested the said mayor and councilman and took them prisoner to Yucatan. And he newly raised other officials, his own servants, to be in charge of our treasury, and he procured for them to hold him as governor there, in order to take revenge on the officials and give the Indians he held to persons of the said town while being paid for them; which he did, selling some native Indians for interests they gave him. And that we are likewise informed that the said <term>Adelantado</term> Montejo is building a sugar mill in Champoton and for it he has taken, and is taking, the land from the Indians of that province, and took away their farmlands, the said towns being mine, agreeing to discharge the said taxpayers by occupying them in trading. And that above all the aforementioned, the said <term>Adelantado</term> has not given any <term>repartimiento</term> <gloss>distribution of indigenous labor</gloss> to any conqueror, but to all his relatives and wives and children, to stepsons and grandsons: they say not only to the legitimate ones, but to the bastards. And they say that he made the Indians of Champoton and Campeche go to war and make slaves, and thus they say that many of them were made, likewise women, contrary to our laws made by us, and that they are sold against all reason and justice, which is the cause of the depopulation of the said provinces. And that the said <term>Adelantado</term>, not content with all the things mentioned above, makes houses, estates, and businesses in the said provinces with our Indians, not being able, nor having the right to do so, and tiring them and making them work excessively. And that likewise other persons have done and committed many and grave crimes in the said provinces worthy of imprisonment and punishment, for which it was fitting to provide and remedy as an important matter."

Such was the report that had been made to the Emperor in the Royal Council of the Indies of what had happened in Yucatan; but it seems to have been excessive, for in what is said there about the <term>Adelantado</term> not having given Indians in <term>encomienda</term> to any conqueror
pages.455:
HISTORIA DE YUCATAN. 438

but to his relatives, there are still today many deposit certificates to the contrary, which were exhibited as soon as they finished being subjected, which their descendants observe originally to further qualify their merits in the conquest. Regarding making slaves of the Indians and selling them, what was happening has already been said and is written in the third book. But as there is never a lack of someone to complain (or it is rare) about those who govern, it had happened at present, and joining the retention of the Indians that the <term>Adelantado</term> enjoyed as a conqueror, having to be removed by the general laws, and the Emperor wishing to certify the truth, this royal provision was dispatched, which by its context seems to be of <term>residencia</term>, and in it, immediately after the aforementioned report, it is said:

"And seen by those of our Council of the Indies, wishing to provide for it, trusting in you that you are such a person that you will guard our service and the right of each of the parties, and that with all care and diligence you will intend to understand what by us will be commanded and committed to you: it is our mercy and will to entrust and commit it to you, and by this present, we entrust and commit it to you. Because we command you that, as soon as you see this, you go with the rod of our royal justice to the said provinces of Yucatan, Cozumél, and above all things, remove the Indians that the said <term>Adelantado</term> Montejo might have, and those of his wife and children, and our officials of the said provinces: except for the male children to whom such Indians were granted, those children already being married and living independently at the time they were granted to them. Which you shall do and fulfill, even if the <term>encomiendas</term> of such wives and sons and daughters have been made before the new laws or after. And because in the said new laws or ordinances we have provided for the good of the conquerors and their children, so that they can live and remain in those parts, that the Indians who were taken away by the disposition of the said new laws and ordinances be placed under the royal crown, and from their tributes
pages.456:
LIBRO QUINTO. 439

it be given for the sustenance and entertainment of the said conquerors, and if they are dead, for their children who do not have <term>repartimientos</term>: you shall provide that the tributes that the towns of Indians yield, which you will thus take away from the said <term>Adelantado</term> and from his wife, sons, and daughters, and from our officials of the said provinces of Yucatan and Cozumél, while we provide for the perpetuity of those provinces as is convenient, you shall distribute among the conquerors who did not have a <term>repartimiento</term>, and among their children and some good settlers. Which you shall do and fulfill, notwithstanding any supplications that may be interposed to this our letter. You shall inform yourself how and in what manner such things contained above in this our letter have passed, and what frauds have been committed against our royal treasury, and what persons did and committed the aforementioned, or any thing or part of it, and of the other crimes that have been committed in the said province, and by whose order they did it, and who gave them advice, favor, and help for it, and those whom you find guilty, arrest their bodies, and thus arrested, having called and heard the parties concerned, you shall do justice upon it by your sentence or sentences, both interlocutory and definitive, etc." And afterwards it proceeds by putting all the clauses that are customary in such commissions. It only specifies that for the execution, as much of what is contained as of any other thing that is committed to him, he should attend for the time that may be assigned by the Viceroy Don Antonio de Mendoza.

By means of this order, the time arrived for the <term>Adelantado</term> to have to give a <term>residencia</term> for the time he had governed Yucatan in war and peace. The judge who was to hold his <term>residencia</term> arrived at Campeche, and once the <term>Adelantado</term> was notified of his arrival, he sent his son Don Francisco with other principal neighbors of the city of Mérida so that, in his name, they might welcome him and receive him. Once arrived in Campeche, they visited the judge, who with many courtesies thanked the <term>Adelantado</term> for what he had done by sending his son, and for what the other gentlemen had manifested by going to
pages.457:
HISTORIA DE YUCATAN. 440

visit him. They came together to the city of Mérida, and by manifesting the superior order that the judge brought, he was received into the exercise of his commission. He published the <term>residencia</term>, and in the interim that it was to be held, the judge assumed the government of this land. Although there were complainants against the <term>Adelantado</term>, the event was generally felt by the religious as well as by seculars and Indians, because he was a very gentlemanly person in his demeanor, a noble person, a friend of the poor, kind, and endowed with many good traits that made him lovable, even if he had some defects as a man: who is perfect in everything? It was already seen in the third book what the principal conquerors wrote together in the council to the Emperor, just after the city of Mérida was founded, when they dispatched the first procurator general to the kingdoms of Spain.

CHAPTER XI.

->The Indians are taken away from the <term>Adelantado</term>. He goes with his <term>residencia</term><-
->to Spain, and dies: and his successors are named.<-

Once the <term>residencia</term> of the <term>Adelantado</term> was published, the administration of justice and government of Yucatan remained in the judge who was conducting it, in whose time it happened that some black slaves of the Spaniards fled to the mountains, and, joined by those who were in open rebellion, a group of up to twenty or more entered some Indian towns, to whom they did much evil and harm, taking what they could from them and committing other crimes that required prompt remedy. So that this would have the necessary end, the judge named the conqueror Alonso Rosado as head and leader of the Spaniards, that they should search for them and bring them in as prisoners, and if they did not surrender, they should use the final remedy by shooting them with arquebuses or killing them by any means possible. Alonso Rosado went out with his men, and suffering some hardships through the mountains, he spotted the fugitive blacks, who, finding themselves without weapons and surrounded by the Spaniards with them, surrendered and were taken as prisoners to the city of Mérida. Delivered
pages.458:
LIBRO QUINTO. 441
<sig>56</sig>

to the judge, he put them in jail until they were legally punished according to their crimes. The imprisonment of these blacks was considered a considerable service to this land because, besides the damages that were avoided by it, a rumor that was already circulating was calmed: that some Indians were attempting to rebel against the Spaniards with the warmth and spirit that those slaves gave them, fearful that they were going to fall into the hands of justice and be punished, as they were afterwards.

It also happened that many Indians from the southern part of this province, which they call the Sierra, had retreated to the interior of the land (which lies between this one and that of Guatemala) fleeing from contact with the Spaniards and from Christian instruction. Considering the great disservice that was being done to God and the King with this flight, the judge ordered Captain Francisco de Montejo, who, as was said, was of the conquest, to enter through those unpopulated areas and try to attract them to the towns of their nature. That captain went out with people from the city and walked through the mountains and villages, gathering many Indians with peaceful means. Some were more than seventy leagues from the city, and forty from the nearest settlement. Among these distant ones, the captain learned of a troop of Indians banded together, and not being able to go, he entrusted it to Alonso Rosado, one of those who went with him, and who had previously captured the blacks, giving him some Spaniards to go with him. They found the Indians, and he persuaded them in such a way that they gave themselves up in peace and he brought them to the captain. A very considerable number of Indians gathered with this outing, who were distributed to the towns of their nature, with which this land of Yucatan remained quiet for then. Both the one and the other are evidenced by the authentic proofs that were made and that I have read.

It is said that the time of the <term>residencia</term> lasted three months, in which the judge ordered some things for the utility of the Indians and their good treatment, and for the increase of their Christianity. He reformed others regarding the Spaniards, who, as in newly founded republics

> If one says it is established as an illusory manifestation,
> The meaning established by logic is not correct.
> What use is the name 'illusory manifestation'?
> This is also, from the demon of grasping at truth,
> Not passed beyond, as the wise assert."

One should understand it as this. Similarly, Subhuti, asked by the great naga, I have not elaborated here as it would turn to another topic, so the main point should be kept in mind.

Therefore, the form that appears in the fundamental scriptural citation is a gathering of appearance and emptiness. Although it is empty of intrinsic nature and not established as such, it appears as form in dependence upon causes and conditions, and by that much, it is established as form.

By that measure, it is the form aggregate; thus it is called "Emptiness is form." It is by no means teaching that the mere negation of <term>satyastong</term> <gloss>emptiness of true existence</gloss>—which cuts off form—is the form that is suitable to be form. It is said extensively in the <term>Ghanavyuha Sutra</term> <gloss>Sutra of the Dense Array</gloss>:

"Thus, it is designated as form, but in the ultimate sense, it is not observed as form, nor is it discarded or conceptualized. Likewise, feeling and perception..." 

Similarly, in the <term>Akshayamati-nirdesa Sutra</term> <gloss>Sutra of the Teaching of Inexhaustible Intellect</gloss>: "Although the <term>dharmadhatu</term> <gloss>realm of phenomena</gloss> is the element of form, the dharmadhatu is not of the nature to be cognized by eye consciousness." This is taught by applying it to all eighteen elements.

Likewise, in the <term>Arya Jnanavati Sutra</term> <gloss>Sutra of the Noble Possessor of Wisdom</gloss>: "Goddess, the five aggregates are designated as the dharmadhatu; the dharmadhatu is these five aggregates."

Thus, because form is the essence of the dharmadhatu, which is empty of intrinsic nature, it is suitable to be called form that has become the object of eye consciousness. Similarly, although the essence of form, which is empty of intrinsic nature, is indeed the nature of form, that which has become the object of eye consciousness as the nature of form is not so.

<note>1) <term>Ghanavyuha Sutra</term> - page 7/b, Sutra section.</note>
<note>2) <term>Akshayamati Sutra</term> - page 12/b, Sutra section.</note>
<note>3) <term>Jnanavati</term> tenth chapter - page 5/b, Tantra section; teaching on emptiness. The translation differs slightly.</note>

<summary>The text clarifies the relationship between form and the dharmadhatu, noting that while form is an aspect of the ultimate nature, it is not grasped by ordinary consciousness.</summary>
<keywords>Dharmadhatu, Emptiness, Aggregates, Eye consciousness</keywords>
pages.128:
<header>Heart Sutra</header>

is so.

Therefore, if one posits that which is empty of the nature of form as form, then since there is nothing else observed as emptiness in that form which is to be emptied, it is taught that the emptiness of the dharmadhatu is not other than that form-to-be-emptied. It is stated, "Emptiness is not other than form." This means that just as that form is not other than being empty of intrinsic nature, that emptiness of intrinsic nature is not other than form.

Likewise, just as the emptiness of intrinsic nature is not other than form, its emptiness is also not other than form, because it is not observed as something else. This is the meaning. For example, it is just as it is not other than the liquid and the wood.

By these four lines of the sutra, it shows that the two truths have the same essence but different attributes. By doing so, it eliminates the two extremes of superimposition and denial regarding the objects of this profound path and also well explains the method of emptiness of those two. By teaching that form and the like are empty and not other than that, the extreme of superimposition is eliminated. By teaching that although empty of intrinsic nature, it is established in dependence upon water and birds <note>a metaphor for dependency</note>, and that this is not other than being empty of intrinsic nature, the extreme of denial is eliminated. Thus, this path is free from the extremes of superimposition and denial. As stated in the commentary on the <term>Pancavimsatisahasrika</term> <gloss>Sutra of Twenty-five Thousand Lines</gloss>: "Form itself is emptiness; emptiness itself is form." This teaches that phenomena and their emptiness are of one intrinsic nature. The former eliminates the extreme of permanence, and the latter eliminates the extreme of annihilation.

<note>1) Commentary on the <term>Pancavimsatisahasrika</term> - page 38, Wisdom section.</note>

<summary>This page explains the non-duality of form and emptiness, using the logic of the two truths to avoid the pitfalls of nihilism and eternalism.</summary>
<keywords>Two truths, Emptiness, Form, Extremes, Non-duality</keywords>
pages.129:
<header>The Essence of the Commentary: A Good Explanation</header>

It is as stated. Similarly, in the <term>Arya-nāmadheya</term> <gloss>Sutra of the Noble Name</gloss>: "Look! Just as form is not other, emptiness also is not other; form itself is emptiness, emptiness is form," and so on. Thus, this abandons the two extremes of positing emptiness and cutting it off.

In this context, Tibetan commentaries have greatly differing views. Since all are pathways of their own philosophical systems, there is not much disagreement, so I have not set them out here for analysis. In short, these are the profound and vast meanings of the precious <term>Prajnaparamita</term> <gloss>Perfection of Wisdom</gloss> sutras. Because their intended meaning is extremely profound and vast, it is impossible for any single commentary to clarify the meaning from all sides; it is extremely difficult. The difficult points of this must be explained as very profound.

This meaning is related to the aspects of meditation on the emptiness path and so forth. Regarding the aspects of the meditation on emptiness, the great omniscient <term>Mikyo Dorje</term> <gloss>the Eighth Karmapa</gloss> made another way of explaining these.

<note>1) <term>Arya-nāmadheya</term> - page 18/3, Wisdom section.</note>
<note>2) The <term>Three Hundred Verses</term> by <term>Mikyo Dorje</term> - in this context, he explains that form and the rest do not exist conventionally and that form is self-empty: "There is no emptiness apart from form, and no form apart from emptiness. The meaning of saying these two are of one nature is this: because form does not exist by its own nature, there is no emptiness apart from form; emptiness is shown to be emptiness because form is not truly present. Saying there is no form apart from emptiness refers to the conventional non-existence of form and the rest." (From the <term>Clarification of the Intent</term> by the Jetsun, page 100/b).</note>

<summary>The author addresses varying interpretations of the Heart Sutra within the Tibetan tradition, specifically citing the perspective of the Eighth Karmapa on the conventional and ultimate nature of form.</summary>
<keywords>Prajnaparamita, Mikyo Dorje, Conventional truth, Emptiness, Commentary</keywords>
pages.130:
<header>Heart Sutra</header>

Method of establishing emptiness from the two truths—above, by citing the sutra "Form is emptiness," etc., and showing that these two are dependent on one another, the meaning of establishing emptiness in the path and the objects of the path is this: form is empty of intrinsic nature. If there were a thing that is other than the form that is empty of intrinsic nature, that would be a view of being established by intrinsic nature. If that which is empty of intrinsic nature were completely separate from form, then that form would be entirely non-existent, like the horns of a rabbit, resulting in a view of annihilation.

Likewise, if the form and the emptiness of the dharmadhatu, which is empty of intrinsic nature, were one in the sense of being inseparable, then since form would become manifest, all ordinary beings would see the truth and quickly attain unsurpassable enlightenment. It is also clear that if they were not one but entirely separate, then for the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who reside on the great stages, all characteristics of volitions <term>samskara</term> <gloss>formations</gloss> would be objects of attachment and would have to be accepted as such. It would be impossible to attain full, perfect enlightenment. The reason for this is that the cause for proceeding to the state of an <term>Arya</term> <gloss>noble being</gloss> is the realization of the inseparability and single taste of volitions and the dharmadhatu, which is empty of intrinsic nature. As stated in the <term>Suvarnaprabhasa-sutra</term> <gloss>Sutra of Golden Light</gloss>:

"That which is the dharmadhatu is emptiness; it cannot be expressed as the five aggregates, nor can it be expressed as being the five aggregates. Why? If the dharmadhatu were the five aggregates, it would lead to a view of annihilation; if..."

<summary>The text explores the Middle Way path by rejecting the extremes of identity and difference between form and emptiness, emphasizing the necessity of their inseparability for the attainment of enlightenment.</summary>
<keywords>Two truths, Emptiness, Form, Dharmadhatu, Volitions, Enlightenment</keywords>
pages.131:
<header>The Essence of the Commentary: A Good Explanation</header>

"...if it were to become five or six, it would lead to a view of permanence," and so forth. Likewise:

"...Why? If these (the five aggregates and the dharmadhatu) were one, they would be different from the dharmadhatu. If they were the same, then ordinary beings would also see the truth of reality and attain the sorrowless state possessed of the unsurpassable truth of reality. Since that is the case, it is not logical that they are one. If one says they are separate, then all characteristics of the volitions of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas would be accompanied by attachment; thus, (those beings) would not be liberated from the shackles of afflictions and would not attain full, perfect, unsurpassable enlightenment. Why? Because all noble beings realize the volitions and the non-volitions as a specific truth; therefore, it is not asserted that they are different."

This is stated extensively. Similarly, the <term>Sandhinirmocana Sutra</term> <gloss>Sutra Explaining the Thought</gloss> also posits that if the two truths are not one in essence but are different, this is based on four logical refutations and the fact that they are not one because they are dependent. Based on eight types of logic, it establishes the two truths as different and based on their characteristics, it establishes how they are different.

<note>1) <term>Suvarnaprabhasa</term> - page 7/b, Tantra section, Beijing Narthang edition 10.</note>
<note>2) <term>Suvarnaprabhasa</term> - page 7/n, same edition.</note>

pages.132:
<header>Prajnaparamita</header>

Based on this, it is explained as a contradiction, as they are explicitly incompatible. By this method, the extremes of superimposition and denial are well eliminated, and the profound conduct is shown as the path of the Middle Way. As the master <term>Aryadeva</term> <gloss>Noble God</gloss> said in his presence:

"Because things transform,
They do not become annihilation.
Because things turn back,
They do not become permanence."

Therefore, because form and the rest become empty,
Form and the rest do not become permanent.
Because emptiness appears as form,
Form and the rest do not become annihilation.

This is the situation. In this context, the great <term>Simhamitra</term> made another way of explaining it: "There are two things regarding these phenomena that appear as form and the rest: the belief that the appearance is a real thing, and the belief in designated existence. The first position is held by the <term>Vaibhashikas</term> <gloss>proponents of great detail</gloss>, the Middle Way proponents, and the <term>Sautrantikas</term> <gloss>sutra followers</gloss>, etc. All of them explain that this form is empty of reality, like the child of a gandharva. The phrase 'Emptiness is form' shows that the form desired by the Vaibhashikas and the analysts is empty of its own essence. The appearance of the mind in the sutras is of the nature of consciousness; therefore, the object that appears as a vessel and the like is empty of the nature of the object itself. The meaning of the <term>Vijnanavada</term> <gloss>Mind-Only school</gloss> is that since it exists, form is other than emptiness..."

<note>1) <term>Catuḥśataka</term> <gloss>Four Hundred Verses</gloss> - Chapter 10, Verse 25.</note>

<summary>This page analyzes the Middle Way view of transformation and permanence, and introduces the interpretation of Simhamitra regarding the nature of appearances and the Mind-Only school's stance.</summary>
<keywords>Aryadeva, Middle Way, Emptiness, Vaibhashika, Vijnanavada, Form</keywords>
pages.133:
<header>The Essence of the Commentary: A Good Explanation</header>

...Thinking this, they [the sutras] refute it: "Form is not other than emptiness; emptiness is not other than form." This is what is refuted here. As it is said, "Thus, what appears as form and the like... is refuted." Such explanations appear extensively, so the material for analysis remains. Although it seems plausible to explain this by applying it to the meaning desired by the sutras and applying the subject matter to form, since the meaning of the sutras such as "Form is emptiness" applies to feelings and the rest just as it does to form, and since those appearances of the mind and the nature of the object cannot be distinguished as separate from the mind, it does not apply to feelings and the like.

"Form is emptiness"—with these words, the meaning of the sutra does not need to be transcended by the philosophical views of the two schools. It is not that it cannot be commented upon; rather, it is that those who assert these as their own system are excellent proponents of tenets of selflessness.

<term>Sautrantika</term> <gloss>sutra follower</gloss> system: In the Sautrantika system, the meaning of the sutra saying "Form is emptiness" refers to the atoms examined in the scriptures of other schools, and the matter included as form-substance; those are empty of intrinsic nature and lack intrinsic essence. Likewise, the "compounded" substance is born from the meeting of feelings with objects and sensory faculties, and the feelings and so forth that arise from that are also empty of intrinsic nature.

<note>1) <term>Panchen Shakya Chokden's</term> commentary - page 255, Wisdom section.</note>

<summary>The author concludes the commentary by examining the Sautrantika perspective on emptiness, particularly their view on atoms and compounded phenomena, and how these relate to the core statement that form is emptiness.</summary>
<keywords>Sautrantika, Emptiness, Atoms, Form, Intrinsic nature, Shakya Chokden</keywords>

The <term>halakhah</term> <gloss>legal ruling</gloss> is that they took for him, regarding that which he drew, the enjoyment of the wine for us; many souls are gathered, and according to the custom of the souls, he saw such and such, and accepted upon himself the wine for us. Moses, for they were acquired from the one, and every one of you shall come to me and show what they brought forth, and they acquired, and they shall divide before Moses, they are equal before him. From where is this? It is from that which is to be taken, a vessel that is made, for there is found one <term>shemerak</term> <gloss>a vessel for measuring grain/flour</gloss> which is sold for that servant, and for every soul and soul from his house. From that which is found, a <term>qasrak</term> <gloss>a specific dry measure</gloss> <term>shemerak</term> which is like that vessel, and it is called an <term>omer</term> <gloss>a unit of dry measure</gloss>. And every soul and soul from his house saw the servant, for there is a <term>qof</term> <gloss>letter Qof</gloss>, behold, it is a living thing, and if it is accepted to be acquired. And it is written: "An omer for a head, according to the number of your souls **all according to** the measure," it is written: "Evening, and you shall know that the Lord brought you out from the land of Egypt," and it is written: "And morning, and you shall see the glory of the Lord." 

Evening, and you shall know, how much they shall know? These, so shall you see, every day there are found burdens received in the <term>pira</term> <gloss>a specialized vessel/measure</gloss> to arouse <term>chesed</term> <gloss>loving-kindness</gloss> in the world. And at that time that there is evening, this hangs in the world, and we have established that at such a time the afternoon prayer was established. What is it expressing? "Evening, the Lord... and you shall know that the Lord, etc." When this is aroused in the world, you shall know that at that time the <term>chesed</term> <gloss>loving-kindness</gloss> of the Lord is for you from pain. "And morning, and you shall see the glory of the Lord," for at that time <term>chesed</term> is aroused in the world, "and he shall give to you to eat **all existence**." What is written above? They are found upon the <term>pir</term> <gloss>measure/distribution</term>, at that time, it is stated: "Evening," for at that time <term>chesed</term> is aroused in the world, behold: "And you shall know that the Lord brought you out from the land of Egypt." You shall know that it is <term>chesed</term> that He did with you in your exodus from Egypt. "And morning, and you shall see the glory of the Lord." The glory of the Lord, truly, why? The soul, the Lord, your souls, the Lord, all the days upon the mouth of the Holy One, blessed be He, burdens. When you live a life... the world supports them, and transforms into mercies for this, just as it is stated: "Blow [the shofar]" for a measure, for the purpose of the measure, and the waters that are established to eat for the World to Come. And life... the world rivers, and it gathers until there is found in it one division, one part for the day, and one for the <term>aqotan</term> <gloss>the small/hidden part</gloss> of the King, in the holiness of the Sabbath. And that night is the union of the Matron with the King, and all two days are blessed, all so, and one alone, in the soul of a man. So, a man, when the way opens in his soul, for the Sabbath, because <term>chesed</term> is upon it, of all from above, and the blessing is not found upon the table of the poor. And that is the holy river of the afternoon, in the King, and their union. Therefore, the disciples of the sages study this, their union from Sabbath to Sabbath: "**Far is the Lord, He has given you the Sabbath.**" What is the Sabbath? The day of the daughter of two others, the all of the all of all those two others.

Rabbi Yissa said: And so also, the Congregation of the Sabbath is called Sabbath, because she is his partner, and this is the bride, and it is written: "And you shall keep the Sabbath, for it is holy unto you, He has given to you and not to the rest of the nations." In it, and so in Israel, it is in it, and this is for <term>chesed</term>, mercies for the people who are complete. Concerning this it is written: "If you turn away your foot from the Sabbath, and do [my] statutes..."
