# And the Lord said to Moses,
"Pass on before the people, and take with you of the elders of Israel, and your rod with which you struck the Nile, take in your hand, and go. Behold, I will stand before you there on the rock in Horeb, and you shall strike the rock, and water will come out of it, and the people shall drink." And Moses did so before the eyes of the elders of Israel. And he called the name of the place Massah and Meribah, because of the contention of the children of Israel, and because of their testing the Lord, saying, "Is the Lord among us, or not?" Then Amalek came and fought with Israel in Rephidim. And Moses said to Joshua, "Choose for us men, and go out, fight with Amalek tomorrow; I will stand on the top of the hill with the rod of God in my hand." And Joshua did as Moses had said to him, to fight with Amalek, and Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill. And it was when Moses lifted his hand, Israel prevailed, and when he lowered his hand, Amalek prevailed. And the hands of Moses were heavy, and they took a stone and put it under him, and he sat on it, and Aaron and Hur supported his hands, one on this side and one on that side, and his hands were steady until the setting of the sun. And Joshua weakened Amalek and his people by the edge of the sword. And the Lord said to Moses, "Write this as a memorial in a book and put it in the ears of Joshua, for I will surely wipe out the memory of Amalek from under the heavens." And Moses built an altar and called its name "The Lord is My Miracle." And he said, "Because the hand is on the throne of God, a war for the Lord against Amalek from generation to generation."

<margin>Rabbi Hiyya opened: "The angel of the Lord camps around those who fear Him and delivers them." Blessed are the righteous, for the Holy One, blessed be He, is in desire [of them] more than everything. Come and see how guilty the people of the world are, who go and transgress above; support for them is <term>tzedek</term> <gloss>justice</gloss> and <term>chesed</term> <gloss>loving-kindness</gloss> from every place. For it is taught: "For not Isaac..." The Holy One, blessed be He, did not ask of him, once He considered him for the Holy One. What is written? "And Amalek came, etc." A serpent, a dark thought, I know this. He sought, he split for him, and praised him, and incensed him, and the Holy One, blessed be He, did not ask of him. As they said, a serpent and he cut upon it, he considered, I know, his hand, and he received. What is written? "And [they] became heavy and he could not." And for this, the Holy One, blessed be He, did not ask of him. He strayed, blasphemed, and cursed, and saw: "Who is the Lord that I should listen to His voice?" And the Holy One, blessed be He, did not ask of him, even though he defiled the throne, for it is written: "A prince and a fool..." The Lord's terror was, and so in every place. And the Holy One, blessed be He, sought the vengeance of the righteous more than everything. Here, Moses, Moses, and the voice went up before Him, He was roused to seek vengeance. And not so? Even "Pass on before the people and the elders..." from... to go, to accept. And is it in his authority to establish? For Him, in His authority. "And your rod with which you struck the Nile," a rod, because it was refined in miracles, and supports the strength, to send to the waters with it, the first... as it is stated: "The way of a serpent upon a rock." ...and so then the gate, take and go. Here, as it is written: "Behold, I will stand before you there on the rock in Horeb, and you shall strike the rock, etc." A rock, just as you say: "The Rock, His work is perfect." And we learned: Moses knew how the serpent stands upon a rock, and takes the law... Rabbi Yehuda: For he should be silent... and so it is written: "And you shall strike the rock for your salvation..." and from the right... and truly this is how it is, for there is no name from those holy names of the Holy One, blessed be He, that does not do miracles and powers, and encompasses all, for He is the secret of the worlds, like that which comes out here from the waters. Rabbi... so here it is written: "The Rock, the Rock, and water comes out from the source of the heavens..."</margin>
pages.125: to the strength of the waters of Solomon, as it is written: "To water the garden." And the cloud is removed and is found, for the <term>maski</term> <gloss>the abundant/thickening</gloss> of <term>gevurah</term> <gloss>power/strength</gloss> is found. And because of this, the rock is strong, and finds the [attribute of] God, this is the illumination of <term>chesed</term> <gloss>loving-kindness</gloss>, and strikes... the world, for he is the illumination to the world. "**Behold, all these** [are] waters without a source." Behold, the consideration and the acceptance of the law in the place of waters was <margin>Do not give water</margin> from <term>gevurah</term> <gloss>power/strength</gloss>, and this is the sign and the business of the acceptance. And for this, the Sabbath of the generation, and the Holy One, blessed be He, said: <term>Chesed</term> <gloss>loving-kindness</gloss> for free, waters, and it implies that [He] reverses the language of the creators... and made rain of Solomon, a pious one, waters, scattering downwards. And what is the name downwards? A rock, as it is written: "And you shall strike among them water from the rock." And what does it bring out? Look, a rock, waters in the going... of the world. **Wine, Chesed.** It is written: "The Rock, His work is perfect," and it strikes, it means perfect, the pious one, as it is written: "Work" <margin>even if it reverses the rock</margin> to perform the work, perfect. And it strikes, he is <term>chesed</term>, as it is written: "Walk before Me and be perfect." And this is the reversal of the flint rock, it means perfect, the work, and this is the pious one. At the time that this is turned, the Rock, perfect work, at the time that <term>chesed</term> is, delight after delight, Moses. And because he brought out waters in this [way], the Rock, in the error of Moses, was not turned as it was previously in him. And who is delighted? Moses, and he said: "The Rock that bore you, you have forgotten," meaning, you acquired it, Moses, for he is in the existence of the building, so for him <term>chesed</term>, perfect. Now, and the rock was made nothing, what was not in his days, your hand, meaning, your world. **Behold, all these**, [is] a strike, as it is written: "Is the Lord among us, or not?" And in their judgment were the foundations that they did not know a word of this. They saw the <term>Shekhinah</term> <gloss>divine presence</gloss> before them, and the burning cloud upon them, that they concealed... and they see, "Is the Lord among us, or not?" The cloud that is the splendor of the glory that shone upon them, the sea, and the smoke, distant, present upon the sea. What is his name? Why, Ezekiel, son of Buzi. And they are found, the business and the observation, "Is the Lord among us, or not?" Not so, heaven forbid! But they heard from the Ancient of Days, the hidden one of all hidden things, of the stature, there is nothing, and between the small, and between the small, the faces. And concerning this it is written: "Is the Lord among us, or not?" Even this they said: "Is the Lord among us, or not?" If it saw, it was delighted, but they made a separation, and made in the testing, as it is written: "And because of their testing the Lord," they said, "If it sees, we shall ask with desire, and if it sees, we shall ask with desire <term>chesed</term> immediately." Then Amalek came. **Rabbi Yossi opened:** It is found the seed of the son of waters, and they did not see delight, how much water and revealed... <margin>waters are found, the righteous</margin> they are Israel, who have none. And the cloud upon the waters, as it is written: "And they traveled there upon the waters." They were the clouds of the [Divine] Attribute, that the [Divine] Attribute has, it has to accept, and he saw upon the pool, and it is strong, and the acceptance that is found, food without [delay], and he is filled with <term>chesed</term> in the ten scales that are found all the days of Amalek. And seventy names, visions, the total, and the return are found in the body that is the Holy One, and they are the seventy branches surrounding them, and this is what is written: "And they came to Elim, and there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees, and they camped there upon the waters." And it has been stated and established, the prophecy downwards, a strike: "And they camped there upon the waters." This is in the time that it sat upon those waters that are the branches that are seen.

distant, the bitter waters, and until there is found his seed upon all waters, "sending out the feet of the ox and the donkey." There is no word that shall go out to freedom like the dawn of my people, and the investigation of the ox and the donkey, and this is what is written: "And I had an ox and a donkey," because in the garden, he is free in the whispers, and in the whisper of the priests and the <term>tannaim</term> <gloss>sages of the Mishna</gloss>, and in the whisper to the companion to the heel, as it is stated: "My secrets to me," and one to be stated, and his spreading and selling, sending the feet, etc., because above upon them, behold, "sending out the feet of the ox and the donkey." The Holy One, blessed be He, will be... and it is taught: "The Lord will arise," for they merit to change evil things, for when the courtyard is checked from the jaw, we see. And when they are mated as one, they cannot stand in them, from their side comes the hardening of them, distant, the dog, the peel/husk from them. Behold, and whoever comes to [the house of the Lord]... the dog, and stealing... I said, "Well, in us," heaven forbid them, even with the ox... and the dog, immediately, "Then Amalek came."

### Then Amalek came. Rabbi Yehuda: "The first of the nations is Amalek." And is Amalek the first of the nations? And were there many nations and languages in the world before Amalek came? Even so, Ishmael and Moab went out, who were crushed, and their heat fell upon them, for the nations from the depths of the field, behold, "nations shall cover," and there was no one who was not afraid of their superior powers, and Amalek did not fear, behold, "and did not fear God," and he hastened, and swept, and there was, "and did not fear God," from your drawing near. And Amalek, "the first of the nations is Amalek," that came to the world, an evil war. Amalek was, and because of this I said, "What for a memory?" As it is written: "For I will surely wipe out the memory of Amalek," and it is written: "You shall wipe out the memory of Amalek," and this is, "I said, what for a memory?" His masculinity is required for him, even though this is the Holy One, blessed be He, and he destroyed to him, meaning, until to accept, [it] shall be, [to] investigate to him, as it is written: "I will surely wipe out," **one** to the evening, and one to the eternity, and this is the work, and He did with them <term>chesed</term> <gloss>loving-kindness</gloss> to open to them, immediately, the Holy One, blessed be He, did not leave [them], as it is written after it, "Then Amalek came." **One vessel opened:** "An evil sickness under the sun, etc." Many people are dull of heart, because they do not look into the Torah. pages.14:
<margin>1613</margin>
to be able to hide a matter of which he was already doubtful; he understood immediately that this journey was intended to bring the *Portuguese* into his kingdom from *India*, that they would make themselves masters of it, and force him to embrace the *Catholic Religion*: upon this, he summoned the Great Men of his court and very secretly shared his thoughts with them; they all agreed that one should not allow the *Ambassador* and me to take this road that we had in mind, as it was the direct one, and that we should be made to take another and very inconvenient route, by many detours and through the Land of *Baly*.

<margin>Were forced to take an arduous detour.</margin>
After many arguments back and forth, he finally said to us in conclusion that he would never let us pass along the road we intended, but indeed through *Baly*, to which we had to settle; for we were determined to continue this endeavor.

<margin>The Kingdom of *Baly*.</margin>
*Baly* is a *Kingdom* that formerly belonged to the *Empire of Ethiopia*; but the *Galles* and *Muslims* possess it at present; it borders on the *Empire of Adel*, and it lies to the East of the *Empire of Narea*. From this, I could easily deduce that I could not complete this journey, and that after I had encountered all these difficulties in the lands of the *Emperor*, I had even greater ones to expect in the lands of the *Kaffers*, who have no other *Law* than their own advantage; nevertheless, considering that it was for the service of *God*, I took the road to *Baly*, trusting myself to His mercy.

<margin>Setting out on the way.</margin>
The *Ambassador* and I, leaving the court of *Narea*, took our way *Eastward*, and arrived on the first day at the place where the *Captain* was, whom the *Benero* had appointed as our *Guide*; in the beginning, he received us quite well, hoping to get a fine gift from us; but that which we presented to him
pages.15:
<margin>1613</margin>
did not correspond to his hope and expectation, and for that reason, he let us wait 8 days for him, after which he gave us 80 men to escort us to the borders of the Kingdom of Narea; with this escort we traveled
<margin>Arriving in a desolate land.</margin>
4 long days through a desolate and deserted land, owing to the raids of the Galles; our escort returned from there, and as the road we still had to cover was very dangerous, we let some scouts go ahead of us to give us a signal as soon as they spotted Galles from afar, so that we might have time to go and hide in the bushes.

At noon we began to climb down a very high and rugged mountain, and the Envoy of Gingiro told us that before we proceeded to climb down, we must hide until evening so that we could pass at night the fields in which the Galles grazed their cattle.

<margin>A very bad road, struggling very miserably.</margin>
At 4 o'clock in the afternoon we set out on the road, under the cover of a dense rainstorm which drove the Galles to their huts, but which also soaked us weary travelers and caused us to suffer much cold. Our worry and anxiety redoubled when night came, because the thicket through which we passed was very dense near the ground, difficult to get through by day, and even worse by night. We lit a fire in the forest and chewed a little roasted barley, which is the common food of travelers of that land, and the next day very early, after we had climbed down a steep mountain, we came to the River Zebée.

<margin>Crossing a very dangerous bridge.</margin>
This stream runs faster than the Nile, and at the place where we had to cross it, it made a terrifying noise, falling from a mountain between very sharp cliffs, between which the water shattered into foam.
pages.16:
<margin>1613</margin>
the bridge, over which we were forced to pass such swift and terrifying currents, was a piece of wood; it went across the river notwithstanding that it was remarkably wide, and the height of this bridge was so great that when one looked down from it, one discovered nothing but an abyss; the great length of the piece of wood caused it to tremble under the feet of our people, and yet everyone wanted to cross it first; for as soon as one is on the other side of this river, one no longer has to fear the Galles, for whom the fear was so great that it numbed all other fears. We thanked God on the other side of the bridge that He had delivered us from the bloodthirsty hands of the Galles; we could not let our mules go over this bridge, so we left them there that night on the bank of the river with 2 men to guard them, with orders to cross the bridge if the Galles came and to break it down behind them; but the next day 2 inhabitants of the land showed them a ford where they still got them across with great difficulty.

<margin>Obtaining an audience with the King of Gingiro.</margin>
The Ambassador arrived shortly thereafter at a dwelling from which we made our arrival known to the King of Gingiro, and we asked him for permission to offer the letters which we had to present to him on behalf of the Emperor of Ethiopia; but this King, being besides very much addicted to his sorcery, made us wait there 8 days, at the end of which we received permission to come to his court, where we arrived in one day; we found this monarch ready to receive us, sitting, or rather enclosed in a cage; for it was a kind of cage or coop of about 25 hand-breadths high and 30 wide; it was round on top, having
pages.17:
<margin>1613</margin>
the shape of a wheel; the King sat on a carpet which was spread out on this wheel; all his Courtiers stood below at this throne, where he gave the audience; he was dressed in a very fine cloth, the whiteness of which made the blackness of his face stand out more, in which one did not otherwise see those features that one notices in the Kaffers. He asked immediately for the letter from the Emperor; he climbed down from his throne to come get it, asked after how he was doing, and climbed back onto his throne,
<margin>Who reads the letter from the Emperor.</margin>
after which he read the letter and spoke for some time with us through an interpreter, to whom, as often as the Emperor or the King said something to be told to us, the interpreter kissed the tips of his fingers, and after he had bowed to the ground, he went to interpret it to me, who was at some distance from the throne, and when he had to bring the answer from me back to the King, he used the same ceremony first; the conversation lasted a long time. Finally, the King let it be said to me and the Envoy that we should go and rest a while, and that the essence of the Emperor's letter consisted of this: that he would certainly welcome us and have us escorted with a good guard to the borders of his Kingdom; that he (said he) very much wished to do.

The next day I presented some Gifts to the King; he showed much pleasure in them, as they were a rare thing in that land. As I stood ready to depart from there, the King sent me, in consideration of my gift, a young daughter of one of the Great Men of his Kingdom to serve me as a slave; I excused myself from receiving her, saying that I was by no means accustomed to carry women with me; the King took satisfaction in the difficulty I made and sent
pages.18:
<margin>1613</margin>
<margin>And a beautiful Mule.</margin>
to me a slave, whom I also accepted, not with the thought of getting any service from him, but rather in the hope of baptizing him; he also gave me a beautiful mule, which came in very handy for me on the journey; as well as people to help us cross the flood **Zebée** again and from there to travel to the Kingdom of **Cambate**.

<margin>Strange kind of ferrymen.</margin>
We departed for that purpose from the court of the King of **Gingiro** and arrived that same day at the bank of the River **Zebée** to cross it; the people that the King had given us, being very skilled at this type of crossing, made a device (**Machine**) that was not much safer than the piece of wood; they slaughtered a cow and put the luggage in the hide, which was to serve two purposes: one to get across, the other to serve as ballast for the **Ship** that they made from the hide of this cow, sewing it shut tightly, then they blew it up stiff, and then fastened 2 pieces of wood or sticks to it, like those of a sedan chair; 4 **People** went to sit on these sticks, 2 in front and 2 behind this raft-work; one forbade them to move, and they arranged them to be of equal weight so that they kept this strange vessel in an even balance: in front of it swam a brave swimmer, who was very well experienced in this art, who had a rope around his body that was also fastened to the equipment, with which he pulled it forward; 2 other swimmers pushed it forward from behind as well; an entire day is spent with this crossing.

<margin>River Zebée.</margin>
<margin>The Kingdom of Gingiro described.</margin>
The Stream **Zebée** surrounds almost the entire Kingdom of **Gingiro** and makes it like a half-island, as one sees in the map of **Ethiopia**, and from there it goes to lose itself in the Sea toward the coast of **Melinde**.

This Kingdom is small; the inhabitants are
pages.19:
<margin>1613</margin>
black, like the Kaffers, but they do not have the facial features like them; they are, like all Heathens, very inclined toward Sorcery, and they have such uncommon customs and habits that I will undoubtedly deserve pardon for having described them.

<margin>Custom of those of Gingiro.</margin>
Gingiro means an Ape or a Monkey, and truly the black color of this monarch, his gestures, face, and manners were entirely equal to those of these animals; these people also have that of the Apes, that they kill their Kings and those of their people who come wounded from the battle; because, they say, that they should rather die than maintain their lives while bearing such marks of reproach for their advantages.

<margin>Which are very ridiculous.</margin>
But although these Kings sitting thus on their <term>Jucquoir</term> <gloss>throne</gloss>, like an owl on a stool, resemble Apes or Monkeys quite nicely, they are nonetheless of an elevated mind and a very sharp understanding; when the King is to go out of his Palace, it is such early in the morning before sunrise; and if it happens that the sun is up before he is out, he keeps himself locked in his Palace that whole day, does not go to the Throne to give audience, nor does he give any order to anyone, because, they say, that 2 Suns cannot endure each other in the world at one time; and because he does not want to grant that precedence to the sun, he avenges himself for it the next day and goes out before the sun is up.</margin>

<margin>Wonderfully strange ceremonies in the election.</margin>
The ceremonies that they observe to elect their Kings are likewise entirely uncommon: they wind the corpse of their dead King in precious fabrics and then put it so into the hide of a cow that has been freshly skinned: immediately, all those who might stand for the crown, like the children of the deceased and the Princes of the blood, go and hide themselves in a
pages.20:
<margin>1613</margin>
desolate forest and behave as if they wanted to flee that honor which they long for; the electors, whom they consider to be great Sorcerers, hold council, go forest-ward, seek the chosen one, and by devilish art make a shape of a Bird of Prey as large as an Eagle, which they call *Liber*, descend; this bird flies with a great scream to the place where the one who is chosen is; the electors also go there immediately and they find him surrounded by Lions, Tigers, Snakes, Panthers, and other similar beasts, which they cause to come around this newly chosen Monarch through Sorcery, who protects and defends himself like a mad Bull against those who want to take him along; he hurts and sometimes even kills them; for those who seek him do not leave him until they have gotten him and have led him along with power and force; leading him along thus, one must fight with the people of a clan who, for a long time, have claimed to have the right to set the chosen Monarch on the Throne; the strongest or the victors have this privilege, which gives them a good share in the favor of the new *Gingiro*.

<margin>As also in the coronation of a King.</margin>
The ceremony of the coronation is to bring the King into the Palace and place him under a tent: On the 7th day after the death of the last King, the Sorcerers bring a worm, which they say came from the nostrils of the dead one, which worm they wrap in a cloth of silk fabric, and the new King pulls the head off it with his teeth; that having been done, they bury the dead King, after they have carried him through the sown fields, which they beg him to be willing to bless: arrived at the burial place of the old Kings, which is in a small grove, they dig a hole in the earth and lay him in it without covering, but he remains exposed to the air,
pages.21:
<margin>1613</margin>
because, they say, that the earth is not worthy to cover the body of their King, who in greatness does not yield to the Sun, and also for that purpose, so that the Heaven might serve as a more glorious Grave-site. On the day of the funeral, they slaughter many cows by the grave, so that the blood of the same drips onto the corpse of the King; they continue to kill a head of cattle there daily as long as the new King is alive, which is to the great advantage of their Priests, or rather of their Sorcerers, who indeed let the blood of the cow-beast run into the grave, but indeed provide their tables with that which remains over.

To come to the new King, while he bites the head off the worm, the people make a cry of joy and cheers to his praise, wishing him a long life; the Feast ends after they have placed him on that construction of a Throne described by us above; for the new King immediately has everyone brought who were favorites of his predecessor, saying to them: that
<margin>Those who served with the murder-death of the previous King were locked up.</margin>
*inasmuch as they were such strong friends of his during his life, it was also fair that they accompany him in the other World, so that they might be able to continue their services,* and he has them all have their necks broken under this pretext; he chooses others again, fills the State-offices that are vacant, and that does not prevent these first and most important positions from being highly coveted, and it makes the Courtiers have very great interest in the preservation of their Prince.

At the time of the election, they put all the houses in which the deceased King has lived, with all his household effects and tools, without excluding anything, however precious it may be, into the ash and coals; they do the same when any special or common person dies,

and forty-nine, in which the venerable father Friar Luis de Villalpando was elected <term>custodio</term> <gloss>custos or guardian of a Franciscan custody</gloss>, exactly one year after the Indians in Maní had intended to burn him along with his companion. The <term>definidores</term> <gloss>councillors of the order</gloss> were the same father <term>custodio</term> as the first, Father Friar Lorenzo de Bienvenida as second, Father Friar Francisco Navarro as third, and Father Friar Miguel de Vera as fourth. Through this same roll, it appears that the convent in the city of Mérida already had a name, its elected guardian being Father Friar Juan de la Puerta, as referred to: that of Campeche, its guardian Father Friar Diego de Bejar; that of Maní, guardian Father Friar Juan de Albalate; that of Cunkal, guardian the venerable father <term>custodio</term>; and that of Ytzamal, guardian the <term>definidor</term> Father Lorenzo de Bienvenida. Not only in this capitular roll are the guardians assigned, but also the companions who were to live with them in each convent: a custom that was observed in this province until the provincial chapter held in the year 1603, from when it seems to have been left to the discretion of the reverend provincial fathers to assign the companions and residents of each convent, according to the need that arises therein. The chapter was presided over by the very Reverend Father Friar Francisco de Bustamante, as is evident from the roll signed with his name and sealed with the seal of his office as commissioner general. This was like the birth of this holy province of San José of Yucatan, for which reason I have written of it with such singularity, in which, with the five convents that have been named, it remained in the form of a <term>custodia</term> <gloss>custody</gloss>, subject while it was one to that of Mexico.

Although Father Friar Juan de la Puerta remained elected guardian of the convent of the city of Mérida in the chapter, since the religious were still so few for such a number of towns as existed in Yucatan, and since for the entire province of Valladolid, so populous and with such a great crowd of people, a foundation of a convent had not been able to be made, it was discussed that a religious of the province should go as a representative to Spain, representing the need that there was for them, and it seems they agreed that the most suitable person for a matter
pages.452:
<header>LIBRO QUINTO. 435</header>

of such importance was Father Friar Juan de la Puerta.
The <term>Adelantado</term> <gloss>governor of a frontier province</gloss> was of the same opinion as the religious, and thus he gave him letters for the Emperor and the Royal Council of the Indies, in which he signified the great fruit being made in the conversion of these Indians and the urgent need they had for the help of ministers.
Father Friar Juan de la Puerta received the dispatches that the province and the <term>Adelantado</term> gave him, and granting him Father Friar Angel Maldonado as his companion, he went to Mexico, where the very Reverend Father Commissioner General, who had great satisfaction in his virtue and prudence, confirmed the office of representative that the province had given him, and entrusted him with other business, for which he gave him instructions and sufficient papers, with which he went to Spain in the fleet of the following year, 1550. I have not found the result of this journey; it only seems to me that this religious was later elected bishop of this bishopric, as was said in the fourth book.

->An order is given to take residency, and to remove the Indians from<-

Nothing notable had happened regarding the secular state until this time: but as in the new laws that had been given for these kingdoms, it was ordered that no governor or royal official should hold Indians in <term>encomienda</term>, and the <term>Adelantado</term>, as a conqueror, retained his, a new order came for them to be taken from him. Father Lizana says that this year of forty-nine, the <term>licenciado</term> <gloss>holder of a law degree</gloss> Herrera came from Spain (with Father Albalate, who brought the religious), assigned as an <term>oidor</term> <gloss>judge of a royal audiencia</gloss> of the Royal <term>Audiencia</term> <gloss>high court</gloss> of Mexico, and that he visited this land and held the <term>residencia</term> <gloss>judicial review of an official's conduct</gloss> of the <term>Adelantado</term>. I persuade myself that the one who held his <term>residencia</term> was the <term>licenciado</term> Santillan, an <term>oidor</term> who resided in the same <term>audiencia</term>, because in a royal provision of the sixteenth day of the month of June of the same year of one thousand five hundred and forty-nine, he is given faculty to
pages.453:
<header>HISTORIA DE YUCATAN.</header>

come to Yucatan, remove the Indians he held, and investigate other excesses that the <term>Adelantado</term> was said to have committed during the time of his government, so that if the other gentleman had been holding his <term>residencia</term>, it seems there would have been no need for this new commission. In it, it is stated as a preamble that, in fraud of the new laws, many Indians were held in <term>encomienda</term> under the names of the wives, sons, and daughters of the governors and royal officials, with which they enjoyed the Indians as if there were no such prohibition of laws, descending to the singular motive of this commission, it is said:

> "And we are informed that, as he wished, although it was provided by our said Royal <term>Audiencia</term> that the said Indians should be taken from the wife, sons, and daughters of the said <term>Adelantado</term> Montejo, it had not been done nor fulfilled: rather, they say that the greater part of that land is with the said <term>Adelantado</term> Montejo and his wife, and Don Francisco de Montejo, and his wife, and a stepson of his, the son of his wife, and for this, many frauds and cavils have been committed. Especially they say that, having given a provision so that the Indians might be taken from the said <term>Adelantado</term> and his sons and daughters, he arranged with the one who carried it to hand it over to him, so that it could not be used, and another provision that he carried, in which it was ordered that they should not interfere in the jurisdiction of the town of La Victoria of the Rio de Grijalva in order to collect from the Indians, who were ordered to be taken from him, all the tributes for a year in advance, which belonged to us. And that the title with which he had made them collect the said tributes had been by saying that he had given them to his nephew, and for that he had shown deposit certificates with the date of them from time back. And that to do the aforementioned, he had the provisions detained. And the fraud that the said governor was committing against us and our royal treasury having been seen by an ordinary mayor of the said town of La Victoria, he and a councilman, who was called Alonso Bazan, as our officials, seized the person who was collecting the tributes for the said <term>Adelantado</term>, and what had
pages.454:
<header>LIBRO QUINTO.</header>

proceeded from them, and they put it in the chest of the three keys. And that, being known by the <term>Adelantado</term>, he went to the said town with an armed hand, after the said provision had been notified to him, so that he would not be judged, and he imprisoned the said mayor and councilman and took them as prisoners to Yucatan. And he newly created other officials who were his servants to have charge of our treasury, and he procured that they should hold him as governor therein, in order to take revenge on the officials and give the Indians he held to persons of the said town by paying for them; which he did, in that he sold some native Indians for interests they gave him. And that likewise we are informed that the said <term>Adelantado</term> Montejo is making a sugar mill in Champoton, and for it he has taken and is taking the land from the Indians of that province, and he took their farmlands from them, the said towns being mine, agreeing to relieve the said tributaries in occupying them in mercantile endeavors. And that above all the aforementioned, the said <term>Adelantado</term> has not given a <term>repartimiento</term> <gloss>allocation of indigenous labor</gloss> to any conqueror, but to all his relatives and wives and sons, to stepsons and grandsons: they say not only to the legitimate ones, but to the bastards. And they say that he made the Indians of Champoton and Campeche go to war and make slaves, and thus they say that many of them were made, likewise as women, against our laws made by us, and that they are sold against all reason and justice, which is the cause of the depopulation of the said provinces. And that the said <term>Adelantado</term>, not content with all the aforementioned things, makes houses, estates, and mercantile endeavors in the said provinces with our Indians, not being able to nor ought to do so, and fatiguing them and making them work excessively. And that likewise other persons have done and committed many and grave crimes in the said provinces worthy of prison and punishment, to which it was fitting to provide and remedy as an important matter."

Such was the report that had been made to the Emperor in the Royal Council of the Indies regarding what had happened in Yucatan; but it appears to have been excessive, for regarding what is said therein about the <term>Adelantado</term> not having given Indians in <term>encomienda</term> to any conqueror,
pages.455:
<header>HISTORIA DE YUCATAN.</header>

but only to his relatives, there are still to this day to the contrary very many deposit certificates that were exhibited as soon as they finished subjugating them, which his descendants observe originally for the greater qualification of their merits in the conquest. Regarding making slaves of the Indians and selling them, what was happening has already been said and remains written in the third book. But as there is never a lack of someone to complain (or it is very rare) about those who govern, it had happened at present, and the retention of the Indians that the <term>Adelantado</term> enjoyed as a conqueror joining with it, it having to be taken from him by the general laws, and the Emperor wishing to certify the truth, this royal provision was dispatched, which by its context appears to be one of <term>residencia</term>, and in it, immediately after the related report, it is said:

"And seen by those of our Council of the Indies, wishing to provide for it, trusting in you, that you are such a person that you will guard our service and the right to each one of the parties, and that with all care and diligence you will intend to understand what by us may be ordered and committed to you: it is our mercy and will to entrust and commit it to you, and by these presents, we entrust and commit it to you. Because we order you that as soon as you see this, you go with the rod of our royal justice to the said provinces of Yucatan and Cozumel, and above all things, take the Indians that the said <term>Adelantado</term> Montejo might have, and those of his wife and sons, and those of our officials of the said provinces: except for the male sons to whom such Indians were entrusted, the such sons already being married and living on their own at the time they were entrusted to them. This, thus do and fulfill, even if the <term>encomiendas</term> of the such wives and sons and daughters have been made before the new laws or after. And because we have provided for the said new laws or ordinances for the good of the conquerors and their sons, so that they may live and remain in those parts, that the Indians that were taken by disposition of the said new laws and ordinances be placed in the Royal Crown, and from their tributes
pages.456:
<header>LIBRO QUINTO. 439</header>

let it be given for the sustenance and entertainment of the said conquerors, and if they are dead, to their sons who do not have <term>repartimientos</term>: you will provide that the tributes that the towns of Indians yield, which you will thus take from the said <term>Adelantado</term> and his wife, sons and daughters, and from our officials of the said provinces of Yucatan and Cozumel, in the meantime that we provide what is convenient for the perpetuity of those provinces, you will distribute among the conquerors who did not have a <term>repartimiento</term>, and among their sons and some good settlers. This, thus do and fulfill, notwithstanding any supplications that may be interposed against this our letter. You will inform yourself how and in what manner such things contained above in this our letter have happened, and what frauds have been committed in our royal treasury, and what persons did and committed the aforementioned, or any thing or part of it, and of the other crimes that have been committed in the said province, and by whose order they did it, and who gave them counsel, favor, and help for it, and those whom you find culpable therein, seize their bodies, and thus imprisoned, after calling and hearing the parties whom it concerns, you will do justice over it by your sentence or sentences, whether interlocutory or definitive, etc." And afterwards it continues by placing all the clauses that are customary to place in similar commissions. It only singularizes that for the execution, as much of what is contained as of any other thing that may be committed to him, he should assist for the time that may be assigned by the viceroy Don Antonio de Mendoza.

Through this order, the time arrived for the <term>Adelantado</term> to give his <term>residencia</term> for the time he had governed Yucatan in war and peace. The <term>oidor</term> who was to hold his <term>residencia</term> arrived in Campeche, and after the <term>Adelantado</term> was given notice of his arrival, he sent his son Don Francisco with other principal residents of the city of Mérida so that, in his name, they might bid him welcome and receive him. Having arrived in Campeche, they visited the <term>oidor</term>, who with many courtesies thanked the <term>Adelantado</term> for the one he had had by sending his son, and for the one that the other gentlemen had manifested by going to
pages.457:
<header>HISTORIA DE YUCATAN.</header>

visit him. They came together to the city of Mérida, and manifesting the superior order that the <term>oidor</term> carried, he was received into the exercise of his commission. He published the <term>residencia</term>, and in the interim that it was to be done, the <term>oidor</term> took the government of this land upon himself. Although there were those complaining of the <term>Adelantado</term>, the event was generally regretted by the religious, as well as by seculars and Indians, because he was a very gentlemanly person in his procedure and a noble person, a friend of the poor, benign, and endowed with many good qualities that made him lovable, even if he had some defects as a man: who is perfect in everything? It was already seen in the third book what the principal conquerors wrote about him and his son Don Francisco together in the <term>cabildo</term> <gloss>town council</gloss> to the Emperor, just after the city of Mérida was founded, when they dispatched the first representative general to the kingdoms of Spain.

CHAPTER XI.

->The Indians are taken from the <term>Adelantado</term>. He goes with his <term>residencia</term><-
->to Spain, and dies: and his successors are told.<-

The <term>residencia</term> of the <term>Adelantado</term> having been published, the administration of justice and government of Yucatan remained in the <term>oidor</term> who was executing it, in whose time it happened that some black slaves of the Spaniards fled to the mountains, and, joined by those who were walking about in revolt, a troop of up to twenty or more; they entered some towns of the Indians, to whom they did much evil and damage, taking from them what they could and committing other crimes that required an immediate remedy. So that this might have the end that was necessary, the <term>oidor</term> named the conqueror Alonso Rosado as captain and leader of the Spaniards, that they should seek them and bring them as prisoners, and if they did not surrender to imprisonment, they should use the last remedy, shooting them with arquebuses or killing them in any way that could be. Alonso Rosado went out with his people, and after suffering some hardships through the mountains, he caught sight of the fugitive blacks, who, finding themselves without arms and surrounded by the Spaniards who had them, surrendered and were brought as prisoners to the city of Mérida. Delivered
pages.458:
<header>LIBRO QUINTO. 441</header>

to the <term>oidor</term>, he put them in jail until they were punished judicially according to their crimes. The imprisonment of these blacks was considered a considerable service in this land; because, besides the damages that were avoided with it, a rumor that was already circulating was calmed: that some Indians were attempting to rebel against the Spaniards with the warmth and spirit that those slaves were giving them, fearful that they were going to fall into the hands of justice and be punished as they later were.

It also happened that many Indians from the southern part of this province, which they call the Sierra, had withdrawn to the interior of the land (which lies between this one and that of Guatemala), fleeing from the communication of the Spaniards and from Christian instruction. The <term>oidor</term>, considering the great disservice that was being done to God and the King with this flight, ordered Captain Francisco de Montejo, who, as was said, was [a captain] of the conquest, to enter through those unpopulated lands and try to attract them to the towns of their origin. That captain went out with people from the city and walked through the mountains and hamlets, gathering many Indians through peaceful means. Some were more than seventy leagues from the city and forty from the nearest settlement. Among these distant ones, the captain learned of a troop of Indians banded together, and not being able to go, he entrusted it to Alonso Rosado, one of those who were going with him, and who had previously imprisoned the blacks, giving him some Spaniards to go with him. They found the Indians, and he persuaded them in such a way that they gave themselves up in peace and he brought them to the captain. A very considerable number of Indians was gathered with this expedition, which was distributed to the towns of their origin, with which this land of Yucatan remained quiet for then. Both the one and the other is evidenced by the authentic proofs that were made and which I have read.

It is said that the time of the <term>residencia</term> lasted three months, in which the <term>oidor</term> ordered some things for the utility of the Indians and their good treatment, and for the increase of their Christendom. He reformed others regarding the Spaniards, who, as in newly founded republics

is what is not established. This is because those <note>referring to conceptual assertions of permanent substances</note> are not established as such. Similarly, the <term>puruṣa</term> <gloss>person/self</gloss> (of the Sāṃkhya school), the <term>vijñāna</term> <gloss>consciousness</gloss> (of the Vaiśeṣika school), and the <term>non-dual cognition</term> (of the Guhyasamāja school), and so forth—those that hold the nature of consciousness to be a permanent substance—are also not established by intrinsic nature and are empty. Thus, one must understand the meaning of "Form is emptiness; likewise, feelings, and so on."

Similarly, the meaning of "Emptiness is form" and so on means that form, which exists as a collection of sounds and coarse substances, is empty of being a permanent substance; it is not established as a permanent substance; it is empty of form that is aggregated by atoms of a permanent substance. It is impermanent. That which serves as the basis for the designation "form," such as form born from karma, is what is meant by "emptiness is form." From that form as well, the emptiness of form, which is asserted as the aforementioned substances or substances with parts, is not something other. This is the meaning of "Emptiness is not other than form." Likewise, the meaning of "Form is not other than emptiness" is that from that emptiness, the form—that which is born from karma—is not something other. This is the understanding of the tenets of the later <term>Sautrāntika</term> <gloss>sutra follower</gloss> school.

The system of one <term>Sautrāntika</term> <gloss>sutra follower</gloss> school: In the system of those [Sautrāntikas], since they accept cognition with aspects, they assert two things: the cognition that appears as the form itself, and the object. Those aspects of cognition are the emptiness of that form as a truly existent entity—

the meaning of "Form is emptiness." Even though the aspect of cognition itself is empty of form, since that which appears as form to it is indeed form, it is said that "emptiness is form." Since it does not make sense to think of form as something other than such form, and empty of form, it is said that "emptiness is not other than form." Because one cannot perceive a form other than that which appears as form in the apprehension of form, which is empty of the characteristics of form, it is said that "form is not other than emptiness." In this way, in the tenets of those sutras, it is not much observed that one interprets them into one's own system. That is because this "profound conduct" taught here is the mother of the noble reasoning. Even though it is considered the mother of reasoning from the perspective of the mind, it is not seen as impossible to apply to tenets as well.

The explanation based on the manner of <term>vijñapti</term> <gloss>consciousness-only</gloss>: The intent of the sutra saying "Form is emptiness" and so on is also explained according to the manner of consciousness-only by the great masters, relying on other sutras. In this system, the characteristics of all phenomena of the path are established as the characteristics of form. The intent of the Mother Sutras, which state that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature, is interpreted. Here, too, relying on the three types of "without nature" and the three types of form, the meaning of the four kinds of emptiness, beginning with "Form is emptiness," is explained for others. As it is said in the sutra:

"Brahmin, a bodhisattva who practices the Perfection of Wisdom and resides in the mastery of interpreting profound phenomena should know how to analyze the depth of form in three ways. Feelings and..." By this, here—
pages.136:
"Imagined form; this is dependent form; this is the form of suchness."

Thus, by relying on these three types of form, the first form is that which is grasped as a real object by childish beings; this is the imagined form, the form that becomes the object of consciousness appearing as an object. The imagined form <note>refers to the dependent nature</note> and the form that is free from the aspects of those two is the perfected form—this is suchness, which is called "the form of suchness."

Therefore, because the nature of dependent form is devoid of the characteristics of imagined form in all respects, it is empty of imagined form, and that emptiness is the meaning of reality itself. As it is said by the great chariot masters:

"What is the characteristic of emptiness? That which is not in it is what it is empty of—this is correctly seen." And, "What is not there? In the aggregates, elements, and sense-spheres, there is no permanent, stable, unchanging phenomenon, nor is there a self or what belongs to a self. In that way, they are empty."

As was said, here "Form is emptiness" means that the form which has the characteristic of dependent nature is devoid of those imagined forms, such as external objects. Therefore, it is empty of those.

Therefore, it is stated that "Form is emptiness." This eliminates the conceptual confusion of distraction and primarily teaches the antidote to the conceptual confusion of superimposition.

Because that very emptiness is perfected form, it is stated that "Emptiness is form." This covers the conceptual confusion of negation. If one thinks that since emptiness and form are distinct because their characteristics are incompatible, emptiness is one thing and form is another, this teaches the antidote to the conceptual confusion of empty-limit and empty-front. That form which has the characteristic of suchness and emptiness does not possess the characteristics of form. As it is said in the Perfection of Wisdom Sutra:

"Shariputra, form is separated from the nature of form." This is taught extensively. Likewise, in the sutra taught by Rab 'byor, it is said, "Even though the <term>dharmadhātu</term> <gloss>dharma-realm</gloss> exists in the realm of form, the <term>dharmadhātu</term> is not the characteristic of consciousness that perceives form."

Thus, one should not think that the form of emptiness or suchness is other than form. Because it is the suchness of form, it cannot be perceived as something other than the phenomenon of form; therefore, it is stated that "emptiness is not other than form." The phenomenon, which is form, is also the basis of that emptiness, and because it is the phenomenon of the form of suchness, it cannot be perceived as other than its own suchness, and because it is its nature, it is not other than emptiness.

<note>1) Twenty-thousand-line, page 146/3, Wisdom section, De-bstan.
2) Inexhaustible Intelligence Sutra, page 13b, Sutra section, De-bstan.</note>

that which is meant. The word "kyaṅ" <gloss>also/even</gloss> is used to include these concepts by the logic of the sutras.

These two teach the antidote to the conceptual confusion of distraction that grasps the phenomenon and the suchness as separate, even when they are not one. As it is said by the great charioteers:

"The teaching intended as an antidote to conceptualization in terms of method is: Form is not other than emptiness. Form is emptiness. Emptiness is form."

That is what was said. These are explanations that accord with the style of the system of sutra commentary. Although the great scholars of Tibet have interpreted this differently regarding the chapters of the commentaries on the Prajñāpāramitā, I have not included the extreme views here. Once the core meaning of these is understood, it is easy to master the way the intent of the Prajñāpāramitā Sutra is interpreted based on the three ways of lacking nature, such as the imagined characteristic being without self-nature. Therefore, one should learn this from various other texts that have commentaries. Here, because the intention is to explain the meaning of the core, that is enough.

The meaning of "Form is emptiness" and so on—

shows that form and the like taught [there] are without self-nature. The logic that establishes this and the manner in which those [logics] overcome wrong views and conceptual projections have been explained in the two stages of method. Even so, if one asks, "What is that self-nature which is said to be 'empty of self-nature'?" and "How should it be identified?", it must be established as established by self-nature. If it were established, it would be refuted by arguments such as "freedom from one or many" and the negation of the four extremes of production. The explanation that "it is without self-nature" is very clear in the Middle Way and Prajñāpāramitā texts. Although it is not taken directly from the <term>Pramāṇavārttika</term> <gloss>Commentary on Valid Cognition</gloss> of the venerable ones, those who wish to understand the texts through the books do not see the way to reach a definitive conclusion based on the aforementioned logical styles.

The ways of explaining the identification of that self-nature which is "empty of self-nature" depend on the various extreme views, as explained above. The explanation of the dependent nature is slightly subtle in the Mahayana scriptures and the commentaries of the great charioteers. The two questions are connected to both the sutras and the tantras, and because they are questions arising from the basis of purification of both, they are so.

Such a self-nature, as in the system of the Perfection of Wisdom, is the nature of form that appears due to the power of imprints of grasping at characteristics, which have been connected to the mental continuum of each sentient being since beginningless time. This is also like a mirage, an illusion, and a magical creation. The way to abandon that form is to remember that all modes of appearance are mixed. The appearance of form, which is spread by imprints of entities, the appearance which is spread by imprints of speech—that very appearance—
pages.140:
appears as the basis for the designation "form." It is the appearance that is born from imprints of grasping at a self, established as appearing in essence. It appears as if established from its own side without relying on others. Even when form does not appear, those three are mixed without distinction and appear as one. As long as the appearance of true existence is not refuted, all three—or the one—are refuted; if the one is not relinquished, all three remain as appearances. Therefore, the nature of form that corresponds to such an appearance is that self-nature which is meant by "empty of its own self-nature." When identifying such a nature of form and the like, as the great noble Aryadeva said—

And in his commentary: "An entity that does not possess the characteristics of the commentary-object, and which remains only as its own nature from causes, is that which is perceived as its self-nature. It is established as such because it is not mixed with other phenomena."

As it is said, the appearance that exists without relying on others is the way it appears established by self-nature, and its establishment as it appears is the way it is established as true and established by essence. As it is said in the same text:

"Whatever entity is from something else,"

As it is said, that is how it is. Therefore, when form appears as a phenomenon, there are three types of "that" in form. Although the two entities are objects of negation by logic, for those who hold form as true and established by self-nature, all three are acceptable because all three are confused appearances born from imprints of unreasonable thinking. At that time, the appearance of form born from the clarity of the self of the entity is an appearance of connection, so it is an object of negation by logic. The second appearance, born from the clarity of the self of verbal designation, is the basis for mixing with names and so forth, so there is no need to negate it by logic. Even if it is clear, it is an appearance like a magical illusion of dependent origination and possesses the mixing of names. Therefore, the appearance of true establishment, the appearance of establishment by self-nature, and the two foundations—the self of the phenomenon that grasps that nature and the object of conceptualization of improper mental engagement, and the grasping at a self—are the roots of cyclic existence, the roots of the unreasonable and of attachment and aversion. Therefore, since they are established and non-existent, they are objects of negation by logic. The conceptualization that grasps them, along with cyclic existence, should be negated. As the son of the Conqueror, Shantideva, said:

"How to see, hear, and know,
Here is not to be negated."

# CHAPTER ONE

The text was prepared on 396 folios: 47 quaternions and 2 quinions (<note>a gathering of 5 sheets</note>; ε fol. 27–36, ια fol. 77–86), which are numbered in the middle of the lower margin of the first folio of each. The quaternions (the quinion is ια) were written most elegantly by the first hand on polished parchment:

| | | |
|:---|:---|:---|
| β – δ | fol. 3–26 | p. 4, 12 – 81, 2 |
| ϛ – η | fol. 37–60 | p. 107, 4 – 186, 15 |
| ι – ιβ | fol. 69–94 | p. 211, 20 – 294, 13 |
| ιε – κγ | fol. 111–182 | p. 347, 17 – 171 C <note>of the Basel edition</note> |
| κε – κϑ | fol. 191–230 | p. 179 A – 216 D |

Thirty-five lines were written on each page of these quaternions. That they were once bound together in a single volume is shown by various evidence, including traces of dampness, which are particularly characteristic of these quaternions compared to the others. Furthermore, I will explain below (p. XI f.) that many quaternions never existed in this codex, nor in the exemplar from which it was copied, nor in the source of the exemplar itself.

The margins are adorned with the most copious and learned <term>scholia</term> <gloss>explanatory notes/commentaries</gloss>, the greatest part of which corresponds with the scholia of codices C or B.

The missing quaternions were supplied in the 15th century by one or two scribes. The former wrote the last two folios of quaternion α (folios 1v and 2 of the codex), quinion ε, and folios 61 and 62r of quaternion ϑ very carelessly. Or perhaps it was one and the same person who, having undertaken the task, performed it with the utmost negligence at the beginning, not undeservedly, as the preparation of folios 1 and 2, 27–36 (to the quinion ε) provided a specimen unworthy of any diligence whatsoever. However, the quaternions ϑ (the whole), ιγ, and ιδ flowed from a sufficiently good source, very similar to codex N, which I believe to be the Marcian codex 190, concerning which compare p. XVII f. To the same book perhaps belong the quaternions κδ (fol. 183–190) and λ–μϑ (fol. 231–387r, which are followed by the blank folios 387v–390), where signs of the <term>recensio uulgata</term> <gloss>common/vulgate revision</gloss> occur.

The interpolated codex exhibits five books of the commentary; but the pages of the good revision, which I judge to be most precious due to the scribe's great diligence, end on

The orthography of this book is generally the same as that of codex C: here and there it has preserved the mute iota (as on p. 112, 5 *syn-d-okei* <note>original: "συνδιῴκει"</note>, p. 117 in the Heraclitean scholium; in contrast, it is wrong on p. 144, 31 *metagein* <note>original: "μετάγειν"</note>). Moreover, in the last line, both the added movable <term>nu</term> <gloss>the letter 'n'</gloss> and the acute accent placed in place of the grave are due to the scribe's pen. Plato's lemmata, according to how many lines they extend, are usually marked with the symbol ˃; passages from poets are distinguished by ˃ or χ or ͂; notes rarely placed in the text to summon scholia are marked ÷ ÷, in the margin ※ or ◡; I have found corrections and additions from the margin joined to the text marked ∴.

Errors arising from <term>itacism</term> <gloss>a pronunciation shift making various vowels sound like 'ee'</gloss> are not lacking. The book returns to an exemplar that seems ancient, written in minuscules <note>see footnote 1</note>, since no certain traces of an uncial exemplar <note>see footnote 2</note> are found.

I believe that besides the beginning of the commentaries, the book *On the Soul of the World and Nature* was inscribed on the first quaternion of the archetype, prefixed as other codices also imitated the philosopher's own exemplar (cf. p. 1, 13 f).

The book belonged to Cardinal Bessarion <note>see footnote 3</note>, as the inscription on folio 1v teaches:

->*Of Proclus the Platonist on the Timaeus. Place 53, book of Bessarion, Cardinal of the Sabines, Nicene*<-

->*Proclus on the Timaeus, place 53, book of Bessarion, Cardinal of the Sabines.*<-

On the middle of folio 1r, a recent hand wrote *Ventiquattro—24.*

I collated these precious quaternions in Venice in the winter of 1899 to 1900, and in Munich in the summer of 1901.

**P** PARISIAN NATIONAL LIBRARY, Greek 1840 [MEDICEAN REG. 2213] (cf. H. Omont, *Inventaire* II p. 151), of very large format 33.6 x 23.6 cm, on paper, written in the 16th century, of 158 folios: nineteen quaternions and one ternion (δ̅), the numbers of which (α̅^ov β̅^ov γ̅^ov) were inscribed by the scribe himself in the lower margins, but have mostly perished due to the binding and cutting of the pages. Because the letters, especially at the beginning, are very small, the number of lines per page varies between 38 and 33. The text breaks off on folio 156r, with the line unfinished. A certain recent hand added in the lower margin: "about ten folios are missing," and wrote on folio 158v, different from this: "Of Proclus the Platonist Successor, three books on Plato’s Timaeus, of which the third is incomplete and nothing more." Another person, slightly later, noted *twenty-four gatherings* below that.

The codex contains the first three books of the work, in excellent condition, up to p. 228 A *and the whole* |. We would judge the large gap from which the Parisinus suffers, from p. 163, 29 *in a unified way* to p. 186, 6 *I suppose* to have arisen from the loss of a single quaternion of the archetype, especially since at the end of the codex two quaternions of the exemplar seemed to be transposed, because from p. 215 C *self-moving* | *for the straight line* until the end of the codex are transmitted in this order — following the word *self-moving* (p. 215 C) are p. 221 E | *one motion of another* up to p. 228 A *and the whole* |, which words are followed by p. 215 C *for the straight line* to p. 221 E *their motion those...* (the final words of the codex) — unless the Vatican Palatine codex 121 prevented this, upon consultation of which it must be determined that two quaternions of the archetype had perished, four transposed.

The iota which we call subscript, although it is usually absent, is correctly transmitted twice in **P** alone (p. 196, 29. 201, 7). Omont, *Inventaire II* p. 151), of very large format 33.1 x 22.6 cm, of 686 pages, written in the 16th century by Ioannes de Otranto; Omont provided a specimen, *Fac-Similés de manuscrits grecs des XV^e et XVI^e siècles*, plate 28; cf. p. 12. It encompasses all the books (p. 1–684). From p. 685 f. I edited in *Musei Rhenani* vol. 54 (1899) p. 196 the beginning of the Melissa of Proclus on Plato's Republic <note>see footnote 1</note>. This codex abounds in faults, lacunae, and gaps, especially at the beginning of the fifth book and at the end. However, I will call to my aid after the failure of the codices **CMPN**, i.e., from p. 228 A | *fitted together harmoniously*, so that codex **Q**, from which it does not differ far, may not lack support, yet in such a way that we might pass over the clear errors of the scribe to be attributed to negligence, so that the image of the tradition may not be obscured.
The Parisian national library, Greek 1841, is a twin. They are very similar, although they were subjected to far fewer errors and were not deformed by reckless conjectures, the Chisian and the Escurial: each preserved the fragment of Melissa — certainly better. For this reason, I am gravely sorry that I could not use either codex as a whole to restore the text: but I am persuaded that neither the Chisian nor the Escurial is as strong as **Q**, which was fully exhausted by me. are not established by [their own] nature. They are not established because those conditions are not established. Similarly, the person <note>(Sāmkhya)</note>, the consciousness <note>(Vaiśeṣika)</note>, and the non-dual consciousness <note>(Guhyasamāja tradition)</note>, and others—those who assert that the nature of consciousness is a permanent substance—are also not established by their own nature and are empty. "Form is empty. Likewise, feeling," and so forth—the meaning of these must also be understood.

Similarly, the meaning of "Emptiness is form," and so forth, is that form is empty of being an inherently existing substantial form, empty of being a permanent substance, empty of being a form composed of permanent substantial atoms, and is impermanent. That which serves as the basis for designating "form," that which is suitable to be a form arising from karma, and so on, is "emptiness is form." From that form, the emptiness of the form which is held to be a substantial entity or a substantial entity with parts is not different. This is the meaning of "Form is not other than emptiness." Similarly, the meaning of "Emptiness is not other than form" is that form which is born of karma is not other than the emptiness of that form which is a substantial entity with parts. This is the understanding according to the tenets of the <term>Sautrāntika</term> <gloss>School of Sutra Followers</gloss> school.

The view of one <term>Sautrāntika</term> <gloss>School of Sutra Followers</gloss> system—The system of the <term>Sautrāntika</term>s: because they accept consciousness as having aspects, they posit both the consciousness that appears in the form of its own aspect and the object as two. Those aspects of consciousness are empty of that form as it is characterized—

<column-break/>
1) "Form born of karma"—this refers to the shape of the body and so forth that is obtained from the ripening of karma.

Since it is unreasonable to think of a form that is empty of form as something other than such a form, it is said that "Form is not other than emptiness." Since one cannot perceive a form other than that which appears as form to one who holds [the concept of] a form empty of the characteristics of form, it is said that "Emptiness is not other than form." In this way, these sutras do not explicitly explain [the path] in terms of one's own body according to these tenets. This is because the 'Profound Practice' shown here is the Mother of the <term>Aryas</term> <gloss>Noble Ones</gloss> based on reasoning. While this is said with the mindset that it is the Mother of Reasoning, I have not seen it as inappropriate to also apply it to tenets.

Explanations relying on the <term>Vijñaptimātra</term> <gloss>Mind-Only</gloss> method—The intention of sutras such as "Form is empty" is also explained in the manner of the <term>Vijñaptimātra</term> <gloss>Mind-Only</gloss> method of the Great Ones, relying on other sutras. In this system, the Great Ones establish the characteristic of form for all phenomena of the path to purification. "Imagined form, this is designated form, this is the form of <term>Dharmatā</term> <gloss>the true nature of phenomena</gloss>."

This is an extensive explanation. Based on these three types of form: the first form is what ordinary people grasp as an object in their <term>vikalpa</term> <gloss>conceptualizing</gloss> minds. That is the imagined form and the form that becomes the object of the consciousness that appears as an object. The <term>paratantra</term> <gloss>dependent</term> form is the designated form, and the form that is free from the characteristics of those two is the <term>pariniṣpanna</term> <gloss>perfected</gloss> form—that is <term>Tathātā</term> <gloss>Suchness</gloss>, which is what is called "the form of <term>Dharmatā</term>."

Therefore, because the nature of the dependent <term>paratantra</term> form is devoid of all characteristics of the imagined <term>parikalpita</term> form, it is empty of imagined form, and that emptiness has the meaning of Suchness. As it is said by the Great Charioteer <note>referring to a great master, likely Nagarjuna or a key commentator</note>:

"What is the characteristic of emptiness? That which is not present in something is seen as being empty of it." And, "What is it that is not present? In the aggregates, elements, and sense spheres, there is no permanent, unchanging phenomenon, no self, and no belonging to a self. Thus, they are empty."

As it is said, here "Form is empty" means that the form which has the characteristic of the dependent <term>paratantra</term> nature is devoid of those imagined forms such as external objects. Thus, it is empty of them.

<note>1) Nyayabindu, 39/a, summarized. 2) Sutrasamuccaya, 37b, Cittamatra section.</note>

<summary>This page elaborates on the three natures (imagined, dependent, perfected) in relation to form, defining emptiness as the absence of imagined characteristics in dependent phenomena.</summary>
<keywords>Three Natures, Emptiness, Form, Aggregates, Dharmata</keywords>

Thus, it is stated "Form is empty." This explains the emptiness of the perfect form, and therefore it is stated "Emptiness is form." This serves as an antidote to the conceptualization of nihilism. If one thinks that since emptiness and form are different in characteristics, emptiness is one thing and form is another, it serves as an antidote to the conceptualization of eternalism and the two extremes. That <term>Dharmatā</term> <gloss>true nature</gloss> form, which has the characteristic of emptiness, does not possess the characteristics of form. As stated in the <term>Prajñāpāramitā</term> sutra:

"Shariputra, form is separated from the nature of form." This is explained extensively. Similarly, in the sutra taught by Rab 'byor <note>Subhuti</note>, it is said, "The <term>Dharmadhātu</term> <gloss>realm of phenomena</gloss> exists in the realm of form, but the <term>Dharmadhātu</term> is not a characteristic of consciousness <note>or "not an object of consciousness"</note>," and so on.

Thinking that "Emptiness or the form of <term>Dharmatā</term> is something other than form" is incorrect. It is the <term>Dharmatā</term> of form, and because it cannot be perceived as something other than the form which is the basis of phenomena, it is stated "Emptiness is not other than form." The basis of phenomena, form, is also the basis of emptiness, and it is the basis of the form of <term>Dharmatā</term>. Because it cannot be perceived as other than its own <term>Dharmatā</term>, and because it is its nature, it is not other than emptiness. The word "also" is used here to encompass both the phenomenon and the <term>Dharmatā</term>.

<note>1) Large Sutra (Nyithri), 146/3. 2) Akṣayamatinirdeśa-sūtra, 13b.</note>

<summary>This page clarifies the non-duality of form and emptiness, emphasizing that emptiness is the true nature (Dharmatā) of form and cannot be separated from it.</summary>
<keywords>Emptiness, Form, Dharmata, Dharmadhatu, Prajnaparamita, Non-duality</keywords>

"This was stated as an antidote to the conceptualization of the two [extremes] as a method: 'Form is not other than emptiness. Form itself is emptiness. Emptiness is form.'"

Nevertheless, if one asks, "What is the intrinsic nature meant by 'Form is empty of intrinsic nature'?" and "How should it be identified?"—it must be established as that which is established by its own nature. If that is established, it is refuted by reasonings such as the separation of one and many, and the refutation of production in the four extremes. Thus, the explanation that "it is devoid of intrinsic nature" is very clear in the <term>Madhyamaka</term> <gloss>Middle Way</gloss> and <term>Prajñāpāramitā</term> texts. Although it is not taken from the <term>Pramāṇavārttika</term> <gloss>Commentary on Valid Cognition</gloss>, those who wish to understand the texts through study of the scriptures will find that, relying on the reasoning mentioned above, a definitive understanding can be reached.

It appears as if established from its own side without depending on others. Even when form does not appear, those three are mixed together inseparably and appear as one. Because it is not mixed with other phenomena."

As stated, appearing as something that exists without depending on others is the mode of appearance of being established by intrinsic nature. And to be established as it appears is to be truly established, and this is the way of being established by its own essence. As it is said in that same text—

As stated. Therefore, when form appears as a phenomenon, there were the three [types of form] mentioned earlier. Although the two entities are objects to be refuted by reason, when it comes to the true and intrinsically established form, all three are targets of refutation. This is because all three are illusory appearances born from the imprints of incorrect reasoning. At that time, the appearance of form arising from the imprint of the entity's reality is an appearance of dependence, so it is an object to be refuted by reason. The second, the appearance arising from the imprints of words, is also a basis for mistaken labeling; it does not need to be refuted by reason, because even if it appears, it is like a magical illusion dependent on conditions, and it involves labeling. Therefore, the appearance of being truly established and established by intrinsic nature, the self that grasps that nature, and the two [graspings of] subject and object [which are] conceptualizations of incorrect mental engagement—these are the root of cyclic existence. Because they are the root of incorrect thought and attachment, they are established as mistaken. Thus, they are objects to be refuted by reason. The conceptualization that grasps them, along with cyclic existence, should be refuted. As stated by the son of the Conqueror, <term>Shantideva</term>:

"Whatever is seen, heard, or known,"
"In this context, should not be refuted."

<note>1) Catuhshataka, Chapter 7, Acharya Chandrakirti’s commentary, 304.</note>

<summary>This page explains that while dependent appearances exist, the appearance of true or intrinsic existence is an illusion and an object to be refuted, marking the root of cyclic existence.</summary>

This manuscript was used primarily by **Chr. Schneider** of Breslau, who published the commentaries in 1847.

**Oxoniensis** <gloss>Manuscript from Oxford</gloss>, Corpus Christi College 98 (see *Catalogus codicum mss. collegii Corporis Christi* <gloss>Catalogue of the manuscript codices of Corpus Christi College</gloss>, p. 34), paper, 16th century, 477 folios.
On the front of the book is read: *This book was purchased from the heirs of William Grocyn in the year of our Lord 1521, for Corpus Christi College, under the presidency of Claimond.* This is the British codex to which <margin>b</margin> **Simon Grynaeus** first published these commentaries in Basel in 1534 together with the works of Plato. Using this Basel edition, **Thomas Taylor** translated the commentaries into the English language (London, 1820).
A specimen was kindly sent by the honorable **Ingram Bywater**.

### EXCERPTS

<margin>L</margin> **Laurentianus** <gloss>Manuscript from the Laurentian Library</gloss>, Greek Plutarch 28, codex 20 (see Bandini II, p. 39 VII), square, paper, 14th century, presents on folio 266r under the title "Excerpts from the Commentary of Proclus on the Timaeus," which begin on p. 192 DE, "And it is to be known that an arithmetic mean is that upon which," and end on p. 193 C, "and they invert one another" (folio 267r).
I will explain the individual details in the preface of the second volume. I collated them in Florence in 1899.

## SYNOPSIS OF CODICES NOT EMPLOYED IN THE RECENSION

VATICANUS PALATINUS Greek 121 (see H. Stevenson, *Codices manuscripti Palatini graeci Bibliothecae Vaticanae* <gloss>Greek Palatine manuscripts of the Vatican Library</gloss>, p. 57), of very large format (30.7 x 24.7 cm), paper, 16th century, 194 folios (23 quaternions, 1 quaternion of three <note>original: "1 trinionis 14"</note>, 1 binion of folios 191—194). It contains the first book of the commentary, corrupted by the same lacuna (folio 187r) as codex P. Moreover, since it gaps in another place (folio 192u)—for there are missing pages from 191, 20 "image of [the] creation" up to 203, 7 "to the Athenians"—which part is half of the former, one might conjecture that both two and one quaternion of the archetype have perished.

I would have held this book to be a twin of codex P (p. 68, 20 "Heraculean" and p. 88, 16 "votive offerings" match P), not a derivative (p. 112, 28 "through these" contrary to P).

I examined it in Rome in 1900.

MARCIANUS Greek 190 (see Zanetti, p. 108), parchment, 31.4 x 22.5 cm, 14th century, 27 quinternions, to which correspond 270 folios of 37 lines. Four blank folios precede the first quinternion, and folios 271r—281r follow the last (to which seven blank ones are annexed), exhibiting Proclus' commentary on the first Alcibiades, which the same hand, which you might easily recognize from the scholia added to the Timaeus commentary, inscribed less diligently with slightly lighter ink. On the reverse side of the first blank folio, these were written by a recent hand:
