Folios 1r—4u, which contain "To Timaeus the Locrian on the Soul of the World and Nature" (the inscription of which booklet is painted in red), follow the five books of commentary, of which the first two stand on the side of codex **N**, which is taught by other things, but especially by a lacuna common to both books, which in this parchment was supplied by one inserted folio (63). Nor is the number of the quinternion's folios disturbed, because two folios are marked with the number 61.

The context of the third, fourth, and fifth books approaches most closely to the vulgate recension. On folio 266u, one meets the same subscription that ends the Munich codex Greek 382: "Up to the matters set forth, the works of Proclus on the Timaeus have been found; whether he also explained the following is unclear."

The inscriptions of the individual books are painted in red lead, and the letters we call initials are artistically gilded, except for the title of the third book (folio 182u), which was decorated only later.
I examined these in Venice in 1899.

Five folios follow, written by a double hand as we said, which exhibit both the end of the commentaries (folio 229r to the middle of 232u) and, with one space of nearly a line left empty, the beginning of the Proclian Melissa <note>A work titled "Melissa" or "The Bee," an anthology of moral/philosophical excerpts</note> (folio 232u, 233). An alien hand in the first and second books of the commentary added a part of the supplements which I published in *Musei Rhenani* vol. 54 (1899) p. 174 ff., both in the margin and in the text above the lines. He who supplemented the Chisian used either codex **N** itself or another very similar to it: the Chisian, augmented, is richer, and nowhere matches the Bourbon, which does not itself contain all those additions.

Otherwise, this book stands on the side of codices **D** and the Escurialensis: the relationship of these books among themselves is easily recognized from the Melissa fragment.

Ernest Lommatzsch inspected them in Rome in 1898 and I did in 1900.

The related codices are **D** and the Chisian (see p. XIV and p. XIX ff.).

<header>CHAPTER ONE</header>

<margin>A</margin> The **Monacensis** [manuscript] of the Royal Greek Library, number 382, of the largest format, paper, 16th century. See Ign. Hardt, *Catalogus codic. Graec. biblioth. reg. Monac.* [Catalog of Greek manuscripts of the Royal Library of Munich], IV, p. 186.
Chr. Schneider, of Breslau, who published the commentaries in 1847, made primary use of this codex.

**Oxoniensis Corporis Christi 98** (see *Catalogus codicum mss. collegii Corporis Christi* [Catalog of manuscripts of Corpus Christi College], p. 34), paper, 16th century, 477 folios.
On the front of the book is written: *this book was purchased from the heirs of William Grocyn in the year of the Lord 1521, for Corpus Christi College, with Claimond as president.* This is the British codex, to which <margin>b</margin> Simon Grynaeus first edited these commentaries at Basel in 1534 along with the works of Plato. Thomas Taylor translated the commentaries into the English language using the Basel edition (London, 1820).
Ingram Bywater, a man of distinction, kindly sent a sample.

### EXCERPTS

<margin>L</margin> **Laurentianus** Greek, Plutarch collection 28, codex 20 (see Bandini II, p. 39, VII), square, paper, 14th century, displays on folio 266^r, under the title *From the commentary of Proclus on the Timaeus*, excerpts that begin at p. 192 D, "and it must be known that there is an arithmetic mean by which," and end at p. 193 C, "and they turn back into one another" (folio 267^r).
I will explain the details in the preface of the second volume. I collated it at Florence in 1899.

### LATIN VERSION

<margin>th</margin> **Niccolò Leonico Tomeo’s** *Opuscula lately brought to light... with privilege*, contains on folio LXXV^r:
*Plato’s [work] from the Timaeus on the generation of souls, with explanation and digression by Proclus Lycius.*
They are inscribed: folio LXXV^u: *Of Niccolò Leonico Tomeo*...

Vatican Palatine Greek 121 (see H. Stevenson, *Codices manuscripti Palatini graeci Bibliothecae Vaticanae* [Palatine Greek manuscripts of the Vatican Library], p. 57), largest format (30.7 x 24.7 cm), paper, 16th century, 194 folios (23 quaternions, 1 quaternion of three <note>original: "trinionis"</note>, 1 binion [set of two] folios 191—194). It contains the first book of the commentary, damaged by the same lacuna [gap] (folio 187^r) as codex P. It also gaps in another place (folio 192^u)—for p. 191, 20 "image of [craftsmanship]" up to p. 203, 7 "the Athenians" are missing—and since this lost part is half of the former, one might conjecture that two quaternions of the archetype have perished.

I have taken this book to be a sibling of codex P (p. 68, 20 "Heraclean" and p. 88, 16 "votive offerings" match P), not a child of it (p. 112, 28 "through these" contradicts P).

I examined it at Rome in 1900.

Marcianus Greek 190 (see Zanetti, p. 108), parchment, 31.4 x 22.5 cm, 14th century, 27 quires [sets of five], which correspond to 270 folios of 37 lines. Four blank folios precede the first quire, and folios 271^r—281^r follow the last (to which seven blank ones are attached), presenting Proclus’s commentary on the first Alcibiades, which the same hand, which you can easily recognize from the scholia added to the Timaeus commentary, wrote out less diligently in slightly lighter ink. *The philosopher's exposition on Plato’s Timaeus, which is my book. Bessarion, Cardinal, Bishop of Tusculum.*

Folios 1^r—4^u, which contain *Timaeus the Locrian on the nature of the soul and the world* (the title of which is painted in red), are followed by the five books of commentary, of which the first two stand on the side of codex **N**, as shown by other things, and especially by a lacuna common to both books, which has been supplied in this parchment by one inserted folio (63). Nevertheless, the number of folios in the quire is not disturbed, because two folios are marked with the number 61.

The context of the third, fourth, and fifth books approaches the vulgate version very closely. On folio 266^u, the same subscription is encountered that ends the Munich Greek codex 382: *Thus far have been found the things on the Timaeus by Proclus; but whether he also commented on the following [parts] is unclear.*

The inscriptions of the individual books are painted in red lead, and the letters we call initials are artistically gilded, except for the title of the third book (folio 182^u), which was adorned only later.
I examined them at Venice in 1899.

Parisinus National Library Greek 1841 [**FONTEBL.-REG. 2095**], paper, 16th century (see Omont, *Inventaire* II, p. 151), is a twin of codex **D**.
I saw it in Paris in 1898.

Chisianus **R VIII 58**, largest format, bombycine [cotton paper], 13th century (?), 233 folios. The context, which faded due to humidity and became lacunose, seems to have been filled in, if any faith is to be placed in the authority of the catalog, by the hand of Laurentius Portius, the scribe of Leo Allatius (folios 1—3 [= folios 4—6 repeated]. 231), and by another much older hand of "another elegant character" (folios 229, 230, 232, 233).

Although five complete books were present at one time, 32 leaves [folia] have now perished before the fourth folio, apparently four quaternions. The ancient book today begins at p. 130, 23, "and..."

<header>PREFACE</header>

"...perishable things," and ends at folio 228^u, "...the following and..." (p. 343 A).
Five folios follow, written by a double hand as we have said, which present both the end of the commentaries (folio 229^r to the middle of 232^u) and, with the space of nearly one line left blank, the beginning of the Proclian Melissa (folios 232^u—233). A foreign hand added to the first and second books of the commentary some of the additions that I published in *Rheinisches Museum* vol. 54 (1899) p. 174 ff., both in the margin and in the text above the lines. The person who supplied the Chisianus [codex] used either codex **N** itself or another very similar to it: it is nowhere near the Bourbon [manuscript], which does not even contain all those additions itself; the augmented Chisianus is richer.

Moreover, this book stands on the side of codices **D** and the Escurialensis: the relationship between these books is easily recognized from the Melissae fragment.

Ernest Lommatzsch inspected it at Rome in 1898, and I did in 1900.

Escurialensis **T III 2** (see E. Miller, *Catalogue des manuscrits grecs de la Bibliothèque de l’Escurial* [Catalog of Greek manuscripts of the Escorial Library], p. 133), square. 402 paper folios were written in the 16th century by various scribes. Although it once contained the whole commentary, the beginning has now perished up to p. 116, 13, "destruction."
Folios 401^u—402^u have been added: *Melissa on the speech of the Muses in the Republic.*

At the foot of folio 402^u the following is read:
*This book is of [name erased] and of his friends, of the beautiful.*

The related codices are **D** and the Chisianus (see p. XIV and p. XIX s).

Bruno Violet examined the book and collated the Melissa for my sake in 1899.

is something else. In thinking this, one also holds that form is not other than emptiness, and emptiness is not other than form. This is what is meant by "refuting" <note>this refers to the refutation of inherent existence</note>, as it is held. Just as it is said, "This appearance of form and the like... is what is refuted," so it is expressed in the explanations. Explanations of this sort appear in detail and remain as subjects for analysis. Even though it seems logical to explain these, while taking the intended meaning of the sutras and the like into account, and applying the basis of explanation to form, when one looks at the intention of the sutra that states "Form is empty," and so on, it is realized that the other [aggregates] such as feeling are quickly transformed like form. Since these do not appear to be separate from the cognitive appearance and the objective reality itself, they do not apply to feeling and so forth.

Regarding the statement "Form is empty," while it is not strictly necessary to differentiate it from the philosophical view of the two schools of the <term>Sutra-system</term> <gloss>Sautrāntika</gloss>, it is still not entirely compatible to explain it as such, because they are proponents of a system that asserts the non-self of those [phenomena].

The System of the <term>Sautrāntika</term> <gloss>Sutra-system school</term>: According to the system of the <term>Sautrāntika</term>, the statement "Form is empty" and the intention of the sutra [are explained as follows]. The atoms examined in the treatises of other schools and the form belonging to the composite material substance are empty by their own nature, and do not exist by their own intrinsic nature. Similarly, feeling, the object, and the senses arise from the substance known as "compilation," and the feelings that arise from these appear as such. These are not established by intrinsic nature.
pages.93:
It refers to that which is not established by nature, because those things are not established as such. Similarly, the "Person" (of the <term>Samkhya</term> school), "Mental Consciousness" (of the <term>Vaisheshika</term> school), and "Non-dual Awareness" (of the <term>Guhyagarbha</term> tradition), which are all considered permanent substances of the nature of consciousness, are also not established by intrinsic nature and are empty. One must also understand the meaning of "Form is empty; likewise feeling and so on."

Similarly, the meaning of "Emptiness is form," and so on, is as follows: form which exists as a coarse substance of sound and so forth is empty of [inherent] form; it is not established as a permanent substance; it is empty of form condensed by permanent atomic substances; it is impermanent; it is the basis for the imputation of the word "form"; it is capable of being form arising from actions—this is what is called "emptiness is form." From that kind of form, the emptiness of the form asserted as the previously mentioned substance and the composite substance is not something else. This is the meaning of "Emptiness is not other than form." Similarly, the meaning of "Form is not other than emptiness" is that the emptiness of the permanent, composite form is also not other than the form arising from action. This is the intended philosophical meaning of the late <term>Sautrāntika</term> school.
pages.94:
"Form is empty," and although the awareness itself is empty of form, since that which appears as form within it is form, it is said that "Emptiness is form." Thinking that a form which is empty of form exists elsewhere from such a form is not logically sound, so it is said that "Emptiness is not other than form." Since there is no form to be observed other than that which appears as form in what is called the apprehension of form, which is empty of the characteristics of form, it is said that "Form is not other than emptiness." In this way, explaining the philosophical tenets of those sutras according to one's own system is not widely seen. This is because the "profound conduct" taught here is the mother of the noble ones' wisdom. Although it is said to be the mother of wisdom in the context of the mind, it is not seen as incompatible with being applied to philosophical tenets as well.

Based on the method of <term>Vijnaptimatra</term> <gloss>Mind-Only</gloss>: The intention of the sutra "Form is empty," and so on, is also explained in the manner of the <term>Vijnaptimatra</term> method of the great ones, based on other sutras. In this system, all phenomena of the path are established with the characteristics of form. They explain the intention of the Mother Sutras, which state that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature. Here too, relying on the three non-existences and the three types of form, they explain the meaning of the four kinds of emptiness, starting with "Form is empty." As it is said in the sutra:

"Brahmin, a Bodhisattva who practices the <term>Prajnaparamita</term> <gloss>Perfection of Wisdom</gloss> and remains skilled in interpreting deep phenomena should realize the three types of form. Feeling and... as for this, in this..."
pages.95:
"[This is the] imagined form. This is the dependent form. This is the form of the nature of reality."

Having explained these in detail, we take these three types of form as the basis. The first form, which childish beings grasp as objects in their various perceptions, is the imagined form, the form that becomes the object of consciousness that appears as an object. The form that is the dependent nature and the form that is free from the two aspects of form is the perfected form—this is <term>Tathata</term> <gloss>Thusness</gloss>, which is called the "form of the nature of reality."

Therefore, the nature of the dependent form is empty of all characteristics of the imagined form, because it does not possess them. Thus, it is empty of the imagined form, and that emptiness is the meaning of emptiness itself. As the great master of the chariot <note>referring to a founder of a lineage</note> has said:

"What is the characteristic of emptiness? That which is not in it is seen as empty, being rightly observed." And, "What is not present? In the aggregates, elements, and sense-spheres, there is no permanent, stable, unchanging phenomenon, nor is there a self or what belongs to a self. In this way, they are empty."

As it is said, here "Form is empty" means that since the imagined form, such as external objects, is not present in the dependent form, which has the characteristics of form, it is empty of those.
pages.96:
Therefore, it is taught that "Form is empty." This suppresses the conceptualizations of distraction and primarily teaches the antidote to the conceptualizations of false projections.

Since that kind of emptiness is the perfected form, it is taught that "Emptiness is form." This suppresses the conceptualizations of denial. If one thinks that because emptiness and form have different characteristics, emptiness is one thing and form is another, then this teaches the antidote to the conceptualizations of nihilism and eternalism. In that form of the nature of reality, which has the characteristic of emptiness, the characteristics of form do not exist. As it is said in the <term>Prajnaparamita</term> sutra:

"Shariputra, form is separated from the nature of form." This is explained in detail, and similarly, in the sutra taught by the noble <term>Rab 'byor</term> <gloss>Subhuti</gloss>: "Although the <term>Dharmadhatu</term> <gloss>Reality-Realm</gloss> exists in the sphere of form, the <term>Dharmadhatu</term> is not the characteristic of consciousness that perceives form."

Thus, thinking that emptiness or the nature of reality is something other than form is not correct. Since it is the nature of reality of form, it cannot be observed as separate from the phenomena of form; therefore, it is said that "Emptiness is not other than form." The phenomena of form is also the basis of that emptiness, and...
pages.97:
that form of the nature of reality is also the phenomenon [of emptiness]. Since it cannot be observed as separate from its own nature of reality, it is also not other than emptiness. The word "also" is used to encompass [the meanings].

By these two [statements], the antidote to the conceptualizations of distraction—which grasp phenomena and the nature of phenomena as separate entities—is taught. Just as it is said by the great teacher:

"The teaching of the antidote to conceptualization is stated as: Form is not other than emptiness. Form itself is emptiness. Emptiness is form."

This is the manner of explanation that accords with the sequence of the sutras. Although the great scholars of Tibet have interpreted this in ways that seem contradictory to the methods of the <term>Prajnaparamita</term> commentaries, I have not included those who hold to extreme views here. Once one has understood the core meaning—that the imagined characteristics have no intrinsic nature, and so on—it is easy to understand the interpretation of the <term>Prajnaparamita</term> sutras based on the three non-existences. Therefore, one should learn from other various treatises. Here, because the intention is to explain the summary of the essence, that is sufficient.

Regarding the "necessity of abandonment": regarding the statement "Form is empty," etc.,
pages.98:
the emptiness of the inherent existence of form and so forth is taught. The reasoning that establishes this, and the manner in which it refutes mistaken concepts, have been taught in the two stages of the method. Nevertheless, if one asks, "What is the nature that is 'empty of inherent existence'?"—to what does this refer? If one asks how it should be identified, it must be established as that which is established by inherent existence. If it is established, it is refuted by reasoning such as the "freedom from one or many" and the "refutation of the four types of arising." Thus, the explanation that "there is no inherent existence" is very clear in the treatises of the <term>Madhyamaka</term> and <term>Prajnaparamita</term>. Although it is not taken directly from the <term>Pramanavartika</term> <gloss>Commentary on Valid Cognition</gloss>, those who wish to understand the treatises through study will see that a conclusive understanding can be reached by relying on the aforementioned reasoning.

In this way, the various ways of explaining the identification of the nature in the statement "empty of inherent existence" have been discussed previously. The slightly clearer way in which it is presented in the words of the Great Vehicle and the commentaries of the great teachers is based on the two [truths], and is a question that arises from the basis of the two.
pages.99: Such a nature is the nature of form as it appears due to the power of the imprints of grasping at characteristics, which have been associated with the continuum of each sentient being since beginningless time. This is also like the reflection of the moon in water; the form is that which is to be abandoned. All modes of appearance are mixed without distinction and are to be abandoned. The appearance that arises from the imprints of entities appears merely as form, and the appearance that arises from the imprints of conventional language—that very appearance
pages.100:
is the basis for the application of the word "form." It is the appearance that arises from the imprints of the view of self, appearing as established and as an essence. It appears to exist from its own side without relying on other things, and even if form is not present, the three are mixed without distinction and appear as one. As long as the appearance of truth is not refuted, all three are refuted, or all three are present; if one does not abandon [the grasping of] one, all three will appear. Therefore, the nature of form that corresponds to such an appearance is that which is "empty of its own nature." When identifying such a nature of form and the like, as the great noble <term>Aryadeva</term> said:

-> "What is seen as not being dependent" <-
-> "is called nature." <-

And in the commentary on this: "It is established that that which is observed merely as an entity, not being dependent on other phenomena, and remaining in its own essence, is its nature; because it is not mixed with other phenomena."

As stated, appearing to exist without relying on others is the mode of appearance of appearing to be established by nature, and appearing as it is is appearing to be established as true, and is the mode of establishment as established by intrinsic nature. Just as it is said in that same text:
"Whatever entity [exists] due to another..."
pages.101:
-> "if it were unchanging," <-
-> "if its own nature were to change," <-
-> "that would not be the case for anything." <-

As it is said. Therefore, when form appears as a phenomenon, there are three types [of appearance] of form, and although the two entities are to be refuted by reasoning, when the truth and inherent existence of form are established, all three are considered to be "good" <note>meaning: they are common misconceptions</note>, because all three are illusory appearances born from imprints of incorrect thought. At that time, the appearance of form arising from the inherent existence of an entity is an appearance to be refuted by reasoning. The second appearance, arising from the inherent existence of language, is also the basis for confusion regarding names and so forth; it does not need to be refuted by reasoning, because although it is clear, it is an appearance like a magical illusion dependent on conditions, and it involves the confusion of names. Therefore, the appearance of being established as true, the appearance of being established by nature, and the two—the self of phenomena that grasps at that nature and the object of incorrect conceptualization—are the root of the two types of grasping at self. As they are the root of cyclic existence and the root of attachment and aversion, because they are established as such, they are to be refuted by reasoning. All conceptualizations that grasp at them, along with the cyclic existence, are to be refuted. As the son of the victorious one, <term>Shantideva</term>, has said:

"Whatever is seen, heard, and known"
"is not to be refuted here."

## OVERVIEW OF MANUSCRIPTS NOT USED IN THIS RECENSION

**Vatican Palatine Greek 121** (see H. Stevenson, *Codices manuscripti Palatini graeci Bibliothecae Vaticanae*, p. 57), very large format (30.7 x 24.7 cm), on paper, 16th century, 194 folios (23 quaternions, 1 trinion $\overline{\iota\delta}$, 1 binion fols. 191—194). It contains the first book of the commentary, damaged by the same <term>lacuna</term> <gloss>gap/missing text</gloss> (fol. 187r) as codex P. Since it also has a gap in another place (fol. 192v)—for pages 191, 20 "image of the work" up to p. 203, 7 "Athenians" are missing—one might conjecture that as this part is half of the former, both two quaternions and one quaternion of the archetype have been lost.

I would consider this book to be a sibling of codex P (p. 68, 20 *Herakleia* and p. 88, 16 *votive offerings* match P), not a child (p. 112, 28 *through these* contradicts P).

I examined this in Rome in 1900.

**Marcian Greek 190** (see Zanetti p. 108), parchment, 31.4 x 22.5 cm, 14th century, 27 quinternions, to which correspond 270 folios of 37 lines. Four blank folios precede the first quinternion; following the last are folios 271r—281r (to which seven blank folios are attached), presenting Proclus’ commentary on the first *Alcibiades*, which the same hand wrote less diligently with slightly lighter ink; one may easily recognize this from the scholia added to the *Timaeus* commentary. Therefore is it said: “The army, being based on a state of order, there is a marvellous result; custom, being based on law, ten thousand changes of circumstances are brought about; a condition of supremacy being based upon the mind, it is outwardly manifested in a condition of preparedness.” If these three points of view are all taken into consideration, the result will be that the strong may be firmly established. Thus orderly government is the necessary result of strength, and strength again of orderly government; orderly government of riches, and riches again of orderly government; riches of strength and strength again of riches. Therefore is it said: “The way to orderly government and strength is to discuss fundamentals.”

## PARAGRAPH 12
### MILITARY DEFENCE

A state that has to fight on four fronts values defence, and a state that rests against the sea values attack. For, if a state that fights on four fronts is fond of raising soldiers, it will be in a dangerous position, as it has to resist four
pages.265: neighbours. As soon as a country with four neighbours begins hostilities, four countries mobilize armies; therefore is it said that the country is in a dangerous position. If a state that has to fight on four fronts is unable to raise, from a city of ten thousand houses, an army of more than ten thousand men, then the state will be in a dangerous position. <margin>6b</margin> Therefore is it said: “A state that has to fight on four fronts should concern itself with defensive warfare.” In defending walled cities, the best way is, with the strength of the worn-out men, to fight the fresh strength of the invaders. It is assaults upon walled cities that wear out the strength of men. So long as the walled cities have not all been razed, the invaders have no means of penetrating the country. This is meant by the saying that the strength of worn-out men should fight the fresh strength of the invading force. But when the walled cities have all been razed and the foreign army thus finds the means of penetrating, then certainly it will be exhausted, and the people within the country will be rested. Fighting with rested strength against those of exhausted strength is said to be: fighting with the strength of fresh men against the worn-out strength of the invading forces. All these are called the misfortunes
pages.266:
attendant upon the besieging of walled cities. It is regarded as a misfortune that always, in capturing cities, the strength of the army is worn out. In these three things, misfortune is due, not to insufficient effort, but to mistaken generalship.

The way to hold a city is to have abundant strength. Therefore is it said: “When the invading force musters its levies, mobilize as many as three armies, and divide them according to the number of the chariots of the invading force.” Of these three armies, one should be formed of able-bodied men, one of able-bodied women, and one of the old and feeble men and women. These are called the three armies. Cause the army of able-bodied men, with abundant provisions and sharp weapons, to marshall themselves, and to await the enemy; cause the able-bodied women, <margin>7a</margin> with abundant provisions and ramparts at their backs, to marshall themselves and to await orders, so as to make, at the approach of the invaders, earthworks as an obstruction, and traps, *chevaux-de-frise* <note>defensive spikes used against cavalry</note> and pitfalls, to pull down the supporting beams and to tear down the houses, to transport what is
pages.267: transportable, and to burn what is untransportable, so that the invaders are not able to make use thereof in their attack. Cause the army of the old and feeble to guard the oxen, horses, sheep, and swine, and to collect all that is consumable of plants and water, to feed them therewith, so as to obtain food for the able-bodied men and women. But see to it carefully that the three armies do not intermingle. If the able-bodied men mingle with the army of the able-bodied women, they will attach great value to the safety of the women and wicked people will have opportunities for intrigue, with the result that the state will perish. Taking pleasure in the women’s company, the men will be afraid of disturbing reports and so not even the brave will fight. If the able-bodied men and women intermingle with the army of the old and feeble, then the old will arouse the compassion of the able-bodied, and the feeble the pity of the strong. Compassion and pity in the heart cause brave people to be more anxious and fearful people not to fight.

### PARAGRAPH 13
## MAKING ORDERS STRICT

<margin>7b</margin> If orders are made strict, orderly government is not delayed, and if laws are equable, officials are not wicked. Once the law is fixed, one should not damage it with virtuous words; if men of merit are appointed to office, people will have little to say, but if men of virtue are appointed to office, people will have much to say. The practice of good government begins with making judgments. Where five hamlets are the unit for judgments, supremacy is attained; where ten hamlets are the unit for judgments, there is merely strength. He who procrastinates in creating order will be dismembered. Govern by punishments and wage war by rewards; seek
pages.269:
transgressors and do not seek the virtuous. Therefore, if the law is fixed and not altered, then... If in the country there are no wicked people, there is no wicked trade in the capital. If affairs are many and secondary things <note>referring to non-essential activities like commerce</note> are numerous, if agriculture is relaxed and criminals gain the upper hand, then the country will certainly be dismembered.

If the people have a surplus of grain, cause them to obtain office and rank by means of their cereals; if through their own efforts they can count upon obtaining office and rank, farmers will not be lazy.

If a tube of no more than four inches has no bottom, it can certainly not be filled; to confer office, to give rank and to grant salaries, without regard to merit, is like having no bottom.

If a state, when poor, applies itself to war, the poison will originate on the enemy's side, and it will not have the six parasites, but will certainly be strong. If a state, when 8a rich, does not apply itself to war, the poison is transferred to
pages.270: its own interior, and it will have the six kinds of parasites and will certainly be weak. If the state confers office and gives rank according to merit, it may be said to be planning with complete wisdom, and fighting with complete courage. Such a country will certainly have no equal. If a state confers office and gives rank according to merit, then government measures will be simple and words will be few. This may be said to be abolishing laws by means of the law and abolishing words by means of words. Let η' and η'' be the indices of probability in two independent ensembles which are each in statistical equilibrium, then η' + η'' will be the index in the ensemble obtained by combining each system of the first ensemble with each system of the second. This third ensemble will of course be in statistical equilibrium, and the function of phase η' + η'' will be a constant of motion. Now when infinitesimal forces are added to the compound systems, if η' + η'' or a function differing infinitesimally from this is still a constant of motion, it must be on account of the nature of the forces added, or if their action is not entirely specified, on account of conditions to which they are subject. Thus, in the case already considered, η' + η'' is a function of the energy of the compound system, and the infinitesimal forces added are subject to the law of conservation of energy.

<margin>||</margin> Another natural supposition in regard to the added forces is that they should be such as not to affect the moments of momentum of the compound system. To get a case in which moments of momentum of the compound system shall be constants of motion, we may imagine material particles contained in two concentric spherical shells, being prevented from passing the surfaces bounding the shells by repulsions acting always in lines passing through the common centre of the shells. Then, if there are no forces acting between particles in different shells, the mass of particles in each shell will have, besides its energy, the <note>The following phrase is circled in the original:</note> moments of momentum about three axes through the centre as constants of motion.

Now let us imagine an ensemble formed by distributing in phase the system of particles in one shell according to the index of probability

-> A - ε/Θ + ω₁/Ω₁ + ω₂/Ω₂ + ω₃/Ω₃, (98) <-

where ε denotes the energy of the system, and ω₁, ω₂, ω₃, its three moments of momentum, and the other letters constants.

<summary>This page explores whether other distributions besides the canonical one possess analogous properties of statistical equilibrium, specifically considering systems where moments of momentum are conserved.</summary>

pages.66:
# CANONICAL DISTRIBUTION

The properties of canonically distributed ensembles of systems with respect to the equilibrium of the new ensembles which may be formed by combining each system of one ensemble with each system of another, are therefore not peculiar to them in the sense that analogous properties do not belong to some other distributions under special limitations in regard to the systems and forces considered. Yet the canonical distribution evidently constitutes the most simple case of the kind, and that for which the relations described hold with the least restrictions.

Returning to the case of the canonical distribution, we shall find other analogies with thermodynamic systems, if we suppose, as in the preceding chapters,\* that the potential energy ($\epsilon_q$) depends not only upon the coordinates $q_1 \dots q_n$ which determine the configuration of the system, but also upon certain coordinates $a_1, a_2$, etc. of bodies which we call *external*, meaning by this simply that they are not to be regarded as forming any part of the system, although their positions affect the forces which act on the system. The forces exerted by the system upon these external bodies will be represented by $- d\epsilon_q / da_1, - d\epsilon_q / da_2$, etc., while $- d\epsilon_q / dq_1, \dots - d\epsilon_q / dq_n$ represent all the forces acting upon the bodies of the system, including those which depend upon the position of the external bodies, as well as those which depend only upon the configuration of the system itself. It will be understood that $\epsilon_p$ depends only upon $q_1, \dots q_n, p_1, \dots p_n$, in other words, that the kinetic energy of the bodies which we call external forms no part of the kinetic energy of the system. It follows that we may write

->$\frac{d\epsilon}{da_{1}} = \frac{d\epsilon_{q}}{da_{1}} = - A_{1}$,      (104)<-

although a similar equation would not hold for differentiations relative to the internal coordinates.

the periods are the same they must be distributed canonically with same modulus in order that the compound ensemble with additional forces may be in statistical equilibrium.

\* See especially Chapter I, p. 4.

pages.67:
# OF AN ENSEMBLE OF SYSTEMS.

We always suppose these external coordinates to have the same values for all systems of any ensemble. In the case of a canonical distribution, i.e., when the index of probability of phase is a linear function of the energy, it is evident that the values of the external coordinates will affect the distribution, since they affect the energy. In the equation

-> $e^{-\frac{ψ}{Θ}} = \int \dots \int_{phases}^{all} e^{-\frac{ε}{Θ}} dp_1 \dots dq_n,$ \quad \quad \quad (105) <-

by which ψ may be determined, the external coordinates, $a_1$, $a_2$, etc., contained implicitly in ε, as well as Θ, are to be regarded as constant in the integrations indicated. The equation indicates that ψ is a function of these constants. If we imagine their values varied, and the ensemble distributed canonically according to their new values, we have by differentiation of the equation:

-> $e^{-\frac{ψ}{Θ}} \left( - \frac{1}{Θ} dψ + \frac{ψ}{Θ^2} dΘ \right) = \frac{1}{Θ^2} dΘ \int \dots \int_{phases}^{all} ε e^{-\frac{ε}{Θ}} dp_1 \dots dq_n$ <-
-> $- \frac{1}{Θ} da_1 \int \dots \int_{phases}^{all} \frac{dε}{da_1} e^{-\frac{ε}{Θ}} dp_1 \dots dq_n$ <-
-> $- \frac{1}{Θ} da_2 \int \dots \int_{phases}^{all} \frac{dε}{da_2} e^{-\frac{ε}{Θ}} dp_1 \dots dq_n - etc.,$ \quad (106) <-

or, multiplying by $Θ e^{\frac{ψ}{Θ}}$, and setting

-> $- \frac{dε}{da_1} = A_1, \quad - \frac{dε}{da_2} = A_2, \text{ etc.},$ <-

-> $- dψ + \frac{ψ}{Θ} dΘ = \frac{1}{Θ} dΘ \int \dots \int_{phases}^{all} ε e^{\frac{ψ - ε}{Θ}} dp_1 \dots dq_n$ <-
-> $+ da_1 \int \dots \int_{phases}^{all} A_1 e^{\frac{ψ - ε}{Θ}} dp_1 \dots dq_n$ <-
-> $+ da_2 \int \dots \int_{phases}^{all} A_2 e^{\frac{ψ - ε}{Θ}} dp_1 \dots dq_n + etc.$ \quad (107) <-

<summary>This page mathematically derives the relationship between the potential function ψ, the modulus Θ, and external coordinates, preparing the ground for connecting these to thermodynamic quantities.</summary>
<keywords>canonical distribution, integration, differential, external coordinates, potential function</keywords>
pages.68:
# CANONICAL DISTRIBUTION

Now the average value in the ensemble of any quantity (which we shall denote in general by a horizontal line above the proper symbol) is determined by the equation

-> $\bar{u} = \int_{\text{phases}}^{\text{all}} \dots \int u e^{\frac{\psi - \epsilon}{\Theta}} dp_1 \dots dq_n.$ (108) <-

Comparing this with the preceding equation, we have

-> $d\psi = \frac{\psi}{\Theta} d\Theta - \frac{\bar{\epsilon}}{\Theta} d\Theta - \bar{A}_1 da_1 - \bar{A}_2 da_2 - \text{etc.}$ (109) <-

Or, since

-> $\frac{\psi - \epsilon}{\Theta} = \eta,$ (110) <-

and

-> $\frac{\psi - \bar{\epsilon}}{\Theta} = \bar{\eta},$ (111) <-

-> $d\psi = \bar{\eta} d\Theta - \bar{A}_1 da_1 - \bar{A}_2 da_2 - \text{etc.}$ (112) <-

Moreover, since (111) gives

-> $d\psi - d\bar{\epsilon} = \Theta d\bar{\eta} + \bar{\eta} d\Theta,$ (113) <-

we have also

-> $d\bar{\epsilon} = - \Theta d\bar{\eta} - \bar{A}_1 da_1 - \bar{A}_2 da_2 - \text{etc.}$ (114) <-

This equation, if we neglect the sign of averages, is identical in form with the thermodynamic equation

-> $d\eta = \frac{d\epsilon + A_1 da_1 + A_2 da_2 + \text{etc.}}{T},$ (115) <-

or

-> $d\epsilon = T d\eta - A_1 da_1 - A_2 da_2 - \text{etc.},$ (116) <-

which expresses the relation between the energy, temperature, and entropy of a body in thermodynamic equilibrium, and the forces which it exerts on external bodies—a relation which is the mathematical expression of the second law of thermodynamics for reversible changes. The modulus in the statistical equation corresponds to temperature in the thermodynamic equation, and the average index of probability *with its sign reversed* corresponds to entropy. But in the thermodynamic equation the entropy (η) is a quantity which is

<summary>This page demonstrates that the equations derived for a canonical ensemble correspond exactly to the thermodynamic equations for temperature, entropy, and energy.</summary>
<keywords>average value, thermodynamic equation, second law of thermodynamics, entropy, temperature, canonical ensemble</keywords>

only defined by the equation itself, and incompletely defined in that the equation only determines its differential, and the constant of integration is arbitrary. On the other hand, the η̄ in the statistical equation has been completely defined as the average value in a canonical ensemble of systems of the logarithm of the coefficient of probability of phase.

We may also compare equation (112) with the thermodynamic equation
->*d* ψ = − η̄ *dT* − *A*₁ *da*₁ − *A*₂ *da*₂ − *etc.*,         (117)<-
where ψ represents the function obtained by subtracting the product of the temperature and entropy from the energy.

How far, or in what sense, the similarity of these equations constitutes any demonstration of the thermodynamic equations, or accounts for the behavior of material systems, as described in the theorems of thermodynamics, is a question of which we shall postpone the consideration until we have further investigated the properties of an ensemble of systems distributed in phase according to the law which we are considering. The analogies which have been pointed out will at least supply the motive for this investigation, which will naturally commence with the determination of the average values in the ensemble of the most important quantities relating to the systems, and to the distribution of the ensemble with respect to the different values of these quantities.

<summary>This page completes the derivation connecting statistical ensembles to thermodynamics, emphasizing the clear definition of entropy within the statistical framework, and sets the stage for further investigation.</summary>

74 قعدت لر وصحبتي بين ضارج .. وبين العذيب بعد ما متأملي

"I sat down with my companions waiting for the rain between Zárij and 'Uzaib after observing the lightning attentively."

<term>صحبتي</term> (plural of <term>صاحب</term>): In the nominative case, coordinated with the first-person pronoun implied in the verb <term>قعدت</term>. <term>ما</term> is an expletive, and <term>متأملي</term> = "my observing attentively." The phrase <term>بعد ما متأملي</term> is also interpreted as: <term>بعد</term> being a shortened form of the past tense verb <term>بَعُدَ</term>; meaning the cloud, the object of my observation, was far away.

Another reading: <term>بعد</term> = (distance) in the object case, treated as a vocative (<term>منادى</term>), with <term>يا</term> (O) implied. It would mean: "O, how great was the distance of that which I watched!"

"In watching for the rain, we guessed that its right downpour was over Qatan, while its left was upon Satár and beyond that, upon Yazbul."

These locations are very far apart, emphasizing the magnitude of the storm.

<term>علي قطن</term>, under the category of <term>ايمن</term>.

Another reading: <term>علي قطنا</term>. It would then mean: "As we guessed from the observation of the lightning and other signs of rain, its right downpour topped Qatan," etc.

<term>يذبل</term>: A diptote (<term>غَيْرُ مُنْصَرِف</term>), being both a verb-form and a proper name, but here used as a triptote to satisfy the rhyme.

->THE SECOND POEM<-

# THE SECOND POEM.

Ascribed to Tarafah, son of 'Abd-il-Bakrí, from the tribe of Bakr-ibn-Wáil. "Tarafah" is his title; his name is 'Amr-bin-ul-'Abd. He was a poet of the pre-Islamic Pagan era and lived after the time of Malik-ul-Zilleel, the author of the first poem.

The story goes that the poet's brother, Ma'bad, reproached him for neglecting their father’s camels to indulge in poetry. Ma'bad taunted him, asking if his poetry could recover the camels if they were ever lost. The poet promised it could. Ma'bad then neglected the camels, which were subsequently stolen by the tribe of Muzar. The poet wrote this piece to appeal to 'Amru, Qáboos, and a chieftain of Yaman for aid; he succeeded in regaining his camels, plus an additional hundred as a reward.

The meter is the second form of <term>الطويل</term> (Long Meter), the same as the first poem; the rhyme (<term>قافية</term>) is also identical.

[Table of metrics omitted in prose: This section outlines the scansion of the opening line.]

1 لِخَوْلَةَ أَطْلَالٌ بِبَرْقَةِ ثَهْمَدِ .. تَلُوحُ كَبَاقِي الْوَشْمِ فِي ظَاهِرِ الْيَدِ

"There are traces of Kholah's encampment in the stony plain of Thahmad, which appear like the faded remains of a tattoo on the back of the hand."

5 يَشُقُّ حُبَابَ المَاءِ حَيْزُومُهَا .. كَمَا قَسَمَ التُّرْبَ الْمُفَايِلُ بِالْيَدِ

“Their prows cleave the ripples of the water, just as the <term>مُفَايِل</term> (divider) separates the dust with his hand.”

<term>مُفَايِل</term>: Agent from the third conjugation verb <term>فَايَلَ</term>, to play the game called <term>فِيل</term>. This game is played by hiding a small object (like a coin) in a sand-heap, which is then divided into smaller piles by the <term>مُفَايِل</term> for the players to guess where the object is hidden.

This line is an instance of the defect in rhyme called <term>الايطاء</term> (Ita’), which is the repetition of the same rhyming word, <term>اليد</term> (hand), used with the same meaning within nine lines.

6 وَفِي الْحَيِّ أَحْوَى يَنْفُضُ الْمُرْدَ شَادِنٌ .. مَظَاهِرُ سِمْطَيْ لُؤْلُؤٍ وَزَبَرْجَدِ

“And in the tribe, there is one like a young gazelle, with deep-colored lips, shaking the Arák tree to get its fruit, while wearing double strings of pearls and emeralds.”

The prose order is: <term>وفي الحي شادن احوى ينفض المرد</term>.
<term>مظاهر</term> and <term>خذول</term> (in the next line) are adjectives to <term>شادن</term>. <term>احوى ينفض</term> etc., is an adjectival sentence to <term>شادن</term>. <term>في الحي</term> is the subject and <term>شادن</term> is the predicate.

suggest that an advance in the systematic study of mind is especially liable to be influenced by, and to mould itself upon, that body of more or less systematic physical knowledge which bulks most impressively in the more thoughtful part of the society of that time and place. For the subject-matter of <term>mental science</term> is, as we know, not accessible to strictly collective observation; <term>introspection</term> is of the individual, and in the individual no two instances of a phenomenon can be shown as absolutely coincident. Hence it is largely—I do not say only—when some onward stride in <term>physical science</term> draws the rest of human knowledge in its wake, that the laws of mind are freshly investigated, as something that must also be brought into the line of march.

Where there is no such advance in <term>psychical investigation</term>, some system of <term>dogmatic metaphysic</term> is probably holding the cultured imagination of the age captive, through the spell of some myth of the Word. When the mind breaks free and looks deeper, there will naturally be a recourse, for its fresh concepts, to more positive ideas as guides and supports.

Now in the healing lore and craft of the day—the only one, I repeat, that comes prominently to the front in episode and in details of rules in the <term>Vinaya</term> <note>The monastic code of Buddhism.</note>—the revolt of thought embodied in the <term>Buddhist movement</term> found its noblest inspiration.

<summary>This page argues that advances in mental science are often shaped by the dominant scientific or medical knowledge of the era, noting that Buddhism’s early psychological insights were linked to its medical focus on 'dukkha'.</summary>

pages.98:
82 BUDDHIST PSYCHOLOGY

ment found its noblest inspiration. The word *dukkha* covers all that is meant by “not well”—ills and pains of body, ills and misery of mind, in a word, dis-ease. Its presence is the doctor’s <term>casus belli</term> <note>Latin: "a cause for war," or here, the reason for the struggle against disease.</note> and <term>raison d'être</term> <note>French: "reason for being."</note>; its cause and extinction is his quest. For its absence there may be several positive expressions. And yet there is nothing else in life so mortally positive as *dukkha*. And it is easy, alas! for many to conceive its mere absence as sufficient for happiness. *Nibbana* itself, a quasi-negative term, was at times employed as “health,” as well as happiness. And the Founder, in one of his more emphatic utterances about his mission, expressed that as one of healing:

“Both then and now just this do I reveal:
—*dukkha* and the extinction of *dukkha*.” <note>Original: "Pubbe chāhaṃ etarahi ca dukkhañceva paññapemi dukkhassa ca nirodhan ti."</note>

The physical healer finds the causes of dis-ease in the mutual interaction of man and his environment. Buddhism too found therein the causes of all that made for unhappiness. Sense-impressions were the avenues whereby came satisfactions (*pasāda*) fraught with peril. Consciousness, with its three main roots or conditions—greed or appetite, enmity, delusion—pushing it, reacted on its impressions as feeling, desire for, grasping after, all that tended to the
pages.99:
FEELING 83

expansion and conceit of this Me and Mine. And as it behooved the physician to keep in view all possible sources of any disease, neglecting none, so was Buddhism searching and exhaustive in its treatment of the avenues of sense, ignoring none of the five that conveyed, nor the sixth that coordinated and revived what the former brought.

The great intermediary between the (relatively) passive reactions to the manifold stimulus of sense and the following more or less deliberate reactions, Buddhism discerned, correctly enough, in Feeling. This might be pleasant, painful, or neither. And it did not follow that where feeling was pleasant (*sukha*), the symptoms of disease (*dukkha*) were absent. For the *sukha* born of sense was the most efficient handmaiden of *dukkha*, if *dukkha* be broadly understood as both physical and moral ill, and all that this does, or may involve of mental suffering and moral deterioration.

As Ledi Sadaw, the eminent Thera (Senior in the Order) writes: “We must distinguish between *dukkha* of the category (or, in Buddhist idiom, of the essential mark) of something unpleasant experienced (by way of sense), physical or psychical, and the *dukkha* we use in the triad: impermanence (*aniccha*), ill, and non-soul (*an-atta*). By this *dukkha*
pages.100:
84 BUDDHIST PSYCHOLOGY

we mean a state of peril and danger, without peace, security, or blessing.”

This, in other words, is the distinction a physician, or at least a patient, might draw between sensations of pain and disease. The presence, the growth, the decline of the pain is not always accompanied by the presence or increase or cessation of the disease. And this distinction we have to draw throughout the whole of Buddhist literature dealing with sense, with feeling, and the effects of feeling. Else we find ourselves landed in much inconsistency of expression, as I shall show.

That feeling is the inevitable response to awareness of new stimulus is affirmed up and down the Nikayas <note>The canonical collections of the Buddha's discourses.</note>, notably in Samyutta-N. on the sphere of sense, e.g.:

“Where there are hands, there taking and setting down appears; where there are feet, there coming and going appears; where there are limbs, there folding and stretching appears; where there is stomach, there hunger and thirst appears. Just so, bhikkhus, where there is sight (or eye), or hearing... there arise subjective pleasure and pain, conditioned by sense-stimulus (literally: contact, *samphassa*).”

The contrary is then stated, both of the analogies and the analogues: “... Where there is not sight, etc., neither pleasure
pages.101:
FEELING 85

nor pain, conditioned by sense-stimulus, arises.”

This quotation is conclusive enough to represent all other passages stating the concomitance of sensations and feeling, understood as our psychology of sense understands pleasure and pain, or at least pleasure and <term>unpleasure</term> <note>A term borrowed from German psychological science referring to the feeling of unpleasantness.</note>. That the senses convey pleasure as well as its opposite is not only allowed and affirmed by doctrinal teaching, but the pleasure is also recognized as very genuine and good by the most eminent of the teachers. The Founder affirmed at times that none lived more at ease (*sukham seti*) than himself, however much he had forsworn most of the so-called good things of life. His chief apostles forgather with him one fine evening in the Gosinga Wood, delighting in the “divine perfumes” of the dewy moonlit scene, where the tall sal-trees stand clad in golden bloom. Temperance was prescribed for maintaining the physical comfort (*phāsuvihara*) of health.

But when the disciple is bidden to look upon *sukha* as, or *quā* <note>Latin: "as" or "in the capacity of."</note> *dukkha*, then we know that the wider concept is to be understood after the *gud*. And this is no
pages.102:
86 BUDDHIST PSYCHOLOGY

less the case when things unpleasant to the “average sensual man” are valued by a different scale and held to constitute higher pleasure:

“Things seen and heard, tastes, odours, what we touch,
Perceive, all, everything desirable,
Pleasant and sweet, while one can say ‘It is,’
These are deemed *Sukha* by both gods and men,
And where these cease to be, they hold it woe.

What other men call *Sukha*, that the saints
Call *Dukkha*; what the rest so name,
That do the Ariyans know as happiness.
Behold a norm that’s hard to apprehend!
Hereby are baffled they that are not wise.”

If we would not be baffled, it is with this wider implication that we must read those passages wherein each sense is declared to be *dukkha*, and not productive of either this or its contrary. If, using Ledi Sadaw’s definition, we read into such passages as “seeing... is sorrow...” the wider sense of *dukkha*, thus:

“The eye, brother, is a faculty of peril and danger, bringing, as such, no peace, security or blessing; it is to understand this that the holy life under the Exalted One is lived...”

and so on for the other senses, why, then we may not be unwilling to admit even for laymen the truth in this “monkish” statement.

CHAPTER V

THE PSYCHOLOGY OF THE NIKAYAS—continued

IV. IDEATION

THE systematic analysis of mind in the Nikayas is pursued no further than the recipient and co-ordinating work of *mano* as <term>sensus communis</term> <note>Latin: "common sense" or the faculty that integrates the various senses.</note>. Sequences in consciousness are occasionally pursued further, but without overmuch terminological consistency, and irregularly. Here are a few instances:

“Because of some tendency there arises perception, opinion, thinking, volition, wish, aspiration. And according as the tendency is low, mediocre or lofty, so will all these be.”

The process of conversion in religion is described as one of “hearing, attending, remembering, comparing, discerning, desire, zeal, pondering, endeavor.”

“Thinking results in desire, through desire objects are divided into what we like and
pages.104:
88 BUDDHIST PSYCHOLOGY

what we dislike, hence envy and selfishness, hence quarrelling and fighting.”

“Conditioned by contact arises feeling; what one feels, one perceives; what one perceives, one thinks about; what one thinks about, one is obsessed withal.”

These samples reveal the persistent effort, in the Suttas, to carry on the method, systematically observed in treating of sense, of setting forth mind and character as orderly, causal process. The method is emphatically Buddhist. The most notable example of it is the important formula of natural causation, as exemplified in the process of life being bound up with *dukkha*. In the mental process, the resolution of afferent or receptive consciousness into efferent or discharging consciousness is clearly affirmed. Sense and feeling stirred by sense are converted into motor presentations, as desire, etc. But we meet with no closer analysis of intellectual process, of what has, in our own psychology, been called representative and re-representative cognition, or <term>ideation</term>. In the last sample, we only hear that “what we perceive,” i.e., notice (the *saññā-kkhandha*), we “think about” (*vitakketi*).

<margin>16</margin> Therefore, let us remove those declamations from the middle: 
"A mind bound by drunkenness has no power over itself. Just as the vats themselves are burst by new wine, and the heat forces everything that lies at the bottom to the top, so when wine effervesces, whatever lies hidden in the depths is brought out and revealed. Just as those loaded with wine cannot keep down their food when they have over-indulged, so they cannot keep a secret. They pour out their own secrets and those of others alike." 

<margin>17</margin> But although this usually happens, it is also common to deliberate on necessary matters with those whom we know to be fond of drinking. Therefore, this argument, which is put forward as a defense, is false: that a man who is often drunk cannot be trusted with a secret. 

How much better it is to frankly accuse drunkenness and expose its vices—vices that even a tolerable person would avoid, let alone a perfect and wise man, who is satisfied with quenching his thirst, and who, even if he is occasionally led further by the gaiety of others, still resists before he reaches the state of drunkenness. 

<margin>18</margin> For we shall see later whether the mind of the wise man is disturbed by too much wine and performs the usual actions of a drunkard. Meanwhile, if you want to prove that a good man should not get drunk, why do you use syllogisms? Say how shameful it is to put into oneself more than one can hold and not to know the measure of one's own stomach; how many things drunkards do that would make a sober person blush; that drunkenness is nothing other than voluntary insanity. Extend that state of the drunkard over several days; would you have any doubt about his madness? It is no less severe now; it is only briefer.

So let us abolish all such harangues as this: “No man in the bonds of drunkenness has power over his soul. As the very vats are burst by new wine, and as the dregs at the bottom are raised to the surface by the strength of the fermentation, so, when the wine effervesces, whatever lies hidden below is brought up and made visible. As a man overcome by liquor cannot keep down his food when he has over-indulged in wine, so he cannot keep back a secret either. He pours forth impartially both his own secrets and those of other persons.” This, of course, is what commonly happens, but so does this—that we take counsel on serious subjects with those whom we know to be in the habit of drinking freely. Therefore, this proposition, which is laid down in the guise of a defense, is false—that secrets are not entrusted to the habitual drunkard.

How much better it is to arraign drunkenness frankly and to expose its vices! For even the reasonably good man avoids them, not to mention the perfect sage, who is satisfied with slaking his thirst; the sage, even if now and then he is led on by good cheer which, for a friend’s sake, is carried somewhat too far, yet always stops short of drunkenness. We shall investigate later the question whether the mind of the sage is upset by too much wine and commits follies like those of the toper; but meanwhile, if you wish to prove that a good man ought not to get drunk, why work it out by logic? <margin>20</margin> When too much wine has taken possession of the mind, whatever evil was hidden emerges. Drunkenness does not make vices, it brings them forth; then the lustful man does not even wait for the bedroom, but gives way to his desires without delay; then the unchaste man proclaims and publishes his disease; then the insolent man does not restrain his tongue or his hand. Haughty pride grows, as does cruelty in the savage and spite in the envious. 

<margin>21</margin> Every vice is loosened and brought to light. Add to this that lack of self-awareness, the doubtful and poorly articulated words, the unsteady eyes, the staggering gait, the dizziness of the head, the roofs themselves moving as if some whirlpool were spinning the whole house, and the torments of the stomach when the wine ferments and distends the very bowels.

Think of Alexander of Macedon, <note>For a dramatic account of the murder of his friend Clitus, see Plutarch’s *Life of Alexander*.</note> who stabbed Clitus, his dearest and most loyal friend, at a banquet; after Alexander understood what he had done, he wished to die, and assuredly he ought to have died.

Drunkenness kindles and discloses every kind of vice and removes the sense of shame that veils our evil undertakings. <note>This is the firm conviction of Seneca, himself a most temperate man.</note> For more men abstain from forbidden actions because they are ashamed of sinning than because their inclinations are good. When the strength of wine has become too great and has gained control over the mind, every lurking evil comes forth from its hiding-place. Drunkenness does not create vice; it merely brings it into view. At such times the lustful man does not wait even for the privacy of a bedroom, but without postponement gives free play to the demands of his passions; at such times the unchaste man proclaims and publishes his malady; at such times your cross-grained fellow does not restrain his tongue or his hand. The haughty man increases his arrogance, the ruthless man his cruelty, the slanderer his spitefulness. Every vice is given free play and comes to the front. Besides, we forget who we are, we utter words that are halting and poorly enunciated, the glance is unsteady, the step falters, the head is dizzy, the very ceiling moves about as if a cyclone were whirling the whole house, and the stomach suffers torture when the wine generates gas and causes our very bowels to swell.

<margin>22</margin> Think of the disasters caused by public drunkenness; it has betrayed the fiercest and most warlike nations to their enemies, it has opened walls defended by the persistent war of many years, it has driven the most stubborn and those who refused the yoke into the power of others, it has conquered the unconquered in battle with wine.

<margin>24</margin> What glory is there in taking a lot? Think of the calamities caused by drunkenness in a nation! This evil has betrayed to their enemies the most spirited and warlike races; this evil has made breaches in walls defended by the stubborn warfare of many years; this evil has forced under alien sway peoples who were utterly unyielding and defiant of the yoke; this evil has conquered by the wine-cup those who in the field were invincible. Alexander, whom I have just mentioned, passed through his many marches, his many battles, his many winter campaigns (through which he worked his way by overcoming disadvantages of time or place), the many rivers which flowed from unknown sources, and the many seas, all in safety; it was intemperance in drinking that laid him low, and the famous death-dealing bowl of Hercules. <note>Legend says Hercules drank from a massive bowl; it became a symbol of dangerous overindulgence.</note>

What glory is there in carrying much liquor? When you have won the prize, and the other banqueters, sprawling asleep or vomiting, have declined your challenge to still other toasts; when you are the last survivor of the revels; when you have vanquished every one by your magnificent show of prowess and there is no man who has proved himself of so great capacity as you—you are vanquished by the cask. Mark Antony was a great man, a man of distinguished ability; but what ruined him and drove him into foreign habits and un-Roman vices, if it was not drunkenness and—no less potent than wine—love of Cleopatra? This it was that made him an enemy of the state; this it was that rendered him

the bull-formed Dionysus “had either been developed out of, or had succeeded to the worship of a bull-totem.”^1 Of course this is possible. But it is not yet certain that the Aryans ever had totemism. On the other hand, it is quite certain that many Aryan peoples have conceived of vegetation deities as embodied in animal forms. Therefore, when we find among an Aryan people like the Greeks a vegetation deity represented as an animal, the presumption must be in favor of explaining this by a principle known to have influenced the Aryan race rather than one which is not. In the present state of our knowledge, therefore, it is safer to regard the bull form of Dionysus as being, like his goat form, an expression of his proper character as a deity of vegetation.

The probability of this view is increased if we can show that, in rites other than those of Dionysus, the ancients slew an ox as a representative of the spirit of vegetation. They appear to have done this in the Athenian sacrifice known as “the murder of the ox” (*bouphonia*). It took place about the end of June or beginning of July, roughly when the threshing is nearly over in Attica. According to tradition, the sacrifice was instituted to end a drought and barrenness that had afflicted the land. The ritual was as follows: Barley mixed with wheat, or cakes made from them, were laid upon the bronze altar of Zeus Polieus on the Acropolis. Oxen were driven around the altar, and the ox that approached the altar and ate the offering was sacrificed. The axe and knife used to slay the beast had been previously wetted with water brought

As soon as he had felled the ox, the first man threw the axe away and fled; the man who cut the beast’s throat apparently did the same. Meanwhile, the ox was skinned, and everyone present partook of its flesh. The hide was then stuffed with straw and sewn up; the stuffed animal was set on its feet and yoked to a plow, as if it were plowing. A trial then took place in an ancient law-court presided over by the King (as he was titled) to determine who had murdered the ox. The maidens who brought the water accused the men who sharpened the axe and knife; those men blamed the ones who handed the tools to the butchers; the men who handed the tools blamed the butchers; and the butchers blamed the axe and knife, which were accordingly found guilty, condemned, and cast into the sea.<sup>1</sup>

This is supported by Varro's statement that killing an ox was once a capital crime in Attica.¹ The method of selecting the victim suggests that the ox which tasted the corn was viewed as the corn-deity taking possession of his own. Passing next to the corn-goddess Demeter, and remembering that in European folklore the pig is a common embodiment of the corn-spirit,¹ we may now ask: could the pig, which was so closely associated with Demeter, be the goddess herself in animal form? The pig was sacred to her;² in art she was represented carrying or accompanied by a pig;³ and the pig was regularly sacrificed in her mysteries, the reason assigned being that the pig injures the corn and is therefore an enemy of the goddess.⁴ But after an animal has been conceived as a god, or a god as an animal, it sometimes happens that the god sloughs off his animal form and becomes purely human in appearance (anthropomorphic). The animal that was once slain as the god then comes to be regarded as a victim offered *to* the god on the grounds of its hostility to the deity—in short, the god is sacrificed to himself on the premise that he is his own enemy. This happened to Dionysus, and it may have happened to Demeter. In fact, the rites of one of her festivals, the Thesmophoria, support the view that the pig was originally an embodiment of the corn-goddess herself, either Demeter or her daughter and double, Proserpine. ### **STANZA XLII.**

But on the other hand, <term>Guru</term> (Jupiter), when combined with <term>Sani</term> (Saturn), not only fails to provide good results but will actively produce evil. <term>Sukra</term> (Venus) does not himself kill the native, although he possesses death-inflicting powers.

### **NOTES.**

It was pointed out (vide Stanza 41) that <term>Guru</term>, being the lord of the 9th and 12th houses, has both good and bad qualities combined within himself. 

Regarding the combination of <term>Sani</term> and <term>Guru</term>, the author tells us that there will be evil in their combination, especially on the part of <term>Guru</term>. This requires explanation. Let us take an example: if a planet is capable of producing one rupee's worth of good and one rupee's worth of evil, the influence should be neutral. However, astrological writers assure us that the result is not neutral but actually bad. They believe that when the good and evil influences of a planet are equal, we must predict evil, though in a milder form. Remembering this principle, we see why <term>Guru</term> is bad in combination with <term>Sani</term>. <term>Guru</term> owns the 9th and 12th houses, while <term>Sani</term> owns the 10th and 11th; the 12th and 11th are evil houses. Here, the evil is equal to the good these two planets possess, as one house for each is good and one is bad. We can understand why the combination is bad, but why should <term>Guru</term> be declared specifically responsible for producing evil while <term>Sani</term> contributes to the result as well? <term>Guru</term> is an auspicious planet by nature, and evil influences seem to affect him more; <term>Sani</term> is an evil planet, and good influences seem to improve him. <term>Guru</term> owns one good and one bad house, which neutralize each other, but he has an evil association—he is in conjunction with <term>Sani</term>. Thus, <term>Guru</term> is declared to produce evil because of this combination. <term>Sani</term> has a better prospect: while his house ownerships also counterbalance, he is in conjunction with <term>Guru</term>, a naturally good planet, and his position is improved.

The reader need scarcely be told that by "constraint" we do not mean an external force moving our limbs without our consent, for in that case we are not agents at all; rather, we mean that constraint which arises from threatening and presenting some evil to make us act in a certain manner. And yet there seems to be a universally acknowledged difference between even this sort of constraint and "obligation." We never say we are "obliged" to do an action we consider base, though we may be "constrained" to do it. We never say that divine laws, by their sanctions, constrain us, but rather that they oblige us; nor do we call obedience to the DEITY "constraint," unless metaphorically, though many admit they are influenced by fear of punishments. Yet, if we suppose an almighty evil being were to require—under grievous penalties—treachery, cruelty, or ingratitude, we would call this "constraint." The difference is plainly this: When any sanctions cooperate with our <term>moral sense</term> in exciting us to actions we count morally good, we say we are "obliged." But when sanctions of rewards or punishments oppose our <term>moral sense</term>, we say we are "bribed" or "constrained." In the former case, we call the lawgiver good, as he is designing the public happiness; in the latter, we call him evil or unjust for his supposed contrary
pages.311:
<header>MORAL GOOD and EVIL.</header>

intention. But if all our ideas of moral good or evil were derived solely from opinions of private advantage or loss in our actions, I see no possible difference that could be made in the meaning of these words.

VI. From this sense, too, we derive our <term>rights</term>.
<margin>Ideas of RIGHTS.</margin>
Whenever it appears to us that a faculty of doing, demanding, or possessing anything—if universally allowed in certain circumstances—would tend to the general good, we say that any person in such circumstances has a "right" to do, possess, or demand that thing. And according to whether this tendency to the public good is greater or less, the right itself is greater or less.

<margin>*Perfect Rights.*</margin>
The rights called "perfect" are of such necessity to the public good that the universal violation of them would make human life intolerable, and it actually makes those people miserable whose rights are thus violated. On the contrary, to fulfill these rights in every instance tends to the public good, either directly or by promoting the innocent advantage of an individual. Hence it follows: "That allowing a violent defense or prosecution of such rights, before civil government is constituted, cannot in any particular case be more detrimental to the public than the violation of them with impunity."
pages.312:
<header>An INQUIRY concerning</header>

And as for general consequences, the universal use of force in a <term>state of nature</term>, in pursuance of perfect rights, seems exceedingly advantageous to the whole by making everyone dread any attempts against the perfect rights of others.

<margin>Right of War and Punishment.</margin>
This is the moral effect that accompanies proper injury, or a violation of the perfect rights of others: namely, a right to war and all violence necessary to force the injurious party to repair the damage and provide security against such offenses in the future. This is the sole foundation for the rights of punishing criminals and for the violent prosecution of our rights in a state of nature. These rights, belonging originally to the injured persons (or their voluntary assistants, according to the judgment of indifferent arbitrators in a state of nature), are transferred to the magistrate in a civil state by the consent of the injured parties. This transfer is the true foundation of the magistrate's right to punish. Instances of perfect rights include: rights to our lives; to the fruits of our labors; to demand performance of contracts from men capable of fulfilling them; to direct our own actions for public or innocent private good before we have submitted them to the direction of others; and many others of a like nature.
pages.313:
<header>MORAL GOOD and EVIL. Sect. 7.</header>

<margin>Imperfect Rights.</margin>
<term>Imperfect rights</term> are such that, if they were universally violated, they would not necessarily make men miserable. These rights tend to the improvement and increase of positive good in any society, but are not absolutely necessary to prevent universal misery. Violating them only disappoints men of the happiness expected from the humanity or gratitude of others, but does not deprive men of any good they previously possessed. From this description, it appears: "That a violent prosecution of such rights would generally occasion greater evil than the violation of them." Besides, allowing force in such cases would deprive men of the greatest pleasure found in actions of kindness, humanity, and gratitude, which would cease to appear amiable if men could be constrained to perform them. Instances of imperfect rights are those which the poor have to the charity of the wealthy; which all men have to favors that require no trouble or expense to the performer; and which benefactors have to returns of gratitude, and such like.

The violation of imperfect rights only shows a man to have such weak benevolence that he does not study to advance the positive good of others when it is even slightly opposed to his own. But the violation of per-
pages.314:
<header>An INQUIRY concerning</header>

<margin>Sect. 7.</margin>
fect rights argues that the injurious person is positively evil or cruel—or at least so immoderately selfish that he is indifferent to the positive misery and ruin of others when he imagines he can find his own interest in it. In violating the former, we show a weak desire for public happiness, which every small view of private interest outweighs. But in violating the latter, we show ourselves so entirely negligent of the misery of others that views of increasing our own good overcome all our compassion toward their sufferings. Now, as the absence of good is more easily borne than the presence of misery, so our good wishes toward the positive good of others are weaker than our compassion toward their misery. He who violates imperfect rights shows that his self-love overcomes only his desire for others' positive good; but he who violates perfect rights betrays such a selfish desire to advance his own positive good that it overcomes all compassion toward the misery of others.

<margin>External Rights.</margin>
Beside these two sorts of rights, there is a third called "external." This occurs when the doing, possessing, or demanding of something is actually detrimental to the public in a particular instance (as being contrary to the imperfect right of another), yet universally denying men this faculty—or the right to use force in its pursuit—would do more mischief than all the evils to be feared from the exercise of this faculty.
pages.315:
<header>MORAL GOOD and EVIL.</header>

<margin>Sect. 7.</margin>
From this it appears:
> "That there can be no right to use force in opposition even to external rights, since it tends to the universal good to allow force in the pursuit of them."

Civil societies substitute legal actions in the place of the force allowed in the state of nature.

Instances of external rights include: that of a wealthy miser to recall his loan from the most industrious poor tradesman at any time; that of demanding the performance of a covenant that is too burdensome on one side; the right of a wealthy heir to refuse payment of any debts contracted while he was a minor (provided there was no fraud by the lender); and the right of taking advantage of a positive law, even when it is contrary to what was equitable before that law existed (such as when a registered deed takes precedence over an unregistered one, even if the latter is prior in time and was known to be so before the second contract).

<margin>What rights can be opposite.</margin>
Now, whereas no action, demand, or possession can be at once necessary to the public good—or conducive to it—and
pages.316:
<header>An INQUIRY concerning</header>

<margin>Sect. 7.</margin>
at the same time have its contrary be necessary or conducive to the same end, it follows:
> "That there can be no opposition of perfect rights among themselves, of imperfect rights among themselves, or between perfect and imperfect rights."

However, it may often tend to the public good to allow a right of doing, possessing, or demanding—and of using force in pursuit of it—even while it would have been more humane and kind for a person to have acted otherwise and not claimed that right. Yet, a violent opposition to these rights would have been vastly more pernicious than all the inhumanity involved in the use of them. Therefore, though external rights cannot be opposite among themselves, they may be opposite to imperfect rights. But imperfect rights, even when violated, give no right to use force. Hence it appears:
> "That there can never be a right to force on both sides, or a just war on both sides at the same time."

<margin>Rights alienable and unalienable.</margin>
