...divine; for through them the bondages of all things, even their solutions and transmutations, the knowledge and prediction of future events, the extermination of evil demons, and the conciliation of good spirits descend from them. Therefore, without these triple elements and the knowledge of them, let no one trust that they can accomplish anything in the hidden sciences of Magick and nature. However, whoever knows how to reduce these into that, the impure into the pure, the manifold into the simple, and knows how to discern and know their nature, virtue, and power in number, degrees, and order without the division of the substance: he will easily obtain the science and perfect operation of all natural and celestial secrets. 

This is He with the *black spaniel* <note>A reference to the dog often accompanying Cornelius Agrippa in legend</note>; or rather, this is he *who from his early youth was a curious and fearless explorer, always around the wonderful effects and operations full of mysteries.* 

Now for your further instruction, hear also the *Dark Disciple* of the more dark *Libanius Gallus*. 
<margin>Johannes Trithemius</margin> 
'The first principle consists in one, not that from which, but through which every virtue of wonderful natural things is produced into effect: we say "through which," because the pure, proceeding from the one, is not composed, nor changed. To it, from the Ternary and Quaternary, the progress is made to the Monad, that the *Denary* may be completed: through it, indeed, is the return of the number to one, together with the descent into four, and the ascent into the *Monad*. It is impossible to complete the *Denary* except through it: the *Monad* is joyfully converted in the *Triad*. All who are ignorant of this principle after the principle of the *Monad* profit nothing in the *Ternary*, nor do they attain to the sacred Quaternary. For even if they possess all the *books* of the wise, and perfectly know the courses, virtues, powers, operations, and properties of the stars, and fully understand their images, rings, and *seals*, and every most secret thing, they can nonetheless achieve no effect of wonders in their operations without the knowledge of this principle from the beginning, into the beginning; whence all whom I have seen working in *natural magick* have either achieved nothing, or have fallen into despair after long and useless operations, arriving only at vain, frivolous, and superstitious things. The second principle, in order—though not indeed in dignity—separated from the First, which being one makes the *Ternary*, is that which works wonders through the *Binary*. For in one is one, and yet it is not one; it is simple, and is composed in the *Quaternary*: when this is purified through *fire* in the sun, *pure water* emerges, and it, returned to its own simplicity, will show the complement of hidden things to the operator. This is the center of all natural *magick*, the circumference of which...
pages.42:
...is a circle representing an immense order to infinity: its virtue is purified above all, and is simple, being less than all, composed on a degree above the Quaternary. The Pythagorean Quaternary, supported by the Ternary, if it observes order and degree, being purified and pure in one, can work the wonders and occult things of Nature through the Binary in the Ternary. This is the Quaternary in whose measure the Ternary, joined to the Binary in one, does all things, which it does miraculously. The Ternary, reduced to unity through aspect, contains all things in itself and can do what it wills. 

The third principle is not a principle in itself, but between it and the Binary is the end of all science and mystical Art, and the infallible center of the medium: in nothing more than in it is one more easily mistaken, since very few live on Earth who understand its profound nature. It is a various composite, and rising by the septenary into the Ternary, multiplied eight times, and remaining fixed. In it is the consummation of number, degrees, and order; through this, all philosophers, true inquirers into the secrets of nature, have achieved wonderful effects; through it, to the simple element reduced in the Ternary, there suddenly occur miraculous cures of infirmities, and naturally of all sicknesses; and the work of the operator in Natural and supernatural Magick achieves its effect through the disposition of the quaternary. 

Prediction of future things is verified through it, and the suggestion of occult things is perceived from Nature nowhere else but through it. By this unique medium, the secret of Nature is opened to alchemists, without which neither the intellect of the Art is acquired, nor the effect of the operation found. They err, believe me, they all err, who trust that they can work anything in the hidden sciences of Nature without these three principles. 

Thus far *Trithemius*; where, for your better understanding of him, I must inform you there is a twofold *Binary, of Light, and of Confusion*: but peruse *Agrippa* seriously *de scalis Numerorum* <note>Latin: "On the Scales of Numbers"</note>, and you may apprehend all, for our *Abbot* borrowed this language from him, the perusal of whose books he had before he published anything in this nature of his own. Now for your further instruction, go along with me, not to *Athens* or *Stagyra*, but to that *Secretary* and *Pen-Man* of *God Almighty*, who stood in a *cleft* of the *Rock* when He made all His *goodness* to pass before him. I am certain the world will wonder I should make use of *Scripture* to establish *physiology*, but I would have them know that secret *physical* and *spiritual* things, all the close connections, and that mysterious *kiss* of God and Nature are clearly and punctually discovered there. Consider that merciful *mystery* of the incarnation wherein the fullness of the Godhead...
pages.43:
...was incorporated, and the *Divine Light* united to the *matter* in a far greater measure than at the first creation. Consider it, I say, and you shall find that no *philosophy* has perfectly united God to His creature but the Christian; wherefore also it is the only true *philosophy*, and the only true *religion*: for without this union there can be neither a *natural temporal* nor a *spiritual eternal life*. 

Moses tells us that in the beginning God created the <margin>+</margin> *Heaven* and the *Earth*, that is, the *Virgin Mercury* and the *Virgin Sulphur*. Now let me advise you not to trouble yourselves with this *Mercury* unless you have a true friend to instruct you, or an *express illumination* from the first *author* of it, for it is a *thing* attained *arte mirabili* <note>Latin: "by a wonderful art"</note>. Observe then what I shall now tell you: there is in every star, and in this elemental world, a certain principle which is *Uxor solis* <note>Latin: "The wife of the sun"</note>. These two in their *coition* do *emittere semen* <note>Latin: "emit seed"</note>, which seed is carried in the womb of *Nature*. But the *ejection* of it is performed invisibly and in a *sacred silence*; for this is the <margin>o</margin> conjugal mystery of *Heaven* and *Earth*, their *act* of *generation*, a thing done in private between particular *males* and *females*, but how much more, think you, between the *two universal natures*? Know therefore that it is impossible for you to extract, or receive any seed from the <insert>Sun</insert> in, without this *feminine principle*, which is the *wife of the Sun*. 

Now then, my small *sophiers* <note>A term often used for shallow or self-styled wise men/alchemists</note> of the stone, you that consume your time and substance in making waters and oils with dirty *caput mortuum* <note>Latin: "dead head"—the useless, burnt residue after distillation</note>: you that deal in gold and *quicksilver*, being infatuated with the legends of some late and former *mountebanks*: consider the last end of such men. Did they obtain anything by it but *diseases* and *poverty*? Did they not in their old age, *inveterati ierum malorum* <note>Latin: "inveterate/hardened by many evils"</note>, fall to *clipping* and *counterfeiting* of *coin*? And for a *period* to their *memory*, did they not die in *despair*, which is the *child* of *ignorance*? Know then for certain that the *Magician's Sun* and *Moon* are two *universal peers, male* and *female*, a *King* and *Queen Regents*, always young, and never old. These two are *adequate* to the whole world, and coextended throughout the universe. The one is not without the other, God having united them in His work of creation in a solemn *sacramental union*. It will then be a hard and difficult enterprise to rob the *husband* of his wife, to put those asunder whom God Himself has put together: for they sleep both in the same bed, and he that discovers the one must needs see the other. The *love* between these two is so great that if you use this *virgin* kindly, she will fetch back her *Cupid* after he has ascended from her on *wings of fire*.

Observe, moreover, that *material principles* can be multiplied but *materially*, that is, by addition of parts, as you see in the *augmentation of bodies*, which is performed by a *continual assumption* of *nutriment* into the *stomach*. But it is not the *body* that *transmutes* the *nutriment* into *flesh and blood*, but that *spirit* which is the *life and light of the body*. *Material principles* are *passive*, and can neither alter nor *purify*, but well may they be altered and *purified*; neither can they communicate themselves to another substance beyond their own extension, which is *finite and determinate*. 

Trust not those *impostors* then who tell you of a *Sulphur Tingens* <note>Latin: "Tincturing Sulphur"—an alchemical agent said to transmute metals</note>, and know not what fables, who pin also that *new* and *narrow name* of *Chemia* <note>Alchemy</note> on a science both *ancient and infinite*. It is the *light only* that can be *truly multiplied*, for this ascends to, and *descends* from the first *fountain of multiplication and generation*. This *light*, applied to any *body* whatsoever, *exalts and perfects* it in *suo genere* <note>Latin: "in its own kind"</note>. If to *animals*, it *exalts animals*; if to *vegetables, vegetables*; if to *minerals*, it *refines minerals*, and translates them from the *worst to the best condition*. Where *note* by the way, that *every body has passive principles in itself* for this light to *work* upon, and therefore needs not *borrow* any from *gold* or *silver*.

Pleased with the sight, he began to wonder whether she would not one day outgrow her plainness. He began to close the door of the women’s apartments, but suddenly feeling that he owed her amends for the harsh opinion of her appearance which he had formed before, he did not quite shut the door. Instead, bringing a low stool toward it, he sat there, putting his disordered head-dress to rights. One of the maids brought him an incredibly battered mirror-stand, Chinese combs, a box of toilet articles, and other things. It amused him to discover that in this household of women, a little male gear still survived, even in such a decrepit state.

He noticed that the princess, who was now up and dressed, was looking quite fashionable. She was, in fact, wearing the clothes which he had sent her before the New Year, but he did not at first recognize them. He began, however, to have a vague idea that her mantle, with its rather conspicuous pattern, was very like one of the things he had given her. "I do hope," he said presently, "that this year you will be a little more conversational. "Poor thing, she really is very ugly," thought Genji in despair.

When he returned to the Nijō-in, he found Murasaki waiting for him. She was growing up to be as handsome a girl as one could wish, and promised well for the future. She was wearing a plain, close-fitting dress of cherry color; above all, the unstudied grace and ease of her movements charmed and delighted him as he watched her come to meet him. In accordance with the wishes of her old-fashioned grandmother, her teeth were not blackened, but her eyebrows were delicately touched with stain. "Why, when I might be playing with a beautiful child, do I spend my time with an ugly woman?" Genji kept on asking himself in bewilderment while they sat together playing with her dolls. Next, she began to draw pictures and color them. After she had painted all sorts of queer and amusing things, "Now I am going to do a picture for you," said Genji, and drawing a lady with very long hair, he put a dab of red on her nose. Even in a picture, he thought, pausing to look at the effect, it gave one a most uncomfortable feeling. He went and looked at himself in the mirror, and as though dissatisfied with his own fresh complexion, he suddenly put on his own nose a dab of red such as he had given to the lady in the picture. He looked at himself in the mirror. His handsome face had in an instant become ridiculous and repulsive. At first the child laughed. "Would you still like me if I were always as ugly as this?" he asked. Suddenly she began to be afraid that the paint would not come off. "Oh, why did you do it?" she cried. "How horrible!" The imperial visit to the Red Sparrow Court was to take place on the tenth day of the Godless Month.<note>The tenth month of the lunar calendar.</note> It was to be a more magnificent sight this year than it had ever been before, and the ladies of the Palace were very disappointed that they could not be present.<note>They were forbidden from leaving the palace.</note> The Emperor, too, could not bear that Fujitsubo should miss the spectacle, and he decided to hold a grand rehearsal in the Palace. Prince Genji danced the "Waves of the Blue Sea." Tō no Chūjō was his partner; but though both in skill and beauty he far surpassed the common run of performers, yet beside Genji he seemed like a mountain fir growing beside a cherry-tree in bloom. There was a wonderful moment when the rays of the setting sun fell upon him and the music grew suddenly louder. Never had the onlookers seen feet tread so delicately nor head so exquisitely poised; and in the song which follows the first movement of the dance, his voice was sweet as that of the Kalavinka,<note>A mythical bird from Buddhist paradise known for its beautiful song.</note> whose music is Buddha’s Law. So moving and beautiful was this dance that at the end of it the Emperor’s eyes were wet, and all the princes and great gentlemen wept aloud. When the song was over and, straightening his long dancer’s sleeves, he stood waiting for the music to begin again and at last the more lively tune of the second movement struck up—then indeed,

Princess Kōkiden<note>The Emperor's consort and mother of the Heir Apparent.</note> did not at all like to see her stepson’s beauty arousing so much enthusiasm and she said sarcastically, "He is altogether too beautiful. Presently we shall have a god coming down from the sky to fetch him away."<note>Alluding to a legend of a beautiful prince carried off by jealous gods.</note> Her young waiting-ladies noticed the spiteful tone in which the remark was made and felt somewhat embarrassed. As for Fujitsubo, she kept on telling herself that were it not for the guilty secret which was shared between them, the dance she was now witnessing would be filling her with wonder and delight. As it was, she sat as though in a dream, hardly knowing what went on around her.

Now she was back in her own room. The Emperor was with her. "At today’s rehearsal," he said, "the 'Waves of the Blue Sea' went perfectly." Then, noticing that she made no response, "What did you think of it?" "Yes, it was very good," she managed to say at last. "The partner did not seem to me bad either," he went on; "there is always something about the way a gentleman moves and uses his hands which distinguishes his dancing from that of professionals. Some of our crack dancing-masters have certainly made very clever performers of their own children; but they never have the same freshness, the same charm as the young people of our class. They expended so much effort on the rehearsal that I am afraid the festival itself may seem a very poor affair. No doubt they took all this trouble because they knew that you were here at the rehearsal and would not see the real performance."

Next morning she received a letter from Genji: "What of the rehearsal? How little the people who watched me knew of the turmoil that all the while was seething in my brain!"

And to this he added the poem: "When sick with love I yet sprang to my feet and capered with the rest, knew you what meant the fevered waving of my long dancing-sleeve?" Next, he enjoined secrecy and prudence upon her, and so his letter ended. Her answer showed that despite her agitation, she had not been wholly insensible to what had fascinated all other eyes: "Though from far off a man of China waved his long dancing-sleeves, yet did his every motion fill my heart with wonder and delight."

To receive such a letter from her was indeed a surprise. It charmed him that her knowledge should extend even to the court customs of a land beyond the sea. Already there was a regal note in her words. Yes, that was the end to which she was destined. Smiling to himself with pleasure, he spread the letter out before him, grasping it tightly in both hands as a priest holds the holy book, and gazed at it for a long while.

On the day of the festival, the royal princes and all the great gentlemen of the court were in attendance. Even the Heir Apparent went with the procession. After the music-boats had rowed around the lake, dance upon dance was performed, both Korean and from the land beyond the sea. The whole valley resounded with the noise of music and drums. The Emperor insisted upon treating Genji’s performance at the rehearsal as a kind of miracle or religious portent and ordered special services to be read in every temple. Most people thought this step quite reasonable; but Princess Kōkiden said crossly that she saw no necessity for it. The Ring<note>The circle of attendants who stand by while the dancers change costumes.</note> was, by the Emperor’s order, composed indifferently of commoners and noblemen chosen out of the whole realm for their skill and grace. # THE TALE OF GENJI 214

in charge of the left and right wings of the orchestra. Dancing-masters and others were entrusted with the task of seeking out performers of unusual merit and training them for the festival in their own houses. When, at last, under the red leafage of tall autumn trees, forty men stood circle-wise with their flutes, and to the music that they made a strong wind from the hills sweeping the pine-woods added its fierce harmonies—while from amid a wreckage of whirling and scattered leaves the Dance of the Blue Waves suddenly broke out in all its glittering splendor—a rapture seized the onlookers that was akin to fear.

The maple-wreath that Genji wore had suffered in the wind, and thinking that the few red leaves which clung to it had a desolate air, the Minister of the Left plucked a bunch of chrysanthemums from among those that grew before the Emperor's seat and twined them in the dancer's wreath.

At sunset the sky clouded over and it looked like rain. But even the weather seemed conscious that such sights as this would not for a long while be seen again, and until all was over, not a drop fell. His Exit Dance, crowned as he was with this unspeakably beautiful wreath of many-colored flowers, was even more astonishing than that wonderful moment on the day of the rehearsal and seemed to the thrilled onlookers like the vision of another world. Humble and ignorant folk sitting afar on tree-roots or beneath some rock, or half-buried in deep banks of fallen leaves—few were so hardened that they did not shed a tear. Next came the "Autumn Wind" danced by Lady Jōkyōden's son,<note>Another illegitimate son of the Emperor; Genji’s step-brother.</note> who was still a mere child. The remaining performances attracted little attention, for the audience had had its fill of wonders and felt that whatever followed could but spoil the recollection of what had gone before.

<summary>The Festival of Red Leaves reaches a climactic peak during Genji's performance, leaving the spectators profoundly moved by its beauty.</summary>
<keywords>Genji, festival, dance, nature, beauty</keywords>

That night Genji was promoted to the First Class of the Third Rank, and Tō no Chūjō was promoted to intermediate standing between the First and Second Classes of the Fourth Rank. The gentlemen of the court were all promoted one rank. But though they celebrated their good fortune with the usual rejoicings, they were well aware that they had only been dragged in Genji's wake and wondered how it was that their destinies had come to be linked in this curious way with those of the prince who had brought them this unexpected piece of good fortune.

Fujitsubo now retired to her own house, and Genji, waiting about for a chance of visiting her, was seldom at the Great Hall and was consequently in very ill odor there. It was soon after this that he brought the child Murasaki to live with him. Aoi heard a rumor of this, but it reached her merely in the form that someone was living with him at his palace, and she did not know that it was a child. Under these circumstances, it was quite natural that she should feel much aggrieved. But if only she had flown into an honest passion and abused him for it, as most people would have done, he would have told her everything and put matters right. As it was, she only redoubled her icy aloofness and thus led him to seek those very distractions of which it was intended as a rebuke. Not only was her beauty so flawless that it could not fail to win his admiration, but also the mere fact that he had known her since so long ago, before all the rest, made him feel toward her a tenderness of which she seemed quite unaware. He was convinced, however, that her nature was not at bottom narrow and vindictive, and this gave him some hope that she would one day relent.

Meanwhile, as he got to know little Murasaki better, he became the more content both with her appearance and her character. She at least gave him her whole heart. For the present, he did not intend to reveal her identity even to the

More than twenty years ago, an attempt was made by a body called the ‘Dialectical Society’ to investigate the phenomena styled spiritualistic. This well-meant essay had most unsatisfactory results.²

First, a committee of inquiry was formed, on the motion of Dr. Edmunds. The committee was heterogeneous. Many of the names now suggest little to the reader. Mr. Bradlaugh we remember, but he chiefly attended a committee which sat with D. D. Home <note>Daniel Dunglas Home, a famous 19th-century physical medium.</note>, and it is admitted that nothing of interest there occurred. Then we find the Rev. Maurice Davies, who was wont to write books of little distinction on semi-religious topics. Mr. H. G. Atkinson was a person interested in mesmerism. Kisch, Moss, and Quelch, with Dyte and Isaac Meyers, Bergheim and Geary, Hannah, Hillier, Reed (their names go naturally in blank verse), were, doubtless, all most estimable men, but scarcely boast of scientific fame. Serjeant Cox, a believer in the phenomena, if not in their spiritual cause, was of the company, as was Mr. Jencken, who married one of the Miss Foxes, the first authors of modern thaumaturgy <note>The working of miracles or magic.</note>. Indeed, according to the same witness, not even inflated air penetrates into the uterus. This, I believe, was the reason why he, proceeding from the interior parts to the exterior, described the history of the uterus. Furthermore, having weighed this structure of the uterus, he denies that semen reaches the cavity of the uterus or constitutes any part of the egg. I readily declare my own name in agreement with this opinion. Indeed, you will find nothing added or changed in a fertile egg (which is not in a subventaneous <note>unfertilized/wind egg</note> one) from which it would be clear that the rooster's semen had entered the uterus and touched the egg. Furthermore, although all eggs are fruitless and subventaneous without the mating of a rooster, yet through his work (even some time after copulation) subsequent eggs, for which there is as yet no beginning or material, become fertile.

<margin>Page 30.</margin>Fabricius, to explain the manner in which the rooster's semen renders eggs fertile, says: *Since semen does not appear in the egg, and yet is offered by the rooster into the uterus; it is asked, why is the rooster's semen inserted into the uterus if it does not enter the egg? ### *On the Ventricle of the Hen and Other Birds.*

### Exercise VII.

From the external orifice therefore, through the vulva, we have reached the uterus or womb of the hen; in which the egg is perfected, is surrounded by albumen, and is covered by a shell: before we speak of its site and position, some things concerning the peculiar <term>anatome</term> <gloss>anatomy</gloss> of the belly of birds must be brought forward here and touched upon first. For I have observed in feathered creatures that the stomach, the intestines, and other viscera are situated and constituted differently in their lower belly than in the class of walking animals.

Almost all birds have a double stomach; of which one is called the *ingluvies* <note>crop</note>, and the other the *ventriculus* <note>gizzard</note> properly so called. In the former, the food taken in is reserved and prepared; in the latter, it is concocted and passes into chyle <note>nutrient fluid</note>: our countrymen call the former *the crop, or craw*; the latter, *the gisard*. In the crop, birds retain whole grains swallowed; thence, when softened by drunk water, macerated, and emollient, they transmit them afterward into the stomach; so that there they may be ground and comminuted. For the sake of which, almost all feathered creatures swallow grains of sand, small stones, and other harder things, and keep them in the stomach together with the food; (while meanwhile no such thing is found in the crop) and they have this stomach [composed] of two very thick...

By this pact they prepare food and create chyle; and afterward, compression being made (just as we are accustomed to express juice or porridge from crushed herbs or fruits), the softer and more liquid part is lifted upward; and they transfer it into the beginning of the intestines (which in them is placed next to the entrance of the gullet, in the upper part of the stomach). That it is done so, appears in many classes of birds; in whose stomachs, if small stones or other harder and rougher things remain longer, they are seen to be so worn down and smoothed by their continuous motion that they are inept for the attrition of food, and therefore are rejected. Hence when birds gather small stones, they test them with their tongue; and, if they feel nothing rough, they reject them. In this way, you will find iron, silver, and small stones worn down and almost consumed in the stomach of the *Struthio* <note>Ostrich</note>, and also in the *Caffovvare* <note>Cassowary</note>. And therefore it is commonly believed that they digest iron and are nourished by it.

In falcons, eagles, and other birds living on prey, if you place your ear near when the stomach is empty, you may perceive manifest noises of small stones ingested there, and colliding with each other. For falcons do not devour small stones for the sake of cooling (which is a vulgar error of falconers).

SINCE IT IS THE CUSTOM of our Academy to attempt to teach everything that the human mind can grasp, it behooves us teachers to have learned everything, a state which we have not yet attained. For I do not see any of us who could have promised that to himself, nor, as I perceive, has anyone promised it.
pages.16: or if he has promised it, he has done so more out of zeal and desire than from the knowledge of a difficult and arduous subject. If someone were to read all the books of Plato, or even those of Aristotle, and even Plutarch, how many are there who do not think they have heard, questioned, and known all things? Yet how many and how great are the things that they lacked? I believe indeed, and I believe truly, that if someone were to collect and arrange in order the doctrines of all the Philosophers—whether they be those Epicureans, or the Academics (both of the old and the new Academy), or the Stoics, and, I say, all of these and the other wise men of all Greece—he would still see that they had wished to know all things rather than having been able to, and that they had divided rather than explained whatever philosophy professes. And if there were nothing else, certainly they could say nothing about God, nothing about the creation of the world, nothing about the nature of man, and nothing about the return of humans to life. The poets dared to name the sons and daughters of Jupiter; but how
pages.17: much they strayed, along with the philosophers, from the pursuit of true knowledge, to say nothing of cognition. Now, in the later subjects of Physics and Mathematics, many things have been discovered which were unknown to the first wise men. And although these things are so, yet since one philosopher professes almost all things, and all have striven to attain this, so that they might know and transmit everything, why should the same thing not be granted to us as to them? Or why can we achieve less through industry than they did? Are books lacking to us? Is leisure lacking? Or stipends or resources? Or, finally, talent? If we yield to the ancients in this, it happens more through the corruption of discipline and our own sloth than through the capacity of nature, whose goodness is no less a gift and benefit of God than that of the crops and the harvest. Truly, ages have brought forth, one after another, more, sharper, and more learned men, just as some years surpass others in fertility. And the Arabs may have more men of talent than Germany
pages.18:

Therefore, learned Athens may have existed, and poets, mathematicians, and philosophers may have flourished there, but they did not always flourish in the same way. Nor is it denied to us for that reason, because that was granted to them before us; and they have left us the monuments of literature, which teach us how many and how great the things are that they encompassed in their doctrine. Learned men understand these things, and consider how much has been added by later generations to the first, and how much can be added by us to later generations. <margin>Concerning unequal marriage.</margin>
The fourth passage is concerning unequal marriage, that is, in which one person is a believer while the other remains in their old religion, whether Jewish or Gentile. The passage contains two parts: a proposition and a cause. The proposition is presented in several ways. For he renders the right equal to both persons. The meaning of the proposition is: even unequal marriage must be kept indissolubly by the pious. He explains how he understands this, concerning the husband who has an infidel wife who nevertheless wishes to live with her Christian husband. Similarly, concerning the wife who has an infidel husband who nevertheless does not think the wife should be abandoned because of the new religion. Thus, the right is made equal, and therefore it pertains only to the faithful persons. For the Apostle could not give commandments to infidels. Furthermore, he says that he speaks these things, because Christ had given no mandate in these cases for the new Christian profession. In the meantime, it is a rule of the Holy Spirit, of whom the Apostle is the organ.

<margin>Why a believer should not abandon an infidel spouse.</margin>
This is a confirmation of the proposition set forth, if a believer should not abandon an infidel spouse. Why? Because the worse part, that is, the infidel, is sanctified by the better, that is, the believing spouse. He takes the argument from the nature of the faith of the better person. It is proper to faith to sanctify us to God, that is, it declares us sanctified by God, and it does not reside only in one person—the believer—but because the believer is one flesh with the infidel spouse, the sanctification consequently flows over to the worse part as well. And indeed, the infidel will have infinite opportunities to repent and convert himself also to Christ the Savior. Nevertheless, the Apostle did not say "will be sanctified" or "let him be sanctified," but "is sanctified." For it is a most certain argument for hoping even for that conversion, since he does not wish to depart. He teaches this learnedly by proposing, explaining, confirming, and concluding. We will resolve the individual points to the proposition.

<term>Πρότασις</term> <gloss>Proposition</gloss>. On account of the profession of the Gospel, it is not necessary to change one’s way of life immediately; rather, each person’s calling must be diligently protected and preserved, provided religion is kept safe. The Apostle said <term>περιπατεῖν</term> <gloss>to walk</gloss> as God has called each, that is, to persist in his own kind of life in which the profession of the Gospel found him. And the word <term>περιπατεῖν</term> <gloss>to walk</gloss> is to produce the fruits of the active life, so that you may understand that it is a matter of piety to produce actions conformable to one's profession. For it is not enough to contemplate and speak much about piety; there is a need for action. And the particle <term>εἰ μὴ</term> <gloss>unless</gloss> is to be connected with <term>ὡς</term> <gloss>as</gloss>. For it is a limited proposition and restricted by a certain condition: "Unless as God has distributed, one must walk," that is, not otherwise; not by our own judgment, a calling is not to be feigned by us, but that which the Lord has imposed is to be retained. In this sense, he censures the superstition of the Corinthians who wanted to change everything immediately on account of the profession of religion.

But let us consider the arguments by which this can be shown which we proposed from the Apostle. One's own station must be kept by each person after the acknowledgment of the truth. Why? Because God has distributed the kinds of life in this way. It is a firm argument from divine ordination and disposition, which must be studiously observed by the pious. The Apostle urges the argument with repetition and the changing of words: <term>θεὸς ἐμέρισεν</term> <gloss>God has distributed</gloss>, and <term>κύριος κέκληκεν</term> <gloss>the Lord has called</gloss>. He indeed says the same thing.

    Submerges his streams born in the Erythraean <note>Red</note> sea;
Whence light winds are born, and why Etna
    Feeds its ruins, having ejected pitch-black globes;
Whence the salty liquor of the sea flows, whence the wholesome vein
    Of Baian water <note>of Baiae</note> draws its warmth.
Having finally searched through all the miracles of the earth,
    He leaves the subject ground with a soaring mind,
And having traversed the Olympus painted with stars,
    He flies through the bright signs of the ethereal home.
Here, the Marathonian Virgin <note>the constellation Virgo</note> offers him her twin scales,
    And the neighboring Lion <note>Leo</note> offers his stars,
And Orion grants the sword taken from his side,
    The rewards owed to *CAESARIAN* warfare.
Here he tracks the path of the Sun, and the hidden causes
    Why pale Cynthia <note>the Moon</note> weeps with black horses;
Why Africans thirst; why the seven kingdoms of the North <note>original: "Trionum"</note>
    Are burned by the frost lingering in the Hyperborean cold;
Why shadows flee Syene <note>Aswan</note> when Cancer is burning;
    Why the greater or lesser boundary varies the day.
But what part of doctrine and your praises is it,
    **AUSTRIAD**, to know the stars of the great pole,
And the lands stretched out with the surrounding sea
    Where the Sun illuminates the East and the West?
If to you even Wisdom, brought forth in eloquent scrolls,
    Is laid open from the history of the Nile,
And the sacred things hidden in reverend shrines do not escape you,
    Nor the marbles ennobled by sculpted beasts.
Indeed, Egypt, having dared to entrust doctrine to rocks,
    Had fashioned foreign effigies,
So that the arcana of the gods, manifest to the masters,
    Might keep the rabble away with doubtful images.
And that late posterity, with the years slipping by,
    Might know the work of ancient art left untouched.
O the vain cares of men! O the breasts blind to the future!
    So many monuments in a royal site.
The barbarian drinker of the Armenian Araxes,
    Cambyses, depopulated the Pharian <note>Egyptian</note> fields,

And was able to overturn the remains that had been saved

But long time shall not take away the eternal honors,
O famous Rome, from your merits,
You who gather the breathing ruins of Pelusian <note>Egyptian</note> pride,

Nor shall black night press upon your genius.

Ancient Memphis <note>original: "Mempheos"</note> reveals its dark bays,
That the father <note>original: "pater"</note> shows the secret faces of the Inachian heifer <note>Io</note>,
That the dog, and the mystical form of the sacred ox,
And what other monsters of famous Canopus besides,
Remain to be seen with ancient marks:
The last dweller of the Nile shall read the titles of the **AUSTRIADS**,
And will shake the jingling sistra with a joyful sound.
Now Solyme <note>Jerusalem</note>, now the Arab shall learn, and the clear marbles
Shall speak of the gifts scattered by the **CAESARIAN** hand.
Am I mistaken? Or will the fates add to the **AUSTRIAN** trophies
Sacred signs torn from Paratonian <note>Egyptian</note> domes?
Or, **FERDINAND**, does Victory already joyfully prepare
To write your name upon the stones of the Pyramids?
Glory, certainly, calls forth the slothful hands of Europe,
Emulous of the Pellaean <note>Alexandrian</note> palms, to pious wars.

## CAESAR,

### THRICE-GREATEST KING,

<note>A decorative drop cap 'O' features a seated scholar or saintly figure writing at a desk, surrounded by ornate scrollwork.</note>

Octavian Augustus Caesar, spurred by the desire to acquire the ancient wisdom which was said to be inscribed on the obelisks erected by him, explored all of Egypt through the work of learned men, so that if he found any interpreter skilled in hieroglyphic doctrine, he might call him to Rome for the office of interpreting arcana. But he could not obtain his wishes, all the mystical doctrine of the Ancients having long since been submerged as if by some river of Lethe. Ferdinand III Caesar Augustus, so much more fortunate than that Octavian, by so much more fortunate auspices attained that which the other could obtain by no vows or expenses, while by some fate Athanasius Kircher fell to him as a new interpreter, a resurrected Oedipus; who, stimulated by Caesar's command, flew with a brilliant intellect to the regions of Wisdom and uncovered treasures hitherto inaccessible. He, first relying on the commands of Ferdinand, entered more deeply into the hidden recesses of the Memphitic shrines, opened the secret seals of the sacraments, and interpreted the mysterious volumes of the ancient Priests, with Caesarean munificence acting as midwife. We therefore proclaim you a happy Caesar, you who, while you burn with the desire for performing great and very grand things, have attained such a person who both wishes and is able to urge the concepts of your great mind into execution: Augustus once placed the scope of his power in the erecting of vast masses of obelisks; but you are even more powerful than he, who not only raise up grand stones, but also this has befallen you above others, that by your aid and work the mute stones of the obelisks

Assemblies and festivals throughout the whole city,
To be affected with honor because of their notable glory of fortitude?
Each and every person will speak this, and other things to this
Opinion,
Nor will glory abandon them, dead or alive.
But obey me now, dearest sister,
Bring help to our parent, bring effort to our brother,
Snatch me and yourself alike from present evils:
Meanwhile keeping before your eyes how shameful it is
To live disgracefully, born of noble stock.

**Cho.** <term>THERE</term> is need of great prudence in these
Matters, both for the one counseling and for the one listening, it is useful.

**Chr.** But before I make an opening of speaking,
O women, if there were even the smallest part of mind
In this one, which she does not have, she would take care of her
Own safety. For with what confidence,
Relying on what hope at last, do you arm yourself with such rash
Audacity, and call me into a partnership of danger?
That you have weighed that you are a woman, not a man, born
To enemies far unequal in strength and power.
Moreover, fortune and the divine powers of the gods favor them,
While we experience adverse things from day to day.
Who would destroy such a man without his own very grave
Damage and extreme calamity?
Look again and again, sister, lest we, by planning such
Deeds, procure for ourselves
Grave evils, if by chance anyone overhearing such sounds
Exposes us.
What would it profit to attain glory and fame,
If we are forced to end our life disgracefully?
Nor do I deem death grave, but, when you
Desire to die, not to be able to attain it.
Therefore, I beg you before we go to destruction,
And our lineage to the depths;
Restrain your anger, and suppress these impulses of your mind.
I, in turn, will ensure that all that has been said by you
Remains unsaid and secret.
Only you, prepare your mind more prudently,
And at last, measuring your own strength, since you can achieve
Nothing, being weak, begin to yield
To the princes and the more powerful.

I pray you, Apollo, hear with a benign divine will.

when salt water departed into the sweetest drink: the crossing of the Israelites dry-shod through the Red Sea, as well as the sprouting of Aaron’s rod, happened in a supernatural manner.

And in sum, the breaking forth of Christ from the sealed sepulcher, that apparition made to the two going into the town of Emmaus, and the manifestation through closed doors, was a divine and supernatural thing. Many other examples could still be brought from the sacred code, if one had to cater to brevity.

To supernatural things are ascribed all the omens of metallic mines, the corporeal apparitions of spirits, phantoms, pygmies, and dwarfs, who very often present themselves to sight, and portend good or evil, ruin or wealth; likewise all the figures and other impressions of metals which are found under the earth among men, formed through the imagination of the three principles, and matured and cooked by the earth and other Elements. To this also belong the monsters of the earth and such things that are given in wondrous forms under the earth at set times, outside of which they can nowhere else be discovered, although at another time they may truly appear again and present themselves to our eyes.

Hither also are referred all visions customarily made through waters, mirrors, crystals, and other media, or through seals and characters, which nevertheless differ greatly; for some are merely natural, yet exhibit supernatural visions. The rest, arising from incantations, are neither natural nor supernatural but Diabolical, and therefore are numbered among Demoniac Magic, and are deservedly forbidden to all Christians.

<summary>This page catalogs supernatural phenomena, including subterranean spirits, omens, and the distinction between natural visions and demonic magic.</summary>

Similarly, all <term>Naiads</term> <gloss>water nymphs</gloss>, <term>Sirens</term>, <term>Succubi</term>, and other <term>Nymphs</term>, and what is akin to them, obtain a place among supernatural things; likewise the earthly spirits, and those who inhabit the air, offering themselves to hearing, sight, and touch, sometimes foretelling death or other evil, at other times signifying fortunes and treasures in certain places by their apparitions. To these, moreover, are added the fiery spirits, exhibiting themselves under the form of fire and a burning torch, all of whom are incorporeal spirits and yet not infernal, who lie in wait for the souls of men as if they were eternal treasures, just as the Stygian <term>Lucifer</term> and his excommunicated companions are wont to do. But they are of such a kind as these Spirits, which are presented to the admiration of men above nature, are uniquely nourished, fed, and pastured by the Elements, and afterward cease in this earthly world, dying and vanishing together, destitute of a redeemed soul. I add no more about these things now, but reserve their further treatment for another time and a more convenient place, where I will compose a singular treatise on visions and their spiritual apparitions, which the greater part of the world judges to be contrary to nature, when in truth they are indeed natural, yet they are detected to be supernatural regarding their operations and their wondrous qualities.

To confirm my proposition more, I assert that there are many things in Medicine that manifest and perform their operation in a supernatural manner, only in a magnetic way, through a certain spiritual attractive virtue, which is attracted by the benefit of the air, because this is the medium between the medicine and the vice, just as the Magnet constantly turns itself toward the southern star, even if it be many thousands of miles distant from it; nevertheless, such a great spiritual operation and inclination intervenes here, that by means of this bond—namely, the air—such distances are joined. Since, however, such attractive virtue is commonly known, it has passed into mere custom, and it serves its turn, nor is any further occult quality observed from which this operating virtue draws its origin. In a like manner, wounds and vices can be healed, even if the person thus oppressed and the Physician are separated by a long interval, not by exorcisms, charms, and other illicit means contrary to **GOD** and nature, but by those in which the magnetic attractive virtue lies hidden. As if a wounded person, departing hence, leaves the weapons with which he was injured, or anything from the gore issued from the wound, to the Physician, from whom legitimate means of healing are afterward duly administered, as is accustomed to be done with the binding of wounds, he will without any doubt recover firmly; these are not charms, but such healing is accomplished solely by the attractive virtue of the medicine, which is carried to the wound by means of the air, to purify the wound and complete its spiritual operation.

There are many living creatures that are devoid of all life in the winter time, but as soon as summer returns, natural heat begets new life, so that the body rises again in that substance in which it previously exerted vital motion, just as an herb that dies in winter revives again in spring. The passing away of these things is therefore judged to be natural, but the reparation of new life through its own knowledge is supernatural. But because man is accustomed to all these things, the smallest part, which further remains to be weighed and searched into, is attempted, with both natural and supernatural things being neglected.

So too, very many are accustomed to pass by with dry feet the character of man, which itself is also supernatural, and likewise those monsters that bring blemishes into the world together; these things are indeed all natural, but they exhibit themselves supernaturally out of an arisen imagination, which supernatural form and character the mother imprinted by accident upon the infant through her own imagination, just as we often see that certain manners are instilled into some men, which they can never renounce, however much they may labor to unlearn them. This instilled power of man is natural; the conception in the mother's womb, which the imagination of these things provided, is supernatural, and subject to those things which the heaven imprinted.

## The First Tincture and Root of Metals.

### Chapter Two.

BUT that I may fulfill my undertaking, **GOD** permitting, and grasp the doctrine concerning the first tincture, root, and generation of Metals and Minerals, it must be known that the tincture and root of all Metals is also a supernatural, volatile, and fiery Spirit, which sustains itself in the air, and naturally seeks its seat in water and earth, where it can rest and operate. This Spirit is found in all Metals, and more abundantly in others than in gold, since that, because of its cooked, matured, and fixed body, is solid, firm, and compact; therefore, beyond what the body requires, it can receive no more. The remaining Metals, however, are destitute of such a fixed body, but their pores are open and widely dispersed; therefore the Spirit of the tincture can penetrate and occupy them the more copiously. Since, however, the bodies of the other Metals are unfixed, the Tincture also cannot subsist with wandering bodies

In chapter 15, regarding the arrogance of the faithful, by which the weaker ones are accustomed to be despised, which topic again pertains to Ethical matters. Afterwards follows the Epilogue, which contains elegant topics, such as a topic of civility, excusing the boldness and prolixity of the writing. Then a topic worthy of knowing is regarding the propagated doctrine of the Gospel in the times of the Apostle. Also a topic regarding his travels. Also regarding the contribution of the faithful for the needs of the poor. Also a topic regarding the intercession of saints, but regarding how the living intercede for the living. Furthermore, there is an elegant topic regarding the custom of greeting received among the pious. Also of commending pious brothers to those absent, and thus the Epistle is concluded.

*Who the Corinthians were.*

Corinth was named after Corinthus, the son of Marathon, who was either the founder or the enlarger of the city. Once it was the most famous and flourishing of the cities of Greece, whence Cicero did not hesitate to call it the light of all Greece. The same author, in his Oration against Rullus, most elegantly describes its situation in these words. Scarcely a trace of Corinth remains. For it was placed in the narrows and throats of Greece, so that it held the bolts of the region by land, and almost joined two seas which were most suited for navigation, while they were separated by a very thin division, etc. <margin>In the Oration for the Manilian Law.</margin>

For their usage, being common, causes one to observe the differences together. And this also is peculiar to both, for they divide the wild ones by male and female, either <gloss>n</gloss> solely or mostly; but the cultivated ones by more forms. It is <gloss>o</gloss> easier to take and number the species of the former; but harder for the latter, because of their multitude. # NOTES

## ON THE FIRST BOOK.

---

### *Constituent parts of Plants.*

#### CAP. I.

"Perhaps not in the same way." Extreme brevity, as correctly observed by **Mr. Moldenhawer**, in the comparison of animals with plants at the end of this chapter; concerning which one should consult Aristotle, History of Animals, v. 3.

"So there is nothing strange." See regarding this matter, *On the Causes of Plants*, ii. 20, 22, 23; v. 2.

"At an equal [distance]," namely, interval. Equidistant.

#### CAP. II.

"They are the first and greatest." Thus Aristotle, *History of Animals*: "As many of the parts, which being whole, have other specific parts within them; for example, the head, etc."

"More enduring in their roots." Those whose roots are perennial. Bot.

"With regard to one," namely, being. To be equipped with a simple trunk. See Pliny, *Natural History*, xiv. 1. 30.

"Homogeneous. Heterogeneous." One should consult Aristotle on this matter, *On the Generation of Animals*, i. 1, and the *Lexicon of Theophrastus*.

"Any part from the same things." Individual parts [consist] of the same vessels, fibers, membranes, etc.

"These are almost the greatest parts." End of chapter ii in the edition of Bodaeus.

"Other things from which these are." The author proceeds to the homogeneous parts.

#### CAP. III.

Menestor. An author on herbal matters, whose works are not extant.

"Namelessly," simply "the moisture."

"Innate moisture and heat." Mr. Moldenhawer treats the warm principle of life most copiously, *Tentamen*, p. 83. He calls it "productive heat."

<summary>This page contains scholarly notes on the first book of Theophrastus, focusing on definitions of homogeneous parts and plant anatomy as interpreted by Moldenhawer, Aristotle, and Pliny.</summary>
<keywords>Theophrastus, Moldenhawer, Aristotle, Pliny, Botany, Plant Anatomy</keywords>
pages.139:
*On the Causes of Plants*, i. 4. Confer also Galen. It is called by Aristotle *natural heat*, ii. 3.

*But there are other different kinds*. Distinct, namely, from *moisture and heat*. Beginning of chapter iv, Bod.

*Fibers—veins*. Remarkable sagacity of the author in describing these most tenuous vessels: which, however, in our own century have been brought to their *pinnacle*. Mr. Moldenhawer treats this matter most copiously, *Tentamen*, p. 91.

*Wood, flesh*. See Mold., p. 108.

*The pith* <note>original: "μήτρα"</note> is compared to *marrow in bones*. But briefly, however, and narrowly, as he is accustomed to do, the author describes the pith of vegetables; clearly, however, if you weigh the force of the words. Mention is made elsewhere, i. 9, iv. 2. *On the Causes of Plants*, v. 6, 7, 24.

### CAP. IV.

*In which it is possible*. In those things which admit of division.

*By way of culture*. By means of cultivation, etc. A frequent usage in Theophrastus.

*Olive groves*. The term *kopades* <note>original: "κοπάδες"</note> is interpreted as coppice wood, but here perhaps refers to a decapitated tree.

### CAP. VI.

*One must always take all*— An obscure reading, if it is sound: the meaning is, *one must always take the differences of all things by their places* regarding climate, etc.

*Another [difference] according to the other genus of liquids*, i.e., aquatic plants differ among themselves regarding *places*.

*Smaller—larger*. The former are Fuci and Ulvae; the latter are called *little trees* elsewhere; Gorgoniae, Corallinae. See iv. 8.

### CAP. VII.

*Thickness*. Here indicates the thickness or mass of the trunk. It is opposed to *thinness*, to gracility.

*From which is the composition*. Regarding the constituent parts. Opposed to *those things according to affections and powers*.

### CAP. VIII.

*Piths*. See cap. iii, p. 9, line 6. N.B. Chapter IX of Bodaeus.

*Some do not have—and the Elder*. In the younger branches of the Elder, pith is not present.

<summary>Scholarly notes continuing the analysis of Theophrastus's terminology regarding plant anatomy, including pith, fibers, and aquatic plants.</summary>
<keywords>Theophrastus, Galen, Aristotle, Botany, Plant Anatomy</keywords>
pages.140:
*All piths are black*. The significance of the word *black* escaped Scaliger. See Bod., p. 24, and the *Lexicon of Theophrastus*.

*In general, some do not have any*. The discussion is about Fungi: see the *Systematic Catalogue*, which have no affinity with other plants. See Bod., p. 27.

*They differ also in their roots*. See on this matter Pliny, xvi. 31.

*Fringed*. Fimbriate; Pliny, but another sense of the word *thysanoi*, ribbons, tufts of fibers. Poll. See *Lexicon of Theophrastus*.

### CAP. IX.

*Those above the earth*, namely, *the parts*.

*For the root*, i.e., the root in general.

### CAP. X.

*Crowning altars*. Perhaps it should be read *collecting heaps*, gathering piles.

*They bear fruit*. Add *below*: under the earth, regarding tubers. See the illustration of *Arachidnas*, Bod., p. 35.

*The fruit*, namely, the tuber from the root.

*Prior to the ones above*, namely, *the parts*.

*These contribute greatly*. It is to be noted that the word *nature* should be taken in the plural.

*The juices of all are similar*. Beginning of the chapter in Bodaeus.

*For from the shoots*. A remarkable description of the habit of the *Ficus Indica* L. (English: "The Banyan Tree").

*If in deep material*. The meaning is, if some material intervenes between the seed and the earth, *it splits the root towards the earth*, it bends the root toward the earth until it touches it.

### CAP. XI.

*In which both are present*, namely, *sexes*. Although a sexual distinction occurs in the Palm, commonly however, the terms *male* and *female* are attributed to varieties of species, as they are observed to be more robust and fruitless, or the contrary.

*Most peculiar are those of the Apple tree*. These words, included in parentheses, **have crept in from the margin**, as I suspect, and interrupt the description of the habit of the *Fir*. Although it is hardly possible to conjecture what the author means regarding the "faces of wild beasts," Pliny interprets the passage thus in *Natural History*, l. xvi, c. 30: "A peculiar kind of branch to Apple trees, for they render the snouts of wild beasts, with smaller ones adhering to one very large one."

<summary>Notes on plant parts, specifically fungi, roots, tubers, the Banyan tree, and sexual characteristics of trees as interpreted by historical commentators.</summary>
<keywords>Theophrastus, Pliny, Botany, Fungi, Tubers, Banyan Tree, Plant sexuality</keywords>
pages.141:
*Of the knots, some are blind*. Observe that the word *ozos* occurs in a double sense, as a branch and as a knot in a trunk.

*Because nothing is placed in between*. Because there are no intervals. Scal.

*Peculiar hollows*. See the word *elos* in the *Lexicon of Theophrastus*. Species of *Hypoxylon*, as I suspect. See iv. 16.

*It is therefore*. A chapter to be added to the previous one as it is a continuation.

*Growing to length*. The discussion is about the trunk: which is either tall and not branched, or which *is split immediately*. I suspect also that what follows, *and the things similar to these*, should be read thus: *a root, similar to these*. Thus Virgil: "As much as it extends its top to the ethereal breezes, so much does it extend its root to Tartarus."

*It becomes thin*, namely, *by cultivation*.

### CAP. XII.

*Furthermore, some are evergreen*. Here begins chapter xv in Bodaeus.

*To partake of winter*. To last until the middle of winter.

### CAP. XIII.

*Like the hand*. Pliny in the same place, xvi. 24, says, *veins on the flat sides*, "incisions underneath," that is, hollow lines, as in the palm of the hand.

*Whichever is towards the twig*, i.e., from the conversion of the leaves it is doubtful which part is the upper and which the lower; *for the hollowness* regarding the position is different from the nature of the leaf.

*Not to be altered in the same way*. Opposed to the conversions *through veins or fibers*, i.e., not in a constant, regular way.

*Going to depth* is to be interpreted as the thickness of the leaf.

*Saw-toothed*. Perhaps *comb-toothed* or *serrated*. See the Preface to the Illustrious Theophrastus, p. v. Also the description of the *Fir*, l. iii.

*Of the Oak from the trunk*. Pliny observes the same regarding the leaves of the Oak, *Natural History*, xvi. 24. Bodaeus says he has never observed it. I suspect an error in the text: it should perhaps be read *Cyprian*. See regarding the *Cyprian Fig*, iv, c. 2.

<summary>Discussion on botanical terminology including knots, leaf structure, and corrections to historical observations on oak and fir trees.</summary>
<keywords>Theophrastus, Pliny, Botany, Philology, Leaves, Oak, Fir</keywords>
pages.142:
"The whole stem is leafless." He accurately describes the scape of the Botanists.

"Through itself." From itself: regarding the sessile leaf. Bot.

"Surrounding in between, the fruit." Fruit in the middle of the leaf.

### CAP. XIV.

"For those [parts] not annual." Persistent parts of the plant, such as the trunk, branches, etc. "For nothing is without this [moisture]."

"Of the flowers, some [are] from the bark." Theophrastus means something strange. Flowers from the bark and nerves. Surely an error in the text, and one should read instead of *of the flowers*, *of the others* (namely, stalks). Regarding flowers, see c. 21, 22.

### CAP. XV.

"The seed immediately after the container." Seed with a simple covering. In this chapter, six types of seeds are noted, the enumeration of which is confused and very long. These are: 1. simple seeds with a covering; Palms. 2. from a stone and flesh—Drupes. 3. in a pod—leguminous. 4. in a certain membrane, membranaceous follicle, such as the Pear, Apple. 5. *angiospermia* <note>original: "ἀγγειοσπέρματα"</note>, with loose, rigid pericarp; Poppy. 6. *gymnospermia* <note>original: "γυμνοσπέρματα"</note>, without a covering; umbelliferous.

"For example, the grape." Here the text is very corrupt. The distinction of Theophrastus of many grains contained in *some common thing*, such as a berry or grape stone: likewise also in a seed. N.B. Pomegranate stones are opposed to the single grains of Wheat, etc. "And the apple ones would least seem to be." By no means, however, should those of the Apples be joined to these, which are wrapped around by membranes in the inner part of the fruit.

"But in the same way also each of these." See the error of the scribe in transcribing above, "since to one taking each..."

### CAP. XVI.

"In those things concerning juices." *History on the Causes of Plants*, l. vi.

"Lettuce." The juice is called *watery* less correctly. Perhaps an error in the text, as above for *milky* one should be placed regarding the juice of the Fig and Poppy.

"Which is proper." The meaning is that the peculiar juice of any plant *has some similarity* within itself before cooking and maturation occurs in the fruit, which is brought about by the aid of the pericarp.

<summary>Botanical notes concerning persistent plant parts, flower classification, and the diverse types of seeds and their coverings as described by Theophrastus.</summary>
<keywords>Theophrastus, Botany, Scape, Drupes, Legumes, Angiosperms, Gymnosperms, Seeds</keywords>
pages.143:
"Of some, sweet-smelling." See more fully regarding odors in Theophrastus, *On the Causes of Plants*, l. i. 6, as well as regarding juices.

### CAP. XVII.

*Outside the sea*. The Red Sea is understood.

*Having a sketch*. The common Columbine is indicated by most botanists under the name *Iasione*; and the description, although intricate, marvelously agrees with the convolutions of the petals: also *it is not separated in the flower*.

N.B. To some, the conjecture of Bodaeus may perhaps be more pleasing, that the *Convolvulus sepium* etc. is indicated here, in which sense *sketching only of the many* is to be interpreted as the amplitude of the flower.

*Appears perforated*. The remarkable *precision* of the author, when the flower is perforated, i.e., falls off without a stigma, the beginning of the fruit remains; when *it is scorched or wetted*, or if it is affected by too much sun or rain, *it loses the fruit along with it*. See the observation below: "as many flowers as have, as it were, a spindle, are fertile."

*On their mouths*. The discussion is about syngenesious plants; therefore, the *mouth* is the common receptacle in this class.

*Like a spindle*. Regarding the stigma of the flower of the Citron or Orange tree.

"Immediately show the fruit," i.e., without a flower or petals.

### CAP. XVIII.

*The wild fig*. The Common Fig, etc., is numbered by Linnaeus among the *Trioeciae*. *The Wild Fig*, from which come *the wild figs* (which are perhaps *the olynthi*), the male tree; *The Fig*, the monoecious tree.

### CAP. XIX.

*And such differences*. A summary and recapitulation of this book.

*More species under each genus*. More species under one genus. A truly Linnaean distinction!

*Cultivated and wild*. Here the distinction is taken from sex: but what does it mean? That wild plants are distinguished by sex, but cultivated ones by *more peculiar properties*; does it indicate varieties of fruits?

<summary>Concluding notes on plant odors, the identification of flower parts like stigmas, and the categorization of fig types, reflecting on early botanical classification methods.</summary>
<keywords>Theophrastus, Columbine, Botany, Stigma, Fig, Linnaeus, Plant classification</keywords>

and reject them. But unless our sins deserve otherwise, they will not prevail in the end. And their madness, according to Paul, will become evident to all, and the fruit of the pious efforts of your Most Serene King—who through you seeks the peace of the churches, provided the controversies are first rightly judged—will one day break forth, even if the devils are unwilling. This hope of a happy harvest should by no means be shaken from us by the fact that the seeds of peace and concord, sown in this embassy of yours, seem to lie hidden for a little while. But to return to the point from which I digressed: indeed, I rejoice with my whole heart that God has kept you safe and sound until the day you wrote to us from England. And I vehemently congratulate you on the many and great testimonies of divine presence that were shown to you by God throughout your entire embassy. And I pray with you to the Son of God, our Immanuel, and the most faithful head and guardian of His Church, that He may bless your most holy labors more each day and keep you safe for a very long time. And likewise that He may strengthen your Most Serene King, another Josiah. Regarding his constancy and fortitude in defending and professing the true religion, the letters of most trustworthy men clearly testify to us, even after your departure from Germany, against the fabrications of the most hollow rumors which, while you were still present in Germany, were spread by wicked and per-
pages.20:
verse men in the courts of many princes to impede the success of your embassy. You mentioned that you knew some of them, and that you had perceived and explored the vanity of those rumors, and that some people, in order to curry favor with others, were willing to believe the fables which facts and time (which is the daughter of truth) would refute. Just as so far, indeed, with God confirming the spirit of His Royal Serenity, the piety of such a great king has, by its own splendor and light, dispelled and scattered all the clouds of lies.

But as I am most fully persuaded that He who began His good work in you and in your Most Serene King will also finish it until the day of Jesus Christ, so, to approve and celebrate that heroic and most holy voice of yours—by which you said to me at the time when various tempests and dangers appeared to threaten you on every side, that in a good cause, one must, with a clear conscience of upright will, despise not only wicked men but the Devil himself, trusting in Divine protection—I believe I can propose no more fitting an epilogue than to append that most noble psalm of Martin Luther, which, as it is most frequently sung in the German churches, so it has an admirable <term>energeia</term> <gloss>efficacy/active power</gloss> for stirring the soul, by which I remember you were also sweetly affected when I once recited a part of it to you, rendered in Stigelian rhythms in this manner:

<quote>
If this world were teeming with demons
Like worms in the earth,
We would not fear anxiously;
We will finally conquer vigorously.
Let the prince of this world be arrogant,
Let him gnash his teeth and rage;
The villain cannot harm,
Since he is broken by even a tiny word.
</quote>

But I also did not mind inserting the entire song into the history of our times as expressed by Sleidan in these words: "God is for us a fortress and a stronghold. That old enemy of the human race now acts with all his strength
pages.21: and employs every kind of device. Our own power is indeed small, and we cannot withstand such an assault for long. But the Hero whom God Himself has chosen for Himself has taken up arms and fights on our behalf. If you ask who He is, know that He is Christ Jesus, in whose hands victory and triumph must reside. Even if this whole fabric of the world were to teem with devils, we would still not be terrified, and with the most certain confidence, we await a joyful outcome. For however much Satan may rage and prowl, he will accomplish nothing against us. For he has been judged, and by a single word, all his armor collapses. Our adversaries will not snatch this Word from us, but will leave it, however unwillingly. For God walks in our camp and in our line of battle, and He protects us with His Spirit and His gifts. If they take away life, if they take away goods, if they take away children and wife, bear it patiently. For nothing is gained by them on account of it, but for us, an immortal kingdom is prepared."
pages.22: I had written this letter privately to you, illustrious and noble Lord Segur, and indeed, I had written it as if I were speaking with you in a present conversation, my spirit jubilant at the auspicious news of your safe return to England. Nevertheless, I could not refuse my friends who wanted this, as a testimony of the true and sincere judgment—not only of myself but of many good men—regarding your virtues, and [filled with] praise, to be printed and prefixed to the book which Lord Brocard had submitted to the press at this same time. In this book, in order to satisfy your commands, he strove to illustrate that mystical Song of Solomon with his own interpretation. I trust that its reading will be neither useless nor unpleasant to pious and learned men who will wish to judge the essence of the matter candidly. And so, I ask and pray with the reverence I owe you, that you do not let this letter, a witness of my respect and love toward you, be a burden or a nuisance to you, and that you continue to hold me in your accustomed benevolence.
pages.23:
Fare you well, Hero most worthy of the perpetual praise and celebration of all good men. And continue to apply yourself vigorously to the work of the Lord, as you are doing, about to receive one day the crown of righteousness which the Lord, the just judge, will return to you and to all who love His appearing. At Bremen, at the beginning of the year of Christ 1585, which I pray to God with my innermost sighs may be beneficial to the entire Church and Republic, and happy and holy for us all.

To Your Illustrious Generosity,

Sincerely honoring and loving,

Christophorus Pezelius, D.
