Whether the intellect disposes [one] to love and to remember, and conversely. Whether the intellect, in one and the same time, can believe and understand. Whether the intellect creates science within itself. It is asked by what [means] the intellect creates a species. Whether the intellect, with its species, commands the will and memory to objectify that species. Just as we apply the questions of the rule to the intellect, so they can be applied to other powers in their own way.

### Concerning questions of the table.

It is asked whether the world is eternal. Go to column b, c, d, and hold the negative [view], and you will find in chamber b, c, t, b that if it is eternal, there are many eternities conflicting with the species, and they are in harmony through chamber b, c, t, e, against chamber b, c, d, which is impossible; whence it follows that the negative question is to be held, and this the rule b proves. It is asked whether God can be infinite as much by his magnitude as by his eternity; go to column c, d, e, and to chamber c, d, t, c, holding the affirmative against chamber c, d, t, d. Whether God can be as much by eternity as by intellect; go to column d, e, f, and to chamber d, e, t, d. Whether God is as powerful through his power as through his understanding and loving; go to column e, f, g, and hold the affirmative for chamber e, f, t, e and for chamber e, f, t, f, and for chamber e, f, t, g, until the entire column is completed. Whether in God his intel-
pages.55:
lect and will are greater than his virtue; go to column f, g, h, and hold the negative for all the chambers of that column, drawing out the meanings of the chambers. Whether divine truth is equally virtuous through equal correlatives as divine will; go to column g, h, i, and hold the affirmative for all the chambers of that column. Whether in God his virtue, his truth, and his grace have that by which they are equal and removed from time, place, and minority; go to column h, i, k, and hold the affirmative for all the chambers.

¶ Concerning questions of the evacuation of the third figure.

In chamber b, c, it is said that goodness is great. Now it is asked whether goodness is great, and what is its magnitude, and goodness and magnitude, in what do they harmonize? And whether they can harmonize without difference. And it must be answered that goodness is great, as is clear from the definition of magnitude. And its magnitude is to have correlatives, as is clear through the second species of rule c, and they harmonize, because goodness is great through magnitude and conversely. Now indeed they could not harmonize without the difference of their correlatives. And let this suffice concerning the evacuation of the third figure for the sake of brevity. For through these things which we have said about it, the artist can solve and make questions through the other chambers.
pages.56:
¶ **Concerning questions of the multiplication of the fourth figure.**

It is asked by what mode the intellect conditions itself to being general through general understanding. Go to the multiplication of the fourth figure and see by what mode the intellect multiplies the conditions with which it multiplies objects and its understanding, so that through many and great sciences it becomes general and clothed in many habits. And let this suffice concerning the multiplication of the fourth figure for the sake of brevity.

**Concerning questions of the mixture of principles and rules.**

It is asked whether goodness is discursive through magnitude, duration, etc., and conversely. And it must be answered that yes, as is signified through the third figure by making the predicate out of the subject. It is asked what goodness is in magnitude, duration, etc. To which it must be answered that it is great in magnitude and durable in duration. It is asked what goodness has in magnitude, etc., to which it must be said that in it it has its correlatives, great in magnitude and durable in duration. And just as we exemplify concerning goodness, so it can be exemplified concerning other principles in their own way. And let this suffice concerning the mixture in its own way.

**Concerning questions of the nine subjects. And first concerning God.**

It is asked whether God is. And it must be answered that yes; it was proven in the questions of the first figure. It is asked, What is God? And it must be answered that God
pages.57:
is a being that acts as much within itself as it itself is. Through the second species of rule c, it is asked what God has in himself essentially. To which it must be answered that he has his correlatives, without which he could not have immense and eternal reasons. Through the third species, it is asked what God is in another. To which it must be said that he is the creator, the governor, and the like. Through the fourth species of rule c, it is asked what God has in another. And it must be said that he has in another power and dominion, and in humans judgment and the act of grace, mercy, patience, and piety. And let this suffice concerning God for the sake of brevity.

¶ Concerning questions of angels.

It is asked whether angels are. And it must be answered that yes. For if that which is less resembles God, it is; and much more, that which is more seen to resemble God is. Furthermore, if there is something which is composed of intellectual and corporal, much more [is] that which is composed of intellectual and intellectual. Moreover, if angels did not exist, the scale of difference and concordance would be evacuated, and consequently the world, which is impossible. It is asked of what the angel is and whose it is. And it must be answered by rule d that it is of itself; its essence, indeed, cannot be punctual nor lineal. And by the second species of the same rule, it is of its spiritual correlatives, that is, of its actives, passives, and acts, from which it is composed
pages.58:
active, and through passives it is receptive, and through the act existing between the actives and passives; by the third species it must be said that the angel is God's. And let this suffice concerning the angels for the sake of brevity.

# Concerning questions of the Heaven.

It is asked whether the heaven moves itself. And it must be answered that yes, so that its principles may have substantial and proper correlatives through their constellations. Whether the heaven moves itself to a place; and it must be answered that yes, in itself and in lower things, circularly, but not outside itself; the reason for this is because outside itself it has no action, nor can it have. Whether an angel moves the heaven; and it must be answered that no, because if it were to move it, the passives would be lower and the actives higher, and also by its form it would not move the elements nor the elementals, but by its matter, which is impossible. It is asked whether the heaven has a motive soul. And it must be answered that yes, for otherwise the sensitive and vegetative would not have motive souls, nor would the elements have motion. It is asked through the first species of rule e, why is the heaven? And it must be said that it is because it is constituted from its form and matter. Through the second species of rule e, it is asked why the heaven is; and it must be said that it is so that lower beings may have motion. And let this suffice concerning the heaven for the sake of brevity.
pages.59:
¶ Concerning the questions of the 4th subject, which is man.

It is asked whether man can have greater knowledge of God by affirming or by denying; and it must be answered that by affirming, for God is not through those things without which he is, but through those without which he cannot be. It is asked why man acts through a specific form; go to the second species of rule e, and there is the implied solution. Whether man, augmenting his acts, augments his essence; and it must be answered that no man acts upon himself. It is asked when a man desires to remember and cannot remember, which of these fails first, or the memory or the intellect; to which it must be said that the memory itself yields the species more quickly to the intellect than to the will. It is asked, of soul and body, by which are humans composed? And it must be answered that in man, corporal and spiritual goodness compose one goodness, and so of others. It is asked what the life of man is; to which it must be answered that it is that form which is composed of the vegetative, sensitive, imaginative, and rational. What is the death of man? It must be answered that it is the dissolution of the elemental, vegetative, sensitive, imaginative, and rational power. It is asked whether man is visible; and it must be said that no, for sight cannot see anything except color and figure. It is asked whether in man the intellect and memory are the same power; and it must be answered
pages.60:
no, because if they were the same power, the intellect would not be successive in acquiring species, nor would it hand them over to oblivion, nor would it be ignorant of them. Again, because it would be too strong in its object against the liberty of the will. And let these things said concerning man suffice for the sake of brevity.

### Concerning questions of the imaginative.

Whether the imaginative imagines imaginable things in its own way, as the sensitive [imagines] sensible things.
It is asked what is the reason why the imaginative abstracts species from sensible things. It is asked what the imaginative is. Whether the imaginative has correlatives. Whether the imaginative augments itself by augmenting its act. Whether the imaginative is a higher power than the sensitive. Whether the imaginative has specific instincts and appetites. By what mode the sensitive hinders the act of the imaginative. Why the imaginative is not as powerful in sensible or sensed things as the sensitive; go to the subject of the imaginative. It is asked whether the sensitive senses the imaginative. And it must be answered that the lower powers do not act upon the higher.

### Concerning questions of the sensitive.

It is asked which power of these senses hunger and thirst, either the gustatory or the tactile? And it must be answered that [it is] that which disposes the object more.
Whether the gustatory senses hunger or thirst with instinct and appetite, just as the visual [senses] the colored with
pages.61:
color. Go to the second species of rule c.
It is asked from what the sensitive senses sensed things. And it must be answered that every particular sense senses its own sensible object through a specific form, just as a colored subject subsisting in crystal colors it. Whether the sensitive has punctual and lineal quantities. And it must be answered that the sensitive attains the object as quickly from far away as from near. Whether the sensitive, just as it has a common sense, so has a common power, instinct, and appetite. It is asked what the sensitive is. The sensitive, with what is it particular and common? The sensitive, from what does it live and is nourished? Whether the sensitive is sensed; go to the subject of the sensitive.

### Concerning the vegetative.

Whether the vegetative acts through its species.
Whether the vegetative has some reason of which it is common and particular, as the sensitive.
Whether the quantity of the vegetative is punctual or lineal. It is asked what the vegetative is and what it has in itself through the second species of rule c.
It is asked from what the vegetative lives and is nourished and grows, and in what subject it is planted. What is the death of the vegetative; go to the subject of the vegetative, in which the solutions to the aforesaid questions are implied.

pages.10:
Sapor, King of the Persians, who proposed to mortals, for eternal memory, the syrup named after apples <note>original: "Syrupum de pomis"</note> (corruptly called by some the King’s Sabor) to dispel the melancholic and black humors offending in the microcosm. I pass over Archelaus, Hiero, and Philemetor, kings who wrote about plants in Greek. I pass over the antidote of that most invincible King Mithridates, praised by the common calculation of all to this day, which was found by Pompey in his sanctuaries. In our own centuries, it is read in the monuments of history that Nicholas and Eusebius V, supreme Pontiffs, were physicians by art and profession. Therefore, as it is most beautiful, it is no wonder if it is also difficult, and on account of this, there seem to be so many and such varied opinions in the medical republic, so that, regarding this, the saying of Horace <note>original: "illud Horatianum"</note> is recited by some: Book 2, Satire 1.

> As many heads as come, so many are the studies.
> A thousand species of men, and a variegated use of things.
> To each his own desire, nor does one live by a single vow.

Yet it should not be believed that this most noble science suffers any shipwreck from this (for by reason of beauty and difficulty, there are indeed various opinions in theory, but in practice, the sense of all is the same, the calculation is the same). Rather, it is directed more and more strengthened toward defending and preserving the human republic and toward repairing and overcoming diseases, which the good also accompanies. Hence, being captivated by the same beauty that is both difficult and beautiful, having proposed certain Theses to be defended by a Physician for the Medical College at Prague in the year 1652, and having given them to the public (as is usually done, promulgated in print), not a few friends, considering them difficult and beautiful for practice, began to exhort me to add—
pages.11:
reasons to corroborate them for the good of mortals. I, who in such an arena <note>a place of contest</note> struggle with difficulty because of so many critics <note>original: "zoilorum" — referencing Zoilus, the archetypal bitter critic</note>, declined the advice. However, having found an opportune moment (since I had also seen very learned men doubting about something in practice), I decided to follow the advice and I record them again in the same order in which I defended them at Prague. If anyone, nauseated, rejects this labor of mine, let him know that I did not write for him, and if he has better things, let him offer them, and let him not doubt that I shall return the greatest thanks to him; and that my intention was none other than that I wished to exercise myself in a matter that is difficult, most beautiful, and necessary for the common good of mortals. For if Emperors, Caesars, Kings, and Pontiffs exercised themselves in the same, because of its beauty and the accompanying good, why should it not be permitted to a physician? Let others enjoy themselves as they please.

# PREFACE TO THE CONCLUSIONS,
### which is
# THE FIRST CONCLUSION.

<note>Large ornamental drop-cap initial 'O' decorated with floral and foliate patterns.</note>
All men naturally desire to know. Some indeed desire to know their own origin, others long to be skilled in knowledge, others have it in mind to learn something else. I, to satisfy such naturalness in some way, bring forth some things from the vast field of the medical faculty, and first, what is formed in the very first formation of man, or shall we say the fetus: whether it is the heart, the fountain of human life; or the liver, the workshop of blood; or the brain, the most divine member, as called by Plato in the Timaeus. And I assert that the liver is formed first, then the heart, and finally the brain.

There are many things, I confess, to be discussed in this Conclusion, namely, how in the introduced seed it is dilated, adheres, lives, and similar things which would pertain to the present matter; furthermore, whether it lives in potentiality or in actuality; whether a natural spirit is given, or whether it proceeds from the liver. But setting these aside, I descend to my main intent (supposing from Aristotle, Book 1 of *Parts of Animals*, chapter 1, that the seed is generation: and generation is the first participation with the warm, nutritive soul, from *On Youth and Old Age*, chapter 14; likewise, Book 1 of *On the Generation of Animals*, chapter 18, if the parts—
pages.13:
are drawn asunder in the seed, how does it live? Likewise, Book 2 of *On the Generation of Animals*, chapter 3, the seed and the conception nonetheless live, as plants do, nor is Galen contrary). See: what is that first member, from the main sayings, that is generated first and more conveniently, and lives with a vegetative life. So that this our conclusion may be firmer, we shall draw authorities from Hippocrates and from others. Afterward, if anything must be brought to the contrary, I shall resolve it.

    Hippocrates, therefore, in his book *On the Formation of the Fetus*, and his faithful interpreter Galen, recount here a certain case (by which he intends to prove that the liver is generated first; I, indeed, shall bring forth both its structure and for what purpose it exists, so that everything may be more corroborated), which is as follows:

    "But indeed, the seed, which had remained in the places for six days, and had afterward fallen out, I saw myself, and from those things which appeared to me in it at that time, I conjecture the rest: how I saw the seed on the sixth day, I shall tell. A certain servant of a woman (she was a distinguished harpist, who used to visit men, whom it was not appropriate to conceive in her womb, lest she be rendered more contemptible; but that harpist had heard what women were accustomed to say among themselves, that when a woman is about to conceive, the man's seed no longer exits the womb, but is contained within. When she had heard this, she paid attention and always observed, and by chance, when she felt the seed had not exited, she manifested it to her mistress; when this had reached our ears, we ordered her to jump onto the ground (another text reads 'onto her buttocks,' and it is better), and she did this about seven times, and the seed, not without a certain noise, was shaken out and flowed down to the ground. When the woman had seen it, she inspected it and was amazed. What it was like, I myself shall say, just as if someone were to tear the outer shell of a raw egg, so that through the inner membrane, the interior humidity would shine through; it was clearly of such a kind in a certain way, and a certain red and round thing was within, but in the membrane, certain white and thick fibers were discerned, indeed wrapped in a thick and red substance, and on the outside around the membrane were bloody bruises: in the middle, something thin gaped, which seemed to me to be the navel, by which the fetus would first breathe, with spirit going both out and in; from it, the membrane which contained the seed was entirely produced." This series of Hippocrates' history, with Galen and Bernardo Feliciano as interpreter. Which, both the same Galen and Felicianus from Galen—
pages.14:
explain in their entirety, and indicate what everything signifies. But, with other things omitted, in chapter 3, around the middle, they interpret that red thing thus, saying, "That red and round thing which appeared in the chorion in the seed, which Hippocrates said was six days old, is to be believed to have been the liver, still indistinct and unformed." And a little later they add: "But before (so Galen and Felicianus from him), when I was writing commentaries on the seed, and was compelled to say something about the order of formation of the individual members, I said the heart, just as the liver, in the first days of the fetus, was, as it were, a certain foundation, based on the use of it itself, which is most necessary in adults and perfect beings, and I was induced to bring this forward: but when I afterward recognized the opinion of all others, both physicians and philosophers (behold the ingenuousness of Galen admitting his own error, behold the foundations upon which he relied to change his opinion), that the fetus is dispersed merely as a plant until formed expression, it seemed more probable to me if we were to maintain that there is no necessity for the heart in the beginning, but that it is formed entirely after the liver." And around the end of the chapter, he adds: "But indeed, just as it is to be believed that the heart was made later than the liver, and therefore the liver was placed closer to the womb of the pregnant woman (which anatomy itself demonstrates most truly), so it was fitting that the brain also be placed further from the heart, inasmuch as it is also fabricated later." Giving the reason why the brain is also fabricated last, he says: "That which is to be done, for this reason must be thought so, because there is no need for the brain for the fetus: for it does not need to see, nor to hear, nor to taste, nor to smell anything, nor likewise to work with its hands or feet, nor to use any other voluntary function at all. In a similar way, there was no necessity for the sense of touch, no necessity for imagination, no necessity for thought, no necessity for memory; therefore, the brain was fabricated third in the order of time." (Beautifully said regarding the necessity of the last formation of the brain itself; if he had provided the same for the heart, it would be less burdensome to us, but we shall demonstrate it with our strength). These both Hippocrates and Galen said. But let it be permitted to me, to confirm this, to add this Case History which I saw.

---

->A certain Marchionilla of Tochau in Bohemia, January 14, 1653, after the tenth day of conception, suffered an abortion.<-
pages.15:
Wishing to see, or rather I should say, being desirous and curious to see the constitution of the fetus, she had me called, and the midwife. In my presence, at my command, and with me demonstrating the method, she cut the abortion into parts, and while she was cutting the chorion, a certain bloody mass was seen, without any motion, without any sense (as appeared from the section), interwoven and divided by various filaments; outside the chorion membrane, other certain filaments were conspicuous. Who will doubt that that bloody mass was the liver, and those filaments were the rudiments of the veins and the navel? It appeared without sense, without motion; what other thing will you present or assign to me than the liver? Wherefore it remains that the liver is generated first, and that nothing more convenient can be devised for the vegetative soul, as a member in which it may reside, than the liver. But let this be confirmed both from the structure of the liver and from its use.

The substance of the liver is fleshy, similar to blood recently poured out and congealed, whence the word *parenchyma* <note>the functional tissue of an organ</note> was deduced by Erasistratus; it is covered by a simple and sufficiently thin membrane, clinging tightly to the organ on all sides; it consists of a double order of veins: the Superior, which are offshoots of the vena cava, and lead the blood into its large trunk, like a royal road; the Inferior, which are more numerous, are branches of the portal vein, from which also the umbilical vein arises in the fetus, by which the fetus is nourished.

Its function and duty is to nourish the body to the very end of life; for from the natural spirit arising from the liver, both the vital and the animal spirits receive nourishment (although Manardus, and with him Ioan. Hier. Bronzerius, in his Treatise, Book 15 of Epistles, first epistle, seem to deny this: yet they conceded, and Bertachius in the third, *On Spirits*, chapter 3, and Galen, Book 1, *On Natural and Spiritual Faculties*—
pages.16: Capiuaccius <note>a Renaissance physician</note> (*Aphorismorum lectione 50* and others from Galen), of whose necessity and use Galen, in the last chapter of the 7th book of *Method*, rightly brings forth these things concerning the liver: "The work of the liver is most necessary for all parts." And in the 16th chapter of the 11th book of *Metaphysics*, he says: "It is most dangerous if the strength of the liver is dissolved, for this is what provides nourishment both to the heart and to the other parts." Hence, infants have more vigorous vegetative faculties, less vigorous sensitive ones, and even less intellectual ones, inasmuch as they obtain such utility from the liver. Wherefore, Franciscus Vlmus Baiensis, in his *Treatise on Urines*, a physician not to be despised, gathering the office and necessity of the liver, did not hesitate to call this the most noble member. Therefore, considering its substance, considering its function, use, and office, what was it fitting to be generated first in the very first formation of the fetus than the liver itself? For the natural faculty (which I do not hesitate to also name the natural spirit) permeates through all members, not only through the arteries themselves and the veins, but also through flesh, nerves, ligaments, even bones, and all the rest that constitute our body. Whence it happens that even in the diseases of all parts, we can have both continuous and certain notes, and also have knowledge of the disposition of the whole, simultaneously from this natural faculty—from the liver, the tinderbox and seat of this and the natural spirit. Why then should we not concede it to be the foundation of the microcosm, and the first principle in the microcosm? From the liver, or from the natural faculty arising from the liver, we not only have the diseases of this principle opened, but also the internal causes of the diseases of the other principle members are represented. Let the brain labor, let the heart itself labor, some pathognomonic signs present themselves (which I neither deny nor is it right to deny) by which you may be able to conclude that these parts are laboring; but, unless the liver cooks the nourishment exhibited to it through the subservient stomach, and carries it to the heart and to the brain, what help will you provide? If you concede it is possible to help those that are laboring by topicals—
pages.17: if you concede that, which to deny is to deny reason itself and experience (you will see, when I demonstrate a single example of a human lacking a liver), why will you not concede that the vegetative principle of the soul, at least, and the first in the formation of the fetus, is more fittingly generated there? Many similar things in the medical field, and better ones, could be elicited for the dignity of such a principle; but, it must be granted to the reader, so that he may refresh his mind, just as it is permitted to me who is writing, therefore, having dismissed the medical study, let us descend into the field of recreation, to the sacred secret fables of antiquity; for from these, perhaps, our opinion will also be corroborated. Those who left behind a written genealogy of the gods fable thus about Venus and Mars: Venus, seen by Phoebus with Mars in adultery, the adultery of his wife was revealed to Vulcan by the same observer. Concerning this matter of such great business among the gods (after iron nets were first taken to catch both adulterers), a Council was convened; Neptune, Mercury, and Apollo were present at the Council; it was decreed that they should have the gods free; Apollo interceded, Mercury interceded, but Neptune interceded in vain. The deities are freed. If it should please one to look accurately into these fictions of fables and veils, we shall easily understand that the heat of fire is very consentaneous to the mystery of Vulcan, that Venus is placed in marriage to our mortality; he is procreated from Jove and Juno, that is from Heaven, acting through motion and light (for such is our native heat, spherical and conformal to the element of the stars, as is judged by the most learned), from the Air, and is precipitated into the circumfluent Island of the Sea, namely into the earth, into the Venus of our mortality, comprised of Water (through generation) into marriage, where it is first nourished from the apes, which it is sufficiently evident are of most prone ingenuity to imitate the actions of rational beings and to feign. Here, I say, he possesses Venus, from the mixture of the humid. By the beauty of this Venus—

all our organs, so that each one may receive as he has done: That there is a resurrection of the dead, & eternal judgment, & the kingdom of heaven, & rest for the righteous, & the inheritance of the faithful, & the rejoicing with the angels, of those who kept the faith, & chastity and hope, & the Lord's commandments. Moreover, it is truly preached, & certainly confirmed, and believed, that some will rise to eternal life, & others to eternal judgment, as it is written in the Gospels. Thus far Epiphanius.

To these must be added what Cyril writes in the Ephesian symbol: We do not say that the flesh is changed into the nature of divinity, nor that the ineffable nature of the Word of God is transferred into the nature of the flesh. For it is entirely immovable & immutable, remaining the same perpetually according to the scriptures. And when he was made visible, still an infant and in the cradle, and at the bosom of his mother the Virgin, he filled every creature, as God, and sat with the Father. For the Godhead is without quantity, & without magnitude, nor can it be circumscribed. Thus far Cyril.

pages.17:
# ABOUT MYSTERIES
## AND SACRAMENTS.

<note>A woodcut depicts a figure in royal robes, likely King Solomon, seated at a desk while writing or studying, framed by ornate architectural elements.</note>About to speak of mysteries, it is necessary before all else to explore what a mystery is, and what it comprises, lest otherwise, by intending to speak many words about mysteries, like one running outside the stadium set for the contestants, he merely wearies himself in vain by laboring, & achieves nothing beyond exhaustion: so he too, not containing himself within the bounds of the mysteries while discoursing, as he wanders from the goal, cannot grasp the palm.

<margin>Prov. 20</margin>
<margin>Ecclus. 27</margin>
<margin>Mat. 13</margin>
First, therefore, it must be observed that "mystery" is a Greek term, although frequently used by the Latins, and it signifies some hidden thing, or that under which something hidden lies, which is not perfected except by some secret method of sacred rites. For mysteries are sometimes called those secret and hidden human affairs, which it is considered sacrilege to speak of in public, as it is in Solomon in Proverbs: Do not associate with one who reveals mysteries, & walks deceitfully, & enlarges his lips. And in Ecclesiasticus: To lay bare the mysteries of a friend, is the despair of an unhappy soul. Likewise, mysteries are called the sacred secrets of God, as it is in Matthew concerning the sower of his seed: where Christ says to his disciples, To you it is given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to the others.
pages.18: <margin>1 Cor. 2</margin> in parables. And in Paul to the Corinthians writing about the preaching of the word of God: We speak the wisdom of God hidden in a mystery, which God predestined before the ages for our glory. <margin>1 Tim. 3</margin> And to Timothy concerning the incarnation of the Word of God he says, Great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifested in the flesh, justified in the spirit, seen by angels, preached to the Gentiles, faith was had in him in the world, he was received in glory. <margin>Rom. 16</margin> And to the Romans concerning the same incarnation, According to the revelation of the mystery kept silent for eternal times, which has been made manifest through the scriptures of the Prophets, according to the commandment of the eternal God for the obedience of faith. Paul also commemorates such secrets of God to the Romans, saying, <margin>Rom. 11</margin> For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, so that you may not be wise in your own estimation, that blindness has happened in part to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, & thus all Israel might be saved. And <margin>1 Cor. 15</margin> he writes to the Corinthians concerning the resurrection, Behold, I tell you a mystery: Not all of us will sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a point of time, in the moment of an eye at the last trumpet. For the trumpet will sound, & the dead will rise incorruptible, & we will be changed. For this corruptible must put on incorruptibility, & this mortal must put on immortality. Writing to the Thessalonians, he recalls that same <margin>1 Thess. 4</margin> mystery, saying: For this we say to you in the word
pages.19:
of the Lord, that we who live and are left for the coming of the Lord, shall in no way precede those who have fallen asleep, because the Lord himself will descend from heaven with a command and the voice of the Archangel, and the trumpet of God, and the dead who are in Christ will rise first: then we who live, who are left, will be taken up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord. And John in the Apocalypse <margin>Apoc. 1</margin> explains the mystery of the seven stars. If Paul and John had not revealed these secrets of God to us, they would still lie hidden from us, unknown.

Sacred signs are also called mysteries by the Greeks, and sacraments by the Latins, as Paul speaking to the Ephesians <margin>Eph. 5</margin> about the union of husband and wife says: This is a great sacrament, but I speak in Christ and the Church. In this sense mysteries are sometimes taken by the Latins: as Paul says to the Corinthians, <margin>1 Cor. 4</margin> Let a man so consider us, as ministers of Christ, and dispensers of the mysteries of God. However, to treat of all kinds of mysteries in this work is not our intention, lest we seem to be wise beyond sobriety: and we are conscious that we have not drawn enough from the spirit of God to be able to either understand, as is proper, all the hidden and latent secrets of God, or to pursue and illustrate each one with fitting words, once understood.

Therefore, in this treatise, we are to assert the truth of the body and blood of the Lord in the sacrament of the Eucharist, if Christ grants it to us, and we will use both terms, of mystery and sacrament, indifferently, but more frequently the name of sacrament, which is more familiar to Latin ears. But before we undertake our purpose, the concordant opinion of the most approved ancients concerning the sacraments must be conveniently opened here, which is of this kind: *Sacraments are sacred signs, & symbols, of God's will toward us. And in the new testament, they are certain & efficacious signs, & vehicles of divine grace, conferring grace upon those who worthily receive them.*

<margin>Wis. 9</margin>
Since sacraments are effective signs of the grace of God & of our sanctification, they consist of two things: namely, of the sign itself, that is, an external element, shadowing forth invisible grace, & of the word, through which the Holy Spirit secretly works that grace. For because on account of our flesh (whose mass the strength of the mind is burdened by), we are dull to receiving the spiritual grace of God, and in need of some external aid, by which our fragility may be at once excited & instructed: therefore for the healing of human infirmity, God has applied the spiritual medicine of his grace, veiled by certain sensible signs: which the Greeks call symbols or mysteries, some Latins call them sacraments, others sacramental signs. These sacraments, lest anyone should doubt their power & efficacy, Christ confirmed with his word, & promise:
pages.20:
the effect of whose divine promise and operation is never wanting to these signs, unless an obstacle intervenes through the vice and unworthiness of the recipient. Of this kind are baptism, the sacrament of penance, the Eucharist, or the sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord, and the other sacraments: each of which has its own promises, based on the word of God as the firmest foundation, and appropriate and suitable to its nomenclature. Baptism has the promise of grace, regeneration, and the kingdom of heaven annexed to it, as in this place:

<margin>John 3</margin>
> *Amen, amen I say to you, unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of heaven:*

and in another place,

<margin>Mark last</margin>
> *He who believes and is baptized will be saved.*

The sacrament of penance has the promise of the remission of sins, and of restoration into the society of the mystical body of Christ, which is the Church: as here,

<margin>John 20</margin>
> *Whose sins you shall forgive, they are forgiven them.*

Furthermore, the Eucharist, or the sacrament of the body and blood, has the promise of eternal life, and of dwelling in Christ: as in John,

<margin>John 6</margin>
> *He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life: and I will raise him up on the last day. For my flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink: he who eats my flesh, and drinks my blood, remains in me, and I in him: as the living Father has sent me, and I live because of the Father: so also he who eats me,*
pages.21:
he himself will also live because of me. Therefore, the worthy reception of the Eucharist constitutes us members of Christ, just as conversely, through an unworthy reception of it which brings judgment upon itself, we make ourselves members of Satan.

Furthermore, the word of God offers us the promise of grace: the sacramental sign is like a seal of the word of God, exhibiting the promised thing. Therefore, just as the promise is useless to us unless it is apprehended by faith: so the sacramental sign is similarly useless to us, unless it is believed that we will receive what is signified. For otherwise, if nothing that does not appear is received through the sign of the sacrament, then the sign itself will be inefficacious, and nothing of more distinguished efficiency, and of greater grace, will be said to have been added to our new testament sacraments from the power of Christ's passion, than was present in those sacraments which were in the old testament.

<margin>Luke 22, Matt. 26</margin>
In the holy sacrament of the Eucharist, however, to the worthy reception of which the promise of grace is annexed, two things must be considered, namely, both the sign exposed to our senses, & at the same time the true body of Christ, to be known not by the judgment of the senses, but by faith, as appears by the very words of the Savior, saying:

> This is my body, which is given for you: This is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins.

Which words, from the very cradles of the Catholic Church after Christ suffered, without any allegory,

while ignorant of these things, could do so much in speaking." "And Catulus," said Antonius, "I am not in the habit of reading the books of these men, and several others, to gain any utility for speaking, but for the sake of pleasure when there is leisure. What then is the result? I will confess: yet something happens by nature, just as when I walk in the sun, even if I walk for a different reason, it happens nevertheless that I am tanned; so, when I have read these books quite diligently at Misenum (for one can hardly do so at Rome), I feel my oratory being colored, as it were, by their strain. But, lest this seem to you to extend more widely, I understand these things only in Greek, which the authors themselves wished to be understood by the common people. If I ever happen upon your philosophers, deceived by the titles of the books, because they are generally inscribed with known and illustrious subjects—on virtue, on justice, on honesty, on pleasure—I do not understand a single word; they are so tied up in narrow and concise disputations. As for the poets, I do not even try to touch them, as if they spoke in some other language. With them, as I have said, I amuse myself, those who have written about history or their own speeches, or those who speak in such a way that they seem to have wished to be familiar to us, who are not the most learned. But I return to that point. Do you see how great a task of the orator history is? I am not sure if it is not the greatest, by the flow of its oratory and its variety. Nor do I find it anywhere separately instructed by the precepts of the rhetoricians; for they lie before our eyes. For who does not know the first law of history, that one must not dare to say anything false; then, that one must not fear to say anything true; that there be no suspicion of favor in the writing, and no suspicion of malice? These, of course, are the foundations

# DE ORATORE
<meta>continues from previous page: known to all. The actual construction itself rests on the facts and the words.</meta>

The arrangement of facts requires the order of times and a description of regions. It also requires that, since in great and memorable affairs councils come first, then actions, and afterwards the outcomes, the writer should indicate what he approves of in the councils, and in the deeds, he should declare not only what was done or said, but also how; and when the outcome is told, all causes—whether of chance, of wisdom, or of rashness—should be explained; and of the men themselves, not only their deeds, but also, concerning those who excel in fame and name, the life and nature of each. The arrangement of words, however, and the style of oratory must be broad and drawn out, flowing with a certain equable gentleness, without this judicial harshness and without the sharp points of forensic reflections. Do you see if any precepts for these many and such great things are to be found in the arts of the rhetoricians? In this same silence, many other duties of the orator have lain, such as exhortations, consolations, instructions, and admonitions; all of which must be treated most eloquently, but have no place in those parts which have been handed down. And in this category is also that infinite forest; because most men (as even Crassus showed) have given the orator two categories for speaking; one concerning a certain and defined cause, such as those that are involved in lawsuits or in deliberations (add to this, if anyone wishes, panegyrics); the other, which almost all writers call by name but no one explains: the infinite question of a kind without time and without person. When they say what this is and how much it is, they do not seem to understand
pages.486:
# LIBER SECVNDVS.
<page-num>57</page-num>

that they do not seem to understand it. For if it belongs to the orator to be able to speak on any subject placed infinitely, he will have to speak on how great the magnitude of the sun is, or what the shape of the earth is; concerning mathematical or musical matters, he will not be able to refuse once he has taken on this burden. Finally, for him who professes that it is his duty to speak not only on those controversies marked by time and persons—that is, on all forensic matters—but also on the infinite questions of kinds, no style of oratory can be excepted. But if we also wish to add to the orator that wandering, free, and wide-ranging part of questions—so that we think the orator should speak on things good or evil, things to be sought or to be avoided, honorable or base, useful or useless; on virtue, on justice, on self-control, on prudence, on greatness of soul, on liberality, on piety, on friendship, on loyalty, on duty, and on other virtues and their contrary vices; and likewise on the Republic, on empire, on military affairs, on the discipline of the state, and on the character of men—let us take on that part as well, but in such a way that it is circumscribed within moderate bounds. Indeed, I think that all things that pertain to the use of citizens, the character of men—which are involved in the customs of life, in the reasoning of the state, in this civil society, in the common sense of men, in nature, in customs—must be embraced by the orator; if not to respond separately on these things in the manner of philosophers, then certainly to be able to weave them prudently into a case; and to speak about these very things in such a way as those who established rights, laws, and states have spoken,
pages.487:
# DE ORATORE

simply and splendidly, without any string of disputations and without the barren contest of words. At this point, let there be no astonishment if no precepts for so many and such great matters are set forth by me: I hold this position, that in other arts, when the most difficult things of each subject have been handed down, the rest do not need to be taught because they are either easier or similar; just as in painting, one who has learned to paint the likeness of a man can paint one of any shape or age, even if he has not been taught; nor is there danger that one who can paint a lion or a bull excellently cannot do the same with many other quadrupeds; nor is there any art at all in which all things that can be accomplished by that art are taught by a master; but those who have learned the very types of the primary and certain things pursue the rest by themselves not unskillfully. Similarly, I think in this reasoning or practice of speaking, whoever has attained that power so that he can move to his own will the minds of those who, whether concerning the Republic or his own affairs, or concerning those against whom or for whom he speaks, listen with some power of deciding; this man will not ask any more about the whole genus of remaining speeches than that famous Polycletus, when he was shaping a Hercules, asked how to shape the skin or the hydra, even if he had never learned to do these things separately. Then Catulus said, "You seem to me, Antonius, to have been able to place before our eyes excellently what he who is to be an orator ought to learn, and what, even if he had not learned it, he would assume from what he had learned. For you have reduced the whole man to only two kinds of causes. The rest you have left
pages.488:

<page-num>58</page-num>
<sig>H ii</sig>

to practice and imitation. But see to it that in those two categories you do not find yourself with a hydra and a skin, while Hercules and other greater works are left in those matters which you pass over. For it seems to me no less work to speak on universal types of defendants than on the causes of individuals, and much greater work to speak on the nature of the gods than on the lawsuits of men." "It is not so," said Antonius, "for I will tell you, Catulus, not as one learned, but as one who is—which is greater—experienced. The oratory of all other subjects, believe me, is child's play for a man who is not dull, not unpracticed, and not inexperienced in common literature and polished humanity. In the contentions of lawsuits, there is a certain great work, and I am not sure if it is not by far the greatest of human works: in which the power of the orator is judged by the uninitiated by its outcome and victory; where an armed adversary is present who must be struck and repelled; where often the one who is to be the master of the case is a stranger, angry, or even a friend to your adversary and an enemy to you; when he must be taught or untaught, repressed or incited, or guided in every way by speech according to the time and the cause: in which often benevolence must be led to hatred, and hatred to benevolence; which, as if by some mechanism, must be twisted now toward severity, now toward remission of mind, now toward sadness, now toward joy. The weight of all reflections and the gravity of all words must be used. There must be added a varied action, vehement, full of spirit, full of passion,
pages.489:
# DE ORATORE
<page-num>82</page-num>

full of severity. If one has grasped that art in these works so that he can create a sign of Minerva like Phidias, he will certainly not labor over how to do those lesser works, just as that same artist might learn to do them on a shield." Then Catulus said, "The greater and more wonderful you make these things, the greater the expectation holds me as to by what reasonings or what precepts such a great power is acquired—not that it concerns me now (for my age does not desire it, and I have followed a different kind of speaking: I never extorted reflections from the hands of the judges by some force of oratory, but rather accepted as much as they themselves allowed, with their minds appeased); but nevertheless, I ask for these things of yours not for my use, but led by the desire to know. And I have no need for some Greek teacher who chants common precepts to me, when he has himself never looked at the forum or any trial; as that Peripatetic Phormio is said to have done: when Hannibal, expelled from Carthage, had come to Ephesus to Antiochus as an exile; and because his name was of great glory among all, he was invited by his hosts to hear that man I mentioned if he wished; and when he had said he was not unwilling: the eloquent man is said to have spoken for several hours on the office of an Emperor and on all military matters. Then, when the others who had heard him were vehemently delighted, they asked Hannibal what he himself judged of that philosopher. The Carthaginian is reported to have replied, not in the best Greek but freely: that he had often seen many doting old men, but none who doted more than Phormio.

And by Hercules, not unjustly. For what could be more arrogant or loquacious than for a Greek man, who had never seen an enemy or a camp and had never touched the smallest part of any public duty, to give precepts on military matters to Hannibal, who had contended for empire for so many years with the Roman people, the conqueror of all nations? This is what all those who give precepts on the art of speaking seem to me to do. For they teach others what they themselves have not experienced: but perhaps they err less in this, that they do not try to teach you, like Hannibal, but boys or very young men." "You are wrong, Catulus," said Antonius. "For I myself have already encountered many Phormios. For who among those Greeks is there who thinks that any of us knows anything? And for me, they are not so troublesome. I easily tolerate and bear them all. For they either bring something that does not displease me, or they cause me not to regret having learned less. But I dismiss them not as insultingly as that philosopher Hannibal: and perhaps I have more trouble for it. But nevertheless, their doctrine, as far as I can judge, is very ridiculous. For they divide the whole subject into two parts: the controversy of the cause and the controversy of the question. They call the cause a matter placed in the discussion of facts and controversy; but the question, a matter placed in infinite doubt. They give precepts for the cause. For the other part of speaking, a wonderful silence. Finally, they make, as it were, five members of eloquence: to find what you say, to arrange what is found, then to adorn with words, then to commit to memory,
pages.491:
# DE ORATORE

then at the end, to perform and deliver. A matter certainly not hidden. For who would not see, of his own accord, that no one can speak aptly unless he has what to say, in what words, and in what order, and remembers them? And I do not criticize these things, but I say they are placed before our eyes, just like those four, five, or six, or even seven parts (since they are divided differently by others) into which all oratory is distributed by them. For they order one to begin in such a way that we make the one who listens well-disposed to us, and docile, and attentive: then to narrate the matter in such a way that the narration is probable, clear, and brief: then to divide the cause or to propose it; to confirm our side with arguments and reasonings, then to refute the contrary. Then others place the conclusion of the speech, or peroration, as it were. Others order one, before concluding, to digress for the sake of adorning or amplifying, then to conclude and perorate. I do not even criticize these things; for they are neatly distributed, but nevertheless, not expertly—as was necessary for men lacking the truth. For the precepts they wished for beginnings and narrations must be preserved in the entire speeches. For I can make a judge well-disposed to me more easily when I am in the course of the speech than when everything is unheard; and docile, not when I promise I will demonstrate, but when I teach and explain; and attentive, we can achieve not by the first announcement, but by frequently rousing the minds of the judges throughout the entire action. Now, indeed, that they order the narration to be probable, and clear, and brief—

pages.18:
spirit that we cultivate in our studies, by writing to each other, having left behind a memory of our own friendship. This king of ours also seems to abide by the aforementioned treaties, both those made with other nations and those with us, insofar as I am able to see. He does not innovate anything before sensing that either you or some others have breached the treaty regarding him, and he acts according to his own counsel. However, if you should decide to write back to me henceforth for the sake of companionship, I would gladly accommodate myself to this favor, since you have begun to love me of your own accord and have provoked me with letters, for which reason I love you wonderfully. Since Linacre and Tunstall have bound me to themselves with this kind of service and have received a reply, I would like you to be persuaded to greet them in my words, and to return a greeting to More, perhaps even with interest, who greeted me in your letters by means of messengers. Farewell, you who are most friendly to letters, and write me into your register. Paris, the fifth day before the Kalends of May, in the year 1518.

### William Budé to Richard Pace, Greetings.

Nicolas Bérauld, who delivered this letter to you, a man most learned in both languages and already having earned no small merit from the humanities, is also otherwise a great friend of mine. When I began to hear that he was going to go there in the company of the Bishop of Paris, I thought it my duty to give him a letter for you, even
pages.19:
though a few days ago I had written a sufficiently long letter to you and entrusted it to a certain relative of mine who is a companion of the same company. For I did not want Bérauld, a man familiar to me and once a guest of your Erasmus, to be in Britain without your knowledge, as you seem to me to be a great lover of studious men yourself. Whatever service and kindness you show him while he is in a foreign province, I shall not refuse to consider it entirely as a favor to me. Although (given the humanity I have found you to possess), I do not doubt that you would have done this of your own accord if you could have learned that a man of such talent and such learning was there, and even when you have the leisure to get to know him, you will desire all things for his sake, so that you do not ask me to count what you bestow upon him as a favor to me. Nevertheless, I would still like him to be recommended to you in my name, as one of my friends whom I am permitted to recommend to you, through your own kindness. Farewell, Paris, the day after the Assumption of the sublime and divine Mother of God.

Good immortal gods, what do I hear? Oh, how many? How great? What panegyrics? What theatrical speeches, which have been celebrated in our midst as a result of the fame of your betrothal and the reception of our embassy, which was accepted so lavishly, elegantly, magnificently, kindly, eloquently, and fluently! Oh, your elegant King, greater than any praise, more excellent than any commemoration of merit! He who has applied such great and ample gifts of body and soul, with such outstanding liberality, with an exceptional will, and with a gracious kindness to all. He who has rendered the munificence of a benign nature more visible, accumulated with a dexterity of manners, august majesty, heroic appearance, and integrity of face. As soon as ours returned from there and began to commemorate that splendid magnificence of the preparations, and how correctly and orderly it was constituted, they were received with the eager ears of all. Then, indeed, every serious man listened with gaping mouth (if I may say so) and amazed expression to the fact that this most serene prince is accustomed to frequenting his retinue with the presence of every most learned man and those most outstanding in the faculty of speech, and to distinguish and adorn his court with such marks, which appearance itself offers to be looked upon by venerable royalty and foreigners. He is, in my opinion, worthy that his fame, illuminated by these lights, should shine forth everywhere that the boundaries of the Christian name extend, and be consecrated to eternal memory by the monuments of the learned. Indeed, as far as I am concerned, I would do nothing more willingly or readily if ever the occasion should arise for writing
pages.20: my essay, so that I might leave to such a great King a memorable eulogy, as a testimony of my mind inclined toward his majesty, for he has indeed deserved excellently and honorably from letters, if what we have heard is true. For he who has raised the honor of the humanities, which had been reduced to the common order by the negligence of other nations and especially by our own customs and institutions, to a height of greater dignity, even by providing an example in himself and establishing a royal eloquence, has most beautifully snatched the glory of this achievement from his contemporaries and from future kings. Indeed, he is the first of kings in many centuries who has understood and seen that such is the power and authority of eloquence that it raises kings to the gods and the underworld, according to their respective merits. If this virtue were to offer itself so easily and be retained with such a certain pleasant immediacy, and if the splendor and appearance of this very virtue could earn applause for itself through all kinds of men, those familiar as well as those ignorant of the liberal arts, then without doubt, princes, nobles, and primary men, taught by such a great example, would soon begin to strive to preserve the majesty of the higher letters, as I see the sense of our own countrymen is now affected since our ambassadors returned. For there is no one among us now who is not ashamed and regretful of his own ignorance. Your own, most learned Richard, speech
pages.21:
delivered in the most ample assemblies of others, is celebrated to such an extent that that opulent and shining preparation used in conducting business is embellished by your eloquence and seemed all the more magnificent. If you hope that we will do the same in this part of preparing things, I fear that we may not be able to satisfy you, among whom the reward of one's eloquence has never remained, due to the remarkable obscurity and indignity of French affairs. Nicolas Bérauld, now most dear to you (as I have understood from your letters), has set out to court with the Bishop of Paris, aided excellently by your votes and recommendations, and is raised from there by no doubtful hope. The King is said to be arriving now, so that he may receive the expected ambassadors from there. Farewell, my Pace, and greet my Tunstall, More, Linacre, and the others for me. Paris, the Nones of November.

## William Budé to Richard Pace, Greetings.

Having now received your third letter, I have marveled at your diligence in this manner of cultivating friendship, to which I have hardly yet experienced an equal in any of my friends. I hope you have been successfully restored from your fever. It will be fitting that this concern pertains to me in the future, as to how successfully you live your life and how firm your bodily health is, since I hold that benevolent mind of yours so dear in it. <unclear>...</unclear>
pages.22: ...with such willingness <unclear>...</unclear> the more so as you have offered yourself to friendship both more voluntarily and more nobly. And indeed, even when I count my friends abroad, you are rightly placed among the very first, and you seem to me not only to have inscribed your name into the catalog of those in me by your own initiative, but also to be performing the customary duties with both hand and spirit. Therefore, I deem that a great addition has been made to my accounts in your name; those more sacred ones, which I have decided to deposit not in the temple of Saturn, but in the citadel of Pallas. Therefore, because you indulge yourself so kindly in the duty of a friend toward me, you have earned a huge debt of gratitude from me. But see how far you have already stepped forward. For what will happen if I call upon you not by formal contract, but by spontaneous promise, when I have been beautifully secured both by the witness of the herald and by letters signed by you? And so that you cannot finally argue that you have been circumvented, you did not hesitate to promise the same thing again after a rather long interval; when those who bind themselves in this way, if they later begin to refuse the duty and make the agreements void, the constitutions of the laws permit one to reproach them with the shame of a repeated promise and the bond of a doubled obligation. Therefore, as I recognize and embrace that candor of your mind where you simply promise yourself to the service, I will truly have such regard for your kindness and generous humanity that I will demand the promise only thus far, and burden your faith: as far as you can
pages.23: cheerfully and without great difficulty fulfill it, and not even at the very first moment, but when I have collected the older debts, of which I still have many good and suitable ones, and whose judgment and dispute I can decide in my own forum if controversies arise from them. I have the calculation of this calendar of names so arranged that I think it is going well with me if I keep the bonds safe at home; as one who rejoices that my wealth is situated in it, so that I can boast for a long time that the day for many rich names has already passed, yet I would not want to sell, nor even if it had come, could I demand them without blushing or sadness. I hear that a most ample embassy is about to go there soon on a matter of both great and peaceful import. I would want it to have been decreed so auspiciously that peace might be confirmed from it for my age and yours, so that I might be able to test and act with you on a more equitable condition (if things turn out that way), by an action for a friend; which, however, anyone might wonder that no such action has been proclaimed by civil law, who certainly might think and note that an action for a partner is most broadly available in the Pandects of the law. But in that embassy, the Bishop of Paris will obtain either the first or second parts, as is the rumor; whether he was to make his way through this city, it was not yet certain when I wrote this, and
pages.24:
he was long among the courtiers, where he spends the greatest part of his time. He is a man learned among few, and endowed with the prudence of many things, an embracer and supporter of the lettered, and a student of your Erasmus, with whom I have a connection more of kinship than of the habit of life, for I dwell in the city. I think you will observe him dutifully, even by the recommendation of this matter, especially since, in fulfilling your duty (as I conjecture), it will often be either necessary or opportune for you to speak with ambassadors. Farewell, and return my greetings a hundredfold to Tunstall, Linacre, and More, who greeted me with your words or letters. Paris, Kalends of August.

->William Budé to Thomas More, Greetings.<-

A pair of British hounds was offered to me on your behalf by the youth Lupset, who is learned in both languages and (as I see) favored among the learned. Although this was a very grateful and pleasant gift to me, and even ample and magnificent in its outcome (for I hope I have produced a clear and happy munificence in gifting each of them), the pair of letters was nonetheless far more pleasant, in the reading of which I recognize and kiss your genius, as I once heard it spoken of and now have come to know it from your Utopia.

# The Portrait of the Concubine

<margin></margin>
Wan'e died at twenty; this is what is meant by a jade person crushed into dust. How sad!
</margin>

The pseudo-Han ruler Chen Youliang had a concubine named Zheng Wan'e, possessing a jade-like quality and icy beauty, the most beautiful of her time. She was also fond of literature and skilled in music and rhythm. The pseudo-Han ruler loved her dearly. She died at the age of twenty and was buried at Pipa Pavilion in Jiangzhou <note>Jiangzhou is now Jiujiang</note>. At the time of her burial, two serving maids were buried with her: one named Xichan and the other Jin'e. Since the concubine was noble and beautiful, even after entering the underworld, her spirit would sometimes appear in the light of day. Those who lived nearby would sometimes see her walking or hear her chanting and playing music, and none were without sorrow. In the early Hongwu years, Shen Shao of Wujiang, a young man who was also beautiful and handsome, studied poetry with Sa Tianxi <note>a master of poetry</note> and calligraphy with Guo Bojing <note>a master of calligraphy</note>, both of whom were admired by their contemporaries. Once, he harmonized with Tianxi's poems, "Passing Jiaxing" and "Inscribed on the scenery of Wuzhong." He wrote: "The Seven Marshes and Three Rivers connect for a hundred miles; willows and lotus blossoms reflect on the lake."

<column-break/>

<margin></margin>
The two poems about Wuzhong, although written according to the scenery, contain deep feelings and longing, and were not written carelessly.

## The Concubine Writes Her Grievance

The Concubine of the Han dynasty was Wang Qiang. She was chosen and entered the land of the Hu barbarians. Because of the pipa, she wrote of her grievances and died there, buried in the green grass of that land. During the Jin dynasty, in the Guiwei year of the Dading era, Wanyan Shouyi of the Shangjing clan was a refined scholar. He had business to go out <note>business</note> and saw the tomb of the concubine. He had feelings in his heart, so he folded his hands and sighed, saying, "Noble! Noble! How the treacherous official misled you! To be in the desert north and drink the bitter hatred of a thousand years, how painful!" After leaving, he left it to the past, and at dusk, he returned. On the road, he passed the concubine's tomb again. When he raised his eyes to look, he saw a magnificent house standing tall <note>tall</note>. The painted beams and carved pillars were not of human standards, and the red curtains and green screens were like those of a celestial residence in heaven. Shouyi was both surprised and suspicious. Before he could investigate, he saw a beautiful woman with teeth like fragrant blossoms and a graceful posture come out from inside, saying, "Young master, please lower yourself to have some tea."
