pages.52: to perfection because it is perfection, and disdain for deficiency because it is a potential deficiency. Since perfection and deficiency are not existent in themselves, but are conditions that attach to things—acting as if they were genera—they only exist within their subjects. Therefore, we must feel humility before every perfection. This is a primary proposition acknowledged by everyone. As to whether this or that is a perfection, that is something requiring demonstration. What is considered a perfection by one group may be a deficiency by another. This is evident to anyone who has examined different laws, opinions, and traditions. Furthermore, something may be a perfection in relation to one thing and a deficiency in relation to another. This is perfection by relation. Such things may be a perfection at one time and not at another. Yet this is not called "perfection," but rather it is given the name "the good." Goods are either synonymous with perfection or more general than it. Things that are perfections may be so by convention or by law. Written and unwritten opinions incorporate perfection by convention, and they exist as perfections by common reputation for everyone. What is by convention is diverse: what is a perfection for one group is not for another. Thus, those who are raised in a certain group have souls that feel humility for things that others disdain. Therefore, if something is a perfection in existence, and a person is among a group accustomed to their soul not feeling humility for that which is a perfection, then even if it becomes clear to him that the thing is a perfection, his soul will not feel humility toward it, nor will he honor it, nor will he see that he has attained anything. That knowledge, for that person, will be cast aside, and he will not heed it except for its necessity in speech. Just as sick people perceive bitter as sweet and see one as two, so too do the sick of soul see perfection as deficiency and deficiency as perfection. Just as there is no way for these sick people to sense the sweet as sweet until they are cured, so too the sick of soul cannot see the good as good until their souls are healthy. Just as among the sick are those who perceive the sweet as bitter and judge it to be bitter, and others who perceive it as bitter yet know it is sweet or judge that the affliction is in themselves—thus it is their duty, even if they do not disdain it, to discard it,
pages.53:
while the second does not merely disdain it. Neither of them understands the sweet as it truly is. Likewise, those who are sick of soul are afflicted with this very thing; they do not know the good, nor are they moved by the good. The spiritual form of things that are good does not move them at all. If they are moved, it is only to flee from those who follow the well-known paths—a state present in the six-hundredth year of the Hijra of Arab history—and all of this deposits illnesses in the souls. Therefore, they do not recognize the perfection that is free from potentiality; they only recognize rest. This is when it is purely in potentiality. Yearning is coupled with them, and they feel it because yearning is a pain. They recognize from perfection only what is coupled with motion, because pleasure is found therein. Thus, when perfection is attained and completed, they do not perceive it. Likewise, the healthy person does not perceive his health and does not see that he has been given something of value, whereas the sick perceive it and see it as the greatest of perceived things, as they were once healthy in potentiality. The perception of the perfection of rest—if it is permissible to call it rest, as it is a rest not accompanied by the potentiality of motion—is a very excellent matter. One must discipline oneself in sensing it until a firm habit is acquired. When this type becomes a habit, it has an immensely valuable effect on human existence. This is a matter that must be prioritized and placed before the discussion on ultimate happiness.

Just as we said regarding affection, we must examine and enumerate in how many ways it is said that the agent acts, and how we sense the appetitive part through action. The appetitive soul is affected, but we do not act through the appetitive soul; rather, we act through another part that is in act, because the appetitive is only in potentiality. It might be thought that the discussion regarding it was not completed in the "Generation and Corruption," just as it appeared in the [discussion of the] right side, for Aristotle only spoke of it in the "Meteorology" regarding what follows.
pages.54: the sea resulting from the elements. Therefore he said in "Book [15]" of the *Animals* that the discussion on the right side was not completed, and that every affected thing—nay, every moved thing—is something else in act. For if it were not something in act at all, potentiality would be something existing in act, and the primary matter would have necessity, and possibility would be self-subsistent and something existing in itself. This is evident to anyone who has practiced natural science even in the slightest. The moved is some substance, or rather, it is some body, for every moved thing is divisible; but that is movement by a middle way between that which is by essence and that which is by accident. Aristotle considers that to be by accident. For if it were by essence in some way, it would not be primary. The mover in potentiality is something by essence and primarily. It moves insofar as it is in potentiality until, if that which is in potentiality were found to be something separate from bodies, it would move itself and that thing would become either substance, quantity, quality, place, or another of the categories. However, that which is in potentiality must, by necessity—as we have said—be something in act. We have said it is something else in potentiality. It is therefore in act one of the categories, and in potentiality one of the categories. Let that which is in potentiality be P and that which is in act be A, and the relation between them be R. It is clear to anyone who has practiced natural science even in the slightest that that which is in potentiality, insofar as it is in potentiality, is not under a category, for everything that is under a category
pages.55: —whatever category it may be—is existing in act. The categories, therefore, are opposed by potentiality just as they are opposed by that which is in act in A, R. If they are under a single category in A, R, they are two opposing species. If they were two substances, they would have no name, but Aristotle and Abu Nasr <insert>al-Farabi</insert> might call them "contraries" when the need arises. However, contraries require a single subject in act. These two have no subject in act. If they are under one of the nine categories that are in potentiality, it exists necessarily as a substance, and it has a third existence by which it is a subject for A, R. In A, L, if they are under quantity, they are more similar to contraries of the first kind. Therefore, growth is said to be motion, and it is more of a change than what is said of rest. The two contrary species of quantity resemble each other in two ways: first, they are species accompanied by the privations of their homogeneous kinds, as found in the form of substances. Second, they have subjects existing in act capable of types of quantity. Substantial types do not have subjects; rather, they are the subjects. If one speaks of subjects for the mover, it is by way of <term>tashkik</term> <gloss>equivocality</gloss>. They differ from contraries in that types of quantity do not have two limited extremes that can be spoken of; the largest dog cannot have the size of an elephant, and the smallest cannot have the size of an ant. The types of size of substances are many and diverse, and their extremes are not limited unless it is in relation to them, in which case opposition occurs, just as it occurs to the extremes of temperament in quality. This has been summarized in "The Temperament"<note>Reference to a lost or specific manuscript of Ibn Bajjah on temperament.</note>. As for A, R, if they are qualities and are under one of the four genera of quality, they have a subject existing in act. Each of the types of that genus is accompanied by a privation homogeneous to it, and in them are two types that are extremes, not by relation but absolutely. It is impossible to find a type further
pages.56:
from that extreme in its opposition, and this is not the case in what is quantity. Let the smallest size be a dog, for example, as S, and the largest size as L. As for what exists in S or T, A, L. Every type of quantity that exists in a dog is closer to L than the size S is to D; there is no size further from S than D. If that existed, it would be smaller than L; let it be E. Thus size L is closer to S than E. So D is not an extreme in M unless M is a universal; it is a type of substance. The sizes S and K are not extremes by relation in reality and essentially to the first subject, which is in potentiality, namely matter, but rather it proceeds in its course because a part of its parts is matter. S and A are not extremes insofar as they are, or from the aspect of a relation that attached to them. They are not, therefore, extremes in existence. For if something has a condition insofar as it is that thing, it has it in existence. And what existed for it while it was in a certain state, and that thing existed for something else that does not have that state, it is not said that it is such in existence. Rather, if it has it in existence, it is by way of analogy. Also, if A, K were not under a single category, it is possible for them of necessity to be A, K; otherwise it would be arbitrary and not an existing thing. If that is not possible, then K and A are not one a subject for the other, except as it is said that the bright is in potentiality cold, because the bright necessitates the hot from the fire. The summary and enumeration of these kinds is easy for whoever desires it, and we suffice with this summary by way of definition.

All opposites, if they are in their subjects, necessitate of necessity the privations of their opposites within them. Privations are of kinds: among them is the privation of substance, the privation of quantity, and the privation of quality. I do not say that substance is privated absolutely, nor quantity. If something is not a quantity, such as intellect, then this is a negation and not a privation. Abu Nasr has <insert>[346 b]</insert> summarized the way in which it is called privation. Privation is attributed to the category in two ways: one is the negation of it, like our saying "The sky is neither heavy nor light"; the second is the removal of the negation of a type of it from
pages.57:
a subject in which that type could exist. This is more deserving of the name "privation" than the first. It is then said in other ways, the most deserving of all being the name "privation": the privation summarized in the opposites in the book *Categories*. This second kind we mentioned is what Abu Nasr <al-Farabi> mentions, saying: Aristotle considers the privation of every category within it: the privation of substance in the category of substance, and the privation of quantity in the category of quantity.

It is clear with the slightest reflection for anyone who has practiced natural science that primary matter cannot be stripped of some categories such that there is not one type of them within it. The first of these is substance. This was demonstrated in the first book of the *Physics*, for if it were stripped of it, the primary matter would be essentially formed. Next is quantity, for it is not a single substance—that is, it is not a body. How far removed is he who composes size from that which is indivisible! For if it were so, a substance would be found that has no quantity. This is impossible. It has been demonstrated in the beginning of the sixth book of the *Physics*, and is even clearer upon reflection. You must know that size is applied to the circular and the straight by <term>tashkik</term> <gloss>equivocality</gloss>, and that circular size is that which has a center. We have summarized this in our interpretation of the meanings of the seventh book of the *Physics*. Then, after that, in matter is the genus of passive quality: such as heat, cold, moisture, and dryness. Therefore, every material substance is a body. Body is applied by <term>tashkik</term> to that which moves circularly and to that which moves in a straight line; their matter is not one in species as he pictured it, but they correspond to the proportion of the forms. The matter that accepts motion in a straight line is matter in the primary sense. As for that which accepts circular motion, it is always a subject and is not matter or a material base. Rather, it is called matter and material base by way of analogy, just as this is called a subject by way of resemblance and analogy. The primary matter is not devoid of the genus of passive quality, and it cannot be stripped of it. Therefore, when Aristotle wants to indicate all of them, he says: "every tangible body." Likewise, the quality of quantity which is shape
pages.58:
and form. Likewise place. Likewise posture. Likewise time. Likewise relation. These nine categories are clear in their nature such that the primary matter is not stripped of them, although some are "whiter" than others.

As for action and affection, there has been doubt about them. But when their nature is examined, it appears it is so. As for the category of "having"<note>The category of *habitus* or possession.</note>, it exists in the soul; and there might be found in inanimate objects what is thought to be "having," although when its nature is examined it appears it is not under this category.

Likewise color: it may be thought that some bodies have no color, such as air and glass. More evident than this are tastes and smells, for their subject may not be free from all their types. However, even if that is so, these are not existing for substance by its essence primarily, but exist secondarily, after various existents under another category precede them in the subject. It is as if these, even if they are not types of those, are like types. An example of this: tastes, for even if they are not types of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness, they are not outside of them, because they are heat to which another thing has attached, by which that heat becomes a type of another genus, as occurred in the discussion of moving spheres: for the study of them is not geometric as applied to geometric study, but it falls under geometric study. We have summarized this in our treatises *On the Soul*.

What we have said has been summarized in another way, which is that every body is composed of form and subject. The subject of eternal bodies is specialized by the subject. The subject of that which generates and corrupts is called matter and material base and things similar to these. Every body
pages.59:
that corrupts is an element or composed of two or more elements. Every compound of things contains what belongs to those things. The things necessary for the elements are necessary for every material body. The things necessary for the elements from the categories are that they are substances, that they are possessors of size, that they are possessors of passive qualities, that they are possessors of postures and places, that they have time, that they are relations, and that they act and are affected. Every body contains these genera of categories of necessity. As for the rest of what exists for material bodies, they return to these—for example: roughness and aridity, hardness and softness, smoothness. As for the rest of what exists for material bodies, they return to these. An example of this <unclear>< . . . ></unclear> for they are kinds of moisture and dryness. For dryness, when an accident attaches to it, becomes roughness and aridity. And from moisture comes smoothness and softness. Aristotle has mentioned this in the second book of *Generation and Corruption*. Likewise taste and smell, for these two genera contain moisture and dryness as matter. As for colors, the discussion on them is another discussion. And when the matter is examined, it appears that this genus exists for the elements. The detailed investigation of this is in another place.

It has been shown in the seventh book of the *Physics* that change occurs only in sensible things. Let whoever wishes refer to that in Aristotle's discourse there, and what the commentators have said about it. Action and affection exist only in the primary qualities, and these are those through which generation and corruption occur, and they are the four, and they have been enumerated in many places. which ceaselessly darted their three-pointed tongues. Countless vipers emerged from his legs and thighs, coiling in various convolutions and spreading along the entire length of his body, with hisses so horrible they astonished the most intrepid. His mouth exhaled only flames; his eyes were burning coals; and his voice was more terrible than thunder. At times he bellowed like a bull, at other times he roared like a lion, and sometimes he barked like a dog. <margin><insert>CaG</insert></margin> The entire upper part of his body was bristled with feathers, and the lower part was covered in scales. Such was this Typhon, formidable even to the Gods, who dared to hurl rocks and mountains at Heaven while letting out frightful howls. The Gods were so terrified that, not believing themselves safe in Heaven, they fled to Egypt and sheltered themselves from the monster's pursuits by hiding in the form of various animals.

Attempts have been made to explain what ancient authors said of Typhon from moral, historical, and physical perspectives. The applications made have sometimes been quite successful, but it has never been possible for mythologists to explain his fable in its entirety within a single system. His marriage to Echidna made him the father of various monsters worthy of their origin, such as the Gorgon, Cerberus, the Hydra of Lerna, the Sphinx, the Eagle that devoured the unfortunate Prometheus, the Dragons guarding the Golden Fleece and the Garden of the Hesperides, etc.
pages.339:
Mythologists, in order to extricate themselves from the difficulty posed by this fable, which became one of the most obscure mysteries of mythology <note>original: "M. l'Abbé Banier Mythol. T. I. p. 468."</note>, decided to claim that the Greeks and Latins, ignorant of the origin of this fable, only obscured it further by attempting to transplant it, according to their custom, from the history of Egypt into their own. Based on traditions learned through their trade with the Egyptians, they turned Typhon into a monster as horrible as it was bizarre, whom the jealous Juno had caused to spring from the earth to avenge herself upon her rival, Latona.

What Diodorus <note>original: "Liv. I."</note> and Plutarch <note>original: "In Iside."</note> report of him is not to the taste of the Abbé Banier, undoubtedly because they are not favorable to his system in this regard. These two authors, he says <note>original: "T. I. p. 468."</note>, "did not fail, according to the genius of their nation, to mingle several ridiculous fictions in what they report; and besides, being inaccurate in chronology and having only a very confused knowledge of the early histories of the world renewed after the Deluge, among which is undoubtedly the one I am explaining (that of Typhon), they are guides that should only be followed with great caution." Although the Abbé Banier is right to think these authors were not versed in the substance of the history of Typhon, it is nonetheless true that they had collected what they
pages.340: say of him from the tradition preserved among the Egyptians. If they mingled some circumstances into it to adapt it to the fables of their own country, they preserved the foundation, which is equally fabulous. It is in vain that Gerard Vossius <note>original: "De Idol. l. 1, 26."</note> claims that Og, King of Bashan, is the same as Typhon, based on the resemblance of the two names; for, he says, that of Typhon comes from <term>τύφω</term> <gloss>to burn, to inflame</gloss>, and that of Og signifies <term>ussit</term> <gloss>burned</gloss> or <term>ustulavit</term> <gloss>scorched</gloss>. It is in vain that M. Huet <note>original: "Demonst. Ev. prop. 4."</note> makes him the legislator of the Hebrews, who became odious to the Egyptians through the loss of their firstborn sons. The Abbé Sevin is no more correct to put him in the place of Cush, nor the Abbé Banier in that of Sebon, in this instance following the sentiment of Plutarch, who relies on the authority of Manethon. It would not be possible to reconcile Plutarch with himself. Bochart succeeded better <note>original: "Chan."</note> than all the authors above by thinking that Typhon is the same as Enceladus; but he guessed without knowing why, since he was ignorant of the reason that led the poets to name them interchangeably for one another, and to have them both perish in the same manner. The poets, much better than the historians, have preserved for us the true basis of the fables and, strictly speaking, have disfigured them less than the historians, because they were content to report them—embellishing them at times, it is true, but without bothering to discuss why, how, and
pages.341:
in what time these things could have taken place; whereas the historians, seeking to adapt them to history, suppressed features, mingled their own conjectures, and sometimes substituted other names, etc.

But finally, what to conclude from so many different opinions? That we must seek what we ought to think of Typhon in the traits upon which historians, poets, and mythologists agree, or in which they differ little. Poets and mythologists all agree that Typhon was cast beneath Mount Etna, and the ancients who did not place his tomb there chose for this purpose sulfurous places known for subterranean fires, such as in Campania or near Mount Vesuvius, as Diodorus claims <note>original: "L. 4."</note>, or in the Phlegraean Fields, as Strabon recounts <note>original: "L. 5."</note>, or in a place in Asia where, according to Pausanias <note>original: "In Arcad."</note>, water sometimes issues from the earth, and at other times fire. In a word, in all the mountains and all other places where there were sulfurous exhalations. The Egyptians finally related that he had been struck by lightning and had perished in a whirlwind of fire.

Let us compare all this with some circumstances of Typhon's life, and unless one wishes to stubbornly close one's eyes to the light, one will be forced to admit that the entire history of this supposed Monster is but an allegory, which is part of that which the priests
pages.342:
of Egypt, or Hermes himself, had invented to veil the <term>Art sacerdotal</term> <gloss>priestly art</gloss>. Since, according to the Abbé Banier himself <note>original: "Mythol. T. I. p. 478."</note>, the Greek and Latin poets and historians have preserved for us, among their most absurd fables, the traditions of Egypt, it is to these primitive traditions that we must hold. They teach us that Typhon was the brother of Osiris; that he persecuted him even to the point of causing him to die in the manner we have mentioned; that he was subsequently vanquished by Isis, aided by Horus; and that he finally perished by fire. Historians also report that the Egyptians held the sea in abomination because they believed it was Typhon himself, and they called it the <term>scum</term> or <term>saliva of Typhon</term> <note>original: "Kirch. Obelif. Pamph. p. 155."</note>, names they also gave to sea salt. Pythagoras, instructed by the Egyptians, said that the sea was a tear of Saturn. Their reason for this was that the sea, according to them, was a principle of corruption, since the Nile, which provided them with so many goods, was corrupted by its mixture with it. These traditions also teach us that Typhon caused Horus to perish in the sea, into which he cast him, and that Isis, his mother, resurrected him after drawing him out.

We have said that Osiris was the igneous, sweet, and generative principle that Nature employs in the formation of mixtures; and that Isis was its radical moisture. For one must not confuse the two, since they differ from one another like
pages.343:
smoke and flame, light and air, sulfur and mercury. Radical moisture is, in mixtures, the seat and food of the innate heat, or natural and celestial fire, and becomes like the bond that unites it with the elemental body. This igneous virtue is like the form and soul of the mixture. This is why it performs the office of the male, and the radical moisture performs, as a moist element, the function of the female. They are therefore like brother and sister, and their union constitutes the base of the mixture. But these mixtures are not composed of radical moisture alone; in their formation, homogeneous, impure, and terrestrial parts join with it to complete the body of the mixture. And these gross and terrestrial impurities are the principle of its corruption, because of their combustible, acrid, and corrosive sulfur, which acts ceaselessly upon the pure and incombustible sulfur. These two sulfurs, or fires, are therefore two brothers, but enemy brothers; and by the daily destruction of individuals, one has reason to be convinced that the impure prevails over the pure. These are the two good and evil principles of which we have spoken in the first and second chapters of this book.

This being established, it is not difficult to conceive why they made Typhon a frightful monster, always disposed to do evil, and who even had the audacity to make war upon the Gods. Metals abound in this impure and combustible sulfur, which gnaws them by turning them into rust, each in its own species. The Gods had given their names to the metals; and this is why
pages.344:
Herodotus <note>original: "In Euterpe."</note> says that the Egyptians counted at first only eight great Gods, that is to say, the seven metals and the principle of which they were composed. Typhon was born of the earth, but of the gross earth, being the principle of corruption. He was the cause of Osiris's death, because corruption occurs only through the solution we explained while speaking of the death of this Prince. The feathers that covered the upper part of Typhon's body and his height, which carried his head to the clouds, indicate his volatility and his sublimation into vapors. His thighs, his legs covered with scales, and the serpents that emerge from them on all sides are the symbol of his corrupting and putrefactive aqueousness. The fire he casts from his mouth marks his corrosive combustibility and designates his pretended brotherhood with Osiris, because the latter is a hidden, natural, and vivifying fire, while the other is a tyrannical and destructive fire. This is why d'Espagnet calls him the tyrant of Nature and the fratricide of natural fire, which suits Typhon perfectly. Among philosophers, serpents are the ordinary hieroglyph for dissolution and putrefaction; thus, it is agreed that Typhon does not differ at all from the serpent Python, killed by Apollo. It is also known that Apollo and Horus were taken for the same God.

This Monster was not content with having caused the death of his brother Osiris; he also cast his nephew Horus into the sea, after seizing him.
pages.345: through the aid of a Queen of Ethiopia. One could not designate more clearly the resolution into water of the Philosophical Horus or Apollo than by saying he was cast into the sea; the blackness, which is the mark of perfect solution and of the putrefaction called death by the Adepts, is seen in this Queen of Ethiopia. This corrupted and putrefied matter is precisely that scum or saliva of Typhon into which Horus was cast and submerged. It is truly a tear of Saturn, since the black color is the Philosophical Saturn. Isis finally resurrected Horus; that is to say, the Philosophical Apollo, after having been dissolved, putrefied, and become black, passed from blackness to whiteness, called resurrection and life in the Hermetic style. The father and mother then reunited to fight Typhon, or corruption, and after vanquishing him, they reigned gloriously—first the mother or Isis, that is to say, the whiteness, and after her, Horus her son, or the redness. Without resorting to so many explanations, the very tombs supposed to belong to Typhon make us understand what was thought of this Monster, father of so many others, which we will explain in the chapters concerning them. Some say that Typhon cast himself into a marsh where he perished; others that he was struck by lightning by Jupiter and that he perished by fire. These two kinds of death are quite different; and only Hermetic Chemistry can resolve this contradiction. ...ugly, and *ḥasanan wajh ab*, and *ḥasan ab*, and *ḥasan wajh ab*. [That] <insert>abstract</insert>, coordinate on "added," meaning "I saw the man, the *ḥasan wajh*," but it is ugly, and *al-ḥasan wajhuhu*, and the other as will come, and "I saw a man *ḥasanan wajhuhu*", but it is ugly, and *ḥasanan wajhuhu*, and *ḥasan wajh*, <insert>and the other, the two complete, in the state of its being with AL will come until tomorrow</insert>. <insert>And from the she-camel to us to it</insert>, so it does not reach the *ḥasan wajh* or *wajh abīhi* or *wajh* or *wajh ab*. And it only <insert>enters</insert> what was mentioned, <insert>so it is in the sentence</insert>. <insert>And it was named</insert>. And that has already preceded as a full explanation, clarifying the meaning in the *ḥasan* <gloss>beauty</gloss> and the *ḍaʿf* <gloss>weakness</gloss> and the *qubḥ* <gloss>ugliness</gloss>, and praise be to God here. <insert>By the Prophet</insert> and to Him [belongs] from him much, other than "How can you disbelieve in God, and you were dead, so He gave you life?" Glory to God, for the dead is he who is not saved, and family for the gods, then to it, to it, and death for the youth is the truth, two descriptions [to which] he pointed by his saying <insert>"O youth, depart"</insert> [in the] state...

pages.74:
...its being by this indefinite if you wanted wonder, and bring with *afʿal*, and it is a predicate in the form of the imperative before its agent, made genitive by a redundant *bāʾ*, necessary. And "tālū afʿal," meaning what is after it, set in the accusative as an object for the first of the verbs of wonder, as preceded, as it is *jalīlan* <gloss>great</gloss>, and *aṣdiq bihima* <gloss>make them truthful</gloss>, and the deletion of what you wondered from and the keeping of the form of wonder is permitted if the meaning is correct upon deletion and is not confused, as His saying, the Almighty: *"asmaʿ bihim wa-abṣir"* <gloss>hear them and see</gloss>. And the saying of Ali, may God be pleased with him: "May God reward on my behalf... by His bounty, Rabiʿah, with good, how chaste and noble [they are]." And in both verbs, *afʿil* and *afʿil bihi*, [they] were advanced, necessary, preventing inflection in each of all of the void, absolutely, meaning certainly and carried out. And they are the equivalent of *laysa* and *ʿasā* and *hab* and *niʿma* and *biʾsa*. And they are from a verb with three letters, contrary to *dahraja* and *inṭalaqa* and *iʿtada* and *istakhraja* and *iḥmarra* and *iḥmārra*, contrary to *madḥa*, contrary to *niʿma* and *biʾsa*...

<column-break/>

...accepting preference <gloss>faḍl</gloss>, meaning increase, like *ʿalama* <gloss>to know</gloss> and *ḥasana* <gloss>to be good</gloss>, contrary to *ʿamāta*, contrary to *kāna* and *kāda*, other than a verb of negation, negated, *kāna* contrary to other than what is wondered by the medicine, and *mā ḍaraba Zaydan*, and other than a verb of a description [that] parallels *ashal* in its being on *faʿlān* of the description that parallels [it], like *suwwida* and *ʿuwira*, and other than a verb walking the path of *fuʿila* in its being constructed for the passive, contrary to the walker like *ḍuriba*, and *niʿma* suffices with a thing, what was intransitive to it, like *khabutha* <gloss>to be foul</gloss> with your need. So it is said *mā aghnāhu* and *ashadduhu* and *asharruhuma* as the majority. And the majority relates in wonder to some of the conditions, [excluding] what was more than three, or a description on *afʿal*, or defective like *mā ashaddu dahrajah* and *jarīyah*, and *ashaddu* by its being future, and likewise if it was negated or constructed for the passive, like *niʿma madḥan*, both are interpreted like *mā akthara*...

pages.75:
...how much is your not saying them, and make great by other than it. And like the looker to what does not accept preference, by *mā anjaḥa* <gloss>how successful</gloss> by his death, and he was afflicted by his death. And Ibn Hisham said: It is not believed absolutely. And the infinitive of the verbs of transmission lacking the conditions, after, meaning whiteness, intensity of accusative, and after *afʿal*, meaning *ashaddu*, by a *jarr* with the *bāʾ*, it is necessary [for] frequency as preceded. And with the *bāʾ*, it is necessary, meaning the separation, judge for other than what was mentioned, like their saying *mā adhraʿahā* <gloss>how skillful she is</gloss> from a woman, *dhirāʿ* <gloss>skillful/light-handed</gloss>, light of hand in spinning, and *mā aḥfarahu* from *iḥtaḍarahu*, and *mā aʿsāhu* and *ʿasā bihi* from *ʿasā*, and *mā aḥmaqa-hu* from *ḥamuqa* so he is *aḥmaq* <gloss>foolish</gloss>. So hear that and do not judge upon what from it was narrated, meaning reported from the Arabs, upon what resembles it. And the detail of this chapter is to advance its object over it, [so it becomes] a connection, necessary, without dispute in both of them. And separating from the object by a *ẓarf* or by a preposition used in poetry and prose, like his saying: "And the prophet of the Muslims said, 'Advance,' the duty of the builders..."

<column-break/>

...is to be advanced. And the saying of Jarir: "And the sons of Maʿdi Karib, how beautiful in the satire." And for us, and the one departing in *AL*, preference—is it permitted or not? It fell, so al-Jurmi and a group went to the permission, and al-Akhfash and al-Mubarrad to the prohibition. This is a chapter on *niʿma* and *biʾsa* and what runs their course in praise and blame, from *ḥabbadhā* and *sāʾa* and the like. Both are two verbs not inflected, *niʿma* and *biʾsa*, for the entry of the silent *tāʾ* upon them in all the dialects and the connection of the pronoun of the nominative to them in a dialect narrated by al-Kisa'i. And the Kufans went, according to what the companions narrated about them in the issues of disagreement, to that both are nouns. And Ibn ʿUsfur said: No one disagreed that both are verbs, and the disagreement is after attributing them to the agent. So the Basrans say *niʿma al-rajul* and *biʾsa al-rajul* are two sentences, two verbs, and al-Kisa'i [says] two nouns narrated in the position of *taʾabbaṭa*...

pages.15:
<header>of the Baron of Trenck.</header>
<sig>A 4</sig>

me, he should have made room for me. He pushed me back with such vehemence that I seized my torch with both hands and smashed it to pieces on his head inside the church. After this, I had to avoid both my order and the school, and learn at home.
We thus traveled to the command that my father had received, which is the <term>Grenz-Festung</term> <gloss>border fortress</gloss> Brod on the Sava river. I and my brothers, however, were sent <term>ad Studia</term> <gloss>to studies</gloss> to the Jesuits in Požega, though against my desire, from where we always returned home during the <term>Vacanzen</term> <gloss>vacation periods</gloss>.

In the year 1725, I had to endure the following mortal danger once again: My father was visited by a certain Colonel of Engineers, Count C***, and his family as neighbors. As there was a pretty young girl in his suite with whom my eldest brother fell in love, we all three decided to escort her back, which we did. But as we were driving back the next day from Djakovo, where we stayed overnight, it happened that the first wheel struck a log, and we all fell out of the carriage. My eldest brother, however, who was steering the horses instead of the coachman, fell under the horses and was crushed so severely that
pages.16:
<header>Life and Deeds</header>
<note>A small decorative flourish flanks the word "und" in the header.</note>

he died two hours later in the forest on the way, after he had given the last sign of life and farewell to my father, who had received news of it and arrived just in time for this misfortune, with open eyes, but spoke no more words, and passed away immediately thereafter.

My grandmother, who was a Countess von Witt and who loved us all tenderly, was so shocked and saddened by this fatal case that she also died of it six weeks later. A similar fate had to befall my mother soon after, namely in the year 1726. Of all these deaths, none saddened me more than that of my dear brother, whom I, for lack of a clergyman, also prepared well for death, with the exception of confession and communion. My old father, however, was inconsolable over three such painful losses, just as he never proceeded to <term>ad vota secunda</term> <gloss>second marriage vows</gloss>. Meanwhile, he still kept both of us brothers studying, though not away from home; which was once again the cause for me to escape a mortal danger. For when once on the Sava river, which flowed hard by our house, during the wintertime, when the marshes were frozen and the ice was floating on the river with a multitude of ducks, I took a small boat,
pages.17:
<header>of the Baron of Trenck.</header>
<sig>A 5</sig>

with which I could steer perfectly, and rowed with my musket through the ice, which I avoided quite skillfully, toward the ducks. I shot three of them dead and shot the wing off one. As I then chased after the wounded duck and forgot the danger in which I was, an ice floe shoved me against another similar large one so violently that I quite accidentally sat upon the other floes and saw my boat smashed to pieces and drifting away. Who would have thought that I would escape this time, too? My father and brother, together with good friends, threw their hands over their heads and called to me that I should commend myself to God, which I also did. I floated downstream for nearly half a mile, and the ice floe, because there was a narrow passage there, wedged itself, and since it was not possible due to the amount of ice to come to my aid with a ship, over 300 people ran along to help with my spectacle. The ice floe had hardly stopped when a <term>Bandur</term> <gloss>member of the Pandur irregular infantry</gloss>, with a rope in his hand, out of love for me, risked himself to reach me and led me safely out of my danger. I remained unpunished by my father here as well.

Several weeks after this danger, however, I was in a boat with my
pages.18:
<header>Life and Deeds</header>

brother, on a duck hunt. And as the boatman steered us both close to the ducks, and my brother, who was kneeling in front of me in the boat, did not want to shoot but wanted to be even closer, I took the musket and shot behind him. I hit the ducks, but at the same time, I shot the clothing off my brother from the right side down to the skin, and two shots of lead into his arm. Had I held my finger a finger's breadth lower, I would have shot his arm off completely. After this, I received heavy blows from my father, and my brother, as the new battalions were raised, became an ensign under Wallis.

Shortly thereafter, namely on July 10, 1727, the now deceased Hungarian Palatine, Count Nicolaus Pálffy, took me into his regiment as an ensign. From this time on, my luck began to contend with misfortune, and misfortune with luck, <term>vice versa</term> <gloss>the other way around</gloss>, as it were. The first misfortune was that, as my father sent me to Osijek to equip myself there, I became so deathly ill with a raging fever that my father sent the money <term>pro funeribus</term> <gloss>for the funeral</gloss> through the then-commissary in Osijek, our secretary at the time, Herr von Hess, and the hussars to accompany my body to Djakovo, where I lay sick. I was, however, soon cured through the help of good medicine,
pages.19:
<header>of the Baron of Trenck.</header>

and thus had to travel to Belgrade to my regiment. I had hardly been in Belgrade for four months when I already had a <term>Rencontre</term> <gloss>duel/encounter</gloss> with an ensign of the regiment, who at first made me yield, but ultimately had to settle with a strike across the nose and skull, then four strikes to the hand. I also received three strikes to the hand, and the hilt of my Parisian sword was hewn off by this strong man, although I was still, so to speak, a child, so that it remained lying on my wounded hand. The same year, I had another affair with a Silesian volunteer, von Gersdorff, whom I wounded through the hand.

In the year 1728, I had an affair with a certain Count Paradiso, from whom I had won 380 florins, and he did not want to pay them to me, over which I insulted him, and he struck at me with his hand, though he only touched my head by a lock of hair. I drew my sword, but he jumped out of the coffee house, where there were about 30 officers, and as I made my way through the officers with my sword in hand and wanted to go out the door, he lunged at me outside the door. I wanted to parry him with my left arm and received a thrust through it; this, however, did not hinder me from attacking him, and
pages.20:
<header>Life and Deeds</header>

and he, or I, would certainly have reached the <term>Extremum</term> <gloss>the end/death</gloss> if about 6 officers had not thrown themselves upon me and prevented the affair in this manner. I subsequently defamed him again and have never been able to find out where he went, as I have still not been paid by him to this day. Perhaps, when this comes before his eyes, he will report himself. I had two more small skirmishes this year, but they ended without injury, so I will make no further mention of them.

In the year 1729, however, I had another affair with the auditor of Prince Alexander of Württemberg's regiment, then stationed in Belgrade, by the name of Beyer, whom I dispatched with two thrusts into the right side, for which he had to be treated for six weeks. It then happened that my battalion, in which I was, had to march to Osijek, and we arrived there in the month of October of that year. Here I must recall that I have hitherto traveled through all of Sicily, the Neapolitan, Apulian, Roman, Venetian, Triestine, Carniolan, Styrian, Lika, Croatian, Slavonian, Serbian, Austrian, Syrmian, Hungarian lands, and a part of Bosnia with my father.
pages.21:
<header>of the Baron of Trenck.</header>

I had hardly arrived in Osijek when I again, although I had never given any cause for it, had an affair with my own cousin, named Tillier, with whom I brawled twice and wounded both times.

In the year 1730, however, I fought again with Baron F***, whom I also wounded through the arm. And although I had been fond of seeing pretty girls since 1727, I was still not skilled enough for intrigues; rather, I satisfied my desire with everything young that came before my eyes without giving myself any trouble. In this year, however, I fell in love with a certain young lady of good lineage. But since the father and mother, in whose house she was, kept a very close watch on her, I had to content myself initially only with the pleasure that I would pass by her window at night and clear my throat sharply—this was the signal—whereupon she would immediately come running to the window and speak a few words with me to console both of us. This <term>Rendez vous</term> <gloss>meeting</gloss> I frequented very diligently and constantly; in such a way that I wished it were always night, just to be able to talk to my beautiful young lady, until I finally managed to find an opportunity for her to let me into her bedroom. What could be more foolish than to see
pages.22:
<header>Life and Deeds</header>

us two lovers? Out of love, I could no longer speak, but only kissed her hands constantly and pressed her to me: she, however, as a young lady of 14 years at the time, smiled. I was not bold enough to involve myself further in love, and so I left my young lady. As great as the love of this person was for me, just as great was the <term>Estim</term> <gloss>esteem</gloss> she bore for me, since I gave her no cause to commit an excess. I was thus loved by her in such a way that I could always come to my beauty at night whenever I wanted. At every <term>Rendez-vous</term> <gloss>meeting</gloss>, I chatted so much to her of love and held her beauty and coldness before her that, at the seventh meeting, she said to me, quite enraptured (which I shall remember for the rest of my life): "Baron Trenck! I am no longer in a state to resist your love; do with me what you will, yet save my honor." Upon this, she fell into my arms, quite enraptured and with eyes full of tears. I kissed her and she me, with which we contented ourselves, whereas certainly another more indiscreet lover than I—who always firmly imprinted the motto upon himself in such cases: *le respect arrête mes désirs* <gloss>respect halts my desires</gloss>—would not have let it rest at that. I believed now that I would be happy for once

and forty-nine, in which the venerable father Fr. Luis de Villalpando was elected custodian, exactly one year after the Indians had tried to burn him and his companion in Maní. The definitors were the same father custodian as first, father Fr. Lorenzo de Bienvenida as second, father Fr. Francisco Navarro as third, and father Fr. Miguel de Vera as fourth. By this same table, the convent of the city of Mérida already seems to have a name, its guardian elected being the aforementioned father Fr. Juan de la Puerta: that of Campeche, its guardian being father Fr. Diego de Bejar: that of Maní, guardian being father Fr. Juan de Albalate; and that of Cunkal, guardian being the venerable father custodian; and that of Ytzamal, guardian being the definitor father Fr. Lorenzo de Bienvenida. Not only are the guardians assigned in this capitular table, but also the companions who were to live with them in each convent: a custom that was observed in this province until the provincial chapter held in the year 1603, since when it seems to have been left to the discretion of the reverend provincial fathers to assign the companions and dwellers of each convent, according to the need that arises in it. The very R. Father Fr. Francisco de Bustamante presided over the chapter, as appears from the table signed with his name and sealed with the seal of his office of Commissary General. This was like the birth of this holy province of San José of Yucatan, for which reason I have written it with such singularity, in which with the five convents that have been named, it remained in the form of a custody, subject while it was such to that of Mexico.

Although Father Fr. Juan de la Puerta remained in the chapter elected as guardian of the convent of the city of Mérida, since the religious were still so few for the great number of towns that were in Yucatan, as for the entire province of Valladolid, so populous and with such a crowd of people, no convent foundation had been able to be established, it was discussed that a religious of the province should go as procurator to Spain, representing the need that existed for them, and it seems that they agreed that the most appropriate person for a matter

of such importance was Father Fr. Juan de la Puerta.
The Adelantado was of the same opinion as the religious, and thus he gave him letters for the emperor and the Royal Council of the Indies, in which he signified the great fruit that was being produced in the conversion of these Indians and the urgent need they had for help from ministers.
Father Fr. Juan de la Puerta received the dispatches that the province and the Adelantado gave him, and granting him Father Fr. Angel Maldonado as his companion, he went to Mexico, where the very R. Father Commissary General, who had great satisfaction with his virtue and prudence, confirmed to him the office of procurator that the province had given him, and entrusted other businesses, for which he gave him instructions and sufficient papers, with which he went to Spain in the Fleet of the following year of 1550. I have not found the result of this trip, I only think that this religious was later elected bishop of this bishopric, as was said in the fourth book.

Nothing notable had happened regarding the secular state until this time: but as in the new laws, which had been given for these kingdoms, it was ordered that no governor or royal official should hold Indians in <term>encomienda</term> <gloss>trusteeship/grant of indigenous labor</gloss>, and the Adelantado, as a conqueror, retained his, a new order came so that they would be removed from him. Father Lizana says that this year of forty-nine, the <term>licenciado</term> <gloss>graduate/lawyer</gloss> Herrera came from Spain (with Father Albalate, who brought the religious) assigned as judge of the <term>real audiencia</term> <gloss>royal high court</gloss> of Mexico, and that he visited this land and took the Adelantado's <term>residencia</term> <gloss>official judicial review of an officeholder</gloss>. I am persuaded that the one who took his residence was the <term>licenciado</term> Santillan, a judge who resided in the same <term>audiencia</term>, because in a royal provision of the sixteenth day of the month of June of the same year of fifteen hundred and forty-nine, he is given faculty to

pages.453:
<header>HISTORY OF YUCATAN. 436</header>

come to Yucatan, to remove the Indians he held, and to investigate other excesses that the Adelantado was said to have committed during the time of his government, so if the other gentleman were already taking his residency, it seems there would have been no need for this new commission. In it, it is referred as a preamble that in fraud of the new laws, many Indians were held in <term>encomienda</term> in the names of the wives, sons, and daughters of the governors and royal officials, with which they enjoyed the Indians as if said prohibition of laws did not exist; descending to the singular motive of this commission, it is said:

"And we are informed that although it was ordered by our said <term>real audiencia</term> that the said Indians be taken from the wife, sons, and daughters of said Adelantado Montejo, it had not been done nor fulfilled: rather they say that the greater part of that land is in the said Adelantado Montejo and in his wife, and in D. Francisco de Montejo, and in his wife, and in a stepson of his, the son of his wife, and for this, many frauds and cavils have been made. Especially they say that having given a provision so that the Indians be taken from said Adelantado and his sons and daughters, he made an arrangement with the one who carried it to hand it over to him so that it could not be used, and another provision he carried in which it was ordered that they should not interfere in the jurisdiction of the town of La Victoria of the Rio de Grijalva in order to collect from the Indians, whom they ordered to be removed, all the tributes for a year in advance, belonging to us. And the title with which he had made the said tributes be collected had been by saying that he had given them to a nephew of his, and for this, he had shown certificates of deposit and the date of them from time past. And that to do the above, he had caused the provisions to be detained. And that the fraud, which said governor did to us and our royal treasury, having been seen by an ordinary mayor of said town of La Victoria: he and a councilman, who was called Alonso Bazan, as our officials, took the person who was collecting the tributes for the said Adelantado, and what from

<summary>The text details the formal grievances against the Adelantado Montejo, alleging that he used fraud to circumvent the new laws regarding the holding of indigenous tributes and officials.</summary>
<keywords>Adelantado Montejo, fraud, new laws, tributes, La Victoria, royal treasury</keywords>
pages.454:
<header>BOOK FIVE. 437</header>

them had proceeded, and put it in the chest with three keys. And that known by the Adelantado, he went to said town with an armed force, after the said provision had been notified to him, so that he would not be judged, and he captured said mayor and councilman and took them prisoner to Yucatan. And he newly created other officials, his own servants, to have charge of our treasury, and he procured that they should hold him as governor in it, in order to avenge himself on the officials and give the Indians he held to persons of said town, paying for them; which he did, as he sold some native Indians for interests they gave him. And that we are likewise informed that the said Adelantado Montejo in Champoton is making a sugar mill and for it has taken, and takes, the land from the Indians of that province, and took their crops away, said towns being mine, it being convenient to unload the said taxpayers by occupying them in gainful businesses. And that above all the aforementioned, the said Adelantado has not given any <term>repartimiento</term> <gloss>allotment of indigenous labor</gloss> to any conqueror, but to all his relatives and wives and children, to stepchildren and grandchildren: they say not only to the legitimate ones, but to the bastards. And they say that he made the Indians of Champoton and Campeche go to war and make slaves, and so they say that many of them were made, likewise as women, against our laws made by us, and that they are sold against all reason and justice, which is a cause for the said provinces to be depopulated. And that the said Adelantado, not content with all the aforementioned things, makes houses, estates, and businesses in said provinces with our Indians: not being able to, nor should he do it, and fatiguing them and making them work excessively. And that likewise other persons have done and committed in said provinces many and grave crimes worthy of prison and punishment, to which it was convenient to provide and remedy as an important thing."

Such was the report that had been made to the Emperor in the Royal Council of the Indies of what had happened in Yucatan; but it seems to have been excessive, for regarding what is said in it about the Adelantado not having entrusted Indians to any conqueror,

<summary>This page recounts specific allegations against the Adelantado, including the illegal enslavement of indigenous people, forced labor on personal projects, and the monopolization of indigenous labor for his own family.</summary>

pages.455:
<header>HISTORY OF YUCATAN. 438</header>

but to his relatives, there are still today many certificates of deposit that were exhibited as soon as they finished subduing the land, which his descendants observe originally for greater qualification of their merits in the conquest. Regarding making slaves of the Indians and selling them, what was happening has already been said and is written in the third book. But as there is never a lack of someone who complains (or it is very rare) about those who govern, it had happened at present, and joining the retention of the Indians, which the Adelantado enjoyed as a conqueror, having to be removed from him by the general laws, and the Emperor wishing to certify the truth, this royal provision was dispatched, which by its context seems to be of residency, and in it, immediately to the referred report, it is said:

"And seen by those of our Council of the Indies, wishing to provide for it, trusting in you that you are such a person that you will keep our service and the right to each one of the parties, and that with all care and diligence you will try to understand what is commanded and committed to you by us: it is our grace and will to entrust and commit it to you, and by the present, we entrust and commit it to you. For we command you that as soon as you see this, you go with the rod of our royal justice to the said provinces of Yucatan, Cozumél, and above all things, remove the Indians that said Adelantado Montejo holds, and his wife and children, and our officials of the said provinces: except the male children to whom such Indians were entrusted, being already married and living on their own at the time they were entrusted to them. The residency of the Adelantado having been published, the administration of justice and government of Yucatan remained with the judge who was acting it, in whose time it happened that some black slaves of the Spaniards fled to the mountains, and gathered a troop of up to twenty or more of those who were uprising; they entered some Indian towns, to whom they did much evil and harm, taking from them what they could and committing other crimes that required prompt remedy. So that this would have the necessary end, the judge appointed Alonso Rosado, a conqueror, as head and leader of the Spaniards, so they might search for them and bring them prisoners, and if they did not surrender for arrest, they should use the final remedy by shooting them or killing them in any way possible. Alonso Rosado went out with his people, and suffering some hardships through the mountains, he spotted the fugitive blacks, who, finding themselves without arms and surrounded by Spaniards who had them, surrendered and were taken prisoners to the city of Mérida. The imprisonment of these blacks was considered a considerable service in this land; because in addition to the damages that were avoided with it, a rumor that was already circulating was calmed, that some Indians were attempting to rebel against the Spaniards, with the heat and encouragement those slaves gave them, fearful that they would fall into the hands of justice and be punished, as they were later.

It also happened that many Indians from the southern part of this province, which they call the Sierra, had retired to the interior of the land (which lies between this and that of Guatemala) fleeing from communication with the Spaniards and from Christian teaching. Considering the great disservice that was being done to God and the King with this flight, the judge ordered Captain Francisco de Montejo, who, as was said, was [a captain] of the conquest, to enter through those uninhabited lands and try to attract them to the towns of their nature. That captain went out with people from the city and walked through the mountains and villages, gathering many Indians with peaceful means. Some were more than seventy leagues from the city and forty from the nearest settlement. Among these distant ones, the captain learned of a troop of Indians gathered together, and not being able to go, he entrusted it to Alonso Rosado, one of those who went with him and who had captured the blacks earlier, giving him some Spaniards to go with him. They found the Indians and persuaded them in such a way that they yielded in peace and he brought them to the captain. A very considerable number of Indians was gathered with this departure, which was distributed to the towns of their nature, with which this land of Yucatan remained quiet for then. Both one thing and the other appear in the authentic proofs that were made and I have read.

It is said that the time of the residency lasted three months, in which the judge ordered some things for the utility of the Indians and their good treatment and for the increase of their Christianity. He reformed others regarding the Spaniards, who, as in newly founded republics

Pass before the people and take with you some of the elders of Israel and your staff, with which you struck the river, take in your hand and go. And Moses did so before the eyes of the elders of Israel. And he called the name of the place <term>Massah</term> <gloss>Testing</gloss> and <term>Meribah</term> <gloss>Contention</gloss> because of the contention of the children of Israel and their testing the Lord, saying, "Is the Lord among us or not?" Then <term>Amalek</term> <gloss>an enemy nation</gloss> came and fought with Israel in <term>Rephidim</term> <gloss>a location</gloss>. And Moses said to <term>Joshua</term> <gloss>a leader/disciple of Moses</gloss>, "Choose men for us and go out, fight against Amalek tomorrow; I will stand on the top of the hill with the staff of God in my hand." And Joshua did as Moses said to him, to fight against Amalek, and Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill. And it was when Moses lifted his hand, Israel prevailed, and when he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed. But Moses' hands were heavy; so they took a stone and put it under him, and he sat on it, and Aaron and Hur supported his hands, one on one side and one on the other, and his hands were steady until the going down of the sun. And Joshua weakened Amalek and his people by the edge of the sword. And the Lord said to Moses, "Write this as a memorial in a book and put it in the ears of Joshua, for I will surely blot out the memory of Amalek from under the heavens." And Moses built an altar and called its name "The Lord is My Banner." And he said, "Because the hand is upon the throne of the Lord, war with the Lord against Amalek from generation to generation."

<margin>Rabbi Hiyya opened: "The angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear Him, and He delivers them." ### And Amalek came.
Rabbi Judah: "The beginning of the nations is Amalek." And is it that the beginning of the nations is Amalek? And are there many nations and tongues to the world before Amalek came? Even so, Ishmael and Moab came out, who were narrow, and their fury fell upon them, that the nations are deepening the field, the gathering, the sun, "The nations will be covered," and there was no one who was not afraid of their power from above, the hard, and Amalek was not afraid, the gathering, and "did not fear God," and he came, the <term>shif</term> <gloss>unknown term</gloss>, and "did not fear God," to approach us, and Amalek, "the beginning of the nations," Amalek, that they came to the world, the evil war, Amalek was, and because of this, "I said, what to the memory?" that which is written, "For I will surely blot out the memory of Amalek," and it is written, "Blot out the memory of Amalek," and this is, "I said, what to the memory?" his manhood he requires. of which he is already suspicious; so he grasped at once that this journey served to cause the *Portuguese* in *India* to come into his kingdom, that they would make themselves masters of it and force him to embrace the *Catholic Religion*: hereupon he caused the Great men of his court to come together and shared his thoughts with them very secretly; they all agreed that one should not allow the *Ambassador* and me to take this road that we intended, as it was the direct one, and that one should make us take another and very inconvenient road, through many detours and the land of *Baly*.

<margin>Were forced into an inconvenient detour.</margin>
After many arguments back and forth, he finally said to us in conclusion that he would never let us pass along the road we were planning, but indeed through *Baly*, to which one had to submit, for we were intent on continuing this undertaking.

<margin>The Kingdom *Baly*.</margin>
*Baly* is a *Kingdom* that formerly belonged to the *Empire of Ethiopia*; but the *Gallas* and *Mohammedans* possess it at present; it borders on the *Kingdom of Adel*, and it lies to the East of the *Kingdom of Narea*. From this I could easily conclude that I could not complete this journey, and that after I had encountered all these difficulties in the lands of the *Emperor*, I had even greater ones to expect in the lands of the *Kaffers* <gloss>pagans/infidels</gloss>, who have no other *Law* than their own advantage; nevertheless, reflecting that it was for the service of *God*, I took the road of *Baly*, trusting in his mercy.

<margin>Set out on the road.</margin>
The *Ambassador* and I, leaving the court of *Narea*, took our way *Eastward*, and arrived the first day at the place where the *Captain* was, whom the *Benero* had appointed as our *guide*; in the beginning he received us very well, hoping to get a fine gift from us, but that which we presented to him,
pages.15:

<margin>1613</margin>
not agreeing with his hope and expectation, he let us wait for him for 8 days, after which he gave us 80 men to accompany us to the borders of the Kingdom of Narea; we went with this escort 
<margin>Arrive in a desolate land.</margin>
4 long days' travel through a desolate and abandoned land, due to the incursions of the Gallas; our escort went back thereafter; and since the road that we still had to cover was very dangerous, we let some scouts run ahead of us to give us a signal as soon as they perceived Gallas from afar, so that we might have time to go and hide ourselves in the woods.

At midday we began to climb down a very high and rugged mountain, and the Envoy of Gingiro told us that before we proceeded to climb down, we must hide until the evening, so that we could pass the fields during the night in which the Gallas grazed their cattle.

<margin>Very bad road, barely managing themselves.</margin>
At 4 o'clock in the afternoon we set off on our way, under the protection of a dense rain squall which drove the Gallas to their huts; but which also soaked us weary travelers and caused us to suffer much cold. Our care and concern doubled when the night came, because the brushwood through which we passed was very dense near the ground, difficult to get through by day, and even worse by night. We lit a fire in the woods and chewed a little roasted barley, which is the common food of travelers of that land, and the next day very early, after we had climbed down a steep mountain, we came to the River Zebée.

<margin>Pass a very dangerous bridge.</margin>
This stream runs faster than the Nile, and at the place where we had to cross it, it made a terrible noise, falling from a mountain between very sharp cliffs, between which the water was crushed into foam;
pages.16:

<margin>1613</margin>
the bridge over which we were forced to pass such fast and perilous waters was made of a piece of wood; this went across the river, notwithstanding that it was remarkably wide, and the height of this bridge was so great that, if one looked down from it, one discovered nothing there but an abyss; the great length of the piece of wood made it tremble under the feet of our people, and yet everyone wanted to be the first to cross; for as soon as one is on the other side of this river, one has no more to fear from the Gallas, for whom the fear was so great that it extinguished all other fears: we thanked God on the other side of the bridge that he had delivered us from the bloodthirsty hands of the Gallas; we could not let our mules cross this bridge, therefore we left them there that night on the bank of the river with 2 men to guard them, with orders to cross the bridge if the Gallas came, and to break it down behind them; but the next day 2 inhabitants of the land showed them a ford where they managed to get them across with great difficulty.

<margin>Get an audience with the King of Gingiro.</margin>
The Ambassador came shortly after this to a dwelling from which we made our arrival known to the King of Gingiro, and asked him for permission to offer him the letters that we had to deliver to him on behalf of the Emperor of Ethiopia; but this King, being besides very given to his sorcery, made us wait there for 8 days, at the end of which we received permission to come to his court, where we arrived in one day; we found this monarch ready to receive us, seated, or rather enclosed in a cage; for it was a type of cage or coop about 25 hand-breadths high and 30 wide; it was round on top, having

<margin>1613</margin>
the appearance of a wheel; the King sat on a carpet which was spread out on this wheel; all his courtiers stood upright below this throne, where he gave audience; he was dressed in a very fine cloth, of which the whiteness made the blackness of his face stand out the more, in which one otherwise did not see those features which one notices in the Kaffers. He asked immediately for the letter from the Emperor; he climbed down from his throne in order to come and get it, asked after how he was doing, and climbed back onto his throne, <margin>Who reads the letter from the Emperor.</margin> after which he read the letter and spoke for some time with us through an interpreter, to whom as often as the Emperor or the King said something to be told to us, the interpreter kissed the tips of his fingers, and after he had bowed himself to the earth, he went to interpret it to me, who was at some distance from the throne, and when he had to bring the answer from me back to the King, he used the same ceremony beforehand; the conversation lasted a long time: finally the King let it be said to me and the Envoy that we should go and rest a little, and that the essence of the Emperor's letter consisted of this: that he would like to entertain us well and have us accompanied by a good guard to the borders of his kingdom; which he (he said) would do very gladly.

The day after, I presented some gifts to the King; he showed much pleasure in them, as they were a rare thing in that land. When I was ready to depart from there, the King sent me, in consideration of my gift, a young daughter of one of the Great men of his kingdom to serve me as a slave; I excused myself from receiving her, saying that I was by no means accustomed to take women along with me; the King took satisfaction in the difficulty I made and sent

<margin>Strange type of ferrymen.</margin>
We departed for that purpose from the court of the King of **Gingiro**, and arrived the same day at the bank of the River **Zebée** to cross it; the people that the King had given us, being very skilled at this type of crossing, made a structure (<term>Machine</term> <gloss>device</gloss>) that was not much safer than the piece of wood; they slaughtered a cow and put the luggage into the hide, which was to serve 2 uses: one to get across, the other to serve as ballast for the **Ship** that they made from the hide of this cow, sewing the same tightly shut, after which they blew it up stiff, and then made 2 pieces of wood or sticks fast to it, like those of a sedan chair; 4 **people** went to sit on these sticks, 2 in front and 2 behind this raft-work; one forbade them to move, and one arranged them to be of equal weight, so that they kept this strange vessel in equal balance: in front of it swam a bold swimmer who was very experienced in this art, who had a rope around his body that was also fastened to the apparatus, with which he pulled it forward; 2 other swimmers also pushed it from behind; a whole day was spent on this crossing.

<margin>River Zebée.</margin>
<margin>The Kingdom of Gingiro described.</margin>
The River **Zebée** surrounds almost the entire Kingdom of **Gingiro** and makes it like a peninsula, as one sees in the map of **Ethiopia**, and from there it goes to lose itself in the sea towards the coast of **Melinde**.

This kingdom is small; the inhabitants are

<margin>1613</margin>
black as the Kaffers, but they do not have the features of the face like them; they are like all heathens, very inclined to sorcery, and they have such uncommon customs and habits that I will doubtlessly deserve forgiveness for having described them.

<margin>Custom of those of Gingiro.</margin>
Gingiro means an ape or a monkey, and truly the black color of this monarch, his gestures, face, and manners were entirely similar to those of these animals; these people also have that of the apes, that they kill their kings, and those of their people who come wounded from the battle; because, they say, they ought to die rather than preserve their lives with such marks of disgrace among their enemies.

<margin>Which are very ridiculous.</margin>
But although these kings thus sitting on their <term>Jucquoir</term> <gloss>stool/throne</gloss>, or throne, like an owl on a perch, resemble apes or monkeys very drolly, they are nonetheless of a lofty mind and of a very sharp perception; when the King is to go outside his palace, it is early in the morning before the rising of the sun; and if it happens that the sun is up before he is out, he keeps himself locked in his palace for that whole day, does not go onto the throne to give audience, and also does not give any order to anyone, because, they say, 2 suns cannot endure each other in the world at one time; and because he does not want to grant that precedence, he takes revenge the next day for it, and goes out before the sun is up.

<margin>Wonderfully strange ceremonies in the election.</margin>
The ceremonies which they observe to elect their kings are likewise entirely uncommon: they wind the body of their dead king in costly fabrics and then put it thus into a hide of a cow which has been freshly skinned: immediately all those who may be in line for the crown, such as the children of the deceased and the princes of the blood, go to hide themselves in a

desolate forest and act as if they wanted to flee that honor which they desire; the electors, who are considered great sorcerers, hold council, go forest-wards, search for the chosen one, and by devil's art cause a form of a bird of prey as large as an eagle, which they call *Liber*, to descend; this bird flies with a great cry to the place where the one who is chosen is; the electors also go there at once, and they find him surrounded by lions, tigers, snakes, panthers, and more similar beasts, which they cause to come around this newly-chosen monarch through sorcery, who protects and defends himself like a mad bull against those who want to take him with them; he wounds and sometimes even kills them; for those who seek him do not leave him until they have gotten him and carried him along by force and violence; leading him along thus, one must fight with the people of a lineage who for a long time have believed they have the right to set the chosen monarch on the throne; the strongest or the victors have this privilege, which gives them a good share in the favor of the new *Gingiro*.

<margin>As also in the coronation of a king.</margin>
The ceremony of the coronation is to bring the King into the palace and to place him under a tent: on the 7th day after the death of the last King, the sorcerers bring a worm, which they say came from the nostrils of the dead man, which worm they wind in a cloth of silk fabric, and the new King pulls the head off it with his teeth; that having happened, they bury the dead King after they have carried him through the sown fields, which they pray for him to be willing to bless: having arrived at the burial place of the old kings, which is in a small grove, they dig a hole in the earth and lay him in it without covering, but he remains exposed to the air,
pages.21:

because, they say, the earth is not worthy to cover the body of their King, who does not yield to the sun in greatness, and also to that end, so that the heaven might serve as a more glorious grave site. On the day of the funeral they slaughter many cows by the grave, so that their blood drips onto the body of the King; they still slaughter a head of cattle there daily as long as the new King is alive, which is to the great benefit of their priests, or rather of their sorcerers, who indeed let the blood of the cow run into the grave, but provide their tables well with what remains of it.

<margin>1613</margin>

To get to the new King while he bites the head off the worm, the people make shouts of joy and acclamations to his praise, wishing him a long life; the feast ends after they have placed him on that frame of a throne described by us above; for the new King immediately has everyone fetched who were favorites of his predecessor, saying to them: *since they have been his friends so strongly during his life, it was also fair that they accompany him into the other world, so that they might be able to continue their services*, and under this pretext he causes them all to have their necks broken; he chooses others again, fills the state offices that are vacant, and that does not prevent these first and foremost positions from being strongly sought after, and it causes the courtiers to have a very great interest in the preservation of their prince.

At the time of the election, they burn the houses in which the deceased King has lived, with all his household effects and tools, without excepting anything, no matter how costly it may be; they do the same when any special or common person dies,
