Similarly, the "Person" <note>of the Sankhya school</note>, the "Mental Consciousness" <note>of the Vaisheshika school</note>, and "Non-dual Awareness" <note>of the Guhyasamaja/Esoteric traditions</note>—all those that posit consciousness as an eternal substance are also not established by intrinsic nature and are empty. One must also understand the meaning of "Form is emptiness; likewise, feelings and..." and so forth.

Similarly, the meaning of "Emptiness is form," and so forth, is that form, which exists as sound and as a coarse substance, is empty of form; it is not established as an eternal substance. It is empty of the form included in the atoms of an eternal substance. It is impermanent. The basis for designating "form," the form born from action, and what is suitable as form is what is meant by "Emptiness is form." Furthermore, the emptiness of the form that is posited as the aforementioned substance and the composite substance is not other than that form itself. This is the meaning of "Emptiness is not other than form." Similarly, the meaning of "Form is not other than emptiness" is that the form born from action is not other than the emptiness of the eternal substance, its parts, and the composite form. This is the understanding of the tenets of the Sautrāntika school.

The System of one Sautrāntika school: As for the system of those who hold that consciousness is accompanied by aspects, they posit the appearance of form and the object as two aspects of consciousness. <note>original: ལས་སྐྱེས་ཀྱི་གཟུགས་- ཞེས་པའི། ལས་ཀྱི་རྣམ་སྨིན་ལས་ཐོབ་པའི་ལུས་ཀྱི་དབྱིབས་སོགས་སོ། །ཆོས་མངོན་བསྡུས་པ་ ཤོག་ ༧ སྤྱད་ཆ་དེབ་ གསལ་བརྗོད་ལུགས།</note>
pages.135:
the meaning of "Form is emptiness." Even though the consciousness itself is empty of form, the appearance of form within it is indeed form, which is why it is said, "Emptiness is form." Since it is not reasonable to think of form as being other than the form that has become emptiness, it is said that "it is not other than form." Since no form is observed beyond that which appears as form, which holds the form empty of the characteristics of form, it is said that "form is not other than emptiness." In this way, these sutras do not appear to be interpreted according to one's own school in terms of philosophical tenets. This is because the "profound practice" taught here is the Mother of the <term>Arya</term> <gloss>Noble Ones</gloss> <note>referring to the perfection of wisdom</note>. Although it is considered the Mother of Reason, I have not seen it as impossible to apply to philosophical tenets as well.

Explanations relying on the method of <term>Vijnaptimatra</term> <gloss>Consciousness-only</gloss>: There are also explanations of the intention of the sutras, such as "Form is emptiness," relying on other sutras, in the manner of the consciousness-only methods of the Great Masters. In this system, all phenomena of the path are established as having the characteristic of form. The intention of the Mother Sutra <note>Prajnaparamita</note>, which states that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature, is interpreted. Here, too, relying on the three non-existences and the three types of form, the meaning of the four types of emptiness, beginning with "Form is emptiness," is explained. As the sutra says:

"Brahmin, one who practices the Perfection of Wisdom and abides in the skill of interpreting profound phenomena, the Bodhisattva, should understand that form is to be examined as profound in three ways. Feelings and..."
pages.136:
This is the imagined form, this is the dependent form, and this is the form of <term>Dharmata</term> <gloss>the true nature of reality</gloss>.

Thus, relying on these three types of form, the first form is what is clung to as an object by children, which is the imagined form and the form that becomes an object of consciousness appearing as an object. The dependent form and the form devoid of the aspects of those two are the perfected form—that is <term>Tathata</term> <gloss>Thusness</gloss>, which is called "the form of Dharmata."

Therefore, the nature of the dependent form is devoid of the characteristics of the imagined form in all respects; thus, it is empty of the imagined form, and that emptiness is the meaning of reality itself. As it is said by the great charioteer <note>Nagarjuna</note>:

"What is the characteristic of emptiness? That which is empty of what is not present is correctly observed." And: "What is it that is not present? In the aggregates, elements, and sense-spheres, there is no eternal, permanent, unchanging phenomenon, nor is there a self or what belongs to a self. Thus, they are empty."

As stated, "Form is emptiness" means that the dependent form, which has the characteristic of the dependent nature, is empty of those imagined forms, such as external objects. <note>original: ཉི་ཁྲི་ ཨེ་ ཤོག་ ༣༩/ན བུམ་ཞུས། མདོ་སྡེ་ཀུན་བཏུས་- ཤོག་ ༣༧བ སེམས་ཙམ་ རཱི་ སྡེ་བསྟན།</note>
pages.137:
Excerpts from the Commentary on the Essence: 95

Because it is empty of them, it is said, "Form is emptiness." This eliminates the conceptual proliferation of distraction and primarily shows the antidote to the conceptual proliferation of superimposition.

Because such emptiness is the perfected form, it is said, "Emptiness is form." This covers the conceptual proliferation of denial. If one thinks that emptiness and form are distinct because their characteristics are incompatible—that emptiness is one thing and form is another—it teaches the antidote to the conceptual proliferation of the two extremes of emptiness. For such a form of Dharmata, which has the characteristic of emptiness, the characteristic of form does not exist. As it is said in the Perfection of Wisdom Sutra:

"Shariputra, form is devoid of the nature of form." As it is stated extensively, and similarly, in the sutra taught by <term>Rab 'byor</term> <gloss>Subhuti</gloss>, it is said, "Although the <term>Dharma-dhatu</term> <gloss>sphere of reality</gloss> exists in the realm of form, the Dharma-dhatu is not the characteristic of consciousness, which is the consciousness of an object."

Therefore, it is not the case that one thinks emptiness or the form of Dharmata is other than form. Because it is the Dharmata of form, it cannot be observed as other than the basis of phenomena, form. Thus, it is said, "Emptiness is not other than form." The basis of phenomena, form, is also the basis of that emptiness. <note>original: ཉི་ཁྲི་། ཤོག་ ༡༤༦/༣ ཤེས་ ཀྱི་ སྡེ་བས། བློ་གྲོས་མི་ཟད་པའི་མདོ། ཤོག་ ༡༣/བ མདོ་ མ། སྡེ་བས།</note>
pages.138:
And because that form of Dharmata is a phenomenon, it cannot be observed as other than its own Dharmata, and because it is its nature, it is not other than emptiness. This is what is meant. The term "also" is used for inclusion in accordance with the logical scriptures.

These two teach the antidote to the conceptual proliferation of distraction that grasps phenomena and their Dharmata as distinct, even though they are not one. As the great charioteer <note>Nagarjuna</note> said:

"It is taught as an antidote to conceptualization in the sense of a method: Form is not other than emptiness. Form itself is emptiness. Emptiness is form."

As it is said, these are explanations consistent with the manner of the sutra commentary style. The great scholars of Tibet have also interpreted this in accordance with the chapters of the commentary on the Perfection of Wisdom, though some have done so contradictorily. I have not included those who hold to extremes here. Once the key point of these is understood, it is easy to understand how the intention of the Perfection of Wisdom sutras is interpreted based on the method of the three non-existences, such as the non-existence of the characteristics of the imagined. One should know this from other various commentaries. Here, I have only explained the essence of the meaning.

The purpose of the joyful state: To that, the "Form is emptiness," etc. <note>original: ཤེས་པ་ཆེན་པོ་བསྡུས་པ- ཤོག་ ༡༥ སེམས་ཙམ་ རི སྟེ་བསྟན། བྱ་སྟོན་ཤེར་ལུང་སྟེ་- ཤོག་ ༣༥ དེབ་གཟུགས་ལ་སྟེར་པས། མཚན་- བཤད་པའི་དག་གཟུགས་རྣམ་གྱི་ལེའུ་ལ་བརྟེན་མོད། བྱམས་རྣམ་གྱི་ལེའུ་ནས་བསྟན་པའི་དངོས་འགྲེལ་གྱི་དགོངས་པ་སེམས་ཙམ་དུ་གཞས་མིན་དཔྱད།</note>
pages.139:
shows that form and the rest have no nature. The reasoning that establishes this, and the manner in which those [reasonings] abandon wrong views and conceptual proliferation, have been taught in the two stages of the method. Nevertheless, one may ask: if it is said, "Form is empty by nature," what is that nature? How should one identify it? The response is: it must be established as being established by nature. If it is established, it is refuted by reasoning such as the "freedom from one or many" and the "refutation of production in the four corners." Therefore, the explanation that "it is devoid of nature" is extremely clear in the scriptures of the Madhyamaka and Prajnaparamita. Although this is not taken directly from the Pramanavartika of the venerable masters, those who wish to understand the scriptures of view by reading the texts will not see how a definitive understanding comes from relying on the aforementioned lines of reasoning.

Thus, the manner of identifying the "nature" in "empty by nature," based on the various extremes, has been explained above. In the Great Vehicle scriptures and the commentaries of the great charioteers, the other aspects are briefly mentioned. The two questions are connected to both the sutras and the tantras, as they are questions derived from the basis of training in both.

That nature, according to the own tradition of the Perfection of Wisdom, is the nature of form that appears due to the power of the imprints of grasping at characteristics, which have been present since beginningless time, connected with the mental streams of sentient beings. This is like a mirage or a magical display. The entire manner of appearance is mixed without separation, and it is abandoned. The appearance of form that is stimulated by the imprints of entities is merely an appearance of form. The appearance stimulated by the imprints of verbal designation is that very appearance.
pages.140:
It appears as the basis for the application of the word "form." It is an appearance born from the imprints of grasping at self, both established and appearing as an entity. It appears as established from its own side without depending on others. Even when form does not appear, those three are mixed without separation, and they appear as one. As long as the appearance of true existence is not refuted, one refutes either the three as one or all three. If one does not abandon the one, the three all remain appearing. Therefore, the nature of form that accords with such an appearance is the nature that is said to be "empty of its own nature." When identifying such a nature of form and the rest, as the great noble <term>Aryadeva</term> <gloss>a great Indian master</gloss> said:

-> "What is seen as not being connected," <-
-> "that is called nature." <-

And as stated in the commentary on this: "What is meant by positing it as an entity that merely abides in its own nature, without being connected to other phenomena, is how much of it is observed. That is its nature, because it is not mixed with other phenomena."

As stated, the appearance of it abiding without depending on others is the way of appearance as established by nature, and the establishment according to appearance is the way of being established as true, and the way of being established by intrinsic nature. As it is said in that same text:
"Whatever entity, from some other..."
pages.141:
"If everything were unchanging,"
"Then its own essence would change."
"That is not the case for anything."

As stated, when form appears as a phenomenon, there are those three types of form, and although two entities are to be refuted by reasoning, when it comes to the form being established as true and by nature, all three are well-suited because all three are illusory appearances born from the imprints of incorrect reasoning. At that time, the appearance of form arising from the clarity of the self of the entity is an appearance of dependence; therefore, it is to be refuted by reasoning. The second appearance, arising from the clarity of the self of verbal designation, is also the basis for the imputation of names and the like; therefore, it does not need to be refuted by reasoning. Because even if it is clear, there exists an appearance like an illusory dependent origination and the imputation of names. Therefore, the appearance of being established as true and established by nature, the self of the phenomenon grasping at that nature, and the two—the object and the grasping at a self—which are the root of incorrect conceptualization and the root of cyclic existence, are the roots of incorrectness, attachment, and aversion. Therefore, since they are established as false, they are to be refuted by reasoning. The conceptualization that grasps at that, together with cyclic existence, is to be refuted. As the son of the Conquerors, <term>Shantideva</term> <gloss>a great master of the Middle Way</gloss>, said:

"Whatever is seen, heard, or known,"
"Is not to be refuted here."

*The philosopher’s exposition on Plato’s Timaeus. Which book is mine.*
*Of Bessarion, Cardinal, Bishop of Tusculum.* 1)
Leaves 1r—4u, which contain *Timaeus the Locrian on the Soul of the World and Nature* (the title of which booklet is painted in red), follow the five books of the commentaries, of which the first two stand on the side of codex **N**, which is taught by other things, and especially by the lacuna common to both books, which in this parchment is supplied by one inserted leaf (63). However, the number of leaves of the quinternion is not disturbed, because two leaves are marked with the number 61.

The context of the third, fourth, and fifth books approaches most closely to the vulgate recension. On leaf 266u one encounters the same subscription that ends the Munich Greek codex 382: *Up to the matters set forth, the writings of Proclus on the Timaeus have been found; whether he explained the following is unclear.*

The inscriptions of the individual books are painted in red lead, and the letters which we call initials are artistically gilded, except for the title of the third book (leaf 182u), which was decorated only later.
I examined them in Venice in 1899.

PARISINUS National Library, Greek 1841 [**FONTEBL.-REG. 2095**], paper, 16th century (cf. Omont, *Inventaire* II p. 151) is a twin of codex **D**.
I saw it in Paris in 1898.

CHISIANUS **R VIII 58**, of the largest format, bombycine <note>cotton paper</note>, 13th century (?), 233 leaves. The context, which faded from humidity and became lacunose, seems to be completed, if any faith is to be placed in the authority of the catalog, by the hand of Laur. Portius, scribe of Leo Allatius (leaves 1—3 [= leaves 4—6 repeated]. 231), and by another much older one in ‘another elegant character’ (leaves 229, 230, 232, 233).

Although five complete books were present at one time, now 32 leaves have perished before the fourth leaf, as it appears, four quires. The old book today begins at p. 130, 23 | <greek>καὶ</greek>

pages.173:
# Fourteenth Chapter

By meditating on that same luminous principle, devoid of any support, one achieves within a year everything that resides within the taste-veil. (17) Contemplating the subtle forms and images mentioned previously, rising upward, one clearly attains all the outcomes resulting from the taste-veil. (18) Therefore, I shall now describe a beautiful and auspicious *dhāraṇā* <term>concentration technique</term> that grants divine vision and is based on the subtle element of form <term>rūpa-tanmātra</term>, for the purpose of achieving all spiritual powers. (19) When a yogi, sitting in solitude with closed eyes, perceives something that appears like the clouds of an autumn twilight, (20) and fixes their consciousness upon it for ten days, they will eventually perceive even the most subtle points of light within it. (21) Some of these are white, some red, others yellow or blue. Upon seeing these, one should meditate with a focused mind, without letting the thought wander. (22) After six months, one sees many forms within these lights. After three years, these same forms become radiant, steady, and brilliant. (23) By practicing this, after three more years, one perceives them in the shape of distinct images. Then, after another year, one sees the light itself, and after six more months, it takes the form of a human figure. (24)

<summary>This page introduces the *dhāraṇā* (meditation) focused on the subtle element of form, detailing a progression of light-based visions over years of practice leading to divine sight.</summary>
<keywords>Yoga, Dhāraṇā, Rūpa-tanmātra, Meditation, Divine Vision</keywords>
pages.174:
# In the Mālinī-Vijayottara Tantra

After practicing for three months, the light spreads throughout the entire body. Through the progression of time, one dwells within the previously mentioned sphere of forms. (25) One obtains all those fruits, and divine vision arises. This is the *dhāraṇā*—a conceptual technique described as a practical means. (26) Fifteen types of variations arise naturally within this practice. Since one attains certainty through this, what is the need for the ostentation of other scriptures? (27) Therefore, I will now tell you about the *dhāraṇā* related to the sense of touch, by which a yogi gains a "diamond-like body." <term>vajradeha</term> (28) One should imagine oneself situated within a hexagonal mandala, resembling dark antimony, with every part of the body vibrating. (29) Then, O Goddess, after ten days, the sensation of ants crawling will occur all over the skin. By meditating on that, (30) one attains a diamond-like body and receives the previously mentioned fruits, contemplating the previously described mandala and form. (31) Who could prevent the knowledge of the sphere of touch from arising? For the sake of the power of the master of that element, one should meditate on oneself within a diminished mandala. (32) Through this success, one will become a knower of all touch. With ears covered and eyes closed, one should practice with effort. (33)

<summary>This page details the practice of the 'diamond-like body' (vajradeha) dhāraṇā, focusing on the sensory perception of touch and the mastery of the hexagonal mandala.</summary>

# Fourteenth Chapter

<margin>Sound</margin>

One should focus their consciousness on the great sound heard therein. After ten days, the internal fire of digestion is ignited. (34) The knowledge of hearing from a distance arises after six months. When the sound heard at the end is faint and perceived bit by bit, (35) that should be known as the *sakala-ātmā* <note>original: "सकलात्मा" - refers to the soul connected to the body/limitations.</note>. Through persistent practice with a focused mind, one gains stability in the knowledge of the sphere of sound. (36) The sound that is heard again, resembling the blowing of a conch at its end, is the form of the *pralayākala* <note>original: "प्रलयाकल" - a stage of spiritual dissolution.</note>; it should be practiced by those desiring that fruit. (37) When that sound covers the subtle sound, it is called the *vijñānākala* <note>original: "विज्ञानाकल" - a stage of consciousness.</note>. That is the "Unconquered" <note>original: "अपराजिते" - referring to a specific state or divinity.</note>. (38) That which is heard at the end of the sound that delights the mind is known to yogis seeking yoga as the *mantra*. (39) Then, another sound is heard that resembles the quiet ringing of a bell. It is called the *mantreśa* <term>Lord of Mantras</term>, granting the fruit of all *siddhis* <term>spiritual powers</term>. (40) The sound that arises at the end of the bell-sound is the state of *mantreśa*; it is the great cause of all perfections. (41) Just as the sound produced by a lute struck by the wind, the sound that is there—one should know that as the *śāmbhava* <term>state of Shiva</term> position. (42)

# PARAGRAPH 11

### THE ESTABLISHMENT OF FUNDAMENTALS

Generally, when utilizing soldiers, there are three stages to victory. Before hostilities break out, laws should be established$^2$; once laws are established, they must become customary; once they are customary$^3$, supplies must be provided. These three things must be accomplished within the country before soldiers can be sent abroad. To perform these three tasks, there are two conditions: the first is to uphold the law so it can be applied$^4$; the second is to appoint the right men so that the law can be established. 

Relying on the masses is merely assembling a mob; relying on outward appearances is just cleverness; relying on fame and sight is deceitfulness. If a leader relies on any of these three, his soldiers may be captured.$^5$ Therefore it is said: “The strong are unbending; they fight for what they desire. By fighting, their strength develops to the full, and thus they are prepared. In this way, they have no rival in the four seas, and since order prevails, products are accumulated.”

---

$^1$ Yen suspects an omission after 使 民 者.
$^2$ Cf. par. 9, p. 238.
$^3$ 俗 成 should be inserted.
$^4$ Wang Shih-jun adds 行 according to the Ch’ung-wen text.
$^5$ Wang Shih-jun suggests that 因 should be 固, which is used for 故.
pages.264:
By the accumulation of products, it is possible for the rewards to be great. If rewards are uniform, rank will be honored; if rank is honored, rewards will bring profit. Therefore it is said: “The army, being based on a state of order, produces a marvelous result; custom, being based on law, allows for ten thousand changes of circumstances; a condition of supremacy being based on the mind, it is outwardly manifested in a state of preparedness <note>The term *shi* (ornament/manifest) is difficult; it is used here in a positive sense. I follow the punctuation of Wang’s text. Yin reads: 'The army is born of order and is different from custom; it is born of law and can adapt to a myriad of changing situations; it is based on the mind and manifested in a state of preparedness.' However, that does not seem as good.</note>.” 

If these three points of view are all taken into consideration, the result will be that the strong may be firmly established. Thus, orderly government is the necessary result of strength, and strength is the result of orderly government; orderly government is the result of riches, and riches are the result of orderly government; riches are the result of strength, and strength is the result of riches. Therefore it is said: “The way to orderly government and strength is to discuss the fundamentals.”

## PARAGRAPH 12
### MILITARY DEFENCE

A state that has to fight on four fronts values defense, and a state that rests against the sea values attack. If a state that fights on four fronts is fond of raising soldiers <note>The word *ju* (raise) should be omitted.</note>, it will be in a dangerous position, as it has to resist four neighbors.
pages.265:
As soon as a country with four neighbors begins hostilities, those four countries mobilize armies; therefore, the country is in a dangerous position. If a state that has to fight on four fronts is unable to raise <note>The text has *she* (to house/stop); I prefer the reading *han* (to contain), as found in the Ch’ung-wen edition.</note>, from a city of ten thousand houses, an army of more than ten thousand men, then the state will be in a dangerous position. Therefore it is said: “A state that has to fight on four fronts should concern itself with defensive warfare.” 

In defending walled cities, the best method is to use the strength of the worn-out men to fight the fresh strength of the invaders. It is assaults upon walled cities that wear out the strength of men. As long as the walled cities have not all been razed, the invaders have no means of penetrating the country <note>Yü suggests reading: 'Unless the cities are entirely razed, the invaders have no way to enter.'</note>. This is what is meant by saying that the strength of worn-out men should fight the fresh strength of the invading force. But when the walled cities have all been razed and the foreign army thus finds the means of penetrating, then certainly it will be exhausted, and the people within the country will be rested. Fighting with rested strength against those of exhausted strength is what is meant by fighting with the strength of fresh men against the worn-out strength of the invading forces. All these are called the misfortunes attendant upon the besieging of walled cities.
pages.266:
It is regarded as a misfortune that, when capturing cities, the strength of the army is always worn out. In these three things, misfortune is due not to insufficient effort, but to mistaken generalship <note>The text seems corrupt; I suggest inserting 'obtain' before 'city'. I read *yue* instead of *ri* (day). The phrase 'It is regarded,' etc., is no doubt a commentary. The expression 'these three things' remains obscure. By the last phrase, one is reminded of the precept in Sun-tzŭ, Chapter 3: 'The worst policy of all is to besiege walled cities; the rule is not to besiege walled cities if it can possibly be avoided.'</note>. 

The way to hold a city is to have abundant strength. Therefore it is said: “When the invading force musters its levies, mobilize as many as three armies, and divide them according to the number of the chariots of the invading force.” Of these three armies, one should be formed of able-bodied men, one of able-bodied women, and one of the old and feeble men and women. These are called the three armies. Cause the army of able-bodied men, with abundant provisions and sharp weapons, to marshal themselves and await the enemy; cause the able-bodied women, with abundant provisions and ramparts at their backs, to marshal themselves and await orders, so as to make—at the approach of the invaders—earthworks as an obstruction, and traps, <term>chevaux-de-frise</term> <note>Portable obstacles made of spiked beams.</note>, and pitfalls, to pull down the supporting beams and to tear down the houses, to transport what is transportable, and to burn what is untransportable <note>The text is corrupt; I follow Sun in reading *zuo* (to clear away) for *geng* (plowing).</note>.
pages.267: ...so that the invaders are not able to make use of them in their attack. Cause the army of the old and feeble to guard the oxen, horses, sheep, and swine, and to collect all that is consumable—plants and water—to feed the others therewith, so as to obtain food for the able-bodied men and women. But see to it carefully that the three armies do not intermingle. If the able-bodied men mingle with the army of the able-bodied women, they will attach great value to the safety of the women, and wicked people will have opportunities for intrigue, with the result that the state will perish. Taking pleasure in the women’s company, the men will be afraid of disturbing reports, and so not even the brave will fight. If the able-bodied men and women intermingle with the army of the old and feeble, then the old will arouse the compassion of the able-bodied, and the feeble the pity of the strong. Compassion and pity in the heart cause brave people to be more anxious and fearful people not to fight <note>The text has been clarified by scholars including Yü and Sun, referencing Mo Ti: 'Up to a hundred paces outside the outer wall, cut away and remove completely all walls and trees... Pull down the houses... carry everything that might be used for the attack inside... burn the wood which cannot be transported.' Regarding the women's role, see also Mo Ti.</note>.
pages.268:
Therefore it is said: “See to it carefully that the three armies do not intermingle.” This is the way to have abundant strength.

### PARAGRAPH 13 <note>This section is largely identical to Han Fei-tzŭ, Chapter 20.</note>
## MAKING ORDERS STRICT <note>The term *chin* refers to a martingale for a horse, used for control.</note>

If orders are made strict, orderly government is not delayed, and if laws are equitable, officials are not wicked. Once the law is fixed, one should not damage it with virtuous words; if men of merit are appointed to office, people will have little to say, but if men of virtue are appointed to office, people will have much to say. The practice of good government begins with making judgments. Where five hamlets are the unit for judgments, supremacy is attained; where ten hamlets are the unit for judgments, there is merely strength <note>Commentators have often misunderstood this; it is not a measurement of distance.</note>. He who procrastinates in creating order will be dismembered. Govern by punishments and wage war by rewards; seek transgressors and do not seek the virtuous.
pages.269:
Therefore, if the law is fixed and not altered, then... If in the country there are no wicked people, there is no wicked trade in the capital. If affairs are many and secondary things <note>i.e., trade and non-essential commerce.</note> are numerous, if agriculture is neglected and criminals gain the upper hand, then the country will certainly be dismembered.

If the people have a surplus of grain, cause them to obtain office and rank by means of their cereals; if through their own efforts they can count upon obtaining office and rank, farmers will not be lazy.

If a tube of no more than four inches has no bottom, it can certainly not be filled <note>As noted in Huai Nan-tzŭ: 'A three-inch tube with no bottom cannot be filled by the whole world.'</note>; to confer office, to give rank, and to grant salaries without regard to merit is like having no bottom.

If a state, when poor, applies itself to war, the poison will originate on the enemy's side, and it will not have the "six parasites" <note>The six internal factors of decay.</note>, but will certainly be strong. If a state, when rich, does not apply itself to war, the poison is transferred to its own interior.
pages.270:
...and it will have the six kinds of parasites and will certainly be weak <note>I follow Yü in altering the text to 'The poison is transferred to the interior and the six parasites are born.' Wang Shih-jun suggests that 'poor' might be better as 'rich,' which aligns with the sense of the passage.</note>. If the state confers office and gives rank according to merit, it may be said to be planning with complete wisdom and fighting with complete courage. Such a country will certainly have no equal. If a state confers office and gives rank according to merit, then government measures will be simple and words will be few. This may be said to be abolishing laws by means of the law, and abolishing words by means of words. But if a state confers office and gives rank according to the six parasites, then government measures will be complicated and words will arise. This may be said to be bringing about laws...

Let η' and η'' be the indices of probability in two independent ensembles which are each in statistical equilibrium, then η' + η'' will be the index in the ensemble obtained by combining each system of the first ensemble with each system of the second. This third ensemble will of course be in statistical equilibrium, and the function of phase η' + η'' will be a constant of motion. Now when infinitesimal forces are added to the compound systems, if η' + η'' or a function differing infinitesimally from this is still a constant of motion, it must be on account of the nature of the forces added, or if their action is not entirely specified, on account of conditions to which they are subject. Thus, in the case already considered, η' + η'' is a function of the energy of the compound system, and the infinitesimal forces added are subject to the law of conservation of energy.

<margin>||</margin> Another natural supposition in regard to the added forces is that they should be such as not to affect the moments of momentum of the compound system. To get a case in which moments of momentum of the compound system shall be constants of motion, we may imagine material particles contained in two concentric spherical shells, being prevented from passing the surfaces bounding the shells by repulsions acting always in lines passing through the common centre of the shells. Then, if there are no forces acting between particles in different shells, the mass of particles in each shell will have, besides its energy, the <note>The following phrase is circled in the original:</note> moments of momentum about three axes through the centre as constants of motion.

Now let us imagine an ensemble formed by distributing in phase the system of particles in one shell according to the index of probability

-> A - ε/Θ + ω₁/Ω₁ + ω₂/Ω₂ + ω₃/Ω₃, (98) <-

where ε denotes the energy of the system, and ω₁, ω₂, ω₃, its three moments of momentum, and the other letters constants.

In like manner, let us imagine a second ensemble formed by distributing in phase the system of particles in the other shell according to the index:

-> A' − ε' / Θ + ω₁' / Ω₁ + ω₂' / Ω₂ + ω₃' / Ω₃, (99) <-

where the letters have similar significations, and Θ, Ω₁, Ω₂, Ω₃ have the same values as in the preceding formula. Each of the two ensembles will evidently be in statistical equilibrium, and therefore so will the ensemble of compound systems obtained by combining each system of the first ensemble with each of the second. In this third ensemble, the index of probability will be:

-> A + A' − (ε + ε') / Θ + (ω₁ + ω₁') / Ω₁ + (ω₂ + ω₂') / Ω₂ + (ω₃ + ω₃') / Ω₃, (100) <-

where the four numerators represent functions of phase which are constants of motion for the compound systems.

Now, if we add to each system of this third ensemble infinitesimal conservative forces of attraction or repulsion between particles in different shells—determined by the same law for all the systems—the functions ω₁ + ω₁', ω₂ + ω₂', and ω₃ + ω₃' will remain constants of motion, and a function differing infinitely little from ε + ε' will be a constant of motion. It would therefore require only an infinitesimal change in the distribution in phase of the ensemble of compound systems to make it a case of statistical equilibrium. These properties are entirely analogous to those of canonical ensembles.*

pages.66:
# CANONICAL DISTRIBUTION

The properties of canonically distributed ensembles of systems—with respect to the equilibrium of the new ensembles which may be formed by combining each system of one ensemble with each system of another—are therefore not peculiar to them in the sense that analogous properties do not belong to some other distributions under special limitations in regard to the systems and forces considered. Yet, the canonical distribution evidently constitutes the most simple case of the kind, and that for which the relations described hold with the least restrictions.

Returning to the case of the canonical distribution, we shall find other analogies with thermodynamic systems if we suppose, as in the preceding chapters,* that the potential energy (εq) depends not only upon the coordinates q₁, q₂, ..., qₙ which determine the configuration of the system, but also upon certain coordinates a₁, a₂, etc., of bodies which we call *external*. By this, we simply mean that they are not to be regarded as forming any part of the system, although their positions affect the forces which act on the system. The forces exerted by the system upon these external bodies will be represented by -dεq/da₁, -dεq/da₂, etc., while -dεq/dq₁, ..., -dεq/dqₙ represent all the forces acting upon the bodies of the system, including those which depend upon the position of the external bodies, as well as those which depend only upon the configuration of the system itself. It will be understood that εp depends only upon q₁, ..., qₙ, p₁, ..., pₙ; in other words, the kinetic energy of the bodies which we call external forms no part of the kinetic energy of the system. It follows that we may write:

-> \frac{d\epsilon}{da_{1}} = \frac{d\epsilon_{q}}{da_{1}} = - A_{1}, (104) <-

although a similar equation would not hold for differentiations relative to the internal coordinates.

* See especially Chapter I, p. 4.

<summary>This page defines the relationship between canonical distributions and thermodynamic systems by introducing "external" coordinates that influence potential energy.</summary>

# OF AN ENSEMBLE OF SYSTEMS.

We always suppose these external coordinates to have the same values for all systems of any ensemble. In the case of a canonical distribution—that is, when the index of probability of phase is a linear function of the energy—it is evident that the values of the external coordinates will affect the distribution, since they affect the energy. In the equation:

-> e^{-\frac{ψ}{Θ}} = \int \dots \int_{\text{phases}}^{\text{all}} e^{-\frac{ε}{Θ}} dp_1 \dots dq_n, (105) <-

by which ψ may be determined, the external coordinates a₁, a₂, etc., contained implicitly in ε, as well as Θ, are to be regarded as constant in the integrations indicated. The equation indicates that ψ is a function of these constants. If we imagine their values varied, and the ensemble distributed canonically according to their new values, we have by differentiation of the equation:

-> e^{-\frac{ψ}{Θ}} \left( - \frac{1}{Θ} dψ + \frac{ψ}{Θ^2} dΘ \right) = \frac{1}{Θ^2} dΘ \int \dots \int_{\text{phases}}^{\text{all}} ε e^{-\frac{ε}{Θ}} dp_1 \dots dq_n <-
-> - \frac{1}{Θ} da_1 \int \dots \int_{\text{phases}}^{\text{all}} \frac{dε}{da_1} e^{-\frac{ε}{Θ}} dp_1 \dots dq_n <-
-> - \frac{1}{Θ} da_2 \int \dots \int_{\text{phases}}^{\text{all}} \frac{dε}{da_2} e^{-\frac{ε}{Θ}} dp_1 \dots dq_n - \text{etc.,} (106) <-

or, multiplying by Θe^(ψ/Θ), and setting:

-> - \frac{dε}{da_1} = A_1, \quad - \frac{dε}{da_2} = A_2, \text{ etc.,} <-

-> - dψ + \frac{ψ}{Θ} dΘ = \frac{1}{Θ} dΘ \int \dots \int_{\text{phases}}^{\text{all}} ε e^{\frac{ψ - ε}{Θ}} dp_1 \dots dq_n <-
-> + da_1 \int \dots \int_{\text{phases}}^{\text{all}} A_1 e^{\frac{ψ - ε}{Θ}} dp_1 \dots dq_n <-

# CANONICAL DISTRIBUTION

Now, the average value in the ensemble of any quantity (which we shall denote in general by a horizontal line above the proper symbol) is determined by the equation:

-> \bar{u} = \int \dots \int_{\text{phases}}^{\text{all}} u e^{\frac{\psi - \epsilon}{\Theta}} dp_1 \dots dq_n. (108) <-

Comparing this with the preceding equation, we have:

-> d\psi = \frac{\psi}{\Theta} d\Theta - \frac{\bar{\epsilon}}{\Theta} d\Theta - \bar{A}_1 da_1 - \bar{A}_2 da_2 - \text{etc.} (109) <-

Or, since:

-> \frac{\psi - \epsilon}{\Theta} = \eta, (110) <-

and:

-> \frac{\psi - \bar{\epsilon}}{\Theta} = \bar{\eta}, (111) <-

-> d\psi = \bar{\eta} d\Theta - \bar{A}_1 da_1 - \bar{A}_2 da_2 - \text{etc.} (112) <-

Moreover, since (111) gives:

-> d\psi - d\bar{\epsilon} = \Theta d\bar{\eta} + \bar{\eta} d\Theta, (113) <-

we have also:

-> d\bar{\epsilon} = - \Theta d\bar{\eta} - \bar{A}_1 da_1 - \bar{A}_2 da_2 - \text{etc.} (114) <-

This equation, if we neglect the sign of averages, is identical in form with the thermodynamic equation:

-> d\eta = \frac{d\epsilon + A_1 da_1 + A_2 da_2 + \text{etc.}}{T}, (115) <-

or:

-> d\epsilon = T d\eta - A_1 da_1 - A_2 da_2 - \text{etc.}, (116) <-

which expresses the relation between the energy, temperature, and entropy of a body in thermodynamic equilibrium, and the forces which it exerts on external bodies—a relation which is the mathematical expression of the second law of thermodynamics for reversible changes. The modulus in the statistical equation corresponds to temperature in the thermodynamic equation, and the average index of probability *with its sign reversed* corresponds to entropy.

<summary>The author identifies the formal correspondence between his statistical mechanical equations and the thermodynamic equations, specifically linking the modulus to temperature and the negative index of probability to entropy.</summary>
<keywords>canonical distribution, average value, entropy, thermodynamic equilibrium, second law of thermodynamics</keywords>
pages.69:
# OF AN ENSEMBLE OF SYSTEMS.

But in the thermodynamic equation, the entropy (η) is a quantity which is only defined by the equation itself, and it is incompletely defined in that the equation only determines its differential, and the constant of integration is arbitrary. On the other hand, the η̄ in the statistical equation has been completely defined as the average value in a canonical ensemble of systems of the logarithm of the coefficient of probability of phase.

We may also compare equation (112) with the thermodynamic equation:

-> dψ = − η̄ dT − A₁ da₁ − A₂ da₂ − etc., (117) <-

where ψ represents the function obtained by subtracting the product of the temperature and entropy from the energy.

How far, or in what sense, the similarity of these equations constitutes any demonstration of the thermodynamic equations, or accounts for the behavior of material systems as described in the theorems of thermodynamics, is a question of which we shall postpone the consideration until we have further investigated the properties of an ensemble of systems distributed in phase according to the law which we are considering. The analogies which have been pointed out will at least supply the motive for this investigation, which will naturally commence with the determination of the average values in the ensemble of the most important quantities relating to the systems, and to the distribution of the ensemble with respect to the different values of these quantities.

<summary>This page clarifies the difference between the arbitrary constant in thermodynamic entropy and the concrete statistical definition provided by Gibbs, while setting the stage for further investigation into these analogies.</summary>
<keywords>entropy, canonical ensemble, probability of phase, thermodynamics, statistical mechanics</keywords>

Or in the objective case, with the <term>ك</term> (like/as) implied; or in the nominative case, serving as the subject to <term>يضيء</term> (it shines), coordinate with <term>سناه</term> (its radiance); or connected to the implied word qualified by the <term>ك</term> in the preceding line.

74 <term>قعدت له وصحبتي بين ضارج .. وبين العذيب بعد ما متأملي</term>

"I sat down for it with my companions between Zárij and 'Uzaib after watching it [the lightning] attentively."

*   <term>صحبتي</term> (my companions, plural of <term>صاحب</term>) is in the nominative case, coordinate to the implied first-person pronoun in <term>قعدت</term> (I sat).
*   <term>ما</term> is an expletive (a filler word for emphasis), and <term>متأملي</term> (my observing) functions as a verbal noun.
*   <term>بعد ما متأملي</term> is also interpreted as: <term>بعد</term> is a shortened form of the past tense verb <term>بَعُدَ</term> (it was far); it means the cloud, the object of my earnest observation, was far away.

Another reading: <term>بُعْدَ</term> (distance) is in the objective case, treated as a vocative (<term>منادى</term>), with <term>يا</term> (O) implied. It means: "O, how great was the distance of the object of my earnest observation!"

75 <term>علي قطن بالشيم ايمن صوبر .. وايسره علي الستار فيذبل</term>

"In looking for the rain, we guessed that the right side of its downpour was over Qatan, while the left side of it was over Satár and beyond that upon Yazbul."

These locations are very far apart, highlighting the massive scale of the storm.
*   <term>علي قطن</term> (over Qatan), with <term>ايمن</term> (right side) implied.

Another reading: <term>عَلَيَّ قَطَنًا</term>. It then means: "As we guessed from observing the lightning and other signs of rain, its right-side downpour was over Qatan, etc."

*   <term>يذبل</term> (Yazbul) is <term>غير منصرف</term> (diptote), due to being a proper noun and having the form of a verb, but it is treated as <term>منصرف</term> (triptote) here due to the requirements of the rhyme.

76 فَأَضْحَى يَسِحُّ المَاءُ حَوْلَ كُثَيْفَةٍ .. يَكُبُّ عَلَى الأَذْقَانِ دَوْحَ الكَنَهْبُلِ

"The storm began to pour its waters around Kuthaifah, overturning the large Kanahbul trees upon their faces [the ground]."

*   <term>أَذْقَان</term> (plural of <term>ذَقَن</term>, literally 'a chin'). Here, it signifies the upper branches of the tree.
*   Another reading is <term>مِنْ كُلِّ دِيقَةٍ</term> (from what collects at each interval of raining); and also <term>مِنْ كُلِّ ثُلْعَةٍ</term> (from each watercourse).
*   <term>يَسِحُّ</term> (it pours) is the predicate after <term>أَضْحَى</term> (it became/commenced). <term>يَكُبُّ</term> (it overturns) is an adverbial sentence of state (<term>حَال</term>). The <term>الهاء</term> (pronoun) refers back to the verb.

77 وَمَرَّ عَلَى القَنَانِ مِنْ نَفَيَانِهِ .. فَأَنْزَلَ مِنْهُ العِصْمَ مِنْ كُلِّ مَنْزِلِ

"Then it passed over the hills of Qanán with such spray that it was so violent it forced the mountain goats to descend from every haunt."

*   He describes the violence of the storm.
*   <term>عِصْم</term> (plural of <term>أَعْصَم</term>) refers to a gazelle or mountain goat with white forelegs above the pastern, or a color distinct from the rest of its body.
*   Another reading of the first hemistich: <term>وَأَلْقَى بِبَيْسَانَ مَعَ اللَّيْلِ بُرْكَةً</term> = "It settled itself on Mount Busyán at night." <term>أَلْقَى بُرْكَةً</term> means it placed its chest down like a camel.
*   <term>بَيْسَان</term> (Busyán) is normally a diptote (<term>غَيْرُ مُنْصَرِف</term>), but used here as a triptote (<term>مُنْصَرِف</term>) by poetic license.

78 وَتَيْمَاءَ لَمْ يَتْرُكْ بِهَا جِذْعَ نَخْلَةٍ .. وَلَا أُطُمًا إِلَّا مُشَيَّدًا بِجَنْدَلِ

*   <term>تَيْمَاءَ</term> is the object of the verb. <term>لَمْ يَتْرُكْ</term> (it did not leave) is directed from the implicit subject to govern the verb. <term>هَا</term> refers back to it. <term>مُشَيَّدًا</term> (strengthened) is an adjective modifying <term>أُطُمًا</term> (building).

# THE SECOND POEM.

Ascribed to Tarafah, son of 'Abd-il-Bakrí, from the tribe of Bakr-ibn-Wáil. "Tarafah" is his title; his name is 'Amr-bin-ul-'Abd. He was one of the poets of the Pagan era, living after the time of Malik-ul-Zilleel, the author of the first Qasidah.

Legend says that the poet's brother, Ma'bad, reproached him for neglecting their father’s camels to indulge in poetry. Ma'bad once asked, "Can your poetry recover the camels if they are lost?" Tarafah insisted it could. To test him, Ma'bad neglected the camels, and they were taken by the tribe of Muzar. Tarafah wrote this poem, seeking assistance from 'Amru, Qáboos, and a Yemeni chieftain, and successfully recovered the camels, plus a hundred more as a reward.

The meter is the second form of <term>الطويل</term> (Al-Tawil), the same as the first poem; the rhyme (<term>قافية</term>) is also the same.

[Table of prosody for the first line]

1 لِخَوْلَةَ أَطْلَالٌ بِبَرْقَةِ ثَهْمَدِ .. تَلُوحُ كَبَاقِي الْوَشْمِ فِي ظَاهِرِ الْيَدِ

"There are traces of Kholah [his mistress] in the stony plain of Thahmad, which appear like the remains of tattooing on the back of the hand."

<summary>This page introduces the second Qasidah by Tarafah, providing biographical background and the circumstances of the poem's composition regarding the lost camels.</summary>
<keywords>Tarafah, 'Abd-il-Bakrí, Bakr-ibn-Wáil, Qasidah, Al-Mu'allaqat, Kholah</keywords>
pages.61:
Kholah is the name of his mistress. Traces refer to the ruins left near a former encampment of her tribe, as in the first poem.
*   <term>خولة</term> (Kholah) is read with a <term>فتحة</term> (a-vowel), acting as a diptote (<term>غير منصرف</term>) due to being a feminine proper noun.
*   <term>أطلال</term> (traces) is the subject (<term>مبتدأ</term>); <term>لخولة</term> (for Kholah) is the predicate.
*   <term>تلوح</term> (they appear) is an adjectival sentence modifying <term>أطلال</term>.

In some manuscripts, the second hemistich is:
> ظَلَلْتُ بِهَا أَبْكِي وَأَبْكِي إِلَى الْغَدِ = "Where I remained weeping and causing others to weep until the next day, due to memories of the past."

2 وَقُوفًا بِهَا صَحْبِي عَلَيَّ مَطِيَّهُمْ .. يَقُولُونَ لا تَهْلِكْ أَسًى وَتَجَلَّدِ

"My comrades, stopping their camels near me there, say, 'Do not die of grief, but bear it bravely.'"

This is a notable example of <term>التوارد</term> (coincidental similarity). Both poets, Imraul-Qais and Tarafah, happened to write the same line independently, differing only in the rhyme. It is said Tarafah had to prove he wrote the line on the same day as Imraul-Qais, but in a different place, to avoid accusations of plagiarism.

3 كَانَ حُدُوجَ الْمَالِكِيَّةِ غُدْوَةً .. خَلايَا سَفِينٍ بِالنَّوَاصِفِ مِنْ دَدِ
4 عَدُولِيَّةٌ أَوْ مِنْ سَفِينِ بْنِ يَامِنٍ .. يَجُورُ بِهَا الْمَلَّاحُ طَوْرًا وَيَهْتَدِي

"As if the Málikian camels, with the howdahs [litters] on the morning of her departure in the water-tracts of Dad, were the big ships of 'Adoal or the vessels of Ibni Yámin, which the sailors at times steer off course and at times guide straight."

<summary>This page analyzes the opening lines of Tarafah's poem, discussing the theme of lost love and the metaphorical comparison of camel litters to ships.</summary>

*   <term>حُدُوج</term> (howdahs, plural of <term>حِدْج</term>, a camel litter for women) is in the objective case, serving as the subject (<term>اسم</term>) after <term>كان</term> (as if); the predicate is <term>خلايا</term> (ships), which is in the nominative.
*   The phrase <term>بالنواصف من دد</term> relates to <term>حدوج</term>, not <term>سفين</term>.
*   <term>عدولية</term> is in the genitive case, acting as an adjective for <term>سفين</term>.
*   <term>يجور بها</term>, etc., is an adjectival sentence describing the ships.

5 يَشُقُّ حُبَابَ المَاءِ حَيْزُومُهَا .. كَمَا قَسَمَ التُّرْبَ المُفَايِلُ بِاليَدِ

"Their bows cleave the ripples of the sea, just as the divider of the sand heaps separates the dust with his hand."

*   <term>المفايِل</term> (the divider) acts as the agent of the action. This refers to the game of <term>فَيَال</term>, where a small object (like a coin) is hidden in sand, and the "divider" separates the sand into heaps to find it.
*   This line is an example of <term>الايطاء</term> (Al-Ita'), a defect where the same rhyming word (<term>اليد</term>) is repeated within nine lines.

6 وَفِي الحَيِّ أَحْوَى يَنْفِضُ المَرِدَ شَادِنٌ .. مُظَاهِرَ سِمْطَيْ لُؤْلُؤٍ وَزَبَرْجَدِ

"And in the tribe there is one like a young gazelle, with deep-colored lips, shaking the Arák tree for fruit, while wearing double strings of pearls and emeralds."

*   The standard word order is: <term>وفي الحي شادن احوى ينفض المرد</term>.
*   <term>مظاهر</term> (wearing) and <term>خذول</term> (next line) are adjectives modifying <term>شادن</term> (gazelle).

7 خَذُولٌ تَرَاءَى رَبْرَبًا بِخَمِيلَةٍ .. تَدَاوَلُ أَطْرَافَ البَرِيرِ وَتُؤْدِي

"A doe who has left her young and is grazing with a herd in a lush thicket, turning over the Arák berries and walking slowly."

suggest that an advance in the systematic study of mind is especially liable to be influenced by, and to mould itself upon, that body of more or less systematic physical knowledge, which bulks most impressively in the more thoughtful part of the society of that time and place. For the subject-matter of mental science is, as we know, not accessible to strictly collective observation; introspection is of the individual, and in the individual no two instances of a phenomenon can be shown as absolutely coincident. Hence it is largely, I do not say only, when some onward stride in physical science draws the rest of human knowledge in its wake, that the laws of mind are freshly investigated, as something that must also be brought into the line of march.

Where there is no such advance in psychical investigation, some system of dogmatic metaphysic is probably holding the cultured imagination of the age captive, through the spell of some myth of the Word. When the mind breaks free and looks deeper, there will naturally be a recourse, for its fresh concepts, to more positive ideas as guides and supports.

Now in the healing lore and craft of the day—the only one, I repeat, that comes prominently to the front in episode and in details of rules in the <term>Vinaya</term>—the revolt of thought embodied in the Buddhist movement

pages.98:
82 BUDDHIST PSYCHOLOGY

The word <term>dukkha</term> <note>Often translated as "suffering" or "ill," but implies a broader state of unsatisfactoriness.</note> covers all that is meant by "not well"—the ills and pains of the body, the ills and misery of the mind; in a word, *dis-ease*. Its presence is the doctor’s *casus belli* <note>original: "cause of war"</note> and *raison d'être* <note>original: "reason for being"</note>; its cause and extinction are his mission. While there may be several positive expressions for its absence, there is, alas, nothing else in life as mortally positive as *dukkha*. It is easy for many to conceive of its mere absence as sufficient for happiness. <term>Nibbana</term> <note>The state of liberation from suffering</note> itself, a quasi-negative term, was at times employed as "health" as well as "happiness." The Founder, in one of his most emphatic statements about his mission, expressed it as one of healing:

"Both then and now, just this do I reveal:
—*dukkha* and the extinction of *dukkha*." <note>Majjhima-Nikaya i. 509; Sutta-Nipata, verse 749.</note>

The physical healer finds the causes of disease in the mutual interaction of a person and their environment. Buddhism also found there the causes of everything that made for unhappiness. Sense impressions were the avenues through which satisfactions (*pasāda*) came, though they were fraught with peril. Consciousness, driven by its three main roots or conditions—greed (appetite), enmity, and delusion—reacted to its impressions through feeling, desire, and grasping after everything that tended toward the expansion and conceit of this "Me" and "Mine."
pages.99:
FEELING 83

Just as it behooved the physician to keep in view all possible sources of a disease—neglecting none—so was Buddhism searching and exhaustive in its treatment of the avenues of sense. It ignored none of the five that conveyed information, nor the sixth that coordinated and revived what the former brought.

Buddhism correctly discerned that the great intermediary between the (relatively) passive reactions to the manifold stimuli of sense and the subsequent, more deliberate reactions, was *Feeling*. This feeling might be pleasant, painful, or neither. It did not follow that where the feeling was pleasant (*sukha*), the symptoms of disease (*dukkha*) were absent. In fact, the *sukha* born of sense was the most efficient servant of *dukkha*, if *dukkha* is understood broadly as both physical and moral ill—and all that this involves regarding mental suffering and moral deterioration.

As Ledi Sadaw, the eminent *Thera* <note>Senior monk</note>, writes: "We must distinguish between *dukkha* of the category (or, in Buddhist terminology, the essential mark) of something unpleasant experienced via the senses—whether physical or psychological—and the *dukkha* we use in the triad: impermanence (*anicca*), ill, and non-soul (*an-atta*). By this *dukkha* we mean a state of peril and danger, lacking peace, security, or blessing." <note>Yamaka, ii. Appendix, p. 248 (London, Pali Text Society, 1913).</note>
pages.100:
84 BUDDHIST PSYCHOLOGY

This is the distinction a physician—or at least a patient—might draw between sensations of pain and the disease itself. The presence, growth, or decline of pain is not always accompanied by the presence, increase, or cessation of the disease. We must maintain this distinction throughout all Buddhist literature dealing with sense, feeling, and the effects of feeling. Otherwise, we will fall into significant inconsistencies of expression, as I shall demonstrate.

That feeling is the inevitable response to the awareness of new stimuli is affirmed throughout the <term>Nikayas</term> <note>The main collections of early Buddhist teachings</note>, notably in the *Samyutta-Nikaya* regarding the sphere of sense:

"Where there are hands, there taking and setting down appears; where there are feet, there coming and going appears; where there are limbs, there folding and stretching appears; where there is a stomach, there hunger and thirst appears. Just so, monks, where there is sight (or eye), or hearing... there arise subjective pleasure and pain, conditioned by sense-stimulus." <note>Samyutta-Nikaya iv. 171.</note>

The converse is then stated for both the analogies and the analogues: "...Where there is no sight, etc., neither pleasure nor pain, conditioned by sense-stimulus, arises."
pages.101:
FEELING 85

This quotation is conclusive enough to represent all other passages stating that sensations and feelings coexist, understood much as our modern psychology of sense understands pleasure and unpleasure. That the senses convey pleasure as well as its opposite is not only allowed and affirmed by doctrinal teaching, but this pleasure is also recognized as very genuine and good by the most eminent of the teachers. The Founder affirmed at times that no one lived more at ease (*sukham seti*) than he, despite having forsworn most of the so-called "good things" of life. His chief apostles gathered with him one fine evening in the Gosinga Wood, delighting in the "divine perfumes" of the dewy, moonlit scene, where the tall *sal*-trees stood clad in golden bloom. Temperance was prescribed for maintaining the physical comfort of health.

However, when the disciple is told to look upon *sukha* as <term>dukkha</term>, then we know that the wider concept is to be understood. 

<note>I owe the term 'unpleasure', borrowed from German science, to my university colleague, Mr. T. H. Pear.</note>
pages.102:
86 BUDDHIST PSYCHOLOGY

This is also the case when things unpleasant to the "average sensual man" are valued by a different scale and are held to constitute a higher pleasure:

"Things seen and heard, tastes, odours, what we touch,
Perceive, all, everything desirable,
Pleasant and sweet, while one can say 'It is,'
These are deemed *Sukha* by both gods and men,
And where these cease to be, they hold it woe.

What other men call *Sukha*, that the saints
Call *Dukkha*; what the rest so name,
That do the <term>Ariyans</term> <note>The Noble ones, those who have attained spiritual realization</note> know as happiness.
Behold a norm that’s hard to apprehend!
Hereby are baffled they that are not wise." <note>Sutta-Nipata, verse 759 f.; cp. Samyutta-Nikaya iv. 127.</note>

If we do not wish to be baffled, we must read those passages wherein each sense is declared to be *dukkha* with this wider implication. If, using Ledi Sadaw’s definition, we read into such passages as "seeing... is sorrow" the wider sense of *dukkha*, it becomes:

"The eye, brother, is a faculty of peril and danger, bringing, as such, no peace, security, or blessing; it is to understand this that the holy life under the Exalted One is lived."

If we do this, we may not be unwilling to admit the truth of this "monkish" statement, even for laypeople.
pages.103:
CHAPTER V

THE PSYCHOLOGY OF THE NIKAYAS—continued

IV. IDEATION

The systematic analysis of the mind in the *Nikayas* is pursued no further than the recipient and coordinating work of *mano* <note>The mind or 'sense-center'</note> acting as a *sensus communis* <note>original: "common sense/shared faculty of perception"</note>. Sequences in consciousness are occasionally pursued further, but without much terminological consistency. Here are a few instances:

"Because of some tendency, there arises perception, opinion, thinking, volition, wish, aspiration. And according as the tendency is low, mediocre, or lofty, so will all these be." <note>Samyutta-Nikaya ii. 153; see Commentary.</note>

The process of religious conversion is described as one of "hearing, attending, remembering, comparing, discerning, desire, zeal, pondering, endeavour." <note>Majjhima-Nikaya i. 480; ii. 173.</note>

"Thinking results in desire; through desire, objects are divided into what we like and what we dislike, hence envy and selfishness, hence quarrelling and fighting." <note>Digha-Nikaya ii. 278 f. (condensed).</note>
pages.104:
88 BUDDHIST PSYCHOLOGY

"Conditioned by contact arises feeling; what one feels, one perceives; what one perceives, one thinks about; what one thinks about, one is obsessed with." <note>Majjhima-Nikaya i., iii.</note>

These samples reveal the persistent effort in the <term>Suttas</term> <note>Buddhist discourses</note> to continue the method—systematically observed in the treatment of sense—of setting forth mind and character as an orderly, causal process. This method is emphatically Buddhist. The most notable example is the important formula of natural causation, exemplified by the process of life being bound up with *dukkha*. In the mental process, the resolution of receptive consciousness into discharging consciousness is clearly affirmed. Sense and feeling, stirred by sense, are converted into motor presentations (such as desire). But we meet with no closer analysis of the intellectual process—what has been called representative cognition, or ideation, in our own psychology. In the last sample, we only hear that "what we perceive," i.e., notice (*sañña-khandha*), we "think about" (*vitakketi*).

<summary>This section explores the Buddhist psychological view of 'feeling' (vedana) as an intermediary between sense-stimuli and deliberate reactions, distinguishing between sensory pain and the broader state of 'dukkha' (unsatisfactoriness), while also introducing the causal mental processes involved in ideation.</summary>
<keywords>Feeling, Dukkha, Sense-stimulus, Psychology, Nikayas, Ideation, Mind, Causality</keywords>

<margin>16</margin> Therefore, let us set aside these declamations:
> "A mind in the bonds of drunkenness is not in its own control. Just as vats are burst by new wine, and the heat of fermentation forces everything that lies at the bottom to the top; so, when wine effervesces, whatever lies hidden at the bottom is brought up and revealed to the world. Just as those who are heavy with wine cannot keep down their food when they have overindulged, so they cannot keep a secret either. They pour out their own <margin>17</margin> and others' secrets alike." But although this often happens, it is also common for us to deliberate on necessary matters with those whom we know to drink more freely. Therefore, this proposition—which is set forward in the place of a defense—that secrets cannot be entrusted to one who is accustomed to getting drunk, is false.

How much better it is to openly accuse drunkenness and expose its vices, which even a tolerable person would avoid, much less a perfect and wise man, who is satisfied with quenching his thirst, and who, even if at times he is led a bit further by cheerfulness induced by another's company, yet resists before he reaches <margin>18</margin> drunkenness. For we shall consider later whether the mind of a wise man is disturbed by too much wine and performs the acts typical of drunks; in the meantime, if you want to prove that a good man should not get drunk, why use syllogisms? Say how base it is to pour more into oneself than one can hold, and not to know the measure of one's own stomach, how many things drunks

So let us abolish all such harangues as this: "No man in the bonds of drunkenness has power over his soul. As the very vats are burst by new wine, and as the dregs at the bottom are raised to the surface by the strength of the fermentation; so, when the wine effervesces, whatever lies hidden below is brought up and made visible. As a man overcome by liquor cannot keep down his food when he has over-indulged in wine, so he cannot keep back a secret either. He pours forth impartially both his own secrets and those of other persons." This, of course, is what commonly happens, but so does this—that we take counsel on serious subjects with those whom we know to be in the habit of drinking freely. Therefore this proposition, which is laid down in the guise of a defence of Zeno's <note>Zeno of Citium, founder of Stoicism</note> syllogism, is false—that secrets are not entrusted to the habitual drunkard.

How much better it is to arraign drunkenness frankly and to expose its vices! For even the middling good man avoids them, not to mention the perfect sage, who is satisfied with slaking his thirst; the sage, even if now and then he is led on by good cheer which, for a friend's sake, is carried somewhat too far, yet always stops short of drunkenness. We shall investigate later the question whether the mind of the sage is upset by too much wine and commits follies like those of the toper; but meanwhile, if you wish to prove that a good man ought not to get drunk, why work it out by logic? Show how base it is to pour down more liquor than one can carry, and not to know the capacity of one's own stomach; show

Even now it is not less, but shorter. Recall the example of Alexander of Macedon, who stabbed Clitus, his dearest and most loyal friend, during a banquet, and upon realizing the crime, wished to die—he certainly ought to have.

Drunkenness both inflames and reveals every vice, removing the sense of shame that hinders evil attempts. For more men abstain from forbidden things out of shame of sinning than from good will. When an excessive amount of wine has taken possession of the mind, whatever evil lay hidden emerges. Drunkenness does not create vices, but draws them out; at that time, the lustful person does not even wait for the bedroom, but yields to his desires as much as they demand without delay; at that time, the unchaste person proclaims and publishes his malady; at that time, the petulant person restrains neither his tongue nor his hand. Arrogance grows in the insolent, cruelty in the savage, malice in the spiteful. Every vice is loosened and comes forth. Add to this the ignorance of oneself, the hesitant and unclear words, the shifting eyes, the staggering gait, the dizziness of the head, and the buildings themselves seeming to move as if some whirlwind were spinning the whole house, and the torment of the stomach when the wine effervesces and distends the very bowels. For more men abstain from forbidden actions because they are ashamed of sinning than because their inclinations are good. When the strength of wine has become too great and has gained control over the mind, every lurking evil comes forth from its hiding-place. Drunkenness does not create vice, it merely brings it into view; at such times the lustful man does not wait even for the privacy of a bedroom, but without postponement gives free play to the demands of his passions; at such times the unchaste man proclaims and publishes his malady; at such times your cross-grained fellow does not restrain his tongue or his hand. The haughty man increases his arrogance, the ruthless man his cruelty, the slanderer his spitefulness. Every vice is given free play and comes to the front. Besides, we forget who we are, we utter words that are halting and poorly enunciated, the glance is unsteady, the step falters, the head is dizzy, the very ceiling moves about as if a cyclone were whirling the whole house, and the stomach suffers torture when the wine generates gas and causes our very bowels to swell.

Consider what disasters public drunkenness has caused; it has betrayed the most spirited and warlike nations to their enemies; it has opened gates defended by the persistent <gloss>tenacious</gloss> warfare of many years; it has forced the most defiant, who rejected the yoke, into the power of others; it has conquered in the field those who were invincible by the wine-cup. Alexander, whom I just mentioned—whom so many marches, so many battles, so many winters through which he had passed by overcoming the difficulties of time and place, so many rivers falling from unknown sources, so many seas, had kept safe—intemperance in drinking and that famous death-dealing cup <gloss>a</gloss> finished off.

What glory is there in taking much? When the victory is yours and others are lying on the floor asleep or vomiting and refusing your toasts, when you have survived the entire banquet, when you have defeated everyone with your magnificent strength and no one was so capable of holding wine as you—you are defeated by the cask. However, at the time, these troubles can be endured, so long as the man retains his natural strength; but what can he do when sleep impairs his powers, and when that which was drunkenness becomes indigestion?

Think of the calamities caused by drunkenness in a nation! This evil has betrayed to their enemies the most spirited and warlike races; this evil has made breaches in walls defended by the stubborn warfare of many years; this evil has forced under alien sway peoples who were utterly unyielding and defiant of the yoke; this evil has conquered by the wine-cup those who in the field were invincible. Alexander, whom I have just mentioned, passed through his many marches, his many battles, his many winter campaigns (through which he worked his way by overcoming disadvantages of time or place), the many rivers which flowed from unknown sources, and the many seas, all in safety; it was intemperance in drinking that laid him low, and the famous death-dealing bowl of Hercules <note>Lipsius quotes Athenaeus as saying that Boeotian silver cups of large size were so called because the Boeotian Hercules drank from them.</note>.

26 Cruelty usually follows wine-bibbing; for the health of the mind is corrupted and exasperated. Just as long-term illnesses make people querulous and difficult <note>1</note>, and drive them to madness at the slightest provocation <note>2</note>, so continuous drunkenness makes spirits savage. # JATAKACHUNDRILA.

[They] join the *Dasanathas* (lords of the major periods) and produce indifferent results. Powerful planets that are not in conjunction with the lords of *Dasas* (major periods) that are evil produce very unfavorable results.

Planets that are capable of giving *Yogam* (favorable planetary combination) and are not connected with the lords of the *Dasas* will give good results in their sub-periods during such *Dasas*.

->NOTES.<-

The idea seems to be repeated here, perhaps to emphasize the point, as the author places great stress on it. However, the author draws a fine distinction. He differentiates between good planets (*Shubhagrahas*) and planets described as powerful or *yoga karakas* (planetary path-makers). The latter term suggests that planets that are not naturally good, but become powerful through association or other means, are called *yoga karakas*. *Guru* (Jupiter), *Sukra* (Venus), *Poornachundra* (the full Moon), and well-associated *Buda* (Mercury) are called *Shubhagrahas*. However, when they are debilitated, poorly associated, or occupying evil houses, they produce evil and can be termed evil planets. There is also a general classification of "evil" planets applied to *Kuja* (Mars), *Ravi* (the Sun), *Sani* (Saturn), poorly associated *Buda* (Mercury), and *Kshinachundra* (the waning Moon) along with *Ravi* and *Kethu*. These may produce good or bad results depending on whether they own good or evil houses, their combinations with other planets, and their exaltation or debilitation. Therefore, *Shubhagrahas* are distinct from *Yogakarakas*.

This distinction must be kept in mind, as the *Phalam* (results) to be predicted depends largely on these considerations. *Sani*, for instance, can own the 9th and 10th houses and thus become very powerful; if he is also exalted and well-associated, he will produce splendid results. The same applies to any other evil planet. In such circumstances, he is called a *yogakaraka* planet rather than a *Shubhagraha*. If *Guru* owns the 8th and 11th houses, he becomes evil and produces bad results. The author seems to contemplate three distinct cases in the treatment of *Dasas* (major periods) and *Bhookties* (sub-periods): (1) Where the lords of the periods are evil and the lords of the sub-periods are favorable but not in conjunction, the result will be unfavorable. (2) Where they join the lords of the periods, they produce indifferent results. (3) Where the lords of the sub-

## NOTES.

Two combinations are contemplated here, which must be kept in mind. First, we must determine which planet is the most likely to inflict death (*Maraka*), and then, if his major period (*Dasa*) is long, we must determine in whose sub-period (*Bhookti*) death is caused. Life is the most important concern, so longevity must be considered and determined first. Only then can other results be predicted. Prospects in life have no value if we do not know the span of our existence. The author states that during the *Dasa* of the *Maraka* planet, the *Bhookti* of a favorable planet in conjunction with him does not produce death, but the *Bhookti* of an evil planet not in conjunction with the *Dasanatha* will cause certain death. The question may arise: does the *Bhookti* of an evil planet in conjunction with the *Maraka Dasanatha* produce death or favorable results? It appears that the periods and sub-periods of even the worst planets, when in conjunction with each other, do not inflict as much evil as when they are not in conjunction. Therefore, there is a protective element in the act of combination that students of astrology should not overlook. I have already discussed the results of the sub-periods of favorable planets when they are not in conjunction with the planet governing the current period.

## NOTES.

These two planets have a peculiar affinity and produce good or evil in an intense form inversely in their *Dasas* and *Bhookties*. If *Sani* (Saturn) is good and his *Dasa* governs a person, the *Bhookti* of *Sukra* (Venus), when well-disposed, produces excellent results. The author notes that even if other *Bhookties* are equally favorable, they will not produce such splendid results as *Sukra*. Thus, in the *Dasas* of *Sani* and *Sukra*, and their intervening sub-periods, the greatest fortune may be expected if they are favorably placed. Regardless of the planets' occupations or associations, *Sani* and *Sukra* produce more intense effects during their periods and sub-periods than any other pair. The author has led us deep into astrology, showing through brief but expressive stanzas the principles guiding the creature's life. ### STANZA XLI Mesha—Aries.

A person born in ***Mesha Lagna*** (Aries rising at birth) finds ***Sani*** (Saturn), ***Buda*** (Mercury), and ***Sukra*** (Venus) ill-disposed. ***Guru*** (Jupiter) and ***Ravi*** (the Sun) are auspicious. The simple combination of ***Guru*** and ***Sani*** produces no beneficial results.

### NOTES.

The author draws attention to three important points for someone born when <term>Mesha</term> is rising. <term>Sukra</term> (Venus) rules the 2nd and 7th houses, <term>Buda</term> (Mercury) rules the 3rd and 6th, and <term>Sani</term> (Saturn) rules the 10th and 11th. It has been established that the lords of the 3rd, 6th, 8th, 11th, and 12th houses are bad. Therefore, Buda, ruling the 3rd and 6th for an Aries native, is evil. Sukra owns the 2nd and 7th; good planets owning quadrants are often considered evil, and the 7th is a quadrant. Sani owns the 10th and 11th—the 11th is bad, but the 10th (a quadrant) owned by an evil planet like Sani is good.

### **STANZA XLII.**

But, on the other hand, *Guru* (Jupiter), when combined with *Sani* (Saturn), not only fails to give good results but will actively produce evil. *Sukra* (Venus) does not himself kill the <term>native</term>, even though he possesses death-inflicting powers.

### **NOTES.**

It was noted (Stanza 41) that *Guru*, being the lord of the 9th and 12th houses, possesses both good and bad qualities.

In the combination of *Sani* and *Guru*, the author warns us not to expect good results, stating instead that their combination will be evil, particularly on the part of *Guru*. Let us take an example. A planet has good and evil influences. If a planet is capable of producing one rupee's worth of good and one rupee's worth of evil, the influence is neutral—the good cancels the evil. However, astrological writers suggest that the result is not neutral but actually bad. They hold that when good and evil influences are equal, we must predict evil, albeit in a milder form. This explains why *Guru* is bad in combination with *Sani*. *Guru* owns the 9th and 12th houses; the 12th for *Guru* and the 11th for *Sani* are evil houses. Here, the evil is equal to the good these planets possess. While the combination is bad, why is *Guru* specifically declared to be the source of evil? *Guru* is an auspicious planet by nature, and evil influences affect him more deeply; *Sani* is an evil planet, and good influences improve him. *Guru* has an evil association—being in conjunction with *Sani*. Because of this, *Guru* is declared to produce evil. *Sani*, however, has a better prospect; his position is improved by being in conjunction with *Guru*, a naturally good planet.

### STANZA XLIII.

Evil planets like *Sani* (Saturn) and others will cause the person's death. Carefully find the good and bad results that might happen to a person born in *Mesha* (Aries) by referring to the principles of astrology.

### NOTES.

In the previous stanza, we pointed out that when *Guru* and *Sani* combine, *Guru* inflicts evil. Now, we must determine who will kill the <term>native</term>. The author says, "Evil planets like *Sani*, etc." He mentions *Sani* first, and includes *Buda* (Mercury) and occasionally *Chundra* (the Moon). *Buda* is bad as he owns the 3rd and 6th houses. *Chundra* is the lord of the 4th; if full, he is classified as good, and his ownership of a <term>quadrant</term> is bad—he may produce death through evil combinations. If he is weak, his ownership of the quadrant is auspicious, and he will do good. These are the planets who determine the death of a person born while <term>Mesha</term> is rising. ### 5.

HISTORY OF ARAB MUSIC.

The early Arab musicians were possibly of the wandering minstrel type, like the "Calenders" we read of in the "Arabian Nights." Such at first was Mabed, one of the most famous of the early Arab musicians. Similar to the Western minstrels, they were as much poets as musicians. "This," says Lane,* "was sufficient to satisfy a people passionately fond of poetry, whose first object is to understand the meaning of the verses which are chanted." Indeed, the song in these days, says Christianowitch,† was a sort of recitative with a light refrain Thus the music of the Arabs, bound in subjection to the words, would necessarily make slow progress. Then again, it is clear from the teachings of Mahomet that music was *tabu*, at any rate as regards

---

† Christianowitch, "Enquisse Historique," etc.
