pages.275:
on anyone but himself. It would be barely reasonable to dispute such a position were it not necessary to show occultists the real messages of the Kabalah on points with which they are concerned. Now, modern students of occult philosophy everywhere reject with disdain the doctrine of vicarious atonement. Let us pass to the question of Messianic atonement, concerning which it is said in the *Vision of the Faithful Shepherd*:

> "This is also exemplified in the history of Job. For the Holy Blessed One, seeing that the entire foundation was sinful, and how Satan appeared to accuse them, said to Him, 'Hast thou considered my servant Job, that there is none like him in the earth' (Job 1:8), to save his generation through him?"

This may be illustrated by the parable of a shepherd who beheld a wolf approaching to rend his sheep and destroy them. What did this shepherd do? Being wise, he gave the wolf the strongest and stoutest bell-wether <note>The leading ram of a flock.</note>, even that which the flock was accustomed to follow; and while the wolf was bearing it away, the shepherd hurried with his sheep to a place of safety, and then, returning, rescued the bell-wether from the wolf. So does the Holy Blessed One deal with a generation: He surrenders a righteous man into the power of the accuser for the salvation of the generation through him. But when such a one is strong like Jacob, it is said, "A man wrestled with him" (Genesis 32:24). But he (Satan) will be unable to prevail, and in the end he will supplicate the righteous man to release him (Ibid. 26), for the righteous man, chosen by the Holy Blessed One, is too strong for the evil one and bears the most
pages.276:
> cruel afflictions willingly for the redemption of his generation; whence also he is held as their savior, and the Holy Blessed One constitutes him shepherd over all the flock, to feed them in this world and to rule over them in the world to come.”*

The clumsy and inadequate parable which thus represents the Almighty fleeing from Satan as the shepherd flies from a wolf, and in accordance with which the just man is first compared to a bell-wether and afterwards to the shepherd of the flock, is something more than a literary failure. Theologians have, I believe, found some trouble in locating the accuser of Job, and it is perhaps most accurate to say with the poet that “He, too, is God’s minister.” However, the Zoharic commentary on Job makes him in most respects a match for the Almighty, who must have recourse to a stratagem in order to save His people. The Kabalah on the problem of evil is therefore, in this place, neither illuminating nor reassuring; it is, in fact, crass and childish. “The ancient pillars of the world [the intellectual luminaries of Israel] differ,” says the same disquisition, as to the nationality of Job. One affirms that he was a righteous Gentile who was chastised for the atonement of the world. At a certain time, Rabbi Hammarumnah met the prophet Elijah and said to him: How is it to be understood that the righteous man suffers while the wicked one has joy of his life? He answered, saying: The just man of few sins receives his punishment for these in this world, and hence it is that he suffers here; but the man whose sins are many, while his good deeds

In this instance, the Kabalah offers an explanation which, shallow though it be, is identical with that accepted by some sections of Christian theology, by which, however, it is applied more mischievously. Thus, not only the sporadic good actions of those who are habitually wicked, but all natural goodness, can find their reward only in this world. The Kabalah is not disfigured by methodized enormities of this kind. There are times also when it loses its grotesqueness for a moment, and by some not unhappy reference to Scripture, illustrates an elementary spiritual truth, as, for example, concerning the change necessary to sinners:

> "Those who are oppressed with sin need a change of place, a change of name, and a change in their actions, even as it was said to Abraham: 'Get thee out of thy country' (Genesis 12:1). Here is a change of place. And: 'Neither shall thy name any more be called Abram, but thy name shall be Abraham' (Genesis 17:5). Here is a change of name. A change of deeds: he changed from his former evil actions to good actions."†

The Christian mystic might develop the significance of this quotation in connection with the new name of the Apocalypse, the new name received in confirmation, ordination, and the monastic and conventual life. Such analogies, though suggestive, are of slender value; the change mentioned in the

Zohar has indeed no special mystical importance; it concerns only the initial fact of spiritual life.

We have seen in the fragments of the *Bahir* that the scriptural history of the Fall of man is disfigured rather than elucidated by Zoharic commentary. The consequences of the first sin are thus described in the *Faithful Shepherd*:

> “Come, see! Had Adam not sinned, man would have known not the taste of death before he ascended to the superior world, but having sinned he became acquainted with the taste of death before ascending to the world above. Through the sin of Adam, the rational spirit (*Ruach*) is separated from the body, which remains in this world. It has to cleanse itself in the river of fire (Daniel 7:10), to receive punishment, after which it goes up to the Garden of Eden, which is above the earth. There, other garments of light are prepared for it, in conformity with the appearance of the body in the present world; it is clothed therein, and therein is its habitation forever.”*

This passage is important because it shows that Jewish theosophy has nothing better to offer us than the old Biblical instruction that sin “brought death into the world and all our woes.” It is not our purpose here to question that doctrine, but simply to demonstrate that the *Zohar*, where it is intelligible, does not improve on accepted religious instruction.

It is said that the relation of the Shekinah to the other lights of creation is like that of the soul to the body, but *she*—for the divine manifestation is presented under a feminine aspect—"stands to the Holy Blessed One as the body stands to the soul." In this, of course, there is nothing profound; the Shekinah is the vestment of the Almighty. But the discourse of the *Faithful Shepherd* adds that all are one—that is, God is one with His manifestation. This may be illustrated by the much more interesting and spiritual doctrine of the Eucharist; the bread is the vestment of Christ, the mode of His manifestation in His Church, but Christ, by the hypothesis of the doctrine, is one with the veil which He assumes. It is otherwise in man, says the *Zohar*: "His body is earth, but the soul is called reason. The one is death, the other is life." This is the ascetic notion which modern occultism has agreed to reject. "But the Holy Blessed One is life, and the Shekinah also is life. Whence it is written: 'She [meaning the Shekinah, but the scriptural reference is to Wisdom] is a tree of life to them that can lay hold upon her'" (Proverbs 3:18). The Shekinah of Kabalism is not, however, merely the visible splendor which shone in the Holy of Holies. The *Faithful Shepherd* affirms that the Holy Blessed One is concealed in the mysteries of the *Thorah* <note>The Law; the Pentateuch.</note> and is known or manifested by the commandments, for these are His Shekinah and this is His image. <header>THE VILLAGE GODS OF SOUTH INDIA</header>

...and to avert epidemics and other calamities from the village, and to ward off the attacks of evil spirits.

Every village in South India is believed by the people to be surrounded by evil spirits, who are always on the watch to inflict diseases and misfortunes of all kinds on the unhappy villagers. They lurk everywhere, on the tops of palmyra trees, in caves and rocks, in ravines and chasms. They fly about in the air, like birds of prey, ready to pounce down upon any unprotected victim, and the Indian villagers pass through life in constant dread of these invisible enemies. So the poor people turn for protection to the guardian deities of their village, whose function it is to ward off these evil spirits and protect the village from epidemics of cholera, small-pox, or fever, from cattle disease, failure of crops, childlessness, fires, and all the manifold ills that flesh is heir to in an Indian village.

The sole object, then, of the worship of these village deities is to propitiate them and to avert their wrath. There is no idea of praise and thanksgiving, no expression of gratitude or love, no desire for any spiritual or moral blessings. The one object is to get rid of cholera, small-pox, cattle disease, or drought, or to avert some of the minor evils of life. The worship, therefore, in most of the villages, only takes place occasionally. Sometimes, as I have stated above, there are daily offerings made to the deity; but, as a rule, the worship is confined to one big sacrifice, which takes place once a year, or on the occasion of some special disaster or outbreak of disease. The general attitude of the villager towards his village deity is “Let sleeping dogs lie.” So long as everything goes on well and there is no disease afflicting man or beast, and no drought nor other great calamity, it seems safest to let her alone. But, when misfortune comes, it is a sign that she is out of temper, and it is time to take steps to appease her wrath.

I have dignified the periodical sacrifices to the village goddesses by the name of festivals. But the term is a misnomer. There is really nothing of a...

<vocab>South India, evil spirits, palmyra trees, guardian deities, cholera, small-pox, sacrifice, village goddesses, festivals</vocab>
pages.49:
festal character about them. They are only gloomy and weird rites for the propitiation of angry deities or the driving away of evil spirits, and it is very difficult to detect any traces of a spirit of thankfulness or praise. Even the term "worship" is hardly correct. The object of all the various rites and ceremonies is not to worship the deity in any true sense of the word, but simply to propitiate it and avert its wrath. A brief description of the sacrifices and offerings themselves will make this clear. But I must premise that, as with the names, images, and shrines, so with the offerings and sacrifices, there is no law of uniformity: the variations of local use and custom are innumerable. Still, the accounts here given will provide a fair idea of the general type of rites and ceremonies prevalent throughout South India in the propitiation of village deities.

# CHAPTER IV

## MODES OF WORSHIP IN THE TELUGU COUNTRY

Let us suppose that an attack of cholera or small-pox has broken out in a village of South India. We will take a village in the Telugu country, in one of the more backward districts, where life is lived under more primitive conditions than in places where large towns, railways, and the influence of the Brāhmans <note>The highest priestly caste in the Hindu social hierarchy.</note> have tended to change old-fashioned ideas and customs.

*A Telugu Village.* The village deity, in this particular village, is called Peddamma, the "Great Mother." The epidemic is a sign that she is angry and requires to be propitiated. So, a collection is made for the expenses of a festival, or a rich man offers to pay all expenses, and a propitious day is selected—which in this village may be any day except Sunday or Thursday. Then, the potter of the village is instructed to make a clay image of the Great Mother, the carpenter is told to make a small wooden cart, and a buffalo is chosen as the chief victim for the sacrifice.

When the appointed day arrives, the buffalo is sprinkled all over with yellow turmeric,¹ while garlands of margosa <note>Also known as the Neem tree, considered sacred and purifying.</note> leaves are hung round its neck and tied to its horns. At about two p.m., it is conducted round the village in procession to the sound of music and the beating of tom-toms. The two sections of the Outcastes, the Mālās and the Mādigās, take the leading...

The potter then takes up the idol, carries it out of the house for a little distance, and gives it to a washerman, who carries it to the place where the canopy has been set up. During the procession, the people flourish sticks, swords, and spears to keep off the evil spirits, and, for the same purpose, cut limes in half and throw them up in the air. The idea is that the greedy demons will clutch at the golden limes and carry them off, and so be diverted from any attack on the man who carries the image.

In the first order, therefore, are the <term>pure elements</term>, which are neither composed, nor changed, nor do they suffer mixture; but they are <term>incorruptible</term>, and they are not things by which, but through which the virtues of all natural things are brought into effect. Their virtues can be explained by no one, because they can do all things in all things. Whoever is ignorant of this can arrive at no operation of miraculous effects. 

In the second order are the <term>composite elements</term>, which are multiple, varied, and impure, yet reducible through <term>art</term> to pure simplicity. When these have returned to their simplicity, they possess a virtue above all things, providing the completion of all hidden operations and the operations of nature: these are the foundation of all <term>natural magic</term>. 

In the third order are the <term>elements</term> which, primarily and in themselves, are not elements, but are varied <term>decomposed</term> [states], multiple, and mutually interchangeable. They themselves are the infallible <term>medium</term>, and therefore are called the media of Nature, or the <term>soul of the middle nature</term>. Few are they who understand their profound <term>mysteries</term>. In them, through certain numbers, degrees, and orders, is the consummation of every effect in whatever thing—natural, celestial, or super-celestial. They are wondrous and full of mysteries that can be worked in magic, both natural and...

<summary>This page defines three orders of elements: pure (incorruptible), composite (reducible by art), and the media of nature (the soul of the middle nature), which are foundational to natural magic.</summary>
<keywords>elements, natural magic, virtue, incorruptibility, occult operations</keywords>
pages.42:
...Divine: for through them the bindings of all things, as well as their dissolutions, transmutations, the knowledge and prediction of future events, and even the extermination of evil demons and the conciliation of good spirits descend. Without these triple elements, therefore, and the knowledge of them, let no one trust that they can work anything in the occult sciences of magic and nature. 

However, whoever knows how to reduce these into that, the impure into the pure, the multiple into the simple, and knows how to discern their nature, virtue, and power in number, degrees, and order without division of the substance: he will easily obtain the science and perfect operation of all natural and celestial secrets. This is he with the *black spaniel*: or rather, this is he <note>original: "Qui ab ineunte ætate semper circa mirabilium Effectuum, & plenas Mysteriorum operationes Curiosus, intrepidusque extitit Explorator."</note> [who from his early youth has always been a curious and fearless explorer of miraculous effects and operations full of mysteries]. 

Now for your further instruction, hear also the *dark disciple* of the more dark <margin>Johannes Trithemius</margin> *Libanius Gallus*. <note>original: "Primum principium in uno consistit, non a quo, sed per Quod omnis mirandorum naturalium virtus producitur in Effectum..."</note> [The first principle consists in the One, not from which, but through which every virtue of miraculous natural things is produced into effect: we say "through which," because the pure, proceeding from the One, is neither composed nor changed. To it, from the ternary and quaternary, the progression is made to the Monad, so that the denary may be completed...]

<summary>The author explains that all magical operations rely on the "triple elements" and cites Trithemius, asserting that mastering these principles is essential for understanding natural secrets.</summary>

pages.43:
[...the denary] is completed: for through it is the regression of the number to the One, at once a descent into four and an ascent into the *Monad*. It is impossible for the *denary* to be completed except through it: the *Monad* is joyfully converted into the *Triad*. All who are ignorant of this principle after the principle of the *Monad* do not profit in the *Ternary*, nor do they reach the sacred *Quaternary*. For even if they possess all the *books* of the sages, and perfectly know the courses, virtues, powers, operations, and properties of the stars, and fully understand their images, rings, and *seals* and everything most secret, they could nevertheless achieve no effect of wonders in their operations without the knowledge of this principle—from the beginning, into the beginning. 

Whence all whom I have seen working in *natural magic* have either achieved nothing, or, after long and useless operations, have collapsed into despair, turning to vain, frivolous, and superstitious things. The second principle, though separated from the first in order and not in dignity, which being one makes the *Ternary*, is that which works wonders through the *Binary*. For in the One there is one, and it is not one; it is simple, and it is composed in the *Quaternary*. When this is purified by *fire* in the sun, the pure *water* comes forth, and it, having returned to its simplicity, will show the complement of hidden things to the operator. This is the center of all *natural magic*, whose circumference...

<summary>Vaughan discusses the failure of those who study magic without understanding the fundamental principles (the Monad, Ternary, and Quaternary), warning that without this foundational knowledge, magical efforts result in vanity and despair.</summary>
<keywords>Ternary, Monad, Quaternary, Natural Magic, Magical operations, Trithemius</keywords>
pages.44:
...represented by the united circle, an immense order to infinity: its virtue is purified above all things, and simple, less than all things, composed on the quaternary degree. But the Pythagorean *Quaternary* number, supported by the *Ternary*, if it observes order and degree, being purified and pure in the One, can work the wonders and occult things of Nature into the *Binary* in the *Ternary*. This is the *Quaternary* in whose measure the *Ternary* joined to the *Binary* makes all things in the One, which it does miraculously. The *Ternary*, reduced to unity by inspection, contains all things in itself and can do what it wills. 

The third principle is not a principle by itself, but between it and the *Binary* is the end of all science and mystical art, and the infallible center of the medium: it is not easier to err in anything than in this, because very few live on Earth who understand its depths. It is a varied composite, rising through the septenary into the *Ternary* multiplied eight times, and remaining fixed. In it is the consummation of number, degree, and order: through this, all philosophers, true inquirers of the secrets of nature, have attained miraculous effects; through it, the miraculous cures of infirmities—and naturally of all sicknesses—suddenly occur as the *Ternary* is reduced to the simple element. And the work of the operator in natural and preternatural magic attains its effect through the disposition of the ternary.

<summary>This page continues the technical exposition of the three principles, focusing on the Quaternary, Binary, and the third principle which acts as the center for miraculous cures and the consummation of natural magic.</summary>
<keywords>Quaternary, Binary, Ternary, Natural Magic, Pythagorean, magical effects</keywords>
pages.45:
[...of the] ternary. The prediction of future events is verified through it, and the suggestion of hidden things is perceived from Nature nowhere else but through it. By this single medium, the secret of Nature is opened to the alchemists, without which neither the intellect of the Art is acquired nor the effect of the operation is found. It becomes an occupation of considerable interest and importance, therefore, to trace the occurrence of these various, but cognate phenomena in the historical records of all nations, ancient and modern; and with this object in view, we shall now proceed to examine the annals of the species, from the earliest period to the present time.

In the early memorials and traditionary history of the primitive Eastern nations, we find the most numerous instances of the manifestation of those peculiar states of the human organism, in which the phenomena of <term>somnambulism</term>, <term>ecstacy</term>, <term>clairvoyance</term>, <term>prophecy</term>, etc., are most prominently, most conspicuously, and most frequently developed. It was in the East, as we have already observed, that magic, in the best and most legitimate acceptation of the term, had its original seat; and, accordingly, it is to the Eastern regions that we must look for the earliest diffusion of that knowledge, divine and human, which it was the primary object of the science to cultivate. Now, there is one characteristic feature in these early records of the human race, which is peculiarly striking and remarkable. We allude to that intimate connection subsisting between science and theology, in consequence of which all human knowledge was rendered subservient to religious worship. This connection is con-

The natural states, which were conceived to be most favorable for the enjoyment of this divine intercourse, were sleep and dreams, somnambulism, and ecstasy.

In process of time, magic became distinguished into two kinds—the *theurgic* or celestial, and the *goetic*, or demoniacal; according as the devotee was supposed to invoke and do homage to the beneficent or to the malevolent being—to the Spirit of Light, or to the Spirit of Darkness—to God or the Devil. It appears, indeed, to have been almost universally held, in the most ancient times, that mankind were placed in intimate connection with a supersensible world, which was governed by the antagonist powers of a good and an evil principle; and that this connection between the sensible and the supersensible world was indirectly maintained through the means of intermediate agents, who were always ready to present their services at the summons of their respective votaries. The pure original idea of magic, as the profound study of nature, and of the power, wisdom, and benevolence of the Deity they worshipped, was gradually lost sight of; and the first of sciences, at length, degenerated into the practice of absurd and superstitious arts and brutalizing ceremonies—as may be observed even in many of the Jewish rites. Even so early as the time of Zoroaster, indeed, magic had begun to be thus deteriorated and abused, as appears from the books of the Zendavesta. Hence, as we have already observed, it ultimately came to be distinguished into the *white* and the *black* art. Even the Jews were with difficulty restrained from the evil practices of this corrupted science. Among the ancient Chaldeans, Medes, Persians, Bactrians, Babylonians, Hindoos, etc., magic was interwoven with their whole physical and intellectual philosophy, and combined with their religious worship and ceremonial observances; and the same combination may be traced in the construction of the Jewish Temple.

The most ancient theological books of the Hindoos, which by some learned men have been considered as the earliest profane records of the human race, are the *Vedas*, or the Brahminical revelations, and the Code of MENU. These books contain the theological notions of this very ancient and remarkable people, their philosophical doctrines, and a continual reference to those magical, or magnetic states of the soul, in which it was supposed to be separated from the body, and to hold immediate intercourse with the original source of all intelligence. These ancient doctrines, narratives, and expositions were, for a long time, regarded by the modern world as empty mystical fables, or, at most, as inscrutable mysteries or fanciful and extravagant inventions; until, in these later times, physiology, at length, afforded the means of a more adequate explanation of their true tenor and genuine purport; and a careful comparison with the recent

Smith, Jones, Brown, and Robinson are sitting with their hands on a table. All of them, *ex hypothesi* <note>original: "by hypothesis"</note>, are honorable men, “above suspicion of intentional deception.” They ask the table where Green is. Smith, Jones, and Robinson have no idea, but Brown firmly believes that Green is in Rome. The table begins to move, kicks, and answers—by the aid of an alphabet and knocks—that Green is at Machrihanish, where, upon investigation, he is proven to be. Later, Brown is able to show (let us hope by documentary evidence) that he had heard Green was going to Machrihanish instead of to Rome as he had intended; however, this remarkable change of plans on Green’s part had entirely faded from Brown’s memory. Now we are to assume, *ex hypothesi*, that Brown is the soul of honor and, like Mr. Facey Rumford <note>a character from a novel by R.S. Surtees, known for his stubborn honesty</note>, “wouldn’t tell a lie if it were ever so.” The practical result is that, while Brown’s consciousness informs him, trumpet-tongued, that Green is at Rome, “the residue of a forgotten impression” makes him (without his knowing it) wag the table, which he does not intend to do, and forces him to say through the tilts of the table that Green is at Machrihanish, while he believes that Green is at Rome.

The table-turners were laughed at, and many, if not all of them, deserved ridicule. But see how even this trivial superstition illuminates our knowledge of the human mind! A mere residue of a forgotten impression—a lost memory which Brown would have sworn in a court of justice had never been in his mind at all—can work his muscles while he supposes that they are *not* working, can

make a table move at which three other honorable men are sitting, and can tell all of them what none of them knows. Clearly, the practice of table-turning in court might be tried by conscientious witnesses who have forgotten the circumstances on which they are asked to give evidence. As Dr. Carpenter remarks, quoting Mr. Lecky, “our doctrine of unconscious cerebration <note>the theory that the brain performs intellectual work without the person being aware of it</note> inculcates toleration for differences not merely of belief, but of the moral standard.” And why not toleration for “immoral” actions? If Brown’s residue of an impression can make Brown’s muscles move a table to give responses of which he is ignorant, why should not the residue of a forgotten impression—that it would be a pleasant thing to shoot Mr. Gladstone or Lord Salisbury <note>prominent British politicians of the Victorian era</note>—make Brown unconsciously commit that solecism <note>a social blunder or mistake</note>? It is a question of degree. At all events, if the unconscious self can do as much as Dr. Carpenter believed, we cannot tell how many other marvels it may perform; we cannot know until we investigate further. If this is so, it is perhaps hardly wise or scientific to taboo all investigation. If a mere trivial drawing-room amusement, associated by some with an absurd “animistic hypothesis” <note>the belief that inanimate objects are imbued with life or spirit</note>, can, when explained by Dr. Carpenter, throw such unexpectedly blinding light on human nature, who knows how much light may be obtained from a research into more serious and widely diffused superstitious practices? The research is, undeniably, beset with the most thorny of difficulties. Yet whosoever agrees with Dr. Carpenter must admit that, after one discovery so singular as “unconscious cerebration” in its effect on tables, someone is bound

# INTRODUCTION.

to go further in the same field and try for more. We are assuming, for the sake of argument, the accuracy of Dr. Carpenter’s facts. ¹

More than twenty years ago, an attempt was made by a body called the “Dialectical Society” to investigate the phenomena styled spiritualistic. This well-meant essay had most unsatisfactory results. ²

First, a committee of inquiry was formed on the motion of Dr. Edmunds. The committee was heterogeneous. Many of the names now suggest little to the reader. We remember Mr. Bradlaugh, but he chiefly attended a committee which sat with D. D. Home <note>a famous 19th-century physical medium</note>, and it is admitted that nothing of interest occurred there. Then we find the Rev. Maurice Davies, who was wont to write books of little distinction on semi-religious topics. Mr. H. G. Atkinson was a person interested in mesmerism. Kisch, Moss, and Quelch, with Dyte and Isaac Meyers, Bergheim and Geary, Hannah, Hillier, Reed (their names go naturally in blank verse), were, doubtless, all most estimable men, but scarcely boast of scientific fame. Serjeant Cox, a believer in the phenomena (if not in their spiritual cause), was of the company, as was Mr. Jencken, who married one of the Miss Foxes—the first authors of modern thaumaturgy <note>the performance of miracles or magic</note>. Professor Huxley and Mr. G. H. Lewes were asked to join, but declined to march to Sarras, the spiritual city, with

the committee. This was neither surprising nor reprehensible, but Professor Huxley’s letter of refusal appears to indicate that matters of interest, and perhaps logic, are differently understood by men of science and men of letters. ¹ He gave two reasons for refusing, and others may readily be imagined by the sympathetic observer. The first was that he had no time for an inquiry involving much trouble and (as he justly foresaw) much annoyance. Next, he had no interest in the subject. He had once examined a case of “spiritualism” and detected an imposture. “But, supposing the phenomena to be genuine, they do not interest me. If anybody would endow me with the faculty of listening to the chatter of old women and curates in the nearest cathedral town, I should decline the privilege, having better things to do.” Thus, it would not interest Professor Huxley if some new kind of telephone should enable him to hear all the conversation of persons in a town (if a cathedral town) more or less distant. He would not be interested by the “genuine” fact of this extension of his faculties, because he would not expect to be amused or instructed by the contents of what he heard. Of course, he was not invited to listen to chatter, which, on one hypothesis, was that of the dead, but to help to ascertain whether or not there were any genuine facts of an unusual nature, which some persons explained by the animistic hypothesis. To mere “belletristic triflers” <note>those concerned with literature for its own sake rather than science</note>, the existence of genuine abnormal and unexplained facts seems to have been the object of inquiry, and we must peni-

tently admit that if genuine communications could really be opened with the dead, we would regard the circumstance with some degree of curious zest, even if the dead were on the intellectual level of curates and old women. Besides, not all old women are imbeciles; history records cases of a different kind, and even some curates are as intelligent as the apes whose anatomy and customs, about that time, much occupied Professor Huxley. In Balaam’s conversation with his ass <note>a reference to the biblical story in Numbers 22</note>, it was not so much the fact that *mon âne parle bien* <note>original: "my donkey speaks well"</note> which interested the prophet, as the circumstance that *mon âne parle* <note>original: "my donkey speaks"</note>. Science has obviously soared very high when she cannot be interested by the fact (if a fact) that the dead are communicating with us, apart from the value of what they choose to say.

However, Professor Huxley lost nothing by not joining the committee of the Dialectical Society. Mr. G. H. Lewes, for his part, hoped that with Mr. Alfred Russel Wallace to aid (for he joined the committee) and with Mr. Crookes (who apparently did not), “we have a right to expect some definite result.” Any expectation of that kind was doomed to disappointment. In Mr. Lewes’s own experience, which was large, “the means have always been proved to be either deliberate imposture... or the well-known effects of expectant attention.” That is, when Lord Adare, the Master of Lindsay, and a cloud of other witnesses thought they saw heavy bodies moving about of their own free will, either somebody cheated, or the spectators beheld what they did behold, because they expected to do so,
pages.44:
# COCK LANE AND COMMON-SENSE.

even when, like M. Alphonse Karr and Mr. Hamilton Aidé, they expected nothing of the kind. This would be Mr. Lewes's natural explanation of the circumstances, suggested by his own large experience.

The results of the Dialectical Society's inquiry were somewhat comic. The committee reported that marvels were alleged, by the experimental sub-committees, to have occurred. Sub-committee No. 1 averred that “motion may be produced in solid bodies without material contact, by some hitherto unrecognized force.” Sub-committees 2 and 3 had many communications with mysterious intelligences to vouch for, and much erratic behavior on the part of tables to record. No. 4 had nothing to report at all, and No. 5, which sat four times with Home, had mere trifles of raps. Home was ill, and the *séances* <note>meetings for communication with spirits</note> were given up.

So far, many curious phenomena were alleged to have occurred, but now Dr. Edmunds, who started the whole inquiry, sent in a separate report. He complained that convinced spiritualists had “captured” the editing sub-committee, as people say, and had issued a report practically spiritualistic. He himself had met nothing more remarkable than impudent frauds or total failure. “Raps, noises, and movements of various kinds,” he had indeed witnessed, and he heard wondrous tales from truthful people, “but I have never been able to see anything worthy of consideration, as not being accounted for by unconscious action, delusion, or imposture.” Then the editors of the *Report* contradicted Dr.

Home, by the Master of Lindsay (Lord Crawford), and by other witnesses who had seen Home grow eight inches longer and also shorter than his average height; fly in the air; handle burning coals unharmed; cause fragrance of various sweet scents to fill a room, and, in short, rival St. Joseph of Cupertino <note>a saint said to have had the power of levitation</note> in all his most characteristic performances. Unluckily, Mr. Home, not being in the vein, did not do one of these feats in the presence of Mr. Bradlaugh and sub-committee No. 5. These results are clearly not of a convincing and harmonious description, and thus ended the attempt of the Dialectical Society. Nobody can do otherwise than congratulate Professor Huxley and Mr. Lewes on their discreet reserve. The inquiry of the Dialectical Society was a failure;

# THE TALE OF GENJI 208

double doors at the end of the eastern wing were wide open, and the roof of the verandah having fallen in, the sunshine poured straight into the house. A little snow was still falling and its brightness made the morning light yet more exquisitely brilliant and sparkling. She watched a servant helping him into his cloak. She was lying half out of the bed, her head hanging a little downwards and her hair falling in great waves to the floor. Pleased with the sight he began to wonder whether she would not one day outgrow her plainness. He began to close the door of the women’s apartments, but suddenly feeling that he owed her amends for the harsh opinion of her appearance which he had formed before, he did not quite shut the door, but bringing a low stool towards it sat there putting his disordered head-dress to rights. One of the maids brought him an incredibly battered mirror-stand, Chinese combs, a box of toilet articles and other things. It amused him to discover that in this household of women a little male gear still survived, even in so decrepit a state.

He noticed that the princess, who was now up and dressed, was looking quite fashionable. She was in fact wearing the clothes which he had sent her before the New Year, but he did not at first recognize them. He began however to have a vague idea that her mantle, with its rather conspicuous pattern, was very like one of the things he had given her. ‘I do hope,’ he said presently, ‘that this year you will be a little more conversational. I await the day when you will unbend a little towards me more eagerly than the poet longs for the first nightingale. If only like the year that has changed you too would begin anew!’ Her face brightened. She had thought of a remark and trembling from head to foot with a tremendous effort she brought out the quotation ‘When plovers chirp and all things grow anew.’ ‘Splendid,’ said Genji, ‘This is a sign that the new year has indeed
pages.218:
begun,” and smiling encouragingly at her, he left the house, she following him with her eyes from the couch on which she lay. Her face, as usual, was half covered by her arm; but the unfortunate flower <note>Referring to the "Saffron-Flower," a nickname for the princess due to her prominent red nose.</note> still bloomed conspicuously. “Poor thing, she really is very ugly,” thought Genji in despair.

When he returned to the Nijō-in, he found Murasaki waiting for him. She was growing up to be as handsome a girl as one could wish, and she promised well for the future. She was wearing a plain, close-fitting dress of cherry color; above all, the unstudied grace and ease of her movements charmed and delighted him as he watched her come to meet him. In accordance with the wishes of her old-fashioned grandmother, her teeth were not blackened, but her eyebrows were delicately touched with stain. 

“Why, when I might be playing with a beautiful child, do I spend my time with an ugly woman?” Genji kept on asking himself in bewilderment while they sat together playing with her dolls. 

Next, she began to draw pictures and color them. After she had painted all sorts of queer and amusing things, “Now I am going to do a picture for you,” said Genji, and drawing a lady with very long hair, he put a dab of red on her nose. Even in a picture, he thought, pausing to look at the effect, it gave one a most uncomfortable feeling. He went and looked at himself in the mirror, and as though dissatisfied with his own fresh complexion, he suddenly put on his own nose a dab of red such as he had given to the lady in the picture. He looked at himself in the mirror. His handsome face had in an instant become ridiculous and repulsive. At first, the child laughed. 

“Should you go on liking me if I were always as ugly as this?” he asked. 

Suddenly, she began to be afraid that the paint would not come off. “Oh, why did you do it?” she cried. “How horrible!” 

He pretended to rub it without effect. “No,” he said ruefully, “it will not come off. What a sad end to our game! I
pages.219:
wonder what the Emperor will say when I go back to the Palace?” 

He said it so seriously that she became very unhappy, and longing to cure him, she dipped a piece of thick, soft paper in the water-jug which stood by his writing-things and began scrubbing at his nose. 

“Take care,” he cried, laughing, “that you do not serve me as Heichū <note>A famous Heian-period lover known for his dramatic gestures.</note> was treated by his lady. I would rather have a red nose than a black one.” 

So they passed their time, making the prettiest couple.

In the gentle spring sunshine, the trees were already shimmering with a haze of new-grown buds. Among them, it was the plum-trees that gave the surest promise, for already their blossoms were uncurling like lips parted in a faint smile. Earliest of them all was a red plum that grew beside the covered steps. It was in full color. 

“Though fair the tree on which it blooms, this red flower fills me with a strange misgiving,” <note>The reference, of course, is to the princess. "Though fair the tree" refers to her high birth.</note> sang Genji with a deep sigh.

We shall see in the next chapter what happened in the end to all these people.

# CHAPTER VII
# THE FESTIVAL OF RED LEAVES

The imperial visit to the Red Sparrow Court was to take place on the tenth day of the Godless Month <note>The tenth month of the lunar calendar, when the gods were believed to leave their shrines to congregate at Izumo.</note>. It was to be a more magnificent sight this year than it had ever been before, and the ladies of the Palace were very disappointed that they could not be present. <note>They were not allowed to leave the palace.</note> The Emperor, too, could not bear that Fujitsubo should miss the spectacle, and he decided to hold a grand rehearsal in the Palace. Prince Genji danced the “Waves of the Blue Sea.” Tō no Chūjō was his partner; but though both in skill and beauty he far surpassed the common run of performers, yet beside Genji, he seemed like a mountain fir growing beside a cherry-tree in bloom. There was a wonderful moment when the rays of the setting sun fell upon him and the music grew suddenly louder. Never had the onlookers seen feet tread so delicately nor head so exquisitely poised; and in the song which follows the first movement of the dance, his voice was sweet as that of the Kalavinka <note>The bird that sings in Paradise.</note> whose music is Buddha’s Law. So moving and beautiful was this dance that at the end of it, the Emperor’s eyes were wet, and all the princes and great gentlemen wept aloud. When the song was over and, straightening his long dancer’s sleeves, he stood waiting for the music to begin again and at last the more lively tune of the second movement struck up—then indeed,
pages.221:
with his flushed and eager face, he merited more than ever his name of Genji the Shining One. The Princess Kōkiden <note>The Emperor’s consort and Genji’s antagonist.</note> did not at all like to see her step-son’s beauty arousing so much enthusiasm, and she said sarcastically, “He is altogether too beautiful. Presently we shall have a god coming down from the sky to fetch him away.” <note>An allusion to a boy-prince of seven years old whom the jealous gods carried off to the sky, as recorded in the Ōkagami.</note> 

Her young waiting-ladies noticed the spiteful tone in which the remark was made and felt somewhat embarrassed. As for Fujitsubo, she kept on telling herself that were it not for the guilty secret which was shared between them, the dance she was now witnessing would be filling her with wonder and delight. As it was, she sat as though in a dream, hardly knowing what went on around her.

Now she was back in her own room. The Emperor was with her. “At today’s rehearsal,” he said, “The ‘Waves of the Blue Sea’ went perfectly.” 

Then, noticing that she made no response, “What did you think of it?” 

“Yes, it was very good,” she managed to say at last. 

“The partner did not seem to me bad either,” he went on; “there is always something about the way a gentleman moves and uses his hands which distinguishes his dancing from that of professionals. Some of our crack dancing-masters have certainly made very clever performers of their own children; but they never have the same freshness, the same charm as the young people of our class. They expended so much effort on the rehearsal that I am afraid the festival itself may seem a very poor affair. No doubt they took all this trouble because they knew that you were here at the rehearsal and would not see the real performance.”

Next morning she received a letter from Genji: “What of the rehearsal? How little the people who watched me knew of the turmoil that all the while was seething in my brain!”
pages.222:
And to this he added the poem: 

“When sick with love I yet sprang to my feet and capered with the rest, knew you what meant the fevered waving of my long dancing-sleeve?” 

Next, he enjoined secrecy and prudence upon her, and so his letter ended. Her answer showed that despite her agitation, she had not been wholly insensible to what had fascinated all other eyes: 

“Though from far off a man of China waved his long dancing-sleeves, yet did his every motion fill my heart with wonder and delight.”

To receive such a letter from her was indeed a surprise. It charmed him that her knowledge should extend even to the Court customs of a land beyond the sea. Already there was a regal note in her words. Yes, that was the end to which she was destined. Smiling to himself with pleasure, he spread the letter out before him, grasping it tightly in both hands as a priest holds the holy book, and gazed at it for a long while.

On the day of the festival, the royal princes and all the great gentlemen of the Court were in attendance. Even the Heir Apparent went with the procession. After the music-boats had rowed round the lake, dance upon dance was performed, both Korean and of the land beyond the sea. The whole valley resounded with the noise of music and drums. The Emperor insisted upon treating Genji’s performance at the rehearsal as a kind of miracle or religious portent, and ordered special services to be read in every temple. Most people thought this step quite reasonable; but Princess Kōkiden said crossly that she saw no necessity for it. The Ring <note>Those who stand in a circle round the dancers while the latter change their clothes.</note> was, by the Emperor’s order, composed indifferently of commoners and noblemen chosen out of the whole realm for their skill and grace. The two Masters of Ceremony, Sayemon no Kami and Uyemon no Kami, were
pages.223:
in charge of the left and right wings of the orchestra. Dancing-masters and others were entrusted with the task of seeking out performers of unusual merit and training them for the festival in their own houses. When at last, under the red leafage of tall autumn trees, forty men stood circle-wise with their flutes, and to the music that they made, a strong wind from the hills sweeping the pine-woods added its fierce harmonies, while from amid a wreckage of whirling and scattered leaves the Dance of the Blue Waves suddenly broke out in all its glittering splendor—a rapture seized the onlookers that was akin to fear.

The maple-wreath that Genji wore had suffered in the wind, and thinking that the few red leaves which clung to it had a desolate air, the Minister of the Left <note>Referring to the Sadaijin.</note> plucked a bunch of chrysanthemums from among those that grew before the Emperor's seat and twined them in the dancer's wreath.

At sunset the sky clouded over and it looked like rain. But even the weather seemed conscious that such sights as this would not for a long while be seen again, and till all was over not a drop fell. His Exit Dance, crowned as he was with this unspeakably beautiful wreath of many-colored flowers, was even more astonishing than that wonderful moment on the day of the rehearsal and seemed to the thrilled onlookers like the vision of another world. Humble and ignorant folk sitting afar on tree-roots or beneath some rock, or half-buried in deep banks of fallen leaves—few were so hardened that they did not shed a tear. Next came the 'Autumn Wind' danced by Lady Jōkyōden's son <note>Another illegitimate son of the Emperor; Genji’s step-brother.</note> who was still a mere child. The remaining performances attracted little attention, for the audience had had its fill of wonders and felt that whatever followed could but spoil the recollection of what had gone before.
pages.224:
That night Genji was promoted to the First Class of the Third Rank and Tō no Chūjō was promoted to intermediate standing between the First and Second Classes of the Fourth Rank. The gentlemen of the court were all promoted one rank. But though they celebrated their good fortune with the usual rejoicings, they were well aware that they had only been dragged in Genji's wake and wondered how it was that their destinies had come to be linked in this curious way with those of the prince who had brought them this unexpected piece of good fortune.

Fujitsubo now retired to her own house and Genji, waiting about for a chance of visiting her, was seldom at the Great Hall and was consequently in very ill favor there. It was soon after this that he brought the child Murasaki to live with him. Aoi <note>Genji’s wife.</note> heard a rumor of this, but it reached her merely in the form that someone was living with him at his palace, and she did not know that it was a child. Under these circumstances it was quite natural that she should feel much aggrieved. But if only she had flown into an honest passion and abused him for it as most people would have done, he would have told her everything and put matters right. As it was, she only redoubled her icy aloofness and thus led him to seek those very distractions of which it was intended as a rebuke. Not only was her beauty so flawless that it could not fail to win his admiration, but also the mere fact that he had known her since so long ago, before all the rest, made him feel toward her a tenderness of which she seemed quite unaware. He was convinced, however, that her nature was not at bottom narrow and vindictive, and this gave him some hope that she would one day relent.

Meanwhile, as he got to know little Murasaki better, he became the more content both with her appearance and her character. She at least gave him her whole heart. For the present, he did not intend to reveal her identity even to the

or that his semen enters the interior cavity of the matrix, is hardly likely; for I could find no path inside with a probe or a bristle, and it did not happen that Fabricius found any either. Indeed, by his own testimony, not even blown air penetrates the matrix. This was the reason, I believe, why he described the history of the matrix by progressing from the interior parts to the exterior. Furthermore, having weighed this structure of the matrix, he denies that the semen reaches the cavity of the matrix or constitutes any part of the egg. In this opinion I also willingly profess my name. Indeed, you will find nothing in a fertile egg (which is not found in an infertile one) either added or changed from which it might be certain that the rooster's semen had entered the matrix and touched the egg. Furthermore, although all eggs are vain and infertile without the rooster's union, yet by his labor (even some time after copulation) the subsequent eggs, of which there is no yet existing principle or matter, turn out fertile.

<margin>Page 37.</margin> Fabricius, in order to explain the manner by which the rooster's semen renders eggs fertile, has these words: *Since semen does not appear in the egg, and yet it is presented by the rooster into the matrix; it is asked, why the rooster's semen is sent into the matrix if it does not enter the egg? Likewise, if it is not present in the egg, how is a fertile egg produced from the rooster's semen, which it does not contain? My opinion is that the rooster's semen, sent into the beginning of the matrix, renders the entire matrix, and at the same time also all the yolks falling into it, and finally the whole egg, fertile; and that it does this by its own faculty, or by a radiating spiritual substance; in the way in which we see,*
pages.76:
<header>On the Generation of Animals.</header>

by witnesses, that other souls are also rendered fertile by semen. For if anyone recalls to memory that incredible transmutation by which an animal is affected when castrated, while it loses the fat, strength, and fertility in its whole body, he will easily grant that which we say happens to the womb of a hen alone. But that it is entirely true that the power of fertilizing eggs and also the womb proceeds from the semen of the rooster is evident from that which women do, having a hen at home deprived of a rooster; they send it to a rooster elsewhere for a day or two: for from this small amount of time the fertility of the juice of all the eggs [is provided] for the whole time of the year. This is what Aristotle also confirms, who holds that when birds have once mated, they persist in having almost all eggs fertile. Furthermore, that the fertilizing power of the semen might not in any way be able to exhale, but might persist longer in the womb and be imparted to the whole, nature itself enclosed and deposited it in a cavity, a bursa <note>an anatomical pouch or sac</note>, near the vent and attached to the womb, and endowed with an entrance so that, with the semen being detained therein, its power might be preserved and communicated to the entire womb.

I, however, suspected the truth of the aforesaid experiment, and the more so because I saw the words of the Philosopher <note>referring to Aristotle</note> recited in bad faith; for he did not say, *Birds, when they have once mated, persist in having almost all eggs fertile*, but, *they persist in having almost all eggs*; Fabricius added <term>to fæcunda</term> <gloss>as fertile</gloss> on his own. But it is one thing for birds to conceive eggs from coitus, and another for eggs to be fertilized from coitus. And that is from the

preceding words of Aristotle more clearly evident, where he says: *In the genus of birds, entirely, not even those eggs which arise through coitus can for the most part be increased, unless the bird's coitus is continued.* The reason for this matter is that, as in women through coitus the male draws out the menstrual excretion (for the warmed womb draws out the humor, and the passages are opened), so it happens in birds while the menstrual excretion gradually approaches, which cannot depart outward because it is little and is contained above at the girdle <note>referring to the narrow part of the oviduct</note>, but it collapses into the womb itself. For this egg is increased, just as the fetus of viviparous animals, because it flows through the navel. For when birds have once mated, they persist in having almost all eggs always, but very small and imperfect, and therefore infertile; if indeed the perfection of an egg is to be fertile. If, therefore, without continued coitus of the bird, not even those eggs which were conceived through coitus are increased, or (as Fabricius has interpreted) are perfected; much less will those eggs which birds persist in having without coitus be rendered fertile.

But lest anyone think that by these words (*for the warmed womb draws out, and the passages are opened*) it is concluded that the womb can draw the rooster's semen into its cavity, it should be known that it is not said by the Philosopher that the womb draws semen from outside; but in women, through veins and passages opened by heat, menstrual blood is drawn from their own body; and similarly in birds, blood is drawn to the womb warmed by continued coitus, and from thence the eggs are increased; just as the fetuses of viviparous animals are accustomed to be through the navel.

But what he adds concerning that cavity, or *bursa*, in which he presumes the rooster's semen is harbored for an entire year; these things have already been refuted by us before; where we asserted that no semen is contained in it, and that it is present in the rooster just as in the hen.

Wherefore, while I could easily believe (if by fertility we understand the production of more and larger eggs) that the hens of poor little women (for whom it is proven there is a lack of an abundance of feed) will produce fewer and smaller eggs unless they are with a rooster (according to that saying of the Philosopher: *But if they have once mated with a rooster, then they will persist in having larger, better, and more numerous eggs throughout the whole year.* To which end the abundance and quality of feed also contribute most). I thought, however, it seemed less likely to me that hens lay all eggs fertile for the whole span of a year from a few matings with a rooster. For if a few coitions were sufficient for such long-term generation, Nature (which does nothing in vain) would have made males in the avian genus less lustful; nor would the rooster so often daily solicit his hens for coitus, even against their will.

We know that a hen, as soon as she has laid an egg and leaves the nest, cries out with a clamorous voice and lures the rooster to coitus; who, responding in like manner with a raised and gasping voice, anxiously seeks her, and having found her, suddenly mounts her: which surely, Nature would not have willed to happen, except for the sake of procreation.

A male *pheasant*, kept in an aviary, is so
pages.79:
<header>EXERCISE VI.</header>

inflamed with intense lust that, unless he has many females (at least six) with him, he maltreats them by frequent repeated coitus, hindering fertility rather than promoting it. I once saw a female pheasant, because of a rooster kept with her (whom she could not avoid either by hiding or by fleeing), so exhausted, and bare of feathers on her back because of his frequent assaults, that at length, agitated in a miserable manner, she failed from sorrow. Yet in the same one, when dissected, I did indeed find the rudiments of eggs.

I also observed a male duck, lacking a mate and living with hens, inflamed with such lust that he would pursue a young hen everywhere for some hours, peck at her with his beak, and at last, when she was exhausted, mount her and perform the act of lewdness.

A rooster, victor in battle, exercises his lust not only on the mates of the defeated, but also on the living bird himself.

Similarly, some females are so inclined to lust that they peck at their males with little bites (as if they were whispering the joys of Venus into their ears), leap upon them, and invite them to coitus with other arts: in which number are pigeons and sparrows.

It does not seem likely, therefore, that a few coitions, celebrated at the beginning of the year, are sufficient for the fertility of all the subsequent eggs throughout its entire course. I, however, sometimes (in order to provide a defense for Fabricius here) in the spring season (intending to investigate something certain about the time and necessity of fertilizing coitus) kept two hens separated from the rooster for four days, which in the meantime each had laid three eggs, no less prolific than other eggs. And again I separated another hen, which on the tenth day from then laid an egg; and another on the twentieth day, and both were fertile. So that it may seem that one or another coition can render the entire year, and all eggs of that year, fertile.

I will also say what I observed at that time. When I restored each hen (separated for some time, as I said) to the rooster; of which one was pregnant with an egg, the other had recently laid, the rooster met the latter more quickly, and greedily mounted her three or four times: the other one, however, he circled often, appearing to greet her by rubbing his feet and wings, and to congratulate her on her arrival; nevertheless, having returned to the former, he mounted her again and again, and repeated the act by force: neglecting meanwhile the pregnant one, whom he in no way solicited for Venus <note>sexual intercourse</note>. I wondered by what signs he could thus distinguish to whom coitus would be beneficial and to whom it would be unwelcome. Truly, it is not at all plain how, whether by sight, hearing, or smell, males (even from afar) understand that females are struck by the gadfly of desire and crave coitus. Some, even if they hear only their voice, or smell the place where they have urinated, or only their tracks, are immediately inflamed with lust and pursue them for coitus. But about this matter elsewhere, in a treatise on the love, lust, and coitus of animals, [it will be] more fully

the place to speak. Now I return to the proposed subject.

### *On the belly of the hen and other birds.*

### EXERCISE VII.

From the external orifice, therefore, through the vulva, we have arrived at the hen's womb, or matrix; in which the egg is perfected, surrounded by albumen, and covered with a shell: concerning whose site and position, before we speak, some things concerning the peculiar *anatomy* of the belly of birds must be brought here and premised. For I have observed in feathered creatures that the stomach, intestines, and other viscera are situated and constituted differently in the lowest part of their belly than in the genus of walking animals.

Almost all birds have obtained a double stomach; of which the one is called the *crop*, the other the *stomach* <note>gizzard</note> properly so called. In the former, eaten food is reserved and prepared; in the latter, it is concocted and passes into chyle: our countrymen call the former *the crop, or craw*; the latter, *the gizzard*. In the crop, birds retain whole grains swallowed; from there, when softened, macerated, and emollient with drunk water, they later transmit them into the stomach; so that they may be ground and broken up in the same place. For the sake of which thing, almost all feathered creatures swallow little grains of sand, pebbles, and other harder things, and keep them in the stomach together with the food (while meanwhile nothing such is found in the crop); and they have this stomach [formed] from two very thick
pages.82:
<header>On the Generation of Animals.</header>

and very robust muscles (in smaller birds, fleshy or ligamentous); so that in this way, as if by two millstones joined by double hinges, they can grind the food and pound it; and the pebbles take the place of molar teeth, which they lack. In this manner they prepare the food and make it into chyle; and afterwards, when compression has been made (just as we are accustomed to express juice or porridge from crushed herbs or fruits), the softer and more liquid part is lifted upward; and they transfer it into the beginning of the intestines (which is placed in them near the entrance of the gullet, in the upper part of the stomach). That it is done so appears in many genera of birds; in whose stomachs, if pebbles or other harder and rough things have remained for a longer time, they are seen to be so worn and smoothed by their continuous motion that they are unfit for the attrition of food, and for that reason are rejected. Hence birds, when they pick up pebbles, test them with their tongue; and, if they have felt nothing rough, they reject them. In this way you will find iron, silver, and pebbles worn and almost consumed in the stomach of the *Ostrich*, and also in the *Cassowary*. And for that reason, it is commonly believed that they digest iron and are nourished by it.

In falcons, eagles, and other birds living on prey, if you place your ear near while the stomach is empty, you may perceive the clear sounds of the pebbles thrown in there, colliding with one another. Nor indeed do falcons swallow pebbles for the sake of cooling (which is the common error of falconers).

SINCE IT IS THE CUSTOM of our Academy to attempt to teach everything that the human mind can grasp, it behooves us preceptors to have learned everything, a state we have not yet attained. For I do not see any of us who could have promised this to himself, nor, as I feel, does anyone keep his promises. Or if he has promised, he has done so more out of zeal and desire than out of knowledge of a difficult and arduous subject. If someone were to read all the books of Plato, or even those of Aristotle and Plutarch, how many are there who would not think they had heard, questioned, and known everything? Yet how many and how great are the things they lacked? I truly believe, and believe it to be the truth, that if anyone were to collect the doctrines of all philosophers—whether they be Epicureans, or Academics of both the old and new Academy, or Stoics—I say, of all these and the rest of the wise men of all Greece, and arrange them in order, he would still see that they wished for everything rather than were able to achieve it, and that they had divided rather than explained whatever philosophy professes. And even if there were nothing else, they were certainly unable to say anything about God, nothing about the creation of the world, nothing about the nature of man, and nothing about the return of men into life. The poets dared to name the sons and daughters of Jove, but how
pages.16:
much they wandered, along with the philosophers, from the pursuit of true knowledge, to say nothing of understanding. Now, in the later physics and mathematics, many things have been discovered that were unknown to the first wise men. And even though this is so, since the philosopher professes, as it were, everything, and all have striven to attain this, so that they might know and transmit everything: why should the same not be granted to us as was to them? Or why should we be less able than they to acquire it through industry? Do we lack books? Do we lack leisure? Do we lack stipends or resources? Or, finally, do we lack talent? If we yield to the ancients in this, it is due more to the corruption of discipline and our own sloth than to the capacity of nature, whose goodness is no less a gift and benefit of God than that of the crops and the harvest. Ages have indeed brought forth others, and more numerous, and sharper, and more learned men, just as some years are surpassed in fertility by others. And though the Arabs may have more men of talent than Germany has, the kindness of God, who is the illuminator of the human mind, must not therefore be taken away. For every light of genius proceeds from God.
Thus, Athens may have been learned, and poets, mathematicians, and philosophers may have flourished there, yet they did not always flourish in the same way. Nor is it denied to us for that reason, because that was granted to them before us, and they left us the monuments of literature which teach us how many and how great are the things they comprised in their learning. Learned men understand these things, and consider how much has been added by those who came later to the first, and how much can be added by us to those who came later. They are the ones who reflect, and who observe the path by which one arrives at this capacity.

But <term>σὺν δύ' ἐρχομένῳ</term> <gloss>when two go together</gloss>, as he says, there is need for <term>συζητήσεως</term> <gloss>discussion</gloss>. And just as he says in a bad matter, so let us speak in a good one: we must offer each other mutual effort, so that if we cannot individually attain everything perfectly, we may nevertheless individually attain things moderately, and each person may cultivate his own path according to his talent, touching upon the others as far as he can, and learning from his other colleagues, so that what individuals do not possess, the whole group may possess. Therefore, if you wish to be the authorities for me and my colleagues, you could bring it about that we institute a distribution among ourselves of the arts and books that we read, so that in a few years, we may possess everything—not just in books and libraries, but in mind and memory—divided, known, and acquired among ourselves, which indeed has been preserved in the books of the ancients. Let the theologians, therefore, divide among themselves the authors whom they read at home, whether they be the Greeks, such as the ecclesiastical historians—like Chrysostom, Basil, Nazianzen, and the rest—or the Latins, such as Tertullian, Lactantius, Cyprian, Jerome, and Augustine.
Let the mathematicians and physicists do the same with their own writers. As for me, to the precepts of speaking, and to Cicero and Demosthenes, I will gladly add this year the books of Plato and Aristotle on the Republic, and on the laws, and what they transmitted about morals. Let others work hard on the historians and poets, so that, instructed by these in daily gatherings and conversations, in disputations and schools, and in rhetorical declamations, it may appear how many and how great are the things the human mind can attain if it tries, and if it enters upon the right reason and path: how many advances the soul of man can make through shared studies, distributed labors, distinct intervals of hours, and, finally, through reason and a good method.

COMMENTARII

First, weigh the type of speech here. "Not I," he says, "but the Lord." Does Paul then proclaim one thing, and the Lord another? By no means: the Apostle put forth the previous points without an explicit word of God, <margin>Matt. 19:11</margin> although Christ had said something similar: "Not all can receive this word; let him who can receive it, receive it." Thus, the Apostle determines the consequences concerning unequal marriage. Where, therefore, he did not have an explicit commandment of God, he attributed the decision to himself. Here, however, he has the command of Christ regarding the constancy of marriage outside the case of adultery, as in lighter cases, in which Moses had even granted indulgences to the Jews; correcting that indulgence, Christ said that it was not so from the beginning, but that the two would be one flesh. The Apostle here commands the same thing, that marriage is indissoluble among the faithful in such cases. In the meantime, both these and the following are decisions of the Holy Spirit. For the Apostle is an instrument of the Holy Spirit, and he pronounces these things through His mouth. He binds the faithful more tightly to preserving the bond of marriage when he introduces the Lord as the author. The Lord says this in Matthew 5 and 19, with which the doctrine of the Apostle agrees. Let not the wife depart from her husband for a light cause, namely, for a pretext of religion, because of a changed way of life, and similar causes. In such cases, a bill of divorce could have had a place according to Moses. Furthermore, if it pleases her to depart altogether, let her remain unmarried, or be reconciled to her husband. He prohibits a new marriage, because the first
pages.228:
IN EPIST. AD COR.

still endures, and cannot be dissolved for a just cause, and therefore he commands widowhood for her in the hope of reconciliation. Thirdly, he commands the husband similarly: "Let not the husband put away his wife": for he might have seemed to grant a certain greater right to the husband than to the wife, which Ambrose also follows; therefore he commands the same to the husband, not to put away his wife, namely for a light cause, after the custom of the Jews, for whom it was customary even to put away pious wives if their manners displeased, or their appearance, or if something else was alleged. And among the Gentiles, too, it was quite common to change unions. In these cases, therefore, the precept of the Apostle is valid: let the husband not put away his wife. But as for that question: Is it then not allowed in any way to repudiate a wife once taken? <margin>That this is not a discourse on divorce by profession.</margin> We answer that this is not being treated here. For the Apostle is not instituting a dispute about divorce, or its legitimate causes, but he is concerned with persuading that marriages must be kept most sacredly and therefore indissolubly. Whoever defends this does not deny that there is a certain mode that can dissolve marriages once entered into sacredly. But what that mode is for which it might be dissolved, Christ indicates in Matthew 5 and 19, namely fornication, for that makes it so that two are no longer one flesh. Likewise, as the Apostle teaches here, if an unbelieving person does not wish to live any longer with a believer, the believer is not bound to servitude. It is beyond controversy that for these causes marriage is broken, and therefore can be lawfully dissolved. But he did not look to just causes of divorce, but rather to unjust ones, and therefore he deals with indissolubility. We have explained the place concerning divorces separately; see our topics.

<margin>Concerning unequal marriage.</margin> The fourth place is about unequal marriage, that is, in which one person is a believer, while the other remains in their old religion, whether Jewish or Gentile. The place contains two parts, <term>protasin</term> <gloss>proposition</gloss> and <term>aition</term> <gloss>reason</gloss>. The proposition is proposed in several ways. For he returns equal right to both persons. The meaning of the proposition is: even an unequal marriage must be preserved indissolubly by the pious. He explains how he understands this regarding a husband who has an unbelieving wife who nonetheless wishes to dwell with a Christian man. Similarly, regarding a wife who has an unbelieving husband who nonetheless thinks his wife should not be abandoned on account of the new religion. And so the right is equalized, and therefore looks only toward the faithful persons. For the Apostle could not give precepts to unbelievers. Furthermore, he says that he speaks these things, because Christ had given no command in these cases for the new Christian profession. In the meantime, it is a rule of the Holy Spirit, whose instrument the Apostle is.
pages.230:
IN EPIST. AD COR.

14. *For the unbelieving husband is sanctified by the wife.*

<margin>Why a believer should not desert an unbelieving spouse.</margin>
This is a confirmation of the proposition set forth, that if a believer ought not to desert an unbelieving spouse. Why? Because the worse part, that is, the unbeliever, is sanctified through the better, that is, the believing spouse. He takes the argument from the nature of the faith of the better person. It is proper for faith to sanctify us to God, that is, it declares us sanctified by God, nor does it reside only in one person, namely the believer, but because the believer is one flesh with the unbelieving spouse, consequently the sanctification flows over even to the worse part. And indeed, the unbeliever will have infinite opportunities of repenting and converting even to Christ the Savior. Nevertheless, the Apostle did not say "will be sanctified," or "let him be sanctified," but "is sanctified." For it is a most certain argument for hoping even for their conversion, since he does not wish to depart. Therefore, that sanctification has a place only in those who do not wish to break the marriage; in the others, it is not the same. Furthermore, the children born from this are holy; if the marriage were broken, they would be rendered impure. Therefore, it should not be broken because of religion. Their children are called holy because, notwithstanding the infidelity of the other part, they belong to the Church of Christ. For it is said to individual believers: "I will be your God, and the God of your children." For the sanctification of the children, therefore, it is enough if one parent is a believer.

is. The children are also called holy because they can also be consecrated to Christ through their education. Therefore, for the benefit of the children also, such a marriage is not to be broken. Thirdly, because God has called you to peace. Therefore, no society established among men for a good end is to be rashly torn apart by the pious. He attaches this reason to the objection. <margin>Question.</margin> For the believer will ask: you do not want me to desert an unbelieving spouse, I being a believer, but what if he does not wish to live with me? Shall I follow him? Or will I be bound to keep celibacy unless I am reconciled to him? The Apostle answers: I do not wish this at all; but I do not want the marriage to be broken at least on your part, provided it remains valid; if the unbeliever does not wish it, very well, let him depart, you will be free from the marriage, he himself deciding thus. God has called us to peace. Therefore, the marriage should not be broken by you. And, He has called us to peace. Therefore, leave the unbelieving one who departs, do not bring them to court, do not pursue your case against them. Preserve peace in both ways.

Fourthly, from the hope of conversion. An unequal marriage should not be broken by the believer, because there is hope that the unbeliever can be gained through honest conduct. For effort must be given so that we may gain anyone for the Lord, let alone a spouse. Therefore, the spouse is to be borne more patiently in this case. It is to be observed in these arguments that the Christian religion does not disturb political matters, so much so that it holds as valid marriages previously entered into: indeed, it teaches one to bear unequal ones patiently.

From which it also follows that the marriages of the impious are by no means holy. For while both persons lack sanctification, they are impure. Thus it must be judged concerning all their works. In the meantime, they have their own political virtues, which, however, do not please God. Fourthly, the great dignity of faith is such that the power of sanctifying is attributed to it, not yet holy, such as sanctifying the unbelieving spouse, children born from an unequal marriage, etc.

17. *Unless as God has distributed to each, as the Lord has called each.*

The fifth place is about each person diligently keeping their own station. For among the Corinthians, some sullen men seemed to exist who, upon the conversion of Jews, immediately imposed an alteration of their whole life in external ceremonies, or, in the case of those converted from gentilism <note>paganism</note>, they immediately demanded a new way of living. Or perhaps there were others who did not seem pious enough to themselves unless they threw away all their previous ceremonies of life entirely. The Apostle meets them in this place, and decides that there is no need for such austerity, that the religion of Christ does not abolish one's state of life; he teaches this learnedly by proposing, explaining, confirming, and concluding. We resolve each part into the proposition.
