pages.233:
COMMENTARII

But let that proposition be.

<term>Protasin</term> <gloss>proposition</gloss>. On account of the profession of the Gospel, it is not necessary to change one's way of life immediately; but each person's own calling, with religion kept safe, must be diligently guarded and preserved. The Apostle said <term>peripatein</term> <gloss>to walk</gloss>, as God has called each one, this is, to persist in his own way of life in which the profession of the Gospel discovered him. And the word <term>peripatein</term> is to produce the fruits of an active life, so that you may understand it to be a matter of piety to produce actions conforming to the profession. For it is not enough to contemplate and speak much about piety: there is a need for action. And the particle "unless" should be connected with "as." It is a limited proposition and restricted by a certain condition: "Unless as God has distributed," one must walk; this is, not otherwise, not by our own judgment, a calling is not to be feigned for ourselves, but the one which the Lord has imposed is to be retained. In this sense, he censures the superstition of the Corinthians who wanted to change everything immediately on account of the profession of religion.

But let us consider the arguments by which this which we have proposed from the Apostle can be shown: each one's station is to be kept after the acknowledgment of the truth. Why? Because God has distributed the kinds of life in this way. It is a firm argument from divine ordination and disposition, which must be studiously observed by the pious. The Apostle urges the argument with repetition and change of words, <term>theos emerisen</term> <gloss>God distributed</gloss> and <term>kurios kekleken</term> <gloss>the Lord has called</gloss>. He indeed says the same thing.

and the fleeting age, with silent centuries, could turn even the saved relics: but long time will not steal the eternal honors from your merits, O renowned Rome, you who collect the breathing ruins of Pelusium, and lift them to the stars in the middle of the forum. Nor will dark night cover your oblivion, O GREATEST CAESAR, nor your genius. For if there is any praise, because under your leadership, antiquity, having been opened, reveals the dark bays of Memphis; because you reveal the secret faces of the Inachian heifer <note>Inachian heifer: Io, often identified with Isis in syncretic Egyptian-Greek thought</note>, because the mystical form of the dog and of the sacred bull, and whatever other monsters of famous Canopus remain to be seen, surpass the ancient notes: the last dweller of the Nile will read the titles of the AUSTRIADS, and will shake the tinkling sistra <note>Sistrum: a sacred percussion instrument used in the cult of Isis</note> with a joyful sound. Now Solyme, now the Arab will learn, and the marbles will speak of the gifts scattered by the CAESAREAN hand. Am I mistaken? Or will the fates add to the AUSTRIAN trophies the sacred signs torn from the Paraetonian vaults? Or, O FERDINAND, does Victory now prepare to write your name upon the stones of the Pyramids? Certainly, glory, emulating the Pellaean <note>Pellaean: referring to Alexander the Great</note> palms, calls the idle hands of Europe to pious wars.

->According to the Greek salutation set forth<-

## BY FRANCISCUS GOZADINUS, BISHOP OF ZAKYNTHOS AND CEPHALONIA.

<note>A large decorative drop cap initial 'Π' featuring a central shield with vertical bars (heraldic pales), surrounded by an ornate frame.</note>

Octavian Augustus, having been seized by a love for the wisdom of Caesar, [sought] the ancient wisdom uncovered in the obelisks raised by him, the whole of Egypt, buried and despaired of, full of rich ministrations and all accompanying sufferings. [He sought] whatever the hieroglyphic experience of learned teachings had published, having sent them to Rome, for the divine service of the revelation of secrets. But the burden fell only upon him, to whom much of the mystical education of all the ancients [was known], as if it had been flooded and submerged by the streams of Lethe. Ferdinand III, O Augustus, more fortunate than that Octavian, obtained what was then hidden, and even then, by that zeal and expense, [he] succeeded in having it successfully accomplished. In the past, Augustus showed the sphere himself, in the <unclear>unbidden</unclear> Obelisks. Octavian AUGUSTUS Caesar, having been struck by the desire to acquire ancient wisdom, which was said to be inscribed upon the obelisks erected by him, explored the whole of Egypt through the work of learned men, so that if he could find an interpreter skilled in hieroglyphic doctrine, he might summon him to Rome for the office of interpreting arcana. But he could not obtain his wishes, all the mystical doctrine of the Ancients having long since been submerged, as if by a certain river of Lethe. FERDINAND III, Caesar Augustus, was so much more fortunate than that Octavian, by how much more fortunate omens he achieved that which the other could not obtain by any wishes or expenses, while by some fate Athanasius Kircher fell to him as a new interpreter, an <term>Oedipus</term> <gloss>riddle-solver</gloss> <term>reborn</term> <gloss>brought back to life</gloss>; who, stimulated by the Caesarean command, flew with a brilliant intellect to the regions of Wisdom and uncovered treasures hitherto inaccessible. He, trusting in the commands of Ferdinand, was the first to enter more deeply into the hidden recesses of the Memphitic shrines, and he opened the secret seals of the sacraments; he interpreted the mysterious volumes of the ancient Priests, with Caesarean bounty acting as midwife. Therefore, we proclaim You, Caesar, fortunate, since you burn with a great and very grand desire to accomplish [great things], and such a man has fallen to You, who both wishes and is able to urge the concepts of your great mind into execution: Augustus once placed the scope of his power in the raising of vast masses of Obelisks; but You are even more powerful than this, who not only raise great stones, but also this has fallen to You beyond others, that by your help and work, the mute stones of the Obelisks

...the matter surpassed it, when salt water turned into the sweetest drink: The dry crossing of the Israelites through the Red Sea, as well as the budding of Aaron’s rod, also came to pass in a supernatural manner.

And in sum, the breaking forth of Christ from the sealed tomb, that appearance made to the two walking to the village of Emmaus, the manifestation through closed doors, was a divine and supernatural event. Many other examples could still be brought forth from the sacred code, if one did not have to sacrifice them for the sake of brevity.

Included among supernatural things are all the prodigies of metallic mines, the bodily apparitions of spirits, phantoms, pygmies, and dwarves, which very often present themselves to sight and portend good or evil, ruin or wealth. Likewise, all the figures and other impressions of metals, which are found under the earth among human beings, fish, and other living creatures, formed through the imagination of the three principles, matured and baked by the earth and other elements; to which also belong the monsters of the earth and things of that kind, which are given in wondrous forms under the earth at set times, outside of which they can be detected nowhere else, although at another time they may truly appear again and present themselves to our eyes.

Hither also are referred all visions, which are accustomed to be made through waters, mirrors, crystals, and other media, by seals and characters, which nevertheless differ greatly; for some are merely natural, yet exhibit supernatural visions. The rest, arising from enchantments, are neither natural nor supernatural, but Diabolical, and are therefore enumerated among Demoniacal Magic, and are deservedly interdicted to all Christia-

<vocab>supernaturalia, miracula, Emmaus, pygmæi, phasmata, metallica, visiones, Magia Dæmoniaca</vocab>
pages.12:
tians, and by right all such media contrary to the sacred scriptures, to the word of GOD, and to His commandment, are rejected and refuted by true and natural <term>Cabalists</term> <gloss>those who study the mystical tradition</gloss>. And I warn of this so that a sure distinction and a certain order may be established between natural, supernatural, and contranatural things.

Likewise, all <term>Naiads</term> <gloss>water nymphs</gloss>, <term>Sirens</term>, <term>Succubi</term>, and other <term>Nymphs</term>, and whatever is akin to them, obtain a place among supernatural things, as do also those earthly spirits that inhabit the air, offering themselves to hearing, sight, and touch, sometimes foretelling death or some other evil, at other times signifying fortunes and treasures in certain places by their apparitions. Added to these, furthermore, are fiery spirits, showing themselves in the form of fire and a burning torch, all of which are incorporeal spirits and yet not infernal, lying in wait for the souls of men as if they were eternal treasures, just as the Stygian <term>Lucifer</term> and his excommunicated companions are accustomed to do. But these are spirits which, presented to men for wonder above nature, are uniquely nourished, fostered, and fed by the elements, and afterwards cease in this earthly world, dying and vanishing together, deprived of a redeemed soul. I will add no more about these things now, but I defer their further discussion to another time and more convenient place, where I will compile a singular treatise on visions and their spiritual apparitions, which the greater part of the world judges to be contrary to nature, when in truth they are indeed natural, but are perceived as supernatural regarding their operations and wondrous qualities.
pages.13:
To confirm my proposal more, I assert that there are many things in medicine that manifest and complete their operation in a supernatural manner, only in a magnetic way, through a certain spiritual attractive virtue, which is enticed by the benefit of the air, because this is the medium between the medicine and the vice, just as the magnet always turns itself toward the northern star <note>original: "australi" (literally 'southern', though traditionally assigned to the pole/star)</note>, even if it be many thousands of miles distant from it. Nevertheless, such great spiritual operation and inclination intervenes here, that by means of this bond, namely the air, such distances concur. But because an attractive virtue of this kind is commonly known, it has passed into mere custom, and it alone sustains its function, nor is any further occult quality observed from which an operating virtue of this kind draws its origin. In a like manner, wounds and vices can be healed, even if the man oppressed by such and the Physician are separated by a long interval, not by incantations, spells, and other illicit means contrary to GOD and nature, but by those in which a magnetic attractive virtue lies hidden. For if a wounded person, departing from here, leaves to the Physician the arms with which he was injured or any of the gore that issued from the wound, from which legitimate means of healing are then duly administered by him, as is accustomed to be done with the binding of wounds, he will recover firmly without any doubt. These are not spells, but such a healing is accomplished uniquely by the attractive virtue of the medicine, which is carried to the wound by means of the air to purify the wound and to complete its spiritual operation.

These words will perhaps seem difficult to most and alien to the powers of nature, and many will fight against this doctrine
pages.14:
as if it were entirely contrary to nature, whence very many will descend into the most serious mutual altercations: whether this remedy is natural or not, whether it is possible or not, or whether it is a fascination <note>a magical influence or sorcery</note>. But this controversy is to be settled by this: that such a cure is indeed natural, but the mode of operating is supernatural and spiritual, because it is done solely by a certain attractive and incomprehensible reason. Furthermore, that this mode of healing proceeds without fascination is proven by this very fact: because it is joined with no fascination nor any other contranatural medium that protests against GOD the creator and His word, but is entirely natural, resulting from its own supernatural, invisible, incomprehensible, spiritual, and attractive virtue, which, having obtained its origin from the stars, completes its operation through the Elements.

Finally, I can defend this cure from fascination, since it is established that the Devil prefers to rejoice in the calamity and misfortune of the human race rather than to provide any help for the salvation of men, which fact, moreover, does not consist in his own powers at all without divine permission. Much more could be added to this magnetic form, but to avoid various errors, I now pause and hold my silence until I have related some things about the natural miracles of the world.

Coarse and rude minds, though stuffed with the opinion of philosophy, and all who have corrupted senses, know no distinction in these things; but the wise and skilled can distinguish natural things from supernatural ones most easily.

Let one note and observe this analogy through a coarser
pages.15:
example. There are many living creatures that are devoid of all life during the winter time, but as soon as summer returns, the natural heat generates new life, so that the body rises again in that substance in which it previously exerted vital motion, just like an herb, which dies in winter and revives anew in spring. The death of these things is therefore judged to be natural, but the restoration of new life through its own knowledge is supernatural. But truly, because man is accustomed to all these things, the smallest part approaches what ought to be further weighed and examined, dismissing both natural and supernatural things.

Very many are also accustomed to pass over the disposition of man with a dry foot <note>a classical idiom for passing over something hastily or without consideration</note>, which itself is also supernatural, as well as those monsters which bring spots into the world together; all these are indeed natural but show themselves supernaturally out of a rising imagination, which supernatural form and disposition the mother imprinted on the infant by accident through her imagination, as we indeed see quite often, that some customs are imbued in certain men, which they can never renounce, however much they may labor to break the habit. This kind of innate force of man is natural, but the conception in the mother’s womb, which the imagination of these things provided, is supernatural and subject to those things which the heaven imprinted.

Finally, neither do I deny this, that no one can support what exceeds the powers of nature with unshaken foundations and undoubted causes to avoid an injury to truth, unless those things are first known which become known to us from their physical course, for they have drawn their birth and their form from supernatural things
pages.16:
; so it will happen afterwards that, having perceived these, an infallible experiment will prove that he has snatched the palm from those who deny all faith to supernatural things. It will likewise refute the opinions of many who, disputing about natural things and not grasping the foundation, do nothing but trifle and rashly produce their contentions.

## The First Tincture and Root of Metals.

### Chapter Two.

BUT so that I may complete my undertaking, with GOD permitting, and take up the doctrine concerning the first tincture, root, and generation of Metals and Minerals, it must be known that the tincture and root of all Metals is also a supernatural, volatile, and fiery Spirit, which sustains itself in the air and naturally seeks its seat in water and earth, where it can rest and operate. This Spirit is found in all Metals, and more abundantly in others than in gold, for the reason that because of its baked, matured, and fixed body, it is solid, firm, and compact, and therefore, besides what the body requires, it cannot receive more. The other metals, however, are destitute of such a fixed body, but their pores are open and widely dispersed; therefore, the Spirit of the tincture can penetrate and occupy them more copiously. But since the bodies of other metals are unfixed, the Tincture also cannot subsist with wandering bodies
pages.17: but is compelled to yield. Since, therefore, the Tincture of gold exists nowhere more abundantly than in Mars <note>Iron</note> and Venus <note>Copper</note>, or the male and female, once their bodies are destroyed, the spirit of the tincture is driven from there, which enriches the enclosed, prepared gold with blood and volatilizes it through food and drink. Hence, the volatile gold, satiated with its food and drink, acquires its own blood and dries it with its native heat by the aid of vaporous fire, and a certain mutual victory is given, which conciliates the greatest fixity, so that gold may turn into a most fixed medicine. Because of the redundancy of blood, it can exhibit no body unless in turn a very large body is added to it, where the superfluous fixed blood is diffused; this added Metallic body, because of the immense heat of the leonine fixed blood, is penetrated like fire, is cleansed from all impurity, and is immediately baked into the fullest maturity and fixity. And so the servant gathers riches for the Lord, because the latter can desire nothing first from his own garment, since nature has bestowed upon him a single garment of honor; nor can the King, in turn, dispense inheritance and lasting courtly attire to his attendants from the kingdom, where he previously collected tribute from his subjects, so that the Lord and the servant may dwell together. Do not, however, wonder that the King needs the mutual help of his attendants, for the cause is the unfixedness of their bodies; for they receive many things into themselves, but can provide little faith. But where the King can become a participant in that matter, he is able to banish cold and heat better than impure metals. Thus, through such reception, he becomes the victor of all the rest, with a glorious
pages.18: triumph of wealth and health for a long life. I believe you have now sufficiently perceived, in place of a principle, this doctrine concerning natural and supernatural things, about the first tincture of the root of Metals and Minerals, upon which the cornerstone has been built and the truest rock in its kind founded, where nature has too deeply hidden and concealed her gifts. In the fiery and tinctured spirits, which color she obtained from the heaven of the stars through the operation of the Elements, and so was able to further tinge and fix those which were not yet tinctured and fixed, since the Moon <note>Silver</note> is destitute of the habit of a golden crown and fixity, as is also Saturn <note>Lead</note>, Jupiter <note>Tin</note>, and Mercury <note>Quicksilver</note>. And although Mars <note>Iron</note> and Mercury may need no garment, but could communicate this to the other five, I say, however, that without the lion <note>the prepared gold/tincture</note>, since they are not sufficiently instructed by the fixity of their Mercury and the subtlety of their salt, they can accomplish nothing that makes for wealth, unless they are conquered by the lion in the contest, so that they might carry off a triumph on both sides, raised moreover to no small improvement, which improvement lies hidden in the signed star or in its magnet, whence all the metals themselves received their gifts. I will proceed now to generation in particular, how the <term>Archaeus</term> <gloss>the vital, formative principle of nature</gloss> exhibits its virtue, pours it out, and draws it into the light, whence all the forms of Metals and Minerals are presented to the eyes and are formed and fortified with bodies by the incomprehensible and volatile fiery spirits of Minerals. Therefore, take this now; attend with study, lest by forgetting you lose great things, nor pass over most useful things and, on the contrary, observe only the bare letters, neglecting the principal way. For whatever I write here, I fear lest the greatest

Since, by the decree of His Sacred Imperial Majesty, it is seriously and firmly forbidden to all and singular printers, booksellers, and others exercising any book trade whatsoever, that any person should dare or presume to reprint—within the borders of the Holy Roman Empire, the kingdoms, and the hereditary dominions of His Sacred Imperial Majesty—any books edited until now or to be edited in the future by our Fathers, whether in the same or another type of character or format, either in whole or in part, or to send them elsewhere to be reprinted, or to bring, sell, and distribute them elsewhere, secretly or openly, without the judgment and testimony of the aforementioned Fathers: I, HERMANNUS BAVINCK, Provincial Superior of the Society of JESUS for the Rhenish Province, by the authority granted to me for this purpose by our Most Reverend Father General, MUTIUS VITELLESCO, grant to Joannes Volmari, printer in Würzburg, the faculty to print the book titled *Catechism in Select Examples, etc.*, written by Father GEORGIUS VOGLERUS, a priest of our Society, and read and approved by the theologians appointed for this purpose. ## Gracious Reader.

<note>A decorative drop cap 'N' is featured, containing intricate foliate scrollwork.</note>Having now taught the Catechism in churches and schools for the twentieth year without cessation by the command of my superiors, and having had to pay—as the saying goes—enough "tuition" <note>meaning practical experience gained through hardship</note> until I found a way that is at once pleasant, useful, and convenient for the still-blossoming youth, and also profitable for the parents, I have, after long practice, arranged this practical Catechism so that the catechist lacks nothing in terms of suitable examples, short explanations, hymns, or other exercises.

Because this book is intended mostly for children, no one should look here for subtle wit or sharp, pedantic matters, since such subtleties are of very little use to dear youth.

Here, Christian teaching is made childish for children and simple for the simple: rightly and
pages.23:
simply laid before the eyes: also, at times, a thing is presented and treated in two, three, or four ways so that the tender youth may grasp the necessary parts for salvation, either in this way or in another. Furthermore, so that the knowledge of divine things may take root more deeply the longer it is impressed upon wax-soft hearts and hold firm, it is presented only through short examples, now through short questions and answers, then through hymns in different melodies, concerts, and rounds: so that the catechist may have many kinds of means, ways, and tricks in hand to help this one or that one with pleasant variety, without which tedium will very quickly arise. The examiner and teacher should by no means be ashamed to be childish with children and simple with simple folk, because the Wisdom of the eternal Father also stooped down and took on our weakness, and chose to align Itself with our understanding, offering milk to some and strong meat to others, with the highest patience and humility.

# NOTES

## ON THE FIRST BOOK.

### *Constituent parts of Plants.*

#### CAP. I.

*Perhaps not in the same way.* Utmost brevity, as **Dr. Moldenhawer** rightly observed, in the comparison of Animals with Plants at the end of this chapter; concerning which Aristotle, Hist. Anim. v. 3, should be consulted.

*So there is nothing strange.* See on this matter Lib. de Caus. Plant. ii. 20, 22, 23. v. 2.

*By an equal distance*, sc. interval. Equidistant.

#### CAP. II.

*And they are first and greatest.* Thus Aristotle, Hist. Anim.: as many parts as, being whole, have other parts of their own within them; for example, the head, etc.

*More durable in the roots.* Those whose root perennates. Bot.

*Regarding the one*, sc. being. To be provided with a simple trunk. See Pliny, Nat. Hist. xiv. 1. 30.

*Homoeomerous. Anhomoeomerous.* Consult Aristotle on this matter, De Gen. Anim. i. 1, and the Lexicon of Theophrastus.

*Any part from the same things.* Individual parts [composed] from the same vessels, fibers, membranes, etc.

*The greatest parts are almost these.* End of chapter ii in Bodaeus.

*Others from which these are*; the Author proceeds to the homoeomerous.

#### CAP. III.

*Menestor.* An author on herbal matters, whose works are not extant.

*Namelessly*, simply the moisture.

*Innate moisture and heat.* Moldenhawer deals very copiously with the warm principle of life in *Tent.* p. 83. He calls it generative heat.
pages.139:
de Caus. Plant. i. 4. Confer also Galen. Called by Aristotle *natural heat*. ii. 3.

*But other different kinds*. Distinct, that is, from *moisture and heat*. Beginning of chapter iv, Bod.

*Fiber—veins*. The Author's remarkable sagacity in describing these most tenuous vessels, which, however, in our century have been brought to their *acme* <gloss>peak/perfection</gloss>. Mold. *Tent.* p. 91 deals very copiously with this matter.

*Wood, flesh*. See Mold. p. 108.

*Marrow* is compared to *marrow in bones*. But briefly, however, and narrowly, as he is accustomed to, the Author describes the *marrow* <gloss>pith</gloss> of vegetables; clearly, however, if you weigh the force of the words. Mention is made elsewhere, i. 9. iv. 2. De Caus. Plant. v. 6, 7, 24.

### CAP. IV.

*In which it is possible*. In those which admit of division.

*Beside the cultivation*. By means of cultivation, etc. A frequent usage in Theophrastus.

*Olive cuttings*. The word *kopades* is interpreted as coppice wood, but here perhaps of a decapitated tree.

### CAP. VI.

*One must always take all*— An obscure reading, if it is sound: the meaning is, *one must always take the differences of all [things] by places* with respect to climate, etc.

*Different according to the different genus of moistures*, i.e., aquatic plants differ among themselves with respect to *places*.

*Smaller—larger*. The former are Sea-wracks and Sea-lettuce; the latter are called elsewhere *small trees*; Gorgonians, Corallines. See iv. 8.

### CAP. VII.

*Thickness*. Here it indicates the thickness or mass of the trunk. It is opposed to *thinness*, slenderness.

*From which is the composition*. With respect to the component parts. It is opposed to *those according to conditions and powers*.

### CAP. VIII.

*Marrows*. See chapter iii, p. 9, l. 6. N.B. Chapter IX in Bodaeus.

*Some do not have—and the Elder*. There is no pith in the younger branches of the Elder tree.
pages.140:
*All marrows are black.* The significance of the word *black* escaped Scaliger. See Bod. p. 24 and the Lexicon of Theophrastus.

*In general some do not have.* The discussion is about Fungi: see the Systematic Catalogue, which have no affinity with other plants. See Bod. p. 27.

*They differ also in roots.* See on this matter Plin. xvi. 31.

*Fringed.* Fimbriated, Pliny, but there is another sense of the word *thysanoi*, ribbons, tufts of fibers. Poll. See the Lexicon of Theophrastus.

### C A P. IX.

*Those above ground*, sc. *parts*.

*For the root*, i.e., the root in general.

### C A P. X.

*Crowning the altars.* Perhaps one should read *gathering heaps*.

*They bear fruit.* Add *below*: under the earth, concerning tubers. See the illustration of *Arachidnas*, Bod. p. 35.

*The fruit*, sc. the tuber from the root.

*Earlier than those above*, sc. *parts*.

*These contribute greatly.* It is to be noted that the word *nature* should be taken in the plural.

*Of all [plants] the juices are likewise.* Beginning of the chapter in Bodaeus.

*For from the shoots.* An amazing description of the habit of the Indian Fig, L. Engl. "The Banyan Tree."

*If the material is deep.* The meaning is, if some material intervenes between the seed and the earth, *it divides the root toward the earth*, it bends the root toward the earth until it reaches it.

### C A P. XI.

*In which are both*, sc. *genders*. Although sexual distinction occurs in the Palm, commonly the words *male*, *female* are attributed to the varieties of the species, as they are observed to be more robust and fruitless, or the contrary.

*Most peculiar are those of the Apple tree.* These words included in parentheses **crept in from the margin**, as I suspect, and interrupt the description of the habit of the *Fir*. Although it is hardly possible to conjecture what the Author means with respect to the *faces of wild beasts*, Pliny interprets the place thus in Nat. Hist. l. xvi. c. 30: "The Apple tree has a peculiar kind
pages.141:
"of branches; for they show the snouts of wild beasts, with smaller ones adhering to one "very large one."

*Of knots, some are blind.* Observe that the word *ozos* occurs in a double sense, as a branch, and a knot in the trunk.

*Because nothing is placed in between.* Because there are no intervals. Scal.

*Peculiar hollows.* See the word *nail* in the Lexicon of Theophrastus. Species of Hypoxylon, as I suspect. See iv. 16.

*There is then.* A chapter to be added to the previous one as it is a continuation.

*Growing in length.* The discussion is about the trunk, which is either tall and not branching, or which *is split straight*. I also suspect that what follows, *those things similar to these*, should be read as follows: *and the root similarly to these*. Thus Virgil: "As much as it extends its top to the ethereal breezes, "so much does it extend its root to Tartarus."

*Becomes thin*, sc. *by cultivation*.

### CAP. XII.

*And further, some are evergreen.* Here begins chapter xv in Bodaeus.

*To partake of the winter.* To last until the middle of winter.

### CAP. XIII.

*Like the hand.* Pliny in passage xvi. 24 says, *veins on the flat sides*, "incisions underneath," that is, hollow lines, as in the palm of the hand.

*Which part toward the twig*, i.e., from the conversion of the leaves, it is doubtful which side is upper, which lower; *for the hollowness* with respect to position is different from the nature of the leaf.

*Not to be altered in the same way.* It is opposed to conversions *by means of veins or fibers*, i.e., not in a constant, regular way.

*Going through the depth* to be interpreted concerning the thickness of the leaf.

*Saw-toothed.* Perhaps *comb-like* or *slaughter-like*. See the Preface to the Illustration of Theophrastus, p. v. Also the description of the *Fir*, l. iii.

*Of the Oak from the trunk.* Pliny observes the same thing about the leaves of the Oak, Nat. Hist. xvi. 24. Bodaeus says he has never observed it. I suspect an error in the text: perhaps it should read *Cyprian*. See concerning the *Cyprian Fig* iv. c. 2.
pages.142:
*The whole stem is leafless.* He accurately describes the scape of the Botanists.

*By itself.* From itself: concerning a sessile leaf. Bot.

*Encompassing between*. Fruit in the middle of the leaf.

### CAP. XIV.

*For those [parts] not annual.* Persistent parts of a plant, such as the trunk, branches, etc. *For nothing [is] without this [moisture].*

*Of the flowers, some from the bark.* An amazing thing, what Theophrastus means. Flowers from the bark and nerves. Surely an error of the text, and one should read for *of the flowers*, *of the others* (sc. stems). Concerning Flowers, see c. 21, 22.

### CAP. XV.

*The seed immediately after the containing part.* Seed with a simple covering. In this chapter six kinds of seeds are noted, the enumeration of which is confused and very long. These are: 1. simple seeds with a covering; Palms. 2. from a nut and flesh—Drupes. 3. in a pod—siliquose. 4. in some membrane, membranous follicle, such as the Pear, Apple. 5. angiosperms <gloss>vessel-seeded</gloss>, with a loose, rigid pericarp; Poppy. 6. gymnosperms <gloss>naked-seeded</gloss>, without a covering; umbelliferous plants.

*Such as the berry.* Here the text of the passage is very corrupt. The distinction of Theophrastus of many grains contained in some common [vessel], such as a berry or grape-stone: and likewise in the seed. N.B. The nuts of the Pomegranate are opposed to the individual grains of Wheat, etc. *Least of all would those of Apples seem [to be].* Yet they should not be joined to the Apples, which are wrapped around by membranes in the inner part of the fruit.

*But similarly each of these.* See the error of the scribe in transcribing above, *since for each one taking [it]*.

### CAP. XVI.

*In those on juices.* Hist. de Caus. Plant. l. vi.

*Of Lettuce.* The juice is said to be watery, which is less correct. Perhaps an error of the text, as above for *milky* <gloss>should be placed</gloss> concerning the juice of the Fig and Poppy.

*Which is proper.* The meaning is that the peculiar juice of any plant *has some likeness* in itself before cooking and maturation happens in the fruit, which is effected by means of the pericarp.
pages.143:
*Some are sweet-smelling.* See more fully concerning odors in Theophrastus, *de Caus. Plant.* l. i. 6, as also concerning juices.

### CAP. XVII.

*Outside the sea.* The Red Sea is understood.

*Having a diagram.* The common Columbine is indicated by most Botanists under the name of *Iasione*; and the description, although intricate, marvelously fits the convolutions of the petals: also *it is not separated in the flower*.

N.B. Perhaps Bodaeus's conjecture will please some more, that the Bindweed, etc., is indicated here, in which sense *only a diagram of the majority* is to be interpreted concerning the amplitude of the flower.

*They appear perforated.* The Author's remarkable *precision*, when the flower is perforated, i.e., falls off without the stigma, the beginning fruit remains; when *it is burnt or soaked*, or affected by too much sun or rain, *it throws off the fruit*. See the observation below: *as many of the flowers as have, as it were, a spindle, are fertile*.

*On the mouths themselves.* The discussion is about syngenesious plants; therefore *mouth* is the common receptacle in this class.

*As if a spindle.* Concerning the stigma of the flower of the Citron tree.

*Immediately to show the fruit*, i.e., without a flower or petals.

### CAP. XVIII.

*The olynthus* <gloss>wild fig</gloss>. The Fig tree, etc., is counted by Linnaeus among the Trioecious plants. *The Oleaster*, from which [come] the *erina* (which perhaps are the *olynthoi*), the Male tree; *the Fig tree* the Monoecious tree.

### CAP. XIX.

*And such are*. A summary and recapitulation of this book.

*More species under each genus*. More species under one genus. A truly Linnaean distinction!

*Cultivated and wild*. Here the distinction is taken from sex: but what does it mean? That wild plants are distinguished by sex, but cultivated ones indeed by *more peculiar things*; does he indicate varieties of fruits?

DISPOSITION OF THE FIRST
Epistle to the
Corinthians.

*Who the Corinthians were.*

Corinth was named after Corinthus, the son of Marathon, who was either the founder or the illustrator of the city. Once it was the most famous and flourishing of the cities of Greece, whence Cicero did not hesitate to call it the light of all Greece. He describes its location most elegantly in the Oration against Rullus <note>original: "In Oratione pro Lege Manilia" <gloss>In the Oration for the Manilian Law</gloss></note>, in these words: "Hardly a trace of Corinth remains." For it was situated in the straits and jaws of Greece, so that the land held the bolts of the region, and it nearly joined two seas that were most navigation-
pages.60:
# IN EPIST. PAVLI. 55
<sig>D. iiii.</sig>

ally distinct, while they were separated by a very narrow interval, etc. By which words he indicates that the Aegean sea washes it from the east, where those sailing from Asia were received in the port of Cenchreae. Indeed, that the Ionian sea is from the west, where those arriving were received in the port of Lechaeum. Hence it is also that Horace sang:

<margin>Horace.</margin>
> "Others will praise glorious Rhodes, or Mitylene,
> Or Ephesus, or the walls of bimarian <note>meaning: between two seas</note> Corinth—"

This suitability of the place, and its wealth, and a singular corruption of morals had brought [people] into this city. For merchants from all of Asia and Europe flocked there as if to a common marketplace. And there was a most famous temple of Venus there, in which women practiced prostitution for profit with their bodies,
pages.61:

whence those noble courtesans, whom Athenaeus and profane authors everywhere mention, were almost all Corinthians. And there exist still today proverbs among authors by which their morals are taxed, such as "to behave like a Corinthian" <note>original: "Corinthiari"</note> and "it is not permitted for everyone to go to Corinth." From this corruption of morals, it flowed undoubtedly that by the just judgment of God it was later destroyed, which we first read in histories was done by the Romans, through Lucius Mummius, before the Numantine war. The occasion for overturning that city was that they had defiled the ambassadors of the Roman people with excrement. Later, however, it was restored by Caesar and again made noble by the studies of humanity, wealth, and corruption of morals. Whoever desires more, let him see Strabo, book 8; Livy, book 5 of the fifth decade;

### OCCASION OF THE
### Epistle.

In this corruption of morals, the Lord also had a Church, the origin of which exists in Acts chapter 18, from which passage, and the first chapter of this Epistle, and likewise chapter 7, the occasion can be gathered, namely that the Apostle wrote this Epistle moved by a grave cause. The occasion, therefore, was offered in this way. The Apostle had taught there for a full year and six months, and that with great fruit and success; for he had done this by divine command, and at the same time it was signaled to him

and they reject it. But unless our sins deserve otherwise, they will not succeed in the end: And their madness, according to Paul, will become evident to all, and will break forth at some time, even if the devils are unwilling, as the fruit of the pious efforts of your most Serene King, who through you seeks the peace of the Churches, if the controversies are correctly judged first. This hope of a happy harvest should not at all be shaken for us by the fact that the seeds of peace and concord, scattered in this your embassy, seem to lie hidden for a while. For nature itself willed that there be one time for sowing and another for reaping.

Reflecting on this, there often comes to mind that most beautiful saying of Nazianzen, who, in the Oration delivered in praise of Cyprian, says: Divine wisdom knows how to lay the foundations of great matters long before, and to procure contrary outcomes through contrary means, so that it might excite greater admiration for itself among mortals <note>original: "οἶδε πόῤῥωθεν καταβάλλεσθαι τῶν μεγάλων πραγμάτων ἡ θεῖα σοφία τὰς ὑποθέσεις"</note>.
pages.19:
and through opposites to govern opposites, so that it may be even more admired.

But to return to where I digressed: Indeed, I rejoice with my whole heart that God has kept you safe and sound until the day you wrote to us from England. And I vehemently congratulate you on the many and great testimonies of divine presence, which have been shown to you divinely throughout your entire embassy. And I pray with you to the Son of GOD, our Immanuel, the head and most faithful guardian of His Church, that He may bless your most holy labors more each day, and keep you safe for a very long time. And likewise that He may strengthen your Most Serene KING, another Josiah. Regarding his constancy and fortitude in defending and professing the true religion, letters from most trustworthy men—even after your departure from Germany—testify to us clearly, contrary to the inventions of the vainest of rumors, which, while you were still present in Germany, had been spread by wicked and per<column-break/>verse men in the courts of many princes to impede the success of your embassy.
pages.20:
Some of whom you said you knew, and that you held the vanity of those rumors to be perceived and proven, and that you said you wanted to believe the tales—which events and time (which is the daughter of truth) were to refute—only to gratify others. As indeed, until now, with GOD confirming the spirit of the Royal Serenity, the piety of such a king has dispersed and scattered all the mists of lies with its own brightness and light.

But as I am most persuaded that He who began His good work in you and in your Most Serene King will also perfect it until the day of JESUS CHRIST, so, to approve and celebrate that heroic and most holy voice of yours—by which you told me at the time when various storms and dangers seemed to hang over you from all sides that in a good cause, the conscience of a right will ought to be despised by Christians no less than the Devil himself, through confidence in Divine protection—I believe I can append no more suitable epilogue to this than that most noble Psalm of Martin Luther, which, just as it is most frequently sung in the German Churches, so it has an admirable <term>energeia</term> <gloss>efficacy/activity</gloss> for stirring the soul, which I remember also affected you sweetly when I once recited a part of it to you, rendered in Stigel’s rhythms in this way:

> If this world were swarming 
> With demons like worms,
> We would not fear anxiously,
> We will win in the end stoutly.
> Let the prince of the world be proud,
> Let him gnash his teeth and rage,
> The scoundrel knows not how to harm,
> Since he is broken by even a little word.

But it did not weary Sleidan to insert that whole song into the history of our times, expressed in these words: GOD is a firm fortress and rampart for us. That ancient enemy of the human race now acts with all his might, and employs all kinds of engines. Our power indeed is small, nor can we withstand such an attack for long. But for our sake that hero whom GOD Himself has chosen for Himself has taken up arms and fights. If you ask who that may be, know that it is CHRIST JESUS, with whom the victory and triumph must rest. Because even if this whole fabric of the world were teeming with devils, we do not grow terrified, and with most certain confidence we await a joyful outcome. For however much Satan may rage and prowl, he will accomplish nothing against us. For he has been judged, and by a word alone all his armor falls. Our adversaries will not snatch this Word from us, but will leave it, however unwillingly. For GOD dwells in our camp and battle line, who protects us and our gifts with His spirit. If they take away life, if goods, if children and wife, you may bear it patiently. For nothing is added to them by that, but for us a kingdom is prepared that is immortal.

pages.23: I had written this letter privately to you, Illustrious and generous Lord SÉGUR, and indeed I wrote it as if I were speaking to you in a present conversation, my mind rejoicing at the auspicious news of your safe return to England. Nevertheless, I ought not to have resisted my friends, who wanted this, as a testimony of the true and not feigned judgment—not just of myself, but of many good men—regarding your virtues, and of praise, to be printed and prefixed to the book which Lord Brocardus had put to the press at this same time. In this book, so that he might satisfy your commands, he sought to illustrate that mystical Song of Solomon with his interpretation. Just as I am confident that its reading will be neither useless nor unpleasant to pious and learned men who will wish to judge the matter as a whole with an open mind, so I ask and pray with the reverence I owe you that you do not let this letter be a burden or a nuisance to you as a witness of my respect and love toward you, and that you continue to embrace me with your accustomed benevolence.

And continue to labor vigorously in the work of the Lord, as you do, to receive at some time the crown of justice, which the Lord, the just judge, will render on that day to you and to all who love His coming. # TO THE MOST AMPLE AND
## *Most illustrious Baron, Jacques Ségur*
## *Pardailhan, Prefect of the King*
## *of Navarre. Greetings.*

<note>A large decorative woodcut initial 'A' is set against a background of intricate foliate and vine patterns.</note>

In the year 1579, and frequently thereafter, you urged me to write something on the Song of Solomon. I, however, who both owe it to you and desire in all things—insofar as I am able and capable—to obey you, always refused for two primary reasons which I brought to you. First, because the exposition of that Song seemed to me at the time to be only for those who existed during a time of peace achieved among the entire Christian people: when the Church had attained her bridegroom, so that she might speak of herself and her own things properly, and those who were rapt in it, above others, in the love of CHRIST. Second, in other books, however I may have exposed them, I seemed to be impelled to write, and an argument was given to my mind, certain and without my own great meditation and deliberation. But because the same did not happen with this Song, such that suddenly to me

pages.10:
<page-num>10</page-num>

that one of Phoebus, the orator, King Sapor of the Persians, who, regarding the melancholic and dark sins of the humors in the microcosm, proposed for the eternal memory of mortals the Syrup of Apples <note>original: "Syrupum de pomis"</note>, <note>a digestive/cordial syrup used to treat imbalances</note> (corrupted by some as King Sabor’s syrup) to be cast down. I pass over Archelaus, Hiero, and Philometor, kings who wrote in Greek about plants. I pass over that antidote of the most invincible King Mithridates, praised by all by common consent to this day, which was found by Pompey in his shrines. In our own centuries, it is read in the monuments of history that Nicholas and Eusebius V, supreme pontiffs, were physicians by art and profession. Since it is so beautiful, it is hardly surprising if it is also difficult, and therefore, in the medical republic, there seem to be so many and such varied opinions that, regarding this, the saying of Horace from Book 2 of his Satires is recited by some:

> There are as many kinds of studies as there are heads.
> A thousand species of men, and a variegated use of things.
> To each his own will, and one does not live by a single vow.

Yet it must not be believed that this most noble science suffers any shipwreck thereby (for while opinions in theory are indeed varied due to the nature of its beauty and difficulty, in practice the judgment of all is the same, the calculation the same). Rather, it is directed and more firmly established for protecting and preserving the human republic and for repairing and defeating diseases, which is accompanied by the good. Hence, captivated by the same beauty, which is both difficult and beautiful, when I had proposed certain Theses for the Medical College at Prague in the year 1652 to be defended—and had published them to the public in print, as is customary—not a few friends who considered them difficult and beautiful for practice began to exhort me to add <catchword>reasons</catchword>
pages.11:
to corroborate them for the good of mortals. I, who struggle with difficulty in such an arena against so many critics, declined the advice. Yet, having found a timely opportunity (since I had seen even the most learned men doubting something in practice), I decided to follow the advice and I set them down in the same order in which I defended them at Prague. If anyone, feeling nauseated, rejects this labor of mine, let him know that I did not write for him. If he has better things, let him offer them, and he need not fear that I shall return the greatest thanks; it was never my intention, other than to have exercised myself on a subject that is difficult, most beautiful, and necessary for the common good of mortals. For if Emperors, Caesars, Kings, and Pontiffs have exercised themselves regarding the same, due to its beauty and the attendant good, why should it not be permitted for a physician, and let others enjoy it as they please.

# PREFACE TO THE CONCLUSIONS,
### which is
# THE FIRST CONCLUSION.

<note>Large ornamental drop-cap initial 'O' decorated with floral and foliate patterns.</note>
All men naturally desire to know. Some indeed desire to know their own origin, others crave to be skilled in science, and others have a mind to learn something else. I, in order to satisfy this natural tendency in some way, bring forward a few things from the vast field of medical faculty. Firstly, as to what is formed in the very first formation of man, or one might say the fetus: whether it is the heart, the fountain of human life; or the liver, the workshop of blood; or the brain, the most divine member, as called by Plato in the *Timaeus*. I assert that the liver is formed first, then the heart, and finally the brain.

There are many things, I admit, to be discussed in this conclusion: namely, how this is dilated in the injected seed, how it adheres, lives, and the like, which would pertain to the present matter; furthermore, whether it lives in potency or in act; whether a natural spirit is given, or whether it proceeds from the liver. However, setting these aside, I descend to my main intent (supposing from Aristotle, Book 1 of *Parts of Animals*, Chapter 1, that seed is generation, and generation is the first participation with the heat of the nutritive soul; from *On Youth and Old Age*, Chapter 14; likewise, Book 1 of *On the Generation of Animals*, Chapter 18, if the parts are dis-
pages.13:
tracted in the seed, how does it live? Likewise, Book 2 of *On the Generation of Animals*, Chapter 3, the seed and the conception live no less than plants, nor is Galen contrary). See: what is that first member, from the stated principles, which is generated first and most conveniently, and lives with a vegetative life? To make this conclusion of ours firmer, we shall draw authorities from Hippocrates and others. Afterward, if anything must be brought to the contrary, I shall resolve it.

Hippocrates, therefore, in his book *On the Formation of the Fetus*, and his faithful interpreter Galen, recount a certain case here (by which he intends to prove that the liver is generated first; I, however, shall bring forward both its structure and its purpose, so that everything may be more corroborated), which is as follows:

"But I saw the seed, which had remained in the place for six days and had subsequently fallen out, and from those things which then appeared to me in it, I conjecture the rest. How I saw the seed on the sixth day after, I shall tell. A certain maid of a woman (she was a notable singer who visited men, whom it did not befit to conceive in her womb, lest she be rendered contemptible; but that singer had heard what women are accustomed to say among themselves: when a woman is about to conceive, the man's seed no longer exits from the womb, but is contained within). When she had heard this, she observed it always, and by chance, when she felt that the seed had not exited, she revealed it to her mistress. When this reached our ears, we ordered her to jump onto the ground (another text reads, 'onto her buttocks,' and it is better). She did this about seven times, and the seed, not without a certain noise, was shaken out and flowed onto the ground. When the woman saw it, she inspected it and was amazed. What it was like, I shall say: just as if one were to tear the outer shell of a raw egg, so that through the inner membrane the inner humidity would shine through, such in a certain way it plainly was. There was a red and round thing inside; in the membrane, however, certain white and thick fibers were discerned, wrapped in a thick and red matter, and externally around the membrane were bloody bruises. In the middle, something thin was gaping, which seemed to me to be the navel, by which the fetus first breathed with the spirit going both out and in. From it, the membrane which contained the seed was entirely produced." This is the series of the history of Hippocrates, according to the interpretation of Galen and Bernardo Feliciano. Which, and the same Galen, and from Galen, Feliciano,
pages.14:
explain in their entirety, and indicate what all things signify. Truly, omitting other things, in Chapter 3, around the middle, they interpret that red thing thus, saying: "It is to be believed that that red, round thing which appears in the chorion in the six-day seed of Hippocrates was the liver, still indistinct and unformed." And shortly after, they add: "Before, however" (thus Galen/Feliciano from him), "when I was writing commentaries on the seed, and was forced to say something about the order of formation of the individual members, I said the heart, just as the liver, in the first days of the fetus, was as if a certain foundation, driven to this by the use of the same, most necessary in adults and perfect ones to be brought forward. But when I subsequently learned that it was the opinion of all others, both physicians and philosophers" (behold the sincerity of Galen admitting his own error, behold the foundations upon which he relied to change his opinion), "that the fetus is dispensed merely as a plant until express formation, it seemed more probable to me if we were to sustain that there is no necessity for the heart in the beginning, but that it is formed after the liver." And toward the end of the chapter, he adds: "But truly, just as it must be believed that the heart was made after the liver, and therefore the liver was constituted nearer to the womb of the pregnant woman (which anatomy itself demonstrates is very true), so it was fitting that the brain also be constituted further from the heart, since it is fashioned later." He gives the reason why the brain also is fashioned last, saying: "It is to be thought that this is done because the fetus has no need for a brain: for it does not need to see, nor hear, nor taste, nor smell anything, nor does it work with its hands or feet, nor use any other voluntary function at all. In a similar way, there was no necessity for the sense of touch, no imagination, no thought, no memory; therefore, in the third order of time, the brain was fashioned." (He speaks beautifully about the necessity of the final formation of the brain; if he had provided the same for the heart, it would be less burdensome for us, but we shall demonstrate it to the best of our ability.) These are the accounts of both Hippocrates and Galen; to me, however, let it be permitted to add this History of a Case which I saw to confirm it.

---

->A certain Marchioness of Tochau in Bohemia, January 14, 1653, after the tenth day of conception, suffered a mis-
pages.15:
carriage. Desiring to see it, or better said, being desirous and curious to see the constitution of the fetus, she had me called, and the midwife. In my presence, by my order and demonstration, she cuts the abortion into parts, and while she was cutting the chorion, a certain bloody mass was seen, without any motion, without any sense (as appeared from the section), interwoven and divided by various filaments. Outside the chorion membrane, other certain filaments were conspicuous. Who will doubt that that bloody mass was the liver, and those filaments were the rudiments of the veins and the navel? It appeared without sense, without motion; what else can you present or assign to me but the liver? Therefore, it remains that the liver is generated first, and nothing more convenient can be conceived for the vegetative soul than the member in which it resides: the liver. But let this be confirmed both from the structure of the liver and from its use.

The substance of the liver is fleshy, similar to blood recently shed and congealed, whence the word *parenchyma* <gloss>the functional tissue of an organ</gloss> was derived by Erasistratus. It is wrapped in a simple and sufficiently thin membrane, clinging tightly to the organ on all sides. It consists of veins in a double order: the Superior, which are branches of the *vena cava* <gloss>great vein</gloss> and lead the blood into its large trunk like a royal road; and the Inferior, which are more numerous and are branches of the *vena porta* <gloss>portal vein</gloss>, from which the umbilical vein also arises in the fetus, by which the fetus is nourished.

Its task and duty is to nourish the body to the very end of life; for from the natural spirit arising from the liver, both the vital and the animal spirits receive nourishment (although Manardus and with him Ioan. Hier. Bronzerius, in his book of letters, Book 15, first letter, seem to deny this in their treatise; yet they conceded it, and Bertachius in his third book, *On Spirits*, Chapter 3, on Galen, Book 1, *On Natural and Spiritual Faculties*).
pages.16: Capiuaccius (in his reading of the *Aphorisms*, 50, and others from Galen), because of whose necessity and use, Galen rightfully proffers these things about the liver in the last chapter of his 7th *Method*, "The work of the liver is most necessary to all parts." And in the 16th chapter of the 11th *Metaphysics*, he says: "It is most dangerous if the strength of the liver is dissolved, for this is what provides nourishment both to the heart and to the other parts." Hence, infants have more vigorous vegetative faculties, less vigorous sensitive ones, and even less intellectual ones, inasmuch as they derive such utility from the liver. Wherefore, Franciscus Vlmus Baiensis, a physician not to be despised, in his *Treatise on Urines*, collecting the duty and necessity of the liver, did not hesitate to call this the most noble member. Considering, therefore, its substance, considering its function, use, and duty, what was necessary to be generated first and most conveniently in the very first formation of the fetus, if not the liver itself? For the natural faculty (which I do not hesitate to call the natural spirit) permeates all members, not only through the arteries themselves and the veins, but also through the flesh, nerves, ligaments, bones, and everything else that constitutes our body. Whence it happens that even in the diseases of all parts, we can have both continuous and certain signs, and from this natural faculty—from the liver, the tinder and seat of this natural spirit—we can have knowledge of the disposition of the whole. Wherefore, shall we not concede that it is the foundation of the microcosm and the first principle in the microcosm? From the liver, or from the natural faculty arising from the liver, we not only have the open diseases of this principle, but also the internal causes of the diseases of the other principle members are represented. Let the brain labor, let the heart itself labor; certain pathognomonic signs present themselves (which it is not right to deny or contradict), by which you can conclude that these parts are laboring. But if the liver does not digest the nourishment presented to it through the subservient stomach, and convey it to the heart and to the brain, what help will you provide? If you believe that you can help those who are laboring with topicals,
pages.17: if you concede that (which to deny is to deny reason itself and experience—you will see, when I demonstrate a unique example, the case of a man lacking a liver), why will you not concede that the vegetative principle of the soul is more appropriately generated first in the fetus formation? Many similar and better things could be elicited in the medical field for the dignity of such a principle; truly, for the sake of the reader, so that he may refresh his mind, it must be granted—as it is permitted to me, the writer—that, leaving aside the medical study, we may descend into the field of recreation to the sacred secret fables of antiquity. From these, perhaps, our opinion will also be corroborated. Those who have left behind a written genealogy of the gods fable thus about Venus and Mars: that Venus was seen by Phoebus in adultery with Mars, and the adultery of the spouse was revealed to Vulcan by that same observer. Upon this matter of such great importance among the gods (having first captured both adulterers with iron nets), a Council was convened. Neptune, Mercury, and Apollo participated in the Council. It was decreed that the gods should have the children; Apollo interceded, Mercury interceded, but in vain did Neptune intercede. The divinities are freed. If it pleases one to accurately examine these fables and veils of fiction, we will easily understand that the heat of fire—that Vulcan—is very consonant with the mystery of our mortality placed in the marriage of Venus. He is procreated from Jove and Juno, that is, from Heaven, by the acting motion and light (for such is our native heat, spherical and considered by the most learned to be conformable to the element of the stars), and is brought forth from the Air and precipitated into the surrounding Island of the Sea—that is, into the earth, into the Venus of our mortality, understood by Water (through generation)—into a marriage, where at first he is nourished by monkeys, which it is sufficiently clear are of a most prone nature for imitating the actions of rational beings and for acting. Here, I say, he possesses Venus through the mixture of the humid. By the beauty of this Venus

pages.54:
Does the intellect organize itself to love and remember, and vice versa? Can the intellect believe and understand at one and the same time? Does the intellect create knowledge within itself? It is asked by what means the intellect creates a species <note>an intellectual representation or image</note>. Does the intellect, with its species, command the will and memory to objectify that species? Just as we apply the questions of the rule to the intellect, they can be applied to other faculties in their own way.

### On the questions of the table.

It is asked whether the world is eternal. Go to column b, c, d, and hold the negative, and you will find in chamber b, c, t, b, that if it is eternal, there are many eternities <note>original: "eternitates"</note> differing by species, and they are concordant through chamber b, c, t, e, against chamber b, c, d, which is impossible; whence it follows that the negative question is to be held, and this the rule b proves. It is asked whether God can be infinite as much by his magnitude as by his eternity; go to column c, d, e, and to chamber c, d, t, c, holding the affirmative against chamber c, d, t, d. Whether God can be as much by eternity as by intellect; go to column d, e, f, and to chamber d, e, t, d. Whether God is as powerful through his power as through his understanding and loving; go to column e, f, g, and hold the affirmative for chamber e, f, t, e, and for chamber e, f, t, f, and for chamber e, f, t, g, until the whole column is finished. Whether in God his intel
pages.55:
lectus and will are greater than his virtue; go to column f, g, h, and hold the negative for all the chambers of that column, extracting the meanings of the chambers. Whether the divine truth is in itself as virtuous through equal correlatives as the divine will; go to column g, h, i, and hold the affirmative for all the chambers of that column. Whether in God his virtue and his truth and his grace possess that by which they are equal, and remote from time, place, and minority; go to column h, i, k, and hold the affirmative for all the chambers.

¶ On the questions of the evacuation of the third figure.
In chamber b, c, it is said that goodness is great. Now it is asked whether goodness is great and what is its magnitude, and goodness, and magnitude, in what they agree. And whether they can agree without difference. And it must be answered that goodness is great as appears by the definition of magnitude. And its magnitude is to have correlatives; as is clear through the second species of rule c, and they are concordant, because goodness is great through magnitude and vice versa. Now, indeed, they could by no means agree without the difference of their correlatives. And let these things suffice concerning the evacuation of the third figure for the sake of brevity. For through these things which we have said about it, the artist can solve and make questions through other chambers.
pages.56:
¶ **On the questions of the multiplication of the fourth figure**
**It** is asked by what mode the intellect conditions itself to be general for general understanding. Go to the multiplication of the fourth figure and see by what mode the intellect multiplies the conditions with which it multiplies objects and its understanding, so that through many and great knowledges it becomes general and clothed in many habits. And let these things concerning the multiplication of the fourth figure suffice for the sake of brevity.

**On the questions of the mixing of principles and rules.**
**It** is asked whether goodness is discursive through magnitude, duration, etc., and vice versa. And it is to be answered that it is so, as is signified by the third figure, making the predicate of the subject. It is asked what goodness is in magnitude, duration, etc. To which it is to be answered that it is great in magnitude and durable in duration. It is asked what goodness has in magnitude, etc., to which it must be said that in it it has its correlatives, great in magnitude and durable in duration. And just as we exemplify about goodness, so it can be exemplified about other principles in their own way. And let these things concerning the mixture suffice in their own way.

**On the questions of the nine subjects. And first of God.**
**It** is asked whether God is. And it must be answered that he is. It is proven in the questions of the first figure. It is asked: What is God? And it must be answered that God
pages.57:
is an entity that acts in itself as much as he is himself. Through the second species of rule c, it is asked what God has in himself essentially. To which it is to be answered that he has his correlatives without which he could not have immense and eternal reasons. Through the third species, it is asked what God is in another. To which it must be said that he is creating, governing, and the like. Through the fourth species of rule c, it is asked what God has in another. And it must be said that he has in another power and dominion, and in men, judgment and the act of grace, mercy, patience, and piety. And let these things concerning God suffice for the sake of brevity.

¶ On the questions of the angels.

It is asked whether angels are. And it must be answered that they are. For if that which is less is seen to be from God, it is; and much more so, that which is seen to be more similar to God. Furthermore, if there is something which is composed of the intellectual and the corporeal, much more so is that which is composed of the intellectual and the intellectual. Moreover, if angels indeed were not, the scale of difference and concordance would be evacuated, and consequently the world, which is impossible. It is asked of what the angel is and whose it is. And it must be answered by rule d that it is of itself; its essence indeed cannot be punctual nor lineal. And by the second species of the same rule, it is of its spiritual correlatives, and of its <unclear>biles</unclear> and <unclear>are</unclear> <note>These terms likely refer to specific technical divisions in Lull's system</note> from which it is composed
pages.58:
correlatives, it is active; and through the <unclear>biles</unclear> it is receptive; and through the <unclear>are</unclear> it is an act existing between the <unclear>tiuos</unclear> and the <unclear>biles</unclear>. By the third species, it must be said that the angel is of God. And let these things concerning the angels suffice for the sake of brevity.

# On the questions of the Heavens.

**It** is asked whether the heaven moves itself. And it must be answered that it is so, so that its principles may have substantial and proper correlatives through its constellations. Whether the heaven moves itself to a place; and it must be answered that it is so in itself and in inferior things, circularly, but not outside itself. The reason for this is because outside itself it has no action, nor can it have. Whether an angel moves the heaven; and it must be answered that it is not, because if it moved, already the <unclear>tiui</unclear> by the movement of the correlatives would be lower, and the <unclear>biles</unclear> higher; and also by its form it would not now move elements nor elementated things, but by its matter, which is impossible. It is asked whether the heaven has a motive soul. And it must be answered that it is so, for otherwise sensitive and vegetative things would not have motive souls, nor would elements have motion. It is asked by the first species of rule d, e, why the heaven is. And it must be said that it is from the fact that it is constituted from its form and matter. Through the second species of rule e, it is asked why the heaven is; and it must be said that it is so that lower entities may be able to have motion. And let these things concerning the heaven suffice for the sake of brevity.
pages.59:
¶ On the questions of the 4th subject, which is man.
It is asked whether man can have greater knowledge of God by affirming or by denying; and it is to be answered that by affirming, for God is not through those ends by which he is, but through those ends by which he cannot not be. It is asked why man acts through a specific form; go to the second species of rule e, and there the solution is implied. Whether man, increasing his acts, increases his essence; and it is to be answered that no man acts upon himself. It is asked when man desires to remember and cannot remember, which of these fails first, either memory or intellect; to which it must be said that memory indeed more quickly renders the ancient species <note>memories/impressions</note> to the intellect than to the will. It is asked of what soul and body men are composed. And it is to be answered that in man, corporeal and spiritual goodness compose one goodness, and so of others. It is asked what the life of man is, to which it must be answered that it is that form which is composed of the vegetative, sensitive, imaginative, and rational. What is the death of man? It must be answered that it is the dissolution of the elementative, vegetative, sensitive, imaginative, and rational power. It is asked whether man is visible, and it must be said that no. For sight can see only color and figure. It is asked whether in man intellect and memory are the same power. And it must be answered
pages.60:
¶ not, because if they were the same power, the intellect would not then be successive in acquiring species, nor would it hand them over to oblivion, nor would it be ignorant of them. Again, because it would be too strong in the object against the liberty of the will. And let these things said concerning man suffice for the sake of brevity.

### On the questions of the imaginative.

Whether the imaginative imagines imaginable things in its own way just as the sensitive senses sensible things. It is asked what is the reason why the imaginative abstracts species from sensible things. It is asked what the imaginative is. Whether the imaginative has correlatives. Whether the imaginative increases itself by increasing its act. Whether the imaginative is a higher power than the sensitive. Whether the imaginative has specific instincts and appetites. Through what mode the sensitive hinders the act of the imaginative. Why the imaginative is not as powerful in sensible things or sensed things as the sensitive; go to the subject of the imaginative. It is asked whether the sensitive senses the imaginative. And it is to be answered that lower powers do not act upon higher ones.

### On the questions of the sensitive.

It is asked which power of these senses hunger and thirst, either taste or touch. And it must be answered that it is the one which more disposes the object. Whether taste thus senses hunger or thirst with instinct and appetite, just as sight senses the colored with
pages.61:
color. Go to the second species of rule c. It is asked from what the sensitive senses sensed things. And it must be answered that every particular sense senses its own sensible object through a specific form, just as a colored subject subsisting in crystal colors it. Whether the sensitive has punctual and lineal quantities. And it must be answered that the sensitive reaches an object from afar just as quickly as from near. Whether the sensitive, just as it has a common sense, so has a common power, instinct, and appetite. It is asked what the sensitive is. The sensitive, with what it is particular and common. From what the sensitive lives and is nourished. Whether the sensitive is sensed; go to the subject of the sensitive.

### On the vegetative.

Whether the vegetative acts through its species. Whether the vegetative has some reason through which it is common and particular just as the sensitive. Whether the quantity of the vegetative is punctual or lineal. It is asked what the vegetative is and what it has in itself through the second species of rule c. It is asked from what the vegetative lives and is nourished and grows, and in what subject it is planted. What is the death of the vegetative; go to the subject of the vegetative, in which the solutions of the aforementioned questions are implied.

# ON MYSTERIES
## AND SACRAMENTS.

<note>A woodcut depicts a bearded man in royal robes and a crown, seated at a desk within an architectural frame.</note>Intending to speak of mysteries, it is necessary before all else to explore what a mystery is, and what it comprehends, lest otherwise, by making many words about mysteries, like one running outside the stadium assigned to the contestants, he merely wearies himself in vain by laboring and achieves nothing but exhaustion: so too, not containing himself within the bounds of the mysteries while discoursing, he who wanders from the goal cannot grasp the palm.

<margin>Prouer. 20</margin>
<margin>Eccle. 27</margin>
<margin>Mat. 13</margin>
In the first place, therefore, it must be observed that "mystery" is a Greek term, although frequently used by the Latins, and it signified something secret, or that under which something secret lies hidden, and which is not perfected except by some hidden reason of sacred rites. For mysteries are sometimes called those things which are secret and hidden among men, which it is considered sacrilege to speak of in public, as is in Solomon in the Proverbs: "Do not associate with him who reveals mysteries, and walks deceitfully, and opens his lips." And in Ecclesiasticus: "To uncover the mysteries of a friend is the desperation of an unhappy soul." In the same way, the sacred mysteries of God are called mysteries, as is in Matthew concerning the one sowing his seed: where Christ says to His disciples, "To you it is given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven, but to others..."
pages.18:

<margin>1.Cor. 2.</margin>in parables. And in Paul writing to the Corinthians about the preaching of the Word of God: "We speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, which was hidden, which God predestined before the ages for our glory." And to Timothy regarding the incarnation of the Word
<margin>1.Timot. 3.</margin>of God, he says: "Great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifested in the flesh, justified in the spirit, seen by angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up in glory." And
<margin>Roma. 16.</margin>to the Romans concerning the same incarnation: "According to the revelation of the mystery kept secret since the world began, which was made manifest through the scriptures of the Prophets, according to the commandment of the eternal God for the obedience of faith." Paul also commemorates such hidden mysteries of God to the Romans, saying:
<margin>Roma. 11.</margin>"For I do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, of this mystery, lest you should be wise in your own opinion, that blindness in part has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter in, and so all Israel should be saved." And
<margin>1.Cor. 15.</margin>he writes to the Corinthians about the resurrection: "Behold, I tell you a mystery: We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, in a point of time, in the moment of an eye, at the last trumpet. For the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall rise incorruptible, and we shall be changed. For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality." The same
<margin>1.Thess. 4.</margin>mystery he also mentions when writing to the Thessalonians, saying: "For we tell you this in the word
pages.19:
<header>IN THE EUCHARIST, BOOK I.</header>

of the Lord, that we who are alive and remain until the coming of the Lord will by no means precede those who have fallen asleep, because the Lord Himself, with a shout, with the voice of an Archangel, and with the trumpet of God, will descend from heaven, and the dead who are in Christ will rise first: then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord." And John in the Apocalypse
<margin>Apoca. 1.</margin>explains the mystery of the seven stars. If Paul and John had not revealed these secrets of God to us, they would still lie hidden from us, unknown.

Sacred signs are also called mysteries by the Greeks and sacraments by the Latins, as Paul says to the Ephesians
<margin>Ephe. 5.</margin>speaking of the union of husband and wife: "This is a great sacrament, but I speak concerning Christ and the Church." In this sense, mysteries are sometimes taken by the Latins, as Paul says to the Corinthians,
<margin>1. Corin. 4.</margin>"Let a man so consider us, as ministers of Christ, and dispensers of the mysteries of God." However, to treat of all types of mysteries in this work is not my intention, lest I seem to be wise beyond sobriety; and I am not conscious of having drawn so much from the Spirit of God that I could either understand all the hidden and secret mysteries of God as is fitting, or pursue each one with apt words and illustrate them once understood.

Therefore, in this treatise, we are to assert that the truth of the body and blood of the Lord is in the sacrament of the Eucharist, if Christ grants it to us, and we shall use both terms, mystery and sacrament, indifferently, but more frequently the name "sacrament," which is more familiar to Latin ears. But before we begin our undertaking, that agreeing opinion of the most approved ancients concerning the sacraments should be set forth here conveniently, which is of this sort: *Sacraments are sacred signs, and symbols, of God's will toward us. And in the New Testament, they are certain and efficacious signs, and vehicles of divine grace, conferring grace upon those who receive them worthily.*
pages.20:
