<margin>Sapien. 9.</margin>
Since sacraments are effective signs of God's grace and our sanctification, they consist of two things: namely, of the sign itself, that is, the external element, shadowing forth the invisible grace, and of the word, through which the Holy Spirit works that grace secretly. For because we are dull toward receiving the spiritual grace of God due to our flesh (by whose mass the strength of the mind is weighed down), and we are in need of some external aid, by which our fragility might be both aroused and instructed: therefore, for the healing of human infirmity, God has applied the spiritual medicine of His grace, veiled by certain sensible signs: which the Greeks call symbols or mysteries, some Latins call sacraments, others call them sacramental signs. Christ confirmed these sacraments with His word and promise, so that no one might doubt their power and efficacy:
pages.21:
<header>IN THE EUCHARIST, BOOK I.</header>
<sig>C</sig>

the effect of which divine promise and operation is never wanting to those signs, unless an obstacle intervenes through the vice and unworthiness of the recipient. Such are baptism, the sacrament of penance, the Eucharist, or the sacrament of the body and blood of the Lord, and other sacraments: each of which has its own promises, supported by the Word of God as the firmest foundation, and appropriate and suitable to its own nomenclature. Baptism has the promise of grace, regeneration, and the kingdom of heaven annexed to it, as in this place:

<margin>Ioan. 3.</margin>
> *Amen, amen, I say to you, unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he cannot enter into the kingdom of heaven:*

and in another place,

<margin>Mar. ult.</margin>
> *He who believes and is baptized will be saved.*

The sacrament of penance has the promise of the remission of sins, and of restoration into the fellowship of the mystical body of Christ, which is the Church: as here,

<margin>Ioan. 20.</margin>
> *Whose sins you remit, they are remitted to them.*

Furthermore, the Eucharist, or the sacrament of the body and blood, has the promise of eternal life, and of abiding in Christ: as in John,

<margin>Ioan. 6.</margin>
> *He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life: and I will raise him up on the last day. For my flesh is food indeed, and my blood is drink indeed: he who eats my flesh, and drinks my blood, abides in me, and I in him: as the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father: so also he who eats me,*
pages.22:
<header>ON THE TRUTH OF THE BODY AND BLOOD OF THE LORD.</header>

he himself also will live because of me. Therefore, the worthy reception of the Eucharist constitutes us as members of Christ, just as, on the contrary, through its unworthy reception, which carries judgment with it, we make ourselves members of Satan.

Furthermore, the Word of God offers us the promise of grace: the sacramental sign is like a seal of the Word of God, exhibiting the thing promised. Therefore, just as the promise is useless to us unless it is apprehended by faith: so the sacramental sign is similarly useless to us unless it is believed that we will receive what is signed. For otherwise, if nothing that does not appear is received through the sign of the sacrament, then the sign itself will be ineffectual, and it will be said that nothing of more distinguished efficiency, or of greater grace, has been added to our New Testament sacraments from the power of Christ's passion than was present in those sacraments that were in the Old Testament.

<margin>Luc. 22. Mat. 26.</margin>
In the holy sacrament of the Eucharist, however, to whose worthy reception the promise of grace is annexed, two things are to be considered: namely, both the sign exposed to our senses, and at the same time the true body of Christ, to be known not by the judgment of the senses, but by faith, as appears through the words of the Savior Himself, saying:

> This is my body, which is given for you: This is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins.

Which words, from the very cradle of the Catholic Church after Christ suffered, without any allegory,

...when he did not know these things, how he could be so powerful in speaking. "And Catulus," said Antonius, "I am not some hunter of utility for speaking when I am in the habit of reading these books and several others, but rather I do it for the sake of pleasure when there is leisure. What then is the case? I will confess: there is something nevertheless—just as when I walk in the sun, even if I walk for a different reason, it happens by nature that I am tanned; so, when I have read those books quite studiously at Misenum (for in Rome it is scarcely permitted), I feel my oration is, as it were, colored by their song. But, lest this seem to you to extend more widely; I understand these things at least in the Greek works which those who wrote them themselves wished to be understood by the common people. If I ever fall upon your philosophers, deceived by the indices of the books, because they are generally inscribed about known and illustrious things, about virtue, about justice, about honesty, about pleasure; I understand absolutely no word: they are so bound up in narrow and concise disputations. As for the poets, I do not attempt to touch them at all, as if they spoke in some other language. With those, as I said, I amuse myself who have written about deeds or their own orations, or who speak in such a way that they seem to have wished to be familiar to us, who are not the most erudite. But I return to that point. Do you see how great a duty of the orator is history? I do not know if it is the greatest in the flow of oration and in variety. Nor do I find it anywhere set apart and instructed by the precepts of the rhetoricians: for they are placed before our eyes. For who does not know that the first law of history is that one should not dare to say anything false: next, that one should not fear to say anything true, so that there is no suspicion of favor in writing, nor any of spite? These, of course, are the foundations
pages.485: note is known to all. But the building itself is placed in matters and words. The rationale of matters requires the order of times and the description of regions: it also desires, since in great matters worthy of memory, first counsels are expected, then acts, then outcomes, that it be signified regarding the counsels what the writer approves, and that in deeds it be declared not only what was done or said, but also in what manner; and, when the outcome is discussed, that all the causes, whether of chance, or of wisdom, or of rashness, be explained; and not only the deeds of the men themselves, but also of those who excel in fame and name, [that one speak] about the life and nature of each one. The rationale of words, however, and the genus of oration must be pursued as diffuse and extended, and flowing with a certain equable gentleness without this judicial harshness and without the barbs of forensic sententiae <note>concise, pointed expressions or arguments</note>. Do you see if there are any precepts for these so many and such great matters that may be found in the arts of the rhetoricians? In the same silence, many other duties of orators have lain dormant: exhortations, consolations, precepts, admonitions: all of which must be treated most eloquently, but have no place in those parts which have been handed down. And in this genre there is also that infinite forest; because most people (as Crassus also showed) have given the orator two genres for speaking: one about a certain, defined cause, such as those that are involved in lawsuits or in deliberations: (let one add, if one wishes, also praise) the other, which almost all writers call by name, but no one explains: the infinite question of a genre without time and without person. When they speak of what this is and how much it is; they do not seem to me to understand
pages.486: to understand. For if it is the orator's duty that, whatever matter is posited infinitely, he can speak about it: it will be necessary for him to speak about how great the magnitude of the sun is, what the shape of the earth is: he will not be able to refuse to speak about mathematics or musical matters once this burden is undertaken. In short, for him who professes that it is his duty to speak not only about those controversies which are marked by times and persons, that is, about all forensic matters, but also about the infinite questions of genera; there can be no genus of oration that is excluded. But if we wish to add that wandering, free, and broadly extending part of questions to the orator; so that we think the orator ought to speak about things good or bad; things to be sought or to be avoided; honest or shameful; useful or useless; about virtue, about justice, about continence, about prudence, about greatness of spirit, about liberality, about piety, about friendship, about faith, about duty, and about other virtues and their contrary vices; and likewise about the state, about empire, about military affairs, about the discipline of the city, about the characters of men: let us assume that part as well, but in such a way that it is circumscribed by modest boundaries. For my part, I think that all things which pertain to the use of citizens, the character of men; which are engaged in the custom of life, in the rationale of the republic, in this civil society, in the common sense of men, in nature, in customs; must be embraced by the orator; if not so that he might answer separately about these things in the manner of philosophers; then certainly so that he can weave them prudently into a cause; but that he should speak about these very things in such a way as those who have established rights, laws, and cities have spoken,
pages.487: simply and splendidly, without any series of disputations and without the barren contention of words. In this place, let there be no surprise if no precepts for so many and such great things are set down by me: I decide it this way, just as in the other arts, when the most difficult things of each matter have been handed down, it is not necessary for the rest to be handed down because they are either easier or similar; as in painting, he who has fully learned to paint the appearance of a man is able, even if he has not learned it, to paint anyone of any form or age; nor is there danger that someone who paints a lion or a bull excellently would not be able to do the same in many other quadrupeds; nor is there any art at all in which all things that can be accomplished by that art are handed down by the teacher; but those who have learned the genera themselves of the primary and certain things pursue the rest by themselves not inconveniently: similarly, I think that in this rationale or practice of speaking, he who has attained that power, so that he can move the minds of those who hear with some power of deciding, whether about the republic, or about his own matters, or about those against whom or for whom he speaks, to his own judgment; this person will not seek more about that whole genre of remaining orations as to what he should say, just as that Polycletus, when he was fashioning Hercules, did not ask how he should fashion the skin or the hydra, even if he had never learned to do these things separately. Then Catulus. You seem to me, Antonius, to have been able to clearly see before your eyes what he who was to be an orator ought to learn; and what, even if he had not learned it, he would take up from that which he had learned. For you have reduced the whole man into only two genres of causes. The rest
pages.488: you have left to practice and similarity. But see to it that in those two genres the hydra and the skin do not become your Hercules, and that other greater works are not left behind in those things which you omit. For it does not seem to me to be less work to speak about the universal genera of the accused than about the causes of individuals, and much greater to speak about the nature of the gods than about human lawsuits. It is not so, said Antonius: for I will tell you, Catulus, not as a learned man, but, which is greater, as one experienced. The oration of all other matters, believe me, is a game for a man who is not dull, not unpracticed, and not experienced in general literature and more polished humanitas <note>refined culture or humanity</note>. In the contentions of causes there is a certain great work, and I do not know if it is by far the greatest of human works: in which the power of the orator is judged by the unskilled for the most part by the outcome and the victory: where there is present an armed adversary who must be both struck and repelled: where often he who is to be the master of the case is a stranger and angry, or even a friend to the adversary and an enemy to you; when he must either be taught or untaught; or repressed or incited; or moderated by every means for the time and the cause by oration: in which often benevolence must be led to hatred, and hatred to benevolence: who must be twisted as if by some machine, now to severity, now to the relaxation of the spirit, now to sadness, now to joy. The weight of all sententiae and the gravity of all words must be used. There must be added a varied action, vehement, full of spirit, full of breath, full of pain, full of severity.
pages.489: full of severity. If anyone in these works has grasped that art, so that he can fashion the statue of Minerva as Phidias could: he will certainly not labor over how the same craftsman learns to do those lesser works on a shield. Then Catulus. The more great and miraculous you have made those things, the greater the expectation holds me as to by what rationales or by what precepts such a great power is acquired: not that it concerns me now: (for my age does not desire it; and we have followed a different genre of speaking: we who have never extorted opinions from the hands of judges by some power of oration, but rather, with their minds calmed, we have received only as much as they themselves allowed) but nevertheless I seek those things of yours for no use of my own, but led only by a desire for knowing. Nor do I have need of some Greek teacher who might chant to me common precepts; when he himself has never looked upon the forum, never looked upon any trial: as that Peripatetic Phormio is said to have done: when Hannibal, expelled from Carthage, had come to Antiochus as an exile; and because his name had great glory among all, he had been invited by his hosts to hear the one I mentioned, if he wished; and when he had said that he did not mind: the man, who was fluent, is said to have spoken for several hours about the duty of a commander and about all military matters. Then, when the others who had heard him were vehemently delighted; they asked Hannibal what he himself judged about that philosopher. This Carthaginian is said to have answered, not in the best Greek, but nevertheless freely: that he had often seen many delirious old men, but he had never seen anyone who was more delirious than Phormio.
pages.490: seen anyone. And by Hercules, not without cause. For what could be more arrogant or loquacious than for a Greek man, who had never seen an enemy, never seen a camp, and in short had never touched the smallest part of any public duty, to give precepts about military matters to Hannibal, who had contended for empire for so many years with the Roman people, the victor of all nations? This, it seems to me, all those who give precepts about the art of speaking do. For they teach others what they themselves have not experienced: but perhaps they err less in this, that they do not try to teach you, like Hannibal, but boys or young men. You err, Catulus, said Antonius. For I myself have already fallen upon many Phormios. For who among those Greeks is there who thinks that any one of us understands anything? And indeed they are not so annoying to me. I easily endure and bear with them all. For they either bring something that does not displease me, or they cause me not to repent less that I have learned. However, I dismiss them not as insultingly as that philosopher did to Hannibal: and perhaps I have more trouble for that reason. But nevertheless, their doctrine, as much as I can judge, is quite ridiculous. For they divide the whole matter into two parts, into the controversy of a cause and that of a question. They call the matter placed in the disceptation of things and controversy a Cause: but they call the matter placed in infinite doubt a Question. They give precepts about the cause. About the other part of speaking, a wondrous silence. Finally, they make, as it were, five limbs of eloquence: to find what you should say: to arrange what has been found: then to adorn with words: then to commit to memory:
pages.491: then at the end to act and to pronounce. A matter surely not hidden. For who would not have seen this on his own, that no one can speak aptly unless he has both what he should say, and in what words, and in what order he should say it, and has remembered these things? And I do not criticize these things, but I say that they are placed before our eyes, just as likewise those four, five, or six parts, or even seven (since they are arranged differently by others) into which all oration is distributed by them. For they bid us to begin in such a way that we make the one who is listening well-disposed to us, and docile, and attentive: Then to narrate the matter in such a way that the narration is verisimilar, open, and brief: After this to divide the cause or to propose; to confirm our side with arguments and rationales, then to refute the contrary. Then, however, others place the conclusion of the oration and, as it were, the peroration. Others bid us, before one reaches the peroration, to digress for the sake of adorning or amplifying, then to conclude and perorate. I do not even criticize these things: for they are neatly distributed, but nevertheless, which was necessary for men inexperienced in truth, not expertly. For what precepts they wanted to be for beginnings and narrations, these are to be preserved throughout the entire oration. For I can also make a judge well-disposed to me more easily when I am in the course of the oration than when all things are unheard; and docile, not when I promise that I will demonstrate, but when I teach and explain; and attentive, indeed, we can achieve through the whole action by stirring up the minds of the judges, not by a first announcement. Furthermore, that they bid the narration to be verisimilar, and open, and brief—

...divine will. We have seen our own, thriving in letters, by writing to one another, leave behind a memory of their friendship. This King of ours seems to abide by the aforementioned treaties, both those concluded with other nations and those with us, at least as far as I can see. He innovates nothing, before having perceived that either you or some others have breached the treaty regarding him, and he acts according to his own counsel.
Otherwise, if you should decide to write to me henceforth for the sake of our spirits, I would gladly accommodate myself to this service, since you began to love me of your own accord and provoked me with your letters, a thing for which I love you wonderfully.
Since Linacre and Tunstall have bound me to themselves by this sort of service, and have received my reply, I would like to ask you to greet them in my name; and render a greeting to More, or rather pay it back with interest, who greeted me in your letters by the messengers with Linacre. Farewell, man most friendly to letters, and write me into your register. Paris, the fifth day before the Kalends of May, in the year 1518.

### Guillaume Budé to Richard Pace. Greeting.

Nicolas Bérauld, who delivered this letter to you, a man most learned in both languages <note>original: "utraque lingua" referring to Latin and Greek</note> and already no mean contributor to good letters, is also otherwise a very dear friend to me. When I began to hear that he was going to travel there in the company of the Bishop of Paris, I thought it my duty to give him a letter for you, even
pages.19:
if I had written a long enough letter to you a few days ago, and entrusted it to a certain kinsman of mine who is a companion of the same retinue. For I did not want Bérauld, a man familiar to me and at one time a guest of your Erasmus, to be in Britain without your knowledge, since you yourself seemed to me to be a very great lover of scholarly men. Whatever service and courtesy you extend to him while he is staying in a foreign province, I shall not refuse to let you charge it all to me. Although (given the humanity I have discovered you possess) I do not doubt that you would have done so of your own accord, if you could once have learned that a man of such talent and such learning was there; and indeed when you have time to get to know him, you will be so desirous of doing everything for his sake that you will not ask me to count what you have bestowed upon him as a favor to me. And yet, I would like him to be commended to you in my name, so that he may be among those whom I am most permitted to commend to my friends through your kindness. Farewell, Paris, the day after the Assumption of the sublime divine Mother of God.

Good immortal gods, what do I hear? Oh, how many? How great? What panegyrics? What theatrical speeches, worthy of applause by you and me, has the celebration of the betrothal excited among us; and the fame of our embassy, received with such richness, splendor, magnificence, kindness, elegance, and eloquence! Oh, your elegant King, greater than any praise, more excellent than any commemoration of merit, who has accommodated such great and ample gifts of body and mind with such noble generosity, remarkable goodwill, and graceful courtesy toward all; who has rendered the munificence of a kind nature worth seeing, embellished by the dexterity of his manners, his august majesty, heroic appearance, and the uprightness of his countenance. Our people, having returned from there, began at once to commemorate that splendid magnificence of the preparations and the proper and orderly arrangement; when they were received by almost all with receptive ears, every serious man indeed followed that account with gaping (so to speak) mouth and awestruck countenance: that this most serene prince is accustomed to frequent his retinue with the presence of every most learned man and every man most excellent in the faculty of speech, and thus to distinguish and adorn his court with those ornaments; which appearance they themselves provide to the venerable royal court, and to be viewed by outsiders; he himself is in my opinion worthy, that his fame, illuminated by those lights, might shine in every direction, as far as the boundaries of the Christian name extend, and might one day be consecrated to eternal memory by the monuments of men of genius. Indeed, as far as I am concerned, I would do nothing more willingly, nor more eagerly, if ever the occasion for writing should arise
pages.20: my intent, so that I may leave behind for such a great King a certain memorable eulogy, as a testimony of my mind inclined toward his majesty: that he has indeed served letters nobly and honorably, if what we have heard is true. For he who has raised the honor of the humanities, which had been reduced to the common level, both by the neglect of other nations and especially by our own customs and institutions, to a height of greater dignity, even by the example set forth in himself and the institution of royal eloquence, he has most beautifully snatched the glory of the thing away from contemporary and future kings alike. For he is the first of kings in many centuries to have understood and seen that the force and authority of eloquence are such that it may raise kings among the gods above and those below, according to the merits of each. If this virtue offered itself so easily to be embraced, and to be retained with a certain immediate sweetness, whose splendor and appearance would earn applause from every kind of man, those acquainted with the liberal disciplines just as those who are ignorant of them, undoubtedly princes, nobles, and primary men, educated by such a great example, would soon begin to strive to preserve the majesty of the higher letters, as I see the sense of our own people is now affected since our ambassadors have returned. For now, there is no one among us who is not ashamed and regretful of his own ignorance. But your speech, most learned Richard,
pages.21:
held in the most ample assemblies of others, is celebrated to such a degree: as that rich and resplendent apparatus employed for the conduct of affairs; your eloquence has been greatly honored by it, and has seemed more magnificent. If you hope that we will do equal things in this part of preparing matters, I fear that we might not be able to satisfy you, for among us the value of industrious work has never stood, due to the notable obscurity of French affairs because of that loss and indignity. Nicolas Bérauld, now most dear to you (as I have understood from your letters), has set out for the court with the President of Paris, aided remarkably by your votes and recommendations, and raised by the hope of it, which is not in doubt. The King is said to be arriving now, to receive the ambassadors expected from there. Farewell, my Pace, and greet my Tunstall, my More, Linacre, and the others for me. Paris, the Nones of November.

## Guillaume Budé to Richard Pace. Greeting.

Having now received your third letter, I have marveled at your diligence in this way of cultivating friendship, the like of which I have scarcely experienced in any of my friends thus far. I wish you are now successfully recovered from your fever. For it will be right for me to be concerned henceforth for how well you spend your life, and how firm a health your body enjoys, since I hold that so benevolent spirit of yours within it. By how much the more <unclear>[...]</unclear>
pages.22: willingly and more nobly you have offered yourself to friendship, by so much more happily... and indeed even when I count up my friends from abroad, you are justly ranked among the very first, and you seem to me not only to have written your name of your own accord into the catalog among those of yours, but also to be performing the customary duties with hand and heart. Therefore, I count a great addition to have been made to my accounts in your name: those indeed more sacred ones, which I have decided to deposit not in the temple of Saturn, but in the citadel of Pallas. Therefore, because you indulge yourself so kindly toward me in the duty of a friend, you have incurred a huge debt of gratitude from me. But see how far you have already stepped forward. For what will happen if I summon you not on the basis of a formal stipulation, but of a spontaneous promise: since I have been beautifully secured, both by the testimony of the herald and by letters signed by you; and so that you cannot finally plead that you were circumvented, you have not hesitated to promise the same thing again, and after a fairly long interval; since for those who bind themselves thus, if they subsequently begin to shirk their duty and make their agreements void, the constitutions of the laws permit the shaming of a repeated promise and the bond of a doubled obligation to be cast against them. Therefore, while I recognize and embrace that candor of spirit with which you promise yourself simply to the service, I will nonetheless take such account of your courtesy and generous humanity, that I shall demand the promise only so far: that your word may be burdened only to the extent that
pages.23: you can happily and without great trouble fulfill it, and not even that at the very first opportunity, but when I have called in older debts; which I still have many good and suitable ones, and whose judgment and adjudication I could establish in my own forum if disputes should arise from them. Moreover, I have the reckoning of this calendar of names arranged in such a way that I think I have done well if I keep the written bonds safe at home; being one who rejoices that my resources are situated in such a way that I can long boast that the day of many wealthy debtors has arrived, and yet I would not want it to come, nor if it had arrived, could I demand it without shame or sorrow. I hear that a most ample embassy regarding a matter both grand and pacificatory is soon to go there. I would like it to have been decreed so auspiciously that peace might be confirmed from it for my age and yours; so that I might be able to test and act on more equal terms with you (if things should turn out that way) by an action on behalf of a friend, which any person might wonder that none is specifically mentioned in the civil law: one who might certainly think and notice that an action for a partner lies most broadly in the Pandects of the law. But in that embassy, the Bishop of Paris will obtain either the first or second place, as is the rumor: whether he was going to make his way through this city, it was not yet certain when I wrote this, and
pages.24:
he had already been among the courtiers for a long time, where he spends the greater part of his time. He is a man learned among the few, and endowed with the prudence of many things, an embracer and supporter of lettered men, and a student of your Erasmus: with whom I have a relationship more than a custom of life, for I dwell in the city. I believe that you will observe him dutifully, even by the recommendation of this very thing, especially since in performing your duty (as I conjecture) it will often be necessary or opportune for you to speak with ambassadors. Farewell, and return a hundredfold greeting to Tunstall, Linacre, and More, who greeted me with your words or letters. Paris, the Kalends of August.

The Scholar asked, "Then, where are you headed?"
Juan replied, "I am going to my uncle’s house to take refuge." 
The Scholar then used these words to tease her, and Juan did not refuse him. The Scholar asked for a marital bond, and Juan agreed. # The Presentation of the Lady of Jieyu

<margin></margin>
The elegant lady died at twenty; this is truly what is called a jade person crushed by the earth. How moving!
</margin>

Chen Youliang of the pseudo-Han dynasty had a Lady of Jieyu <note>an imperial concubine title</note> named Zheng Wane. She possessed a jade-like constitution and an icy grace, with a beauty unmatched in her time. She was also familiar with literature and skilled in music and rhythm. The pseudo-Han treated her with the utmost favor. She died at the age of just twenty and was buried at the Pipa Pavilion in Jiangzhou <gloss>Jiangzhou is modern-day Jiujiang</gloss>. At that time, two serving maids were buried with her: one named Xichan and the other named Jin’e. Although the Lady of Jieyu was noble and beautiful, after entering the underworld, her spirit would sometimes appear in broad daylight. Those living nearby would occasionally see her walking about or hear the sound of her playing music, and none were without feelings of grief. In the early Hongwu era, Shen Shao of Wujiang, a young man of twenty, was also handsome and talented. He studied poetry under Sa Tianxi <gloss>a master of poetry</gloss> and calligraphy under Guo Bojing <gloss>a master of calligraphy</gloss>, both of whom were praised by their contemporaries. Once, he harmonized with Tianxi’s two poems about passing through Jiaxing and writing on Wu: The first said, "The Seven Marshes and the Three Rivers connect for a hundred li; the willows and lotuses reflect the lake—"

<column-break/>

<margin></margin>
These two poems about Wu, although using the scenery to express his feelings, also contain gratitude and longing; they were not written lightly.
</margin>

"—water. Past the water gate, then it is Pan Gate; behind half-hidden red curtains in the painted towers, the *miwu* herbs have grown over the mandarin ducks. The east wind has blown away all the pear blossoms; in the Guanwa fragrance path, deer run, and in the clear night, lanterns can be seen. Below the Temple of the Three Worthies <gloss>a shrine to three sages</gloss>, the eastern flow continues; above the grave of Zhenniang, the wind blows through the bamboo. After Xi Shi left, the wooden sandals were overturned; year after year, the spring deepens, and the fire-scars turn green. In the prosperous region of the southeast, a stretch of flute and string music brushes the river water. The young maiden writes of spring on a white ramie shirt; the magnolia oars and orchid paddles are in the mirror’s reflection. The dance stages and song pavilions face the gull sands; the whitewashed walls are half-hidden by cherry blossoms. The butterflies picking fragrance do not leave, fluttering down on the light, round silk fans. Who will continue the Wu songs tonight? In the willow shadows, the flute blows through the Ke Pavilion bamboos. Fan Li’s flat boat is gone and will not return; only the spring waves reflect the green of the people."
His other poems were of this same class. However, because his family was wealthy, he did not wish to serve in office. People knew this, and those who coveted his wealth—some wishing to recommend him as a filial and incorrupt official, others wanting to nominate him as a student—caused such a constant disturbance that he had no peace. <margin>Sighing at the tomb, lamenting the mistake of the treacherous official—this has been the public sentiment for a thousand years.</margin>

## The Beautiful Concubine Writes of Regret

The Honorable Concubine of the Han was Wang Qiang. Because she entered the barbarian lands according to the registers, she wrote of her regret using the *pipa*. Later, she was buried in that land, and the grass on her tomb turned green. In the Guiwei year of the Dading era of the Jin Dynasty, Wanyan Shouyi, a refined scholar from the capital, had business to attend to <gloss>circumstances</gloss>. He saw the tomb of the Honorable Concubine and felt moved in his heart. He cupped his hands and sighed, saying, "How heroic! How heroic! The treacherous official ruined you! Han lies in the northern desert, drinking the sorrow and regret of a thousand years! How bitter!" After he left, he simply let it pass as a thing of the past. By evening, he was returning and passed by the Concubine’s tomb. He raised his eyes to look and saw a magnificent residence standing tall and alone <gloss>kui means tall</gloss>. The painted beams and carved rafters were not of human standards; the red curtains and emerald screens resembled the celestial abodes of heaven. Shouyi was both surprised and suspicious. Before he could investigate in detail, he saw a beautiful woman with fragrant breath and a graceful figure come out from within, saying, "Young master, would you like to humble yourself and come in for tea?" Shouyi—

<column-break/>

<margin></margin>
Shouyi wrote that the Honorable Concubine lived among the barbarians; the barbarians were like a cold moon. He looked at her from afar and fell in love. He actually met her and talked; once the words were finished, he was completely captivated. This was also a strange encounter.
</margin>

—had not yet spoken when the beautiful woman requested it again. He had no choice but to follow her. He entered the main hall, took the host’s seat, and they had tea, followed by wine. The beautiful woman rose and thanked him, "During the day, I was honored to receive your clear gaze and the expression of your indignant words. Although I have been in the Nine Springs <gloss>the afterlife</gloss> for so long that even the grass and trees have rotted, I am touched and will not forget it." Shouyi was just about to ask her name and about her words during the day when the beautiful woman rose suddenly and said, "I beg to describe my own inner feelings; young master, please do not be surprised. I am not a person of this living world. I am Wang Qiang, Zhaojun, of the Great Han Dynasty. Because of the traitorous official <gloss>referring to Mao Yanshou of the Han</gloss>, I was forced to harmonize with the barbarians. I left the Emperor, and the Emperor felt regret when he saw my appearance, but I had already been sent to the barbarians; what could be done about his regret? I arrived at the barbarian court, holding the *pipa* every day to write of my regret, and died of depression. Even today, I am still a ghost lingering in the direction of my hometown." She chanted a seven-character four-line regulated poem to lament herself, saying:

> The *pipa* is silent, the moon is lonely. The Wang Pass—

<header>Folio 345b</header>

for perfection due to it being perfection, and holding imperfection in contempt due to it being imperfection. Since perfection and imperfection are not in themselves existing entities, but rather conditions that attach to things—as if they were genera—they only exist within their subjects. Therefore, every perfection demands our humility <term>al-khushu'</term> <gloss>humility/reverence</gloss>. This is a primary proposition acknowledged by all. As for whether this or that is a perfection, that requires clarification. What is a perfection for one group may be an imperfection for others. This is evident to anyone who has examined the various laws, opinions, and traditions. A thing may be a perfection in relation to one thing and an imperfection in relation to another. This is perfection by relation. Something may be a perfection at one time and not a perfection at another. However, this is not called perfection; rather, the name "good" is applied to it. For "goods" are either synonymous with perfection or more general than it. Things that are perfections may be so by convention and law; thus, written and unwritten opinions contain perfection by convention. Consequently, they are perfection according to some, and according to recognized perfection, they are so for everyone. What exists by convention varies: what is perfection to one group is not perfection to others. Therefore, those raised among a certain people have souls that feel humility <term>al-khushu'</term> <gloss>humility/reverence</gloss> for things that others hold in contempt <term>al-istihana</term> <gloss>disdain/contempt</gloss>. Thus, if there is something that is a perfection in existence, and a human being among a certain people has become accustomed to not feeling humility <term>al-khushu'</term> <gloss>humility/reverence</gloss> for that thing which is a perfection, and it is then clarified to him that it is indeed a perfection, his soul will not feel humility <term>al-khushu'</term> <gloss>humility/reverence</gloss> for it, nor will he honor it, nor see that he has attained anything. Such knowledge, for that person, remains disregarded; he cares nothing for it except for the sake of the argument, just as the sick perceive the bitter as sweet and see one thing as two. Likewise, the sick of soul see perfection as imperfection and imperfection as perfection. Just as there is no way for these sick people to perceive the sweet as sweet until they are cured, the sick of soul cannot see the good as good until their souls are healthy. Just as among the sick there are those who perceive the sweet as bitter and judge it to be bitter, and others who perceive it as bitter yet know it to be sweet—or judge that the defect is in themselves—it is incumbent upon the latter, even if he does not hold it in contempt <term>al-istihana</term> <gloss>disdain/contempt</gloss>, to discard it.
pages.53:
<header>‘Abd al-Raḥmān Badawī [40]</header>

The second does not merely hold it in contempt. Neither of them understands the nature of the sweet as it should be understood. Likewise, the sick of soul are afflicted with this very same state; they do not know the good, and the good does not move them. The spiritual image <note>original: "al-ṣūra al-rūḥāniyya"</note> of things <note>(1)</note> that are good does not move these people at all. If it does move them, it is only toward fleeing from the followers of the well-known paths and the things present in the year six hundred <note>(2)</note> of the Hijra of Arab history. All of this deposits diseases in the souls. Therefore, they do not know the perfection that is devoid of potentiality, but only know rest <note>term: <term>sukūn</term> <gloss>rest/immobility</gloss></note>. This is when it is purely in potentiality. Excitement accompanies this for them; they feel it because excitement is a form of pain. They recognize of perfection only that which is accompanied by motion, because pleasure exists at that point. If perfection is attained and completed, they do not feel it. Similarly, the healthy person does not feel his health, nor does he see that he has been given something of value; the sick, however, feel it and see it as the greatest of all perceptions, as they were healthy in potentiality. The feeling of "perfectional rest"—if it is permissible to call it rest, as it is a rest not accompanied by the potentiality of motion—is a very noble matter. One must discipline oneself in sensing it until it becomes a habit. If this type becomes a habit, it has an immensely valuable influence on human existence. This is a matter that must precede the discussion on the supreme happiness <note>term: <term>al-sa‘āda al-quṣwā</term> <gloss>supreme happiness</gloss></note>.

Just as we said regarding affection <note>term: <term>infi‘āl</term> <gloss>affection/being acted upon</gloss></note>, we must examine and count in how many ways it is said that the agent acts, and how we sense the desiderative part <note>term: <term>al-juz’ al-nuzū‘ī</term> <gloss>the desiderative or appetitive part of the soul</gloss></note> in action. For the desiderative soul is acted upon; we do not act through the desiderative soul, but through another part that is in actuality, because the desiderative part is only in potentiality. It might be thought that the discussion on this was not finished in *On Generation and Corruption*, just as happened in the case of the "right side," for Aristotle only spoke of it in *Meteorology* regarding what follows.

<note>Footnotes: (1) ‘T’ reads: "things". (2) ‘T’ reads: "the years of the seven hundredth [year] of the Hijra of history".</note>

<header>New Epistles by Ibn Bājja [41]</header>

the sea formed from the elements <note>term: <term>usṭuqusāt</term> <gloss>elements</gloss></note>. For this reason, he said in [book] "Y" <note>note: i.e., the 15th book of *On Animals*</note> of *Animals* that the discussion on the right side was not finished, and that every thing acted upon—in fact, every thing in motion—is in actuality [346a] something else. For if it were not something in actuality at all, potentiality would be something existing in actuality, and prime matter <note>term: <term>hayūlā</term> <gloss>prime matter</gloss></note> would necessarily exist, and possibility would be subsistent by itself and something subsistent in its own essence. This is evident to anyone who has practiced natural philosophy, even if only slightly. The thing in motion is some essence, or rather some body, because every thing in motion is divisible; but that is due to motion in a way that is intermediate between what is by essence and what is by accident. Aristotle considers that to be among the accidental. For if it were by essence in some way, it would not be first. The mover in potentiality is something by essence and first. It moves insofar as it is in potentiality, such that if what is in potentiality were found to be something separate from bodies, it would move by itself and that thing would become either an essence, a quantity, a quality, a place, or some other of the categories <note>term: <term>maqūlāt</term> <gloss>categories</gloss></note>. However, what is in potentiality necessarily requires—as we have said—that it be something in actuality. We have said it is something else in potentiality. It is therefore in actuality one of the categories, and in potentiality one of the categories. Let what is in potentiality be P, what is in actuality be A, and the thing by account be C. It is clear to anyone who has practiced physical science, even if only slightly, that what is in potentiality, insofar as it is in potentiality, is not under a category, for everything that is under a category—

<note>Editorial note: The translator lists various references to Aristotle's works *On the Parts of Animals* and *On the Progression of Animals* where the right side is discussed, noting it is considered more noble, warmer, stronger, and the initiator of motion.</note>
pages.55:
<header>‘Abd al-Raḥmān Badawī [42]</header>

—whatever category it may be—is something existing in actuality. The categories are therefore contrasted by potentiality just as they are contrasted by what is in actuality in A, C. If they were under one category in A, C, they would be two contrasted types. If they were two essences, they would have no name, but Aristotle and Abū Naṣr <insert>al-Fārābī</insert> might call them "contraries" when the need arises. However, contraries require one subject in actuality. These two do not have a subject in actuality. If they are under one of the nine categories that are in potentiality, they necessarily exist as an essence <note>term: <term>jawhar</term> <gloss>essence/substance</gloss></note>, so they have a third existence through which they are a subject for A, C. In A, L, if they are under quantity <note>term: <term>kam</term> <gloss>quantity</gloss></note>, they are more similar to contraries than the first type. For this reason, it is said that growth is motion, and that it is change more than is said of rest. The two contrary types of quantity are similar in two ways: first, they are types accompanied by the privations of their homogeneous counterparts, as is found in the form of essences. Second, they have subjects existing in actuality that are capable of receiving types of quantity. Essence types do not have subjects; rather, they are the subjects. Indeed, if the mover is said to have subjects, it is by way of skepticism. They differ from contraries in that types of quantity do not have two limited extremes from which one can speak. The largest dog cannot have the size of an elephant, and the smallest cannot have the size of an ant. Thus, types of the size of essences are many and varied, and their extremes are not limited except in relation to one another, so a contrariety occurs to them, as occurs to the extremes of temperament <note>term: <term>mizāj</term> <gloss>temperament/mixture</gloss></note> in quality. This has been summarized in *On Temperament*. As for A, C, if they are qualities and under one of the four genera of quality, they have a subject existing in actuality. Accompanied by each type of that genus is a privation homogeneous to it, and in them are two types that are extremes, not by relation but absolutely. It is impossible to find a type further

<note>Footnotes: (1) i.e., in the treatise "On Temperament". (2) ‘T’ reads: "its homogeneous counterparts".</note>
pages.56:
<header>New Epistles by Ibn Bājja [43]</header>

from that extreme than its counterpart, and this is not the case for what is quantity. Let the smallest size be that of a dog, for example, upon A, and the largest size be upon R. What exists in A or T, A, R. Every type of quantity that exists in a dog is closer to R than the size A is to D; there does not exist a size further from A than D. If that were found, it would be smaller than R; let it be E. The size R is closer to A than E. Thus D is not an extreme in Q, unless Q is universal, for it is a type of essence. The sizes A and C are not extremes by relation in reality and by essence to the first subject, which is in potentiality, i.e., the prime matter; rather, they behave as it does, because one of its parts is matter. A and A are not extremes in terms of what they are, or from the aspect of a relation that has attached to them. Thus they are not extremes in existence. For everything that exists and has some state from the aspect of being that thing, that thing exists for it. And what exists for it while it is in a certain state, and that thing exists for something else that does not have that state, it is not said to be such in existence. Rather, if it has it in existence, it is by way of analogy. Also, if A and C are not under one category, it is possible for it necessarily to be A, C; otherwise, it would be arbitrary and nothing existing. If that is impossible, then C, A are not one of them a subject for the other, except as it is said that the light is cold in potentiality, because the light implies the hot from the fire. The summary and enumeration of these types is easy for anyone who desires it, and we suffice with this summary by way of definition.

All contraries, if they are in their subjects, necessarily require in them the privations of their opposites. Privations are of types: among them is the privation of essence, the privation of quantity, and the privation of quality. I do not say that essence is ever non-existent, nor quantity. If there is something that is not a quantity, such as the intellect, this is a negation and not a privation. <insert>[346b]</insert> Abū Naṣr has summarized the mode by which it is called privation. Privation is attributed to the category in two ways: among them is its negation, as we say: "The sky is neither heavy nor light"; and among them is the lifting of the negation of a type of it from
pages.57:
<header>‘Abd al-Raḥmān Badawī [44]</header>

a subject that could contain that type. This is more deserving of the name "privation" than the first. It is then said in various ways, the most deserving of which is the privation summarized in the contraries in the book *Categories* <note>original: "Categoriae" or "Qāṭāghūrīyās"</note>. This second type that we mentioned is what Abū Naṣr <Fārābī> mentions, saying: Aristotle considers the privation of every category within it: the privation of essence is in the category of essence, and the privation of quantity is in the category of quantity.

It is clear upon the slightest reflection by anyone who has practiced natural science that prime matter cannot be devoid of some categories such that it would not contain one type of them. The first is essence. This was made clear in the first book of *Physics* <note>original: "Sama‘ Ṭabī‘ī"</note>, for if it were devoid of it, prime matter would possess a form. Following this is quantity, for it is not a single essence—because it is not a body. How far removed is he who composes size from what is not divisible! For if it were so, there would exist an essence without quantity. This is impossible. This has been made clear in the beginning of the sixth book of *Physics*, and made more clear upon reflection. You must know that "size" is said of the spherical and the straight by ambiguity, and that the spherical size is what has a center. We have summarized this in our commentary on the meanings of the seventh book of *Physics*. Then, after that, in the matter <note>term: <term>hayūlā</term> <gloss>prime matter</gloss></note> is the genus of qualitative affection: such as heat, cold, moisture, and dryness. Therefore, every material essence is a body. "Body" is said by ambiguity of what moves in a circle and what moves in a straight line; their matter is not one in type, as it depicts it, but they relate as the relation of forms. The matter that accepts motion in a straight line is the matter by priority. As for that which accepts circular motion, it is always a subject and is not matter, nor prime matter. Rather, it is called matter and prime matter by analogy, just as this is called a subject by similarity and analogy. Prime matter is not devoid of the genus of qualitative affection, and it cannot be stripped of it. Therefore, when Aristotle wants to indicate all of them, he says: "every tangible body." Likewise, the quality of quantity, which is shape

and form. Likewise for "where" <note>term: <term>ayna</term> <gloss>where/place</gloss></note>, position, "when," and relation. It is clear that prime matter is not devoid of these nine categories, though some are clearer than others.

As for action and passion <note>term: <term>fi‘l wa-infi‘āl</term> <gloss>action and passion/being acted upon</gloss></note>, there has been skepticism regarding them. However, when the matter is examined, it appears to be so. As for the category of "having" <note>(1)</note>, it is found in the soul; and it may be found in inanimate objects that which one thinks is "having," except that when the matter is examined, it appears it is not under this category.

Likewise for color: it may be thought of some bodies that they are devoid of color, such as air and glass. More evident than this are tastes and smells <note>(2)</note>, for their subject may not be devoid of all their types. Even so, these are not present to the essence in itself first; rather, they are found secondarily, and after various things under <note>(3)</note> another category have preceded them in the subject. It is as if these, even if they are not types of those, are like types. An example of this is tastes; for even if they are not types of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness, they are not outside of them, because they are heat to which another matter has attached, by which <note>(4)</note> that heat became a type of another genus, as occurred in the discussion on moving spheres: for the consideration of them is not a geometrical one resulting in geometrical theory, but it is rather under geometrical theory. We have summarized this in our remarks in *On the Soul*.

What we have said has been summarized in another way, which is that every body is composed of form and subject. The subject of the eternal bodies is specific to the subject. The subject of the generated and corruptible is called prime matter and matter and things similar to these. Every body

that is corruptible is an element <note>term: <term>usṭuqus</term> <gloss>element</gloss></note> or composed of two or more elements. Everything composed of things contains what belongs to those things. The things necessary for the elements are necessary for every material body. The things necessary for the elements from the categories are that they are essences, possess sizes, possess qualitative affections, possess positions and places <note>(1)</note>, that they have "when," that they are relative, and that they act and are acted upon. Every body necessarily contains these genera of categories. As for the rest of what is found in material bodies, they revert to these—an example of this: roughness and dryness <note>(2)</note>, hardness, softness, and smoothness. As for the rest of what is found in material bodies, they revert to these. An example of this <unclear><...></unclear> <note>(3)</note> is that they are varieties of moisture and dryness. For when dryness is joined by an accident, it becomes roughness and dryness. From moisture comes smoothness and softness. Aristotle has mentioned this in the second book of *On Generation and Corruption*. Likewise for taste and smell, for these two genera contain moisture and dryness as matter. As for colors, the discussion on them is a different discussion. When the matter is examined, it appears that this genus is found in the elements. A full investigation of this is in a place other than this.

It has been made clear in the seventh book of *Physics* that alteration only occurs in the sensible things. Let anyone who wishes refer to that in the words of Aristotle there, and what the commentators have said about it. Action and passion are only in the primary qualities, which are those by which generation and corruption occur, and they are the four, and they have been enumerated in many places. We have clarified in places other than this that "potentialities" are said by equivocation of: the passive and the active, and we have defined each of these two genera. which constantly darted their three-pointed tongues. Countless vipers emerged from his legs and thighs, and, folding themselves in various convolutions, extended along the entire length of his body, with hissings so horrible that they astonished the most intrepid. His mouth exhaled only flames; his eyes were burning coals, with a voice more terrible than thunder; sometimes he bellowed like a bull, sometimes he roared like a lion; and sometimes he barked like a dog. <margin><insert>CaG</insert></margin> The upper part of his body was bristling with feathers, and the lower part was covered in scales. Such was this Typhon, formidable even to the Gods, who dared to throw rocks and mountains against Heaven while making hideous howls; the Gods were so terrified by this that, not believing themselves safe in Heaven, they fled to Egypt and took shelter from the pursuit of this monster by hiding there in the form of various animals.

Attempts have been made to explain what the ancient authors said about Typhon morally, historically, and physically. The applications that have been made of it have sometimes been quite successful; but it has never been possible for mythologists to explain his fable in its entirety within the same system. His marriage with Echidna made him the father of various monsters worthy of their origin, such as the Gorgon, Cerberus, the Hydra of Lerna, the Sphinx, the Eagle that devoured the unfortunate Prometheus, the Dragons guarding the Golden Fleece and the Garden of the Hesperides, etc.

Mythologists, in order to get out of the embarrassment into which this fable threw them—which for them became one of the most obscure mysteries of mythology <note>(a)</note>—have taken it upon themselves to say that the Greeks and the Latins, ignorant of the origin of this fable, only obscured it further by wanting to transfer it, according to their custom, from the history of Egypt into their own. Based on traditions they had learned through their trade with the Egyptians, they made Typhon into a monster equally horrible and bizarre, whom the jealous Juno had caused to emerge from the earth to take revenge on her rival, Latona.

What Diodorus <note>(b)</note> and Plutarch <note>(c)</note> report to us about this is not to the taste of the Abbé Banier; no doubt because they are not at all favorable to his system in this regard. These two authors, he says <note>(d)</note>, "did not fail, according to the genius of their nation, to mingle several ridiculous fictions into what they report; and furthermore, they are not very exact in their chronology, and knowing only very confusedly the first histories of the world renewed after the Deluge, among which is undoubtedly that which I am explaining (of Typhon), they are guides that should only be followed with great caution." Although the Abbé Banier is right to think that these authors were not well-versed in the essence of the history of Typhon, it is nonetheless true that they had collected what they

If they mixed in some circumstances to adapt it to the fables of their own country, they preserved the foundation, which is found to be equally fabulous. In vain does Gerard Vossius <note>(a)</note> claim that Og, King of Bashan, is the same as Typhon, based on the resemblance of the two names; for, he says, that of Typhon comes from <term>τύφω</term> <gloss>to smoke, to burn, to kindle</gloss>, and that of Og means *he burned, he scorched*. In vain does M. Huet <note>(b)</note> make him the legislator of the Hebrews, who became odious to the Egyptians through the loss of their firstborn sons: the Abbé Sevin is no more correct to put him in the place of Cush; nor the Abbé Banier in that of Sebon, following on this occasion the sentiment of Plutarch, who relies on the authority of Manetho. It would not be possible to reconcile Plutarch with himself. Bochart succeeded better <note>(c)</note> than all the aforementioned authors by thinking that Typhon is the same as Enceladus; but he guessed without knowing why, since he was ignorant of the reason that led the poets to name them interchangeably for one another, and to have them both perish in the same manner. The poets, much better than the historians, have preserved for us the true foundation of the fables, and have, strictly speaking, defaced them less than the historians, because they were content to report them, embellishing them, it is true, sometimes, but without bothering to discuss why, how, and

But finally, what can one conclude from so many different opinions? That one must seek what we ought to think of Typhon in the traits upon which the historians, the poets, and the mythologists are in agreement, or in which they differ little. The poets and the mythologists all say in concert that Typhon was precipitated under Mount Etna, and the ancients who did not place his tomb there chose for this purpose sulfurous places known for their subterranean fires, such as in Campania, or near Mount Vesuvius, as Diodorus claims <note>(a)</note>, or in the Phlegraean Fields, as Strabo recounts <note>(b)</note>, or in a place in Asia where water sometimes issues from the earth, and at other times fire, according to Pausanias <note>(c)</note>. In a word, in all the mountains and all the other places where there were sulfurous exhalations. Finally, the Egyptians recounted that he had been struck by lightning and that he had perished in a whirlwind of fire.

Let us compare all this with some circumstances of Typhon’s life, and unless one wishes to stubbornly close one's eyes to the light, one will be forced to admit that the entire history of this alleged monster is but an allegory, which is part of the one that the priests

Since, according to the Abbé Banier himself <note>(a)</note>, the Greek and Latin poets and historians have preserved for us among their most absurd fables the traditions of Egypt, it is to these primitive traditions that we must hold. They teach us that Typhon was the brother of Osiris; that he persecuted him until he caused him to die in the manner we have mentioned; that he was then conquered by Isis, aided by Horus; and that he finally perished by fire. The historians also report that the Egyptians held the sea in abomination because they believed it was Typhon himself, and called it *foam* or *spittle of Typhon* <note>(b)</note>, names they also gave to sea salt. Pythagoras, instructed by the Egyptians, said that the sea was a tear of Saturn. The reason they had for this was that the sea, according to them, was a principle of corruption, since the Nile, which provided them with so many goods, was corrupted by its mixture with it. These traditions also teach us that Typhon caused Horus to perish in the sea, into which he threw him, and that Isis, his mother, resurrected him after drawing him out.

We have said that Osiris was the igneous, gentle, and generative principle that Nature employs in the formation of mixtures; and that Isis was its radical moisture; for one must not confuse the one with the other, since they differ from each other like

smoke and flame, light and air, sulfur and mercury. The radical humor is, in mixtures, the seat and nourishment of the innate heat, or natural and celestial fire, and becomes like the bond that unites it with the elemental body; this igneous virtue is like the form and soul of the mixture. This is why it performs the office of the male, and the radical humor, as moisture, performs the function of the female; they are therefore like brother and sister, and their reunion constitutes the base of the mixture. But these mixtures are not composed of the radical humor alone; in their formation, homogeneous, impure, and earthly parts join with it to complete the body of the mixture; and these gross and earthly impurities are the principle of its corruption, because of their combustible, acrid, and corrosive sulfur, which acts constantly upon the pure and incombustible sulfur. These two sulfurs, or fires, are therefore two brothers, but enemy brothers; and by the daily destruction of individuals, one has reason to be convinced that the impure prevails over the pure. These are the two good and evil principles of which we have spoken in the first and second chapters of this book.

This being posited, it is not difficult to conceive why Typhon was made into a terrifying monster, always disposed to do evil, and who even had the audacity to make war against the Gods. Metals abound in this impure and combustible sulfur, which gnaws at them by turning them into rust, each in its own species. The Gods had given their names to the metals; and this is why

Herodotus <note>(a)</note> says that the Egyptians counted at first only eight great Gods, that is to say, the seven metals and the principle of which they were composed. Typhon was born of the earth, but of the gross earth, being the principle of corruption. He was the cause of the death of Osiris, because corruption is only effected through the solution that we have explained while speaking of the death of this Prince. The feathers that covered the upper part of Typhon's body, and his height, which carried his head to the clouds, indicate his volatility and his sublimation into vapors. His thighs, his legs covered with scales, and the serpents that emerge from them on all sides are the symbol of his corrupting and putrefactive aqueousness. The fire he throws from his mouth marks his corrosive adustibility and designates his pretended brotherhood with Osiris, because the latter is a hidden, natural, and vivifying fire, while the other is a tyrannical and destructive fire. This is why d'Espagnet calls him the tyrant of Nature and the fratricide of the natural fire, which fits Typhon perfectly. Among the philosophers, serpents are the ordinary hieroglyph for dissolution and putrefaction; thus, it is agreed that Typhon does not differ from the serpent Python, killed by Apollo. It is also known that Apollo and Horus were taken for the same God.

This monster was not content with having caused his brother Osiris to die; he also cast his nephew Horus into the sea after seizing him.

One could not have designated the resolution into water of the Philosophical Horus or Apollo more clearly than by saying he was precipitated into the sea; the blackness which is the mark of the perfect solution and of the putrefaction called death by the Adepts is seen in this Queen of Ethiopia. This corrupted and putrefied matter is precisely that foam or spittle of Typhon, in which Horus was thrown and submerged. It is truly a tear of Saturn, since the black color is the Philosophical Saturn. Isis finally resurrected Horus; that is to say, the Philosophical Apollo, after having been dissolved, putrefied, and become black, passed from blackness to whiteness, called resurrection and life in the Hermetic style. The father and mother then reunited to fight Typhon, or corruption, and after having conquered him they reigned gloriously, first the mother or Isis, that is to say, the whiteness, and after her Horus her son, or the redness. Without resorting to so many explanations, the very supposed tombs of Typhon make us understand what was thought of this monster, father of so many others, which we will explain in the chapters that concern them. Some say that Typhon threw himself into a marsh where he perished; others that he was struck by lightning by Jupiter, and that he perished by fire. I have worked, fought, and conquered by sea and by land, and I have extirpated the race of the vicious, of the seditious, and of the traitors.
How did you arrive at being a Knight?
By five swords.
How were they placed?
One on my head ready to pierce my skull, brains, tongue, and throat, and the others were on my heart and my hands in the form of a cross ready to pierce me if I had been found false in my past works.
What happened to you?
I was purified by the fire and the water of sanctification.
Where does this water come from?
From the Jordan; water salutary through the operation of St. John and which gives to the Knights of the Orient <note>original: "ch.. cl.."</note> the courage and the zeal necessary to fight the infidels.
What is the name of the Knight of the Orient: <term>Nishmat Chayim</term> <note>original Hebrew: "נשמת חיים"</note>
Give the signs of...
How old are you? 70.....7070

I will let the kind reader judge for himself at the conclusion of this work: only let him not lose sight of the first concept and description of what playful thoughts, symbols, and allegories are—namely, that they can be drawn, interpreted, compared, and explained in various ways and to various things—but rather pay close attention to it when I paint before the eyes, and place in the hands, at least in the main points, and upon which most depends, that this or that thesis can only be drawn in this way, and in no other possible ways, or interpreted in many ways, consequently it cannot be a mere play of thoughts.

H. It has not happened by chance that the all-wise Creator of all things, when He wished to make Himself known to the created creatures, also explained Himself through measure and number, having specified such Himself, for example, in the erection of the Tabernacle in the desert, the Temple at Jerusalem, and the New Jerusalem, and having wanted everything arranged so precisely according to them: There must be something in the measure and numbers which bears witness to the Divine Wisdom; otherwise it would have been all the same to God, or could have been, whether the Tabernacle

# And the Lord said to Moses
Pass on before the people, and take with you some of the elders of Israel, and your staff, with which you struck the river, take in your hand, and go. Behold, I will stand before you there upon the rock at Horeb, and you shall strike the rock, and water shall come out of it, and the people shall drink. And Moses did so before the eyes of the elders of Israel. And he called the name of the place Massah and Meribah, because of the quarrel of the children of Israel and because they tested the Lord, saying: "Is the Lord among us or not?" Then came Amalek and fought with Israel in Rephidim. And Moses said to Joshua: "Choose for us men, and go out, fight with Amalek; tomorrow I will stand on the top of the hill with the staff of God in my hand." And Joshua did as Moses said to him, to fight with Amalek; and Moses, Aaron, and Hur went up to the top of the hill. And it was when Moses lifted up his hand, Israel prevailed; and when he let down his hand, Amalek prevailed. But Moses' hands were heavy; and they took a stone, and put it under him, and he sat on it; and Aaron and Hur supported his hands, one on one side, and one on the other; and his hands were steady until the going down of the sun.
