He also shoved me back with such impetuosity that I, in anger, grabbed my taper with both hands and smashed it to pieces on his head in the church, whereupon I had to avoid both my <term>sodal</term> <gloss>confraternity member</gloss> status and the school and study at home. In this manner we traveled to the command that my father had received, which is the <term>border fortress</term> of Brod on the Sava River; but I and my brothers were sent to Possega <term>ad studia</term> <gloss>for studies</gloss> with the Jesuits, though against my desire, from where we always came home for the <term>vacancies</term> <gloss>vacations</gloss>.

Anno 1725 I had to endure the following danger to my life again: My father was visited by a certain engineer colonel, Count C*** and his family, as a neighbor; and since there was a pretty young girl in his retinue, with whom my eldest brother fell in love, we all three decided to escort her back, which also happened. But as we were driving back the next day from Diacovar, where we stayed overnight, it happened that the first wheel struck a log and we all fell out of the carriage. My eldest brother, however, who was steering the horses in place of the coachman, fell under the horses and was broken on the wheel in such a way that

<meta>catchword: er</meta>
pages.16:
<header>Life and Deeds</header>

<note>Small ornamental flourishes flank the word "und" in the header.</note>

he died two hours later on the way in the forest, after he had given the final sign of life and farewell to my father, who had received news of it and arrived at this misfortune just in time, with open eyes, but spoke no more words, and passed away immediately thereafter.

My grandmother, who was a Countess von Witt and loved us all tenderly, was so frightened and saddened by this fatal case that she also died of it 6 weeks later. My mother also had to succumb to a similar fate shortly thereafter, namely in the year 1726. Of all these deaths, none saddened me more than that of my dear brother, whom I also, for lack of a clergyman, prepared quite well for death, with the exception of confession and communion. My old father, however, was inconsolable over three such sensitive losses, as indeed he never proceeded to <term>vota secunda</term> <gloss>second marriage vows</gloss>. Meanwhile, he still kept both us brothers at our studies, though not away from home; which was once again the cause that I had to escape a danger to my life. For once, on the Sava River, which flowed right past our house, in wintertime, when the marshes were frozen and the ice was floating on the river with a multitude of ducks, I took a small boat,
pages.17:
<header>of the Baron von Trenck.</header>
<sig>A 5</sig>

with which I could travel perfectly, and drove with my shotgun through the ice, which I avoided quite skillfully, at the ducks, and shot three of them dead and one’s wing off. As I then chased the wounded duck, and forgot the danger in which I was, an ice floe shoved me with such force onto another like it, that I sat quite by accident on the other floes and saw my little boat shattered into pieces and drifting away. Who would have thought that I would escape this time too? My father and brother, together with good friends, threw their hands over their heads and called out to me that I should commend myself to God, which I also did. I floated in this way soon half a mile downstream, and the ice floe, because there was a narrow place there, wedged itself; and since it was not possible due to the amount of ice to come to my aid with a ship, over 300 people ran to help my <term>spectaculum</term> <gloss>spectacle</gloss>. The ice floe had hardly stopped when a Pandur <note>A member of the irregular infantry serving under Baron von Trenck.</note> with a rope in his hand, out of love for me, dared to reach me and safely led me out of my danger. I remained unpunished by my father here as well.

A few weeks after this experienced danger, I was in a boat with my
pages.18:
<header>Life and Deeds</header>

brother on a duck hunt, and as the boatman steered us both close to the ducks, and my brother, who was kneeling in the boat before me, did not want to shoot but wanted to be even closer, I took the shotgun and shot behind him; I hit the ducks, but at the same time I shot the garment from my brother from the right side down to the skin, and two lead pellets into his arm. If I had held a finger lower, I would have shot his arm completely away. Hereupon I received severe beatings from my father, and my brother, when the new battalions were raised, became an ensign under Wallis.

Shortly thereafter, namely on the 10th of July, 1727, the now deceased Hungarian <term>Palatinus</term> <gloss>Palatine</gloss>, Count Nicolaus Palfi, took me into his regiment as an ensign. From this time on my luck began to contend with misfortune, and misfortune with luck, <term>vice versa</term> <gloss>conversely</gloss>. The first misfortune was that, when my father sent me to Esseg to equip myself there, I became so deathly ill with a fever that my father, through the provision administrator still in Esseg at the time, our secretary at the time, Herr von Hess, sent the money <term>pro funeribus</term> <gloss>for the funeral</gloss>, and the hussars to accompany my body, to Diacovar, where I lay sick; but I was, through the help of good medicine,
pages.19:
<header>of the Baron von Trenck.</header>

soon cured, and thus had to travel to Belgrade to my regiment. I was barely 4 months in Belgrade when I already had a <term>rencontre</term> <gloss>encounter/duel</gloss> with an ensign of the regiment, who at first made me retreat; but finally, with a blow over the nose and skull, then four blows to the hand, he had to settle down. I also received three blows to the hand, and the hilt of my Parisian sword was hacked down by this strong man, although I was, so to speak, a child, so that it remained lying on my wounded hand. The same year I again had an affair with a Silesian volunteer named Gersdorff, whom I wounded through the hand.

Anno 1728 I had an affair with a certain Count Paradiso, from whom I had won 380 florins, and he did not want to pay me, over which I insulted him, and he struck at me with his hand, though he only touched my head by the tip of the hair. I drew my sword, but he jumped out of the coffee house, in which there were about 30 officers, and as I made my way through the officers with my sword in hand and wanted to go out the door, he lunged at me outside the door; I, however, wanted to parry him with my left arm and received a thrust through it; but this did not stop me from attacking him, and
pages.20:
<header>Life and Deeds</header>

and he, or I, would certainly have reached the <term>extremum</term> <gloss>end/fatal conclusion</gloss> had not about 6 officers thrown themselves upon me and hindered the affair in such a way. I later defamed him again, and could never learn where he went, for I have not been paid by him to this day. Perhaps, when this comes before his eyes, he will announce himself. I had two more small skirmishes in this year, which however ended without injury, consequently I will not make further mention of them.

Anno 1729, however, I again had an affair with the Auditor of the Prince Alexander of Württemberg’s regiment then stationed in Belgrade, by the name of Beyer, whom I finished off with two thrusts into his right side, for which he had to have himself cured for 6 weeks. It then happened that my battalion, in which I served, had to march to Esseg, and we arrived there in the month of October of this year. Here I must recall that I have hitherto traveled with my father through all of Sicily, the Neapolitan, Apulian, Roman, Venetian, Triestine, Carniolan, Styrian, Licanian, Croatian, Slavonian, Serbian, Austrian, Sirmian, Hungarian, and a part of Bosnia.
pages.21:
<header>of the Baron von Trenck.</header>

I had barely arrived in Esseg when I again, although I had never given any cause for it, got into an affair with my own cousin, named Tillier, with whom I fought twice, and wounded him both times.

Anno 1730, however, I fought again with Baron F***, whom I also wounded through the arm, and although I had liked to see beautiful girls since the year 1727, I was still not skilled enough for intrigues, but rather I satisfied my desire with everything young that came before my eyes, without giving myself any trouble. In this year, however, I fell in love with a certain young lady of good lineage, but since the father and mother, in whose house she was, kept a very good watch on her, I had to content myself initially only with the pleasure that I walked past her window at night and, this was the signal, cleared my throat sharply, whereupon she immediately came running to the window and spoke a few words with me to comfort us both. This <term>rendezvous</term> <gloss>meeting</gloss> I frequented very diligently and constantly; in such a way that I had wished that it were always night, in order to be able to talk with my beautiful young lady, until I finally brought it so far that she found the opportunity to let me into her bedroom. What could be more foolish than the two of us
pages.22:
<header>Life and Deeds</header>

lovers to see? I could not speak anymore for love, but only kissed her hands constantly and pressed her to me: she, however, as a young lady of 14 years at that time, smiled. I was also not bold enough to involve myself further in love, and thus left my young lady. As great as the love of this person for me was, so great also became the <term>esteem</term> <gloss>respect</gloss> she held for me, as I gave her no cause to commit an excess. I was thus loved by her in such a way that I could always, and whenever I wanted, come to my beauty at night. I chatted so much of love with her at every rendezvous, and held her beauty and coldness up to her, that she said to me at the seventh rendezvous, quite enraptured: (of which I will also remember my life long,) "Baron Trenck! I am no longer in a position to resist your love, do with me what you want, yet save my honor." Hereupon she fell into my arms quite enraptured and with tear-filled eyes; I kissed her, and she me again, with which we were satisfied, whereas certainly another more indiscreet lover than I, who had the motto <term>le respect arrête mes désirs</term> <gloss>respect stops my desires</gloss> always firmly imprinted, would not have let it rest there. I believed now that I would once be happy

to be able to hide a matter from one about whom he is already suspicious; he immediately concluded that this journey served to bring the *Portuguese* into his kingdom, that they would make themselves masters of it, and force him to embrace the *Catholic Religion*: upon this, he summoned the great lords of his court and very secretly shared his thoughts with them; they all agreed that one should not permit the *Ambassador* and me to take this road which we had planned, as it was the direct one, and that we should be made to take another and very inconvenient route through many detours and the land of *Baly*.

<margin>Forced to take an inconvenient detour.</margin>
After much debate back and forth, he said to us finally in conclusion that he would never let us pass along the road we intended, but certainly through *Baly*, to which one would have to adjust, for we were determined to continue this undertaking.

<margin>The Kingdom of *Baly*.</margin>
*Baly* is a *Kingdom* that formerly belonged to the *Empire of Ethiopia*; but the *Galles* and *Mahometans* possess it at present; it borders the *Kingdom of Adel*, and it lies to the east of the *Kingdom of Narea*. From this, I could easily conclude that I could not complete this journey, and that, after I had encountered all these difficulties in the lands of the *Emperor*, I had even greater ones to expect in the lands of the *Kaffers*, who have no other *Law* than their own advantage; nevertheless, considering that it was for the service of *God*, I took the road to *Baly*, trusting in His mercy.

<margin>Set out on the road.</margin>
The *Ambassador* and I, departing from the court of *Narea*, took our road eastward and arrived on the first day at the place where the *Captain* was, whom the *Benero* had assigned us as a guide; in the beginning he received us quite well, hoping to get a fine gift from us, but that which we presented to him,
pages.15:
# ANTONIO FERNANDEZ.

<margin>1613</margin>
did not correspond to his hope and expectation. Because of this, he let us wait for him for 8 days, after which he gave us 80 men to accompany us to the borders of the Kingdom of Narea. We went with this escort

<margin>Entering a wild land.</margin>
for 4 long days' journey through a wild and deserted land to avoid the raids of the Gallas. Our escort then turned back, and since the road we still had to cover was very dangerous, we let some scouts run ahead of us to give us a signal as soon as they spotted Gallas from afar, so that we might have time to go and hide in the woods.

At midday, we began to climb down a very high and rugged mountain, and the Envoy of Gingiro told us that, before we continued to climb down, we must hide until evening so that we could pass by night through the fields where the Gallas grazed their cattle.

<margin>A very bad road, suffering great poverty.</margin>
At 4 o'clock in the afternoon, we set out on the road under the cover of a dense rainstorm, which drove the Gallas to their huts, but also soaked us weary travelers and caused us to suffer much cold. Our care and distress doubled when the night came because the brush through which we passed was very dense near the ground, difficult to get through by day, and even worse by night. We lit a fire in the woods and chewed a little roasted barley, which is the common food of travelers in that land. The next day, very early, after we had climbed down a steep mountain, we came to the river Zebée.

<margin>Crossing a very dangerous bridge.</margin>
This stream flows faster than the Nile, and at the place where we had to cross it, it made a terrifying noise, falling from a mountain between very sharp rocks, between which the water was crushed into foam.
pages.16:
# VOYAGIE VAN A.

<margin>1613</margin>
The bridge over which we were forced to pass such fast and dangerous waters was made of a piece of wood. This went across the river, notwithstanding that it was remarkably wide, and the height of this bridge was so great that, when one looked down from it, one discovered nothing there but an abyss. The great length of the piece of wood caused it to tremble under the feet of our people, and yet everyone wanted to be the first across, for as soon as one is on the other side of this river, one no longer has to fear the Gallas, for whom the fear was so great that it numbed all other fears. We thanked God on the other side of the bridge that He had delivered us from the bloodthirsty hands of the Gallas. We could not let our mules go over this bridge, therefore we left them there that night on the bank of the river with 2 men to guard them, with orders to cross the bridge if the Gallas came, and to break it down behind them. But the next day, 2 inhabitants of the land showed them a ford where they managed to get them across with great difficulty.

<margin>Obtaining an audience with the King of Gingiro.</margin>
The Ambassador arrived shortly after this at a dwelling from which we made our arrival known to the King of Gingiro, and we asked for permission to present to him the letters which we had to deliver on behalf of the Emperor of Ethiopia. But this King, being besides that very devoted to his sorcery, made us wait there for 8 days, at the end of which we received permission to come to his court, where we arrived in one day. We found this monarch ready to receive us, sitting or rather enclosed in a cage, for it was a type of cage or crate of about 25 hand-breadths high and 30 wide. It was round on top, having
pages.17:
# ANTONIO FERNANDEZ.

<margin>1613</margin>
the appearance of a wheel. The King sat on a carpet which was spread out on this wheel. All his courtiers stood below this throne upright, where he gave the audience. He was clothed in a very fine cloth, the whiteness of which made the blackness of his face stand out all the more, in which one otherwise did not see those features that one notices in the Kaffers. He immediately asked for the letter from the Emperor. He climbed down from his throne to come and get it, asked how he was doing, and climbed back onto his throne,

<margin>Reading the Emperor's letter.</margin>
after which he read the letter and spoke for some time with us through an interpreter, to whom, as often as the Emperor or the King said something to be told to us, the interpreter kissed the tips of his fingers and, after he had bowed down to the earth, went to interpret it to me, who was at some distance from the throne. And to bring the answer from me back to the King, he first used the same ceremony. The conversation lasted a long time. Finally, the King let it be said to me and the Envoy that we should go and rest, and that the substance of the Emperor's letter consisted of this: that he would certainly like to entertain us, and would like to have us escorted with a good guard to the borders of his Kingdom, which (he said) he would do very gladly.

The day after, I presented some gifts to the King. He showed much pleasure in them, as they were a rare thing in that land. As I stood ready to depart from there, the King sent me, in consideration of my gift, a young daughter of one of the great men of his kingdom to serve me as a slave. I excused myself from receiving her, saying that I was by no means accustomed to taking women with me. The King was satisfied with the difficulty I made, and sent
pages.18:
# VOYAGIE VAN

<margin>1613</margin>
<margin>And a fine mule.</margin>
me a slave, whom I also accepted, not with the thought of getting any service from him, but in hope of baptizing him. He also gave me a fine mule, which served me very well on the trip, as well as people to help us cross the river Zebée again and from there to travel to the Kingdom of Cambate.

<margin>Strange kind of ferrymen.</margin>
We departed for that purpose from the court of the King of Gingiro, and arrived that same day at the bank of the river Zebée to cross it. The people that the King had given us, being very skilled in this kind of crossing, made a device (machine) that was not much safer than the piece of wood. They slaughtered a cow and put the luggage in the hide, which would serve two purposes: the one to get across, the other to serve as ballast for the ship that they made from the hide of this cow, sewing it tightly closed. After that, they blew it up stiff and then made 2 woods or sticks fast to it, similar to those of a sedan chair. 4 people went to sit on these sticks, 2 in front and 2 behind this raft-work. One forbade them to move, and one arranged them to be of equal weight so that they kept this strange vessel in an equal counterweight. In front of it swam a brave swimmer, who was very well experienced in this art, who had a rope around his body that was also fastened to the apparatus with which he pulled it forward. 2 other swimmers also pushed it from behind. A whole day was spent on this crossing.

<margin>River Zebée.</margin>
<margin>The Kingdom of Gingiro described.</margin>
The stream Zebée surrounds almost entirely the Kingdom of Gingiro and makes it like a peninsula, as one sees in the map of Ethiopia, and from there it goes to lose itself in the sea towards the coast of Melinde.

This Kingdom is small; the inhabitants are
pages.19:
# ANTONIO FERNANDEZ.

<margin>1613</margin>
black like the Kaffers, but they do not have the facial features of the latter. They are, like all heathens, very inclined to sorcery, and they have such uncommon customs and habits that I shall surely deserve to be excused for having described them.

<margin>Custom of those of Gingiro.</margin>
Gingiro means an Ape or a Monkey, and truly the black color of this monarch, his gestures, countenance, and manners were entirely similar to those of these animals. These people also have that of the apes, that they kill their kings, and those of their people who come wounded from the battle, because, they say, they ought to die sooner than keep their lives with such marks of reproach of the advantages of their enemies.

<margin>Which are very ridiculous.</margin>
But although these kings, sitting thus on their <term>Jucquoir</term> <gloss>throne</gloss> like an owl on a perch, look very oddly like apes or monkeys, they are nevertheless of a high spirit and of a very sharp perception. When the King is to go outside his palace, it is early in the morning before the sun rises. And if it happens that the sun is up before he is out, he keeps himself locked in his palace for that whole day, does not go onto the throne to give audience, and does not give the same order to anyone, because, they say, two suns cannot endure each other in the world at one time. And because he does not want to grant that precedence, he takes revenge for it the next day and goes out before the sun is up.

<margin>Wonderfully strange ceremonies in the election.</margin>
The ceremonies they observe to elect their kings are likewise entirely uncommon: they wrap the corpse of their dead king in precious fabrics and then put it in the hide of a cow that has been freshly skinned. Immediately, all those who might aspire to the crown, such as the children of the deceased and the princes of the blood, hide themselves in a
pages.20:
# VOYAGIE VAN

<margin>1613</margin>
wild forest and pretend as if they wanted to flee that honor, which they crave. The electors, who are held to be great sorcerers, hold council, go towards the forest, search for the chosen one, and by devilish art make a shape of a bird of prey as large as an eagle, which they call *Liber*, descend. This bird flies with a great cry to the place where the one who is chosen is. The electors also go there immediately, and they find him surrounded by lions, tigers, snakes, panthers, and more such beasts, which they make come around this newly chosen monarch by sorcery, who defends himself and resists like a mad bull against those who want to take him along. He wounds and sometimes even kills them, for those who search for him do not leave him until they have gotten him and have led him along with force and violence. Leading him thus, one must fight with the people of a clan who, from long ago, claim to have the right to put the chosen monarch on the throne. The strongest or the victors have this privilege, which gives them a good share in the favor of the new *Gingiro*.

<margin>As also in the coronation of a king.</margin>
The ceremony of the coronation is to bring the King into the palace and to set him under a tent. On the 7th day after the death of the last King, the sorcerers bring a worm which they say came out of the nostrils of the dead one, which worm they wind in a cloth of silk fabric, and the new King pulls the head off it with his teeth. That having been done, they bury the dead King after they have carried him through the sown fields, which they beg him to bless. Having arrived at the burial place of the old Kings, which is in a small grove, they dig a hole in the earth and lay him in it without covering him, but he remains lying exposed to the air,
pages.21:
# ANTONIO FERNANDEZ.

because, they say, the earth is not worthy to cover the body of their King, who in greatness does not yield to the sun, and also for that purpose so that the Heaven might serve as a more glorious grave-site. On the day of the funeral, they slaughter many cows by the grave so that the blood of these drips onto the corpse of the King. They still slaughter a head of cattle there daily as long as the new King is alive, which is to the great advantage of their priests, or rather their sorcerers, who do let the blood of the cow flow into the grave but well provide their tables with what remains of it.

<margin>1613</margin>

To get to the new King while he bites the head off the worm, the people make a cry of joy and acclamations to his praise, wishing him a long life. The feast ends after they have placed him on that construction of a throne described by us above, for the new King immediately has everyone fetched who were favorites of his predecessor, saying to them: *whereas they were his friends so strongly during his life, it was also fair that they accompany him in the other world, so that they might be able to continue their services*, and he has them all under this pretext have their necks broken. He elects others again, fills the state offices that are vacant, and that does not prevent these first and most important offices from being sought after strongly, and it causes the courtiers to have a very great interest in the preservation of their Prince.

At the time of the election, they lay all the houses in which the deceased King lived, with all his furniture and implements, without excluding anything, however precious it may be, in ashes and charcoal. They do the same when any private or common person dies,

and forty-nine years, when the venerable father Friar Luis de Villalpando was elected custodian, exactly one year after the Indians in Maní had tried to burn him along with his companion. The definitors were the said custodian himself as the first, Father Friar Lorenzo de Bienvenida as second, Father Friar Francisco Navarro as third, and Father Friar Miguel de Vera as fourth. By this same record, it appears that the city of Mérida already had the name of a convent, with the aforementioned Father Friar Juan de la Puerta elected as its guardian; Campeche, with Father Friar Diego de Bejar as its guardian; Maní, with Father Friar Juan de Albalate as guardian; Cunkal, with the venerable custodian as guardian; and Ytzamal, with the definitor Father Friar Lorenzo de Bienvenida as guardian. Not only are the guardians assigned in this chapter table, but also the companions who were to live with them in each convent: a custom that was observed in this province until the provincial chapter held in the year 1603, from which time it seems to have been left to the discretion of the reverend provincial fathers to assign the companions and residents of each convent according to the need that arises there. The chapter was presided over by the Very Reverend Father Friar Francisco de Bustamante, as evidenced by the table signed with his name and sealed with the seal of his office of Commissary General. This was like the birth of this holy province of San José de Yucatan, for which reason I have written about it with such detail, as it remained in the form of a custody with the five convents that have been named, remaining subject to that of Mexico while it was one.

Although Father Friar Juan de la Puerta was elected guardian of the convent of the city of Mérida at the chapter, since the religious were still so few for the number of towns that existed in Yucatan—as for the entire province of Valladolid, which was so populous and had so many people, a convent foundation had not been able to be made—it was discussed that a religious from the province should go as a procurator to Spain to represent the need for them, and it seems that they agreed that he was the most suitable for a matter
pages.452:
LIBRO QUINTO. 435

of such importance.
The <term>Adelantado</term> <gloss>governor/military commander</gloss> was of the same opinion as the religious, and thus he gave him letters for the Emperor and the Royal Council of the Indies, in which he expressed the great fruit being made in the conversion of these Indians and the urgent need they had for the help of ministers.
Father Friar Juan de la Puerta received the dispatches that the province and the <term>Adelantado</term> gave him, and, being granted Father Friar Angel Maldonado as his companion, he went to Mexico, where the Very Reverend Father Commissary General, who had great satisfaction in his virtue and prudence, confirmed the office of procurator that the province had given him and entrusted him with other business, for which he gave him sufficient instructions and papers, with which he went to Spain in the Fleet of the following year, 1550. I have not found the result of this trip; it only seems to me that this religious was later elected bishop of this bishopric, as was said in the fourth book.

->CHAPTER X.<-
->The order is given to take the <term>residencia</term> <gloss>judicial review of an official's conduct</gloss>,<-
->and to remove the Indians from the <term>encomienda</term> <gloss>grant of native labor</gloss> of the<-
-><term>Adelantado</term>, and the reason for both.<-

Nothing notable had occurred regarding the secular state until this time, but since the new laws that had been given for these kingdoms commanded that no governor or royal official should hold Indians in <term>encomienda</term>, and the <term>Adelantado</term>, as a conqueror, retained his, a new order came for them to be taken away. Father Lizana says that in this year of forty-nine, the Licentiate Herrera came from Spain (with Father Albalate, who brought the religious), assigned as a judge of the Royal <term>Audiencia</term> <gloss>high court</gloss> of Mexico, and that he visited this land and held the <term>residencia</term> of the <term>Adelantado</term>. I am persuaded that the one who took his <term>residencia</term> was the judge Licentiate Santillan, who resided in the same <term>audiencia</term>, because in a royal provision of the sixteenth day of the month of June of the same year of one thousand five hundred and forty-nine, he is given the authority to
pages.453:
HISTORIA DE YUCATAN. 436

come to Yucatan, remove the Indians he held, and investigate other excesses that the <term>Adelantado</term> was said to have committed during the time of his government, so if the other gentleman were holding his <term>residencia</term>, it does not seem there would be a need for this new commission. In it, it is stated as a preamble that, in fraud of the new laws, many Indians were held in <term>encomienda</term> under the names of the wives, sons, and daughters of the governors and royal officials, whereby they enjoyed the Indians as if there were no such prohibition of laws. Descending to the singular motive of this commission, it is said:

> "And we are informed that, although it was ordered by our said Royal <term>Audiencia</term> that the said Indians be taken away from the wife, sons, and daughters of the said <term>Adelantado</term> Montejo, it had not been done or fulfilled. Instead, they say that the greater part of that land is in the hands of the said <term>Adelantado</term> Montejo and his wife, and Don Francisco de Montejo and his wife, and a stepson of his, the son of his wife, and for this, many frauds and ruses have been committed. Especially they say that having given a provision so that the Indians be taken away from the said <term>Adelantado</term> and his sons and daughters, he found a way with the person carrying it to have it handed over, so that it could not be used, along with another provision he was carrying, in which it was ordered that they should not interfere in the jurisdiction of the town of La Victoria del Rio de Grijalva in order to collect from the Indians, whom they ordered to be taken away, all the tributes of a year in advance, which belonged to us. And the title with which he had had the said tributes collected had been by saying that he had given them to a nephew of his, and for this, he had shown deposit certificates with dates from long before. And that to do the aforementioned, he had had the provisions detained. And that the fraud, which the said governor was committing against us and our royal treasury, having been seen by an ordinary mayor of the said town of La Victoria, he and a councilman, who was called Alonso Bazan, as our officials took the person who was collecting the tributes for the said <term>Adelantado</term>, and what had proceeded
pages.454:
LIBRO QUINTO. 437

from them, and put it in the chest of the three keys. And that when the <term>Adelantado</term> found out, he went to the said town with an armed hand, after the said provision had been notified to him, so that he would not be judged, and he arrested the said mayor and councilman and took them prisoner to Yucatan. And he newly raised other officials, his own servants, to be in charge of our treasury, and he procured for them to hold him as governor there, in order to take revenge on the officials and give the Indians he held to persons of the said town while being paid for them; which he did, selling some native Indians for interests they gave him. And that we are likewise informed that the said <term>Adelantado</term> Montejo is building a sugar mill in Champoton and for it he has taken, and is taking, the land from the Indians of that province, and took away their farmlands, the said towns being mine, agreeing to discharge the said taxpayers by occupying them in trading. And that above all the aforementioned, the said <term>Adelantado</term> has not given any <term>repartimiento</term> <gloss>distribution of indigenous labor</gloss> to any conqueror, but to all his relatives and wives and children, to stepsons and grandsons: they say not only to the legitimate ones, but to the bastards. And they say that he made the Indians of Champoton and Campeche go to war and make slaves, and thus they say that many of them were made, likewise women, contrary to our laws made by us, and that they are sold against all reason and justice, which is the cause of the depopulation of the said provinces. And that the said <term>Adelantado</term>, not content with all the things mentioned above, makes houses, estates, and businesses in the said provinces with our Indians, not being able, nor having the right to do so, and tiring them and making them work excessively. And that likewise other persons have done and committed many and grave crimes in the said provinces worthy of imprisonment and punishment, for which it was fitting to provide and remedy as an important matter."

Such was the report that had been made to the Emperor in the Royal Council of the Indies of what had happened in Yucatan; but it seems to have been excessive, for in what is said there about the <term>Adelantado</term> not having given Indians in <term>encomienda</term> to any conqueror
pages.455:
HISTORIA DE YUCATAN. 438

but to his relatives, there are still today many deposit certificates to the contrary, which were exhibited as soon as they finished being subjected, which their descendants observe originally to further qualify their merits in the conquest. Regarding making slaves of the Indians and selling them, what was happening has already been said and is written in the third book. But as there is never a lack of someone to complain (or it is rare) about those who govern, it had happened at present, and joining the retention of the Indians that the <term>Adelantado</term> enjoyed as a conqueror, having to be removed by the general laws, and the Emperor wishing to certify the truth, this royal provision was dispatched, which by its context seems to be of <term>residencia</term>, and in it, immediately after the aforementioned report, it is said:

"And seen by those of our Council of the Indies, wishing to provide for it, trusting in you that you are such a person that you will guard our service and the right of each of the parties, and that with all care and diligence you will intend to understand what by us will be commanded and committed to you: it is our mercy and will to entrust and commit it to you, and by this present, we entrust and commit it to you. Because we command you that, as soon as you see this, you go with the rod of our royal justice to the said provinces of Yucatan, Cozumél, and above all things, remove the Indians that the said <term>Adelantado</term> Montejo might have, and those of his wife and children, and our officials of the said provinces: except for the male children to whom such Indians were granted, those children already being married and living independently at the time they were granted to them. Which you shall do and fulfill, even if the <term>encomiendas</term> of such wives and sons and daughters have been made before the new laws or after. And because in the said new laws or ordinances we have provided for the good of the conquerors and their children, so that they can live and remain in those parts, that the Indians who were taken away by the disposition of the said new laws and ordinances be placed under the royal crown, and from their tributes
pages.456:
LIBRO QUINTO. 439

it be given for the sustenance and entertainment of the said conquerors, and if they are dead, for their children who do not have <term>repartimientos</term>: you shall provide that the tributes that the towns of Indians yield, which you will thus take away from the said <term>Adelantado</term> and from his wife, sons, and daughters, and from our officials of the said provinces of Yucatan and Cozumél, while we provide for the perpetuity of those provinces as is convenient, you shall distribute among the conquerors who did not have a <term>repartimiento</term>, and among their children and some good settlers. Which you shall do and fulfill, notwithstanding any supplications that may be interposed to this our letter. You shall inform yourself how and in what manner such things contained above in this our letter have passed, and what frauds have been committed against our royal treasury, and what persons did and committed the aforementioned, or any thing or part of it, and of the other crimes that have been committed in the said province, and by whose order they did it, and who gave them advice, favor, and help for it, and those whom you find guilty, arrest their bodies, and thus arrested, having called and heard the parties concerned, you shall do justice upon it by your sentence or sentences, both interlocutory and definitive, etc." And afterwards it proceeds by putting all the clauses that are customary in such commissions. It only specifies that for the execution, as much of what is contained as of any other thing that is committed to him, he should attend for the time that may be assigned by the Viceroy Don Antonio de Mendoza.

By means of this order, the time arrived for the <term>Adelantado</term> to have to give a <term>residencia</term> for the time he had governed Yucatan in war and peace. The judge who was to hold his <term>residencia</term> arrived at Campeche, and once the <term>Adelantado</term> was notified of his arrival, he sent his son Don Francisco with other principal neighbors of the city of Mérida so that, in his name, they might welcome him and receive him. Once arrived in Campeche, they visited the judge, who with many courtesies thanked the <term>Adelantado</term> for what he had done by sending his son, and for what the other gentlemen had manifested by going to
pages.457:
HISTORIA DE YUCATAN. 440

visit him. They came together to the city of Mérida, and by manifesting the superior order that the judge brought, he was received into the exercise of his commission. He published the <term>residencia</term>, and in the interim that it was to be held, the judge assumed the government of this land. Although there were complainants against the <term>Adelantado</term>, the event was generally felt by the religious as well as by seculars and Indians, because he was a very gentlemanly person in his demeanor, a noble person, a friend of the poor, kind, and endowed with many good traits that made him lovable, even if he had some defects as a man: who is perfect in everything? It was already seen in the third book what the principal conquerors wrote together in the council to the Emperor, just after the city of Mérida was founded, when they dispatched the first procurator general to the kingdoms of Spain.

CHAPTER XI.

->The Indians are taken away from the <term>Adelantado</term>. He goes with his <term>residencia</term><-
->to Spain, and dies: and his successors are named.<-

Once the <term>residencia</term> of the <term>Adelantado</term> was published, the administration of justice and government of Yucatan remained in the judge who was conducting it, in whose time it happened that some black slaves of the Spaniards fled to the mountains, and, joined by those who were in open rebellion, a group of up to twenty or more entered some Indian towns, to whom they did much evil and harm, taking what they could from them and committing other crimes that required prompt remedy. So that this would have the necessary end, the judge named the conqueror Alonso Rosado as head and leader of the Spaniards, that they should search for them and bring them in as prisoners, and if they did not surrender, they should use the final remedy by shooting them with arquebuses or killing them by any means possible. Alonso Rosado went out with his men, and suffering some hardships through the mountains, he spotted the fugitive blacks, who, finding themselves without weapons and surrounded by the Spaniards with them, surrendered and were taken as prisoners to the city of Mérida. Delivered
pages.458:
LIBRO QUINTO. 441
<sig>56</sig>

to the judge, he put them in jail until they were legally punished according to their crimes. The imprisonment of these blacks was considered a considerable service to this land because, besides the damages that were avoided by it, a rumor that was already circulating was calmed: that some Indians were attempting to rebel against the Spaniards with the warmth and spirit that those slaves gave them, fearful that they were going to fall into the hands of justice and be punished, as they were afterwards.

It also happened that many Indians from the southern part of this province, which they call the Sierra, had retreated to the interior of the land (which lies between this one and that of Guatemala) fleeing from contact with the Spaniards and from Christian instruction. Considering the great disservice that was being done to God and the King with this flight, the judge ordered Captain Francisco de Montejo, who, as was said, was of the conquest, to enter through those unpopulated areas and try to attract them to the towns of their nature. That captain went out with people from the city and walked through the mountains and villages, gathering many Indians with peaceful means. Some were more than seventy leagues from the city, and forty from the nearest settlement. Among these distant ones, the captain learned of a troop of Indians banded together, and not being able to go, he entrusted it to Alonso Rosado, one of those who went with him, and who had previously captured the blacks, giving him some Spaniards to go with him. They found the Indians, and he persuaded them in such a way that they gave themselves up in peace and he brought them to the captain. A very considerable number of Indians gathered with this outing, who were distributed to the towns of their nature, with which this land of Yucatan remained quiet for then. Both the one and the other are evidenced by the authentic proofs that were made and that I have read.

It is said that the time of the <term>residencia</term> lasted three months, in which the judge ordered some things for the utility of the Indians and their good treatment, and for the increase of their Christianity. He reformed others regarding the Spaniards, who, as in newly founded republics

are not established by [their own] nature. They are not established because those conditions are not established. Similarly, the person <note>(Sāmkhya)</note>, the consciousness <note>(Vaiśeṣika)</note>, and the non-dual consciousness <note>(Guhyasamāja tradition)</note>, and others—those who assert that the nature of consciousness is a permanent substance—are also not established by their own nature and are empty. "Form is empty. Likewise, feeling," and so forth—the meaning of these must also be understood.

Similarly, the meaning of "Emptiness is form," and so forth, is that form is empty of being an inherently existing substantial form, empty of being a permanent substance, empty of being a form composed of permanent substantial atoms, and is impermanent. That which serves as the basis for designating "form," that which is suitable to be a form arising from karma, and so on, is "emptiness is form." From that form, the emptiness of the form which is held to be a substantial entity or a substantial entity with parts is not different. This is the meaning of "Form is not other than emptiness." Similarly, the meaning of "Emptiness is not other than form" is that form which is born of karma is not other than the emptiness of that form which is a substantial entity with parts. This is the understanding according to the tenets of the <term>Sautrantika</term> <gloss>sutra follower</gloss> school.

The view of one <term>Sautrantika</term> <gloss>sutra follower</gloss> system—The system of the <term>Sautrantika</term>s: because they accept consciousness as having aspects, they posit both the consciousness that appears in the form of its own aspect and the object as two. Those aspects of consciousness are empty of that form as it is characterized—

<column-break/>
1) "Form born of karma"—this refers to the shape of the body and so forth that is obtained from the ripening of karma.

the meaning of "Form is empty." Even though the aspect of consciousness itself is empty of form, since that which appears as form to it is indeed form, it is said that "Emptiness is form." Since it is unreasonable to think of a form that is empty of form as something other than such a form, it is said that "Form is not other than emptiness." Since one cannot perceive a form other than that which appears as form to one who holds [the concept of] a form empty of the characteristics of form, it is said that "Emptiness is not other than form." In this way, these sutras do not explicitly explain [the path] in terms of one's own body according to these tenets. This is because the 'Profound Practice' shown here is the Mother of the <term>Aryas</term> <gloss>Noble Ones</gloss> based on reasoning. While this is said with the mindset that it is the Mother of Reasoning, I have not seen it as inappropriate to also apply it to tenets.

Explanations relying on the <term>Vijñaptimātra</term> <gloss>Mind-Only</gloss> method—The intention of sutras such as "Form is empty" is also explained in the manner of the <term>Vijñaptimātra</term> <gloss>Mind-Only</gloss> method of the Great Ones, relying on other sutras. In this system, the Great Ones establish the characteristic of form for all phenomena of the path to purification. They interpret the intention of the Mother sutras, which state that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature. Here too, relying on the three non-existences and the three types of form, they explain the meaning of the four types of emptiness, beginning with "Form is empty." As stated in the sutra:

"Brahmin, a <term>Bodhisattva</term> <gloss>enlightenment-being</gloss> who practices the <term>Prajñāpāramitā</term> <gloss>Perfection of Wisdom</gloss> and dwells in skill in interpreting profound phenomena should know to investigate form through three aspects. Feeling..." and so on. Thus, regarding this

pages.136:
"Imagined form, this is designated form, this is the form of <term>Dharmatā</term> <gloss>the true nature of phenomena</gloss>."

This is an extensive explanation. Based on these three types of form: the first form is what ordinary people grasp as an object in their <term>vikalpa</term> <gloss>conceptualizing</gloss> minds. That is the imagined form and the form that becomes the object of the consciousness that appears as an object. The <term>paratantra</term> <gloss>dependent</term> form is the designated form, and the form that is free from the characteristics of those two is the <term>pariniṣpanna</term> <gloss>perfected</gloss> form—that is <term>Tathātā</term> <gloss>Suchness</gloss>, which is what is called "the form of <term>Dharmatā</term>."

Therefore, because the nature of the dependent <term>paratantra</term> form is devoid of all characteristics of the imagined <term>parikalpita</term> form, it is empty of imagined form, and that emptiness has the meaning of Suchness. As it is said by the Great Charioteer <note>referring to a great master, likely Nagarjuna or a key commentator</note>:

"What is the characteristic of emptiness? That which is not present in something is seen as being empty of it." And, "What is it that is not present? In the aggregates, elements, and sense spheres, there is no permanent, unchanging phenomenon, no self, and no belonging to a self. Thus, they are empty."

As it is said, here "Form is empty" means that the form which has the characteristic of the dependent <term>paratantra</term> nature is devoid of those imagined forms such as external objects. Thus, it is empty of them.

<note>1) Nyayabindu, 39/a, summarized. 2) Sutrasamuccaya, 37b, Cittamatra section.</note>

Thus, it is stated "Form is empty." This explains the emptiness of the perfect form, and therefore it is stated "Emptiness is form." This serves as an antidote to the conceptualization of nihilism. If one thinks that since emptiness and form are different in characteristics, emptiness is one thing and form is another, it serves as an antidote to the conceptualization of eternalism and the two extremes. That <term>Dharmatā</term> <gloss>true nature</gloss> form, which has the characteristic of emptiness, does not possess the characteristics of form. As stated in the <term>Prajñāpāramitā</term> sutra:

"Shariputra, form is separated from the nature of form." This is explained extensively. Similarly, in the sutra taught by Rab 'byor <note>Subhuti</note>, it is said, "The <term>Dharmadhātu</term> <gloss>realm of phenomena</gloss> exists in the realm of form, but the <term>Dharmadhātu</term> is not a characteristic of consciousness <note>or "not an object of consciousness"</note>," and so on.

Thinking that "Emptiness or the form of <term>Dharmatā</term> is something other than form" is incorrect. It is the <term>Dharmatā</term> of form, and because it cannot be perceived as something other than the form which is the basis of phenomena, it is stated "Emptiness is not other than form." The basis of phenomena, form, is also the basis of emptiness, and it is the basis of the form of <term>Dharmatā</term>. Because it cannot be perceived as other than its own <term>Dharmatā</term>, and because it is its nature, it is not other than emptiness. The word "also" is used here to encompass both the phenomenon and the <term>Dharmatā</term>.

<note>1) Large Sutra (Nyithri), 146/3. 2) Akṣayamatinirdeśa-sūtra, 13b.</note>

<summary>This page clarifies the non-duality of form and emptiness, emphasizing that emptiness is the true nature (Dharmatā) of form and cannot be separated from it.</summary>
<keywords>Emptiness, Form, Dharmata, Dharmadhatu, Prajnaparamita, Non-duality</keywords>
pages.138:
These two points serve as the antidote to the conceptualization that mistakenly holds phenomena and their <term>Dharmatā</term> to be different, as if they were two separate things. As the Great Charioteer said:

"This was stated as an antidote to the conceptualization of the two [extremes] as a method: 'Form is not other than emptiness. Form itself is emptiness. Emptiness is form.'"

This is an explanation that accords with the sutra’s style of progressive steps. Although great Tibetan masters have disagreed on whether this explanation depends on the chapters of the <term>Prajñāpāramitā</term> commentary or not, I have not included those extremes here. Once one has grasped the crux of these points, it is easy to understand how the intention of the <term>Prajñāpāramitā</term> sutra is interpreted based on the three modes of non-existence, such as the imagined characteristic being devoid of intrinsic nature. Therefore, one should learn more from other existing commentaries. Here, I only intend to summarize the meaning of the Essence <note>Heart Sutra</note>, so that is enough.

Regarding the antidote—In the statement "Form is empty," etc.,

Nevertheless, if one asks, "What is the intrinsic nature meant by 'Form is empty of intrinsic nature'?" and "How should it be identified?"—it must be established as that which is established by its own nature. If that is established, it is refuted by reasonings such as the separation of one and many, and the refutation of production in the four extremes. Thus, the explanation that "it is devoid of intrinsic nature" is very clear in the <term>Madhyamaka</term> <gloss>Middle Way</gloss> and <term>Prajñāpāramitā</term> texts. Although it is not taken from the <term>Pramāṇavārttika</term> <gloss>Commentary on Valid Cognition</gloss>, those who wish to understand the texts through study of the scriptures will find that, relying on the reasoning mentioned above, a definitive understanding can be reached.

How the intrinsic nature in "empty of intrinsic nature" is identified varies according to different schools of thought, as explained above. However, the explanations that are somewhat clear in the Mahayana sutras and the commentaries of the Great Charioteers are a bit different. As stated. Therefore, when form appears as a phenomenon, there were the three [types of form] mentioned earlier. Although the two entities are objects to be refuted by reason, when it comes to the true and intrinsically established form, all three are targets of refutation. This is because all three are illusory appearances born from the imprints of incorrect reasoning. At that time, the appearance of form arising from the imprint of the entity's reality is an appearance of dependence, so it is an object to be refuted by reason. The second, the appearance arising from the imprints of words, is also a basis for mistaken labeling; it does not need to be refuted by reason, because even if it appears, it is like a magical illusion dependent on conditions, and it involves labeling. Therefore, the appearance of being truly established and established by intrinsic nature, the self that grasps that nature, and the two [graspings of] subject and object [which are] conceptualizations of incorrect mental engagement—these are the root of cyclic existence. Because they are the root of incorrect thought and attachment, they are established as mistaken. Thus, they are objects to be refuted by reason. The conceptualization that grasps them, along with cyclic existence, should be refuted. As stated by the son of the Conqueror, <term>Shantideva</term>:

Folios 1^r—4^u, which contain *Timaeus the Locrian on the nature of the soul and the world* (the title of which is painted in red), are followed by the five books of commentary, of which the first two stand on the side of codex **N**, as shown by other things, and especially by a lacuna common to both books, which has been supplied in this parchment by one inserted folio (63).
